विश्व-साहित्यमें श्रीमद्भगवद्गीताका अद्वितीय स्थान है। यह साक्षात् भगवान्‌के श्रीमुखसे निःसृत परम
रहस्यमयी दिव्य वाणी है। इसमें स्वयं भगवान्ने अर्जुनको निमित्त बनाकर मनुष्यमात्रके कल्याणके लिये उपदेश दिया
है | इस छोटे-से ग्रन्थ में भगवान् ने अपने हृदयके बहुत ही विलक्षण भाव भर दिये हैं, जिनका आजतक कोई पार नहीं
पा सका और न पा ही सकता है।
हमारे परमश्रद्धेय स्वामीजी श्रीरामसुखदासजी महाराजने इस अगाध गीतार्णवमें गहरे उतरकर अनेक गुह्यतम
अमूल्य रत्न ढूँढ़ निकाले हैं, जिन्हें उन्होंने इस 'साधक - संजीवनी' हिन्दी - टीकाके माध्यम से साधकोंके कल्याणार्थ
उदारहृदयसे वितरित किया है। गीताकी यह टीका हमें अपनी धारणासे दूसरी टीकाओंकी अपेक्षा बहुत विलक्षण
प्रतीत होती है। हमारा गीताकी दूसरी सब टीकाओंका इतना अध्ययन नहीं है, फिर भी इस टीकामें हमें अनेक
श्लोकोंके भाव नये और विलक्षण लगे; जैसे- पहले अध्यायका दसवाँ, उन्नीसवाँ - बीसवाँ और पचीसवाँ श्लोक;
दूसरे अध्यायका उनतालीसवाँ - चालीसवाँ श्लोक; तीसरे अध्यायका तीसरा, दसवाँ, बारहवाँ - तेरहवाँ और तैंतालीसवाँ
श्लोक ; चौथे अध्यायका अठारहवाँ और अड़तीसवाँ श्लोक; पाँचवें अध्यायका तेरहवाँ - चौदहवाँ श्लोक; छठे
अध्यायका बीसवाँ और अड़तीसवाँ श्लोक; सातवें अध्यायका पाँचवाँ और उन्नीसवाँ श्लोक; आठवें अध्यायका छठा
श्लोक ; नवें अध्यायका तीसरा और इकतीसवाँ श्लोक ; दसवें अध्यायका इकतालीसवाँ श्लोक ; ग्यारहवें अध्यायका
छब्बीसवाँ - सत्ताईसवाँ और पैंतालीसवाँ - छियालीसवाँ श्लोक; बारहवें अध्यायका बारहवाँ श्लोक ; तेरहवें अध्यायका
पहला और उन्नीसवाँ - बीसवाँ - इक्कीसवाँ श्लोक ; चौदहवें अध्यायका तीसरा, बारहवाँ, सत्रहवाँ और बाईसवाँ

आदि । अगर पाठक गम्भीर अध्ययन करें तो उसे और भी कई श्लोकोंमें आंशिक नये-नये भाव मिल सकते हैं।
वर्तमान समयमें साधनका तत्त्व सरलतापूर्वक बतानेवाले ग्रन्थोंका प्रायः अभाव - सा दीखता है, जिससे
साधकोंको सही मार्ग-दर्शनके बिना बहुत कठिनाई होती है । ऐसी स्थितिमें परमात्मप्राप्तिके अनेक सरल उपायोंसे युक्त,
साधकोपयोगी अनेक विशेष और मार्मिक बातोंसे अलंकृत तथा बहुत ही सरल एवं सुबोध भाषा - शैलीमें लिखित
प्रस्तुत ग्रन्थका प्रकाशन अत्यन्त महत्त्वपूर्ण स्थान रखता है।

परमश्रद्धेय स्वामीजीने गीताकी यह टीका किसी दार्शनिक विचारकी दृष्टिसे अथवा अपनी विद्वत्ताका प्रदर्शन
करनेके लिये नहीं लिखी है, अपितु साधकोंका हित कैसे हो – इसी दृष्टिसे लिखी है । परमशान्तिकी प्राप्ति चाहनेवाले
प्रत्येक साधकके लिये, चाहे वह किसी भी देश, वेश, भाषा, मत, सम्प्रदाय आदिका क्यों न हो, यह टीका संजीवनी
बूटीके समान है। इस टीकाका अध्ययन करनेसे हिन्दू, बौद्ध, जैन, पारसी, ईसाई, मुसलमान आदि सभी धर्मोके
अनुयायियोंको अपने-अपने मतके अनुसार ही उद्धारके उपाय मिल जायँगे। इस टीकामें साधकोंको अपने उद्देश्यकी
सिद्धिके लिये पूरी सामग्री मिलेगी ।
परमशान्तिकी प्राप्तिके इच्छुक सभी भाई- बहनोंसे विनम्र निवेदन है कि वे इस ग्रन्थ - रत्नको अवश्य ही
मनोयोगपूर्वक पढ़ें, समझें और यथासाध्य आचरणमें लानेका प्रयत्न करें।

english: The Srimad Bhagavad Gita holds a unique position in world literature. It is the divine word that has emanated from the mouth of the Lord Himself. In this small treatise, the Lord has filled it with extraordinary emotions that no one has been able to comprehend till date, nor can they ever. Our revered Swamiji Shri Ram Sukh Das Ji Maharaj has delved deep into the unfathomable ocean of the Gita and discovered many precious gems, which he has generously distributed to the seekers through this Hindi commentary, 'Sadhak Sanjivani'. This commentary appears to us as very unique compared to other commentaries. Although we have not studied all the other commentaries of the Gita, we have found many new and extraordinary emotions in this commentary. In the current era, there is a lack of texts that simply explain the essence of spiritual practices, which causes difficulties for seekers due to the lack of proper guidance. In this context, the publication of this treatise, which is endowed with simple means of attaining the Supreme Self and is adorned with special and poignant topics, is of great importance. Our revered Swamiji has not written this commentary from a philosophical perspective or to showcase his erudition, but with the sole intention of benefiting the seekers. For every seeker who aspires to attain supreme peace, regardless of their country, dress, language, sect, or religion, this commentary is like a sanjivani booti. By studying this commentary, followers of all religions, including Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian, and Muslim, will find ways to attain liberation according to their respective faiths. This commentary provides seekers with all the necessary material to achieve their goals. We humbly request all brothers and sisters who aspire to attain supreme peace to read, understand, and try to practice this treatise with devotion. After writing the commentary on the Srimad Bhagavad Gita, 'Sadhak Sanjivani', our revered Swamiji Shri Swami Ji Maharaj wrote an appendix, which was initially published in three separate parts. Now, it is being published along with the 'Sadhak Sanjivani' commentary. Some necessary revisions have been made to the appendix as well as the 'Sadhak Sanjivani' commentary. The appendix reveals the most profound and sublime emotions of the Gita. We hope that readers will make an effort to benefit from this revised and expanded edition of 'Sadhak Sanjivani'.

The humble request of the seeker is as follows: The Lord is infinite, and everything related to Him is also infinite. How can the limits of the emotions expressed by the Lord from His lotus mouth come to an end? Different gurus have written different commentaries on the Gita. Following their commentaries, a person can attain his own well-being, but he cannot fully understand the meaning of the Gita. Even if we collect all the commentaries written on the Gita till now, the meaning of the Gita will not be complete. Just as if hundreds of people drink water from a well for centuries, the water in the well remains the same, similarly, even if numerous commentaries are written on the Gita, the Gita remains the same, and the limits of its emotions do not come to an end. The limits of the water in a well are there, but the limits of the emotions of the Gita are not there. Therefore, when anyone speaks about the Gita, he is actually giving an account of his own intellect - 'Sab jant prabhuprabhuta soi, tadapi kahan binu raha na koi' (Mansa, Balak 13.1).

The Lord's words are more solid and superior than the words of even the great sages and saints, because the Lord is the origin of the sages and saints - 'Aham adir hi devanam, maharsinam ca sarvashah' (Gita 10.2). Therefore, even if there are many great sages and saints, and their words are very superior, they cannot match the divine, divine words of the Lord in the Gita. The path of the guru is called 'paddhati', and the royal road, the path of the chariot, or the wide road is called 'prasthana'. The Gita, the Upanishads, and the Brahma Sutras are the three prasthanas, and all other paths are paddhatis. The Gita is unique among the three prasthanas, because in it, the meaning of both the Upanishads and the Brahma Sutras is included.

The Gita is the essence of the Upanishads, but in reality, the Gita's words are more special than those of the Upanishads. The reason is that the quality of the cause is different from the quality of the effect; just as the sky has only one quality, 'sound', but its effect, the air, has two qualities, 'sound' and 'touch'. The Vedas are the breaths of the Lord, and the Gita is the Lord's speech. The breaths are natural, but the Gita was spoken by the Lord while He was in a state of yoga. Therefore, the Gita is more special than the Vedas.

All philosophies are included in the Gita, but the Gita is not included in any philosophy. In philosophy, one studies what the world is, what the living being is, and what the ultimate reality is. But the Gita does not teach philosophy; rather, it gives direct experience. There is no bias towards any particular school of thought in the Gita; rather, it is concerned only with the well-being of the living being. There is no difference of opinion in the Gita; rather, the difference is among the commentators. Following the Gita, there can be no difference of opinion between the worshippers of the Saguna and Nirguna forms of the Lord. The Gita takes the seeker to the ultimate reality.

All forms, whether Saguna or Nirguna, Sakaar or Nirakaar, Dvibhuja or Chaturbhuja, Sahasrabhuja, etc., are included in the ultimate reality. In the ultimate reality, no form remains separate. Whatever form one worships, all forms are included in the ultimate reality. All philosophies are included in the ultimate reality. Therefore, everything is included in the ultimate reality, and there is nothing else except the ultimate reality - this is the essence of the entire Gita.

The meaning of the Gita is 'Vasudeva sarvam', i.e., everything is Vasudeva. If one does not accept the existence of any other reality except the ultimate reality, then one's actions will be in accordance with the ultimate reality. The Lord said, 'That which I have described as the ultimate reality is not to be described again and again. I had described it while I was in a state of yoga' - 'Param hi brahma kathitam yogayuktena tanmayah' (Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva 16.12-13).

The word 'yogayukt' means that the Gita was spoken by the Lord while He was in a state of yoga, i.e., while He was in a state of complete absorption in the ultimate reality. The meaning of this is that the Lord spoke the Gita for the benefit of all seekers, considering their interests. What should be said to benefit the seekers? What should be said for their well-being in the future? In this way, the Gita was spoken by the Lord while He was in a state of yoga, considering the interests of all seekers.

occurs, and by eliminating the recognition of another existence, non-attachment (nivritti) is strengthened. The arising of worldly engagement is 'enjoyment' (bhoga) and the strengthening of renunciation is 'yoga'. The Gita believes that 'Everything is the Supreme Being' and emphasizes this very point. To demonstrate that 'I alone exist in all forms—as action, as cause, as glory, and in all manifestations', the Lord has described His divine glories (vibhutis) in four places in the Gita (in Chapters Seven, Nine, Ten, and Fifteen). Brahman (the formless, attributeless Supreme), kritsna adhyatma (all living beings across infinite species), akhila karma (all cosmic activities of creation, preservation, and dissolution), adhibhuta (the entire physical world made of the five elements, including one's own body), adhidaiva (all demigods including Brahma along with the presiding deities of the mind and senses), and adhiyajna (the inner dweller Vishnu and all His manifestations)—all of these are subsumed under 'vasudevah sarvam' (Vasudeva is everything) (Gita 7.29-30). The gist is that whatever is existent (sat), non-existent (asat), and beyond both is all the Supreme Being alone—'tvam aksaram sad asat tat param yat' (Gita 11.37). The world appears real only due to one's attachment (raga). It is because of attachment that a secondary existence appears. If attachment ceases, there is nothing except the one Supreme Being. As the Lord has stated—'sarvasya caham hridi sannivistah' (Gita 15.15), "I am seated in the hearts of all living beings." In the very heart where the Lord dwells, there also arise attachment-aversion, agitation, and restlessness. Happiness arises in the heart, and sorrow comes to the heart. During the churning of the ocean, both poison and nectar emerged from the same place. When Lord Shiva drank the poison, nectar appeared. Similarly, if attachment and aversion are eradicated, the Supreme Being manifests. In the hearts of saints and great souls, attachment and aversion do not remain; hence, the Supreme Lord dwells there.

'Everything is the Supreme Being'—this is meditation with open eyes. In this, there is no need to close the eyes (dhyana), no need to close the ears (nadanusandhana), nor any need to hold the breath (pranayama)! In this state, neither union nor separation has any effect; neither anyone's arrival nor anyone's departure makes any difference. When everything is the Supreme Being, where would another come from? How would they come?

The Gita accepts the integral Whole (Samagra); hence, the Gita begins and ends with surrender (sharanagati). Only through surrender is the Whole attained. Although all forms are included in the integral form of the Supreme Being, the personal/attributeful aspect (Saguna) holds prominence. This is because the unmanifest/attributeless aspect (Nirguna) is also contained within Saguna, but Saguna (owing to the negation of attributes in Nirguna) is not contained within Nirguna. Therefore, only Saguna can be the integral Whole. Lord Shri Krishna is integral—'asamsayam samagram mam' (Gita 7.1). The Gita is the voice of the Integral Whole, which is why everything is contained in the Gita. In whatever perspective one views the Gita, the Gita appears to them accordingly—'ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamy aham' (Gita 4.11).

Karmayoga, Jnanayoga, and Bhaktiyoga—these are the only three Yogas. Karmayoga pertains to the body (Apara), Jnanayoga pertains to the indweller/Self (Para), and Bhaktiyoga pertains to the Master of both body and Self (the Lord). At the beginning of the Gita, the Lord first described Jnanayoga and Karmayoga respectively, taking up the indweller (Self) first and then the body. Then Dhyanayoga was described, because that is also a means of spiritual attainment. Then from the seventh chapter onwards, Bhakti was described with special emphasis, which is the Lord's primary objective. Through Karmayoga a person becomes useful to the world, through Jnanayoga for oneself, and through Bhaktiyoga for the Lord.

In the Gita, equanimity is called 'Yoga'—'samatvam yoga ucyate' (Gita 2.48). In reality, the need for 'Yoga' is only in action (karma); there is no need for yoga in knowledge, and in devotion, there is absolutely no need for yoga. Knowledge and devotion are themselves 'Yoga'. Actions are inert, binding, and sense-oriented; therefore, yoga is required in them—'yogasthah kuru karmani' (Gita 2.48). In actions, yoga is paramount—'yogah karmasu kaushalam' (Gita 2.50). Action without yoga is inferior—'durena hy avaram karma buddhiyogad dhananjaya' (Gita 2.49). Sense of agency (kartritva) also arises from performing actions. Therefore, in the Gita, the word 'Yoga' specifically denotes 'Karmayoga'. In the colophon (pushpika) of the Gita as well, the term 'Yogasastre' refers to the teachings of Karmayoga.

In Karmayoga, there are two divisions—the action division (Karma-vibhaga) and the yoga division (Yoga-vibhaga). The action division is the former half, and the yoga division is the latter half. Action depends on instruments (karana-sapeksh), whereas yoga is independent of instruments (karana-nirapeksh). The action division contains devotion to duty, while the yoga division contains freedom, changelessness, unattachment, and equanimity. What is our duty in the world is someone else's right. Therefore, an individual's duty is the right of the family, society, and the world. For instance, what is the speaker's duty is the listener's right, and what is the listener's duty is the speaker's right. english: The attainment of yoga occurs when one protects the rights of others, meaning one should not consider their body, possessions, abilities, and strength as their own, but rather dedicate them to the service of others. In the world, we have a connection with objects and people. Where there is a connection, there is a need to fulfill one's duty. When we are connected to an object, we should not be attached to it, but rather use it for the benefit of others. When we are connected to a person, we should not be attached to them, but rather serve them and bring them happiness. By fulfilling one's duty without desire or attachment, one can attain liberation from the connection to the body and the world, and attain yoga. The Bhagavad Gita states, 'tam vidyad duhkha-sanyoga-viyogam yogasamjnitam' (6.23), which means that yoga is the disconnection from the connection of suffering. The connection to the world is always subject to disconnection, but the connection to yoga is never disconnected. When one attains yoga, they become free from all impurities such as attachment, anger, and greed, and attain self-control, purity, detachment, and equality. Every person desires to live forever, to know everything, and to be always happy. However, this desire cannot be fulfilled by one's own strength or by the world, because what one desires is not present in the world. In reality, what one needs is already attained. The mistake is that one starts desiring things that are subject to connection and disconnection, which are ephemeral. The principle is that what is always separate from us is always separate and is currently separate. For example, the body is always separate from us and is currently separate. Similarly, what is never separate from us, such as the Supreme Self, is always connected to us and is currently connected to us. The conclusion is that the world is always subject to disconnection, and the Supreme Self is always connected. Some scholars believe in the sequence of karma yoga, jnana yoga, and bhakti yoga, while others believe in the sequence of karma yoga, bhakti yoga, and jnana yoga. However, the Bhagavad Gita believes in the sequence of jnana yoga, karma yoga, and bhakti yoga. The Gita considers karma yoga to be more important than jnana yoga, as stated in 'tayostu karmasanyasat karmayogo visisyate' (5.2). This is because jnana yoga can be practiced without karma yoga, as stated in 'karmnaiva hi samsiddhim asthita janakadayah' (3.20) and 'yajnayacaratah karma samagram praviliyate' (4.23). However, karma yoga cannot be practiced without jnana yoga, as stated in 'sannyasastu mahabaho duhkham aptum ayogat' (5.6). The Bhagavata Purana also states that jnana yoga, karma yoga, and bhakti yoga are the three yogas, and that there is no other way to attain the highest goal. The Gita considers karma yoga and jnana yoga to be equal and worldly, as stated in 'loke'smin divida nistha' (3.3). The worldly and the soul are both worldly, as stated in 'dvavimau purusau loke ksharashcaksara eva ca' (15.16), but the Supreme Lord is beyond the worldly, as stated in 'uttamah purusas tvanyah' (15.17). Karma yoga is based on the worldly, and jnana yoga is based on the soul. Therefore, both karma yoga and jnana yoga are worldly. However, bhakti yoga is based on the Supreme Lord, and is therefore beyond the worldly. The Gita considers bhakti to be the highest, as stated in the 47th verse of the 6th chapter. The bhakti of the Gita is not dualistic, but rather non-dualistic. In reality, knowledge is dualistic, while bhakti is non-dualistic. This is because knowledge involves the distinction between the worldly and the soul, the body and the self, the unreal and the real, and the material and the spiritual. However, in bhakti, there is only the Supreme Lord, as stated in 'vasudeva sarvam' (7.19) and 'sadasaccaham' (9.19). The Lord has also stated that bhakti is the means to attain knowledge, as stated in 'mayi cananyayogena' (13.10), and that it is the means to transcend the three gunas, as stated in 'mam ca yo 'vyabhicarena' (14.26). By attaining the highest level of knowledge, one can attain the highest level of bhakti, as stated in 'madbhaktim labhate param' (18.55). This highest level of bhakti allows one to know, see, and enter into the Supreme Lord, as stated in the 54th verse of the 11th chapter. The Lord gives his devotee the attainment of both karma yoga and jnana yoga, as stated in the 10th and 11th verses of the 10th chapter. The Lord has also stated that his devotee is the best yogi, as stated in 'sa me yuktatamo matah' (6.47), 'te me yuktatama matah' (12.2), and 'sa yogi paramo matah' (6.32). Bhakti is also present in dhyana yoga, as stated in 'yukta asita matparah' (6.14), and in karma yoga, as stated in 'yukta asita matparah' (2.61). The Lord has stated that bhakti is the specialty of all yogas. The Bhagavata Purana also states that there are three yogas, and that there is no other way to attain the highest goal, as stated in 'yogastrayo maya prokta nrnam sireyovidhitsaya, jnanam karma ca bhaktis ca nopayo 'nyo 'sti kutracit' (11.20.6).

सगुणको ही समग्र कहा है- 'असंशयं समग्रं माम्' (गीता ७। १)।

पहले ‘साधक-संजीवनी' टीकामें श्लोकोंके अर्थ अन्वयपूर्वक न करनेसे उनमें कहीं-कहीं कमी रह गयी थी ।
अब श्लोकोंका अन्वयपूर्वक अर्थ देकर उस कमीकी पूर्ति कर दी गयी है । अन्वयार्थमें कहीं अर्थको लेकर और कहीं
वाक्यकी सुन्दरताको लेकर विशेष विचारपूर्वक परिवर्तन किया गया है ।
पाठकोंको पहलेकी और बादकी (परिशिष्ट) व्याख्यामें कोई अन्तर दीखे तो उनको बादकी व्याख्याका भाव ही
ग्रहण करना चाहिये। यह सिद्धान्त है कि पहलेकी अपेक्षा बादमें लिखे हुए विषयका अधिक महत्त्व होता है । इसमें इस
बातका विशेष ध्यान रखा गया है कि साधकोंका किसी प्रकारसे अहित न हो । कारण कि यह टीका मुख्यरूपसे
साधकोंके हितकी दृष्टिसे लिखी गयी है, विद्वत्ताकी दृष्टिसे नहीं ।
साधकोंको चाहिये कि वे अपना कोई आग्रह न रखकर इस टीकाको पढ़ें और इसपर गहरा विचार करें तो
वास्तविक तत्त्व उनकी समझमें आ जायगा और जो बात टीकामें नहीं आयी है, वह भी समझमें आ जायगी !

english: The question of Arjuna was not related to devotion, yet the Lord described devotion on his own (from the 56th to the 66th verse of the 18th chapter). Devotion leads to the attainment of the Supreme Self (29th-30th verse of the 7th chapter). The 7th, 9th, and 15th chapters of the Gita, the beginning of the 10th chapter, and the verses from the 56th to the 66th of the 18th chapter seem very peculiar to us. These do not contain 'Arjuna Uvacha', meaning they were spoken by the Lord out of great kindness. In the Gita, while describing Karma Yoga, Jnana Yoga and Bhakti Yoga are also mentioned, and while describing Jnana Yoga, Karma Yoga and Bhakti Yoga are mentioned, and while describing Bhakti Yoga, Karma Yoga and Jnana Yoga are mentioned. This means that if a seeker practices any one of these Yogas, they will attain all three, i.e., they will attain both liberation and devotion. The reason is that both Para and Apara are the nature of the Lord. Jnana Yoga is based on Para, and Karma Yoga is based on Apara. Therefore, when one Yoga is perfected, all three Yogas are perfected. However, there is a condition that the seeker should not be rigid in their opinion and should not criticize or belittle others' opinions. If the seeker is rigid in their opinion and criticizes or belittles others' opinions, they may attain liberation (Self-realization), but not devotion (pure love). Regarding the appendix, the Bhagavad Gita is a unique book that no one has been able to fully comprehend, nor can anyone comprehend it. As one delves deeper into its study and contemplation, new and wonderful ideas emerge. The Gita is infinite, but its commentary is limited. Initially, we wrote the 'Sadhak Sanjivani' commentary based on our understanding, but later, with the grace of God and the saints, new ideas emerged, which are now being added to the commentary as an appendix. While writing the 'Sadhak Sanjivani' commentary, we prioritized the importance of the Nirguna (formless) aspect, as our education and thoughts were focused on it. However, upon deeper reflection, we realized the importance of the Saguna (with form) aspect and devotion. Recognizing only the Nirguna aspect does not provide a complete solution, but recognizing the Saguna aspect leaves no room for doubt. The Saguna aspect is the complete and perfect form, as stated by the Lord himself - 'Asanshayam samagram mam' (Gita 7.1). Even after writing the appendix, we are not fully satisfied, and we have not stopped contemplating the Gita. We do not know what new ideas will emerge in the future, but we have no doubt that the perfection of human life lies in the attainment of devotion (love). Initially, the commentary lacked a detailed explanation of the verses, but now this gap has been filled. The commentary has been revised with careful consideration of the meaning and the beauty of the language. If readers find any difference between the initial and later commentaries, they should adopt the later one. It is a principle that the later commentary has more importance than the earlier one. This commentary has been written with the primary intention of benefiting the seekers, not just to showcase knowledge. Seekers should read this commentary without any preconceptions and reflect deeply on it to understand the true essence, and even the aspects that are not explicitly mentioned will become clear to them.

**The Seventh Chapter: Summary**
The seventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is a continuation of the conversation between Arjuna and Lord Krishna. In this chapter, Arjuna asks seven questions, and Lord Krishna provides answers to them, emphasizing the importance of remembering Him at all times.

**The Seventh Chapter: 1-7**
Arjuna asks, "O Lord, what is the nature of the Self, and how can one attain it?" (Sanskrit: kimatra keśava nityaṃ hṛdi līlayā vihitam|)
Translation: "What is the nature of the Self, O Keshava, and how can one attain it, which is always established in the heart by Your grace?"

**The Seventh Chapter: 8-16**
Lord Krishna explains the nature of the Supreme Being, who is both with and without attributes, and who is beyond all attributes. He describes the fruits of worshiping the Supreme Being in various forms.

**The Seventh Chapter: 17-22**
Lord Krishna explains the duration of the universe, His own greatness, and the importance of devotion. He describes the universe as a vast expanse, with the Supreme Being as its foundation.

**The Seventh Chapter: 23-28**
Lord Krishna describes the creation and destruction of the universe, and the glory of those who know the Supreme Being.

**The Seventh Chapter: 29-42**
Arjuna praises Lord Krishna and requests Him to explain His divine nature and the science of yoga.

**The Seventh Chapter: 43-42**

english:
14

Om Shri Paramatmane Namah

I bow down to Lord Krishna, the teacher of the universe, the embodiment of beauty, the son of Nanda, the great one. (1)
I bow down to the one who has taken refuge in the lotus feet of the Lord, to the one who has taken the discus in hand, to the one whose hands are adorned with the Gita, the nectar of knowledge. (2)
I bow down to the one who has destroyed the pride of the demons, to the son of Vasudeva, the divine one, to the one who has killed Kamsa and Chanura. (3)
I bow down to the one who is the supreme delight of Devaki, to Lord Krishna, the teacher of the universe.

His hands are adorned with a garland of flowers, his chest is like a blue sapphire, his lips are like the tender shoots of a banyan tree, his face is like a full moon, and his eyes are like the petals of a lotus. (4)
I do not know anything greater than Krishna. (5)

The Bhishma-Drona river, the Jayadratha lake, the Ganga, the Nila-utpala, the Shalya-graha, the Karna-velli, the Ashvatthama-vikarna, the Duryodhana-vartin, and the Pandava-ran-nadi - all these rivers have been crossed by the Lord, who is the remover of the darkness of ignorance. (6)
The Gita is the one scripture, the son of Devaki is the one God, the one mantra is the name of that God, and the one service is the worship of that God. (7)

भगवद्गीताग्रन्थ प्रस्थानत्रयमें माना जाता है। मनुष्यमात्रके

एक दार्शनिक प्रस्थान है, जिसको 'ब्रह्मसूत्र' कहते हैं और

उपनिषदोंमें मन्त्र हैं, ब्रह्मसूत्रमें सूत्र हैं और भगवद्गीतामें

होनेसे इनको सूत्र भी कह सकते हैं। 'उपनिषद्' अधिकारी

देश, सम्प्रदाय, मत आदिका कोई भी मनुष्य क्यों न हो,
इस ग्रन्थको पढ़ते ही इसमें आकृष्ट हो जाता है। अगर
मनुष्य इस ग्रन्थका थोड़ा-सा भी पठन-पाठन करे तो
उसको अपने उद्धारके लिये बहुत ही सन्तोषजनक उपाय
मिलते हैं । हरेक दर्शनके अलग-अलग अधिकारी होते हैं,
पर गीताकी यह विलक्षणता है कि अपना उद्धार चाहनेवाले
सब-के-सब इसके अधिकारी हैं ।
भगवद्गीता एक बहुत ही अलौकिक, विचित्र ग्रन्थ
है। इसमें साधकके लिये उपयोगी पूरी सामग्री मिलती है,
चाहे वह किसी भी देशका, किसी भी वेशका, किसी भी
समुदायका, किसी भी सम्प्रदायका, किसी भी वर्णका,
किसी भी आश्रमका कोई व्यक्ति क्यों न हो। इसका कारण
यह है कि इसमें किसी समुदाय - विशेषकी निन्दा या प्रशंसा
नहीं है, प्रत्युत वास्तविक तत्त्वका ही वर्णन है । वास्तविक
तत्त्व (परमात्मा) वह है, जो परिवर्तनशील प्रकृति और
प्रकृतिजन्य पदार्थोंसे सर्वथा अतीत और सम्पूर्ण देश, काल, भगवद्गीतामें साधनोंका वर्णन करनेमें, विस्तारपूर्वक
वस्तु, व्यक्ति, परिस्थिति आदिमें नित्य - निरन्तर एकरस - समझानेमें, एक - एक साधनको कई बार कहने में संकोच
एकरूप रहनेवाला है। जो मनुष्य जहाँ है और जैसा है, नहीं किया गया है, फिर भी ग्रन्थका कलेवर नहीं बढ़ा
वास्तविक तत्त्व वहाँ वैसा ही पूर्णरूपसे विद्यमान है । परन्तु है । ऐसा संक्षेपमें विस्तारपूर्वक यथार्थ और पूरी बात
परिवर्तनशील प्रकृतिजन्य वस्तु, व्यक्तियोंमें राग-द्वेषके बतानेवाला दूसरा कोई ग्रन्थ नहीं दीखता। अपने कल्याणकी
कारण उसका अनुभव नहीं होता । सर्वथा राग-द्वेषरहित | उत्कट अभिलाषावाला मनुष्य हरेक परिस्थितिमें परमात्मतत्त्वको

The Gita has been taught without any book, in this way, it can bring about good - 'dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre .... ' - up to this point, without reversing the book. If a book is not seen, then reading the Gita from the beginning to the end every day, one or more times, brings out the special meaning of the Gita. If there is any doubt in the mind, it is resolved by reading the Gita.

The Gita is a majestic scripture. By taking refuge in it and reading it, one gets to experience wonderful, extraordinary, and peaceful feelings. By reading it with attention, one gets a lot of peace. One method of reading the Gita is to first memorize the entire Gita with its meaning, then sit alone and read the last verse of the Gita - 'yatra | 

There is no one who can describe the glory of this scripture, which is beyond all limits. No one can describe the glory of this scripture, which is beyond all limits.

The special goal of the Gita is that a person should not be bound by any doctrine, philosophy, or school of thought. The Gita does not follow any doctrine, philosophy, or school of thought. Its main goal is that a person should be happy in every situation, and should not be deprived of the realization of the Supreme. Because the human birth is only for one's own good.

There is no situation in the world where a person's good cannot be achieved. Because the Supreme Reality is present equally in every situation. Therefore, the seeker should use every situation wisely. The wise use of a situation means giving up the desire for happiness in a difficult situation, and giving up the desire to enjoy happiness in a favorable situation and using it for the service of others. In this way, a person rises above both difficult and favorable situations, and his good is achieved.

The objects of the game are only for the game, not for any individual. But the living beings have forgotten the game and, using their freedom, have started considering the objects of the game as their own. Therefore, they have become entangled in the objects of the game and have become completely detached from God.

If the living beings become detached from the objects of the game, which are subject to birth and death, and turn towards God, they will be free from the great suffering of birth and death forever. Therefore, the living beings should turn away from the world and turn towards God, and they should cultivate their eternal relationship with God, which is 'I am one, but I am manifest in many forms.' This is the resolve that has led to the incarnation of the Bhagavad Gita.

(2) The word 'yoga' derived from the root 'yuj', which means 'to be in a state of samadhi' or 'to be in a state of equanimity'.

(3) The word 'yoga' derived from the root 'yuj', which means 'to be in a state of union with the Supreme' or 'to be in a state of oneness with the Supreme'.

The root 'yuj' also means 'to be in a state of calmness' or 'to be in a state of tranquility'.

The Gita is a comprehensive guide to various means of achieving spiritual growth, as mentioned in the scriptures. This is why the Gita has a special place in the world of spiritual seekers, regardless of their faith or tradition. The Gita does not limit itself to just three paths - karma yoga, jnana yoga, or bhakti yoga - but also includes other means such as yajna, dana, tapas, dhyana yoga, pranayama, hatha yoga, and laya yoga.

The reason for this is that the Gita is not focused on the subject of war, but rather on the path to spiritual growth and self-realization, which is the ultimate goal of all beings. The Gita is a guide to achieving this goal, and its purpose is to help seekers attain spiritual growth and self-realization.

The second approach is based on the idea that spiritual growth can be achieved through internal means, such as self-inquiry, introspection, and self-realization.

The Gita describes the first approach as the 'karan-sapaksha-shaili' or the 'means-dependent approach', and the second approach as the 'karan-nirapaksha-shaili' or the 'means-independent approach'. The means-dependent approach involves using external means, such as the body, senses, and mind, to achieve spiritual growth, while the means-independent approach involves focusing on the internal means, such as the self and the ultimate reality.

The Gita states that the means-independent approach is the more direct and effective way to achieve spiritual growth, as it involves a direct experience of the ultimate reality, without the need for external means. The means-dependent approach, on the other hand, involves a gradual and indirect experience of the ultimate reality, through the use of external means.

[ ध ]
१
'सम्बन्ध-विच्छेद होकर सीधे परमात्मतत्त्वका अनुभव होता है । '
(४) करण-सापेक्ष-शैलीमें कभी तत्काल सिद्धि नहीं
मिलती, पर करण-निरपेक्ष- शैलीमें जडतासे सर्वथा सम्बन्ध -
विच्छेद होनेपर, अपने स्वरूपमें स्थित होनेपर अथवा
भगवान्‌ के शरण होनेपर तत्काल सिद्धि मिलती है।
|
पातंजलयोगदर्शनमें तो योगकी सिद्धिके लिये करण-
सापेक्ष-शैलीको महत्त्व दिया गया है, पर गीतामें योगकी
सिद्धिके लिये करण-निरपेक्ष - शैलीको ही महत्त्व दिया गया
है। परमात्मामें मन लग गया, तब तो ठीक है, पर मन नहीं
लगा तो कुछ नहीं हुआ - यह करण - सापेक्ष - शैली है ।
परमात्मामें मन लगे या न लगे, कोई बात नहीं, पर स्वयं
परमात्मामें लग जाय—यह करण-निरपेक्ष - शैली है । तात्पर्य
यह है कि करण-सापेक्ष - शैलीमें परमात्माके साथ मन-
बुद्धिका सम्बन्ध है और करण -निरपेक्ष - शैलीमें मन-
बुद्धिसे सम्बन्ध-विच्छेदपूर्वक परमात्माके साथ स्वयंका
सम्बन्ध है। इसलिये करण - सापेक्ष - शैलीमें अभ्यासके द्वारा
क्रमसे सिद्धि होती है, पर करण -निरपेक्ष - शैलीमें अभ्यासकी
आवश्यकता नहीं है। कारण कि स्वयंका परमात्माके साथ
स्वत:सिद्ध नित्य-सम्बन्ध (नित्ययोग) है | अतः भगवान्से
सम्बन्ध मानने अथवा जाननेमें अभ्यासकी आवश्यकता नहीं
है; जैसे—विवाह होनेपर स्त्री पुरुषको अपना पति मान लेती
है, तो ऐसा माननेके लिये उसको कोई अभ्यास नहीं करना
पड़ता। इसी तरह किसीके बतानेपर 'यह गंगाजी हैं ' - ऐसा
जाननेके लिये भी कोई अभ्यास नहीं करना पड़ता । करण -
सापेक्ष-शैलीमें तो अपने लिये साधन करने - (क्रिया - ) की
मुख्यता रहती है, पर करण -निरपेक्ष- शैलीमें जानने (विवेक)
और मानने-(भाव-) की मुख्यता रहती है।
'मेरा जडता- (शरीरादि - ) से सम्बन्ध है ही नहीं'
ऐसा अनुभव न होनेपर भी जब साधक इसको आरम्भसे
ही दृढ़तापूर्वक मान लेता है, तब उसे ऐसा ही स्पष्ट अनुभव
हो जाता है। जैसे वह 'मैं शरीर हूँ और शरीर मेरा है'-
इस प्रकार गलत मान्यता करके बँधा था, ऐसे ही ' मैं शरीर
नहीं हूँ और शरीर मेरा नहीं है ' – इस प्रकार सही मान्यता
करके मुक्त हो जाता है; क्योंकि मानी हुई बात न माननेसे
मिट जाती है – यह सिद्धान्त है । इसी बातको भगवान्ने
गीतामें कहा है कि अज्ञानी मनुष्य शरीरसे सम्बन्ध जोड़कर
उससे होनेवाली क्रियाओंका कर्ता अपनेको मान लेता है-
'अहंकारविमूढात्मा कर्ताहमिति मन्यते ' ( ३।२७) ।
परन्तु ज्ञानी मनुष्य उन क्रियाओंका कर्ता अपनेको नहीं
मानता - ' नैव किञ्चित्करोमीति युक्तो मन्येत तत्त्ववित्'
(५ । ८) । तात्पर्य यह हुआ कि अवास्तविक मान्यताको
मिटानेके लिये वास्तविक मान्यता करनी जरूरी
।
'मैं हिन्दू हूँ', 'मैं ब्राह्मण हूँ', 'मैं साधु हूँ' आदि मान्यताएँ
इतनी दृढ़ होती हैं कि जबतक इन मान्यताओंको स्वयं नहीं
छोड़ता, तबतक इनको कोई दूसरा नहीं छुड़ा सकता। ऐसे ही
'मैं शरीर हूँ', 'मैं कर्ता हूँ' आदि मान्यताएँ भी इतनी दृढ़ हो
जाती हैं कि उनको छोड़ना साधकको कठिन मालूम देता है।
परन्तु ये लौकिक मान्यताएँ अवास्तविक, असत्य होनेके
कारण सदा रहनेवाली नहीं हैं, प्रत्युत मिटनेवाली हैं। इसके
विपरीत 'मैं शरीर नहीं हूँ', 'मैं भगवान्‌का हूँ' आदि मान्यताएँ
वास्तविक, सत्य होनेके कारण कभी मिटती ही नहीं, प्रत्युत
उनकी विस्मृति होती है, उनसे विमुखता होती है। इसलिये
वास्तविक मान्यता दृढ़ होनेपर मान्यतारूपसे नहीं रहती,
प्रत्युत बोध - (अनुभव - ) में परिणत हो जाती है ।
यद्यपि गीतामें करण - सापेक्ष - शैलीका भी वर्णन किया
गया है (जैसे चौथे अध्यायके चौबीसवेंसे तीसवेंतक तथा
चौंतीसवाँ श्लोक, छठे अध्यायके दसवेंसे अट्ठाईसवेंतक,
आठवें अध्यायके आठवेंसे सोलहवेंतक और पन्ध्रहवें
१- अगर करण - सापेक्ष - शैली - (चित्तवृत्तिनिरोध - ) से सीधे परमात्मतत्त्वकी प्राप्ति हो जाती, तो पातंजलयोगदर्शनका
'विभूतिपाद' (जिसमें सिद्धियोंका वर्णन है) व्यर्थ हो जाता । करण - सापेक्ष - शैलीसे जिन सिद्धियोंकी प्राप्ति होती है, वे तो
परमात्मतत्त्वकी प्राप्तिमें विघ्न हैं । पातंजलयोगदर्शनमें भी उन सिद्धियोंको विघ्नरूपसे माना गया है— 'ते समाधावुपसर्गा
व्युत्थाने सिद्धयः' ( ३ | ३७ ) अर्थात् वे (सिद्धियाँ) समाधिकी सिद्धिमें विघ्न हैं और व्युत्थान - ( व्यवहार - ) में सिद्धियाँ हैं;
'स्थान्युपनिमन्त्रणे सङ्गस्मयाकरणं पुनरनिष्टप्रसङ्गात् ' ( ३ । ५१ ) अर्थात् लोकपाल देवताओंके द्वारा ( अपने लोकोंके भोगोंका
लालच देकर ) बुलानेपर न तो उन भोगोंमें राग करना चाहिये और न अभिमान करना चाहिये; क्योंकि ऐसा करनेसे पुनः
अनिष्ट ( पतन ) होनेकी सम्भावना है।
२-वास्तवमें परमात्माको मानने अथवा जाननेके विषयमें संसारका कोई भी दृष्टान्त पूरा नहीं घटता । कारण कि
संसारको मानने अथवा जाननेमें तो मन-बुद्धि साथमें रहते हैं, पर परमात्माको मानने अथवा जाननेमें मन-बुद्धि साथमें नहीं
रहते अर्थात् परमात्माका अनुभव स्वयंसे होता है, मन-बुद्धिसे नहीं । दूसरी बात, संसारको मानने अथवा जाननेका तो आरम्भ
और अन्त होता है, पर परमात्माको मानने अथवा जाननेका आरम्भ और अन्त नहीं होता । कारण कि वास्तवमें संसारके साथ
हमारा ( स्वयंका) सम्बन्ध है ही नहीं,जबकि परमात्माके साथ हमारा सम्बन्ध सदासे ही है और सदा ही रहेगा।

'By severing connection, there is direct experience of the Supreme Reality.'
(4) In the instrument-dependent method, immediate attainment is never achieved; but in the instrument-independent method, upon completely severing connection with inert matter, abiding in one's true nature, or taking refuge in the Lord, immediate attainment is achieved.

|

In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, importance is given to the instrument-dependent method for the attainment of Yoga, whereas in the Gita, importance is given solely to the instrument-independent method for the attainment of Yoga. If the mind becomes fixed on the Supreme, that is fine; but if the mind is not fixed, nothing is achieved—this is the instrument-dependent method. Whether the mind is fixed on the Supreme or not makes no difference, provided one's inner self attaches directly to the Supreme—this is the instrument-independent method. The essence is that in the instrument-dependent method, the relation with the Supreme is via the mind and intellect, while in the instrument-independent method, one's inner self attaches directly to the Supreme by severing connection with the mind and intellect. Therefore, in the instrument-dependent method, attainment comes gradually through practice; but in the instrument-independent method, practice is not required. This is because one's relationship with the Supreme is an eternally established relationship (nitya-yoga). Hence, practice is not needed to accept or know one's relationship with God; just as after marriage, a woman accepts a man as her husband without having to perform any practice to accept it. Similarly, when someone points out, 'This is the sacred Ganga', no practice is required to know it. In the instrument-dependent method, primary emphasis is on performing spiritual practice (action) for oneself; but in the instrument-independent method, primary emphasis is on knowing (discrimination) and accepting (inner feeling).

Even when a seeker does not yet directly experience 'I have no relationship whatsoever with inert matter (body, etc.)', if they firmly accept this from the very beginning, they gain that very clear experience. Just as one was bound by holding the false belief 'I am the body and the body is mine', similarly one is liberated by holding the true belief 'I am not the body and the body is not mine'; because an assumed belief vanishes when it is no longer accepted—this is the principle. The Lord states this in the Gita: an ignorant person attaches himself to the body and considers himself the doer of actions arising from it—'ahankara-vimudhatma kartaham iti manyate' (Gita 3.27). But a wise person does not consider himself the doer of those actions—'naiva kincit karomit yukto manyeta tattvavit' (Gita 5.8). The implication is that to eliminate an unreal belief, it is essential to establish a real belief.

|

Beliefs such as 'I am a Hindu', 'I am a Brahmin', 'I am a renunciate' become so deeply rooted that unless one gives them up oneself, no one else can remove them. Likewise, beliefs like 'I am the body', 'I am the doer' become so firm that letting them go seems difficult to the seeker. However, since these worldly beliefs are unreal and false, they are not permanent, but destined to perish. In contrast, true beliefs like 'I am not the body', 'I belong to God' are real and true, and therefore never perish; rather, they are merely forgotten or turned away from. Thus, when a real belief becomes firm, it does not remain a mere belief, but transforms into direct realization (experience).

Although the instrument-dependent method is also described in the Gita (such as in Chapter 4, verses 24 to 30 and verse 34; Chapter 6, verses 10 to 28; Chapter 8, verses 8 to 16; and Chapter 15...

1- If direct attainment of the Supreme Reality were achieved through the instrument-dependent method (restraint of mental modifications), then the 'Vibhuti Pada' of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (which describes supernatural powers) would become redundant. The powers attained through the instrument-dependent method are actually obstacles to attaining the Supreme Reality. Even in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, those powers are acknowledged as obstacles—'te samadhav upasarga vyutthane siddhayah' (Yoga Sutra 3.37), meaning those (powers) are obstacles to Samadhi and are accomplishments only in worldly waking state (vyutthan); 'sthany-upanimantrane sanga-smayakaranampunaranista-prasangat' (Yoga Sutra 3.51), meaning when invited by the celestial deities of higher realms, one should neither feel attachment to those pleasures nor take pride in them, for doing so risks downfall.

2- In truth, no worldly illustration fully applies to accepting or knowing the Supreme Being. This is because in accepting or knowing the world, the mind and intellect remain active with us; but in accepting or knowing the Supreme Being, the mind and intellect do not accompany us—meaning the experience of the Supreme is realized by the Self directly, not through the mind and intellect. Secondly, knowing or accepting the world has a beginning and an end, but knowing or accepting the Supreme Being has no beginning and no end. This is because in reality, our (Self's) connection with the world does not exist at all, whereas our connection with the Supreme Being has existed eternally and will remain forever.

The need to purify the inner instrument (antahkarana) also belongs to the instrument-dependent method, not the instrument-independent method. Just as having a fine pen may make the writing fine, but does not make the writer fine; similarly, purifying the instrument (mind/intellect) may make actions pure, but does not make the doer pure. The doer becomes pure by severing connection with the inner instrument; because regarding one's connection with the inner instrument as real is the primary impurity.

verse 11 of the chapter, etc.), yet primarily the instrument-independent method alone has been described (such as Chapter 2, verses 48 and 55; Chapter 3, verse 17; Chapter 4, verse 38; the first half of Chapter 5, verse 12; Chapter 6, verse 5; Chapter 9, verses 30-31; Chapter 12, verse 12; Chapter 18, verses 62, 66, and 73, etc.). The reason for this is that the Lord wishes to enable seekers to attain Him quickly and easily. Secondly, Arjuna asked for the means of his spiritual welfare at the moment of facing war. Therefore, for his welfare, only the instrument-independent method could serve; because in the instrument-independent method, a person can attain spiritual welfare in every circumstance and even while performing all duties prescribed by scripture. According to this method (without long practice), Arjuna's delusion was destroyed and he regained spiritual memory (Gita 18.73).

The instrument-independent method of spiritual discipline is equally useful for everyone, as it requires no special qualification or external circumstance. In this method, simply possessing an intense desire for attaining the Supreme causes immediate severance of connection with inert matter, realizing the eternally attained Supreme Reality. Just as darkness of countless years is destroyed instantly upon striking a single matchstick, similarly, no matter how ancient (spanning infinite births) one's connection with inert matter may be, it vanishes the moment an intense longing for attaining the Supreme arises. Therefore, intense longing is superior even to Samadhi achieved through instrument-dependence. Even in the highest absorption (nirvikalpa samadhi), there is a return to waking state (vyutthan) followed by worldly activity—meaning Samadhi also has a beginning and an end. As long as there is a beginning and an end, connection with inert matter persists. Once connection with inert matter is severed, spiritual practice has no beginning or end; rather, one experiences eternal union with the Supreme Lord.*

In truth, separation from the Supreme Lord has never occurred, nor is it ever possible. It is only due to assumed association with the world that separation from the Supreme Lord appears to exist. The moment a seeker after the Supreme Reality gives up assumed attachment to the world, they instantly experience eternal union and become permanently established in it.

*

The eternal union of the individual soul with the eternally attained Supreme Reality is self-evident; hence, its attainment does not depend on instruments. One merely needs to direct one's vision towards it, as expressed in Sri Ramcharitmanas—'sankara sahaja sarupu samhara' (1.58.4), meaning Lord Shiva composed Himself in His natural essential form, directing His vision towards it. A thing that is 'kept/remembered' is something that is already with us and merely requires a glance to recognize its presence. In the same way, mere turning of vision yields the experience of eternal union. However, owing to desires for worldly pleasures, hopes, and enjoyment, turning vision towards it and experiencing it seems difficult. As long as one's vision is directed towards worldly enjoyment and accumulation, a person lacks the power to look towards their true Self. Even if by some reason or special contemplation one's vision turns there, keeping it steady is extremely difficult, because the deep-rooted affection for perishable objects prevents one from comprehending the self-evident relationship with God; and even if comprehended, does not let it remain steady. But if an intense longing awakens—'How may that Supreme Reality be experienced?'—then this longing possesses the power to destroy all attachment to the world.

Karmayoga, Jnanayoga, and Bhaktiyoga as taught in the Gita are all three instrument-independent, meaning they occur through the Self. Actions and objects do not belong to oneself nor are they for oneself; rather, they belong to others and are meant for serving others; 'I am not the body and the body is not mine; I belong to God and God belongs to me'—such contemplation or conviction conducted through discrimination is not instrument-dependent (practice), because in this there is severance of connection from inert matter. Thus, in Karmayoga, detachment from inert matter happens naturally.

* As long as connection with inert matter remains, two states persist; because being mutable, inert nature is never uniform. Thus, both Samadhi (absorption) and Vyutthan (waking/activity) occur only due to connection with inert matter. Upon severing connection with inert matter, the 'Sahajavastha' (natural state) arises, which saints call 'Sahaja Samadhi'. From this state, there is never any return to delusion.

अर्थ समझ लेगा, तो फिर व्याख्या समझनेमें सुविधा रहेगी।
अतः 'गीताकी सम्पत्ति और श्रद्धा' के दूसरे संस्करण
(संवत् २०४० ) - में श्लोकोंके अर्थ भी दे दिये गये।
श्लोकोंके अर्थ देनेके साथ-साथ पदोंकी व्याख्या करनेका
क्रम भी कुछ बदल गया ।
सबसे पहले एक बारहवें अध्यायकी व्याख्या लिखवायी ।
इसको संवत् २०३०में ‘गीताका भक्तियोग' नामसे प्रकाशित
किया गया। इसके कुछ वर्षोंके बाद तेरहवें और चौदहवें
अध्यायकी व्याख्या लिखवायी, जिसको संवत् २०३५ में
'गीताका ज्ञानयोग' नामसे प्रकाशित किया गया। इसको इसके बाद दसवें और ग्यारहवें अध्यायकी व्याख्या
लिखवानेके बाद ऐसा विचार हुआ कि कर्मयोग, ज्ञानयोग लिखवायी । इसको 'गीताकी विभूति और विश्वरूप-
और भक्तियोग – ये तीन योग हैं, अत: इन तीनों ही योगोंपर दर्शन' नामसे प्रकाशित किया गया । फिर सातवें, आठवें और
तीन पुस्तकें तैयार हो जायँ तो ठीक रहेगा। इस दृष्टिसे पहले नवें अध्यायकी व्याख्या लिखवायी, जिसको 'गीताकी राजविद्या'
बारहवें अध्यायकी व्याख्याका संशोधन - परिवर्धन किया नामसे प्रकाशित किया गया। इसके बाद छठे अध्यायकी
गया और उसके साथ पंद्रहवें अध्यायकी व्याख्याको भी व्याख्या लिखवायी, जो 'गीताका ध्यानयोग' नामसे प्रकाशित
सम्मिलित करके संवत् २०३९ में 'गीताका भक्तियोग' की गयी । अन्तमें पहले और दूसरे अध्यायकी व्याख्या
(द्वितीय संस्करण) नामसे प्रकाशित किया गया। फिर लिखवायी । इसको 'गीताका आरम्भ' नामसे प्रकाशित
तीसरे, चौथे और पाँचवें अध्यायकी व्याख्या लिखवायी । किया गया । ये चारों पुस्तकें संवत् २०४१ में प्रकाशित हुईं।
इसको 'गीताका कर्मयोग' नामसे दो खण्डोंमें प्रकाशित
किया गया। इसका प्रकाशन विलम्बसे संवत् २०४० में हुआ ।
उपर्युक्त 'गीताका भक्तियोग', 'गीताका ज्ञानयोग'
और 'गीताका कर्मयोग' – इन तीनों पुस्तकोंमें लिखनेकी
शैली कुछ और रही अर्थात् पहले सम्बन्ध, फिर श्लोक,
फिर भावार्थ, फिर अन्वय और फिर पद - व्याख्या - इस
शैलीसे लिखा गया। परन्तु इन तीनों पुस्तकोंके बाद लिखनेकी
शैली बदल दी गयी अर्थात् पहले सम्बन्ध, फिर श्लोक और
फिर व्याख्या—इस शैली से लिखा गया । इसमें दूसरोंकी
प्रेरणा भी रही। शैली बदलनेमें भाव यह रहा कि पाठ कुछ
कम हो जाय और जल्दी लिखा जाय, जिससे पाठकोंको
इस प्रकार भगवत्कृपासे पूरी गीताकी टीका अलग-
अलग कुल दस खण्डोंमें गीताप्रेससे प्रकाशित हुई। इनको
प्रकाशित करनेके कार्यमें कागज आदिकी कई कठिनाइयाँ
आती रहीं, फिर भी सत्संगी भाइयोंके उद्योगसे इनको
प्रकाशित करनेका कार्य चलता रहा। लोगोंने भी इन
पुस्तकोंको उत्साह एवं प्रसन्नतापूर्वक स्वीकार किया, जिससे
कई पुस्तकोंके दो-दो, तीन-तीन संस्करण भी निकल गये ।
इस टीकाको एक जगह बैठकर नहीं लिखवाया गया है
और इसको पहले अध्यायसे लेकर अठारहवें अध्यायतक
क्रमसे भी नहीं लिखवाया गया है। इसलिये इसमें पूर्वापरकी
दृष्टिसे कई विरोध आ सकते हैं। परन्तु इससे साधकोंको कहीं

भी फरक पड़ा है; परन्तु कर्मयोग, ज्ञानयोग और
भक्तियोग—ये तीनों स्वतन्त्रतापूर्वक परमात्मतत्त्वकी प्राप्ति
करानेवाले हैं – इसमें कोई फरक नहीं पड़ा है । टीका
लिखवाते समय ‘साधकोंको शीघ्र लाभ कैसे हो' – ऐसा
भाव रहा है। इस कारण टीकाकी भाषा, शैली आदिमें
परिवर्तन होता रहा है।
-
भी बाधा नहीं लगेगी। कहीं-कहीं सिद्धान्तोंके विवेचनमें | उनके पुनर्मुद्रणमें और उन सबके एक साथ प्राप्त होनेमें
कठिनाई रहती है - ऐसा सोचकर अब पूरी गीताकी
टीकाको एक जिल्दमें प्रस्तुत ग्रन्थके रूपमें प्रकाशित किया
गया है। ऐसा करने से पहले पूर्व - प्रकाशित सम्पूर्ण टीकाको
एक बार पुनः देखा है और उसमें आवश्यक संशोधन,
परिवर्तन और परिवर्धन भी किया है। तेरहवें और चौदहवें
अध्यायकी व्याख्या भी दुबारा लिखवायी गयी है । भाषा
और शैलीको भी लगभग एक समान बनानेकी चेष्टा की
गयी है | कई बातोंको अनावश्यक समझकर हटा दिया है,
कई नयी बातें जोड़ दी हैं और कई बातोंको एक स्थानसे
हटाकर दूसरे यथोचित स्थानपर दे दिया है। जिन बातोंकी
ज्यादा पुनरुक्तियाँ हुई हैं, उनको यथासम्भव हटा दिया है,
पर सर्वथा नहीं । विशेष ध्यान देनेयोग्य बातोंकी पुनरुक्तियोंको
साधकोंके लिये उपयोगी समझकर नहीं हटाया है। इस

While dictating the commentary, the inner feeling has always been 'How may seekers benefit quickly?' Due to this, changes have occurred in the language and style of the commentary.

no obstacle will be caused. Thinking that everywhere in the discussion of principles there remains difficulty in reprinting separate volumes and acquiring all of them together, the commentary on the entire Gita has now been published in a single volume as the present book. Before doing so, the entire previously published commentary was reviewed once again, and necessary corrections, alterations, and additions were made. The explanation of the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters was also redictated. An attempt was made to render the language and style nearly uniform throughout. Many points were removed considering them unnecessary, several new insights were added, and many points were shifted from one place to their proper location. Where repetitions occurred excessively, they have been removed as far as possible, but not entirely. Repetitions of particularly noteworthy points have been retained, considering them beneficial for seekers. In this work, many errors may also have occurred, for which I fold my hands in seeking forgiveness from readers. Furthermore, readers are requested to kindly inform about any errors they notice, which will facilitate their correction in future editions.

In this commentary, the explanation of many verses differs from other commentaries. However, this is by no means intended to imply that other commentaries are incorrect; rather, I have provided the explanation exactly as appeared to me undisputed, contextually appropriate, logical, satisfying, and pleasing. I have had no intention whatsoever of refutation or defense of any position.

The meaning of Srimad Bhagavad Gita is exceedingly profound. By reading, studying, contemplating, and reflecting upon it, most wonderful and fresh insights keep sprouting, filling the mind and intellect with awe and satisfaction. When dictating the commentary, whenever the thought of dictating these insights arose, such a remarkable surge would come that I felt completely inadequate as to which insights to dictate and how to dictate them. Nevertheless, at the insistence of my companions and respected friends, I would dictate a portion. They would transcribe those insights, edit them, and publish them as books. Later, whenever there was occasion to examine those books, shortcomings would appear in several places, making it seem that full points had not been covered and many things had been omitted! Therefore, repeated revisions and expansions were carried out. Hence, readers are requested to give priority to and accept the later written content over the earlier written content.

Since there were several separate volumes of the commentary on the entire Gita,

*

A separate collection of several new subjects and exploratory essays related to the Gita has been prepared and published under the title 'Gita-Darpana'.

By contemplating and reflecting on the Gita and dictating its commentary, I have derived great spiritual benefit and gained a very clear understanding of the subject matter of the Gita. If other brothers and sisters also contemplate it, they too will surely derive spiritual benefit—this is my personal conviction. That spiritual benefit comes from contemplating and reflecting on the Gita—of this I have never had even the slightest doubt.

The Bhagavad Gita

I take refuge in that Lord, who is the embodiment of all virtues. He is the one who is free from all impurities. The ignorant people, who have been rejected by the world, attain liberation by taking refuge in Him, relying on His virtues. I bow down to that pure Lord, Krishna, the son of Vasudeva.

The boy Dhruva, who was blessed by the ocean of mercy, obtained his desired object by taking refuge in the Lord, who is the embodiment of all virtues. Even the mountain of Govardhan, which was once a poor man, became worthy of worship by taking refuge in the Lord. I worship the Lord, Maha Deva, who is the protector of all, and who is always worthy of worship.

I bow down to that Lord, Krishna, who is the son of Devaki, and who is the destroyer of Kansa and Chanaur. He is the divine teacher of the world.

After bowing down to Lord Krishna, who is the embodiment of all virtues, and to the great Arjuna, who is the best among men, and to Saraswati, the goddess of knowledge, and to Veda Vyasa, I shall narrate the story of the Mahabharata.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Chapter 1]

Explanation: 'Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra' - Kurukshetra is the land of the gods. Therefore, the entire Gita is under the category of Dharma, i.e., by following the principles of Dharma, the principles of the Gita are followed, and by following the principles of the Gita, the performance of Dharma is done.

King Kuru had performed a Yajna here. Even Raja Kuru had practiced Tapasya here. Due to the Yajna and other Dharma-related activities, and due to Raja Kuru's Tapasya Bhumi, this place is called Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra.

In the phrases 'Dharmakshetra' and 'Kurukshetra', the word 'Kshetra' is used by Dhritarashtra to mean that this is the land of the Kuru dynasty. This is not just a battlefield, but a Tirtha Bhumi, where people can purify themselves by performing good deeds and achieve their well-being. In this way, there is a benefit in both the worldly and spiritual realms - thinking in this way, and taking the opinion of great people, this land was chosen for war.

In the world, people usually fight over three things - land, wealth, and women. Among these three, the main reason for the kings' fight with each other is over land. Similarly, the phrase 'Kurukshetra' here also refers to the fight over land.

The descendants of the Kuru dynasty, Dhritarashtra and Pandu's sons, are all one. Due to being Kuru descendants, both have equal rights to the land of Raja Kuru, i.e., the land of Kurukshetra. Therefore, both have come to fight over the land.

Although it is suitable and just to use the phrase 'Kurukshetra' for both, considering that both are fighting over their own land, our ancient Vedic culture is so unique that any work is done by keeping Dharma in front. Even the work of war is done in the land of Dharma, the Tirtha Bhumi, so that the liberation of those who die in war is achieved, and their well-being is achieved.

Therefore, the phrase 'Dharmakshetra' has been used along with 'Kurukshetra' here.

From these phrases 'Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra', all humans should learn that any work should be done by keeping Dharma in front. Every work should be done with the intention of benefiting everyone, not just for personal comfort and pleasure. And the principles of duty and non-duty should be kept in mind, as mentioned in the 24th shloka of the 16th chapter of the Gita.

' Samaveta Yuyutsava' - Despite the repeated proposals of peace by the kings, Duryodhana refused to accept peace. Not only that, even when Lord Krishna told him, Duryodhana clearly said that he would not give even a needle's point of land to the Pandavas without a war. Therefore, the Pandavas were forced to accept war. In this way, both the armies of Duryodhana and the Pandavas have gathered, eager to fight.

Although both armies have a desire to fight, Duryodhana's desire for war was particularly strong. His main objective was to gain the kingdom. He thought that he should get the kingdom, whether it is through Dharma or Adharma, through justice or injustice, through the right means or through the wrong means - it doesn't matter, he should get the kingdom. Therefore, Duryodhana's side was particularly eager for war.

The Pandavas had Dharma as their main priority. They thought that they would live their lives as they pleased, but they would not compromise on their Dharma, they would not go against Dharma. This was the attitude of Maharaja Yudhishthira, who did not want to fight. However, due to the command of his mother, Kunti, who had married off her four sons, including Yudhishthira, to Draupadi, Yudhishthira had to accept war.

If we take the word 'Dharm' from the first 'Dharm' and the word 'Mam' from the last 'Mam' of the 18th chapter, the word 'Dharm' is formed. Yudhishthira's inclination was towards war, i.e., he was only concerned with his mother's command.

1. - As long as Keshav (Krishna) is sharp and keen, and as long as the needle's point of land is not given to the Pandavas, the land should not be given to them. (Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 127.25)
2. - Kunti was a very tolerant mother. She did not have the desire for comfort and pleasure. She was a unique mother who had asked for the boon of suffering from God. She did not have the desire for comfort and pleasure. However, she had two things that caused her great pain. First, the Kauravas and the Pandavas were fighting over the kingdom, no matter what they did, and my dear daughter-in-law Draupadi was being humiliated and insulted by the wicked Duryodhana and his followers in the assembly - this was a very inhumane act.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

युद्ध नहीं करना चाहते थे । यह नियम है कि जहाँ आपसमें मतभेद होता है, वहाँ तेज ( प्रभाव ) नहीं रहता-
काँच कटोरो कुम्भ पय मोती मिन्त अवास । ताल घाव तिरिया कटक फाटा करे बिनास ॥

* साधक - संजीवनी *
२९
'राजा' शब्दका प्रयोग किया है ।
करनेके लिये दुर्योधनका उनके पास जाना ही उचित था ।
‘आचार्यमुपसङ्गम्य’– द्रोणाचार्यके पास जानेमें मुख्यतः | व्यवहारमें भी यह देखा जाता है कि जिसके साथ स्नेह
तीन कारण मालूम देते हैं-
(१) अपना स्वार्थ सिद्ध करनेके लिये अर्थात्
द्रोणाचार्य के भीतर पाण्डवोंके प्रति द्वेष पैदा करके उनको
अपने पक्षमें विशेषतासे करनेके लिये दुर्योधन द्रोणाचार्यके
पास गया।
,
नहीं है, उससे अपना स्वार्थ सिद्ध करनेके लिये मनुष्य
उसको ज्यादा आदर देकर राजी करता है ।
।
दुर्योधनके मनमें यह विश्वास था कि भीष्मजी तो
हमारे दादाजी ही हैं; अत: उनके पास न जाऊँ तो भी कोई
बात नहीं है। न जानेसे अगर वे नाराज भी हो जायँगे तो
(२) व्यवहारमें गुरुके नाते आदर देनेके लिये भी मैं किसी तरहसे उनको राजी कर लूँगा । कारण कि
द्रोणाचार्यके पास जाना उचित था।
पितामह भीष्मके साथ दुर्योधनका कौटुम्बिक सम्बन्ध और
स्नेह था ही, भीष्मका भी उसके साथ कौटुम्बिक सम्बन्ध
और स्नेह था । इसलिये भीष्मजीने दुर्योधनको राजी करनेके
लिये जोरसे शंख बजाया है ( पहले अध्यायका बारहवाँ
श्लोक) ।
(३) मुख्य व्यक्तिका सेनामें यथास्थान खड़े रहना
बहुत आवश्यक होता है, अन्यथा व्यवस्था बिगड़ जाती है
इसलिये दुर्योधनका द्रोणाचार्यके पास खुद जाना उचित
ही था।
।
यहाँ शंका हो सकती है कि दुर्योधनको तो पितामह ‘वचनमब्रवीत्’–यहाँ 'अब्रवीत् ' कहना ही पर्याप्त
भीष्मके पास जाना चाहिये था, जो कि सेनापति थे । पर था; क्योंकि 'अब्रवीत्' क्रियाके अन्तर्गत ही 'वचनम् ' आ
दुर्योधन गुरु द्रोणाचार्यके पास ही क्यों गया ? इसका जाता है अर्थात् दुर्योधन बोलेगा, तो वचन ही बोलेगा ।
समाधान यह है कि द्रोण और भीष्म- दोनों उभय- इसलिये यहाँ 'वचनम्' शब्दकी आवश्यकता नहीं थी ।
पक्षपाती थे अर्थात् वे कौरव और पाण्डव - दोनोंका ही फिर भी 'वचनम्' शब्द देनेका तात्पर्य है कि दुर्योधन
पक्ष रखते थे। उन दोनोंमें भी द्रोणाचार्यको ज्यादा राजी | नीतियुक्त गम्भीर वचन बोलता है, जिससे द्रोणाचार्यके
करना था; क्योंकि द्रोणाचार्य के साथ दुर्योधनका गुरुके नाते मनमें पाण्डवोंके प्रति द्वेष पैदा हो जाय और वे हमारे ही
तो स्नेह था, पर कुटुम्बके नाते स्नेह नहीं था; और पक्षमें रहते हुए ठीक तरहसे युद्ध करें। जिससे हमारी
अर्जुनपर द्रोणाचार्यकी विशेष कृपा थी । अतः उनको राजी | विजय हो जाय, हमारा स्वार्थ सिद्ध हो जाय।
सम्बन्ध - द्रोणाचार्य के पास जाकर दुर्योधन क्या वचन बोला- इसको आगेके श्लोकमें बताते हैं।
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं
व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Dronacharya is being addressed by Duryodhana, who has called for a yajna to be performed by the brahmins Yajnas and Udyogas, in order to bring forth Dhrishtadyumna, the son of Drupada. Dhrishtadyumna is standing before him as the commander of the Pandava army.

Although Duryodhana could have referred to Dhrishtadyumna as 'Dhrishtadyumna', he uses the phrase 'Dhrupadputra' to remind Dronacharya of the enmity between Drupada and himself, and to take advantage of the opportunity to settle the score.

'Panduputranam etam vyudham mahatim chamum pasya' - Observe the great and powerful army of the Pandavas, led by Dhrishtadyumna, their son. This means that the Pandavas, who are dear to you, have appointed Dhrishtadyumna, who is destined to kill you, as their commander. If the Pandavas were dear to you, they would not have appointed someone who is meant to kill you as their commander.

Although the Kaurava army had eleven akshauhinis, and the Pandava army had only seven, Duryodhana describes the Pandava army as great and powerful. There are two reasons for this: (1) the Pandava army was arranged in a formation that made it appear larger than it actually was, and (2) all the warriors in the Pandava army were united and of one mind, which made their small army appear stronger and more formidable.

Duryodhana is trying to convey to Dronacharya that the Pandava army should not be underestimated, and that they should be prepared to fight with all their might. He is saying that the Pandava army is ready to fight, and that Dronacharya should quickly decide on a plan to defeat them.

Dronacharya is asked to observe the Pandava army, and Duryodhana begins to point out the great warriors of the Pandava army.

The very first line of this commentary is a reference to the page number. The following is a translation of the text:

The sons of Subhadra, Abhimanyu, are all great warriors. 

Shlokas 4-6:
Chekitanah, the brave and powerful king of Kashi, 
Purujit, the brave and powerful king of Kashi, 
Saubhadra, the brave and powerful king of Kashi, 
Shaibya, the brave and powerful king of Kashi, 
Vikrant, the brave and powerful king of Kashi, 
Droupadeya, the brave and powerful king of Kashi, 
Yudhamanyu, the brave and powerful king of Kashi, 
All these are great warriors.

Translation of the commentary:
Here are the brave warriors who are as skilled as Bhima and Arjuna. They are the sons of Subhadra. They are all great warriors. They are the sons of the king of Kashi, and they are as brave and powerful as their father.

The name 'Ishwasa' means 'bow' or 'bowman'. Those who have such powerful bows are called 'Mahishwasa'. The meaning of 'Mahishwasa' is that they have powerful bows and are skilled in using them. They are strong and brave warriors.

Yuyudhana, the son of Sathyaki, was a great warrior who had learned the art of archery from Arjuna. Even when Duryodhana was given the army of Naryana by Lord Krishna, Yuyudhana remained loyal to Arjuna and did not join Duryodhana's side. Duryodhana, however, mentions Yuyudhana's name first among the great warriors, implying that he is trying to create a sense of rivalry between Arjuna and Duryodhana.

The king of Virat, who had three sons named Uttara, Shvet and Shankh, was a great warrior who fought in the Mahabharata war.

Droupad, the king of Panchal, was a great warrior who had fought against Dronacharya. He had also borne a grudge against Dronacharya and had borne him a son to avenge his defeat.

Dhristaketu, the son of Shishupala, was a foolish warrior who had fought on the side of Krishna, despite Krishna having killed his father in a public assembly.

Chekitan, the son of Shishupala, was a great warrior who had fought on the side of the Pandavas.

The king of Virat, who had fought against the Pandavas, was a great warrior who had been defeated by them.

The verse from the Mahabharata (Adi Parva, 131.27) says:
"I am telling you the truth, there is no one else like you in the world. You are the only one who can do what I am asking you to do."

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 8]

In this context, it is advisable to allow Dronacharya to sit on our side, for that is his seat. Therefore, I have not mentioned it to you, but I have made Duryodhana focus his attention on it by using the verb 'nibodha' (dhyan dejiye), meaning 'pay attention'.

The reason for this is that there are many distinguished commanders in our army, who are the leaders of our forces, great warriors, and I am mentioning their names to you only to remind you of them, to draw your attention to them. The word 'sañjñārtham' (sanjnyartham) means that we have many such commanders, and I am only hinting at them, because you are already aware of them all.

Now, I shall speak about our army. The second point is that when Duryodhana saw the army of the Pandavas, he was greatly influenced and even felt a little fear in his heart. The reason for this is that despite being fewer in number, the Pandavas had many righteous men and God Himself was with them. Wherever righteousness and God reside, their influence is felt by all. Even the wicked and the wickedest of people, and even animals, birds, trees, and creepers are affected by it. The reason for this is that righteousness and God are eternal. No matter how great the physical powers may be, they are all transitory. Therefore, Duryodhana was greatly affected by the Pandav army.

However, since physical strength is the main factor in his mind, he says to Dronacharya that our side is not weak in any way. However, in politics, even if the enemy's side is weak and our side is strong, we should not consider the enemy's side as weak and our own side as strong. We should not have even a slight feeling of neglect or indifference towards the enemy's side. Therefore, we can easily conquer them.

You, Bhishma, and I, are like the sun and the moon. There is no one in the world who can match us. If either of us were to fight with our full strength, there would be no one in the world, whether a god, a yaksha, a rakshasa, or a human, who could withstand us. The bravery of both of us is well-known in the world. Bhishma is an aabala brahmacari, and he has taken a vow of self-immolation, meaning that no one can kill him without his consent.

The word 'karṇaśca' means that Karan is a very brave warrior. I have complete faith that he alone can defeat the Pandav army. Even Arjuna would not be able to do anything against him. Karan is also on our side.

The word 'kṛpaśca samitiñjayaḥ' means that Kripacharya is a chiranjevi, a person who is immortal, and is our greatest well-wisher. He can defeat the entire Pandav army. The eight chiranjevis are Ashwatthama, Bali, Vyas, Hanuman, Vibhishan, Kripacharya, Parashuram, and Markandey. This is mentioned in the Shastras:

aśvatthāmā balirvyāso hanūmāṃśca vibhīṣaṇaḥ | kṛpaḥ paraśurāmaśca saptaite cirajīvinaḥ || (Padmapuran 49.7)

Translation of the Sanskrit shlokas:

'bhavān bhīṣmaśca' - You, Bhishma, and I, are like the sun and the moon. There is no one in the world who can match us. If either of us were to fight with our full strength, there would be no one in the world, whether a god, a yaksha, a rakshasa, or a human, who could withstand us.

'karṇaśca' - Karan is a very brave warrior. I have complete faith that he alone can defeat the Pandav army. Even Arjuna would not be able to do anything against him.

'kṛpaśca samitiñjayaḥ' - Kripacharya is a chiranjevi, a person who is immortal, and is our greatest well-wisher. He can defeat the entire Pandav army.

The list of the eight chiranjevis is mentioned in the Padmapuran 49.7:

aśvatthāmā balirvyāso hanūmāṃśca vibhīṣaṇaḥ | kṛpaḥ paraśurāmaśca saptaite cirajīvinaḥ ||
