Chapter 1

Although Dronacharya and Bhishma are ahead of Duryodhana, our great-grandfather Shantanu's brother Bhalika's grandson and Somadatta's son Bhurishravas are also great devotees. They have performed many great sacrifices with large donations. They are great warriors and maharathis.

It would have been proper to mention Kripacharya's name, but Duryodhana had as much faith in Karna as he did in Kripacharya. Therefore, Karna's name slipped out in the middle. Dronacharya and Bhishma should not think that Kripacharya was insulted, so Duryodhana wants to please Kripacharya by calling him 'sangramvijayi'.

'Asvatthama' - these are also immortal and your own sons. They are great warriors. They have learned the art of weapons from you. They are very skilled in the art of weapons.

[In the war, Vikarna was killed by Bhima and Bhurishravas was killed by Satyaki.]

By mentioning the names of these great warriors, Duryodhana's intention is clear that, O teacher! Our army has great warriors like you, Bhishma, Karna, Kripacharya, etc. such great warriors are not seen in the army of the Pandavas. In our army, Kripacharya and Asvatthama are two immortal ones, while in the army of the Pandavas, there is not even one such. There is no shortage of devotees in our army. Therefore, do not think that only the Pandavas are devotees, my brother Vikarna is a great devotee and warrior, and there is no fear of defeat.

Shloka 10:
That which is insufficient for us, protected by Bhishma, is sufficient for these, protected by Bhima. 10

Translation of the commentary:
Dronacharya, observing Duryodhana's thoughts, thought to himself that in reality, our army is protected by Bhishma, who is impartial, and hence, insufficient for victory. However, the army of the Pandavas, protected by Bhima, is sufficient for victory.

Explanation: Duryodhana thought that despite Bhishma being the protector of our army, it is insufficient for victory. This is because Bhishma is impartial and has a soft spot for both the Kauravas and the Pandavas. He is a great devotee of Krishna and has a lot of respect for Yudhishthira and Arjuna. Therefore, despite being the commander-in-chief of our army, he secretly wishes well for the Pandavas. Hence, our army is not capable of defeating the Pandavas.

On the other hand, the army of the Pandavas, protected by Bhima, is sufficient for victory. This is because their army is well-organized and united, with no internal conflicts. Bhima, the protector of their army, is a powerful warrior who has been a thorn in my side since childhood. He has even vowed to kill all my hundred brothers. His body is as strong as a thunderbolt, and I have not been able to defeat him.

Note: The commentary explains that Duryodhana refers to Bhishma as the protector of our army, and Bhima as the protector of the Pandavas' army, because he is more familiar with Bhima's strength and power. This is also evident from the fact that Duryodhana goes to Dronacharya to see the Pandavas' army, whereas Arjuna goes to see the Kauravas' army.

Special note: The commentary also points out that Duryodhana's heart is filled with fear, which is evident from the fact that he goes to Dronacharya to see the Pandavas' army, whereas Arjuna goes to see the Kauravas' army. This shows that Duryodhana is not confident in his own army's strength.

The verse translation of the Sanskrit text is as follows:

* Arjuna has the principle of dharma and justice within him. He is never fearless. But the one who has the principle of dharma and takes refuge in God, he is not deceitful, nor is he fearful; but he is full of enthusiasm and bravery. He is never fearful. His strength is true. Therefore, he remains always confident and fearless, like a brave warrior, to inspect the army. Therefore, God instructs Arjuna to say to Him, "Oh, the imperishable one! Leave the two armies of the seekers of dharma and adharma, and place my chariot in the middle" (after having performed the first chapter and taking refuge only in the one God, for the sake of devotion to God, the 21st verse of the 7th chapter of the Mahabharata).

The commentary in Hindi is as follows:

The meaning of this is that the one who has the principle of dharma and takes refuge in God, he is not deceitful, nor is he fearful; but he is full of enthusiasm and bravery. He is never fearful. His strength is true. Therefore, he remains always confident and fearless, like a brave warrior, to inspect the army. Therefore, God instructs Arjuna to say to Him, "Oh, the imperishable one! Leave the two armies of the seekers of dharma and adharma, and place my chariot in the middle" (after having performed the first chapter and taking refuge only in the one God, for the sake of devotion to God, the 21st verse of the 7th chapter of the Mahabharata).

The commentary further explains that the one who has the principle of dharma and takes refuge in God, his heart is strong because God's strength is true. But the one whose vision is on worldly wealth, his heart is weak because worldly strength is fragile.

Now, Duryodhana tells his grandfather Bhishma to be pleased with him, saying:

"O, you all, who are stationed on all the battlefields, as per your respective positions, protect Bhishma, and all of you will be protected" (11th verse).

The translation of the Sanskrit text is as follows:

"O, you all, who are stationed on all the battlefields, as per your respective positions, protect Bhishma, and all of you will be protected" (11th verse).

The commentary explains that Duryodhana is saying this to Bhishma to please him, and to make him a part of his side. The second meaning of this is that when Bhishma goes to war, make sure that Shikhandi does not come in front of him from any angle. If Shikhandi comes in front of him, Bhishma will not fight with him. This is because Shikhandi was a woman in his previous birth and in this birth as well, and he was born to kill Bhishma. Therefore, if Shikhandi is protected, then Bhishma will be killed, and our victory will be certain.

The commentary further explains that Duryodhana is saying this to Bhishma to please him, and to make him a part of his side.

The verse translation of the Sanskrit text is as follows:

"Thus, Kunti's son, Dhanañjaya, was pleased with Keshava, and he chose to fight in the battle, leaving his army, which was equipped with weapons, and taking refuge in the unarmed Keshava" (21st verse of the 7th chapter of the Mahabharata).

The commentary in Hindi is as follows:

When Shri Krishna says this, Kunti's son, Dhanañjaya, chooses to fight in the battle, leaving his army, which was equipped with weapons, and taking refuge in the unarmed Keshava.

[Verse 12]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The Critical Translation of the Gita Press edition of Srimad Bhagavad Gita is as follows:

After that, the conch shells, drums, and mridangas were blown. They were blown all at once, and a tumultuous sound arose. (13)

Explanation: Although Bhishma did not blow the conch shell to announce the beginning of the war, but to please Duryodhana, the Kaurava army, however, took it as a declaration of war. Therefore, when Bhishma blew the conch shell, all the instruments of the Kaurava army were blown simultaneously.

The conch shells are called 'shankha' and are born from the ocean. They are kept in the worship of the Lord and are used in the aarti ceremony. They are blown with the mouth and are considered auspicious for the beginning of any work or war.

The drums are called 'panav' and are made of wood or metal. They are covered with the skin of a goat and are blown with a stick. They are considered auspicious for the beginning of any work or war.

The mridangas are called 'gomauka' and are made of wood. They are covered with the skin of a goat and are blown with the hands. They are considered auspicious for the beginning of any work or war.

The sound of the conch shells, drums, and mridangas was very loud and tumultuous. The Kaurava army was very enthusiastic, and therefore, when Bhishma blew the conch shell, all the instruments of the Kaurava army were blown simultaneously without any delay or effort.

The sound of the conch shells, drums, and mridangas was very loud and tumultuous, and it filled the entire battlefield.

Now, Sanjaya will describe what the Pandavas did.

After that, the white horses were yoked to the great chariot, and Madhava (Krishna) and the Pandavas were seated on it. They blew the divine conch shells. (14)

Translation: After that, Lord Krishna, seated on a chariot with white horses, was accompanied by Arjuna, who also had divine horses. These horses had a special characteristic: no matter how many of them were killed in battle, their number remained the same, and they never decreased. They could travel to all places, including earth and heaven. Among these hundred horses, four beautiful and well-educated white horses were yoked to Arjuna's chariot.

The verse 14 continues:

Mahati Syandane Sthitau - Yajno Agnir Upahartya Ahutim Grahayatah.

Translation: Seated on the great chariot, Lord Krishna and Arjuna were like the gods, for they had been fed with the oblation of ghee, which had been offered to the fire in the yajna. The fire had become impure due to the consumption of the ghee, and it was trying to purify itself by consuming the trees of the Khanda-vana forest. However, the gods, led by Indra, were protecting the forest, and the fire was unable to burn it. Finally, with Arjuna's help, the fire was able to burn the entire forest, and it was pleased with Arjuna, who was then given this magnificent chariot.

The chariot was equipped with nine carts, each carrying various weapons and armor. It was made of gold and was extremely powerful. Its wheels were strong and large. Its flag was shining like lightning and was visible from a distance of one yojana (four kos). Despite its great length, the flag did not weigh down or get stuck in any trees. Hanuman was seated on the flag.

The verse 14 continues:

Sthitau - The presence of Lord Krishna and Arjuna on the chariot made it even more magnificent and powerful.

The verse 14 continues:

Madhava Pandavashchaiva - Madhava is the name of Lord Krishna, and Dhava is the name of his consort, Lakshmi. Therefore, Madhava is the name of Lord Krishna. Pandava is the name of Arjuna, as he was the chief of the Pandavas. Arjuna was the human incarnation of Nar, and Lord Krishna was the divine incarnation of Narayana.

The verse 14 continues:

Divyaau Shankau Pradadhmatah - The divine conch shells in the hands of Lord Krishna and Arjuna were blown loudly.

It may seem strange that Lord Krishna, who was the chief of the Pandava army, blew the conch shell first, while the chief of the Kaurava army, Bhishma, was also present. However, Lord Krishna was the supreme commander of the Pandava army, and he was the one who controlled the entire army. As the supreme commander, he was always the chief, regardless of his position or location. This is because he was the supreme being, and he was never defeated.

The verse 14 continues:

Jo Svayam Chhota Hota Hai, Vahi Uchch Sthan Par Niyojit Hone Se Bada Mana Jata Hai. Atah Jo Uchch Sthan Ke Kaaran Apne Ko Bada Manaata Hai, Vah Svayam Vashikam Hi Hota Hai.

Translation: The one who is small in stature is considered great when appointed to a high position. However, the one who considers himself great due to his high position is actually small-minded.

The Lord Krishna, being the one who is great, is considered to be great wherever He resides. The reason for this is that whatever He does, others also follow in His footsteps. Just as the Lord Krishna has become the charioteer here.

Connection: Now, Sanjaya will explain the previous shloka by describing the other warriors who blew their conch shells.

Panchajanya, the conch shell of Lord Krishna, Devadatta, the conch shell of Arjuna, Paundra, the conch shell of Bhima, and Mahashankha, the conch shell of Nakula and Sahadeva, were blown.

Sanskrit:
pāñcajanyaṃ hṛṣīkeśo devadattaṃ dhanañjayaḥ|
pauṇḍraṃ dadhmau mahāśaṅkhaṃ bhīmakarmā vṛkodaraḥ || 15 ||

English Translation:
Panchajanya, the conch shell of the Lord of the senses (Krishna), Devadatta, the conch shell of Arjuna, Paundra, the conch shell of Bhima, and Mahashankha, the conch shell of Nakula and Sahadeva, were blown.

Explanation: 'Panchajanya, the conch shell of the Lord of the senses' - This conch shell was the one that could see into the hearts of all beings, and it would make the enemy's army tremble. Arjuna, the son of Lord Krishna, blew this conch shell.

The Lord Krishna, being the charioteer, blew the 'Panchajanya' conch shell. The Lord had taken the form of Panchajana, a demon, and had killed him, and then taken his conch shell, which is why it is called 'Panchajanya'.

'Bhima, the one with great deeds, blew the Mahashankha conch shell' - Bhima had killed many demons, including Hidimba, Bakasura, and Jatasura, and many powerful warriors, including Kichaka and Jarasandha. Therefore, Bhima's name is 'Bhima-karma'. He also had a conch shell called 'Paundra', which was very large.

Arjuna had a conch shell called 'Devadatta', which was given to him by Indra. Arjuna had won many battles and had collected a lot of wealth. Therefore, his name is 'Dhananjaya'. He also had a conch shell called 'Pauundra', which was very large.

Sanskrit:
anantavijayaṃ rājā kuntīputro yudhiṣṭhiraḥ |
nakulaḥ sahadevaśca sughoṣamaṇipuṣpakau ||16||

English Translation:
The king, the son of Kunti, Yudhishthira, blew the conch shell called 'Anantavijaya'. Nakula and Sahadeva blew the conch shells called 'Sughosh' and 'Manipushpaka'.

Explanation: 'The king, the son of Kunti, Yudhishthira' - Arjuna, Bhima, and Yudhishthira are the three sons of Kunti, and Nakula and Sahadeva are the two sons of Madri. This distinction is made here to show that Yudhishthira is the son of Kunti.

Yudhishthira, being the king, blew the conch shell called 'Anantavijaya'. Nakula and Sahadeva blew the conch shells called 'Sughosh' and 'Manipushpaka'. Before their exile, Yudhishthira was the king of half of the kingdom (Indraprastha), and according to the rules, he should have been the king after twelve years of exile and one year of incognito life. Therefore, Sanjaya is indicating that Yudhishthira will be the king of the entire world.

Note: The reference to the Mahabharata is given in the original text.

Kashyash (the king of Kashyap), the most excellent archer, Shikhandi, the great warrior, Dhrishyadhyumna, Virata, the unconquerable Sathyaki, and Drupada, the king of the earth, and all the sons of Drupada, and Subhadra's son Abhimanyu, all of them, with their long arms, blew their conch shells separately.

Shloka 19:
S Ghosho Dhartarashtranan Hridayani Vyadaryat |
Nabhashcha Prithivi chaiva Tumulo Vyanunadayat || 19 ||

Translation:
That sound of the conch shells, which was so loud and terrifying, shook the hearts of the unjust Dhartarashtras, and the sound echoed through the sky and the earth.

Commentary:
The great warrior Shikhandi was a woman in his previous birth, the daughter of King Kashyap. He had obtained his manhood by killing the yaksha, Stunakarana. Bhishma, the great warrior, knew all these facts and mentioned the names of the brave warriors. It seems that Sanjay, the narrator, considered Shikhandi to be a woman and did not consider him to be a worthy opponent. Therefore, he did not mention him among the brave warriors of the Kaurava army. Arjuna, however, considered him to be a brave warrior and led him to the front in the battle. Bhishma, on the other hand, was a great warrior and was considered to be invincible. He was the only one who was not afraid of Arjuna's conch shell sound. He was the only one who was not afraid of Arjuna's conch shell sound.

The sound of the conch shells of the Pandava army was so loud and terrifying that it shook the hearts of the unjust Dhartarashtras. The sound echoed through the sky and the earth, causing a great commotion.

The text from the Gita Press edition of Srimad Bhagavad Gita is as follows:

The warriors who unjustly seize the kingdom, they are filled with enthusiasm, they become brave. The Pandavas and those who stood in their support, they were the ones who had previously ruled the kingdom with justice and righteousness before going into exile. The hearts of the kings were shattered. This means that the pain they experienced was similar to the pain of being pierced by an arrow from a weapon, just as the hearts of the Kauravas were shattered when they were ruled by the Pandavas with justice and righteousness.

The sound of the conch shell, which was a symbol of the Kaurava army, had a different effect on the Pandava army. It filled them with enthusiasm and bravery. This is because the Kaurava army was on the side of injustice, while the Pandava army was on the side of justice and righteousness.

On the other hand, those who commit injustice, sin, and unrighteousness, their hearts become weak by nature. They do not have fearlessness and confidence in their hearts. Their own sinful actions and unrighteous behavior make their hearts weak. Unrighteousness consumes the unrighteous person. Duryodhana and others had made a great effort to kill the Pandavas unjustly. They had taken away their kingdom through deceit and treachery and had caused them great suffering. Therefore, their hearts had become weak and feeble. This means that the Kaurava army was on the side of unrighteousness.

Therefore, when the Pandava army, which was seven akshauhinis strong, heard the sound of the conch shell, their hearts were shattered, and they experienced great pain.

Sanjaya is narrating these events to Dhritarashtra. If Sanjaya had said that he had shattered the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons or relatives, it would not have been a civilized or reasonable statement. Therefore, Sanjaya should have said "tavakinaam" (your sons or relatives) instead of "dhartarashtranaam" (the sons of Dhritarashtra). This would have been a more civilized and reasonable statement.

In this context, the phrase "dhartarashtranaam" can be interpreted as "those who have unjustly seized the kingdom". This interpretation is more reasonable and civilized.

The sages should be cautious and aware of the fact that the sound of the conch shell, which is a symbol of the army, can have a different effect on different people. If the army is on the side of justice and righteousness, the sound of the conch shell can fill them with enthusiasm and bravery. On the other hand, if the army is on the side of injustice and unrighteousness, the sound of the conch shell can fill them with fear and anxiety.

The example of Ravana is given to illustrate this point. Ravana, who was a great warrior, was feared by the three worlds. However, when he was on the side of justice and righteousness, his heart was filled with courage and bravery. He was not afraid of anyone.

Similarly, those who are on the side of justice and righteousness, their hearts are filled with courage and bravery. They are not afraid of anyone. They should never engage in unrighteous and unjust behavior.

1. The phrase "anyayen dhritam rashtram yais te dhritarashtrah" (the kingdom was unjustly seized by them, who are the sons of Dhritarashtra) is a compound sentence. After breaking down the compound sentence, the phrase "dhritarashtrah" (the sons of Dhritarashtra) was formed by adding the suffix "an" to the root "dhritarashtra". This is an example of the use of the sixth case (vibhakti) in Sanskrit.

2. It is not possible for Duryodhana to have had eleven akshauhinis on his side. However, when the Pandavas went into exile, Duryodhana adopted the policy of ruling the kingdom with justice and righteousness, just like Yudhishthira. He treated the people with kindness and justice, just like Yudhishthira. As a result, he was able to gather a large army of nine akshauhinis, which was previously on the side of the Pandavas. He also managed to win over the army of one akshauhini led by Lord Krishna and the army of one akshauhini led by King Shalya, which were previously on the side of the Pandavas. Therefore, Duryodhana had eleven akshauhinis on his side, while the Pandavas had seven akshauhinis.

तब एक दिन अकस्मात् वायुने एक दिव्य सहस्रदल कमल
लाकर द्रौपदीके सामने डाल दिया । उसे देखकर द्रौपदी

द्रौपदीकी इच्छा पूर्ण करनेके लिये भीमसेन वहाँसे चल
पड़े। जब वे कदलीवनमें पहुँचे, तब वहाँ उनकी
हनुमान्जी से भेंट हो गयी। उन दोनोंकी आपसमें कई बातें
हुईं । अन्तमें हनुमान्जीने भीमसेनसे वरदान माँगनेके लिये
आग्रह किया तो भीमसेनने कहा कि 'मेरेपर आपकी कृपा
बनी रहे'। इसपर हनुमानजीने कहा कि 'हे वायुपुत्र ! जिस
समय तुम बाण और शक्तिके आघातसे व्याकुल शत्रुओंकी
सेनामें घुसकर सिंहनाद करोगे, उस समय मैं अपनी
गर्जनासे उस सिंहनादको और बढ़ा दूँगा । इसके सिवाय
अर्जुनके रथकी ध्वजापर बैठकर मैं ऐसी भयंकर गर्जना
किया करूँगा, जो शत्रुओंके प्राणोंको हरनेवाली होगी,
सो दससीस स्वान की नाईं । इत उत चितइ चला भड़िहाईं ॥
इमि कुपंथ पग देत खगेसा । रह न तेज तन बुधि बल लेसा ॥
(मानस ३। २८ । ४-५ )

25

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 23]

Arjuna says, "I will not look, until you keep the chariots in their place. I want to see who among them are strong, who are weaker than me, and who are stronger than me. I will just take a look at all of them."

Here, Arjuna is saying that we had thought of a peaceful resolution, but Duryodhana did not accept it. His mind is eager for war. Therefore, I will see how many warriors he has with him and how strong they are.

I will examine those who have come here eager to fight, the foolish Duryodhana's followers, who have come to fight in his war.

Translation of Shloka 23:
yotṣyamānān avēkṣe 'haṃ ya ete 'tra samāgatāḥ |
dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbudheryuddhe priyacikīrṣavaḥ || 23 ||

Translation of the commentary:
Here, "dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbudheryuddhe priyacikīrṣavaḥ" means that Arjuna is calling Duryodhana foolish-minded. He is saying that Duryodhana has been plotting to destroy us in many ways. He has humiliated us and has been working against us. Although we are entitled to half the kingdom, he wants to take it all for himself. This is his foolish thinking. And these kings have come to support him in his war, without thinking about his well-being in this life or the next.

If they were to advise Duryodhana to keep half the kingdom for himself and give the other half to the Pandavas, it would be beneficial for him, both in this life and the next.

Translation of Shloka 24:
sañjaya uvāca
evamuktaḥ hṛṣīkeśo guḍākeśena bhārata |
sēnayōrubhayōrmadhya sthāpayitvā rathōttamam || 24 ||

Translation of the commentary:
Sanjaya says that after Arjuna said this, Lord Krishna, the charioteer, placed the best chariot in the middle of the two armies.

Translation of Shloka 25:
bhīṣmadrōṇapramukhatḥ sarveṣāṃ ca mahīkṣitām |
uvāca pārtha pashyaitān samavētān kurūnitīti || 25 ||

Translation of the commentary:
Sanjaya says that Lord Krishna then said to Arjuna, "Look at these Kurus, who have come together to fight."

Note: The term "dhārtarāṣṭra" has two meanings - (1) the sons or relatives of Dhritarashtra, and (2) those who unjustly hold the kingdom. In this context, it refers to Duryodhana, the son of Dhritarashtra.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 26]

The Lord, having set up the chariot, awakened Arjuna's confusion. This is the same feeling. In family affection, the action and the object are considered, and one says, "See the Kurus" (these Kuruvanshi people). But in the Lord's love, the main thing is the feeling. In family affection, there is ignorance (confusion), and in the Lord's love, there is intimacy. In family affection, there is darkness, and in the Lord's love, there is light. In family affection, a man becomes detached from his duties, and in the Lord's love, due to absorption, one may forget one's duties, but a devotee never becomes detached from his duties. In family affection, one's family members are considered one's own, and one never thinks of their faults; similarly, the Lord's love for His devotees is such that He never thinks of their faults, but only says, "This is Mine." 

There is a great difference between family affection and the Lord's love. In the family, affection becomes mixed with attachment, and one never thinks of the family's faults; but in the Lord's love, the Lord's supremacy is established.

Translation of the commentary from the Gita Press edition of Srimad Bhagavad Gita:

As per the previous shloka, Arjuna had seen those who were standing on the battlefield, including his relatives, Bhaluki, Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandi, Suraatha, and others, as well as his maternal uncles, Jayadratha, and other relatives, standing in both armies. The phrase 'sa kaunteya kripaya parayavishat' implies that it was Kunti's son, who had been sent to fight by his mother's message, and who had shown bravery by saying, 'Who among my relatives will fight alongside me?' - such main warriors were to be seen by Lord Krishna, who was to be placed in the middle of both armies, and Arjuna, the son of Kunti, becomes extremely cowardly.

On seeing the relatives and friends in both armies, Arjuna's mind was filled with the thought that, 'Whether the people of this side die or the people of that side die, it will be our loss, our family will be destroyed, and our relatives will be killed!' This thought of Arjuna's made his desire to fight disappear, and cowardice took hold of his heart. This cowardice is referred to by Lord Krishna as 'kashmalam' and 'hridaya-daurbalyam' in the next two shlokas (2.2-3), and Arjuna himself has acknowledged it in shloka 2.7 as 'karpunya-doshopahata-svabhava'.

*

Chapter 2
Arjuna is overcome with cowardice - 'kripaya parayavishat'.

This shows that this cowardice was not present earlier, but has arisen now. Therefore, it is an adventitious fault. Due to being adventitious, it will not remain. However, bravery is a natural quality of Arjuna; therefore, it will remain.

What is extreme cowardice? It is to condemn, despise, and insult others without any reason, to cause pain and suffering to others, to harbor enmity towards others, and to try to destroy others. Seeing Duryodhana, Dushasana, Shakuni, and others, who are bent on harming him, standing in front of him, ready to fight, and not thinking of killing them, not making an effort to destroy them - this is a sign of extreme cowardice.

Here, Arjuna is being surrounded by the fault of cowardice, to the extent that even those who are bent on harming him and are constantly trying to harm him are being shown mercy by him.

(Gita - First chapter, 35th and 38th shlokas)

'Vishidannidam bravit' - Arjuna is extremely distressed about the fate of his family, clan, and country in the outcome of the war, and in that state, he utters the words that are described in the next shlokas.

Arjuna said:

Drishtvam sva-janam krishna yuyutsam samupasthitam (2.28)
Sedanti mam gatraani mukham cha parishusyati
Vepathushcha sharire me romaharshashcha jayate (2.29)
Gandiva sransate hastat tvak chaiva paridahyate
Na cha shaknomi avasthatum bhramatiiva cha me manah (2.30)

Translation of the shlokas:

Arjuna said:
Oh Krishna, seeing my relatives, who are eager to fight, standing in front of me,
My limbs are trembling, my face is drying up,
And I am experiencing palpitations in my body, and my hair is standing on end.
My bow, Gandiva, is slipping from my hand, my skin is burning,
And I am unable to stand, my mind is wavering.

[Verse 31]

Arjuna, seeing his kinsmen, Krishna, who are eager for battle, standing before him, is bewildered, like a person whose skin is burning.

*Translation of Shloka 31:*

From my hand, the Gāṇḍīva bow, the Gāṇḍīva bow, is slipping, and my skin is burning, and my skin is burning, and my mind is bewildered, like a person whose skin is burning.

*Translation of Commentary:*

The word 'Kṛṣṇa' was very dear to Arjuna. This address occurs nine times in the Gita. No other address to Lord Krishna occurs as many times as this. Similarly, the word 'Pārtha' was very dear to Lord Krishna. Therefore, Lord Krishna and Arjuna used to call each other by these names in their conversation, and this was well-known to people. From this perspective, Sanjaya has mentioned the names 'Kṛṣṇa' and 'Pārtha' at the end of the Gita: 'Yatra Yogeshvaraḥ Kṛṣṇo Yatra Pārthaḥ Dhanaurdharaḥ' (18.78).

Dhritarashtra had said 'Samaveta Yuṣṭhavaḥ' earlier, and Arjuna has said 'Yuṣṭhavaḥ Samupasthitam' here; but there is a big difference in their perspectives. Dhritarashtra's perspective is that my sons, Duryodhana, etc., and the sons of Pandu, Yudhishthira, etc., are on opposite sides - there is a distinction. Therefore, Dhritarashtra said 'Māmakaḥ' and 'Pāṇḍavāḥ' there. But Arjuna's perspective is that there is no distinction. Therefore, Arjuna has said 'Svajanam' here, which includes people from both sides. The meaning is that Dhritarashtra is afraid of the death of his sons in the war, and he is sorrowful; but Arjuna is sorrowful because of the possibility of the death of his kinsmen on both sides, and he is thinking that if anyone dies, it will be his own kinsman.

*Translation of Shloka 31:*

I do not see any good in killing my kinsmen in this war, and I see only evil.

*Translation of Commentary:*

The word 'Dṛṣṭvā' has occurred three times earlier - 'Dṛṣṭvā Pāṇḍavānīkam' (1.2), 'Dṛṣṭvā Gira Padūṅga' (1.20), and 'Dṛṣṭvā Emam Svajanam' (1.28). In all these places, Arjuna has seen the warriors on the opposite side, but now he is seeing his own kinsmen, and he is thinking that it would be a great evil to kill them. The connection is that in the previous shloka, Arjuna described the eight signs of his body due to sorrow, and now he is explaining the inauspicious signs of war, which are indicative of the future consequences of war.

*Translation of Shloka 31:*

I see inauspicious signs, Keshava, and I do not see any good in killing my kinsmen in the war.

*Translation of Commentary:*

The phrase 'Cintā Cita Samān' is mentioned in the commentary, which means that worry and grief are similar. The commentary further explains that worry burns a living person, and grief burns a dead person.

english:
51
[Verse 33-34]

If we assume that we have won the war, then we would have the entire earth as our kingdom, and we would have the authority to rule over it. We would also get many kinds of pleasures. However, I do not desire any of these things, i.e., I do not have any longing for victory, kingdom, or pleasures.

'kiṃ no rājyena govinda kiṃ bhogairjīvitena vā'-
Even if we get a vast kingdom, or if we get many beautiful pleasures, what is the use of them? What is the benefit of them? We can live for many years, enjoying the pleasures of the kingdom, but what is the use of it? The implication is that these victories, kingdoms, and pleasures can only bring happiness when there is a desire for them, when they are cherished, and when they are valued. But we do not have any desire for them. Therefore, what happiness can they bring to us?

We do not even have a desire to live after killing our relatives. Why? Because when our relatives die, what will be the use of the kingdom and pleasures? The kingdom and pleasures are meant for the family, but when the family members die, who will enjoy them? It is not even a question of enjoying them; on the contrary, we will have more worries and sorrows.

Relation - Arjuna does not desire victory and other things, and the reason for this is explained in the next shloka.

yeṣāmarthe kāṅkṣitaṃ no rājyaṃ bhogāḥ sukhāni ca |
ta ime'vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṃstyaktvā dhanāni ca ||33||

Translation:
For whom we desire the kingdom, pleasures, and happiness, those very people are standing in the battlefield, having given up their lives and wealth.

Explanation: We do not have a desire for the kingdom and pleasures for our own sake, but for the sake of our relatives, friends, and loved ones. We want them to be happy, to be comfortable, and to be served. We want them to be pleased, and we want to serve them. We want to live for their sake, and we want to give up our lives and wealth for their sake.

'ta ime'vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṃstyaktvā dhanāni ca'-
These very people, who are dear to us, are standing in the battlefield, having given up their lives and wealth. They have thought, "Let us go, but we will not run away from the battle." If they had a desire for life and wealth, they would not have come to the battlefield to give up their lives and wealth.

The implication is that they have given up their desire for life and wealth, and they are standing in the battlefield, ready to give up their lives and wealth for our sake.

Relation - Arjuna will now describe the people for whom he desires the kingdom, pleasures, and happiness.

ācāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrāstathaiva ca pitāmahāḥ |
mātulāḥ śvaśurāḥ pautrāḥ śyālāḥ sambandhinastathā || 34||

Translation:
The preceptors, fathers, sons, grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and relatives are all standing in the battlefield.

Explanation: The people for whom Arjuna desires the kingdom, pleasures, and happiness are his preceptors, fathers, sons, grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and relatives.

[Verse 36]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The relationship here is that Arjuna is wondering why Duryodhana and others are not considering the consequences of their actions, just like he is. They are his relatives, and he is thinking of withdrawing from the war, but they are not thinking of withdrawing. What is the reason for this?

Yad yadi phalani labhante lopahutachetasah
Kulakshayakritam dosham mitradrohe cha patakam || 38 ||
Even if they do not see the fault in their actions, driven by greed, they are destroying their family and committing a sin by betraying their friends.

Katham na jneyam asmaabhih papaat asman nivartitum
Kulakshayakritam dosham prapashyadbhir janardan || 39 ||
How can we not know that we should withdraw from sin, O Janardan? Even if they see the fault in their actions, they are destroying their family.

Translation of the commentary:

The phrase "yad yadi phalani labhante" means "even if they are getting the fruits of their actions." The phrase "lopahutachetasah" means "driven by greed." The phrase "kulakshayakritam dosham" means "the fault of destroying their family." The phrase "mitradrohe cha patakam" means "and committing a sin by betraying their friends."

The commentary explains that the greed-driven nature of Duryodhana and others has led to the loss of their discriminative power, and therefore they are not able to see the consequences of their actions. They are so blinded by their greed that they are not able to think about the destruction of their family and the sin of betraying their friends.

The commentary also explains that the destruction of the family is a result of the greed-driven nature of Duryodhana and others. They are so focused on their own interests that they are not able to see the consequences of their actions. They are not able to think about the destruction of their family and the sin of betraying their friends.

The commentary also mentions the example of the enmity between Drupada and Drona. Drupada and Drona were childhood friends, but after Drupada became the king, he insulted Drona and broke their friendship. Drona then became his enemy and helped Arjuna to defeat Drupada. Drupada then performed a yajna to destroy Drona, and as a result, Dhristadyumna and Draupadi were born. The commentary says that this is an example of how enmity between friends can lead to great suffering.

The commentary also explains that the greed-driven nature of Duryodhana and others is leading them to commit great sins. They are so blinded by their greed that they are not able to see the consequences of their actions. They are not able to think about the destruction of their family and the sin of betraying their friends.

The commentary also mentions that the time, wealth, and power are lost in the war. The commentary says that the people are suffering from various worries and troubles. The commentary also says that the people are not able to see the consequences of their actions. They are so blinded by their greed that they are not able to think about the destruction of their family and the sin of betraying their friends.

The commentary also explains that the people are not able to see the consequences of their actions because they are not able to see the impermanence of things. They are so blinded by their greed that they are not able to see that everything is temporary and that the pleasure of getting something is short-lived, but the pain of losing it is long-lasting. The very thought of separation from them is painful. However, a person who is devoid of the things he considers essential, continues to strive to acquire them due to greed. On reflection, it can be seen that the things whose absence he feels, will still be absent even if he acquires them in accordance with his past deeds. Therefore, our state remains the same as it was before acquiring the things. In the meantime, he toils only in the pursuit of the things he desires, and suffers only suffering. The little happiness he experiences in the meantime is also due to greed. If greed, the root of all vices, did not exist within him, he would not experience happiness even in the presence of the things he desires. Similarly, if the vice of attachment did not exist, he would not experience happiness even in the company of his family members. And if the vice of greed did not exist, he would not experience happiness even in the accumulation of wealth. The implication is that happiness in the world is always accompanied by some vice or the other. Without any vice, happiness is not possible. However, due to greed, a person is unable to think in this manner.

He knows the evil that arises from hatred and enmity, but if his friends cause him suffering, it is not detrimental to him. The reason is that suffering leads to the destruction of his past sins and purifies him. However, if hatred and enmity arise in his heart, they will remain with him even after death and will continue to incite him to commit sins, leading to his downfall. Therefore, why should he not think of avoiding this evil that is like a war? In other words, he should certainly think of avoiding this evil after reflection.

Arjuna's gaze is directed towards the greed of Duryodhana and others, but they are speaking from a place of familial affection and attachment. Their gaze is not directed towards their own evil. This is why they do not understand their duty. It is a rule that a person's gaze remains directed towards the faults of others as long as it does not see its own faults. Instead, an inflated sense of self-importance arises, thinking that the other person has this fault, but not us. In this state, he cannot think that if the other person has a fault, he too may have another fault. Even if the other person does not have another fault, the fault of seeing the faults of others is itself a fault. The fault of seeing the faults of others and the fault of self-importance due to good qualities are always together. Arjuna too sees the faults of Duryodhana and others, and has an inflated sense of self-importance due to good qualities (good qualities cast a shadow of self-importance).

"kathaṃ na jñeyamasmābhiḥ... prapaśyadbhirjanārdana" - Now, Arjuna says, "Although Duryodhana and others do not see the evil of their family's destruction and the evil of enmity with friends, we should see the evil of our family's destruction and the evil of enmity with friends."

We should see the evil of our family's destruction and the evil of enmity with friends because we know the evil of our family's destruction and the evil of enmity with friends. What are the evils of our family's destruction that we know? We will describe them in the next five verses.

"kulakṣaye praṇaśyanti kuladharmāḥ sanātanāḥ | dharme naṣṭe kulaṃ kṛtsnamadharmo'bhibhavatyuta || 40 ||"

When the family is destroyed, the eternal family virtues are destroyed. When the virtues are destroyed, the entire family is overwhelmed by vice.
[Verse 40]

[Verse 41]

When a family's values and traditions are not followed, and instead, they are led astray by immoral actions, the entire family is affected. The family's values and traditions, which have been passed down through generations, are lost, and the family's reputation is tarnished.

The question arises, "When the family is destroyed, who will uphold the values and traditions?" The answer is that those who are capable of fighting in a war will be destroyed, and those who are not capable will be left behind. These individuals will be influenced by the immoral actions of others and will lose their values and traditions.

When the family's values and traditions are lost, the individuals who are left behind will be without guidance and will follow their own desires, leading to a decline in their moral character. This is why it is said, "When the family's values are lost, the entire family is consumed by immorality" (Dharmo na hanyate kulaṃ kṛṣṇaḥ).

The Sanskrit shloka is:

adharmābhibhavātkṛṣṇa praduṣyanti kulastriyaḥ |
strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇasaṅkaraḥ || 41 ||

Translation:

Due to the prevalence of immorality, the women of the family become corrupted.
In corrupted women, the varṇasamkara is born.

Explanation:
When the family's values and traditions are lost, the women of the family become corrupted. This is because when the family's values and traditions are not followed, the individuals who are left behind will be without guidance and will follow their own desires, leading to a decline in their moral character. This is why it is said, "In corrupted women, the varṇasamkara is born."

The Sanskrit term "varṇasamkara" refers to the mixing of different castes or classes. When individuals from different castes or classes intermingle and have children, the resulting offspring are considered to be of mixed caste or class.

Arjuna addresses Krishna, saying, "Oh Krishna, you are the one who attracts everyone, so you are called Krishna. You are also known as Vārṣṇeya because you are the avatar of the Vṛṣṇi dynasty. But when our family is destroyed, what will happen to our descendants? Will they be considered part of the Vṛṣṇi dynasty or will they be considered part of another family?"

Krishna's response is that when the family's values and traditions are lost, the individuals who are left behind will be without guidance and will follow their own desires, leading to a decline in their moral character. This is why it is said, "In corrupted women, the varṇasamkara is born."

The different norms and practices are known as 'Jati-Dharma' or 'Varṇa-Dharma', which is a general term for 'Kul-Dharma', the norms of the community. All these norms are complete and fixed by the scriptures. The norms that are mentioned in relation to the community and the collective of clans are all the norms of 'Jati-Dharma', and these norms are lost if they do not follow the practices of 'Jati-Dharma'.

O Janārdana, O Janārdana, we have heard that the men whose family norms are destroyed, their abode is in hell for a long time.

Translation of Sanskrit Shloka:
O Janārdana, O Janārdana, we have heard that the men whose family norms are destroyed, their abode is in hell for a long time.

Sanskrit Shloka:

Janārdana = O Janārdana
utsannakuladharmāṇām = of those whose family norms are destroyed

aniyataṃ = for a long time

bhavati = is
hotā hai = becomes

The Lord has given man the power of discrimination and the authority to perform new actions. Therefore, man is free to perform or not perform actions, to do good or bad, and to act wisely or foolishly. Therefore, one should always perform actions with discrimination and wisdom. However, man is often swayed by the desire for pleasure and wealth, and he disregards his own discrimination and becomes a slave to his passions and hatred. As a result, his actions become contrary to the scriptures and the norms of his community. This leads to criticism and disrespect in this world, and in the next world, he suffers from bad karma and is born in hell. He suffers in hell for a long time due to his own sins. This is what we have heard from our elders.

The word 'manuṣyaṇām' includes all men, including those who have committed sins in the past, those who are present, and those who will be born in the future.

We, on the other hand, are aware of our duties and the consequences of our actions. We have studied the scriptures and know what is right and wrong. Therefore, it is not right for us to engage in this war.

In this page, Arjuna expresses his astonishment and grief at having decided to engage in the war, which is a great sin. He says that it is a sin to engage in war, even if one's own family members are to be killed. Arjuna's attention is focused on the consequences of war, and he is worried about the harm that will be caused to his family and himself.

The two words 'aho' and 'bata' in this shloka convey Arjuna's astonishment and grief. 'aho' is an expression of wonder, and Arjuna is amazed that he and his family members have decided to engage in war despite knowing its consequences. 'bata' is an expression of sorrow, and Arjuna is grieved that they are willing to kill their own family members for the sake of a kingdom and pleasure.

The reason behind their decision to engage in war is their attachment to a kingdom and pleasure. Arjuna says that if they win the war, they will get a kingdom, wealth, and respect, and their influence will spread across the land. They will be able to live a life of luxury and pleasure, and no one will be able to stop them from doing so.

However, Arjuna's attention is focused on the consequences of war, and he is worried about the harm that will be caused to his family and himself. He says that if they engage in war, they will be responsible for the destruction of their own family and the harm that will be caused to themselves.

In this shloka, Arjuna is expressing his attachment to a kingdom and pleasure, and he is worried about the consequences of war. He is not considering the moral implications of war, but rather the consequences that will affect him and his family.

The shloka can be translated as:

"If I were to be killed unarmed, even by those who are armed with weapons, it would be better for me than to kill my own family members in the war."

The Lord has not made Arjuna fight, but has instead imparted to him the knowledge of his duty. The duty of fighting was already inherent in Arjuna. Therefore, the thought of war was Arjuna's own. He himself was inclined to fight, and it was he who brought the Lord to the battlefield by inviting Him. However, Arjuna, considering his own thought to be unwholesome, was turning away from the war, i.e., he was abandoning his duty. On this, the Lord said, "This reluctance of yours to fight is due to your attachment." Therefore, it is not proper to abandon the duty that has become one's own at the right time.

Translation of Shloka 46:
yadi mām kṣemataraṃ bhavet

If I were to abstain from the war, perhaps my well-being would be ensured. The Lord's high-mindedness is such that if I were to renounce the war entirely, the worldly-minded people would perhaps understand that I am doing so for the sake of my own well-being. They would think that I am renouncing the war because I do not want to fight, and therefore, they would not accept the Lord's words. They would think that I am not willing to fight, and hence, they would not fight either. But perhaps, in a moment of enthusiasm, they would think that they are fighting on my behalf, and thus, they would not be deterred from fighting.

Translation of Shloka 46 (continued):
sadāke liye hamāre rāstekā kā~ṭā nikala jāya, vairī samāpta ho jāya

If I were to renounce the war, perhaps the obstacle in our path would be removed, and the enemy would be vanquished. The worldly-minded people would think that if I were to renounce the war, it would be beneficial for me, and they would not be deterred from fighting. They would think that I am renouncing the war because I do not want to fight, and hence, they would not fight either. But perhaps, in a moment of enthusiasm, they would think that they are fighting on my behalf, and thus, they would not be deterred from fighting.

Commentary:
The worldly-minded people would think that if I were to renounce the war, it would be beneficial for me, and they would not be deterred from fighting. They would think that I am renouncing the war because I do not want to fight, and hence, they would not fight either. But perhaps, in a moment of enthusiasm, they would think that they are fighting on my behalf, and thus, they would not be deterred from fighting.

62

The Bhagavad Gita

Chapter 1

Here, I have come. Therefore, without your participation in this war, these enemies, including your brother Dhritarashtra's son Duryodhana and my five sons, along with Abhimanyu, will not be able to stand as warriors. (This is mentioned in the 32nd shloka of the 11th chapter of the Gita.) Therefore, this massacre is inevitable. This massacre would have occurred even if you, Arjuna, had not participated in the war. If you had not participated in the war, then those who had accepted the proposal of your mother (Kunti) to marry their five brothers, including Yudhishthira, along with Draupadi, would have certainly fought the war as per their mother's command. Bhima, your brother, would never have retreated from the war, as he had taken an oath to kill the Kauravas. Draupadi had even said that if her husbands, the Pandavas, did not fight the Kauravas, then her father, Drupad, would not be worthy of being called a father. Therefore, there were many reasons that made it impossible to avoid the war.

It is not possible to stop a person who is destined to do something. However, a person can attain salvation by performing his duty and can also meet with destruction by abandoning his duty. The meaning is that a person is free to decide his own fate. Therefore, the Lord has imparted knowledge of duty to Arjuna and has given a sermon to humanity that they should remain prepared to perform their duty as per the command of the scriptures.

Sanjaya said:

Thus, Arjuna, having spoken in this manner, sat down on the chariot in the battlefield, having discarded his bow and arrow, and having been overcome with grief. (47)

Translation of Sanskrit Shloka:

Arjuna, having spoken in this manner, sat down on the chariot in the battlefield, having discarded his bow and arrow, and having been overcome with grief.

Commentary:
Arjuna's statement and his subsequent actions are a result of his being overcome with grief. He has been told that if he fights the war, he will have to kill his relatives and friends, which will lead to great suffering and ultimately to hell. Arjuna's mind is filled with grief and anxiety, and he is unable to take a decision.

Sanjaya continues to narrate the events that unfolded after Arjuna's statement.

The translation of the next part of the text is as follows:

If Bhima and Arjuna, who are both skilled in archery and are eager to make peace, and if I, Krishna, who am a devotee of the Lord, were to fight on their side, then their father, who is old and experienced, would fight along with his sons, who are all skilled warriors. My five sons, including Abhimanyu, would also fight on the side of the Kauravas, being encouraged by them. (This is mentioned in the Mahabharata, Chapter 8, Section 82, Shlokas 37-38)

इस प्रकार ॐ, तत्, सत्— इन भगवन्नामोंके उच्चारणपूर्वक ब्रह्मविद्या और योगशास्त्रमय श्रीमद्भगवद्गीतोपनिषद्रूप

प्रत्येक अध्यायकी समाप्तिपर महर्षि वेदव्यासजीने जो
उपर्युक्त पुष्पिका लिखी है, इसमें श्रीमद्भगवद्गीताका
विशेष माहात्म्य और प्रभाव ही प्रकट किया गया है।
‘ॐ, तत्, सत्*’– ये तीनों सच्चिदानन्दघन परमात्माके
पवित्र नाम हैं। ये मात्र जीवोंका कल्याण करनेवाले हैं ।
इनका उच्चारण परमात्माके सम्मुख करता है और
शास्त्रविहित कर्तव्य-कर्मोंके अंग- वैगुण्यको मिटाता है।

और अक्षरोंके उच्चारणमें जो-जो भूलें हुई हैं, उनका

भगवत्-सम्बन्धकी याद आनेके लिये प्रत्येक अध्यायके
अन्तमें ‘ॐ तत्सत्' का उच्चारण किया गया है।
इसमें सम्पूर्ण उपनिषदोंका सारतत्त्व संगृहीत है और
यह स्वयं भी भगवद्बाणी होनेसे उपनिषद् - स्वरूप है,
इसलिये इसे 'उपनिषद्' कहा गया है।
वर्ण, आश्रम, सम्प्रदाय आदिका आग्रह न रखकर
प्राणिमात्रका कल्याण करनेवाली सर्वश्रेष्ठ विद्या होनेके
कारण इसका नाम 'ब्रह्मविद्या' है। इस ब्रह्मविद्यास्वरूप
गीतामें कर्मयोग, ज्ञानयोग, ध्यानयोग, भक्तियोग आदि
योगसाधनोंकी शिक्षा दी गयी है, जिससे साधकको
परमात्माके साथ अपने नित्य-सम्बन्धका अनुभव हो जाय ।
इसलिये इसे 'योगशास्त्र' कहा गया है।
यह साक्षात् पुरुषोत्तम भगवान् श्रीकृष्ण और भक्तप्रवर
अर्जुनका संवाद है। अर्जुनने निःसंकोच - भावसे बातें पूछी
महर्षि वेदव्यासजीके द्वारा अध्यायके अन्तमें 'ॐ' के हैं और भगवान्‌ने उदारतापूर्वक उनका उत्तर दिया है।
उच्चारणका तात्पर्य है कि मेरी रचनाका अंग - वैगुण्य मिट | इन दोनोंके ही भाव इसमें हैं । अतः इन दोनोंके नामसे
जाय, ‘तत्’के उच्चारणका तात्पर्य है कि मेरी रचना | इस गीताशास्त्रकी विशेष महिमा होनेके कारण इसे
भगवत्प्रीत्यर्थ हो जाय और 'सत्' के उच्चारणका तात्पर्य 'श्रीकृष्णार्जुनसंवाद' नामसे कहा गया है।
है कि मेरी रचना सत् अर्थात् अविनाशी फल देनेवाली हो
जाय। ‘इति’–बस, मेरा यही प्रयोजन है। इसके सिवाय
मेरा व्यक्तिगत और कोई प्रयोजन नहीं है ।

जो ‘श्रीमत्' अर्थात् सर्वशोभासम्पन्न हैं और जिनमें
सम्पूर्ण ऐश्वर्य, धर्म, यश, श्री, ज्ञान और वैराग्य – ये छ:
'भग' नित्य विद्यमान रहते हैं, उन भगवान्‌के मुखसे निकली
हुई होनेके कारण इसको 'श्रीमत् भगवत्' कहा गया है ।
जब मनुष्य मस्तीमें, आनन्दमें होता है, तब उसके |
मुखसे स्वतः गीत निकलता है । भगवान् ने इसको मस्तीमें
आकर गाया है, इसलिये इसका नाम 'गीता' है। यद्यपि
संस्कृत व्याकरणके नियमानुसार इसका नाम 'गीतम्' होना
चाहिये था, तथापि उपनिषद् - स्वरूप होनेसे स्त्रीलिंग शब्द
'गीता' का प्रयोग किया गया है।
इस पहले अध्यायमें अर्जुनके विषादका वर्णन है। यह
विषाद भी भगवान् अथवा सन्तोंका संग मिल जानेपर
संसारसे वैराग्य उत्पन्न करके कल्याण करनेवाला हो जाता
है । यद्यपि दुर्योधनादिको भी विषाद हुआ है, तथापि उनमें
भगवान् से विमुखता होनेके कारण उनका विषाद 'योग'
नहीं हुआ । केवल अर्जुनका विषाद ही भगवान्‌की सम्मुखता
होनेके कारण 'योग' अर्थात् भगवान् के नित्य - सम्बन्धका
अनुभव करानेवाला हो गया । इसलिये इस अध्यायका नाम
'अर्जुनविषादयोग' रखा गया है।
प्रत्येक अध्यायके अन्तमें पुष्पिका देनेका तात्पर्य
है कि अगर साधक एक अध्यायका भी ठीक तरहसे मनन-
विचार करे, तो उस एक ही अध्यायसे उसका कल्याण
हो जायगा ।

The Bhagavad Gita is a part of the Upanishads, which includes the knowledge of Brahman (Brahmavidya or Jnana Yoga), the science of Yoga (Yogashastr or Karma Yoga), and the dialogue between Sri Krishna and Arjuna (Sri Krishna Arjuna Samvada or Bhakti Yoga).

The Gita begins and ends with devotion. At the beginning, Arjuna, being perplexed, seeks refuge in Lord Krishna. He says, "I am your disciple, protect me, I have taken refuge in you" (2.7). At the end, Lord Krishna inspires Arjuna to take complete refuge by saying, "Come to me alone for shelter" (18.73). Arjuna had asked for the means to attain his own good (2.7, 3.2, 5.1), so Lord Krishna has also described Jnana Yoga and Karma Yoga in the Gita.

The first chapter of the Gita has 503 words, 12 lines, and 13 phrases in the Pushpika.

(1) In this chapter, there are three lines, "Ath Prathamah Adhyayah", twelve lines, "Dhritarashtra Uvacha", "Sanjaya Uvacha", etc., 505 words, and 13 phrases in the Pushpika. In total, the sum of all the words is 578.

(3) In this chapter, there are six "Uvacha" - one "Dhritarashtra Uvacha", three "Sanjaya Uvacha", and two "Arjuna Uvacha".

The Second Chapter

Introduction-

Duryodhana told Dronacharya about both armies, but Dronacharya did not say anything. This made Duryodhana unhappy. To please Duryodhana, Bhishma loudly blew his conch shell. After Bhishma's conch shell was blown, the conches of the Kauravas and the Pandavas were also blown. Following this (from the twentieth verse), the conversation between Arjuna and Krishna began.

Arjuna asked the Lord to place his chariot in the middle of both armies. The Lord placed the chariot in the middle of both armies, in front of Bhishma, Drona, and others, and asked Arjuna to see the Kauravas. Seeing their own relatives in both armies, Arjuna's domestic attachment was awakened, which led to his grief. As a result, Arjuna abandoned the fight, laid down his bow and arrows, and sat in the middle of the chariot.

Sanjaya then begins the second chapter, to tell Dhritarashtra what the Lord said to Arjuna in his grief.

Sanjaya said:

That Arjuna, who was overcome with compassion, whose eyes were filled with tears, and who was lamenting, was thus overcome with compassion. (1)

Sanjaya said:

The Lord, whose eyes were filled with tears, spoke to Arjuna.

Translation of Sanskrit Shlokas in English:

That Arjuna, who was overcome with compassion, whose eyes were filled with tears, and who was lamenting, was thus overcome with compassion. (1)

Sanjaya said:

The Lord, whose eyes were filled with tears, spoke to Arjuna.

Explanation:
The phrase 'taṃ tathā kṛpayāviṣṭamaśrupūrṇākulekṣaṇam' means that Arjuna, who was overcome with compassion, had tears in his eyes, and was lamenting. The phrase 'viṣīdantamidaṃ' means that he was lamenting, and the phrase 'tathā kṛpayā āviṣṭam' means that he was thus overcome with compassion. The phrase 'tam viṣīdantam' means that he was lamenting, and the phrase 'vākyamuvāca madhusūdanaḥ' means that the Lord, whose eyes were filled with tears, spoke to Arjuna.

Sanjaya said:

The Lord, who was overcome with compassion, spoke to Arjuna, whose eyes were filled with tears, and whose face was pale. His body was trembling, his hair was standing on end, and his hands were shaking. He was unable to see, and his mind was confused. How can this be? Arjuna, who was known for his bravery and never fled from a fight, was now overcome with fear and was sitting in the chariot, unable to see or fight. This is a great wonder, and Sanjaya is expressing this wonder through the above words.

Explanation:
The phrase 'aśrupūrṇākulekṣaṇam' means that Arjuna's eyes were filled with tears, and his face was pale. The phrase 'madhusūdanaḥ' means that the Lord was overcome with compassion. The phrase 'vākyam' means that the Lord spoke, and the phrase 'uvāca' means that he spoke to Arjuna. Sanjaya is expressing his wonder at how Arjuna, who was known for his bravery, was now overcome with fear and was unable to see or fight.

The Bhagavad Gita, a sacred Hindu text, is a direct and piercing blow to the heart. It is a message of self-realization, which is the ultimate goal of human life. Arjuna, the warrior, was overcome with grief and fear due to his cowardice in the face of war. Lord Krishna, the divine teacher, decided to awaken Arjuna from his slumber and guide him towards the path of self-realization. In this context, Lord Krishna spoke the following words, which are a direct attack on Arjuna's cowardice.

The words "viṣīdantamidaṃ vākyamuvāca madhusūdanaḥ" can be translated to "Lord Krishna, the slayer of Madhu, spoke these words to Arjuna, who was overcome with grief." The word "madhusūdanaḥ" means "the slayer of Madhu," which refers to Lord Krishna's ability to destroy the evil forces of the world.

The phrase "yahā~ 'viṣīdantamuvāca' kahanese hī kāma cala sakatā thā, 'idaṃ vākyam' kahanekī jarūrata hī nahīṃ thī" can be translated to "It would have been enough to say 'viṣīdantamuvāca,' but the need to say 'idaṃ vākyam' was felt." This means that the phrase "idaṃ vākyam" was used to emphasize the importance of Lord Krishna's words.

The phrase "arjunakā yuddhase kāyaratāke kāraṇa viṣāda karate hue arjunase bhagavān uparāma honekā jo nirṇaya thā, usameṃ khalabalī macā denevālī madhusūdanane ye (āge dūsare-tīsare ślokoṃmeṃ kahe jāne vāle) vacana kahe" can be translated to "Lord Krishna, the slayer of Madhu, spoke these words to Arjuna, who was overcome with grief and fear due to his cowardice in the face of war."

The phrase "yahā~ 'viṣīdantamuvāca' kahanese hī kāma cala sakatā thā, 'idaṃ vākyam' kahanekī jarūrata hī nahīṃ thī" can be translated to "It would have been enough to say 'viṣīdantamuvāca,' but the need to say 'idaṃ vākyam' was felt." This means that the phrase "idaṃ vākyam" was used to emphasize the importance of Lord Krishna's words.

The phrase "arjunako apane doṣakā jñāna karākara apane kalyāṇakī jijñāsā jāgrat karā denevālī hai" can be translated to "These words will awaken Arjuna to his own faults and inspire him to seek his own well-being."

The phrase "isa gambhīra arthavālī vāṇīke prabhāvase hī arjuna bhagavān‌kā śiṣyatva grahaṇa karake unake śaraṇa ho jāte haiṃ" can be translated to "It is the effect of these profound words that Arjuna accepts Lord Krishna as his teacher and takes refuge in him."

The phrase "saṃjayake dvārā 'madhusūdanaḥ ' pada kahanekā tātparya hai ki bhagavān śrīkṛṣṇa 'madhu nāmaka' daityako māranevāle arthāt duṣṭa svabhāvavāloṃkā saṃhāra karanevāle haiṃ" can be translated to "The word 'madhusūdanaḥ' means that Lord Krishna is the destroyer of the evil forces of the world, the slayer of Madhu."

The phrase "sambandha - bhagavānne arjunake prati kauna-se vacana kahe- ise āgeke do ślokoṃmeṃ kahate haiṃ" can be translated to "The connection - Lord Krishna speaks the following words to Arjuna, which are explained in the next two verses."

**Shloka 2**

śrībhagavānuvāca
kutastvā kaśmalamidaṃ viṣame samupasthitam |
anāryajuṣṭamasvargyamakīrtikaramarjuna
||2||

**Translation**

Lord Krishna spoke:

"Arjuna, where did this weakness come from? This weakness is not suitable for a warrior, nor is it worthy of a noble person. It is not a quality that brings fame, nor is it a quality that leads to heaven."

**Explanation**

The word "kutastvā" means "where did this come from?" The word "kaśmalamidaṃ" means "this weakness." The word "viṣame" means "in this difficult situation." The word "samupasthitam" means "has come to you." The word "anāryajuṣṭam" means "not suitable for a noble person." The word "asvargyam" means "not worthy of heaven." The word "akīrtikaram" means "not a quality that brings fame."

The phrase "yaha sambodhana denekā tātparya hai ki | hai, jisase arjunakā dhyāna apane kartavyapara calā jāya" can be translated to "This address is meant to awaken Arjuna to his duty."

The phrase "tuma svaccha, nirmala antaḥkaraṇavāle ho" can be translated to "You are a person with a pure and clean heart."

The phrase "ataḥ tumhāre svabhāvameṃ kāluṣya—kāyaratākā ānā bilakula viruddha bāta hai" can be translated to "Therefore, the presence of cowardice in your nature is completely opposed to your true nature."

The phrase "phira yaha tumhāremeṃ kaise ā gayī ?" can be translated to "How did this weakness come to you?"

The phrase "kutaḥ" kahanekā tātparya yaha hai ki mūlameṃ yaha kāyaratārūpī doṣa tumhāremeṃ (svayaṃmeṃ) nahīṃ hai" can be translated to "The word 'kutaḥ' means that this weakness is not inherent in you."

The phrase "yaha to āgantuka doṣa hai, jo sadā rahanevālā nahīṃ hai" can be translated to "This weakness is an extrinsic fault, which is not permanent."

The phrase "samupasthitam" kahanekā tātparya hai ki yaha kāyaratā kevala tumhāre bhāvoṃmeṃ aura vacanoṃmeṃ hī nahīṃ āyī hai; kintu tumhārī kriyāoṃmeṃ bhī ā gayī hai" can be translated to "The word 'samupasthitam' means that this weakness has not only come to your thoughts and words, but also to your actions."

The phrase "yaha tumhārepara acchī tarahase chā gayī hai, jisake kāraṇa tuma dhanuṣa-bāṇa chor̤akara rathake madhyabhāgameṃ baiṭha gaye ho" can be translated to "This weakness has completely taken over you, causing you to abandon your bow and arrow and sit in the middle of the chariot."

The phrase "kutastvā kaśmalamidaṃ viṣame samupasthitam " - bhagavān āścarya prakaṭa karate hue arjunase kahate haiṃ ki aise yuddhake maukepara to tumhāremeṃ śūravīratā, utsāha ānā cāhiye thā, para isa bemaukepara tumhāremeṃ yaha kāyaratā kahā~se ā gayī" can be translated to "Lord Krishna, in a state of wonder, asks Arjuna, 'How did this weakness come to you in this difficult situation, when you should have been filled with courage and enthusiasm?'"

The phrase "apane na jānaneke kāraṇa aura dūsareko cetāneke liye" can be translated to "This wonder is caused by not knowing oneself and by being awakened to the other."

The phrase "arjunako cetāneke liye hī paidā hote haiṃ, ve apane kalyāṇake uddeśyako lekara hī hote haiṃ" can be translated to "These wonders are created to awaken Arjuna, and they are meant to bring about his own well-being."

**Note**

The phrase "yahā~ 'bhagavān' padameṃ 'bhaga' śabdameṃ jo 'matup ' pratyaya kiyā gayā hai, vaha nityayogameṃ kiyā gayā hai" can be translated to "In the word 'bhagavān,' the suffix 'matup' is used in a permanent sense."

The phrase "arthāt samagra aiśvarya, dharma, yaśa, śrī, jñāna aura vairāgya- ye chahoṃ 'bhaga' bhagavān‌meṃ nitya rahate haiṃ" can be translated to "This means that the six qualities of the divine - sovereignty, duty, fame, prosperity, knowledge, and detachment - are always present in the Lord."

The phrase "anāryajuṣṭam" padameṃ jo 'nañ' samāsa hai, vaha 'āryairjuṣṭamāryajuṣṭam ' – isa tṛtīyā samāsake bāda hī karanā cāhiye" can be translated to "The phrase 'anāryajuṣṭam' is a compound word that should be used in the third case."

The phrase "agara 'nañ' samāsa tṛtīyā samāsake pahale kiyā jāya ki 'na āryā anāryāḥ anāryairjuṣṭamanāryajuṣṭam' to yahā~ yaha kahanā banatā hī nahīṃ" can be translated to "If the compound word 'nañ' is used before the third case, it would not be suitable in this context."

The phrase "kyoṃki anārya puruṣoṃke dvārā jisakā sevana kiyā jātā hai, vaha dūsaroṃke liye ādarśa nahīṃ hotā" can be translated to "Because what is used by unworthy people is not a model for others."

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 5]

The Lord has already killed those who harbor enmity and do evil, even such enemies. However, in front of me, there stand my grandfather Bhishma and preceptor Drona, who are the epitome of virtue, extremely fond of me, and lovingly imparting knowledge to me. How can I kill such well-wishers of mine?

The Adityas, too, have been killed by the Lord, and those who have come to me with great affection and love. Preceptor Drona is revered by us due to his association with knowledge. He is my preceptor. His affection for me is so great that he has not taught his own son Ashwatthama in the same way as he has taught me. He has taught both of us how to use the Brahmastra, but he has taught me alone how to withdraw it. He has also given me the boon that 'among my disciples, there will be none greater than you in the arts of warfare and other sciences.'

In the context of reverence, both my grandfather Bhishma and preceptor Drona are revered and worthy of worship. They have the right to attack me, but how can I attack them with arrows? Engaging in a duel with them as their adversary would be a grave sin. They are both worthy of service and, in fact, more worthy of worship than service.

There are two main types of relationships in the world: relationships based on birth and relationships based on knowledge. My grandfather Bhishma is revered by us due to our relationship based on birth. Since childhood, I have been nurtured in his lap. When I used to call him 'Pitaji - Pitaji' in my childhood, he would lovingly say, 'I am also the father of your father's father.'

In the context of reverence, both my grandfather Bhishma and preceptor Drona are worthy of reverence and worship. They have the right to attack me, but how can I attack them with arrows? Engaging in a duel with them as their adversary would be a grave sin. They are both worthy of service and, in fact, more worthy of worship than service.
