The Bhagavad Gita
Chapter 2

Arjuna, who had earlier stood with the Kauravas without understanding his duty, now presents his case, taking into account his own side. He says that if he does not fight along with Bhishma, Drona, and other revered individuals, Duryodhana will not fight with him alone either. As a result, he will not get the kingdom, and he will suffer distress. His livelihood will also become difficult. To the extent that begging, which is forbidden for a Kshatriya, may become necessary for his livelihood, he prefers to beg rather than kill the gurus.

The phrase "in this world" (iha loke) implies that although begging may bring him shame and ridicule in this world, he considers it better than killing the gurus.

The word "api" (api) implies that both killing the gurus and begging are forbidden for him; however, he considers killing the gurus more forbidden.

Now, Arjuna, looking at the Lord's words, says that if he fights according to the Lord's command, he will be stained with the blood of the gurus and will enjoy the fruits of their labor, which are driven by the desire for wealth and other material possessions. He will enjoy these fruits, and there will be little liberation or peace for him.

A question arises here: If Bhishma, Drona, and other gurus were bound to the Kauravas through wealth, then why not consider the phrase "artha-kama" (arthakāma) as a qualifying word for "gurus" (gurūn)? The answer is that it would not be proper to consider gurus who are not driven by the desire for wealth as being driven by the desire for wealth. The patriarch Bhishma, the preceptor Drona, and others were not driven by the desire for wealth; they were bound to Duryodhana through his behavior. Therefore, abandoning Duryodhana in the midst of war would be a good thing.

Another point is that Arjuna has used the phrase "mahānubhāvān" (mahānubhāvān) to describe Bhishma, Drona, and others. Therefore, it is not possible to describe such noble individuals as being driven by the desire for wealth. The implication is that those who are noble cannot be driven by the desire for wealth, and those who are driven by the desire for wealth cannot be noble.

Special Note

The Lord had given Arjuna the command to fight in the second and third shlokas, considering his welfare. However, Arjuna has misunderstood this and thinks that the Lord is giving the command to fight for the sake of enjoying the kingdom. Earlier, Arjuna had only one reason for not fighting, which was that he was afraid to fight. He had laid down his arms and sat in the chariot, overcome with grief (Chapter 1, verse 47). However, the reason for fighting has come from the Lord's words. The implication is that Arjuna thinks that he and the others know the dharma, but Duryodhana and others do not know it. Therefore, they are ready to fight for the sake of wealth and kingdom. Now, Arjuna is saying the same thing for himself: If I fight according to the Lord's command, I will get the kingdom and wealth, which are stained with the blood of the gurus. In this way, Arjuna sees only evil in fighting.

It is easier to eliminate the evil that appears as evil. However, it is difficult to eliminate the evil that appears as good. Just as Ravana and Kumbhakarna, who were disguised as sages, were not recognized by Sita and Hanuman, respectively, Arjuna's perception is that fighting is evil, and not fighting is good. He thinks that he and the others know the dharma, which is the renunciation of violence, and that Duryodhana and others do not know it.

The Lord's command to fight is not for the sake of enjoying the kingdom, but for Arjuna's welfare. Arjuna's perception is limited to the physical world, and he sees the body and other physical objects as the main thing. He is caught in the web of family attachment and sees the dharma as a physical thing. He does not have the vision of the spiritual realm, and his perception is not beyond the physical kingdom. Therefore, he thinks that the Lord is giving the command to fight for the sake of enjoying the kingdom, whereas the Lord is actually trying to benefit him.

[Verse 6]

In the garb of duty, the evil of self-sacrifice has come. One's gaze does not go towards the consequence of this. Similarly, people do not consider the vices of deceit, cunning, dishonesty, cheating, and betrayal, etc. as vices, all these vices have come in the garb of duty. Here, Arjuna has considered the killing of great souls like Bhishma and Drona as a sin, because he knows the duty of a warrior. The implication is that Arjuna has considered what he considers to be good, to be evil in reality; but due to the perception of goodness, it does not appear to be evil. The evil of self-sacrifice does not appear to be evil because of the attachment to the bodies within them. Therefore, to eliminate this evil, a great effort is being made by God, and time is taking its course.

In today's society, an attempt is being made to eliminate the varna and ashrama system, using the pretext of unity, so this evil does not appear to be evil in the garb of goodness. Therefore, the result of eliminating the varna and ashrama system will be the downfall of people, and the increase of asuric nature in people.

Commentary: 'Mahānubhāvān' - The great souls, like Bhishma, Drona, etc., are considered to be of high character, because even while fighting, they do not have any bias.

Relation: The words of God have such a unique effect that they are influencing Arjuna from within, making him more doubtful about not fighting the war. In this state, Arjuna says:

I do not know which of the two is superior, whether we should fight or not fight. If we fight, we may win, or if we do not fight, they may win us. I do not know this. We do not know whether we will live or die, if we kill them, or if we do not kill them, they will be standing in front of us, the main enemies of the Dhritarashtra clan. 6.

Translation of Sanskrit Shloka:

na caitad vidmaḥ kataranno garīyaḥ yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ |
etad ca na vidmaḥ naḥ yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣāmaste'vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ || 6||

Translation of Sanskrit words:

- na caitad vidmaḥ = I do not know this.
- kataranno garīyaḥ = Which of the two is superior.
- yadvā jayema = Whether we will win.
- yadi vā no jayeyuḥ = Or if we will lose.
- etad ca na vidmaḥ = I do not know this.
- naḥ = We.
- yāneva = In this way.
- hatvā = By killing.
- na jijīviṣāmaḥ = We will not live.
- aste'vasthitāḥ = They will be standing.
- pramukhe = In front of us.
- dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ = The Dhritarashtra clan.

Explanation: 'na caitad vidmaḥ kataranno garīyaḥ ' - I do not know which of the two is superior, whether I should fight or not fight. The reason is that there is uncertainty about the future; whether we will win or lose. On one hand, your opinion is that fighting is superior, but on the other hand, my opinion is that killing the gurus is a sin, so not fighting is superior. When I consider both these points, I am unable to decide which one is more superior. In this way, the opinion of God and my own opinion have become equal in my mind.

'yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ ' - If we fight as per your order, we may win or they may win us - we do not know this.

'yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣāmaḥ ' - We do not even want to live by killing our relatives. We do not want to enjoy the world, nor do we want to rule and give orders, because if we kill our relatives, what will we do? We will only be left with grief and sorrow, and we will not be able to live.

'te'vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ ' - The relatives whom we do not even want to kill, are standing in front of us, the main enemies of the Dhritarashtra clan.

Arjuna, being unable to decide on his duty, is now anxiously praying to Lord Krishna, beset with worry.

I am inquiring from you, O Lord, whose mind is bewildered by the complexities of duty, what is certain to be beneficial for me. Teach me, I am your disciple, and I have taken refuge in you. (7)

Translation of Sanskrit Shloka:
karpṇyadōṣopahatasvabhāvaḥ pṛcchāmi tvāṃ dharmasammūḍhacetāḥ |
yacchreyaḥ syān niścitaṃ brūhi tan me śiṣyaḥ te 'haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam || 7 ||

Explanation:
Arjuna is inquiring from Lord Krishna, whose mind is bewildered by the complexities of duty, what is certain to be beneficial for him. He is saying that he is a disciple of Lord Krishna and has taken refuge in him, and he is seeking guidance from him.

The word "karpṇyadōṣopahatasvabhāvaḥ" means that Arjuna's nature has been affected by the fault of cowardice. The word "dharmasammūḍhacetāḥ" means that his mind is bewildered by the complexities of duty.

In the commentary, it is explained that Arjuna is seeking guidance from Lord Krishna because he is unable to decide on his duty. He is saying that he is a disciple of Lord Krishna and has taken refuge in him, and he is seeking guidance from him.

The commentary also explains that Arjuna's mind is bewildered by the complexities of duty, and he is seeking guidance from Lord Krishna to help him make a decision.

[Verse 8]

In this critical juncture, Arjuna's attitude undergoes a significant transformation. Initially, when asked about his well-being, Arjuna thinks that seeking guidance from a guru is the right approach, but not from a charioteer. This notion, which led him to ask Krishna to position the chariot between the two armies, is now replaced by a desire to seek guidance from Krishna as his guru. Arjuna says, "Maharaj! I am your disciple, worthy of receiving knowledge, please guide me."

However, this apparent surrender to Krishna is not a complete submission. Arjuna is still not fully convinced that Krishna will guide him in the right direction. He is still uncertain about the outcome of the war and the consequences of his actions. This is evident from the fact that he is still hesitant to fight and is seeking Krishna's guidance.

The verse "śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam" - "Teach me, I have come to you as a disciple" - is a significant one. Arjuna is seeking Krishna's guidance, but he is not willing to completely surrender to him. He wants Krishna to teach him, but he also wants to be in control of his own actions.

In this context, it is interesting to note that Arjuna is not fully aware of the implications of his actions. He is still uncertain about the consequences of his decisions and is seeking Krishna's guidance to navigate this complex situation.

The verse "na hi prapaśyāmi mamāpanudyād yacchokamucchoṣaṇamindriyāṇām" - "I do not see any benefit in killing my kin, which would lead to great sorrow and distress" - highlights Arjuna's continued hesitation and uncertainty. He is still not convinced that fighting is the right thing to do and is seeking Krishna's guidance to resolve this dilemma.

The Sanskrit verse is:

śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam

English translation:
Teach me, I have come to you as a disciple.

The Sanskrit verse is:

na hi prapaśyāmi mamāpanudyād yacchokamucchoṣaṇamindriyāṇām

English translation:
I do not see any benefit in killing my kin, which would lead to great sorrow and distress.

The Sanskrit verse is:

avāpya bhūmāvasapatnamṛddhaṃ rājyaṃ surāṇāmapi cādhipatyam

English translation:
Even if I were to gain a prosperous kingdom on earth, with a beautiful wife and a rich treasury, and even if I were to become the ruler of the gods, I do not see any benefit in killing my kin.

The Lordship of the Devas

What is this sorrow of mine? 7.4

* The Bhagavad Gita *

Why is it that even if I acquire the lordship of the gods (in heaven), the riches and prosperity of the earth, a kingdom, and a kingdom free from enemies, I still do not see my sorrow disappearing?

The transliteration and translation of the relevant Sanskrit shloka is:

avāpya bhūmāvasapatnamṛddhaṃ rājyam

English translation: Acquiring a kingdom that is prosperous, free from enemies, and rich in wealth and grain.

The Lordship of the Gods

Even if I acquire the lordship of the gods, which is a divine kingdom, I still do not see my sorrow disappearing.

The transliteration and translation of the relevant Sanskrit shloka is:

surāṇāmapi cādhipatyam

English translation: Even if I acquire the lordship of the gods, which is a divine kingdom.

Arjuna's thoughts are that if he wins the war, he will acquire a kingdom that is prosperous, free from enemies, and rich in wealth and grain. However, he does not see how this will alleviate his sorrow.

The commentary explains that Arjuna's thoughts are that even if he acquires a kingdom that is prosperous and free from enemies, he will still not be able to alleviate his sorrow. This is because his sorrow is not due to the lack of material possessions, but rather due to the fear of losing his loved ones.

The commentary also notes that Arjuna's thoughts are different from his previous thoughts in the first chapter, where he said that he did not want to win the war, nor did he want to acquire a kingdom or enjoy its pleasures. However, in this chapter, Arjuna's thoughts are driven by a desire to alleviate his sorrow, which is a more selfish motivation.

The commentary concludes that Arjuna's thoughts are still driven by a desire for personal gain, rather than a desire to fulfill his duty or to achieve spiritual growth.

Sanjaya's commentary continues in the next shloka:

Sanjaya said:

Thus spoken to Hrishikesha (Krishna), the slayer of the demon Gouda (Arjuna) remained silent, having spoken thus to Govinda (Krishna). 9.

The transliteration and translation of the relevant Sanskrit shloka is:

evamuktvā hṛṣīkeśaṃ guḍākeśaḥ parantapa |
na yotsya iti govindamuktvā tūṣṇīṃ babhūva ha || 9 ||

English translation: Thus spoken to Hrishikesha (Krishna), the slayer of the demon Gouda (Arjuna) remained silent, having spoken thus to Govinda (Krishna).

[Verse 10]

As Arjuna had spoken to Lord Krishna, keeping both his own and the Lord's perspectives in view, and after considering them, they finally reached the conclusion that, although they would gain more kingdoms, fame, and praise in the world by fighting, Arjuna's heart would still be filled with sorrow, anxiety, and grief. Therefore, it seemed to Arjuna that he should not fight.

Although Arjuna respects and wants to follow Lord Krishna's words, yet the idea of fighting does not seem right to him. Therefore, Arjuna clearly and distinctly expresses his own thoughts and decision, saying, "I will not fight." By doing so, Arjuna has said what he wanted to say to the Lord, and there is no need for him to say anything else.

Relation - Now, Sanyaji will tell in the next shloka what happened after Arjuna refused to fight.

Lord Krishna spoke to Arjuna, laughing, as if in amusement, in the middle of the two armies, saying:

"O descendant of Bharata, Arjuna, who was sorrowful, spoke these words, sorrowful, spoke these words." (10)

Translation of Sanskrit Shloka:

Translation of Hindi Commentary:

Lord Krishna spoke to Arjuna, laughing, as if in amusement, in the middle of the two armies, saying: "O descendant of Bharata, Arjuna, who was sorrowful, spoke these words, sorrowful, spoke these words." The word "prahassanniva" means that Lord Krishna laughed, even though he was laughing loudly, but he was smiling while speaking.

Explanation - Arjuna had asked Lord Krishna to place the chariot in the middle of the two armies so that he could see the warriors. Now, Arjuna is sorrowful and speaking these words in the middle of the two armies. It would have been proper for Arjuna to stand in the middle of the two armies with the intention of fighting, but instead, he is sorrowful and speaking these words. Therefore, Lord Krishna starts giving him a sermon in the middle of the two armies.

The word "prahassanniva" also means that Lord Krishna was amused to see Arjuna's change of heart. Arjuna had earlier said that he would follow Lord Krishna's words and do what he said, but now he has made up his mind to not fight without even consulting Lord Krishna. This is why Lord Krishna is amused.

Lord Krishna could have said to Arjuna, "Do as you please," but instead, he understood that when a person is overcome with sorrow and anxiety, he often says things without thinking. This is what Arjuna is doing. Therefore, Lord Krishna's heart is filled with compassion for Arjuna. Lord Krishna looks at Arjuna's emotions rather than his words. Therefore, Lord Krishna does not pay attention to Arjuna's words and starts giving him a sermon.

A person who takes refuge in the Lord, even by saying a single word, is accepted by the Lord. Lord Krishna's heart is filled with love for Arjuna, and he starts giving him a sermon.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 11]

The inevitable separation of the gross and subtle bodies of all beings is a natural phenomenon. Some have already experienced this separation, while others will experience it in the future. Therefore, one should not grieve for them. The grief you have experienced is your own fault.

Some will say that you should only take refuge in Me and grieve. But I say, "Mā śucchaḥ" (18.66). This is because taking refuge in Me will lead to the downfall of those who are of mixed varṇa and their family. The reason is that taking refuge in Me is only a means of grieving, and if you do so with ananya-bhāva (exclusive devotion), you will also lead to the downfall of your ancestors. But if you take refuge in Me with the intention of being free from grief, then your grief, anxiety, and other emotions will all be eliminated.

This is also evident from the fact that the body is ephemeral, and the only two things in the world are the eternal and the ephemeral. If the body were eternal, then it would not be a cause for concern, and there would be no fear of the downfall of the family and ancestors. But since the body is ephemeral, it is a cause for concern, and there is a fear of the downfall of the family and ancestors. Therefore, it is not suitable to grieve for the body, which is ephemeral.

[Verse 12]

The one who remains in the body is constantly in a state of death. You do not suffer any loss, even a tiny bit, due to the damage to the body. Therefore, you should not feel sorrow, anxiety, fear, and the like, taking the body with you.

The body is not attached to any body, hence it is said to be 'sarvagatah' (2.24), 'yena sarvam idam tatam' (2.17). The implication is that the nature of the seeker is only consciousness; therefore, in reality, he is not a body (shariri) but is unembodied (ashariri). That is why the Lord has also called him 'avikta' (2.25), 'aviktaadin bhutani' (2.28). The body is constantly being destroyed and is unreal. There is no existence of the unreal - 'nasato vidyate bhava' (2.16). If there is no existence, how can the unreal body be considered a body (shariri)? Therefore, the seeker is neither a body (shariri) nor a body (shariri). However, in this context, the Lord has called the seeker 'shariri' (dehi) for the purpose of explaining to the seekers. 'Shariri' means that you are not a body.

When we think of the body and the body (shariri), they are the same at the time of thinking and the same at the time of not thinking. The state of the body and the body (shariri) does not change due to thinking or not thinking. The seeker's attachment is removed, and his human birth is successful.

The human body is endowed with discrimination. Therefore, the realization 'I am not a body' can only be achieved in the human body. Considering the body as 'I' is not a human intellect but an animal intellect. That is why Shri Shukadeva Maharaj says to King Parikshit:

"O King! Now, give up this animal intellect that says 'I will die.' Just as the body was not born before and will not be born after, similarly, you were not born before and will not be born after - this is not true."

Relation - Why is it inappropriate to grieve for the eternal truth?

To answer this question, the Lord says in the next two verses:

We were never born, nor will we ever die. You were never born, nor will you ever die. Neither we nor you nor the kings will ever be born or die. 12.

Explanation - Only two things exist in the world - the eternal (shariri) and the body (shariri). Both are unobjectionable, i.e., it is not possible to grieve for either the eternal (shariri) or the body (shariri). The reason is that the eternal (shariri) never ceases to exist, and the body (shariri) never exists. The term 'ashochyam' in the previous verse is explained here as the eternal (shariri) and the body (shariri) are eternal and non-eternal, respectively.

The two verses say that we, you, and the kings will never be born or die. This is not true. The Lord says that I was not present in this form before I took an incarnation, and you were not present in this form before you were born. Similarly, these kings were not present in this form before they were born. However, even if we were not present in this form, we were still present in some form.

The statement that we were not there, is not true. 

The Gita Press edition of Srimad Bhagavad Gita states that the phrase "we were not there" is not being used here. The reason for this is that if we say "we were not there," it implies that we were there before. The meaning of "jatu" is that the eternal truth is always eternal and has never been absent in any time, place, situation, event, or object. 

Here, the Lord has used the word "aham" to convey a unique message. In the fourth chapter, fifth verse, the Lord tells Arjuna that "we have had many births, but I know them, you do not." In this way, the Lord has revealed His divine nature and distinguished Himself from the living beings. However, in this verse, the Lord is stating His unity with the living beings. The meaning is that there, in the fourth chapter, fifth verse, the Lord's intention was to reveal His greatness and uniqueness, while here, His intention is to explain the eternal truth.

"Na caiva vayam atah param" - In the future, these bodies will not exist, and one day these bodies will not exist at all; but even in such a state, we will not be absent - this is not the case. The reason is that the eternal truth has never been absent and will never be absent.

You and the kings - we were not there, this is not the case, and we will not be there in the future, this is also not the case - in this way, the Lord has stated that we were not there in the past and will not be there in the future. However, He has not stated that we are not present in the present. The reason for this is that from the perspective of the body, we are all present in the present moment, and there is no doubt about it. Therefore, there is no need to say "we were not there, this is not the case."

If we look at the eternal truth from a philosophical perspective, we are all present in the present moment, and the bodies are constantly changing. In this way, we should experience the separation from the body in the present moment. The meaning is that just as there is no absence of our existence in the past and future, similarly, there is no absence of our existence in the present moment - this should be experienced.

Just as every living being experiences that "we are present" before falling asleep and after waking up, so we were present in the past and will be present in the future. The only difference is that the external means of perception were absent, but our existence was not absent. Similarly, my, you, and the kings - we were not present in the past, and we will not be present in the future, but our existence is present in the present moment, and the bodies are constantly changing. Our existence is the eternal truth, because we are aware of all three times - past, present, and future.

The Lord has said this verse to explain the eternal truth. A special point is that we were not there in the past, and we will not be there in the future - this statement implies that when these bodies were not present, we were present, and when these bodies will not be present, we will still be present. This means that these bodies are impermanent, and we are permanent.

The impermanence of the bodies has been established by the fact that they were not present in the past and will not be present in the future. Similarly, the permanence of our existence has been established by the fact that we were present in the past and will be present in the future. These two facts establish the principle that what exists in the beginning and end also exists in the middle, and what does not exist in the beginning and end also does not exist in the middle.

The question arises as to how what does not exist in the beginning and end can exist in the middle, because it is visible to us. The answer is that the way in which we perceive the visible object is through the mind, intellect, and senses, which are constantly changing. These means of perception are not permanent for even a moment. When we identify ourselves with the visible object and the means of perception, we become the observer. However, when the means of perception and the visible object are both impermanent, how can the observer be permanent?

The meaning is that the name "observer" is given to us in relation to the visible object and perception. If there is no relation between the visible object and perception, then there is no name for the observer, but the eternal truth that is the foundation of the observer remains.

Sanskrit Shloka: 
na caiva vayamataḥ param

English Translation:
Nor even in the future will we be.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The concept of the soul's transmigration is a subject of great sorrow. Another point to consider is that just as the body and senses experience rejuvenation during childhood and youth, but not during old age, so too does the subtle body undergo a change. This is evident from the fact that the state of rest or relaxation is not the same in old age as it is in childhood and youth. In this way, the change in the causal body is also established.

Just as the physical body undergoes various stages of development, such as childhood, youth, and old age, so too does the subtle body undergo a change. This is evident from the fact that the subtle body is not the same in childhood as it is in youth, and so on. In fact, there is no moment when the physical body does not undergo a change. Similarly, the subtle body also undergoes a change at every moment, which is evident in the transmigration of the soul.

We have knowledge of the physical body, but we do not have knowledge of the subtle body. Therefore, it is not possible for us to have knowledge of the change in the subtle body. The knowledge of the subtle body is based on its various states, just as the knowledge of the physical body is based on its various stages of development.

The states of the physical body are 'jagrat' (wakefulness), the state of the subtle body is 'swapna' (dreaming), and the state of the causal body is 'sushupti' (deep sleep). A person in childhood sees himself as a child in his dreams, a person in youth sees himself as a youth in his dreams, and a person in old age sees himself as an old person in his dreams. This shows that the subtle body undergoes a change along with the physical body.

In the same way, the state of sushupti (deep sleep) is more pronounced in childhood, less pronounced in youth, and almost non-existent in old age. Therefore, the change in the causal body is also established.

When a person acquires a new body, he experiences the new body as 'I am this' due to the phenomenon of deha-adhyasa (identification with the body). This is a change in the subtle body. Similarly, the causal body has a nature or tendency, which is known as 'adat' (habit) in the physical world. This adat is determined by the type of body one acquires, whether it is a divine body, an animal body, or a bird body. This is a change in the causal body.

If the change in the body were to occur, then even when the stages of development change, the knowledge of 'I am the same' would not arise. However, even when the stages of development change, the knowledge of 'I was a child, I was a youth, and now I am the same' arises. This shows that there has been no change in the self.

A question may arise that if the knowledge of the physical body's stages of development changes, then why does the knowledge of the previous body not arise when one acquires a new body? The reason for this is that there is great suffering at the time of death and birth. Due to this suffering, the memory of the previous life is not retained in the mind.

Just as a person who has suffered a stroke or is very old does not retain the same level of knowledge as before, so too does a person at the time of death and birth not retain the memory of the previous life. However, if a person dies without suffering, and acquires a new body without any effort, then the memory of the previous life may be retained in the mind.

Now, let us consider the knowledge that arises at the time of transmigration. 

1. At the time of transmigration, the physical body is left behind, but the subtle and causal bodies are not left behind. As long as one has not attained liberation, the subtle and causal bodies remain connected to the self.

2. The knowledge of transmigration is known as 'pratyabhijna' in the scriptures. 'Tat-tadan-tavagahi jnanam pratyabhijna' (The knowledge of the self is the knowledge of transmigration).

3. 'Manushya rodate rudantam svanam uru vedenayastadhih' (The person becomes unconscious due to intense suffering and dies). (Shrimad Bhagavat 3.30.18)

4. 'Vinishkranti krichchhrena niruchchhvaso hatasmiti' (The person's breath stops and the memory of the previous life is lost). (Shrimad Bhagavat 3.31.23)

5. 'Ye mrite sahassa martya jayante sahassa punah. Tesam pauranikabhyasah kanchit kalam hi tisthati' (The dead are born again immediately, and their memories of the past life remain for a short time). 'Tasmat jatismarah lokah jayante bodhasamyuta' (Those who are born with memories of their past life are born with knowledge). 'Tesam vivardhatam sanjna svapnavat sa pranashyati' (Their knowledge grows, but eventually fades away like a dream). (Mahabharat, Anushasan Parva 145)

The understanding of the impermanent nature has dawned. A man of great wisdom is never deluded by this subject, nor does he ever harbor any doubts about it. This does not mean that such a wise man attains transmigration of the soul. The cause of birth in high or low castes is the association with good or bad qualities, and when one is separated from these qualities, a wise man can never attain transmigration of the soul.

It is true that the knowledge of the transmigratory state does not arise in this way; but the knowledge of one's own existence, 'I am,' remains in all beings. Just as, in deep sleep, one has no knowledge of anything, but when one wakes up, one says, 'I had such a deep sleep that I had no knowledge of anything,' the knowledge of 'I had no knowledge' is still there. Before falling asleep, I was what I am now, and after waking up, I am the same. In this way, the knowledge of one's own existence remains unbroken and continuous. The knowledge of the absence of one's own existence never arises in anyone. The existence of the embodied soul remains unbroken and continuous, and that is why liberation is attained, and in the state of liberation, it remains so.

However, in the state of liberation, one may not have knowledge of the transmigratory state, but one experiences, 'I am separate from the three bodies.' A man of great wisdom is not deluded in this matter. He knows that the body is perishable, and the soul is imperishable. The body is subject to change, but the soul remains the same. The soul is beyond all changes and transformations. A wise man knows that the body is a mere change, and the soul is the eternal and unchanging reality. He knows that the body is perishable, and the soul is imperishable. He knows that the body is a mere change, and the soul is the eternal and unchanging reality.

The jiva (soul) experiences the fruits of its actions in various bodies, and it goes to various worlds - this is self-evident. If this were not the case, then the eighty-four lakhs of bodies would be left behind, and the heavens and hells would be left behind, but the soul itself would remain. The bodies change, but the soul does not change. The soul remains the same, and it experiences various bodies. The soul is not attached to any body, and it is not bound by any body. If it were bound, then who would experience the eighty-four lakhs of bodies? Who would go to the heavens and hells? Who would be liberated?

Birth and death are not our duty, but the duty of the body. Our life is eternal and infinite, and within it, various bodies are born and die. Just as we change our clothes, but our essence remains the same, similarly, we experience various bodies, but our soul remains the same. Our independence and detachment are self-evident. Our life is not bound by any body. We are not attached to any body, and we are not bound by any body. We experience various bodies, but our soul remains the same. Our independence and detachment are self-evident.

The association with the impermanent is the cause of sorrow, and to get rid of this sorrow, it is said, 'Those who attain death and then take birth again, their old habits or tendencies remain for some time. Therefore, they are born in the world with the knowledge of their past deeds and are known as jatismar.' As they grow, their old memories, like a dream, gradually fade away.

The connection between these two concepts is that they are based on the idea of adaptability to favorable and unfavorable circumstances. Just as fatigue arises in every moment of wakefulness, so too do these objects of the senses appear to be capable of causing pleasure and pain. This is evident from the fact that even in sleep, freshness arises in every moment. Therefore, the Lord has said "sukhaduhkhadaḥ" (those who are the causes of pleasure and pain). The senses are constantly changing.

The objects of the senses are "āgama-apāyinaḥ" (those who are born and die), that is, they are ephemeral and fleeting. They do not remain permanent because they did not exist before their birth and will not exist after their death. Therefore, they are "āgama-apāyinaḥ".

If someone were to say that even though they may not exist before their birth and after their death, they still exist in the middle, the Lord says that they do not even exist in the middle. They are constantly changing at such a rapid pace that no one can see them in the same form again. Therefore, the Lord has called them "anityaḥ" (those who are ephemeral).

[Here, the objects of the senses are called "āgama-apāyinaḥ" in a gross sense and "anityaḥ" in a subtle sense. To describe them as even more subtle than ephemeral, they will be called "asat" in the 16th verse, and the description of the eternal and unchanging reality will be called "sat".]

The Lord says, "tāṃs-ti-ti-kṣaṣva" (bear them patiently). The knowledge that these objects of the senses are favorable or unfavorable is not a fault, but the attachment and aversion that arises from them is a fault. Therefore, even when one has knowledge of what is favorable or unfavorable, one should not allow attachment and aversion to arise. This patience is what the Lord has called "titi-kṣaṣva".

The second point is that the actions, states, and qualities of the body, senses, and mind are constantly arising and ceasing. These actions, states, and qualities are not in you; you are the one who knows them and is separate from them. You remain as you are, unchanged. Therefore, remain unchanged in these actions, states, and qualities. This is what is meant by patience.

Only the objects of the senses are ephemeral and changing, but the senses and the mind, from which one gains knowledge of them, are also ephemeral and changing. How can one understand their change? Just as one becomes tired from working during the day and fresh after sleeping, so too do the senses and mind become tired and fresh in turn. Therefore, one must sleep again to regain freshness and to alleviate tiredness.

Similarly, the objects of the senses are constantly changing, their union and separation with the self is a constant process. When we experience the union of the objects of the senses, we experience pleasure, and when we experience their separation, we experience pain. The objects of the senses are ephemeral and changing, and so are the senses and mind, from which one gains knowledge of them, and the pleasure and pain that arise from them. However, the self remains unchanged, eternal, and unchanging. Therefore, one should bear them patiently, that is, one should not experience pleasure and pain from their union and separation, but rather remain unchanged.

Pleasure and pain, joy and sorrow, attachment and aversion, desire and anger, and so on, are all ephemeral and changing. However, the self remains unchanged, eternal, and unchanging. The mistake of the seeker is that he sees the changing states, but not the self.

The concept of 'dasha' (state or condition) is discussed in the previous shloka. Now, the effect of 'titi-ksha' (tolerance) in such a state is explained in the next shloka.

The Sanskrit shloka is:

yaṃ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣaṃ puruṣarṣabha |
samaduḥkhasukhaṃ dhīraṃ so'mṛtatvāya
kalpate || 15 ||

English transliteration and translation:

yam hi na vyathayantye te purusham purusharshabha |
samadukh-sukham dhiram so 'mritatvaya kalpate || 15 ||

Translation:
For one who is not perturbed by these material contacts, O best of men (Arjuna), who is even-minded in happiness and distress, and who is wise, it is possible to attain immortality.

The meaning of 'purusharshabha' is that a person usually thinks of changing the circumstances that cannot be changed and are not meant to be changed. Arjuna, in the face of war-like circumstances, has not thought of changing them, but has instead thought of his own well-being. This is the mark of a superior person.

The phrase 'samadukh-sukham dhiram' means that a wise person remains even-minded in happiness and distress. The distinction between happiness and distress is perceived through the inner disposition of the mind. The person who experiences happiness and distress is the one who is subject to the material contacts. But the one who remains even-minded is not affected by these material contacts.

The phrase 'yam hi na vyathayantye te purusham' means that these material contacts do not perturb the wise person. The happiness and distress that arise from material contacts are not felt by the wise person. The reason is that the wise person has not identified himself with the material contacts. He has realized that the happiness and distress that arise from material contacts are not his true nature.

The phrase 'so 'mritatvaya kalpate' means that the wise person becomes eligible for immortality. The reason is that he has not identified himself with the material contacts, and therefore, he is not affected by them. He has realized that the happiness and distress that arise from material contacts are not his true nature.

The commentary explains that the wise person remains even-minded in happiness and distress because he has not identified himself with the material contacts. He has realized that the happiness and distress that arise from material contacts are not his true nature. Therefore, he is not affected by them, and he becomes eligible for immortality.

The commentary also explains that the wise person's even-mindedness is not due to a lack of feeling or emotion, but rather due to his realization that the happiness and distress that arise from material contacts are not his true nature. He has realized that the material contacts are external to him, and therefore, he is not affected by them.

The commentary concludes that the wise person becomes eligible for immortality because he has not identified himself with the material contacts. He has realized that the happiness and distress that arise from material contacts are not his true nature, and therefore, he is not affected by them.

[Verse 15]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 16]

The very poignant truth is that we can only see the world once, not twice. This is because the world is constantly changing; therefore, what appears to be a certain way in one moment is not the same in the next. Just as in a movie, the scenes on the screen appear to be stationary, but in reality, they are constantly changing due to the rapid movement of the film. The speed of the film is so great that our eyes cannot capture it. Even more poignant is the fact that the world is not even visible at all. This is because the very instruments through which we perceive and experience the world - the body, senses, mind, and intellect - are themselves part of the world. Therefore, it is only the world that appears to us as the world. That which is completely detached from the world, its true form, is never visible to us. The implication is that the true nature of the world is not perceived in its true form. It is only through its relationship with the world that we perceive the world. This establishes that the true nature of the world has no connection with the world.

Another point is that the world (body, senses, mind, intellect) is of no help to the consciousness (true nature) in performing any action. This establishes that all action takes place in the world, not in the true nature. Since the true nature has no connection with action, it is established that the entire world, including the body, senses, mind, and intellect, is non-existent. Only the essence of the Supreme Being, which is the source of all light and the foundation of all, exists.

Great souls have realized this truth and have distilled it to the essence that only one eternal truth exists.

The essence of the world (body, senses, mind, intellect) and the essence of the non-existent (non-being) are both eternal. This means that the essence of both is one and the same, eternal. Therefore, the eternal truth that is realized by great souls is one and the same, eternal. The power that appears to be non-existent is, in reality, eternal. The eternal is the source of the power that appears to be non-existent. This eternal is referred to as the "para prakriti" (7.5), "kshetrajna" (13.1-2), "purusha" (13.19), and "akshara" (15.16). The non-existent is referred to as the "apara prakriti", "kshetra", "prakriti", and "kshara".

Arjuna is lamenting the fact that all these bodies will perish in the war. On this, the Lord says, "Will they not perish even if they do not engage in war?" The non-existent will certainly perish and is constantly perishing. However, the eternal essence within it will never perish. Therefore, Arjuna's lamentation is a sign of his ignorance.

In the eleventh shloka, it is said that wise men do not lament for those who have died and those who are alive. In the twelfth to thirteenth shlokas, the eternal nature of the body is described, and the word "dhira" (wise) is used. In the fourteenth to fifteenth shlokas, the impermanence of the world is described, and the word "dhira" is used again. Similarly, in this sixteenth shloka, the discussion of the eternal and non-existent is presented, and the word "tattvadarshi" (wise) is used. The use of the words "pandit", "dhira", and "tattvadarshi" in these shlokas implies that only the wise and intelligent do not lament.

If someone laments, it means that they are not wise and intelligent. The verse "ubhayorapi drsto'ntastvanyosattvadarshibhi" (those who have realized the true nature of both the eternal and non-existent) implies that only those who are wise and intelligent do not lament.

Supplementary note - The eternal truth is only the essence of the eternal, and everything else that is part of the world and its activities (action and material) is non-existent, i.e., constantly changing. Those great souls who have realized the true nature of the eternal and non-existent, i.e., those who have experienced their own eternal and self-existent state, have a vision that the power of the non-existent is always present.

The verse "yadapi prati-kshan hi sharirani bhavanti na bhavanti cha, kala-nalaksya-vegen suukshmatvaat tann drishyate" (11.22.42) states that although the bodies are constantly being born and dying, their birth and death are not visible due to the extremely subtle movement of time.

The words "na anushochanti panditah" (2.11), "dhira-statra na muh-yati" (2.13), and "samduhkh-sukham dhira" (2.15) refer to those who are wise and intelligent, and they are referred to as "tattvadarshi" in this context.

The Bhagavad Gita

Chapter 2

It is not that the non-existent exists, nor is the existent non-existent. This means that, apart from the essence of existence (sat-tattva), nothing else exists. 

In the 14th and 15th shlokas, the Lord described the impermanence of the body, which is stated here as 'nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ'. In the 12th and 13th shlokas, the Lord described the permanence of the body, which is stated here as 'na bhāvo vidyate satḥ'.

The phrase 'nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ na bhāvo vidyate satḥ' - consisting of 16 syllables - contains the essence of all the Vedas, Puranas, and Shastras. The non-existent and the existent are described by various names such as nature and person, perishable and imperishable, body and embodied, impermanent and permanent, and so on.

Whatever is perceived, heard, understood, thought, or decided upon is non-existent. The one by whom we perceive, hear, think, or decide is also non-existent. The one that is perceived is also non-existent.

In this 16-syllable phrase, three verbs are used:

(1) 'bhū' - like 'abhāvaḥ' and 'bhāvaḥ'.

(2) 'as' - like 'asat' and 'sat'.

(3) 'vid' - like 'vidyate' and 'na vidyate'.

Although the root meaning of these three verbs is 'sat-tattva' (existence), they each have their own subtle meaning. For example, the verb 'bhū' means 'origin' or 'birth', 'as' means 'existence' or 'being', and 'vid' means 'existence' or 'being present'.

The phrase 'nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ' means 'asat-kī sat-tā na vidyate', i.e., the existence of the non-existent is not present, but rather its absence is present. This is because the non-existent is constantly changing and has no permanent existence. The non-existent is not present, not available, not obtained, not acquired, not available, not permanent. Whatever is born will eventually perish, and its destruction is inevitable. The destruction of a thing occurs so quickly that it cannot be seen twice in the same state.

The principle is that if a thing has no existence at any moment, it has no existence at all. Therefore, the world is always in a state of non-existence. No matter how much existence or importance is attributed to it, the world is not actually present. The non-existent is not obtained, was never obtained, and will never be obtained. It is impossible for the non-existent to be obtained.

The phrase 'na bhāvo vidyate satḥ' means 'sat-kī bhāva na vidyate', i.e., the existence of the existent is not absent, but rather its existence is present. This is because the existent is constantly present and has no absence. The existent is always present, always existing, always available, always obtained, always acquired, always available, and always permanent. In any place, time, thing, person, action, event, situation, or state, the existence of the existent is not absent. This is because the existent is always the same and has no change or deficiency.

The wise and enlightened people who have seen the truth have not created the existent, but rather have seen it. They have realized that the non-existent and the existent are both aspects of the same existent. They see only one existent, which is the ultimate reality. The non-existent and the existent are both aspects of the same existent, and there is no separate existence of the non-existent.

[Verse 17]

The savior of seekers is the understanding that the absence of the non-existent and the absence of the existent are both nonexistent. The conclusion is that the non-existent does not exist, and the existent is the existent. In the existent reality, there is no distinction between the body and the self.

As long as the non-existent is present, there is discrimination. When the non-existent is eliminated, discrimination transforms into knowledge of the ultimate reality. The wise ones who have realized the truth see both the existent and the non-existent within themselves. They have realized the ultimate reality and have experienced it. Discrimination has transformed into knowledge of the ultimate reality, and only the existent remains.

The existent is the only reality – this is the supreme truth of the path of knowledge.

It is also true that the non-existent does not exist, and it is also true that the absence of the existent does not exist. The seeker must accept the existent. Whether the seeker has experienced it or not, they must accept the existent. Accepting "is" and rejecting "is not" is the essence of Vedanta, the ultimate conclusion of the Vedas.

In the world, both existence and non-existence appear to exist, but non-existence is the primary reality. In the ultimate reality, both existence and non-existence appear to exist, but existence is the primary reality. In the world, non-existence is the primary reality, and within it, there are existence and non-existence. In the ultimate reality, existence is the primary reality, and within it, there are existence and non-existence. In other words, in the world, there is a mixture of existence and non-existence, and in the ultimate reality, there is a mixture of existence and non-existence.

The relationship between existence and non-existence will be explained in the next two verses.

Avyaya, the imperishable, is to be known as that by which all this is pervaded. There is no one who can cause the destruction of the imperishable. 17

Translation of Sanskrit shloka:

Avyaya tu tadvidhi yena sarvam idam tatam
Vinasam avyayasya asya na kascit kartum arhati

Explanation:
"Avyaya tu tadvidhi" - This verse is a continuation of the previous verse, where it was said that the non-existent does not exist. Here, the imperishable is to be known as that by which all this is pervaded. The word "tu" is used to indicate that the imperishable is to be known as that which is beyond the duality of existence and non-existence.

"Yena sarvam idam tatam" - This phrase means that the imperishable is the reality that pervades all this, the entire universe.

"Vinasam avyayasya asya na kascit kartum arhati" - This phrase means that there is no one who can cause the destruction of the imperishable. The word "avyaya" means imperishable, and the word "asaya" means of that. The phrase "na kascit kartum arhati" means that there is no one who can cause the destruction of the imperishable.

उसीको लक्ष्य करके भगवान्ने यहाँ ' अस्य' पद दिया है।
परिशिष्ट भाव—व्यवहारमें हम कहते हैं कि 'यह मनुष्य है, यह पशु है, यह वृक्ष है, यह मकान है' आदि,
तो इसमें 'मनुष्य, पशु, वृक्ष, मकान' आदि तो पहले भी नहीं थे, पीछे भी नहीं रहेंगे तथा वर्तमानमें भी प्रतिक्षण अभावमें
जा रहे हैं। परन्तु इनमें ‘है' रूपसे जो सत्ता है, वह सदा ज्यों-की-त्यों है। तात्पर्य है कि 'मनुष्य, पशु, वृक्ष, मकान'
आदि तो संसार (असत्) है और 'है' अविनाशी आत्मतत्त्व (सत्) है। इसलिये 'मनुष्य, पशु, वृक्ष, मकान' आदि
तो अलग-अलग हुए, पर इन सबमें ' है ' एक ही रहा । इसी तरह मैं मनुष्य हूँ, मैं पशु हूँ, मैं देवता हूँ आदिमें शरीर
तो अलग-अलग हुए पर 'हूँ' अथवा 'है' एक ही रहा ।
‘येन सर्वमिदं ततम्’— ये पद यहाँ जीवात्माके लिये आये हैं और आठवें अध्यायके बाईसवें श्लोकमें तथा अठारहवें
अध्यायके छियालीसवें श्लोकमें यही पद परमात्माके लिये आये हैं । इसका तात्पर्य है कि जीवात्माका सर्वव्यापक
परमात्माके साथ साधर्म्य है। अतः जैसे परमात्मा संसारसे असंग हैं, ऐसे ही जीवात्मा भी शरीर - संसारसे स्वतः-
स्वाभाविक असंग है—‘असङ्गो ह्ययं पुरुषः ' (बृहदा० ४। ३ । १५), 'देहेऽस्मिन्पुरुषः परः' (गीता १३ । २२ ) ।
जीवात्माकी स्थिति किसी एक शरीरमें नहीं है । वह किसी शरीरसे चिपका हुआ नहीं है । परन्तु इस असंगताका अनुभव
न होनेसे ही जन्म-मरण हो रहा है ।
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः ।

original:
श्लोक १८ ]
* साधक-संजीवनी *
केवल श्रद्धाका विषय है', प्रमाणका विषय नहीं ।
शास्त्र और सन्त किसीको बाध्य नहीं करते कि तुम
हमारेमें श्रद्धा करो। श्रद्धा करने अथवा न करनेमें मनुष्य
स्वतन्त्र है। अगर वह शास्त्र और सन्तके वचनोंमें श्रद्धा करेगा,
तो यह तत्त्व उसकी श्रद्धाका विषय है; और अगर वह श्रद्धा
नहीं करेगा, तो यह तत्त्व उसकी श्रद्धाका विषय नहीं है।
'नित्यस्य' '– यह नित्य-निरन्तर रहनेवाला है । किसी
कालमें यह न रहता हो—ऐसी बात नहीं है अर्थात् यह सब
कालमें सदा ही रहता ।
'अन्तवन्त इमे देहा उक्ताः शरीरिणः' – इस अविनाशी,
अप्रमेय और नित्य शरीरीके सम्पूर्ण संसारमें जितने भी
शरीर हैं, वे सभी अन्तवाले कहे गये हैं । अन्तवाले कहनेका
तात्पर्य है कि इनका प्रतिक्षण अन्त हो रहा है। इनमें अन्तके
सिवाय और कुछ है ही नहीं, केवल अन्त - ही - अन्त है ।
उपर्युक्त पदोंमें शरीरीके लिये तो एकवचन दिया है
और शरीरोंके लिये बहुवचन दिया है। इसका एक कारण
तो यह है कि प्रत्येक प्राणीके स्थूल, सूक्ष्म और कारण -
ये तीन शरीर होते हैं। दूसरा कारण यह है कि संसारके
सम्पूर्ण शरीरोंमें एक ही शरीरी व्याप्त है । आगे चौबीसवें
श्लोकमें भी इसको 'सर्वगतः ' पदसे सबमें व्यापक
बतायेंगे । यह शरीरी तो अविनाशी है और इसके कहे
जानेवाले सम्पूर्ण शरीर नाशवान् हैं। जैसे अविनाशीका कोई
विनाश नहीं कर सकता, ऐसे ही नाशवान्‌को कोई
अविनाशी नहीं बना सकता । नाशवान्‌का तो विनाशीपना ही

The eighteenth shloka is the essence of devotion, not a matter of proof. The scriptures and saints do not compel anyone to have faith in them. A person is free to have faith or not. If he has faith in the scriptures and saints, then this truth is his subject of faith; and if he does not have faith, then this truth is not his subject of faith.

"'Nityasya' - This is the eternal and continuous one. It does not cease to exist at any time; that is, it always exists.

"'Antavant ime deha uktah sharirinah' - All the bodies in this imperishable, incomprehensible, and eternal world, which are called perishable, are indeed perishable. The meaning of 'perishable' is that their end is constantly approaching. There is nothing but their end; only end after end.

In the above verses, the word 'deha' (body) is used in the singular form, and 'sharirinah' (bodies) is used in the plural form. The reason for this is that each living being has three bodies - the gross, subtle, and causal. The other reason is that the same body dweller pervades all the bodies in the world. In the twenty-fourth shloka, we will also see that it is called 'sarvagatah' (all-pervading).

The body dweller is imperishable, and the bodies that are said to be perishable are indeed perishable. Just as the imperishable one cannot be destroyed, so the perishable one cannot be made imperishable. The perishable one will always be perishable, and its destruction will always be its nature.

Special note:

Here, 'antavant ime deha' means that all the bodies that are seen are perishable. But what are these bodies? 'Nityasya', 'anashinah' - these bodies are eternal, imperishable. The meaning is that the eternal truth has taken these bodies as its own, and has kept them as its own. Keeping oneself in the body and keeping the body in oneself - this is the meaning.

By keeping oneself in the body, 'ahamta' (I-ness) is born, and by keeping the body in oneself, 'mamatva' (my-ness) is born. The one who keeps himself in these things, in these things, 'I-ness' is born; just as - keeping oneself in wealth, 'I am wealthy'; keeping oneself in the kingdom, 'I am the king'; keeping oneself in knowledge, 'I am learned'; keeping oneself in wisdom, 'I am wise'; keeping oneself in spiritual powers, 'I am a sage'; keeping oneself in the body, 'I am the body'; and so on.

The one who keeps these things in himself, in these things, 'my-ness' is born; just as - keeping the family in oneself, 'the family is mine'; keeping wealth in oneself, 'wealth is mine'; keeping wisdom in oneself, 'wisdom is mine'; keeping the body in oneself, 'the body is mine'; and so on.

The birth of 'I-ness' and 'my-ness' with the jiva (the individual self) is the cause of all vikaras (disturbances). The meaning is that the body and the self are separate, and if this discrimination is not given importance, then only vikaras are born. But those who give importance to this discrimination are pandits. Such pandits never grieve, because they have the right understanding that the true is true and the false is false.

"'Tasmad yudhyasva' - The Lord gives the order to Arjuna to fight, understanding the true and the false. That is, perform the duty that has to be done. The meaning is that the body is perishable and the body dweller is imperishable. From this point of view, grief cannot be born. Therefore, give up grief and fight.

Special note:

In the seventeenth and eighteenth shlokas, the special feature is the discussion of the truth of the true. The reason is that the Lord's goal in this whole section is to make Arjuna aware of the true. When the true is understood, the false automatically disappears.

1. At first, this truth is a matter of faith, but later, when its direct experience is obtained, it is no longer a matter of faith.

2. Here, the word 'tasmad' is used in the sense of 'yukti' (reason). That is, when the reason is understood, then fight. This is the way the word 'tasmad' is used in the Gita, usually at the end of a section or at the end of a reason.

english:
95
[Verse 20]

The one who thinks that this body is being killed and also thinks that it is being killed, does not know. This is because the one who thinks that this body is being killed, does not know that this body is not being killed, and the one who thinks that it is being killed, does not know that it is not being killed. 

This body cannot perform any action, just like it cannot exist without a body. It cannot do anything by itself. Therefore, in the 13th chapter, the Lord says that all actions are done through the nature - one who experiences this, experiences the body as non-doer (13th chapter, 31st shloka). The meaning is that there is no doer in the body, but by associating with the body and linking it with oneself, one considers oneself as the doer of the actions that happen through the body. If one does not associate with the body, then it is not the doer of any action.

The question arises here, if the one who thinks that this body is being killed and also thinks that it is being killed, does he know? The answer is that he does not know. The reason is that this body is not like that. It is not a killer and it is not being killed. It is eternal and unchanging, existing in its original form. Therefore, one should not grieve for this body.

The one who thinks that this body is dead, does not know. Just like this body is not a killer, it is not a dead body either; because it does not have any defects. Where there are defects, there is change, i.e., where there is birth and death, that is a dead body. This body is free from all defects and changes.

Here, the context of the war in front of Arjuna has led to the explanation that this body is free from the actions of being killed and killing. In reality, this body is not a killer and is not killed - this is the meaning. It does not have any actions and does not have any defects. The people who consider this body as a killer and a dead body, do not give importance to the body and its wisdom, but rather give importance to ignorance.

The question arises here, why is this body not a dead body? The answer is that it is not born, it does not die, it is not created, and it is not destroyed. It is eternal, unchanging, and ancient. It is not affected by the changes in the body.

The shloka says:

na jāyate mriyate vā kadācit nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ |
ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre || 20 ||

This body is not born, it does not die, it is not created, and it is not destroyed. It is eternal, unchanging, and ancient. It is not affected by the changes in the body.

The explanation of this shloka is that the body has six defects - birth, change, growth, decrease, and death. This body is free from all these defects.

The shloka says:

jāyate asti vipariṇamate vardhate apakṣīyate vinaśyati | (nirukta 1 | 1 | 2 )

This body is not born, it does not change, it does not grow, it does not decrease, and it does not die.

कहा है; और जिसको पहले 'न म्रियते' कहा, उसीको
दुबारा ' न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे' कहा
है।
'अयं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ' - यह अविनाशी
नित्य-तत्त्व पैदा होकर फिर होनेवाला नहीं है अर्थात् यह
स्वत:सिद्ध निर्विकार है । जैसे, बच्चा पैदा होता है, तो पैदा
होनेके बाद उसकी सत्ता होती है । जबतक वह गर्भमें नहीं
आता, तबतक ‘बच्चा है' ऐसे उसकी सत्ता (होनापन )
कोई भी नहीं कहता । तात्पर्य है कि बच्चेकी सत्ता पैदा
होनेके बाद होती है; क्योंकि उस विकारी सत्ताका आदि
और अन्त होता है। परन्तु इस नित्य-तत्त्वकी सत्ता
स्वत: सिद्ध और निर्विकार है; क्योंकि इस अविकारी
सत्ताका आरम्भ और अन्त नहीं होता ।
'अज: ' – इस शरीरीका कभी जन्म नहीं होता ।
इसलिये यह ‘अज:' अर्थात् जन्मरहित कहा गया है।

शाश्वतः '– यह नित्य-तत्त्व निरन्तर एकरूप, एकरस
रहनेवाला है। इसमें अवस्थाका परिवर्तन नहीं होता अर्थात्
यह कभी बदलता नहीं । इसमें बदलनेकी योग्यता है ही
नहीं ।
'पुराण : ' - यह अविनाशी तत्त्व पुराण (पुराना )
अर्थात् अनादि है । यह इतना पुराना है कि यह कभी पैदा
हुआ ही नहीं । उत्पन्न होनेवाली वस्तुओंमें भी देखा जाता
है कि जो वस्तु पुरानी हो जाती है, वह फिर बढ़ती नहीं,
प्रत्युत नष्ट हो जाती है; फिर यह तो अनुत्पन्न तत्त्व है,
इसमें बढ़नारूप विकार कैसे हो सकता है ? तात्पर्य है कि
बढ़नारूप विकार तो उत्पन्न होनेवाली वस्तुओंमें ही होता
है, इस नित्य-तत्त्वमें नहीं।
'न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे' – शरीरका नाश होनेपर
भी इस अविनाशी शरीरीका नाश नहीं होता । यहाँ 'शरीरे'
पद देनेका तात्पर्य है कि यह शरीर नष्ट होनेवाला है। इस
नष्ट होनेवाले शरीरमें ही छ: विकार होते हैं, शरीरीमें नहीं ।
इन पदोंमें भगवान्ने शरीर और शरीरीका जैसा स्पष्ट
वर्णन किया है, ऐसा स्पष्ट वर्णन गीतामें दूसरी जगह नहीं
आया है।
अर्जुन युद्धमें कुटुम्बियोंके मरनेकी आशंकासे विशेष
शोक कर रहे थे। उस शोकको दूर करनेके लिये भगवान्
कहते हैं कि शरीरके मरनेपर भी इस शरीरीका मरना नहीं
होता अर्थात् इसका अभाव नहीं होता । इसलिये शोक करना
अनुचित है।
।
'नित्यः '– यह शरीरी नित्य - निरन्तर रहनेवाला है;
अतः इसका कभी अपक्षय नहीं होता । अपक्षय तो अनित्य
वस्तुमें होता है, जो कि निरन्तर रहनेवाली नहीं है । जैसे,
परिशिष्ट भाव – हमारा ( स्वयंका) और शरीरका स्वभाव बिलकुल अलग-अलग है। हम शरीरके साथ चिपके
हुए नहीं हैं, शरीरसे मिले हुए नहीं हैं। शरीर हमारे साथ चिपका हुआ नहीं है, हमारेसे मिला हुआ नहीं है । इसलिये
शरीरके न रहनेपर हमारा कुछ भी बिगड़ता नहीं । अबतक हम असंख्य शरीर धारण करके छोड़ चुके हैं, पर उससे
हमारी सत्तामें क्या फर्क पड़ा ? हमारा क्या नुकसान हुआ ? हम तो ज्यों-के-त्यों ही रहे — 'भूतग्रामः स एवायं भूत्वा
भूत्वा प्रलीयते' ( गीता ८ । १९) । ऐसे ही यह शरीर छूटनेपर भी हम स्वयं ज्यों-के-त्यों ही रहेंगे।
जैसे हाथ, पैर, नासिका आदि शरीरके अंग हैं, ऐसे शरीर शरीरी (स्वयं) - का अंग भी नहीं है । जो बहनेवाला
और विकारी होता है, वह 'अंग' नहीं होता *; जैसे - कफ, मूत्र आदि बहनेवाले और फोड़ा आदि विकारी होनेसे
शरीरके अंग नहीं हैं, ऐसे ही शरीर बहनेवाला (परिवर्तनशील) और विकारी होनेसे शरीरीका अंग नहीं है ।
* अद्रवं मूर्त्तिमत् स्वाङ्गं प्राणिस्थमविकारजम् । अतत्स्थं तत्र दृष्टं च तेन चेत्तत्तथायुतम्॥

This is a commentary on the 13th verse of the 2nd chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, which says that a wise person does not grieve about the change of bodies. The author is explaining this concept using the example of a person changing clothes.

The author says that clothes are changed by humans, not animals, and therefore, the example of changing clothes is used to illustrate the concept of changing bodies. The word "naraḥ" (nara) means a human being and includes both men and women, children and adults, and all others.

Just as a person discards worn-out clothes and takes on new ones, similarly, the embodied soul discards worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. The author says that the soul is not attached to the body and therefore, it does not grieve about the change of bodies.

The author also explains that the body is discarded when its life is over, and a new body is taken on when the soul is reborn. The soul continues to take on new bodies as long as it is connected to nature and its karma.

The author also clarifies that the use of the plural form "śarīrāṇi" (sharirani) in the verse means that the soul continues to take on new bodies until it attains its true nature.

The author then addresses a question that may arise - why is the example of changing clothes used to illustrate the concept of changing bodies, when the body is not like a piece of clothing that can be changed at will? The author responds that the example is used to illustrate the concept of detachment from the body, not to suggest that the soul has control over the body.

The author also explains that the verse is not suggesting that the soul is attached to the body and therefore, it grieves about the change of bodies. Rather, it is suggesting that the soul is not attached to the body and therefore, it does not grieve about the change of bodies.

The author also addresses another question that may arise - why is the example of changing clothes used to illustrate the concept of changing bodies, when the change of clothes is a pleasant experience, while the change of bodies is a painful experience? The author responds that the pain of changing bodies is not due to the change itself, but due to the attachment to the body. When one is attached to the body, one grieves about its change, but when one is detached from the body, one does not grieve about its change.

The author concludes by saying that the verse is not suggesting that the soul is attached to the body and therefore, it grieves about the change of bodies. Rather, it is suggesting that the soul is not attached to the body and therefore, it does not grieve about the change of bodies.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[ Verse 24 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
The body may be burnt by the fire of Varuna's weapon, but the soul within the body is not burnt. Even if the body is destroyed by weapons or dies, the soul within it does not die. If the body is dissolved, the soul within it does not dissolve. If the body is dried up by the wind, the soul within it does not dry up. Therefore, to mourn for it is utter foolishness on your part. Appendix - We say that the body is subject to change, but the soul within it is not. Just as a piece of wood may be cut or burnt, but the fact that it "is" remains unchanged. The wood may be wet or dry, but the fact that it "is" remains unaffected. This soul is indestructible, cannot be burnt, cannot be made wet, and cannot be dried up. It is eternal, all-pervading, immovable, and unchanging. Word-by-word breakdown:
achchhedyo 'yam = this soul is indestructible, cannot be cut
adahyo 'yam = this soul cannot be burnt
akledyo 'yam = this soul cannot be made wet
ashoshyah = this soul cannot be dried up
nityah = this soul is eternal
sarvagatah = this soul is all-pervading
sthanuh = this soul is immovable
achalah = this soul is unchanging
sanatanah = this soul is eternal

Explanation - [This verse explains why weapons and other means cannot affect the soul.] The soul cannot be cut or pierced by weapons, nor can it be burnt by fire. This does not mean that weapons or fire are ineffective, but rather that the soul is not capable of being affected by them. The soul cannot be cut or pierced by any means, including mantras or curses. Just as the body can be affected by mantras or curses, but the soul remains untouched. The soul is not susceptible to burning, wetting, or drying, and it remains unchanged and eternal. The Lord emphasizes that the soul is indestructible, cannot be burnt, cannot be made wet, and cannot be dried up, and that it is eternal, all-pervading, immovable, and unchanging. This is why Arjuna's mourning is unnecessary. The soul is not something that can be affected by any means, and it remains unchanged and eternal.
