* 
Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
*
The term 'sarvagatah' (omnipresent) means that the Atman (the eternal soul) remains the same in all times. The word 'nityah' (eternal) is used to indicate that it is always present. If it is present everywhere, then it must be present in some place. In response to this, it is said that the Atman is present equally in all beings, objects, and bodies. The term 'achal' (immovable) means that the Atman is stable in nature, i.e., it does not have the ability to come and go. The term 'sthānūḥ' (unshakable) means that the Atman does not have the ability to shake or tremble, just like a tree that stands firm in one place and does not move, but may still sway slightly. However, the Atman does not even have this slight movement. The term 'sanātanāḥ' (eternal) means that the Atman is eternal, without beginning, and has always existed. It is not possible for it to not exist at any point in time. Special Note
[ Chapter 2 ]
[Verse 25]
The term 'sarvagataḥ' is used to indicate the all-pervading nature of the Atman, which is present in all objects, beings, and matter that we see, hear, read, and understand in the natural world. All objects, beings, and matter in the world are transient. The term 'achalḥ' is used to indicate the Atman, which remains unchanged and unmoving despite being present in these transient objects. The natural world is constantly changing, with creation and destruction occurring every moment. The term 'sthānūḥ' is used to indicate the Atman, which remains stable and unchanging amidst this flux. Only natural objects are born and die, and they did not exist before and will not exist after. However, the Atman is not born and does not die, and it has always existed and will continue to exist. The term 'sanātanāḥ' is used to indicate this eternal nature of the Atman. The five terms used to describe the Atman (omnipresent, immovable, unshakable, eternal, and imperishable) indicate that the body and the world are transient and do not remain stable even for a moment. However, the Atman remains stable and unchanged, and it is always present. Appendix - The term 'sarvagataḥ' means that the Atman is not limited to the body but is all-pervading. To realize this is to attain liberation. Just as the body sits in the world, we are not sitting in the body. We have never been connected to the body, we are not connected, and we will never be connected. The body is far removed from us, but due to desire, attachment, and identification, we perceive ourselves as being connected to it. In reality, the Atman does not need the body and can exist independently. The Atman is said to be avyakta (not visible), achintya (beyond thought), and avikārya (unchanging). Therefore, knowing this, you should not grieve for it. Commentary - The term 'avyakta' means that the Atman is not visible to the senses, just like the body and the world are visible in a gross form. The term 'achintya' means that the Atman is beyond the reach of the mind and intellect.

* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
The subject is the body. However, this is not a subject for contemplation; 
because it is devoid of subtle creation. Coming, but as soon as it comes into contemplation, it is all 
about contemplation, that is, this body is described by the four 
adjectives - Nitya (eternal), Sarvagata (all-pervading), Sthánu (immovable), 
and Sanátana (eternal). However, in reality, its description is not possible; 
because it is not a subject of speech. How can speech and other 
things illuminate the body from which they originate? Therefore, experiencing this body is the only way to describe it. 'Avikáryo'yam uchyate' - This body is called unchanging, 
meaning that it never undergoes any transformation. The cause of 
everything is nature, and even in that causal nature, there is 
transformation. But in this body, there is no transformation of any kind; 
because it is devoid of causal creation. Here, in the 24th and 25th verses, the body is described by eight 
adjectives - Achchhedya (indivisible), Ada (imperishable), Akledya (impermeable), 
Ashóshya (unshriveling), Achal (unmoving), Avyakta (unmanifest), 
Achintya (inconceivable), and Avikárya (unchanging) - and also by 
'Tasmád evam viditvainam nánushochitum arhasi' - Therefore, 
knowing this body as indivisible, imperishable, unchanging, etc., 
one should not grieve. Connection - Even if the body is considered to be changing 
(contrary to the established doctrine), grief is not justified - this 
will be explained in the next two verses. Athá cha enám nitya-játam nityam vá manyase mrítam. Tathápi tvam mahá-báho naivam shochitum arhasi. If you think that the body is always born or always dies,

Here, in the alternative, 'Athá cha' and 'manyase' are used to

always dying, contrary to the established doctrine (as stated in 
the 20th verse of the second chapter of the Gita), you should not

born and always dying, even then grief is not justified. For example, a seed germinates, grows into a tree, and eventually 
dries up. The seed is never the same for a moment; it is always 
changing. If the seed remained the same for a moment, how could 
it go through the process of growth and decay? When it gives up 
its original form, it is said to have died, and when it takes on a new 
form, it is said to have been born. Similarly, the body is like a seed; 
it is born, grows, decays, and dies. If the body is considered to be 
always changing, like the seed, then grief is not justified.

Commentary - 'For one who is born, death is certain, and for one who has died, birth is certain.' - Even if we consider the body to be eternal, with constant birth and death, it is still not a cause for grief. The reason is that for one who is born, death is certain, and for one who has died, birth is certain. 'Therefore, you should not grieve over the inevitable.' - Because no one can prevent this cycle of birth and death, which has been going on since time immemorial and will continue forever. From this perspective, it is not fitting for you to grieve. These sons of Dhritarashtra have been born, so they will certainly die. You do not have the means to save them. Those who have died will certainly be born again. You cannot prevent this either. So, what is the point of grieving? Similarly, if you think that these bodies, including Bhishma and Drona, will die, then they will also be reborn. Therefore, from this perspective as well, grief is not justified. The Lord has stated in these two verses (26 and 27) that this is not His actual doctrine. Therefore, using the phrase 'atha cha' (and now), the Lord presents the view of another party (those who consider the body to be eternal), saying that even if one accepts this doctrine, grief is still not justified. The meaning of these two verses is that the things of this world are constantly changing, taking on new forms and leaving their old ones. This process of change is what we call birth and death. The one who is born will certainly die, and the one who has died will certainly be born again. This cycle is always in motion. From this perspective, what is the point of grieving? Grieve only for what is unlikely to happen. What is meant to happen will happen. Just as everyone knows that the sun will set after it rises, and it will rise again after it sets, we should not grieve over the inevitable. Appendix - When a loved one dies or wealth is lost, people grieve. Similarly, they worry about the future, thinking, "What will happen if my wife dies? What will happen if my son dies?" and so on. These feelings of grief and worry arise because we do not give importance to our own wisdom. Change is necessary in this world. If circumstances do not change, how can the world function? How can a child grow into a youth? How can an ignorant person become wise? How can a sick person become healthy? How can a seed become a tree? Without change, the world would become stagnant like a static picture. In reality, only the perishable (the changing) dies, while the imperishable (the eternal) never dies. It is a common experience that when someone dies, their body remains before us, but the soul (the owner of the body) departs. If we give importance to this experience, then grief and worry cannot arise. When a child dies, Lord Rama points to this experience, saying:
"O Tara, do not cry. The body is like a tree, and the soul is like the wind. The body is consumed by fire, but the soul is not touched. The soul is eternal, and the body is transient."

* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
When the knowledge arose, then I attained the highest devotion and prayed for it. (Manas, Kishkindha 11.2-3)
One should consider that when none of the 8.4 million bodies remain, then how can this body remain? When none of the 8.4 million bodies are mine, then how can this body be mine? This discernment can occur in a human body, not in other bodies. Connection - After discussing the other side in the previous two verses, Lord Krishna now speaks from a very ordinary perspective in the next verse. The beings, O Bharata, are unmanifest before birth and manifest in the middle; they are unmanifest again after death. What is the cause for lamentation in this? 28
 Commentary:
'Avyaktadini bhutani' - All the beings (bodies, etc.) that can be seen, heard, and understood are unmanifest before birth, i.e., they are not visible. 'Avyaktanidhanani' - All these beings will become unmanifest after death, i.e., they will perish and become non-existent. 'Vyaktamadhyani' - All these beings are manifest in the middle, i.e., after birth and before death. Just like a dream is not present before sleeping and not present after waking, but is present in between, similarly, these beings' bodies were not present before and will not be present after, but are present in between. However, in reality, their destruction is happening every moment. 'Tatra ka paridevana' - What is the point of lamentation for something that is not present in the beginning and end? The principle is that what is not present in the beginning and end is also not present in the middle. All beings' bodies were not present before and will not be present after; therefore, they are not present even in the middle. However, this body (the self) was present before and will be present after; therefore, it will be present in the middle as well. The conclusion is that the bodies are always non-existent, and the self is never non-existent. Therefore, there can be no lamentation for either of them. Appendix - Whatever is not present in the beginning and end, its 'non-existence' is eternal and continuous. Whatever is present in the beginning and end, its 'existence' is eternal and continuous. Whatever has eternal and continuous 'non-existence' is 'asat' (the body), and whatever has eternal and continuous 'existence' is 'sat' (the self). We have eternal separation from the asat and eternal union with the sat. Connection - Now Lord Krishna describes the transcendence of the self. 1 - That which is not present in the beginning and end is also not present in the middle. (Mandukya Karika 4.31)
2 - (a) Whatever is present in the beginning and end is also present in the middle, and that is the truth. (Srimad Bhagavatam 11.24.17)
(b) Whatever is present in the beginning and end of this world, whatever is its root cause and illuminator, that is also present in the middle. (Srimad Bhagavatam 11.28.18)
(c) Whatever is not present before creation and not present after destruction, one should understand that it is not present in the middle either, but is merely a concept, a mere name. (Srimad Bhagavatam 11.28.21)

Commentary:
The phrase "ashcharyavat pashyati kashchid enam" means that someone sees this (the Self) as a wonder. This implies that the Self is not known in the same way as other objects, which can be seen, heard, or read about. The Self is not an object of the senses or the mind, but is known directly, through self-awareness. This self-awareness is not like ordinary knowledge, but is a unique and extraordinary experience. The word "pashyati" has two meanings: seeing with the eyes and knowing through self-awareness. In this context, it refers to knowing the Self through self-awareness. In ordinary perception, there are three factors: the seer (the subject), the seen (the object), and the act of seeing (the process). However, in self-awareness, there is no such triad, as the Self is not an object of the senses or the mind. The Self is known directly, without the need for any external means. The example of a lamp is given to illustrate this point. When we want to see an object in a dark room, we need a lamp and our eyes to see it. However, when we want to see the lamp itself, we do not need another lamp or our eyes, because the lamp is self-luminous. Similarly, the Self is self-aware and does not need any external means to know itself. There are three types of bodies: the gross body (sthula sharira), the subtle body (sukshma sharira), and the causal body (karana sharira). The gross body is made up of food and water and is an object of the senses. The subtle body is made up of the five senses, the five organs of action, the five vital breaths, the mind, and the intellect, and is not an object of the senses but of the intellect. The causal body is beyond the intellect and is the source of the subtle body. When we reflect on these three bodies, we realize that the gross body is not our true nature, as it is constantly changing and is an object of the senses. The subtle body is also changing and is an object of the intellect, so it is not our true nature either. The causal body is the source of the subtle body, but it is not our true nature, as we are beyond it. When we transcend the causal body and establish ourselves in our true nature, we come to know ourselves directly. This self-knowledge is unique and extraordinary, and is not like the knowledge of ordinary objects. Therefore, it is said that someone sees this (the Self) as a wonder.
[Verse 29]

[ Verse 29 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
Here, the word 'anyah' implies that the listener (the inquirer of the truth) is different from the one who knows and the one who speaks. The doer is only one - 'kashchit' - and it further illuminates the subject. Therefore, in the seventh chapter, third verse, it is also stated that the listener listens with wonder. Only one person knows me in reality - 'kashchin maam vetti tattvatah.' These words indicate that knowing this indestructible truth is very difficult, rare. However, this is not the case. Knowing this truth is not difficult, nor is it rare; rather, there is a lack of genuine interest in knowing it. This lack is due to a lack of curiosity about knowing. 'Aashcharyavad vadati tathaiva cha anyah' - another person describes this body with wonder; because this truth is not a subject of speech. That which illuminates speech itself cannot be described by speech. The great person who describes this truth only gives a hint through speech, like the Chandrayana vow, so that the listener's attention is drawn to it. Therefore, its description is always with wonder. The word 'anyah' used here does not mean that the speaker is different from the one who knows; because one who does not know themselves cannot describe it. Therefore, the meaning of this word is that among those who know, only one can describe it. This is because all experienced, truth-knowing great persons cannot, through their explanations, bring the listener to that truth, nor can they completely resolve their doubts and arguments. Therefore, the word 'anyah' is used to indicate the unique ability of the describer. 'Shrutvaapyenam veda na chaiva kashchit' - even after hearing, no one knows it. This does not mean that after hearing, one will not know it. It means that no one can know it simply by hearing. After hearing, when one is established in it, they will know it by themselves. If someone says that knowledge is gained by listening to scriptures and gurus, then why is it said here that 'no one knows it even after hearing'? Reflecting deeply on this subject, we see that scriptures and gurus do not create faith in themselves; rather, the seeker themselves has faith in scriptures and gurus. If knowledge were possible without being present before them, then with so many incarnations of God and great liberated beings, no one should remain ignorant. In other words, everyone should have attained truth-knowledge. Listening with faith and trust helps in being established in one's true nature, but one becomes established in their true nature by themselves. Therefore, the meaning of the above words is not to indicate the impossibility of knowing the truth but to show that it is beyond the means (one knows it by themselves). No matter how hard a person tries to know the truth, ultimately, they will know it by themselves. Hearing, reflection, etc., can be considered traditional means of knowing the truth, but the actual realization is beyond means (it happens by itself). 'Aashcharyavach chainam anyah shrunoti' - another person hears this body with wonder. This means that the listener, who has heard so many things from scriptures and the world, finds this body's truth to be extraordinary. What is it to know oneself by oneself? The reason is that everything else one has heard is related to the senses, mind, and intellect, and is a subject of action, seeing, and knowing. However, this body is not a subject of the senses, etc., but rather it is the one that knows through the senses, etc. The idea of knowing oneself by oneself is mentioned in the Gita in several places, such as:
(1) Atmanyevatmanaa tushthah sthitaprajnastaduchyate. (2.55)
(2) Yastvaatmaratireva syaadatmatruptashcha maanavah, atmanyeva cha santushtastasya kaaryam na vidyate. (3.17)
(3) Yatra chaivaatmanaatmaanam pashyannatmani tushyati. (6.20)
(4) Yatanto yoginashchainam pashyantyaatmanyavasthitam. (15.11)

* 
Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
*
[ Chapter 2 
[Verse 30]
It is not possible to know through the senses, but rather through direct experience. I have no connection with objects, and what I know through my own self is of two types: one is the connection with the body and the world, and the other is the eternal, unchanging connection with the Supreme Atman (the eternal soul). After knowing this, one experiences the distinction between the self and the body. This experience cannot be described in words, and even the intellect becomes silent. Appendix - One cannot know the truth by merely listening or practicing, but by inquiring and learning from experienced and knowledgeable persons. As stated in the Gita (7.3), "Even among those who strive, only a few know me in reality." The statement "one speaks in wonder" means that even among those who experience the truth, only a few can describe it. Just as marriage does not occur simply by listening, but by the mutual acceptance of the man and woman as husband and wife, one cannot know the truth of the Supreme Atman merely by listening. One must listen, then accept and realize it within themselves. Therefore, one can learn and teach about knowledge by listening, but cannot experience it. The truth of the Supreme Atman cannot be known merely by listening, but by listening and then worshiping - as stated in the Gita (13.25), "Having heard, others worship." If the speaker is experienced and the listener is devoted and inquiring, knowledge can be attained immediately. Connection - The topic of the body and the embodied self, which has been discussed so far, is being concluded in the next verse. The embodied self, which is eternal and indestructible, is present in every body, O descendant of Bharata. Therefore, you should not grieve for any living being. Breakdown:
- dehi: the embodied self
- nityam: eternal
- avadhyah: indestructible
- tasmat: therefore
- sarvani: all
- bhutani: living beings
- tvam: you
- socitum: to grieve
- arhasi: should

Explanation - The embodied self, which is present in all bodies, is eternal and indestructible. No one can destroy it, and it cannot be destroyed - as stated in the Gita (2.17), "No one can destroy the indestructible." Therefore, you should not grieve for any living being, as the embodied self is eternal and indestructible, and the destructible body is always changing. The word "avadhyah" has two meanings: (1) it should not be killed, and (2) it cannot be killed. Just as a cow is not to be killed, as it is a sin, the embodied self's destruction is not possible in any way. The use of the plural "sarvani bhutani" (all living beings) means that no living being should be excluded, and one should not grieve for any of them. The body is destructible, as it is always changing and being destroyed moment by moment. However, the self, which is one's own, is eternal and indestructible.

[ Verse 30 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
The eternal soul is imperishable and never undergoes destruction. If one understands this reality, then sorrow cannot occur. The special topic of this chapter is to distinguish between the eternal and the non-eternal, the existent and the non-existent, and the imperishable and the perishable. This is necessary for the practice of Karma Yoga, Jnana Yoga, Bhakti Yoga, and other yogas. Even for attaining heaven and other worlds, it is essential to understand the difference between the body and the soul. All philosophers, whether they are non-dualists or dualists, accept the distinction between the body and the soul. Here, Lord Krishna explains this distinction. He does not use philosophical terms like Atman (the eternal soul), Brahman (Supreme Consciousness), Prakriti (nature), Purusha (the absolute), Maya (illusion), and Avidya (ignorance). Instead, He uses simple words like body and soul, imperishable and perishable. One can experience the difference between the body and the soul through direct experience. The body changes, but the soul remains the same. For example, the body goes through different stages of life, such as childhood, youth, and old age, and it may become sick or recover, but the soul remains unchanged. There is a significant difference between studying philosophy and experiencing it. Studying philosophy involves acquiring knowledge about Brahman, God, the soul, nature, and the world. However, experiencing it involves realizing the distinction between the body and the soul, and understanding the imperishable and the perishable. In this chapter, Lord Krishna explains that the distinction between the body and the soul is not just a matter of philosophical knowledge but a direct experience that anyone can have. He uses simple words like body and soul to convey this idea, rather than complex philosophical terms. If one understands the distinction between the imperishable and the perishable, they can attain true knowledge. However, if one only acquires philosophical knowledge without experiencing it, they will not be able to overcome sorrow. The appendix explains that Lord Krishna has described the distinction between the body and the soul from the 11th to the 30th verse. He has not used philosophical terms like Brahman, soul, nature, and illusion, as He wants to emphasize the importance of direct experience rather than mere knowledge. In this chapter, Lord Krishna has used simple words like body and soul to explain the distinction between the imperishable and the perishable. This is because He wants to make it accessible to everyone, regardless of their philosophical background. If one applies the distinction between the imperishable and the perishable to their own body, they become a seeker of truth. However, if they apply it to the world, they become a scholar. One who applies this distinction to their own body can attain true knowledge, whereas one who applies it to the world only acquires book knowledge. Note that although the word "Purusha" is used twice in this chapter, it is not used in the philosophical sense of "Prakriti-Purusha" but rather in the sense of "human being".

Srimad Bhagavad Gita
*
[ Chapter 2 
The distinction between the body and the embodied self is useful and worth learning, and the analysis of the ultimate reality is also useful. Therefore, if the seeker wants to experience, he should first experience his separation from the body, that is, the body is devoid of physical relationships and the physical is devoid of bodily relationships, meaning "I am not the body." He should consider the existence and greatness of the body with the same sincerity, firmness, faith, and certainty with which he has considered the existence and greatness of the body, and experience the existence and greatness of the self (his true nature). The body is merely an instrument for performing actions, and actions are only for the sake of the world. Just as a writer takes up the pen when he sits down to write and puts it back in its place when he finishes writing, similarly, the seeker should accept the body while performing actions and put it back in its place when the actions are finished - he should become detached from it. Because if we do not do anything, what is the need for the body? A special thing for the seeker is to renounce the known unreal. If the seeker renounces what he knows to be unreal, his spiritual practice will become easy and will be quickly accomplished. The seeker's love for his spiritual practice is what is called his spiritual practice. This love is not obtained through any object, person, ability, or power, nor is it obtained through any practice, but it is obtained through a sense of ownership in the spiritual practice. The seeker's love for something arises spontaneously when he considers it his own. However, true ownership can only be with that which has the following four qualities:
1. With which we have a relationship of unity of nature. 2. With which our relationship is eternal. 3. From which we do not desire anything. 4. To which we can dedicate everything we have. These four things can only be found in God. Because our relationship with the body and the world is not eternal, and we do not have a unity of nature with them. How can there be unity between something that changes every moment and something that never changes? The unity we seem to have with the body is not real, but rather assumed. This assumed unity is for the purpose of fulfilling our duties. In other words, we can serve that with which we have an assumed unity, but we cannot have a sense of ownership with it. To renounce the known unreal, it is necessary for the seeker to renounce relationships that are contrary to wisdom. Considering something as one's own or for one's own sake, with which we do not have an eternal relationship or a unity of nature, is a relationship contrary to wisdom. From this perspective, considering the body as one's own or for one's own sake is contrary to wisdom. As long as a relationship contrary to wisdom exists, no spiritual practice can be successful. Even if one performs intense austerities, attains deep meditation, or travels to other worlds while maintaining a relationship with the body, one will not be able to destroy attachment or attain the true reality. As soon as one renounces relationships contrary to wisdom, attachment is destroyed and the true reality is attained. Therefore, the seeker should not rest until he has renounced relationships contrary to wisdom. If we do not renounce the body, which is a relationship contrary to wisdom, the body will eventually renounce us! What is the difficulty in renouncing that which will eventually renounce us? Therefore, any seeker, regardless of the path he follows, must accept the fact that the body is not "I", the body is not mine, and the body is not for me, because I am bodiless and my true nature is unmanifest. As long as the seeker maintains a relationship of "I" and "mine" with the body, he will not attain success even while performing spiritual practices, and he will remain bound by good deeds, meaningful thoughts, and attachment to his state. Even if he performs great good deeds like sacrifices, austerities, and charity, or contemplates the soul or the Supreme Soul, or even attains a state of deep meditation, his bondage will not be completely destroyed. This is because considering the body as one's own is the root bondage, the root defect, from which all other defects arise. If the seeker's assumed relationship with the body is completely destroyed, he will not perform bad deeds, and he will not be attached to good deeds. He will not engage in meaningless thoughts, and he will not be attached to meaningful thoughts.

[ Verse 31 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
The restlessness will cease to exist, and there will be no attachment in samadhi, stability, or the state of nirvikalpa. In this way, when the attachment to actions performed by the gross body, thoughts performed by the subtle body, and stability performed by the causal body is destroyed, one's spiritual practice will be perfected, and the truth will be realized. Therefore, the Lord has described the distinction between the body and the Self at the beginning of His teachings to completely eliminate the relationship with the body. Connection - Arjuna had grief in his mind due to the death of his relatives and the fear of sinning by killing his gurus. In other words, he was afraid of the sorrow that would come from the separation of his relatives and the fear of suffering in the afterlife due to sin. Therefore, the Lord explained the topic from the eleventh to the thirtieth verse to remove Arjuna's grief, and now He begins the next topic to remove Arjuna's fear, related to the duty of a warrior. svadhar-mam api cha-avekshya na vikam-pitum arhasi |
dharmya-ad dhi yuddha-chchhre-yo 'nyat kshatri-yasya na vidyate || 31 ||
And
svadharma (one's own duty) - the duty of a warrior
api (also)
cha (and)
avekshya (considering)
na (not)
vikam-pitum (to be perplexed)
arhasi (you should be);
dharmyat (from a righteous war)
hi (certainly)
yuddhat (than war)
kshatri-yasya (for a warrior)
anyat (other)
shre-yah (better)
na (not)
vidyate (exists)
Commentary - In the first two verses, the Lord describes the benefits of war. 'svadhar-mam api cha-avekshya na vikam-pitum arhasi' - This (the Self) is a part of the Supreme Self. When it identifies with the body, it considers its duty to be 'svadharma' (one's own duty). For example, if someone considers themselves a Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, or Shudra, their duty is to follow the rules of their respective varna. If someone considers themselves a teacher or a servant, their duty is to fulfill the responsibilities of that role. If someone considers themselves a father or a son, their duty is to fulfill the responsibilities towards their family. The Lord says that even if you consider your own duty, you should not be perplexed, because for a warrior, there is no other duty more beneficial than a righteous war. 'dharmya-ad dhi yuddha-chchhre-yo 'nyat kshatri-yasya na vidyate' - There is no other duty more beneficial for a warrior than a righteous war. This means that for a warrior, following their duty is the most important thing. Arjuna had asked the Lord to tell him what was the best course of action for him. The Lord replies that the best course of action is to follow one's own duty. Giving up one's duty is not beneficial. Therefore, Arjuna should not be perplexed and should follow his duty as a warrior. Here, the duty of a warrior is referred to as 'dharma' (duty). The specific duty of a warrior is not to be perplexed in war. Arjuna is a warrior, and therefore, his duty is to fight. Appendix - After describing the distinction between the body and the Self, the Lord now describes the fulfillment of one's duty from this verse to the thirty-eighth verse. The reason is that the principle that is obtained from the distinction between the body and the Self is the same principle that is applied to the fulfillment of one's duty. * In the eighteenth chapter (18.42-48), the duties of the four varnas are described, and the word 'dharma' is also used - 'shre-yansva-dharmo viguna-h para-dharmat svanushthita-t' (18.47). This shows that the words 'karma' (action) and 'dharma' (duty) are synonymous.

[ Chapter 2 ]
The main idea is that one can attain the same goal through the pursuit of one's own Dharma (righteous duty) as through the pursuit of knowledge. In the pursuit of knowledge, "knowing" is the main thing, and in the pursuit of one's own Dharma, "doing" is the main thing. Although knowledge is the primary thing for a human being, which is useful in both worldly and spiritual matters, for one who does not understand the distinction between the body and the self, the Lord speaks of the pursuit of one's own Dharma, so that one may experience the true nature of reality. The idea is that if a person wants to know the ultimate reality but cannot do so through the path of knowledge due to lack of sharp intellect and detachment, then they can know it through the path of action (Karma Yoga); because the experience that one gets through the path of knowledge can also be obtained through the path of action (as stated in the 4th and 5th verses of the 5th chapter of the Gita). Arjuna was a Kshatriya, so the Lord speaks of the duty of a Kshatriya in this context. Actually, the duty of a Kshatriya mentioned here is a symbol of the duties of all four varnas (classes). Therefore, the other varnas, such as Brahmins, should also understand their respective duties (as stated in the 42nd, 43rd, and 44th verses of the 18th chapter of the Gita). The term "Svadharma" (one's own Dharma) is also known by other names such as "Svabhavaja Karma" (natural action), "Sahaja Karma" (easy action), and "Svakra" (one's own action). To perform actions without selfishness, pride, and desire for reward, and to do so for the benefit of others, is one's own Dharma. The pursuit of one's own Dharma is Karma Yoga. If, by chance, a war comes to them, which is like an open door to heaven, then the Kshatriyas, who are fortunate, obtain such a war. yadṛchchhāyā chopapannam: that which has come by chance, 
svargadvāram apāvṛtam: an open door to heaven, 
[Verse 32]
[Verse 33]
sukhinaḥ kṣhatriyāḥ pārtha: O son of Pritha, the Kshatriyas who are happy, 
labhante yuddham īdṛśam: obtain such a war. Commentary: 
The phrase "yadṛchchhāyā chopapannam svargadvāram apāvṛtam" means that the war has come to them by chance, and it is like an open door to heaven. The Lord is saying to Arjuna that this war has come to you by chance, and for a Kshatriya who dies fighting bravely in this righteous war, the door to heaven is open. The phrase "sukhinaḥ kṣhatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddham īdṛśam" means that the Kshatriyas who are fortunate obtain such a war. The word "sukhinaḥ" here means those who are fortunate, and the phrase as a whole means that the Kshatriyas who are fortunate obtain such a war. The idea is that the Pandavas had played a game of dice with Duryodhana, and as a result, they had to go into exile for 12 years and then live in hiding for 1 year. After the 13th year, they would get their kingdom back. However, if they were found during their hiding, they would have to go into exile again for 12 years. The Lord is saying that the war that has come to them by chance is like an open door to heaven, and the Kshatriyas who are fortunate obtain such a war. The idea is that the happiness that comes from performing one's duty is not the same as the happiness that comes from worldly pleasures. The happiness that comes from performing one's duty is a higher kind of happiness, and those who obtain such a war are indeed fortunate. Connection: 
The next four verses describe the harm that comes from not fighting the war. athā chet tvam imam dharmyam saṅgrāmam na kariṣyasi, 
tataḥ svadharmaṁ kīrtim cha hitvā pāpam avāpsyasi. If you do not fight this righteous war, then you will abandon your duty and your reputation, and you will incur sin.

[ Verse 34-35 ]
* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
If you will not fight this righteous war, then, having abandoned your own Dharma (righteous duty), you will incur sin and lose your reputation. The word "ath" is an indeclinable word indicating a change of direction, and "chet" is an indeclinable word indicating possibility. Their meaning is that although you cannot remain without fighting, being under the control of your Kshatriya (warrior) nature, you will certainly fight (Gita - 18th chapter, 60th verse). However, if we assume that you will not fight, then you will abandon your Kshatriya Dharma (warrior duty). If, being afraid of death, you abandon your duty, what will you achieve? By abandoning your own Dharma (righteous duty), you will have to accept another's Dharma (paradharma), which will bring you sin. If you abandon the war, others will think that even a great warrior like Arjuna is a coward. All creatures will also speak of your dishonor, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death. The word "avayam" means permanent or eternal. The meaning is that even those creatures who have no relation with you, neither friendship nor enmity, will also speak of your dishonor, saying, "Look, Arjuna was so cowardly that he abandoned his Kshatriya Dharma (warrior duty)!" 
In the world's view, what is considered great, when such a person's reputation is tarnished, that dishonor is more painful than death. The reason is that in death, one's life ends, but in dishonor, one's reputation is lost due to their own actions, having deviated from Dharma (righteous duty) and duty. The word "avayam" means that the reputation and dishonor of a person who is considered great are more lasting. The meaning is that the more a person is renowned for their greatness, the more their reputation and dishonor will be lasting. The great chariot-warriors will think you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear, and you will lose their respect, even though you were previously highly esteemed by them.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle due to fear of being killed. You, who were considered great by many, will be considered insignificant by them. Those who were your admirers, such as Bhishma, Dronacharya, Kripacharya, and Shalya, will now think that you are a coward. You, who were considered a great warrior, will now be considered weak. Your enemies will speak ill of you, saying that you are a coward and that you ran away from the battle. They will say that you are not a true warrior and that you are not capable of fighting. What could be more painful than this? Your enemies, such as Duryodhana, Dushasana, and Karna, will speak ill of you and say that you are not a true warrior. They will say that you are a coward and that you ran away from the battle. You will not be able to bear their insults and you will be forced to fight. Even if you do not want to fight, you will be compelled to do so. Now, the Lord explains the benefits of fighting. [ Verse 38 ]
If you are killed in the war, you will attain heaven, and if you win, you will enjoy the kingdom of the earth. Therefore, arise, O son of Kunti, with determination, and engage in the war. The commentary explains that Arjuna had expressed his doubt about the outcome of the war, saying that they did not know whether they would emerge victorious or be defeated. Lord Krishna clarifies that if Arjuna is killed in the war, he will attain heaven, and if he wins, he will enjoy the kingdom of the earth. Thus, Arjuna has nothing to lose and everything to gain by engaging in the war. The Lord's intention is that one should not abandon their duty under any circumstances, but rather perform it with enthusiasm and dedication. By performing one's duty, one can attain success in both this world and the next. Appendix - The performance of one's duty leads to the betterment of both this world and the next. This means that by performing one's duty and avoiding that which is not one's duty, one can attain success in this world and also attain liberation. Considering gain and loss, victory and defeat, and pleasure and pain to be the same, engage in the war. You will not incur sin by doing so. The commentary explains that Arjuna was concerned that by killing his kin in the war, he would incur sin. However, Lord Krishna says that the cause of sin is not the war itself, but rather one's desires. Therefore, by renouncing one's desires and performing one's duty without attachment, one can engage in the war without incurring sin. The phrase "considering pleasure and pain to be the same" means that one should not be motivated by a desire for pleasure or a fear of pain. Rather, one should perform their duty with equanimity, without being swayed by these factors. The performance of one's duty is essential, regardless of whether one is motivated by a desire for reward or not. One who is motivated by a desire for reward shouldn't be lazy or negligent in performing their duty, and one who is not motivated by a desire for reward should still perform their duty with dedication and enthusiasm.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
One should not abstain from doing his duty, but rather perform it with enthusiasm. Even one who desires his own welfare and has a selfless attitude should perform his duty with enthusiasm. Happiness is pleasing when it comes and unpleasant when it goes, and suffering is unpleasant when it comes and pleasing when it goes. Therefore, what is good and what is bad among these? In other words, both are equal. Thus, one should perform his duty, maintaining equanimity in the face of happiness and suffering. Your engagement in any action should not be motivated by a desire for happiness, nor should you abandon an action out of fear of suffering. Your engagement and disengagement in actions should be in accordance with the scriptures (Gita - 16th chapter, 24th verse). 'Naivam papam avapsyasi' - Here, the word 'pap' refers to both sin and virtue, whose result is the attainment of heaven and hell, which is a bondage that deprives a person of his welfare and leads to repeated birth and death. The Lord says, "O Arjuna, by performing your duty in a state of equanimity, you will not be bound by sin or virtue." 
Special topic-related discussion 
From the 31st to the 38th verses, the Lord has expressed several unique ideas, such as: 
(1) If one wants to explain something to someone, the Lord teaches the art of explanation in these eight verses. For example, if one wants to explain the rules and prohibitions of duty, one should first explain the rules, then the prohibitions, and finally the rules again to conclude the explanation. The Lord has also done this, first explaining the benefits of performing one's duty in the 31st and 32nd verses, then explaining the harm of not performing one's duty in the 33rd to 36th verses, and finally explaining the benefits of performing one's duty again in the 37th and 38th verses. (2) In the first chapter, Arjuna presented his arguments from his own perspective, which the Lord has refuted in these eight verses. For example, Arjuna says, "I do not see any good in fighting" (first chapter, 31st verse), and the Lord says, "For a Kshatriya, there is no better means of attaining welfare than a righteous war" (second chapter, 31st verse). Arjuna says, "How can we be happy by fighting?" (first chapter, 37th verse), and the Lord says, "Those Kshatriyas who get such a war are indeed happy" (second chapter, 32nd verse). (3) Arjuna was insistent that giving up the terrible duty of war and living on alms would be more beneficial for him (second chapter, fifth verse), but the Lord ordered him to fight (second chapter, 38th verse). Similarly, when Udadhava desired to stay with the Lord, the Lord ordered him to go to the Uttarakhand region and perform austerities (Srimad Bhagavata, 11th skandha, 29th chapter, 41st verse). This means that one cannot attain welfare without giving up one's stubbornness, regardless of the method. (4) The Lord has elaborated on the ideas presented in the second and third verses of this chapter. For example, what was said briefly as 'anaryajushtam' is elaborated as 'dharmyad yuddhachchhreyo 'nyat', what was said as 'asvargyam' is elaborated as 'svargadvaram apavritam', and what was said as 'akirtikaram' is elaborated as 'akirtim cha api bhutanam kathayishyanti te 'vyayam'. The Lord's order to fight, 'tyaktvottishtha parantap', is repeated as 'tato yuddhaya yujyasva'. [ Chapter 2 ]

* Sadhak Sanjivani *
Appendix / Parishishta Bhaav - The Gita describes the extraordinary art of supreme truth in worldly dealings, by which a person can attain their own welfare while remaining in every situation and performing all kinds of duties prescribed by the scriptures. Other scriptures usually say that if you want to attain your own welfare, you should renounce everything and become a sage, go to a secluded place; because worldly dealings and supreme truth cannot go together. But the Gita says that you can follow the Gita's teachings while remaining in your current situation, following your own beliefs, principles, Dharma (righteous duty), sect, caste, and stage of life, and still attain welfare. The same attainment that sages and seers used to achieve by practicing austerities for years in seclusion can be achieved by following the Gita's teachings while engaging in worldly dealings. According to the Gita, performing one's duties with a sense of detachment and without desire is the key to achieving welfare. What situation can be more terrible than war? If a person can attain their welfare even in such a terrible situation, then what situation can be so bad that a person cannot attain their welfare? According to the Gita, one can attain welfare by meditating in seclusion (as described in the sixth chapter, from the tenth to the thirteenth verse) and also by performing one's duties in the world, like Arjuna did by fighting in the war. Arjuna did not desire heaven or kingdom (as mentioned in the first chapter, thirty-second, thirty-fifth, and second chapter, eighth verse). He only wanted to avoid the sin of killing his relatives (as mentioned in the first chapter, thirty-sixth, thirty-ninth, and forty-fifth verse). Therefore, the Lord is saying that if you do not desire heaven or kingdom but want to avoid sin, then perform your duty of fighting with equanimity, and you will not incur sin - "You will not incur sin." The reason for incurring sin is not the act of war itself, but rather partiality, desire, self-interest, and ego. War is your duty (Dharma). Not performing one's duty and performing undesirable actions are what lead to sin. In the previous verse, the Lord told Arjuna that if he desired to attain kingdom and heaven, he should still perform his duty. In this verse, the Lord is saying that even if Arjuna does not desire kingdom and heaven, he should still perform his duty with equanimity. The meaning is that giving up one's duty is not justified under any circumstances. Connection - In the previous verse, the Lord mentioned equanimity, and in the next two verses, He will describe its glory and instruct Arjuna to listen to it. The Lord says:
Esha te abhihita sankhye buddhiryoge tvimam shrinu |
Buddhya yukto yayaa paarth karmanbandham prahasyasi || 39 ||
Oh Paarth, this samabuddhi (equanimity) that was previously described in the context of Sankhya Yoga, now listen to it in the context of Karma Yoga, with which you will be able to transcend the bondage of karma. Explanation - The word "esha" refers to the samabuddhi mentioned in the previous verse. The description of samabuddhi has already been provided in the context of Sankhya Yoga (from the eleventh to the thirtieth verse). Now, the Lord is instructing Arjuna to listen to the same samabuddhi in the context of Karma Yoga, with which he will be able to transcend the bondage of karma. The word "tu" is used to distinguish between the two contexts. The Lord is saying that just as samabuddhi was described in the context of Sankhya Yoga, now Arjuna should listen to it in the context of Karma Yoga.

[ Chapter 2 
The meaning of saying 'imam' is that this samabuddhi (equanimity) is for the sake of loka-sangraha (welfare of the world), i.e., for maintaining the social order and leading people from the wrong path to the right path by performing actions selflessly. By performing actions for the sake of loka-sangraha, one can easily attain equanimity. With the attainment of equanimity, a karma-yogi can easily get liberated from the bondage of karma. Regarding karma-yoga, it is said that this samabuddhi is attained through karma-yoga. What is its nature? What is its glory? To explain these things, Lord Krishna has asked to listen to this buddhi (intellect) in the context of yoga. "With the intellect (buddhi) endowed with which, O Partha, you will cast off the bondage of karma" -

Arjuna had the apprehension of incurring sin by fighting the war (as mentioned in the 36th and 45th verses of the first chapter). However, according to Lord Krishna, sin is incurred only when there is viṣama-buddhi (unequal intellect, i.e., attachment or aversion) in actions. With samabuddhi, there is no sin. Just as in the world, there are many actions that are considered sinful or virtuous, but we do not incur sin or virtue by them because we have samabuddhi, i.e., we do not have any attachment or aversion towards them. Similarly, if you are endowed with samabuddhi, these actions will not bind you. In the 7th verse of this chapter, Arjuna had asked about his welfare. Therefore, Lord Krishna explains the main means of achieving welfare. First, Lord Krishna explained the means of sānkhya-yoga and emphasized the importance of performing one's duty (as mentioned in the 31st verse of the second chapter). Then, He said that by fighting with samabuddhi, one does not incur sin (as mentioned in the 38th verse of the second chapter). Now, He explains the same samabuddhi in the context of karma-yoga. A karma-yogi performs all actions for the sake of loka-sangraha - 
"Considering also the maintenance of the world, you ought to perform action" (Gita -

This (39th) verse fits perfectly after the 30th verse, and it should have come here. The reason is that this verse describes two types of nishthā (devotion). First, from the 11th to the 30th verse, the nishthā of sānkhya-yoga (equanimity) is explained, and now the nishthā of karma-yoga (equanimity) is explained. Therefore, it seems inappropriate to insert the eight verses from the 31st to the 38th here. However, the reason for inserting these eight verses here is that before explaining the samatā (equanimity) in karma-yoga, it is necessary to explain what is one's duty (kartavya) and what is not (akartavya). For Arjuna, fighting the war is his duty, and not fighting is his akartavya. Therefore, Lord Krishna explains the kartavya and akartavya in the above-mentioned eight verses (from the 31st to the 38th verses of the second chapter) and then explains the samatā. The meaning is that from the 11th to the 30th verse, the sat (real) and asat (unreal) are explained, and through this explanation, samatā is shown, i.e., sat is sat, and asat is asat; no one can change them. Then, from the 31st to the 38th verse, the kartavya and akartavya are explained, and from the 39th verse onwards, the renunciation of akartavya and the performance of kartavya, as well as the attainment of success and failure in actions and the reception and non-reception of their fruits, are explained with equanimity. Appendix - There are two divisions of karma-yoga: kartavya-vijñāna (knowledge of duty) and yoga-vijñāna (knowledge of yoga). Lord Krishna has explained kartavya-vijñāna from the 31st to the 37th verse, which describes the benefits of performing one's duty and the harm of not performing it. Now, from here to the 53rd verse, He explains yoga-vijñāna. The samatā that Lord Krishna has explained in the previous verse can be attained through both sānkhya-yoga and karma-yoga. Sānkhya-yoga is the knowledge of the body and its divisions, and the separation from the body and its divisions. Karma-yoga is the knowledge of kartavya and akartavya, and the renunciation of akartavya and the performance of kartavya. A person should attain this samatā by following either of these two paths. The reason is that with the attainment of samatā, a person gets liberated from the bondage of karma. There are two śāstras: one is the dharma-śāstra (Pūrva-mīmāṁsā), and the other is the mokṣa-śāstra (Uttara-mīmāṁsā). From the 31st to the 37th verse, the dharma-śāstra is explained, and from the 39th to the 53rd verse, the mokṣa-śāstra is explained. Dharma leads to both worldly and spiritual progress. In dharma-śāstra, the performance of one's duty is the main thing. Dharma and kartavya are the same thing. "That which leads to the attainment of abhyudaya (worldly prosperity) and niḥśreyasa (spiritual prosperity) is dharma" (Vaiśeṣika 1.3).

[ Verse 40 ]
* Sadhaka-Sanjivani *
The act of not doing what one should do is also a mistake, and doing what one should not do is also a mistake. That which brings happiness to others by sacrificing one's own desires and is beneficial to both oneself and others is called "duty" (Karma). By following one's duty, one can attain "Yoga" (union with the Supreme) naturally. Without following one's duty, a person cannot attain Yoga (Gita - 6.3). When one attains Yoga, they also attain self-realization, which is the result of both Karma Yoga and Jnana Yoga (Gita - 5.4-5). iha asya dharmasya abhikramanaashah na asti - 
In this world, the destruction of the commencement of this duty (of self-realization) does not occur. nehaabhikramanaasho'sti pratyavaayo na vidyate - 
There is no loss in commencing this duty, and there is no fear of an opposite result. swalpamapyasya dharmasya trayate mahato bhayat - 
Even a small portion of this duty protects one from great fear. Commentary:
The commencement of this duty (of self-realization) means the development of a desire to attain self-realization. This desire is the beginning of self-realization, and it is never destroyed. The reason is that the desire for a true thing is also true. The opposite result (pratyavaaya) refers to the occurrence of an undesirable outcome. In the world, the opposite result is the occurrence of inequality (vishamata), which is characterized by attachment (raga) and aversion (dvesha). This inequality leads to the cycle of birth and death. However, when a person develops self-realization, they are no longer affected by attachment and aversion, and therefore, they are not subject to the opposite result. Even a small portion of this duty (of self-realization) protects one from great fear, which is the cycle of birth and death. This self-realization is not destroyed even after enjoying the fruits of one's actions, such as wealth and prosperity. The self-realization that develops in a person's heart is permanent and cannot be destroyed at any time. For example, a person who has fallen from the path of Yoga (yogabhraasta) still retains the self-realization they had developed, and it is not destroyed. The word "iha" (in this world) indicates that only humans have the ability to develop self-realization. Other living beings are not capable of developing self-realization because they are driven by attachment and aversion. If a person performs actions with attachment and aversion, they will experience an opposite result. For example, if a person performs a ritual (yajna) with the desire to have a son, but makes a mistake in the ritual, they may experience an undesirable outcome, such as the death of a family member or the birth of a child with disabilities. However, if a person develops self-realization and performs actions without attachment and aversion, they will not experience an opposite result. The reason is that they do not have a desire for a specific outcome, and therefore, they are not subject to the opposite result. This self-realization, which is the result of Karma Yoga and Jnana Yoga, is permanent and cannot be destroyed, even after enjoying the fruits of one's actions in heaven or on earth (Gita - 6.41 and 44).

* 
Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
*
[ Chapter 2 ]
Even a little effort in this direction does not go in vain; rather, it always remains intact. One who has attained a state of equilibrium in the Supreme Self, which is eternal and unchanging, remains unaffected by the world. This is because it is the ultimate reality, always present. The term 'Dharma' (righteous duty) refers to two things: (1) performing acts of charity, building public wells, and other selfless deeds, and (2) diligently following one's duties as prescribed by the scriptures, in accordance with one's social order and stage of life. By performing these duties selflessly, one naturally develops a state of equilibrium, which is the true nature of the Self. This equilibrium is referred to as 'samatadharm' or the 'dharma of equilibrium'. Special consideration of equilibrium: 
People often believe that devotion and remembrance of God can only be achieved with a focused mind. However, according to the Bhagavad Gita, a focused mind is not the highest goal. The Gita considers equilibrium to be the highest goal. Even if other qualities are not present, if one has attained equilibrium, the Gita considers them to be perfected. On the other hand, if one possesses all other qualities but lacks equilibrium, they are not considered perfected. There are two types of equilibrium: inner equilibrium and equilibrium of one's true nature. The Supreme Self is all-pervading and perfect. One who has attained this state has achieved victory and is liberated. However, the recognition of this state is through inner equilibrium (as mentioned in the 19th verse of the 5th chapter of the Gita). Inner equilibrium means remaining unchanged in success or failure (as mentioned in the 48th verse of the 2nd chapter of the Gita). One should not be affected by praise or criticism, success or failure, gain or loss of wealth, and should not experience happiness, sorrow, joy, or grief (as mentioned in the 20th verse of the 5th chapter of the Gita). This equilibrium is never destroyed and yields only beneficial results. Any meritorious act, such as austerity, charity, pilgrimage, or vow, will eventually bear fruit and then cease. However, if even a little equilibrium is attained through these practices, it will not be destroyed and will instead bring about liberation. Therefore, equilibrium is a higher goal than mental concentration. Mental concentration can lead to the attainment of supernatural powers, but not liberation. On the other hand, the attainment of equilibrium allows one to be freed from worldly bondage (as mentioned in the 3rd verse of the 5th chapter of the Gita). Appendix: The glory of equilibrium has been described by Lord Krishna in four ways in the 39th-40th verses: 
(1) 'Karman bandham prahasyasi' - Through equilibrium, one is freed from the bondage of karma (action). (2) 'Neha abhikrama nasho'sti' - Even the initial effort towards equilibrium is never destroyed. (3) 'Pratyavayo na vidyate' - The practice of equilibrium never yields adverse results. (4) 'Svalpam api asya dharmasya trayate mahato bhayat' - Even a little practice of this dharma (equilibrium) provides great protection from the fear of birth and death. Although the first point encompasses the other three, there is a subtle difference between them. For example: 
(1) Lord Krishna first states that a person endowed with equilibrium is freed from the bondage of karma. The cause of this bondage is the association with the gunas (qualities) and their effects, which is considered a relationship with nature and its workings (as mentioned in the 21st verse of the 13th chapter of the Gita). With the attainment of equilibrium, this relationship ceases to exist, and one is freed from the bondage of karma. Just as various good and bad actions occur in the world without affecting us, because we have no connection with them, similarly, a person endowed with equilibrium has no connection with the actions performed by their body. (2) If one merely begins to cultivate equilibrium, or even develops a desire to attain it, this initial effort is never destroyed. This is because the desire for the eternal and unchanging is itself eternal and unchanging, whereas the desire for the ephemeral is also ephemeral. The desire for the ephemeral leads to destruction, but the desire for equilibrium leads to liberation - 'Jijnasur api yogasya shabda brahmativartate' (Gita 6.44). (3) The practice of equilibrium never yields adverse results. When actions are performed with a selfish motive, the results can be unfavorable. However, the practice of equilibrium always yields beneficial results.

[ Verse 40 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
If there is any flaw in the method, then the opposite result is obtained. However, if there is any mistake in the application or lack of caution in the equalized state (samatā) that has been achieved in the practice and in life, then the opposite result (bondage) does not occur. For example, if someone working for us accidentally breaks a lantern while lighting it in the dark, we get angry with them. But if our friend, who never asks for anything from us, breaks the lantern, we do not get angry; instead, we say, "Even we sometimes drop things, so it's okay if you did." Therefore, for one who performs actions with a desire for results (sakāma), the opposite result can occur, but for one who does not desire any results, the opposite result cannot occur. Even a little practice of equality (samatā) or a slight development of the sense of equality can protect one from the great fear of birth and death, i.e., it can bring about liberation. Just as a desirable action (sakāma karma) bears fruit and then disappears, a small amount of equality, once it bears fruit, does not disappear; rather, it is only used for liberation. Yajña (sacrifice), dāna (charity), tapas (austerity), and other virtuous actions, if performed with a desire for results, yield perishable fruits (such as wealth, property, and attainment of heaven), but if performed without desire for results, they yield imperishable fruits (Moksha, or liberation). Thus, these virtuous actions can have two outcomes, but equality has only one outcome - liberation. Just as a traveler who has stopped or fallen asleep on the way does not return to the starting point but continues from where they stopped, the equality that has been achieved in life is never lost. "A little of this Dharma (righteous duty) delivers one from great fear" - even a small amount of selfless (nishkāma) action is true, and great fear is false. Just as a spark of fire can burn a large amount of cotton, a small amount of selflessness can burn away great fear. As cotton, whether a small or large quantity, can be burned by a single spark, so too can a small or large amount of ignorance be burned away by a small spark of knowledge. Just as darkness cannot stand before light, so too cannot ignorance stand before knowledge. Can great fear stand before fearlessness (abhaya)? There is a story that Tvashtar performed a yajña (sacrifice) with the desire to have a son who could kill Indra. In this yajña, the sages chanted the mantra "Indrashatruṁ vīvṛdhasva" (increase the enemy of Indra). If the word "Indrashatru" is interpreted as a ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa compound (Indra's enemy), its meaning would be different from that of a bahuvrīhi compound (one whose enemy is Indra). Due to the difference in compounding, the pronunciation of the word also changes. The ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa compound "Indrashatru" would be pronounced with an udātta (high pitch) on the last syllable "tru", while the bahuvrīhi compound would be pronounced with an udātta on the first syllable "in". The sages intended to pronounce the word as a ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa compound with an udātta on the last syllable, but they actually pronounced it as a bahuvrīhi compound with an udātta on the first syllable. Due to this mistake in pronunciation, the result of the mantra was reversed, and Indra ended up killing Tvashtar's son (Vritrāsura). Therefore, it is said:

"A mantra that is defective in sound, syllable, or pronunciation does not convey its meaning; it is like a thunderbolt of speech that injures the sacrificer, as in the case of 'Indrashatru', where the mistake in pronunciation led to the opposite result." (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā)

[ Chapter 2 
[Verse 41]
Even if it is small, it is complete, and even if the fear is great, it is incomplete. A little equality is also great; because it is true, and great fear is also small (insignificant); because it is immature. What is the meaning of calling equality and desirelessness 'small'? Desirelessness is great, but in our understanding, in our experience, it has been called small because it has come a little. In reality, the understanding has become a little, not the equality. On the other hand, our vision has decreased, so there is a decrease in our vision, not in the reality. Similarly, we have given more respect to the unreal, so the unreal has not become great, but our respect has become great. Therefore, if we give more respect to the real, the real will become great, i.e., its importance will be experienced, and if we do not give respect to the unreal, the unreal will become small. In reality, whether the unreal is great or small, it has no existence - 'there is no existence of the unreal', and whether the real is great or small, its existence is always present - 'there is no non-existence of the real'. Therefore, in the Upanishads, the Supreme Reality has been called smaller than an atom and greater than the great - 'anoraniyan mahato mahiyan' (Katha 1.2.20; Shvetashvatara 3.20). Connection - In the forty-ninth verse, the Lord had said to listen to the same equanimity in yoga, and in the next verse, he explains the means of attaining that equanimity. vyavasayatmika buddhir ekeha kuranandana, 
bahushakha hy anantash ca buddhayo 'vyavasayinam 
= There is only one resolute (determined) intellect, O son of Kuru. For those who do not have a resolute intellect, their intellects are many, infinite, and have many branches. Explanation: The resolute intellect of a karma yogi is the goal (target) that one has to attain, which is the nature of the Supreme Reality. For the attainment of that Supreme Reality, the equilibrium of the mind is the means, and the attachment to the world is an obstacle to that equilibrium. The single determination to remove that attachment or to attain the Supreme Reality is called a resolute intellect. Why is the resolute intellect only one? Because in it, there is a renunciation of the desire for worldly things, which is the same whether one renounces the desire for wealth or the desire for honor and prestige. However, in the case of acceptance, there are many things; because one thing can be of many types; for example, one sweet can be of many types. Therefore, the desires for these things are also many and infinite. In the Gita, the description of the resolute intellect has come in the context of karma yoga (the present verse) and bhakti yoga (the thirtieth verse of the ninth chapter), but not in the context of jnana yoga. The reason is that in jnana yoga, the knowledge of the nature comes first, and then, as a result, the intellect becomes resolute on its own, whereas in karma yoga and bhakti yoga, the intellect is resolute first, and then the knowledge of the nature comes. Therefore, in jnana yoga, knowledge is primary, and in karma yoga and bhakti yoga, resoluteness is primary. 'Bahushakha hy anantash ca buddhayo 'vyavasayinam' - 
Those who are not resolute are the ones who have a desireful attitude, who are attached to enjoyment and accumulation. Due to desire, the intellects of such people are infinite and have many branches, i.e., even one intellect has infinite branches. For example, the desire to have a son is one intellect, and the means to fulfill that desire, such as taking medicine, chanting mantras, performing rituals, seeking the blessings of saints, etc., are the infinite branches of that intellect. Similarly, the desire to acquire wealth is one intellect, and the means to fulfill that desire, such as doing business, working, stealing, robbing, cheating, etc., are the infinite branches of that intellect. The intellect of such people does not have a resolute determination for attaining the Supreme Reality.

[ Verse 42-43 ]
* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
[Verse 43]
Appendix - The real objective is one. As long as a person does not have one objective, they have many objectives, and each objective has many branches. They have countless desires, and there are many ways to fulfill each desire. Connection - The reason why the intellect of idle people is infinite will be explained in the next three verses. Those who are not wise, who are fond of Vedic debates, say that there is nothing else, and they speak with flowery language. The self-centered, who are devoted to heaven, consider heaven as the ultimate goal, and they are attached to actions that lead to birth, karma, and the enjoyment of heavenly pleasures. Explanation - 'Kamatmanah' - They are so engrossed in desires that they become one with their desires. They do not see any difference between themselves and their desires. Their belief is that without desires, a person cannot live, and without desires, no work can be done. The self is eternal and unchanging, but desires come and go, and they increase and decrease. The self is a part of the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman), while desires are a part of the worldly illusion (Maya). Therefore, the self and desires are completely different. However, people who are engrossed in desires do not have a sense of their own true nature. 'Swargapara' - They consider heaven as the ultimate goal because it provides the best divine pleasures, and they strive day and night to attain it. The term 'Swargapara' refers to those people who have faith in the heavenly worlds described in the Vedas and scriptures. 'Vedvadaratah' - They are fond of the Vedas, but their understanding is limited to the enjoyment of worldly pleasures and the attainment of heaven. They believe that there is nothing beyond these pleasures, and they are attached to the rituals and actions that lead to them. 'Yamimam pushpitam vacham pravdanty avipashchitah' - The unwise, who lack the discernment between the real and the unreal, the eternal and the transient, speak with flowery language, describing the worldly pleasures and enjoyments. The term 'pushpitam' means that their language is like flowers and leaves, but it does not bear fruit. Only the fruit provides satisfaction, not the flowers and leaves. Their language does not provide lasting fulfillment.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
The fruit of speech, which is the enjoyment of heaven and other worlds, looks beautiful only in appearance, but it is not permanent. 'Janmakarmaphalpradam' - the speech that gives birth to fruit is the one that gives importance to worldly enjoyments, because it is the cause of future births (Gita - 13.21). -
*
[ Chapter 2 
The showy speech that describes the sakama (desire-driven) rituals for the attainment of enjoyment and wealth has many actions, i.e., it involves many methods, many actions to be performed, many materials are required, and there is also a lot of physical labor (Gita - 'Kriyavisheshabahulam bhogaiswaryagatim prati' - that showy speech, 18.24). For those who are attached to enjoyment and wealth, 
their intellect is carried away by that showy speech (and they) 
bhogaiswaryaprasaktanam: who are attached to enjoyment and wealth, 
tayapahritachetasam: whose minds are stolen away by that showy speech, 
vyavasayatmika buddhih: the intellect that is focused on the main goal, 
samadhau: in samadhi (deep meditation), 
[Verse 44]
na vidhiyate: is not possible. Commentary - Tayapahritachetasam - those whose minds are stolen away by the showy speech described in the previous verses, i.e., the speech that describes the great joy of heaven, the divine Nandana forest, the apsaras, and the nectar. 'Bhogaiswaryaprasaktanam' - the five senses (sound, touch, form, taste, and smell), physical comfort, pride, and the pursuit of fame - all these are the means of enjoying worldly pleasures. The accumulation of wealth, money, and property for the sake of these pleasures is called 'aiswarya' (wealth). Those who are attached to these pleasures and wealth are called 'bhogaiswaryaprasaktanam'. Those who are engaged in worldly pleasures and wealth are asuric (demonic) in nature. The reason is that 'asu' refers to the life force, and those who strive to maintain it are called 'asurs'. They prioritize the body and want to enjoy worldly pleasures or those of heaven. 'Vyavasayatmika buddhih samadhau na vidhiyate' - the intellect that is focused on the main goal of human life, which is to attain the Supreme Self, is not possible for those who are attached to worldly pleasures and wealth. The point is that due to the impressions of past enjoyments, the intellect becomes tainted, and as a result, one is not able to renounce the world and move towards the Supreme Self with a firm determination. Similarly, those who are attached to the enjoyment of knowledge, arts, and other worldly pursuits, and who take pride in their accomplishments, also do not have a firm determination to attain the Supreme Self. Special Note 
The all-merciful Lord has bestowed upon human beings a unique power of discernment, by which they can rise above worldly pleasures and pains, attain liberation, and serve others to win the Lord's favor. Here, the rajasik (passionate) individuals being described are those who have been called 'asuric' by the Lord in the sixteenth chapter, where it is said, 'Kamopabhogaparama etavaditi nishchitah' (16.11), 'Prasaktah kambhogeshu' (16.16), etc. Therefore, those who only desire to enjoy worldly pleasures are indeed asuric in nature.

[ Verse 45 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
The essence is that if one disregards the discriminative power bestowed by the Lord and becomes attached to perishable worldly pleasures and accumulation, it is considered animalistic. This is because even animals and birds are engrossed in pleasures. If humans also remain engrossed in pleasures like animals and birds, then what difference is there between humans and animals? Animals and birds are driven by their instincts; hence, the question of duty does not arise for them. However, human birth is solely for the purpose of performing one's duties and attaining liberation, not for indulging in pleasures. Therefore, any favorable or unfavorable circumstances that arise before humans are meant to be utilized as a means to achieve their goals, not for indulgence. Those who consider these circumstances as opportunities for indulgence lack a focused mind on the Supreme. In reality, worldly objects do not hinder one's progress toward the Supreme; rather, it is the importance attached to these objects in one's mind that creates the obstacle. The attachment to worldly objects is not as significant a hindrance as the importance one assigns to them. The primary factor in creating obstacles is one's own inclination and intention. If one attempts to attain the Supreme while still having a fondness for worldly pleasures and accumulation, they will not only fail to achieve their goal, but they will also be unable to make a firm resolve to do so. This is because where there is a desire for the Supreme, there is also a desire for worldly pleasures. As long as one has a fondness for worldly pleasures, accumulation, pride, and comfort, they cannot focus on the Supreme with determination, for their mind is preoccupied with these desires, and their energy is spent on them. Appendix - The only obstacle to one's welfare is the desire for worldly pleasures and accumulation. Just as a fish caught in a net cannot move forward, a person entangled in worldly pleasures and accumulation cannot advance toward the Supreme. Moreover, such a person cannot even make a firm resolve to attain the Supreme. One who considers the world to be real can quickly attain success through Karma Yoga. A Karma Yogi performs their duties selflessly, serving the world and doing every action solely for the benefit of others, without any desire for personal gain. They find joy in the happiness of others and are compassionate toward those who suffer. By rejoicing in the happiness of others, they do not develop a desire for worldly pleasures, and by being compassionate toward those who suffer, they do not develop a desire for accumulation. Connection - To establish a point, it is customary to present both sides of the argument before affirming it. Here, Lord Krishna intends to emphasize the importance of selflessness; therefore, after describing those who are driven by desire in the previous three verses, He now encourages selflessness in the following verse. Traigunya-vishaya vedah nistraigunyo bhava Arjuna, 
nirdvandvo nitya-sattva-stho niryoga-kshema atmavan. (4.45)

Translation: The Vedas deal with the three modes of material nature, O Arjuna. Be transcendental to these three modes, be free from the duality of life, be always fixed in truth, and never think in terms of gain or loss. Be self-controlled and balanced in mind. Explanation - Here, the term "Vedas" refers to that part of the Vedas which describes the three modes of material nature and their effects, such as the heavenly planets. "Nistraigunyo bhava" means to transcend the three modes of material nature. "Nirdvandvah" means to be free from the duality of life, such as pleasure and pain, or gain and loss. "Nitya-sattva-sthah" means to be always fixed in truth, or to be always situated in the mode of goodness. "Niryoga-kshemah" means to be free from the desire for gain or the fear of loss. "Atmavan" means to be self-controlled and balanced in mind. In essence, this verse emphasizes the importance of selflessness and detachment from worldly desires. Just as the description of glass is often used to highlight the beauty of a diamond, the description of the Vedas here is used to emphasize the importance of transcending the three modes of material nature. The true service to others can only be performed by one who has renounced all desires for worldly pleasures and accumulation. Although imitation service may also be beneficial, it is only through selfless service that one can truly achieve their goals.
