*
[ Chapter 2 
The Vedas describe the sakama bhava (desire-oriented approach), not for criticism, but to guide. The Vedas are not limited to describing the workings of the three gunas (qualities) in the world. They also describe the Supreme Being and the means to attain Him. 'Nistraigunyo bhava arjuna' - Oh Arjuna, give up the desire for the worldly objects, which are the manifestations of the three gunas, and become asamsari (above the worldly influences), i.e., rise above the world. 'Nirdvandvah' - To rise above the world, it is essential to be free from the dualities like attachment and aversion, as they are the real enemies of man, binding him to the world (Gita - 3.34). Therefore, become completely free from all dualities. Here, Lord Krishna is instructing Arjuna to be free from dualities because they lead to infatuation and entanglement in the world (Gita - 7.27). When the seeker is free from dualities, he can perform devotion with determination (Gita - 7.28). Being free from dualities, the seeker can easily liberate himself from worldly bondage (Gita - 5.3). Freedom from dualities also removes ignorance (Gita - 15.5). Moreover, being free from dualities, the seeker can perform actions without being bound by them (Gita - 4.22). In essence, the seeker's spiritual practice should be free from dualities. Another point is that if there is attachment to any object, person, etc., in the world, there will be aversion to other objects, persons, etc. - this is a rule. Such attachment and aversion will lead to neglect of the Lord, which is also a form of aversion. However, when the seeker develops love for the Lord, he will naturally become detached from the world, not with aversion, but with a sense of transcendence. The first stage of detachment is that the seeker will not have aversion to unfavorable situations, but rather indifference. After indifference comes detachment, where attachment and aversion are completely eradicated. In this process, if we examine closely, we find that in indifference, there are still remnants of attachment and aversion, but in detachment, there is a complete absence of attachment and aversion. 'Nityasattvasthah' - The means to be free from dualities is to constantly abide in the eternal, all-pervading, and perfect Supreme Being. 'Niryogksemah' - Do not even desire for yog (acquisition) and ksem (preservation), for I myself take care of the yog and ksem of those who are devoted to me (Gita - 9.22). 'Atmavam' - Be solely devoted to the Supreme Being. This devotion is what makes one steadfast. Therefore, Lord Krishna instructs Arjuna to have the sole goal of attaining the Supreme Being, being free from dualities. Appendix - 
'Nirdvandvah' - In reality, the distinction between the inert and the conscious, the existent and the non-existent, the eternal and the transient, is also a duality. Desiring yog (acquisition) and ksem (preservation) is also a duality. As long as one is caught in dualities, one cannot experience the reality that everything is the Supreme Being. For when everything is the Supreme Being, how can there be dualities like the inert and the conscious? Therefore, Lord Krishna has stated that both the immortal and the mortal, the existent and the non-existent, are His manifestations - 'Amrtam caiva mrtyus ca sad acchahamarjuna' (Gita - 9.19). Connection - The next verse will explain what happens when one becomes free from the three gunas, free from dualities, etc. 1. Having two opposing attitudes towards the same subject or object is called duality. However, when the subjects or objects are different, it is not duality, such as understanding 'prakriti' (nature) and 'purush' (the conscious being) as separate entities. Similarly, turning away from the world and towards the Lord is not duality. But having two opposing attitudes (like attachment and aversion, joy and sorrow, pleasure and pain, etc.) within the world is duality, and it is this duality that entangles man. 2. The acquisition of something not yet attained is called 'yog', and the preservation of something already attained is called 'ksem'. 3. Although this context is about karma yoga, the term 'niryogksemah' seems to imply bhakti yoga (the path of devotion). This is because Lord Krishna has instructed Arjuna to be devoted to Him at various places and has also accepted Arjuna as His devotee (4.3). Lord Krishna has also stated that He takes care of the yog and ksem of His devotees (9.22).

[ Verse 46-47 ]
* Sadhaka-Sanjivani *
As much purpose is served by a small pond when there is a large lake full of water everywhere, 
so much purpose is served by all the Vedas for a Brahmin who knows the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman). =
The purpose (of having a small pond) remains 
when there is a large lake full of water everywhere, 
i.e., there is no purpose (in having a small pond). For a Brahmin who knows the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman), 
all the Vedas have as much purpose as a small pond has when there is a large lake full of water everywhere. =
Explanation — "As much purpose is served by a small pond when there is a large lake full of water everywhere" - 
When a person gets a large, pure, and clean lake, they do not need small ponds. This is because if one washes their hands and feet in a small pond, the water becomes muddy and unfit for bathing; 
if one bathes in it, the water becomes unfit for washing clothes; and if one washes clothes in it, the water becomes unfit for drinking. However, when one gets a large lake, they can do all these things without affecting its purity and cleanliness. "So much purpose is served by all the Vedas for a Brahmin who knows the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman)" - 
Similarly, for great souls who have attained the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman), all the virtuous acts mentioned in the Vedas, 
such as sacrifices, charity, austerity, pilgrimage, and vows, become as insignificant as small ponds. This is also illustrated in the 70th verse, where it is said that a wise and great soul is like the ocean, 
which remains unaffected by the numerous pleasures that come before it. For one who knows the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman) and the essence of the Vedas and scriptures, 
such a great soul is referred to here as "Brahmin who knows the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman)". The word "so much" implies that upon attaining the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman), one becomes free from the three gunas (qualities) 
and becomes nir-dvandva (free from duality), i.e., they are not affected by attachment or aversion. They become established in the eternal essence and become free from the desire for gain or the fear of loss. They remain always devoted to the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman). There are countless worlds and countless pleasures, but if one renounces them and becomes detached, 
their significance comes to an end. Similarly, desires are endless, but if one renounces them and becomes desireless, 
their significance also comes to an end. Connection — The Lord had instructed Arjuna to listen to the concept of equal vision (sama-buddhi) in the 39th verse. Now, in the next verse, He instructs Arjuna to perform actions to attain it. You have the right to perform your duty, but never consider yourself the cause of the results of your actions. You have no claim to the results of your actions; therefore, do not be attached to them. Your right is to perform your duty, never to consider yourself the cause of the results of your actions. Do not be attached to inaction, and do not be the cause of the results of your actions.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Explanation - 'karmanyevadhikaraste' - 
You have the right to perform your duties, and in this, you are independent. The reason is that humans are meant for action. No other being, apart from humans, can perform new actions. Animals, birds, and other living beings, whether movable or immovable, cannot perform new actions. The gods have the power to perform new actions, but they only enjoy the fruits of their previous good deeds, such as yajnas and charity, and provide the means for humans to perform their duties according to the Lord's plan. However, due to being engrossed in enjoying pleasures, they do not perform new actions themselves. The beings in hell are also only experiencing the fruits of their evil deeds and cannot perform new actions. Only humans have the right to perform new actions. The Lord has given this final human birth to perform new actions in the form of service, and if one performs actions for personal gain, they will be bound, and if they do not perform actions and remain idle, they will be reborn repeatedly. Therefore, the Lord says that you only have the right to perform your duty in the form of service. The word 'karmani' is in the singular form, which means that although the duties prescribed by the scriptures may vary according to time, place, and circumstances, a person can only perform one action at a time with complete dedication. For example, as a Kshatriya, Arjuna has the duty to fight, give charity, and perform other duties, but at the time of war, he can only perform the duty of fighting, not other duties. A significant point to note is that human life has two aspects: experiencing the fruits of past actions and performing new actions. Other beings, such as animals, birds, and gods, only experience the fruits of their past actions. Therefore, the scriptures do not provide instructions for them, saying "do this and do not do that." The actions performed by animals, birds, and other beings are also a result of their past actions, and the experiences they have in their lives, whether favorable or unfavorable, are also a result of their past actions. [ Chapter 2 ]
However, human life is meant for performing new actions, which can lead to liberation. Human life has two parts: one is the experience of favorable or unfavorable circumstances due to past actions, and the other is the performance of new actions. The future is shaped according to the new actions performed. Therefore, the scriptures, the instructions of saints, and the rules of the state are only for humans, as they have the ability to perform new actions and are independent in doing so. However, they are dependent on the circumstances that arise due to their past actions. The key point is that humans are independent in performing actions but dependent on the fruits of those actions. However, by making good use of the circumstances that arise, whether favorable or unfavorable, humans can use them as a means to achieve liberation. This is because human life is meant for liberation, and both the new actions performed and the circumstances that arise due to past actions can be used for this purpose. There is a special understanding to be had here: in human life, whatever circumstances arise due to past actions, whether good or bad, can be seen as either pleasurable or painful. However, in reality, the experience of pleasure or pain is not the result of the circumstances, but rather the result of foolishness. The circumstances arise from outside, and the experience of pleasure or pain is internal. By identifying with the circumstances, one becomes the experiencer of pleasure or pain. If one does not identify with the circumstances and instead makes good use of them, they can become a means to achieve liberation. The good use of pleasurable circumstances is to serve others, and the good use of painful circumstances is to renounce the desire for pleasure. When painful circumstances arise, one should not become anxious, but rather reflect on the fact that they had previously committed sins due to the desire for pleasure, and those sins are now being destroyed in the form of painful circumstances. There are two benefits to this: the sins are being atoned for, and one is becoming purified. Another benefit is that one becomes aware of the fact that...

[ Verse 47 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
It is warned that if we commit sins for the sake of enjoying pleasures, we will continue to face painful situations. Therefore, we should not perform any action with the desire for pleasure, but rather for the benefit of all living beings. This means that for animals, birds, insects, and other species, the fruits of past actions and new actions are both in the form of enjoyment, whereas for humans, the fruits of past actions and new actions (purushartha) are both means of liberation. The phrase "ma phaleshu kada chan" means that you have no right to the fruits, i.e., you have no independence in achieving the fruits. The ordinance of the fruits is under my control. Therefore, perform your duties without desiring the fruits. If you perform actions with the desire for fruits, you will be bound - "phale sakto nibadhyate" (Gita 5.12). This is because the desire for fruits, or the tendency to enjoy, is the basis of action. When the desire for fruits is completely eliminated, the tendency to act also disappears, and when the tendency to act disappears, a person is not bound even while performing actions. In reality, a person is not as entangled in the tendency to act as they are in the desire for fruits, or the tendency to enjoy. Another point is that all actions are performed through the combination of material objects and individuals. Without this combination, one cannot perform actions; therefore, it is not honest to desire the fruits of actions performed through this combination for oneself. Hence, desiring the fruits of actions is not beneficial for humans. The statement "you have no right to the fruits" proves that humans are free and capable of either associating with the fruits or not. They are not dependent or weak in this regard. The use of the plural form "phaleshu" implies that a person performs one action but desires many fruits. For example, by performing a certain action, one desires to attain merit, gain fame in the world, be respected by people, receive wealth, and so on. The means to attain a state of desirelessness (niskama) are: 
(1) Understanding that desire leads to lack, fulfillment of desire leads to dependence, and unfulfilled desire leads to suffering. Additionally, enjoying the pleasure of fulfilled desire gives rise to new desires, and the tendency to perform new actions with desire increases. By thoroughly understanding this, desirelessness arises naturally. (2) Actions are not eternal, as they have a beginning and an end, and their fruits are also not eternal, as they are subject to union and separation. However, the Self (Atman) is eternal. Eternal nature is not benefited by transient actions and their fruits. By understanding this, desirelessness arises. Desirelessness leads to liberation from the world and the attainment of the Supreme Reality (Brahman). To be desireless in actions, a seeker should possess the virtues of discernment (viveka) and a service-oriented attitude (sevabhava), as these are essential for the proper practice of Karma Yoga. Otherwise, there will be actions, but no Yoga. This means that discernment should be primary in renouncing one's own pleasure and comfort, and a service-oriented attitude should be primary in bringing pleasure and comfort to others. The phrase "ma karma-phala-hetur bhuh" means do not be the cause of the fruits of actions. This implies that one should not have any attachment to the body, senses, mind, intellect, and other instruments of action, as attachment to these makes a person the cause of the fruits of actions. In the eleventh verse of the fifth chapter, Lord Krishna also states that one should not have any attachment to the body, mind, intellect, and senses, using the word "kevalaih". Even if one does not desire the fruits of good actions, the thought "I have done good to someone, I have benefited someone, I have brought happiness to someone" can make one the cause of the fruits of actions. This is because such thoughts create a connection with the mind, intellect, senses, and other instruments of action, which is an association with the unreal (Asat). In reality, we have no connection with the inner and outer instruments or actions, as their connection is with the collective world. Just as the tendency to enjoy (bhoktritva) is more pronounced in another person's mind, a person considers actions to be the cause of attaining God (Bhagavatprapti), knowledge (Tattvajnana), and love (Prema). However, in reality, these attainments do not depend on actions, but rather on attitude (Bhava) and understanding (Bodha). This is because the attainment of unattained objects depends on actions, but the attainment of the eternally present Reality (Brahman) does not depend on actions.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
If something benefits others, we do not consider it our own, nor do we consider ourselves the cause of it. Similarly, if our so-called body, etc., benefits someone, we should not consider ourselves the cause of it. When we do not consider ourselves the cause of any action, we will not be the cause of the fruit of that action either. 'Ma te sango 'stv akarmani' - You should not have attachment to not performing actions. Because attachment to not performing actions leads to laziness, negligence, etc. Attachment to the fruit of action binds, and similarly, laziness and negligence resulting from not performing actions also bind, as they are a kind of enjoyment, a pleasure that is Tamasic (related to darkness or ignorance) - 'Nidralasyapramadottham tattamasamudahritam' (Gita 18.39), and its result is a downward journey - 'Adho gacchanti tamasah' (Gita 14.18). In short, wherever there is attachment, it will bind - 'KaranaM gunasango 'sya sad asad yonijanmasu' (Gita 13.21). * 
[ Chapter 2 
In this verse, Lord Krishna implies that the seeker should be completely detached from all changing things, persons, objects, actions, events, circumstances, states, and gross, subtle, and causal bodies. The seeker should not have any relationship with them, not even to the slightest extent. This verse has four parts: (1) you have the right to perform actions, (2) you never have the right to the fruit, (3) do not be the cause of the fruit, and (4) do not have attachment to not performing actions. The first and fourth parts are the same, and the second and third parts are the same. The first part states the right to perform actions, and the fourth part prohibits attachment to not performing actions. The second part prohibits desire for the fruit, and the third part prohibits being the cause of the fruit. In short, having an interest in not performing actions leads to a relationship with Tamasic tendencies like laziness and negligence. Having a relationship with actions and their fruits leads to a relationship with Rajasic (related to passion) tendencies. Not having a relationship with actions, their fruits, laziness, and negligence, and instead having a relationship with the joy, light, and knowledge that comes from discernment, leads to a relationship with Sattvic (related to purity) tendencies. Having a relationship with these tendencies is the cause of birth and death. Therefore, the seeker should not have a relationship with or attachment to actions, their fruits, or the joy of renouncing them. Performing actions without having a relationship with them is Karma Yoga. We should not have any worldly or spiritual goals, such as gaining worldly benefits or achieving a high spiritual state, by performing or not performing actions. In short, even the idea that 'not performing actions will lead to worldly and spiritual progress' is an attachment to not performing actions, because the true principle is beyond performing or not performing actions. Appendix - There are two divisions: the division of action and the division of fruit. A person has the right to the division of action, not to the division of fruit. This is because a new effort (purushartha) is under human control, and the enjoyment of past actions is under the control of destiny (prarabdha). From the perspective of Karma Yoga, the means (objects, qualifications, and abilities) one has received are due to destiny, and utilizing them properly, i.e., not considering them as one's own or for one's own sake, but rather for others and for their sake, is the new effort. The main point of Karma Yoga is to protect others' rights through one's duties and to renounce one's own rights, i.e., the fruit of action. By protecting others' rights, old attachment is destroyed, and by renouncing one's own rights, new attachment is not created. Thus, the Karma Yogi becomes free from attachment. When one becomes free from attachment, one attains knowledge of the truth. This is because attachment to impermanent, unreal things is the only obstacle to attaining knowledge - 'Rago lingamabodhasya chittavyayamabhoomishu. Kutah shadvalata tasya yasyagnih kotare taroh.'
In short, the attachment or inclination of the mind towards objects, persons, and actions is a special sign of ignorance. Just as a tree with a fire in its hollow does not remain green but becomes dry, similarly, one who has the fire of attachment within cannot have peace.

* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
Connection - After ordering to perform actions in the previous verse, Lord Krishna now explains how to remain balanced while performing actions. Established in yoga, perform actions, having abandoned attachment, O Dhananjaya. Becoming equal to success and failure, balance is called yoga. Dhananjaya = O Dhananjaya! Asiddhime = in failure
karmāṇi = actions
(tū) = you
samaḥ = equal
= be equal
kuru = perform
saṅgam = attachment
= attachment
tatykṭvā = having abandoned
samatvam = balance
yogaḥ = yoga
ucyate = is called
= perform actions; (because)
= balance (is)
= yoga
= is called
Commentary - 'Having abandoned attachment' - there should be no attachment to any action, any caste, any country, any time, any event, any circumstance, any inner or outer object. Only then can you perform actions with detachment. If you get attached to any action or its result, how can you remain detached? And without detachment, how can that action lead to liberation? 'Becoming equal to success and failure' - what is the result of abandoning attachment? One becomes equal to success and failure. The completion or non-completion of an action, its result being favorable or unfavorable from a worldly perspective, receiving respect or disrespect, praise or criticism, purification of the mind or not - one should remain balanced in all these successes and failures. A karma yogi should have such balance, i.e., selflessness, that whether the action is completed or not, whether the result is achieved or not, whether one attains liberation or not, one should only perform their duty. If a seeker has not experienced detachment and balance, even then their goal is to attain balance, i.e., balance of the mind - 'then you will attain yoga' (2.53). 'Established in yoga, perform actions' - after becoming equal to success and failure, one should remain steadfast in that balance. This is what it means to be 'established in yoga'. Just as one performs a ritual at the beginning of a task, one should not think that they can perform actions without remaining in that balance. Therefore, Lord Krishna says that one should perform their duty while remaining established in balance. 'Balance is called yoga' - balance is the nature of the Supreme Self. This balance should remain in the mind at all times. Later, in the fifth chapter, nineteenth verse, Lord Krishna will say that those whose minds are established in balance have conquered the world while still alive, because Brahman is flawless and balanced; therefore, their state is that of Brahman. 'Balance is the name of yoga' - this is the definition of yoga. One should be detached and balanced. This is what will be said later in the sixth chapter, twenty-third verse. In this regard, Shankaracharya says - 
"Established in yoga, perform actions only for the sake of God, having abandoned attachment. Actions performed by a person devoid of desire for results, with a pure mind, lead to knowledge and are considered success. The opposite is failure. Perform actions, considering both success and failure to be equal. What is that yoga in which one should remain established and perform actions? It is this very balance between success and failure that is called yoga."

[ Chapter 2 ]
The union that has separation from the conjunction of sorrows is called Yoga. 'Vyasito hi sah' (9.30) and that is the seeker. These two definitions are actually the same. Just as in the disease of ringworm, there is the pleasure of itching and the pain of burning, but both are painful due to the disease, similarly, the pleasure and pain arising from the connection with the world are both actually painful. The separation from such a world is called 'duhkha-sanyoga-viyoga' (separation from the union of sorrows). Therefore, whether we call it the separation from the union of sorrows, i.e., being free from pleasure and pain, or being equal in success and failure, i.e., being equal in pleasure and pain, it is the same thing. The meaning of this verse is that one should perform actions related to the gross, subtle, and causal bodies only for the service of the world, not for oneself. By doing so, equality will be achieved. Special discussion on intellect and equality
Equality is of two types - equality as a means and equality as an end. Equality as a means is related to the inner self, and equality as an end is related to the Supreme Self. Remaining equal in success and failure, favorability and unfavorability, etc., means not having attachment and aversion in the inner self, which is equality as a means, described in the Gita. The equality as an end, which is achieved through this equality as a means, is the inherent equality, described in this chapter's 57th verse as 'Tada yogam avapsyasi'. Now, let's understand these four aspects: there is a worldly person and a seeker, a means and an end. The one whose goal is to enjoy and accumulate worldly pleasures is a worldly person. He does not have a resolute intellect, but rather an intellect with infinite desires. The intellect is of two types - resolute and irresolute. The intellect that has the goal of achieving worldly pleasures, enjoyment, comfort, honor, etc. is irresolute. The intellect that has the goal of achieving equality, saying "I will achieve equality, no matter what" is resolute (Gita, 2nd chapter, 44th verse). When such a seeker enters the practical field, he remains equal in the face of success and failure, gain and loss, favorability and unfavorability, without attachment and aversion. This equality as a means leads to the achievement of the Supreme Self - 'Ihaiva tairjitah sargo yesam samye sthitam manah' (Gita 5.19). The intellect that is resolute leads to the achievement of the Supreme Self, and the one that is irresolute is worldly. Appendix - In Patanjali's Yoga Darshan, the means of controlling the mind is called 'Yoga' - 'Yogash chittavritti-nirodah' (1.2). As a result of this Yoga, the seer attains a state of being established in his own nature - 'Tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam' (1.3). The Gita calls this result of Yoga as 'Yoga' - 'Samatvam yogah uchyate', 'Tam vidyad duhkha-sanyoga-viyogam yogasamjnitam' (6.23). This means that the Gita calls the natural state of being established in equality, having completely severed all connections with the mind, as 'Yoga'. Once established in this Yoga, i.e., equality, one never falls away from it, hence it is also called 'Nitya Yoga' (eternal Yoga). When the mind is controlled, there is a state of 'nirvikalpa' (without thoughts), but when one experiences the natural state of equality, there is 'nirvikalpa bodh' (thoughtless awareness), which is not a state, but rather the illuminator of all states and the result of all Yoga practices. States can be both with and without thoughts, but awareness is always without thoughts. Thus, the Yoga of the Gita is very different from the Yoga of Patanjali's Yoga Darshan.

* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
The authority on yoga in the Patanjali Yoga Darshana is one who is not of a dull and restless temperament, but rather of a restless temperament. However, all human beings who desire to attain the Lord are eligible for the yoga of the Gita. Moreover, a person who does not give importance to worldly enjoyment and accumulation, but rather gives importance to this yoga and desires to attain it, even such a seeker of yoga transcends the sakama karmas (actions with desire) described in the Vedas - 'jijnasur api yogasya shrutibrahmativartate' (Gita 6.44). Connection - The superiority of the same intellect, which has been described from the 39th to the 48th verse, in comparison to sakama karma, will be explained in the next verse. For action is far inferior to the yoga of intellect, O Dhananjaya. Seek refuge in the intellect, for those who are motivated by the desire for fruit are indeed miserable. buddhiyogat = the yoga of intellect (equanimity)
karma = action
duren = far superior
avaram = inferior
dhnanjaya = O Dhananjaya
buddhau = in the intellect
sharanam = refuge
anvichchha = seek
krpanah = miserable
phalahetavah = those who are motivated by the desire for fruit
The yoga of intellect and sakama karma can never be equal, just like darkness and light. There is a great difference between the two, like day and night. The reason is that the yoga of intellect leads to the attainment of the Supreme, while sakama karma leads to birth and death. Commentary - 'duren hyavaram karma buddhiyogat' - Action with a desire for fruit is far inferior to the yoga of equanimity. This is because actions are also subject to creation and destruction, and their fruits are also subject to association and dissociation. However, yoga (equanimity) is eternal and never subject to dissociation or distortion. Therefore, actions with a desire for fruit are far inferior to equanimity. 'buddhau sharanam anviccha' - Seek refuge in the intellect (equanimity). To be constantly established in equanimity is to seek refuge in it. By being established in equanimity, one experiences one's own state. 'krpanah phalahetavah' - To be motivated by the desire for fruit is indeed miserable. To be motivated by the desire for fruit means to be associated with actions, their fruits, and the means of performing them, as well as to identify oneself with the body and its instruments. Therefore, the Lord has forbidden being motivated by the desire for fruit in the 47th verse, saying 'ma karmaphalahetur bhu'. In all actions, equanimity is the highest. Without equanimity, living beings simply perform actions and experience their consequences, taking birth and death, and suffering. This is because without equanimity, actions lack the power to liberate. Equanimity is the skill in actions. If there is no equanimity in actions, then the sense of 'I' and 'mine' arises in the body, and this is animal-like intelligence. In the Bhagavata, Shukadeva Ji told King Parikshit - 'tvam tu rajan marishyati pasubuddhimimam jahi' (12.5.2), meaning "O King, give up this animal-like intelligence that you will die."
The word 'duren' means that just as light and darkness can never be equal, yoga and action can never be equal. Just as an atom is far removed from a mountain, yoga and action are far removed from each other, and their comparison is not possible. Yoga is the skill in actions - 'yogah karmasu kaushalam' (Gita 2.50). There is a distinction between action and its fruit, and the eternal essence that is beyond both is distinct from them. If this eternal essence were to become dependent on the transient fruit of action, what could be more inferior than that?

* 
Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
*
[ Chapter 2 ]
[Verse 50]
Therefore, without yoga, actions are inferior, meaningless, and obstructive - 'karmna badhyate jantu' (action binds the living being). In karma yoga, 'karma' (action) is dependent on the instrument, but 'yoga' is independent of the instrument. The attainment of yoga does not come from action, but from selfless service and renunciation. Thus, karma yoga is not action; it is a means that is independent of the instrument, i.e., it is a wisdom-based practice. If there is no emphasis on selfless service and renunciation, then it is mere action, not karma yoga. Equanimity leads to the attainment of the Supreme Reality, while actions with desires lead to birth and death. Therefore, the seeker should take refuge in equanimity and remain established in it. By being established in equanimity, one becomes fulfilled, knowing what is to be known, and attaining what is to be attained. However, one who performs actions with a selfish motive remains bound and miserable. In the Gita, three terms are used for karma yoga: buddhi (intellect), yoga, and buddhi-yoga. In karma yoga, the emphasis is not on action, but on 'yoga'. Yoga, intellect, and buddhi-yoga all have the same meaning. Karma yoga is called 'buddhi' because it emphasizes the intellect in worldly activities, and it is called 'yoga' or 'buddhi-yoga' because it emphasizes renunciation with discernment. In dhyana yoga (meditation), the mind is prominent, while in karma yoga, the intellect is prominent. In controlling the mind, there is a great distance between stability and restlessness, as the seeker tries to withdraw the mind from the world and engage it in the Supreme. Even when the mind is withdrawn from the world, the world's influence remains. It is a principle that as long as there is a notion of a second reality, the mind cannot be completely controlled. Therefore, even after attaining samadhi (a state of deep meditation), there are two states: samadhi and vyutthana (the state of being outside of samadhi). However, in karma yoga, where the intellect is prominent, discernment is primary. Discernment involves both the real and the unreal. The karma yogi uses the unreal (worldly) things as a means for selfless service, thereby easily and quickly renouncing the unreal. The mind cannot be controlled continuously; it can only be controlled at times and in solitude. However, the intellect, which is engaged in worldly activities, remains steady and firm. Connection - The previous verse mentioned taking refuge in the intellect; the next verse explains the result of taking refuge in that intellect. Buddhi-yukto jahati iha ubhe sukrtaduskrtre |
Tasmad yogaya yujyasva yogah karmasu kausalam || 50 ||
Buddhi-yuktah = one who is endowed with the intellect (of equanimity)
Iha = in this life
Jahati = renounces
Ubhe = both
Sukrtaduskrtre = good and bad deeds
Tasmad = therefore
Yogaya = to yoga
Yujyasva = engage in
Yogah = yoga
Karmasu = in actions
Kausalam = skill

Commentary - 'Buddhi-yukto jahati iha ubhe sukrtaduskrtre'
A person endowed with the intellect of equanimity renounces both good and bad deeds in this life, i.e., they are not affected by them. Just as the all-pervading Supreme Reality is not affected by good and bad deeds, similarly, one who remains established in equanimity is not affected by them (Gita, 2.38). Tasmad yogaya yujyasva, yogah karmasu kausalam
Therefore, engage in yoga, for yoga is skill in actions. Equanimity is a knowledge that enables a person to remain unaffected by the world while living in it. Just as a lotus leaf is born in water, lives in water, but remains unattached to water, similarly, a person endowed with equanimity remains unattached to the world. Good and bad deeds do not touch them; they become untouched by them. * Without yoga, both action and knowledge are meaningless, but devotion is not meaningless. This is because devotion involves a relationship with the Lord; therefore, the Lord Himself grants the devotee yoga - 'dadami buddhi-yogam tam' (Gita 10.10).

[ Verse 50 ]
* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
In reality, this Self (consciousness) is untouched by virtue and vice. It is only when a relationship is established with impermanent things like the body that virtue and vice come into play. If it does not establish a relationship with these impermanent things, it remains unattached, like the sky, and is not affected by virtue and vice. In these verses, the Lord has not defined yoga, but rather described its glory. If we interpret these verses to mean that skill in actions is yoga, what is the harm in that? If we interpret it in this way, then even the act of stealing, if done with great skill and caution, would be considered yoga. Therefore, it is not proper to interpret it in this way. The Lord says, "Therefore, strive to be in yoga," meaning, remain in a state of equilibrium. In reality, equilibrium is your true nature. Someone may say that we consider skill in performing prescribed actions to be yoga. However, this is not correct, because if you are always in a state of equilibrium, you will not be bound by the results of your actions. If you are not in a state of equilibrium, you will be bound by the results of your actions, and your state will not be one of equilibrium. Therefore, here, the meaning of "yoga is skill in actions" is not appropriate, because actions and yoga are two different things. When performing actions, if you have knowledge, you will remain in a state of equilibrium, and you will not be bound by the results of your actions. This is the experience of equilibrium that you should have. The meaning of "yogah karmasu kausalam" is that yoga, or equilibrium, is the skill in actions. This means that remaining in a state of equilibrium while performing actions, and not being affected by their success or failure, is the skill in actions. In impermanent actions, there is no other importance than yoga. Another point is that in the previous two verses, as well as in the first part of this verse, the topic is yoga, or equilibrium, and not skill. Therefore, it is also appropriate to interpret "yoga is skill in actions" in this way. Appendix - In this verse, the words "yogah karmasu kausalam" can be interpreted in two ways: 
(1) "karmasu kausalam yogah" meaning that skill in actions is yoga. (2) "karmasu yogah kausalam" meaning that yoga, or equilibrium, is the skill in actions. If we interpret it in the first way, that skill in actions is yoga, then even the act of stealing or cheating, if done with great skill and caution, would be considered yoga. However, this is not appropriate, and the topic of prohibited actions is not being discussed here. If we consider that performing good actions with skill is yoga, then the person will be bound by the results of those actions, and their state will not be one of equilibrium. Therefore, their suffering will not be eliminated. The scriptures say, "karmana badhyate jantuh" meaning that a person is bound by their actions. Therefore, the actions that naturally bind a person should be the ones that lead to liberation. This is the true skill in actions. Liberation is achieved through yoga, or equilibrium, and not through skill in actions. Yoga, or equilibrium, has no beginning or end, but actions, no matter how good they are, have a beginning and an end, and their results also have a beginning and an end. How can liberation be achieved through something that has a beginning and an end? How can the impermanent lead to the permanent? Equilibrium is the nature of the Supreme Self - "nirdosam hi samam brahm" (Gita 5.19). Therefore, the importance is of yoga, not of actions. If we consider the first interpretation to be correct, then we must also consider equilibrium and selflessness to be part of the skill in actions. If skill in actions is yoga, then what is skill? The answer would be that yoga, or equilibrium, is the skill. In this case, why not interpret "yoga is skill in actions" directly? When the word "yoga" is used in the phrase "yogah karmasu kausalam", there is no need to interpret the meaning of skill as yoga. If we consider the context, the topic is yoga, or equilibrium, and not skill in actions. [ Chapter 2 ]
[Verse 51]
Having said 'samatvam yogah uchyate' (equanimity is called Yoga), they have also explained the definition of Yoga. Therefore, in this context, Yoga is the main subject, not skill in actions. Yoga itself is the skill in actions, meaning that while performing actions, the heart remains equipoised, without attachment or aversion - this is the skill in actions. Hence, 'yogah karmasu kausalam' (Yoga is the skill in actions) - this is not the definition of Yoga, but rather the glory of Yoga. In the first half of this (50th) verse, the Lord has said that a person endowed with equanimity becomes free from both merit and demerit. If a person becomes free from both merit and demerit, then which action will be performed with skill? Therefore, being free from merit and demerit does not mean that one does not perform any action; because no human being can remain without performing any action, even for a moment (Gita - 3.5). Hence, being free from merit and demerit means being free from their consequences. In the Gita, the word 'kushal' (skill) is also used in the 10th verse of the 18th chapter. There, 'akushal karma' (unskillful action) includes actions performed with desire and prohibited by scripture, and 'kushal karma' (skillful action) includes actions performed without desire and prescribed by scripture. Unskillful and skillful actions have a beginning and an end, but Yoga has no beginning or end. It is attachment and aversion that bind, not skillful or unskillful actions. Therefore, even if actions are performed with attachment, no matter how good they may be, they are binding; because even if they lead to the attainment of the realm of Brahman, one will still have to return (Gita - 8.16). In the 10th verse of the 18th chapter of the Gita, it is said that a person who does not abandon unskillful actions with aversion and does not perform skillful actions with attachment is truly a renunciate, wise, and free from doubt, and established in their own nature. From the above explanation, it is clear that the phrase 'yogah karmasu kausalam' (Yoga is the skill in actions) should be understood as 'Yoga is the skill in actions'. The Lord also commands us to perform actions while established in Yoga - 'yogastah kuru karmani' (2.48). The meaning is that actions are not important, but rather Yoga (equanimity) is important. Therefore, Yoga is the skill in actions. Connection - Now, to confirm the previous verse, the Lord gives an example in the next verse. Karmanjam buddhiyuktah hi phalam tyaktva manishinah |
Janmabandhavinirmuktah padam gacchantyanamayam || 51 ||
= For
hi
buddhiyuktah = endowed with intellect, i.e., 
samatayuktah = endowed with equanimity
manishinah = wise
sadhak = seekers
karmanjam = resulting from action
phalam = fruit, i.e., 
tyaktva = having abandoned
janmabandha = the bond of birth
vinirmuktah = liberated
anamayam = stainless
padam = state
gacchanti = attain

Explanation - 'Karmanjam buddhiyuktah hi phalam tyaktva' - Those who are endowed with intellect, i.e., equanimity, are the ones who truly abandon the fruit of action. As it is said, "what is sown will surely grow". Similarly, if one performs an action, its consequence will surely follow. 'Manishinah' - those who are endowed with equanimity are truly wise. In the 10th verse of the 18th chapter, it is said that one who does not have aversion for unskillful actions and does not have attachment for skillful actions is a wise person (medhavi). One who performs actions without desire, will surely attain the fruit of action, but it will not be binding. Hence, the abandonment of the fruit of action means the abandonment of the desire, longing, attachment, and craving for the fruit of action. Everyone is capable of abandoning these. Action will inevitably yield its consequence. 'Janmabandhavinirmuktah' - wise seekers who are endowed with equanimity become liberated from the bond of birth. Because, when one is established in equanimity, they are free from attachment, aversion, desire, craving, and possessiveness.

[ Verse 52 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
The primary impurities are completely eliminated; therefore, the cause of rebirth is also eliminated. They, being free from impurities, become liberated from the bondage of birth and death, even though they have a body prone to impurities. When the Self (Atman) identifies with the body, it considers itself impure as well. However, when it renounces its connection with the body, it experiences its natural, impureless state. This experience of the natural, impureless state is referred to as attaining the Anamay Pad (the state of being free from diseases or impurities). The term "Anamay" means being free from diseases or impurities. A state where there is not even a slight impurity is called Anamay. Wise men, endowed with equanimity, attain this impureless state. This impureless state is also referred to as "Avyay Pad" in the fifteenth chapter, verse 5, and "Shashwat Avyay Pad" in verse 56 of the eighteenth chapter. The use of the plural form implies that all those who abide in equanimity attain the Anamay state and become liberated. Although the Gita refers to Sattva Guna as Anamay (14.6), the true Anamay (impureless state) is the Supreme Self (Atman) or the Brahman (Supreme Consciousness), which is beyond the three Gunas. Once this state is attained, one is no longer bound by the cycle of birth and death. The attainment of the Supreme Self is the cause of liberation. Appendix - The essence of this verse is that equanimity (Sama) is the key to liberation. The Gita states that the result of Sattvic actions is pure, Rajasic actions lead to suffering, and Tamasic actions result in ignorance (Gita, Chapter 14, Verse 16). A person with equanimity renounces the desire for the fruits of actions and remains unaffected by the consequences of actions. In reality, the entire world is nothing but the result of actions. When one renounces the fruits of actions, there is no longer any bondage. The term "Manishi" means a wise or intelligent person. According to the previous verse, performing actions with equanimity is the mark of intelligence (Gita 4.18). The phrase "Padam gachchanti anamayam" means attaining the impureless state. The word "Gachchanti" has three meanings: knowledge, movement, and attainment. Here, it refers to the attainment of the impureless state, which is the state of being free from birth and death. This verse establishes that Karma Yoga is an independent means of achieving liberation and attaining the Supreme Self. Through Karma Yoga, one can attain liberation from the world and realize the Supreme Self. Connection - The next two verses will explain the process of attaining the Anamay state mentioned in the previous verse. When your intellect will completely cross the ocean of delusion, then you will attain detachment from the world and the heard scriptures. (52)

* 
Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
*
[ Chapter 2 ]
Explanation - 'When the intellect crosses the mire of delusion, then it will cross' - Considering the body as 'I' and 'mine', and having attachment to relatives like mother, father, brother, sister, wife, son, and to objects and wealth, is 'delusion'. The reason is that there is no real 'I' and 'mine' in these bodies and relatives, it is just an assumption. Being pleased when favorable objects, things, or people are obtained, and being disturbed when unfavorable ones are obtained, and having unevenness, partiality, and jealousy in the world and in the family - all this is a 'mire' or a quagmire. When the intellect gets stuck in this delusion, a person becomes perplexed and unable to decide what to do. This (Atman) (the eternal soul), being conscious, considers itself attached to inert objects like the body, and assumes a relationship with them. But in reality, the things it relates to cannot stay with it forever, and it cannot stay with them either. However, due to delusion, it does not see this, and instead, it gets more and more entangled in the world by creating new relationships. Just like a traveler who sets up camp on the way and spends time in play and laughter before reaching the destination, a person gets caught up in collecting perishable objects and enjoying them, and in having attachment to individuals and family, and thus derives pleasure from them. This is the intellect getting stuck in the mire of delusion. The more intense the feeling of giving happiness to others, the more one's desire for personal happiness will be renounced. Just as a student, son, or servant has the desire to make their teacher, parents, or master happy, and their own desire for comfort and happiness is automatically mitigated, similarly, a Karma Yogi's desire to serve the world leads to the automatic renunciation of their desire for personal enjoyment. Using discrimination and reflection to renounce one's desire for enjoyment is a bit difficult. The reason is that if the discrimination and reflection are not very strong, they are effective only as long as the enjoyment is not present. When the enjoyment is present, the seeker usually gets distracted by it. However, one who has a sense of service, even when faced with the best of enjoyments, uses them for the service of others. Therefore, their desire for personal comfort and happiness is easily renounced. That's why Lord Krishna has stated that Karma Yoga is superior (5th chapter, 2nd verse), easier (5th chapter, 3rd verse), and quicker to attain perfection (5th chapter, 6th verse) compared to Sankhya Yoga. 'Then you will cross the mire of delusion, having heard and having known' - All the enjoyments that one has heard of, experienced, and thoroughly understood, are included in the term 'having known'. The enjoyments of heaven, Brahma's world, and others that can be heard of, are included in the term 'having heard'. When your intellect crosses the mire of delusion, you will develop detachment from these worldly and other-worldly enjoyments and objects. In other words, when the intellect crosses the mire of delusion, the sharp discernment of the intellect awakens, realizing that the world is constantly changing, and 'I' remain the same; therefore, how can I find peace in this world? How can my lack be alleviated? Then, one automatically develops detachment from all these objects of enjoyment. Should we just sit here, having attachment to the body and family, and thus deprive ourselves of our true well-being? We should not get stuck in these and deprive ourselves of our real progress. We should not get stuck in these, but rather, we should make a firm decision to achieve our own well-being - this is what it means to cross the mire of delusion. The reason is that with such a firm decision, the intellect will not get stuck in worldly relationships and will not get attached to the world. There are two ways to cross the mire of delusion - discrimination and service. Discrimination (described from the 11th to the 30th verse of the 2nd chapter) becomes sharp and creates a dislike for unreal objects. If the mind is filled with the desire to serve others and give them happiness, the attraction to objects is automatically reduced. Here, instead of 'having heard' and 'having known', it would have been better to say 'enjoyed' and 'to be enjoyed'. However, not saying so implies that the terms 'having heard' and 'having known' are indicative of the five objects of sense perception - sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

[ Verse 53 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
In these, listening is the most important thing for liberation from the world and worldly objects. There is no rule that detachment will occur in so many years, months, and days, but rather, the moment the intellect transcends worldly delusion, detachment from worldly objects and pleasures will occur. There is no delay in this. Where the path of knowledge and devotion are described, listening is also considered the most important. The essence is that listening is the primary aspect, whether it is about the world or the Supreme Self. The phrase "yada" and "tada" implies that when the intellect, afflicted by the contradictions of the scriptures, becomes steady, and the mind becomes unwavering in samadhi, then one will attain yoga. The verse says: 
"shrutivipratipanna te yada sthasyati nishchala, 
samadhavachala buddhistada yogam avapsyasi" 
- When your intellect, afflicted by the contradictions of the scriptures, becomes steady, and your mind becomes unwavering in samadhi, then you will attain yoga. In this context, the Lord is inspiring Arjuna to transcend the worldly delusion and the contradictions of the scriptures. Arjuna's mind is afflicted by the contradictions of the scriptures, such as whether to follow his duty as a warrior or to protect his family. The Lord is encouraging Arjuna to make his intellect steady and unwavering in the pursuit of the Supreme Self. Initially, the seeker is uncertain about whether to focus on worldly affairs or the attainment of the Supreme Self. Once they decide to dedicate themselves to the service of the world without any attachment, they begin to develop detachment and a sense of renunciation. As they progress on the path to the Supreme Self, they encounter various scriptural contradictions regarding the goal and the means to achieve it. This can make it challenging to decide which path to follow. However, when the seeker determines their inclination, faith, and eligibility through the company of the wise, or seeks refuge in the Lord, their intellect becomes steady. The essence of all scriptures and traditions is that, despite the different descriptions of the individual self, the world, and the Supreme Self, there is a consensus that the individual self should be realized, the world should be renounced, and the Supreme Self should be attained. By making this determination, the seeker's intellect becomes steady, and they can easily attain yoga, the union with the Supreme Self. The Lord is stating that the seeker's intellect should be steady and unwavering in the face of worldly and scriptural contradictions, and that their mind should be fixed on the attainment of the Supreme Self. The two types of snares are worldly and scriptural. The worldly snare is like a tangled thread, while the scriptural snare is like a tangled rope of a hundred threads. The Lord is emphasizing that the seeker's intellect should be steady and unwavering in the face of these snares, and that their mind should be fixed on the attainment of the Supreme Self, come what may.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
* 
However, when the intellect becomes stable and immovable in both of these, one experiences perpetual union with the Supreme Self. To sever one's connection with the world, the intellect must be 'immovable', as stated in the 23rd verse of the 6th chapter with the phrase 'duhkha-sanyoga-viyogam', and to establish a connection with the Supreme Self, the intellect must be 'stable', as stated in the 48th verse of the 2nd chapter with the phrase 'samatvam yogah uchyate'. [ Chapter 2 ]
The more uncertainty there is, the more delay there will be. The state of knowing is called 'yoga', meaning the actual state of being perpetually united with the Supreme Self. This actual state is so unique that it can never be separated from; it is impossible for separation to occur. In this state, words like union, separation, and yoga do not apply. The term 'yoga' is used here to describe the renunciation of assumed relationships with the unreal. In reality, this yoga refers to perpetual union. If this perpetual union is experienced through actions (service), it is called 'karmayoga'; if through discernment and reflection, it is called 'jnanayoga'; if through love, it is called 'bhaktiyoga'; if through contemplation of the dissolution of the world, it is called 'layayoga'; and if through pranayama, it is called 'hathayoga'. The attainment of yoga described in the phrase 'tada yogam avapsyasi' is not a state where there was previously separation from the Supreme Self, which is then eliminated, resulting in yoga. Rather, it is the complete separation from unreal objects that were mistakenly considered to be related. This is called 'ashtangayoga'. Appendix - There are two divisions of delusion: 'mohakalil', or worldly delusion, and 'shrutivipratipatti', or scriptural (philosophical) delusion. Worldly delusion refers to attachment to the body, wife, children, wealth, and property, while scriptural delusion refers to being entangled in philosophical debates such as dualism, non-dualism, and so on. When both of these are renounced, a person develops detachment from worldly pleasures and their intellect becomes stable. When the intellect is stable, one attains yoga, meaning the distance from the Supreme Self is eliminated, and closeness is achieved. Karmayoga leads to closeness, jnanayoga leads to non-difference, and bhaktiyoga leads to oneness. If a seeker achieves either karmayoga or jnanayoga, they will attain the fruits of both (Gita, 5th chapter, 4th-5th verses). If a person's sole intention is their own welfare and they have no self-interest in wealth, property, family, and so on, they will transcend worldly delusion. If their goal is not to study books or learn scriptural concepts, but rather to experience the truth, they will transcend scriptural delusion. In other words, a seeker should not prioritize worldly delusion or scriptural debates, meaning they should not be attached to any particular doctrine or tradition. When this happens, they become eligible for yoga, liberation, or devotion. No other special qualification is required. [ Verse 55 ]
* Sadhaka-Sanjivani *
Explanation - Arjuna had asked questions about the characteristics of a person with stable wisdom (Sthitaprajna). Before asking these questions, Arjuna had doubts about action (Karma) and intellect (Buddhi) from the 47th to the 50th verse of the second chapter. However, Lord Krishna said in the 52nd and 53rd verses that when your intellect transcends the darkness of ignorance and the contradictions of the scriptures, you will attain Yoga. Hearing this, Arjuna wondered what his characteristics would be when he attains Yoga and becomes a Sthitaprajna. Therefore, Arjuna asked about his personal doubts first and later asked about the doctrine (Siddhanta) related to action and intellect in the first and second verses of the third chapter. If Arjuna had asked about the doctrine here in the 54th verse, he would have missed the opportunity to ask about the Sthitaprajna. The word "Samadhisthasya" refers to a person who has attained the Supreme Self (Paramatma). The term "Sthitaprajnasys" refers to both the seeker (Sadhaka) and the perfected one (Siddha). A seeker who is firm in their resolve and never deviates from their spiritual practice is also called Sthitaprajna, and a perfected one whose intellect is stable due to the experience of the Supreme Self is also called Sthitaprajna. Therefore, the term "Sthitaprajna" here refers to both the seeker and the perfected one. Earlier, from the 41st to the 45th verse and from the 47th to the 53rd verse, the characteristics of the seekers were described; hence, in the following verses, the characteristics of both the seekers and the perfected ones are described. Here, a doubt arises that Arjuna had asked about the perfected Sthitaprajna using the term "Samadhisthasya," but Lord Krishna explained that a seeker of Jnana Yoga (the path of knowledge) usually becomes detached from actions even during their spiritual practice, and in the state of perfection, they become even more detached. A seeker of Bhakti Yoga (the path of devotion) also has a tendency to perform devotional actions like chanting, meditation, and self-study during their spiritual practice, and these actions increase in the state of perfection. Similarly, a seeker of Karma Yoga (the path of action) does not experience a difference between their spiritual practice and the state of perfection, as their actions continue uninterrupted. This is because their actions during spiritual practice are the primary cause of their attainment of Yoga. Therefore, Lord Krishna described both the characteristics of the perfected ones and the means for the seekers to attain perfection. The question arises, what language does a person with stable wisdom (Sthitaprajna) use, i.e., what are their characteristics? (The answer is given by Lord Krishna in the following verses.) What does a person with stable wisdom say? (The answer is given by Lord Krishna in the 56th and 57th verses.) How does a person with stable wisdom sit, i.e., how do they become detached from the world? (The answer is given by Lord Krishna from the 58th to the 63rd verse.) How does a person with stable wisdom walk, i.e., how do they behave? (The answer is given by Lord Krishna from the 64th to the 71st verse.)

Connection - Now, Lord Krishna answers Arjuna's first question in the following verse. The Supreme Lord said:
When one gives up all desires that arise from the mind, and being satisfied in the Self by the Self, they are called a person with stable wisdom (Sthitaprajna). (55)

1. Here, the term "Samadhi" refers to the Supreme Self (Paramatma), which was also mentioned in the 44th verse as "Samadhi."
2. "Kaya bhashaya" means "what language does one use?" or "what does one say?"

Jis sadhan (karmyog, bhaktiyog aadi) ke dwara siddh 
Hota usi sadhan se uski poornata ka varnan kiya jata hai. Jaise, bhaktiyog mein sadhak Bhagwan ke siway aur kuchh hai hi nahin—aise ananya-yog se upasana karta hai (barahwan adhyay ka chhatha shlok); atah siddhavastha mein vah sam-purn praniyon mein dwesh-bhav se rahit ho jata hai (barahwan adhyay ka terahwan shlok). Jnanayog mein sadhak swayen ko gunon se sarvatha asambaddh evam nirlipat dekhta hai (chaudhwan adhyay ka unniswan shlok); atah siddhavastha mein vah sam-purn gunon se sarvatha atit ho jata hai (chaudhwan adhyay ke baiaswan se pachiswan shlok tak). Aise hi karmyog mein kaman ka tyag ki baat mukhya kahi gayi hai; atah siddhavastha mein vah sam-purn kamanon ka tyag kar deta hai—yeh baat is shlok mein batati hain.]

'Prajahati yada kaman sarvan Partha manogatan' – In padon ka tatparya yeh hua ki kaman na toh swayam mein hai aur na man mein hi hai. Kaman toh aane-jane wali hai aur swayam niranter rahne wala hai; atah swayam mein kaman kaise ho sakti hai? Man ek karana hai aur usmein bhi kaman niranter nahin rehti, pratyut usmein aati hai - 'manogatan'; atah man mein bhi kaman kaise ho sakti hai? Parantu sharir - indriyan - man - buddhi se tadatmya hone ke karan manushya man mein aane wali kamanon ko apne mein maan leta hai. 'Jahati' kriya ke sath 'pra' upasarg dena ka tatparya hai ki sadhak kamanon ka sarvatha tyag kar deta hai, kisi bhi kaman ka koi bhi ansh kinchit matra bhi nahin rehta. Apne swarup ka kabhi tyag nahin hota aur jisse apna kuchh bhi sambandh nahin hai, uska bhi tyag nahin hota. Tyag usi ka hota hai, jo apna nahin hai, par usko apna maan liya hai. Aise hi kaman apne mein nahin hai, par usko apne mein maan liya hai. Is manyata ka tyag karne ko yahan 'prajahati' pad se kaha gaya hai. Sthitaprajnah
Uchyate
San-tusht rehta hai,

jata hai. Yahan 'kaman' shabd mein bahuvachan hone se 'sarvan' pad usi ke antargat aa jata hai, fir bhi 'sarvan' pad dena ka tatparya hai ki koi bhi kaman na rahe aur kisi bhi kaman ka koi bhi ansh baki na rahe. 'Aatmany eva aatmana tushtah' - Jis kalmen sam-purn kamanon ka tyag kar deta hai aur apne-aap se apne-aap mein hi san-tusht rehta hai arthat apne-aap mein sahaj swabhavik san-tosh hota hai. San-tosh do tarah ka hota hai - Ek san-tosh gun hai aur ek san-tosh swarup hai. Antah-karan mein kisi prakar ki koi bhi ichha na ho – yeh san-tosh gun hai aur swayam mein asan-tosh ka atyant abhav hai - yeh san-tosh swarup hai. Yeh swarup-bhut san-tosh swatah sarvada rehta hai. Iske liye koi abhyas ya vichar nahin karna padta. Swarup-bhut san-tosh mein prajna (buddhi) swatah sthir rehti hai. 'Sthitaprajnah tadochyate' - Swayam jab bahushakhaon wali anant kamanon ko apne mein maanta tha, us samay bhi vastav mein kamanayein apne mein nahin thin aur swayam sthitaprajnah hi tha. Parantu us samay apne mein kamanayein maan ne ke karan buddhi sthir na hone se vah sthitaprajnah nahin kaha jata tha arthat usko apni sthitaprajnata ka anubhav nahin hota tha. Ab usne apne se sam-purn kamanon ka tyag kar diya arthat unki manyata ko hata diya, tab vah sthitaprajnah kaha jata hai arthat usko apni sthitaprajnata ka anubhav ho jata hai. Sadhak to buddhi ko sthir banata hai. Parantu kamanon ka sarvatha tyag hone par buddhi ko sthir banana nahin padta, vah swatah - swabhavik sthir ho jati hai. Karmyog mein sadhak ka karmo se jyada sambandh rehta hai. Uske liye yog mein aarudh hone mein bhi karm kaaran hain - 'Aarurukshor muney yogam karm kaaranam uchyate' (Gita 6.3). Isliye karmyogi ka karmo ke sath sambandh sadhak-avastha mein bhi rehta hai aur siddhavastha mein bhi. Siddhavastha mein

[ Verse 55 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
The Karma Yogi performs actions according to the norms, renounces the world, and becomes an ideal for others, as stated in the 21st verse of the 3rd chapter of the Gita. Lord Krishna has also said in the 4th chapter that the Karma Yogi remains unattached while performing actions and performs actions while remaining unattached - "He who sees inaction in action and action in inaction" (4.18). In the 57th verse, Lord Krishna mentioned two aspects of the intellect for attaining Yoga: the intellect should be unwavering in renouncing the world and firm in devotion to the Supreme Self. The same two aspects are being discussed here using the words "yada" and "tada", stating that when the seeker is completely free from desires and remains satisfied in their own self, they are called "Sthitprajna". This means that as long as there is a trace of desire, one is called a seeker, and when all desires are completely eliminated, one is called "Siddha". Lord Krishna has described these two aspects from the beginning of this chapter to the end, such as stating the renunciation of the world with the words "prajahati yada kaman sarvan" and the establishment in the Supreme Self with the words "atmany evatmana tushtah" in the first part of the 56th verse. In the 57th and 58th verses, the renunciation of the world is described first, followed by the establishment in the Supreme Self with the words "tasya prajna pratishtita". In the first part of the 59th verse, the renunciation of the world is described, and with the words "param drishtva", the establishment in the Supreme Self is described. From the 60th to the 61st verse, the renunciation of the world is described first, followed by the establishment in the Supreme Self with the words "yukta asita matparah". From the 62nd to the 65th verse, the renunciation of the world is described first, followed by the establishment in the Supreme Self with the words "buddhih paryavatishthate". From the 66th to the 68th verse, the renunciation of the world is described, and then the establishment in the Supreme Self is described with the words "tasya prajna pratishtita". In the 69th verse, the renunciation of the world is described with the words "ya nisa sarvabhutanam" and "yasyam jagrati bhutan", and the establishment in the Supreme Self is described with the words "tasyam jagarti sanyami" and "sa nisa pasyato muneh". In the 70th and 71st verses, the renunciation of the world is described first, followed by the establishment in the Supreme Self with the words "sa santim adhigacchati". In the 72nd verse, the renunciation of the world is described with the words "nainam prapya vimuhya", and the establishment in the Supreme Self is described with the words "brahmanirvanam ricchati". Appendix - There are two categories: one with unstable intellect and the other with stable intellect. The topic of those with unstable intellect was discussed from the 41st to the 44th verse, and now the topic of those with stable intellect is being discussed from the 55th to the 71st verse. When the seeker renounces worldly desires and remains established in their own self, they are called one with a stable intellect. One who has the goal of the Supreme Self has a resolute intellect, as the Supreme Self is one. However, one who has the goal of the world has an intellect with countless desires, as worldly objects are countless (Gita - 2nd chapter, 41st verse). For attaining equanimity, the stability of the intellect is very essential. In the Patanjala Yoga Darshana, the stability of the mind (vritti-nirodha) is given importance, but the Gita gives importance to the stability of the intellect (uddeshya-ki-dridhata). The reason is that the stability of the mind is not as important for attaining liberation as the stability of the intellect. The stability of the mind leads to worldly accomplishments, while the stability of the intellect leads to spiritual accomplishment (liberation). In Karma Yoga, the stability of the intellect is the main thing. If the mind is stable, how can the Karma Yogi perform their duties? The reason is that when the mind is stable, external actions cease. Lord Krishna also instructs to perform actions while established in Yoga (equanimity) - "Yogastah kuru karmani" (2.48). The purpose of using the words "prajahati" and "kaman sarvan" is that not even a trace of desire should remain, but rather a complete renunciation should take place. The reason is that desire is a major obstacle to attaining the Supreme Self. Connection - Now, in the next two verses, the answer to the second question, "How does the Sthitprajna speak?" will be given.

= Is called a sage. Explanation - [Arjuna had asked, 'How does a person of steady wisdom speak?' The question was raised with the importance of action, but the Lord answers with the importance of emotions, saying 'devoid of attachment, fear, and anger'. This is because the world's objects have an effect on the mind, which is called attachment. Emotions are primary in actions. If a strong person destroys those objects, fear arises in the mind. If that person is weak, anger arises. However, one who has the emotion of doing good to others, serving them, and benefiting them, has no attachment, fear, or anger. 'Duḥkheṣvanudvignamānāḥ' - One who is not disturbed by the attainment of sorrows, i.e., when performing duties, the primary duty is to do good to others, to perform actions without any attachment, ego, or desire - being cautious in this matter. By doing so, a sense of satisfaction remains in the mind. Due to this satisfaction, even if many adversities arise, the mind remains undisturbed. 'Sukheṣu vigataspṛhāḥ' - One who has no desire even when happiness is attained, i.e., when actions are performed, and immediate respect and praise are received, and favorable results are obtained, there is no desire for the situation to remain the same or to always receive favorable results. As long as there is some disturbance, desire, attachment, fear, or anger, one is a seeker. When one is completely free from these, they become accomplished. [Desire, attachment, and other emotions are all forms of attachment. They have different names due to varying degrees of attachment. The attachment that remains hidden in the mind is called 'desire'. Another name for this desire is 'attachment' and 'love'. The desire for an object is called 'desire'. The possibility of fulfilling a desire is called 'hope'. When a desire is fulfilled, and there is a desire for more objects or an increase in objects, it is called 'greed'. An increase in greed is called 'craving'. The point is that the attraction to ephemeral objects is called 'craving'. * In the Gita, wherever Arjuna has asked questions with the importance of action, the Lord has answered with the importance of emotions and knowledge. This is because emotions and knowledge are primary in actions. Actions occur according to emotions and knowledge. For example, Arjuna asked in the fourteenth chapter what the conduct of a person beyond the three gunas is like. The Lord answered, emphasizing the importance of emotions, that their conduct is equal in all situations. [ Chapter 2 ] 
A person of steady wisdom is one who is not disturbed by sorrows and is free from desires in happiness, one who is devoid of attachment, fear, and anger, and is steadfast. Karpanya-dosha-upahata-svabhavah: a heart afflicted by cowardice. Dharmasya glanir: the decline of righteousness. Sthitaprajna: one with steady wisdom. [ Verse 57 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
The best and most important thing is the intellect, which is not affected by desires, cravings, etc., as stated in the 17th chapter, 16th verse. -
'Sthitadhirmunirucyate' - The intellect of such a contemplative Karma Yogi becomes stable and unwavering. The word 'muni' refers to one who has control over their speech. However, the word 'muni' is not limited to just control over speech. In the 17th chapter, the word 'maun' (silence) is used to describe mental austerity. The term 'muni' is used here to describe a contemplative Karma Yogi because the context is about Karma Yoga. Contemplation means being mindful and cautious, so that no desires or attachments arise in the mind. Constantly remaining unattached is the caution of a perfected Karma Yogi, as stated in the 3rd chapter, 19th verse of the Gita. He who is unattached everywhere, 
- who meets with good or bad fortune 
- does not rejoice or hate; 
his intellect is well-established. =
=
=
=
=
A person who is unattached everywhere 
- meets with good or bad fortune 
- does not rejoice or hate; 
his intellect is well-established. Commentary - [In the previous verse, Lord Krishna explained how to remain unattached while performing one's duties. In this verse, He explains how to remain unattached in favorable or unfavorable circumstances that arise due to one's actions.]
'Yah sarvatra anabhisnehah' - One who is unattached everywhere, meaning one who has no attachment to their body, senses, mind, intellect, wife, children, home, wealth, etc. The attachment that arises due to the existence of these things, thinking "I exist because they exist, and I will cease to exist if they cease to exist" - this is called 'abhisneh'. A stabilized Karma Yogi has no such attachment to any object or person. Even when they are surrounded by external objects or people, they remain internally unattached. 'Tat tat prapya shubhashubham na abhinandati na dveshti' - When such a person encounters favorable or unfavorable circumstances, they do not rejoice or hate. They do not become elated when faced with favorable circumstances, nor do they become dejected when faced with unfavorable ones. The elation that arises in the mind and is expressed through words and external celebrations is called 'abhinandan' (rejoicing). Similarly, the dejection that arises in the mind and is expressed through words and actions is called 'dvesh' (hate). A person who is unattached everywhere does not rejoice or hate in such circumstances. 'Tat, tat' refers to the various favorable and unfavorable objects, people, events, and circumstances that can cause disturbances in a person. Even when these circumstances arise, the person who is unattached everywhere does not rejoice or hate. 'Tasya prajna pratishtita' - Their intellect is well-established, stable, and unwavering. The intellect that was previously engaged in worldly activities is now firmly established in the Supreme Self. The person has realized that they have no real connection with the good or bad things of the world.

[ Chapter 2 
The circumstances are changing, but my nature is not changing. Why not? Because with the changing, the unchanging also exists; therefore, how can there be a relationship between the changing and the unchanging? In reality, if we look, there is no difference in the nature, nor in the body, senses, mind, and intellect. The reason is that the nature that is ours never changes, and the material nature and its effects, such as the body, are always changing. So where is the difference? The difference occurs in the intellect due to identification with the body. When this identification is removed, the difference that occurred in the intellect is also removed, and the intellect becomes established. No matter how much one thinks, one cannot bring the Supreme (Paramatma) within the range of the intellect. The reason is that the intellect is limited, and the Supreme is unlimited and infinite. However, when the intellect becomes absorbed in that unlimited Supreme, then in that limited intellect, there is no other existence except the Supreme - this is the establishment of the intellect in the Supreme. -
[Verse 58]
A Karma Yogi is active. Therefore, in the fifty-sixth verse, the Lord has spoken about being devoid of desire and agitation in the success or failure of actions, and in this verse, He speaks about obtaining favorable or unfavorable circumstances according to one's destiny. Another idea is that no matter how sharp someone's intellect may be, it is necessary to be free from praise and dislike. Connection - Now, from the next verse, the Lord begins to answer the third question, "How does a Sthitaprajna (one with established intellect) sit?"
As,
the tortoise
withdraws
its limbs
completely,
when
it withdraws,
its limbs,
the intellect of that person becomes established, having withdrawn the senses from the sense objects. = In the same way,
this (Karma Yogi)
withdraws
the senses
from the sense objects
completely,
when
he withdraws,
his intellect becomes established. Commentary - The example of the tortoise is given to illustrate that just as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs - four legs, one tail, and one head - when it moves, and only its back is visible when it withdraws them. Similarly, a Sthitaprajna withdraws the five senses and the mind - these six - from their respective objects. If he still has any mental connection with the senses, etc., he is not a Sthitaprajna. "Pratishthita" - Here, the meaning is that the experience that occurs when the senses are completely withdrawn from their objects is not bound by time or limited by time. The reason is that this experience is not the result of any action or renunciation. It is not a produced thing. Therefore, there is no need to use the word "tada" (then) here, which indicates time. The need for "tada" arises when one thing is dependent on another. For example, when the sun is in the sky, even if we close our eyes, the sun is not visible, and when we open our eyes, the sun becomes visible. Here, there is no relationship of cause and effect between the sun and the eyes, meaning that the sun is not produced by opening the eyes. The sun was already there, and it remains the same whether the eyes are open or closed. We just didn't experience it when our eyes were closed. Similarly, here, the experience of the Self (Atman) that occurs when the senses are withdrawn from their objects is not an object of the mind and senses. The meaning is that this Self is self-evident and not dependent on the mind and senses. The use of the word "sanharate" (withdraws) here means that the Sthitaprajna withdraws the senses from their objects, meaning he does not even think about them with his mind. In this verse, the word "yada" (when) is used, but not "tada" (then). Although according to "yattador nitya sambandhah," where "yada" is used, "tada" is implied, yet here the use of "tada" is not made. However, there is a deep meaning in not using "tada" here.
