* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
The connection with the objects of enjoyment remains, and due to this connection, the experience of the Self is not obtained. Even while enjoying the objects, the experience remains the same. However, as soon as the veil of connection with the objects is removed, the experience is obtained. Connection—Merely withdrawing the senses from the objects is not the characteristic of a sthitaprajna (one who is established in the Self). This will be explained in the next verse. The objects of enjoyment withdraw from one who has controlled the senses, but the taste (or attachment) for them does not withdraw. However, upon seeing the Supreme, even the taste for them withdraws. Niraharasya = one who has controlled the senses (i.e., one who has withdrawn the senses from the objects of enjoyment)
Rasvarjam = devoid of taste (or attachment)
Rasah = taste (or attachment)
Api = also
Asya = of this person
Param = the Supreme
Drshtva = upon seeing
Nivartate = withdraws
Vishayaha = the objects of enjoyment
Vinivartante = withdraw
Drshtva = upon seeing
Anubhav ho jana = the experience is obtained
This verse is for those sadhakas (aspirants) who are engaged in contemplation and have withdrawn their senses from the objects of enjoyment. It is said that even after withdrawing from the objects of enjoyment, the taste (or attachment) for them does not withdraw. The taste (or attachment) of this sthitapragna (one who is established in the Self) withdraws upon experiencing the Supreme. This is for the sadhakas who have withdrawn their senses from the objects of enjoyment. The withdrawal of taste (or attachment) leads to the state of sthitaprajna. The word "niraharasya" indicates that the person has controlled the senses. However, this is not a rule. The rule is that the taste (or attachment) withdraws after attaining the state of sthitaprajna. A patient thinks, "What can I do? I am not capable of enjoying objects due to my illness, but when I recover, I will enjoy them." In this way, the taste (or attachment) remains within. Similarly, when the senses are withdrawn from the objects of enjoyment, the objects may withdraw, but the taste (or attachment) for them does not withdraw quickly. The word "raso'pyasya" indicates that the taste (or attachment) remains in the ego (ahamkara) of the sadhaka. This taste (or attachment) takes the form of intense attachment (raga). Therefore, the sadhaka should remove the taste (or attachment) from their ego by thinking, "I am niskama (without desire); it is not my duty to have attachment or desire."
In this way, the taste (or attachment) withdraws, and the experience of the Supreme is obtained. For those sadhakas who are naturally detached from the objects of enjoyment and have intense vairagya (dispassion), the taste (or attachment) withdraws during the state of sadhana (spiritual practice). Appendix—The concept of "ras" (taste or attachment) arises from considering the objects of enjoyment as real and important. This creates a subtle attraction, fondness, or sweetness in the mind. When a greedy person receives money or a lustful person meets a woman, they feel a inner joy, which is the "ras". After enjoying the objects, a person says, "It was great fun," which is a memory of the "ras". This "ras" resides in the ego (ahamkara). The gross form of "ras" is attachment (raga) or pleasure (sukha). As long as the taste (or attachment) remains for the enjoyment of objects, one remains bound to the objects and their creator (prakriti). When the taste (or attachment) withdraws, the bondage is completely removed, and one is no longer enslaved by the pleasure of objects.

* 
Srimad Bhagavad Gita
* 
[ Chapter 2 ]
As long as there is even a slight presence of worldly pleasures and their importance in the mind, and as long as there is a taste for them, the divine taste of the Supreme Self (Paramatman) does not manifest. Not to mention the divine taste of the Supreme Self, there is not even a determination to attain the Supreme Self (Gita - 2.44). Even when the senses are withdrawn from their objects, i.e., when worldly pleasures are renounced, the taste for them remains within. This taste is eradicated and subsides when one gains knowledge of the ultimate reality (Tattva) - 'param drishtva nivartate'. This means that when one experiences their distinction from the world and their non-difference from the Supreme Self, the transient (samyogaja) taste subsides. With the subsidence of the transient taste, the imperishable (akhand) taste awakens. When one gains knowledge of the ultimate reality, the taste is completely eradicated. However, even before gaining this knowledge, the taste can be subdued through neglect, reflection, good company, and the grace of saints. The taste can also subside through the company of great souls whose taste has already been subdued. The imperishable taste can be subdued through the three means of Karma Yoga, Jnana Yoga, and Bhakti Yoga. As one progresses in Karma Yoga, the taste for service; in Jnana Yoga, the taste for experiencing the ultimate reality; and in Bhakti Yoga, the taste for love, increases, the transient taste automatically subsides. Just as in childhood, one finds joy in toys, but as one grows up and finds joy in money, the joy in toys automatically subsides. Similarly, when one finds joy in spiritual practices, the joy in worldly pleasures automatically subsides. When one experiences the taste for worldly pleasures and obtains them, their mind becomes infatuated and they become enslaved by these pleasures. However, after the taste has subsided, even when one obtains worldly pleasures, the mind of a great soul who has gained knowledge of the ultimate reality remains unaffected (Gita 2.70). No impure thoughts arise within them that could attract them to worldly pleasures. For instance, if a bag of money is placed before an animal, it does not arouse any greed, and if a beautiful woman is seen, it does not arouse any lust. The animal is unaware of money and women, but a great soul who has gained knowledge of the ultimate reality is aware of both and yet remains unaffected (Gita 2.69). Just as when we scratch our body with our finger, the itch subsides without any effect on the finger, similarly, when a great soul indulges in worldly pleasures through their senses, their mind remains unaffected and free from impurities. This is because, with the subsidence of the taste, they do not engage in worldly pleasures for their own enjoyment. All their actions are for the benefit and happiness of others. Even thinking about worldly pleasures for one's own enjoyment leads to downfall (Gita 2.62-63), and indulging in them for one's own enjoyment is binding (Gita 2.64-65). The transient taste is fleeting and does not last long. The joy that arises when one obtains worldly pleasures like women or money does not last. The joy that arises when one eats food decreases with each bite and eventually disappears, leaving one with a dislike for food. However, the imperishable taste never decreases and remains constant. Indulging in the transient taste leads to various impurities like dullness, absence, sorrow, disease, fear, and anxiety. One who indulges in worldly pleasures cannot escape these impurities, as they are the inevitable consequences of such actions. Therefore, the Lord has advised us to contemplate on the miseries of worldly life - 'duhkha-dosha-anudarshanam' (Gita 13.8). Only when one is free from the impurities of lust and other desires can they engage in actions that lead to their welfare (Gita 16.21-22). Connection - What is the consequence if the taste is not subdued? This will be explained in the next verse. [ Verse 60 ]
Even a wise person, O son of Kunti, has their mind forcibly stolen away by the senses, which are like a group of robbers.

Oh Kunti's son, the senses (indriyani) of a person (purushasya), even of a wise and learned one (vipashchitah), are so powerful (pramathini) that they forcibly (prabhavam) seize his mind (manah) while he is making efforts (yatatah) to control them. Commentary - The senses of even a wise and learned person, who is making efforts to control them, can forcibly seize his mind and drag it towards worldly objects. This is because as long as the intellect (buddhi) is not fully established in the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman), the senses, which are related to worldly objects, can overpower the mind. Many examples can be cited of even great sages who were distracted by worldly objects. Therefore, a seeker (sadhak) should never be confident that his senses are under control and should never be proud of being a conqueror of his senses. A person who makes efforts (yatatah) to control his senses, performs his duties (karma) with discernment (vivek), and is free from attachment (asakti) and desire for fruits (phalechchha), and who has the well-being of others in mind, can still be overpowered by his senses. This is because the senses are so powerful that they can drag even a wise and learned person towards worldly objects. Connection - In the previous verse, it was stated that even a wise and learned person's senses can seize his mind while he is making efforts to control them, due to the presence of attachment to worldly objects (rasabuddhi). The question arises as to how to overcome this attachment. The answer will be provided in the next verse. One who has controlled all his senses (tani sarvani sanyamya) and is united with Me (matparah), with his intellect (prajna) firmly established (pratishthita), should sit in a balanced state (yuktah). For one who has his senses under control (vase hi yasyendriyani), his intellect is firmly established. Commentary - The verse states that one who has controlled all his senses and is united with the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman), with his intellect firmly established, should sit in a balanced state. This means that when a seeker controls his senses, he should not be proud of his achievement, but rather should remain humble and united with the Supreme Consciousness. Note - Here, Lord Krishna has described the senses as "pramathini" (powerful), and in the 34th verse of the 6th chapter, Arjuna has described the mind as "pramathi" (powerful). This indicates that both the senses and the mind are powerful and can distract a person. Therefore, a seeker should control both the senses and the mind to become a true conqueror. Quote from Manu Smriti (2.215) - "One should not sit alone with his mother, daughter, or sister, for a strong group of senses can overpower even a wise person."

Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
The Lord gives the hands. Therefore, the seeker should never be proud of his own strength in controlling the senses, nor should he consider his own effort as the cause. Rather, he should consider only the Lord's grace as the cause, thinking, "The success I have achieved in controlling the senses is due to the Lord's grace alone." In this way, by being devoted to the Lord alone, his spiritual practice becomes successful. Here, the phrase "mat-parah" means that the attainment of a human body, interest in spiritual practice, engagement in spiritual practice, and the success of spiritual practice - all these depend on the Lord's grace. However, due to pride, a person's attention is diverted from this fact. In the case of a Karma Yogi, the emphasis is on performing actions, and he considers his own effort as the primary factor. Therefore, the Lord, out of special grace, is telling the Karma Yogi seeker to be devoted to Him. Being devoted to the Lord means having a sense of importance and belonging only to the Lord, thinking, "The Lord is mine, and I am the Lord's; the world is not mine, and I am not the world's." This is because the Lord is always with me, whereas the world is not. In this way, the seeker's sense of "I-ness" is focused only on the Lord. * 
[ Chapter 2 ]
[Verse 62]
[Verse 63]
Since this chapter deals with Karma Yoga, the Lord should have explained the means of Karma Yoga. However, from the study of the Gita, it appears that devotion to the Lord is the only cause of success in spiritual practice. Therefore, the Gita extols the glory of devotion to the Lord, as in the verse, "Among all the yogis, the one who worships Me with devotion and love is the best" (6.47). The verse "vase hi yasyendriyani tasya prajna pratishthita" - previously, in the 61st verse, the Lord said that even if the senses are disconnected from their objects, one may not attain a stable state of wisdom. In this verse, He says that one whose senses are under control is a stable and wise person. This means that in the previous verse, although the senses are disconnected from their objects, the sense of enjoyment remains within; hence, the senses are not under control. However, in the case of a stable and wise person, the senses are under control, and the sense of enjoyment has ceased. Therefore, it is not a rule that the senses will automatically come under control when they are disconnected from their objects, as the sense of enjoyment may still remain. But it is a rule that when one becomes a stable and wise person, the senses will definitely come under control. Appendix - The Lord has said that even for a Karma Yogi, devotion to Him is necessary, which is a special characteristic of devotion. This is because without being devoted to the Lord, it is difficult to bring the senses completely under control. In Karma Yoga, there is renunciation, and through renunciation, one attains peace and happiness. However, this is not the happiness of attainment, but rather the happiness of the cessation of suffering. In devotion, one experiences the happiness of attainment. Therefore, without experiencing the happiness of devotion, the senses cannot be completely controlled. Another point is that in Karma Yoga, the senses come under control only when there is intense detachment, whereas in devotion, the senses can be easily controlled even with a little detachment. Connection - If one is devoted to the Lord, the senses will come under control, and the sense of enjoyment will cease. But what happens if one is not devoted to the Lord - this is explained in the next two verses. Dhyayato vishayan pumsah sangas teshu upajayate. Sangat sanjayate kamah kamat krodho 'bhijayate. (2.62)

[ Verse 62-63 ]
From desire (Kama) arises anger (Krodha), and from anger, delusion (Sammodha) is born. Due to delusion, the memory (Smriti) is destroyed, and from the destruction of memory, the intellect (Buddhi) is lost. With the loss of intellect, one's downfall occurs. Explanation: When a person meditates on worldly objects, attachment to those objects arises. This is because the individual has two options: either to take refuge in the Supreme Being (Paramatma) or in the world (Samsara). When one abandons the refuge of the Supreme Being, they take refuge in the world and contemplate worldly objects. As a result, attachment, affection, and love for those objects develop. This attachment leads to the desire to possess those objects, and the desire to possess them gives rise to anger when faced with obstacles. Desire (Kama) is a passion-driven tendency, delusion (Sammodha) is a darkness-driven tendency, and anger (Krodha) is a tendency that arises from the interplay of passion and darkness. Whenever anger arises, it is rooted in attachment. For instance, when one becomes angry upon seeing someone act unjustly, it is because they are attached to justice. When one becomes angry at being disrespected, it is because they are attached to respect. Anger gives rise to delusion, which leads to a loss of memory. This loss of memory refers to the forgetfulness of one's resolutions, such as the determination to perform certain actions, follow specific practices, or strive for self-improvement, as guided by scriptures and noble thoughts. In reality, delusion can arise from four sources: desire (Kama), anger (Krodha), greed (Lobha), and possessiveness (Mamata). 1. Delusion born from desire leads to a loss of discernment, causing individuals to engage in inappropriate behavior. 2. Delusion born from anger causes people to speak and act irrationally, even towards their friends and respected individuals. 3. Delusion born from greed leads to a disregard for truth, righteousness, and morality, causing individuals to deceive and cheat others. 4. Delusion born from possessiveness creates partiality and a lack of equanimity. Although delusion can arise from all four sources, the Supreme Being has specifically mentioned anger in this context. This is because, unlike desire, greed, and possessiveness, which are driven by self-interest, anger is driven by a desire to harm others. Therefore, the delusion born from anger is more dangerous than the delusion arising from the other three sources.

152  
* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

“Smṛti‑bhr̥śhā‑d‑buddhi‑nāśa:” – When memory is destroyed, the discernment that appears in the intellect disappears; consequently a person loses the power to generate new thoughts. “Buddhi‑nāśāt‑praṇaśati” – With the loss of discernment a person falls from his position. Hence, to avoid this decline every aspirant must develop a profound reliance on the Lord. Thus,

[ Chapter 2 ]

Only by giving attention to the various objects does attachment arise; attachment gives rise to desire; desire gives rise to anger; anger gives rise to delusion; delusion gives rise to loss of memory; loss of memory gives rise to loss of intellect; and loss of intellect leads to downfall. The exposition of this sequence may take time, but the emergence of all these tendencies and the resulting downfall occurs instantly, like an electric current. Relation – In the following verse the Lord answers the fourth question: “How does the person of steady wisdom act?”

**[ Verse 64 ]**  
rāga‑dveṣa‑viyuktaiḥ tu ātma‑vaśyair vidhēyātmā viṣayān indriyaiḥ śṛṇan  
*When free from attachment and aversion, the self‑controlled one, having mastered the inner self, moves among the objects of the senses.*

**[ Verse 65 ]**  
prasāde sarva‑duḥkhānāṁ hāni‑rasya upajāyate | prasanna‑cetaso hy āśu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣṭhate  
*In the state of grace the destruction of all suffering arises; for one whose mind is serene, intellect quickly remains steady.*

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- adhigacchati = attains, obtains  
- caran = by indulging, by partaking, gives rise to  
- vidheyātmā = the inner self that is under one’s control (the “inner instrument”)  
- prasād = grace, inner purity (the inner‑instrument of the karmayogi)  
- prasannacetas = one whose mind is pleasant, serene  
- buddhi = intellect, clarity of mind (when purified, it quickly steadies)  
- āśu = instantly, swiftly  
- paryavatiṣṭhate = remains, stays firm  
- rāga‑dveṣaviyuktaiḥ = free from attachment and aversion  
- ātma‑vaśyaiḥ = by self‑control, by mastery over the self  
- viṣayān = objects, sense‑objects  
- indriyaiḥ = through the senses  
- hāni = destruction, loss  
- sarva‑duḥkhānām = of all suffering  
- sthira = steady, fixed

Thus, a pure‑hearted aspirant whose intellect is free from doubt quickly attains the steady wisdom that remains fixed in the Supreme (Brahman). **Commentary**

The connective “tu” signals a shift from the previous verse, where the Lord spoke of attachment. The term “vidheyātmā” refers to mastering the inner instrument (the heart‑mind). Merely contemplating objects while still attached leads to downfall; when attachment ceases, the use of the senses brings upliftment. Earlier the loss of intellect was described; here the intellect’s residence in the Supreme is emphasized. The word “ātma‑vaśyaiḥ” again means bringing the senses under control. The implication is that during action the senses must be subjugated, and for that subjugation they must be free of attachment and aversion. Hence a sense should not grasp an object with attachment, nor renounce an object with aversion. The importance lies not in the act of grasping or renouncing, but in keeping the senses free from attachment and aversion. In Chapter 3, Verse 34, the Lord warns the aspirant that each sense‑object carries attachment and aversion, which are the aspirant’s enemies. In Chapter 5, Verse 3, the Lord states that a seeker who is free from such dualities must keep the inner instrument (the heart‑mind) under control. Without mastering the inner instrument, the perfection of karmayoga cannot be attained; acting while still attached to objects leaves the possibility of decline. In practice, keeping the inner instrument under one’s control is essential for every aspirant, and especially critical for the karmayogi. When the aspirant is “ātma‑vaśyaiḥ rāga‑dveṣa‑viyuktaiḥ indriyaiḥ,” he becomes effortlessly liberated, his intellect residing in the Supreme.

[ Verse 64-65 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

“Vishayan charan” – whose inner self is under one’s control. It implies that with contentment two results occur: separation from worldly attachment and steadiness of intelligence in the Supreme Self. The Lord already expressed this in the sixteenth verse, using the words *nischala* (immovable) and *achala* (steady), indicating that his intellect becomes unmoving in the world and unshakable in the Supreme. The aspirant whose senses are free from attachment and aversion and are under his control may still engage with objects through the senses, i.e., perform all kinds of actions, but does not indulge in their enjoyment. Consumption driven by the desire for enjoyment is the cause of downfall. To forbid such enjoyment‑driven intellect, the terms *vidheyatma*, *atmavashaih* etc., appear here. “Prasadamadhigacchati” – by consuming objects without attachment or aversion, the aspirant attains inner contentment (purity). This contentment is a mental austerity (Bhagavad Gita Chapter 17 Verse 16), superior to physical and verbal austerities. Hence the aspirant should neither consume objects with attachment nor abandon them with aversion, because both attachment and aversion bind one to the world. When one consumes objects with senses free from attachment and aversion, the resulting contentment, if not followed by further indulgence, leads to the attainment of the Supreme Self. “In contentment, the loss of all suffering arises” – when the mind attains contentment (purity), all suffering disappears; no sorrow remains. This is because attachment creates mental agitation, which gives rise to desire, and desire is the source of all suffering. When attachment is removed, the mind becomes content, and that contentment eradicates all suffering. Here “the loss of all suffering” does not mean that no painful circumstances will ever arise; according to one’s karma, adverse events may occur, but the inner self will remain free from sorrow, distress, or agitation. “For one whose mind is content, intelligence quickly becomes established” – the intellect of a pure mind swiftly becomes fixed in the Supreme; the aspirant himself becomes steady in the Supreme, and his intellect harbors no doubt. A poignant point: whether devotion manifests as contentment or agitation, if either intensifies excessively it swiftly leads to the Supreme. For example, when the gopis were prevented by parents, brothers, husbands, and confined at home, their agitation to meet the Lord destroyed their rajas and tamas qualities, and the contentment arising from meditating on the Lord eliminated their sattva quality. Thus, free from attachment to qualities, they left the body and first attained the Lord. However, the contentment and distress arising from worldly objects both reinforce the impressions of enjoyment, strengthening the bondage to the world. Ordinary worldly beings exemplify this, trapped in the world by both pleasure and sorrow. All suffering originates from nature and its functions, which are linked to the body‑world relationship, and this relationship is driven by the desire for pleasure. Desire for pleasure arises from distress. When contentment arises, distress disappears, and consequently the desire for pleasure ceases. Without desire, the bond with body and world dissolves, and the absence of bond eliminates all suffering – “the loss of all suffering.” The subtle color becomes permanent, and the inner self melts. In contentment and agitation (distress) the inner self melts, just as adding color to melted wax gives the wax an inner form. “Those afflicted by the intense heat of separation, whose minds are burnt by the fire of desire, are inauspicious. By attaining meditation, the delusion of material existence is removed, and even an aged intellect becomes united with the Supreme. The body, being composed of the three qualities, immediately becomes diminished and inauspicious. The bonds are cut.” (Srimad Bhagavata 10.29.9‑11)

(For a detailed exposition of these verses, refer to the article “Alaukik Prem” in the Gita Press publication *Mere to Giridhara Gopal*.)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 2 ]

When one attains the most cherished object of the world, the feelings that arise become permanent. Once permanent, those feelings no longer bring joy, and when an undesirable object is obtained, the emotions rise and fall. Therefore the aspirant should not become agitated. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – One part of existence belongs to the enjoyer (bhogika) and another part to the yogi. A person of the enjoyer type, whose mind is colored by attachment and aversion, falls when he even thinks about material objects (see Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 2, verses 56‑66). In contrast, a yogi whose mind is free from attachment and aversion does not fall even if he partakes of material objects; instead, he attains the Supreme Self. A person free from attachment and aversion does not consume the sensory pleasures (rasa) that arise from material enjoyment, because such enjoyment is not his aim. He experiences sense‑objects without desire and then relinquishes them (see Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 3, verse 34). Consequently his inner consciousness becomes pure. Relinquished enjoyment is, in reality, no enjoyment at all. To the external observer it may appear that he is still engaged in enjoyment; hence the term “vishayaṇ caran” (one who walks among objects) is used. When one is free from attachment and aversion, “prasada” (grace) is attained. The mind remains ever‑cheerful, never sorrowful, never dull—this is true grace. If one does not cling to this grace or consume it, the realization of the Supreme Self comes swiftly. **Sambandh (Connection)** – The two preceding verses state a principle that is reinforced in the next two verses:

*“There is no intelligence in one whose mind and senses are uncontrolled, nor is there any feeling in such a person. Without this, there is no peace; and how can peace bring happiness to one who is restless?”* (Verse 2.66)

Explanation: This passage deals with Karma‑yoga. In Karma‑yoga, controlling the mind and the senses is essential. Without self‑restraint, desire is not destroyed; without the destruction of desire, the stability of intelligence does not arise. Therefore a Karma‑yoga practitioner must first discipline mind and senses. The verse describes a person whose mind and senses are not disciplined. Because the mind and senses are uncontrolled, such a person lacks a decisive intellect that is fixed solely on attaining the Supreme Self. His attention remains on transient worldly enjoyments and accumulations. He alternately seeks honor, comfort, wealth, and sensual pleasure. Without the transformation of the ego (“I‑ness”), the senses cannot be mastered, and without mastering the senses a decisive intellect cannot arise. When the ego transforms into the understanding “I am the seeker and my task is to practice,” the mind and senses become naturally subservient, requiring no forced control.

[ Verse 67 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

Thus, within it many different desires arise. If a sage, teacher, Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra, etc., are not diligent in performing their respective duties, they do not obtain peace. This is because lack of steadfastness in duty creates unrest. Consequently, its intellect is not decisive. “Na chāyuktasya bhāvanā” – the mind that is not attached does not possess a business‑oriented intellect; such a mind does not hold the attitude “I must only perform my duty and renounce desire for results, cravings, attachments, etc.” The reason this attitude is absent is that the goal is not fixed. “Na cābhāvayataḥ śāntiḥ” – one who is not devoted to his duty cannot attain peace. Likewise, “aśāntasya kutaḥ sukham” – how can a restless person be happy? Because his heart is constantly agitated. Even if he receives countless favorable external enjoyments, the agitation in his heart does not cease; therefore he cannot be happy. **Connection** – why the intellect of an unattached person is not decisive is explained in the following verse. **Sanskrit verse (67)**  
*indriyāṇāṁ hi charatāṁ yan mano anuvidhīyate*  
*tadasya harati prajñāṁ vāyuḥ nāvam iva ambhasi*

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- indriyāṇāṁ – of the senses  
- hi – indeed  
- charatāṁ – wandering, moving about  
- yan – which  
- mano – mind  
- anuvidhīyate – follows, is drawn along  
- tadasya – of that (mind)  
- harati – destroys, removes  
- prajñāṁ – wisdom, intellect  
- vāyuḥ – wind, breath (the subtle force that carries)  
- nāvam – boat  
- iva – like  
- ambhasi – in water

**Explanation** – Human birth is granted solely for the attainment of the Supreme Self. Among the senses, the one that becomes attached to its object is the cause of birth. Therefore one’s purpose must be firmly fixed on attaining the Supreme Self, whatever may happen. When the purpose is firm, the importance of worldly enjoyments disappears from the aspirant’s mind. With the removal of worldly importance, the business‑oriented intellect becomes steady. Until that intellect becomes steady, its condition is described here. The sense makes the mind its follower, taking the mind along. Consequently, the mind begins to enjoy the object; a sense of pleasure and desire arises in the mind, and the mind becomes colored by that object and its importance settles. For example, when eating, the taste of a food item attracts the gustatory sense. Once attached, the taste also draws the mind: “indriyāṇāṁ hi charatāṁ yan mano anuvidhīyate” – the mind becomes delighted and satisfied with that taste. When the aspirant engages in all kinds of activity, then “tadasya harati prajñāṁ” – when the mind places importance on objects before the senses, the solitary mind alone destroys the aspirant’s intellect. In the first half of this verse, before applying the doer‑action construction, the sentence was active: “charatām indriyāṇām indriyam yat manḥ anuvidhīyati.” Here the senses were the agent and the mind the action. To simplify, the term “karmakartṛ” (doer of action) is used, making the action itself the agent; consequently the senses are treated as the doer. This emphasizes the primacy of the mind—without the senses the mind does everything—so the mind is presented as the doer. Because the mind is in the first person, the verb “anuvidhīyate” is employed. When the original agent (the senses) is omitted, the sentence becomes “indriyāṇāṁ hi charatāṁ yan mano anuvidhīyate,” which is the line of the verse. The implication of using the doer‑action construction is that among the objects in which the senses wander, the mind is drawn to any one of them, begins to take pleasure, and that solitary mind alone destroys wisdom; i.e., the mind becomes dominated by sense‑enjoyment.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 2 ]

The passage explains that when the seeker is no longer devoted to duty‑oriented action, a sense of enjoyment‑buddhi (pleasure‑mind) arises and becomes the follower (anugami) of the senses. In that state the solitary mind itself becomes the boat fashioned in the form of wisdom. Because of this enjoyment‑mind, the seeker no longer retains the business‑oriented wisdom that declares “I must attain the Supreme”. Such an analysis may take time, but the distraction of the intellect is instantaneous: as soon as the senses make the mind their follower, enjoyment‑buddhi is generated and the intellect is slain at the same moment. The mind is thus carried away toward the world, and the seeker’s mind acquires a happiness‑buddhi concerning material objects and a significance‑buddhi concerning useful substances. Wind can disturb a boat in two ways—by leading it off course or by sinking it. A skilful sailor, however, adapts the wind’s action to his own purpose, preventing the wind from diverting the boat and instead using it to reach the destination. In the same manner, the mind that follows the senses distracts intellect in two ways: it suppresses the resolve for Supreme‑Self attainment and creates an enjoyment‑buddhi, or it attaches the mind to prohibited pleasures and causes downfall. When the mind and the senses are under control, the mind does not distract intellect; rather, it assists in reaching the Supreme (see Chapter 2, verses 64‑65). The expression “vayur‑nava‑miv‑ambhasi” (the wind takes the boat as water does) illustrates how intellect is seized: just as wind can take a boat moving on water, the mind can take intellect. Imagine a person crossing a river or sea by boat toward a destination; if a contrary wind blows, it pushes the boat away from the intended point. Likewise, the seeker, mounted on the boat of business‑oriented intellect, crosses the ocean of worldly existence toward the Supreme. A question arises here: why does the verse use the terms “yat” and “tat” to refer to the mind rather than the senses, when the senses are the ones that seize the intellect? The answer lies in Chapter 2, verse 60, where the senses are described as seizing the mind, and in Chapter 3, verse 42, where the relationship among senses, mind, and intellect is detailed as subtle, superior, and powerful. This demonstrates that the senses seize the mind, and the mind seizes the intellect. The primary agent in the seizure of intellect is the mind, not the senses, because a sense without its accompanying mind lacks even knowledge of its own object (as stated in Gita 15.9: “Adhishthaya manas ca yaṁ viṣayān upasevate”). The Srimad Bhagavatam records Dattatreya Maharaj’s words (SB 11.9.13):

*tadai‑vam‑ātman‑yavaruddha‑citto na veda kiñcid bahir‑antarāṁ vā*  
*yatheṣu‑kāro nṛpatiṁ vrajantam iṣau gatātmā na dadarśa pārśve*

“Whose consciousness is completely absorbed in the Self, such a person perceives nothing external or internal. He saw a craftsman so absorbed in making an arrow that, as he worked, the king’s carriage passed by without his noticing.”

The craftsman’s ear‑sense existed and his object was the word “arrow,” yet because his mind was not directed toward the ear, the sound was not perceived. This illustrates that the mind’s presence is required for a sense to know its object; without the mind, a sense cannot even recognize its own object, let alone seize the intellect. The preceding discussion explained why a person without attachment (nishchayatmika‑buddhi) lacks decisive intellect. The next verse describes the condition of one whose senses are fully restrained:

[ Verse 68 ]  
*tasmād yasy mahā‑bāho nigṛhītāni sarva‑śaḥ*  
*indriyāṇi indriya‑arthebhyaḥ tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitaḥ*

“Therefore, for the great‑armed one (Arjuna), whose senses are completely restrained, the wisdom (prajña) that is established is beyond the objects of the senses.”

[ Verse 69 ]

**Commentary (preceding the verse)**

*tasmāt* – “therefore”. Arjuna is addressed as “Mahābāho, O great‑armed one!”

*yasya* – “of the person whose”. *indriyāṇi* – “senses”. *indriyārthebhyḥ* – “for the sake of the senses”. *sarvaśaḥ* – “completely”. *viṣayair* – “by material objects”. *prājña‑pratiṣṭhita* – “the intellect is firmly established”. *nigṛhītāni* – “subjugated, brought under control”. The word *tasmāt* concludes the previous discussion about subduing the mind and the senses. It declares that when the attraction of the world no longer dwells in the mind and senses, the intellect becomes steady and firmly established. Because the mind no longer assigns importance to material objects, the intellect remains unshaken. *nigṛhītāni* means that the senses are completely mastered over the objects of sense‑pleasure; they retain no trace of desire, attachment, or tension. It is like a snake whose fangs have been removed – even if it bites, no poison remains. In the same way, removing desire and aversion from the senses is akin to extracting their poisonous teeth. Once this is done, the senses lose the power to lead the seeker toward downfall. The term *sarvaśaḥ* indicates that whether one is engaged with the world or meditating in solitude, the senses never become inclined toward pleasure or material objects. No matter how many objects come into contact with the seeker, they cannot distract him. The mind, together with the senses, cannot disturb his intellect. Just as a mountain cannot be toppled, his intellect becomes so firm that the mind cannot shake it in any condition; thus the intellect remains steady. The import of this verse is that the aspirant must resolutely decide that his goal is the attainment of the Supreme Self, not the enjoyment of sense‑pleasures or the accumulation of wealth. If such vigilance is continuously maintained, the difference between a person whose senses are completely subjugated and an ordinary human being will be explained in the following verse. **Verse 69**

yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṁ tasyāṁ jāgarti saṁyamī |  
yasyaṁ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ || 69 ||

*Translation*: “The night in which the self‑controlled one awakens while all beings are asleep, that night is the night perceived by the sage who sees the Supreme.”

**Commentary (following the verse)**

*sarvabhūtānām* – “of all living beings”. *jāgarti* – “is awake, is alert”. *yā* – “which”. *niśā* – “night (the state of being turned away from the Supreme Self)”. *tasyām* – “in that”. *bhūtāni* – “beings”. *saṁyamī* – “the self‑controlled person”. The expression “yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṁ” refers to those whose senses and mind are not under the sway of sense‑objects; they are attached to worldly pleasures and therefore remain asleep with respect to the Supreme Self. The “night” symbolizes the darkness of ignorance that blinds them to the nature of the Supreme Self, to the true knowledge (tattva‑jnana), to the cause of suffering, to the burning of desire, and to the consequences of their actions. By refusing to look in that direction, their night is complete darkness. The phrase *bhūtānām* is used to illustrate that, just as animals and birds spend the whole day occupied with eating and drinking, many humans spend day and night absorbed in food, comfort, and material enjoyment. For such people, the sage’s “night” is the darkness that covers their vision of the Truth. Those who are preoccupied with accumulation and wealth are counted among the same class of animals and birds. Their turning away from the Supreme Self makes no essential difference between them and the lower creatures; both are asleep with respect to the Supreme Self. If a difference exists, it is that animals and birds lack the awakened discriminative power (viveka‑śakti) that humans can develop through the grace of the Divine. This awakened discrimination enables a person to work for the welfare of all, to serve living beings, and to attain the Supreme Self, rather than remaining trapped in mere material pursuit.

[ Chapter 2 ]

Misusing the power of discrimination, a person begins to hoard material objects. He becomes satisfied with the notion that he has obtained a great profit, and he immerses himself in acquiring and enjoying them, becoming more harmful to the world than even animals. Animals and birds eat only enough to fill their stomachs and do not accumulate; but a human, wherever he finds any material thing, gathers it whether it is useful to him or not, and thereby obstructs the use of that thing by others. “tasyām jāgarti saṁyamī” – In that condition the self‑controlled person is awake. This is the “night” of humanity, i.e., the state of turning away from the Supreme Self and from one’s own welfare. The self‑controlled individual has mastered the senses and mind, is unattached to enjoyment and accumulation, and his sole aim is the Supreme Self; such a person is the self‑controlled man. Truly knowing the Supreme Self, his own nature, and the world as they really are constitutes his awakening in that night. “yasyām jāgrati bhūtāni” – In which beings are awake. Those who are extremely vigilant about enjoyment and accumulation keep a ledger of every penny, watch every inch of land, and rejoice whether the wealth they acquire is justly or unjustly obtained, thinking, “We have secured such capital; the profit is ours.” Thus they devote themselves to gathering fleeting worldly pleasures and to gaining honor, respect, and prestige; their vigilance in these pursuits is what they call awakening. “sā niśā paśyato muneḥ” – That is the night for the sage. Humans who consider themselves clever and skillful because they indulge in worldly enjoyment and accumulation view the world and the Supreme Self as complete darkness. If they do not obtain what they desire, they lament a great loss. Yet a wise person who does not assign importance to stones, pebbles, or similar trivialities asks, “What benefit did I gain from acquiring these stones, and what loss did I suffer by not acquiring them?” Even if children receive stones, how long will they keep them? In the same way, people engrossed in enjoyment and accumulation fight, lie, cheat, and act dishonestly to obtain more, then celebrate their “great profit.”

The contemplative, self‑controlled person who knows the Supreme Self, his own nature, and the results of the world sees clearly that once pleasures, honor, comfort, food, and adornment are obtained, what remains? What truly benefits humanity? How long will these pleasures be retained? How long will the tendencies produced by them endure? To such a mind, the awakening of beings is like night. The contemplative, self‑controlled individual knows the Supreme Self, his own nature, and the outcomes of the world, and he also understands material objects well enough to discern which are beneficial, how much they help others, and he employs each material thing appropriately in its proper place, dedicating them to the service of others. Just as a defect in the eyes makes the sky appear as a net, and even when the eyes are closed the net resembles a peacock feather, the intellect remains steadfast that there is no net in the sky. Similarly, when the senses and inner mind present the world, children playing with pebbles, glass, and yellow pieces argue over them, yet the contemplative, self‑controlled mind remains firm that, in reality, the world does not exist—it is only an appearance. **Appendix —** The worldly person remains occupied day and night with enjoyment and accumulation, assigning them supreme importance. He becomes highly vigilant and skillful in worldly activities, learns various arts and crafts, invents many things, regards the acquisition of material objects as his progress, sings praises of worldly greatness, performs great austerities to enjoy lasting happiness, worships deities, chants mantras, and so on. However, to the liberated, philosophically enlightened great souls and true seekers, he is pure darkness; even a speck of his existence holds no significance. In their view, the entire universe up to Brahmaloka does not truly exist—*na‑sato vidyate bhāvaḥ* (Bhagavad Gita 2.16) “The unreal has no existence,” and *ā‑brahma‑bhuvanāl‑lokāḥ punar‑āvartino ’rjuna* (Bhagavad Gita 8.16) “O Arjuna, the worlds of the material are repeatedly traversed.”

Worldly people continue to create and consume within the world, believing that what exists is only what they perceive—*na‑anya‑dasti* “There is nothing else.”

[ Verse 70 ]
* Sadhaka-Sanjivani *
The worldly-minded persons are convinced that the enjoyment of desires is the ultimate goal (Gita 2.42), (Gita 16.11). Their intellect does not go beyond worldly matters. However, a seeker of spiritual truth understands both spiritual and worldly matters, which is why the word "pashyatah" (sees) is used for them. Worldly people see only the night (ignorance), not the day (knowledge), but a yogi sees both. For example, a child has only experienced childhood, not youth, but an old man has experienced childhood, youth, and old age. A person who accumulates wealth does not know the value of renunciation, but one who renounces wealth understands both accumulation and renunciation. The principle is that a person engrossed in the world cannot understand the world. One can understand the world only by detaching from it, because in reality, the world is separate from the self. Similarly, a person can understand the Supreme Self only by becoming one with it, because in reality, the self is one with the Supreme Self. One who is established in the state of "being" (existence) understands both "being" and "non-being", but one who is established in "non-being" (non-existence) cannot truly understand "non-being" and therefore cannot understand "being". The one who understands "being" does not have a conflict with the one who acknowledges "non-being", but the one who acknowledges "non-being" has a conflict with the one who understands "being". Connection: To a contemplative and self-controlled person, the world appears like night. This raises the question of whether such a person comes into contact with worldly objects at all. If not, how do they sustain their life? And if they do come into contact, what is their state? The next verse explains these points. Just as the waters of the rivers flow into the ocean, which remains unmoved and unchanging, in the same way, all desires enter the person who has attained peace, and they do not become a slave to desires. Explanation: The ocean remains unmoved and unchanging, even when the waters of the rivers flow into it. The ocean does not increase or decrease due to the influx of river water. It remains full and does not transgress its boundaries. Similarly, the person who has attained peace remains unmoved and unchanging, even when all desires enter them. The word "kama" here refers to the objects of desire, not the desires themselves.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 2 ]

The self‑realized, self‑controlled person who knows the ultimate principle attains that principle; he is infinite, eternal, and the material objects of worldly enjoyment are inert. They may appear before him, but they cannot create pleasure‑pain disturbances in his body or inner consciousness. Consequently he attains supreme peace. That peace arises from the Supreme Self (Paramatma), not from material objects (Gita – Chapter 2, Verse 46). All things are impermanent, unreal, limited, and ending. The second difference is that river water reaches the ocean, whereas the sthitaprajna who abides in the ultimate reality is not reached by worldly objects of enjoyment; only his designated body and inner consciousness are affected. Hence the analogy of the ocean and rivers given here applies only to his designated body; it is not intended to describe the inner state of the self‑realized, self‑controlled person. The water that fills the ocean is the water of the same species; it is not a metaphor that reveals the true nature of the ultimate. The desire‑driven (kāmaka) being, whose mind craves material objects, cannot be satisfied even if all worldly enjoyments are gathered; his thirst, yearning, and anguish cannot be quenched by any analogy. Therefore the analogy cannot hold. The conscious principle in which the sthitaprajna abides is the conscious (Chetan) principle, which is eternal, true, and cannot be satisfied by inert material substances. Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav) – The world appears inert only because of desire; in reality it is the luminous Supreme Self – “Vāsudevaḥ sarvam” (Gita 7.19), “Satya‑saccā‑aham‑arjuna” (Gita 9.19). When a person becomes free of desire, all objects become pleased with him. The sign of objects being pleased is that the self‑less great soul automatically attracts the necessary objects. Objects become eager to come to him for success. Yet because desire is absent, neither the acquisition nor the non‑acquisition of objects creates any disturbance (joy, etc.) within him. In his view objects have no value (importance). Conversely, a desire‑driven person remains restless whether objects are obtained or not. Relation (Sambandh) – In the next verse we conclude the answer to the question “How does the sthitaprajna act?”

**Verse 71**  
vihaya kāmānyah sarvān pumān ścarati nispṛhaḥ | nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ sa śāntim adhigacchati || 71 ||

- **vihaya** – having abandoned  
- **kāmānyah** – all desires (kāma = desire, -ānyah = others)  
- **sarvān** – all, every  
- **pumān** – person, human being  
- **ścarati** – moves about, roams  
- **nispṛhaḥ** – without attachment, free from longing  
- **nirmamo** – without cruelty, free from malice  
- **nirahaṅkāraḥ** – without ego, free from pride  
- **sa** – he  
- **śāntim** – peace  
- **adhigacchati** – attains, reaches

**Translation:** “Having abandoned all desires, the self‑realized person roams the world without attachment; free from cruelty and ego, he attains peace.”

[ Verse 71 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

He does not even partake of material objects. By completely renouncing the items needed for subsistence, he renounces everything; that is, if the sense of “I‑self” refrains from consumption, he also observes the distinction between permissible and forbidden. In other words, in the initial stage of practice he treats the body and the like exactly as he did before; only now, as long as the body remains, it is fine, and as long as the means of livelihood continue to be available, it is fine—there is no attachment to any of these within him. In the fifty‑fifth verse of this chapter the words “prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān” expressed the principle of renouncing desire; the same idea is reiterated here with the phrase “vihāya kāmāny an sarvān”. The implication is that in Karma‑yoga one cannot become a Sthitaprajna without completely abandoning all desires, because desire is the very link that binds one to the world. If all desire is utterly relinquished, no relationship with the world can remain. “Nirmamaḥ” – the Sthitaprajna completely gives up affection (Mamata). The objects that a person claims as his own are in fact not his; they are merely gifts received from the world. To consider such received objects as one’s own is a mistake. When this mistake disappears, the Sthitaprajna becomes free of attachment to objects, persons, substances, the body, the senses, etc. “Nirahaṅkāraḥ” – the notion “the body is I” is ego‑clinging. In the Sthitaprajna this ego‑clinging does not exist. The body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, etc., appear in a certain light, and even the “I‑self” appears in that light. Hence, from the standpoint of illumination, the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the ego (“I‑self”) are all visible phenomena. The seer is distinct from the seen – this is a universal rule. Once this experience is realized, the Sthitaprajna becomes nirahaṅkāra (ego‑free). “Sa‑śāntim adhigacchati” – the Sthitaprajna attains peace. When one is free of desire, craving, affection, and ego, peace naturally arises; it is not something that has to be artificially obtained. In fact, peace is self‑evident in the human mind. Only the desire to enjoy pleasure from transient, created objects and the attachment to them generate unrest. When all worldly desire, craving, affection, and ego are completely abandoned, the innate, self‑evident peace is experienced. In this verse the four mental tendencies—desire (Kāma), craving (Spṛhā), affection (Mamata), and ego (Ahaṁkāra)—are discussed, with ego being the primary one. If ego disappears, the sense of “my‑self” also disappears, and consequently there is no “I” to generate desire or to act for any purpose. When merely uttering “nirahaṅkāra” already implies the renunciation of desire, why then describe the renunciation of desire separately? The answer is that among the four tendencies, desire is the grossest. From desire arises subtle craving; from craving arises subtle affection; from affection arises subtle ego. Therefore, if the practitioner first abandons desire, craving, and affection, the abandonment of ego becomes easy. From a scriptural viewpoint, the sequence is first the renunciation of desire, then craving, then affection, and finally ego. From the practitioner’s perspective, however, it is more effective to first abandon affection, then desire, craving, and finally ego. Affection pertains to objects already obtained, whereas desire pertains to objects not yet obtained. Abandoning affection is therefore the most accessible step. Man — being first entangled by affection for the objects he possesses — gains the capacity for self‑lessness (niḥsākam) by relinquishing affection, the capacity for desire‑lessness (niḥspṛhā) by relinquishing desire, and the capacity for ego‑lessness (nirahaṅkāra) by relinquishing craving. Following the scriptural path makes a person learned; following the practitioner’s path gives direct experience. Method for eliminating ego and affection (from the standpoint of Karma‑yoga): “I have nothing.” Because I have no independent right over any object, person, circumstance, event, or state. When I have nothing, I need nothing; if the body were truly mine, I would need food, water, clothing, etc., but when the body is not mine, I need nothing of anyone. When I have nothing and desire nothing, what remains of “I”? The sense of “I” exists only by clinging to some object, body, or condition. The body that is called “mine” is entirely inseparable from the world. Hence, whatever must be done with this so‑called body is to be done solely for the welfare of the world, because I desire nothing. When this attitude arises, the one‑pointedness of “I” dissolves into self‑effacement.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 2 ]

Thus the ego (Ahanta) of the Karma‑yogi becomes free of attachment (Mamata). In the same way, the ego of the Sankhya‑yogi becomes free of attachment. From the Sankhya‑yogi’s point of view, even the mere breath is identified as “I am,” and this knowledge of one’s own self‑existent reality (the state of being) is self‑evident. In this view, “I” is a fragment of Prakriti, while “am” is the power of existence. The power “am” actually refers to the “I.” If the “I” were absent, the power “am” would disappear, and only “is” would remain. From the Bhakti‑yogi’s perspective, everything that one calls “mine” or “my” belongs entirely to the Lord. The reason is that I have no even the slightest right over the object I call “my,” whereas the Lord has complete authority over it. Whatever the Lord wishes to do with an object, it becomes so; therefore everything is the Lord’s. This must be offered in service to the Lord. The body, senses, mind, and intellect that I possess are also His, and I am also His. When this feeling arises, the Bhakti‑yogi’s ego becomes free of attachment. “I am,” “you are,” “this is,” and “that is” refer to the four categories of person, place, and time. If these four are not grasped, only “is” remains, and the state of “is” alone persists. Because of the presence of “is,” the earlier appendix stated, “So one attains immortality” (2.15), indicating the attainment of Jnana‑yoga (knowledge). Now it says, “Thus one attains peace,” indicating the attainment of Karma‑yoga. The implication is that abiding in one’s true nature (Chit‑maya) leads to the nectar of immortality, while the renunciation of ego (Ahanta) leads to peace. The ego is imagined as real in one’s own perception, but it is not real in actuality. If it were truly real, we could never become self‑less, and the Lord does not speak of being self‑less. Yet the Lord declares “Nirahaṅkāra” (self‑lessness), therefore we can be free of ego. Our experience confirms that the true nature is indeed free of ego. During deep sleep, the feeling of ego’s absence and the sense of one’s own existence are experienced by everyone, becoming clearly known upon waking. In sleep, the ego becomes immersed in ignorance, yet the self remains. Hence, upon waking (by recollection), one says, “I slept in such bliss that I knew nothing.” This recollection proves that the one who experiences bliss and the one who says “I knew nothing” are the same; otherwise, who experienced bliss and who knew nothing? Therefore, “I knew nothing” signifies the absence of ego, and the knowledge of this absence belongs to the self‑less nature. A woman’s nose fell into a well. To retrieve it, a man descended into the well and, after searching in the water, felt the nose in his hand, feeling great joy. Yet at that moment he could not speak, because fire (speech) and water are opposed. Only when he emerged from the water could he say, “The nose is found!” In the same way, when one is immersed in the ego during sleep, a person experiences bliss but cannot express it, because the instrument of expression is lacking. Upon waking, the memory of that bliss appears. Memory is experiential: “Experiential knowledge is memory.” Thus, everyone experiences the lack of ego in sleep, but no one experiences that lack directly. Ego cannot exist without us, but we can exist without ego, and indeed we do. Our true nature is pure consciousness (Chit‑maya). This eternal consciousness has no need for anyone’s expectation, yet everyone expects consciousness. If we were not separate from the ego and were only the form of ego, we would not even exist when immersed in ego during sleep. Hence, even without ego, our existence is established. In the waking state and in dreams, ego appears; in deep sleep, ego merges, yet the self remains continuously. What is neither manifested nor merged is our true nature. Even after renouncing desire, some object, person, or substance is needed merely for bodily sustenance; this is called “Spṛhā” (attachment). In a person of steady wisdom (Sthitaprajña), even the need for bodily sustenance disappears; the body itself is no longer required. The need for a body makes a person subordinate. Need arises only when a person accepts something that is not his own. The Karma‑yogi does not consider any object as his own or for his personal use; rather, he regards it as belonging to the world and for the world. Consequently, he has no need for any object.

[ Verse 72 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

The renunciation of both kāmanā (desire) and spṛhā (craving) means that one should have no longing for external objects and also no desire even for mere subsistence (the body’s necessities). Even the desire for subsistence is a form of pleasure‑seeking. Moreover, the wish to attain peace, liberation, philosophical knowledge, etc., is also a desire. Hence, in a self‑less state one should not even desire liberation. This verse declares the prohibition of the external nature (apara prakṛti). Because of ego, the living being has taken on the external nature (the world) – “yad evam dhāryate jagat” (Gita 7.5). Therefore, when ego‑lessness (nirahaṅkāra) arises, the external nature is relinquished (relationship‑severance) and the soul is freed from the cycle of birth and death. Even when all objects are renounced, ego remains; but when ego itself is abandoned, all renunciation is accomplished. Relationship—what is the state when desire, craving, affection, and ego‑attachment are absent—will be described in the following verse, concluding this subject. eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtḥ naināṁ prāpya vimuhyati | sthitvā hy āsya māntakāle api brahma‑nirvāṇam ṛcchati || 72 ||

Translation: “This is the Brahmi state, O Partha; having attained it, one is no longer deluded. Even while remaining in this state at the time of death, one attains Brahma‑nirvāṇa.”

The term brahmi signifies that one becomes established in Brahma‑nirvāṇa (peaceful liberation). Partha is the address to Arjuna (son of Pritha). “Nainaṁ prāpya vimuhyati” means that as long as ego remains in the body, delusion is possible; when ego is completely absent and one experiences one’s position in Brahma, the personality is destroyed and delusion ceases. Not distinguishing correctly between sat (the real) and asat (the unreal) is delusion. Even while being sat, regarding oneself as united with asat is delusion. When the seeker fully discerns asat, the relationship with asat is severed and one experiences the true state of sat. Once this state is realized, delusion never returns (Gita 4.35). The phrase “sthita vāsya‑māntakāle api brahma‑nirvāṇa‑mṛcchati” is spoken by the Lord: “When your intellect is freed from the fog of delusion and from the confusion of hearing, you will attain yoga.” Hearing this, Arjuna wondered what that state would be. He asked four questions about the sthita‑prajña (steady‑wise one). By answering those questions, the Lord explained that the state is the brahmi state. It is not a personal state; the individual personality, body, and mind exist only as instruments for attaining the Supreme. Knowing asat (leads to) the cessation of asat, because asat has no independent existence. Only through sat does asat obtain any semblance of existence. If knowledge of asat does not bring about its cessation, then one has not truly known asat; one has merely learned about it. Mere intellectual knowledge does not eliminate asat, since the notion of asat persists in the mind.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 2 ]

Therefore the Lord gives this opportunity that even the most ordinary person—whether through prior practice, a good samskara, or even a sinner—if at the time of death he attains the state of the Supreme Self, i.e., severs his attachment to material nature, he also attains the peaceful Brahman and becomes free from birth and death. A similar statement is found in Chapter 7, Verse 30, where the Lord says, “The embodied, the divine, and the knower of the Vedas are all one God—those who realize this even at the moment of death truly know Me and attain Me.”

In Chapter 8, Verse 5 it is said, “One who departs this world remembering Me attains Me; there is no doubt about this.”

Secondly, from those verses the Lord describes the glory of the Brahmi state, stating that if one attains it even at the time of death, one attains the peaceful Brahman. Just as in the subject of equal intelligence the Lord said that even a small ritual protects one from great fear (Chapter 2, Verse 40), here He says that even at death, if the Brahmi state is attained and the attachment to material nature is severed, one attains Nirvana Brahman. The attachment (raga) to material nature is the obstacle to experiencing this state. If this attachment is abandoned even at the moment of death, the self‑realized state is automatically experienced. One may wonder how an experience that has not been realized during life can occur at death. In a healthy state the seeker’s intellect, thought‑power and mindfulness enable the experience of the Brahmi state; but at the moment of death the intellect becomes disturbed and mindfulness ceases, raising the question of how the Brahmi state can be realized. The answer is that at the instant of death the body automatically severs its attachment. If the mind then turns toward the self‑realized principle, the experience arises effortlessly. While attaining the non‑dual (Nirvikalpa) state requires intellect and discrimination, attaining the transcendental principle requires only a focus. Once the focus is established—whether by the Lord’s grace or the saint’s benevolent grace—the attainment is self‑evident. - Here the word “api” means that if this state is attained before death, i.e., while alive, one becomes liberated; and even if it is attained at death, i.e., becoming beyond ego, one is also liberated. This implies that the state arises instantly; no practice, meditation or samadhi is required to attain it. In the discourse on Karma‑yoga the Lord uses the term “Brahma‑Nirvana”. This means that just as the Sankhya‑yogi attains Nirvana Brahman (Gita, Chapter 5, verses 24‑26), the Karma‑yogi also attains Nirvana Brahman. This is affirmed in Chapter 5, Verse 5, which states that the position attained by the Sankhya‑yogi is the same as that attained by the Karma‑yogi. **Special Note** – Matter (jada) and consciousness (chetana) are the two substances. The essence of the soul (prana) is consciousness, yet it is associated with matter. Attraction toward matter leads to decline, while attraction toward the conscious principle leads to upliftment and welfare. The former is dominated by “moha” (attachment), the latter by “viveka” (discrimination). For understanding, moha and viveka can be divided into two categories each: (1) ego‑driven moha (with affection) and desire‑driven moha; (2) discrimination between sat (real) and asat (unreal), and discrimination of duty versus non‑duty. The attained object, such as the body, is acted upon by ego‑driven affection—this is ego‑affection moha; the unattained object, such as events or circumstances, is pursued by desire—this is desire‑driven moha. The “shariri” (the one residing in the body) is distinct from the body itself; the shariri is sat (real) while the body is asat (unreal). The shariri is conscious. In the attainment of the non‑dual (Nirvikalpa) state, practice, contemplation, and meditation are effective, but in attaining the transcendental Brahmi state, intellect does not function; it falls away. This is because Nirvikalpa awareness is independent of action (karaṇa), requiring no causal effort. The separation from causation is what enables its attainment.

* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

The soul exists while the body is inert; it cannot be cleanly separated. The body was never distinct, will not remain distinct in the future, nor even in the intermediate state. Discriminating between sat (truth) and asat (untruth) and knowing what is duty changes every moment, just as the body passes through youth, middle‑age and old age. What is “akarma” (non‑duty), what is dharma (righteous duty), what is adharma (unrighteousness) also changes with these stages. As a person understands these changes, he discards the non‑duty and embraces the duty; this is the wisdom of akarma. In the first chapter Arjuna is shown to be afflicted by two kinds of attachment (moha): one rooted in ego‑pride and the other in affection. He says, “We are dharmic souls who know our faults,” and, “Our families will die.” This is ego‑affection‑laden attachment. He also wishes that no sin may fall upon him, that his lineage may not be destroyed, that no betrayal of friends may occur, that he may not go to hell, that his ancestors may not fall – a desire‑laden attachment. To remove these two kinds of attachment, the Lord, in the second chapter, explains two discriminations:

* The bodily discrimination (the distinction of the body), covering verses 11 to 30 of chapter 2, which is the sat‑asat discrimination. * The discrimination of duty versus non‑duty, covering verses 31 to 39 of chapter 2. While describing the bodily discrimination, the Lord says that you and these kings were not existent before; the same applies to the future. While describing the duty‑non‑duty discrimination, the Lord declares that for a Kshatriya there is no dharma higher than war. An unexpected war is the open door to heaven. If you do not follow your war‑related svadharma, you incur sin. If you treat victory and defeat, gain and loss, pleasure and pain as equal while fighting, you incur no sin. Your right lies in performing action, not in its fruits. Do not become the cause of the results of your actions, and do not cling to inaction. Therefore, act with equanimity, immersed in the success‑failure continuum, because equanimity itself is yoga. One who works with a balanced mind becomes free from merit and demerit while still alive. The statement “there will be no further existence” means that when your intellect crosses the mire of illusion and the opposition to hearing, you have always been and will always be; the body will transcend the leaf‑like existence, and then you will attain yoga. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – By becoming ruthlessly self‑less (nir‑mama) and free of ego (nir‑ahankara), the practitioner’s attachment to the asat (untruth) division is severed, and he experiences his innate, self‑existent state in the sat (truth) division, i.e., Brahman. In this “Brahmi‑sthiti” (Brahma‑state) no one claims ownership of the body; the sense of “I‑am” disappears, and personality is erased. Hence our condition no longer depends on ego. Even when ego vanishes, the Brahmi‑state remains. Once this perpetual yoga is realized, delusion never returns (see Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 4, Verse 35). If, at the moment of death, a person attains the Brahmi‑state through ruthlessness and ego‑lessness, immediate nirvāṇa and union with Brahman are attained. Ruthlessness and ego‑lessness lead to the realization of Brahman, i.e., true philosophy. The person becomes free of affection, desire, and personal duty. The world is sustained only because of the sense of “I‑am” – “the ego‑deluded soul thinks ‘I am the doer’” (Bhagavad Gita 3.27) and “the living beings, O mighty‑armed, support the world” (Bhagavad Gita 7.5). If one abandons the ego, the world would cease. When Brahman is realized (especially if devotional impressions are present), the complete Supreme Self is automatically attained, for the Supreme Self is the very establishment of Brahman. Accepting “I have nothing” makes a person ruthlessly self‑less; accepting “I desire nothing” makes a person self‑less (nishkama); accepting “I have nothing to do for myself” makes a person ego‑less. Om Tat Sat. In the Srimad Bhagavad Gita, within the Brahma‑vidyā section of the Yoga‑Shāstra, in the dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna, the Sankhya Yoga is the second chapter. [ Verse 2 ]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 2 ]

Thus, through the precise pronunciation of the divine names Om, Tat, Sat, the second chapter called **Sankhya Yoga** is completed in the dialogue of Shri Krishna and Arjuna, which presents the Srimad Bhagavad Gita as an Upaniṣad‑like treatise on Brahma‑knowledge and Yoga‑shastra. In all practices—Karma Yoga, Sankhya Yoga, Bhakti Yoga, etc.—discernment (**Viveka**) is of great importance. In Sankhya Yoga this discernment is paramount, and it is through Sankhya Yoga that the Lord began His teaching; therefore this chapter is named “Sankhya Yoga.”

(1) In this chapter there are three verses of “Atha Dvitiya Adhyāya” (Thus, the second chapter), fourteen utterances such as “Sanjaya Uvacha” and “Shri Bhagavān Uvacha,” 977 verses, and thirteen verses attributed to Pushpika. Hence the total number of verses is 977. (2) The chapter contains seven “Atha Dvitiya Adhyāya” verses, forty‑five utterances of “Sanjaya Uvacha,” “Shri Bhagavān Uvacha,” etc., 2,403 verses, and forty‑five letters of Pushpika. Consequently the total number of letters is 2,500. Among the seventy‑two verses of this chapter, verses 5, 7, 8, 20, 22, and 70 each consist of forty‑four letters; verse 6 consists of forty‑six letters; and verse 29 consists of forty‑five letters. The remaining sixty‑four verses each contain thirty‑two letters. (3) This chapter contains seven utterances—two “Sanjaya Uvacha,” three “Shri Bhagavān Uvacha,” and two “Arjuna Uvacha.”

The meters employed in the second chapter are described as follows: among the seventy‑two verses, verses 5, 6, 7, 8, 20, 22, 29, and 70 are composed in the **Upajati** meter. In the second chapter, the 51st and 66th verses in their first pāda use the **na‑gaṇa**, producing a “na‑vipula” (abundant with “na”). The 12th, 26th, and 32nd verses in their first pāda, as well as the 61st and 63rd verses in their third pāda, employ the **ra‑gaṇa**, yielding a “ra‑vipula.” The 64th and 66th verses in their first pāda use the **bha‑gaṇa**, giving a “bha‑vipula.” The 71st verse in its first pāda and the 31st verse in its third pāda use the **ma‑gaṇa**, resulting in a “ma‑vipula.” The 46th verse in its first pāda uses the **sa‑gaṇa**, producing a “sa‑vipula.” The 35th verse in its first and third pādas uses the **na‑gaṇa**, creating a “jāti‑paksha‑vipula.” The 47th verse in its first and third pādas employs the **bha‑gaṇa** and **na‑gaṇa**, respectively, giving a “saṅkīrṇa‑vipula” (mixed abundance). The remaining ninety‑five verses are in the standard **Pāthyāvaktra** Anushtubh meter, exhibiting its characteristic features.

[ Chapter 3 ]

Now

Om Shri Paramatmane Namah

The teaching of the *Srimad Bhagavad Gita* is based on the experience of ordinary human beings. When the divine instruction begins (from the 11th verse of Chapter 2), the Lord first makes clear that the body (śarīra) and the soul (śarīrī) are completely distinct. The body is impermanent, unreal, limited to one place, and perishable; the soul is eternal, real, all‑pervading, and indestructible. Hence, seeing the destruction of a perishable object without sorrow, and not desiring to preserve an indestructible object, is called **viveka** (discrimination). All three yogic paths—Karma Yoga, Jñāna Yoga and Bhakti Yoga—require great viveka. Only when one truly discerns “I am wholly different from the body” does the longing for liberation arise. Even the desire for heaven or other attainments appears only after recognizing one’s separateness from the body. For this reason the Lord opens his discourse with a description of viveka. The above discussion of viveka in the Gita starts with the 11th verse of Chapter 2 and ends with verse 30. In this section the Lord does not employ philosophical terms such as Atman, Anātman, Prakṛti, Purusha, Brahman, Avidyā, Īśvara, Jīva, Jagat, Māyā, etc.; instead he explains in a manner that every person can readily understand. The implication is that only a human being is qualified for the attainment of the Supreme Self, because the human body is provided precisely for that purpose. By giving importance to the described viveka, only a human can achieve the Supreme Self. The Lord also refrains from using the word “buddhi” (intellect) in this passage. In reality, to distinguish the eternal from the non‑eternal, the real from the unreal, the indestructible from the destructible, the soul from the body, **viveka alone** is required; intellect is not sufficient. Viveka transcends intellect. Just as Prakṛti and Purusha are beginningless (Bhagavad Gita 13.19), the discrimination that reveals their difference is also beginningless. This same discrimination manifests in the intellect. The discrimination given by the Lord is universally available to all beings. Animals and birds also recognize the difference between edible and inedible substances. Plants sense seasonal changes and the contrast between favorable and unfavorable conditions. Because humans are primarily intellect‑driven, they uniquely acquire this viveka. In lower beings the discrimination is limited to the identification of inert matter for mere survival, whereas a human, by virtue of his viveka, can free himself forever from the cycle of birth and death and attain eternal peace. This is the special characteristic of human viveka. When viveka awakens—that is, when the experience of the body‑soul distinction arises—the attachment to the body, senses, mind and intellect, together with the whole world, is completely severed. The intellect becomes pure and balanced; its previous unevenness disappears. In Karma Yoga, a decisive intellect is paramount—“vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ ekā” (Bhagavad Gita 2.41). When a person’s sole resolve is the welfare of the self or the attainment of the Supreme Self, neither favorable nor adverse circumstances can hinder him, and his intellect naturally becomes balanced without any effort. The intellect remains unbalanced only as long as it is attracted to the importance, allure, and pull of the world. A decisive intellect (nishchayātmikā buddhi) is the hallmark of Sankhya Yoga’s viveka, of Bhakti Yoga’s faith‑trust, and of Karma Yoga’s decisive intellect. Karma Yoga does not lack faith or viveka; rather, its primary feature is the presence of a decisive intellect. The same decisive intellect characterizes both Sankhya Yoga and Bhakti Yoga.
