* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Because the one who creates a being has the duty to protect that being, Brahmā creates the progeny, remains ever ready to protect them, and constantly thinks of their welfare. Hence he is called “Prajāpati.”

At the beginning of creation Brahmā fashioned humans endowed with the capacity for duty‑action and with discernment. Proper use of both favorable and unfavorable circumstances brings welfare. Therefore Brahmā gave the discernment to make proper use of both kinds of conditions while creating humans. Animals, birds, trees, etc., which are incapable of distinguishing truth from falsehood, act naturally in self‑less service (duty). Man, however, has received a special power of discernment through divine grace. Thus, if he gives importance to his discernment and does not act against duty, even his actions can be naturally for the welfare of the world. Deities, sages, ancestors, humans and other animals, birds, trees, etc., are all “prajā” (beings). Because of their qualifications, rights and means, the responsibility for caring for all other beings rests on humans. Hence the term “prajāḥ” is used here especially for humans. It is arriving. This is not a new matter. [ Chapter 3 ]

In the fourth chapter (from verses 24 to 30) every means for attaining the Supreme Self is described as “yajña” (sacrifice); e.g., material‑yajña, austerity‑yajña, yoga‑yajña, pranayama, etc. Commonly the word “yajña” is known only for fire‑offering actions, but in the Gītā the word also denotes all prescribed ritual actions performed according to scriptural injunction. The duties appropriate to one’s varṇa, āśrama, dharma, caste, nature, country, time, etc., fall under “yajña.” All actions performed with the feeling of benefiting others are also “yajña.” Such yajña (duty) is the responsibility of man alone. —  
**anena prasavishyadhva meṣaḥ vo ’stviṣṭakāmadhuk?** 2

Brahmā tells humans: “By this you shall be born; you are the one who seeks the desired object.”

Brahmā says to humans that by performing their respective duties each of you should increase and progress. By doing so you will always obtain the material needed for duty, never lacking. To remove Arjuna’s reluctance to act, the Lord says that even the words of Prajāpati Brahmā should teach you to perform duty. Performing duty for the benefit of others brings both worldly and transcendental advancement. Karmayoga has existed since the beginning of time. In the third verse of the fourth chapter the Lord says with the word “purātanaḥ” that this Karmayoga had almost disappeared. The same point is expressed here with the word “pura” in another way: “I have not only said it, but Brahmā also, at the beginning of creation, created beings with duties and instructed them to practice this Karmayoga.” The implication is that the tradition of Karmayoga—performing duty without selfish desire—has existed from the very beginning. Acting with self‑less (Nishkama) attitude fulfills duty and liberates the person; acting with desire (Sakama) binds the person. The present section analyses duty performed with self‑less attitude. Therefore the term “iṣṭakāma” (desired material) which indicates a Sakama attitude is not appropriate here. Here the term means “yajña” (duty‑action). 1. It should be understood that by the Lord’s command and His power Brahmā creates the progeny. Hence truly the original creator of the universe is the Lord (Gītā 4.13; 17.23). 2. The word “iṣṭa” is formed from the root “yaj” with the suffix “‑kta,” denoting yajña (duty‑action), and the word “kāma” is formed from the root “kam” with the suffix “‑aṇ,” denoting material (object). 3. In the preceding verse the Lord said that apart from yajña, a person entangled in actions performed with desire becomes bound; and in the thirteenth verse it is also said that those who act for themselves (with desire) eat only sin. Thus both earlier and later verses stress renunciation of desire, so the middle verses (10, 11, 12) should also stress renunciation of desire. If “iṣṭakāma” were taken to mean “desired material,” the passage would be contradictory, because actions performed to obtain desired material are, in the Lord’s view, binding. Therefore “iṣṭakāma” means “material necessary for duty” only.

[ Verse 10-11 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

The karmayogi is ever ready to serve or benefit others. Consequently, according to the decree of the creator Brahma, he never lacks the material, capability, or bodily necessities required for serving others. These useful items are constantly provided to him with ease. As per Brahma’s law, every individual who receives the means for performing his duty‑action obtains them completely; no one ever possesses an incomplete set of resources for duty‑fulfilment. Since Brahma has fixed the rule for performing duty‑action, the provision of sufficient material depends solely on him. In reality, the human body is not meant merely for sensual enjoyment: “ehi tana kara phala viṣaya na bhāī” (Manusmṛti 7.44.1). Therefore, no scripture commands “enjoy worldly pleasures,” nor does society grant a free licence to indulge. On the contrary, both scripture and society command the propagation of happiness to others. For example, a father is enjoined to nurture his son, but there is no injunction that a son must serve his father. The same understanding applies to sons, wives, and other relationships. The karmayogi constantly maintains the attitude of giving, never of taking, because the desire to take binds the mind. This attachment hinders both spiritual welfare and the acquisition of material goods. Experience shows that those who cling to receiving find no one willing to give them anything. Hence Brahma declares that a person can advance only by performing duty‑action selflessly, without any desire for reward. “deVān bhāvayatane” – here the word “deva” is inclusive; it signifies all beings—human, divine, sage, ancestors, etc. The purpose of the karmayogi is to bring happiness to all sentient beings through his duty‑action. Accordingly, Brahma orders humanity to perform a sacrificial duty‑action that uplifts all creatures. By fulfilling one’s own duty, a person automatically attains personal welfare (Bhagavad Gita Chapter 18 Verse 45). Humans alone are fully authorized to preach the observance of duty‑action, and they alone possess the freedom to act; therefore they must use this freedom wisely. “te devā bhāvayantu vaḥ” – just as trees and vines naturally bear flowers and fruit, they produce abundant blossoms when given fertilizer and water. Similarly, worship and sacrifice strengthen the gods, making their actions just and effective. When humans neglect to honor the gods through their duty‑action, the gods lose their support, leading to a decline in their own performance of duty. This shortfall precipitates cosmic disturbances such as droughts or floods. “parasparaṁ bhāvayantaḥ” – this does not mean that we should serve only those who serve us. Rather, irrespective of whether another serves us, we must serve him through our own duty. What the other does or does not do, whether he brings us joy or sorrow, is irrelevant; focusing on another’s duty distracts us from our own and leads to our downfall. It is not our right to compel others to perform their duties. Our sole responsibility is to fulfil our own duty, thereby bringing happiness to all. In service we must not retain even a small portion of our understanding, ability, time, or material for ourselves; otherwise all relational bonds will be severed. All worldly relationships—parents, wife, children, brothers, sisters, etc.—must be served. These relationships are not for our personal pleasure. According to the nature of each relationship, we must serve and bring happiness within the bounds of propriety. Expecting anything from them or claiming a right over them is a grave error. We are indebted to them, and our birth exists to repay that debt. Thus, by serving our relatives selflessly, we discharge our obligations.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 3 ]

This is our foremost necessary duty. Service leads us to experience the divine consciousness. Therefore it is improper to imagine exaggeration in the words of Prajapati Brahmaji. We must serve everyone, but those relatives for whom we bear responsibility should be served first. The body, senses, mind, intellect, material objects, etc., are neither ours nor for our own use—this is the principle. Consequently, by performing each one's own duty, the progress of one another automatically follows. **Duty and Right – a profound matter**  
Karmayoga occurs only when a person, while faithfully performing his duty, protects the rights of others. For example, serving one's parents is the son's duty and the parents' right. Whatever is another's right is our duty. Hence each person must, through his duty, protect the rights of others and must not look at another's duty. Observing another's duty causes a person to become devoid of his own duty, because seeing another's duty is not our duty. The implication is that doing another's welfare is our duty and his right. Although rights are subordinate to duty, a person should not even consider his own right; rather, he should renounce his own right. One should perform his duty solely for the protection of another's right. Seeing another's duty and accumulating one's own right leads to great downfall in this world and the next. The present unrest, discord, and conflict in homes and society stem from the fact that people demand their rights but do not fulfill their duties. Hence Brahmaji instructs gods and humans that doing each other's welfare is your duty. ‘Shreyah paramavapsyatha’ – there is a common belief that the statement about attaining supreme welfare here is an exaggeration, but in reality it is not. If anyone doubts, he can verify it himself. Just as a custodian who returns an heirloom no longer has any relation with the heirloom or its owner, similarly, when one dedicates worldly objects to the service of the world, one ceases to have any relation with the world and its objects. The moment the perceived connection with the world is severed, the principle holds that as long as a person acts for himself, his actions never cease and he remains bound by them. The true work is that which one never does for oneself. Not doing anything for oneself also prevents sinful conduct, because sin arises from desire (Chapter 3, Verse 33). Therefore, a seeker who wishes his own welfare should, in accordance with the scriptures, abandon desire for fruits and attachment, and eagerly perform his duty‑action; then welfare is automatically attained. Renouncing one's desire benefits only the world. One who, out of attachment, indulges in enjoyment to satisfy his desire harms himself (causing his own downfall) and also harms those who lack material enjoyment, i.e., causes suffering. This is because seeing a person with material enjoyment naturally makes a deprived person feel the pain of lacking that enjoyment. Thus, a person who enjoys personal pleasure can never escape violence. Conversely, seeing a person walking the selfless path brings immediate peace to others, because everyone has equal right to selfless wealth. The conclusion is that if a person renounces desire and attachment and continues to perform his duty‑action, he will inevitably attain supreme welfare as Brahmaji states. There is no doubt. Here, the attainment of supreme welfare is described primarily for humans, not for gods, because the gods were not created to pursue their own welfare. Humans perform actions, and gods were created to dispense the results of those actions, provide the material for action, and receive the fruits of each one's virtuous deeds. It is not the case that the gods give material for selfless action. However, even among those gods, if any develop a desire for their own welfare, there is no prohibition on that welfare; i.e., if someone wishes his own welfare, he may pursue it. [ Verse 12 ]  
* Seeker’s Life‑Giving *

If there is no prohibition, how can there be a prohibition for the gods (who, even when they dwell in the realm of merit, have the sole purpose of continual enjoyment) to save themselves? This is because they generally lack a desire for their own welfare. **Appendix (Parishishta) meaning** – Human beings belong to the realm of action, while there are eighty‑four lakh (8.4 million) other realms: those of the gods, of demonic beings, of various other enjoy‑realms, etc. A person driven by desire goes to heaven merely to experience enjoyments. Hence the divine beings, without cultivating a self‑less attitude, perform their duty and keep the cosmic order; therefore the discussion of welfare must be understood as applying to humans. Liberation is natural; bondage is unnatural. The human realm exists for the purpose of one’s own welfare. Consequently, a person who performs his prescribed duty automatically attains welfare – “by mutual contemplation one obtains the supreme good.” No new work is required for welfare; whatever work one is already doing, if performed without selfishness, pride, or desire for fruit and dedicated to the benefit of others, results in welfare. Even without self‑lessness, merely fulfilling one’s duty leads to the attainment of heavenly and other virtuous worlds. The heavens that are attained by performing great sacrifices can be attained by a Kshatriya solely by performing his prescribed duty – warfare. Just as Brahmā has instructed the gods and humans to act for each other’s benefit, the four varnas must likewise understand the principle of mutual benefit. When each varna performs its own prescribed duties for the welfare of the others, they will attain the highest welfare. The entire creation is arranged so that nothing belongs to the self; everything belongs to the other – “this is Brahman’s, not mine.” A devoted wife exists for her husband, not for herself. A woman’s body gives pleasure to a man, but not to herself; a man’s body gives pleasure to a woman, but not to himself. A mother’s milk is for the child, not for herself, and the child’s actions bring joy to the mother, not to the child. Parents exist for their offspring, and the offspring exist for the parents. The listener exists for the speaker, and the speaker exists for the listener. The implication is: do not seek personal pleasure; give pleasure to others. Creation is not for enjoyment, but for liberation. Even the gods can act for the benefit of others by renouncing selfishness; thus sages such as Narada appear among the gods. Although no one is forbidden by the Lord, the primary and self‑appointed guardian of welfare is the human being. A possible doubt: if we do good to others, but the other does not reciprocate and harms us, how can “mutual contemplation” occur? The answer is that when we do good to others, the other will be unable to harm us because we will have removed the power to do so. Even if the other attempts harm, remorse and tears will follow. If the other harms us, many who share our empathy and goodwill will arise. In reality there is no script for harming another; only humans, driven by hatred, cause harm. “Mutual contemplation” is a human principle; its absence is the source of human suffering. **Sanskrit verse (with transliteration and word‑by‑word meaning)**

iṣṭān‑bhogān‑hi‑vaḥ devā‑dāsyante yajñabhāvitaḥ |  
tair‑dattān‑apradāyai‑bhyo yo bhunkti stena eva saḥ || 12 ||

- **iṣṭān** – desired, chosen enjoyments  
- **bhogān** – enjoyments, pleasures  
- **hi** – indeed, certainly  
- **vaḥ** – they (referring to the gods)  
- **devā** – gods  
- **dāsyante** – become servants, serve  
- **yajñabhāvitaḥ** – imbued with the spirit of sacrifice (yajña)  
- **tair** – by them (the gods)  
- **dattān** – given, bestowed  
- **apradāyai** – without giving, ungranted  
- **bhyo** – to (the recipients)  
- **yo** – who  
- **bhunkti** – consumes, enjoys  
- **stena** – thief, one who takes without right  
- **eva** – only, precisely  
- **saḥ** – he, that person

Thus the verse teaches: “The gods, filled with sacrificial spirit, become servants to the desired enjoyments; the one who partakes of what is given without giving in return is nothing but a thief.”

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Commentary – “iṣṭān‑bhogān hi vo devā” (the gods indeed give you the enjoyments you desire). The phrase “iṣṭabhoga” cannot be understood merely as “desired material objects”. In the preceding (eleventh) verse the attainment of supreme welfare is mentioned, and verse twelve explains the means for that welfare. As long as one is attached to worldly enjoyments, supreme welfare can never arise. Hence the word “iṣṭa” (desired) is derived from the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), and the word “bhoga” (enjoyment) signifies the essential material needed for sacrifice. Consequently the meaning of the line is: the gods will continually provide you with the material required for performing yajña (the duty‑action). The expression “yajñabhāvitāḥ devā” (the gods imbued with the spirit of sacrifice) implies that the deities, considering it their right, supply humans with the necessary material; it is the humans who must perform their duty. In the clause “tair‑dattān‑pradāyaiḥ yo bhūṅkte” the author of the Brahma‑sūtras uses the term “te devāḥ” (those gods) because before them stood humans, not other gods. Here the word “ebhyaḥ” (from “idam”) functions as a proximate‑demonstrative, indicating that all that is near to the Lord is near to Him (see Chapter 7, Verse 26). This shows that the Lord’s words begin from this point. The verb “bhūṅkte” does not refer only to eating food; it denotes the use of the entire body’s necessities—food, clothing, wealth, shelter, etc.—for one’s own pleasure. The body is received from mother and father, and its nourishment also comes from them. Knowledge is received from teachers. The gods supply everyone with the material required for duty‑action. The rishis give knowledge. The ancestors point out the means for human comfort. Animals, birds, trees, vines, and the like sacrifice themselves for the happiness of others (although they may not consciously realize they are performing charity, their actions automatically benefit others). Thus everything we possess—strength, ability, position, authority, wealth, property, etc.—has been received from others. Therefore these should be offered in selfless service to those from whom they came. The body, senses, mind, intellect and all other substances are obtained from the world. They are never truly ours, nor will they ever become ours. To consider them as one’s own and to enjoy them is bondage. The simple remedy for this bondage is to regard the donors of these substances as the true owners and to serve them with a selfless attitude. This is our highest duty. Often a seeker’s mind generates the feeling that if we serve the world we will become attached to it and become trapped. Yet the Lord’s words demonstrate that the cause of entrapment is not service but the desire to take for oneself. Hence, abandoning the motive of taking and, like the gods, bringing happiness to others is the supreme duty of humanity. In the doctrine of karma‑yoga, the proper use of acquired material, capability, time and discernment is prescribed. Desiring more than what has already been obtained (new material, etc.) contradicts the principle of karma‑yoga. Therefore the material already received should be employed solely for the benefit of others; no excess is required. Logically, one can hope only as much as one’s own power permits; how can the Lord or the gods expect more? “stena eva sa” – in the phrase “sa‑stenaḥ” the singular indicates that a person who neglects his duty appropriates the share of material (food, water, clothing, etc.) that belongs to everyone, keeping it for himself without giving it to others. Such a person is a thief. A man who, without sharing any portion, consumes everything alone is a thief; likewise, a man who seeks any personal gain by converting material into service for the purpose of receiving honor or prestige is also a thief in that respect. The inner self of such a person can never be pure or peaceful. The body, being a part of the total world, is subject to the rule “1‑ bhuj‑pālanābhyavahāra‑yoḥ” (from *Siddhānta‑Kaumudī* 1548). The root *bhuj* has two meanings—‘to sustain’ and ‘to consume’. Here the sense of ‘to sustain’ (to take) is appropriate. 2‑ The non‑causative form of the root *bhuj* yields the verb “bhūṅkte” (to consume), meaning to take an object for one’s own purpose.

[ Verse 12 ]  
* Seeker - Sanjivani *

It is not separate and cannot become separate; because, on the contrary, the more understanding, time, capability and resources we possess, the more we serve others, the more welfare inevitably results, and even without desiring material objects, comfort, prestige, honor, etc., they begin to be attained. However, a Karmayogi does not have desires for honor, prestige, etc.; because such desires and sensual enjoyment are the very cause of bondage. The part of the whole is called the individual (vyakti). Hence, regarding the individual (the body) as one's own and the whole (the world) as not one's own is the cause of attachment, aversion and other dualities, and this is ego, personality or disparity. Through the practice of Karmayoga, all such attachment and aversion are smoothly eliminated. This is because the Karmayogi maintains the attitude that whatever he does is not for himself, but solely for the world. Moreover, a profound point is that the Karmayogi performs all actions not even for his own welfare, but solely for the welfare of the world. Considering one's own welfare as separate from the welfare of all gives rise to personality and disparity, which hinders the aspirant's advancement. The body, senses, mind, intellect and everything we possess have all been received from the world. Using the objects obtained from the world solely for selfish fulfillment is not honest. **Special point concerning duty**

The sole purpose of Hindu culture is the welfare of humanity. For this purpose, Brahma (the primordial creator) commands humans, with selfless attitude, to bring happiness to one another through the performance of their respective duties (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 3, Verse 10). - “How can I obtain happiness?” – solely desiring this leads a person to abandon duty and fall. Therefore, the Karmayogi must always maintain the attitude, “How can others obtain happiness?”

Within the family, parents, siblings, wife, children and all members should consider each other's welfare. Often the servant makes the mistake of thinking, “I serve,” “I give things,” and takes false pride. In reality, the servant gives to the served exactly what the served needs. Just as a mother’s milk is not for herself but for the child, likewise everything a person possesses is not for himself but for others. Therefore, a person has no right to cherish the acquired material as his own or for himself. Even if he cherishes it, the material will not remain forever; only the bond of attachment will persist. For this reason, the Lord says that one who claims ownership of objects and enjoys them himself is a thief. Deities, sages, ancestors, animals, birds, trees and vines are all naturally inclined to do service. Humans are indebted to them for the cooperation they receive. To be freed from this debt, the doctrine of the Panchamahayajna (Rishiyajna, Devayajna, Bhutayajna, Pitriyajna and Manushyajna) is prescribed. Man is the only being who can, with intelligence, satisfy everyone through his duties and actions. Hence the greatest responsibility rests on humanity. This grants a freedom that, when properly utilized, leads to the highest merit. Family members such as brothers, sisters, mothers, etc., all perform actions; however, their great mistake is that they act under the domination of desire, affection, attachment, selfishness, etc. Consequently, they gain neither worldly nor transcendental benefits, only loss. Acting selfishly for oneself creates conflict, strife, jealousy in the world and leads to downfall in the afterlife. When one serves others and then desires something in return, a relationship with objects and persons forms. Attaching selfish motive to any action makes that action trivial and binding. A selfish person is not regarded as good in the world. The one who desires receives no greater giving. Often it is observed that deities, etc., simply fulfill their duties. Even at home, possessions are hidden from the attached and pleasure‑seeking person. If a person does not fulfill his duty then

* “Even this body is not mine, nor is the whole earth mine.” (Maha‑Ashvamedhika 32.11) *

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]

The disturbance is not limited to the gods; it spreads throughout the three worlds. When the karmic yogi severs his connection with the body, natural calamities such as excessive rain, drought, earthquakes, famine, etc., begin to arise. In the twenty‑third and twenty‑fourth verses of Chapter 3, the Lord says that if He does not carefully observe His duty, all worlds will become corrupted and ruined. Just as a single broken wheel jolts an entire bull‑cart in motion, a single person who neglects his duty creates a contrary effect that impacts the whole creation. Conversely, when even one afflicted limb of the body heals, the entire body benefits; similarly, when a man faithfully performs his duty, the whole universe benefits automatically. Praja‑pati Brahma instructed both the deities and humans to fulfill their respective duties. The gods act within their limits; only humans, through ignorance, transgress those limits. They mistake the material possessions acquired for the purpose of serving others as their personal right. Although humanity has been granted freedom to escape the bondage of endless karmic cycles, it misuses this liberty, clinging to karma and its fruits. Consequently, new bonds are created, trapping the individual and preparing him for further suffering in many future births. Therefore, a person must employ whatever material resources he has for the service of the three worlds—that is, devote those resources to God, the deities, the sages, ancestors, humans, and all beings. He should regard the world not as his own but as belonging to the world, and dedicate himself to its service. His vision remains fixed on the imperishable Self, not on the perishable body. One whose vision is fixed on the body can doubt how a karmic yogi will sustain his life. As long as the desire for enjoyment persists, the wish to live and the fear of death remain. The desire for enjoyment does not reside in the karmic yogi, because all his actions are performed not for himself but for the service of others. Hence the karmic yogi does not concern himself with his own livelihood; the question “How will I sustain my life?” never arises for him. In reality, the one whose heart does not need the world finds that the world provides for his sustenance. When the lives of all creatures—animals, birds, insects, vines, trees, and even the simplest beings—are provided for, how can a human, who expends all material resources for the welfare of beings, lack provision for his own livelihood? By the boundless grace of the Lord who sustains everything, material provisions are equally available to all creatures. A clear example is the mother’s body: where only blood circulates, sweet, nourishing milk is spontaneously produced for the infant’s sustenance. Thus, whether by destiny or divine grace, the material needed for human livelihood appears automatically. There should be no doubt, anxiety, sorrow, or contemplation about it. In the Lord’s kingdom, even the most sinful and atheistic individuals receive sustenance. The doubt that arises is only about the body; therefore, questioning the karmic yogi’s livelihood because he identifies himself with the body is itself a mistake. The real question is: how can the karmic yogi’s livelihood be maintained when all his acquired material is wholly devoted to the service of others? **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – The term “Yajna‑bhavita” means “nourished, worshipped, and enriched by sacrifice.” Because a human can nourish beings in the upper, middle, and lower worlds, he is placed in the middle world solely to benefit all. Hence humanity is entitled to welfare. **Relation (Sambandh)** – In Verse 9 the Lord states, “Acts performed for sacrifice are not binding.” He thus commands the performance of sacrificial duty. By reinforcing this command with Brahma‑ji’s words, the Lord, in Verse 9, affirms his own statements and, in the following verses, gives a clear exposition of the results of performing or not performing the sacrificial (duty‑related) action.

[ Verse 13 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

**Sanskrit shloka (transliteration & meaning)**  
yajña‑śiṣṭa‑āśinaḥ santo mucyante sarva‑kilbiṣaiḥ |  
bhuñjate te tvaghaṁ pāpā ye pacanty ātma‑kāraṇāt ||13||

“Saints who subsist on the remnants of the sacrifice are liberated from all sins; they enjoy the imperishable (agham), whereas the sinners who act for self‑interest become bound by sin.”

**Explanation**

The saints who have tasted the residue of the sacrifice (yajña‑shesh, i.e., the state of yoga) are the highest‑minded persons. Because they have experienced this residue, they are freed from every sin and become completely liberated. Their actions, though performed, do not bind them. In contrast, those who act out of selfish motive “cook” (perform) for the sake of the self; they feed on the agham (the sin) and therefore become bound. Even deeds done with desire for reward become binding because they generate fruit. When one experiences the equanimity that is the remainder of the sacrifice, both sin and merit disappear, as the Bhagavad‑Gita states: “The wise discard both good and bad deeds” (Gita 2.50). Yajña‑shishṭa‑ashina saints are freed from all forms of bondage that arise from duty‑bound actions. When sinful deeds are performed selflessly, what remains is yoga or equanimity (yajña‑shesh). In Karma‑yoga, material activity is the instrument of action; thus, dedicating one’s service to the world makes the activity itself a yajna. After the yajna is completed, the residual “yoga” becomes one’s own. This yoga (equanimity) is the yajña‑shesh, which the Lord calls “amrita” in Chapter 4, Verse 31: “yajña‑shishtāmṛta‑bhujaḥ.”

The phrase “mucyante sarva‑kilbiṣaiḥ” uses the plural “kilbiṣaiḥ” to denote all sins, i.e., all bonds. The addition of “sarva” emphasizes that, upon experiencing yajña‑shesh, no form of bondage remains. All accumulated, destined, and ongoing karmas are annihilated (Gita 4.23). When all karmas are destroyed, one attains the eternal Brahman (Gita 4.31). The true cause of bondage is desire. Desire is the root of every sin (Gita 3.37); therefore, its renunciation is essential. Desire is not an independent entity; it arises from a perceived lack, but the Self (Sat) is never lacking. The sense of lack appears only when the individual mistakenly identifies the Self with the body and other non‑self (asat) objects. Consequently, the desire for non‑self objects can never satisfy the perceived lack. A seeker must realize that only actions that arise from beginnings and end in destructions produce transient substances; such impermanent substances can never fulfill the lack. Hence, seeking them is a mistake. In Chapter 3, Verse 9, the Lord declares that actions performed for the sake of yajna become binding elsewhere, and in Chapter 4, Verse 23, He states that all actions of a yajna‑performer are annihilated. These verses convey the same teaching expressed by “sarva‑kilbiṣaiḥ”: the experience of yajña‑shesh naturally leads to the cessation of desire. When desire ceases, accumulated karmas are destroyed. As long as the body persists, destiny brings favorable and unfavorable circumstances, yet the person remains unaffected—this is the dissolution of destined karma. When the longing for fruit disappears, ongoing actions become non‑action, i.e., they no longer yield results—this is the dissolution of active karma.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Yes, by never regarding the body and other material objects that are called “mine” as belonging to oneself or for oneself, and by offering them in the service of others, one automatically severs one’s attachment to these objects, and thereby immediately perceives one’s true divine nature. No sense of lack remains. The person whose mind harbors no notion (desire) of any kind of lack is, while still alive, already liberated from the world. The expression “pachanti‑ātmakāraṇāt” (the desire to obtain anything for oneself, i.e., selfishness, craving, affection, attachment, and even the slightest feeling of being called good) falls under the term “ātmakāraṇāt” (self‑caused, Atman). The greater the selfish intellect in a person, the more sinful he becomes. Here the word “pachanti” is used in a broader sense, not merely “to cook” but to denote all worldly activities such as eating, drinking, walking, sitting, etc. There is no affection‑attachment. [ Chapter 3

A human being must experience the fruits of his own actions; however, the effect of those actions falls upon the entire world. The person who acts “for himself” becomes detached from his duty, and when people become detached from their duty, great calamities such as famine, epidemics, and death arise in the nation. Therefore it is proper for a person to do nothing for himself, to consider nothing as his own, and to desire nothing for himself. Taking refuge in the results of action (the produced and destroyed material objects) is included in “cooking for oneself”. Hence, in the first verse of the sixth chapter, Lord Krishna says “anāśritaḥ karma‑phalam” (unattached to the fruits of action) to instruct the karmayogi not to rely on the results of action. Only when one becomes completely unattached does a person cease to do anything for himself and thereby attains yoga. “bhunjate te tvaghaṁ pāpāḥ” – in these words the Lord censures, in refined language, those who act “for themselves”. By acting for oneself one accumulates so much sin that even after enduring the suffering of 48 million wombs and countless hells, the sin is not exhausted; it remains as a stored residue. The human womb is an extraordinary field in which any seed of sin or merit sown yields fruit for many births. Consequently, a person must immediately resolve, “I will no longer commit sin (action for myself).” This resolution carries great power; indeed, when one makes a firm determination to move toward the Supreme (Paramātma), sinful actions automatically cease. A selfish person who seeks his own interest “cooks for himself” (acts) either for himself or for others, but in reality he cooks only for himself. Conversely, the seeker who renounces selfishness and performs duty‑action for the sake of duty, “cooks for the body called his own” or for others, but in reality he cooks for others. Whatever material wealth we have received from the world, placing it in the service of the world rather than in our own pleasure is “cooking for oneself”. Even the smallest portion of the world that we consider as our own and as for ourselves is a great sin. Yet, by not treating the body as our own, and by providing it with food, water, clothing, etc., as needed, and by not allowing it to become lazy, indulgent, or a mere enjoyer, we are serving the body. Appendix note – A person possesses body, ability, position, authority, knowledge, strength, etc., all of which are given and will be taken away. Hence they are not for oneself but for the service of others. This reflects the complete principle of Indian culture: just as all organs of the body exist for the body’s welfare, all human beings exist for the welfare of the world. A person, regardless of nation, dress, caste, or ashrama, can promote his own well‑being smoothly by serving others through his actions. All the special qualities we possess are for others, not for ourselves. If every person acted thus, no one would remain bound; all would become liberated. When the things we have received are offered in service to others, what expense is incurred for our own household? Welfare will be attained freely. Apart from this, there is no further need for any action for liberation. One’s responsibility is to devote exactly what one possesses—material goods, abilities, and capacities—to service; there is no responsibility beyond that, nor can a person do more than he possesses. If we expend all that we have in service, welfare will be complete. In reality, human birth is both the first and the final birth of all births. If a person attains the Supreme (Paramātma), this final birth is the same; if he does not attain the Supreme, the first birth of endless cycles is also this same human birth.

[ Verse 14-15 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

In reality the body serves only the world; it has no purpose of its own, because the body is not even for us. The body is needed merely to perform some activity. If we do nothing, what need is there for the body? Hence, using the body to do something for oneself is a fault. With the material that is given to us we cannot act for ourselves; rather, through it we can serve the world. The body is a part of the world; therefore whatever comes from it is for the world. Beyond the world the body, the senses, the mind and the intellect cannot go; they cannot be separated from the world. Thus acting for one’s own pleasure is not humaneness but demonic (asur) behavior! Truly, a human being is one who works for the welfare of others. One who works for his own pleasure feeds on sin, remains perpetually sorrowful, whereas one who works for the benefit of others is freed from all sins and becomes eternally happy – “Those who partake of the remnants of sacrifice attain the immortal Brahman” (Bhagavad‑Gītā 4.31). **Connection** – “Why do you bind me to terrible action?” (Arjuna’s question). In answer, the Lord gives many reasons and, in the next two verses, establishes the necessity of performing sacrifice (duty‑action) for the protection of the cosmic cycle. ---

### Verse 14

**Sanskrit (transliterated)**  
Annamād bhavanti bhūtāni ; parjanyād annasambhavah . Yajñād bhavati parjanya ; yajñaḥ karmasamu‑dhavah . **English meaning**  
All beings arise from food; food arises from rain. Rain arises from sacrifice; sacrifice is born of action. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- *Annamād* – from food  
- *bhavanti* – arise, become  
- *bhūtāni* – all beings (creatures)  
- *parjanyād* – from rain  
- *annasambhavah* – origin in food  
- *Yajñād* – from sacrifice (the act of offering)  
- *bhavati* – arises, is produced  
- *parjanya* – rain  
- *yajñaḥ* – sacrifice (duty‑action)  
- *karmasamu‑dhavah* – born of action (karmas)

### Verse 15

**Sanskrit (transliterated)**  
Karma brahmodbhavam viddhi Brahma aksharasamu‑dhavah . Tasmāt sarvagatam Brahma nityam yajñe pratiṣṭhitam . **English meaning**  
Know that action is born of Brahman, and Brahman is born of the imperishable (Akshara). Therefore the all‑pervading Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice. - *Karma* – action, duty‑action  
- *brahmodbhavam* – born of Brahman  
- *viddhi* – know, understand  
- *Brahma* – the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman)  
- *aksharasamu‑dhavah* – born of the imperishable (Akshara)  
- *Tasmāt* – therefore  
- *sarvagatam* – all‑pervading, universal  
- *nityam* – eternally, always  
- *yajñe* – in sacrifice  
- *pratiṣṭhitam* – established, fixed

### Explanatory notes (parishishta‑bhāva)

- All creatures are generated from **food** (annam). The material that sustains a being is called *ann* (food). For example, a soil‑dwelling worm lives on soil; soil is its *ann*. - Four categories of beings—*jarāyuja* (humans, animals), *udbhijja* (trees, etc.), *aṇḍaja* (birds, snakes, insects) and *svedaja* (lice, etc.)—are all produced from food and survive by food. - Consequently, the all‑pervading Supreme (Brahman) eternally resides in sacrifice (duty‑action). - “*Parjanyād annasambhavah*” – the origin of all edible substances is water. Grass, grains, etc., are water‑based; even the formation of soil depends on water. Food, water, clothing, shelter—every material needed for bodily sustenance—has a water component, and water’s source is rain. - “*Yajñād bhavati parjanya*” – the term *yajña* primarily denotes the act of offering. In the context of the Gītā’s doctrine and the chapter on Karma‑yoga, *yajña* signifies the totality of prescribed duties. Sacrifice therefore implies renunciation (the root *adh‑* “to eat” + *kṛ* “to do”) leading to the word *ann* (food) as explained in the Aṣṭādhyāyī (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.68). - Footnote 1: From the root *ad* “to eat” with the suffix *‑kṛ* the term *ann* (food) is derived; otherwise the root would yield *jagdh* (“to burn”). - Footnote 2: “All beings are indeed born of food; they live by food” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.2).

Srimad Bhagavad Gita
*
[ Chapter 3

is paramount. In offering oblations, there is renunciation of grains, ghee, etc.; in giving charity, there is renunciation of material goods; in performing austerity, there is renunciation of one's own comfort and enjoyment; in performing duty (karma), there is renunciation of selfishness and personal ease. Therefore, the word 'Yajna' signifies all scripturally ordained activities such as ritual sacrifice (havan), charity, and austerity.

There is a story in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: Prajapati Brahma, having created devas (gods), humans, and asuras (demons), imparted to them the single syllable 'Da' (द). Owing to the abundance of enjoyment available to gods, they understood 'Da' to mean 'Damyata' (exercise self-control). Due to the hoarding tendency among humans, they understood 'Da' to mean 'Datta' (give in charity). Because demons possessed a strong inclination toward violence and causing distress to others, they understood 'Da' to mean 'Dayadhvam' (be compassionate). Thus, the underlying intent of the instruction given to devas, humans, and demons alike was to act for the welfare of others. When rain clouds thunder 'Da, Da, Da...', even today it serves as a reminder of Brahma's instruction (control yourselves, donate, show mercy) regarding one's duties (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Chapter 5, Brahmana 2, Mantras 1–3).

'Why should we fall behind in fulfilling our duty?' Thinking thus, peacocks also began to call out. Hearing the peacocks' calls, the clouds thought: 'Why are peacocks calling today without hearing our thunder?' Learning the whole matter, the clouds thought: 'Why should we shrink back from our duty?' And they too began to thunder. Hearing the thundering clouds, Indra wondered what was happening. Upon learning that they were performing their duty, Indra thought: 'Why should I lag behind in performing my duty?' So thinking, Indra ordered the clouds to rain down.

'Yajnah karma-samudbhavah'—all scripturally prescribed secular and spiritual duties performed without desire for results are called 'Yajna'. For a brahmachari (celibate student), performing daily agnihotra is 'Yajna'. Similarly, cooking meals for the family is 'Yajna' for women*. If an expert in Ayurveda practices medicine solely for the welfare of people, that very practice becomes 'Yajna' for him. Likewise, a student can regard his studies and a merchant his trade as 'Yajna' (provided it is carried out selflessly for the benefit of others). Thus, all duty-bound actions performed in accordance with scriptural ordinances while respecting the boundaries of varna, ashrama, place, and time are of the nature of 'Yajna'. Whatever form Yajna takes, it is generated through action.

When physicians purify toxic substances such as arsenic or marking nut and administer them as medicine, those poisons become like nectar and cure severe diseases. Similarly, desires, mine-ness, attachment, partiality, inequality, selfishness, and pride act like poison within actions. Once this poisonous element is eliminated from actions, those actions become ambrosial and cure the great disease of the cycle of birth and death. Such ambrosial actions alone are called 'Yajna'.

How does performing one's duty lead to rainfall? Example and action naturally have a greater impact on others than mere words—'yad yad acarati sresthas tat tad evatero janah' (Gita 3.21). When human beings perform their respective duties, it influences the devas as well, prompting them to fulfill their duties and bring rain (Gita 3.11). In this context, there is a story: There were four young peasant boys. Even when the month of Ashadha arrived, there was no rain. They reasoned: 'It is time to plow the fields; even if rain hasn't fallen, let us fulfill our duty on time.' Thinking thus, they went to the fields and started plowing. Seeing them plow, peacocks thought: 'Rain hasn't fallen yet, why are they plowing?' Upon learning that the boys were performing their duty, the peacocks thought...

'Karma brahmodbhavam viddhi'—the Vedas describe the method of performing duty-bound actions (Gita 4.32). Because humans acquire knowledge of how to perform duties from the Vedas, actions are said to originate from the Vedas.

* Vaivahiko vidhih strinam samskaro vaidikah smritah | Patiseva gurau vaso grihartho 'gniparikriya || (Manusmriti 2.67)
'For women, marriage itself is declared to be the sacred Vedic rite (sacred thread ceremony), serving one's husband is residence in the gurukula (study of Vedas), and household duties constitute agnihotra (yajna).'

Under the term 'Veda', besides the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda, there are also included Smritis, Puranas, and Itihasas (Ramayana, Mahabharata, etc.)...

* Sadhaka-Sanjivani *
Verse 16 ]
Mahabharata), as well as the experiential words of Acharyas of various traditions, and all righteous scriptures aligned with the Vedas should be accepted.

'Brahmaaksarasamudbhavam'—Here the word 'Brahma' signifies the Vedas. The Vedas originated from the Supreme Lord of Sacchidananda (Gita 17.23). Thus, the Lord is the root of all. From the Lord originate the Vedas. The Vedas describe the method of performing duty. Human beings perform that duty according to scriptural ordinance. Through the performance of duty-bound actions, Yajna arises, and from Yajna comes rain. Rain produces food, food sustains creatures, and among those creatures, humans perform Yajna by discharging their duties*. Thus this cosmic wheel keeps revolving.

'Tasmat sarva-gatam brahma nityam yajne pratisthitam'—Here the word 'Brahma' refers to the Imperishable (saguna-nirakara Supreme Being). Therefore, the Supreme Being is all-pervading (sarva-gata), not the Vedas. Even though all-pervading, the Supreme Being is ever-present in a special manner within 'Yajna' (duty-bound action). The meaning is that wherever duty is performed with a desireless attitude, God resides there. Therefore, human beings seeking God-realization can easily attain Him through their duties—'svakarmana tam abhyarcya siddhim vindati manavah' (Gita 18.46).

197

Question—If God is all-pervading, why is He said to be eternally established specifically in Yajna? Is He not eternally established elsewhere?

Answer—God is indeed eternally present equally everywhere. He is neither temporary nor localized. That is why He is called 'sarva-gata' (all-pervading) here. Saying He is eternally established in Yajna (duty) implies that Yajna is the locus of His realization. Even though water is present everywhere beneath the ground, it is accessible through a well, not everywhere. Even though water is present throughout a pipe, it is obtained only where there is a tap or opening. Similarly, though all-pervading, God is realized through Yajna.

By acting for oneself and assuming a relationship with inert matter (body, etc.), an obstacle (veil) arises in realizing the all-pervading God. By performing one's duty selflessly solely for the benefit of others, this obstacle is removed, and the ever-attained God is naturally realized. This is why the Lord is placing special emphasis on performing duty through various arguments to Arjuna, who wished to shrink from his duty.

Context—The responsibility of moving according to the cosmic wheel—that is, performing one's duty—rests solely upon human beings. Therefore, the Lord reprimands in the following verse the person who does not perform his duty.

Evam pravartitam cakram nanuvartayatiha yah |
Aghayur indriyaramo mogham partha sa jivati || 16 ||

partha = O son of Kunti (Partha)!
yah = a person who
iha = in this world
evam = in this manner
pravartitam = set in motion (from tradition)
cakram = cosmic wheel
na, anuvartayati = does not follow,
sah = he
indriyarama = delighting in sense pleasures through senses
aghayuh = leads a sinful life (aghayu)
manusyah = human being
mogham = in vain
jivati = lives.

Commentary——'Partha'—Concluding the section begun in verse 9, the Lord addresses Arjuna as 'Partha', as if saying: "You are the son of that very Pritha (Kunti), who endured lifelong hardships yet fulfilled her duty. Therefore, neglect of duty should not come from you either. The battle which you call a dreadful act is not a dreadful act for you, but rather a Yajna (duty). Fulfilling it is acting in accordance with the cosmic wheel, and failing to fulfill it is acting contrary to the cosmic wheel."

* Through all non-human stationary and moving creatures, Yajna (welfare of others) happens naturally, but they cannot perform Yajna consciously. Only human beings can consciously perform Yajna, because humans alone possess the capability and right for it.

[ Chapter 3

acting according to the cosmic wheel; and failing to perform it is acting contrary to the cosmic wheel.

'Evam pravartitam cakram nanuvartayatiha yah'—just as when even a small part of a chariot wheel breaks, a severe jolt affects all parts of the chariot along with the rider and charioteer; similarly, a person who does not live in harmony with the cosmic wheel described in verses 14 and 15 creates an obstacle in the operation of the entire creation.

The world and the individual are not two alien entities. Just as there is an intimate relationship between the body and its limbs, so there is an intimate bond between the world and the individual. When an individual abandons desire, mine-ness, attachment, and egoism to perform their duty, happiness naturally flows to all creation.

'Indriyaramah'—a person who, possessed of desire, mine-ness, and attachment, indulges in sense pleasures through their senses is called here 'one who delights in sense pleasures'. Such a person is lower even than an animal; because an animal does not commit new sins, but rather moves toward purity by merely exhausting the fruits of past sins. In contrast, an 'indriyaraam' (sense-delighter) person commits new sins leading to moral downfall, and by disrupting the cosmic wheel, inflicts suffering on the entire universe.

'Aghayuh'—the life of a person who does not live in harmony with the cosmic wheel is purely sinful. This is because a person who indulges in sense enjoyment with a pleasure-seeking attitude cannot escape the sin of harm/violence. A selfish, arrogant person seeking luxury and accumulation harms others; therefore, their life is inherently sinful.

Goswami Tulsidas Ji says:
'Par drohi par dar rata par dhana par apabada |
Te nara pamvara papamaya deha dharem manujada ||' (Ramcharitmanas 7.39)
"Those men who harm others, covet others' wives, steal others' wealth, and slander others are wretched, sinful demons in human form."

'Mogham partha sa jivati'—censuring and reprimanding the person who fails to do his duty in refined language, the Lord says that such a person lives in vain in this world—meaning it were better if he died! The implication is that if he cannot bring happiness to creation by performing his duty, he should at least not cause distress. Just as during Lord Rama's exile, when the residents of Ayodhya visited Chitrakoot, the forest dwellers (Kols, Kirats, Bhils) told them: "That we do not steal your clothes and utensils is our greatest service to you" (Ramcharitmanas 2.251.2); similarly, if those who do not perform their duty refrain at least from disrupting the cosmic wheel, that itself is their service.

Regarding a person who does not align with the cosmic wheel, the Lord earlier stated: 'stena eva sah' (Gita 3.12), "he is indeed a thief", and 'bhunjate te tv agham' (Gita 3.13), "they eat only sin"; and now in this verse, calling him 'aghayur indriyarama' ("sinful in life and delighting in senses"), He declares his very living to be futile.

Goswami Tulsidas Ji Maharaj has also said:
'Teja krisanu rosa mahisesa | Agha avaguna dhana dhani dhanesa ||
Udaya keta sama hita sabahike | Kumbhakarana sama sovata nike ||' (Ramcharitmanas 1.4.3)

Appendix Sentiment—The description from verse 9 up to this point emphasizes serving others selflessly.

Context—The preceding verse reprimanded a person who does not perform his duty to sever connection with the world. But in the following two verses, the Lord describes the state of a great soul who has severed connection with the world by fulfilling his duty:

Yastvatmaratir eva syad atmatriptasca manavah |
Atmanyeva ca santustas tasya karyam na vidyate || 17 ||

Commentary——'Yastvatmaratir eva .... ca santustas tasya'—Here the word 'tu' (but) is used to highlight the extraordinary distinction of a great soul who has attained perfection through selfless action compared to the person described in the previous verse who fails to perform his duty.

As long as a person regards his relationship with the world as real, he considers his 'rati' (delight/love) to lie in sense pleasures and in wife, children, family, etc., his 'tripti' (satisfaction) in food and water, and his 'santusti' (contentment) in wealth. However, in these things, his delight, satisfaction, and contentment are neither ever complete nor ever continuous. This is because the world changes every moment, is inert, and perishable; whereas the 'Self' is ever uniform, conscious, and imperishable. The point is that the 'Self' has not even the slightest connection with the world. Therefore, how could the Self's delight, satisfaction, and contentment ever come from the world?

No person's love for the world remains forever—this is everyone's lived experience. The mutual love or attraction felt between husband and wife at the time of marriage wanes after having one or two children. In some cases, women even remark about their elderly husband: "It would be better if the old man died!" The satisfaction derived from eating food lasts only for a short time; the contentment a person feels upon acquiring wealth is also fleeting, because the greed for wealth keeps growing continuously. Thus, a deficiency always persists. The essence is that delight, satisfaction, and contentment can never remain permanent in the world. Human beings merely perceive an illusion of delight, satisfaction, and contentment in worldly objects, but it does not truly exist; if it did, disinterest, dissatisfaction, and discontentment would never arise again. By essential nature, delight, satisfaction, and contentment are self-evident. The Self is Existence (Sat). In Sat, there is never any non-existence—'na bhavo vidyate satah' (Gita 2.16); and without deficiency, no desire arises. Therefore, desirelessness in the Self is self-evident. But when the individual soul mistakenly considers its relationship with the world as real, it begins searching for delight, satisfaction, and contentment in the world, desiring worldly objects for this purpose. After desiring, when that object (wealth, etc.) is obtained, once the existing desire leaves the mind (before a new desire is born), one's state becomes desireless, and one experiences the joy of that desirelessness. However, by mistake, a person attributes that joy to the acquisition of the worldly object and calls that joy by the names of delight, satisfaction, and contentment. If that joy came from acquiring the object, then after receiving it, as long as the object remained, joy would persist forever, sorrow would never occur, and desire for objects would not arise again. But because complete (eternal) delight, satisfaction, and contentment can never be gained from worldly objects, and because attachment to the world persists, one begins making new desires again. When desire arises, one feels deficiency; and when the desired object is attained, one feels dependence. Therefore, a person filled with desire is ever miserable.

It is worth noting here that spiritual seekers consider desirelessness to be the root cause of happiness and desire to be the cause of sorrow; whereas worldly attached people consider acquiring objects to be happiness and non-acquisition to be sorrow. If an attached person were also to view reality with true insight like a seeker, they could quickly experience self-evident desirelessness.

Desire-bound persons are declared eligible for Karmayoga—'karmayogastu kaminam' (Shrimad Bhagavatam 11.20.7). The delight, satisfaction, and contentment of desire-bound persons lie in the world. Therefore, describing the state of selfless great souls perfected through Karmayoga, the Lord states that their delight, satisfaction, and contentment do not lie in the world like desire-bound persons, but in their own Self (Gita 2.55), which is already present by essential nature.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Although they are not separate, the various aspects of the world appear as distinct. Therefore, when a great soul becomes completely detached from the world, his love, satisfaction and contentment merge into a single principle (nature). [ Chapter 3

In reality, love, satisfaction and contentment are three different things— for society, for the nation and for the world. When one performs all duties for the whole, his attachment to the world is cut off. When the attachment to the world is entirely removed, no duty remains for him, because in his true nature no action occurs. Any action that does occur is only because of his relationship with the world and is performed through material objects. Hence, only those who are still bound to the world have any duty. The Lord uses the words “eva” and “ca” twice in this verse and once again in verse 18. This indicates that the love, satisfaction and contentment of the Karma‑yogi never lack any element, and no other requirement exists beyond the principle itself (Gita – Chapter 6, Verse 22). “tasyāḥ kāryaṁ na vidyate” – for a human being, whatever duty or action has been prescribed, its purpose is to attain the Supreme (Brahman) as the ultimate welfare. Once the goal is achieved by any means—Karma‑yoga, Jnana‑yoga or Bhakti‑yoga—there remains nothing further to do, to know or to obtain; that is the highest success of life. Karma arises when there is a desire to obtain something, and desire is born of lack. A perfected great soul knows no lack, so there is nothing for him to do. When the love, satisfaction and contentment of a great soul attained through Karma‑yoga become internal, the categories of “doer‑do‑able”, “known‑to‑be‑known” and “attainable‑to‑be‑attained” disappear, and he rises above all prohibitions. Although scriptural injunctions no longer govern him, all his actions remain naturally in accord with the scriptures and become exemplary for others. Here the phrase “tasyāḥ kāryaṁ na vidyate” does not imply that the great soul is completely devoid of any capacity for action. Even when nothing remains for him to act upon because of his detachment, actions arise automatically for the welfare of the world, as he identifies the body with “I” and “mine”. Just as the eyelids act for themselves, his duties of falling, rising, breathing and digesting food continue. Yet when even those self‑directed functions cease, the great soul, considering himself as the body, senses, mind and intellect, performs all scripturally‑approved ideal actions for the benefit of all beings—parents, spouse, children, family—without any sense of personal ownership. Appendix (Parishishta) – The Karma‑yogi, out of self‑lessness, performs all actions solely for the service of the world. Just as one worships the Ganga with Ganga‑water, dedicating the body, senses, mind, intellect and ego to the service of the world leaves only the pure, luminous nature. Hence his love, satisfaction and contentment reside in his very nature. Both worldly rules and prohibitions are in fact prohibitions, because they are themselves impermanent. Therefore, when detachment from the world is complete, no rule or prohibition remains for the Karma‑yogi – “tasyāḥ kāryaṁ na vidyate”. naina tasyāḥ kṛtenārtho nākṛtena eha kaścana

[ Verse 18 ]

(With any creature), some *Sadhak‑Sanjivani* = its 201 material support = relation of selfishness = not even the slightest amount remains. Explanation – “There is no purpose for it” – applies to every human being. Consequently, from the body onward a tendency to act, to do something, is inherent. As long as that tendency is directed toward acquiring a worldly object, the impulse to “do” for oneself persists. Man is bound by the desire to obtain something for himself. To extinguish that desire, the performance of duty‑action (Karma) becomes necessary. Karma is performed in two ways: for the fulfillment of desire and for the renunciation of desire. The ordinary person works for desire‑fulfillment, whereas the Karma‑yogi works for desire‑renunciation. Therefore, in a great soul perfected by Karma‑yoga, no desire remains, and consequently no relationship of even the slightest degree exists with any duty. By self‑less (Nishkarm) feeling, all actions are performed automatically for the welfare of the whole creation. When purpose (Purushartha) is absent, the great soul’s actions naturally become exemplary for others. Actions performed with a purpose are not ideal actions – this is the principle. “‘Na‑kṛtena‑eha kaścana’ – one who identifies himself with body, senses, mind, intellect, etc., and who is attached to laziness, negligence, etc., does not wish to act; because his purpose is the pleasure that arises from negligence, laziness, comfort (Gita, Chapter 18, Verse 48). Yet this great soul, who has risen above even sattvic pleasure, cannot become inclined toward tamasic pleasure, because he has no relationship of any kind with the body. Hence the question of attachment to laziness or comfort does not arise. A poignant point: aspirants often give importance to non‑action. They wish to remain in meditation, free from any thought. This is noble and beneficial, but it is not a principle. Although the tendency toward renunciation (non‑action) is considered superior to the tendency toward action, it is not an absolute truth. In a great soul perfected by Karma‑yoga, there is no personal (individual) connection to actions for personal pleasure or comfort. Such a soul experiences that matter, body, senses, inner organ, etc., belong only to the world and are derived from the world; they are not personal. Therefore, actions are performed solely for the world, not for oneself. The reason is that no action can be performed without the assistance of the world. Moreover, the relationship of the acquired karmic material is also with the totality of the world, not with the individual. Hence there is nothing personal to claim. The whole cannot be used for the individual; the individual’s attempt to use the whole for himself creates unrest. If one uses the body, senses, mind, intellect, matter, etc., for the whole, great peace can be attained. In a great soul perfected by Karma‑yoga, the so‑called body, senses, mind, intellect, matter, etc., are employed only for the world. In essence (consciousness), both tendency (action) and renunciation (non‑action) belong to the state of nature. Both tendency (action) and renunciation (non‑action) are states of Prakṛti. The state of non‑dual absorption (Nirvikalpa Samādhi) is a state of nature, because even from non‑dual absorption arises transformation. Action exists only within Prakṛti—‘prakṛṣaṇena karaṇam (bhāve lyut) iti prakṛtiḥ’—and without action, transformation cannot occur. Hence walking, speaking, seeing, hearing, as well as sleeping, sitting, standing, remaining silent, being motionless, and being in meditation are all actions. The real nature is continuously active; therefore, any being, while related to nature, cannot remain even a moment without some action (Gita 3.5; 18.11). Consequently, as long as there is a relationship with Prakṛti, meditation itself is an action, comprising the two phases of meditation and emergence. When the relationship with nature is severed, the two phases disappear, giving rise to ‘sahaja‑samādhi’ or ‘natural state’, in which emergence never occurs. The distinction of states lies in nature, not in essence. Hence the natural state is described as the highest, the intermediate as meditative concentration, the lower as scriptural contemplation, and the lowest as pilgrimage.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 3 ]

The great soul is beyond both activity (pravrtti) and renunciation (nivṛtti); there is no trace of selfishness, expectation of reward, or pride in him. The feeling of ego‑clinging never arises. When one identifies with the body, the duality of “to do” and “not to do” appears, but in reality both belong to the same category. Even “not doing” while related to the body is, in fact, a form of doing. Just as “gacchati” (goes) is an action, “tiṣṭhati” (stands) is also an action. From a gross perspective, the action in “gacchati” seems evident, while “tiṣṭhati” appears inert; yet a subtle view shows that the same body that performed the “going” now performs the “standing.” Similarly, any desire to “do” or “not do” contains action. Hence, the apparent outward manifestation of action (pravrtti) is inherent in nature, and the apparent lack of outward action (nivṛtti) is likewise inherent in nature. Because nature and its functions have no material, spiritual, worldly, or transcendental purpose, the great soul accrues no selfish motive from either doing or refraining. The question of doing or not doing arises only when there is attachment (jaḍatā) to the body, for without such attachment no action occurs. This great soul is completely detached from attachment, and both activity and renunciation naturally dissolve into the timeless, effortless state of pure being. Therefore, the seeker must sever all ties with attachment (the ego‑clinging and affection residing in the body). The absolute reality remains ever‑present as it is. “na ca asya sarvabhūteṣu kaścidarthavyapāśrayaḥ” – because there is no slightest selfish dependence on the body or the world, all of this great soul’s actions automatically serve the welfare of others. Just as every organ of the body works instinctively for the body’s benefit, his so‑called body (a tiny part of the world) works instinctively for the world’s benefit. His attitude and all his movements are directed toward the welfare of the world. When one washes one’s own face with one’s own hands, no feeling of selfishness, expectation of reward, or pride arises; likewise, when his designated body works for the world’s welfare, no such feeling arises. In the preceding verse, the Lord said that the realized great soul has no duty—“tasya kāryaṁ na vidyate.” Explaining his purpose, the Lord states three points for that great soul: (1) performing actions yields no personal gain, (2) refraining from actions yields no personal gain, and (3) he has no slightest selfish relation to any being or material, meaning that even acquiring something gives him no purpose. In essence, in pure form there is no purpose in doing or not doing, and there is no relation to any person or object, because pure form itself performs no action. Any action that occurs arises only through nature and nature‑derived substances. Hence there is no prescription for acting for oneself. As long as a human harbors desire for action, longing for acquisition, hope for continued existence, and fear of death, duty remains imposed upon him. However, when one is free from any desire to act or not act, free from any wish to obtain any worldly object, free from hope of continued life, and free from fear of death, duty does not bind him; yet duties automatically continue to manifest. Where the possibility of non‑duty exists, the motivation for duty also persists. **Special Note**  
The Lord’s style in the Gita is to describe the characteristics of perfected souls according to the varied qualities of seekers who progress toward the Supreme through different means. This same method is employed in verses seventeen and eighteen. The path that begins at a certain point also ends at that point. Although the chapter on Karma‑yoga formally begins with verse forty‑seven of the second chapter, the fundamental principle of Karma‑yoga is analyzed in verse forty‑four of the second chapter. 203  
[ Verse 19 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

The commentary explains that when one has no right (adhikāra) to act, attachment disappears and there is no longer any relationship of desire, satisfaction or contentment. In such a state the fruits of action (karma‑phala) never arise in themselves. In verse 16 the text says that there is no right; the Lord’s words “moghāṁ pārtha sa jīvati” indicate that duty must be performed even when the result seems futile. In verse 17 the statement “mā karma‑phal‑hetur bhūḥ” (do not act for the sake of results) shows that a person who does not act for the sake of results lives a meaningless life; therefore in verse 17 the phrase “yaḥ tu” is used to explain that a realized great soul, even if he does not perform prescribed duties, is free from attachment. Verse 18 says “mā te saṅgo ’stvakarmaṇi” (your attachment does not arise from inaction). If a perfected sage refrains from duty, no attachment is created. His life is not meaningless; rather it is supremely meaningful because he has fulfilled the purpose of human birth. Consequently, for him nothing remains to be done. The eighteenth verse (the one under discussion) precisely states the principle of the preceding discussion. In the forty‑third verse of the second chapter, the second and third stages address the seeker; in the latter half of the present verse the same principle is applied to the perfected sage, declaring that he has no selfish relationship with any creature or material object. In the first and fourth stages of the earlier chapter the teaching was directed to the seeker; in the first half of the present verse it is directed to the perfected sage, stating that whether he acts or does not act, no purpose is attached to either. Thus verses 17‑18 describe the characteristics of a great person who has attained perfection through Karmayoga. When no duty remains for a person, even an ordinary human can attain that state by performing his prescribed duties in every circumstance with wholehearted, self‑less dedication, because the attainment is open to all who are free and qualified. Duty is linked to every situation; therefore duty is inherent in every circumstance. Only the pursuit of personal pleasure causes a person to forget duty. If one eliminates selfish desire by serving others without expectation, all worldly sorrows are relinquished and supreme peace (param śānti) can be attained. This supreme peace is equally available to everyone. The highest material objects, positions, etc., cannot be equally shared by all, but supreme peace, viewed as the goal of Karmayoga, requires that verse 18 precede verse 17 in the logical order. When a great soul has become perfect through Karmayoga, neither acting nor refraining from action serves any purpose, and he has no selfish relationship of any kind with any being or thing. ---

**Appendix (Parishishta Bhāva)** – In the world, “to do” and “not to do” are both relative. Hence the statement “I have nothing to do” is itself an act of doing. In the nature of the Supreme Atman, “not doing” is absolute and natural. The divine, immutable reality (cintamaya sattā) is unrelated both to action and to inaction. Therefore a Karmayoga‑realized great soul has no relationship with any object, no relationship with any person, and no relationship with any action—“yo ’vasthiti nīṅgate” (Bhagavad Gītā 14.23). In his vision, only the immutable divine reality remains. The two preceding verses describe the state of the great soul; the Lord now explains the means by which the seeker should proceed:

**tasmād asaktaḥ satataṁ kāryaṁ karma samācar**  
**asaktaḥ hy ācaran karma param āpnoti pūruṣaḥ** (19)

*Word‑by‑word breakdown*

- **tasmād** – therefore  
- **asaktaḥ** – unattached, free from attachment  
- **satataṁ** – constantly, continuously  
- **kāryam** – duty, prescribed action (Dharma)  
- **karma** – action, work  
- **samācar** – perform, practice diligently  
- **asaktaḥ** – unattached (repeated for emphasis)  
- **hi** – indeed, certainly  
- **ācaran** – to act, to perform  
- **karma** – action (again)  
- **param** – supreme, highest  
- **āpnoti** – attains, reaches  
- **pūruṣaḥ** – a man, a human being

Thus, “Therefore, being unattached, constantly perform your prescribed duty; indeed, a man who acts without attachment attains the supreme.”

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
Commentary – ‘tasmād asaktaḥ satataṁ kāryaṁ karma samācara’

To explain the connection of this verse with the preceding verses, the word ‘tasmāt’ is used here. In the earlier verses, the Lord said that even when there is no need to act for oneself, the great sages still perform actions for the welfare of the world. Hence, for Arjuna, the Lord also uses the word ‘tasmāt’ to command him to perform his duty without desire, so as to attain the Supreme Self. The reason is that acting or not acting for one’s own nature (‘sva’) serves no purpose. Action is always for ‘para’ (others), not for ‘sva’. Therefore, performing action for others removes the attachment to action and establishes one’s true nature. Attraction of the innate (inert) material elements toward one’s true nature is called ‘āsakti’ (attachment). To become free of attachment, one must understand its cause. Believing ‘I am the body’ or ‘the body is mine’ imprints the importance of the perishable body and similar substances in the heart, leading to attachment to them. Attachment, not action, leads to downfall. Because of attachment, a person regards the body, senses, mind, intellect and other inert substances as his own, and performs various actions for comfort and pleasure. Thus, the attachment‑based relationship with inertia is the cause of repeated birth and death—**kāraṇaṁ guṇasaṅgo ’sya sad‑asat‑yoni‑janmasu** (Gita 13.21). Acting without attachment severs the connection with inertia. A person bound by attachment cannot work for the welfare of others, whereas a person free of attachment naturally promotes the welfare of all beings. All his actions are solely for the benefit of others. * [ Chapter 3 ]  
By doing nothing for oneself and desiring nothing, no new debt is created. Thus, when the old debt is cleared and no new debt arises, there is no cause for bondage, and the person becomes automatically liberated. No action remains continuous, but attachment (in the heart) persists continuously. Therefore the Lord uses the expression ‘satataṁ asaktaḥ’ to urge perpetual detachment. One must constantly maintain the awareness ‘I must not be attached anywhere’. While remaining continuously unattached, any prescribed action that arises should be performed merely as duty. In reality, attachment does not remain constant in anyone’s heart. Since the world is ever‑changing, its attachment cannot stay continuous. Yet, due to the sense of ‘aham’ (I), attachment appears to persist. The term **kāryam** (duty) denotes that which one is capable of doing and must certainly do. In other words, duty means renouncing one’s own selfishness to serve others, i.e., fulfilling the scripturally prescribed, just demand of others that we are able to meet. Hence duty is related to altruism. Everyone is free and capable of observing duty; no one is subordinate or incapable. However, due to negligence and laziness, the habit of shirking duty and the desire for fruit make duty‑performance seem difficult in the present, though otherwise nothing is as easy as fulfilling duty. Duty depends on circumstances. In every situation a person can freely observe duty
