[ Verse 19 ]  
* Sadhak – Sanjivani *

A slightest carelessness in performing one’s prescribed duty (dharma‑karm) nullifies the worldly benefits of karmayoga for oneself; it can become an obstacle to success. According to a person’s varna, ashrama, nature (svabhava) and circumstances, the duty prescribed by the scriptures is his *sahaja karma* (natural action). Even if a flaw appears in that natural action, it must not be abandoned (Gita – Chapter 18, Verse 48); for a person who performs his natural action does not incur sin (Gita – Chapter 18, Verse 44). Hence here the Lord seems to tell Arjuna: you are a Kshatriya; therefore fighting (even if it looks dreadful) is your natural duty, not a dreadful act. Consequently, one should perform the arising natural duty without attachment. Only through non‑attachment does equanimity arise. **Special Note**  
When a living being is born in a human womb, he receives body, wealth, land, house, etc.; when he departs, all these material possessions are left behind. From this simple fact it follows that body and other possessions are received, not owned. Just as a man who goes to an office receives a chair, desk, papers, etc., solely for the purpose of office work—not to take them home as his own—so too a human being receives body and all material things in this world only for the service of the world, not for personal ownership. When he works in the office with readiness and enthusiasm, he receives a salary in return. The work belongs to the office and the salary belongs to him. In the same way, when all work is done for the world, one becomes detached from the world and experiences yoga (the constant relationship with the Supreme Self). ‘Karma’ and ‘yoga’ together constitute **karmayoga**. Karma is performed for the world; yoga is for the self. Yoga is, in effect, the salary. The world is the field of practice. Here every material thing is obtained for practice, never for enjoyment or accumulation. When one attains the supreme reality—Parmatma—there remains no desire for any other object (Gita – Chapter 6, Verse 22). Yet, however many worldly objects one acquires, the desire for them never ceases; it even intensifies. When a person regards the obtained objects as his own, he becomes bound by this mistake. The proper remedy is the observance of karmayoga, which is both easy and supreme. A karmayogi does not consider any object as his own; he offers it in the service of others (regarding it as theirs). Thus he is smoothly liberated from worldly bondage. All beings act, but there is a great difference between the actions of ordinary beings and those of a karmayogi. An ordinary person (karmi) performs actions while retaining attachment, affection, desire, etc.; a karmayogi performs actions after abandoning attachment, affection, desire, etc. The flow of a karmi’s actions is directed toward himself, whereas the flow of a karmayogi’s actions is directed toward the world; therefore the karmi becomes bound and the karmayogi becomes free. “‘Asakto hy acharan karma’ – a person, not the world, attaches himself to the world. Hence a person’s duty is to act solely for the welfare of the world without seeking any fruit. By acting without attachment—‘I desire nothing from anyone’—the very act of serving the world creates an automatic separation from the world. The karmayogi, by serving the world and desiring nothing of the present or future, severs his relationship with worldly objects. In a fair, a volunteer, considering service his duty, assists travelers all day and asks for nothing in return; therefore, when he sleeps at night, no one’s memory troubles him, because he asked for nothing while serving. Likewise, one who performs all actions for others out of a spirit of service, without seeking honor or praise, does not recall the world. He is smoothly freed from worldly bondage.

[ Chapter 3 ]

All beings engage in Karma (action), but only the true seeker recognizes Karma‑Yoga. Consequently, if one limits service to the body alone, how can there be any pride of doership when actions are performed without attachment for the benefit of others? Attachment can be eliminated only by performing the duty‑Karma prescribed in the scriptures—“Dharma (righteous duty) leads to detachment” (Manas 3.16.1). Attachment never disappears when one engages in prohibited actions. The statement “Parama‑apnoti puruṣaḥ” (as in Chapter 13, Verse 34, where the Lord says that the word “parama” denotes the attainment of the Supreme Self by the Sankhya‑yogi) is used here to indicate that the word “parama” also signifies the attainment of the Supreme Self by the Karma‑yogi. The implication is that a seeker, according to his inclination, faith and qualification, may follow any path—Karma‑yoga, Jnana‑yoga or Bhakti‑yoga—and the ultimate object to be attained on every path is the same Supreme Self (Gita, Chapter 5, Verse 4). The object that can be attained must be free of alternatives, doubt and despair, and must be ever‑present, everywhere, at all times, for everyone, belonging to all, and inseparably identical with all beings at all stages. **Question:** How can the doership pride of a Karma‑yogi be eradicated while performing actions? Because without the removal of doership pride, the experience of the Supreme Self is impossible. **Resolution:** An ordinary person performs all actions for himself, which sustains a sense of doership. A Karma‑yogi does not act for himself. He regards the body, senses, mind, intellect, material possessions, money, etc., that he has received from the world as belonging to the world, not to himself. Whenever an opportunity arises, he offers that material, time, capability, and so on to the service of the world, considering them as the world’s property that he is employing in its service. By holding this view, the sense of doership does not arise. It is a rule that a person becomes absorbed in the very goal that motivated his action as soon as the action ends. For example, a merchant trades solely for the purpose of earning money; when the shop closes, his attention automatically turns to counting the rupees, and he does not think about which customers came, what castes they belonged to, etc., because the customers have no purpose for him. A person who works with the aim of worldly objectives may become deeply engrossed in the world, yet he cannot achieve unity with the world, because the world is ever‑changing and inert, whereas the “self” (one’s true nature) is immutable and conscious. In contrast, one who works with the aim of the Supreme Self inevitably attains unity with the Supreme Self (whether or not the seeker experiences it), because the “self” is intrinsically identical with the Supreme Self. Thus, when the doer becomes the “duty‑bearer” and merges with his purpose—the Supreme Self—there is no longer any question of doership pride. A Karma‑yogi performs every action for the purpose of attaining the Supreme Self; in that purpose there is no doership pride or sense of ownership. Consequently, at the beginning and end of every activity, the experience of oneness with that purpose eliminates any doership pride. Every action performed by the body has a beginning and an end; no action is perpetual. Therefore, no doership is perpetual; as soon as an action ends, the sense of doership also ends. Human error lies in continuing to identify oneself as the doer even after the action has ceased, which reinforces doership pride. For instance, a man is a speaker while delivering a lecture, but even when he is not lecturing he still perceives himself as a doer—now as a listener. A Karma‑yogi does not act with the expectation of enjoyment. A person who acts hoping for pleasure is not a Karma‑yogi. Just as washing one’s own face with one’s own hands does not evoke a feeling of great merit—because the hands and the face are both considered one’s own limbs—a Karma‑yogi also regards the body as the world’s instrument and does not regard himself as the ultimate doer.

[ Verse 19 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

The impression does not disappear. By constantly considering oneself a lecturer, one simultaneously attains renunciation; likewise the sense of doership in a karmayogi remains, like a mask, limited only to the act of doing. Just as an actor playing Harishchandra performs all the deeds of Harishchandra yet does not truly regard himself as the real Harishchandra, the karmayogi, while performing all scripturally prescribed actions, does not regard himself as the true doer of those actions. The karmayogi does not treat the body and other material elements as his own; he regards them as belonging to the world and devotes himself to the service of the world. Consequently, in any state the karmayogi can have no trace of doership‑pride. His mind adopts the attitude: “Let the listeners serve me, honor me, fulfill my needs,” and “How can I sit among these ordinary people? How can I perform such ordinary work?” Thus his sense of identity remains continuously linked to the activity of lecturing. The reason is that the lecturing activity carries with it a desire for wealth, honor, prestige, comfort, or some other gain. When that desire disappears, doership is confined to the mere performance of action, and as soon as the action ends, doership merges into its purpose. Just as a person, while eating, identifies himself as the consumer of the food, but not after the meal, the karmayogi regards himself as the doer only at the moment of action, not otherwise. For example, the karmayogi is a lecturer and enjoys great reputation among people. Yet when the occasion arises to listen to a lecture, he can sit anywhere and listen with ease. At that moment he needs neither respect nor a lofty seat, because he now sees himself as a listener, not as a lecturer. Similarly, after delivering a lecture, if he is asked to clean a room, he performs the cleaning with the same readiness with which he delivered the lecture. No thought arises in his mind such as, “How can a great lecturer do this trivial cleaning? What will people say? My reputation will be sullied.” He sees himself as a lecturer while lecturing, as a listener while hearing, and as a cleaner while cleaning. Hence his sense of doership‑pride is not continuous. Anything that is not continuous, but keeps changing, does not truly exist, and its relation is also not continuous—this is a fundamental principle. When the seeker turns his attention to this principle, he directly experiences reality free from the ego‑centered sense of doership. The karmayogi performs every action with the same attitude that an actor assumes a role in a play. In the drama, the mask of Harishchandra exists only for the performance; once the drama ends, the mask‑like doership ceases to be identified with the self. Likewise, the karmayogi does not continuously identify himself with relationships such as parent‑child, husband‑wife, brother‑sister, etc. He acknowledges those relationships only while serving. For instance, if a man is a husband, his wife may be harsh, unattractive, or quarrelsome, yet having accepted her as his wife, it becomes his duty to provide for her according to his capacity. As a husband he must point out her shortcomings, whether she accepts the advice or not. He does not constantly see himself as a husband, because before this birth he was a wife—how can that be known? And after death he may still be a wife—what certainty is there? In the present life he is also a mother to someone, a daughter to someone, a sister, a sister‑in‑law, a sister‑in‑law’s sister, and so on. He is never only a wife. Recognizing this eliminates any desire to extract pleasure from the relationship, and the conviction that “the wife exists solely for my support (service)” becomes firm. Thus, the karmayogi fulfills each worldly role—father, son, husband, brother, etc.—exactly as prescribed, without being swayed by whether the other party performs his duty. The presence of doership‑pride in oneself directs attention toward others’ duties; once the mind focuses on others’ duties, it falls away from its own duty, because observing another’s duty is not one’s own duty. Just as the karmayogi does not regard his relationship with all beings of the world as continuous, he likewise does not regard his relationship with caste, ashrama, community, circumstance, or any other condition as permanent.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]

The relationship is not regarded as continuous. That which is not continuous, though it may appear, is called “prapta” (attained). Its lack of perception (seeing‑hearing) is automatic. Hence, for the karmayogi, the sense of doership and pride that arise at the outset are erased by the ever‑changing world of perception. The ever‑present, all‑pervading Supreme Self (Paramatman) is “attained” everywhere. The Supreme Self, identical with Brahman, is inherently attained by every being, from the smallest ant onward. **Essential point** – In that which has no doership, there is an automatic, self‑realized unity with the Supreme Self. The seeker often makes the mistake of not directing his attention toward this reality. Just as a swing, no matter how rapidly it moves forward and backward, always returns to a state of equilibrium (the point where the rope is attached), each action is followed by a state of non‑action (equilibrium). In other words, between the end of the first action and the beginning of the second, and between every intention and its alternative, equilibrium persists. Secondly, if one looks with true vision, even while the swing appears to move irregularly, it remains continuously in equilibrium: while moving forward‑backward it stays aligned with the straight line of the rope. In the same way, the living being remains in equilibrium in every action. Its unity with the Supreme Self remains continuous. Even when the equilibrium is not visible during action, it actually remains; when the action ceases, the experience of that equilibrium is immediate. If the seeker remains constantly vigilant on this point, he experiences the ever‑present equilibrium or his unity with the Supreme Self, where there is no sense of doership. To eliminate the false pride of doership, it is necessary to understand the distinction between “pratiti” (perception) and “prapta” (attainment). What is seen but not obtained is called “pratiti”; what is obtained is “prapta”. The apparent “pratiti” is constantly disappearing, moment by moment, into the invisible. The senses, mind, intellect, etc., that give rise to perception are themselves merely “pratiti”. The immutable, ever‑present “swayam” (Self) does not acquire “pratiti”. The Supreme Self, ever‑present in all, eternally “attains” the “swayam”. Hence “pratiti” is the form of non‑existence and “prapta” the form of existence – “na asti vedyo bhavo na bhavo vedyo sat” (Gita 2.16). Only matter and action are “pratiti”. Action alone merges into the state of non‑action. At the beginning and end of every action, a self‑evident, non‑active principle remains. What exists at the beginning and end also exists in the middle – this is the principle. Therefore, even during action, the unbroken, self‑evident non‑active principle remains exactly as it is. This self‑evident non‑active principle (the conscious nature or Supreme Self) illuminates both the inactive and active states; it is beyond both doing and not‑doing. Because “pratiti” (place, time, object, person, action, etc.) is the basis of attachment, the experience of the ever‑attained Supreme Self does not arise while attachment exists. When attachment is destroyed, the experience of the ever‑attained Supreme Self naturally arises. Thus, by being free of attachment and offering the perceived bodies and other material forms to the service of “pratiti” (the world alone), the flow of perceived materiality is directed solely toward the world, and the self‑attained Supreme Self remains untouched. **Relation (Sambandh)** – By acting without attachment, i.e., performing action for no personal gain, does one attain the Supreme Self? The Lord answers this in the following verse. karmaṇaiḥ hi saṁsiddhim āsthita janakādayaḥ  
loka‑saṅgraha‑m evāpi sampaśyankartum arhasi ||20||

*Transliteration*: “karmaṇaiḥ hi saṁsiddhim āsthita janakādayaḥ; loka‑saṅgraha‑m evāpi sampaśyankartum arhasi.”

*Translation*: “It is through action alone that perfection is established for the progenitors and for all beings; even for the purpose of gathering the world, you ought to see (understand) this.”

209  
[ Verse 20 ]

The expression “janakādayaḥ” denotes King Janaka, who exemplifies perfect attainment. It is called the practitioner’s life‑giving elixir for achieving the highest perfection. Many great souls—both before and after Janaka—have attained this supreme state through their deeds, such as the Sun, the sage Vaivasvata Manu, King Ikshvaku, etc., as mentioned in the first two verses of Chapter 4. The word “ādi” can signify either “origin” or “type.” If taken as “origin,” “janakādayaḥ” would mean “those whose origin is King Janaka,” i.e., Janaka and the great men who followed him. This sense is inappropriate because numerous eminent beings had already reached the supreme state through their actions before Janaka’s time. Therefore “ādi” must be understood in the sense of “type,” and the phrase means: great persons who, like King Janaka, lived in the householder’s stage, performed all actions with self‑less attitude, and attained the highest perfection, both before and after Janaka up to the present. Karmayoga is an ancient path by which many saints such as Janaka have realized the Supreme Self. Consequently, anyone now or in the future who wishes to attain the Supreme Self through karmayoga must regard all material objects received by the body (the body itself, etc.) as not belonging to oneself. In reality they are not “mine”; they belong to the world and to the service of the world. Recognizing this truth and offering worldly possessions to the service of the world creates a smooth disconnection from worldly ties and leads to the attainment of the Supreme Self. Hence karmayoga is an easy, superior, and independent means of attaining the Supreme Self—there is no doubt about this. The phrase “karmṇā eva” in this verse is linked to the earlier line “asakto hy ācharan karma” (perform action without attachment). Only by acting without attachment does a person become free from the bondage of action; merely acting does not liberate. Action performed with self‑less attitude alone is the proper qualification: “karmṇā eva (nishkāmabhāvasya) karma karṇe yogyaḥ”—one must certainly act in a self‑less way. The Gita’s style is to restate in a later verse the essential teaching of a previous verse in a concise form. After commanding detached action in verse 19, verse 20 summarizes the same idea with the words “karmṇā eva.” Similarly, in Chapter 12 the main teaching of verse 6 is briefly repeated in verse 7 with “mayy āveśita‑cetasām” (devotees who fix their mind on Me). The Lord could have said “yogena eva” instead of “karmṇā eva,” but Arjuna’s request focuses on renouncing the very nature of action, so the text uses “karmṇā eva.” Thus, according to the preceding verse, the intended meaning is the performance of karmayoga without attachment. In reality, the realization of the luminous Supreme Self does not arise from inert actions. The obstacles that prevent constant experience of the Supreme Self disappear when one acts without attachment. Then the ever‑present, self‑existent experience of the Supreme Self manifests automatically. Hence the commentary states that through action one can achieve the highest perfection—realization of the Supreme Self. A poignant observation on attaining the Supreme Self: people often regard even the attainment of the Supreme Self as something produced by effort, just as they consider the acquisition of worldly objects to be the result of labor. They think that meeting a high‑ranking person requires great exertion, so meeting the infinite Lord of the universe must demand even greater austerities (penance, fasts, etc.). This is the greatest mistake of the seeker.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]

The individual soul (Atman) is not fragmented, whereas the Supreme Soul (Paramatma) is indivisible. To try to experience the ever‑present, ever‑attainable Paramatma by employing the same logical arguments and reasoning that are used for acquiring material objects is nothing but self‑deception. Human beings are intimately linked with actions (Karma). Hence even the “I” that appears in the world of the body is extremely close to the Paramatma. The “I” of the embodied being is described as “Karmasangi”, i.e., one attached to actions—“Having entered the realm of destruction, one is born again among the Karmasangi” (Gita 14.15). Consequently, a person’s special tendency is to seek desired objects through actions, and when one is bound by destiny, one even obtains worldly objects through actions, reinforcing the belief that every object is obtained only by performing actions. The same attitude persists regarding the Paramatma, and one attempts to acquire the conscious Paramatma also through material actions. Yet the reality is that the Paramatma cannot be obtained by actions; this point must be understood with utmost seriousness. Actions lead to the acquisition of perishable things (the world), not to the acquisition of the imperishable (the Paramatma). All actions are connected with perishable entities—body, senses, mind, etc.—whereas the realization of the Paramatma occurs only when all ties with the perishable are completely severed. Each action has a beginning and an end; therefore the object obtained as a result of an action is also subject to birth and destruction. Actions bring about objects that, from the standpoint of space‑time and beyond, remain unattainable. A worldly object exists within a particular place, time, etc., is generated, destroyed, and constantly changing; consequently its attainment is achievable through action. In contrast, the Paramatma pervades all places, times, objects, and persons, is eternally present, and is completely free from birth, destruction, and change. Hence its realization is self‑evident, not dependent on action. This explains why the acquisition of material substances does not occur through contemplation, whereas contemplation is central to attaining the Paramatma. Through contemplation one can obtain only that which is extremely near. In truth, even the contemplation‑based activity does not bring about the Paramatma. The value of contemplating the Paramatma lies solely in relinquishing all other (worldly) contemplations. When all worldly contemplation ceases, the experience of the ever‑present Paramatma automatically arises. The all‑pervading Paramatma is never distant from us, nor can it become distant. Because we do not perceive any distance, the acquisition of a worldly object is not achieved merely by desire; however, the attainment of the Paramatma can be realized by an intense longing alone. The only obstacle to the awakening of this intense longing is the desire for worldly enjoyment and accumulation; no other obstacle exists. If the intense longing for Paramatma awakens now, the experience of the Paramatma follows immediately. The purpose of human life is not merely to act and reap the results. Only when the aspirant abandons the desire for worldly enjoyment and accumulation can an intense longing for Paramatma arise, provided that the aspirant’s sole lifelong aim becomes the attainment of the Paramatma. No other activity retains significance once the Paramatma is attained. In fact, beyond the attainment of the Paramatma, human life has no other purpose. The sole requirement is to recognize this purpose and fulfill it. It is essential to distinguish between “purpose” and “desire for fruit”. The eternal purpose is the realization of the Paramatma principle; the desire for fruit pertains to transient (born‑and‑perishable) material objects. The purpose is fulfilled, whereas the desire for fruit inevitably fades. “Self‑realization” and “attainment of the Divine” are purposes, not fruits. Actions performed for the sake of attaining the purpose are not “desire‑driven”. Therefore, a self‑less (Nishkama) person—the karmayogi—performs all actions with purpose, not with desire for fruit. In karmayoga, actions are performed in accordance with scriptural injunctions, aiming at the severance of attachment to material actions (inertia). A desire‑driven (Sakam) person works for personal gain, whereas the karmayogi relinquishes personal desire and works (serves) for others. Action inevitably yields fruit; thus fruit is linked to action, not the other way around. Purpose is not linked to action. When one acts selflessly for the welfare of others, the notion that “the Paramatma is distant” disappears. “Desh kāla disi bidisi hu māhīṁ; kahahu so kahā̃ jahā̃ prabhu nāhī̃” (Manas 1.185.3) – “The world, time, directions, and all places are but a fleeting illusion; where can one say that the Lord is absent?”

[ Verse 21 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

‘Lokasaṅgraha‑meva‑api samapśyankartumarhasi’ – “Lok” (world) is understood as the duty that arises according to one’s opportunity, varṇa, āśrama, sect, etc.; that duty is the great action. The size or severity of an action is judged only by its nature and its result. By renouncing the desire for fruit, every action becomes a means for attaining purpose. Hence, when one severs attachment to inertia, both small and large actions are equal. Words have three senses: (1) the worlds such as the human world, (2) the beings who inhabit those worlds, and (3) the scriptures (all scriptures besides the Vedas). According to the limits of the human world, its inhabitants, and the scriptures, the totality of conduct (mere way of life) is called **Lokasaṅgraha**. **Lokasaṅgraha** means: for preserving social order, to turn people away from *asat* (untruth) and toward *sat* (truth) through self‑less action. In the Gītā this is also termed **yajña‑artha karma**. Turning people away from untruth and toward truth by one’s deeds and speech is a great service, because facing truth brings about their improvement and liberation. No human life can function without the assistance of others. The body is received from mother and father; knowledge, skill, education are received from teachers. The food one eats is produced by others; the clothing one wears is made by others; the house one lives in is built by others; the road one walks on is constructed by others, and so on. Thus every person’s livelihood depends on others. Consequently each person owes a debt to others, which must be repaid by serving others self‑lessly as far as possible. No duty or action is inherently small or large. When even the smallest or the largest worldly objects (body, etc.) are regarded merely as duties, and nothing is claimed as one’s own, a person acting out of service is the same. By performing one’s duty according to one’s varṇa, āśrama, sect, etc., one becomes free from debt. Performing one’s duty merely to display it to others is **not** Lokasaṅgraha. Whether observed or not, Lokasaṅgraha automatically arises when each person follows his own duty in accordance with social order. **Appendix (Pariśiṣṭa‑Bhāva)** – The statement *karmanaiva hi saṁsiddhim āsthitaḥ* demonstrates that Karma‑yoga is an independent means of liberation. Even kings such as Janaka attained the supreme perfection through Karma‑yoga, because they ruled only to serve others and bring them happiness, not for personal gain. The meaning of *Lokasaṅgraha‑meva‑api samapśyankartumarhasi* is that you must establish in people the ideal of Karma‑yoga, for its practice leads to the supreme perfection. **Relation** – How action produces Lokasaṅgraha is explained by the Lord in the following verse. [ Verse 21 ]

**Sanskrit:** śreṣṭhas tattadeve tvaro janah kurute lokas tad anuvartate

**Transliteration:** shreshṭhas tattadeve tvaro janah kurute lokaḥ tad anuvartate

**English meaning:** The best among men, who is devoted to the Supreme, performs actions; the world then follows his example. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- **śreṣṭhaḥ** – the best, superior  
- **tattadeva** – devoted to the Truth (the Supreme)  
- **tva‑** – his (possessive suffix)  
- **janah** – person, human  
- **kurute** – performs, does  
- **lokaḥ** – the world, society  
- **tat** – that, the same action  
- **anuvartate** – follows, imitates

Thus, the world imitates the conduct of the most virtuous person. **Illustration** – From the standpoint of the nature of action, sweeping a floor appears as a small deed while delivering a lecture appears as a large deed; and from the standpoint of fruit, giving a little charity yields little merit, whereas giving generously yields greater merit.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Commentary – “Yadyad‑ācharati śreṣṭhas tattadeve‑taro janaḥ” – The “person” (purusha) is the one who knows the material world (body, etc.) and the “self” (one’s true nature) as the ultimate reality. He naturally experiences that the body, senses, mind, intellect, wealth, family, land and other objects belong to the world; they are not his own. Moreover, the great person does not consider renunciation, dispassion, love, knowledge, virtue, etc., as his own, because regarding them as his own strengthens the ego, which obstructs the attainment of truth. Statements such as “I am a renunciate,” “I am dispassionate,” “I am a servant,” “I am a devotee,” etc., also reinforce the ego and therefore hinder the realization of truth. In a great person, the “individual ego” (the ego arising from attachment) does not exist at all, and the “collective ego” functions only for practical dealings, remaining engaged in service to the world; even ego is a product of the world (Gita – Chapter 7, verse 4 and Chapter 13, verse 5). All material possessions—body, wealth, family, position, qualifications, authority—are given solely for their proper use, i.e., for serving others, not for personal consumption or for amassing one’s own rights. Whoever treats these as his own and consumes them is called a thief by the Lord: “Yo bhuktas tenaiva saḥ” (Gita 3.12). These objects belong to the whole, never to the individual. In reality we have no personal relationship with them. The great person’s body and other material aspects, being part of the world, automatically become instruments of service to the world. His natural inclination is for the welfare of all beings. The attitude of “giving” creates unity and love in society, whereas the attitude of “taking” generates conflict. “Giving” is uplifting; “taking” is degrading. When one regards the body as “I,” “mine,” or “for me,” the desire to take arises. Because the great person does not identify with the body, the feeling of taking is completely absent. Consequently, every action of his is directed toward the welfare of others. The mere sight, touch, conversation, or contemplation of such a great person automatically benefits people. Even the breath that passes through his body benefits those who inhale it. [ Chapter 3 ]

Great persons are of two kinds: (1) the avadhuta class and (2) the acharya class. Avadhuta‑class great persons serve as ideals only for avadhutas, not for ordinary people. In contrast, acharya‑class great persons are ideals for ordinary humanity. The present description concerns the acharya‑class great persons, whose conduct always conforms to scriptural propriety. Whether observed or not, because there is no ego‑attachment, they naturally fulfill their duties. For example, a flower that blooms in a forest and later withers and falls unnoticed still spreads fragrance in all directions, eliminating foul odor. Similarly, a great person, because of his boundless compassion for others, naturally renders great service to the world, whether people recognize it or not. This is because the dissolution of personal ego (self‑attachment) unites him with the Lord’s sustaining power, which works for the welfare of the world alone. Just as all limbs of a single body remain one despite being different (e.g., pain in any limb is felt as one’s own pain), all beings of the world, though diverse, are essentially one. When any afflicted limb of the body heals, the whole body benefits; likewise, a person who, within the limits of propriety, performs his duty according to the circumstances, time, and conditions, automatically promotes the welfare of the entire world. The impact of a great person’s actions and words, being manifested through the gross body, is limited. However, the impact of his attitudes operates in a subtle, limitless manner. Action is finite; attitude is infinite. The attitudes that a great person brings into his conduct exert a strong influence on other humans. Because he faithfully observes the customs of his caste, ashrama, and sect, his spoken words also profoundly affect people of other castes, ashramas, and sects. Although a great man performs no actions for personal gain and harbors no sense of ownership, he nevertheless influences people…

[ Verse 21 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

Because a person appears to be practicing visibly, here the lakh‑patis (millionaires) are regarded as superior. Yet the daily “practice” (ācharati) of chanting the Lord’s name is employed. By this, those who chant the Lord’s name a hundred‑thousand times are not considered superior. They view such actions as spontaneous acts of charity. They do not think that when a lakh‑pati dies, even a single coin will remain with him, because there is no selfish motive attached to his small or large possessions; whereas the act of chanting the Lord’s name is inherently self‑beneficial. Even after death, the complete wealth represented by the Lord’s name does not become a duty for anyone—“tasyāḥ kāryaṁ na vidyate” (Gita 3.17). No trace of the Lord’s name will be left behind! There is also no pride in performing it—“nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ” (Gita 2.71). Nevertheless, by this spontaneous, flawless practice, one fulfills his duty. In this way, a spontaneous, natural collection of the world (lokasaṅgraha) occurs. **Special observation**  
It is often seen that in any society, sect, caste, varna, or ashrama where certain persons are called “superior” and are respected, the conduct of those “superior” people influences the rest of the community to adopt the same behavior. Because of the inner importance attached to wealth and position, and because of greed, people regard the richer (lakh‑patis, crore‑patis) and the higher‑ranked (leaders, ministers, etc.) as superior and treat them with great respect. Those whose hearts are attached to material objects—wealth, rank, etc.—are in reality neither superior themselves nor capable of recognizing a truly superior person. The person they deem superior is, in fact, not superior either. If their hearts esteem wealth above all, they are more easily swayed by the wealthy, just as thieves are influenced by the chief of thieves. Although such wealthy or high‑ranking individuals are not truly superior, society automatically propagates their conduct because they are regarded as superior. Consequently, the methods by which they acquire and accumulate wealth are also propagated among people, no matter how secret those methods may be. This is why, in the present age, falsehood, hypocrisy, dishonesty, deceit, theft, and other evils spread in society without any formal instruction. In every locality, the persons who are considered the chief—teachers, lecturers, acharyas, gurus, leaders, rulers, mahatmas, storytellers, priests, etc.—must exercise great caution in their conduct so that they exert a positive influence on others. Likewise, the head of a family (the mukhiya) must also be extremely careful in his behavior, because all eyes are on the chief. Just as a train driver bears special responsibility, the chief of a group must remain ever‑vigilant. The passengers may even sleep, but the driver must stay awake; a moment’s negligence can cause an accident. Therefore, all men who are regarded as superior in their respective fields must pay special attention to their conduct. “Yad yathā pramāṇaṁ kurute lokas tad anuvartate” – When a person’s heart is free of desire, affection, attachment, selfishness, bias, and has no regard for perishable things, the words spoken by such a person automatically affect others, and they begin to act in accordance with his statements. One may wonder why, after speaking of conduct, it is necessary to speak of proof, and why, after speaking of proof, it is necessary to speak of conduct. The answer is that although conduct is primary, it is impossible for a single individual to embody the conduct appropriate to all varṇas, ashramas, sects, etc. Hence a superior person fully practices conduct only according to his own varṇa, ashrama, or sect, and for people of other varṇas, ashramas, or sects he can only convey the teachings through his words, scriptures, history, etc. It is a sorrowful and astonishing fact that today people are taught by proof to do nothing for themselves…

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]

The welfare of all beings is best served when each person, according to his own varna, ashrama, sect, etc., performs his prescribed duties by personal example. This is the most effective and noble means of promoting well‑being (as stated in the 45th verse of Chapter 18). Inspired by those words, people of other varnas, ashramas and sects begin to observe their own duties as instructed. Although the sphere of personal conduct is limited while the sphere of preaching (the spoken word) is broad, the Lord’s description of the conduct of a great man includes five elements—‘yat’, ‘yat’, ‘tat’, ‘tat’ and especially ‘eva’—to indicate that his conduct influences society five times more, whereas the two elements ‘yat’ and ‘tat’ in preaching signify that the influence of preaching is only about twice as strong. Hence, in verse 20 the Lord emphasizes the importance of personally performing one’s duty for the benefit of the world. If a great person merely gives verbal instruction without living according to his own varna, ashrama, etc., his impact on people will be negligible. Listeners may think the statements are only words, because the speaker himself is not fulfilling his own duties. Such an attitude can breed disbelief and disinterest in one’s own responsibilities. By both speaking and acting, a great person guides each individual to fulfill his own duty, thereby promoting collective welfare. Only those who regard him as great will follow the conduct of a great person. Consequently, even if a person is truly great, those who do not recognize his greatness will be unable to emulate his actions and teachings. In the present age, despite the presence of many teachers who propagate devotional (Bhagavata) sentiments, the effect of those sentiments on the masses appears minimal. This is because speakers often do not embody what they preach. A statement delivered after personal practice is like a gun loaded with a bullet—it makes a sound and also inflicts damage when the bullet is fired. In contrast, a statement made without personal practice is like a gun loaded only with gunpowder—it produces only a noise and then falls silent. Nevertheless, devotional teachings never cease to have some effect; they always leave a trace. Discussions of the Lord, narratives, kirtans, etc., inevitably influence everyone. When the listeners possess faith and are inclined to practice (or wish to practice), the impact of the verses is amplified by their devotion and interest. Relation – Now the Lord, in the next three verses, confirms the principle of gathering the world by giving his own example. [ Verse 22 ]  
n na me pārt h āsti kartavyaṁ triṣu lokeṣu kiñcana  
na anāvaptaṁ avāptavyam vartā eva ca karmaṇi

Translation: “O Partha, I have no duty whatsoever in the three worlds; there is nothing that I have not already attained, yet I remain engaged in action.”

Breakdown of key terms (Roman transliteration + English meaning):

- **Partha** – O Partha (address to Arjuna)  
- **kartavyam** – duty, prescribed action  
- **me** – to me, my  
- **asti** – exists, is present  
- **anāvaptaṁ** – not attained, unacquired  
- **karmani** – in action, in deeds  
- **triṣu** – in the three (worlds)  
- **lokeṣu** – worlds, realms of existence  
- **na** – not, no  
- **eva** – indeed, only  
- **avāptavyam** – that which is to be attained, goal  
- **kincana** – not even a little, anything at all  
- **vartā** – remains, continues

Explanation – The Lord declares that He is not confined to any single world; therefore He says He has no duty in the three worlds. For the Lord, no duty remains in the three‑world system because He has already attained everything that can be attained. All beings (humans, animals, birds, etc.) act because they seek to obtain something; the Lord, having obtained all, still engages in action to set an example, illustrating the supreme principle of selfless duty.

[ Verse 22 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

Even when there is nothing left to do or to obtain, I still act. The Lord incarnates not because He has any personal duty, but for the welfare of others; He performs actions to rescue the saintly, to destroy the sinful, and to establish Dharma (righteousness) (Gita 4.8). Apart from incarnations, the Lord’s creation of the universe is also solely for the liberation of living beings. Heaven exists as the reward for meritorious deeds, and the 84 lakh worlds together with hell serve as the arena for the results of sinful deeds. Human existence—both virtuous and sinful—provides the opportunity to rise above one’s own welfare. This is possible only when a person does nothing for himself. All actions—gross‑body activity, subtle‑body contemplation, and causal‑body stability—must be performed solely for the benefit of others, not for personal gain. The three bodies (gross, subtle, causal) that enable all deeds belong to the world, not to the individual. Consequently, the karmayogi regards the body, senses, mind, intellect, material elements, and all other substances (which in reality are only the world) as belonging to the world and devotes them to the service of the world. If a person uses worldly objects for his own pleasure instead of for the world’s service, he commits a grave error. Recognizing worldly objects as his own creates desire for fruit, and fruit‑seeking necessitates action. As long as a person works driven by the desire to obtain something, the duty of “doing” remains for him. A serious examination reveals that a human being has no duty for himself. The object to be attained (the supreme soul, Atman) is eternally present, and the self (svarupa) is also eternal, whereas action and its results are transient, arising and perishing. How can the transient (action and result) be related to the eternal (self)? Action is related to the external (body and world), not to the self. Action always occurs through and for the external. Hence there is nothing for a person to do for himself. When a human has no personal duty, how can the Lord have any duty? The great souls who have attained perfection through karmayoga are described in verses 17‑18 of this chapter as having no duty, because their desire, satisfaction, and contentment reside within themselves. Consequently, they have no purpose in acting or refraining in the world, and they bear no selfish relation to any creature. Yet even such a great soul performs actions for the collection of the world. In the same way, the Lord declares that even when there is no duty and nothing remains to be obtained, He acts for the collection of the world. This implies that the realized great soul is one with the Lord—“Mama sādharmyām āgatāḥ” (Gita 14.2). Just as the Lord is the ideal man in the three worlds (Gita 3.23 and 4.11), the realized man is the ideal in this world (Gita 3.25). “Varta eva ca karmaṇi” – the word “eva” indicates that the Lord acts with enthusiasm, readiness, without laziness, carefully and completely in all prescribed duties. He neither abandons nor neglects his actions. As the wheels of an engine move the attached carriages, so the Lord and saint‑great souls—who have no desire to act or to acquire—function like the engine, prompting other humans to follow them. Ordinary people retain the desire to act and to acquire; these desires disappear only through selfless performance of duty. If the Lord and saint‑great souls ceased their duties, other people would also abandon theirs, leading to negligence and laziness, and they would begin to act without duty. Their desires would then persist. Therefore, for the welfare of all humanity, the Lord and saint‑great souls naturally perform their duties. The Lord is ever devoted to duty and never deviates from it. Hence a devotee of the Lord must also never deviate from duty, for deviation deprives one of the experience of the divine reality. Constant devotion to duty enables the seeker to readily experience the divine reality.

Appendix – In the Mahābhārata the Lord also tells the great sage that He performs His duty in the three worlds for the protection of Dharma and the establishment of Dharma. Thus, in the three worlds He assumes various forms and attires, O Bharadvaja. (Mahābhārata, Āśvamedha Parva, Chapter 54, verses 13‑14)

Translation: O Partha, if I were to become inattentive, if indeed I should not act, then all men would follow my conduct, O Partha, in every way. utsīdeyur ime lokā na kuryāṁ karma ced aham. saṅkarasya ca kartā syām upahanyām imāḥ prajāḥ. [ Verse 24 ]  
Translation: If I were to abandon these worlds and not perform action, I would become the cause of mixing and would destroy these peoples. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

**Commentary translation**

Explanation – In verse 22 the Lord stresses the necessity of dutiful performance. In verses 23‑24 He explains the harm that follows from neglecting duty. The conditional phrase “yadi hy ahaṁ na varteyaṁ jātu karmaṇy atandrītaḥ” is used to illustrate that it is inconceivable for the Divine not to act carefully; however, if we imagine that He were to refrain from action, the word “jātu” (become) is employed. The term “atandrītaḥ” means that one must not perform duty with laziness or negligence; duty must be carried out with great care and readiness. Acting without such care leads a person into laziness and negligence, destroying precious life. The commentator notes that the doer (kartā) would become the destroyer of all beings. By performing actions without slackness, one severs attachment to the results of action, just as a partially broken branch hangs longer than a fully broken one. Careful, prompt action creates separation from the fruits of action, whereas lazy, negligent action does not. Hence the Lord uses “samāchara” in verse 19 and “atandrītaḥ” here. If a particular action repeatedly comes to mind, it indicates an unremoved fault (desire, attachment, incompleteness, laziness, negligence, neglect, etc.) that prevents complete detachment from that action.

[ Verse 23-24 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

In these verses the Lord appears to say that only those who follow My path are truly worthy of being called human. Those who do not regard Me as an ideal, who, out of laziness and negligence, shirk their prescribed duties and instead seek power, are not truly human even though they may look human in form. “mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ” – “All men, O Partha, follow My way.” This statement must be free of attachment – “mā te saṅgo ’stv akarmaṇi” (Gita 2.47). Hence the Lord gives an example: even when nothing is to be gained, He still performs action. If He, according to the varna‑ashrama in which He incarnated, were to neglect His duty, all humanity would become corrupted and fall into ruin. Abandoning one’s duty brings about a tamasic (dark) nature in people, leading to their degradation – “adhoga chanti tāmāsāḥ” (Gita 14.18). In verse 21 of this chapter the Lord said that all men follow the conduct and proof of the supreme person, and here He says that men follow My path in every way. The implication is that the supreme person is an ideal in a single world (the human world), whereas the Lord is the ideal in all three worlds. The Lord incarnates in the human world to show how a man should live in this material existence. Living only for oneself is not the true science of existence. The world is essentially a school where we must learn to renounce desire, affection, selfishness, etc., and act for the welfare of others, thereby attaining our own liberation. All relationships in the world exist for mutual service (benefit). Consequently, fathers, sons, husbands, wives, brothers, sisters, and so on should protect each other’s rights, perform their respective duties, and strive for each other’s welfare. “utsīdeyur ime lokā na kuryām karma ced aham” – “If I did not act, I would not create these worlds.” In verse 23 the Lord warned, “yadi hy ahaṁ na varteyaṁ jātu karmaṇy atandrītaḥ,” that carelessness in action brings loss. In the present (verse 24) He again stresses the danger that arises from not performing action. Although it is impossible for the Lord to refrain from duty, He uses the conditional particle “chet” to indicate that, were He to neglect duty, the entire three‑fold world would fall into decay, and He Himself would be the cause of that destruction—though such a situation cannot occur. When two mutually contradictory dharmas (principles) merge, the result is called “saṅkara” (mixing). In verses 40 and 41 of the first chapter, Arjuna argued that if he fought, his lineage would be destroyed; the destruction of the lineage would annihilate the eternal family dharma, leading to the spread of sin throughout the family, the corruption of women, and consequently the emergence of varna‑mixing (caste inter‑breeding). Thus Arjuna’s view was that war would generate varna‑mixing. The Lord, however, states the opposite: the failure to perform the war‑related duty itself creates varna‑mixing. He illustrates that if He were to abandon duty, all categories—karma, dharma, worship, varna, ashrama, caste—would automatically become mixed. The meaning is that non‑performance of duty is the very cause of mixing. Therefore, the Lord tells Arjuna that even according to Arjuna’s own reasoning, the true cause of varna‑mixing is the neglect of duty. The ruin of the lineage and the corruption of women arise precisely because duty is abandoned; abandonment of duty brings about mixing. If women believed that their husbands had sacrificed their lives while performing the war‑duty but had not abandoned their own duty, why should they abandon theirs? In that case they would not be duty‑abandoned, their chastity would remain protected, and varna‑mixing would never arise.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]

The war‑like form of duty‑action, if not performed, gives rise to caste mixing. In this incarnation you have accepted the role of charioteer and I have become the driver, not by fighting as you imagine. **Special note** – Arjuna’s fundamental question (“Why do you bind me to such terrible action?”) is answered by the Lord in verses 22, 23 and 24, where He gives three examples to show that He is the one who engages you in action; He does not say that He himself is also engaged in action, because in reality He has no duty or desire in the three worlds. Having accepted that you will be the charioteer and I the driver, see that even as a Kshatriya I am now your driver and I am carefully and promptly performing the duty I have accepted. My performance of this duty will also affect the three worlds, because I am the ideal man in them. All beings follow my path. Likewise, you must not neglect your own duty‑action; you should perform it with the same care and promptness that I demonstrate. The Lord signals to Arjuna that prompt, careful observance of duty is required. **Relation** – In the three preceding verses the Lord described the need for caution in performing one’s own actions; in the next two verses He inspires the wise great soul to act with similar caution. **Verse 25**  
*Transliteration*:  
karmany asaktah karmanyavidvanso yatha kurvanti bhārata |  
kurvād vidvān sthā asaktaḥ icchanti lokasaṅgraham

*Meaning*:  
O Bharata, those who are attached to action perform it in the same way as the learned (who are unattached). The learned, though unattached, also desire the welfare (collection) of the world. **Verse 26**  
*Transliteration*:  
na buddhi‑bhedam janayet jnanam karmasankhinam |  
josayet sarvakarmani vidvan yuktaḥ samacaran

*Meaning*:  
One should not create a division of intellect that leads to ignorance among those attached to action; rather, the wise, acting with proper understanding, should perform all actions diligently. **Commentary on Verse 25**

- *saktāḥ* – those attached to action; they have full faith in the scriptures, follow scriptural duties, and are confident of the results prescribed by the scriptures. They are not philosophers nor sinners, but they are attached to actions, pleasures and material objects. - *avidvāns* – ignorant persons; although they know the scriptures, their desire for personal gain makes them ignorant in the true sense. They are scholars but not sages. - *asaktaḥ* – unattached; the true sage who is free from attachment. - *vidvān* – the learned, who act without attachment because they desire the welfare of the world (lokasaṅgraha). Thus, the learned perform all actions with care, avoiding negligence or laziness, because any lapse in action would diminish the fruits of those actions. The Lord holds this method of action as an ideal and encourages even the unattached learned to act for the benefit of the world. **Commentary on Verse 26**

- One must not let the confusion of intellect (buddhi‑bheda) give rise to ignorance among those attached to action. - The wise, equipped with proper understanding, should perform every action (sarva‑karmāṇi) with diligence (yuktaḥ samācaran). - Such conduct prevents the loss of results that would follow from careless or half‑hearted action. **Relation – Continued**

The verse stresses that desire, affection, attachment, passion, bias and selfishness are the obstacles that bind a person to action. The Lord advises that by cultivating detachment and wisdom, one can act for the collective good without being ensnared by personal cravings.

english:
219  
[ Verse 25-26 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

When the primordial source is completely absent, how can the welfare of the body and other material elements be ensured? From this attitude there is no attachment even to a single duty; when such a knower acts, the propagation of noble sentiments in the world occurs spontaneously. For a great soul, the terms **asakta** (detached) and **vidvan** (scholar) appear here. In verse 20 the phrase “lokasaṅgrahmevāpi samśyan” is used, and in verse 21 the same meaning is explained; here it is expressed with the words “lokasaṅgraham cikirsuh”. All conduct of the noble person (the **asakta vidvan**) is naturally oriented toward sacrifice and the preservation of propriety. Just as a sensual person is attached to pleasures, a materialistic person to family, and a greedy person to wealth, the noble person is attached only to the welfare of living beings. In his heart there is no explicit thought “I work for the world”; nevertheless, his actions automatically serve the world. Because of complete disconnection from material nature, even the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc., which are called the body of that wise great soul, fall under the term “lok” in “lokasaṅgrah”. To others such a wise great soul appears to desire “lokasaṅgrah”, but in reality he has no desire for it. The body, senses, mind, intellect, material elements, position, authority, wealth, qualifications, and abilities that he has obtained from the world are never regarded as his own; they are regarded solely for the service of the world, and due to this continuous flow, even in the state of realization the so‑called body and other elements act automatically, without any personal desire, in the service of the world. In this verse the words “yathā” and “tathā” denote the mode of action. It means that just as an ignorant (**sakam**) person performs duties with caution and eagerness for his own benefit, the wise person should also act for “lokasaṅgrah”, i.e., for the welfare of others. The wise person must continuously perform all worldly and Vedic duties with the intention of benefiting living beings. The ignorant man performs prescribed duties with care and eagerness to obtain results, whereas the wise man has no attachment to results and no duty toward them. Therefore, neglect of action by him is possible. For this reason, the Lord commands even the wise person to act in the same way as the ignorant (**sakam**) person. In verse 21 the scholar was described as an “ideal”, but here he is called a “follower”. The meaning is that whether the scholar is an ideal or a follower, lokasaṅgrah occurs automatically through him. Just as Lord Shri Rama instructs the people and also obeys his father’s command to go into exile, in both situations his actions constitute lokasaṅgrah, because his actions are not driven by personal purpose. When the scholar, free from attachment, performs his duties, his actions automatically influence the hearts of those whose minds are attached, whether or not they perceive “this great soul is acting without desire”. The self‑less attitude of a person naturally affects others—this is a principle. Hence the influence of an unattached scholar’s thoughts and conduct extends not only to humans but also to animals, birds, and other beings. **Special note** – As long as a person does not perform prescribed duties without desire, his cycle of birth and death cannot be terminated. As long as he acts for himself, he remains a doer; his “doing” never ends because the self is eternal while action and its results are transient. Therefore every person has a profound need to perform duty selflessly (not for oneself but solely for the welfare of others). * Although upon attaining the Supreme Self the Sankhya yogi and the Karma yogi become one (Gita 5.4‑5), because their means of practice differ in the preparatory stage, a slight difference remains in their characteristics and nature even in the state of realization. The Sankhya yogi retains a special superiority over actions, whereas the Karma yogi retains a special readiness for action, since the habit of acting persists for him. This difference appears in certain respects.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Because we regard worldly objects as valuable, the practice of Karma‑yoga (performing one’s duty without desire for personal gain) appears difficult. If we accept that we must act for the welfare of others without asking anything for ourselves, the observance of Karma‑yoga becomes easy today. In reality, the importance lies not in the objects themselves but in the conduct (their use). Conduct matters only when the heart does not attach importance to material things. No material thing is personal; it is personal only for the purpose of use. When we treat a material thing as personal, relinquishing it for the benefit of others seems hard. Neither any material nor any action is a cause of bondage; rather, their relationship creates the sense of bondage. Even learned persons perform all actions for the collection of the world (Lok‑sangraha). Yet they do not harbor the pride “I am collecting the world.” This is because the body, senses, mind, intellect, knowledge, abilities, position, etc., all belong to the world and have been received from the world. Offering the material received from the world back to the world is an act of honesty. It must be offered with utmost truthfulness and sincerity. Such offering is not a great deed. For example, if someone had kept money with us as a trust and, when asked later, we returned the money, what great act have we performed? Our obligation is fulfilled; we become debt‑free. Likewise, by offering worldly objects to the world, our obligation ends, we become free from the debt of birth and death, and we are liberated from the bondage of existence forever. Therefore, using worldly substances in the service of the world is not about earning merit; it is about freeing the self from those substances. In verse 25, the phrase “na buddhi‑bhedam … vidvān‑yuktaḥ samācaran” describes the unattached scholar as “yukta, vidvān.” The scholar whose inner heart possesses natural equanimity, whose state is unchanged, whose senses are perfectly mastered, and for whom earth, stone, and gold are alike, is called “yukta, vidvān” (Gita, sixth chapter, eighth verse). [ Chapter 3 ]

In the preceding (25th) verse, the terms “sakta, avidvān” refer to those who are attached and ignorant; they are labeled “karmasaṅgina, ajñāna” because they perform scriptural duties for personal gain—pleasure, honor, fame, etc. A great person bears a special responsibility because others naturally follow his example. Hence the Lord commands the learned, through the above verses, not to adopt any conduct or utter any words that would cause the downfall of ignorant (desire‑driven) persons from their present state. Creating such a downfall (bringing them down) generates “buddhi‑bheda” (division of intellect). Consequently, the learned should, keeping the welfare of all in mind, continue to perform scripturally prescribed auspicious actions according to their varna‑ashrama‑Dharma, thereby inspiring others to act duty‑bound without desire. The same principle applies to the principal members of society and family; they must carefully and consistently practice their duties so that a positive impact spreads through society and family. Examples that create “buddhi‑bheda” are:

1. Preaching such statements as “What is there in actions? Actions bind the soul; actions are inferior; one should abandon actions and turn to knowledge,” thereby sowing doubt and disbelief in others regarding duty. 2. Declaring “Self‑interest is everywhere; without self‑interest no one can live; everyone works for self‑interest; whenever a person acts, there is always a desire for fruit; if there is no desire for fruit, why act at all?”

3. Teaching that “Acting with desire for personal fruit leads to repeated births for enjoying those fruits.”

Such teachings cause desire‑driven individuals to lose faith in the results of actions. Consequently, their attachment to fruit does not cease, while auspicious actions are abandoned. The cause of bondage is attachment, not the actions themselves.

[ Verse 27 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

The realized sage should not create a division of intellect among people. He must act in accordance with his own varna‑ashrama‑dharma and cause others to act likewise. By his conduct and speech he should uplift the ignorant, who are presently trapped in delusion, step by step, without generating further confusion in their intellect. When ignorant persons are performing scripturally prescribed auspicious deeds, the sage should specially praise those deeds and point out the mistakes inherent in their performance, so that they may correct the errors and carry out the rites in full accordance with the prescribed method. In addition, the wise teacher should instruct that performing yajña, dāna, pūja, recitation, etc., is indeed meritorious, but it is improper to cling to the desire for fruit. Just as it is foolish to sell a diamond for ordinary stones, so too is it unwise to retain a selfish motive. Renouncing selfish desire and performing auspicious actions yields benefit far more quickly. Thus, moving from a selfish (sākāma) attitude to a self‑less (niṣkāma) attitude is not a division of intellect; it is the very reality. No human being is completely devoid of qualities; every person possesses some virtues. Therefore, the great realized master should, when giving instruction or explanation to anyone for his advancement, refrain from criticism or insult and instead extol that person’s virtues. Instruction delivered with respect to the praised qualities will have a special impact on the recipient. The same principle should guide the chief members of society and family when they educate others. The terms “samācaran” and “joṣayet” give two commands to the learned: (1) to perform, with utmost care, the scripturally prescribed duties; and (2) to cause even the attached, ignorant persons to perform those duties in the same way. Acting merely to display one’s deeds is “dambha” (pretension), a characteristic of the degrading demonic nature (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 16, Verse 4). Hence the Lord commands action not for display but for the welfare of the world. The realized man must continue to perform all prescribed duties efficiently even when there is no personal gain, so that the attached individuals awaken a sense of the importance of self‑less action and begin to act without attachment themselves. In other words, by observing the unattached conduct of the great soul, others are inspired to emulate it. Similarly, in matters of worship the sage must not create an intellectual split. Often people claim that chanting the divine name is futile if the mind is not fixed on God. The enlightened teacher should counter this by teaching that chanting can never be futile, because any chanting presupposes at least a modicum of feeling toward the Divine. Without feeling, there is no inclination to chant. Therefore, chanting should never be abandoned in any state. The statement “if the mind wanders in all directions, it is not remembrance” actually means that lack of mental focus does not negate the act of chanting; the chant still occurs, though with less efficacy. Concentrated, mindful chanting yields rapid benefit. **Appendix –** Neither the great realized master nor the Lord possess a sense of personal ownership over action. Consequently, they perform duties solely for the welfare of the world, not for themselves. The seeker likewise should not act for personal gain, because in essence there is no doer. Guiding people away from erroneous paths toward the righteous path constitutes world‑service. World‑service is achieved by observing scriptural conduct while internally maintaining the attitude “I do nothing for myself.” The seeker must not proclaim, “I do nothing for myself,” to others. Thus, the wise man should respectfully explain to the attached individuals the futility of prohibited actions and inspire them to abandon selfish desire altogether, while encouraging the abandonment of selfish motive even in permitted actions. **Relation –** What is the difference between the wise and the ignorant? The Lord explains in the following verse:

prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ | ahaṅkāravimūḍhātmā kartāham iti manyate || 27 ||

All actions performed in accordance with nature are conditioned by the three modes of material nature; the ego‑deluded soul thinks, “I am the doer.”

Karmāṇi sarva‑śaḥ = all actions, complete actions, of every kind, performed by the qualities (guṇas) of Prakṛti (nature). * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
(but) Ahankāravimūḍh‑ātmā = the ego‑deluded soul, “I am” (aham) = I

[ Chapter 3 ]

The ignorant person, whose inner mind is bewildered by ego, regards himself as the doer of actions. Explanation – “Karmāṇi are actions performed by the qualities of Prakṛti.” The one called “Ahankāravimūḍh‑ātmā” is said to be possessed by ego. This assumed ego is the universal power that creates, sustains and transforms bodies, trees, rivers such as the Ganga, houses, and all material changes. By the same universal power the human perceives, hears, eats, drinks, etc. All these activities are functions of that power. However, under the influence of ego and ignorance, a person divides the activities of that single universal power into two categories:

1. **Spontaneous activities** – those that happen automatically, e.g., the formation of the body, digestion of food, etc. 2. **Knowledge‑guided activities** – those performed consciously, e.g., seeing, speaking, eating, etc. The ego‑deluded person, in ignorance, claims the knowledge‑guided activities as his own deeds. The qualities (guṇas) that arise from Prakṛti – sattva, rajas and tamas – give rise to intellect, ego, mind, the five great elements, the ten senses and the sense‑objects (sound, etc.). These are also called the qualities of Prakṛti. In the verses quoted, the Lord makes clear that every action, whether universal (samastikī) or individual (vyastikī), is performed through the qualities of Prakṛti, not through the self‑nature (svarūpa). “Ahankāravimūḍh‑ātmā” – ego is a tendency of the inner mind (antar‑kara). “Self” (svarūpa) is the knower of that tendency. Because of mistake, the self is identified with that tendency and is taken as one’s own nature; therefore the person is called a deluded soul. Just as the body is “idam” (this), ego is also “idam”. “Idam” can never become “aham” (I) – this is a principle. When a person mistakenly identifies “idam” (this) with “aham” (I), he does not cease to act; even in action the ego remains. The assumed ego disappears only by non‑acceptance (by refusing to acknowledge it). **Special note** – “Aham” exists in two forms:

1. **Real (foundational) aham** – e.g., “I am” in the sense of pure existence. **Imagined aham** – e.g., “I am the body”. The real aham is natural and eternal; the imagined aham is unnatural and transient. Hence the real aham can be forgotten but never destroyed; the imagined aham may appear but cannot endure. The human error is to forget the real aham (one’s true nature) and to accept the imagined aham (“I am the body”) as truth. “Kartāham iti manyate” – although all actions of every kind are performed through the qualities of Prakṛti, the ego‑bewildered ignorant inner mind regards itself as the doer of certain actions. This is because he takes ego as his own nature. Because of ego, the human identifies himself with body, senses, mind, etc., and claims to be the agent of their activities. This opposite belief is self‑created; therefore only the same person can eradicate it. The way to eradicate it is through discernment – to consciously refuse to accept the false identification. *The “real aham” mentioned here is not the ego‑self but the true sat‑rūpa, cit‑rūpa (existence‑form, consciousness‑form) – the immutable reality. It is called “real aham” because it never changes, whereas the imagined aham changes. For example, an illiterate person may say, “I am a fool, I am unlearned,” while a learned person says, “I am a scholar, I am educated.” In both cases the underlying “I am” does not change. The permanence of the imagined aham gives rise to the term “real aham.” When the imagined aham is relinquished, i.e., when the vision shifts away, the “real aham” becomes the pure sat‑citananda (existence‑consciousness‑bliss) form.

[ Verse 27 ]

Because it is only through belief that belief is cut off. *The Seeker’s Revitalizer*

There is a “to‑do” and a “not‑to‑do”. Just as “to‑do” is an action, “not‑to‑do” is also an action. Sleeping, waking, sitting, walking, remaining in meditation, etc., are all actions. Action exists only in Prakṛti (nature). In “Svayam” (the conscious Self) there is neither doing nor not‑doing, because the Self is beyond both. The Self is inert (akriya) and the illuminator of all. If even the Self performed actions, how could it be the knower of those actions (the transformations of the body and the like)? Doing and not‑doing occur where the “Aham” (the sense of “I”) resides. When the “I‑sense” is absent, there is no relation to action. Both doing and not‑doing are manifested in the inert principle (its own nature); this is the natural condition of the human being. Yet, because of the “I‑sense”, man identifies himself with the actions of Prakṛti. The relationship that is assumed with the inert (the material) nature is called “Aham”. **Special point**

Just as a wave is part of the ocean and therefore shares the ocean’s identity, likewise the body, being a part of the world, shares the world’s identity. Man does not consider the world to be “I”, but through forgetfulness he mistakenly regards his body as “I”. The body has no independent existence. However, when a person, deluded by ego‑attachment, regards the body as his own nature, many desires arise: to obtain a woman, a son, wealth, to be regarded as good, to receive respect, to have others act in his favor, etc. His attention never turns to the fact that, by taking the body as his own nature, he is already bound; by adding desires he only deepens his bondage and brings himself into further distress. In the period of practice, even if one does not experience the truth “I (Svayam) am completely beyond the qualities of Prakṛti”, when the seeker accepts this statement, it becomes his experience. Thus, just as he was bound by a false belief, he is liberated by a true belief; the false belief disappears when it is no longer accepted—this is the principle. In Chapter 5, Verse 8, the Lord says:

*naiva kimcit karomi iti yukto manyeta tattvavit* – “One who, being wise, thinks ‘I do nothing’, does not consider himself the doer.”

To eradicate this unreal belief one must adopt the real belief: “I do nothing.”

False identifications such as “I am the body; I am the doer” become so firm that they seem impossible to abandon. Conversely, how can true identifications like “I am not the body; I am the non‑doer” become firm? Once they are firm, there is no separate existence, just as there is no separate existence without the world. Just as a wave has no existence without the ocean, the body has no existence without the world. ---

**Appendix –** All actions belong to the inert (material) division. In the conscious division there is never even a trace of action. Because of ego‑attachment, the ignorant person declares “I am the doer”. Ego‑attachment means that the individual, being a fragment of the non‑material nature, assumes the material fragment as his own nature—that is, he identifies himself with the ego. This is called *tādātmyam* (identification). The one who regards himself as the doer is, in fact, the conscious principle, but he mistakenly takes the inert ego as his nature. In other words, the one who identifies the ego as his nature is, in fact, a fragment of the Supreme Self. In that very Self, agency is impossible (see Gita Chapter 13, Verse 29). In reality the Self can never act through the body—*śarīrastho ’pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate* (Gita 13.31). Yet the person assumes “I am the doer”. In reality there is no *tādātmyam*; only the notion of *tādātmyam* is imagined. The Self does not become the doer; he merely, without discrimination, accepts the notion of agency—*manyate*. As soon as one assumes himself to be the doer, scriptural injunctions of prohibition apply, and he becomes the experiencer of the results of his actions. In the true nature (Svayam) there is no action. Action occurs only where there is an empty space. How can action exist in a completely solid nature? Yet, by taking himself to be the doer, the person attaches his sense of agency to the actions of Prakṛti, and that is the source of all subsequent activity.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 3 ]

For the individual, action (Karma) becomes the source of its own result, and he must endure that result. The doer is therefore also the enjoyer. The essential nature (Swarupa) is completely disconnected from mere activity; even the slightest modification of the essential nature does not constitute agency. Agency belongs to a separate category. To date, among the many bodies (yoni) of gods, humans, animals, birds, yakṣas, rakṣasas, etc., none of the actions performed have ever reached the essential nature, nor has any body reached the essential nature, because the categories of action and of material (body) are distinct, and the category of essential nature is distinct as well. Because one does not give importance to this discernment, a person becomes bound by action and its results. As long as “to do” exists, there is a connection with ego, for action cannot be realized without ego‑hood (the sense of doership). When the intention to act arises, the pride of agency inevitably appears. That pride of agency gives rise to action, and action reinforces the pride of agency. Consequently, a seeker can never become completely free of ego through any attained means. An action performed with ego can never bring welfare, because ego is the root of all miseries, birth, and death. By refraining from doing anything for oneself, the link with ego ceases, i.e., the connection with Prakṛti alone is severed. Therefore the seeker should de‑emphasize action and give priority to discernment (Viveka). When discernment is given importance, it remains self‑evident and continuously guides the seeker. Over time this discernment itself matures into true philosophical knowledge. tattva‑vittu mahābāho guṇakarma‑vibhāgayoḥ | guṇā guṇeṣu vartanta iti matvā na sajjate || 28 ||
*Translation of Verse 28*: “O mighty‑armed one, knowing that the divisions of qualities and actions are themselves the qualities, one does not become attached.”

Mahābāho = “O mighty‑armed one!”  
tattva‑vittu = “the knower of the ultimate reality” (the one who knows the true nature). The verse explains that a great soul, who knows the ultimate reality, does not cling to the division of qualities (guṇas) and actions (karma). In the preceding commentary, “tattva‑vittu” is used to distinguish a true knower of the ultimate reality from an ego‑deluded soul (ahankāra‑vimuḍhātmā) described earlier. Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities inherent in Prakṛti. Their operation makes the entire creation a tri‑guṇic entity. Hence body, senses, mind, intellect, living beings, and material forms are all suffused with qualities. This is called the “guṇa‑division.” Actions arising from these (body, etc.) constitute the “karma‑division.”

Guṇa and karma—that is, matter and activity—are constantly changing. Matter is created and destroyed; actions have a beginning and an end. Direct, precise experience of this is what constitutes true knowledge of the guṇa‑ and karma‑divisions. In pure consciousness (Swarupa) no action ever occurs; it remains ever free of attachment and change. When an ignorant person identifies himself with the guṇa‑division and the karma‑division, he becomes bound. Scripturally, the primary cause of this bondage is ignorance (Ajnana); from the seeker’s perspective, the primary cause is attachment (Rāga). Attachment arises from lack of discernment. When discernment awakens, attachment is destroyed. This awakened discernment is a special faculty of human beings. The only requirement is to give importance to this discernment and awaken it. Thus the seeker, having awakened discernment, must specifically eradicate attachment. Even a seeker who wishes to know the ultimate reality, if he does not consider himself related to guṇa (matter) and karma (action), also comes to know the guṇa‑ and karma‑divisions through the ultimate reality. Whether one knows the guṇa‑ and karma‑divisions through the ultimate reality, or knows the “self” (the conscious essence) through the ultimate reality, the result is the same.
