* Sadhaka – Sanjivani *

Our inherent, self‑evident relationship is with the immutable Supreme Self (Paramātma). There is essentially no relationship with the mutable Prakṛti; it is only imagined. When the imagined relationship with Prakṛti is erased through contemplation, it is called *jnāna‑yoga* (the yoga of knowledge). When the same relationship is erased by self‑less action, it is called *karmayoga* (the yoga of action). Only when the connection with Prakṛti is severed does true *yoga* (the experience of an eternal relationship with the Supreme Self) arise; otherwise there is merely *jnāna* and *karm* alone. Hence, the one who, after cutting off the tie with Prakṛti, recognises his perpetual relationship with the Supreme Self is the true *tattvavit* (knower of reality). [ Verse 28 ]

The method of knowing the division of qualities (guṇas) and actions (karmas) from the ultimate reality is described as follows. 1 – Even while residing in the body, the conscious principle (svarūpa) remains completely inactive and unattached (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 13, Verse 31). The functions of Prakṛti—body, senses, mind, intellect, etc.—are called *idam* (“this”). *Idam* never becomes *aham* (“I”). When “this” (the body and its functions) is not “I,” how can the actions occurring in “this” be “my” actions? The implication is that the body, senses, mind, intellect, and so on are merely activities of Prakṛti, while the *svayam* (conscious Self) is entirely unaffiliated and detached from them. Consequently, how can the *svayam* be the doer of those actions? In this way, one does not become bound by identifying oneself with material forms and actions. In every state one experiences the feeling “naiva kiñcit karomīti” (“I do nothing”) (Bhagavad Gita 5.8). To feel that one is distinct from actions is to know and experience oneself as separate from activity. “Guṇā guṇeṣu vartante” – because qualities arise from the qualities inherent in Prakṛti, the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc., are themselves called *guṇas* and all actions are produced by these qualities. Due to lack of discrimination, an ignorant person assumes a relationship with these qualities and regards himself as the doer of the actions that arise from them. Yet the *svayam* (ordinary light of consciousness) cannot experience the notion “I am the doer” when its self‑evident state is realized. An analogy: a locomotive’s engine moves, i.e., it performs work; however, the pulling power comes from the combination of engine and driver. In reality the pulling power belongs to the engine, but only when the driver operates it does the train reach its destination. The engine has no senses, mind, or intellect; therefore it does not possess those faculties. 2 – Senses (seeing, hearing, eating, drinking, etc.) are actions, while the objects of seeing, hearing, food, drink, etc., are *dravyas* (materials). We refer to these actions and materials as the senses (eyes, ears, mouth, etc.). The senses are known through the mind, the mind through the intellect, and the intellect through the assumed *aham* (“I‑ness”). This *aham* itself is illuminated by the ordinary light of consciousness, which is the knower, illuminator, and foundation of all. How can one know one’s true nature (consciousness) beyond the *aham*? Even in deep sleep, when intellect is immersed in ignorance, a person upon waking says, “I slept very peacefully.” Thus, after waking, the experience “I am” is present for everyone. This proves that even during sleep one possessed one’s own existence. If that were not true, there would be no memory such as “I slept peacefully; I knew nothing.” Memory is experiential; therefore, in every state each person has an uninterrupted experience of his own existence. In no state is there an experience of non‑existence (“I am not”). Those who have detached even the assumed *aham* and realized their true nature (the state of “is”) are the *tattvavits*. 1 – The memory of an experienced object is a “samskara” (Yogadarshana 1.11). 2 – Example: speech is a *dravya* (material), the tendency to speak is an *action*, and speaking occurs through the collective power of qualities; thus qualities act through qualities. Yet, out of ignorance, a person identifies both material and action as his own and thereby becomes the apparent *doer*.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

All people follow the conduct of a great man. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, the knower‑great soul, explains how the world is gathered by such a great person, saying that just as that great soul “abides in the qualities while remaining unattached to them,” the seeker likewise should regard himself in the same way and not become attached. **Nature – Person – Relational Insight**

Attraction always occurs within the same species; for example, attraction is found in the sound of the ears, the touch of the skin, the form seen by the eyes, the taste of the tongue, and the smell of the nose. Thus each of the five senses is attracted only to its own objects. One sense never attracts the object of another sense. The implication is that the fundamental cause of attraction of one thing to another is their common nature (sajatiyata). Attraction, tendency, and the principle of tendency (pravrttiki‑siddhi) exist only within the same nature. In objects of a different nature there is neither attraction nor tendency nor the principle of tendency. Hence attraction, tendency, and pravrttiki‑siddhi arise in nature because of its sameness. However, in the conscious person (purusha‑cetanā) the apparent attraction of inert nature (prakṛti‑ja, the material) is also, in reality, only a fragment of nature being drawn toward nature. The acts of doing and enjoying belong to nature alone, not to the person. The person remains ever unchanged, eternal, immovable, and uniform. In Chapter 13, Verse 31 the Lord states that even while residing in the body, the person actually does nothing and is not entangled—“śarīrastho ’pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate.” The person is merely “prakṛti‑stha” (situated in nature); because of this identity with nature, he becomes the cause of experiencing pleasure and pain—“purushaḥ sukha‑duḥkhānāṁ bhoktṛtve hetur ucyate” (Gita 13.20) and “purushaḥ prakṛti‑stho hi bhunktē prakṛti‑jñānagūṇān” (Gita 13.21). In other words, although all actions, their results, and attraction reside in nature, the identification of the person with nature makes him think “I am happy,” “I am sorrowful,” and thus he becomes the cause of enjoyment and suffering. The experience of being happy or sorrowful cannot arise in inert nature (prakṛti‑ja) alone; without the conscious person (cetanā) nature cannot become the enjoyer of pleasure or pain. The person does not undergo any change or disorder; however, he possesses the capacity to acknowledge or deny relation. He is not a lifeless stone; he is knowledge‑itself. If the person lacked the capacity to accept or reject relation, how could he consider himself related to nature? How could he regard nature’s activity as his own? How could he accept the role of doer or enjoyer? Recognizing or denying relation is a “feeling” (bhāva), not an “action” (kriyā). The person can choose to associate or not associate, but he lacks the capacity to act. The capacity to act resides in that which undergoes change (vikar). The person has no nature of change, whereas nature is inherently changeable; activity is natural to nature. Therefore, only when the person relates himself to nature does he consider the activity as his own—“kartāham iti manyate” (Gita 3.27). The absence of change in the person is not a weakness or deficiency; rather, it is his significance. He remains continuously uniform and unvarying. Change is not his nature, just as ice has no nature or capacity to become hot. Change‑driven activity is the nature of material existence, not of the person. Yet the person possesses full freedom to deny any relation to nature, because fundamentally there is no inherent relation to nature. When the person, as the conscious self, identifies himself with the fragment of nature that is his body, attraction, actions, and their fruits continue to arise in that fragment of homogeneous nature. This is indicated by the verse “guṇāḥ guṇeṣu vartante” (qualities dwell in qualities). By assuming his position within the qualities, the person (cetanā) remains apparently happy or sorrowful. In reality, there is no separate existence of pleasure or pain. Hence the Lord emphasizes the need to sever the perceived relation with the qualities. From a philosophical standpoint, the separation of relation is ever‑present; it is only through ignorance that relation is imagined. Thus, by rejecting the imagined relation, one recognizes that only the qualities themselves remain.

[ Verse 29 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The task is to recognise that the qualities (guṇas) are merely a manifestation of reality. The expression “iti matvā na sajjate” uses the verb *matvā* in the sense of “knowing”. The enlightened great soul discerns nature (prakṛti, the inert) and the conscious principle (puruṣa) as inherently distinct; therefore he is not attached to the qualities that arise from nature. By employing the word *matvā*, the Lord appears to command seekers to regard the natural qualities as separate and not become attached to them. **Special note** – The practice systems of the karmayogi and the sāṅkhya‑yogi are not unified. The karmayogi strives to erase the sense of unity that arises from the qualities (the body, etc.), which is why the Śrīmad‑Bhāgavatam states “karmayogas tu kāminām” (Bhāgavatam 11.20.7). Accordingly, the Lord emphasizes for the karmayogi the necessity of action: “Without the initiation of deeds a person does not attain non‑action” (Bhagavad‑Gītā 3.4) and “For the aspirant who wishes to mount yoga, performing action is the sole purpose” (Bhagavad‑Gītā 6.3). The karmayogi does act, but not for personal gain; he acts solely for the welfare of others. Hence he does not become the enjoyer (*bhokta*) of those actions. When the role of enjoyer disappears, the role of doer (*kartṛ*) also vanishes automatically. In other words, the sense of doership exists only for the sake of fruit; when there is no fruit, doership ceases. Consequently, even the karmayogi is not truly a doer. In sāṅkhya yoga, discernment (*viveka*) and contemplation dominate. Knowing that “the natural qualities are merely qualities in operation,” the sāṅkhya yogi does not consider himself the agent of those actions. The Lord will later state in Chapter 13, Verse 29 that the person who sees all actions as performed by nature alone and perceives the *Atman* (the eternal soul) as non‑acting is the one who sees reality. Thus the sāṅkhya yogi destroys the notion of doership, and the disappearance of doership automatically eliminates enjoyership. From the very beginning of Chapter 3, the Lord repeatedly stresses the importance of action through numerous examples: great sages such as Janaka performed self‑less action and attained the highest perfection (3.20); “I also act” (3.22); even the wise perform worldly actions for the purpose of gathering material results, just as the ignorant do (3.25‑26). These passages demonstrate that action, performed with the proper attitude, is always commendable. **Appendix (Pariśiṣṭa‑Bhāva)** – One who is not deluded by ego is called *tattva‑vit* (knower of the ultimate reality). The same person is referred to as *tattva‑darśī* in Chapter 2, Verse 16. The *tattva‑vit* transcends both the division of qualities and the division of action, i.e., material and kinetic aspects. As long as the seeker remains attached to the world, he cannot become *tattva‑vit*. One cannot truly know the world while still bound to it; only when completely detached can the world be known. Similarly, one cannot know the Supreme (*Brahman*) while remaining separate from it; only by becoming one with the Supreme can one truly know the Supreme. The underlying principle is that, in reality, we are distinct from the world yet one with the Supreme. The body is united with the world; our *Atman* is united with the Supreme. **Verse 29 (Sanskrit with word‑by‑word breakdown)**

> prakṛteḥ guṇa‑sammūḍhāḥ sajjante guṇa‑karmaṣu |  
> tān akṛtsna‑vido mandān kṛtsna‑vinna vichālayet || 29 ||

- **prakṛteḥ** – of material nature (prakṛti)  
- **guṇa‑sammūḍhāḥ** – deluded by the modes (qualities)  
- **sajjante** – remain attached / stay engrossed  
- **guṇa‑karmaṣu** – in the modes and their actions  
- **tān** – those  
- **akṛtsna‑vido** – who are not fully aware (akṛtsna = not fully known)  
- **mandān** – of dull intellect  
- **kṛtsna‑vinna** – without discrimination / without true knowledge  
- **vichālayet** – should not be disturbed / should not deviate

Thus, those whose minds are clouded by the qualities and who lack true knowledge become attached to actions, while the enlightened *tattva‑vit* remains undisturbed.

[ Chapter 3 - Commentary – ‘Prakṛtigeruṇasammūḍhāḥ sajjante guṇakarmasu' ]

Sattva, rajas and tamas – the three gunas born of Prakṛti – are the bonds that bind a person. The sattva‑guna binds through attachment to happiness and knowledge, the rajas‑guna binds through attachment to action, and the tamas‑guna binds through delusion, laziness and sleep. (This explanation refers to verses 6‑8 of Chapter 14.)

The verses quoted above describe those ignorant persons who are completely deluded by the gunas of Prakṛti; nevertheless they have faith in the scriptures, in the prescribed auspicious actions, and in the fruits of those actions. In verses 25‑26 of this chapter such ignorant men are called “saktāḥ, avidvānsaḥ” and “karmasaṅginām, ajñānām”. Because of desire for worldly and transcendental enjoyments, these men remain attached to material objects and actions. Consequently they cannot comprehend how to rise above these attachments, and therefore the Lord calls them ignorant. “tān‑kṛtsna‑vido mandān” – ignorant persons perform auspicious actions, but they do so for the acquisition of perishable, non‑lasting objects. They cling to wealth and other obtained objects and crave what they have not obtained. Thus, bound by affection and desire, they cannot fully understand the essence of the gunas (objects) and actions. Such ignorant persons know the scriptural duties and their procedures correctly, but because they do not fully grasp the essence of the gunas and actions, they are termed “akṛtsna‑vidaḥ” (those who do not know completely). Their preoccupation with worldly enjoyments and accumulation makes them “mandān” (of dull intellect). A person should not cause these previously described ignorant, desire‑driven men to deviate from auspicious actions, lest the dull‑intellect individuals fall from their present state. In verses 25‑26 the wise men are described as “asaktaḥ, vidvān” and “yuktaḥ, vidvān”. In verse 25 the Lord instructed the knower of the truth (tattvajña) with the word “kuryāt” (let him act), and in verse 26 with the word “joṣayet” (let him incite) that even the ignorant should perform the same actions. However, here the Lord says “na vicālayet” (do not cause deviation), implying that the wise should, at most, refrain from disturbing the ignorant with their signals, words or deeds. This is because the liberated soul (jīvanmukta) is beyond the governance of the Lord and the scriptures; actions for the natural gathering of the world arise automatically from the body. Whether the tattvajña is a karmayogī or a jñānayogī, even while performing all actions, his relationship with actions and material objects is not of the ordinary kind; in reality there is no such binding relationship. Ignorant persons perform auspicious actions only to attain heaven. Therefore the Lord commands that such persons should not be disturbed—that the great souls should not, through their signals, words or deeds, create doubt, disbelief or disinterest in the scripturally prescribed auspicious actions of these desire‑driven men, lest they abandon those actions and fall. Thus, to free them from the bondage of birth and death, it is appropriate to divert them from desire‑driven attachment, not from scriptural duties. The phrase “kṛtsnavinna vicālayet” (one who fully knows the gunas and actions and is free from desire and attachment) describes a wise and necessary person. **Appendix (Pariśiṣṭa‑bhāva)** – Arjuna asked why the Lord engages me in severe actions. The Lord answers in many ways, indicating that His purpose is not to bind me to severe actions but to sever my attachment to actions. Severing attachment to actions is the purpose of karmayoga. *Action and Karma* – There is a distinction between the two. When an action is performed with the sense “I am the doer,” it becomes karma and yields three types of results: desirable, undesirable, and mixed (see Gita 18.12). When the sense “I am not the doer” is present, the activity does not become karma and yields no fruit. The tattvajña’s activities are not karmic; they are merely movements (see Gita 3.33).

229  
[ Verse 30 ]  
* Sadhaka – Sanjeevani *

Relation – What a person should do to free himself from attachment to actions and their results, which bind him, is explained by the Lord in the following verse. **Verse (Sanskrit transliteration)**  
mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi sannyasyādhyātma‑cetasa  
nirāśīr nirmamo bhūtvā yudhyasva vigata‑jvaraḥ

**English translation**  
Abandon all duties to Me, O one whose mind is spiritual; having become free of hope and without selfish desire, fight without fever (without the burning passion of desire). **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- *adhyātma‑cetasa*: (you) discerning, spiritual‑mindful  
- *mayi*: in Me  
- *sarvāṇi*: all, complete  
- *karmāṇi*: actions, duties  
- *sannyasy*: having relinquished, having offered  
- *nirāśīr*: free from hope, without expectation of results  
- *nirmamo*: without selfish desire, unattached  
- *bhūtvā*: becoming, having become  
- *yudhyasva*: fight, engage in battle  
- *vigata‑jvaraḥ*: without fever, without the feverish heat of desire

**Commentary**

The aspirant often believes that actions bind him and that one cannot live without performing them; therefore, he fears that acting will imprison him. The Lord tells Arjuna that, with a spiritual mind, one should offer all prescribed duties to the Divine, regarding them as having no personal claim. In reality, the power that operates behind every worldly activity is the Lord’s alone. The body, senses, material objects, and even the power itself belong to Him. Hence, when one earnestly thinks “everything belongs to the Lord and the Lord is Himself,” the duties performed will no longer bind but will become liberating. The body, senses, mind, intellect, and material elements have no independent claim; they are merely aspects of nature—*prakṛti‑sthāni*. The true Self is the Supreme (*Paramātmā*), as expressed in “mamaivaṁśo jīvaloke” (Gita 15.7). Recognizing that the apparent ownership of these bodies is a mistake and offering them to the Lord is called *arpana* (offering). By valuing one’s discernment and renouncing the foolish sense of personal connection to matter and action, one fulfills the true meaning of offering. **Instruction on duty**

Perform the duty of fighting, but let the inner self remain guided by discernment. From any philosophical or scientific standpoint, it cannot be proved that the physical body and other material substances are truly one’s own. In fact, they are not owned by anyone; they are provided for proper use. Because they are not “mine,” no one can claim dominion over them. The world belongs wholly to the Supreme; yet the living being mistakenly appropriates the Supreme’s property as his own, leading to bondage. By erasing this error through discernment, one accepts all matter and actions as expressions of the Supreme’s spiritual principle and thereby offers them. **Explanation of “adhyātma‑cetasa”**

The phrase emphasizes that without discernment, the body (the transient world) appears as one’s own. When viewed through the lens of discernment, the body does not appear as personal; instead, an imperishable Supreme reality is seen. Seeing the world as one’s own is downfall; not seeing it as one’s own is upliftment. **Quoted verse**

dvyakṣarastu bhavēn mṛtyus tr̥akṣaram brahma śāśvatam  
mame'ti ca bhavēn mṛtyurna mame'ti ca śāśvatam

*Translation* – “The two‑letter word ‘mam’ (this is mine) denotes death, while the three‑letter word ‘na‑mam’ (this is not mine) denotes the immortal, eternal Brahman.” (Maha 0, Shanti 0 13.4; Ashvamedhika 0 51.29)

**Special note on offering**

The Lord’s use of “adhyātma‑cetasa” indicates that any seeker, regardless of the path, must aim for the spiritual, not the worldly. The ultimate purpose is always the eternal principle; desire is always directed toward the transient. The seeker must have purpose, not mere craving. By offering all actions through the instruction “mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi sannyasy,” one relinquishes personal claim to body, senses, mind, intellect, and life‑force, dedicating them wholly to the Divine.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]

The offering (Arpana) concerns the instruments (the material useful for performing actions) and the actions themselves. When a person regards objects as his own and offers them to God, God returns many more objects; for example, the earth yields many times more grain than the seeds sown, yet even after receiving manyfold, the yield remains limited. But when one does not consider the objects as his own (regarding them as belonging to God) and offers them to God, God gives Himself and the devotee becomes indebted. The implication is that by treating objects as one’s own, their value is found only in the objects themselves, whereas by offering them without self‑attachment, one receives God Himself. One mistakenly regards the self and one’s possessions as belonging to oneself—things that never truly were, are not, will not be, and cannot become so. What relation does the perishable have with the imperishable? Hence, whether one offers actions to the world, to nature, or to God, the result is the same; the world is the activity of nature, and God is the master of nature. From this viewpoint both the world and nature belong to God. Therefore, “I am God’s, and the only things called mine belong to God”; consequently everything should be offered to God, i.e., one must relinquish personal attachment. After doing so the seeker need not desire anything from the world or from God, because whatever is required is automatically arranged by God. After the offering, even the body and other material appearances should no longer seem to belong to the self. If they still appear as one’s own, the offering has not truly taken place. For this reason, even the father’s house, the courtyard, and the key are regarded as belonging to the father when the mind is discriminative and contemplative. The teaching on offering to God is so unique that even a half‑hearted offering yields only benefit. The reason is that actions and objects are never truly one’s own. After performing actions, they can still be offered, but a genuine offering occurs only when there is a complete disassociation from objects and actions. Such disassociation arises when one fully experiences that the body (including the senses), the material instruments, actions, and the “self” are all God’s. Practitioners often err by trying to regard only the instruments as God’s, neglecting that the body and the self are also God’s; consequently their offering remains incomplete. Hence the seeker must regard the body, instruments, actions, and the self as exclusively God’s, for they truly belong to Him. God is exceedingly pleased by a genuine offering. This does not mean that the offering assists God; rather, the one who offers becomes free from the bondage of Karma, and that liberation pleases God. Just as a small child gives a key lying in the courtyard to his father and the father rejoices, the child’s act of giving, however simple, delights the divine. The Supreme Soul (Atman) has fashioned the human body in a remarkably subtle manner. All material necessities required for human livelihood and practice are abundantly available, and divine discernment (Viveka) is also present. When a person fails to value this discernment and does not make proper use of the acquired objects, instead treating them as his own and using them for personal gain while also developing attachment to them and longing for unattained things, he becomes bound by the cycle of birth and death. In the present age, renouncing the very forms of objects, persons, circumstances, events, abilities, powers, bodies, senses, actions, and material substances—offering mind, life‑force, intellect, etc.—is not something that has ever existed. Recognizing that the objects of God are truly God’s is the authentic understanding. Such objects were never truly ours, nor will they ever remain ours in the future.

[ Verse 30 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

Because they never remain uniform and change every moment, this reality is known to man. If a person accepts exactly what he knows and acts accordingly, there is not the slightest doubt of his liberation. To accept as one knows means not to regard the body and other material things as one’s own or for oneself, not to become dependent on them, and not to give them importance thereby accepting subordination. Giving importance to material things is a great mistake. Considering oneself fulfilled by acquiring material things is a great bondage. By giving importance to perishable material things, new desires arise. Desire is the root of all sins, heats, sorrows, misfortunes, hells, etc. Desires do not obtain material objects, and even if they are obtained by destiny, they do not endure, because material objects are transient while Atman (the eternal soul) is ever‑lasting. Hence, by renouncing desire a person should perform his duty‑Karma. A doubt may arise here: how can there be inclination toward actions without desire? The answer is that both the fulfillment and the renunciation of desire involve inclination toward actions. Ordinary persons are inclined toward actions for the fulfillment of desire, while the seeker, for the purpose of self‑purification, is inclined toward the renunciation of desire (Gita – Chapter 5, Verse 11). In reality, inclination toward actions is only for the renunciation of desire, not for its fulfillment. From taking a relationship with rigidity (jaddatā) the origin of both necessity and desire arises. When the relationship with the world is completely abandoned, the fulfillment of necessity and the renunciation of desire occur. ‘Nirāśir‑nirmamo bhūtvā yudhya sv vigat‑jvaraḥ’ – “Having become dispassionate and self‑less, fight, free from past fever.” Even after reflecting all actions and material (Karma‑sāmagrī) in the mirror of the Divine, a fragment of desire, affection and distress may remain. For example, we gave someone a book. Seeing him read the book, a feeling arises in our mind that he is reading *my* book. This is a partial affection that remains after the offering. To abandon this fragment, the Lord tells Arjuna: do not desire a new object, do not develop affection for the obtained object, and do not feel distress for the destroyed object. The test of my offering is that even the fragments of desire, affection and distress should not remain. Seekers who, even after offering everything to the Divine, still see desire, affection and distress toward body and other material things because of past conditioning, should never become despondent. Where desire appears, that very place is desire‑free; where affection appears, that very place is affection‑free; and where distress appears, that very place is distress‑free. Similarly, the one who regards the body as “I” (aham) is the one who is without body (ahantāriha). Hence, a mere human is fully entitled to be free of desire, affection and distress. The word “jvara” (fever) appears only here in the Gita. In war, familial love, etc., can give rise to distress. Therefore, when performing duty‑Karma in the form of war, the Lord, to caution specially, uses the term “vigat‑jvara” and tells Arjuna to fight without distress. Man – the body – is obtained only for the fulfillment of purpose. When the purpose is fulfilled, nothing remains to be done. The inclination toward actions for the fulfillment of desire belongs to those who have forgotten their real purpose (the attainment of the eternal principle, Brahman). The Lord calls such persons “kripan” (the pitiable, the object of compassion) – “kripanāḥ phala‑hetavaḥ” (Gita 2.49). In contrast, those who, keeping the purpose before them (for the renunciation of desire), are inclined toward actions, the Lord calls them “manishi” (the wise) – “phalaṁ tyaktvā manīṣiṇāḥ” (Gita 2.51). Service, self‑realisation and the feeling of attaining the Divine are the purpose, not desire. The feeling of acquiring perishable material things is desire. Hence, it is a mistake to think that without desire there is no inclination toward actions. Actions also proceed smoothly for the fulfillment of purpose. Having turned away from the Supreme in one’s part, the world becomes “vigat‑jvara” (past fever); because the pleasure that arises from suitability…

Arjuna faced duty‑Karma in the form of war; therefore the Lord, using the word “yudhya sv” (fight), gives him the command to fight. The Lord’s intention is not to fight per se, but to perform duty‑Karma. Consequently, whenever a duty‑Karma arises, the seeker must perform it selflessly, without desire, without distress, with the intellect of reflecting the Divine. He should not look at the result (success or failure). He should remain equanimous regarding success‑failure, favorable‑unfavorable, and similar dualities.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 3 ]

Both the anxiety that arises from adversity and the anxiety itself are fevers, and its vision departs only when one performs action. Distress, attachment–aversion, joy–sorrow, desire–anger, etc., are also fevers. In short, all mental disturbances (viksas) such as attachment–aversion, anxiety, agitation, restlessness, etc., are fevers, and being free from them is the meaning of the term “vigata‑jvara” (fever‑free). Special point: When the aspirant’s sole purpose becomes the attainment of the Supreme Self, everything that he possesses (objects, circumstances, etc.) becomes a means (instrument). Then there is no distinction of good and bad within that means. Therefore, whatever the means are, they must be offered to God exactly as they are. One must return to God exactly what God has given. Even after offering all actions to God, any desire, affection, and distress that appear within oneself must also be offered to God. By offering to God, one becomes attached to God. Therefore, in the present verse God commands the performance of duty‑action through the word “yudhyaḥ” (fight). Just as in the forty‑eighth verse of the previous chapter God instructed to act with equanimity in success and failure, here (in verse 30) He commands to fight without desire, without malice, and without distress—that is, to perform duty‑action. If even a fierce act such as war can be performed with equanimity, what other act cannot be performed with equanimity? Equanimity arises only when the attitude “the body is not mine, the self is not mine, and nothing is for me” becomes real. - The observance of duty‑action is possible only when the aspirant’s aim shifts from the world to the sole Supreme Self. As the aspirant becomes increasingly devoted to duty for the purpose of attaining the Supreme Self, desires, affection, attachment, and similar faults automatically disappear, and one experiences one’s natural state of equanimity. When the full experience of equanimity is attained, the sense of doership vanishes completely and merges with the purpose. The rule is that when there is no desire to obtain or do anything for oneself, the ego (Ahm) is automatically destroyed. In the state of a yogi, action itself is said to be the means—“Arurukshormuner yogaṁ karma kāraṇam ucyate” (Gita 6.3). The reason is that by performing duty‑action the aspirant discovers what lacks within him (desire, affection, etc.). Therefore, in verse 12 of chapter 12, renunciation of the fruits of action (Karma‑yoga) is praised over meditation, because in meditation the aspirant’s focus remains primarily on the mind’s restlessness, and merely fixing the mind on the object is considered success. However, beyond the mind’s restlessness, other deficiencies (desire, affection, etc.) also arise, as does the need for devotion‑yoga. - Arjuna seeks his own welfare, but apart from the war‑like duty‑action. Hence, when Arjuna asks about his welfare, the Lord commands him to perform the war‑like duty‑action; because, according to the Lord, performing duty‑action (Karma‑yoga) also leads to welfare, and the supplemental aspect of Jnana‑yoga—so far the Lord has answered Arjuna’s question (Why do you engage me in such terrible action?) in many ways. In this verse the Lord now explains the method of action according to divine will. The instruction to offer all actions to Me means to regard both the action and the material not as belonging to oneself but as belonging to Me and for Me. The reason is that the Lord is all‑encompassing and all actions and material (the created world) are subsumed within the all‑encompassing Lord (Gita – Chapter 7, verses 29‑30). For that all‑encompassing Lord the word “mayi” (in Me) appears here. In this verse, the phrase “mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi sannyasya” refers to devotion‑yoga, the term “adhyātma‑cetasā” refers to Jnana‑yoga, and the expression “nirāśīr‑nirmamo bhūtvā yudhyaḥ vigata‑jvaraḥ” pertains to Karma‑yoga. * For example, a person works earnestly in a service committee, but when he receives respect or a reward, he may develop attachment to it—this indicates a deficiency. Such deficiencies become apparent only when one acts.

[ Verse 31 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

Relation – In the preceding verse He presented His doctrine; now He confirms that doctrine in the next two verses. These humans constantly uphold this doctrine of Mine. The faithful, free from fault‑finding, are also liberated by their actions. **Explanation** – “These humans constantly uphold this doctrine of Mine” means they follow it continuously. By invoking the term “śraddhāvanta‑anasūyasaḥ” (Gita 18.71), the Lord tells the listener to be full of faith and free from any tendency to find fault. ‘Anasūyantaḥ’ refers to a person who harbors no suspicion toward any caste, ashrama, dharma, or sect. Anyone who wishes to be freed from karmic bondage must accept this principle and follow it. The body, senses, mind, intellect, material objects, actions, etc., are not truly his own; realizing this truth releases all beings from the bonds of karma. A person who possesses unquestionable, direct confidence and reverence for the Lord and His doctrine is called a “śraddhāvanta”. When one does not regard the body and other inert substances as his own, he becomes free; faith in this reality makes it easy to renounce attachment to the perceived relationships of materiality. A faithful seeker (śraddhāvanta) listens to the true scriptures, true discussions, and the teachings of holy company, and puts them into practice. The human body is given solely for the purpose of attaining the Supreme Self. Therefore, when the sole, intense longing is to attain the Supreme Self, faith, readiness, and control of the senses arise automatically in the seeker. Hence the seeker’s primary aim must be the intense desire for Supreme Self‑realization. In the previous (third) verse the Lord gave His doctrine; to avoid a fault‑viewing attitude He uses the word “anasūyanta”. The tendency to see faults in qualities is called “asūya”. Here those free from such fault‑viewing are termed “anasūyanta”. Even where faith exists, a trace of fault‑viewing may remain. Consequently the Lord pairs the term “śraddhāvanta” with “anasūyanta” to urge the person to be completely free of fault‑viewing (a fully faithful one). Thoughts such as “the Lord’s doctrine is excellent, but the Lord boasts, saying everything should be offered to Him” or “the doctrine is good, but how can one attain the Lord through actions? Actions are binding and inert” represent a fault‑viewing of the Lord’s teaching. The seeker must not develop a fault‑view of either the Lord or His doctrine. In reality everything belongs to the Lord; however, by mistakenly treating the Lord’s possessions as his own, a person becomes bound, driven by desire and attachment, and suffers. By relinquishing this sense of ownership, a person is liberated and attains lasting happiness. The Lord, out of his innate compassion, offers everything as his own offering; it is improper to view this with suspicion. This is the Lord’s supreme benevolence, compassion, and parental love—offering all his deeds for the welfare of humanity even though he needs nothing. The Lord’s doctrine is called “principle” (siddhānta) in the world. The supreme principle is referred to as “matam” (doctrine). Because of His natural simplicity and lack of ego, the Lord names the supreme principle “mat”. This doctrine remains unchanged through the three ages; it does not alter whether one has faith or not. Here the word “nityam” is not an adjective of “matam”; it qualifies the verb “anutiṣṭhanti”. The Lord is eternal; therefore all that is related to Him is also eternal. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- ye – those  
- me – my  
- matam – doctrine, opinion  
- idam – this  
- nityam – always, eternally  
- anutiṣṭhanti – uphold, stand firm in  
- mānavāḥ – humans  
- śraddhāvantaḥ – faithful, devoted  
- anasūyantaḥ – free from suspicion, without fault‑finding  
- mucyante – are liberated  
- te – they  
- api – also  
- karmabhiḥ – by actions

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The doctrine of the Lord is eternal. It is supreme and not for one’s own personal benefit. A principle is that which never perishes. Hence the Lord’s doctrine is eternal, and its observance must also be perpetual. The adverb “nityam” (eternal) therefore signifies remaining constantly (always) in the Lord’s doctrine and acting in accordance with it. **Question:** What is the Lord’s doctrine, and how should its perpetual observance be performed? **Answer:** Any object that has been obtained is not truly one’s own—this is the Lord’s doctrine. The body, senses, mind, intellect, life‑force, wealth, property, material substances, etc., are all functions of nature, and the world itself is a function of nature. Consequently these objects are united with the world, and because they contain a fragment of the Supreme Atman, the individual self is united with the Supreme Atman. Thus these objects are not personal (not “mine”); only the right to use them is personal. Likewise virtues, moral conduct, renunciation, dispassion, compassion, forgiveness, etc., are not personal; they belong to the Lord. They are divine wealth—Bhagavata‑acquired wealth (capital)—and therefore belong to the Lord alone. If such virtues and moral qualities were truly personal, we would have complete ownership over them, and no one else could acquire them without our permission. Claiming them as one’s own breeds pride, which is the root of demonic (asuri) attachment to wealth. [ Chapter 3 ]

The material objects we acquire—body, senses, etc.—cannot be taken with us, nor can we retain them permanently; even now they are constantly separating from us. The things that appear to belong to us in the present are meant for noble use, i.e., for the benefit of others, not for hoarding personal rights. Therefore we have only the right to make proper use of acquired objects, not to claim them as ours. The Lord has bestowed these objects so generously that they seem to be our own. Treating them as our own is an abuse of the Lord’s generosity. When one mistakenly regards what is not his as his own, the seeker must, through deep spiritual contemplation, offer those mistakenly‑claimed objects back to the Lord—removing the false sense of ownership. The sole purpose of this offering is the attainment of the spiritual principle (the Supreme Atman). A sincere seeker who reflects seriously will clearly understand that any obtained object is never truly his; it is always destined to be relinquished. The body, position, authority, education, qualifications, wealth, property, land, etc., that one has received have come from the world and belong to the world. Whether one calls these objects “world‑property,” “nature‑property,” or “Lord‑property,” the essential truth remains that they are not one’s own. How can something that is not yours be yours? Claiming a non‑personal object as one’s own and performing actions to acquire it creates bondage. The body and similar objects are neither “own” nor “for oneself.” If they were for oneself, their acquisition would bring complete satisfaction and a sense of wholeness. Yet, no matter how many worldly objects one obtains, satisfaction never arises. True satisfaction or the experience of completeness occurs only upon receiving the object that is truly one’s own—the Lord. When the genuine object is attained, even the desire for anything further disappears, as in a dream where nothing else is sought. Just as every woman who bears children is a mother, a child does not find contentment in being with all mothers; only the child’s own mother brings satisfaction. Similarly, as long as the desire for more persists, one must understand that the true object has not yet been obtained. Even if one mistakenly regards acquired objects as personal, they are in fact not, and therefore cannot provide true satisfaction. Consequently, any acquired object remains merely an object of thought. Thus the Lord alone is the sole reality of the universe. The seeker must neither regard any “object” as his own nor perform any “action” for his own sake. Actions performed for one’s own benefit become binding (see Gita – Chapter 3, Verse 9), i.e., sacrifices performed selfishly. Apart from self‑less sacrifice (yajna) performed for the welfare of others, all other actions done for personal gain bind the individual. The totality of a seeker’s actions, including accumulated karma, is dissolved when performed as yajna (see Gita – Chapter 4, Verse 23). The Lord is the great sovereign of all worlds—*sarvalokamaheshvaram* (Gita 5.29). When a person regards himself as the master of objects, he forgets his true Master, because he identifies himself with the very objects he claims to own.

[ Verse 32 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

The seeker, while regarding the Supreme as his Master, must remain a servant in the world and continuously perform his duty. This is the ever‑required attitude prescribed by the Lord. Even while carrying out all the tasks of his Master, the servant must follow without ever considering himself the Master. Consequently, the seeker should not regard his body, senses, mind, intellect, material possessions, etc., as his own; he should regard only the Lord as his own and fulfill his duty, becoming merely an instrument for action. He must not be proud of any sense of mastery over himself. After reflecting the entire self as the Lord’s mirror, whatever profit or loss, honor or dishonor, pleasure or pain that arises should also be regarded as belonging to the Lord, with no personal purpose attached. One should perform only the duty appropriate to the given circumstances. ‘Mucyante te ’pi karmabhiḥ’ – the Lord, speaking to Arjuna, seems to say: “I am giving you my entire self as an offering and issuing a clear command to perform your prescribed duties; therefore there is no doubt that obeying my command will lead to your liberation.” Even those to whom I do not give such an explicit command will be liberated if they follow this principle – that one should perform one’s duty without considering oneself as the doer. Whether one accepts the Lord or not, liberation follows simply by adhering to this view. By joyfully acting in accordance with the circumstances, a person frees himself. ---

Appendix Note – The Lord’s view is the ultimate and supreme *principle* (siddhānta) under which all various opinions fall. Yet the Lord, without pride, modestly calls his principle a “view” (mat). This means the Lord does not impose his own or anyone else’s view; he presents his teaching impartially. A view is not supreme; it is individual. Each person may express his own view, but the principle is supreme and must be accepted by all. Hence, even a guru‑disciple relationship may have differences of view, but never a difference of principle. Rishis, philosophers, and teachers also call their own views “principles,” while in the Gita the Lord calls his principle a “view.” Differences of view exist among sages, but there is no difference of principle in the Lord’s view. Translation of the verse (32):

ye tv etad abhyasūyanto nā nutiṣṭhanti me matam /  
sarvajñāna vimūḍhān tān viddhi tu

“Yet those who, out of envy, do not stand by my teaching, are deluded even in all knowledge; understand them.”

Explanation – The use of the particle “tu” after describing the benefits of those who follow the principle (as in verse 31) serves to set apart those who do not follow it. Just as selfish people in the world desire that all material gain belong to them, the Lord likewise wishes that all actions be offered to Him and that He alone be regarded as Master; to accuse the Lord for this is to ascribe fault to Him. The phrase “avivekī manuṣyān — naṣṭa‑āchetasaḥ viddhi” means “understand that the unintelligent, deluded persons are already destroyed in consciousness.” Without desire, worldly activity cannot proceed; complete renunciation of affection is impossible, and freedom from attachment, aversion, and similar mental disturbances is unattainable. To label this as a fault against the Lord’s view is to misinterpret his teaching. Those who, driven by desire for enjoyment and accumulation, consider the body and material objects as theirs and perform all actions for personal gain do not walk according to the Lord’s view. ‘sarvajñāna vimūḍhān tān viddhi’ – those who do not follow the Lord’s view are lost in all worldly pursuits.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]

People become enamoured of all kinds of knowledge (sciences, arts, etc.). Yet, if the disposition of such persons in the present remains the same in future inventions such as motors, airplanes, radios, television, etc., they will inevitably be destroyed, being deprived of divine grace because they are absorbed in learning new techniques and inventions. Consequently, they remain entangled in creation and destruction. For those who attempt to float on water, build houses, or engage in painting, sculpture, and other crafts, the Lord has employed mantras and rituals. They devote themselves to acquiring knowledge of tantra, yantra, and other mystic devices, and to displaying extraordinary miracles, as well as to learning foreign languages, scripts, customs, cuisine, and so on. Their sole conviction is expressed in the eleventh verse of Chapter 16 of the Gita: “Such persons are said to be bewitched by all knowledge.”

Thus, they are described as being “bewitched by all knowledge.”

‘Achetasaḥ’ – persons who do not follow the Lord’s doctrine lack discernment of ultimate realities such as sat‑asat (truth‑falsehood), sār‑asār (essence‑non‑essence), dharma‑adharma, bondage‑moksha, etc. They are unconscious like animals, driven by futile hope, futile action, and futile knowledge; they are scattered‑minded, deluded men—“Moghāśā moghakarmāṇo moghajñāna vichetasḥ” (Bhagavad Gita 9.12). ‘Viddhi naṣṭān’ – even if a human obtains a body, if he does not act according to the Lord’s doctrine, he should be considered destroyed. This implies that such a person remains trapped in the cycle of birth and death. A person who does not follow the Lord’s doctrine performs all actions with attachment (rāga) or aversion (dveṣa). Both attachment and aversion are the greatest enemies of humanity—“Tau hy asya paripanthinau” (Bhagavad Gita 3.34). Because material objects and actions are impermanent, attachment‑or‑aversion‑driven deeds bind the individual to selfishness, affection, and desire, repeatedly leading him to low realms and hells. Hence the Lord declares that such persons are already destroyed. In verses 31 and 32 the Lord states that a person who lives according to His principles is freed from the bondage of karma, whereas one who does not follows a path of ruin. This indicates that whether a person acknowledges the Lord or not, the Lord makes no demand for personal devotion; however, one must certainly observe the Lord’s doctrine (principle). This is the Lord’s command. If a person fails to do so, his downfall is inevitable. Indeed, if a seeker reveres the Lord and faithfully practices His doctrine, liberation remains possible until the end of life; the Lord will then bestow Himself. Conversely, if one disregards the Lord and merely performs ritual without embracing His doctrine, the Lord will still rescue him in the present, and ultimately, through the influence of satsaṅga (good association) and similar factors, those who accept the Lord’s doctrine will attain love and the Lord’s guidance, leading to liberation. Those who accept the doctrine attain moksha (liberation). **Connection** – According to the Lord’s doctrine, non‑performance of righteous action leads to a person’s downfall. Why is this so? The answer is given in the following verse. **Verse 33**  
sadr̥śaṁ ceṣṭate svasyāḥ prakṛtirjñānavāṇapi |  
prakṛtiṁ yānti bhūtāni nigrahaḥ kiṁ kariṣyati || 33 ||

*Transliteration and word‑by‑word meaning*  
- sadr̥śaṁ – similar, alike  
- ceṣṭate – strives, acts, makes an effort  
- svasyāḥ – of one’s own, one’s own nature  
- prakṛtiḥ – nature, material world  
- jñānavān – the knowledgeable, the wise (a great sage)  
- api – also, even  
- prakṛtiṁ – nature (as object)  
- yānti – attain, reach, are drawn to  
- bhūtāni – all beings, creatures  
- nigrahaḥ – restraint, control  
- kiṁ – what  
- kariṣyati – will do

*Literal rendering*: “Even a wise person, acting in accordance with his own nature, strives for what is similar to his nature; beings are drawn to nature; what will restraint accomplish?”

**Glossary of explanatory notes**  
- bhūtāni = all creatures  
- prakṛtim = nature, the material world  
- yānti = are obtained, are drawn toward  
- jñānavān = a learned great soul  
- api = also, even  
- svasyāḥ = of one’s own  
- prakṛtiḥ = one’s own nature  
- sadr̥śam = similar, alike  
- ceṣṭate = makes an effort, acts  
- nigrahaḥ = (any) restraint, self‑control  
- kiṁ = what  
- kariṣyati = will do

Thus, the verse questions the efficacy of mere self‑restraint when even the wise, acting according to their inherent nature, are inevitably attracted to the material world.

* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

Explanation – “All beings move according to Prakriti” – one who regards every action as his own deed and considers himself the doer of those deeds. These deeds are performed in view of nature or principle (Gita, third chapter, verse 27). Material objects are acted upon. Nature is of two kinds – free of attachment‑aversion and imbued with attachment‑aversion, the latter arising from identifying oneself with actions. For example, while walking on a road enmity may arise, producing the bondage of birth and death. If a board is shown and its writing is read, the seeker who does not relate himself to nature never reads it out of attachment‑aversion or any principle; he sees himself as the non‑doer (Gita, thirteenth chapter, verse 29), yet the reading occurs spontaneously from a nature free of attachment‑aversion (a verse of a friend). When a letter from a friend arrives, one reads it with attachment; when a letter from an enemy arrives, one reads it with aversion; thus this reading is done from an attachment‑aversion nature. Reading the Gita, Ramayana and other sacred scriptures is done according to principle. Human life exists for attaining the Supreme Self; therefore, actions performed with the purpose of attaining the Supreme Self must also be in accordance with principle. Thus seeing, hearing, smelling, touching, etc., are actions that arise from both nature and principle. A nature free of attachment‑aversion is not culpable, whereas a nature imbued with attachment‑aversion is culpable. Actions performed with attachment‑aversion bind the person because they render nature impure, while actions performed according to principle liberate because they purify nature. Because nature is impure, the perceived relationship with the world is not severed. When nature becomes pure, the perceived relationship with the world is smoothly dissolved. In a wise great soul, actions occur automatically through the body that is called his, because he lacks the ego of doership. The seeker who desires the Supreme Self acts according to principle. Just as a greedy person remains ever watchful lest he incur loss, the seeker remains constantly vigilant so that no action is performed with attachment‑aversion. With such vigilance the seeker’s nature quickly becomes pure, and consequently he is liberated from the bondage of action. The chief defect in nature is attachment to material objects; as long as attachment remains, actions remain impure. Hence, for the seeker, attachment is the primary cause of bondage. Attachment resides in the sense of “I‑am” and manifests in mind, intellect, senses and their objects. “I‑am” has two forms: (1) the identity‑type “I‑am” arising from the conscious association with the inert, and (2) the inert‑nature’s elemental “I‑am” – the “Mahabhuta‑nigraha‑ego” (Gita 13.5). In the elemental “I‑am” of inert nature there is no fault, because this “I‑am” is merely a cause like mind, intellect, senses, etc. Hence all faults reside in the sense of “I‑am” that is identified. In a wise great soul the identity‑type “I‑am” is completely absent; therefore all actions performed through his so‑called body arise from the elemental “I‑am” of nature. In reality, all beings’ actions arise from this elemental “I‑am”, but the ignorant person who regards the inert body as “I” and “mine” appropriates those actions as his own and becomes bound, because claiming actions as one’s own generates attachment. “Even one who is knowledgeable of his own nature acts similarly” – although the inner heart is free of attachment‑aversion, the wise great soul’s nature remains faultless and he is not enslaved by nature; yet even though actions naturally arise from nature, he acts in accordance with his own nature. In contrast, the ignorant person relates himself to actions. For example, a wise great soul may not know the English language and …

1 – Principle is that which conforms to the scriptures and the Lord’s command. A principle contrary to the scriptures and the Lord’s command is not valid. 2 – Just as the body’s growth, change, etc., are natural, the practical actions of sustaining the body also occur naturally; however, when attachment‑aversion is present, ordinary persons remain entangled in these practical actions, whereas a wise great soul, free of attachment‑aversion, does not become entangled.

[ Verse 34 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

One should not engage in mere collection but should aim solely at attaining the Supreme Self; then the ever‑present experience of the Supreme Reality is realized. In contrast, a person who acts without keeping an ideal before him performs all actions driven by attachment and aversion, thereby strengthening attachment and aversion and leading to his downfall—“destroyed” (Bhagavad Gita 3.32). Just as we cannot stop the flow of a river but can divert it by constructing a canal, likewise we cannot stop the flow of actions but can redirect it. Acting selflessly solely for the welfare of others is the way to divert the stream of actions. Performing even a minute action for oneself does not alter the flow. The implication is that when actions are performed only for others’ benefit, the current of actions turns toward the world, and all feelings, thoughts, deeds, etc., become supportive of one’s advancement. Therefore the seeker must first set the goal of attaining the Supreme Self, and then, for the realization of that goal, perform duty‑action free from attachment and aversion. An easy means to be free from attachment and aversion is to regard the body and other material objects not as one’s own, to serve others, and to desire nothing in return. To remain beyond the sway of nature, the seeker should perform duty‑action with an ideal before him. Two kinds of ideals are possible—(1) the doctrine (principle) of God and (2) the conduct of great saints. When one acts with an ideal in mind, his nature becomes pure and the seeker is liberated from the bondage of actions. **Appendix note** – Even a wise great soul, when he acts, does so according to his nature, because no action can occur without a cause. Just as a teacher, entering a child’s situation, teaches him the alphabet (ka‑kha‑ga), likewise a wise great soul, entering the condition of an ordinary person, explains and acts accordingly. The term *cheshtate* implies that he does not act; rather, action arises automatically according to nature. As the leaves of a tree flutter without generating any karmic fruit (sin or merit), similarly, because there is no sense of doership, no auspicious or inauspicious action is produced. Even wise great souls remain engaged in the welfare of others, because even in the stage of practice their nature is devoted to the welfare of all beings—“immersed in the welfare of all creatures” (Bhagavad Gita 5.25; 12.4). Hence, even when there is nothing left to do, know, or acquire, they continue to have the disposition to serve all. The implication is that when, in serving others, they become completely detached from the world, they no longer need to act for others; the prior flow of their being automatically benefits others. **Relation** – Every human is born with his own nature; therefore he must act according to his nature. Hence, in the following verse, the Lord explains the method of purifying nature. **Sanskrit verse (transliterated)**  
indriyasya‑indriyasya‑arthē rāga‑dveṣau vyavasthitau | tayor na vasham āgacchet tau hy asya paripanthinau || 34 ||

**English meaning**  
In each sense of the senses, attachment and aversion are established; let them not be brought under control, for they are the obstacles on the spiritual path. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- **indriyasya** – “of the senses” (repeated to stress each individual sense)  
- **arthē** – “in respect to, in the sense of” each sense  
- **rāga‑dveṣau** – “attachment and aversion” (the two mental tendencies)  
- **vyavasthitau** – “are established, are set” in the mind of the sense‑holder  
- **na** – “not”  
- **vasham** – “control, subjugation”  
- **āgacchet** – “should come under” (i.e., be brought under control)  
- **tau** – “the two” (referring to attachment and aversion)  
- **hy** – “indeed, for this reason”  
- **asya** – “of this” (the spiritual path)  
- **paripanthinau** – “obstructors of the path”, i.e., the enemies that hinder progress.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

According to the doctrine of suitability‑and‑unsuitability in each sense‑organ (hearing, skin, sight, taste and smell) and in each of their objects (sound, touch, form, flavor and odor), a person’s attachment‑aversion (rāga‑dveṣa) persists. When an object is judged suitable, the person develops attachment (rāga) toward that object; when it is judged unsuitable, aversion (dveṣa) arises. In reality, attachment‑aversion does not reside in the sense‑objects themselves. If it did, a single object would be perceived uniformly as either pleasant or unpleasant by everyone. That is not the case: rain is pleasant to a farmer but unpleasant to a potter; a cool breeze feels pleasant in summer but unpleasant in winter. Thus every object appears pleasant or unpleasant only because of the mind’s perception of suitability or unsuitability. Consequently, the individual projects his own favorable or unfavorable attitude onto objects, labeling them as good or bad, and thereby generates rāga‑dveṣa. For this reason the Lord states that attachment‑aversion is situated in every object of every sense. [ Chapter 3 ]

When one renounces worldly activity, the underlying attachment does not renounce. That attachment ceases only upon direct realization of the Supreme Self (Paramātma). tayoḥn vaśam āgacchet: “May the aspirant become subject to the two (attachment and aversion).”  
These words assure the seeker that when the tendency toward attachment‑aversion arises, he must never become disheartened with the means (sādhan) or the goal (sādya). Rather, he should become master of the tendency itself and neither become overly active nor overly withdrawn in any action. Activity or withdrawal must follow scriptural prescription (Bhagavad Gita – Chapter 16, Verse 24). If one’s actions are driven solely by attachment or aversion, it indicates that the seeker has fallen under their control. Action motivated by attachment strengthens rāga; action motivated by aversion strengthens dveṣa. Thus, the strengthening of attachment‑aversion inevitably leads to downfall. When the seeker abandons worldly duties and engages in devotional worship, many pleasant and unpleasant mental impressions arise, causing anxiety. The Lord reassures the seeker that he should not be disturbed by these impressions. In reality, such impressions have no substantive existence; they arise and, being transient, disappear. A careful observation shows that impressions are not newly appearing but are receding. The reason is that, while engaged in worldly activity, lack of pause suppresses impressions; once worldly activity ceases, the pause allows old mental impressions to surface as fleeting sparks. Therefore, the seeker must not develop attachment‑aversion toward either pleasant or unpleasant sparks, but should, with mindful detachment, remain neutral. The same principle applies to material objects, persons, and subjects. Attachment‑aversion actually resides in the sense of “aham” (the ego‑sense of “I”). The identification with the body constitutes the aham. As long as this bodily identification persists, attachment‑aversion remains, manifesting in the intellect, mind, senses and their objects. From verses 33 to 44 of this chapter, the Lord refers to these same attachments as “kāma” (desire) and “krodha” (anger). The gross forms of rāga and dveṣa are indeed kāma and krodha. Verse 40 explains that this “kāma” dwells in the senses, mind and intellect. Just as the sense‑objects give the appearance of desire, the senses, mind and intellect give the appearance of attachment‑aversion. These faculties are merely instruments for action; they do not themselves contain desire, anger, or attachment‑aversion. Only when one becomes subject to attachment‑aversion and acts under its influence do these qualities become operative. In Chapter 26, the Lord states that when the impure nature (prakṛti) becomes strong, a person who does not accept sense‑objects as his own takes on the form of that nature. **Means to overcome attachment‑aversion**

[ Verse 34 ]  
* Sadhaka – Sanjivani *

Subservience persists. Such subservience arises from an impure nature. Therefore, when performing the pind‑dan during Śrāddha, even if the father’s hand is visibly present, Bhīṣma Pitāmah offered the pind on a kusha grass in accordance with scriptural injunction (Mahābhārata, Anuśāsana Parva, chapter 84, verses 15‑20). Hence the sadhaka must perform all Karma (action) strictly according to scriptural directives. Karma binds a person. Consequently, one should not act or withdraw under the sway of attachment (rāga) and aversion (dveṣa) – this remedy is explained here. Earlier, the Lord has said that one who follows His view is freed from the bondage of Karma (Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 3, Verse 31). Thus, by performing Karma in accordance with the Lord’s view rather than being driven by the cycles of attachment and aversion, rāga‑dveṣa gradually disappear. The implication is that the sadhaka should reflect perfectly in the mirror of the Lord all his actions and consider them not as his own but as belonging solely to the Lord; the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc., are also of the Lord, and the sadhaka himself is also of the Lord. Then, acting selflessly, without desire, without malice, and without pain, the attachment and aversion vanish. In this way, one must engage or disengage from any activity only after placing the Lord’s doctrine (principle) before oneself. The entire creation is the work of Prakṛti, and the body is a part of that creation. As long as affection for the body remains, attachment and aversion persist; that is, the human being accepts and rejects objects with interest (ruchi) or disinterest (arucci). This interest‑disinterest is the subtle form of rāga‑dveṣa. When actions are performed with attachment or aversion, those tendencies are reinforced; but when actions are undertaken with the scriptures as the guide, attachment and aversion are eliminated because, according to the scriptures, one’s preferences do not dominate. If a person does not know the scriptures, the words of the great sage Vyāsa become his guide. For aspirants who wish to eradicate rāga‑dveṣa, scriptural authority is required for action, yet a great soul whose inner self is completely pure and immaculate perceives the meaning of the Vedas spontaneously, whether he has studied them or not. Whatever arises in his inner self conforms to the scriptures. Because of the total absence of rāga‑dveṣa, such a great soul never commits actions prohibited by the scriptures; his nature automatically aligns with scriptural precepts. Consequently, his conduct and speech become ideals for other humans (Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 3, Verse 21). By following the conduct and words of such a great soul, the sadhaka’s own attachment and aversion also disappear. Some claim that rāga‑dveṣa are inherent qualities of the inner self and therefore cannot be removed. This view is not logically sound. In reality, rāga‑dveṣa are disorders (vikāras) of the inner self, not its dharma (righteous duty). If they were intrinsic dharmas, they would be constantly present whenever the inner self is awakened, but their manifestation is intermittent. Practitioners observe that with sustained practice, attachment and aversion diminish progressively; what diminishes eventually disappears. This further proves that rāga‑dveṣa are not dharmas of the inner self. The Lord has called rāga‑dveṣa “manogat” – “the thoughts that arise in the mind” (Bhagavad Gītā 2.55) – indicating they are transient, not permanent. Moreover, the Lord described them as disorders (Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 13, Verse 6). Even a liberated great soul respects scriptural limits and constantly steadies the mind in the reception of the pleasant and the unpleasant:

*Śruti is the entirety of Dharma (righteous duty); having heard it, one should contemplate it. One should not act against one’s own self nor towards others.*

(Padma Purāṇa, Sṛṣṭi 19, verses 355‑356)

“ O human being! Hear the essence of Dharma and internalize it: do not do to others what you do not wish for yourself.”

A man who never abandons Dharma (righteous duty) attains a pure inner self. While describing King Duṣyanta, the great poet Kālidāsa wrote:

*Where doubt exists, the inclination of the virtuous person’s inner self is the proof.* (Abhijñānaśākuntalam 1.21)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]  
Gita – Chapter 13, Verse 9

If the attraction of the inert (jada) is regarded as attachment (rāga), then when the aspirant’s body‑rāga‑dveṣa (attachment and aversion) become the Dharma of the inner self, he identifies himself solely with the balanced‑mind form of the inert (jada). In that state he cannot become a means (sādhan). Dharma remains permanent, and eliminating rāga‑dveṣa appears difficult. Yet these mental disturbances are temporary, coming and going. When the mind (caitanya) focuses on its true nature, the fleeting nature of rāga‑dveṣa in the inner self becomes evident, and their removal no longer seems arduous. Rāga‑dveṣa are not self‑evident; they arise from the relationship between the inert (asat) and the conscious (caitanya). Nature (jada) and the person (caitanya) are distinct, and the discrimination between them is self‑evident. The person, ignoring this discrimination, merges with the material body and assumes a one‑sided identity. This identity of jada‑caitanya is called “aham” (the I‑sense), within which attachment and aversion reside. Thus, in the sense of “I‑ness” (aham‑tā), rāga‑dveṣa exist and are reinforced by the sense of “I‑ness”. These attachments appear in the intellect, causing the intellect to favor its own doctrines and reject others. Consequently, they appear in the mind, making agreeable thoughts pleasant and disagreeable thoughts unpleasant. They also manifest in the senses, so that objects pleasing to the senses are liked, while those displeasing are disliked. The senses experience words, touch, form, taste, and smell with corresponding favorable and unfavorable feelings. Therefore, when the identity of jada‑caitanya (the “I”) is dissolved, all rāga‑dveṣa disappear, because they exist only in that identity. “I am a servant; I am curious; I am a devotee”—the servant, the seeker, and the devotee all dwell in the same “I”, and so does rāga‑dveṣa. Attachment and aversion are not confined solely to the inert nor solely to the conscious; they exist in the relationship understood between jada and caitanya. Even within that relationship, they are primarily situated in the inert. The attraction of the inert is present only in the inert portion, yet because of their unity, it becomes visible in the conscious. If satsaṅga, bhajana, and dhyāna are performed with attachment (rāga), they generate aversion toward the world; but when performed with love, aversion toward the world does not arise, and instead a natural indifference (vīmr̥ta) toward the world develops. Attachment to any single worldly object creates aversion toward other objects, whereas love for the Divine produces detachment from the world. Detachment eliminates the desire to derive pleasure from the world, and the body, senses, mind, intellect, and even the “I‑sense” automatically turn to the service of the world. As a result, when the “I‑sense” also separates from the world, the remaining rāga‑dveṣa are completely eradicated. Human actions are based on nature (svabhāva) or principle (dharma). Performing actions solely for spiritual advancement means acting according to principle. Nature is of two kinds: pure (free of rāga‑dveṣa) and impure (laden with rāga‑dveṣa). One cannot annihilate nature, but one can purify it, i.e., render it free of attachment and aversion. Just as the Ganga emerges from Gangotri: if a dam equal to or higher than the height of Gangotri is constructed, the river’s flow can be halted—though this is not an easy task. However, one can divert the river through canals and alter its course. Similarly, the flow of innate actions cannot be stopped, but it can be redirected, i.e., transformed into a flow free of attachment and aversion—this is the essential teaching of the Gita. Actions driven by attachment and aversion are not as restrictive as the aspirant’s attachment (rāga) or love in satsaṅga, bhajana, or dhyāna. This can be illustrated: if a person encounters resistance in satsaṅga, bhajana, or dhyāna, anger arises, indicating that there is attachment in the spiritual gathering; if instead tears arise without anger, it shows love in the gathering. Lack of determination (dṛḍhatā) within oneself creates obstacles in practice, leading the aspirant to weep upon perceiving this deficiency. Likewise, when another religion or sect appears disagreeable, it reflects our own attachment to our tradition. In reality, having attachment in satsaṅga, bhajana, or dhyāna is not inherently negative, because whatever the circumstance, devotion to the Divine is always beneficial—“tasmāt kenāpyupāyena manaḥ kṛṣṇe niveshayet” (Srimad‑Bhāgavatam 7.1.31).

[ Verse 34 ]
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

Raga‑dvesha (attachment and aversion) are obstacles. Therefore the Lord first abandons raga‑dvesha; service originates from that abandonment, for all these are merely portions of the world. When the doer alone is called a true renouncer (Bhagavad Gita — Chapter 18 Verse 10), attachment and aversion can arise. Identifying the body and other material elements as “mine” prevents the aspirant’s concentration, so genuine inclination and true service become impossible; such identification breeds affection and withdrawal rooted in raga‑dvesha. Consequently a self‑less attitude free of raga‑dvesha arises. Hence, to deal with these material elements, the aspirant must first establish the principle that everything belongs to the one whose service is performed, just as a devotee performs devotional actions. Then his nature automatically regards all material objects as belonging to the Lord and offers them to the Lord in accordance with the principle, becoming pure. Thus the karmayogi, seeing material objects as the world, offers them to the world, saying “I surrender to You, O Govinda, what is yours alone.”

When raga‑dvesha‑infused impulses arise, acting according to them strengthens raga‑dvesha; acting contrary to them, in line with the principle, eliminates raga‑dvesha. In both auspicious and inauspicious mental impulses, raga‑dvesha must be absent. The aspirant should not identify these impulses with himself, nor attach any relationship to them; he should neither support nor oppose them. If the aspirant finds himself unable to remove raga‑dvesha, he should take refuge in the all‑powerful, ever‑friendly Lord. By the Lord’s grace his raga‑dvesha disappears (Bhagavad Gita — Chapter 7 Verse 14) and he attains supreme peace (Bhagavad Gita — Chapter 18 Verse 52). The body, senses, mind, intellect, prana and all worldly substances, together with the sense of “I‑am,” are all the Lord’s; recognizing this is true surrender. Then, for the Lord’s pleasure, one should serve only the Lord’s people with the material given by the Lord, desiring nothing in return. Any desire for return creates a bond with material attachment. Self‑less service to the world is a surefire means of eradicating raga‑dvesha. One should devote everything he possesses—gross body, subtle body, causal body, and even the sense of “I‑am”—to worldly service, because these substances are essentially inseparable from the world. Treating them as separate (as “my own”) is bondage. One must not seek the pleasure of actions and objects through the gross body, the contemplation pleasure of the subtle body, or the stability pleasure of the causal body. In reality, the human body is not meant for personal pleasure—“the fruit of this body is not for oneself” (Manas 7.44.1). Furthermore, only one who desires nothing for himself can truly serve. The desire for wealth or other objects is a wish; the desire to serve is also a wish, because the wish to serve generates the wish for material means. When opportunity and qualification arise, one should serve without cultivating a wish to serve. Finding happiness by making others happy, thinking “people receive happiness through me,” and seeking praise or satisfaction for one’s service turns service into a pursuit of pleasure, not service. When service is performed for personal pleasure, that pleasure creates importance and intellect attached to material wealth, leading gradually to affection and desire. The notion “I give something to someone” is rarely understood; no one can easily explain that the material employed in service belongs to the very one being served.
