* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 3 ]

The discourse here is at the gross level; in truth it is the spirit of service, not mere action (Karma). Action gives rise to rule. A person who serves from a sincere heart attains liberation from the bondage of a coarse outlook through service. When the attitude of service is present, the objects that one possesses automatically become instruments of service. Because of this attitude, one can render complete service with whatever one already has; therefore there is no need to desire additional objects. True service is possible precisely because there is no sense of importance attached to objects. Even gross objects can be used for the same service when the mind does not assign them significance. If one serves while regarding objects as important, the pride of service arises. As long as the inner heart regards objects as valuable, the servant retains a sense of enjoyment (bhoga‑buddhi), whether he is aware of it or not. In reality, service arises from the feeling of service, not from the objects themselves. Objects give rise to action, not to service. Hence merely giving away objects is not service. A shopkeeper also gives away goods, but without the attitude of giving, no merit accrues. Similarly, the people give the king material wealth in the form of tribute, but that is not donation. When one says, “I gave him water, and then he became happy,” that attitude is merely shopkeeping. We do not seek praise, yet the belief “by giving water merit is earned” or “by giving charity merit is earned” implants the importance of water, wealth, etc., in the heart because merit is linked to results. Once the importance of objects is imprinted, genuine service ceases; the desire to receive something in return maintains a connection with the material, whether conscious or unconscious. Therefore, one must not use others’ service as a means for donation‑merit; instead, one must sever the personal attachment to those objects. A thing can be given only to the one who has the right over it—that is, to the true owner. Giving the object relieves our debt. If another person has a greater need (hunger) for a thing, that person is the rightful holder and may take it. Our own rightful possession cannot be taken by another. It is especially important to note that when one serves others from a true heart, the feeling of service awakens in the heart of the one being served. This appears as if the material object is being used for the service of the servant, but from a subtle viewpoint it actually awakens the spirit of service in the served’s heart. If the served’s heart does not develop this feeling, the practitioner must understand that there is a fault in the service—namely, a desire to gain something for oneself. Hence the practitioner must exercise special caution, serve others sincerely, and eliminate his own faults. The attitude “let others call me good” must never be entertained in service; as soon as it arises it should be eradicated, because it inflates pride. For every practitioner, the world is merely a field for performing duty, not a realm of happiness or sorrow. The world exists for service. In the world the practitioner must practice only service. The foremost attitude in service must be that no harm, however slight, should be caused by one’s actions. Some beings in the world are sorrowful, others are joyful. Feeling sorrow upon seeing a sorrowful being, and feeling joy upon seeing a joyful being, is also service, because it allows both the sorrowful and the joyful to experience happiness and to realize that they are not alone. When another is sorrowful, we should share his grief, ask how his suffering may be alleviated, speak and listen with love, and tell him not to panic when adverse circumstances arise. Such situations have befallen great personalities like Lord Rama, King Nala, King Harishchandra, and many others; today many are even more distressed than you. If we can be of help, we should offer it. These words will satisfy him. Likewise, when we meet a joyful person, we should let our heart rejoice, saying “how wonderful,” which will please him. In this way we can serve both sorrowful and joyful individuals. By empathizing with both their sorrow and joy, we can bring happiness to others. Continuous concern for the welfare of others is essential. Those who become sorrowful because of others’ sorrow and become joyful because of others’ joy are saints. As Goswami Tulsidas Maharaj described the characteristics of saints: “He sees both sorrow and joy, sorrow and joy alike” (Manas 7.38.1).

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Chapter 3

Therefore, one who performs his duty, following his own dharma, is a follower of dharma. If any hardship comes, that hardship too becomes a means of advancement. In reality, that hardship is not hardship, but tapas. The hardship from tapas is even more beneficial than the tapas itself. This is because tapas is performed for oneself, whereas duty is performed for others. The benefit from tapas performed out of knowledge is not as much as the benefit from the hardship that comes naturally, in the form of tapas. Those who have borne hardships in the performance of their duty and who have died following their duty are dharmatmas, who have become immortal. Even from a worldly perspective, one who remains steadfast in his duty, even in the face of hardship, is greatly praised and revered. Just as those who have suffered hardships for the sake of their country's freedom and have been imprisoned and hanged are still greatly praised and revered today.

On the other hand, those who have committed bad deeds and have been imprisoned are condemned everywhere. The implication is that even if one dies following his duty, he will attain salvation in this world and liberation in the next.

The duty of a person is to follow his dharma, and the power to attain salvation comes from the instructions of the Lord, the Vedas, the Shastras, the Rishis, the Munis, and the saints. Just as it is said in our scriptures that a woman's salvation comes from following the dharma of pativratya, it is the power of the Lord, the Vedas, and the Shastras that brings about her salvation, not the power of her husband. Similarly, it is the instructions of the Lord, the Vedas, the Shastras, the Rishis, the Munis, and the saints that guide one in following his dharma, and it is their power that brings about one's salvation, even if one dies following his duty.

2 - It is also established by the Puranas and histories that following one's dharma brings about salvation. For example, King Harishchandra did not waver from his duty of speaking the truth, even in the face of many hardships, insults, and humiliation. As a result, he went to the supreme abode, taking all his subjects with him, and is still greatly praised and revered today.

3 - In the present time, many true incidents of rebirth are seen, heard, and read, which reveal the fate of the soul after death.

4 - If one follows one's duty without any attachment, even an atheist will have a sense of satisfaction and peace in his heart.

Question - How can we be certain that salvation comes from following one's duty?

Answer - The Gita is the direct word of God, so there is no room for doubt. Furthermore, this is not a matter that can be seen with the eyes or touched with the hands, but rather a matter of faith and trust. However, some points are worth noting.

1 - The knowledge of the scriptures is the only means of knowing what is unknown. It is said in the Manu Smriti, "Dharma protects the protector of dharma" (Manu Smriti 8.15). Therefore, it is the duty of a person to follow his dharma, and it is the duty of dharma to protect him.

2 - The benefit of following one's duty is that it leads to the ultimate goal of life, which is moksha or liberation. This is evident from one's own experience, as one who gives up all attachment and follows his duty will attain salvation.

Marmik Baat (A Marmic Point)

Since one is a part of the Supreme Being, one's own duty is to attain one's own salvation, to consider oneself as a servant of God, and to consider oneself as a seeker of truth. This is because these are the true duties, and not the duties of the mind or intellect.

1 - The scripture is the eye of all, and it is the only means of knowing the unknown. One who does not have knowledge of the scripture is blind.

2 - See Markandeya Purana, Devi Bhagavat, etc.

3 - See the special issue of the magazine "Kalyan" (March 1968) on the topic of "Parlok and Punarjanma".

The verse 35 reads:

"Sadhak - Sanjivani"
Dharma are, they are one's own duty to be performed, yet they are also paradharm. For, they are all considered as dharma, not one's own; and in all of them, there is a need for the support of others, i.e., there is a state of dependence; but in one's own real dharma, there is no need for the support of anyone, i.e., there is independence. Therefore, a lover is one's own, an inquirer is one's own, and a servant is one's own. Thus, a lover becomes one with the beloved by love, an inquirer becomes one with the knowable by inquiry, and a servant becomes one with the served by service. Similarly, a sadhak becomes one with the siddhyasvarupa by siddhi alone.

The translation of the following text reads:

"It is said that 'I' remains even when the body remains, and 'I' does not remain even when the body does not remain. If the body were 'mine', then there would be no desire to acquire anything else after acquiring it. If there is a desire, it is clear that the real 'mine' has not been acquired, and the acquired body is not 'mine'. One should not take the body along, nor can one take it along, nor can one change it according to one's desire, then how can it be 'mine'? In this way, 'the body is not 'I' and 'mine' is not' is the knowledge (vivikta) that all sadhaks possess. However, if they do not give importance to this knowledge, their attachment and aversion do not subside. If 'I' and 'mine' appear in the body even once, the sadhak should not give importance to it, but rather give importance to his own knowledge, i.e., 'the body is not 'I' and 'mine' is not'. By giving importance to one's own knowledge, one attains the real knowledge of the ultimate truth. When one attains the real knowledge, attachment and aversion do not remain. When attachment and aversion do not remain, the knowledge of one's own dharma and paradharm becomes manifest in the heart, and one acts accordingly.

The translation of the following text reads:

"The sadhak who has the resolve to attain his own well-being, does not have the desire to acquire wealth, fame, respect, honor, comfort, etc. Therefore, he is not disturbed even if he does not get these things, and if he gets them, he is not pleased. Because his goal is to attain the ultimate truth, not to acquire wealth, fame, etc. Therefore, he performs his worldly duties in a proper and pure manner. All his actions are for the sake of the ultimate truth. Just as a businessman gives up comfort when his goal is to acquire wealth, and endures hardships, and just as a doctor remains focused on the result of the surgery, saying 'this will be good', so that the patient's heart remains pleased, similarly, when the sadhak's goal is to attain the ultimate truth, he remains pleased even in the face of defeat, loss, hardship, etc. in the world. For him, favorable and unfavorable circumstances are means of attaining the ultimate truth.

The translation of the following text reads:

"When the sadhak is determined to attain his own well-being, and is engaged in the performance of his own dharma with great enthusiasm, he is not distracted even if he faces difficulties, sorrows, hardships, etc. In fact, he considers these difficulties, sorrows, hardships, etc. as means of spiritual practice, and they bring him joy.

The translation of the following text reads:

"The body is considered 'I' and 'mine' due to which attachment and aversion arise in the world. When attachment and aversion arise, one does not attain the knowledge of one's own dharma and paradharm. If one's own dharma is considered 'paradharm', then it is said that 'paradharm is terrible' - although it appears to be easy to perform in the present, it is terrible in its consequences. If one gives up one's own self-interest and performs one's own dharma for the benefit of others, then there is no fear for oneself.

The translation of the following text reads:

"The solution is that the restraint of the mind, the control of the senses, etc. are common dharma (Gita - 13th chapter, 7th to 11th shlokas, and 16th chapter, 1st to 3rd shlokas) which all should perform, because these are one's own dharma. These common dharma are the 'swabhavik karma' of the brahmin because they do not require much effort to perform; but for other varnas, their performance requires effort.

The translation of the following text reads:

"The 42nd, 43rd, and 44th shlokas of the 18th chapter describe the natural duties of the brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, and shudra. Therefore, when it is said here that another's natural duty is terrible, it is not in accordance with the shlokas of the 18th chapter, where it is said that even the natural duties of the brahmin are terrible for others (kshatriyas, etc.). Therefore, the shlokas of the 18th chapter are not in accordance with the shlokas of the 18th chapter.

The translation of the following text reads:

"The solution is that the restraint of the mind, the control of the senses, etc. are common dharma (Gita - 13th chapter, 7th to 11th shlokas, and 16th chapter, 1st to 3rd shlokas) which all should perform, because these are one's own dharma. These common dharma are the 'swabhavik karma' of the brahmin because they do not require much effort to perform; but for other varnas, their performance requires effort.

The natural duty and general relationship are the causes of a little effort. Both the duty related to the body and the duty that arises from the general relationship come under the category of 'Svadharma' (one's own duty). Except for the general duty, even if one appears to be committing a sin in one's natural duty, it is not actually a sin. For example, a warrior's natural duty is to fight courageously and selflessly, without any personal interest or hatred, and this is not a sin, as it is said in the Gita, "Svabhāvaniyataṃ karma kurvannāpnoti kilbiṣam" (Gita 18.47).

The general duty of others (paradharma) is frightening because it is against the scriptures and takes away the livelihood of others. The duty of others is frightening because it is against the scriptures and leads to sin, and it is specific to a particular place and a particular species. Therefore, the Lord seems to say to Arjuna that it is not good for you to live on alms, as it would mean taking away the livelihood of others, which is against the scriptures and is not good for a warrior. Instead, it is better for you to follow your natural duty, which is to fight in a war.

The distinction between Svadharma and Paradharma is that the former is eternal and the latter is transitory. The former is the duty of the Self, while the latter is the duty of the body and the world. The Self is eternal and unchanging, while the body and the world are transitory and changing.

The three yogas - Karma Yoga (the yoga of action), Jnana Yoga (the yoga of knowledge), and Bhakti Yoga (the yoga of devotion) - are all self-evident and come under the category of Svadharma. Svadharma is the duty of the Self, while Paradharma is the duty of the body and the world.

A yogi is one who follows Svadharma, while a bhogi (one who indulges in worldly pleasures) is one who follows Paradharma. To remain detached is Svadharma, while to be attached is Paradharma. To serve is Svadharma, while to desire is Paradharma. To be a lover is Svadharma, while to be a lover of worldly pleasures is Paradharma. To be unattached, unmotivated, and unpossessive is Svadharma, while to be attached, motivated, and possessive is Paradharma.

In other words, everything that happens without the influence of nature (prakriti) is Svadharma, while everything that happens due to the influence of nature is Paradharma. Svadharma is the duty of the Self, while Paradharma is the duty of the body and the world.

The Self is the essence of the Self, while the body is the essence of nature. The Self has two meanings - one is 'I' (sama) and the other is 'my own' (sva). From this perspective, the desire to know one's own nature and the desire to know the Self are both Svadharma.

The duty of a person (purusha) is to be in a state of self-evident existence, while the duty of nature (prakriti) is to be in a state of self-evident changeability. The duty of a person is Svadharma, while the duty of nature is Paradharma.

There are two kinds of desires in a person - one is the desire for worldly pleasures and the other is the desire for one's own well-being. The desire for worldly pleasures is Paradharma, while the desire for one's own well-being is Svadharma. This is because the desire for worldly pleasures arises from the attachment to the body, while the desire for one's own well-being arises from the attachment to the Self.

One is free to follow Svadharma, as one does not need the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc. to achieve one's own well-being. However, one is not free to follow Paradharma, as one needs the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc. to achieve worldly pleasures. The body, senses, mind, intellect, etc. are necessary for following Paradharma.

The Self is the essence of the Self, while the body is the essence of nature. One does not need to practice (abhyasa) to know the Self, as one is the Self. When one considers oneself to be the Self, one is free from the cycle of birth and death, as it is said in the Nirukta, "Jāyate 's ti viparīṇamate 'rthate 'rthate 'paksīyate vināśyate" (Nirukta 1.1.2).

[Verse 36]

When a person considers his own duty as the ultimate goal, it becomes his 'swadharma', and when he considers the world as his own, it becomes his 'paradharma', which is the duty of the body. When a person performs actions without considering his own relationship with the body, those actions become his 'swadharma'. All means to attain the ultimate reality or one's own true nature are 'swadharma', and all actions that lead to worldly attachments are 'paradharma'. From this perspective, karma yoga, jnana yoga, and bhakti yoga – all three paths – are 'swadharma' for a human being. On the other hand, considering the body as one's own and being attached to worldly pleasures and accumulation is 'paradharma' for a human being.

The special duty of a human being is to be detached from 'paradharma' and to be engaged in 'swadharma'. Only a human being can do this. A human being has obtained a body for the sake of realizing 'swadharma'. 'Paradharma' is present not only in human beings but also in other living beings and in the pleasure-oriented heavens. In 'swadharma', a human being is powerful, eligible, and independent, whereas in 'paradharma', a human being is weak, ineligible, and dependent.

The pain of absence is caused by the desire for worldly objects, and the bondage of attachment is caused by the attainment of those objects, which is 'paradharma'. However, when the desire for worldly objects is destroyed, the pain of absence and the bondage of attachment are destroyed forever, which is 'swadharma'. Even if a person faces many difficulties and loses his body, remaining in 'swadharma' is beneficial. On the other hand, even if a person experiences pleasure and comfort in 'paradharma', it is terrifying and leads to repeated birth and death.

All the sufferings, sorrows, and worries in the world arise from taking refuge in 'paradharma'. By abandoning 'paradharma' and taking refuge in 'swadharma', one attains eternal, universal, and perpetual bliss, which is self-evident.

All virtuous actions, such as pilgrimage, vows, donations, austerities, contemplation, meditation, and concentration, performed with a sense of attachment are 'paradharma', whereas those performed without attachment are 'swadharma'. This is because the nature of the ultimate reality is detached, and attachment arises from a relationship with the world. Therefore, actions motivated by attachment are 'paradharma', and those motivated by detachment are 'swadharma', which liberates and binds, respectively.

Supplementary note: A person considers his own 'sw' or self as his duty, which is his 'swadharma', and what is prohibited for him is 'paradharma'. For example, a person considers himself a student or a teacher, so studying or teaching becomes his 'swadharma'. He considers himself a servant, an inquirer, or a devotee, so serving, inquiring, or devoting becomes his 'swadharma'. Whatever action involves harming or harming others is not 'swadharma' but 'adharm' or 'kut-dharma'.

Arjuna said:

What force compels a person to commit sin, even unwillingly, like a person forced by power? (36)

Note: The three aspects of every duty are kut-dharma (immoral), adharma (unrighteous), and paradharma (duty of another). Immorality and unrighteousness are present in every duty, and the duty of another is present in every duty. These three do not lead to well-being. Well-being arises from the duty that involves the renunciation of one's own interests and pride and the well-being of others in the present and future.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 37]

The very first step is to understand the nature of desires. We consider it difficult to renounce desires, but if we think about it, is it not even more difficult to fulfill them? No one in the world has been able to fulfill all their desires. Not even the father of Lord Krishna, Dasharatha, could fulfill all his desires. Therefore, it is impossible to fulfill all desires, but it is not impossible to renounce them. If we consider renouncing desires to be difficult, then the expectation of fulfilling desires becomes even more difficult. Because, renouncing desires is possible, but fulfilling them is not. Therefore, the expectation of fulfilling desires makes renouncing desires seem easy.

There are four types of desires:

1. The desire for the necessary means of sustenance for the body.
2. The desire that is personal and just, but beyond one's capacity, should be offered to God and abandoned.
3. The desire to fulfill the just and beneficial desires of others, which one has the capacity to fulfill.
4. All other desires should be abandoned through contemplation.

The desire is a fierce enemy that cannot be pacified by gifts, worship, or flattery. It is like a fire that cannot be extinguished. Just as wealth increases the desire for more wealth, so too, the more one enjoys worldly pleasures, the more one's desires increase. Therefore, desire is called 'great enemy' (mahashan).

Desire is the root cause of all sins. Theft, robbery, and violence are all caused by desire. Therefore, desire is called 'great sinner' (mahapapma).

As soon as desire arises, a person becomes detached from his duties, his true nature, and his Lord. He becomes a fleeting being in the world, and due to this, he commits sins, which lead to hell and lower birth.

The world appears to be permanent due to the desire for sensual pleasure. People consider the worldly objects to be stable, and they enjoy them, thinking that they will remain the same. However, the world is constantly changing, and the body is also constantly dying. How can one desire to enjoy the world, which is constantly dying?

The four characteristics of a desire are:

1. The desire should be present in the present moment (e.g., the desire for food when one is hungry).
2. The means to fulfill the desire should be available in the present moment.
3. The desire should be such that one cannot live without fulfilling it.
4. The fulfillment of the desire should not harm oneself or others.

One should fulfill the necessary desires for the means of sustenance for the body. Fulfilling necessary desires gives the strength to renounce unnecessary desires. However, one should not enjoy the fulfillment of necessary desires, because new desires will arise, and there will be no end to them.

For example, the desire for justice in the world is a strong personal desire, but it is beyond one's capacity. Therefore, one should offer it to God and be detached from it. Such a desire may be fulfilled in the future if God so wills.

The Gita Press edition of Srimad Bhagavad Gita presents a profound understanding of the human condition, where even the sight of abundant fruits does not evoke a desire to eat them if the body is not in a state of hunger. This illustrates that we have indeed considered the self to be stable. However, when we consider the ever-changing world as stable, we fail to perceive the true, eternal reality. As a result, we become detached from it and get entangled in fleeting worldly pleasures.

This understanding reveals that one cannot experience true bliss without being detached from worldly desires. Furthermore, indulging in worldly pleasures out of attachment leads to detachment from the divine. The Gita emphasizes that a person who is driven by the desire for worldly pleasures cannot escape the consequences of harming others, as he is himself a victim of his own desires.

The Gita explains that a person who is driven by the desire for worldly pleasures is unable to escape the consequences of harming others, as he is himself a victim of his own desires. He causes harm to himself and others by misusing worldly resources and perpetuating their scarcity. The Gita states that the only exception to this rule is the jivanmukta, or the liberated soul, who is not driven by desires and performs actions without attachment.

The Gita emphasizes that the desire for worldly pleasures is not a necessity, but rather a product of ignorance. It is the root cause of all suffering, and it is the source of all evil. The Gita states that the desire for worldly pleasures is a form of ignorance, which leads to attachment and ultimately to suffering.

The Gita provides a solution to this problem by suggesting that one should focus on serving others and bringing them happiness. This is the key to overcoming the desire for worldly pleasures and achieving true bliss. The Gita states that one should not consider the body, senses, mind, intellect, and breath as one's own, but rather as instruments to be used for the service of others.

The Gita explains that the three aspects of karma yoga - action, thought, and stability - are not for personal gain, but rather for the benefit of others. The Gita states that the body, senses, and mind are connected to the physical, subtle, and causal worlds, respectively. Therefore, one should use them to serve others, rather than to indulge in personal desires.

[Verse 38]

The verse 38 reads:

As the fire is covered by smoke, as the mirror is covered by dust, as the embryo is covered by the womb, similarly this (world) is covered by the three gunas (sattva, rajas, and tamas).

English translation of the Sanskrit verse:
dhūmenāvriyate vahniryathādarśo malena ca|
yatholbenāvṛto garbhastathā tenedamāvṛtam || 38 ||

The commentary explains that the three gunas (sattva, rajas, and tamas) are the causes of worldly attachments and desires. The sattvic guna is associated with knowledge and wisdom, the rajasic guna with passion and attachment, and the tamasic guna with ignorance and darkness. The verse suggests that just as a fire is obscured by smoke, a mirror by dust, and an embryo by the womb, the world is similarly obscured by these three gunas.

The commentary further explains that a seeker of spiritual knowledge (sadhak) must be detached from these three gunas and their effects. This detachment is achieved by cultivating a sense of service (seva) and selfless concern for others (parahit-chintan). The seeker must also be free from attachment to pleasure and pain, and must not seek to enjoy the fruits of their actions (sukh lene). By doing so, they will be able to attain spiritual knowledge and liberation.

The commentary also notes that the three gunas are the causes of all worldly attachments and desires, and that the rajasic guna is the primary cause of all evil. It is the rajasic guna that gives rise to the concept of "kam" or desire, which is the root of all suffering. The commentary concludes that as long as the rajasic guna remains, a person cannot be free from suffering and cannot attain spiritual knowledge and liberation.

As the smoke covers the fire, so too does desire cover the intellect.

Just as a mirror covered with soot no longer reflects its image, so too does the intellect become obscured by desire.

The intellect is of three types: sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. In sattvic intellect, one has clear knowledge of duty and non-duty. In rajasic intellect, one does not have clear knowledge of duty and non-duty, and in tamasic intellect, one has knowledge that is opposite to reality. When desire arises, even sattvic intellect becomes obscured, like a fire covered with smoke. What to say of rajasic and tamasic intellects?

As soon as worldly desires arise, the path of spiritual growth becomes shrouded in darkness. If one is not cautious in this state, desire only grows stronger. In this state, the path of spiritual growth becomes even more obscure.

The origin of desire is the attachment to perishable objects, which are valued for their beauty, utility, and other qualities. This attachment is the root cause of the obscuration of the intellect. In the human body, the intellect is more prominent than in other bodies, but due to the influence of desire, it does not function properly. As soon as desire arises, the intellect becomes clouded.

Just as a fire can still function even if it is covered with smoke, so too can the intellect function even if it is clouded by desire, if the seeker is cautious from the very beginning. The simple way to eliminate desire is to reflect on the fact that the object of desire is not always present with us, nor will it always be present in the future. In fact, it is always absent from us, and there is a constant separation between us and the object of desire.

If one reflects on this, desire does not arise.

This is the state in which the intellect is covered by desire.

Just as a mirror covered with soot no longer reflects its image, so too does the intellect become obscured by desire.

As the dirt on a mirror prevents the reflection of one's image, so too does the increase of desire prevent the knowledge of one's duty and non-duty. The more one values perishable objects, the more one's intellect becomes clouded.

The value of perishable objects is not in themselves, but in their proper use. Wealth, knowledge, strength, etc. are not valuable in themselves, but in their proper use. When one understands this, desire for these objects does not arise, because one knows that one is responsible for their proper use. One should use these objects properly, and not desire more than what one needs.

As one's attachment to perishable objects decreases, one's attachment to the Supreme Being increases. When one's attachment to perishable objects is completely eliminated, one experiences the Supreme Being, and desire is completely eliminated.

Just as a mirror covered with dirt still retains its identity as a mirror, so too does the intellect retain its knowledge of its duty and non-duty, even when it is clouded by desire.

Just as a womb covered with a layer of mucus does not reveal whether it is carrying a male or female child, so too does the intellect, when clouded by desire, lose its knowledge of its duty and non-duty.

When desire increases, the intellect becomes completely clouded, and one's knowledge of duty and non-duty is lost.

When one is overcome by desire, anger arises. From anger, delusion arises. From delusion, the intellect is destroyed. When the intellect is destroyed, one does not perform one's duties, and one engages in activities that are not in accordance with one's duty, such as falsehood, deceit, injustice, and other evil actions. Such people are not even considered human beings by the Lord.

This is why the Lord says in the sixteenth chapter of the Gita...

[Verse 38]

In the chapter where the description of such people is given, the Lord has not used any word referring to humans from the eighth to the eighteenth shlokas. The Lord has said to those who desire the heavenly world, 'kamātmānāḥ' (Gita 2.43), because such people are in the form of desire. Due to being in the form of desire, they are convinced that there is nothing greater than worldly pleasure (Gita - Sixteenth Chapter, Eleventh Shlok).

Although in this third stage of desire, a person's vision does not turn towards his true objective (attainment of the Supreme), yet if due to some past impressions, good company in the present, or any other reason, he becomes aware of his objective, then his well-being can also be achieved.

The Lord has given three examples in this shlok about covering wisdom by one desire. Therefore, the meaning of the above words is that wisdom is covered by one desire, and due to this, all three stages of desire become awakened.

These three stages of desire arise in everyone's heart when desire is born. However, those people who consider desire as the cause of pleasure and take its shelter, and do not consider it as something to be abandoned, do not recognize desire. But those who are interested in the ultimate goal and are engaged in practice, recognize this desire. He who recognizes desire can also destroy it.

The Lord has described the three stages of desire in this shlok with the intention of destroying it, and has given the order to destroy it in the forty-first and forty-third shlokas. In reality, the increase of desire is so rapid after its birth that even to describe its three stages is a delay, but there is no delay in its increase. When desire increases, only the sequence of evil habits begins. All sins, troubles, and sorrows arise due to desire. Therefore, a person should keep his wisdom awakened and not allow desire to arise in the first place. If desire arises, he should destroy it in the first or second stage. He should never allow it to reach the third stage.

Special Note

259

Just as the presence of smoke proves the existence of fire, because if there were no fire, smoke would not arise, similarly, just as the presence of malice proves the existence of ignorance, because if there were no ignorance, malice would not arise. In the same way, just as the presence of a veil proves the existence of a mirror, because if there were no mirror, the veil would not arise, similarly, just as the presence of a veil proves the existence of a womb, because if there were no womb, the veil would not arise, in the same way, just as the presence of desire proves the existence of ignorance, because if there were no ignorance, desire would not arise. Therefore, just as wisdom remains present even when covered by smoke, malice, or a veil, similarly, wisdom remains present even when covered by desire, but it is not put to use due to desire.

According to the scriptures, there are three obstacles to the attainment of the Supreme: malice, distraction, and veil. These obstacles arise from the relationship with the non-existent (samsara). The relationship with the non-existent arises from desire. Therefore, the root obstacle is desire itself. When desire is completely destroyed, the relationship with the non-existent is severed. When the relationship with the non-existent is severed, all obstacles are eliminated, and wisdom is revealed.

The main obstacle to the attainment of the Supreme is considering worldly objects as ephemeral and giving them importance. As long as the inner self considers worldly objects as ephemeral and they appear to be true, beautiful, and pleasant, the three obstacles - malice, distraction, and veil - remain present. Among these three, malice is considered the most obstructive. Malice is the main cause of the malice-dosh (sin), because all sins arise from desire. When a seeker firmly decides, 'I will not commit sin from now on', at that very moment, the root of all obstacles is cut off, and the malice-dosh begins to disappear. When one becomes completely detached, the malice-dosh is completely destroyed.

The Lord has said in the Shrimad Bhagavatam that the means of the well-being of those who are attached to desire is Karma Yoga (detached action) - 'karmayogastu kāminām' (11.20.7). Therefore, those who are attached to desire should not become hopeless about their well-being, because the one in whom desire has arisen will also become detached. Through Karma Yoga, the destruction of desires becomes easy. If one is careful in every small or big worldly or spiritual action, 'Why am I doing this and how am I doing it?' - such awareness arises. When one remains constantly aware of the ultimate goal, one does not commit evil actions, and one also does not become attached to good actions, and one experiences the state of detachment, and one's well-being is achieved.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 39]

The desire for worldly objects is the very source of 'lust' or 'craving'. It is the desire for things that have been given to us. As this desire increases, it turns into 'prayer'. All these are forms of 'work' or 'karma'.

The 'enemies of the wise' - This phrase refers to the wise and discerning seekers who have taken up the path of self-realization. It is they who can recognize this 'karma' as an enemy and destroy it. Others, who have not taken up the path of self-realization, do not recognize it as an enemy, but rather as a source of happiness.

The Lord says that this 'karma' is the constant enemy of the wise and discerning seekers. As soon as the desire arises, the wise seeker thinks, "Some calamity will surely come!" The desire for worldly objects keeps the importance and dependence of the world in the mind, which is a great obstacle on the path of self-realization. The desire is a constant thorn in the side of the wise seeker. Ultimately, it brings suffering to all.

To the ignorant, who are attached to worldly objects, this desire appears as a friend. This is because the desire for worldly objects makes them feel happy. Without desire, worldly objects cannot give happiness. But ultimately, they bring suffering, pain, anxiety, bondage, and hell. Therefore, this desire is also the constant enemy of the ignorant.

However, the ignorant do not have the awareness that this desire is their enemy. On the other hand, the wise and discerning seekers have this awareness. They are always vigilant.

The 'knowledge that is veiled' - This refers to the discriminative faculty, which is present in human beings. In other animals and birds, this faculty is not developed, and their life is limited to mere existence. But in human beings, if there is no desire, this faculty can be developed. This is because the desire for worldly objects veils the discriminative faculty.

The discriminative faculty is veiled because of the desire for worldly objects. As a result, human beings cannot move towards their ultimate goal of self-realization. The desire for worldly objects does not allow them to move towards the ultimate reality, but rather keeps them attached to the material world.

When someone speaks something unpleasant and untrue about us, we feel bad about it. On the other hand, when someone speaks something pleasant and true about us, we feel good about it. This means that the knowledge of good and bad, right and wrong, is present in all human beings. However, if someone does not follow their duty and speaks something unpleasant and untrue, it is because their discriminative faculty is veiled due to their desire for worldly objects.

The knowledge that 'renunciation is bliss' - This is not a knowledge that can be acquired through desire. Human beings think that happiness comes from acquiring worldly objects. But in reality, happiness comes from renouncing them. This is an experience that everyone has. In wakefulness and dreams, we experience both happiness and suffering due to our attachment to worldly objects. But in deep sleep, we do not even remember worldly objects, and we experience only happiness.

Therefore, it is clear that happiness comes from renouncing worldly objects. When we acquire worldly objects, we think that we are happy. But in reality, happiness comes from renouncing them. If acquiring worldly objects brought happiness, then we would never experience suffering while we have them. But even when we have worldly objects, we experience suffering.

When a person desires something, he becomes a slave to it. For example, if someone desires a watch, he becomes a slave to it. As soon as the desire arises, he starts to feel unhappy without the watch. This is an example of slavery. He thinks that if he gets the money, he can buy the watch and become free. But this is a wrong assumption. In reality, he becomes a slave to the money. Money is also a 'par' (something external), not 'swa' (something internal). Just as the desire for a watch makes him a slave to the watch, the desire for money makes him a slave to the money. The slavery is the same in both cases. However, due to the veil of desire, he experiences the slavery of the watch, but not the slavery of the money. On the other hand, he experiences the freedom of the money. The slavery that appears as freedom is very difficult to overcome.

The world is transitory. The body, wealth, land, and house are all ephemeral.

The Lord warns us to be cautious of the enemy that is 'kama' or desire, which is the root cause of all suffering and sin. Just as a man searching for his wife is told not to worry, as she will surely come to him, but the man is actually a thief, so too is the case with desire. It is the root cause of all suffering and sin.

The Lord says, "As long as one is attached to desire, one cannot attain true happiness, even in dreams. Desire is never satisfied, and the more one desires, the more one experiences the pangs of lack. This is why the wise man says, 'Kama achhat sukh sapnehu nahin' (Mans 7.90.1). The Lord also says, 'Analen, dushpurenen' (Gita 5.22), meaning that desire is never fulfilled, and the more one desires, the more one experiences the pangs of lack.

The Lord explains that the root cause of all suffering is the attachment to desire. Just as a man who desires wealth will stop at nothing to get it, and will even commit crimes, so too is the case with desire. The more one desires, the more one experiences the pangs of lack, and the more one is driven to commit sin.

The Lord says, "The senses, mind, and intellect are the abode of the Lord. This kama (desire) deludes the embodied being by covering the knowledge." (Gita 3.40)

The Lord explains that the senses, mind, and intellect are the abode of the Lord, and that desire deludes the embodied being by covering the knowledge. This means that desire is the root cause of all suffering and sin, and that it deludes the embodied being by covering the knowledge of the Lord.

The Lord warns us to be cautious of the enemy that is 'kama' or desire, which is the root cause of all suffering and sin. The Lord says, "One who is attached to desire cannot attain true happiness, even in dreams. Desire is never satisfied, and the more one desires, the more one experiences the pangs of lack." (Gita 5.22)

श्लोक ४० ]
* साधक-संजीवनी *
मुच्यते'–काम पाँच स्थानोंमें दीखता है– (१) पदार्थोंमें
(गीता—तीसरे अध्यायका चौंतीसवाँ श्लोक), (२) इन्द्रियोंमें,
(३) मनमें, (४) बुद्धिमें और (५) माने हुए अहम् (मैं)
अर्थात् कर्तामें (गीता—दूसरे अध्यायका उनसठवाँ श्लोक) ।
इन पाँच स्थानोंमें दीखनेपर भी काम वास्तवमें माने हुए
‘अहम्'-(चिज्जडग्रन्थि- ) में ही रहता है । परन्तु उपर्युक्त
पाँच स्थानोंमें दिखायी देनेके कारण ही वे इस कामके
वास-स्थान कहे जाते हैं।
२६३
व्याख्या– 'इन्द्रियाणि मनो बुद्धिरस्याधिष्ठान - | उत्पन्न होता है - ' कामात् क्रोधोऽभिजायते' (२ । ६२)
और क्रोधसे सम्मोह (अत्यन्त मूढ़भाव) उत्पन्न होता है—
'क्रोधाद्भवति सम्मोहः ' (२ । ६३) । इससे यह समझना
चाहिये कि कामनामें बाधा पहुँचनेपर तो क्रोध उत्पन्न होता
है, पर यदि कामनामें बाधा न पहुँचे, तो कामनासे लोभ और
लोभसे सम्मोह उत्पन्न होता हैं । तात्पर्य यह है कि कामनासे
पदार्थ न मिले तो 'क्रोध' उत्पन्न होता है और पदार्थ मिले
तो 'लोभ' उत्पन्न होता है। उनसे फिर 'मोह' उत्पन्न होता
है। कामना रजोगुणका कार्य है और मोह तमोगुणका कार्य ।
रजोगुण और तमोगुण पास-पास रहते हैं । अतः काम,
क्रोध, लोभ और मोह पास-पास ही रहते हैं । काम इन्द्रियों,
मन और बुद्धिके द्वारा देहाभिमानी पुरुषको मोहित (बेहोश )
कर देता है । इस प्रकार 'काम' रजोगुणका कार्य होते हुए
भी तमोगुणका कार्य 'मोह' हो जाता है ।
-
समस्त क्रियाएँ शरीर, इन्द्रियों, मन और बुद्धिसे ही
होती हैं। ये चारों कर्म करनेके साधन हैं। यदि इनमें काम
रहता है तो वह पारमार्थिक कर्म नहीं होने देता। इसलिये
कर्मयोगी निष्काम, निर्मम और अनासक्त होकर शरीर,
इन्द्रियों, मन और बुद्धिके द्वारा अन्तःकरणकी शुद्धिके लिये
कर्म करता है (गीता — पाँचवें अध्यायका ग्यारहवाँ श्लोक) ।
वास्तवमें काम अहम्-(जड-चेतनके तादात्म्य - ) में ही
रहता है। अहम् अर्थात् 'मैं' - पन केवल माना हुआ है । मैं
अमुक वर्ण, आश्रम, सम्प्रदायवाला हूँ – यह केवल मान्यता
है। मान्यताके सिवाय इसका दूसरा कोई प्रमाण नहीं है । इस
माने हुए सम्बन्धमें ही कामना रहती है । कामनासे ही सब
पाप होते हैं। पाप तो फल भुगताकर नष्ट हो जाते हैं, पर
अहम्' से कामना दूर हुए बिना नये-नये पाप होते रहते
हैं। इसलिये कामना ही जीवको बाँधनेवाली है। महाभारतमें
कहा है—
'
कामबन्धनमेवैकं नान्यदस्तीह बन्धनम् ।
कामबन्धनमुक्तो हि ब्रह्मभूयाय कल्पते ॥
( शान्तिपर्व २५१ । ७)
'जगत् में कामना ही एकमात्र बन्धन है, दूसरा कोई
बन्धन नहीं है। जो कामनाके बन्धनसे छूट जाता है, वह
ब्रह्मभाव प्राप्त करनेमें समर्थ हो जाता है । '
कामना उत्पन्न होनेपर मनुष्य पहले इन्द्रियोंसे भोग
भोगनेकी कामना करता है । पहले तो भोग- पदार्थ मिलते
नहीं और मिल भी जायँ तो टिकते नहीं। इसलिये उन्हें
किसी तरह प्राप्त करनेके लिये वह मनमें तरह- तरहकी
कामनाएँ करता है । बुद्धिमें उन्हें प्राप्त करनेके लिये तरह-
तरहके उपाय सोचता है। इस प्रकार कामना पहले
इन्द्रियोंको संयोगजन्य सुखके प्रलोभनमें लगाती है । फिर
इन्द्रियाँ मनको अपनी ओर खींचती हैं और उसके बाद
इन्द्रियाँ और मन मिलकर बुद्धिको भी अपनी ओर खींच
लेते हैं। इस तरह काम देहाभिमानीके ज्ञानको ढककर
इन्द्रियों, मन और बुद्धिके द्वारा उसे मोहित कर देता है
तथा उसे पतनके गड्ढेमें डाल देता है।
यह सिद्धान्त है कि नौकर अच्छा हो, पर मालिक
तिरस्कारपूर्वक उसे निकाल दे तो फिर उसे अच्छा नौकर
नहीं मिलेगा । ऐसे ही मालिक अच्छा हो, पर नौकर उसका
तिरस्कार कर दे तो फिर उसे अच्छा मालिक नहीं मिलेगा ।
इसी प्रकार मनुष्य परमात्मप्राप्ति किये बिना शरीरको सांसारिक
भोग और संग्रहमें ही खो देता है तो फिर उसे मनुष्यशरीर
नहीं मिलेगा । अच्छी वस्तुका तिरस्कार होता है अन्तःकरण
अशुद्ध होनेसे और अन्तःकरण अशुद्ध होता है कामनासे ।
दूसरे अध्यायमें भगवान्ने कहा है कि कामनासे क्रोध | इसलिये सबसे पहले कामनाका नाश करना चाहिये ।
'एतैर्विमोहयत्येष ज्ञानमावृत्य देहिनम् ' - कामनाके
कारण मनुष्यको जो करना चाहिये, वह नहीं करता और
जो नहीं करना चाहिये, वह कर बैठता है । इस प्रकार
कामना देहाभिमानी पुरुषको मोहित कर देती है ।

english:
263

The concept of desire (kama) is often misunderstood. It is not just a physical or sensual desire, but a complex phenomenon that manifests in five different places: (1) in material objects, (2) in the senses, (3) in the mind, (4) in intelligence, and (5) in the ego (aham).

Even when it appears in these five places, desire is ultimately rooted in the ego, which is the true abode of desire. The ego is a mere concept, a notion that we have created for ourselves. It is not based on any concrete reality. The ego is a product of our imagination, and it is the source of all desires.

The Gita explains that when the ego is not satisfied, it gives rise to anger (krodha), and when anger is not satisfied, it gives rise to delusion (sammmoha). The phrase 'dehinam vimohayati' - the meaning of this phrase is that it binds the one who believes, but not the one who is in their pure form. The one who does not consider themselves related to the body cannot be bound by it. It is only when one considers the body as 'I', 'mine', and 'for me' that they attribute importance to transitory and perishable material things, which leads to attachment to materiality. Attachment to materiality arises when one attributes importance to material things, and when one is attached to materiality, one's desires are born. When desires are born, the individual becomes entangled in the cycle of birth and death. This is what binds the person who is attached to the body.

The one who considers the body as 'I' and 'mine' is the one who is attached to the body. The Lord has already discussed the distinction between the body and the one who inhabits it in the beginning of his teachings (Gita - Chapter 2, verses 11-30). Both the body and the one who inhabits it are distinct, and this is the experience of all. This is what the body-attached person cannot understand, as it is covered by ignorance.

Therefore, O Arjuna, the one who is the embodiment of the Bharata dynasty, you should first control your senses. The wicked one who is the destroyer of knowledge and wisdom should be killed by you. (Gita - Chapter 3, verse 41)

The meaning of this verse is that one should control the senses by not allowing them to be driven by the desire for pleasure, but rather by allowing them to function in a neutral and detached manner. This is what is meant by controlling the senses. (Gita - Chapter 18, verse 10)

The reason for saying that one should control the senses first is that as long as one is under the control of the senses, one's vision is not directed towards the ultimate reality. And it is only when one's vision is directed towards the ultimate reality that one can truly understand the nature of the self and the world. Without this understanding, the destructive force of desire cannot be eliminated.

Therefore, O Arjuna, you should kill this great sinner, the destroyer of knowledge and wisdom. (Gita - Chapter 3, verse 41)

The phrase 'enam jñānavijñānanāśanam' - the meaning of this phrase is that one should first destroy the knowledge and wisdom that is the root cause of desire. The word 'jñāna' here refers to the knowledge of the scriptures, and the word 'vijñāna' refers to the knowledge of the ultimate reality. However, in this context, the word 'jñāna' refers to the ability to distinguish between right and wrong, and the word 'vijñāna' refers to the knowledge of the ultimate reality.

Both the ability to distinguish between right and wrong and the knowledge of the ultimate reality are self-evident. However, not everyone has the experience of the ultimate reality, but everyone has the experience of the ability to distinguish between right and wrong. This ability to distinguish between right and wrong is particularly prominent in humans. Arjuna's question - why does a person commit sin even when they do not want to? - is answered by the fact that a person's behavior is determined by their senses. Therefore, the phrase 'anicchannapi' - even when one does not want to - also confirms this.

[Verse 42-43]

The verse 42-43 of the Gita states:

The one who has discrimination (vivēka) knows both good and bad deeds, and does not want to commit evil. The desire not to commit evil is not possible without discrimination. However, 'kāma' (desire) covers this discrimination and does not allow it to be awakened.

When discrimination is awakened, a person performs all actions with a view to the future consequences. However, due to the influence of desire, he does not have a view towards the consequences. The lack of a view towards consequences is the reason he commits evil.

Everyone experiences the effect of this discrimination, but when desire does not allow it to be awakened, no one experiences the effect of this discrimination. Therefore, when desire does not allow the awakening of discrimination, how can one experience the effect of the ultimate truth (tattva-jñāna)?

Therefore, here, desire is said to be the destroyer of both knowledge (vivēka) and wisdom (bodha). In reality, desire does not destroy knowledge and wisdom, but covers them, i.e., it does not allow them to manifest.

Just as when clouds come in front of the eyes, it is said that the clouds have covered the sun, but in reality, the eyes are covered, not the sun, similarly, it is said that desire has covered knowledge and wisdom, but in reality, the intellect is covered, not knowledge and wisdom.

A person thinks that living a household life is not good, and that he should become a sādhu and live in solitude, but he does not give up desire. If he gives up desire, all his actions will become right. When a person dies with the desire to live and other desires, these desires become the cause of his birth in the next life. The meaning is that as long as a person has desire, he remains bound by the cycle of birth and death.

When a person is attracted to worldly objects, desire is born in him. When desire is born, discrimination and insight are suppressed, and the senses become dominant. The senses only engage a person in enjoying worldly objects. Even animals and birds are engaged in enjoying worldly objects up to their senses.

However, due to the influence of desire, a person's discrimination and insight are suppressed, and he becomes engaged in enjoying worldly objects. He then becomes engaged in accumulating wealth for the sake of worldly objects, and then his attention is focused on counting and accumulating wealth. He then becomes engaged in increasing his wealth, and for this purpose, he commits sinful actions like deceit, theft, and cheating.

As his wealth increases, he develops pride, which is the root of all evil. In this way, a person is led to great downfall due to desire. Therefore, the Lord gives the command to destroy this great evil desire, which is the root of all sins.

The verse 42 states:

The senses are said to be superior to the senses, the mind is said to be superior to the senses, and the intellect is said to be superior to the mind. 42

The verse 43 states:

Thus, knowing the intellect to be superior, and controlling oneself with the help of oneself, O mighty-armed one, destroy the great and difficult enemy, desire. 43

* साधक-संजीवनी *
२६७
जडमें सुखी - दुःखी होना नहीं बनता। तात्पर्य यह है कि | ( कामनाओं - ) की निवृत्ति और पारमार्थिक इच्छा-
(संसारसे छूटनेकी इच्छा, स्वरूपबोधकी जिज्ञासा और
भगवत्प्रेमकी अभिलाषा - ) की पूर्ति होती है । लौकिक
इच्छाएँ उत्पन्न हो सकती हैं, पर टिक नहीं सकतीं । परन्तु
पारमार्थिक इच्छा दब सकती है, पर मिट नहीं सकती ।
कारण कि लौकिक इच्छाएँ अवास्तविक और पारमार्थिक
इच्छा वास्तविक है। इसलिये साधकको न तो लौकिक
इच्छाओंकी पूर्तिकी आशा रखनी चाहिये और न पारमार्थिक
इच्छाकी पूर्तिसे निराश ही होना चाहिये ।
'अहम्' में जो जड-अंश है, उसके साथ तादात्म्य कर
लेनेसे चेतन भी अपनेको 'मैं भोक्ता हूँ' ऐसा मान लेता
है। परमात्मतत्त्वका साक्षात्कार होते ही रसबुद्धि निवृत्त हो
जाती है - 'रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते' ( गीता २ ।
५९)। इसमें 'अस्य' पद भोक्ता बने हुए 'अहम्' का
वाचक है और जो भोक्तापनसे निर्लिप्त तत्त्व है, उस
परमात्माका वाचक ‘परम' पद है। उसके ज्ञानसे रस
अर्थात् ‘काम' निवृत्त हो जाता है। कारण कि सुखके लिये
ही कामना होती है और स्वरूप सहजसुखराशि है । इसलिये
परमात्मतत्त्वका साक्षात्कार होनेसे 'काम' (संयोगजन्य
सुखकी इच्छा ) सर्वदा और सर्वथा मिट जाता है ।
मार्मिक बात
स्थूलशरीर 'विषय' है, इन्द्रियाँ 'बहिःकरण' हैं और
मन-बुद्धि 'अन्तःकरण' हैं । स्थूलशरीरसे इन्द्रियाँ पर
(श्रेष्ठ, सबल, प्रकाशक, व्यापक और सूक्ष्म) हैं तथा
इन्द्रियोंसे बुद्धि पर है। बुद्धिसे भी पर ' अहम्' है, जो कर्ता
है। उस ‘अहम्’-(कर्ता - ) में 'काम' अर्थात् लौकिक
इच्छा रहती है।
वस्तुतः मूलमें इच्छा एक ही है, जो अपने अंशी
परमात्माकी है । परन्तु जडके सम्बन्धसे इस इच्छाके दो भेद
हो जाते हैं और मनुष्य अपनी वास्तविक इच्छाकी पूर्ति
परिवर्तनशील जड - ( संसार - ) के द्वारा करनेके लिये जड-
पदार्थोंकी इच्छाएँ करने लगता है, जो उसकी भूल है ।
कारण कि लौकिक इच्छाएँ ' परधर्म' और पारमार्थिक
इच्छा 'स्वधर्म' है । परन्तु साधकमें लौकिक और पारमार्थिक—
दोनों इच्छाएँ रहनेसे द्वन्द्व पैदा हो जाता है । द्वन्द्व होनेसे
साधकमें भजन, ध्यान, सत्संग आदिके समय तो पारमार्थिक
इच्छा जाग्रत् रहती है, पर अन्य समयमें उसकी पारमार्थिक
अपनी सत्ता (होनापन) अर्थात् अपना स्वरूप चेतन, इच्छा दब जाती है और लौकिक ( भोग एवं संग्रहकी )
निर्विकार और सत्-चित्-आनन्दरूप है। जब वह जड - इच्छाएँ उत्पन्न हो जाती हैं। लौकिक इच्छाओंके रहते हुए
(प्रकृतिजन्य शरीर - ) के साथ तादात्म्य कर लेता है, तब साधकमें साधन करनेका एक निश्चय स्थिर नहीं रह
'अहम्' उत्पन्न होता है और स्वरूप 'कर्ता' बन जाता है सकता। पारमार्थिक इच्छा जाग्रत् हुए बिना साधककी
इस प्रकार कर्तामें एक जड - अंश होता है और एक चेतन- उन्नति नहीं होती । जब साधकका एकमात्र परमात्मप्राप्ति
अंश। जड-अंशकी मुख्यतासे संसारकी तरफ और चेतन - करनेका दृढ़ उद्देश्य हो जाता है, तब यह द्वन्द्व मिट जाता
अंशकी मुख्यतासे परमात्माकी तरफ आकर्षण होता है * । है और साधकमें एक पारमार्थिक इच्छा ही प्रबल रह जाती

[Verse 42-43]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

english:
268

When one considers himself to be related to the world, then the mind is controlled by the senses, the intellect is controlled by the mind, and the intellect is controlled by 'kama' (lust). At that time, 'prem' (love) is suppressed, and 'kama' is generated. As long as 'kama' exists, 'prem' does not awaken. As long as 'prem' does not awaken, 'kama' is not completely destroyed. The primary aspect of the jiva (individual self) is the jada (insentient) part, in which the desire for worldly pleasures (kama) remains. In this jiva, the primary aspect of the chetana (sentient) part is the desire for the Paramatma (Supreme Self). Therefore, the true residence of 'kama' is in the jada part, but it is related to the chetana part. When the connection with the chetana part is severed, the destruction of 'kama' occurs. The meaning is that when the chetana part separates from the jada part, the 'aham' (I-consciousness) is destroyed, and with the destruction of 'aham', 'kama' is also destroyed.

The jada part in 'aham' is where 'kama' resides - this is a strong argument. The visible world, the senses that perceive it, and the intellect that understands it, and the one who experiences it - all three are connected by a fundamental unity (sajatiyata). Without this unity, the experiencer cannot be attracted to the experienced. This is because attraction occurs only among similar things, not among dissimilar things. For example, the eyes are attracted to forms, not to words. This applies to all senses. The intellect is also attracted to its own subjects of understanding (vivek-vichar), not to external subjects (if it is attracted to external subjects, it is only with the help of the senses). Similarly, the self (chetana) is attracted to the Paramatma due to a fundamental unity (tattvika ekata). This unity is experienced only when the jada part is completely renounced, i.e., when the connection with the jada part is completely severed. When this unity is experienced, 'prem' awakens. In 'prem', the jada part (asat) is completely absent, i.e., the absence of jada is extreme.

The 'karanasharira' (causal body) is the subtle part of the prakriti (nature) that is the essence of the 'aham' (I-consciousness). This 'karanasharira' is where 'kama' resides. Due to the unity with the 'karanasharira', 'kama' appears to be present in the self. When this unity is severed, there is no trace of 'kama' left. In that state, one experiences one's own pure form. When one experiences one's own pure form, 'kama' is completely destroyed.

The meaning of the above statements is that 'kama' is present in the 'aham' (I-consciousness), but it is not present in one's true form. If 'kama' were present in one's true form, it would never be destroyed. 'Kama' is generated only when the jada part is connected with the self. Even if 'kama' appears to be present in the self, it is only in the jada part. Therefore, one should know this 'kama' that is beyond the intellect and destroy it.

The means to destroy 'kama' that resides in the 'aham' (I-consciousness) beyond the intellect is to control oneself by oneself, i.e., to maintain a connection only with one's pure form or with one's part (aspect) of the Paramatma. This is what the Lord has said in the sixth chapter, fifth shloka, 'udhareda atmanam atmanaa' (control oneself by oneself), and in the sixth shloka, 'yena atmaiva atmanaa jita' (conquer oneself by oneself).

The self (svarupa) is the direct part of the Paramatma, and the body, senses, mind, and intellect are parts of the world (samsara). When the self is turned away from its part (aspect) of the Paramatma and faces the world, desires (kamanas) are generated. Desires are generated from the absence of something, and this absence is due to the connection with the world. The world is essentially an absence (abava), as it is said in the second chapter, sixteenth shloka, 'nasato vidyate bhava' (there is no existence in non-existence). When the connection with the world is severed, the destruction of desires occurs, as it is said in the second chapter, sixteenth shloka, 'na bhavo vidyate sat' (there is no absence in existence).

Even when one considers oneself to be related to the world, the true desire (avashyakta or bhukh) of the jiva is to attain the Paramatma. 'I want to live forever; I want to know everything; I want to be happy forever' - this is the true desire of the jiva, which is to attain the Paramatma, who is the essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss. However, due to the connection with the world, one mistakenly wants to fulfill these desires through the world. This is what 'kama' is. This 'kama' can never be fulfilled. Therefore, one must destroy this 'kama'.

One who has connected with the world can also sever this connection. Therefore, the Lord has said, 'evam buddheh param buddhvaa' (first control the body and then the senses).

[Verse 42-43]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Chapter 3

It is not difficult to renounce desires. However, due to attachment to worldly objects, a person considers worldly pleasures to be the ultimate goal and thus finds it difficult to renounce desires. To get rid of the desire for pleasure, God sends suffering at various times, saying, "Do not desire pleasure; if you desire, you will only get suffering." A person attached to worldly objects can never escape suffering - this is a rule; because worldly pleasures are the causes of suffering (Gita - 5th Chapter, 22nd Shloka).

In its true form, it has infinite power. Its existence and power are the causes of the existence and power of the intellect, mind, and senses. However, due to attachment to worldly objects, it forgets its own power and considers itself to be under the control of the intellect, mind, and senses. Therefore, it is essential to know oneself and one's own power in order to defeat the enemy of desire.

Desire is a product of attachment to worldly objects and is itself a product of worldly objects. Due to similarity, it appears to be present in oneself. If attachment to worldly objects is removed, desire does not exist. Therefore, the meaning of defeating desire is to completely eliminate it. On the other hand, if one tries to eliminate desire by considering it to be a separate entity, it becomes difficult to eliminate. Because, in reality, desire is not an independent entity. Desire arises and the object of desire will be destroyed - this is a rule. If one does not create new desires, the old desires will automatically be destroyed.

Therefore, the meaning of eliminating desire is to not create new desires.

A person who is attached to worldly objects wants to enjoy worldly objects. However, in reality, worldly objects can never fulfill one's desires. Because, the self is eternal and worldly objects are ephemeral. Even though the self is eternal, to desire ephemeral objects is of no benefit and causes no harm. Therefore, God considers desire to be an enemy and orders its destruction.

Through the practice of karma yoga, the destruction of desire is easily achieved. Because, a karma yogi performs every action with the intention of attaining God and for the benefit of others, not for the fulfillment of one's desires. He performs every action without attachment and for the benefit of others, never for his own benefit. Whatever time, knowledge, resources, and strength he has, he considers them to be given to him and not his own. Therefore, he uses them for the benefit of others without attachment.

A karma yogi never performs actions for his own benefit, never desires anything for himself, and never considers anything to be his own. Therefore, the destruction of desires is easily achieved in him. When the destruction of desires is complete, his goal is achieved, and he attains self-realization, becoming a knower, a known, and a possessor of all that is to be known.

The attachment to worldly objects is the cause of the experience of "I" and "mine". The Lord has named the senses, mind, and intellect, but not the "I". The "I" is beyond the intellect. In the 7th Chapter, 4th Shloka, the Lord has also mentioned the "I" after the intellect - "bhumi, apo, analo vāyuḥ, khaṃ manaḥ buddhir eva ca | ahaṅkāra itīyam me..." . Therefore, here also, the "I" should be taken as the one in whom the "kam" resides, indicated by the word "saha".

As long as there is no direct experience of the self, the "kam" remains in the "I". When the self is directly experienced, the "kam" does not remain in the "I" - "parāṃ dṛṣṭvā nivartate" (Gita 2.59). The pleasure is in the self, but due to the presence of "kam", a person considers the attachment to worldly objects to be a source of pleasure. As long as there is attachment to worldly objects, "kam" exists; when there is a complete separation from worldly objects, "prem" (love) exists.

The "kam" is in oneself - "raso 'py asya" (Gita 2.59). Being in oneself, it becomes a hindrance. If it were not in oneself, but in others (senses, mind, intellect), what would be the hindrance? Being in oneself, it becomes a hindrance.
