रहता है। अतः जबतक अहम् है, तबतक अहम्की जातिका आकर्षण अर्थात् 'काम' होता है और जब अहम् नहीं
रहता, तब स्वयंकी जातिका आकर्षण अर्थात् 'प्रेम' होता है। काममें संसारकी तरफ और प्रेममें परमात्माकी तरफ
आकर्षण होता है।
सम्पूर्ण त्रिलोकी, अनन्त ब्रह्माण्ड 'विषय' है । विषय इन्द्रियोंके एक देशमें हैं, इन्द्रियाँ मनके एक देशमें हैं, मन
बुद्धिके एक देशमें है, बुद्धि अहम्के एक देशमें है और अहम् चेतन (स्वरूप) - के एक देशमें है। अतः चेतन अत्यन्त
महान् है, जिसके अन्तर्गत सम्पूर्ण त्रिलोकी, अनन्त ब्रह्माण्ड विद्यमान हैं । परन्तु अपरा प्रकृतिके एक अंश अहम्के
साथ अपना सम्बन्ध जोड़नेके कारण मनुष्य अपनेको अत्यन्त छोटा ( एकदेशीय) देखता है !

[Verse 42-43]

The one who is happy or unhappy, the doer or the enjoyer, is seen to be so only when viewed from a superficial perspective.  In reality, the sense of 'I' is not within oneself, but is perceived as such.  It is only when this sense of 'I' is perceived that the sense of 'I' is considered to be within oneself.  Therefore, the sense of 'I' is not within oneself, but is perceived as such.

A person considers the things that reside within him to be his own.  He considers the sense of 'I' to be his own and resides within it.  As long as the sense of 'I' exists, there is attraction to its own kind, i.e., 'lust'.  When the sense of 'I' does not exist, there is attraction to its own kind, i.e., 'love'.  Lust is an attraction to the world, while love is an attraction to the Supreme.

The entire universe, the infinite cosmos, is a 'subject' (viṣaya).  The senses reside in one place, the mind in another, the intellect in another, the intellect in another, and the sense of 'I' in another.  Therefore, the sense of 'I' is extremely great, and the entire universe, the infinite cosmos, resides within it.  However, due to the association of the inferior nature (aparā prakṛti) with the sense of 'I', a person considers himself to be extremely small (ekadeśīya).

Thus, the third chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, known as 'Karma Yoga', comes to an end with the recitation of the names 'Om', Tat, and Sat, which are the essence of the Bhagavad Gita, the Upanishads, and the science of yoga.  This chapter is called 'Karma Yoga' because it contains four 'Uvach' (statements) - two 'Arjuna Uvach' and two 'Shri Bhagavan Uvach'.  This is not found in other chapters of the Gita.

The words, syllables, and Uvach of the third chapter are as follows:

(1) This chapter contains three 'Ath Tretiyah Adhyayah', eight 'Arjuna Uvach' and five hundred and forty-two words, and thirteen 'Puspika' words.  In this way, the total number of words is five hundred and fifty-five.

(2) This chapter contains seven 'Ath Tretiyah Adhyayah', twenty-six 'Arjuna Uvach', one thousand three hundred and seventy-seven words, and forty-five 'Puspika' words.  In this way, the total number of words is one thousand four hundred and twenty-two.  All the shlokas of this chapter have thirty-two words.

The meter used in the third chapter is as follows:

In the forty-three shlokas of this chapter, the meter 'Raganya' is used in the first and thirty-seventh shlokas, and in the third shloka of the eleventh shloka.  The meter 'Naganya' is used in the fifth shloka, and the meter 'Bhaganya' is used in the nineteenth, twenty-sixth, and thirty-fifth shlokas, and in the third shloka of the eighth and twenty-first shlokas.  The meter 'Sankirtana-Vipula' is used in the seventh shloka, and the meter 'Pathya-Avaktara' is used in the remaining thirty shlokas.

25

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

॥ ॐ श्रीपरमात्मने नमः ॥
अथ चतुर्थोऽध्यायः
अवतरणिका-
श्रीभगवान्ने दूसरे अध्यायके उनतालीसवें श्लोकमें अर्जुनसे कहा कि ज्ञानयोगमें अपने विवेकके अनुसार
विचारपूर्वक चलनेसे जिस समबुद्धिकी प्राप्ति होती है, उसीको तू कर्मयोगके विषयमें सुन अर्थात् कर्मयोगमें
निष्कामभावपूर्वक परहितार्थ कर्तव्य-कर्म करनेसे यह समबुद्धि कैसे प्राप्त होती है, इसे सुन- 'एषा तेऽभिहिता
साङ्ख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां शृणु ।' फिर कर्मयोगका वर्णन करते हुए प्रसंगानुसार अर्जुनके प्रश्न करनेपर स्थितप्रज्ञके
लक्षण बताकर अध्यायका विषय समाप्त किया।
तीसरे अध्यायके आरम्भमें अर्जुनने प्रश्न किया कि आपके मतमें जब बुद्धि श्रेष्ठ मान्य है, तो फिर आप
मुझे घोर कर्म - (युद्ध-) में क्यों लगाते हैं? इसके उत्तरमें भगवान् ने चौथे श्लोकसे उनतीसवें श्लोकतक विविध
प्रकारसे कर्तव्य-कर्म करनेकी आवश्यकताका प्रतिपादन करते हुए सिद्ध किया कि कर्तव्य-कर्म करनेसे ही समबुद्धि
प्राप्त होती है। फिर तीसवें श्लोकमें भगवन्निष्ठाके अनुसार कर्तव्य-कर्म करनेकी विशेष विधि बतायी कि
विवेकपूर्वक सम्पूर्ण कर्मोंको मेरे अर्पण करके तथा निष्काम, निर्मम और नि:सन्ताप होकर शास्त्रविहित कर्तव्य-
कर्मोंको करना चाहिये । कर्तव्य-कर्म करनेकी इस विधिको 'अपना मत' कहते हुए भगवान्ने इकतीसवें - बत्तीसवें
श्लोकोंमें अन्वय और व्यतिरेक विधिसे अपने इस मतकी पुष्टि की तथा पैंतीसवें श्लोकमें इस विधिके पालनपर
विशेष जोर देते हुए कहा कि अपने कर्तव्यका पालन करते हुए मरना भी श्रेयस्कर है - 'स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः ।'
इसपर अर्जुनने छत्तीसवें श्लोकमें प्रश्न किया कि मनुष्य न चाहते हुए भी किससे प्रेरित होकर पाप (अकर्तव्य)
कर बैठता है ? इसके उत्तरमें भगवान्ने 'काम' अर्थात् कामनाको ही सारे पापों, अनर्थोंका हेतु बताकर अन्तमें
कामरूप शत्रुको मार डालनेकी आज्ञा दी।
यद्यपि तीसरे अध्यायके सैंतीसवें श्लोकसे भगवान् लगातार उपदेश दे रहे हैं, तथापि तैंतालीसवें श्लोकमें
अर्जुनके प्रश्नका उत्तर समाप्त होनेपर महर्षि वेदव्यासजी तीसरे अध्यायकी समाप्ति कर देते हैं और नया (चौथा )
अध्याय आरम्भ कर देते हैं। इससे ऐसा मालूम देता है कि अर्जुनके प्रश्नका उत्तर समाप्त होनेपर भगवान् कुछ
समयके लिये रुक जाते हैं; फिर दूसरे अध्यायके सैंतालीसवें - अड़तालीसवें श्लोकोंसे जिस कर्मयोगका विषय चल
रहा था, उसीको चौथे अध्यायके पहले श्लोकमें 'इमम्' पदसे पुनः आरम्भ करते हैं। अत: चौथा अध्याय तीसरे
अध्यायका ही परिशिष्ट माना जाता है।
कर्मयोगमें दो बातें मुख्य हैं- १ - कर्तव्य-कर्मोंका आचरण और २ – कर्तव्य-कर्मोंके विषयमें विशेष

The Lord said: 'This wisdom, which has been explained in the Sankhya, listen to it, O Arjuna, as it is also applicable in the path of Yoga.' Then, while describing the path of Karma Yoga, the Lord, in response to Arjuna's questions, explained the characteristics of the one who is established in their wisdom and thus concluded the chapter.

In the beginning of the third chapter, Arjuna had asked the Lord, "If wisdom is considered superior, then why do you engage me in this terrible war?" In response to this, the Lord, from the fourth verse to the twenty-ninth verse, presented the necessity of performing duties in various ways, thereby establishing that it is through the performance of duties that one attains equanimity. Then, in the thirtieth verse, the Lord explained the special method of performing duties according to the principle of devotion to Him, saying, "Offer all actions to Me, and perform all actions without attachment, without ego, and without anxiety." The Lord, in the thirty-first to thirty-second verses, confirmed His own view through the method of analogy and contrast, and in the thirty-fifth verse, He emphasized the importance of following this method, saying, "It is more auspicious to die in the performance of one's duty."

Arjuna then asked in the thirty-sixth verse, "What drives a person to commit evil actions, even though they do not want to?" In response, the Lord identified "kama" or desire as the root cause of all evil and misfortune, and ultimately instructed Arjuna to vanquish the enemy in the form of desire.

Although the Lord has been continuously teaching in the third chapter from the thirty-seventh verse, Maharishi Vedavyasa concludes the third chapter and begins the fourth chapter in the forty-third verse, after responding to Arjuna's question. This implies that the Lord pauses for a while after completing His response to Arjuna's question, and then begins the fourth chapter again, from the forty-fourth verse, continuing the discussion on Karma Yoga that was ongoing in the second chapter from the forty-first to the forty-eighth verses. Therefore, the fourth chapter is considered an appendix to the third chapter.

In Karma Yoga, there are two main aspects: 1) the performance of duties, and 2) the special knowledge about duties. Arjuna wants to renounce the nature of actions, which is why, in the beginning of the third chapter, he asks the Lord, "Why do you engage me in this terrible war?" Therefore, in the third chapter, the Lord emphasizes the necessity of performing duties in various ways and also explains the theoretical aspects of Karma Yoga; but in this fourth chapter, the Lord emphasizes the theoretical aspects of Karma Yoga, while also emphasizing the necessity of performing duties. In other words, both the third and fourth chapters discuss these two aspects, but in the third chapter, the main emphasis is on the performance of duties, and in the fourth chapter, the main emphasis is on the special knowledge about duties - "I shall explain to you the action in the performance of which one attains liberation from evil" (4.16).

The Lord, beginning again from the forty-fourth verse, describes the path of Karma Yoga, which, although eternal, had become rare on this earth due to the non-existence of a special person who knew it. The Lord, in the first three verses, explains the tradition of Karma Yoga and establishes its eternity.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 1]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 2]

The one who performs the duty that leads to the accomplishment of the ultimate goal is certain to achieve it. The one who does not perform it is not. Just as the sound produced by the radio can be broadcast through a specific frequency, but the responsibility of broadcasting it lies with no one, and the sound spreads everywhere, but one should not broadcast a sound that one should not, similarly, there are two states - one of non-action or non-performance, and the other of performing the duty that one should.

When a karma yogi renounces the sense of personal gain and performs only the duty that one should, then the entire universe is benefited by his actions. The all-pervading and benevolent power of the Lord unites him with the ultimate goal, and his actions become extraordinary. The power of the Lord works through him, and through him, the welfare of others is achieved. Therefore, there is no obstacle or effort in performing one's duty.

Duty is performed naturally and spontaneously, as it is one's inherent nature. However, when one performs duty with a sense of personal gain, attachment, or ego, then it becomes a source of bondage. The Lord has described such actions as being laborious (Gita - 18th chapter, 24th shloka). In karma yoga, there is no need to rely on anyone. One should perform one's duty according to the circumstances that arise.

If one helps someone in need, it is considered service. For example, if someone's car breaks down, and they are trying to push it, then one can help them. However, if one searches for opportunities to serve, then it is not service, but rather a means to achieve one's own selfish goals. Service is that which is done according to the circumstances. A karma yogi does not change the circumstances or seek them out. Instead, they make the most of the circumstances that arise.

Just as the Lord's power benefits all living beings, similarly, the power of the Lord's power is always engaged in the welfare of all living beings. This is karma yoga.

Thus, the great kings, such as Surya, Manu, and Ikshvaku, knew the karma yoga well and practiced it themselves and also taught it to their subjects. This tradition of karma yoga was passed down through the generations of kings. However, in this human world, this tradition has been lost.

This knowledge is a special and unique one, and therefore, every king should know it. Similarly, the leaders of families, communities, and villages should also know this knowledge.

In ancient times, the kings who knew karma yoga well ruled their kingdoms.

The Bhagavad Gita

[Chapter 4]

The natural inclination of those who perform actions for the benefit of their subjects is always present. The great poet Kalidasa writes about the kings of the solar dynasty:

"They (the kings) used to take from their subjects only what was necessary for their well-being, just as the sun takes water from the earth to produce a thousandfold. They would not use the wealth collected from their subjects for their own benefit, but would instead use it for the benefit of their subjects."

The implication is that these kings would use the wealth collected from their subjects for the benefit of their subjects, without any personal gain. They would also engage in separate activities for their personal sustenance. The practice of karma yoga was inherent in their actions, and as a result, they possessed extraordinary knowledge and devotion. This is the reason why great sages of the past would often visit these kings to seek knowledge.

The principle of karma yoga is eternal, and its essence is described in sacred texts. However, due to the passage of time, this knowledge has become rare in this world. In the 20th verse of the third chapter, the Lord mentions that the practice of karma yoga was first taught to the sun, and then passed down to the royal sages. Over time, the practice has become distorted, and now it is rare to find someone who practices karma yoga.

The Lord instructs Arjuna to follow the example of his ancestors and practice karma yoga in accordance with their tradition. Additionally, the knowledge of karma yoga is easily accessible to him, and he should therefore acquire it. The Lord further explains that karma yoga, jnana yoga, and bhakti yoga are eternal and cannot be destroyed. They are the means to attain the ultimate reality, and their existence is guaranteed.

Even though the practice of karma yoga has become rare, its underlying principle remains eternal. This principle is that one should not engage in actions for personal gain. Without this principle, it is impossible to practice any form of yoga, including jnana yoga, bhakti yoga, and others. The Lord further explains that a jnana yogi renounces worldly attachments by realizing the impermanence of worldly actions, and a bhakti yogi renounces worldly attachments by realizing the impermanence of worldly actions.

The following verse from the Chandogya Upanishad is relevant in this context:

"There is no thief in my kingdom, no miser, no drunkard, no one who does not perform the agnihotra, no one who is ignorant, and no one who is a paramour. How then can there be a prostitute?"

The Lord's words are eternal and cannot be contradicted.

[Verse 3]

Thus, the followers of knowledge and devotion will have to accept the principles of karma yoga. This is what is meant by the 'loss' of 'yoga'. They will have to accept it, even if they do not perform the rituals of karma yoga. In reality, the principles of karma yoga are still present, even though they are on the verge of being lost.

The human body is meant for the practice of karma yoga, i.e., for serving others selflessly. However, today people are engrossed in their own comforts, prestige, and other worldly pursuits. Due to the increase of self-interest, their attention is not towards serving others. Thus, forgetting the purpose for which the human body is given, is what is meant by the 'loss' of karma yoga.

In reality, it is not the 'karma' that has been lost, but the 'yoga' has been lost. The 'yoga' is the flow of actions towards oneself. Just as the objects of the world are obtained through actions, similarly, the Lord is also obtained through actions. This is a firmly established notion in the minds of seekers. However, due to this, their attention is not towards the reality that the Lord is always present.

The 'karma' is always for the benefit of the world, and the 'yoga' is always for one's own benefit. The 'yoga' is not obtained through actions, it is self-existent. Therefore, to consider that 'yoga' is obtained through actions is a misconception.

A person can control animals, birds, humans, gods, ancestors, sages, saints, and even the Lord through service. However, due to the absence of a service mentality, a person becomes a slave to his own desires, which results in his downfall in hell and in 84 lakhs of species.

This is the ancient yoga that has been declared by me. You are my devotee and friend, and this is the greatest secret. (3)

Translation of the Sanskrit verse:
This is the ancient yoga that has been declared by me.
You are my devotee and friend, and this is the greatest secret. (3)

Translation of the Sanskrit verse with transliteration:
yogaḥ proktaḥ purātanaḥ |
bhakto'si me sakhā ceti rahasyaṃ hyetaduttamam || 3 ||

Translation of the commentary:
The verse 'bhakto'si me sakha ceti' is revealed to Arjuna in the presence of his teacher, who has taken the form of a friend. Arjuna had considered Krishna as his friend since the eleventh chapter of the Gita, but he became a devotee only in the second chapter, seventh verse. The teacher or guru gives instructions only to his disciple or servant, not to his friend. When Arjuna surrendered to Krishna, the instructions began.

Krishna says, 'I am your teacher, therefore, teach me.' Therefore, Krishna reveals himself to Arjuna and discloses the secret. Arjuna had a special affection for Krishna, which is why he accepted Krishna as his charioteer, even though Krishna had given up his divine army and divine weapons.

The verse 'arurukshor muner yoga' means that the practice of yoga is the fulfillment of one's duty. Therefore, the practice of duty is not for its own sake, but for the sake of its cessation. The practice of duty should be done with a service mentality, not with a selfish mentality. When one performs duties for the benefit of others, the tendency to perform duties for one's own benefit decreases, and when one performs duties for one's own benefit, the tendency to perform duties for others increases. When the tendency to perform duties for one's own benefit is eliminated, the self-existent yoga is experienced.

Translation of the Sanskrit verse from the Mahabharata:
Thus, Krishna spoke to Arjuna, the son of Kunti, who was eager to fight in the battle. (Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, 7.21)

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

english:
281

(1) I am nothing. This is because my true nature is Sat (the eternal and unchanging reality). Therefore, my form is eternal and unchanging, and whatever I have obtained is transient and meant to be separated from the world for the sake of others. How can the transient be mine? The duty is to act. This is the path of action (Karma Yoga). When the path of action is realized, how can the transient be connected with the eternal? The attachment to action, the desire to possess, the desire to live, and the fear of death all disappear.

(2) I do not need anything. This is because my true nature is Sat, and it is never incomplete or lacking. Therefore, why should I desire anything? The eternal and unchanging reality is uncreated and imperishable. How can a transient and perishable thing be of any use to it?

(3) I should not do anything for myself. The first reason for this is that I am a part of the conscious and eternal Paramatma (the supreme self), and action is of the nature of the material world. I am eternal and unchanging, while action and its fruits are transient and have a beginning and an end. Therefore, by doing action for myself, I become connected with the transient and the impermanent. Action and its fruits come to an end, but their effects remain, which are the causes of birth and death (Gita 13.21). The second reason is that the duty to act belongs to one who can act, that is, one who has the capacity to act. Since I am conscious, eternal, and unchanging, and I do not need anything, I do not have the capacity to act. Therefore, it must be accepted that I should not do anything for myself. The third reason is that my true nature is Sat, and it is complete and perfect. Therefore, there is no possibility of incompleteness or lack in it. Since there is no lack, there is no desire to possess anything. This itself proves that I do not have the duty to act, that is, I should not do anything for myself.

In the path of action (Karma Yoga), 'action' is for the world, and 'yoga' is for myself. However, by doing action for myself, I do not experience 'yoga'. I experience 'yoga' only when the flow of action is completely directed towards the world. This is because the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, wealth, and possessions that I have are all part of the world and are not separate from it. Just as people perform many actions in the light of the sun, but the sun has no connection with those actions, so too, in the light of the conscious and eternal self, all actions take place, but the self has no connection with them. This is because the self is conscious and unchanging, while action is material and changing. However, when the self mistakenly identifies with those objects and actions, they inevitably bind it.

It is a remarkable fact that the Gita describes the human experience (vivikta) from the eleventh shloka to the thirtieth shloka of the second chapter. This is not just a human experience, but a universal experience of all living beings, because all living beings have the experience of 'I am'. Even trees and mountains have this experience, but they cannot express it. In animals and birds, it is even more evident, as they fight with each other, taking pride in their own existence. If they did not have the experience of their own existence, they would not fight.

The verse translation is as follows:

It is a direct experience of a man that the more he gets entangled, the more he gets confused. However, he does not look at his own experience. When self-interest, desire, and the intellect of accumulation are not present, then his duty becomes clear and all kinds of confusions are automatically resolved.

He does not even respect his own experience. This experience is called wisdom or self-knowledge. This wisdom is inherent in all and is bestowed by God.

The senses, mind, and intellect are parts of nature, so the knowledge obtained from them is also of nature. The knowledge obtained by reading and listening to scriptures through these senses, mind, and intellect is also of a kind of nature. The truth of the Supreme Being is far more extraordinary than this natural knowledge. Therefore, the Supreme Being can be known only through self-knowledge (the knowledge that arises from oneself). By giving importance to self-knowledge, one gets the power to know 'What am I? What is mine? What is the difference between the inert and the conscious? What is nature and what is the Supreme Being?' This is the power of wisdom that works in the path of action (Karma Yoga).

In the path of action, there are two main things related to wisdom: (1) There should be no doubt about 'I am' and (2) one should not consider the things that have been obtained as one's own; because they were not one's own in the beginning and will not be one's own in the future. I (the self) remain permanent, and these obtained things - the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc. - are constantly changing and are constantly separate from me. Just as the beginning and end of actions occur, similarly, the union and separation of their fruits also occur. Therefore, the relationship of actions and objects is with the world, not with the self. In this way, as soon as wisdom awakens, the destruction of desires occurs.

The destruction of desires occurs, and self-sufficiency (niskamata) is automatically revealed, i.e., Karma Yoga is fully accomplished.

The external situation is formed according to actions, i.e., it is the fruit of actions. Wealth, poverty, praise, blame, respect, disrespect, fame, infamy, gain, loss, birth, death, health, and disease, etc. are all under the control of actions. Favorable and unfavorable situations arise due to the fruits of good and bad actions; but linking oneself with that situation and considering it as one's own and being happy or unhappy is foolishness. The meaning is that the occurrence of favorable and unfavorable situations is the fruit of actions, and being happy or unhappy due to it is the fruit of ignorance and foolishness. It is not possible to eliminate the fruit of actions, but it is possible to eliminate ignorance and foolishness. One does not eliminate the ignorance that can be eliminated, and one tries to change the situation that cannot be changed - this is a great mistake! Therefore, by giving importance to one's wisdom, one should eliminate ignorance and by utilizing favorable and unfavorable situations, one should rise above them, i.e., one should become detached. One who uses favorable and unfavorable situations without linking oneself with them, i.e., one who serves others in favorable situations and does not get unhappy in unfavorable situations, i.e., one who does not have the desire for happiness, becomes free from the bondage of the world with ease.

The unfavorable situation that a person does not want is the fruit of the bad actions done in the past. Therefore, one should not do bad actions. One should not do such a thing that causes harm to someone even in a dream. However, even if one does not do new bad actions, the unfavorable situation arises due to the fruits of old bad actions, and then anxiety, sorrow, fear, etc. arise in the heart. The reason for this is that we have made anxiety and sorrow familiar to ourselves. Just as the cow that has been sold is covered with old desires (Gita - Third Chapter, Thirty-eighth to Forty-fifth verses), so the self-interest, desire, and intellect of accumulation cover wisdom. A person does not make a proper decision about his duty due to self-interest, desire, and the intellect of accumulation. He wants to resolve the confusions by means of the body, senses, mind, and intellect, and therefore, he tries to change the present situation. However, changing the situation is not in one's power, and therefore, the confusion remains. The situation comes back to the same place due to familiarity with the place.

O, Bhagavan, the Munis have said: 'It is not in our hands to get or lose, to live or die, to be good or bad, to be virtuous or vicious.' (Mansarovar, 2.171)

283
[Verse 4-5]

But, just as a life-giving medicine is administered repeatedly to a patient, and he eventually stops taking it, similarly, if one repeatedly thinks about the changing circumstances of life, one will eventually stop doing so. Therefore, let us firmly decide today and now that thinking about and worrying about the circumstances of life is a wrong approach, and we will not make this mistake again. If we firmly decide on this, we will stop worrying and thinking about the circumstances of life.

Even without full realization of discrimination, a resolute mind remains in the path of karma yoga, thinking that one should separate oneself from what is not one's own and serve without enjoying worldly pleasures. The reason for this resolute mind is that the importance of worldly pleasures does not remain in one's heart. Therefore, one is not deceived by the idea that 'pleasure lies in enjoyment.' Thus, by firmly holding on to this one decision, one's well-being is achieved. This resolute mind is strengthened by association with the wise and self-study. Therefore, every seeker must certainly form this beneficial decision. One is free to form this decision; no one is bound. There is no need for even a little help from anyone else, because one is self-sufficient.

Context - Arjuna is naturally curious to know how the Lord, who is sitting in front of him, had given a discourse to the Sun in the beginning of creation. Therefore, Arjuna asks the Lord a question in the next shloka.

Arjuna said:
"Your birth is very recent, and the birth of the Sun is very ancient. How can I understand that you had given a discourse to the Sun in the beginning of creation?" (4)

Translation of Sanskrit shloka:
"aparṃ bhavato janma param janma vivasvataḥ
katham etad vijānīyāṃ tvām ādau proktavān iti"

Explanation: Arjuna is saying that your birth is very recent, and the birth of the Sun is very ancient. Therefore, how can I understand that you had given a discourse to the Sun in the beginning of creation?

Arjuna's question is not based on doubt or criticism but on curiosity. He is asking the Lord about the mystery of the Lord's birth in order to understand it easily. Since the Lord is all-knowing, Arjuna is confident that the Lord will reveal the mystery of the Lord's birth.

The next shloka is the Lord's response to Arjuna's question.

The Lord said:
"Many births have passed for you, O Arjuna, and I know all of them. You do not know them, O best of men." (5)

Translation of Sanskrit shloka:
"bahūni me vyatītāni janmāni tava charjuna
tāny ahaṃ veda sarvāṇi na tvam vettha parantapa"

Explanation: The Lord is saying that many births have passed for you, O Arjuna, and I know all of them. You do not know them, O best of men.

The Lord said:

"Many births have passed for Me, and for you as well. I know all of them."

- The Lord has already been referred to as Arjuna's friend and beloved companion in the third shloka, so in the subsequent shlokas, Arjuna asks questions freely from his heart. Arjuna has a strong desire to know the Lord's birth secret, so the Lord reveals it to him as a friend. This is a rule that a speaker cannot hide himself when the listener has a strong desire to know. Even saints and sages can reveal themselves to those who have a special faith in them.

As it is said in the Mānasa (1.110.1):

gūu tattva na sādhu durāvahiṃ |
ārata adhikārī jaha~ pāvahiṃ ||

- "The wise do not hide their true nature from those who are worthy and deserving."

The Lord says, "Many births have passed for Me, and for you as well." However, My birth and your birth are of different kinds. My birth is of a different nature (which will be described in the sixth shloka), and your birth (the birth of the jiva) is of a different nature (which will be described in the eighth chapter, nineteenth and thirteenth shlokas, and the twenty-first and twenty-sixth shlokas of the twenty-sixth chapter).

In the twelfth shloka of the second chapter, the Lord said to Arjuna, "We were not present before, and we will not be present after." This means that the Lord and the jiva (the individual soul) are both eternal and uncreated.

The Lord says, "I know all of them." However, you do not know. There are some jivas in the world who have knowledge of their past births, known as "yunjana yogis" or "jatismaras." These great souls have achieved their goal through their sadhana (spiritual practice) and have developed a strong will. Their consciousness is so strong that they can know the past and present of any place where they focus their consciousness. However, they can only know up to a certain limit of their past births, not all of them. On the other hand, the Lord is a "yukta yogi," who is naturally self-realized and eternal. He does not need to practice sadhana to achieve his goal. He has knowledge of all his past and future births, as well as the present, without any effort. His knowledge is not limited to the past, present, or future; it is all-pervading and eternal.

As it is said in the Gita (7.26), "Their knowledge is not limited to the past, present, or future; it is all-pervading and eternal."

The Lord's words, "I know all of them," should bring joy to the seekers, knowing that they are known by the Lord and that He is always watching over them.

The Lord says, "You do not know." The reason for not knowing is the attraction and importance given to ephemeral things in the heart. This is the root cause of not knowing. Arjuna's heart was attracted to ephemeral things and the importance of individuals, which is why he was hesitant to fight the war.

Even saints and sages hide themselves and do not reveal themselves to everyone. However, they reveal themselves in the following three situations:

1. When a person with great faith comes before them and has a strong desire to know them.
2. When a person's beloved body is about to leave them.
3. When a saint's or sage's own body is about to leave them.

In the second and third situations, even if the person does not have great faith, if they have respect for the saint or sage and want to know them, the saint or sage will reveal themselves to them.

[Verse 6]

In the previous shloka, Arjuna said that those who have a desire for our kingdom, enjoyment, and happiness are the ones who have left their family and wealth behind to fight in the war. This shows that Arjuna had a desire for the kingdom, enjoyment, and happiness. Therefore, due to the desire for perishable objects, they did not know their previous births.

The attachment to one's own happiness and comfort, and the accumulation of wealth and other material possessions for the sake of enjoyment and relaxation, is called "parigraha" (accumulation). On the other hand, the complete renunciation of parigraha, i.e., not accumulating any material possessions for the sake of one's own happiness and comfort, is called "aparigraha" (non-accumulation). When one has the firmness of aparigraha, one gains knowledge of one's previous births.

As stated in the Patanjali Yoga Darshan (2.39), the world (action and objects) is always changing and impermanent, and therefore, it is certain to have a lack (deficiency). Due to the connection with the world, a person starts to see a lack in himself. This lack creates a desire to fill it, and then to seek something new. This desire to fill the lack is the cause of a person's constant engagement in worldly activities. However, this desire is never fulfilled. Due to this desire, a person becomes unconscious and unaware of his present duties and the knowledge of his past and future lives is also lost.

Relation - In the previous shloka, the Lord mentioned that He and Arjuna have had many births. Now, in this shloka, the Lord explains the uniqueness of His birth (avatara).

I am the unchanging and imperishable Self, the Lord of all beings, and yet, I am born (appear) through my own power (maya) by establishing myself as the ruler of nature (prakriti). (6)

Translation of Sanskrit Shloka:

ajah api sannavyyatma bhutanam isvarah api san
prakritim svam adhisthaya sambhavami atma-maya ya
= I am (ajah) unborn (and)
bhutanam isvarah = the Lord of all beings
prakritim svam adhisthaya = by establishing myself as the ruler of nature
sambhavami = I am born (appear)
atma-maya ya = through my own power (maya)

Explanation - This is the sixth shloka, and in it, the Lord explains six points about Himself. The first three points are about the Lord's three forms - aj, avyay, and ishvara. The Lord has explained these three forms in the Gita as follows:

1. Aj - The Lord's unborn form:
Whoever knows Me as the unborn and imperishable, the Lord of the universe, is not bewildered among the people of the world, and is freed from all sins. (10.3)
On the other hand, the ignorant do not know Me as the unborn and imperishable. (7.25)

2. Avyay - The Lord's imperishable form:
Those who, with their minds not attached to anything, worship Me, knowing Me as the imperishable and the oldest of all beings, attain Me. (9.13)
On the other hand, those who do not know My imperishable and supreme form are deluded. (7.24)

3. Ishvara - The Lord's form as the Lord of all beings:
One who knows Me as the enjoyer of all sacrifices and austerities, the Lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all living beings, attains peace. (5.29)
On the other hand, the foolish do not know Me as the Lord of all beings, who has taken this human form. (9.11)

The Lord says in these words that I am not born like ordinary humans and nor do I die. Humans are born and die, but I am 'ajam' (unborn) and yet I manifest, and I am 'avinas' (unending) and yet I disappear. Manifesting and disappearing are my supernatural play. All living beings were unmanifest (avyakta) before birth and will become unmanifest (avyakta) after death, but they are manifest (vyakta) in between. However, the Lord is always manifest like the sun. The implication is that just as the sun remains the same before and after sunrise and sunset, the Lord remains the same always, but people see His manifestation and disappearance according to their perspective.

Other living beings are bound by their actions and are born, but the Lord's birth is not like that. When they are born, they have age and experience happiness and sorrow, but the Lord does not have these. When other living beings are born, they are first infants, then grow into youth, then become old, and then die. But the Lord does not undergo any change. He plays as a child and grows up to be a youth, and then remains eternally youthful. Even after hundreds of years, the Lord remains as beautiful and youthful. Therefore, the pictures of the Lord that are made do not depict His beard and moustache (although some may depict them!). The Lord is not born like other living beings, does not undergo change, and does not die.

'bhutananam isvaro'api san' - The Lord is the supreme ruler of all living beings. Even when the Lord incarnates as a small child, He remains the supreme ruler. His divine nature (shashakatva) does not diminish even when He incarnates. Just as Lord Krishna killed the demon Pootana on the sixth day, if He did not have divine nature, how could He have killed her? The Lord killed Shakatasura at three months, Trinavart at one year, and Aghasura at five years. In this way, the Lord killed many demons even in His childhood. At seven years, He lifted the Govardhan mountain on His finger! Even when the Lord is the supreme ruler of all living beings, He incarnates as a small child and performs small tasks. This is the true nature of the Lord's divinity.

The Lord's divine nature is that He can perform any task, even as a small child. Even when the Lord is the charioteer of Arjuna and hails his horses, He remains the supreme ruler of Arjuna and all other living beings. As the charioteer, He gives Arjuna the great teachings of the Gita. Lord Rama does not disobey his father's orders and goes to the forest for fourteen years, but the Lord's divine nature remains the same towards Rama and all other living beings.

'prakritim swamadhisthaya' - The Lord's pure nature is that which is beyond the three gunas (satva, rajas, and tamas). This pure nature is the Lord's own true, conscious, and blissful form. This is also known as the sakti (power) of the Lord, which is the sambhuti (creative) power, the sambhuti (manifesting) power, and the ahladi (delighting) power. This is also known as the chitmayi (conscious) power, the kripa (compassionate) power, and other names. The Lord's consort, Radha, and His devotee, Sita, are also this same power. The Lord's devotee, Bhakti (devotion), and the knowledge of Brahman (Brahma-vidya) are also this same power.

The nature of the Lord is His power. Just as fire has two powers - the illuminating power and the burning power - the illuminating power dispels darkness and fear, and the burning power burns and cooks. These two powers are the sambhuti (creative) power, the sambhuti (manifesting) power, and the ahladi (delighting) power. 

1. The sambhuti (creative) power is the power of existence, the sambhuti (manifesting) power is the power of manifestation, and the ahladi (delighting) power is the power of delight.

2. When the Lord incarnates, He comes with His pure nature and powers. During the incarnation, He uses these powers to perform tasks. Radha is the Lord's power, and His many female companions are also His powers, which are all forms of devotion and are devoted to devotion. A person without devotion cannot know them. They can be known only through the Lord's and Radha's mercy.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 6]

The verse 6 reads:

O, stay close to your heart! 
* The elixir of the devotee *

When the king of the Videhas, Janaka, saw the beauty of Lord Rama, he too became a Videha, i.e., devoid of sense and reason—
Murti Madhura Manohar Dheki Bhayo Bidehu Bidehu Viseshi (Mānasa 1.2.15.4)
And it is said:
Sahaj Biragarup Manu Mora (Mānasa 1.2.16.2)
Even the forest-dwelling Kol and Bhil tribes become enchanted when they see the form of the Lord—

Karahu Joharu Bhenat Dhari Aage (Mānasa 2.13.3)
They look at the Lord with great love and affection, their bodies tremble, and their eyes overflow with tears, as if they are drawing a picture.

As for the devotees, it is not surprising that they are drawn to the Lord's divine beauty. But even those who harbor enmity towards the Lord, like Ravana and Khar-Dushan, are amazed by the Lord's beauty and say—

Nag Asur Sur Nar Munijete Dekhe Jite Hate Hum Kete (Mānasa 3.19.2)
We have seen, fought, and killed many beings, but we have never seen such beauty. (Mānasa 3.19.2)

In essence, the divine beauty of the Lord attracts the minds of all, including the devotees, the detached, the wise, the foolish, the enemies, the demons, and the rakshasas.

The phrase "Sambhavamy Atma Maya" means that those who are averse to the Lord remain unaware of His presence, even when He is standing right in front of them, hidden behind the veil of His Yogamaya. The ordinary human being, like the chandrama (moon), appears to be exhausted, but the Lord, like the lotus flower, remains unaffected.

The two veils that remain before the foolish person are their own ignorance and the Lord's Yogamaya. Even when the Lord's presence is right in front of them, they fail to recognize Him, just like the example of Dushasana, who was unable to see the Lord's presence despite His divine form being revealed in the assembly.

The Lord's presence is not revealed to the foolish person, even when they are in His presence, because their ignorance remains unremoved. However, if the individual removes their ignorance, they will attain knowledge of their true nature or the ultimate reality. But even then, they will not see the Lord's presence.

The Lord's presence is revealed only when He removes the veil of His Yogamaya. The individual can remove their ignorance, but they cannot remove the veil of Yogamaya. However, if the individual surrenders to the Lord, He can remove their ignorance and reveal His presence.

The Lord performs all His leelas (pastimes) with the aid of His Yogamaya. Therefore, only those who have the capacity to see the Lord's leelas can experience them. If the Lord were to abandon His Yogamaya, no one would be able to see or experience His leelas.

Special Point about Avatars

The term "Avatar" means to descend or come down. The all-pervading, blissful, and eternal Lord, who is the embodiment of truth, descends to a particular place, especially to fulfill the desires of His exclusive devotees. In doing so, He becomes small and takes on a human form.

The reason for this is that the Lord's power or influence becomes greater when He is in a higher form, but it becomes lesser when He is in a lower form. The Lord performs His leelas with the aid of His Yogamaya, as stated in the verse:

The Lord, like the lotus flower, remains unaffected, even when He is surrounded by the darkness of night. He is the embodiment of the divine, and His mind is engaged in the play of Yogamaya.

The Lord says:

My darshan (vision) is the most rare and precious fruit, and it is only when the individual sees the Lord that they attain knowledge of their true nature. (Mānasa 3.36.5)

The Lord, though infinite and boundless, can manifest Himself in a limited form. Even the great sages and saints do not know the secrets of His divine play. This is His unique characteristic. Just as the Lord sustains infinite universes, yet He is known as Giridhari (the remover of mountains) because He lifted a single mountain, so too, when He manifests Himself in a limited form, it is no great feat, but rather a small one. However, in this small form, He reveals His great power. Similarly, His incarnation is His unique characteristic.

The ignorant and the wise alike are amazed by His divine play. Only those whom the Lord Himself chooses to reveal the secrets of His play can understand it. As it is said, "Soi janai jehi dehu janai" (Mānās 2.127.2). Even while grazing cattle or playing with the cowherd boys, the Lord performs great and powerful deeds. He can destroy even the most powerful demons with a mere gesture. Even in the form of a small child, He retains His full power.

Just as a great scholar teaches a child the alphabet by holding its hand and making it write the letters "ka," "kha," "ga," and so on, and also making it speak the sounds, yet the scholar himself does not learn the alphabet, so too, the Lord, the master of infinite universes, manifests Himself in our midst and teaches us in our own form, making it easy for us to learn. His divine play is full of wonders and is beyond human comprehension. Even the great sage Brahma, the greatest of the wise, was bewildered by the Lord's play.

The Lord's play is not limited to His divine form; He can also manifest Himself in a simple and childlike form. While playing with the cowherd boys, He can be defeated by one of them, and He can become a horse, while the boy becomes the rider. This is His unique characteristic. The wise and knowledgeable ones, who understand the Lord's power, remain immersed in His divine form. However, for the devotees, His simple and childlike form is full of wonder and sweetness. The devotees are not bound by the limitations of their own understanding; they can see the Lord's play in all its glory.

When the decline of righteousness and the rise of unrighteousness occur, the Lord incarnates. The Lord's incarnation is for the establishment of righteousness and the destruction of unrighteousness.

The phrase "yada yada hi dharmasya" implies that whenever the need arises, the Lord incarnates. In one yuga, the Lord can incarnate as many times as the need and opportunity arise. For example, during the churning of the ocean, the Lord took the form of Ajita and churned the ocean, took the form of Kaccha and held Mount Mandara, and took the form of Sahasrabahu and pressed Mount Mandara from above. Then, the Lord took the form of Mohini to distribute nectar to the gods. In this way, the Lord took multiple forms at the same time.

The main reason for the rise of unrighteousness and the decline of righteousness is the attraction to ephemeral things. Just as the body is formed from the mother and father, similarly, the creation is formed from nature and the Supreme Being. In this creation, nature and its activities are constantly changing, never remaining the same for even a moment, while the Supreme Being and His part, the individual soul, remain eternal and unchanged. When the individual soul, which is ephemeral and subject to birth and death, begins to desire pleasure from ephemeral things and considers their attainment as pleasure, its downfall begins. As people become more attached to worldly pleasures and accumulation, unrighteousness increases in society, and as unrighteousness increases, so do sinful behavior, conflict, and other vices.

When the decline of righteousness and the rise of unrighteousness occur, the Lord incarnates. Therefore, the main purpose of the Lord's incarnation is to establish righteousness and destroy unrighteousness.

When people's behavior becomes unrighteous, it is a natural consequence of their actions. The Lord is the supreme well-wisher of all living beings. Therefore, to prevent them from falling, He Himself incarnates.

The decline of righteousness and the rise of unrighteousness occur when people become motivated by selfish desires and abandon their duties to engage in prohibited behavior. All unrighteousness, sin, and injustice arise from these desires (Gita, 3.31). Therefore, the Lord incarnates to destroy these desires and spread the quality of detachment.

There may be a question as to why the Lord does not incarnate in the present time when righteousness is declining and unrighteousness is increasing. The answer is that the time has not yet come, considering the era. In the Treta Yuga, the demons killed the sages and rishis and piled their bones. This has passed even beyond the Treta Yuga, but righteous people still exist, and no one is harming them. There is another point. When righteousness declines and unrighteousness increases, saints come to the earth as per the Lord's command or special seekers of truth manifest on this earth and establish righteousness. Sometimes, great souls who have attained the Supreme Being come to the world to save it. The seekers of truth and saints who reside in a particular country prevent unrighteousness from increasing and establish righteousness in that country.

Looking at the four yugas - Satya Yuga, Treta Yuga, Dwapara Yuga, and Kali Yuga - we see that in each yuga, righteousness declines. In the Satya Yuga, all four stages of righteousness remain, in the Treta Yuga, three stages remain, in the Dwapara Yuga, two stages remain, and in the Kali Yuga, only one stage remains. When the decline of righteousness goes beyond the limits of the yuga, the Lord incarnates to re-establish righteousness.

When people do not follow the saints and sages, but instead seek to destroy them, and when there are very few who preach righteousness and the expected righteousness for that yuga is also very little, then the Lord Himself incarnates.

उसे महत्त्व देनेसे कामनाएँ पैदा होती हैं। ज्यों-ज्यों
कामनाएँ नष्ट होती हैं, त्यों-त्यों साधुता आती है और
ज्यों-ज्यों कामनाएँ बढ़ती हैं, त्यों-त्यों साधुता लुप्त होती
है। कारण कि असाधुताका मूल हेतु कामना ही है । साधुतासे
अपना उद्धार और लोगोंका स्वतः उपकार होता है ।
साधु पुरुषके भावों और क्रियाओंमें पशु, पक्षी, वृक्ष,
पर्वत, मनुष्य, देवता, पितर, ऋषि, मुनि आदि सबका हित
भरा रहता है—
हेतु रहित जग जुग उपकारी । तुम्ह तुम्हार सेवक असुरारी ।
(मानस ७। ४७। ३)
यदि लोग उसके मनके भावोंको जान जायँ तो वे
उसके चरणोंके दास बन जायँ । इसके विपरीत यदि लोग
दुष्ट पुरुषके मनके भावोंको जान जायँ तो दिनमें कई बार
लोगोंसे उसकी पिटाई हो ।
कि साधु पुरुषोंकी रक्षाका तात्पर्य उनके भावोंकी रक्षा है;
शरीर, धन-सम्पत्ति, मान - बड़ाई आदिकी रक्षा नहीं; कारण
कि वे इन सांसारिक पदार्थोंको महत्त्व नहीं देते। भगवान्
भी इन वस्तुओंको महत्त्व नहीं देते; क्योंकि सांसारिक
पदार्थोंको महत्त्व देनेसे ही असाधुता पैदा होती है।
|
भक्तोंमें सांसारिक पदार्थोंका महत्त्व, उददेश्य होता ही
नहीं; तभी तो वे भक्त हैं। भक्तलोग प्रतिकूलता- (दुःखदायी
परिस्थिति - ) में विशेष प्रसन्न होते हैं; क्योंकि प्रतिकूलतासे
जितना आध्यात्मिक लाभ होता है, उतना किसी दूसरे
साधनसे नहीं होता। वास्तवमें भक्ति भी प्रतिकूलतामें ही
बढ़ती है । सांसारिक राग, आसक्तिसे ही पतन होता है और
प्रतिकूलतासे वह राग टूटता है। इसलिये भगवान्का भक्तोंके
लिये प्रतिकूलता भेजना भी वास्तवमें भक्तोंकी रक्षा करना
है।
'विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् ' – दुष्ट मनुष्य अधर्मका
प्रचार और धर्मका नाश करते हैं, इसलिये उनका विनाश
करनेके लिये भगवान् अवतार लेते हैं ।
जो मनुष्य कामनाके अत्यधिक बढ़नेके कारण झूठ,
कपट, छल, बेईमानी आदि दुर्गुण - दुराचारोंमें लगे हुए हैं,
जो निरपराध सद्गुण, सदाचारी, साधुओंपर अत्याचार
किया करते हैं, जो दूसरोंका अहित करनेमें ही लगे रहते
हैं, जो प्रवृत्ति और निवृत्तिको नहीं जानते, भगवान् और
वेद-शास्त्रोंका विरोध करना ही जिनका स्वभाव हो गया
है, ऐसे आसुरी सम्पत्तिमें अधिक रचे- पचे रहकर वैसा
ही बुरा आचरण करनेवाले मनुष्योंके लिये यहाँ 'दुष्कृताम्'
यहाँ शंका हो सकती है कि यदि भगवान् साधु पद आया है। भगवान् अवतार लेकर ऐसे ही दुष्ट

The Lord now explains the purpose of His incarnation. He says, "To protect the righteous, to annihilate the wicked, and to re-establish the institution of dharma, I appear in every age."

paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām|
dharmasaṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge || 8 ||

Translation of the shloka:

To protect the righteous (sādhu) and to annihilate the wicked (dūṣkṛta), and to re-establish the institution of dharma, I appear in every age.

Explanation: The term "sādhu" refers to a person who has dedicated his life to the pursuit of spiritual growth and has renounced worldly attachments. The term "dūṣkṛta" refers to a person who is engaged in wicked and sinful activities. The Lord appears in every age to protect the righteous and to annihilate the wicked, and to re-establish the institution of dharma.

The Lord's incarnation is not for the protection of the body, wealth, or prestige of the righteous, but for the protection of their spiritual well-being. The righteous person's spiritual well-being is not dependent on external factors, but on their internal state of mind. The Lord's protection of the righteous is not a physical protection, but a spiritual protection, which means that He protects their spiritual well-being and guides them on the path of spiritual growth.

The Lord's incarnation is also not for the protection of the wicked, but for their spiritual transformation. The wicked person's spiritual transformation is not possible without the Lord's intervention, and the Lord's incarnation is a manifestation of His will to transform the wicked and to guide them on the path of spiritual growth.

The Lord's incarnation is also for the re-establishment of the institution of dharma. Dharma refers to the universal law of righteousness, which is the foundation of all spiritual growth. The institution of dharma is not just a set of rules and regulations, but a way of life that is based on the principles of righteousness, compassion, and selflessness. The Lord's incarnation is a manifestation of His will to re-establish the institution of dharma and to guide humanity on the path of spiritual growth.

The question arises, "If there is no enmity towards anyone (as stated in the Gita, 9.29: 'samoham sarvabhuteshu na me dveshyah'), then why do the gods destroy the wicked?"

This question is raised by the devotees. The gods and saints, who are like a mother to their devotees, explain the truth. However, if a person does not give up their wickedness, then the gods have to take an incarnation to destroy them. If they give up their wickedness, then there is no need to destroy them.

The solution to this question is that since the gods are the supreme well-wishers of all living beings, they have no enmity towards anyone. However, those who commit crimes against their devotees are considered enemies of the gods.

Listen, O king, Raghunath, the lord of the gods, does not tolerate the crimes committed against his devotees. (From the Ramayana, 2.218, 2-3)
The name of the god is 'bhaktabhaktiman' (Shrimad Bhagavatam, 10.86.59). Therefore, the gods themselves destroy those who cause suffering to their devotees. The devotees destroy the wicked, and the gods destroy the wicked who commit crimes against them.

The gods have as much mercy on the wicked as they do on the righteous in saving them from destruction. By destroying the wicked, the gods purify and sanctify them.

The saints and mahatmas establish the path of dharma, but they do not engage in the destruction of the wicked. The destruction of the wicked is the responsibility of the gods, just as a compounder applies ointment to a wound, but a civil surgeon performs a major operation himself.

A mother and father both want the best for their child. If the child does not study and behaves badly, the mother and father both try to correct him. If the child does not listen, the father punishes him. However, if the child is afraid, the mother stops the father from punishing him. Although the mother is a devoted wife, she does not abandon her duty to follow her husband. However, this does not mean that she will also punish the child if the father does.

The father does not want to punish the child, but rather to remove his bad habits and behavior. Similarly, the gods are like a father to all living beings and do not want to destroy anyone. They are the opponents of ignorance, Maya, and other negative forces, but they are not opposed to the creation itself.

The gods do not have any enmity towards any living being, but rather they give them strength and nourishment. They are the creators of the universe and give everyone an equal place to live. The earth, food, water, air, and sun all give everyone an equal share, without any partiality.

If the earth, food, water, air, and sun were to stop giving everyone an equal share, then the wicked would not be able to survive. In the same way, the gods, who are the creators of the universe, have infinite mercy and equality. They are the embodiment of compassion and kindness.

The gods do not have any enmity towards the wicked, but rather they are opposed to their evil deeds. The wicked deeds of the wicked harm not only the world but also themselves. The gods are the well-wishers of all living beings and destroy the wicked to benefit them.

Those who are destroyed by the gods are sent to their own abode, which is a manifestation of the gods' infinite mercy. (From the Pandav Gita)
'O king, those who are killed by the lord Janardan, the king of the three worlds, are all sent to the abode of Vishnu. Even the anger of the gods is like a blessing.'

The question may arise that if we consider sinful actions as 'nitya' (eternal) and continue to perform them, then will God have to come to kill us? If this is the case, then our well-being would be ensured by being killed by God; therefore, why should those who need to practice self-control, such as those who follow the path of righteous conduct, exert themselves to follow it? The answer to this is that God indeed comes to kill only those who are sinful and cannot be killed by anyone else except God. The second point is that the more we engage in virtuous actions, the more we will accumulate merit, but if we continue to engage in sinful actions, even if we die in the middle or are killed by someone else, it will be difficult. How can we attain liberation by being killed by God's hands? Therefore, we should not engage in sinful actions.

The establishment of dharma (righteous conduct) is the teaching, command, and propagation of the principle of nishkama (selfless) behavior. For, it is only through the propagation of nishkama behavior that the establishment of dharma is ensured. The refuge of dharma is God (Gita, 14th chapter, 27th shloka). Therefore, God incarnates to establish eternal dharma. The establishment of dharma means establishing it in its proper form. The meaning is that dharma is never destroyed, but only its glory is diminished. When the glory of dharma is diminished, God establishes it again in its proper form (Gita, 4th chapter, 1st to 3rd shlokas).

"Sambhavami yuge yuge" - God incarnates in every age as and when necessary. In one age, God incarnates as many times as is necessary. God's incarnations as karka purusha (the creator) and as great saints are also considered as avatars. However, the avatar of God and karka purusha is 'naimittik' (conditional), but the avatar of great saints is 'nitya' (eternal).

[Chapter 4]

Here, the question arises that if God is all-powerful, then why does He need to incarnate to protect saints, destroy the wicked, and establish dharma? The answer is that God cannot perform these tasks without incarnating. Although God can perform these tasks without incarnating and does so, yet He incarnates to benefit the jivas (living beings) with special mercy. The jivas benefit from seeing, touching, and conversing with God during the time of incarnation, as well as from hearing about and contemplating God's divine pastimes and following His teachings. In this way, the jivas are easily liberated. Therefore, God incarnates in this way to benefit the jivas.

There are many devotees of God who want to play with God, live with God, and fulfill their desires. God incarnates to fulfill their desires and plays with them, becoming like them. God incarnates in the age and in the form that is necessary to fulfill the task at hand. Therefore, there is a difference in God's incarnations, but God Himself is always complete and unchanged.

God has no duties to perform and nothing to gain (Gita, 3rd chapter, 22nd shloka). Yet, God incarnates at different times to benefit the world. Therefore, humans should also perform their duties for the benefit of others.

In the 4th shloka of the 10th chapter of the Bhagavatam, it is said: "Anugrahaya bhutanam manusham deham aasthitah...". God incarnates as a human being to benefit the jivas and performs such pastimes that, when heard, the jivas become devoted to God.

[Verse 9]

(1) The divine nature of the Lord is manifest in all beings, both human and divine, due to His yogamaya. They have all been born from the fourth chapter onwards. However, they know this, but the Lord knows it (4.5).

(2) Human beings are born due to their attachment to nature, to enjoy the fruits of their good and bad deeds, and to attain the ultimate goal of realizing the Supreme Lord after enjoying the fruits of their actions. However, the Lord is born with His own nature, unattached and free from the influence of nature.

(3) In their actions, human beings generally work to fulfill their desires, which is not the ultimate goal of human life. However, the Lord works solely for the welfare of living beings (4.7-8).

Context: In the fourth chapter, the Lord had begun to describe His divine nature in response to Arjuna's question. Now, with the intention of explaining the concept of nishkam-karma (action without attachment), He also explains the glory of knowing His divine nature and the divine nature of His actions.

Arjuna, tell me,
My birth and actions are divine, indeed.
One who knows this truth, O Arjuna,
Abandoning the body, does not take birth again and attains Me. 9

Translation of Sanskrit Shlokas:

janma karma cha me divyam evam yo vetti
tattvatah tyaktva deham punarjanma naiti mameeti so 'rjuna

= O Arjuna!
My birth and actions are divine, indeed.
Thus, one who knows this truth, O Arjuna,
Abandoning the body, does not take birth again and attains Me.

vyakhya—'janma karma cha me divyam' - The Lord is birthless, deathless, and free from the cycle of birth and death. His divine nature is eternal, pure, and beyond human comprehension. His divine actions are also beyond human understanding. The Lord's birth and actions are not bound by the laws of nature, and He is not affected by the consequences of His actions.

Commentary:
The Lord's birth and actions are not like those of ordinary human beings. His divine nature is beyond human comprehension, and His actions are not bound by the laws of nature. The Lord's birth and actions are not driven by desires or attachments, but are solely for the welfare of living beings. His divine nature is beyond human understanding, and His actions are not subject to the consequences of good or bad deeds.

Uddhava says:

When the Lord incarnates as Rama and Krishna, He is not born from the womb of Devaki or Kausalya. First, He appears in His divine form, and then He takes on a human form to play with the children. (Mansaghar, 4.26)

When the Lord incarnates, He is not bound by the laws of nature. He is the Supreme Being, beyond human comprehension, and He takes on a human form by His own will. (Mansaghar, 4.26)

The Lord says:

You are the supreme being, beyond human comprehension, and you are the creator of the universe. You have incarnated in this world by your own will, and you have taken on a human form. (Mansaghar, 11.11.28)

The Lord's incarnation is not like that of ordinary human beings. His divine nature is beyond human comprehension, and His actions are not bound by the laws of nature. The Lord's incarnation is solely for the welfare of living beings, and He takes on a human form by His own will.

Tulsidas says - 
When Lord Krishna was born, He appeared in a divine form, with four arms, and was very kind and compassionate. His eyes were very attractive, and His body was dark and handsome. He wore a garland of flowers around His neck and had a beautiful face. 
His mother, Devaki, said, 'My child, please hide Your divine form, which is adorned with a conch, disc, mace, and lotus.' 
Then, in front of His parents, Lord Krishna assumed the form of an ordinary child. 
When Lord Rama was about to leave for His divine abode, He disappeared from sight, and His body did not remain on earth. Instead, He entered the divine realm with His body. 
Lord Krishna also did the same, and His story is mentioned in the Bhagavad Gita. 
Valmiki says to Lord Rama, 'Your body is full of bliss and knowledge, and You are the Lord of the universe. You have taken a human form to fulfill the duties of the gods and to show the world Your divine play.' 
Once, the sage Sanaka and his brothers were on their way to Vaikuntha, the divine abode of Lord Vishnu. The gatekeepers stopped them, and Sanaka cursed them. When Lord Vishnu heard about this, He came to the spot and was pleased with Sanaka's devotion. Sanaka and his brothers were overjoyed to see the Lord and bowed down at His feet. 
The fragrance of the Lord's feet, mixed with the fragrance of the tulsi leaves, entered the nostrils of Sanaka and his brothers and disturbed their minds, even though they were always absorbed in the Lord's divine form. 
The Lord's divine body is full of wonder, and His garments, ornaments, and weapons are all divine and full of knowledge. 
Listening to, reading, and remembering the Lord's divine plays purify the heart and remove ignorance. Even Lord Shiva, Brahma, and other great sages like Sanaka and Narada are absorbed in the Lord's divine plays. 
Living in the places where the Lord's divine plays took place, with faith and devotion, and having His darshan, also brings liberation to humans. The Lord takes incarnations only to liberate the souls. 
With His divine and beautiful form, which is the object of meditation and contemplation, the Lord entered His divine abode, without being cremated by the fire of yoga. 
The great sages and the Lord's divine plays are full of wonder, and reading and listening to them brings the highest liberation to humans.

english:
297

As one listens and contemplates on the words of the Lord, it becomes natural to have a sense of benevolence towards all living beings and detachment from actions. This is the realization of the ultimate goal. In reality, it is the knowledge of the Lord's birth and the nature of actions that is to be known.

Here, the Lord begins to speak about actions on His own initiative, without Arjuna's inquiry, after Arjuna had asked only about the Lord's birth in the fourth shloka. It appears that the Lord's intention is that just as His actions are divine, so should be the actions of Arjuna. For, a human being's birth is not divine, but his actions can be divine because it is for his sake that he was born. Divinity in actions arises from yoga. Those actions that bind are those in which divinity does not arise. When divinity arises in actions, they become liberating. When actions are divine (free from attachment and desire), the doer is not bound by them; nor is he bound by his past actions - he becomes free; and his actions also benefit others.

On careful consideration, it becomes clear that the association with perishable objects is the cause of impurity in actions, and they become binding. When one associates with perishable objects, the mind, actions, and objects - all three become impure, and when one disassociates from them, they become pure by themselves. Therefore, the association with perishable objects is the root cause of bondage.

'And he who knows the truth' - although the Lord is unborn and imperishable, and the Lord of all living beings, He takes incarnation in the form of a human being, and other beings, for the sake of the welfare of living beings. To know this truth is to know the divinity of the Lord's birth. The Lord is the doer of all actions, yet He is not attached to the fruits of actions - this is the truth. He does not desire any fruit of actions - this is the truth. (Gita - 4th chapter, 13th shloka and 14th shloka). Yet, He takes incarnation on this earth out of compassion, and performs wondrous deeds. By listening to, reading, and contemplating on these deeds, one becomes associated with the Lord. When one becomes associated with the Lord, one's association with the world is broken. When one's association with the world is broken, one is not reborn - one becomes free from the cycle of birth and death.

In reality, actions do not bind. The binding power in actions is the creation of the individual's own desires. When one performs actions with attachment, one becomes bound by them. As one's desires increase, one becomes more and more attached to worldly things, and one's actions become more and more impure, leading to rebirth in lower states and hells. But when one performs actions without attachment, for the sake of others, one's actions become pure, and one becomes free from the cycle of birth and death.

'He who says "I am of the Lord" - because of associating with perishable objects, even the Lord appears to be unattainable. When one performs all actions without attachment, for the sake of others, the flow of actions is only towards the world, and one experiences the presence of the Lord. The Lord's incarnation is due to His great compassion - to know this truth is to know the divinity of the Lord's birth. When one knows this truth, one's devotion to the Lord arises. When one knows the divinity of the Lord's actions, one's own actions also become divine, and one becomes a means of welfare to all beings, just as the Lord's actions are.

* "One who knows this truth is not attached to worldly things. He should renounce worldly attachments and not have any attachment to worldly things." (Mansa 5.34.2)
