Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 10]
The world is sustained by the Lord in the form of Jiva - 'Jivabhutam Mahabaho Yayedam Dharyate Jagat' (Gita 7.5). To remove this sustenance, the seeker should firmly believe that what is visible is the form of the Lord and what is happening is the play of the Lord. By accepting this, the world will not remain in its worldly form, and one will experience that there is nothing except the Lord. In other words, the world will disappear, and only the Lord will remain. The reason is that by considering every object and person as the form of the Lord and every action as the play of the Lord, there will be no attachment or aversion. When attachment disappears, the actions that previously seemed worldly will appear as the divine play of the Lord, and where there was previously attachment, there will be love for the Lord. The Lord performs actions according to the form He assumes. When He assumes the form of an idol, He performs the action of remaining still like an idol. If He does not remain still, how can He be an idol? The Lord has assumed various forms like Rama, Krishna, and others, and has also assumed forms like Matsya and Kurma. He performs actions according to the form He assumes. For example, in the Varaha avatar, He performed the action of a boar, and in the Vamana avatar, He performed the action of a brahmin. From this, the seeker should understand that whatever is happening now is also the play of the Lord. The relationship is that the Lord protects and establishes dharma in the three worlds by assuming various forms and behaviors. When the Lord is in the form of a deva, He behaves like a deva; when He is in the form of a gandharva, He behaves like a gandharva; and when He is in the form of a naga, He behaves like a naga. The verse says: 'Vitaragabhayakrodhah, manmaya, mamupashritah, bahavo jnanatapasaputa, madbhavamagatah' (10). This means that those who are free from attachment, fear, and anger, and are devoted to the Lord, have attained the Lord's state through the fire of knowledge. The commentary explains that attachment, fear, and anger are obstacles to realizing the Lord. Attachment leads to anger, and anger leads to greed. The Lord's devotees, who are free from these obstacles, have attained the Lord's state.

The Bhagavad Gita teaches us that if we have attachment to worldly things, then fear arises. Such attachments are fleeting and ephemeral, as stated in the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra (70): "tanmāyāḥ" (those who are attached to worldly things). These attachments are born from our love for worldly objects, and they lead to the birth of fear, anger, greed, attachment, desire, and other vices. When these attachments are removed, these vices also disappear. 

The removal of attachments occurs when we serve others and the world without considering them as our own or for our own benefit. This is because our relationship with worldly objects and actions is not genuine. 

Even when there is no personal benefit, the Lord incarnates only for our well-being. This is because the Lord is the ultimate well-wisher of all living beings, and His actions are solely for their benefit. As a result, when we have faith in the Lord's benevolence, we are drawn to Him. When we are drawn to the Lord, our attachment to the world (raga) automatically disappears. 

Just as children are attracted to stones and pebbles in their childhood and fight over them, but as they grow up, their attraction to these things disappears and they become attracted to money. Similarly, when a person's attachment to the world disappears and he becomes attached to the Lord, the world loses its charm for him. His fear and anger also disappear, as these are born from attachment to the world. 

The Bhagavad Gita states that when we are attached to the Lord, we become "manmayāḥ" (those who are absorbed in the Lord). When we are attached to worldly objects, we become "kāmātmānāḥ" (those who are absorbed in worldly desires). 

The Bhagavad Gita also states that when we are attached to the Lord, our thoughts, actions, and everything else are centered on Him. This is because of the abundance of love in our hearts. As a result, we become one with the Lord, and it seems as if we have no separate existence. 

The Bhagavad Gita contrasts this with the attachment to worldly objects, which is a separation from the world. The Bhagavad Gita states that a person cannot exist without taking shelter in someone or something. If a person takes shelter in someone other than the Lord, that shelter is temporary and will eventually disappear. 

Taking shelter in worldly objects, such as wealth, is a fleeting and destructive thing. Even taking shelter in good deeds, such as spiritual practices, will not lead to the Lord's realization if one does not take shelter in the Lord Himself. As long as a person does not take shelter in the Lord, his bondage to the world will not be broken, and he will continue to suffer. 

The Bhagavad Gita states that a person's attachment to worldly objects and his taking shelter in them are different. For example, a person's attachment to a woman or a child is different from his taking shelter in his elders. However, when a person is attached to the Lord, his attachment is to the Lord alone, and his shelter is also in the Lord alone. This is because the Lord is the most dear and the greatest of all. 

The Bhagavad Gita states that even if a person is purified through the practice of knowledge (jnāna-yoga), he is still not purified if he does not know the Lord's divine nature. This is because the Lord is the most pure and the most sacred. The Lord's own part is within the living being, and therefore, the living being is inherently pure and sacred. However, when the living being attaches himself to worldly objects and considers them as his own, he becomes impure. 

The Bhagavad Gita quotes from the Shrimad Bhagavatam (10.30.3): "gatismitaprakshanabhashanadishu priyah priyasya pratirudhamurtayah" (those who are dear to the Lord are also dear to the Lord's dear ones). The Bhagavad Gita states that the Lord's dear ones, such as the gopis, become identical with the Lord and follow His ways. They forget their own existence and become one with the Lord, saying "I am the Lord" and imitating the Lord's behavior.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The subject matter here is the shelter or refuge of devotees. The behavior of a person towards others is imitated by others. As stated in the 21st shloka of the 3rd chapter of the Gita, "Just as a person behaves, others also behave in the same way." Since God is the supreme being, everyone follows His path. This very same idea is also mentioned in the latter part of the 23rd shloka of the 3rd chapter.

Therefore, there is no scope for any doubt in this matter. However, let us ponder over this a bit. The meaning of accepting God is to benefit or to do good to someone. The way someone accepts God, God also behaves in the same way and ultimately benefits that person.

God is the supreme well-wisher of all living beings (Gita, 5th chapter, 29th shloka). Therefore, whoever has the well-being of someone, God also takes care of that person's well-being. Even those who harbor enmity and hatred towards God, God still benefits them if it leads to their well-being.

As mentioned in the Ramayana, when Lord Rama sent Angad to Ravana's assembly, He said, "Speak in such a way that it benefits both us and Ravana" (Mansa, 6.17.4). This is an example of how God benefits those who harbor enmity and hatred towards Him.

Not only is God the well-wisher of all living beings, but even His devotees are the well-wishers of all living beings (Shrimad Bhagavatam, 3.25.21). If the devotees do not harm anyone, even God cannot harm anyone. Any relationship established with God is beneficial, as God is all-compassionate, all-loving, and all-knowing.

Just as bathing in the Ganges during the month of Vaisakha is equally beneficial as bathing during the month of Magh, but the joy experienced during Vaisakha is greater than during Magh, similarly, those who establish a relationship with God through devotion and love experience greater joy than those who do so through hatred and enmity.

As stated in the Gita, "Just as all men follow the path of a great soul, O Partha, so do all men follow the path that thou followest" (Gita, 3rd chapter, 21st shloka). The great souls who have a certain kind of relationship with God, God also has the same kind of relationship with them. Maharaja Dasharatha accepted Lord Rama as his son, and God became his true son and was obedient to him.

This kind of behavior is a manifestation of God's secret, that if someone has a certain kind of affection for someone, they should establish a similar relationship with God. For example, if someone has affection for their mother, they should consider God as their mother, if they have affection for their father, they should consider God as their father, and so on.

God teaches us through His behavior that just as He becomes whatever someone considers Him to be, we should also become whatever someone considers us to be. For example, we should become a good son for our parents, a good husband for our wife, a good brother for our sister, and so on. But we should not expect anything in return.

As stated in the Shrimad Bhagavatam, "Many people have attained God through their devotion, just as they have attained Him through their attachment, hatred, fear, and love" (Shrimad Bhagavatam, 7.1.29).

Lord Rama says, "I can enter the fire even if it is blazing, I can drink poison even if it is deadly, and I can jump into the ocean even if it is turbulent" (Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda, 18.28-29). This shows that God is all-powerful and can do anything.

The Sanskrit shloka and its translation are:

1. kāmād dveṣād bhayāt snehād yathā bhaktyeśvare manaḥ | āveśya tadaghaṃ hitvā bahavastadgatiṃ gatāḥ ||
Translation: "Just as many people have attained God through their devotion, just as they have attained Him through their attachment, hatred, fear, and love."

2. ahaṃ hi vacanād rājñaḥ pateyamapi pāvake | bhakṣayeyaṃ viṣaṃ tīkṣṇaṃ pateyamapi cārṇave ||
Translation: "Lord Rama says, 'I can enter the fire even if it is blazing, I can drink poison even if it is deadly, and I can jump into the ocean even if it is turbulent.'"

है, तब उसे भगवान् से अपने नित्य-सम्बन्धका अनुभव हो
जाता है ।
भगवान्के नित्य-सम्बन्धको पहचानना ही भगवान्के
शरण होना है । शरण होनेपर भक्त निश्चिन्त, निर्भय,
नि:शोक और नि:शंक हो जाता है । फिर उसके द्वारा
जीवमात्रका परमात्माके साथ स्वतः नित्य-सम्बन्ध है भगवान्‌की आज्ञाके विरुद्ध कोई क्रिया कैसे हो सकती है ?
(गीता—पन्द्रहवें अध्यायका सातवाँ श्लोक) । परन्तु जबतक उसकी सम्पूर्ण क्रियाएँ भगवान्‌के आज्ञानुसार ही होती हैं-
जीव इस सम्बन्धको पहचानता नहीं और दूसरा सम्बन्ध | 'मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते ।'
-
|
परिशिष्ट भाव — यद्यपि यह संसार साक्षात् परमात्माका स्वरूप है, तथापि जो इसको जिस रूपसे देखता है,
भगवान् भी उसके लिये उसी रूपसे प्रकट हो जाते हैं । हम अपनेको शरीर मानकर अपने लिये वस्तुओंकी आवश्यकता
मानते हैं और उनकी इच्छा करते हैं तो भगवान् भी उन वस्तुओंके रूपमें हमारे सामने आते हैं, हम असत्में स्थित
होकर देखते हैं तो भगवान् भी असत् - रूपसे ही दीखते हैं । जैसे बालक खिलौना चाहता है तो पिता रुपये खर्च करके
भी उसको खिलौना लाकर देता है, ऐसा ही हम जो चाहते हैं, परम दयालु भगवान् (स्वयं सदा सत्स्वरूप रहते हुए
भी) उसी रूपसे हमारे सामने आते हैं। अगर हम भोगोंको न चाहें तो भगवान्‌को भोगरूपसे क्यों आना पड़े? बनावटी
रूप क्यों धारण करना पड़े ?
भगवान्के स्वभावमें ‘यथा - तथा' होते हुए भी जीवपर उनकी बड़ी भारी कृपा है; क्योंकि कहाँ जीव और कहाँ
भगवान्! अभिमानके सिवाय जीवमें और क्या सामर्थ्य है ? फिर भी जीवका भगवान्‌में आकर्षण होता है तो भगवान्‌का
भी जीवमें आकर्षण होता है । जैसे, विदुरानीजी अपने-आपको भूल गयीं तो भगवान् भी अपने-आपको भूल गये
और केले के छिलके खाने लगे तथा उसीमें आनन्द लेने लगे !
भगवान्के स्वभावमें ‘यथा - तथा' केवल क्रियामें है, भावमें नहीं । भगवान्का आस्तिक-से-आस्तिक व्यक्तिके प्रति
जो स्नेह है, कृपा है, वैसा ही स्नेह, कृपा नास्तिक - से - नास्तिक व्यक्तिके प्रति भी है। इसलिये भगवान्‌के ‘यथा-तथा’
में स्वार्थभाव नहीं है, प्रत्युत यह तो भगवान्‌की महत्ता है कि कहाँ जीव और कहाँ भगवान् ! फिर भी वे जीवको
अपना मित्र बनाते हैं, उसको अपने समान दर्जा देते हैं! भगवान् अपनेमें बड़प्पनका भाव नहीं रखते - यह उनकी
महत्ता है।
सम्बन्ध - पूर्वश्लोकमें भगवान्ने बताया कि जो मुझे जिस भावसे स्वीकार करता है, मैं भी उसे उसी भावसे स्वीकार
करता हूँ अर्थात् मेरी प्राप्ति बहुत सरल और सुगम है। ऐसा होनेपर भी लोग भगवान्‌का आश्रय क्यों नहीं लेते-
इसका कारण आगेके श्लोकमें बताते हैं ।
काङ्क्षन्तः कर्मणां सिद्धिं यजन्त इह देवताः ।
क्षिप्रं हि मानुषे लोके सिद्धिर्भवति कर्मजा ॥ १२ ॥

The Bhagavad Gita

Chapter 4

The moment one develops love for the Lord, one's attachment to others is quickly dispelled, and one's love for the Lord becomes established. This is the way to attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death, and to attain the Lord.

A Special Point

When one acts selflessly, without attachment to one's ego, love is automatically directed towards the Lord. The reason is that one's ego and self-interest are obstacles to loving the Lord. When these two are renounced, one's love becomes all-encompassing. As a result, all artificial relationships are dissolved, and the natural, eternal relationship with the Lord is established.

The bondage of the ego is two-fold: one, the ego does not recognize its eternal relationship with the Lord, and two, it mistakenly considers its artificial relationships as eternal. When the ego recognizes its eternal relationship with the Lord, as stated in the verse "ye yatha māṁ prapadyante" (those who approach me with devotion), it experiences the Lord's eternal relationship.

Recognizing the eternal relationship with the Lord is the same as taking shelter in the Lord. When one takes shelter in the Lord, one becomes fearless, free from anxiety, and free from doubt. Then, how can one go against the Lord's will and perform any action? (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 15, Verse 7)

However, as long as one's actions are not in accordance with the Lord's will, one does not recognize the eternal relationship.

The Lord's eternal relationship is not just a concept, but a direct experience. The Lord's will is not just a command, but a natural law.

The Lord's nature is such that He is pleased with one who approaches Him with devotion, regardless of whether one is a devotee or a non-devotee. The Lord's love is not limited to devotees, but is equally present for non-devotees. The Lord's nature is not one of pride or arrogance, but one of humility and equality.

Chapter 4

(6.3) How can the path of action (karma yoga) not be tainted by action? (Gita 2.47)

The solution to this dilemma is that in the path of karma yoga, a person is bound by actions and the materials used for those actions (Gita 3.9). Actions are performed to sever the bond of attachment, and through yoga and selfless actions, one becomes free (Gita 3.9).

The relationship between the individual and the Supreme is eternal and natural (Gita 4.23). Therefore, the path of yoga or the attainment of the Supreme is not tainted by actions. Even when all actions are performed for others, the individual remains unattached (Gita 3.25).

In reality, actions are not true, but rather a means to sever the bond of attachment, which is the experience of yoga (Gita 6.3). The provision of actions as a means to attain the Supreme is true. When any action is performed for the sake of the Supreme, its result is also the Supreme, and the name of that action also becomes the Supreme (Gita 17.27).

The experience of yoga (eternal relationship with the Supreme) does not arise from performing actions for oneself, but rather from performing actions for others (Gita 3.25). In the path of karma yoga, all actions are performed for others, not for personal gain or attachment to the fruits of action.

In karma yoga, one has to rely on the help of the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, individuals, time, and space, which are all subject to change (Gita 3.9). Relying on these changing factors is a form of bondage. The Supreme, on the other hand, is eternal and unchanging. In the experience of the Supreme, there is no need for the help of the body and other changing factors.

The relationship between the individual and the Supreme is eternal and natural (Gita 4.23). Therefore, the path of yoga or the attainment of the Supreme is not tainted by actions. Even when all actions are performed for others, the individual remains unattached (Gita 3.25).

Now, the Lord explains the divine nature of His actions, which is the reason for His teaching the path of karma yoga.

By My will, I have created the four varnas (castes) with their respective qualities and actions (Gita 4.13).

One who knows Me as the creator of the universe and its various forms, and who knows Me as the unchanging and eternal, should consider Me as the ultimate reality (Gita 4.14).

Translation of Sanskrit shlokas:

mayā cāturvarṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇakarmavibhāgaśaḥ (Gita 4.13)
By My will, I have created the four varnas (castes) with their respective qualities and actions.

tasya kartāramapi māṃ viddhyakartāramavyayam (Gita 4.13)
One who knows Me as the creator of the universe and its various forms, and who knows Me as the unchanging and eternal, should consider Me as the ultimate reality.

na māṃ karmāṇi limpanti na me karmaphale spṛhā (Gita 4.14)
My actions do not taint Me, and I do not have any attachment to the fruits of action.

iti māṃ yo'bhijānāti karmabhirna sa badhyate (Gita 4.14)
One who knows Me in this way, through actions, is not bound by actions.

Explanation:
The four varnas (castes) were created by the Lord with their respective qualities and actions. The Lord is the creator of the universe and its various forms, and He is the unchanging and eternal reality. One who knows the Lord in this way, through actions, is not bound by actions.

[Verse 13-14]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 15]

The Lord's creation and the universe's existence are mere play, as stated in the Brahma Sutra (2.1.33): "Lokavattu leelakaiyavalyam." This means that just as the world appears to exist despite not actually being so, the Lord's creation and other activities are also mere play. In other words, the Lord appears to be the doer despite not being so.

This is further supported by the phrase "Chaturvarnyam maya srishtham gunakarmavibhagashah" from the Gita, which indicates that the Gita considers birth (utpatti) as the basis for caste. A person's caste is determined by the caste of their mother and father, and the word "jati" itself is derived from the root "janipradurbhavah," which signifies birth. The word "karma" is derived from the root "dukri-karane," which signifies action. However, the protection of one's caste is only ensured through the performance of one's duties.

Context - In the previous shloka, the Lord provided an example of himself. Now, in this shloka, the Lord provides an example of mukhya purushas (great souls) who have attained liberation and gives Arjuna the command to perform his duties without attachment.

Evam jnata krtam karma purvaipimukshubhih.
Kuru karmev tasmat tvam purvaipurvataram krtam.

Translation:
Having known that the karma performed by the great souls in the past was also done with the same intention, you should perform your karma, for it has been done by them in the same way.

Explanation - Arjuna was a mukhya purusha (great soul) who desired liberation. However, he did not see his duty as a means to attain liberation, but rather as a ghora karma (heinous deed). Therefore, the Lord provides an example of the great souls who have performed their duties in the past and attained liberation. He tells Arjuna that he should also perform his duties in the same way.

Kuru - The Lord says that Arjuna should perform his karma, just like the great souls in the past.

Shastras say that a mukhya purusha should abandon karma after attaining self-realization, as they are no longer bound by karma. However, the Lord says that the great souls have performed karma with the intention of attaining liberation. Therefore, Arjuna should also perform his duties without attachment.

The essence of karma yoga is to perform karma while being established in yoga and to perform karma while being established in yoga. Karma is for the world, and yoga is for the self. There are two states of karma: to perform karma and not to perform karma. Therefore, one should perform karma until one attains detachment.

1. The Gita has also referred to this as "cheshta" - "Sadrisam cheshtate" (3.33).
2. One should continue to perform karma until one attains detachment or until one develops faith through hearing and contemplating the Lord's teachings - "Tavat karmaani kurvita n nirvidyeta yavata" (11.20.9).

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

311

If a person performs actions with the intention of achieving a specific goal, then that action is considered to be of the rajasic type. On the other hand, remaining detached from such actions is considered to be a state of akarma, or non-action. If a person performs actions with the intention of harming others, then those actions become tamasic. Similarly, if a person performs actions without attachment to the fruits of their labor, without being driven by desires or attachment, then those actions become akarma, or non-binding.

However, the mere knowledge of external actions or inactions does not provide a true understanding of the nature of karma. Even scholars who are well-versed in the scriptures are often misled in this regard. They may consider certain actions to be karma, while others may consider them to be akarma, and yet others may consider them to be vikarma, or counterproductive. This is because the nature of an action is determined by the attitude of the person performing it.

Therefore, the Lord seems to be saying that He will explain the true nature of karma, which binds or liberates, and how one can attain liberation through actions. Arjuna considers inaction in the form of war to be beneficial, and therefore the Lord seems to be saying that mere abandonment of war-like actions will not lead to liberation. On the other hand, one can attain a state of akarma, or non-action, even while engaging in war-like actions.

If a person is driven by desires, attachment, and attachment to the fruits of their labor, then even inaction is considered to be a form of karma, or action. Conversely, if a person is free from these attachments, then even action is considered to be a form of akarma, or non-action.

The Lord has explained that there are two types of abandonment of karma: tamasic and rajasic. Tamasic abandonment is motivated by fear of physical suffering, while rajasic abandonment is motivated by a desire to avoid the consequences of one's actions. However, neither of these types of abandonment leads to a complete separation from karma.

On the other hand, sattvic abandonment of karma, which involves renouncing attachment to the fruits of one's labor and cultivating a sense of detachment, is considered to be a true form of akarma, or non-action. This is because sattvic abandonment leads to a complete separation from karma.

Therefore, the Lord is saying that the true nature of akarma, or non-action, is to perform actions while remaining detached from them, or to remain detached while performing actions. This is the true meaning of the Lord's statement, "I will explain the nature of karma, which binds or liberates."

The Lord is also saying that there are two paths to karma: the path of engagement (pravritti-marga) and the path of disengagement (nivritti-marga). The path of engagement involves performing actions, while the path of disengagement involves abandoning actions. However, both paths are binding, as long as one is driven by desires, attachment, and attachment to the fruits of one's labor.

If one is free from these attachments, then one can remain detached while performing actions, or perform actions while remaining detached. This is the true meaning of the Lord's statement, "The true nature of karma is to perform actions with skill and detachment."

As the Lord has said in the second chapter, verse 50, "Yoga is skill in action." This means that the true nature of karma is to perform actions with detachment and skill, rather than being driven by desires, attachment, and attachment to the fruits of one's labor.

312

The true method of liberation is 'yoga', which means equanimity. However, Arjuna was unable to grasp this truth, and therefore, the Lord is reiterating it.

A special point to note is that 'karma yoga' is not an action, but rather service. The primary aspect of service is renunciation. Service and renunciation are not actions themselves, but rather they are governed by discrimination. We possess various things such as the body, senses, mind, intellect, and so on, which are all interconnected and transient.

We cannot claim ownership of the things that are given to us. The things we possess are meant to be used for the service of the world. The things that are truly ours, such as our true nature or the Supreme Being, cannot be renounced, and the things that are not ours, such as the body or the world, are to be renounced naturally.

Therefore, renunciation is of that which is not truly ours, but which we mistakenly consider as our own. This is a matter of discrimination. The things that are not truly ours are meant to be used for the service of others.

The material for action (body, senses, mind, intellect, etc.) is not for our own use, but rather for the use of others. Its relation is with the world, not with the self. Since the self is eternal, unchanging, and unattached, it has no relation with the material for action. The material for action was not present with us initially, will not be present with us in the future, and is constantly being separated from us.

Therefore, any action performed through this material is for the benefit of others, not for our own benefit. There is a poignant point to note here: no action can be performed without the material for action. Even a great writer cannot write without a pen, ink, and paper.

Since no action can be performed without the material for action, it must be accepted that no action is performed for our own benefit. The reason is that the material for action is related to the world, not to the self. Therefore, actions and the material for action are always for the benefit of others, which is what is meant by service. If the material for action were to be used for our own benefit, it would not be service.

Discrimination is not a result of any action, but rather it is a natural attribute of all living beings from time immemorial. If discrimination were a result of a good action, then who would perform that action without discrimination? It is through discrimination that a person knows the difference between good and bad actions and renounces the bad actions to perform the good ones.

Therefore, discrimination is the cause of good actions, not the result. It is self-evident, and hence, karma yoga is also self-evident, meaning that no effort is required for it. Similarly, jnana yoga is self-evident because the self is already detached from all things, and bhakti yoga is self-evident because the relationship with the Lord is already established.

The Lord says, "One who knows this truth will be liberated from the cycle of birth and death." This is the conclusion of the discussion on the nature of actions, which is stated in the 32nd verse as "Evam jñātvā vimokṣyase."

A poignant point to note is that the essence of karma yoga is that 'karma' is for the world, and 'yoga' is for the self. The two meanings of 'karma' are to do and not to do. Both of these are natural states. In both states, the ego remains. In the state of doing, the ego remains as the doer, and in the state of not doing, the ego remains as the reason.

As long as the ego remains, there is a relationship with the world, and as long as there is a relationship with the world, the ego remains. However, 'yoga' transcends both states. To experience 'yoga', it is necessary to be free from the ego. The way to be free from the ego is to remain established in 'yoga' while performing actions or not performing actions, and to remain established in 'yoga' while experiencing the world.

The Lord says, "I will describe the truth of actions, which, when known, will liberate you from the cycle of birth and death."

[Verse 17]

The essence of the matter is that whether one performs actions or does not perform them, one should remain detached in both states. A person should consider himself to be the same as the Supreme Being in whichever state he finds himself. As mentioned in the verse, "yogasthah kuru karmani" (Gita 2.48), one should perform actions while remaining in a state of yoga.

However, the relationship with the Supreme Reality remains the same in both states. The reason we do not experience this reality is because we consider our connection with the natural world and its phenomena to be the only reality.

Performing actions leads to involvement in the world, while not performing actions leads to involvement with the Supreme Reality. Considering this, even remaining alone in meditation and samadhi is a form of action. Through this, one will have a direct experience of the Supreme Reality. In this way, the desire to attain the Supreme Reality in the future is also a subtle form of action. This is because the foundation for future attainment is laid in the present.

However, the Supreme Reality is beyond both action and inaction. The Lord says that He will reveal the truth about action and inaction, which will lead to the immediate attainment of the Supreme Reality. There is no need to wait for the future; as long as the sense of "I" and "mine" persists, the ego remains unbroken, regardless of whether it is in its gross or subtle form.

The sense of "I" and "mine" is present even in the statement "I do not perform actions." When we do not perform actions for our own sake, but rather for the benefit of others, the sense of "I" and "mine" dissolves into the world.

Now, the Lord encourages us to understand the truth about action.

karmaṇo hyapi boddhavyaṃ boddhavyaṃ ca vikarmaṇaḥ |
akarmaṇaśca boddhavyaṃ gahanā karmaṇo gatiḥ || 17 ||

Translation:

It is necessary to understand the truth about actions, and also the truth about inactions. It is also necessary to understand the truth about inactions, because the path of actions is profound and difficult to comprehend.

Explanation: The phrase "karmaṇo hyapi boddhavyam" means that even in the midst of actions, one should understand the truth about inaction. This is described in the 18th verse, "karmaṇyakarma yaḥ paśyet" (Gita 2.50).

Actions, in their true nature, appear to be one thing, but according to the inner attitude, they are divided into three categories: action, inaction, and counter-action. An action performed with the intention of gaining a specific fruit is considered "action." An action performed without any attachment or desire for fruit, solely for the benefit of others, is considered "inaction." An action performed with the intention of harming others or causing them suffering is considered "counter-action." Prohibited actions are also considered "counter-action."

The phrase "akarmaṇaśca boddhavyam" means that one should understand the truth about inaction, which is described in the 18th verse, "akarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ" (Gita 2.50).

The phrase "boddhavyaṃ ca vikarmaṇaḥ" means that one should understand the truth about counter-actions, which are actions performed with the intention of gaining a specific fruit. When desires increase, counter-actions (papakarm) arise.

In the 38th verse of the second chapter, the Lord explains that even a violent action like war, if performed according to the scriptures and with equanimity (samata), does not lead to sin. The implication is that actions performed with equanimity are considered "inaction" (akarma).

The Bhagavad Gita

Chapter 4
The Desire is the Motive (Gita - 3rd Chapter, 38th - is; because desire is the main motive for sinful actions. Therefore, to abandon desire and to describe sinful actions as inferior, the Lord has used the term 'sinful actions'.

Thus, the essence of sinful actions is desire; and to know the essence of sinful actions is to abandon it and to understand its cause, which is desire. 'The path of actions is very deep' - which action is liberating and which is binding - this is a very difficult decision to make. What is action, what is inaction, and what is sinful action - the true nature of these is not known even by the great scholars and learned men. Arjuna also considers his warlike duty as a very difficult action due to not knowing the truth of these.

Doubt - In this (17th) shloka, the Lord has said that the essence of sinful actions should also be known. However, from the 19th to the 23rd shlokas, the Lord has not said anything about 'sinful actions'! Why has the Lord only mentioned sinful actions in this shloka?

Solution - From the 19th to the 23rd shlokas, the Lord has mainly discussed 'action and inaction', so that all actions become inaction, i.e., no bondage is created. Sinful actions are very close to actions.

The desire from which 'action' is born, when it increases, sinful actions start to occur. But when desire is destroyed, all actions become inaction. The special significance of this discussion is to know 'inaction', and 'inaction' is the destruction of desire. Desire is not destroyed, so there is no need to discuss sinful actions. Therefore, sinful actions have not been mentioned in this discussion. Another reason is that sinful actions are to be completely rejected due to being the cause of sin and hell. Therefore, its discussion has not been expanded.

However, the idea of abandoning the root cause of sinful actions, 'desire', has been mainly discussed in this shloka, just like - 'free from the desire of sensual pleasure' (4.19), 'abandoning the attachment to the fruits of actions' (4.20), 'being detached' (4.21), 'being equal in both success and failure' (4.22), 'one who has renounced all attachments' (4.23), 'one who performs sacrifices without attachment' (4.23).

Thus, this shloka has been said to describe the root cause of sinful actions, 'desire', for the sake of abandoning it.

Additional Note - It is very difficult for us and others to understand the results of actions in the future. A person thinks that a particular action is beneficial for him, but it becomes a harm. He does it for his benefit, but it becomes a loss. He does it for happiness, but it brings unhappiness. The reason is that due to the ego of being the doer and the desire for pleasure, a person cannot understand the path of actions.

Relation - Now, the Lord praises the person who knows the essence of actions.

karmanyaakarmanyaah paashyedakarmanyaakarmani cha karmanyaah |
sa bhoodhimaaanmaanushyaeshu sa yuktaa krttsnakarmakrit || 18 ||

Translation:
The person who sees action in inaction and inaction in action, he is a wise man among men, and he is a yogi, and he is the one who has performed all actions.

In the 16th chapter, where the description of the asuric wealth is given, the word 'kam' (desire) has appeared nine times from the 8th to the 23rd shloka. This proves that 'kam' (desire) is the cause of all asuric wealth (sinful actions).

३१५
व्याख्या–'कर्मण्यकर्म य: पश्येत्' – कर्ममें अकर्म | कारण कि जबतक वह लेनेकी इच्छासे वस्तुएँ देता रहेगा,
तबतक दूकान चलती ही रहेगी, उठेगी नहीं।
देखनेका तात्पर्य है-कर्म करते हुए अथवा न करते हुए
उससे निर्लिप्त रहना अर्थात् अपने लिये कोई भी प्रवृत्ति
या निवृत्ति न करना। अमुक कर्म मैं करता हूँ, इस कर्मका
अमुक फल मुझे मिले - ऐसा भाव रखकर कर्म करनेसे
ही मनुष्य कर्मोंसे बँधता है। प्रत्येक कर्मका आरम्भ और
अन्त होता है, इसलिये उसका फल भी आरम्भ और अन्त
होनेवाला होता है। परन्तु जीव स्वयं नित्य - निरन्तर रहता
है। इस प्रकार यद्यपि जीव स्वयं परिवर्तनशील कर्म
और उसके फलसे सर्वथा सम्बन्धरहित है, फिर भी वह
फलकी इच्छाके कारण उनसे बँध जाता है । इसीलिये
चौदहवें श्लोकमें भगवान् ने कहा है कि मेरेको कर्म नहीं
बाँधते; क्योंकि कर्मफलमें मेरी स्पृहा नहीं है । फलकी
स्पृहा या इच्छा ही बाँधनेवाली है— 'फले सक्तो निबध्यते'
( गीता ५ । १२) ।
फलकी इच्छा न रखनेसे नया राग उत्पन्न नहीं होता
और दूसरोंके हितके लिये कर्म करनेसे पुराना राग नष्ट
हो जाता है। इस प्रकार रागरूप बन्धन न रहनेसे साधक
सर्वथा वीतराग हो जाता है। वीतराग होनेसे सब कर्म
अकर्म हो जाते हैं ।
अपने लिये कुछ भी न करने और न चाहनेसे असंगता
स्वतः प्राप्त हो जाती है। कारण कि करण (शरीर, इन्द्रियाँ,
मन, बुद्धि, प्राण) और उपकरण (कर्म करनेमें उपयोगी
सामग्री) संसारके हैं और संसारकी सेवामें लगानेके लिये
ही मिले हैं, अपने लिये नहीं । इसलिये सम्पूर्ण कर्तव्य-
कर्म (सेवा, भजन, जप, ध्यान, समाधि भी ) केवल
संसारके हितके लिये ही करनेसे कर्मोंका प्रवाह संसारकी
ओर चला जाता है और साधक स्वयं असंग, निर्लिप्त रह
जाता है । यही कर्ममें अकर्म देखना है ।
जबतक प्रकृतिके साथ सम्बन्ध है, तबतक कर्म करना
अथवा न करना - दोनों ही 'कर्म' हैं । इसलिये कर्म करने
अथवा न करने — दोनों ही अवस्थाओंमें कर्मयोगीको
निर्लिप्त रहना चाहिये । कर्म करनेमें निर्लिप्त रहनेका तात्पर्य
है - कर्म करनेसे हमें अच्छा फल मिलेगा, हमें लाभ होगा,
हमारी सिद्धि होगी, लोग हमें अच्छा मानेंगे, इस लोकमें
और परलोकमें भोग मिलेंगे - इस प्रकारकी किसी भी
इच्छाका न होना । ऐसे ही कर्म न करनेमें निर्लिप्त रहनेका
तात्पर्य है— कर्मोंका त्याग करनेसे हमें मान, आदर, भोग,
शरीरका आराम आदि मिलेंगे - इस प्रकारकी किंचिन्मात्र
भी इच्छाका न होना ।
जीवका जन्म कर्मोंके अनुबन्धसे होता है । जैसे, जिस
परिवारमें जन्म लिया है, उस परिवारके लोगोंसे ऋणानुबन्ध
है अर्थात् किसीका ऋण चुकाना है और किसीसे ऋण दुःख समझकर एवं शारीरिक क्लेशके भयसे कर्म न
वसूल करना है। कारण कि अनेक जन्मोंमें अनेक लोगोंसे करना राजस त्याग है और मोह, आलस्य, प्रमादके कारण
लिया है और अनेक लोगोंको दिया है। यह लेन-देनका कर्म न करना तामस त्याग है । ये दोनों ही त्याग सर्वथा
व्यवहार अनेक जन्मोंसे चला आ रहा है । इसको बंद किये त्याज्य हैं। इसके सिवाय कर्म न करना यदि अपनी
बिना जन्म-मरणसे छुटकारा नहीं मिल सकता। इसको बंद विलक्षण स्थितिके लिये है, समाधिका सुख भोगनेके लिये
करनेका उपाय है—आगेसे लेना बंद कर दें अर्थात् अपने है, जीवन्मुक्तिका आनन्द लेनेके लिये है तो इस त्यागसे

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

317
[Verse 19]

The question arises, how can one attain this state? The one who has entered the cave of kajal (kohl) and yet remains unaffected by it is not an ordinary intelligent person. Similarly, the one who performs all actions (karma) and yet remains unaffected by them is not an ordinary intelligent person. Therefore, the Lord calls such a person wise (buddhimān) among humans. In the 10th shloka of the 18th chapter, the Lord has also called him 'medhāvī' (wise).

In the previous 17th shloka, the Lord had explained the nature of karma, akarma, and vikarma. Here, by saying 'manuṣyeṣu buddhimān' (among humans, the wise one), the Lord seems to be saying that the one who has understood the nature of karma and akarma has understood everything, i.e., he has become jñāta-jñātavya (the one who has knowledge and the one who is to be known).

The one who is yukta (in yoga) remains in a state of siddhi-asiddhi (success and failure) - he remains equanimous, whether he gets the fruit of his actions or not. This is because he has renounced the desire for fruit (phala-icchā). Equanimity is the name of yoga. He remains in a state of eternal equanimity, therefore, he is a yogi.

317

The one who is yukta (in yoga) has renounced the desire for fruit, attachment, and attachment to worldly things, and performs actions only for the benefit of others. This breaks his bond with the world and he experiences the realization of his eternal and self-existent yoga with the Supreme. Therefore, he is called a yogi.

The phrase 'yuktaḥ' implies that he has attained the knowledge of the attainable and the unattainable. When there is no desire to attain something, there is no attachment to the act of attaining it. As long as there is a desire to attain something, the attachment to the act of attaining it remains. The fruit of worldly actions is also ephemeral. As long as there is a desire for ephemeral fruit, the attachment to the act of attaining it remains. But when the attachment to the ephemeral fruit is renounced, the attachment to the act of attaining it also disappears. The one who has renounced the attachment to the act of attaining ephemeral fruit is the one who has renounced the attachment to the act of attaining the eternal fruit. Therefore, he is the one who has renounced all actions.

317

The phrase 'kṛtsna-karma-kṛt' means that as long as there is a desire to attain something, there is an attachment to the act of attaining it. As long as there is a desire to attain something, the attachment to the act of attaining it remains. The fruit of worldly actions is ephemeral. As long as there is a desire for ephemeral fruit, the attachment to the act of attaining it remains. But when the attachment to the ephemeral fruit is renounced, the attachment to the act of attaining it also disappears. The one who has renounced the attachment to the act of attaining ephemeral fruit is the one who has renounced the attachment to the act of attaining the eternal fruit. Therefore, he is the one who has renounced all actions.

317

The one who is yukta (in yoga) has renounced all actions, and therefore, he is free from the bondage of the world. (Gita, 4th chapter, 16th and 32nd shlokas).

The eternal and self-existent yoga with the Supreme is the nature of all living beings. But the human being has considered his bond with the world to be his true nature, and therefore, he has forgotten his eternal and self-existent yoga with the Supreme. The implication is that considering one's bond with the world to be one's true nature is the same as forgetting one's eternal and self-existent yoga with the Supreme.

317

The implication is that the bond with the world is a separate entity, and the eternal and self-existent yoga with the Supreme is a separate entity. The bond with the world is a part of karma, and the eternal and self-existent yoga with the Supreme is a part of akarma. Therefore, the one who sees karma in akarma (i.e., the one who remains unaffected by actions) and the one who sees akarma in karma (i.e., the one who remains unaffected by actions) has renounced all actions, knowledge, and attachment. Just as one performs the ritual of worshiping Ganesha at the beginning of a task, but does not worship him continuously while performing the task, so too, one should not assume that one has become unaffected by actions just because one has renounced attachment at the beginning of a task. Therefore, the Lord has explained these two points here.

317

The implication is that one should never have attachment (phala-icchā and kartṛtva-abhimāna) in oneself, i.e., one should always remain unaffected. In the 8th shloka of the 3rd chapter, the Lord has said that performing actions is better than not performing actions - 'karma jyāyo hy akarmaṇaḥ'. Here, the Lord is saying that seeing akarma (non-attachment) in karma (actions) is even better, and the one who sees akarma in karma has renounced all actions, knowledge, and attachment. This proves that humans should not have attachment (phala-icchā and kartṛtva-abhimāna), because these two attachments bind humans.

317

Now, the Lord will describe the wise and intelligent person who has understood the nature of karma and akarma.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The very first line of this commentary is a crucial one, as it sets the tone for the discussion of the nature of karma and the state of a person who has transcended it. The verse 20 of chapter 3 of the Bhagavad Gita states:

"Mahapurushake dwara harik karm suchaaruropase, sangopaang aur bhi keval anukool ya pratikool paristhiteke roopmein uske tatparataapoorvaka hota hai. Dusra ek bhaav hai ki saamne aakar nashat ho jaate hain; parantu phalase asang honeke uske karm shastrasmmit hote hain. Uske dwara karneyogya karan vaahinke bhokta nahin banta, arthath kinchitmatra bhi karm hi hota hai. Jisse kiseeka ahit hota hai, vah sukhya ya dukhi nahin hota. Isliye prarabd-karm bhi karm usse kabhi nahin hota."

Translation:
"By the great person, every action is done in a well-ordered manner, in detail, and also in a favorable or unfavorable situation, with complete dedication. The second aspect is that they are destroyed as soon as they appear; but their actions are in accordance with the scriptures, as they are not attached to their fruits. The person who performs actions through them does not become their enjoyer, i.e., they do not have any attachment to them. Whatever action causes harm to someone, they do not experience happiness or sorrow. Therefore, the actions of a person who has transcended karma are not considered as karma."

The next part of the commentary explains that the actions of a person who has transcended karma are not bound by the law of karma, and they do not have any attachment to their fruits. The verse 20 of chapter 3 of the Bhagavad Gita states:

"Karmonka sambandh par (sharir-sansar-) ke saath hai, swa-rup (svaroop-) ke saath nahin; kyunki karmonka aarambh aur ant hota hai, par svaroop sabse jyokataiyon rahta hai - is tatvko thik-thik jaanana hi 'jnaan' hai. Is jnaan-rup agnise sampann karmon bhassm ho jaate hain, arthath karmonmein phal deneki (baandhneki) shakti nahin rehti (Gita - chauteh adhyayaka 16va aur 32va shlok)."

Translation:
"The relationship of actions is with the body and the world, not with the Self. Because the beginning and end of actions are in the body and the world, but the Self remains unchanged - this is the truth that is known as 'knowledge'. This knowledge, like a fire, burns all actions, i.e., there is no power to bind actions with their fruits."

The commentary then explains that a person who has transcended karma is not attached to their actions, and they do not have any attachment to their fruits. The verse 20 of chapter 3 of the Bhagavad Gita states:

"Jo karmonka svaroop se tyag karke paramatma mein lagaa hua hai, us manushyako samajhna to sugam hai, par jo karmonse kinchitmatra bhi lipat hue bin tatparataapoorvaka karmon kar raha hai, usko samajhna kathin hai."

Translation:
"It is easy to understand a person who has transcended karma and is attached to the Supreme, but it is difficult to understand a person who is performing actions without any attachment to them, even if they are slightly involved in karma."

The commentary then quotes a verse from the Astavakra Gita, which states:

"Moodh purushaki nivritti bhi pravritti ko utpann karne wali hoti hai, aur jnaani purushaki pravritti bhi nivritti-rup phal ko denewali hoti hai."

Translation:
"The inaction of a foolish person also gives rise to action, and the action of a wise person also gives rise to the fruit of inaction."

"Karmonse nirliptataka anubhav aur uske varataman karmon hi nasht nahin hote, bhaav hai ki aisa karmonyogi pratyut sanchit karmon bhi sarvathaa nasht ho jaate hain."

[Chapter 4]
Explanation: When one performs actions, there is no absence of the Self. (Gita 2.16) However, the sense of ownership remains, i.e., "This body and its limbs are mine, I am performing the action, and the action is for me, and I will get a certain fruit from it." This sense of ownership makes the action a cause of attachment to its fruit. A great person who has achieved the state of karma yoga experiences a complete separation from all natural phenomena, so he does not have even a slight attachment to the means of action, the action itself, or its fruit. Therefore, he is not a cause of attachment to the fruit of action.

An army fights a war with the intention of victory. However, when the war is won, the victory is not attributed to the army, but to the king, because the king has made arrangements for the army's livelihood, provided them with the means to fight, and has motivated them to fight. The army fights for the king. Similarly, when one attaches oneself to the means of action, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and other factors, one becomes a partner in the fruits of their actions.

A great person who has achieved the state of karma yoga does not attach himself to the means of action, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and other factors. Therefore, he is not a partner in the fruits of their actions. In fact, there is no relationship between the Self and the fruits of action. The reason is that the Self is conscious, eternal, and unchanging, while action and its fruits are both material and changing. There is no action or fruit that is always present with the Self. This misconception that there is a relationship between the Self and the fruits of action is the cause of bondage. When this misconception is removed, one experiences the natural state of being free from the fruits of action.

'Nirashrayah' - To have no reliance on anything, including the country, time, object, person, or situation. Even a great king or emperor has to rely on the country, time, and other factors. However, a great person who has achieved the state of karma yoga does not rely on anything. He is not concerned whether he gets support or not. Therefore, he is nirashrayah.

'Nityatruptah' - The Self is a part of the eternal and infinite Paramatma. The Self is always full and complete. When the Self identifies itself with the non-Self, it experiences a sense of lack or insufficiency. To fill this lack, it starts desiring worldly objects. The satisfaction obtained from these objects is temporary and fleeting, because everything in the world is constantly changing and impermanent. The Self can never be satisfied with the non-Self. A great person who has achieved the state of karma yoga is nirashrayah, and therefore, he experiences the natural state of being always full and complete.

4
'Karmanyabhipravrttahapi naiva kinchitkaroti sah'
'Abhipravrttah' - A great person who has achieved the state of karma yoga performs all actions, but he does not perform any action in the sense that he is not attached to the fruits of action. His actions are done for the benefit of the world. One who is attached to the fruits of action cannot perform actions in a complete and perfect way, because the attachment to the fruits of action makes him think about the fruits while performing the action, and this attachment wastes his energy, making it impossible for him to perform the action perfectly.

'Api' - Even though he performs all actions in a complete and perfect way, he does not perform any action in the sense that he is not attached to the fruits of action. His actions are not actions in the true sense, because he is completely detached from them. When he does not perform any action, he cannot be bound by the fruits of action. This is why the Lord says in the 18th chapter, 12th verse, that a karma yogi who renounces the fruits of action does not get any fruit from his actions - 'Na tu sannyasinam kvacit'.

Nature is always active. Therefore, as long as one identifies with nature, one is bound by its actions. A great person who has achieved the state of karma yoga is not bound by nature's actions, because he has transcended nature.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:

The same applies to the karma yogi, whether they are in the householder or renounced stage, as long as they have a firm conviction in the three aforementioned principles. 
People generally believe that the karma yogi is in the householder stage and the jnana yogi (sankhya yogi) is in the renounced stage. However, this is not the case in reality. 
The verse is: 
Yadrichchalabhasantushto dwandwatito vimatsarah, 
Samah siddhavasiddhau cha kritwapy na nibadhyate. 
The karma yogi is content with whatever comes their way, is beyond duality, and is free from envy. They are equal in success and failure and are not bound by their actions. 
The karma yogi performs their duties without desiring the fruits of their actions, and they are not affected by the results. They are content with whatever they receive, whether it is favorable or unfavorable, and they do not have any regrets. 
The term 'labha' (gain) in this context refers to whatever is obtained, not just gain or favorability. 
The karma yogi considers themselves one with all living beings and does not have any envy towards anyone. They are cautious not to have any envy, as it can hinder their actions, which are meant for the benefit of all living beings. 
Envy is a subtle defect that can arise even among friends. For example, if one friend's business is doing better than the other's, the latter may feel envious. This defect can arise even in relationships where there is love, unity, and friendship. Therefore, the seeker should be especially cautious to avoid this defect. 
The karma yogi is beyond duality, such as gain and loss, honor and dishonor, praise and criticism, and happiness and sorrow. They do not have any attachment or aversion to these dualities and are not bound by their actions.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 24]
The seventeenth verse states that there are three types of actions: good, bad, and inaction. The main purpose of this chapter is to describe inaction. Therefore, the Lord has described the renunciation of desire, the root cause of both good and bad actions, and inaction in each verse from the nineteenth to the twenty-third verse, and at the end of the thirty-second verse, one should understand the essence of all three. Then, in the eighteenth verse, the Lord mainly explained the essence of actions, or inaction. Desire leads to action, increased desire leads to bad action, and a complete lack of desire leads to inaction. This concludes the chapter. 
Additionally, there are three types of actions: physical, mental, and spiritual. The body grows from childhood to youth and then to old age - this is a physical action. This action does not result in sin or virtue, bondage or liberation. For example, the flow of the Ganges is a physical action; if someone drowns or benefits from it, the Ganges does not incur sin or virtue. When a person becomes attached to an action and performs it for personal gain, it becomes a mental action that yields results. This mental action leads to bondage, as stated in the Gita (3.9): 'The world is bound by actions other than those performed for the sake of sacrifice.' To be free from this bondage, one must perform actions selflessly, without attachment, and only for the benefit of others. This is spiritual action, which leads to liberation and the experience of a constant connection with the Supreme. 
The twenty-third verse is the main verse for spiritual action. Just as the Lord stated that knowledge burns away all sins (4.37) and that He will free the devotee from all sins (18.66), this verse states that spiritual action destroys all sins. 
The connection is that the previous verse explained how performing actions for the sake of sacrifice leads to the destruction of all actions. Since seekers have different tastes, beliefs, and abilities, the means to achieve this goal also vary. Therefore, in the next seven verses (from the twenty-fourth to the thirtieth), the Lord describes various means in the form of sacrifice. 
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, the fire is Brahman, and the one making the offering is Brahman. The goal to be attained is also Brahman, and it is achieved through the union of Brahman and action.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The sages who have realized the Self and the Self-revivers are constantly dying and ultimately die. Let us consider this further. In this way, man is constantly dying, his life is constantly going towards death. The visible is constantly going towards the invisible. This is the nature of destruction, and therefore, only destruction remains. The power of destruction has taken the form of existence, and thus, only one existence, the formless Brahman, remains. Therefore, it is said, "All this is Brahman" (Chandogya Upanishad 3.14.1). "Vasudeva is the only one who is the sequence of creation and destruction, and there is no actual existence" (Chandogya Upanishad 3.14.1). If a man's entire life is fifty years, then after twenty years, his life is only thirty years. Let us consider this further, and we will see that there is only destruction, destruction, and no creation. Just as the years that have passed are the years of death for a man. (Gita 7.19)
