Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The study of the Bhagavad Gita is a good material for the practice of duty. Therefore, tolerating unfavorable circumstances with a cheerful heart is another form of tapas (austerity) that is not inferior to any other. Due to attachment to worldly pleasures, one finds it difficult to tolerate favorable and unfavorable circumstances alike. Therefore, the importance of tolerating unfavorable circumstances does not strike one.

The term 'yogayajna' here refers to the state of equanimity of the mind. Equanimity means remaining unaffected by the fulfillment and non-fulfillment of one's work, the attainment and non-attainment of one's desired fruits, favorable and unfavorable circumstances, praise and criticism, respect and disrespect. This state of equanimity is the true 'yogayajna'.

Chapter 4
'Svadhyaya-jnanayajnah' - The study of the Gita, the Ramayana, the Bhagavata, and the Vedas, as well as the Upanishads, is a form of 'svadhyaya' or self-study, which is a 'jnanayajna' or a sacrifice of knowledge.

In the end of the Gita, the Lord says that whoever studies this Gita-Shastrak, I will be worshiped by him through the sacrifice of knowledge - such is my opinion (18th chapter, 70th shloka). The meaning is that the study of the Gita is a 'jnanayajna'. Studying the Gita with a deep understanding of its meaning, trying to understand its essence, and so on, all these are forms of 'svadhyaya' or self-study, which is a 'jnanayajna'.

[Verse 29-30]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 32]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

[Verse 34]

The Lord says in the 35th verse, "One who attains knowledge in this way, without depending on any other means, will attain it by performing their duties (karma yoga) and will attain it by themselves, without going to anyone else."

To attain knowledge, one should go to a guru and, with humility and devotion, bow down to them with sixteen types of prostrations (sastang dandavat pranam). This means that one should behave like a lowly person and serve the guru with humility, simplicity, and a desire to learn. One should surrender oneself to the guru and become their disciple. One should offer one's body and possessions to the guru and serve them with one's body and possessions.

The service of a guru is to serve them with one's body and possessions, so that they may be pleased. One should do such work that pleases the guru and makes them happy. This is the true service of a guru.

The greatest service of a saint or a great person is to live one's life according to their principles. Because the principles are dearer to them than their own body, they are willing to give up their body for the sake of their principles. Therefore, a true servant follows their principles with firm determination.

To attain knowledge, one should ask questions to the guru with simplicity, humility, and a desire to learn, but not to show off one's knowledge or to test the guru. One should ask questions like "Who am I?" "What is the world?" "What is bondage?" "What is liberation?" "How can I experience the ultimate reality?" "What are the obstacles in my path?" "How can I overcome them?" and so on.

The phrase "tattvadarshi" means that the guru has experienced the ultimate reality, and the phrase "jnani" means that they have a deep understanding of the Vedas and the scriptures. One should go to such a guru who is both a tattvadarshi and a jnani.

There are three types of people who are eligible to receive knowledge: the uttama, the madhyama, and the kanishtha. The uttama is one who receives knowledge simply by hearing it. The madhyama receives knowledge by hearing, thinking, and meditating. The kanishtha asks questions and seeks clarification. To answer the questions of the kanishtha, one needs to have a deep understanding of the Vedas and the scriptures.

Therefore, a guru should be both a tattvadarshi and a jnani. If a guru is a tattvadarshi but not a jnani, they may not be able to answer the questions of the disciple. If a guru is a jnani but not a tattvadarshi, their words may not be convincing and may not lead to knowledge.

The Lord says in the 35th verse, "Those who bow down to the guru, serve them, and ask questions with simplicity will be taught knowledge by the guru."

The scriptures say, "First, one should perform the duties prescribed for one's varna and ashrama, and then, with a pure mind, one should give up those duties and go to a guru to attain self-knowledge." (Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttar 5.7)

The scriptures also say, "To attain knowledge, one should go to a guru who is a Brahmin, a scholar, and a devotee of the ultimate reality, with a humble heart and a desire to learn." (Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.12)

The scriptures also say, "The one who is eager to attain knowledge should go to a guru who is a scholar and a devotee of the ultimate reality, with a humble heart and a desire to learn." (Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.12)

The uttama is one who has a strong desire to attain knowledge and does not consider the future to be a barrier to attaining it.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

दृष्टि है (गीता - तेरहवें अध्यायका सत्ताईसवाँ श्लोक) ।
परिशिष्ट भाव — तत्त्वज्ञान अथवा अज्ञानका नाश एक ही बार होता है और सदाके लिये होता है । तात्पर्य है
कि तत्त्वज्ञानकी आवृत्ति नहीं होती । वह एक बार अनुभवमें आ गया तो सदाके लिये आ ही गया ! कारण कि जब
अज्ञानकी स्वतन्त्र सत्ता ही नहीं है, तो फिर पुनः अज्ञान कैसे होगा ? अतः नित्यनिवृत्त अज्ञानकी ही निवृत्ति होती
है और नित्यप्राप्त तत्त्वकी ही प्राप्ति होती है।
स्वयं सत्तामात्र तथा बोधस्वरूप है। बोधका अनादर करनेसे हमने असत्को स्वीकार किया और असत्को स्वीकार
करनेसे अविवेक हुआ । तात्पर्य है कि बोधसे विमुख होकर हमने असत्को सत्ता दी और असत्को सत्ता देनेसे विवेकका
अनादर हुआ। वास्तवमें बोधका अनादर किया नहीं है, प्रत्युत अनादिकालसे अनादर है । अगर ऐसा मानें कि हमने
बोधका अनादर किया तो इससे सिद्ध होगा कि पहले बोधका आदर था । अतः अब आदर करेंगे तो पुनः अनादर
हो जायगा। परन्तु बोध एक ही बार होता है और सदाके लिये होता है
।
तत्त्वज्ञान होनेपर फिर मोह नहीं होता; क्योंकि वास्तवमें मोह है ही नहीं । मिटता वही है, जो नहीं होता और
मिलता वही है, जो होता है।
जगत् जीवके अन्तर्गत है और जीव परमात्माके अन्तर्गत है, इसलिये साधक पहले जगत्को अपनेमें देखता है—

(कर्मयोग तथा ज्ञानयोग ) - से आत्मज्ञानका अनुभव होता है और अलौकिक निष्ठा ( भक्तियोग) - से परमात्मज्ञानका
अनुभव होता है।
सब कुछ भगवान् ही हैं - इस प्रकार समग्रका ज्ञान 'परमात्मज्ञान' है। आत्मज्ञानसे मुक्ति तो हो जाती है, पर
सूक्ष्म अहम्की गन्ध रह जाती है, जिससे दार्शनिकोंमें और उनके दर्शनोंमें मतभेद रहता है। अगर सूक्ष्म अहम्की गन्ध
न हो तो फिर मतभेद कहाँसे आया ? परन्तु परमात्मज्ञानसे सूक्ष्म अहम्की गन्ध भी नहीं रहती और उससे पैदा होनेवाले
सम्पूर्ण दार्शनिक मतभेद समाप्त हो जाते हैं । तात्पर्य हुआ कि जबतक 'आत्मनि' है, तबतक दार्शनिक मतभेद हैं।

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 37]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

परन्तु यही पद यदि 'मासेन अधीते' इस प्रकार तृतीयामें प्रयुक्त होता है, तो इसका अर्थ है कि एक मासमें पूरा पढ़ लिया ।

कर्मयोगसे अवश्य फलप्राप्ति ( सिद्धि ) होती है।

The Gita Press edition of Srimad Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 4, verse 35 states: "This process of acquiring knowledge is fraught with uncertainty and delay. However, through the practice of karma yoga, one can experience the ultimate truth without any external expectation or delay. Therefore, I consider karma yoga to be the most suitable path for you, and I will not teach you the conventional method of acquiring knowledge."

The verse continues: "One who acquires knowledge through the practice of karma yoga, by serving and inquiring with humility, and by listening, reflecting, and meditating in accordance with the teachings, will attain the ultimate knowledge. This knowledge can only be acquired through the practice of karma yoga, and not through any other means."

The commentary further explains: "I had previously encouraged Arjuna to seek knowledge from the wise sages, but it is not certain that he will attain the ultimate knowledge even if he does so. This is because the wise sages are also subject to the limitations of the world, and their knowledge may not be absolute."

The commentary then quotes the verse: "śraddhāvā~llabhate jñānaṃ tatparaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ | jñānaṃ labdhvā parāṃ śāntimacireṇādhigacchati || 39 ||"

Translation: "One who is endowed with faith, who is dedicated to his spiritual practice, and who has controlled his senses, will attain knowledge. Having attained knowledge, he will soon attain the supreme peace."

The commentary explains: "The word 'śraddhāvān' (shraddhavan) means one who has faith. The word 'tatparaḥ' (tatparah) means one who is dedicated to his spiritual practice. The word 'saṃyatendriyaḥ' (samyatendriyah) means one who has controlled his senses. These three qualities are essential for attaining knowledge and spiritual growth."

The commentary further explains: "As long as one has not experienced the ultimate reality, one should have faith in its existence. The ultimate reality is not distant from us, but our perception of it is limited by our ignorance. Therefore, faith is essential for spiritual growth."

The commentary concludes: "Even a person who is not spiritually inclined can attain the ultimate knowledge if he has faith in its existence and is dedicated to his spiritual practice. The key to spiritual growth is not the external circumstances, but the internal attitude of the individual."

The commentary then explains the meaning of the word 'paramātmā' (paramatma), which means the ultimate reality. It is not a distant entity, but a reality that is present within us. The commentary further explains that the ultimate reality is not limited by space and time, but our perception of it is limited by our ignorance.

The commentary concludes: "Therefore, faith is essential for spiritual growth. One who has faith in the ultimate reality and is dedicated to his spiritual practice will soon attain the supreme peace."

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The Srimad Bhagavad Gita is instructing Arjuna to stand ready for battle. This is where attachment arises, and it is through these actions that we become bound. The Lord has already explained this in the 48th verse of the second chapter, stating "yogasthah kuru karmani" (perform actions while established in yoga). The meaning of yoga is "samatvam" or equanimity, as stated in the Gita (2.48) - "samatvam yogah uchyate" (equanimity is called yoga).

Arjuna considered war to be a sin (Gita, first chapter, 36th and 45th verses). Therefore, the Lord is instructing Arjuna to fight while established in equanimity, because when one fights with equanimity, they do not incur sin (Gita, second chapter, 38th verse). Thus, performing one's duties while established in equanimity is the means to become free from the bondage of actions.

In the world, numerous actions are constantly taking place, day and night. However, if we do not have attachment or aversion towards these actions, we do not become bound to them. Instead, we remain unattached. When we perform actions with attachment or aversion, our relationship with those actions becomes entangled. But when equanimity arises, our relationship with actions does not become entangled, and thus, we become free from the bondage of actions.

If we reflect on our true nature, we will find that equanimity is inherently present. We should consider that every action has a beginning and an end, and the fruits of those actions also have a beginning and an end. However, our true nature remains unchanged. Actions and their fruits are numerous, but our true nature remains one. Therefore, when we do not perform actions for our own sake and do not consider anything as our own, our relationship with the world of actions and objects is severed, and we naturally experience the state of equanimity.

Om, tat, sat - with these names of the Lord, the fourth chapter of the Srimad Bhagavad Gita Upanishad, which is a dialogue between Sri Krishna and Arjuna, and is a treatise on the science of yoga and the knowledge of Brahman, comes to an end. This chapter is named "Jnanakarmasannyasa Yoga" (the yoga of knowledge and the renunciation of actions).

The fourth chapter describes the path of karma yoga and sankhya yoga for the attainment of true knowledge. All the verses in this chapter have 32 syllables. There are three instances of "uvacha" (said) in this chapter - two "Sri Bhagavan uvacha" (the Lord said) and one "Arjuna uvacha" (Arjuna said).

The fourth chapter has a total of 533 words, with 3 words in the phrase "atho chaturtho'dhyayah", 6 words in the phrases "Arjuna uvacha" and others, 511 words in the verses, and 13 words in the phusphika (colophon). The total number of syllables in this chapter is 1421, with 7 syllables in the phrase "atho chaturtho'dhyayah", 20 syllables in the phrases "Arjuna uvacha" and others, 1344 syllables in the verses, and 50 syllables in the phusphika.

The meter used in the fourth chapter is primarily "pathyavaktra" anustup, with some variations. The 31st and 38th verses have the "nagana" meter, the 6th verse has the "ragana" meter, and the 24th and 30th verses have the "bhagana" meter. The remaining 33 verses follow the "pathyavaktra" anustup meter.

The fifth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita begins with the following verse:

Arjuna said:
"I am confused, O Krishna, as you praise both renunciation of actions (sannyasa) and the practice of yoga (yoga). Tell me, which of these two is superior and beneficial for me?" (1)

In the previous chapter, Krishna had praised the path of knowledge (jnana yoga) and the path of action (karma yoga). Arjuna was initially inclined towards the path of knowledge, but after hearing Krishna's praise for karma yoga, he became confused and sought clarification.

The verse "sannyāsaṃ karmaṇāṃ kṛṣṇa punaryogaṃ ca śaṃsasi" can be transliterated as "sannyāsaṃ karmaṇāṃ kṛṣṇa punaryogaṃ ca śaṃsasi" and translated as "I am confused, O Krishna, as you praise both renunciation of actions (sannyasa) and the practice of yoga (yoga)".

The word "sannyāsaṃ" (sannyāsaṃ) means "renunciation of actions" or "sannyasa", while "karmaṇāṃ" (karmaṇāṃ) means "of actions". "punaryogaṃ" (punaryogaṃ) means "the practice of yoga again" or "karma yoga", and "ca" (ca) is a conjunction. "śaṃsasi" (śaṃsasi) means "you praise" or "you recommend".

The verse "yacchreya etayorekaṃ tanme brūhi suniścitam" can be transliterated as "yacchreya etayor ekam tanme brūhi suniścitam" and translated as "Tell me, which of these two is superior and beneficial for me?"

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The Lord says, "Both renunciation and the path of action are means to achieve ultimate liberation. However, among these two, the path of action is superior to renunciation."

The Lord says, "Both renunciation and the path of action are means to achieve ultimate liberation. However, among these two, the path of action is superior to renunciation."

Explanation:
The Lord explains that both renunciation and the path of action are means to achieve ultimate liberation. However, among these two, the path of action is superior to renunciation. This is because the path of action is more accessible and practical for all individuals, regardless of their social class, stage of life, or creed.

The Lord further explains that the path of action is not just about renouncing worldly attachments, but about performing actions without attachment to their fruits. This is the essence of the path of action, which is also known as 'karma yoga'.

The Lord says that the path of action is more superior to renunciation because it is more accessible and practical for all individuals. This is because the path of action does not require one to renounce worldly attachments, but rather to perform actions without attachment to their fruits.

The Lord also explains that the path of action is more effective in achieving ultimate liberation because it is more practical and accessible. This is because the path of action does not require one to renounce worldly attachments, but rather to perform actions without attachment to their fruits.

In conclusion, the Lord says that the path of action is superior to renunciation because it is more accessible, practical, and effective in achieving ultimate liberation.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 4]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 5]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Chapter 5

One who is free from attachment attains happiness and is liberated from bondage - 'sukham bandhat pramucyate' (Gita 5.3). Therefore, the path of Karma Yoga is easy, quick, and independent.

Relationship - Now, Lord Krishna describes the characteristics of a Karma Yogin.

The one who is united with yoga, whose soul is pure, whose soul is conquered, and whose senses are conquered, performs actions without being tainted by them. 7

Translation of Sanskrit Shloka:
yoga-yuktah vishuddha-atma vijita-atma jita-indriyah |
sarva-bhuta-atma-bhuta-atma kurvan na api lipyate || 7 ||

Meaning: The one who is united with yoga, whose soul is pure, whose soul is conquered, and whose senses are conquered, performs actions without being tainted by them.

[Verse 7]
Explanation - 'Jita-indriyah' - The meaning of 'jita-indriyah' is that the senses are under control. When the senses are free from attachment and aversion, they do not have the power to disturb the mind. The practitioner can control them as per his will.

For a Karma Yogin, it is essential to have control over the senses. That's why Lord Krishna emphasizes the importance of controlling the senses in the context of Karma Yoga, as seen in the following verses: 'yastvindriyani manasa niyamya' (3.7); 'tasmad tvam indriyani adau niyamyah' (3.41). A Karma Yogin has a deeper connection with his actions; therefore, the possibility of being distracted exists if the senses are not under control. To perform Karma Yoga, it is essential to serve others for their benefit, which requires having control over the senses. Without controlling the senses, the path of Karma Yoga becomes difficult.

Having a strong desire to attain the ultimate reality is essential for the purification of the mind. The faster and more profound the purification of the mind, the faster and more profound the purification of the heart. Therefore, the glory of having a single-minded goal in Karma Yoga is unparalleled.

'Vijita-atma' - In Karma Yoga, it is essential to renounce the attachment to the body's comforts and pleasures. If the body is not under control, the practice of Karma Yoga cannot be established. Therefore, Lord Krishna emphasizes the importance of controlling the body.

'Sarva-bhuta-atma-bhuta-atma' - A Karma Yogin experiences unity with all living beings. Just as when one part of the body is injured, the other parts serve it without any sense of pride or attachment, similarly, a Karma Yogin serves all living beings without any attachment or pride.

'Vishuddha-atma' - The impurity of the heart is due to the attachment to worldly objects. A Karma Yogin, by serving others for their benefit, experiences a natural detachment from worldly objects. When the attachment to worldly objects is absent, the heart becomes pure.

Manu Smriti 2.98 states: 'Shrutva sprishthva cha drishthva cha bhukthva ghraathva cha yo narah, na hrisyati glayati va sa vijneyo jita-indriyah' - The one who, having heard, touched, seen, eaten, and smelled, does not get delighted or distressed, is considered to be a person with controlled senses.

1. Whether one is detached from the body or considers oneself to be one with all living beings, the outcome is the same. A Jnani is detached from the body, and a Karma Yogin considers himself to be one with all living beings. This unity makes him liberal.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

The ultimate goal of a karma yogi is the same as that of one who is bound - to benefit others. However, a karma yogi can achieve this while remaining detached, and he can be with everyone and remain with everyone forever. The goal that is achieved by some and not by others, and that exists at some time and not at others, is not the goal of a karma yogi. From this perspective, the ultimate goal is always the realization of the Paramatma.

The Paramatma is not the result of any action, practice, or other such thing. The Paramatma is eternal, while the results of actions are born and perish. A karma yogi does not desire the results of actions, which are born and perish, because his desire itself becomes an obstacle to the realization of the Paramatma. Therefore, the ultimate goal of a karma yogi is the realization of the Paramatma alone.

A karma yogi is called 'yogayukta' because his ultimate goal is the realization of the Paramatma.

He is not bound by actions. His actions are like 'guna guneshu vartante' - they are done for the benefit of others.

Here, the word 'api' also implies that a karma yogi is detached not only when performing actions, but also when not performing them (Gita - 4th chapter, 18th shloka). There is no purpose in performing or not performing actions for him (Gita - 3rd chapter, 18th shloka). He remains detached always.

In essence, a sannyasi renounces the attachment to the material world and identifies himself with the consciousness, while a karma yogi identifies himself with the material world - the body, mind, senses, etc. He does not consider them as his own, but rather as belonging to the world and for the benefit of the world. When a karma yogi considers the body, mind, senses, etc. as belonging to the world and for the benefit of the world, then if some benefit is derived from them, some happiness is given to someone, some service is done to someone, he cannot say 'I did it' or 'it happened through me'. Therefore, he is not the doer of actions, and hence, he is not bound by actions.

The one who is called 'yogayukta' is also referred to as 'yogarudha' in the 6th chapter, 4th shloka.

'Kurvannapi nalipyate' - a karma yogi is not bound by actions even when performing them. The reasons for being bound by actions are attachment to actions, desire for the fruits of actions, desire for the happiness resulting from actions, and the sense of doership. In essence, the desire to gain something from actions is the reason for being bound. Since a karma yogi does not have even a slight desire to gain something from actions, he is not bound by them, and hence, his actions become neutral.

A sannyasi, on the other hand, considers the senses to be operating in their respective objects, and hence, does not get bound by actions (Gita - 3.28).

[Verse 8-9]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 8-9]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 8-9]

If one starts to perceive himself as a doer, then what is the wonder in that? In reality, at the time when one considers himself as a doer and enjoyer, he is not a doer and enjoyer even then. 'Though seated in the body, the embodied soul does not act nor is it tainted' (Gita 13.31). This is because his true nature is mere existence. Existence is not 'I' and 'I-ness' is not existence. Therefore, even if one's conviction that 'I am a doer' is very strong, it is still a mistake. One can rectify a mistake by acknowledging it as a mistake. Just as darkness in a cave for hundreds of years is dispelled by light and disappears immediately, without taking any time, similarly, the conviction that 'I am a doer' can be rectified by firmly believing that 'I am not a doer.' This conviction will not remain as a mere belief, but will be transformed into an experience.

The use of 'I' is for both the jiva (embodied soul) and the true nature (svarupa). Just as 'I am a doer' implies a focus on the jiva, 'I am not a doer' implies a focus on the true nature. One who focuses on the jiva is 'ahankarvimoodh-atma' (a person bound by ego), and one who focuses on the true nature is 'tattvavit' (a person who has realized the truth).

When a seeker tries to experience himself as not doing anything in the present moment, he faces a big problem. When he remembers the good deeds he did in the past, he feels happy, thinking, 'I did a great job!' and when he remembers the forbidden deeds, he feels sad, thinking, 'I did a terrible thing!' In this way, the impressions of past deeds make him happy or unhappy. There is a significant point to consider here. The true nature is not a doer in the past, present, or future. Therefore, the seeker should see that just as he is not a doer in the present, he was not a doer in the past either. This is because the present is the past. The true nature is mere existence, and existence cannot perform any actions. Actions are performed by the ego-bound, ignorant person (Gita 3.27).

The memory of past deeds that brings happiness or sadness is a memory of the ego-bound person, not the true nature. 'I do not perform any actions' means that there is no action, but there is existence. Therefore, the seeker's focus should be on the existence. Existence is consciousness and is blissful, being unchanging and one-pointed.

Due to the identification with the body, one thinks that 'I am doing this' or 'I am doing that.' However, the body performs actions, but the true nature does not perform any actions. It is free from both action and inaction (Gita 3.18). Therefore, even when the body performs actions, the seeker should focus on the true nature, thinking, 'I am not doing anything.'

Relation: In the seventh shloka, the Lord explained the non-attachment of the karma yogi, and in the eighth and ninth shlokas, He explained the non-attachment of the sanyasi. Now, the Lord explains the non-attachment of the bhakti yogi.

[Verse 10]
Bhagavan said: He who dedicates all actions to the Supreme, renouncing attachment, is not tainted by sin, like a lotus leaf untouched by water. 10

Translation of Sanskrit Shloka:
brahmaṇyādhāya karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā karoti yaḥ |
lipyate na sa pāpena padmapatramivāmbhasā || 10 ||

Translation of Sanskrit words:
brahmaṇyādhāya = dedicates to the Supreme
karmāṇi = actions
saṅgaṃ = attachment
tyaktvā = renouncing
karoti = performs
yaḥ = he who
lipyate = is tainted
na = not
sa = he
pāpena = by sin
padmapatramiva = like a lotus leaf
ambhasā = by water
lipyate = is tainted
na = not

Explanation:
The verse emphasizes the importance of dedicating all actions to the Supreme and renouncing attachment. This allows one to remain untainted by sin, just like a lotus leaf remains untouched by water. The lotus leaf is a symbol of spiritual purity and detachment.

The commentary explains that the verse is referring to the Bhakti Yoga path, where one dedicates all actions to the Supreme and renounces attachment. [Verse 11]

The absence of attachment (asakta) is essential for the non-existence of desire (kama). Therefore, a devotee who practices bhakti-yoga is not attached to any kind of sinful actions, and thus the possibility of sin does not remain. There is no attachment.

Just as smoke clings to fire, all actions are tainted by some kind of sin or virtue (papa-punya). However, one who has renounced attachment, hope, and desire, and is a devotee of bhakti-yoga, is not affected by these virtues and vices. This is because he is free from attachment and does not get bound by them. This is also mentioned in the 38th verse of the 18th chapter of the Gita, which states that the effects of actions (karma) in the next birth are the cause.

Similarly, as mentioned in the 23rd verse of the 17th chapter of the Gita, the devotee who has renounced attachment is not affected by the fruits of actions (shubha-shubha-phala). This is also mentioned in the 27th-28th verses of the 9th chapter of the Gita, which state that one who performs actions with devotion will be freed from the bondage of karma.

In the commentary, it is explained that the term "Brahma" refers to the Supreme Being who is both saguna (with attributes) and nirguna (without attributes). The Bhagavatam also mentions that Brahma (nirguna), Paramatma (saguna-nirakara), and Bhagavan (saguna-sakara) are all one. The term "saguna" includes Brahma, Paramatma, and Bhagavan, while "nirguna" only includes Brahma, as it is devoid of attributes.

The Vaisnavas call the festival of the saguna-sakara Bhagavan "Brahmotsav". Arjuna also referred to Lord Krishna as "Brahma" in the Gita, saying "Param Brahma Param Dham Pavitra Param Bhavan" (10.12). The Gita also mentions three names of Brahma: "Om", "Tat", and "Sat" (17.23). The relationship between the names and the Supreme Being is also saguna.

Now, the Lord explains the way of performing actions for the karma-yogi.

The karma-yogi performs actions with his body, mind, intellect, and senses, but without attachment. He renounces attachment for the sake of self-purification.

The verse is:

kayena manasā buddhyā kevalair indriyair api
yoginah karma kurvanti saṅgam tyaktvātmaśuddhyai || 11 ||

Translation:

The yogis (karma-yogis) perform actions with their body, mind, intellect, and senses, but without attachment. They renounce attachment for the sake of self-purification.

Explanation: The term "yoginah" refers to the karma-yogis who perform actions with devotion. However, those who perform actions without devotion, solely for the sake of serving the world, are called karma-yogis. The karma-yogis do not consider their body, senses, mind, and intellect as their own, but rather as a means to serve the world. This is because the body, senses, mind, and intellect are all connected to the world.

The verse "kayena manasā buddhyā kevalair indriyair api" means that the karma-yogis perform actions with their body, mind, intellect, and senses, but without attachment. The term "kevalair" means "without attachment" or "without desire". The karma-yogis do not consider their body, senses, mind, and intellect as their own, but rather as a means to serve the world.

The commentary explains that the body, senses, mind, and intellect are all connected to the world and are not our own. We should not consider them as our own, but rather as a means to serve the world. This is because the body, senses, mind, and intellect are all subject to the laws of nature and are not under our control.

The verse "yoginah karma kurvanti saṅgam tyaktvātmaśuddhyai" means that the karma-yogis perform actions with their body, mind, intellect, and senses, but without attachment, for the sake of self-purification. The term "saṅgam" refers to attachment, and the term "tyaktvā" means "renouncing". The karma-yogis renounce attachment for the sake of self-purification.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.
