Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 2]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 3]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[Verse 4-5]

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

Maharshi Vedavyasa had a lot of affection for Dhritarashtra. Due to this affection, he went to Dhritarashtra and said, "War is inevitable and a great massacre of warriors is certain. This cannot be avoided. If you want to see the war, I can give you divine vision, so that you can see the war clearly sitting here." Dhritarashtra replied, "I have been blind since birth, I do not want to see the destroyers of my family, but I want to know how the war is happening - I want to hear the news of it." Then Vedavyasa said, "I will give divine vision to Sanjaya, so that he can see the entire war, all the events, the thoughts of the warriors, and he will tell you everything."

As per the fixed time, the war started in Kurukshetra. Sanjaya stayed at the war site for ten days. When grandfather Bhishma was thrown off his chariot by arrows, Sanjaya went to Hastinapura (where Dhritarashtra was sitting) and told him this news. After hearing this news, Dhritarashtra was very sad and started crying. Then he asked Sanjaya to tell him the entire story of the war. In the beginning of the 25th chapter of the Bhishma Parva, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya-

Dhritarashtra said:
In the field of dharma, in Kurukshetra,
The gathered warriors, eager for battle,
My sons, the Pandavas, and the Kauravas too,
What were they doing, Sanjaya? 1

Dhritarashtra said:
1. In the Mahabharata, there are eighteen parvas. Among them, this 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Parva' is a part of the Bhishma Parva, starting from the 13th chapter and ending at the 42nd chapter. 2. The conversation between Vaisampayana and Janamejaya is 'Dhritarashtra - Sanjaya - Sambandh', and the conversation between Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya is 'Shri Krishna Arjuna - Sambandh'. 3. Sanjaya was born from Gavalgana, a Suta. He was a wise and righteous person, like a sage - 'Sanjayo munikalpa stu jajneya sutah gavalganaat' (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 63.97). He was Dhritarashtra's minister.

[ Verse 16 – 18 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
Commentary – [Just as hungry people have the same hunger and the same satisfaction after eating, but their taste in food is different. Similarly, people who are attached to the impermanent and ephemeral world, no matter what they do, are never satisfied and remain deprived. When they turn away from the world and move towards the Supreme Self alone, they attain satisfaction, i.e., they become fulfilled, knowing what is to be known, and achieving what is to be achieved. However, their taste, qualifications, faith, and trust are different, so their methods of worship are also different.]

[Verse 17]
[Verse 18]
'Jnana-yajnena chaapyanye yajanto mamupasate ekatvena' - Many knowledge-seekers, through the sacrifice of knowledge, i.e., by renouncing the unreal with discernment, and considering the all-pervading Supreme Self and their own true nature as one, worship my formless and attributeless nature. Since this world was initially non-existent and is still heading towards non-existence, it is essentially non-existent. The existence of the world is perceived only due to the existence of the Supreme Self, from which it originates, on which it depends, and by which it is illuminated. To constantly focus on that Supreme Self, considering our unity with it, is to worship with a sense of oneness. Here, the word 'yajantah' means that they have reverence only for the Supreme Self within themselves - this is their worship. 'Prithaktvena bahudha vishvatomukham' - Many action-seekers, considering themselves as servants and the world as the vast form of the Lord, dedicate all their bodily, sensory, mental, and intellectual activities, as well as all objects, to the service of the world. With the thought of how everyone can be happy, how everyone's suffering can be alleviated, and how they can serve everyone, they remain engaged in the service of the Lord, using their body, mind, and wealth, and attain fulfillment through divine grace. Appendix - All seekers, according to their taste, qualifications, and faith, worship the Lord through different means, which is actually the worship of the Lord's complete form. The description of this complete form will be given from the sixteenth to the nineteenth verse. Connection - If all methods of worship are different, then how can they all be yours? The next four verses answer this question. I am the ritual, I am the sacrifice, I am the offering to the ancestors, I am the healing herb. I am the mantra, I am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation. 16

I am the father of this universe, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather. I am the knowable, the purifier, the syllable Om, the Rig Veda, the Sama Veda, and the Yajur Veda. 17

I am the goal, the supporter, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend. I am the origin, the dissolution, the foundation, the treasure, the seed, and the imperishable. 18

According to one's own inclination, faith, and conviction, one can consider anyone as the direct form of the Supreme Lord and associate with them. If one does so, then this association is indeed true. There should be no slightest doubt in one's mind. Just as a person knows the Supreme Lord through knowledge, he knows that everything in the world is one and the same. There is no independent existence of anything else except the Supreme Lord - he should have no doubt about this. Similarly, the Lord is manifesting in various forms, so everything is the Lord Himself - one should have no doubt about this. If one has any doubt about this, then he will be deprived of the true reality and will be entangled in great suffering. Therefore, one should firmly believe that everything is the Lord Himself. The Lord's all-pervading nature is described from the sixteenth to the nineteenth verse. 'I am the doer, I am the sacrifice, I am the oblation, I am the medicine' - whatever is done according to Vedic rituals, that is 'kṛta' (ritual). That kṛta is I myself. Whatever is done according to smārta (Pauranic) rituals, that is 'yajña' (sacrifice), and the smārta-karma (rituals) are known as panchamahāyajña (five great sacrifices). That yajña is I myself. The offering of food to the ancestors is called 'svadhā'. That svadhā is I myself. The herbs, grains, and other substances required for yajña and svadhā, those are also I myself. ' I am the mantra, I am the yajña, I am the fire, I am the oblation' - the mantra through which kṛta, yajña, and svadhā are performed, that mantra is I myself. The ghee required for yajña is also I myself. The fire in which the oblation is offered is also I myself, and the act of offering the oblation is also I myself. 'What is to be known is the imperishable Brahman, the syllable Om, the Rudra, the Sāma, and the Yajur' - the method of performing kṛta, yajña, and svadhā, as described in the Vedas, is to be known. This means that whatever is done for the fulfillment or removal of desires through Vedic and scriptural rituals, that should be done with complete knowledge of the method. Therefore, all the things that are to be known are my own form. Yajña, dāna (charity), and tapas (austerity) - these three are the great purifiers of the niskāma (selfless) person - 'yajño dānaṃ tapaścaiva pāvanānī manīṣiṇām' (18.5). In these, the things that are spent in niskāma-bhāva (selfless attitude) are purified, and the actions that are performed in niskāma-bhāva are also purified. This purification is my own form. The recitation of the mantras for the performance of kṛta, yajña, etc. begins with the recitation of 'Om' only. By reciting 'Om', the mantras give the desired results. The Vedic scholars perform all their rituals, including yajña, dāna, and tapas, by reciting 'Om' only. Therefore, the Lord has described 'Om' as His own form. The Vedic scholars have described the method of performing kṛta, yajña, etc. in the Rigveda,

* The Nourisher of Seekers *

The three Vedas are the Samaveda and the Yajurveda. The ones that contain the fixed-letter mantras are called the Rigveda. The ones that contain mantras with sounds are called the Samaveda. The ones that contain mantras without fixed letters are called the Yajurveda. These three Vedas are the very form of God Himself. "I am the Father of this world, the Mother, the Creator, and the Grandfather" - I am the one who brings forth this entire world of inert and conscious beings, "I am the origin of this entire world" (Gita 7.6). And I am the one who protects it by taking birth again and again. Therefore, I am the Father. Arjuna has also said in the 43rd verse of the 11th chapter that you are the Father of this world of living beings - "Pitasasi Lokasya Characharasya". I am the one who sustains this world in all ways and I am the one who creates the laws of the world. Therefore, I am the Creator. I am the Mother who gives birth to living beings in various forms and bodies according to their karma. Therefore, I am the Mother of the entire world. The ultimate reality that is the highest goal for all living beings is I myself in the form of "Gati" (destiny). I am the one who sustains and nourishes the world and I am the Lord of the world. I am the witness who knows everything at all times. Since all living beings are my parts, they are always present in me and I am their abode. I am the one who is the refuge and the protector of all living beings. I am the well-wisher who benefits all living beings without any reason. "I am the origin, the destruction, the place, the treasure, and the seed that is never exhausted" - The entire world is born from me and it is also dissolved in me. Therefore, I am the origin and the destruction. I am the place where the world resides and I am the treasure that contains everything. The seed that gives rise to the world is also me, but it is not exhausted. I am eternal and I do not undergo any change. Brahma is considered to be the creator of the world, but He is born from me. Therefore, I am the grandfather of Brahma and the father of all living beings. Arjuna has also called God the creator of Brahma and all living beings - "Brahmano 'py Adikarta" (11.37). Commentary - Just as knowledge is seen to be operating within the realm of qualities, "guna guneshu vartante" (Gita 3.28), similarly, from the perspective of devotion, God's property is being offered to God Himself. Just as one offers worship to Ganga with Ganga water, to the sun with a lamp, to the earth with flowers, similarly, God's property is being offered to God Himself. In reality, it is seen that the one being worshipped, the worship material, the worship itself, and the worshipper are all God Himself. The worldly seed is born from a field, but the divine seed is not born from anywhere. Therefore,

1. The mantras that describe worldly knowledge and the creation of weapons, houses, etc. are called the Atharvaveda. Although the word "cha" (and) is used to denote the Atharvaveda, it is not included in the rituals of the Veda. Therefore, in the 20th and 21st shlokas, the words "trividya" and "trayi dharmmanuprpanna" also refer to the three Vedas - Rig, Sam, and Yajus. 2. The place where all living beings reside in the creation stage is called the "nivas" and the place where the entire world resides in the destruction stage is called the "sthana". This is the difference between nivas and sthana.

[ Chapter 9 ]
Lord Krishna had stated in the seventh chapter that He is the 'Sanatana Bija' (eternal seed) - 'Bijam mam sarvabhutanam viddhi partha sanatanam' (7.10). Now, here Lord Krishna says that He is the 'Avyaya Bija' (indestructible seed). The reason is that worldly seeds, after producing a sprout, get destroyed, but the divine seed, in the form of Lord Krishna, remains unchanged even after creating infinite universes. In other words, Lord Krishna exists at the beginning and at the end of the universe. Whatever exists at the beginning and at the end also exists in the present - this is a fundamental principle. Just as various objects are created from earth, exist in earth, and ultimately merge into earth, similarly, all the seeds of the universe are born from Lord Krishna, exist in Him, and ultimately merge into Him (Gita, 10th chapter, 39th verse). The implication is that worldly seeds are destroyed after producing, but the indestructible seed, in the form of Lord Krishna, remains unchanged at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end. Therefore, in the present, Lord Krishna is the only reality, and nothing else exists. Arjuna
=
[Verse 19]
I heat up (as the sun) and I withhold (the rain) and release it. I am the immortality and death, and I am the existence and non-existence, O Arjuna (19). Explanation - I (Lord Krishna) heat up as the sun and withhold the rain, and I release it. I am the one who causes the separation of the body and the soul (death). Whatever exists in the world, whether it is sat (existence) or asat (non-existence), I am the one who is behind it. The sun, in the form of Lord Krishna, heats up the earth and absorbs the dirty water, making it pure and clean. Then, when the time is right, He releases the rain, which is essential for the survival of all living beings. In other words, Lord Krishna is the one who is behind everything, whether it is existence or non-existence, sat or asat, cause or effect. Just as great souls see everything as Vasudeva (Lord Krishna), 'Vasudevah sarvam', similarly, Lord Krishna sees everything as Himself. However, worldly people see things as separate and distinct - life and death, creation and destruction, gross and subtle, satva, raja, and tama (the three gunas), cause and effect, and water and ice, all appear as separate entities. But in reality, everything is a manifestation of Lord Krishna. The implication is that just as the sun is the cause of health and longevity, 'Arogyam bhaskarad ichchet' (Laukakshisamhita), similarly, Lord Krishna is the one who is behind everything, and everything is a manifestation of Him.

[ Verse 19 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
Everything is just the form of God. Except for God, nothing has an independent existence. Just as all clothes made from a thread are nothing but the thread, everything is just God. Appendix: Before creation, God existed, and in the end, God will still exist. So, where did anything else come from in between? Therefore, even immortality is God's form, and mortality is also God's form. The supreme nature (Para Prakriti) is God's form, and the inferior nature (Apara Prakriti) is also God's form. Just as in the offerings of a food festival, there are sweet dishes like rasgullas and gulabjamuns, and also bitter dishes like methi and karela. Similarly, what pleases our mind is God's form, and what does not please is also God's form. The sun's act of absorbing water and then pouring it back is also God's work. Not only that, but the water being absorbed and the water being poured are also God, and the act of pouring is also God. The world is a mixture of the eternal (Sat) and the transient (Asat). The world is Asat, and the divine element within it is Sat. The body is Asat, and the soul within it is Sat. The body and the world are subject to change, while the soul and God are unchanging. The body and the world are perishable, while the soul and God are imperishable (Gita, Chapter 2, Verse 12). God says that the changing and the unchanging, the perishable and the imperishable, are all God. The essence is that everything is just God, and there is nothing beyond God (Gita, Chapter 7, Verse 7). The verse "Nasato vidyate bhavo..." implies discernment, but "Sadasachaham" implies faith. The faith that everything is God is sharper than discernment. Discernment works only when there is a consideration of both the eternal and the transient. When there is no transient, what can discernment do? If we acknowledge the transient, there is discernment, but if we do not acknowledge it, there is faith. In discernment, there is a distinction between the eternal and the transient, but in faith, there is no distinction. In faith, there is only the eternal, i.e., only God. In the path of knowledge, discernment is primary, while in the path of devotion, faith and love are primary. In the path of knowledge, the distinction between the eternal and the transient, the inert and the conscious, and the permanent and the impermanent, is primary, which leads to duality. However, in the path of devotion, the faith in one God is primary, which leads to non-duality. The essence is that true non-duality is found only in devotion. In the path of knowledge, the seeker negates the transient. This negation can lead to a sense of existence of the transient. The more the seeker emphasizes the negation of the transient, the more the sense of its existence becomes firm. Therefore, negating the transient is not as good as ignoring it. And ignoring it is not as good as having the attitude that everything is God. Hence, the devotee neither removes the transient nor ignores it but sees God in everything, because, in reality, everything is God. God says, "I was present even before creation, and there was nothing else. After creation, everything that is seen is also me. I am the eternal, the transient, and what is beyond both. I am what remains after creation and what will remain after destruction" (Shrimad Bhagavat, 2.9.32). The body, senses, mind, intellect, life force, ego, and everything else are all God. Just as when we think of Haridwar, the stairs, the bell tower, and everything else become a mental concept, and the Ganges, the fish swimming in it, and the people bathing also become a mental concept. Similarly, the eternal is also God, and the transient is also God.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita
*
[ Chapter 9 
The real and the unreal—these two divisions are in our view, that is why the Lord says to us for explanation— 'I am the real and the unreal' . In the Lord's view, there is nothing except Him. Even from the highest philosophical view, the reality is one only. There cannot be two realities. Accepting a second reality is the cause of delusion (Gita - 13th verse of the 7th chapter). Attachment and aversion also arise from accepting a second reality. Connection—The creation of the world and its various transformations occur under my supervision; however, foolish people who do not understand my influence take refuge in demonic, monstrous, and deluding nature and disregard me, so they head towards downfall. Those devotees who understand my influence take refuge in my divine qualities and worship me single-mindedly in various ways, so they experience that everything, real and unreal, is the one Supreme Being. But those whose minds are filled with desires for worldly pleasures and accumulation do not know the true reality and, turning away from the Lord, perform sacrifices and other rituals with a motivated attitude to attain the pleasures of heaven and other worlds, so they are subject to the cycle of birth and death—The Lord describes this in the next two verses. Those who are versed in the three Vedas, who drink the Soma juice, and who are purified of sins, worship me through sacrifices and pray for heaven. They attain the world of Indra and enjoy divine pleasures. 20. Surendra-loka: the world of Indra
Te: they
Punyam: merit
Asadya: attain
Trai-vidya: those who know the three Vedas
Mam: me (in the form of Indra)
Istva: having worshiped
Svargatim: heaven
Prarthayante: pray for
Somapah: those who drink Soma juice
Puta-papa: purified of sins
Divyan: divine
Deva-bhogan: pleasures of the gods
Ashnanti: enjoy
Commentary—Here, the word 'Trai-vidya' has been used. Most people in the world are engrossed in worldly pleasures. Even the most intelligent among them, whose hearts are filled with the importance of ephemeral things, when they hear the descriptions of motivated actions and their results in the three Vedas (Rig, Sama, and Yajur), they become greedy for the pleasures of heaven and engage in the performance of sacrifices described in the Vedas. Such people are subject to the cycle of birth and death. *

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 9 ]
[ Verse 21 ]
The sages call the juice of the Soma plant Soma ras, and those who perform sacrifices pray for the attainment of heaven by drinking it after it has been sanctified with Vedic mantras. Therefore, they are called Somapa (Soma drinkers). Those who perform the sacrifices described in the Vedas and drink the Soma ras sanctified with Vedic mantras have their sins, which hinder their attainment of heaven, destroyed. Hence, they are called Putapapa (those whose sins have been destroyed). Prayer means to praise and worship the lord of heaven, Indra, with the desire of attaining heaven and to ask him for a place in heaven. By performing sacrifices with a desire for rewards, according to Vedic and Puranic rituals, and worshiping Indra, they attain heaven and enjoy divine pleasures, which are far superior to the pleasures of the mortal world. They experience the five divine senses - sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Apart from these, they also enjoy roaming in divine gardens like Nandana, taking pleasure, and receiving respect. The Lord has said in the previous verse that He is everything, sat and asat, so Indra is also a form of the Lord. Therefore, the word 'Mam' (me) should be understood to refer to Indra, as those who perform sacrifices with a desire for rewards worship Indra, the lord of heaven, and ask him for heaven. Appendix - This verse describes those who are attached to the worldly life and perform worship without following the proper rules (as described in the 23rd verse of the 9th chapter of the Gita). The result of such worship is ephemeral (as described in the 23rd verse of the 7th chapter of the Gita). Since everything is a part of the Lord, the word 'Mam' is used for Indra. The word 'Punyam' is used for Indra's world because it is more sacred than the mortal world. They, having enjoyed that vast heaven, enter the mortal world when their merit is exhausted. Thus, those who are attached to the three Vedas and driven by desires, attain birth and death. Having enjoyed that vast heaven, they enter the mortal world when their merit is exhausted. This Soma creeper is very rare and has fifteen leaves. Its shape is like a serpent, and the nodes from which the leaves emerge are red. If the five parts (root, stem, leaves, flowers, and fruit) of this creeper are brought on the full moon day and used to bind mercury, it can make even a person who is bound by the cycle of birth and death, a Lakshavedhi (one who can pierce the target of a hundred thousand). The Soma tree, which also has the five parts, can also bind mercury on the full moon day. However, the Soma creeper is more potent. Its leaves fall one by one during the dark half of the month and grow back one by one during the bright half. If the root of the creeper is extracted on the full moon day, it is very beneficial. When this root is combined with Datura, it can make the body strong like iron and the bound mercury can make one lakh times more gold than iron. This Soma creeper is very rare.

[ Chapter 9 ]
Then, they keep revolving in the cycle of birth and death in the mortal world. They never get liberated from this cycle. Commentary—'te tam bhuktvā svargalokam kāmākāmā'—Those who repeatedly perform sakama (desire-motivated) good deeds and go to heaven, where they enjoy the pleasures of heaven. The heaven is vast, the lifespan there is long, and the enjoyments are also plentiful. Therefore, the heaven is called 'vishala' (vast). Those who desire to attain heaven do not take shelter of the Lord, nor do they take shelter of any means of attaining the Lord. They only take shelter of the sakama dharma (desire-motivated rituals) mentioned in the three Vedas. Therefore, they are said to be under the shelter of trayi dharma (the three Vedas). The word 'gatāgatam' means going and coming. Those who perform sakama anushthana (rituals) and attain heaven due to the fruits of their merits, when their merits are exhausted, they return to the mortal world. Thus, they keep revolving in the cycle of birth and death. If we interpret the word 'pūtāpāḥ' from the previous verse to mean those whose all sins have been destroyed, and the word 'kṣīṇe puṇye' to mean those whose all merits have been exhausted, then they should be liberated (since both their sins and merits are exhausted). However, they do not get liberated; instead, they are subject to the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, the word 'pūtāpāḥ' refers to those whose sins that hinder their attainment of heaven have been destroyed by performing yajna (sacrifices), and the word 'kṣīṇe puṇye' refers to those whose merits that lead to heaven have been exhausted after enjoying the pleasures of heaven. Thus, the idea of the destruction of all sins and merits is not implied here. Connection—Those who take shelter of trayi dharma have to pray to the deities for their needs, but those who take shelter of Me alone do not need to worry or pray for their maintenance and protection—this is what the Lord will explain in the next verse. ananyāḥ cintayanto māṃ ye janāḥ paryupāsate |
teṣāṃ nityābhiyuktānāṃ yogakṣemaṃ vahāmy aham || 22 ||
= Those who, having no other thought (ananyāḥ), meditate on Me (cintayanto māṃ) and worship Me (paryupāsate) with their entire being, I bear the responsibility of their yogakṣema (yogakṣemam vahāmy aham), i.e., I take care of their needs and protection. Commentary—'ananyāḥ cintayanto māṃ ye janāḥ'—The Lord, apart from Himself, is the only reality for them; they see everything as a manifestation of the Lord. Whatever they see, hear, or understand, they consider it to be the Lord's form, and the changes and movements they observe are all the Lord's līlā (play). They have no other thought or affection apart from the Lord. Since they have no other thought or affection, they naturally meditate on the Lord. The word 'ananyāḥ' also means that their means and end are both the Lord alone. They have no desire other than to take shelter in the Lord, think of the Lord, worship the Lord, and attain the Lord, because everything else is perishable. Therefore, they have no desire for their own maintenance or even their own life. Hence, they are ananyāḥ (having no other thought). Whatever actions they perform, such as eating, walking, talking, or engaging in any activity, they consider it all to be worship of the Lord, because they do everything for the Lord's pleasure. 'teṣāṃ nityābhiyuktānām'—This phrase refers to those who, having no other thought, meditate on the Lord and perform all actions for the Lord's pleasure. This can also be understood in another way: those who are ananyāḥ (having no other thought) and are engaged in the Lord's worship, considering everything to be the Lord's manifestation, and performing all actions for the Lord's pleasure...

* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
The Lord has come before them - this is their 'contemplation', and they have become devoted to the service of the Lord in all active and inactive states - this is their 'worship'. Those in whom these three things occur are the ones who are 'nitya-abhiyukt' (always engaged). The Lord says, "I carry the yoga-kshema of my devotees who are always engaged in me." 'Yog' means providing what is not obtained, and 'kshem' means protecting what has been obtained. Those who have turned away from the Lord - this is their 'ananyata' ( exclusivity), they think that whatever the Lord has done is right, and whatever the Lord has not done is also right, and that is where our welfare lies. We do not need to think about what should or should not happen. Because we are always in the Lord's hands, and the Lord is always doing what is truly in our best interest. Therefore, our misfortune can never occur. In other words, if the devotee's desires are fulfilled, it is for their welfare, and if their desires are not fulfilled, it is also for their welfare. The devotee's likes and dislikes have no value; the value lies in the Lord's decree. Therefore, if someone is pleased in favorable circumstances and displeased in unfavorable circumstances, they are not the Lord's servant, but rather a servant of their own mind. In reality, 'yog' refers to the relationship with the Lord, and 'kshem' refers to the welfare of the living being. From this perspective, the Lord strengthens the relationship between Himself and the devotee - this is the devotee's 'yog', and the Lord makes efforts for the devotee's welfare - this is the devotee's 'kshem'. The Lord has instructed Arjuna in the 45th verse of the second chapter to become 'niryogkshem', meaning to not worry about yoga and kshem. In reality, the Lord's 'yog' is involved in both the attainment and non-attainment of something, because the Lord sees what is in the best interest of the devotee and does what is beneficial for them. Similarly, the Lord's 'kshem' is involved in both the protection and non-protection of something, because if the devotee's devotion increases and their welfare is ensured, the Lord will protect what has been obtained; if the protection of what has been obtained does not increase the devotee's devotion or ensure their welfare, the Lord will destroy it, because that is what is best for the devotee. Therefore, the Lord's devotees remain extremely pleased in both favorable and unfavorable circumstances, because they have unwavering faith in the Lord's support. They believe that whatever circumstances arise, they are sent by the Lord. Thus, their attitude of "favorable circumstances are good and unfavorable circumstances are bad" disappears. Their attitude is that the Lord's statement "I carry the yoga-kshem" means that just as a mother understands what her child needs and happily provides it, the Lord understands what His devotees need and happily provides it, meaning that the Lord Himself does all the work for His devotees. The underlying idea is that the Lord is explaining the special nature of His devotees, as compared to the Vedic ritualistic people mentioned in the previous verse and the worshippers of other deities mentioned in the next verse. The Lord's exclusive devotees do not recognize Indra or other deities. Those who worship other deities receive limited fruits according to their desires, but the worshipper of the Lord receives unlimited fruits. The worshipper of other deities is like a laborer, while the worshipper of the Lord is like a member of the family. A laborer works and receives limited wages, but a family member works and receives everything. Exclusive devotees are those who see no other power except the Lord - "In my mind, there is no one except the Supreme Lord, not even in my dreams" (Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 5.6). The Lord provides the necessary means for the devotee and protects what has been obtained - this is the Lord's yoga-kshem. Although the Lord carries the yoga-kshem of all devotees, He specially carries the yoga-kshem of His exclusive devotees, just as a mother takes care of her beloved child herself, not through servants. Just as the devotee finds joy in the Lord's service, the Lord also finds joy in the devotee's service - "In whatever way people approach me, I reward them in the same way" (Gita 4.11).

[ Chapter 9 ]
[Verse 23]
Connection - Having spoken about His own worship in the previous verse, Lord Krishna now talks about the worship of other deities. Ye 'py anya-devata bhakta yajante shraddhay anvitah |
Te 'pi mam eva kaunteya yajanty avidhi-purvakam || 23 ||
Kaunteya = O son of Kunti! Aanya-devatah = of other deities
Ye = who
Yajante = worship
Api = also
Te = they
Bhaktah = devotees
Api = also
Shraddhaya = with faith
Anvitah = endowed with
Mam = Me (Lord Krishna)
Eva = only
Avidhi-purvakam = not according to the rules (i.e., not knowing that the deities are not separate from Me)

Explanation - 'Ye 'py anya-devata' - The devotees who worship other deities with faith, thinking them to be separate from Me, are actually worshiping Me actually, but not according to the rules. 'Avidhi-purvakam' means that they worship the deities, considering them to be separate from Me, and not knowing that everything is a manifestation of Me. The conclusion of this verse is that (1) if one has no desires and has the knowledge of the Lord, then one can worship any being, human, or deity as a manifestation of the Lord, and that worship will be considered as worship of the Lord Himself; and (2) if one has desires and worships the Lord with the intention of fulfilling those desires, then one will be considered as an artharthi (one who worships for material gain) or an artharthi-bhakta (a devotee who worships for material gain), as mentioned in the 18th verse of the 7th chapter. In reality, everything is the Lord. Therefore, worshiping or serving anyone, or doing good to anyone, is ultimately worshiping the Lord. Just as the water that falls from the sky eventually reaches the ocean, similarly, worshiping any deity or being is ultimately worshiping the Lord. 'Te 'pi mam eva kaunteya yajanty avidhi-purvakam' - The worshipers of other deities are also worshiping Me, but not according to the rules, because they consider those deities to be separate from Me. However, in reality, there is nothing separate from Me, and those deities are also My manifestations. Therefore, worshiping them is also worshiping Me, but it is not according to the rules. The meaning of 'avidhi-purvakam' is not that the worship is incorrect in terms of rituals or procedures, but that the worshipers do not know that the deities are not separate from the Lord. They worship the deities, considering them to be separate, and this is the reason for their worship being 'avidhi-purvakam'. Appendix - The words 'Traividyam mam' (9.20), 'Ananyash chintayanto mam' (9.22), and 'Te 'pi mam eva' (9.23) all refer to the Lord, indicating that everything is the Lord. If one has no desires and has the knowledge of the Lord, then worshiping anyone or anything is ultimately worshiping the Lord. As stated in the Laghu Smriti, "Just as the water that falls from the sky eventually reaches the ocean, similarly, worshiping any deity or being is ultimately worshiping the Lord."

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The worship will not be without rules, but it will be the worship of the Lord Himself. In the seventh chapter, the word 'devayaj' (7.23) was used, and here it is said with the word 'yajante'. Connection - What is the worship of the gods by those who worship without rules? It is said:
I am the enjoyer (bhokta) of all sacrifices (yajna) and the Lord (prabhu) of all, but they do not know me in essence (tattvatah), and therefore they fall. Because I am the enjoyer of all sacrifices, and the Lord of all; but they do not know me in essence, and therefore they fall. Whatever good deeds they perform, and whatever duties they perform according to their varna and ashrama, I am the enjoyer (bhokta) of all those deeds. The reason is that in the Vedas, shastras, Puranas, and Smriti-granthas, the rules for good deeds for living beings have been made by me, and I have made them to be given to me, so that these living beings may remain completely unattached to their duties and their fruits, and may not deviate from their true nature, and may remain devoted to me alone. Explanation - [In the second chapter, the Lord said that those who are very much attached to sacrifices, charity, austerity, pilgrimage, vows, enjoyment, and wealth, cannot decide to move towards the Supreme Self alone (second chapter, verse 44). Therefore, there are two main obstacles to moving towards the Supreme Self: considering oneself the enjoyer of pleasures and considering oneself the owner of wealth. Both of these turn the mind away, and the person becomes completely averse to the Supreme Self. For example, in childhood, a child cannot live without its mother; but when it grows up and gets married, it becomes the enjoyer and owner of its wife, and then it does not love its mother as much. Similarly, when this living being becomes attached to enjoyment and wealth, i.e., becomes the servant of pleasures and wealth, and becomes averse to the Lord, it forgets that the Lord is the enjoyer and owner of all. This is the cause of its downfall. But when this living being realizes that the Lord is the true enjoyer of pleasures and the owner of wealth, it becomes devoted to the Lord and comes to the right path, and then it does not fall. 'Aham hi sarvayajnanam bhokta cha prabhureva cha' - Just as I am the enjoyer (bhokta) of all sacrifices, so I am also the owner (prabhu) of the entire world, i.e., all lokas, objects, persons, events, circumstances, actions, and the bodies, minds, intellects, and senses of living beings. The reason is that I have created this entire universe out of my own being for my own pleasure; therefore, being the creator of all, I am the owner of all. Special Note
What is it to become the enjoyer (bhokta) of the Lord? The Lord has said that in the eyes of the great souls, everything is the Lord's (Atman, the eternal soul); here, the word 'yajnanam' (sacrifices) includes all duties (Karma, action), and yet the word 'sarva' (all) is used to indicate that no duty, whether scriptural, physical, or worldly, is left out.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
*
[ Chapter 9 ]
Vasudeva is the ultimate reality (as stated in the 19th verse of the 7th chapter), and He has dominion over the entire universe. I am the creator of the universe, and in my view, everything, whether real or unreal, is me (as stated in the 19th verse of the 9th chapter). When everything is me, then if someone performs a sacrifice to worship a deity, that sacrifice ultimately nourishes me in the form of the deity. If someone donates to others, the recipient's needs are fulfilled, and that is my assistance. If someone practices austerity, the resulting peace and tranquility are mine, as I am the one who experiences them in the form of the ascetic. If someone feeds others, I am the one who is satisfied in the form of the nourished beings. If someone cleanses themselves, I am the one who is pleased in the form of that person. If someone nurtures plants and trees, the nourishment they provide reaches me in the form of those plants and trees, and I am the one who is nourished. If someone serves the poor, the crippled, or the afflicted, that service is ultimately rendered to me. If a doctor treats a patient, the treatment is mine. If someone feeds dogs, pigeons, or cows, or provides food and water to the hungry and thirsty, all such service is rendered to me, as I am the one who receives it in all those forms. Just as serving any part of a person's body or their family is equivalent to serving that person, similarly, any service rendered to any being is ultimately service to me, because I am the only reality that exists. I have manifested in numerous forms - "bahusyam prajayeya" (Taittiriya 2.6). The essence of this is that to consume everything in all forms is to become the enjoyer, the Bhokta, of the divine. What does it mean to be the master, the Malika, of the divine? In the view of devotees who understand the divine essence, the ultimate reality, the supreme consciousness, is the only true master of the universe. Whether the universe is maintained or not, whether it is dissolved or not, whether beings are placed anywhere, governed in any way, utilized in any manner, or transformed at will, the divine has absolute freedom in all these matters. This means that just as an enjoyer has the freedom to utilize their possessions as they wish (although this freedom is only apparent, not real), the divine has real and absolute freedom to transform and govern the universe as it pleases. This freedom is the true nature of the divine, the essence of being the master, the Malika. As stated, "Na tu mam abhijananti tattvenatashcyavanti te" - I am the ultimate reality, the essence of everything, real and unreal, conscious and unconscious. Therefore, I am the enjoyer of all actions and their fruits, and I am also the master of all resources. However, those who do not understand this essence think that the actions they perform and the fruits they bear are enjoyed by other beings. For instance, they believe that when they perform sacrifices, the deities are the enjoyers; when they give charity, the recipients are the enjoyers; when they feed dogs or cows, these animals are the enjoyers. They do not recognize me in all these forms, and this ignorance leads to their downfall. Therefore, one should always consider me, the divine, as the enjoyer and master of all, and offer everything to me, saying, "Whatever belongs to you, O Govinda, I offer back to you."

Another perspective is that all the wealth and luxuries one possesses belong to me, and I, in my universal form, have the freedom to utilize them as I wish. There is a story about Shri Namdevji Maharaj, who once went on a pilgrimage. During his journey, he prepared some bread under a tree and turned around to get some ghee from his luggage. Meanwhile, a dog snatched a piece of bread and ran away. When Namdevji saw this, he chased after the dog, ghee in hand, saying, "O Lord, you are the one who should be offered the bread, so why are you running away with dry bread? Let me at least put some ghee on it for you." As soon as Namdevji said this, the dog transformed into the Lord. What else could the dog have been but the Lord? Namdevji realized this and bowed down. This story illustrates that the divine essence is present in all beings. Therefore, whatever is given to anyone is ultimately received by the divine.

[ Verse 25 ]
* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
The purpose of life is to serve, but those who are attached to worldly pleasures and wealth fall. The meaning is that knowing me as the enjoyer and owner of all sacrifices leads to liberation, and not knowing me leads to downfall. The word "chyavanti" means that not attaining me leads to their downfall. Even if they perform good deeds and go to higher realms, it is still their downfall because they will have to return; they are not liberated and are subject to the cycle of birth and death. People do not understand the true nature of things and consider worldly pleasures and wealth as their own, thinking that they are meant for their enjoyment and that they are the masters. However, they become slaves to these things. The more they consider these things as their own, the more they become dependent on them. Eventually, they start to identify their own existence with the rise and fall of these things. The appendix to this idea is that in the fifth chapter, Lord Krishna has stated that he is the enjoyer of all sacrifices and austerities - "bhoktaaram yajna-tapasam" (5.29). There, he mentioned that those who know him as the enjoyer of all sacrifices attain peace, and here, he says that not knowing him leads to downfall. Becoming the enjoyer oneself is the cause of downfall. Considering Lord Krishna as the enjoyer of all good deeds eliminates the desire for enjoyment and leads to peace. In reality, Lord Krishna is the supreme doer and enjoyer of all actions, but he is not affected by them - "tasya kartaaram api maam viddhy akartaaram avyayam" (Gita 4.13), "na maam karmmani limpanti na me karma-phale sprihaa" (Gita 4.14). Connection - Those who do not consider Lord Krishna as the enjoyer and owner of all sacrifices and worship other deities with a selfish motive will be described in the next verse. They who worship the devas faithfully go to the devas; they who worship the pitrs go to the pitrs; they who worship the bhutas go to the bhutas; and they who worship me come to me. Explanation - [In the previous verse, Lord Krishna explained that he is the enjoyer and owner of all sacrifices, but those who do not consider him as such and become enjoyers themselves fall. Now, in this verse, he explains their downfall.] "They who worship the devas faithfully go to the devas" - those who desire worldly pleasures and wealth, not knowing Lord Krishna properly, worship their chosen deities according to the rules, vows, mantras, and rituals prescribed in the Vedas and scriptures. They perform these rituals and become completely devoted to their deities. These deities will give their devotees the highest fruit, which is to take them to their own realms, which Lord Krishna has called recurring (8.16). In the 23rd verse, Lord Krishna stated that worshiping the devas is also worshiping him, but if it is not done according to the proper rules, it leads to the worshiper going to the devas.

[ Chapter 9 ]
In that worship, being devoid of rules means that they do not know, do not believe, and do not accept that God is the only one. They worship deities and desire to attain worldly pleasures and luxuries. Therefore, they face downfall. If they considered deities as a form of God and did not desire anything from them, then even if they wanted to give something, they would say, "Oh Lord, you are ours and we are yours. What more could we ask for than this relationship with you?" In this way, they would become a source of joy for God and would not attain the lower and ephemeral realms of the deities. 'Yanti mad-yajino 'pi mam' - Those who engage in my worship, puja, and contemplation with an unwavering mind, undoubtedly attain me. Special Note:
People who desire worldly pleasures and luxuries are diligent in worshiping their chosen deities and performing tasks to please them. However, they repeatedly attain trivial worldly pleasures, hells, and the 8.4 million species, instead of attaining the essence that is achieved through devotion to God. Thus, humans who have the opportunity to form a loving relationship with God and bring joy to Him, become entangled in worldly desires and the cycle of lower deities and ancestors, and consequently, attain great misfortune. Therefore, humans should be extremely cautious and solely devote themselves to God. If one has the understanding that God is present in deities, ancestors, sages, and humans, and selflessly serves and worships them for their nourishment and well-being, then they attain God. Considering these deities as separate from God and having a selfish motive is the cause of downfall. 'Pitrin yanti pitr-vratah' - Those who worship ancestors with a selfish motive receive various forms of assistance from them. Hence, people who seek worldly accomplishments diligently follow the vows, rules, and worship rituals of their ancestors and consider them as their chosen deities. The highest reward they can attain is that their ancestors will take them to their realm. Therefore, it is said that those who worship ancestors attain the realm of ancestors. 'Bhutan yanti bhutejyah' - People with a tamasic nature worship ghosts and spirits with a selfish motive and follow their rules. For example, using a donkey's ghost, a preta, or a pishacha for mantra recitation, and using an uttk's teeth to create a thread for worship, are all highly impure. Those who worship in this manner cannot have the understanding of God, nor can they be selfless. Consequently, they face complete downfall. In this context, there is a true story from a few years ago. A person was worshiping a 'karnapishachini' and would answer questions without being asked. If a devotee has the understanding that God is present in a ghost or spirit, then that ghost or spirit can attain liberation, and the devotee can have a vision of God. For instance, when a tall and terrifying ghost appeared before the devotee Namdev, he considered it to be a form of God and said with joy:
"Welcome, oh tall lord! Your feet are on the earth, your head is in heaven, and your arms are a yojan long. Even the great sages like Sanak cannot reach you, and you have innumerable ornaments with you. You are the lord of Namdev, please save me today."

This led to the liberation of the ghost, and God appeared in its place.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 9 ]
[ Verse 26 ]
The question is, and this is its answer. From this, he earned a lot of money. When he ran towards the Narmada, Karnapishachini killed him on the banks of the Narmada before he could reach it. The reason was that if he had died in the Narmada, he would have attained a good fate. However, Karnapishachini did not let him attain a good fate and killed him on the banks of the Narmada, taking him with her. Now, seeing the miracle of this knowledge, a gentleman started following him, saying, "Teach me this knowledge, I want to learn it too." He simply said, "This knowledge is indeed miraculous, but its real benefit is that it is not conducive to the well-being of deities, ancestors, etc." He was asked if the worship of ghosts, spirits, and goblins was not to be abandoned; however, the worship of deities, ancestors, etc., is not to be abandoned, but the worship of ghosts, spirits, and goblins is to be abandoned. The reason is that those who worship them never attain a good fate, but rather a bad one. He was asked how he knew the questions and answers of others. He said, "I keep the dung of a divine being in my ear. When someone comes to ask a question, Karnapishachini comes at that time and whispers the question and answer in my ear, and I repeat it."

Then he was asked, "How will you die?" He said, "I will die on the banks of the Narmada." After his body was calm, it was found that when he was about to die and was going to the Narmada, Karnapishachini, in the form of a she-pig, came before him. Seeing her, he ran towards the Narmada, but she killed him on the banks. Appendix - The word "vrat" means a rule or vow. Therefore, the word "devavrat" means to follow the rules of worshiping deities (Gita, 7.20). Worshiping the Lord by doing actions for His sake is the real worship - "swakarmana tam abhyarchya siddhim vindati manavah" (Gita 18.46). Offering all actions to the Lord is His worship (Gita 9.27). With a selfless attitude and devotion to God, no action can be prohibited, because prohibited actions are the result of desire (Gita 3.36-37). In reality, everything is a form of the Lord. However, one who believes in any other independent power apart from the Lord will not attain liberation. Even if one reaches the highest realms, one will still have to return to the world (Gita 8.16). Connection - In the worship of deities, many materials, rules, and procedures are required. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 9 ]
- 
Commentary: The two functions of the Lord's inferior Prakriti are: matter and action. When the living being identifies itself with these two, considering them to be its own, it begins to think of itself as the enjoyer and controller of these objects and actions, forgetting that the Lord is the actual enjoyer and controller. To remove this misconception, the Lord says that one should offer all objects and actions to Him, and in doing so, one will be freed from all troubles (9.27-28). Another point is that the worship of deities requires rituals, mantras, and other formalities. However, the Lord's relationship with the living being is one of natural affection, and therefore, no formalities are necessary for His attainment. Just as a child can approach its mother without any formalities, simply due to their affectionate relationship, similarly, one can attain the Lord through a strong sense of affection and devotion. The verse says: "patram pushpam phalam toyam yo me bhaktya prayacchati" - If a devotee offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or even water, I accept it. The Lord eats what is offered to Him with love, just as He ate the leaf offered by Draupadi, the flower offered by Gajendra, and the fruit offered by Shabari. "tad aham bhaktyupahritam ashnami prayat-atmanah" - I eat what is offered to Me with devotion by one who has controlled his mind. The Lord not only accepts but also eats what is offered to Him with love, regardless of whether it is edible or not. This shows that when the devotee has the desire to give, the Lord has the desire to receive. The mention of leaf, flower, fruit, and water in this verse is symbolic of all objects, as they are all products of water and are, therefore, mere representations of the objects of the world. The Lord is saying that one should offer all objects to Him. In this verse, the word "bhakti" appears twice, once as "bhaktya" and once as "bhaktyupahritam". The first refers to the devotee's act of offering with devotion, and the second refers to the object being offered with devotion. This means that when something is offered with devotion, it becomes an embodiment of devotion, and the Lord accepts it as such, for He is hungry for devotion. A special point to note is that when the devotee's desire to give increases, they forget themselves, and the Lord, too, becomes so absorbed in the devotee's love that He forgets Himself. In such a state of intense devotion, the devotee does not think about what they are offering, and the Lord does not think about the object being offered. The devotee's sentiment is what matters, for the Lord is hungry for devotion, not objects. The quote from Vinay Patrika says: "When I went to my in-laws' house, I did not find any taste in Shabari's fruits, but the Lord found it delicious." Another quote says: "The Lord, who has eaten throughout the three worlds, found taste only twice - once at Shabari's house and once at Vidura's house."

[ Chapter 9 ]
[ Verse 27 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
It should be done with devotion. Just as a highly devoted disciple, who serves his guru with his time, resources, and actions, feels immense joy and satisfaction, similarly, a devoted wife feels great pleasure in serving her husband, as she sees her life's success and fulfillment in his service. Likewise, a devotee's love for the Lord brings him immense joy in offering anything, big or small, ordinary or precious, to the Lord. His attitude is that everything belongs to the Lord, and he feels grateful that the Lord has given him the opportunity to serve and worship Him. The Lord certainly accepts the offerings made with devotion, whether we see it or not. A teacher once said that in their temple, they used to offer pistachios, almonds, walnuts, cashews, and charoli to the Lord during the festival of Diwali. However, when they started offering peanuts, one night the Lord appeared in a dream and said, "Will you only offer peanuts?" From that day on, they resumed offering other nuts. They became convinced that the Lord accepts the offerings made to Him. When the Lord accepts the offerings, the items become extraordinary, their taste increases, they emit a fragrance, and they bring immense satisfaction when consumed. These items do not spoil even after many days. However, this is not a guaranteed test. Sometimes, the devotee's attitude can make the offered items extraordinary, as we have heard from the saints. When people offer materials, it becomes a yajna (sacrifice); when they give to others, it is called dana (charity); when they abstain from their desires, it is tapa (austerity); and when they offer to the Lord, it establishes a connection with Him. All these are different names for the same act of tyaga (renunciation). Appendix - In the worship of deities, many rules need to be followed (Gita, 7.20); however, in the worship of the Lord, there are no rules. The primary aspect of the Lord's worship is love and affection, not rituals - "bhaktya prayacchati," "bhaktyupahritam." Just as an innocent child puts whatever he gets into his mouth, the Lord also accepts whatever is offered to Him with innocence. As it is said, "ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamy aham" (Gita 4.11); for example, Vidura's wife offered the Lord a banana peel, and He accepted it. The phrase "bhaktya prayacchati" means that the devotee offers materials to the Lord with love, not with any desire. In the worship of deities, specific materials are required, but in the worship of the Lord, there is no need for specific materials; instead, love is required. Connection - The world has two forms: materials and actions. Both can lead to downfall if one becomes attached to them. Therefore, the previous verse discussed offering materials, and the next verse will discuss offering actions. Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer as sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kunti, do it as an offering to Me. yat karoshi = whatever you do
