* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 9 ]
The Lord's rule is that whoever controls their senses from worldly objects, performs their duties while being content in favorable and unfavorable circumstances, and dedicates all their spiritual activities such as pilgrimage, vows, devotion, meditation, chanting, listening, reflection, and samadhi to Me, I provide them shelter in the same manner they approach Me (Gita, 4.11). Whoever dedicates their belongings to Me, I give them My belongings. The devotee offers limited things, but I give infinitely more. However, whoever dedicates themselves to Me, I dedicate Myself to them. In reality, I have already given Myself to the entire world (Gita, 9.4) and granted everyone the freedom to do everything. If a person dedicates the freedom given by Me back to Me, I also dedicate My freedom to them, meaning I become subordinate to them. Therefore, the Lord tells Arjuna to dedicate that freedom to Him. The word "yat karoshi" is unique, encompassing all actions, whether they are scriptural, physical, worldly, social, or spiritual. The Lord says to dedicate all these actions to Him, meaning to dedicate oneself to Him, and all actions will automatically become dedicated to Him. Now, the Lord categorizes those actions:
"Yad ashnasi" includes all physical actions, such as eating, drinking, avoiding unhealthy food, taking medicine, wearing clothes, protecting the body from cold and heat, sleeping and waking up at the right time, walking, bathing, and other similar activities, which should be dedicated to Him. This is the first category of physical actions. "Yaj juhoshi" includes all scriptural actions related to sacrifices, such as collecting materials, igniting the fire, reciting mantras, and making offerings, which should be dedicated to Him. "Dadasi yat" refers to actions like serving others, helping them, and fulfilling their needs, which should be dedicated to Him. The above three phrases are the second category of scriptural and spiritual actions. "Tat kurushva mad arpanam" - Here, the Lord uses the word "kurushva" in the Atmanepada form instead of the Parasmaipada form "kuru". This implies that dedicating all actions to Him does not mean that He needs them to fulfill His own lack, but rather, when one dedicates all actions to Him, their sense of "I" and "mine" will be eliminated, which is the cause of bondage. As a result of dedicating all actions to Him, one will attain perfection, which is the greatest gain possible, and in which one cannot be disturbed even by great sorrow (Gita, 6.22-23). In this verse, the word "yat" is repeated five times, indicating that dedicating each action has immense significance, and dedicating all actions is even more profound. Special note: In the 26th verse, the Lord mentioned dedicating leaves, flowers, etc., which can be obtained without much effort. However, in this 27th verse, the Lord says that one does not need to acquire new things, perform new actions, or make new efforts. Instead, one should dedicate the natural, worldly, and spiritual actions that one already performs to the Lord. This means that the Lord does not require any specific objects or actions to be dedicated to Him; rather, one should dedicate themselves to Him. By dedicating oneself, one attains the greatest gain.

[ Chapter 12 ]
[ Verse 28 ]
* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
All actions will become spontaneous offerings to the Lord, in accordance with His will. Just as a child plays in front of his mother, sometimes running away and then returning to her lap, and whatever the child does, the mother is pleased with that action, because the child's intention is to please the mother. Similarly, the devotee's intention is to please the Lord, and therefore, all their actions will be in accordance with the Lord's will. If someone says, "We will also offer forbidden actions to the Lord," this is the rule: whatever is offered to the Lord becomes infinite. Therefore, if you offer forbidden actions to the Lord, you will also receive the consequences of those actions infinitely. Here, the word "yad" is used with the verb "karoshi," which means "whatever you do." This could include forbidden actions as well. However, at the end, it is said "tad kurushva mad arpanam," which means "offer that to me." Therefore, whatever is offered to the Lord must be in accordance with His will. Appendix - To offer something with respect, and to give only what is acceptable, is called "arpan." The Lord has spoken about giving objects - "prayachchhati" - and about offering actions - "tad kurushva mad arpanam," because actions cannot be given. A jnana yogi renounces their connection with the world, but a devotee does not recognize any other reality except the Lord. In other words, a jnana yogi renounces the sense of "I" and "mine," while a devotee accepts "you" and "yours." Therefore, a jnana yogi renounces objects and actions, while a devotee offers them to the Lord, considering them to be the Lord's and not their own. It is easier to offer something to someone than to renounce it, considering it to be false. If the object of one's devotion is the most revered and lovable Lord, then it is even easier to offer everything to Him. Moreover, a renouncer may develop pride in their renunciation, but one who offers everything to the Lord cannot become proud, because they are simply giving back what belongs to the Lord. "Tvädiyam vasu govinda tubhyameva samarpaye" - all objects have always belonged to the Lord. Offering them to the Lord is simply a matter of correcting one's mistake of considering them to be one's own. When this mistake is corrected, one feels joy, not pride. When one considers the world to be the Lord's, their connection with the world is severed, and the world's independent existence ceases to be. In reality, the world has no independent existence anyway. Therefore, the devotee does not need to use their discernment to sever their connection with the world. Instead, they consider the world to be the Lord's and offer it to Him, because the material world is the Lord's (as stated in the fourth verse of the seventh chapter of the Gita). Connection - Having described the offering of objects and actions to the Lord in the previous two verses, the next verse describes the result of such an offering. You will be freed from the bonds of actions, which are the causes of good and bad results. With your self united with the yoga of renunciation, you will be liberated and attain me.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 9 ]
Thus, by dedicating (all actions to Me), you will be liberated from the bondage of actions and their good and bad results. With your heart dedicated to Me, you will be completely free from all the results of actions. The commentary explains: 'By dedicating all actions and their results to Me, you will be liberated from the bondage of actions and their good and bad results.' This means that by dedicating all things and actions to Me, you will be free from the good and bad results of actions that have been accumulated over countless births. Those results will not cause you to be born and die again. Being completely free (from the results of actions), you will attain Me. This is because the one who dedicates all actions to Me is called 'sannyasa-yoga-yuktatma' (one who is united with Me through the yoga of renunciation). Although the word 'sannyasa' often refers to the path of knowledge (in the Gita), it is also used in the context of devotion, as in 'mayi sannyasya' (18.57). Just as a follower of the path of knowledge remains established in their own nature, having placed all actions in the body with nine gates (Gita 5.13), a devotee places their relationship with actions in Me. In other words, just as a noble person deposits their wealth in a safe place, a devotee deposits their accumulated actions, their results, and their relationships with Me. This is why it is called 'sannyasa-yoga'. 'Being free from (the results of actions), you will attain Me.' The previous verse instructed, 'tat kurusva mad-arpanam' (dedicate all actions to Me). Here, it is said that 'by dedicating (all actions to Me), you will be free from the good and bad results of actions, and having become free, you will attain Me.' This means that being free from all results is a means to attain love, and attaining Me is the attainment of love. Here, 'shubha' and 'ashubha' (good and bad) refer to the accumulated actions of countless births. The reason is that a devotee dedicates to Me only those actions that are performed in accordance with My instructions, and such actions are always good, never bad. However, if a devotee were to perform some bad action due to some circumstance or past habit, the Lord, who dwells in their heart, would destroy that bad action. All actions are external, performed by the body, mind, intellect, and senses. Therefore, the results of those actions, whether favorable or unfavorable, are also external. Humans mistakenly identify with those circumstances and experience happiness or sorrow, which is the bondage of actions, causing them to be born and die. However, a devotee's focus is on the Lord's grace, not on the favorable or unfavorable circumstances. They consider all actions, whether good or bad, to be the Lord's ordinance and do not consider their results. Therefore, they are free from the bondage of actions, which is the result of identifying with favorable or unfavorable circumstances. 'Sannyasa-yoga-yuktatma' means dedicating all actions to the Lord. This is a special point: what is the bondage of good and bad actions? 1. Even a little bad action, which arises somehow, destroys everything (when it is not dedicated to the Lord). 2. Just as bad actions are binding, good actions are also binding. For example, whether a chain is made of iron or gold, it still binds. Good actions are binding because they lead to birth, and bad actions are binding because they forcefully bind.

[ Verse 28 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
When one identifies with their actions, they become connected to the fruits of those actions. This is stated in the phrase "vimukto mam upaishyasi" (you will attain me, being liberated). Although the connection between actions and their fruits is not inherent, the doer accepts this connection as their own. The doer, being eternal in nature, considers this connection as eternal as well. The doer desires the fruits of good actions, which manifest as favorable circumstances. They find happiness in these circumstances. As long as they crave this happiness, they cannot escape sorrow. This is because happiness is preceded and followed by sorrow, and one is constantly separated from it. The separation that one does not desire inevitably occurs, and this is a fundamental principle. In other words, one cannot abandon the desire for happiness, and sorrow cannot abandon them. When the individual surrenders themselves to the Lord, they become one with Him, and their connection with the body, which was based on ignorance, is severed. This oneness with the Lord was always present, but it was not experienced due to the individual's egoistic actions. Now, by dedicating all actions to the Lord, the individual's sense of doership is eliminated, and they attain selfless love. When the individual surrenders to the Lord, the favorable and unfavorable circumstances that arise are transformed into manifestations of the Lord's grace and mercy. In other words, when favorable circumstances arise, the individual sees them as the Lord's mercy, and when unfavorable circumstances arise, they see them as the Lord's grace. The difference between mercy and grace is that the Lord sometimes bestows mercy by showing love and affection, liberating the individual from the bondage of actions, while at other times, He bestows grace by disciplining and punishing the individual, destroying their sins. Through these means, the Lord makes the devotee strong and tolerant. However, the devotee remains pleased in both situations, as their focus is solely on the Lord, rather than on the favorable or unfavorable circumstances. As it is said:
"Lalane tadane maturna karunya yatharbhake,
Tad vadeva maheshasya nianthur guna-doshayoh."
"Just as a mother's love is not limited to either nurturing or disciplining her child, the Supreme Lord's control over the virtues and vices of living beings is not limited to either mercy or grace."

Appendix - The Lord concludes the discussion that began with the phrase "yanti mad-yajino 'pi mam" (9.25), stating that by dedicating all actions and objects to Him, one becomes liberated from the bondage of actions and the fruits of both good and bad actions, ultimately attaining Him. Actions and their fruits can be either good or bad. Performing actions for the benefit of others is considered a good action, while performing actions for personal gain is considered a bad action. Favorable circumstances are considered good fruits, while unfavorable circumstances are considered bad fruits. The Lord's devotee dedicates good actions to the Lord, refrains from performing bad actions, and remains unaffected by either favorable or unfavorable circumstances. The accumulated good and bad actions of countless past lives are destroyed, just like a burning piece of grass is reduced to ashes. By dedicating everything to the Lord, the connection to the world (and its qualities) is severed, and only the connection to the Lord remains, which is eternal - "mamaivamsho jivaloke jivabhutah sanatanah" (Gita 15.7). Considering something that is not one's own as one's own leads only to bondage. The devotee, having no sense of ownership or attachment to any object, person, or action, becomes liberated. Here, the path of surrender is referred to as "Sannyasa Yoga". The phrase "mam upaishyasi" means that the devotee becomes one with the Lord, losing their individual identity - "jnanI tvatmaiv me matam" (Gita 7.18). This is known as the path of love and non-duality.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 9 ]
Connection - Now a doubt arises that those who are devoted to the Lord are liberated by Him, and those who are not devoted to Him are not liberated. In this, the Lord's kindness and impartiality are not seen, but rather partiality and bias. To this, it is said -
I am equal to all beings; no one is hateful or dear to me. But those who worship me with devotion, I am in them and they are in me. 29. Aham: I, 
sarvabhuteshu: in all beings, 
samah: am equal, 
na: not, 
me: to me, 
dveshyah: hateful, 
asti: is, 
na: not, 
priyah: dear. Those who worship me with devotion, 
te: they, 
bhajanti: worship, 
tu: indeed, 
mam: me, 
bhaktya: with devotion, 
mayi: in me, 
te: they, 
teshu: in them, 
ca: and, 
api: also, 
aham: I. Explanation - 'I am equal to all beings' - I am not a subject of the stationary or moving world. The meaning is that I am equally present in all beings, and my merciful glance is on all. The meaning is that I am all-pervading, perfect, and equally present in all - 'Maya tatam idam sarvam jagad avyaktamurtina' (Gita 9.4), and my merciful glance is equally on all - 'Suhridam sarvabhutanam' (Gita 5.29). I am not less in one and more in another, meaning I am not less in an ant because it is small, and more in an elephant because it is big; I am not less in a low-born and more in a Brahmin; I am not less in those who are opposed to me and more in those who are favorable to me. This is not the case, because all beings are my parts, my forms. Since they are my forms, they can never be separated from me, and I can never be separated from them. Therefore, I am equal to all, and I have no partiality. The meaning is that even though there is inequality among beings due to birth, actions, circumstances, and various other factors, I am still equally present in all, and I am not more or less in any. 'No one is hateful or dear to me' - The Lord previously said that He is equal to all beings, and now, explaining this further, He says that no being is an object of His love or hatred. Even if a being performs many auspicious actions like Vedic sacrifices and charity, it is not an object of His love, and even if another being performs many inauspicious actions like injustice and cruelty, it is not an object of His hatred. The reason is that the Lord is equally present in all beings and has equal mercy on all, and all beings are equally dear to Him because they are His parts. However, it is true that one who performs actions with a desire for results will attain a higher state, and one who performs inauspicious actions will attain a lower state, i.e., hell or one of the 8.4 million species. But even then, the virtuous and the sinful are not objects of His love or hatred. The material elements created by the Lord, such as earth, water, fire, air, and space, also do not show partiality in providing a place for beings to live, quenching their thirst, giving them light, or providing them with space to move. Then how can beings become objects of His love or hatred due to their good or bad actions? The reason is that they are all parts of the Lord, His forms. Just as when one hand of a person is in pain, the person does not hate that hand; rather, they try to alleviate its pain. 1. This verse has two parts - the first part describes those who do not worship, and the second part describes those who do worship. 2. Here, the word 'priya' (dear) should be understood as an object of love, because the Lord has equal love for all beings - 'All are my dear, all are my creation' (Ramayana 7.86.2). Therefore, the Lord cannot deny this. Another point is that the word 'dveshya' (hateful) is accompanied by the word 'raga' (love), because love and hatred are a pair of opposites. This pair of opposites is denied here.

* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
[ Chapter 9 ]
[ Verse 29 ]
Just as a hand that is afflicted with pain does not perform its functions, and hinders one's work and sleep, while the other hand performs all the functions of the body. However, the person does not have any liking or disliking for either hand, considering both as their own limbs. Similarly, for one who follows my words and principles, and is a virtuous person, and another who contradicts my words and principles, and is a wicked person, I do not have any liking or disliking for them. The difference in their behavior and conduct will result in a difference in their consequences, but I do not have any liking or disliking for anyone. If I had liking or disliking, then it would not be possible for me to say, "I am the same in all beings" (Samo'ham sarvabhuteshu), because liking and disliking arise due to inequality. Those who worship me with devotion, who have no attachment, liking, or affection for the world, who consider me as their only goal, and who work day and night only for my satisfaction, using their body, senses, mind, and speech, are in me, and I am in them (Gita, 9.14 and 10.9). This does not mean that those who are ordinary beings and do not follow my instructions are not in me, and I am not in them. Rather, they do not consider themselves to be in me, saying, "We are worldly beings, living in the world!" They do not understand that the world and the body are always changing, so how can they remain stable in such a world and body? Due to this lack of understanding, they consider themselves to be established in the world and the body. On the other hand, those who are engaged in my remembrance and worship, day and night, and consider me to be present everywhere, in all countries, at all times, in all things, in all persons, in all events, and in all circumstances, are in me in a special way, and I am in them in a special way. Another meaning is that those who establish a relationship with me, saying, "I am the Lord's, and the Lord is mine," become so intimate with me that we become one - "there is no difference between us" (Narada Bhakti Sutra 41). Therefore, they are in me, and I am in them. A third meaning is that they do not have any sense of "I-ness" or ego, because "I-ness" is a limitation. When this limitation is removed, they remain in me alone. Now, if someone asks, "Lord, you are specially present in your devotees, and less so in others. Is this not a sign of inequality in you?" The Lord replies, "My dear, this inequality is due to the devotees themselves. If someone worships me, takes refuge in me, and I do not show them special love, or manifest specially in them, then that would be inequality on my part. It would not be just if I remained equal in both those who worship me and those who do not. This would make the worship and devotion of the devotees meaningless. To avoid this inequality, I respond to each one according to their approach - 'ye yatha mam prapadyante, tams tathaiva bhajamy aham' (Gita 4.11). Therefore, this inequality is due to the devotees' own feelings and approaches. For example, a son who does good deeds is called a good son, and one who does bad deeds is called a bad son. This distinction between a good son and a bad son is due to their actions, not due to any difference in the parents' love for them. A cow's udders may be infested with leeches that suck blood instead of milk, but this is not the cow's fault, but rather the leeches' own doing. Electricity can produce both ice and fire, but this is not due to any inequality in the electricity itself, but rather due to the instruments used. Similarly, those who do not recognize me, do not worship me, and do not follow my instructions, are not unequal due to me, but due to their own actions. As it is said, "Even the liberated ones, who have no desires, may have preferences for certain people or things, based on their qualities, feelings, and actions" (Kirata 3.12).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
A piece of wood, a glass shard, and a lens - there is no difference in the sun's rays as they fall on these three objects; however, when placed in the sun, the piece of wood blocks the sun's rays, the glass shard does not block them, and the lens concentrates the rays to produce fire. The implication is that this difference is not in the sun, but in the objects that come into contact with it. The sun's rays fall equally on all objects, and they are revealed in those objects to the extent that they are capable of receiving them. Similarly, God is equally present in all living beings, perfect and complete. However, those who come into contact with God and are devoted to Him experience a special manifestation of God's presence and grace. The more they love God, the more God's love is revealed to them. When they surrender themselves to God, God also surrenders Himself to them. Thus, God's special grace and love are revealed according to the devotion of His devotees. [ Chapter 9 ]
The implication is that human beings consider themselves to be part of the world due to their attachment to worldly things. When they begin to worship God with love, their worldly attachment disappears, and they see themselves in God and God in themselves. From God's perspective, they were always in God and God was in them; it was only their attachment that prevented them from realizing this. Here, God uses the word "ye" (those who) to indicate that anyone, regardless of their country, dress, state, sect, caste, or stage of life, can worship Him with devotion and experience His presence. If God had specified any particular caste, sect, or stage of life, it would have implied partiality on His part. However, God has given everyone the freedom to worship Him and experience His presence. Appendix - "Samoham sarvabhuteshu" (I am equally present in all living beings) - whether a living being offers their actions and objects to God or not, it makes no difference to God. God remains the same. No particular caste, sect, caste, or action has any effect on God. Therefore, anyone from any caste, sect, or stage of life can approach God, become His devotee, and attain Him. "Na me dweshyo'sti na priyah" (I have no one I hate or love) - from God's perspective, there is no one other than Himself. How can there be any object of hatred or love? It is the living being who becomes bound to the world due to their attachment to good or bad actions and their consequences, and who becomes liberated by renouncing this attachment. Therefore, bondage and liberation are the experiences of the living being, not God. The living being is the one who creates differences, not God. In the eleventh verse of the fourth chapter, God said, "Ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamy aham" (I reward those who approach Me in the same way that they approach Me). Here, God says the same thing: "Ye bhajanti tu mam bhaktya mayi te teshu chapay aham" (Those who worship Me with devotion, I am in them and they are in Me). God is equally present in all living beings, without any difference. However, those who worship Him with love are in God and God is in them, meaning that God is specially revealed in them. Just as water is present everywhere in the earth, but is specially revealed in a well, God is present everywhere in the world, but is specially revealed in His devotees. This special revelation is due to the devotee's love and God's grace. Just as the ghee (clarified butter) present in the body of a cow is of no use to the cow, but the ghee extracted from its milk is useful, God's presence in the world is of no use to people unless they approach Him with love and devotion. Only then can their sins be removed. Ordinary people do not see God even though they are under His jurisdiction, but devotees see God everywhere (Gita 6.30). Devotees love God, and God loves His devotees - "Priyo hi jnanino'tyartham aham sa cha mama priyah" (Gita 7.17). Therefore, devotees are in God and God is in His devotees. When the living being turns towards Me, their millions of sins are destroyed (Ramayana, Sundar Kand 44.1).

The meaning is that there is no inequality in God, but the inequality is in the living beings who are averse to God. In reality, God is 'samo 'ham sarvabhuteshu' (I am equally present in all beings), but in experience, God is 'mayi te teshu chapyaham' (I am in them and they are in me). The meaning is that even though God is equally and fully present in all beings, only the devotees experience Him, not others. In fact, the power to experience Him is also obtained from God. The only task of a human being is to come before God. In the Ramayana, it is said:
"Satawan sam mohi may jag dekhA, moten sant adhik kari lekha" (Manas, Aranya 36.2)
The meaning is that God's equal presence, love, mercy, and affection are present in all beings, but they are especially visible in the devotees. This special quality in the devotees comes from their love for God, which is a result of God's mercy and is given by God. The devotees have a unique absorption, love, and affection for God, which is not found in others. Therefore, God also has a special love for the devotees. The mutual love between the devotees and God is expressed in the words "mayi te teshu chapyaham". Srimad Bhagavad Gita

[ Chapter 9 ]
He is completely wicked. This means that even if he has been committing evil deeds in the past and is still doing so in the present, but is now devoted to me with an unwavering mind, his wicked deeds have not completely ceased. In other words, due to his past habits, he may still commit sinful acts in certain situations. Even in such a state, he is devoted to me because his goal is no longer to attain wealth, prosperity, respect, comfort, or other worldly pleasures. His sole objective is to be devoted to me alone. Now, a question arises as to how such a wicked person can be devoted to the Lord. There could be several reasons for this, such as:

(1) He may fall into a difficult situation where he finds no support or help from anyone. In such a state, he may suddenly remember the words he had heard earlier, "The Lord is the helper of all, and by taking refuge in Him, all problems are solved."

(2) He may come into contact with a good environment where great saints and mahatmas have lived and are still living, and their influence may inspire him to develop an interest in the Lord. (3) He may hear the stories of sinful people like Valmiki, Ajamila, and Sadan, the butcher, who became devotees of the Lord and underwent a transformation due to the power of devotion. This may awaken a good impression from his past, which is present in all living beings. (4) He may experience a situation where he is saved from a great calamity, and this may lead him to believe in the existence of a extraordinary power that saves him. He may realize that this power is the Lord, and therefore, he should surrender to Him. (5) He may have the darshan (vision) of a saint, and the saint's mercy may fall upon him, as in the case of Valmiki and Ajamila. There are many such stories in the Puranas and Bhaktamal, where people's hearts changed suddenly, and they became great devotees of the Lord. Now, a question arises as to how the mind of a wicked person can be fixed on the Lord, when even those who have been practicing devotion and meditation for years are not able to fix their minds on the Lord. The answer lies in the fact that the term "ananyabhak" does not mean that one's mind is constantly fixed on the Lord like a stream of oil. Rather, it means that one does not worship or take refuge in anyone else except the Lord. The wicked person's sole support and refuge is the Lord, just like a devoted wife's sole love and devotion are for her husband. She remains faithful to him even in her dreams. The key aspect of being an "ananyabhak" is to change one's ego and realize that "I belong to the Lord, and the Lord belongs to me." This transformation of ego brings about purification much faster than practices like japa (chanting), tapa (austerity), yajna (sacrifice), and dana (charity). There are three aspects to this transformation of ego:

(1) Eradicating the ego: This can be achieved through jnana yoga (the path of knowledge). In the state of self-realization, one understands that the "I" or the ego is not one's true nature. The ego is a product of the mind and is not the ultimate reality. (2) Purifying the ego: This can be achieved through karma yoga (the path of action). For example, a son may say, "I am a son, and these are my parents." This means that his duty is to serve his parents, regardless of whether they acknowledge him as their son or not. Similarly, one's relationship with others, such as mother, brother, wife, children, and family members, is based on the principle of duty and service. As the Ramayana says, "Good and bad thoughts are present in everyone's heart, and the Lord is the ancient and eternal one who is beyond all this." (Manas 5.40.3)

[ Verse 30 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
If we look at him, he is not unrighteous. The reason is that he has become 'ananyabhak', meaning 'I am only the Lord's and the Lord is only mine; I do not belong to the world and the world does not belong to me.' In this way, he has become the Lord's from within, and he has changed his ego from within. Therefore, his behavior will improve soon, as all behavior is based on one's ego. One should follow their duty. I should not look at their actions towards me or towards the world. It is not my duty to look at others' duties, as one who looks at others' duties deviates from their own duty. Therefore, they have complete authority over me, but I do not have the authority to make them act according to my will. In this way, by not looking at others' duties and only following one's own duty, the ego becomes pure, as the ego becomes impure due to the desire for one's own happiness and comfort. (3) Changing the ego - the ego changes through Bhakti Yoga. Just as a woman's ego changes after marriage, and she considers her husband's house as her own, his Dharma (righteous duty) as her own, and becomes devoted to him, similarly, a person's ego changes when they become one with the Lord, thinking 'I am the Lord's and the Lord is mine.'

'Sadhur Eva Sa Mantavyah' - Now, a question arises that if someone was previously unrighteous and still has not completely pure behavior, should we consider them unrighteous based on their past actions or righteous based on their current devotion? The Lord says that we should consider them righteous. Here, 'Mantavyah' (should be considered) is a command, meaning it is the Lord's special instruction. The instruction to consider someone as righteous is given only when their righteousness is not apparent. If they had no unrighteousness at all, why would the Lord say 'consider them righteous'? This shows that they still have some unrighteousness, but the Lord says to consider them righteous anyway. The reason for this is that people usually look at someone's external behavior and judge them based on that, without considering their inner intentions. For example, if someone is known to be a devotee and has good behavior for 20-25 years, but is seen coming out of a prostitute's house one night, people immediately think that they are not as good as they thought, and their previous good impression is lost. Similarly, if someone is known to be unjust and sinful, but is seen taking a bath on the banks of the Ganges and sitting with a peaceful face, people may think they are a good person, but others who know their past may say that they are just pretending. In this way, people judge others based on their external behavior, without considering their inner intentions. But the Lord's vision is different, and He looks at the inner intentions of a person.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The Lord does not forget the devotion of His devotees, 
even if they have committed mistakes in the past. As stated in the Ramayana (1.29.3), 
"Rahati na prabhu chit chook kie ki, 
Karta surati say bar hiye ki."
This is because the Lord is a knower of the inner feelings of the devotees - 
"bhavagrahi janardanah."
In the second chapter, while discussing Karma Yoga, 
it is mentioned that the intellect of a Karma Yogi is 
"vayasayatmika buddhi" (Gita 2.41, 2.44), 
meaning that the intellect is resolute and determined. This determination arises from the fact that the Karma Yogi 
has made a firm resolve to perform their duties without 
attachment or aversion, and to remain equipoised in success or failure. However, in the case of a devotee, the determination is not 
just of the intellect, but of the self - "samyagvyavasitah" (Gita 2.41). This means that the devotee has made a firm resolve to dedicate 
themselves to the Lord, and this resolve is not just a mental 
decision, but a deep-seated conviction of the self. [ Chapter 9 ]
The Lord says that one who has made this resolve is indeed a 
sadhaka, and will soon become a dharmatma (Gita 9.31). Where the resolve is based on intellectual conviction, 
it may not be stable, but when the self is firmly resolved, 
it becomes unshakeable. For example, a woman who has gotten married 
makes a resolve to dedicate herself to her husband, 
and this resolve remains firm and unshakeable. Similarly, when a devotee makes a resolve to dedicate 
themselves to the Lord, it becomes an integral part of their being, 
and they will not waver from it. In the case of Jnana Yoga and Karma Yoga, the emphasis is on 
the intellect - "esa te abhita sankhye buddhir yoge tvimam shrinu" (Gita 2.39). However, in Bhakti Yoga, the emphasis is on the self, 
and the devotee becomes firmly resolved - "samyagvyavasitah". What is resolved in the mind and intellect can be forgotten, 
but what is resolved in the self cannot be forgotten. This is because the mind and intellect are not always present, 
but the self is always present. Therefore, when a devotee makes a resolve to dedicate 
themselves to the Lord, it becomes a part of their very being, 
and they will not forget it. The realization that "I am the Lord's and the Lord is mine" 
is a conviction that arises from the self, not from the mind or intellect. Once this conviction is established, it can never be shaken; 
because the self is an integral part of the Lord, and the Lord is 
the very essence of the self. However, due to ignorance, the self may mistakenly identify 
itself with the material world (Gita 15.7). But when this ignorance is removed, the self realizes its true 
nature and its eternal relationship with the Lord - 
"nasto mohah, smritir labdha" (Gita 18.73).

Vyakhya - 'Kshipram bhavati dharmaatma' - he immediately becomes dharmaatma, i.e., extremely pure. Because this jiva (living being) is a part of the Supreme Self, and when its goal is also to attain the Supreme Self, then what delay can there be in its becoming dharmaatma? How can it remain paapaatma (sinful)? Because it was inherently dharmaatma, but due to its connection with the world, it had become paapaatma, which was a temporary condition. Now, when its ego changes and its connection with the world is severed, it remains in its original state (dharmaatma). This jiva, when it was not paapaatma, was pure, and when it became paapaatma, it was still pure. Because, being a part of the Supreme Self, the jiva is always pure. It was only due to its connection with the world that it became paapaatma. As soon as its connection with the world is severed, it remains pure in its original state. It is true that as long as a person has the desire to commit sin, he cannot make a firm resolve to move towards God. However, it is not a rule that a sinful person cannot make such a resolve. Because, being a part of the Supreme Self, every jiva is inherently pure. It is only due to its attachment to the world that it develops temporary impurities. If it develops a dislike for sin and makes a firm resolve to worship God, it can quickly become dharmaatma. Because, where there is a desire for the world, there is also an inclination towards God. If the inclination towards God becomes strong, desire and attachment are destroyed, and there can be no delay in attaining God. The statement "he quickly becomes dharmaatma" means that any impurities or bad habits that he may have will not persist. Because all impurities arise from giving importance to the world. But when he becomes free from worldly desires and longs only for God, the importance of the world disappears, and only the importance of God remains. This is what makes him dharmaatma. A profound truth is that when the doer changes, the actions also change automatically. For example, if someone wants to become dharmaatma by performing virtuous actions, it may take time. But if he changes his ego, i.e., his sense of self, he can quickly become dharmaatma. Similarly, even a great sinner can become dharmaatma, a saint, or a devotee by changing his ego and realizing "I am God's, and God is mine." This means that when a person identifies himself with the body and the world, and seeks pleasure through attachment, he becomes kaamaatma (controlled by desires). * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
One who has a firm conviction in their ego that 'I am not a thief', cannot commit theft. The implication is that a change in ego leads to a change in actions. These two examples prove that the doer is as they are, and their actions are accordingly, and the doer's conviction becomes stronger based on their actions. Similarly, here, even a wicked person, by becoming 'ananyabhak' (exclusive devotee), i.e., having an exclusive relationship with the Lord, saying 'I belong only to the Lord, and the Lord alone belongs to me', their ego becomes firmly established in the fact that 'I belong to the Lord, not to the world', which is the absolute truth. In this way, when the ego changes, even if there is a slight decrease in actions, one quickly becomes a righteous person (Dharmatma). Here, a doubt may arise that in the previous verse, the Lord referred to the person as 'suduracharah' (very wicked), so why does the Lord call them 'Dharmatma' (righteous person) now? The solution is that if the wickedness of the wicked person is eradicated, they will become a righteous person. Therefore, whether you call them a righteous person or a Dharmatma, it's the same thing. -
'Shashvachchanti nigachchhati' - one who becomes a Dharmatma through mere religious actions, due to the presence of desires for worldly pleasures and wealth, may attain those, but not eternal peace. When the wicked person's ego changes and they become one with the Lord, their desires and worldly attachments cease to exist. Hence, they attain lasting peace. |
[ Chapter 9 ]
'Kaunteya pratijanihi na me bhaktah pranashyati' - here, the Lord makes Arjuna take an oath that 'my devotee will not perish'. The implication is that war is about to begin, and the Lord has already taken an oath not to take up arms. However, when Bhishma later takes an oath that 'if I do not take up arms against Hari, I will be ashamed to call myself the son of Ganga', the Lord's oath will be broken, but the devotee's (Bhishma's) oath will not. The Lord has already accepted Arjuna as His devotee in the third verse of the fourth chapter, saying 'bhakto'si me sakha cheti' (you are my devotee and friend). Therefore, the Lord asks Arjuna to take the oath, because if Arjuna takes the oath, even the Lord cannot break it. The statement 'my devotee will not perish' means that when the devotee stands before the Lord, there is no possibility of their downfall. The reason for downfall was the ego's attachment to the body. When the devotee becomes exclusively devoted to the Lord, their ego changes, and there is no possibility of downfall. If a wicked person can become a devotee, then it is possible for a devotee to become wicked again - this is what justice says. To refute this, the Lord says that this justice does not apply here. In the Lord's justice, even the most wicked can become devotees, but once they become devotees, they will not fall again, i.e., they will not become wicked. Thus, the Lord's justice is also filled with mercy, and He is both just and merciful. -
Another implication is that being a part of the Supreme Self, one is 'chetan amal sahaj sukharsi' (conscious, pure, and naturally blissful). Therefore, the eternal peace that is inherent in the Self is attained when one becomes a Dharmatma, i.e., has an exclusive relationship with the Lord. This peace was not being experienced due to attachment to the world. Appendix - just as a patient forms a relationship with a doctor, a person forms a relationship with the Lord when they have faith in their own weakness and the Lord's omnipotence. The implication is that when a person is troubled by worldly sorrows and feels helpless, yet has faith that the Lord's merciful power can remove their weakness and save them from worldly sorrows, they immediately become a devotee - 'kshipram bhavati dharmatma' (quickly becomes a righteous person). Will a hungry person delay eating when they are given food? As long as a person sees some strength, capability, or specialty in themselves, they do not become 'ananyabhak' (exclusive devotee).

[ Chapter 9 ]
[ Verse 31 ]
The term "ananyabhak" (exclusive devotee) refers to one who has no other recourse to alleviate their suffering. When one becomes an exclusive devotee, they become a righteous person, a devotee of the Lord. A devotee does not fall from their path because they are steadfast in their devotion to the Lord, and their means and end are both the Lord. They do not rely on their own strength but rather on the Lord's strength. A question may arise as to why the Lord says in the 18th chapter, "If you do not listen to me due to pride, you will fall" (18.58), even though Arjuna is considered a devotee (Gita 4.3). The resolution to this is that a devotee can only fall when they abandon the Lord's shelter and take refuge in pride. As long as they remain under the Lord's shelter, they will not fall. Devotees are like the Lord's young children, while the wise are like the older children. Just as a mother loves all her children equally but takes care of the younger ones, the Lord takes care of His devotees, who are completely dependent on Him. The Lord Himself bears the burden of their spiritual journey (Gita 9.22). However, the wise, who are self-sufficient, do not require the Lord's care. Therefore, a seeker of knowledge can fall, but a devotee cannot. The gods say to the Lord:
"Those who are not devoted to You, who are not purified in their intellect, and who consider themselves liberated, are actually bound. Even if they attain the highest state through great effort, they will still fall down." (Srimad Bhagavatam 10.2.32)

The gods further say:
"But, Lord, those who are Your devotees, who have genuine love for You, do not fall from their path. Protected by You, they move about fearlessly, even among great obstacles, and no hindrance can stop them." (Srimad Bhagavatam 10.2.33)

The Vedas praise the Lord, saying:
"Those who are proud of their knowledge and do not respect devotion to You, even if they attain a high state, will still fall. But those who have faith in You, who abandon all other hopes, and who become Your servants, can cross the ocean of existence without effort by chanting Your name."

The Lord says:
"Even if My devotee is tempted by sense objects and has not yet controlled their senses, they will still not be overwhelmed by sense objects due to their strong devotion." (Srimad Bhagavatam 11.14.18)

In this way, the Lord explains that a devotee who has not yet controlled their senses can still be saved by their devotion, whereas a seeker of knowledge can fall due to their pride.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
*
[ Chapter 9 ]
Even if the senses, which are always attracted to their respective objects, try to drag one towards them, still, due to the increasing power of My devotion, one is not defeated by the senses. 'No inauspiciousness ever befalls the devotees of Vasudeva.' (Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva 149.131)
'Who can harm one who has the great Lord Rama as their protector?' (Ramayana, Bala Kanda 126.4)
'Kunti, take a vow' - The Lord asks Arjuna to take a vow, because even the Lord cannot refuse a vow taken by a devotee. Devotion is the Lord's weakness. That is why the Lord told Durvasa, 
'I am completely dependent on My devotees, I am not independent. My heart is controlled by the devotees, and I am very fond of them.' (Srimad Bhagavata 9.4.63)
[Verse 32]
The words 'Kunti, take a vow, for My devotee will never perish' should give the seeker firm faith that they will never fall, because they belong to the Lord. Connection - In this context, the Lord has described seven types of people who are eligible for devotion. Among them, He has described the wicked in two verses. Now, in the next verse, He describes four types of people who are eligible for devotion. Even those who take refuge in Me, though they may be of sinful birth, women, Vaishyas, or Shudras, they too attain the highest goal. (32)
O son of Pritha, 
those who 
take refuge 
in Me, 
though they may be 
of sinful birth, 
women, 
Vaishyas, 
or Shudras, 
they too 
attain 
the highest goal. Commentary - 'Those who take refuge in Me' - The Lord refers to those whose behavior is bad in this life, i.e., those who are sinners in this life, whom He called 'wicked' in the 30th verse. Those whose behavior was bad in their previous life, i.e., those who are sinners of their previous life and are born in lower species to suffer the consequences of their past sins, are called 'of sinful birth' here. As it is said, 'All living beings, from the lowest to the highest, are eligible for devotion.' (Shandilya Bhakti Sutra 78) Just as kindness, forgiveness, and generosity are common virtues that all humans are eligible for, similarly, all living beings, from the lowest to the highest, are eligible for the Lord's devotion. The reason is that since all living beings are parts of the Lord, they are not ineligible to move towards the Lord, to practice devotion, or to stand before Him. The term 'of sinful birth' is so broad that it can include demons, Rakshasas, animals, birds, etc. All these are considered eligible for the Lord's devotion. Shandilya Rishi has said, 'Even those born in contemptible species, such as cows, trees, animals, snakes, and other foolish-minded beings, have easily attained Me through single-minded devotion.' (Srimad Bhagavata 11.12.8)

[ Verse 32 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
The reason is that the fruits of past sinful actions are in the form of unfavorable circumstances of birth and experience; therefore, they cannot hinder one's progress towards the Lord. The fact that one may not be able to attach oneself to the Lord due to lack of qualification is no reason. All living beings are the Lord's; hence, everyone can come before Him. In other words, whoever yearns for the Lord with a sincere heart is eligible for devotion to Him. Even those born of sinful wombs can attain the highest state and become supremely pure by taking refuge in the Lord. From a worldly perspective, impurity is considered to be the result of corrupt behavior. However, in reality, all impurity arises from being averse to the Lord. Just as embers become coal as soon as they are separated from the fire, and no amount of soap can remove the blackness of coal, but if it is put back into the fire, it regains its glow. Similarly, the impurity or blackness in the living being, who is a part of the Lord, is due to being averse to the Lord. If it comes before the Lord, its impurity is completely eradicated, and it becomes supremely pure and radiant. It becomes so pure that the Lord makes it His crown jewel. When someone cries out to the Lord in distress, the power of that cry can move the Lord's heart, which is not possible through good deeds. Just as a mother loves her child who does good deeds, but when her child cries out to her in distress, she cannot bear to see it cry and immediately takes it in her arms. Similarly, even the most wicked person, if they cry out to the Lord in distress, the Lord takes them in His arms and loves them. This proves that when one's heart is turned towards the Lord, even the sins of this life cannot hinder one's progress, let alone past sins. The word "striyah" (women) is used here to indicate that women of any caste, stage of life, country, or dress can attain the highest state and become supremely pure by taking refuge in the Lord. Examples include Devahuti, Shabari, Kunti, and Draupadi in ancient times, and Mirabai, Karmabai, and Phoolibai in recent times. Similarly, many men from the Vaishya and Shudra castes, such as Samadhi, Tuladhara, Vidura, Sanjaya, and Nishada, have become devotees of the Lord. In other words, all those who are considered to be of low birth, women, Vaishyas, and Shudras can attain the highest state by taking refuge in the Lord. Special Note
In this verse, the word "papayonayah" (those born of sinful wombs) is used independently. This word cannot be considered as an adjective for women, Vaishyas, and Shudras, as it would lead to many contradictions. Women can be from any of the four castes, and they have the right to participate in Vedic rituals along with their husbands. Therefore, women cannot be considered as being born of sinful wombs. The fact that the Lord has mentioned women separately indicates that they can take refuge in Him independently, without being dependent on their husbands. Women should take refuge in the Lord alone, without relying on anyone else. If the word "papayonayah" is considered as an adjective for Vaishyas, it is also not logical, as according to the Shruti, Vaishyas are not considered to be born of sinful wombs. The Shruti states that those with good character are born in the castes of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas, while those with bad character are born in the wombs of dogs, pigs, and Chandals.

* 
Srimad Bhagavad Gita
* 
[ Chapter 9 ]
For the Vaishyas, there is the right to read the Vedas and perform Vedic rituals like yajna, which leads to the attainment of Brahman (Brahman) - 'Brahmaiva san brahmapyeti' (Brihadaranyaka 4.4.6). If the term 'papayonayah' is considered to be an adjective for Shudras, it is not logical; because Shudras are included among the four varnas. Therefore, the term 'papayonayah' should be applied to those low-caste people, such as Yavanas, Hunas, and Khas, who are outside the four varnas. Just as there is no restriction for any child to go to its mother's lap, because they are her own children, similarly, since all living beings are parts of God, there is no restriction for them to move towards God. Although animals, birds, trees, and creepers do not have the understanding or capability to move towards God, they can still come before God due to their past karma or some other reason. Hence, the term 'papayonayah' can also be applied to animals and birds in an exceptional sense. There have been devotees like Gajendra and Jatayu among animals and birds. A thought-provoking point
The body does not have pride in itself. Where the body has pride, there is no discernment that 'I am separate from the body', and one remains a slave to the body, which is a machine that produces flesh, blood, urine, and feces. This is ignorance, and due to the dominance of ignorance, a person cannot follow the path of devotion or knowledge. Therefore, the behavior towards the body is essential for worldly dignity, and one should follow that dignity. However, in moving towards God, the importance is of the self, not the body. The essence is that one who desires devotion or liberation is the self, not the body. Although the self identifies with the body due to its nature, the self can never become the body, and the body can never become the self. The self is always the self, and the body is always the body. The self has unity with the Supreme Soul, and the body has unity with the world. As long as one identifies with the body, one is not eligible for devotion or knowledge and cannot resolve all doubts. This identification with the body is removed through emotions. When a person has emotions for God, their mind does not go towards the body or other things; they become completely absorbed in God, which removes their identification with the body. Hence, they do not need to use their discretion, and no doubts arise in them regarding varna or ashrama. Similarly, discretion also removes identification with the body. When identification with the body is removed, one does not have pride in their varna or ashrama, because the self does not have varna or ashrama. In moving towards God, emotions are primary, not birth. One who gives importance to birth does not have emotions, and devotion to God does not arise in them. This is because one who considers birth to be primary has a strong sense of 'I' related to the body, which does not allow them to be devoted to God. The body is not a devotee of God, and the devotee is not the body; rather, the self is the devotee. Similarly, the Jiva (individual soul) cannot attain Brahman; only Brahman can attain Brahman, meaning that the Jiva does not have the nature of Brahman, and Brahman does not have the nature of Jiva. The Jiva is associated with life forces, while Brahman is not. Therefore, only Brahman can attain Brahman, meaning that the Jiva nature is removed. Appendix - In this context, 'vyapashraya' refers to a special refuge that has no other refuge. Previously, the sinful person of this life was mentioned (in the 30th-31st verses); now, the sinful person of the past life is being mentioned in this verse - 'ye 'pi syuh papayonayah'. Connection - The description of the remaining two eligible persons for devotion will be given in the next verse.

* Sadhak Sanjivani *
What to say of the pious Brahmins, the devotees, and the royal sages? Having obtained this impermanent and unhappy world, worship Me. (33)

(Those who are) pure in conduct, 
devotees,

and royal sages - what to say of them? Having obtained (this world), 
-
This is an obvious fact. -

-
Brahmins and royal sages. 'Imam lokam' (this world) refers to the human body. -
Worship Me. -
The reason is that actions are performed through external means (mind, intellect, senses, and body), so the purity obtained through them is also external. The terms 'pious Brahmins' and 'royal sages' are used to indicate this external purity. However, for those who take refuge in the Lord from within, the term 'devotees' is used. -
'Anityamasukham lokam imam prapya bhajasva mam' 
This human birth is the last of countless births, and it is possible to attain the Lord and bring joy to Him in this life. Therefore, this human birth is pure but impermanent - 'anitiam', meaning it is not eternal; it can end at any moment. Hence, one should strive for their liberation as soon as possible. This human body is not a source of happiness - 'asukham'. In the fifteenth verse of the eighth chapter, the Lord has described the human birth as a place of suffering. Therefore, one should not crave for sensual pleasures or waste their time and emotions on them when they obtain a human body. For the pious Brahmins and the royal sages, the term 'imam lokam' refers to the human body, which is obtained only for the purpose of attaining the Lord. The presence of the term 'bhaktah' (devotees) in between indicates that those who have pure conduct in their previous birth and are also pure in this birth, if they become devotees of the Lord, there should be no doubt about their liberation. The terms 'pious Brahmins', 'royal sages', and 'devotees' convey that the purity of this birth and the previous birth, as well as the purity of conduct in this birth, are all external. However, the Lord has not ordained that one will have another birth after attaining Him. On the contrary, this human birth is given only for the purpose of attaining the Lord. If one fails to attain the Lord and secure their liberation in this birth, they will not get such an opportunity in other bodies. Therefore, the Lord says, "Having obtained this human body, worship Me alone." 
Whatever uniqueness is present in humans is due to the Lord's grace. Here, the term 'bhaktah' (devotees) is used for both Brahmins and royal sages, like the example of a lamp in a house.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The Lord's intention in saying 'Māṁ bhajasva' (Worship me) is not that I will gain something by your worship, but rather that you will attain great benefit. Therefore, be eager to devote yourself solely to me, with me as your only goal and objective. The coming and going of worldly objects will continue automatically according to my will, but do not set your sights on ephemeral objects or consider them important. Turn away from them and focus solely on me. A profound statement: Just as a mother's gaze is upon her child's body, the Lord and his devotees focus on the true nature of living beings. This nature, being a part of the Lord, is pure, conscious, and indestructible. However, due to its connection with nature, it becomes involved in various behaviors. In the 29th verse, the Lord stated that he is equally present in all beings and has no affection or aversion towards anyone. Even the most wicked, who act contrary to the Lord's principles, can attain liberation by taking refuge in him and worshiping him. The Lord cannot consider them impure, for they are inherently pure as his parts. They are only temporarily afflicted by ephemeral flaws. The Lord has described two types of people: the presently wicked and those who were wicked in their previous birth. Even those born in lowly species, such as outcastes, or in animal species, can attain liberation by taking refuge in the Lord. [ Chapter 9 ]
The Lord now describes people of middle and higher classes. First, he mentions women, which includes the wives of Brahmins and Kshatriyas, who are also revered by Vaishyas. Next, he mentions Vaishyas, who are not as pious as Brahmins and Kshatriyas but are still twice-born. Then, there are Shudras, who are not twice-born and are not as pure as Vaishyas. Even women, Vaishyas, and Shudras can attain the highest goal by taking refuge in the Lord. It is obvious that Brahmins and Kshatriyas, who are of higher classes, can also attain the highest goal by taking refuge in the Lord. The Lord has mentioned seven types of people who are eligible for devotion: the wicked, those born in lowly species, women, Vaishyas, Shudras, Brahmins, and Kshatriyas. It would have been expected that the Lord would first mention the most qualified, such as pious Brahmins or Kshatriyas. However, the Lord first mentions the wicked, because in devotion, the more humble and free from pride one is, the more dear they are to the Lord. The wicked do not have the pride of being virtuous, so they naturally possess humility. This is why the Lord first mentions the wicked. Similarly, in the 12th chapter, the Lord states that he is more fond of devotees who have attained perfection and even more fond of those who are still striving (verses 13-20). An important point to note is that the Lord has categorized the seven types of devotees based on their social class (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra), behavior (wicked and those born in lowly species), and individuality (women). This shows that the Lord's devotion is not affected by social class, behavior, or individuality, as these are related to the body. However, the Lord's relationship is with the true nature, not the body. All beings are parts of the Lord and can attain liberation by taking refuge in him and worshiping him. With this understanding, the Lord has used the word 'bhajasva' (worship me) in the first person, indicating that the devotee should worship him directly.

[ Verse 33 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
There is not even a slight difference; because all are entitled to devotion, being parts of the Lord. Yes, no one is impure or unworthy because they are not with the Lord; rather, they are pure and worthy of liberation. The implication is that the uniqueness and speciality that has come to the seven entitled ones of devotion has not come from any varna, ashrama, emotion, conduct, etc., but from the relationship with the Lord, from devotion to the Lord. In the sixteenth verse of the seventh chapter, the Lord has described four types of devotees based on their emotions, and here, the seven types of entitled ones of devotion are described based on varna, conduct, and personality. The implication is that there is a difference among devotees based on their emotions, but from the Lord's side, no one is unworthy of devotion. Only humans can establish a relationship with the Lord because humans have turned away from the Lord, but the Lord has never turned away from any human. Therefore, all humans who have turned away from the Lord are free, capable, and entitled to turn towards the Lord and establish a relationship with Him. Therefore, no one should be disappointed in turning towards the Lord. There is no difference based on varna, conduct, etc. -
Appendix - From the thirtieth to the thirty-third verse, the Lord has mentioned the seven entitled ones of devotion and attainment of the Lord - the wicked, those born of sin, women, vaishyas, shudras, brahmins, and kshatriyas. There is no living being outside of these seven. Whatever one's birth, caste, or past sins, all humans are entitled to the Lord and His devotion. The names of the four varnas - brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, and shudra - have been mentioned in these verses. The name of women has been mentioned separately so that one does not think that only men are included in the four varnas. Those who are below the four varnas, such as yavanas, hunas, and khasas, are all included in the category of those born of sin. Animals and birds can also be considered as those born of sin because all living beings are parts of the Lord, and there is no restriction for anyone to turn towards the Lord. One who is currently committing sin is a "durachari" (wicked), and one who has been born in a low caste due to past sins is a "papyoni" (one born of sin). The implication is that even the most wicked and those born in the lowest caste are entitled to attain the Lord. Therefore, one should not be disappointed in attaining the Lord based on caste or conduct. Caste and conduct are temporary and artificial, but the relationship between humans and the Lord is eternal and real. Therefore, the Lord only considers the relationship of devotion, not caste or conduct. As stated in the Ramayana - "Oh Raghupati, listen to my words, I consider only devotion as a relationship." 
Caste, family, dharma, pride, wealth, strength, relatives, virtues, and cleverness - what is the use of these for a person devoid of devotion? He looks like a garden without water. -
People in the world look at external caste and conduct, not the inner essence. But the Lord looks at the essence, that this is My eternal part. In the sixteenth verse of the seventh chapter, the Lord has described four types of devotees based on their inner emotions - artharthi, artha, jijnasu, and jnani. And here, seven types of devotees are described based on external varna and conduct. In the seventh chapter, the Lord talks about those devotees who are already devoted to Him, and here, He talks about those humans who can become devoted to Him. The implication is that despite differences in varna, ashrama, dress, caste, and sect, all humans can become one of the four types of devotees - artharthi, artha, jijnasu, and jnani - and attain the Lord. In the matter of attaining the Lord, all are equal; there is no high or low. There is no one in any yoni who is unworthy of attaining the Lord, has been, or will be. -
The word "bhaktah" in the verse "Kimbhunar brahmanah punya bhakta rajarsayas tatha" implies that the glory is not of the pure conduct of brahmins or the kshatriya rsis, but of the devotion within them. The implication is that the Lord has no hatred for the wicked or those born of sin, nor does He have any partiality for the pure brahmins and kshatriyas.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 9 ]

All living beings are fundamentally the same (see Gita 9.29). Yet anyone who sings the Lord’s name with love—regardless of country, dress, caste, ashrama, community, or sect—has an intimate relationship with the Divine, expressed in the verse “mayi te teṣu cāpyaham” (Gita 9.29). Consequently, even the most sinful, the outcast, women, Vaishyas, Shudras, Brahmins, and Kshatriyas become united in devotion; no distinction remains. For this reason the Lord commands, “bhajasva mām” (chant My name). The term “bhajan” here means to be in the presence of the Lord, to feel beloved by Him, and to have the purpose of attaining Him. Acting with divine wisdom—serving others, feeling the urge to give, helping the destitute—is also considered bhajan. “Anityam‑asukhaṁ lokam imaṁ prāpya bhajasva mām” teaches that after attaining this transient, joy‑less body we should abandon the desire to keep living and enjoying pleasure, and instead devote ourselves to the Lord. The world offers no real happiness; pleasure is an illusion, and even the notion of “living” is an illusion—we die a little every moment. In verse 29 the Lord said that those who love‑filledly chant Him are already in Him, and He is in them. Hence He again commands, “bhajasva mām.”

From verse 29 through verse 33 the discussion centers on devotional service; the next verse (34) describes the form of that devotion. [ Verse 34 ]

**Sanskrit (Roman transliteration) and word‑by‑word meaning**  
mān‑manaḥ bhava: become one whose mind is fixed on Me  
mad‑bhaktaḥ: become My devotee  
mad‑yājī: become My worshipper  
mām namaskuru: salute Me  
mām eva iṣyasi: you will obtain Me alone  
yuktvā eva: having united  
am‑ātmanam: your own self  
mat‑parāyaṇaḥ: devoted to Me

**Explanation** – The Lord is speaking directly to the heart, where there is no blame toward the listener and only reverence exists. Arjuna is free of blame, which is why the Lord calls him “anasyave” (Gita 9.1). Thus the Lord shares his innermost counsel with Arjuna. The phrase “mad‑bhaktaḥ” (My devotee) implies that the seeker should develop exclusive intimacy with the Lord, forming a relationship that is eternally self‑evident. Human beings mistakenly identify themselves with external labels—caste, ashrama, sect, name—treating these as their true identity. The teaching urges the removal of this false, unreal identity and its replacement with the true identity: “I am yours, and you are mine.” This creates a natural, inherent closeness with the Divine. “mān‑manaḥ bhava” stresses that the mind dwells where love resides. The Lord’s unbroken connection with the devotee cannot be forgotten by Him, but the devotee may forget; therefore the Lord asks the devotee to become “mind‑fixed in Me.”

“mad‑yājī” (My worshipper) directs the devotee to perform every activity—eating, drinking, sleeping, waking, moving, working—as an act of worship to the Lord. All actions become worship when performed with that consciousness. “mām namaskuru” (salute Me) means that the devotee should remain perfectly content in all circumstances—whether favorable, adverse, or ordinary. Even if the Lord’s decision opposes the devotee’s personal wishes, the devotee must remain pleased.

[ Verse 34 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The man who, fearing loss and the after‑life, takes refuge in My feet—who is the supreme friend of the living being—experiences such events. He becomes My refuge, and in reality his happiness and decline are bound to My feet. In the same way, O Arjuna, you too must become entirely a refuge in My feet, not in any other refuge. Take shelter in Me; remain ever delighted in every decree of Mine. If anyone wishes to obtain any pleasure or comfort, that desire is never a true refuge in Me, because as long as one seeks some pleasure or comfort, he regards himself as possessing an independent existence. Only the one who has completely surrendered to My feet, who abandons all personal doctrines and merges his mind with My will, is truly considered to be in My feet. In such a person, not only My presence but also the entire world retains no trace of pleasure, comfort, or even a hint of respect. Even when he knows about favorable and unfavorable circumstances, none of that affects him; when any favorable or adverse event occurs by My will, the devotee who remains devoted to Me perceives no disparity in that event. Knowledge of the duality of favorable and adverse does not make the event appear in two forms; it appears solely as My grace. Whether My decree is favorable to the body or adverse, whatever event transpires from My decree should be regarded as My gift, and one should remain supremely delighted. If an adverse event arises due to the mind’s opposition, it must be recognized as My special grace, because that event lacks the devotee’s consent. In favorable events, the portion that has his consent becomes impure for him; in adverse events, only My pure decree exists, and one should be supremely pleased with this fact. Man does not desire adverse events, does not cause them, and does not approve them, yet such events occur. No matter what cause is assigned to bring about the event—though anyone may call it a cause—in reality it is My hand, My will, that brings the event about. Therefore the man should not be sorrowful or anxious about that event; rather, he should become increasingly delighted. His delight must not be because of My decree, but because of Me, the decreer. If the man’s welfare is absent, then…

For example, when someone commits a crime, he goes before the offender and says, “Whether you punish, reward, rebuke, or do anything, my supreme delight lies in that.” He does not think that the offender must decide in his favor. Likewise, the devotee becomes wholly surrendered to the Lord and says, “O Lord! I do not know in how many births I have acted contrary to You, nor the deeds I have performed. Yet the circumstances You send, in accordance with those deeds, will be wholly beneficial to me. Hence I shall have no dissatisfaction in any circumstance, only delight.”

“O Lord! How attentively You consider my deeds, that I do not know in which births or circumstances I have acted, and yet You devise such wondrous decrees to remove all those deeds! I cannot even comprehend Your decree, nor possess the power to understand it. Therefore, O Lord, why should I apply my intellect there? I must look only toward You. Whatever decree You make, Your hand is in it; it is Your work, which is supremely auspicious for me. This is the meaning of ‘Māṁ namaskuru’ (salute to Me).”

‘Mām evaiṣyasi yuktvā evam ātmānaṁ matparayanaḥ’ – here “evam” signifies that the devotee has offered himself to Me; “manmanaḥ” indicates that his inner self has become devoted to Me; “mad‑yāji” shows that his actions and material become My worship material; and “māṁ namaskuru” means his body is offered at My feet. Thus, having become devoted to Me, you will obtain Me. ‘Yuktvā evam ātmānaṁ’ (by attaching oneself to Me) means “I am of God”; upon this transformation, body, senses, mind, intellect, material, and action—all become attached to Me. (Manas 1.128.1)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 9 ]

The state that will arise is called **sharanagati** (complete surrender). When such surrender occurs, one is wholly devoted. The sense of “I” and “mine” disappears; even the faint scent of “I” and “my” no longer remains within. No longer does one think, “I am something, I have a principle, I hold certain beliefs,” etc. There is no doubt that only **my** attainment will occur. Doubt about my attainment appears only where the desire, respect, or sense of importance of another exists besides me. Because of desire, sense of importance, attachment, etc., even when one is perfectly fulfilled everywhere, one’s own attainment does not happen. The term **matparayanah** means that without the Lord’s will there is not even the slightest impulse to act or cause action. One becomes completely inseparable from the Lord, like a toy in His hand. **Special point (1)**  
When a person becomes a devotee of the Lord, identifies with the Lord, and declares “I am the Lord’s,” a rapid transformation takes place. The transformation is that the person becomes mentally united with the Lord, becomes a worshipper of the Lord, and remains pleased only with the Lord’s pure ordinance. These four aspects complete sharanagati, but the primary aspect is becoming the Lord’s devotee. The one who becomes the Lord’s own no longer possesses an independent mind‑intellect, material nature, action, or even a separate body. In worldly view, everything that is said to be “own”—which is created and perishable—does not remain truly one's. When one’s self is wholly offered, all natural things become the Lord’s; personal affection disappears. The mistake of personal affection is completely erased. **Special point (2)**  
No matter how much a human claims unity with the world, the world cannot be fully known. Likewise, no matter how much one claims unity with the body, one cannot become one with the body or truly know it. In reality, only by remaining distinct from world and body can they be known. In the same way, remaining separate from the Supreme Soul (Paramatma) prevents true knowledge of the Supreme Soul; only those who have become one with the Supreme Soul can truly know Him. When “I” and “mine” are entirely surrendered to the Lord, the joys and sorrows of the body appear as one’s own joys and sorrows, and the sense of an existence separate from the body disappears. Likewise, when a devotee experiences the self‑evident unity with the Lord, even the tiniest sense of separate existence vanishes. Just as changes that occur in the world by the Lord’s will do not affect the devotee, changes in the gross, subtle, and causal bodies likewise have no effect on the devotee. The body’s actions continue automatically as expressions of the Lord’s will. This is the true devotion to the Lord. To attain the Lord means to become inseparable from Him, which is the ultimate reality. This inseparability can arise through discrimination as well as through non‑discrimination. For example, Sriji (the revered form of the Lord) is inseparable from Lord Krishna. Fundamentally, Lord Krishna is both Sriji and Krishna, manifested in these two forms. Though two forms exist, Sriji is not different from the Lord, nor is the Lord different from Sriji. Yet, for the exchange of divine love (rasa), a play of union (yoga) and separation (vigraha) continuously occurs. In their union there is also separation, and in their separation there is also union; thus union strengthens separation and separation strengthens union, leading to an ever‑growing, indescribable love. Attaining this indescribable, ever‑increasing love is precisely attaining the Lord. **Unity of the themes of the Seventh and Ninth chapters**  
At the beginning of the Seventh chapter the Lord pledged to disclose complete knowledge together with its application—“I will now speak to you of knowledge with its full application, without omission” (7.2). The flow of the Lord’s discourse in the Seventh chapter continued until a question from Arjuna at the start of the Eighth chapter introduced a shift. Consequently, when the subject of the Eighth chapter concluded, the Lord, without further prompting from Arjuna, said, “Now I shall reveal to you the most secret teaching, the knowledge together with its application” (9.1).
