[ Verse 34 ]
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

In the thirteenth verse of Chapter 7, the Lord described all beings as being deluded by the three gunas, and in the eighth verse of Chapter 9 He said that all beings are subject to nature. He then begins to speak again, this time with scientific knowledge, in the fourth and fifth verses of Chapter 9. The subject that He elaborated in detail in Chapter 7 is repeated, from the beginning of Chapter 9 up to the eleventh verse of Chapter 10, continuously. The statements made in those verses have a great impact on Arjuna, causing him, from the twelfth to the eighteenth verse of Chapter 10, to offer praise and prayer to the Lord. In other words, what was said in Chapter 7 is summarized, expanded, or presented in a different form in Chapter 9. In the first verse of Chapter 7, the brief statement “mayy‑asakta‑manaḥ …” is expanded slightly in the thirty‑fourth verse of Chapter 9 with the words “man‑manaḥ …”. In the second verse of Chapter 7 the Lord says that He will speak knowledge together with science, knowledge that once known leaves nothing else to be known. The same promise appears in the first verse of Chapter 9, where He says that this scientific knowledge will free the listener from the inauspicious world (samsara). Once liberated, there is nothing further to learn. Thus, at the beginning of both Chapter 7 and Chapter 9 the Lord pledges to give knowledge together with science and describes the result of that pledge. In the third verse of Chapter 7 the Lord says that among thousands of people only one strives for true perfection, and among those who strive, only one truly knows Him. The reason for this is given in the third verse of Chapter 9: without faith in this scientific knowledge a person does not attain the Lord and wanders on the path of death, i.e., is repeatedly born and dies. In the sixth verse of Chapter 7 the Lord declares Himself to be the cause (prabhava) and dissolution (pralaya) of the entire universe. The same idea is expressed in the eighteenth verse of Chapter 9 with the words “prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ”. In the tenth verse of Chapter 7 the Lord calls Himself the eternal seed (sanātana‑bīja); in the eighteenth verse of Chapter 9 He calls Himself the imperishable seed (avyaya‑bīja). In the twelfth verse of Chapter 7, using the concise phrase “na tv aham teṣhu te mayi …” He summarized a royal science; the same concise description appears in the eleventh verse of Chapter 9 as “ava‑jānanti māṁ mūḍhāḥ” (the ignorant do not recognize Me). In the fifteenth verse of Chapter 7 the Lord said “na māṁ duṣkṛtino mūḍhāḥ” (the foolish do not perform evil deeds for Me); the same idea is rendered in the eleventh verse of Chapter 9 as “ava‑jānanti māṁ mūḍhāḥ”. In the fifteenth verse of Chapter 7 the Lord spoke of those who cling to demonic nature with the words “āsura‑bhāva‑māśritāḥ”. The identical notion is repeated in the twelfth verse of Chapter 9 as “rākṣasīm‑āsurīm caiva prakṛtiṁ mohinīṁ śritāḥ” (those attached to demonic, devilish nature). In the sixteenth verse of Chapter 7 He called certain persons “sukṛtinaḥ” (the doers of good); the thirteenth verse of Chapter 9 refers to the same persons as “mahātmānaḥ” (great souls). From the sixteenth to the eighteenth verses of Chapter 7 the Lord described four types of devotees based on desire‑bound (sākāma) and desire‑free (niṣkāma) attitudes. From the thirtieth to the thirty‑third verses of Chapter 9 He describes seven categories of devotees according to their color, conduct, and personality. In the nineteenth verse of Chapter 7, from the perspective of a great soul, He says “Vāsudevaḥ sarvam” (Vasudeva is all). In the nineteenth verse of Chapter 9, He states from His own perspective “satya‑saccā‑aham” (I am truth, existence, and consciousness). Turning away from the Lord and worshipping other deities occurs for two main reasons: desire and failure to recognize the Lord. In the twentieth verse of Chapter 7 the desire‑based reason for seeking refuge in other deities is mentioned; in the twenty‑third verse of Chapter 9 the reason of not recognizing the Lord and thus worshipping other deities is given. In the twenty‑third verse of Chapter 7 the Lord says that desire‑bound men receive a finite (destructive) fruit, and the corresponding passage appears in Chapter 9…

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 9 ]

In the 21st verse of the chapter, the movement of desire‑driven persons is described; the same idea of attainment is expressed in the latter half of the 24th verse of the 7th chapter. The statement “parāṁ bhāvaṁ ajānanto mama‑avyaya‑mānuttamam” (the supreme state is unknown to those who do not know My imperishable supreme) appears, and in the latter half of the 11th verse of the 9th chapter it is rendered as “parāṁ bhāvaṁ ajānanto mama‑bhūta‑maheshvaram” (the supreme state is unknown to those who do not know Me as the Lord of all beings). In the 23rd verse of the 7th chapter, the Lord says that the devotees of the gods obtain the gods, and My devotees obtain Me; the same assertion is repeated in the 25th verse of the 9th chapter. In the 27th verse of the 7th chapter the Lord says “sarge yānti” (they go to the world); in the 3rd verse of the 9th chapter the phrase “mṛtyu‑saṁsāra‑vartmani” (in the cycle of death and rebirth) is used. In the first half of the 24th verse of the 7th chapter the Lord declares “avyaktaṁ vyaktim‑āpannaṁ manyante mām‑buddhiḥ” (the unmanifest is considered to have become manifest by those of discerning intellect); this idea is highlighted in the first half of the 11th verse of the 9th chapter, and in the 34th verse the expression “avajānanti māṁ mūḍhā mānuṣīṁ tanum‑āśritam” (the foolish, attached to the human body, do not know Me) is given. The main point of these verses is the offering to the Lord. **Appendix meaning** – This verse emphasizes the transformation of ego. The devotee adopts the attitude “I am the Lord,” thereby converting his ego and linking himself with the Divine. He becomes devoted to the Lord rather than to external practices; consequently, renunciation of worldly ties is not required, as they fall away automatically. Although distinctions of caste, ashrama, birth, qualification, authority, action, and qualities are all provisional, the relationship with the Divine is not provisional; it is beginningless, eternal, and self‑evident. Om Tat Sat is cited in the Srimad Bhagavad‑Gītā‑Upaniṣad, the treatise on Brahma‑vidyā and Yoga‑śāstra, in the dialogue of Krishna and Arjuna. The ninth chapter is titled **Rajavidyā‑Rājaguhya‑Yoga**. Thus, by the proper pronunciation of the divine names “Om Tat Sat,” the Brahma‑vidyā and Yoga‑śāstra are embodied in the Gītā‑Upaniṣad, completing the ninth chapter named “Rajavidyā‑Rājaguhya‑Yoga.”

In this chapter the Lord says “mayā tatam‑idaṁ sarvam” (All this is pervaded by Me). The chapter contains 1,171 verses; the 34 verses of this chapter are the king of all teachings. Verses 20 and 21 (out of the 44 verses) are the two verses in which the Lord reveals Himself to Arjuna through His own letters; the remaining 32 verses consist of 32 letters each. The chapter contains the utterance “Śrī‑Bhagavān uvāca” (the Lord said). It is the king of all secret meanings. When the two aspects—**Rajavidyā** (royal knowledge) and **Rājaguhya** (royal secret)—are understood in essence, the experience of **Yoga** (eternal Yoga) arises. Hence the chapter is named “Rajavidyā‑Rājaguhya‑Yoga.”

**Verses, syllables and utterances of Chapter 9**

The meters employed in Chapter 9 are listed. Among the 34 verses, verses 20 and 21 are composed in the *upajāti* meter. Of the remaining 32 verses:

* In the first stanza of the first verse, the syllable groups “bhagaṇa” and “na‑gaṇa” appear, giving a “narrow‑wide” pattern. * In the first stanza of the second verse, the group “ra‑gaṇa” yields an “r‑wide” pattern. * In the first stanzas of the third and tenth verses, “bhagaṇa” produces a “bh‑wide” pattern. * In the first stanza of the seventeenth verse, and in the thirteenth and twenty‑sixth verses, the use of “na‑gaṇa” in the third stanza of the verse “Śrī‑Bhagavān uvāca” creates a “n‑wide” pattern. These verses together amount to 1,112 instances of the *saṁjñā* meter, while the remaining 25 verses follow the *pāthyā‑vaktra* pattern, each containing 51 letters of the *puṣpika* meter. Consequently, all letters conform to the characteristics of the *anuṣṭup* meter. In this chapter there are three occurrences of “Atha navamo ’adhyāyaḥ” (Now the ninth chapter), two occurrences of “Śrī‑Bhagavān uvāca,” 466 verses, and thirteen *puṣpika*‑type lines. The total count of all lines is 468.

Ninth Chapter Summary

In Chapter 7 the Lord began to speak of *jnana* (knowledge) and *vijnana* (realization). *Jnana* liberates one from the world, while *vijnana* engenders love for the Divine. After Arjuna’s question, Chapter 8 introduced a different theme, but in Chapter 9 the Lord returns to the same subject. In Chapter 7 He explained the cause of the world’s origin, stating that the conjunction of the higher (*para*) and lower (*apara*) aspects of My nature gives rise to all beings (verse 6). In Chapter 9 He describes the condition of the world: for those whose vision perceives the reality of the world, the world exists in Me and I exist in the world (verses 4‑6). Chapter 6 contains the statement, “He who sees Me everywhere, sees everything in Me” (6.30). Yet for the realized great souls who do not see the world as an independent reality, the vision is “I am alone—Vasudeva is all.”

The Lord says that although I am the source and sustainer of all beings, I am not dependent on them; rather, the beings are dependent on Me (Chapter 9, verse 5). Just as air in the sky depends on the sky, while the sky does not depend on the air, the *para* and *apara* natures, being My own disposition, are subordinate to Me, but I am not subordinate to them. Consequently, as air originates from the sky, remains in the sky, and merges into the sky, all creatures arise from the Lord in the great creation, dwell in the Lord, and merge back into the Lord at the final dissolution (verse 7). This implies that all creatures depend on nature, while nature depends on the Lord (verse 8). In other words, a portion of the Lord is nature, and a portion of nature is the creature. Hence, even when the act of creation is performed, the Lord is not bound by the karmic activity of creation (verse 9), because the actual work of creation is carried out by the nature that is dependent on the Lord (verse 10). Because this mystery is not known, ignorant people regard the Lord as dependent on a body (*apara*), just as we cannot exist without a body; thus they think the Lord cannot exist without a body (verse 11). Such people are attached to demonic, rakshasi, and alluring natures (verse 12). In reality, whereas a human being has a distinction between body and subtle body, the Lord has no such distinction—“I am the eternal truth, O Arjuna” (9.19). Therefore, those who do not consider the Lord as dependent on nature are actually dependent on the divine nature; they are not dependent on nature but on the Lord (verse 13). Because they are dependent on the Lord, they are called *mahātman* (great souls). *Karmayoga* primarily operates through the body (*apara*), while *jnanayoga* primarily operates through the subtle body (*para*). When one is attached to a single body—whether gross or subtle—the karmic and knowledge yogis become one‑pointed. In contrast, *bhakti‑yoga* operates primarily through the Lord Himself. Hence the devotee is called *mahātman*—the great soul—by the Lord. The devotee sings the Lord’s praises with exclusive devotion, because in his vision no other independent reality exists besides the Lord; therefore his mind never departs from the Lord. He remains ever‑attached to the Lord, never separating—“ever attached” (9.14), “ever engaged” (9.22). Practitioners are of many types and worship various deities by different means, yet in truth all such practitioners worship the one universal Lord—“They worship Me” (9.15), “the three Vedas are My” (9.20), “even they are My” (9.23), “I am the enjoyer and Lord of all knowledge” (9.24). The same Lord manifests in many forms (9.16‑19). Because this mystery is not understood, those who regard their chosen deity as separate from the Lord and worship with selfish desire actually worship the Lord in a distorted manner.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Summary

Practices performed without proper procedure are improper; therefore they lead to downfall, i.e., they become subject to birth and death (Chapter 9, verses 23‑24). However, those who worship the Supreme Lord attain Him alone. Those who abandon the Lord and worship other deities require many rules, rites, etc., which involve great difficulty. In worship of the Lord, only devotion (bhava) is needed; actions—rules, rites, etc.—are not required (Chapter 9, verses 26‑27). The Lord does not accept actions; He accepts devotion—‘Bhava‑grāhi Janardana’ (the Lord who receives devotion). Hence the devotee easily attains the Lord. Moreover, a person of any conduct, caste, ashrama, or birth can, by becoming a devotee, readily attain the Lord (Chapter 9, verses 30‑33). At the end of Chapter 9 the Lord says, ‘Mann‑mana bhava’ (9.34). Its meaning is: I am everything that exists; nothing exists apart from Me (Chapter 7, verses 29‑30). Firmly accepting this is the sense of ‘Mann‑mana bhava’ and similar statements.

Om Shri Paramatmane Namah

[ Chapter 10 ]

**Introductory commentary**  
In Chapter 7 the Supreme Lord spoke of the truth of the heart together with scientific knowledge. When, at the very beginning of Chapter 8, Arjuna asked a question, the Lord’s discourse shifted slightly. Consequently, the Lord commenced Chapter 9 to again present knowledge with scientific insight and concluded it with devotion to Him. Yet the Lord still felt a desire to say more; He was not completely satisfied with His own statements. Just as a devotee does not become fully satiated by hearing the Lord’s words (Gita 10.18), the Lord, while expressing the innermost feelings of His heart to His beloved devotee Arjuna, also did not attain complete satisfaction. The reason is that the secret matters of the Lord’s heart have no listener in this world except the devotee. Therefore, without waiting for Arjuna’s request, the Lord graciously began the subject of Chapter 10. **Shloka 1**  
*Transliteration*:  
bhūya eva mahābāho śṛṇu me paramaṁ vacaḥ  
yatte ’haṁ prīyamāṇāya vakṣyāmi hitakāmyayā

*English meaning*:  
Again, O Maha‑Bāho (the one of great arms), listen to my supreme word:  
what I shall utter for the one who loves Me, I speak with the desire for his welfare. **Commentary on the shloka**  
The Lord addresses Arjuna as “Maha‑Bāho” (the mighty‑armed one), then says “again” (bhūya) to indicate that He is about to repeat a supreme teaching. The phrase “prīyamāṇāya” denotes the Lord’s deep affection for Arjuna, while “hitakāmyayā” expresses that the forthcoming instruction is intended for Arjuna’s benefit. The expression “bhūya eva” underscores the Lord’s manifold glories; the particle “eva” emphasizes that the knowledge being imparted is a direct result of divine manifestation. By invoking “paramaṁ vacaḥ,” the Lord signals that what follows is the highest truth, a secret of His own majesty and heart, which He now wishes Arjuna to hear. **Further exposition**  
The term “bhūya” also alludes to the Lord’s countless divine manifestations (vibhūti). Through sincere inquiry, one attains devotion (bhakti) and love for the Lord. Consequently, out of grace, the Lord enumerated seventeen divine manifestations in Chapter 7 (from verse 8 to verse 12) and thirty‑three manifestations in Chapter 9 (from verse 16 to verse 19). In the present chapter He proceeds to describe additional manifestations, as also mentioned in Chapter 8, verse 14; Chapter 9, verses 22, 24, and 34, to further illuminate the special qualities of devotion. Whenever the Lord reveals His supreme significance, influence, and sovereignty to Arjuna, He employs terms such as “parama vacaḥ” (supreme word) and “rahasyam” (secret), for example in Chapter 4, verse 3: “rahasyam hy etat uttamam” (this secret is indeed supreme). **Notes**  
1. In this tenth chapter the Lord has already disclosed forty‑five manifestations from verses 4 to 6. 2. The Lord declares that, by His grace, He bestows knowledge upon those devotees who seek His compassion—“teṣāme‑ānukampārtham” (Gita 10.11)—which is His supreme promise.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

The one who once instructed the Sun is the same as the charioteer of your carriage; therefore the expression “parama‑vacha” (supreme word) is used here. I am seated before you, neighing like a horse. In Chapter 18, Verse 66, the words “śṛṇu me parama‑vacaḥ” (listen to my supreme instruction) convey that you should abandon the entanglements of adjudicating all dharmas and take refuge in Me; I will liberate you from all sins, so do not worry. Through the phrase “śṛṇu me parama‑vacaḥ,” the Lord indicates that the myriad emotional states of beings arise from Him, and that the seven great sages, the four Sanakas, and the fourteen Manus are all born of His mind. In other words, He is the source of everything. The verse “yatte ’haṁ prīyamāṇāya vakṣyāmi hitakāmyayā” (for the one who loves me, I speak with the desire for welfare) means that when the listener possesses faith and love for the speaker, and the speaker feels compassionate goodwill toward the listener, the speaker’s words become firmly implanted in the listener’s mind. This automatically awakens the listener’s interest in the Lord, engenders devotion, and creates love. A possible doubt about the term “hitakāmyayā” (desire for welfare) is that the Gita repeatedly forbids desire, yet the Lord appears to retain desire Himself. The resolution is that personal longing for pleasure, comfort, and ease is indeed “kāma” (desire). Desire for the welfare of others, however, is not desire at all; it is self‑sacrifice and the principal means of extinguishing one’s own cravings. Consequently, the Lord, as an ideal, advises that just as He speaks from the desire for welfare, a human should act solely from the desire for the welfare of all living beings. When personal desire is eliminated, the Lord’s grace is attained effortlessly. Those who cultivate desire for the welfare of all creatures also obtain My personal (saguna) form, as expressed in “te prāpnuvanti mām eva sarva‑bhūta‑hite rataḥ” (Gita 12.4), and they also realize the impersonal (nirguna) form, as stated in “labhate sarva‑bhūta‑hite rataḥ” (Gita 5.25). Just as in Chapter 13 the Lord, while speaking of knowledge, promises at the beginning of Chapter 14 to describe knowledge again, similarly in Chapters 7 and 9 He discusses knowledge‑science, yet at the start of Chapter 10 He again pledges to return to the same theme. At the opening of Chapter 14 He says “paraṁ bhūyaḥ pravakṣyāmi jñānānāṁ jñānam uttamam” (I shall now speak the supreme knowledge among all knowledge), and at the opening of Chapter 10 He repeats “śṛṇu me parama‑vacaḥ.” Their implication is that the path of knowledge emphasizes understanding and discrimination; therefore the seeker, by hearing the verses, discerns the truth thoughtfully. Hence the expression “jñānānāṁ jñāna‑uttamam” (the highest knowledge among knowledge). The devotional path, by contrast, places faith and trust at its core; thus the seeker, by hearing the verses, accepts them with faith and trust. **Appendix (Parishishta‑Bhava)** – Even after arriving on the battlefield, Arjuna does not desire victory but seeks his own welfare; consequently he is addressed as “mahābāho” (great‑armed). This address signifies Arjuna’s superiority, his capacity to receive instruction, and his rightful authority. “Parama‑vacha” – Because the Lord’s words are aimed at the welfare of every living being, they are supremely excellent. By being concerned solely with the welfare of beings, the Gita becomes beloved and revered by the whole world. “vakṣyāmi hitakāmyayā” – Arjuna represents the collective of living beings and seeks only his own welfare. Hence the Lord, speaking for the welfare of all beings, utters the supreme instruction. Apart from welfare, no other interest exists for a being. The Lord’s words are also welfare‑oriented, and their purpose is to promote welfare; therefore the Lord’s speech is filled with the supreme good (parahita) for beings. No other entity can provide as much benefit to beings as the Lord can. Uma, Rama, and all alike are equally beneficent in the world; there is no guru, father, mother, brother, or lord beyond them. “yac chreyaḥ syān nishchitaṁ brūhi tan me” (Gita 2.7) – “Tell me definitively what is truly beneficial.”  
“tad ekaṁ vad niścitya yena śreyo ’ham āpnu yām” (Gita 3.2) – “Declare one thing firmly, by which I may attain the highest good.”  
“yac chreya etayo rekam tan me brūhi niścitam” (Gita 5.1) – “State clearly which of the two is the true benefit for me.”

(Reference: Manas, Kiskinda 12.1)

[ Verse 2 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The words of other beings often differ, but the words of the Lord are universally agreed. The Lord, situated in yoga, is speaking the Gita; therefore His utterances are especially beneficent. What does it mean that the Lord is “situated in yoga”? In ordinary sense the Lord is the supreme friend of all living beings, but when a distressed soul takes refuge in Him, special sentiments for that soul’s welfare arise in the Lord’s heart—this is the Lord’s being “situated in yoga.” It is like the milk that, at the sight of a calf, instantly flows into the calf’s udder. From the verses “yatte ’ham prīyamāṇāya vakṣyāmi hitakāmyayā,” the Lord says that within you there is love for Him and within Him there is goodwill toward you; therefore He will repeat the knowledge together with its science that He taught in the seventh and ninth chapters. This shows that in the seventh, ninth, and tenth chapters the Lord expressed, from the heart, the desire for the welfare of all living beings. Relation—Concerning the supreme word that I shall speak later, no one besides Me can fully disclose it. Why? The Lord explains this in the following verse. na me vidoḥ suragaṇāḥ prabhavam na maharṣayaḥ  
aham ādir hi devānāṁ maharṣīṇāṁ ca sarvaśaḥ || 2 ||

*na* – not  
*me* – of Me  
*vidoḥ* – know (the gods)  
*suragaṇāḥ* – the divine beings (gods)  
*prabhavam* – origin, source  
*na* – not  
*maharṣayaḥ* – the great sages  
*aham* – I  
*ādir* – the primal cause, source  
*hi* – indeed  
*devānāṁ* – of the gods  
*maharṣīṇāṁ* – of the great sages  
*ca* – and  
*sarvaśaḥ* – in every way

Translation of the verse: “The gods do not know My origin, nor do the great sages; I alone am the primal source of both the gods and the sages in every respect.”

Explanation – Although the bodies, intellects, realms, and material aspects of the deities are divine, they do not comprehend My manifestation. My universal manifestation includes incarnations such as fish, tortoise, etc., and the display of action, feeling, and divine powers in creation. Even the deities are unaware of the full purpose, aim, and cause of My appearance. Their knowledge of My manifestation is far from complete; even beholding Me is extremely difficult for them. Consequently they are ever yearning for a glimpse of Me (as mentioned in the 45th verse of the eleventh chapter of the Gita). Similarly, the great sages who have revealed countless hymns, mantras, and extraordinary powers—who are elevated above the world and endowed with divine experience—also do not fully comprehend My manifestations, My various pastimes, or My greatness. Here the Lord mentions both “devas” and “maharshis.” The names are invoked from the standpoint of high position (devas) and from the standpoint of knowledge (maharshis). The reason they do not know My manifestation is that I am the source of all deities and sages—“aham ādir hi devānāṁ maharṣīṇāṁ ca sarvaśaḥ.” In the Mahabharata (Ashvamedh Parva 16, verses 12‑13) it is stated that the supreme Brahman, described by one who is united with yoga, is beyond My reiteration. ( The Lord speaking to Arjuna: ) “To repeat everything again in the same form is no longer within My power; at that time, only while being united with yoga, did I describe the supreme soul‑principle.”

2 – “Bruhīḥ snigdhasy śiṣyasya guravo guhya‑mapi yutaḥ” (Śrīmad‑Bhāgavatam 1.1.8; 10.13.3): The gurus even reveal the most secret matters to their beloved disciple. “gūḍha‑tattva na sādhū durāvahiḥ | ārata adhikāri jahāṁ pāviḥ ||” (Manasa‑Bala 110.1): The profound truth is not to be shunned by the saint; the rightful seeker attains it.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

There is some intelligence, power, capability, rank, influence, greatness; these cannot be measured. Because even before the manifestation of these deities and great sages the Lord was exactly as He is, and after their dissolution He will remain exactly as He is. Hence those whose bodies have a beginning and an end cannot, by their limited intellect, aptitude, or power, comprehend the beginning‑less and end‑less—that is, the infinite Supreme Soul (Atman). They cannot bring the infinite within the limits of their finite mind. All that they know has been received from Me. Therefore, the influence, power, and capability that they have obtained from Me cannot enable them to fully know Me. It is like a child who does not know the marriage of the mother from whom he was born; similarly, the deities and great sages have originated from Me, and thus they do not know My manifestation nor the cause of My appearance. Their work may become absorbed in its cause, but they cannot know the cause itself. In the same way, because the deities and great sages are generated from Me and arise from My activity, they cannot know Me as the cause, though they may become absorbed in Me. In the fourteenth verse of this chapter Arjuna also says to the Lord that he does not know the gods or the demons, because the gods are preoccupied with material enjoyment and the demons are preoccupied with the power of illusion (Maya). The implication is that attachment to enjoyment prevents the gods from having time to know Me, and the deceptive power of Maya occupies the demons. Thus the gods and great sages cannot know the Lord’s beginning, end, and present manifestation; they can only take limited incarnations and therefore cannot know Me. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – In the third verse of Chapter 7 the Lord said “manuṣyāṇāṁ sahasreṣu …” (among thousands of humans …). Here He says “na me viduḥ …” (they do not know Me). The reason given is that I am the origin of all deities and great sages. In the twenty‑sixth verse of Chapter 7 the Lord also says that I know all beings of past, present, and future, but no one knows Me. Consequently, in verses fourteen and fifteen Arjuna states that neither the gods nor the demons know the Lord; only the self‑knowing individual knows himself. In this verse the Lord reveals the “raja‑guhya” (supreme secret). The Lord is not known through knowledge, intellect, aptitude, or power; He is known only through the devotee’s faith, trust, and divine grace. **Relation (Sambandh)** – The preceding verses state that even the gods and great sages cannot at all know the Lord’s manifestation; therefore, how can a human know the Lord and attain welfare? The remedy is given in the following verse:

*Yo māṁ ajam anādiṁ ca vetti loka‑maheśvaram |  
sarva‑pāpaiḥ asammūḍhaḥ sa martyēṣu pramucyate || 3 ||*

**Word‑by‑word translation**  
- *Yo* – who  
- *māṁ* – Me (the Lord)  
- *ajam* – unborn, without birth  
- *anādiṁ* – beginningless  
- *ca* – and  
- *vetti* – knows  
- *loka‑maheśvaram* – the Lord of all worlds (Supreme Consciousness)  
- *sarva‑pāpaiḥ* – by all sins  
- *asammūḍhaḥ* – free from delusion  
- *sa* – he  
- *martyēṣu* – among mortals  
- *pramucyate* – is liberated

**Interpretation** – One who, without any doubt, knows the unborn, beginningless Lord who is the sovereign of all worlds, is freed from all sin and attains liberation among mortals. This implies that the Lord is beyond birth and beyond time; He is the timeless reality in which even time itself has a beginning and an end.

[ Verse 3 ]
* Sadhak - Sanjeevani *

The three worlds (triloka) exist, and in those three worlds all creatures reside; over those creatures there are many deities, each possessing distinct authority. Among those deities there is a supreme God, Bhagavan. Thus, by knowing—i.e., by firmly believing with faith—a person never harbors even the slightest doubt about God's eternal, imperishable, and universal lordship. Great God refers to the forms of heaven, earth and the netherworld which, when one firmly acknowledges the Lord of the universe, also truly perceives the transitory nature of the world; consequently the sense of “I” and “mine” cannot remain in this world. One's belonging shifts entirely to the sole God. Hence, if one is not freed from sins, what else can happen? Only a man without folly truly knows God as eternal, imperishable, and universal, and such a man is liberated from all sins. All his ongoing, accumulated and other karmas are destroyed. Man must experience this reality; mere rote learning, like a parrot, is insufficient. Knowledge acquired like a parrot does not fully work. “An unconfused mortal is liberated from all sins.” Knowing God as eternal, imperishable, and universal frees a person because God is unborn and deathless, i.e., never undergoes any change. The unborn, unconfused state is beyond the body that remains with everyone while the supreme God remains eternal for all. Neither the supreme God nor any being can remain forever in this world; the Supreme Being is never separate from anyone, yet also beyond all. This reality admits no doubt; there is no trace of doubt. Simultaneously, knowledge itself is the unconfused state, and realizing it is the truth. This fleeting world constantly changes; that impermanent state is where man resides, and whatever form is seen at any moment is called unconfused. Such an unconfused person cannot see that form again in another moment; he perceives the formless, manifest, and unmanifest reality, because he does not remain in the same form. Thus he knows the world in its true nature—its play, mystery, influence, sovereignty, etc.—without any doubt, including himself. Appendix - In Chapter 9 Verse 24 God, by way of exception, says that one who does not know Me falls into ruin, and by implication states that one who knows Me is freed from all sins. Here “vetti” means to accept firmly without doubt, because the senses—mind and intellect—cannot know God (Gita 10.2). Therefore God is not an object of knowledge but an object of acceptance and experience. Knowledge itself is not even nature; how then can past nature become an object of knowing God? To experience means to merge oneself in God, to become inseparable from Him. Only by becoming inseparable can one know God, because in reality they are already one. Likewise, only by being separate from the world can one know the world, because in reality they are separate. Great sages may not know the origin of God, but they do know that God is eternal—without beginning. Since the Atman is a portion of God, the Atman is also eternal—without beginning. Hence, one who knows God as eternal without beginning will also know oneself as such, because the Atman knows God by being inseparable from Him. When one knows oneself as eternal without beginning, one becomes free of folly; then how can sin remain? Sin is born later, whereas the eternal without beginning is ever‑present. “Liberated from all sins” signifies freedom from the association of qualities. While attached to qualities, a person cannot be freed from sin, because attachment to qualities is the root cause of sin. From verses four to six the discussion continues on the unconfused state, wherein God declares Himself as the “origin” of all. God Himself is Anadi (without beginning) and is the origin of emotions and of the great sages.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

Connection—In the first verse the Lord gave the instruction to listen to the supreme word; in the following three verses He now explains that instruction. **Verse 4**  
*Transliteration:* buddhiḥ jñānam asammohaḥ kṣamā satyaṃ damaḥ śamaḥ | sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ bhavo ’bhāvo bhayaṃ cābhayam eva ca ||4||  
*Translation:* Intelligence, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, self‑control, and tranquility; pleasure, pain, existence, non‑existence, fear and fearlessness. **Verse 5**  
*Transliteration:* ahiṃsā samatā tuṣṭiḥ tapo dānaṃ yaśo ’yaśaḥ | bhavanti bhāvā bhūtānāṃ matta eva pṛthak‑vidhāḥ ||5||  
*Translation:* Non‑violence, equality, contentment, austerity, charity, fame and infamy; these become the various states of beings, all originating from Me alone. **Term‑by‑term explanation**

- **buddhiḥ** – intelligence, the faculty that decides purpose; the name of “truth.”  
- **jñānam** – knowledge, the essence of discernment between the real and unreal, permanent and impermanent, right and wrong, duty and non‑duty; the discriminative wisdom that humans receive from the Lord. - **asammohaḥ** – freedom from delusion; knowing that the body and the world are subject to creation and destruction, yet not identifying with “I” and “mine.”  
- **kṣamā** – forgiveness; the willingness, within one’s capacity, to bear any offense without seeking punishment for the offender in this life or beyond. - **satyaṃ** – truth; speaking in accordance with the ultimate reality of the Supreme Self, abandoning selfishness and ego, and acting for the welfare of others exactly as perceived. - **damaḥ** – self‑control; withdrawing the senses from their objects and bringing them under one’s command for the purpose of attaining the Supreme. - **śamaḥ** – tranquility; withdrawing the mind from contemplation of worldly pleasures. - **sukhaṃ** – happiness; the pleasant feeling that arises in the heart when body, mind, and senses are in harmonious conditions. - **duḥkhaṃ** – sorrow; the unpleasant feeling that arises when conditions are adverse. - **bhavaḥ** – existence; the arising of worldly objects, persons, events, circumstances, emotions, etc. - **abhāvaḥ** – non‑existence; the dissolution or cessation of those same things. - **bhayaṃ** – fear; the inner apprehension that one’s conduct, feelings, etc., may be contrary to scriptural or societal standards. - **abhayaṃ** – fearlessness; when one’s conduct aligns with scripture and the teachings of the saints, the heart is free from such apprehension. - **ahiṃsā** – non‑violence. - **samatā** – equality, impartiality. - **tuṣṭiḥ** – contentment, satisfaction. - **tapaḥ** – austerity, disciplined effort. - **dānaṃ** – charity, giving. - **yaśaḥ** – fame, reputation. - **ayashaḥ** – infamy, disgrace. - **bhāvā** – states, conditions. - **bhūtānāṃ** – of beings. - **matta** – from Me (the Lord). - **pṛthak‑vidhāḥ** – various distinct categories. **Further commentary**

The word “buddhi” denotes the faculty that determines purpose and declares it as “truth.” The term “jñānam” refers to the essential discriminative knowledge that distinguishes the eternal from the non‑eternal, the knowable from the unknowable, the appropriate from the inappropriate, and duty from non‑duty. This knowledge (discernment) is granted to humanity by the Lord. “asammoha” signifies the absence of delusion; even while recognizing that the body and the world are subject to creation and destruction, the identification with “I” and “mine” is called delusion, and its negation is “asammoha.”

“kṣamā” is the attitude of bearing any wrongdoing against oneself, within one’s capacity, and wishing that the offender receives no punishment from either the divine or worldly realms. “satya” is the truthful speech required for attaining the Supreme Self: speaking exactly as one has heard, seen, and understood, relinquishing selfishness and ego, and acting for others’ benefit precisely as it is. “dama” is the control of the senses by withdrawing them from their objects and bringing them under one’s mastery, while “śama” is the calming of the mind away from contemplation of material enjoyments. “Happiness (sukha) arises when the body, mind, and senses find favorable conditions; sorrow (duḥkha) arises when conditions are unfavorable.”

“Bhava” denotes the arising of worldly objects, persons, events, circumstances, emotions, etc.; “abhāva” denotes their dissolution. “Fear (bhaya) and fearlessness (abhaya)” refer to the inner anxiety that one’s conduct or feelings may be contrary to scriptural or societal norms; when conduct aligns with the teachings of the scriptures and saints, that anxiety disappears, resulting in fearlessness.

[ Verse 4-5 ]  
* Sadhaka – Sanjivani *

He fears no one; this state is called **Abhaya** (fearlessness). **Ahimsa** (non‑violence) is the principle of causing not even the slightest suffering to any creature, in any country, time or circumstance, through body, mind or speech. **Samata** (equanimity) is the condition of having no inner discord when various favorable and unfavorable objects, persons, events or situations arise. **Tusti** (contentment) is the attitude of being satisfied even when one receives less than needed, or when one receives more than needed, and of having no desire for more. In other words, whether one gets a lot or a little, whether one gets or does not get, one remains pleasant in every condition. **Tapah** (austerity) is the pleasant endurance of any hardship, adverse circumstance, or difficulty that comes while performing one’s duty. Observing fasts such as Ekadashi is also called tapah. **Dana** (charitable giving) is the act of giving a portion of one’s pure earnings to a worthy recipient, without any desire for return or fruit, gladly and without expectation (Gita, Chapter 17, Verse 20). **Yash** and **Ayash** (glory and disgrace) – the fame, praise, etc., that arise in the world because of a person’s good conduct, feelings and virtues are called **Yash** (glory). The condemnation, criticism that arise because of a person’s bad conduct, feelings and vices is called **Ayash** (disgrace). *“bhavanti bhāva‑bhūtānāṁ matta eva pṛthag‑vidhāḥ”* – The various and many states of beings arise only from Me, each being distinct. All the separate and manifold emotions, powers, foundations and illuminations of creatures are derived from Me, the Lord of the worlds. Hence the essence of all is Me. Here the word **mattaḥ** points to the Lord’s yoga, potency and influence, while **pṛthag‑vidhāḥ** indicates the many different manifestations that should be known. Whatever is prescribed or prohibited in the world, whatever is auspicious or inauspicious, and all the good and bad tendencies in the world, are all the play (lila) of the Lord. When the devotee understands the Lord in his true nature, his yoga with the Lord becomes unwavering (Gita, Chapter 10, Verse 7). The twenty bhavas (states) of beings are described. Twelve of them are singular and arise in the inner heart; fear accompanied by its opposite, **Abhaya**, also arises in the inner heart. The remaining seven are mutually contradictory. Among them, birth (utpatti), non‑existence (abhava), glory (yash) and disgrace (ayash) are the results of past actions, while happiness, sorrow and fear are the results of folly. This folly can be eradicated by man. The Lord’s intention in enumerating the twenty bhavas is to show that although they are distinct, their source is one and the same – Me. All of them originate from Me, receive their power and illumination from Me. In Chapter 7, Verse 12, the Lord says with the words **matta eva** that the sattvic, rajasic and tamasic qualities also arise from Me; their root is Me, they are from Me and obtain their potency from Me. Hence the purpose here is to direct the seeker’s view toward the fundamental principle of all manifestations. **Special note** – How should the seeker view the world? He should see the world as the form of the Lord. Whether it is creation, dissolution, favorable or adverse, nectar or death, heaven or hell, all are the Lord’s play. The Lord’s lila includes the childhood episode, the Ayodhya episode, the forest episode and the Lanka episode. In various cities the Lord’s manifestation is evident: in Ayodhya the Lord appears as king, queen and subjects with affectionate feeling; in Janakpur King Janaka, Queen Sita and the people display extraordinary devotion toward Lord Rama, treating him as a son, playing with him, entertaining him. In the forest (Aranyaka) there are meetings with devotees as well as with demons. In Lanka there is war, killing, rivers of blood. Thus, in different cities and episodes, the Lord’s diverse lila are present, yet despite the variety the Ramayana remains one.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

All pastimes are limbs of a single Ramayana; from these limbs one being lives while another dies, and so on. In the world beings display countless moods and actions: some laugh, some weep, some hold scholarly gatherings, some fight, some are born. At the root of everything is the Supreme Soul. Physical activities are nothing but the Divine’s pastimes. Those who enact the pastimes are forms of the Divine. Hence a devotee’s vision must ever remain fixed on God. Appendix meaning – From the standpoint of knowledge, all moods arise from nature; from the standpoint of devotion, all moods arise from God. If these moods are regarded as the living entity, then the living entity, being of the Supreme Nature, is inseparable from God; therefore these moods belong to God. In God they are ever‑present; in the living entity they appear and disappear according to association with the Supreme. Because they originate from God, all moods are of the Divine form. The expression “pṛthag‑vibhidhāḥ” means that just as a hand is one but its fingers are distinct, so God is one, yet the moods manifested from Him are distinct. In the one God many mutually opposite moods coexist. saptam ahṛṣayaḥ pūrve catvāraḥ tathā mahārṣayaḥ sapta pūrve catvāro manavastathā  
= madbhavaḥ mānasā yātā yeṣāṁ loka imāḥ prajāḥ [ Verse 6 ]

**Transliteration:** madbhavaḥ mānasā yātā yeṣāṁ loka imāḥ prajāḥ  
**Meaning:** By My divine feeling, these worlds are created from the mind; they are My creations. Seven great sages (Mahārṣis) and four earlier sages, together with the fourteen Manus, are all born of My mind; they constitute the total creation. Those who bear My feeling (faith‑devotion) are appointed to uphold Dharma and to perform the duties of the progenitor. These seven sages are called Mahārṣis here. In the two preceding verses the Lord described twenty elemental forms of beings as forms; in this verse He enumerates twenty‑five elemental forms of the individual, which are especially influential in beings and are the cause of the world. ‘Pūrve caturāḥ’ – Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana; ‘Mahārṣayaḥ sapta’ – the long‑lived sages who revealed the mantras, including Sanatkumāra, etc. These four are the foremost of Brahmā’s austerities, the wealthy, the divine‑eyed, and the first to manifest qualities, knowledge, etc. They are the Bhagavat‑forms. The elders who directly uphold Dharma and propagate lineages are also counted among them. The seven sages, endowed with the seven qualities, are remembered as the Saptarṣis and remain forever in the form of a child. They wander the three worlds spreading devotion, knowledge, and renunciation (Marīci, Angirā, Ātri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha). Their speech constantly chants “Hariḥ śaraṇam”. [ Verse 7 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

The commentary continues, describing three listeners who become participants in the narration and hearing of the Divine story. “Manavas‑tathā” – In one day of Brahmā’s kalpa there are fourteen Manus. In the present kalpa of Brahmā the fourteen Manus are named Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, Vaivasvata, Sāvarṇi, Dakṣasāvarṇi, Brahmasāvarṇi, Dharmasāvarṇi, Rudrasāvarṇi, Devasāvarṇi and Indrasāvarṇi. All of them, by Brahmā’s command, are the creators and initiators of the universe. “Mad‑bhāvāḥ” – All of them dwell within me as feeling, that is, as devotion‑love. “Yeṣāṁ lokamimāḥ prajāḥ” – In the world there are two kinds of beings: those born from the union of woman and man, and those born from the word (initiation, mantra, teaching, etc.). The beings born from union are called **binduj** (point‑born) and the beings born from the word are called **nādaj** (sound‑born). The binduj lineage continues through sons and hereditary succession, while the nādaj lineage continues through disciples and teaching succession. “Mānasā yātā” – Creation arises merely from the divine intention of the Lord. Yet here it is said that the Saptarṣis and others were born from the mind of the Lord. This is because those who expand the creation have pre‑eminence within it, and because they themselves are products of Brahmā’s mind, i.e., of divine intention. The Lord Himself manifested in Brahmā‑form for the purpose of creation. Hence the twenty‑five entities – the seven great sages, the four Sanakas, and the fourteen Manus – may be called the mind‑children of Brahmā or of the Lord; they are all nādaj beings. The Saptarṣis and the fourteen Manus married, therefore the progeny that arose from them is binduj. The Sanakas, however, never married; consequently the beings that arise from their teachings, who follow the transcendental path, are nādaj. All renunciates – past, present and future great saints – are, by their very nature, inseparably linked to the Lord because they are born of the Lord’s mind, as expressed in the appended description of the seven great sages, the four Sanakas and the fourteen Manus. **Relation** – From the fourth to the sixth verse the Lord has described his divine manifestations (vibhūti) and his yogic power (yoga) as they appear in various beings and personalities. In the following verse He now explains the fruit of truly knowing this reality. *“etāṁ vibhūtiṁ yogaṁ ca mama yo vetti tattvataḥ | so ’vakampena yogena yujyate nātra saṁśayaḥ || 7 ||”*

**Word‑by‑word translation**

- **etāṁ** – “this” (accusative plural)  
- **vibhūtiṁ** – “divine manifestation, glory”  
- **yogaṁ** – “yoga, spiritual power”  
- **ca** – “and”  
- **mama** – “my”  
- **yo** – “who”  
- **vetti** – “knows”  
- **tattvataḥ** – “from the absolute truth”

*“so ’vakampena”* – “he, unshaken, without doubt”  
- **vakampena** – “without tremor, steadfast”

*“yogena yujyate”* – “is united with yoga (devotional practice)”  
- **yogena** – “by yoga”  
- **yujyate** – “becomes united, is attached”

*“nātra saṁśayaḥ”* – “there is no doubt”  
- **nātra** – “not here, there is no”  
- **saṁśayaḥ** – “doubt, uncertainty”

Thus: “Who knows this divine manifestation and my yoga from the absolute truth is united with yoga without any doubt.”

**Explanation of the terms**

- **vibhūti** denotes the Lord’s sovereign splendor and divine attributes. - **yoga** denotes the Lord’s supramundane, extraordinary power, the infinite potency that manifests those attributes. The commentary notes that the description of these powers appears in detail in the eighth Canto of the Srimad‑Bhāgavatam, chapters five and thirteen. According to the text, a day of Brahmā consists of one thousand **caturyugas**. Within one **caturyuga** a Manu’s reign lasts a little more than seventy‑one **caturyugas**. At the present moment Brahmā is in his fifty‑first year, and the seventh Manu, **Vaivasvata**, is presently ruling.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

The term **Vibhuti** (divine opulence) is explained up to verses four through six as a state in which one transcends ordinary experience and attains supreme bliss. All the various Vibhutis are manifestations that arise from the Lord’s power and influence; they are said to be “born of Me” (mattah, mānasā jāta). This is the Lord’s Yoga, His divine effect. The same idea is expressed in Chapter 9, verse 5 with the words *pashy me yogam‑aishvaram* (“see My supreme divine Yoga”). Later, in Chapter 11, verse 8, when the Lord reveals His universal form to Arjuna, He again uses *pashy me yogam‑aishvaram* to invite Arjuna to behold His sovereign Yoga. **Special note**  
When a person enjoys pleasures through the intellect of enjoyment, he derives happiness from those pleasures, but his own power diminishes and the objects of enjoyment are exhausted, causing loss on both sides. If, however, he does not enjoy pleasures through the “enjoyment‑mind”—that is, if no desire for pleasure arises within him—his power and capacity remain intact and continuous. True happiness is not found in the mere enjoyment of pleasures; it lies in the **restraint of pleasures**. This restraint is of two kinds: (1) **governance over others** and (2) **self‑governance**. Governance over others means “let others’ suffering cease and they become happy,” i.e., rescuing others from the wrong path and placing them on the right path. Self‑governance means “renounce one’s selfishness and pride and refrain from any personal pleasure.” Both forms of restraint are called **Yoga** or **Prabhava** (divine effect). Such Yoga or effect is naturally inherent in the Supreme Soul (Paramatma) and can be attained by others. When one rules over others driven by selfishness and pride, the ruler experiences a certain pleasure, but his own power wanes while the ruled become subservient. Therefore, by completely abandoning selfishness and pride and acting for the welfare of others—so that mortals do not become trapped in transient pleasures, for humanity has been suffering endless sorrow since time immemorial—one attains a higher, unparalleled form of governance (restraint). The ultimate limit of this governance is the Lord’s rule, i.e., **Samyama** (self‑control). This is called **Yoga**. The name **Yoga** signifies equality, relationship, and capacity. It is rooted in the immutable essence of the Supreme Soul, from which boundless capacity flows. The Supreme Soul is a flawless, all‑powerful reality; no other being can match its capacity. Humans possess a partial share of this capacity when they act selflessly, because desire (kāma) depletes power, whereas selflessness (nishkāma) accumulates it. Just as a person who works becomes fatigued and regains strength through rest, a speaker who talks excessively regains eloquence through silence, and a living being who dies is revived by the impulse to live again, so creation is a phase of power depletion and dissolution is a phase of power accumulation. In other words, power diminishes through attachment to the material world and returns in abundance when one severs that attachment. **“Yo vetti tattvataḥ”** – to know Vibhuti and Yoga in their essence means to recognize that all the influence, power, and special qualities that appear in the world—whether in objects, beings, inner feelings, or the distinguished knowledge, discernment, and cosmic order of great personalities—originate from the Lord, who is the source of everything. Whoever truly understands this sees the Lord as the root of all distinctions; his consciousness resides solely in the Lord, not in the particular attributes of objects or individuals. Just as a goldsmith’s eye focuses on ornaments while recognizing that, in essence, they are all gold, similarly, wherever a special quality appears, the vision should be directed toward the Lord, for that quality belongs to Him; the object, person, or action is merely an expression of the Divine.

[ Verse 7 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjivani *

In this world, action and material objects are constantly changing. Whatever special quality appears in them is, in reality, the immutable, all‑pervading quality of the Supreme Self. Wherever marvels, super‑natural features, etc., are seen, the object or person is taken to be the source of that marvel; the mind then becomes entangled in it and gains nothing. The reason is that the marvel seen in objects is merely a reflection of the unchanging Supreme Self, not of the mutable object. Thus, directing one’s sight toward that original principle is what is meant by “knowing the principle” – i.e., accepting it with firm faith. Knowing the principle of the divine manifestations (vibhūti) means recognizing that their special quality belongs to the Supreme Self. Therefore, the seeker’s vision must be directed only toward that Supreme quality. This is precisely what is meant by “knowing the principle” – i.e., accepting it. “so’ avikampena yogena yujyate” – (so’ avikampena yogena yujyate: “He is united with the unshakable yoga”) – engenders steadfast devotion to Me. “Steadfast” here implies that, apart from Me, no other thing possesses even a trace of significance. Consequently, his attraction is not toward any other, but solely toward Me. “na‑atra saṁśayaḥ” – (na‑atra saṁśayaḥ: “There is no doubt”) – means that if any doubt existed, he would not have truly accepted Me as the principle. The reason is that he would have regarded My yoga, i.e., the marvelous effect, and the resulting divine powers (vibhūti, i.e., wealth) as separate from Me and given them importance. After truly knowing Me, if any worldly marvel were to appear before him, it could not affect him; his vision would not turn toward that marvel but remain fixed on Me, resulting in natural, unwavering devotion. The description of vibhūti here signifies that they are fully pervaded by the Supreme Self’s divine power. The manifested wealth is nothing but the Supreme Self’s power of yoga. Hence, wherever a marvel appears, that marvel is the result of the Supreme Self’s yogic power (vibhūti), not of the object itself. Thus yoga and vibhūti are of the Supreme Self, and the appended note explains:

In this world, any marvel or special quality that is perceived is the “yoga” of the Lord – the extraordinary effect or potency. From that extraordinary effect arises the specific manifestation called “vibhūti.” Consequently, a person who truly knows the Lord’s vibhūti and yoga develops firm devotion to the Lord. There is no other reality besides the Lord; accepting this without doubt is what “knowing the principle” means. Hence, one who knows the principle is called “the knower” (as stated in the Gita, Chapter 7, Verse 19). “avikampa (avichala) yoga” – (avikampa yoga: “the unshakable yoga”) – signifies that the path of devotion itself does not move and cannot be moved, because there is no other entity besides the Lord. Just as all objects can be bought with money, an ordinary person places value only in money and becomes attached to it. Similarly, whatever influence or importance appears is ultimately the Lord’s; realizing this makes one’s devotion to the Lord unshakable. “na‑atra saṁśayaḥ” – (na‑atra saṁśayaḥ: “there is no doubt”) – means that when there is no other reality besides the Lord, how can doubt arise? Because this is a chapter on devotion, the phrase “tattvataḥ vetti” (to know in essence) should be understood as “tattvataḥ maṇa” (to accept in essence). The Lord’s statement that “knowing in essence yields firm devotion” is reiterated in later verses, e.g., “I am the sole cause of the material world, and all of creation acts through Me.” Thus, just as knowledge becomes firm, acceptance also becomes firm, yielding the fruit of true philosophy. Assertions such as “I am Hindu,” “I belong to a certain caste,” etc., persist only while one clings to them; they do not vanish until one relinquishes them. In the same way, the belief that “the Lord is the source of all vibhūti” never fades. Social labels like caste or sect are provisional, tied to the body, and ultimately perish, whereas the Supreme Self at the root of all is eternal and real. Consequently, this belief never disappears; it transforms into true knowledge (knowledge of the principle).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 10 ]

There is no room for doubt; wherever two entities exist, doubt arises. When only one Supreme Being exists and nothing else, where can the mind go, why would it go, into what, and how would it go? Hence unwavering devotion settles in the one Supreme Being—there is no doubt about this. Relation – In the preceding verse the Lord explained that one who knows His opulences (vibhūti) and yoga from their true nature becomes endowed with steadfast devotion. Therefore, what does it mean to know opulences and yoga from their true nature? The explanation follows in the next verses. [ Verse 8 ]

ahaṁ sarvasya prabhavo  
ahaṁ – I  
sarvasya – of all  
= prabhavaḥ – source, cause  
iti matvā bhajante māṁ – thinking “I am the source of all,” they worship Me  
samsāramātraka – of the material world only  
= prabhava (original cause)  
pravartate – operates, manifests  
mattḥ sarvaṁ pravartate – from Me everything proceeds  
buddhā bhāvasamanvitāḥ – the wise, united in feeling, are devoted

Thus, the mind is engaged, the wise act, saying “I am,” and they worship Me, considering the whole universe as originating from Me, with love and devotion aligned within. The intelligent devotee worships only Me—everything, in every form, takes refuge in Me. Explanation – The present verse repeats the message of the previous one: every action in the world has its root cause in the Lord. In “ahaṁ sarvasya prabhavo,” the term “sarvasya” denotes the Lord’s opulence; everything that is seen, heard, or understood is His opulence. In “mattḥ sarvaṁ pravartate,” “mattḥ” signifies the Lord’s yoga (influence) by which all manifestations appear. The teachings of Chapters 7, 8, and 9 are already encompassed in the first half of this verse. “Ahaṁ sarvasya prabhavo” – the mind, sound, points, embryos, sprouts, insects, eggs, sweat, i.e., all material and subtle beings, originate from the Supreme Father, the Supreme Lord. Here “prabhava” means that I am the inseparable cause‑effect‑instrument of everything, i.e., I alone manifest as creation. “mattḥ sarvaṁ pravartate” – all creations, states, dissolutions, sustenance, protection, and every activity in the world arise from Me. Their power, vigor, and all that they receive come from Me, just as all work is performed by the power of electricity. The statement “ahaṁ sarvasya prabhavo, mattḥ sarvaṁ pravartate” instructs the seeker not to focus on the external forms of beings, conduct, or actions, but to look toward the Lord who is the underlying source of all. The fundamental principle behind work, cause, feeling, action, object, substance, and person must be the focus of the devotee’s vision. The repeated use of “mattḥ” in Chapter 7, verses 7 and 12; Chapter 10, verse 5; and this verse (Chapter 10, verse 8) emphasizes that all feelings, actions, and persons arise from the Lord, reside in the Lord, and merge into the Lord. Consequently, everything is essentially divine; recognizing this establishes an unshakable yoga (relationship) with the Lord. Here the double occurrence of “sarva” in “sarvasya” and “sarvam” underscores that, apart from the Lord, there is no other creator or controller of this universe. As in Chapter 7, verse 6 the Lord described Himself as the cause of the upper and lower natures, and in Chapter 14, verse 4 He is called the seed‑giving Father; similarly, here He declares Himself the producer of all.

[ Verse 8 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

“Considering this, those whose minds are aligned with the feeling that everything in the world originates from the Lord and that all existence—gross, subtle, and causal—derives its power from the Lord, firmly accept that the Lord alone is supreme; no one is equal to Him, none has been, none is, none will be, and none can possibly become equal.”  
When their intellect is fixed solely on the Lord, their attraction, faith, trust, love, etc., become directed toward Him alone. By taking refuge in the Lord, they naturally acquire equanimity, freedom from change, freedom from sorrow, carefree confidence, fearlessness, and similar qualities. Wherever the Divine (Paramatma) is present, divine wealth naturally appears. The wise (buddhāḥ) recognize that no other reality exists apart from the Lord, that the Lord is the foundation of everything, and that devotion and love should be offered to Him alone. This is why they are called wise. In the 15th chapter, verses 18‑19, it is stated that one who knows the Lord to be beyond the perishable (the world) and superior to the imperishable (the soul) is all‑knowing and worships Him with every possible feeling. ‘Mām bhajante’ – chanting the Lord’s name, singing His glories, meditating on His form, listening to His stories, and studying the scriptures related to Him (the Gita, Ramayana, Bhagavata, etc.) are all forms of worship. True worship, however, is that which draws the heart irresistibly toward the Lord, wherein only the Lord appears dear, the thought of forgetting Him feels painful, and immersion in the Lord alone constitutes genuine devotion. **Special note**  
The Supreme Self (Paramatma) is the basis of all beings, and from the Supreme Self all objects, persons, substances, and events receive their existence and vitality. This understanding is essential for every aspirant seeking the Supreme. Since the Supreme is the root of everything, the seeker’s aim must also be directed toward the Supreme. Guiding the aim toward the Supreme is the purpose of all divine powers and the knowledge of yoga, as repeatedly indicated in the Gita—for example, the 18th chapter, verse 46, advises worship of the Supreme through one’s duties, and the 18th chapter, verses 66‑56, urges complete surrender to the Supreme who dwells in every heart and inspires all beings. Karmayoga, Jnanayoga, and Bhakti‑yoga may differ according to individual inclination, but the foregoing knowledge is indispensable for all aspirants. **Appendix**  
People value money because it can procure material things. Money can obtain objects but does not create them; the Lord, however, both creates and provides all things. Those who comprehend the Lord’s supremacy do not become trapped by the greed for trivial money but devote themselves wholly to the Lord—“sarvavid bhajati māṁ sarvabhāvena bhārata” (Gita 15.19). The Lord declares that material substances and persons arise from Him (ahaṁ sarvasya prabhavaḥ) and that all actions proceed from Him (mattḥ sarvaṁ pravartate). Yet the soul, by identifying with substances and actions, assumes ownership, becoming both consumer and doer, thereby binding itself. When the soul becomes a consumer, substances become binding; when it becomes a doer, actions become binding. If the soul refrains from being either consumer or doer, no bondage exists. All phenomena observed in the world are ultimately the Lord’s work, a truth expressed repeatedly in the Gita with the term “mattḥ,” for example:  
- “mattḥ paraṁ nānyat kiñcid asti” (7.7) – “Apart from Me, nothing else exists.”  
- “matt‑eva eti tān viddhi” (7.12) – “Know that they are from Me alone.”  
- “bhavanti bhāvā bhūtānāṁ matt eva pṛthag‑vidhāḥ” (10.5) – “The various states of beings arise from Me, each distinct.”

= “Those whose minds are fixed in Me,  
= the souls who have taken refuge in Me,  
= who enlighten one another,  
= and who constantly speak of Me,  
= are ever satisfied and delight in Me.”

Explanation of the verse (six points)

1. **macchittāḥ** – “mind‑fixed in Me.” The devotee’s mind merges with the Divine; the self‑identification “I am the Lord” causes the mind, intellect, and senses to automatically rest in the Lord. 2. **mad‑gat‑prāṇā** – “souls devoted to Me.” When a seeker sincerely aspires for the Supreme, his very being (prāṇa) is offered to the Lord, and all other activities become expressions of the Divine. 3. **bodhayantaḥ parasparam** – “they enlighten each other.” Mutual instruction arises when minds fixed in the Lord meet; the illumination is a result of their shared devotion. 4. **kathayantāḥ** – “they constantly speak of Me.” Continuous remembrance and verbal expression of the Lord are the natural outcome of the previous three qualities. 5. **tuṣyanti** – “they are satisfied.” Contentment is the fruit of the preceding qualities. 6. **ramanti** – “they delight.” Delight (spiritual joy) follows satisfaction. All beings originate from the Lord and act through the Lord; therefore the Supreme Self (Atman) is the substratum of everything. For those who have firmly realized this, nothing remains to be acquired, known, or performed except to remain wholly absorbed in the Lord in every possible way. Further clarification of **macchittāḥ**

The phrase denotes a mind that is already situated in the Lord. When one declares “I am the Lord,” the mind, intellect, and all faculties automatically align with the Divine. The doer (the self) and the instrument (mind, intellect) become inseparable; wherever the doer is placed, the instrument follows. Thus, a sincere aspirant whose heart is fixed on the Supreme finds his mind automatically engaged in the Divine practice, and all other actions become expressions of the Lord. Conversely, a person who continues to identify himself with worldly roles—“I am a householder, I am a mortal”—cannot sustain a mind constantly fixed in the Lord; the mind remains attached to the material world. The mind settles where affection (priyata) exists. Affection arises from a sense of belonging (sambandha) with the Lord. When one truly regards himself as belonging wholly to the Lord—“I am only the Lord’s, the Lord is only mine; the body and the world are not mine”—the Lord has complete authority over him, and the devotee surrenders himself entirely. In such surrender, the mind naturally rests in the Lord. Hence, the term **macchittāḥ** includes the mind (manas) as its integral part; the Gita treats “citta” and “manas” as synonymous in several places (e.g., “bhūmir āpo ’nalo vāyuḥ khaṁ manas caitanyam eva ca” — 3.4). In the present context, “citta” subsumes “manas.”
[Verse 9]

[ Verse 9 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjivani *  
[ Chapter 6 ] [ Verse 14 ] – In ordinary discourse the mind (manas) and the consciousness (citta) are treated as separate entities. In the term “mac‑citta” of this verse they are identified as one and the same. “mad‑gat‑prānāḥ” – Their life‑force has been offered to Me. The life‑force consists of two aspects: living and activity. For those devotees, both the act of living and every bodily activity (kriyā) are performed for the Lord. All actions of the body—sacrificial rites, scriptural worship, meditation, narration of pastimes, singing of hymns, as well as mundane activities such as eating, drinking, farming, trade, service, etc.—are ultimately for the Supreme. Though the actions differ in type, their purpose is identical: they are all directed toward the Lord, which makes them “Bhagavad‑gat‑prānāḥ”. Whether healthy or sick, honored or disrespected, happy or sorrowful, none of these affect the devotee; his only concern is the Lord. When this firm purpose arises, the seeker becomes a “Bhagavad‑gat‑prān”. “bodhayantaḥ parasparam” – When devotees who have attained the divine mood meet each other, the Lord’s presence spreads among them. They begin to disclose to one another the Lord’s nature, mysteries, qualities, and influences, creating a remarkable satsaṅga. In such heartfelt exchanges, spontaneous divine insights arise. It is like two lamps placed opposite each other: the darkness beneath each lamp disappears. Likewise, when two bhaktas converse about the Lord, each generates a fresh divine feeling that is expressed, and the other responds with another feeling, leading to a continual emergence of new sentiments. In solitary contemplation, such feelings are far fewer and remain unshared. As the gopīs say in the “Gopī‑gīta” – “We have offered our very souls to You” (Srimad Bhagavata 10.31.1). Thus the devotees’ souls dwell exclusively in the Lord; their attachment to the Lord exceeds any attachment to their own lives. Every being harbors the desire “May my life never be relinquished in any state,” which is the attachment and affection of the life‑force. The Lord’s devotees, however, are free from such attachment. They do not cling to the Lord’s stories or fear death; they are wholly absorbed in the Lord alone. When a devotee hears the Lord’s pastimes, the desire “May I continue to live” disappears, and the fear of death loses its grip. Their sole concern is the Lord. They speak and listen to the Lord’s narratives without hesitation, for they have realized that the speaker and the three listeners become one. Death separates only the life‑force, never the soul from the Lord. Hence a true lover of the Lord never experiences separation. Their relationship with the life‑force is replaced by an innate, self‑evident intimacy with the Lord, expressed through the narration of His qualities, pastimes, and mysteries. “satāmayaṁ sārabhūtāṁ nisargo yadarthavāṇīśruticetasām api. pratikṣaṇaṁ navyavadacyutasya yat striyā viṭānām iva sādhu‑vārta” (Srimad Bhagavata 10.13.2) – “Those whose nature is rooted in the essence of truth have ears, speech, and inner mind solely for singing, hearing, and contemplating the Lord’s pastimes. Just as a frivolous man finds novelty in women’s chatter, the devotee finds perpetual novelty in the Lord’s pastimes and stories.”

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

“nityaṁ tuṣyanti ca” – thus the story of the Lord is told, “tasmaiṁs tajja‑ne bhedābhāvāt” (Nārada‑Bhakti‑Sūtra 41). At times a devotee becomes the devotee of the Lord; at other times the Lord becomes the devotee of his devotee. In this way the play of mutual love between the Lord and the devotee continues eternally, and love increases every moment. Play, qualities, influence, mysteries, etc., generate one another, and by contemplating and narrating them the devotees remain perpetually satisfied. The implication is that only the Lord can be the source of their satisfaction; no one else exists apart from Him. “ramanti ca” – they delight (raman) in the Lord, i.e., they love Him. The aspirant must therefore recognize that every action, feeling, and impulse flows from this love. In this love there is no distinction between the devotee and the Lord – it is directed solely toward the Lord. Appendix meaning — Here the Lord describes the unshakable bhakti‑yoga mentioned in the seventh verse. The mind of the Lord’s devotees never leaves the Lord. In their view, when nothing exists except the Lord, the mind has nowhere else to go, how to go, or why to go. The devotees live for the Lord, and all their efforts are for the Lord. When a listener arrives, they impart the extraordinary knowledge of the Lord’s qualities, influences, etc.; they narrate the Lord’s pastimes. When a speaker arrives, they listen with love. Neither the speaker nor the listener attains satisfaction; there is no satiation – this is separation, and a constantly new rasa (taste) arises – this is yoga. Because of this separation and yoga, love expands every instant. The Nārada‑Bhakti‑Sutra states:

kāṇṭhāvarodharomāñcāśrabhih parasparaṁ lapamānāḥ pāvayanti kulāni pṛthivīṁ ca (68)

“Such exclusive devotees, with throats blocked, throbbing hearts, and tear‑filled eyes, converse with each other and thereby purify their lineages and the earth.”

Relation — In the previous verse the type of bhajana (devotional singing) performed by the devotees was described; in the next two verses the Lord explains the special grace He bestows upon them. [ Verse 10 ]  
teṣāṁ satata‑yuktānāṁ bhajatāṁ prītipūrvakam  
dadāmi buddhi‑yogaṁ taṁ yena mām upayānti te

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- teṣāṁ – of those  
- satata‑yuktānāṁ – constantly united, ever‑devoted  
- bhajatāṁ – who worship  
- prītipūrvakam – with love (lovingly)  
- dadāmi – I give  
- buddhi‑yogaṁ – the yoga of wisdom (intelligent action)  
- taṁ – that  
- yena – by which  
- mām – me  
- upayānti – they attain  
- te – those

**Translation** – “To those ever‑devoted worshippers, I grant the yoga of wisdom by which they attain Me.”

The phrase “prītipūrvakam” (lovingly) indicates that the Lord’s responsibility is to give whatever is required to those devotees—what to do, what to receive, etc. Hence, in these two verses the Lord explains that He imparts equality (samata) and philosophical knowledge (tattva‑jñāna) to the devotees. Explanation – “Bhaktas who are attached to the Lord desire neither equality nor philosophical knowledge nor anything else; their sole aim is to remain constantly attached to the Lord. Apart from attachment to the Lord, they have no other work.”

1 – “Thus, O king, those who are devoted to the Lord are devotees of the Lord.” (Srimad Bhagavatam 10.86.59)  
2 – “Neither the supreme ruler nor Indra nor the universal sovereign nor the lord of rasa, nor the attainment of yoga, nor any other boon is desired by the devotee who offers himself to Me, except Me.” (Srimad Bhagavatam 11.14.14)

[ Verse 11 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The expression “satat‑yuktānām” (those who are continuously united) refers, as explained in the ninth verse, to devotees whose inner mind remains unmoved by any external circumstance—whether gain or loss, honor or dishonor, praise or criticism, health or disease, or any other mutually contradictory situation. Their equanimity (buddhi‑yoga) enables them to stay perfectly balanced. “bhajataam preetipūrvakam” (let them worship with love) describes devotees who seek neither intellectual knowledge nor renunciation. Because they do not desire supreme knowledge, renunciation, worldly pleasures, the eight siddhis, or the nine treasures, their vision never turns toward such objects. They place no value on achievements or honors; they simply regard the Supreme as their own and naturally engage in loving devotion. No relationship with any material object or person arises; their sole devotion is to remain constantly absorbed in the Divine. Their love for the Divine is so complete that even in dreams no desire other than the Divine awakens. The term “dadāmi” (I give) indicates that the guru does not claim the buddhi‑yoga as his own; he acknowledges it as a gift from the Divine. Consequently, the devotee does not consider the buddhi‑yoga a personal merit. “yen” (by which) introduces the specific buddhi‑yoga that the guru bestows, the very yoga through which the devotee attains the Guru. “mām upayānti te” (they come to Me) means that once the devotees have become mind‑ and life‑identical with the Divine, are eternally satisfied in Him, and love Him, there is nothing left to obtain. Their perceived lack disappears; they experience the fullness of the Divine, as expressed in “dadāmi buddhi‑yogam tam” (I give them that perfect realization). **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – As long as attachment and aversion (rāga‑dveṣa) persist, the world appears and the Divine remains unseen; the Divine is beyond duality. While duality exists, two things are perceived and the third is hidden. When attachment and aversion are eradicated, only the Divine is seen. Thus, the removal of duality brings the experience that “everything is the Divine.” The Divine therefore grants equanimity (samata) to His devotees. Samata itself is the buddhi‑yoga, i.e., karma‑yoga, as stated in the Gita: “samataṁ yoga ucyate” (2.48). The Gita calls karma‑yoga “buddhi‑yoga” (2.49, 18.57). Upon attaining buddhi‑yoga, a devotee empathizes with another’s suffering and strives to bring happiness. A thought that is performed is artificial; a thought that arises spontaneously is genuine. Voluntary thought is intermittent, whereas spontaneous thought flows continuously like breath—hence “satat‑yuktānām.” When the body is attached to objects, one must consciously contemplate the Divine; the body’s contemplation is automatic. In the Divine, attachment (apnapan) does not require effort—devotion arises spontaneously and never ceases. Therefore the text emphasizes loving devotion: “bhajataam preetipūrvakam.”

**Verse Translation**  
For those devotees, out of compassion, I dispel the darkness of ignorance that dwells within their own‑nature, illuminating them with the lamp of self‑realized knowledge. **Word‑by‑Word Breakdown**  
- teṣām: of those devotees  
- eva: indeed, only  
- anukampārtham: for the sake of compassion  
- aham: I  
- ajñāna‑jatam: born of ignorance  
- naśayāmi: I destroy  
- ātmabhāvastha: residing in the state of the Self (Atman)  
- jñāna‑dīpena: with the lamp of knowledge  
- bhāsvatā: shining, illuminating.
