* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

I am the one who dwells within them – the darkness that arises from ignorance. Explanation – “For their compassion I, the darkness born of ignorance, become their light.” In the hearts of those devotees there is no worldly desire. Moreover, they do not even long for liberation apart from me. The meaning is that they desire neither material objects nor transcendental goals such as Moksha or self‑realisation; they simply sing my praises out of pure love. Seeing this self‑less love and devotional singing melts my heart. I wish that, through my grace, I may become a service to them and that they may receive something from me. If they do not take anything from me, my melted heart, moved by compassion, dispels their ignorance‑born darkness. My heart is melted because there is not even the slightest lack in any of my devotees. ‘Ātmabhāvasthaḥ’ – Humans usually identify their existence (“I am”) with the changing body (prakṛti). They say “I am a child, I am young, I am strong, I am weak,” etc., linking their sense of self to the body. Removing these adjectives, from the standpoint of the ultimate reality, the being’s true existence is free from prakṛti. In that immutable existence the Lord, who eternally abides, is called ‘ātmabhāvasthaḥ’. “Bhāsavtā jñāna‑dīpena nāśayāmi” – By the radiant lamp of knowledge I eradicate the darkness of ignorance in those beings. In other words, I destroy the ignorance that makes one ask, “Who am I? What is my true nature?” and I grant them self‑realisation (tattva‑bodha). The glory of such self‑realisation, praised in the scriptures, is attained through hearing, contemplation and meditation, without any external practice or effort; I directly bestow it upon them. Special note: When a devotee remains wholly absorbed in the Lord, he naturally attains equanimity in worldly success and failure. The Lord Himself gives this equanimity, and He alone can grant the purest self‑knowledge (tattva‑bodha). Because the Lord gives it directly, the devotee needs no desire or effort; the divine grace automatically brings equanimity and self‑knowledge. Where devotion (bhakti) is present as a mother, renunciation and knowledge appear as her sons. Thus, when bhakti arises, both equanimity—detachment from the world—and the knowledge of one’s own nature arise spontaneously. The perfection achieved by divine grace surpasses any perfection obtained through personal effort; it is flawless and without any trace of imperfection. Just as the Lord bears the welfare of devotees who sing His name with exclusive devotion (see Chapter 9, Verse 22 of the Gita), He likewise grants equanimity and self‑knowledge to those who are devoted solely to Him, even if they receive no material benefit or if nothing remains for them. Even while giving, the Lord remains indebted to those devotees. In the Bhagavata, the Lord says that the debt He owes to the pure, innocent gopis—who associate with Him without any ulterior motive—cannot be repaid even with a long life like the gods, because even great sages and renunciates could not easily break the bonds of familial attachment, but He has broken them for them. Devotees so absorbed in the Lord’s worship do not accept any worldly gifts, even the five liberations (sālokya, sāṣṭi, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya). **Verse 1** (Bhāgavata 3.29.13):  
sālokyasāṣṭisāmīpyasārūpy aikatvam apy uta | dīyamānaṁ na gṛhṇanti vinā matsa‑sevanam janāḥ ||  
Translation: “People do not accept the gifts of the five higher worlds—sālokya, sāṣṭi, sāmīpya, sārūpya, and even unity—without first having tasted the nectar of devotion to the Lord.”

**Verse 2** (Manasa 7.119.4):  
asa bicāri hari bhagata sayāne | mukti nirādara bhagati lubhāne ||  
Translation: “One who contemplates the Lord with a wise devotee does not seek liberation through disrespect; instead, he is drawn by pure devotion.”

**Verse 3** (Bhāgavata 10.32.22):  
na pāra ye ahaṁ niravadyasaṁyujāṁ svasādhukṛtyaṁ vibudhāyuṣāpi vaḥ | yā mabhajana durjara‑gehabhṛṅkhalaḥ saṁvṛścya tad vaḥ pratiyātu sādhunā ||  
Translation: “I do not abandon those who, without any hindrance, perform their own righteous deeds; even the wise, long‑lived ones, if they worship Me, the formidable bonds of worldly existence are broken, and they return to the path of the virtuous.”

[ Verse 11 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

They are unaware that equanimity (samatā) has arisen within us. They pray to the Lord, saying, “O Lord! You are equanimous; we have realized our true nature. If ever we fail to realize, even if we were granted the right to liberate the world, we would be astonished that this equanimity and realization should be unknown to me—how could it have entered me! They claim that no special quality appears in them, yet that very claim is a quality. I remain absorbed only in your worship and contemplation.”

Appendix: Although Karma Yoga and Jnana Yoga are both means and Bhakti Yoga is attainable, the Lord also bestows Karma Yoga upon his devotees—“I give you the Yoga of intellect”—and likewise bestows Jnana Yoga—“May the lamp of knowledge illuminate you.” Both the lower (Apara) and higher (Para) natures belong to the Lord. Hence, by His grace, He provides the devotee with Karma Yoga, which is primarily of the lower nature, and Jnana Yoga, which is primarily of the higher nature. Consequently the devotee readily attains the essential element of Karma Yoga, **Nishkama‑bhāva** (self‑less attitude), and the essential element of Jnana Yoga, **Svarūpa‑bodha** (realization of one’s true nature). When Karma Yoga is attained, the devotee renders service to the world; when Jnana Yoga is attained, the devotee’s ego‑attachment to the body disappears. The devotee, absorbed in contemplation of the Lord and in love, remains satisfied and immersed. He perceives no deficiency in himself nor any need to acquire anything. Just as a child is wholly dependent on his mother—his gaze never turns to his own shortcomings; the mother cares for him, bathes him, removes his dirty clothes and gives him clean ones—the devotee becomes entirely dependent on the Lord, saying, “Whatever I am, I belong to the Lord, and the Lord belongs to me.” He does not look inward. Therefore the Lord destroys the ignorance residing within him through true knowledge. In a child, folly is prominent; in a devotee, discernment is prominent. The devotee’s special duty is to regard the Lord as his own. When the devotee fulfills his duty, the Lord also fulfills His duty and, without any request or desire, grants the power of both Karma Yoga and Jnana Yoga, leaving no deficiency in him. In Karma Yoga there is the rasa of peace (**Shānta‑rasa**); in Jnana Yoga the rasa of indivisibility (**Akanda‑rasa**); and in Bhakti Yoga the rasa of the infinite (**Ananta‑rasa**). Peace and indivisibility do not contain the infinite, but the infinite contains both peace and indivisibility. Karma Yoga and Jnana Yoga are worldly means, whereas Bhakti Yoga is a transcendental means. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

Relation— After hearing about the Lord’s transcendental, extraordinary acts of grace, Arjuna’s attention turns toward the Lord’s compassion; impressed by this compassion, he proceeds to extol the Lord in the following verses. Arjuna said:

**Verse 12**  
*paraṁ brahma paraṁ dhāma pavitraṁ paraṁ bhavān*  
*purushaṁ śāśvataṁ divyam ādidevam ajaṁ vibhum*

Translation: “You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the most holy, the supreme Lord; the eternal, divine Person, the primordial God, unborn and all‑pervading.”

**Verse 13**  
*ahūstvāmṛṣayaḥ sarve devaṛṣir nāradas tathā*  
*asito devalo vyāsaḥ svayaṁ caiva bravīṣi me*

Translation: “All the sages, the celestial seers, Nārada as well, Asita, the sage Devala, and Vyāsa himself, address you as ‘my Lord.’”

---

**Explanation of the epithets**

- *paraṁ brahma* – the highest Brahman, the ultimate reality. - *paraṁ dhāma* – the highest abode, the supreme dwelling of all. - *pavitraṁ* – the most sacred, the purest. - *paraṁ* – supreme, unsurpassed. - *purushaḥ* – the eternal Person, the divine being. - *śāśvataṁ* – everlasting, without beginning or end. - *divyam* – divine, of the nature of the gods. - *ādidevam* – the primordial deity, the source of all gods. - *ajaṁ* – unborn, not subject to birth. - *vibhum* – all‑pervading, the lord of the universe. The sages mentioned—Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa—have all called the Lord “my Lord” in the scriptures. **Commentary**

Arjuna, seated before the Lord, praises Him, saying that the one whom the Lord himself described as the supreme Brahman (see Bhagavad‑Gita 8.3) is indeed the supreme Brahman Himself, the substratum in which the whole universe exists. That supreme Brahman is also the supreme abode, the ultimate place (see Bhagavad‑Gita 8.10). In the form of the eternal, divine Person (see Bhagavad‑Gita 2.9 and 9.18), He is the greatest of the holy—“the holy among the holy” (see Bhagavad‑Gita 8.10). The great sages have spoken of Him as follows:

1. **Mārkaṇḍeya Rishi**: “Lord Krishna is the embodiment of sacrifice, austerity, and the past, present, and future.” (Maha 0, Bhīṣma 68.3)  
2. **Bṛhu Rishi**: “He is the deity of the gods and the ancient Vishnu.” (Maha 0, Bhīṣma 68.4)  
3. **Aṅgiṛa Rishi**: “He is the creator of all living beings.” (Maha 0, Bhīṣma 68.6)  
4. **Sanatkumāra and others**: “From His head spring the sky, and from His arms the earth; the three worlds rest in His belly. He is the eternal Person; only a purified heart can perceive Him. Even the most realized sages consider Him the supreme. He is the ultimate destination of the generous royal sages who never turn their backs in battle.” (Maha 0, Bhīṣma 68.8‑10)  
5. **Nārada Rishi**: “Lord Krishna is the origin of all worlds and the knower of all states of being. He is the Lord of both the perfected beings and the gods.” (Maha 0, Bhīṣma 68.2)  
6. **Asita and Devala Rishis**: “Lord Krishna alone is the progenitor of creation and the sole creator of all worlds.” (Maha 0, Vana 12.50)  
7. **Maharshi Vyāsa**: “You are the Vasudeva of the Vasu, the bestower of Indra’s rulership, and the supreme deity even among the gods.” (Maha 0, Bhīṣma 68.5)

Thus, through the testimonies of the great seers, Arjuna’s description of the Lord as the supreme Brahman, supreme abode, most holy, eternal divine Person, primordial and unborn, is fully corroborated.

* Sadhak’s Reviving Elixir *

The sages and the primordial rishis are described as “Ādi‑Deva” (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 10, Verse 3). In that aspect the Lord is called “Aja” (the unborn) (Chapter 2, Verse 2). The ignorant consider me to be unborn and pervading the whole universe in an unmanifest form (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 9). The enlightened, however, know that I am truly unborn (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 10, Verse 4). In the same vein the Lord is also called “Vibhū” (the manifest) and directly addresses me. **Appendix** – For the attributeless, formless reality the term “para‑Brahman” is used; for the attributeless yet non‑formless reality the term “para‑dhāma” is employed; and for the embodied, manifest reality the phrase “pavitraṁ paramṁ bhavān” (the most holy, supreme you) is applied. By using these expressions Arjuna is told that the whole Supreme Self is none other than the Lord Himself (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 7, Verses 29‑30; Chapter 8, Verses 1‑4). One who is pure in himself and purifies others is called “para‑pavitra” (the supreme holy). The Lord is the supreme holy, and his name, form, etc., are likewise supreme holy. In Chapter 4, Verse 28 the Gītā declares knowledge to be the most sacred thing in this world—“nahi jñānena sadr̥śaṁ pavitram iha vidyate” (there is nothing as pure as knowledge). Yet that knowledge itself is encompassed within the Supreme Lord; therefore the Lord is even more sacred than knowledge itself. **Verse Translation**  
*sarva‑metad‑ūtaṁ manye yan‑māṁ vadasi Keśava*  
*na hi te bhagavan‑vyaktiṁ vidur‑devā na dānavāḥ*

“I consider everything you have spoken to me, O Keśava, to be true. Neither the gods nor the demons know your personal manifestation.”

**Commentary on the Verse**

- “Keśava” is a compound of the letters K‑E‑Ś‑A‑V, representing the names Brahmā (K), Viṣṇu (A), Śiva (E), and the essential nature (V). Thus the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva are collectively addressed as “Keśava”. Arjuna’s use of “Keśava” signifies that the Lord is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the universe. - The phrases “yat” (that which has been said) and “etat” (that which you have just described in Chapter 10 concerning your glories and yoga) are both accepted by Arjuna as truth. This affirms that the Lord alone is the origin and regulator of all. No other being can be supreme; the Lord is the ultimate source of everything. - The statement “na hi te bhagavan‑vyaktiṁ vidur‑devā na dānavāḥ” (also found in Chapter 4, Verse 5) emphasizes that countless births of both the speaker and the listener have passed, known to the speaker but unknown to the listener. Likewise, in Chapter 10, Verse 2 the Lord says that even the gods and great sages do not know his manifestation. Whatever the Lord has said about his own appearance is therefore correct. - Human expectations of divine perfection do not aid in realizing the true nature of the Lord; such expectations are temporal, arising and perishing. Consequently, even the gods cannot fully comprehend the principle and purpose of the Lord’s manifestation. If the gods cannot know, how could demons? The term “dānavāḥ” (demons) here highlights the extraordinary maya (illusion) that demons possess, which can produce strange effects but cannot reveal the Lord. In the presence of the Lord, the demons’ maya is utterly dispelled.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10

The supreme Being is beyond nature. He is infinite, limitless, and the power of demons, however marvelous, is material, finite, and subject to creation and destruction. A finite and perishable object cannot comprehend the infinite and imperishable principle. The forces of nature and the powers inherent in nature cannot be known. Human capacity for knowledge, ability, and special qualities are all material, whereas the Divine is beyond material nature. Practices such as renunciation, dispassion, austerity, and self‑study purify the inner self, yet even through these means the Divine cannot be known. The Divine can be known only by surrendering with exclusive devotion and by His grace (Gita – Chapter 10, verse 11 and verse 11). Appendix: No one can know the Divine by his own power; only by the Divine’s grace can one know Him—

**Transliteration and meaning**  
sōi jānai jehi dehu tumharihi kṛpā̃ tumhahi jehi deh janāī. jānat tumhahi tumhai hoī jāī. *One who knows only by the body that is given by your grace, knowing you, becomes you.*

raghunandan. jānahi bhagat bhagat ur candan. *Raghunandan, the devotee knows the devotee, the sandalwood of the heart.*

(Manas 2.127.2)

At the Divine’s abode, miracles of intellect and siddhis cannot operate. No amount of material invention can reveal the Divine. **Verse (Chapter 15, Verse 15)**  
svayam evātmanātmānaṁ vettha tvaṁ bhūtabhāvan bhūteśa devadeva puruṣottama jagatpate

*You alone know yourself; you are the origin of all beings, the Lord of beings, the Supreme Person, the Lord of the universe.*

Breakdown of epithets:

bhūtabhāvan = “O Origin of beings!”  
purūṣottama = “O Supreme Person!”  
ātmanā = “by oneself”  
bhūteś = “Lord of beings!”  
deva‑deva = “O God of gods!”  
tvaṁ = “you”  
svayam = “yourself”  
jagatpate = “O Lord of the world!”

These five designations are employed together for the Divine. Explanation: Because the Divine is the origin of all beings, He is addressed as “bhūtabhāvan.” As the master of all beings and gods, He is called “bhūteś” and “deva‑deva.” As the sustainer of the inert, mobile, and all‑worldly creation, He is “jagatpate.” As the supreme among all persons, He is “puruṣottama” (Gita – Chapter 15, Verse 18). The phrase “svayam evātmanātmānaṁ vettha tvaṁ” means that the Divine knows Himself directly, without any material instrument, without any mental tendency or curiosity, and without any internal or external cause. Footnote 1: In poetry the Divine is also called “puruṣottama” – “the unique supreme person” (Raghuvamsa 3.49). Footnote 2: The five epithets—bhūtabhāvan, bhūteś, deva‑deva, jagatpate, and puruṣottama—can be associated respectively with Surya, Śiva, Ganesha, Śakti, and Viṣṇu. By invoking these names, Arjuna is essentially saying that these five deities are, in essence, the Divine Himself.

[ Verse 16 ]  
* Sadhak - Sanjivani *

There is no necessity at all. They have no sense of a body or bodily existence. The soul also knows itself solely from itself; it is not something other than itself. They naturally, spontaneously know themselves. Their knowledge is cause‑independent, not cause‑dependent. The sense of this verse is that, just as the Lord must know His own nature, the knowledge of one’s own self is entirely cause‑independent. Hence the senses, mind, intellect, etc., cannot reveal one’s true nature. Being a fragment of the Lord, you know yourself directly, just as the Lord knows Himself; likewise the soul’s knowledge is cause‑independent. Appendix meaning: You alone know yourself from yourself—meaning the knower, the one who is known, and the act of knowing are all you; everything is you. If there is no other than you, who can know whom? If one strives to know the Absolute, one moves away from the Absolute, because one makes the Absolute an object of knowledge; only then does one desire to know it! The Absolute is the knower of all, not an object to be known. No other can be the knower of everyone’s knowledge. For example, the eye sees everything, yet the eye cannot see the eye, because the eye’s power of seeing is not an object of the senses; the senses themselves are beyond the senses. Therefore the Supreme Self is its own knower. Connection – Knowledge of the Lord’s divine manifestations (vibhūti) fosters firm devotion to the Lord (Gita 10.7). Hence, in the next three verses Arjuna prays to the Lord to describe His manifestations in detail. **Shloka (Verse 16)**  
*Transliteration:*  
vaktumarhasya‑śeṣeṇa divyā hy ātma‑vibhūtayaḥ | yābhiḥ‑vibhūtibhir‑lokān imān tvam‑vyāpya tiṣṭhasi || 16 ||

*Translation:*  
“O Lord, you are worthy of being described by the inexhaustible divine manifestations of the Self; by those very manifestations you pervade all the worlds and remain established.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- hi – indeed, thus  
- yābhiḥ – by those  
- vibhūtibhir – by the divine manifestations  
- lokān – the worlds  
- imān – these  
- tvam – you  
- vyāpya – pervading, pervade  
- tiṣṭhasi – remain established, stay  
- asheṣeṇa – inexhaustibly, without limit  
- vibhūtayaḥ – manifestations, powers  
- divyāḥ – divine  
- ātma‑ – of the Self

**Explanation**  
Because you pervade all the worlds through those divine manifestations, the mind is naturally drawn toward the Lord and devotion awakens spontaneously within the devotee. Arjuna seeks his own welfare and sees devotion as the supreme means to attain it. Therefore he says that the Lord, who abides in those wondrous, transcendent manifestations that pervade all the worlds, is the very source of that devotion. In the seventh verse the Lord had already declared that a person who knows His manifestations and yoga from the standpoint of the Absolute attains unwavering devotional yoga. Hearing this, Arjuna realizes that firm devotion is the easiest and highest path, for knowing the Lord’s manifestations and yoga from the standpoint of the Absolute expands the mind. He cites two scriptural supports:

1. “nānanyo ’to ’sti draṣṭā” (Bṛhad‑Aranyaka 3.7.23) – “There is no other seer.”  
   “vijñātāramare kena vijānīyat” (Bṛhad‑Aranyaka 2.4.14) – “Who can know the knower of all?”

2. The senses that see are not themselves senses; the mind sees, but the mind that sees is intellect; the intellect that sees is the ego (ahaṃ); the ego that sees is the Self; the Self that sees is the Self itself. Thus the Lord’s divine manifestations are the means by which Arjuna can attain steadfast devotion.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

You alone are capable of describing your own divine manifestations; no one else can enumerate them completely. The phrase “divya‑hy‑ātmavibhūtayaḥ” (the manifestations are divine) means that every special quality seen in the world ultimately belongs to the Supreme Self, not to the material world. Observing worldly qualities is merely sensual enjoyment, whereas perceiving the Supreme Self’s qualities is true divine manifestation and constitutes yoga. In earlier chapters (the 7th, 9th, and at the beginning of this 10th chapter) you already listed your manifestations and declared that knowing them leads to steadfast devotion (Bhakti‑yoga). I therefore wish to learn all of your manifestations so that my devotion may become equally firm. Arjuna asks you, “You alone can describe your complete set of manifestations, because you are the knower of yourself” (Gita 10.15). He also notes that it is impossible for anyone else to know you fully (Gita 10.2, 10.14). Hence you should proclaim your entire spectrum of divine powers, enabling me to attain unwavering devotion. **[ Verse 17 ]**  
*katham vidyām aham yogiṁ tvāṁ sadā paricintayan*  
*keṣu keṣu ca bhāveṣu cintyo ’smi bhagavān mayā*

- *katham* – how  
- *vidyām* – may I know  
- *aham* – I  
- *yogiṁ* – the yogi (the one who is devoted)  
- *tvāṁ* – you  
- *sadā* – always  
- *paricintayan* – by continual contemplation  
- *keṣu keṣu* – in which, in what  
- *ca* – also  
- *bhāveṣu* – states, conditions  
- *cintyo ’smi* – I am the object of contemplation  
- *bhagavān* – the Supreme Lord  
- *mayā* – by me

**Translation:** “How can I, ever contemplating you, the yogi, know you? In which states or conditions am I to contemplate you, O Supreme Lord?”

Arjuna’s question “How may I know you, O Lord?” reflects the teaching of verse 7, where the Lord says that one who truly understands his divine manifestation and yoga becomes endowed with unshakable devotion. He therefore asks, “How shall I constantly contemplate you?”

In verse 8.14 the Lord replies that the yogi who constantly remembers him with exclusive devotion is easily attained. Later, in verse 9.22, the Lord states that he supports the welfare of those exclusive devotees who perpetually think of him. Hearing this, Arjuna wonders where and how he should contemplate the Lord—what objects, persons, places, or times are appropriate for such contemplation. He asks: “In which objects, persons, countries, or moments should I meditate on you?” The answer given is that wherever you meditate, you will understand the Lord. This implies that the Supreme Self pervades all objects, persons, places, and times; therefore, wherever the mind turns, the contemplation is of the Lord’s own nature. Recognizing worldly qualities leads to worldly thinking, whereas recognizing the Lord’s qualities leads to contemplation of the Lord himself. Consequently, worldly contemplation must be transformed into divine contemplation. **Appendix (Parishishta‑bhab)** – Arjuna’s underlying query is, “O Lord, in which forms have you manifested so that I may contemplate you?” He asks this gently, aiming at direct realization of the Divine. Arjuna represents the aspirant seeker; his question is intended for all seekers.

[ Verse 18 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

Arjuna knew Lord Shri Krishna, but he did not know the Lord’s total, all‑encompassing form. His curiosity to perceive that total form led him to ask, “How may I know your total form? In what forms should I contemplate you?” This shows that the divine manifestations (vibhutis) are not merely secondary; because they are the means of attaining the Lord, they become primary. In the form of vibhutis the Lord Himself is directly present. As long as a person does not know the Lord, he retains a notion of something being secondary or primary. When the Lord is known, that notion disappears, for apart from the Lord there is nothing, so the distinction of secondary versus primary has no meaning. The distinction exists only in the seeker’s mind, not in the view of the Lord or the realized sage. **Sanskrit verse and word‑by‑word rendering**

vistarena‑ātmanaḥ yogaṁ vibhūtiṁ ca Janārdana |  
bhoayah kathaya tṛptir hi śṛṇvataḥ nāsti me amṛtam

- *vistarena* – by expansion  
- *ātmanaḥ* – of the self  
- *yogaṁ* – yoga (the means of union)  
- *vibhūtiṁ* – divine manifestations  
- *ca* – and  
- *Janārdana* – O Janardana (Krishna)  
- *bhoayah* – again  
- *kathaya* – speak  
- *tṛptir* – satisfaction  
- *hi* – indeed  
- *śṛṇvataḥ* – hearing  
- *nāsti* – is not  
- *me* – my  
- *amṛtam* – immortal (nectar‑like)

**Commentary translation**

The Lord, in the seventh and ninth chapters, had already spoken extensively about knowledge and wisdom. Yet even after that, his satisfaction was not complete, so he began the tenth chapter of his own accord. Commencing the tenth chapter, the Lord said, “Listen again to my supreme words.” Hearing this, Arjuna’s attention turned especially toward the Lord’s grace and greatness, and he prayed to hear the Lord’s teachings once more. Arjuna says, “Please recount your yoga and your vibhutis in detail once again, for while listening to your immortal words I am not satisfied; I wish to keep listening.”

Because hearing the Lord’s vibhutis intensifies a direct attraction toward the Lord, Arjuna felt that acquiring knowledge of these vibhutis would deepen his special attraction to the Lord and naturally strengthen his steadfast devotion. Hence he earnestly requests the Lord to elaborate again. “Listening, my satisfaction is not attained by your immortal words.” (Arjuna, verse 7 of chapter 10)

For Arjuna, learning about the vibhutis seemed very simple: he need not undertake any new work or new contemplation; wherever a special quality of the Lord is perceived, the mind’s natural pull aligns with that quality. Consequently, the flow of mental tendencies will shift from the world to the Lord, resulting in firm devotion and effortless welfare. Arjuna likens this to a person who sits down to eat and discovers a favorite dish; the desire for that dish grows, and the person repeatedly asks for it. Two obstacles arise: if the dish is offered in a small quantity, it does not fully satisfy; if it is offered in excess, the stomach cannot accommodate more. In contrast, the desire to hear the Lord’s vibhutis and yogic teachings never ends. The immortal words have no terminus, and no satisfaction is achieved merely by hearing them. Therefore Arjuna implores the Lord, “Again, speak, for I am not satisfied while listening to your immortal words.”

Arjuna seeks the supreme means (sādhan) mentioned in the second chapter, seventh verse; the third chapter, second verse; and the first verse of the fifth chapter. The Lord explains that the fruit of truly understanding vibhuti and yoga is steadfast devotion (Bhakti).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

Appendix Note – Just as food pleases a hungry person and water pleases a thirsty person, the inquisitive Arjuna finds the divine verses exceedingly wonderful. The more the Lord’s words appear wondrous to him, the more a special feeling toward the Lord manifests. Connection – Having accepted Arjuna’s prayer, the Lord now begins, in the following verses, to speak of his divine manifestations and yoga. Sri Bhagavan said:

**Verse 19**  
hanta te kathayiṣyāmi divyāḥ ātma‑vibhūtayaḥ | prādhānyataḥ Kuru‑śreṣṭha nāsty antaḥ vistaraḥ me || 19 ||

Translation: “Yes, I will now tell you of my divine manifestations. Primarily, O chief of the Kuru, there is no limit to my expansion.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- hanta = yes, alright  
- te = to you  
- kathayiṣyāmi = I will speak, I shall tell  
- divyāḥ = divine, celestial  
- ātma‑vibhūtayaḥ = my self‑manifestations, divine powers  
- prādhānyataḥ = primarily, chiefly  
- Kuru‑śreṣṭha = O best of the Kuru (chief of the Kuru)  
- na = not  
- asti = there is  
- antaḥ = end, limit  
- vistaraḥ = expansion, extent  
- me = of mine

**Explanation** – “hanta te kathayiṣyāmi divyāḥ ātma‑vibhūtayaḥ” means that the divine manifestations have no end. In the eleventh chapter, the term *vibhūtayaḥ* (manifestations) is used to answer Arjuna’s request for a description of the Lord’s yogic powers. The adjective *divyāḥ* indicates that whatever special quality appears in any object, person, or event is essentially the Lord’s own; thus perceiving it as divine is to see the divine, whereas perceiving it as ordinary is to see the non‑divine, i.e., the worldly. When Arjuna timidly says, “I wish to see your universal form; if it is possible for me to see it, please show it,” the Lord replies, “Observe my forms, Partha” (11.5). The Lord does not limit the number of forms to two or four; he invites Arjuna to behold hundreds or thousands of forms. Similarly, after hearing Arjuna’s request to hear the Lord’s manifestations in detail, the Lord says he will describe them briefly, and after hearing Arjuna’s request to see a single form, the Lord invites him to see hundreds and thousands of forms. The phrase “prādhānyataḥ Kuru‑śreṣṭha nāsty antaḥ vistaraḥ me” expresses a great marvel: although a man may hear the Lord’s many manifestations, his eyes cannot fully perceive them; the capacity of sight is limited compared to that of hearing. Hence the Lord will summarize his manifestations, because his expansion is inexhaustible. **Footnotes**  
1. *Gita‑Darpan* (twelve‑th article) – “The Lord appears in many diverse forms in the Gita.”  
2. The ear deals with *śabda* (sound). Words are of two kinds – descriptive and phonetic. Through hearing, we gain direct knowledge as well as indirect knowledge (of heaven, hell, etc.). Thus in the Vedantic process (śravaṇa, manana, nididhyāsana, etc.) “śravaṇa” (hearing) comes first. Likewise in devotional practice (śravaṇa, kīrtana, smaraṇa, pāda‑sevana, etc.) “śravaṇa” is primary. The knowledge of the Supreme (parātmā) described in the scriptures is indirect knowledge that we obtain through the ears; by hearing we come to understand, accept, and realize the Supreme. **Sanskrit quotation**  
śabda‑śakteḥ acintyatvāḥ śabda‑deva‑āparokṣadhīḥ | prasuptaḥ puruṣo yad‑vachchabdenaiva‑avabudhye || (Sadācārānusandhānam 19)

Translation: “The power of the word is inconceivable; the word alone is the means to indirect knowledge. A dormant person is understood only through the word.”

[ Verse 20 ]  
* Sadhak – Sanjivani *

The Lord, after briefly stating His power, instructed that one should listen succinctly; He gave permission to behold His many forms. When Arjuna modestly expressed his inability to see even a single form, the Lord urged him to view the multitude of forms. This is because Arjuna’s understanding of the Divine subject matter gradually expands throughout the Gita. In Chapter 10, when the Lord declared that His divine manifestations are endless, Arjuna’s vision turned toward the Lord’s infinitude. He realized that, regarding the Divine, he knows nothing, for the Lord is infinite, boundless, and immeasurable. Yet Arjuna mistakenly asked the Lord to enumerate all His manifestations. Consequently, Arjuna later becomes more cautious and, with humility, prays to the Lord to reveal only one form. Even though the power of the eyes is limited, the Lord bestows divine sight—granting extraordinary capability to the subtle eyes—so that whatever is received is received in abundance. Another point concerns the difference between asking a personal question of the Lord and earnestly praying, out of ignorance and unworthiness, to learn. Here Arjuna, wishing to hear an extensive list of manifestations, sought the Lord’s clarification, but the Lord replied that He would speak briefly, for He has no exhaustive list of His manifestations. In Chapter 11, Arjuna, acknowledging his ignorance and unworthiness, prayed to see the Lord’s immutable form; the Lord then granted permission to view His infinite forms and also gave the divine vision required to perceive them. Therefore, a seeker should make no claim of personal effort, ego, or intellect, but should rely wholly on the Lord, because dependence on the Lord is the essential supplement— the Lord is infinite, and thus His manifestations are infinite as well. No one can fully describe or even hear the totality of His manifestations; if someone could, they would cease to be infinite. Hence the Lord says He will speak of His manifestations only in brief. When the Lord calls Arjuna “Kuru‑shreshtha” (the best among the Kauravas), He means that Arjuna’s mind now desires to know Him, and therefore he is deemed the best. Relation – Manifestations and Yoga: From the twentieth to the forty‑seventh verse, the Lord enumerates eighty‑two of His manifestations. **Sanskrit verse (transliterated and rendered):**  
*aham‑ātmā guḍākeśa sarva‑bhūtāśaya‑sthitaḥ* – I, the Atman (the eternal soul), am the indwelling essence of all beings. *aham‑ādiś ca madhyaṁ ca bhūtānām anta‑eva ca* – I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of all created things. When a person sleeps, the senses contract, the mind contracts, the intellect contracts, and finally ignorance (avidyā) prevails. Yet, even though the senses are deeply withdrawn in sleep, calling the name of a sleeping person awakens him. The word (śabda) possesses such power that it can rouse even one immersed in avidyā; therefore, the word is infinitely potent. Vision ceases at material objects, but the word does not stop at the ear—it returns to its source. The eyes capture forms: just as a face appears in a mirror when light passes through glass, the eye contains a “glass” through which material forms become visible. The eyes have a special ability to perceive a second form while still holding the first; thus, when a fan rotates on three blades, the eyes perceive a single circular motion rather than three separate motions. Even so, the ears possess less power than the eyes. The senses can grasp only their respective objects; they cannot apprehend the Supreme (Paramātma). The Supreme is not an object of the senses, for it is self‑existent; its knowledge is self‑evident. Hence, in this chapter the Lord says, “You know yourself by yourself” – *svayameva ātman ātmanam vettha tvam* (Gita 10.15). In another chapter the Lord explains that when one renounces all desires, the mind becomes satisfied with itself – *prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān partha manogatān ; ātmanyeva ātmanā tuṣṭaḥ* (2.55). This implies that knowledge of the Supreme is independent of action. The eyes cannot grasp that knowledge, but the ears, through the word, convey it directly to the self.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

Gudakesha (Arjuna), O conqueror of sleep! In the innermost core of every creature, the self (Atman) dwells; I am that self, I am the heart‑essence, I alone am the soul. The opening of this chapter explains that the Supreme Self (Parmatma) is the source, the midpoint, and the end of all beings. By stating “I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of all creatures,” the Lord declares that His divine manifestations (vibhūti) pervade the whole of creation. In the twentieth verse He says, “I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of all beings.” In the thirty‑second verse He says, “I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of all creations.” In the forty‑seventh verse He says, “I am the seed of all beings; without Me no animate or inanimate entity exists.” These statements constitute the essence of the vibhūti. The implication is that whatever particular qualities (such as “beginning”) are ascribed to the divine manifestations, any other manifestation that appears is also a manifestation of the Lord. Hence He identifies Himself as existing in the beginning, the middle, and the end of all animate and inanimate beings. From the ultimate standpoint, everything is the Supreme Self – “Vasudeva is all” (Gita 7.19). The vibhūti are cited to illustrate this goal. Explanation – The Lord’s contemplation operates in two ways:

1. The seeker should fix his mind solely on the chosen deity (Ishta‑Deva) and, if other thoughts arise, withdraw the mind and return to that devotion. 2. When the mind dwells on worldly attributes, those attributes must be recognized as expressions of the Lord’s own nature. The present description of vibhūti serves this second mode of contemplation. In other words, wherever the mind latches onto a particular attribute, the contemplation must be of the Lord, not of the object or individual. This is why the Lord enumerates His vibhūti. ‘Aham ādiś ca madhyaṃ ca bhūtānām anta eva ca’ – “I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of all beings.” This verse summarizes the totality of the Lord’s manifestations: He alone pervades the beginning, the middle, and the end of every creature. A universal principle holds that for any transient entity, the underlying reality that exists at its origin and its dissolution also remains present in its middle, whether visible or not. Thus, the substance that gives rise to a thing and into which it dissolves is constant throughout its existence. For example, a jewel made of gold is gold in its essence before it is fashioned, remains gold while it is a jewel, and returns to gold when it is melted. In the twentieth verse the Lord identifies the soul (Atman) as the gold‑like essence present in all beings. In the thirty‑second verse He identifies Himself as the gold‑like essence of creation itself. Only the name, form, function, measure, weight, etc., are described, while the underlying reality – the immutable, conscious, and dynamic principle – remains the same in all its manifestations. The Lord declares, “I become many forms, yet I am always the same gold.” Thus, even when the myriad forms merge back into the source, the Supreme Self remains unchanged. The terms ‘Ādi’ (beginning) and ‘Anta’ (end) are used in the masculine gender, indicating that at the absolute beginning and at the absolute end alone the Supreme Lord resides (cf. Gita 10.2, “Aham ādiḥ hi devānāṃ mahārṣīṇāṃ ca sarvaśaḥ”). In the middle, i.e., during creation, masculine, feminine, and neuter entities coexist. Consequently, the neuter gender is employed for the word ‘Madhyam’ (middle) to signify that the neuter encompasses all three genders. This grammatical choice is repeated in the thirty‑second verse.

[ Verse 21 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

(Gita 9.19); because the principle that exists at the beginning and at the end (the seventeenth verse) is the object of contemplation of any thing or person, that same principle is present in the middle. At the end, in the forty‑eighth verse, it is not in the subject. The Lord declares, in the form of seed (cause), that He alone is the seed of all; without Him no creature exists. Thus, in these three places—three verses—the principal divine manifestations (vibhūti) are described, and in other verses the manifestations that dominate the community, that have supremacy over the community, or possess special qualities, are also described. However, the seeker should not dwell on the importance, specialness, beauty, or supremacy of these manifestations; rather, remember that all these manifestations appear only from the Lord. Their significance belongs solely to the Lord; these manifestations are themselves the divine form. The reason is that Arjuna’s question concerns the object of contemplation of the Lord. Appendix meaning: the beginning, middle, and end of all beings are the Lord—implying that apart from the one Lord, nothing else exists; everything is the Lord. I, the Atman, the ever‑present Self, reside in all beings. How should the seeker use these manifestations? When the seeker’s vision turns toward beings, he should contemplate that “the Lord is present as the Self‑form in all beings.” When the seeker’s vision turns toward creation, he should contemplate that “in the beginning, middle, and end of the ever‑born, ever‑destroyed, ever‑changing creation, there is one Lord.” When his vision turns toward the root of beings, he should contemplate that “the Lord is the seed; without the Lord no moving or unmoving creature exists or can exist.”

Lord Krishna is the totality, and the soul is His manifestation. The soul is the Lord’s “para‑nature” and the inner self is the “apara‑nature” (Gita 7.4‑5). Both para and apara are inseparable from the Lord. **Shloka (21)**  
ādityānām ahaṁ viṣṇur jyotiṣāṁ ravi raṁśumān | marīcir marutām asmi nakṣatrāṇām ahaṁ śaśī || 21 ||

*Translation*: “Of the sons of Aditi I am Vishnu; of the luminous bodies I am the sun‑rayed Ravi; of the winds I am the illusory Marīci; of the stars I am the moon‑like Śaśī.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- ahaṁ – I  
- adityānām – of the sons of Aditi (the celestial deities)  
- viṣṇuḥ – Vishnu (the dwarf‑form Vāmana) is the chief among them  
- jyotiṣāṁ – of the luminous objects (moon, stars, fire, etc.)  
- ravi – the sun, the one bearing rays  
- raṁśumān – radiant, shining  
- marīciḥ – the illusory one, a name of the wind‑spirit  
- marutām – of the winds (the eighty‑nine winds)  
- asmi – I am  
- nakṣatrāṇām – of the stars  
- śaśī – the moon

**Explanation of the use of the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī)**  
In this passage the sixth case serves both a determinative (definitive) function and a relational function. Where it is determinative, Hindi uses the postposition “mein”; where it is relational, Hindi uses “ka/ki”. For example, in the first half of the verse the sixth case is used determinatively, while in the second half it is relational. - “ādityānām ahaṁ viṣṇuḥ” – among the sons of Aditi, I am Vishnu. - “jyotiṣāṁ ravi raṁśumān” – among the luminous bodies, I am the sun‑rayed Ravi. - “marīciḥ marutām asmi” – I am the chief brilliance of the eighty‑nine winds. - “nakṣatrāṇām ahaṁ śaśī” – among the stars, I am the moon. Thus, the Lord identifies Himself as the supreme principle in each category of cosmic entities. **Additional note**  
Among the twelve solar deities that preside over the twelve months, the sun of the Kartik month is also called “Vishnu.”

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

The verse “I am the moon among the twenty‑seven constellations” is explained as a declaration of the Lord’s divine manifestations. He says that, just as He is Vāmana among the sons of Aditi (Verse 21), He is Rāma among the wielders of weapons (Verse 31), and among the most eminent manifestations He is Vāsudeva (Krishna) among the Yādavas and Dhananjaya (Arjuna) among the Pandavas (Verse 37). All such manifestations belong to the Lord. [This section describes the various divine manifestations (vibhūti).]

[ Verse 22 ]  
**Transliteration:**  
*vedānāṁ sāma‑vedaḥ asmi, devānāṁ vāsavaḥ;  
indriyāṇāṁ manaḥ ca asmi, bhūtānāṁ cetanā.*

**Literal meaning:**  
“I am the Samaveda among the Vedas, I am Vasava among the gods; I am the mind among the senses, and I am consciousness among all beings.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown:**  
- *vedānāṁ* – of the Vedas  
- *sāma‑vedaḥ* – the Samaveda (the Veda of chants)  
- *asmi* – I am  
- *devānāṁ* – among the gods  
- *vāsavaḥ* – Vasava (the divine controller)  
- *indriyāṇāṁ* – of the senses  
- *manaḥ* – the mind  
- *ca* – also  
- *asmi* – I am  
- *bhūtānāṁ* – of the living beings  
- *cetanā* – consciousness

**Commentary:**  
‘I am the Samaveda of the Vedas’ means that the Vedas’ hymns do not function without the mind; the senses can perceive objects only when the mind is present. The mind’s special quality originates from the Lord, therefore He calls the mind one of His manifestations. The Samaveda, sung with melody, contains praises of the Lord in the form of Indra; hence the Samaveda itself is a manifestation of the Lord. ‘I am Vasava among the gods’ indicates that among all deities—Sun, Moon, etc.—Indra is the chief, and the Lord identifies Himself with that chief. ‘I am the mind among the senses’ shows that the eyes, ears, etc., operate only together with the mind; they have no independent power. ‘I am consciousness among all beings’ refers to the vital consciousness that distinguishes a sleeping person from a dead one; this consciousness is another of the Lord’s manifestations. The Lord further declares:

[ Verse 23 ]  
**Transliteration:**  
*rudrāṇāṁ śaṅkaraḥ ca asmi, vitteśo yakṣa‑rakṣasām;  
vasūnām pāvakaḥ ca asmi, meruḥ śikhariṇām aham.*

**Literal meaning:**  
“I am Śaṅkara among the Rudras, I am Vitteśa among the yakṣas and rakṣasas; I am the purifier fire among the waters, and I am Meru, the peak of the mountains.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown:**  
- *rudrāṇāṁ* – of the Rudras  
- *śaṅkaraḥ* – Śaṅkara (Shiva)  
- *ca* – also  
- *asmi* – I am  
- *vitteśaḥ* – Vitteśa (Kuber, the treasurer)  
- *yakṣa‑rakṣasām* – among the yakṣas and rakṣasas (nature‑spirits and demons)  
- *vasūnām* – of the waters  
- *pāvakaḥ* – the purifier fire  
- *ca* – also  
- *asmi* – I am  
- *meruḥ* – Meru (the sacred mountain)  
- *śikhariṇām* – of the peaks  
- *aham* – I

**Commentary:**  
‘I am Śaṅkara among the Rudras’ means that among the eleven Rudras—such as Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka—Śaṅkara (Shiva) is the supreme lord, the source of welfare. ‘I am Vitteśa among the yakṣas and rakṣasas’ indicates that Kuber, the chief of the yakṣas and rakṣasas, is appointed as the treasurer of wealth; his pre‑eminence makes him a manifestation of the Lord. ‘I am the purifier fire among the waters’ refers to the fire that purifies the eight waters (earth, air, fire, water, ether, etc.), signifying the Lord’s role as the purifier. ‘I am Meru, the peak of the mountains’ declares that the Lord is the highest summit, the cosmic mountain Meru, embodying the ultimate elevation.

[ Verse 24-25 ]  
* Saadhak‑Sanjeevani *

In the world of the elements, fire (the heat of the sun) is the lord of all. It is the store‑house of gold and jewels; therefore the Lord has declared it to be His own manifestation. The fire is the one that carries the sacrificial offerings of the gods and is described as the Lord’s mouth; hence He calls it His own splendour. The four divine manifestations mentioned in these verses derive their special significance from the Supreme Self itself. Their essential nature is a reflection of the Supreme, whose “peak is the summit of the mountains” – among the many peaks of gold, silver, copper, etc., Mount Meru is the chief. Contemplation of this truth is required. **Explanation of Verse 24**

> **Sanskrit (transliterated):**  
> *purohitoḥ ca mukhyaṁ māṁ viddhi pārtha brihaspatim |*  
> *senānīnāma ahaṁ skandaḥ sarasām asmi sāgaraḥ*

> **Literal meaning:**  
> “O Partha, consider Me the chief among all priests, the Brahma‑guru (Brihaspati). I am called Skanda among the commanders, and I am the ocean among all lakes.”

- *purohitoḥ* – among the priests (priests = priests of the Vedic rites)  
- *mukhyaṁ* – the chief, the foremost  
- *brihaspatim* – Brihaspati, the preceptor of the gods, the universal teacher and priest of Indra; the greatest among all learned and wise beings. The Lord therefore asks Arjuna to recognise Brihaspati as His own divine manifestation. - *senānīnāma* – “by the name of commander”  
- *skandaḥ* – Skanda (also known as Kartikeya), the son of Shiva; he possesses six heads and twelve arms, is the commander of the celestial armies, and is supreme among all earthly and divine commanders. The Lord therefore declares Skanda as His own manifestation. **Explanation of Verse 25**

> **Sanskrit (transliterated):**  
> *bhṛgur ahaṁ girām asmy ekam akṣaram |*  
> *yajñānāṁ japa‑yajño'smi sthāvārāṇāṁ himālayaḥ*

> **Literal meaning:**  
> “I, the sage Bṛhaspati, am the one syllable (Akṣara) that is the mountain; I am the chanting‑sacrifice among all sacrifices and the immovable Himalaya among the mountains.”

- *bhṛgur* – the great sage Bṛhaspati (one of the revered ṛṣis)  
[Verse 25]
- *ekam akṣaram* – the single indivisible syllable, the primordial “Om” (the first three‑mora sound that gave rise to the Gayatri, the Vedas, the scriptures, the Puranas and the whole literary world). - *yajñānāṁ japa‑yajño'smi* – “I am the japa‑sacrifice (repetitive chanting) among all sacrifices”  
- *sthāvārāṇāṁ himālayaḥ* – “I am the Himalaya, the immovable mountain, among all stable (unchanging) things.”

Thus, the four divine forms—fire, Brihaspati, Skanda, and the ocean—are not merely their own powers; they are expressions of the Supreme Self. When one beholds them, the memory of the Lord Himself arises. The sage Bṛhaspati, described as “the one syllable,” is the origin of the sacred sound *Om*, from which the three‑fold Gayatri emerged, then the Vedas, and subsequently all scriptures, Puranas and the entire corpus of sacred literature. Consequently, the Lord identifies Himself with this single, all‑encompassing syllable.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[Verse 26]
Pranava is presented as His own manifestation. The Gita also contains such references; for example – “Pranavaḥ sarva‑vedeṣu” (7.8) – “I am the Pranava in all the Vedas”; “Om ity ekākṣaraṁ brahma vyāharann mām anusr̥maraṇ yaḥ prayāti tyajand dehaṁ sa yāti paramāṁ gatim” (8.13) – “He who, by uttering the single syllable Om and remembering the Lord, abandons the body, attains the supreme destination”; “tasmād om ity udāhṛtya yajña‑dāna‑tapaḥ kriyāḥ pravartante vidhāno‑khyatāḥ satataṁ brahmavādinām” (17.24) – “The Vedic rites of sacrifice, charity and austerity are initiated by the utterance of Om.”

“Yajñānāṁ japayajño’smi” – All sacrificial rites performed with mantras require various substances and procedures, and some defect inevitably arises. In contrast, the japayajña (the chanting of the Lord’s name) needs no material or procedural requirement; no defect can occur, and all existing defects are eliminated. Anyone may perform it. Though different sects use different divine names, the act of name‑chanting brings welfare—this is accepted by Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists, Jains, etc. Hence the Lord declares the japayajña as His own manifestation. [ Chapter 10 ]

“sthāvārāṇāṁ Himālayaḥ” – All immovable mountains are represented by the Himalaya, which, being the site of intense austerity, is supremely sacred and the sovereign of all mountains. The most holy pilgrimage rivers such as the Ganga and Yamuna chiefly emerge from the Himalaya. The Himalaya greatly assists in attaining the Lord. Even today, long‑lived yogis and saints practice meditation and devotion in its caves. Sage Nara‑Narayana also continues austerities there for the welfare of the world. The Himalaya is the father‑in‑law of Lord Shankara, and Shankara himself dwells on its summit, Mount Kailāsa. Thus the Lord calls the Himalaya His own manifestation. In this world, whatever appears special is taken as worldly; the mind becomes trapped in it, leading to downfall. The Lord, however, offers a simple method: wherever the mind is attracted to any particular quality, consider that quality as belonging to the Lord, as originating from Him, not from this transient, perishable world. If you understand and accept this, your attraction will be directed toward the Lord, your mind will recognize only His greatness, worldly concerns will fade, and love for Him will arise. Ashvattha – sarva‑vṛkṣāṇāṁ devarṣīṇāṁ ca Nāradaḥ | gandharvāṇāṁ citrarathaḥ siddhānāṁ kapilo muniḥ || 26 ||

- ashvattha = the sacred fig (peepal) tree, considered the supreme among all trees  
- devarṣīṇām = among the divine sages (the term also includes Nārada)  
- gandharvāṇām = among the celestial musicians (citraratha = “the splendid chariot”)  
- siddhānām = among the perfected beings (kapila = the sage Kapila)  
- muniḥ = sage

Translation of the verse: “The peepal tree is the supreme among all trees; among the divine sages is Nārada; among the gandharvas is the splendid‑chariot; among the siddhas is the sage Kapila.”

Explanation: The peepal is a gentle, ever‑growing tree that spreads its roots everywhere, even on hard places such as mountains, walls, and roofs. Its worship holds great merit; Ayurveda attributes to it the power to eliminate many diseases. For these reasons the Lord declares the peepal His own manifestation. “devarṣīṇāṁ ca Nāradaḥ” – There are many divine sages and many Nāradas, yet “Devarṣī Nārada” refers to a single entity: the mind of the Lord, pre‑arranged for a specific role. Hence Nārada is called the Lord’s mind. He eternally carries a veena and sings the Lord’s glories while traveling. He instructed Valmiki and Vyāsa, inspiring them to compose the Rāmāyaṇa and Bhāgavata. All beings—humans, gods, demons, serpents—trust his words and seek his counsel. The Mahābhārata and other scriptures describe his numerous virtues.

[ Verse 27-28 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
It has been stated here that Lord Krishna has described Kapila as His own vibhuti (divine manifestation). Kapila is a born Siddha (one who has attained perfection) and is considered the foremost among the Siddhas. He is also the chief of the Gandharvas, the heavenly musicians. Kapila was born to Kardama and Devahuti, and Arjuna learned the art of music from him. Therefore, Lord Krishna has described Kapila as His own vibhuti. The uniqueness of these vibhutis is essentially a manifestation of the Lord Himself. Hence, the seeker's vision should always be focused on the Lord. Of horses, know Me to be the Ucchaisravas, born of nectar, and of mighty elephants, Airavata, and among men, the king. (27)
Ucchaisravas is the horse that emerged during the churning of the ocean, and it is the vehicle of Indra, the king of the gods. Therefore, Lord Krishna has described it as His own vibhuti. Among men, the king is the most exalted, as he is responsible for the protection, governance, and welfare of his subjects. Hence, the Lord has described the king as His own vibhuti. Airavata is the foremost among elephants, and it is also the vehicle of Indra. The strength and power that reside in these vibhutis are essentially a manifestation of the Lord Himself. Of weapons, I am the thunderbolt, and of cows, I am the wish-fulfilling cow Kamadhenu. I am Prajan, the god of love, and among serpents, I am Vasuki. (28)
The thunderbolt is the most powerful weapon, and Kamadhenu is the wish-fulfilling cow that grants all desires. Prajan, the god of love, is the deity of procreation, and Vasuki is the king of serpents. The Lord has described these as His own vibhutis, and the seeker should always contemplate on the Lord's divine manifestations.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

The Lord is brilliance; therefore He has declared the thunderbolt (vajra) to be His own manifestation. In the eleventh chapter, the Lord also describes desire (kāma) as His cow, saying “I am the desire that is contrary to dharma among beings, O Bharata; I am the cow of desire.” Among all cows, the wish‑fulfilling cow (Kamadhenu) is supreme; it is like an ocean, meaning that among all creatures He is the desire that conforms to dharma. This cow emerged from the churning of the ocean and fulfills the wishes of all gods and humans, hence it is a manifestation of the Lord. “I am Vasuki among the serpents” – Vasuki is the lord of all serpents and a devotee of the Lord. During the ocean‑churning, the rope used for the churning was fashioned from him; therefore the Lord has named him His manifestation. “I am Kandarpa among the progenitors” – The creation of the world arises only from desire. When desire is employed in accordance with dharma, renouncing personal pleasure for the sake of progeny, that desire is the Lord’s manifestation. The extraordinary nature of these manifestations is not limited to the individual beings; it originates from and belongs to the Lord Himself. Consequently, they reflect the Lord’s own thought. [ Verse 29 ]  
**Transliteration:** anantaś ca asmi nāgānāṁ varuṇo yādāsām aham | pitṝṇām aryamā ca asmi yamaḥ saṁyamatā aham |  
**Translation:** “I am the infinite among the Nagas; I am Varuna, lord of the waters; I am the compassionate one among the ancestors; I am Yama, the controller of restraint.”

**Commentary on the verse:**  
- *naganam* – “among the Nagas.”  
- *varuṇo* – “lord of the waters (Varuna).”  
- *yādāsām* – “of the waters.”  
- *ananta* – “infinite.”  
- *pitṝṇām* – “among the ancestors.”  
- *aryamā* – “compassionate.”  
- *yamaḥ* – “Yama, the judge of beings.”  
- *saṁyamatā* – “controller of restraint.”

The Nagas are ruled by their king, who possesses a thousand hoods. They forever lie on the ocean of milk as the Lord’s couch, constantly bringing Him pleasure. They have repeatedly taken incarnations with the Lord and participated in His pastimes; therefore the Lord has declared them His manifestation. “I am Varuna among the waters” – Varuna is the sovereign of all water‑creatures and water‑deities and a devotee of the Lord; thus He is named a manifestation of the Lord. “I am Yama, the controller of restraint” – Among the rulers who govern beings, Yama is the chief. He purifies beings by making them experience the results of their deeds; his rule is just and dharmic. He is also a devotee of the Lord and a guardian of the world, hence He is a manifestation of the Lord. The uniqueness displayed by these manifestations does not belong to the individual beings; it comes from the Lord and is His alone. Therefore, they embody the Lord’s own contemplation. “pitr̥ṇām aryamā ca asmi” – refers to the seven paternal figures such as Kavyavāha, Anala, Soma, etc.; among them is the compassionate one named Aryama. [ Verse 30 ]  
**Transliteration:** prahlādaś ca asmi daityānāṁ kālaḥ kalayatām aham | mṛgāṇāṁ ca mṛgendro ’ham vainateyaś ca pakṣiṇām |  
**Translation:** “I am Prahlada, the destroyer of demons; I am the time (kāla) that subdues the demons; I am the lion among the beasts; I am Vainateya among the birds.”

* A snake (sarp) lives on the earth, whereas a naga lives in water—this is the difference between a snake and a naga.

[ Verse 31 ]

Explanation – “I am Prahlada among the demons.” The instruments used for measuring time—clocks, days, seasons, months, years, etc.—are called demons. Among those demons, Prahlada is the chief and the best. He is the Lord’s supreme devotee and a self‑less lover of God; therefore the Lord has declared him as one of His divine manifestations. Prahlada existed long ago, yet the Lord says in the present tense, “I am Prahlada among the demons.” This shows that the Lord’s devotees remain ever‑present and can appear according to the faith of the worshipper. After merging in the Lord, if someone remembers Him and seeks His vision, He assumes a form and grants darshana. “Kalah kalayatam aham” – In astrology, time (kala) is the basis for calculating lifespan; thus a moment or period is a manifestation of the Lord. “Mriganam ca mrigendro aham” – Among all beasts such as tiger, elephant, cheetah, lynx, etc., the lion is the strongest, radiant, influential, heroic and courageous. The lion is the king of beasts, so the Lord calls this his manifestation. “Vaineteyashcha pakshinam” – Garuda, the son of Vinata, is the king of all birds and a devotee of the Lord. He is Vishnu’s vehicle, and when he flies his wings produce the sounds of the Samaveda verses. Hence the Lord calls him his manifestation. In all these manifestations, the particular forms described are essentially the Lord Himself; therefore, when the mind turns toward them, contemplation of the Lord should arise automatically. **Shloka (transliteration and word‑by‑word meaning)**

**English rendering** – “I am the wind among the purifiers; I am Rama among those who bear weapons; I am the crocodile among the fishes; I am the Ganga among the streams.”

Explanation – “pavanah pavataam asmi.” All things become pure through air; air brings health, so the Lord designates air as his manifestation among the purifiers. “ramah shastrabhṛtām aham.” Though Rama is an incarnation of the Lord Himself, among all weapon‑bearers he is supreme; thus the Lord calls Rama his manifestation. “jhṣāṇām makaraḥ ca asmi.” Among water‑dwelling creatures, the crocodile is the strongest; therefore the Lord declares the crocodile his manifestation. “srotasām asmi jāhanavī.” Among all flowing waters—rivers, streams, waterfalls—the Ganga is pre‑eminent. She is the Lord’s special life‑giving water; immersing the bones of the dead in the Ganga grants their souls salvation. Hence the Lord calls her his manifestation. Indeed, the essence of these manifestations is not separate from the Lord; their greatness originates from Him. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The means of knowing Me (the various attitudes in which I may be contemplated) are twofold: contemplate Me in My divine manifestations, and the result of that contemplation is to know the Supreme Reality of God at the root of all manifestations. For example, among the warriors God revealed Himself as Shri Rama, and among the Vṛṣṇas as Vasudeva (His own self). This was shown so that those communities could meditate on the divine forms of Shri Rama and Vasudeva, and the fruit of that meditation would be to recognize Shri Rama and Vasudeva as the Supreme Reality. Such meditation and the direct knowledge of God must be understood in the context of all divine manifestations. [ Chapter 10 ]

Wherever in the world a special quality, uniqueness, or beauty appears, treating it as a separate object entangles the mind; the person becomes trapped by identifying that quality or beauty as the whole world. Therefore, the Lord tells humanity not to regard that special quality or beauty as an independent object, but to consider it as originating from Me and belonging to Me. If you adopt this view and meditate on Me, your worldly preoccupations will cease and I will appear to you. The result will be that you will know Me directly; knowing Me directly will engender in you steadfast devotion (as expressed in the seventh verse of this chapter). [ Verse 32 ]

sargaṇām ādi antaś ca madhyam caiva aham arjuna  
adhyātmavidyā vidyānāṁ vādaḥ pravadatām aham

Translation:  
“I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of all creations, O Arjuna; I am the spiritual knowledge among all knowledge, and I am the discourse that is proclaimed.”

Word‑by‑word breakdown:  
- sargaṇām – of all creations  
- ādi – beginning  
- antaḥ – end  
- ca – and  
- madhyam – middle  
- caiva – also indeed  
- aham – I  
- arjuna – O Arjuna  
- adhyātmavidyā – spiritual knowledge (the knowledge of the Atman)  
- vidyānām – of all knowledge  
- vādaḥ – discussion, argument  
- pravadatām – I declare, I proclaim

Explanation of “sargaṇām ādi antaś ca madhyam caiva aham”: In every creation and every great creation—i.e., in every being’s origin—I am present; I am present in the middle of their existence, and I am present at their dissolution (when they merge). Hence, everything is Vasudeva. Merely seeing the world or living beings should evoke remembrance of the Lord. “adhyātmavidyā vidyānām” – The science that brings about human welfare is called spiritual knowledge. No amount of worldly learning can exhaust the quest for knowledge, but once spiritual knowledge is attained, there is nothing left to learn. Therefore the Lord has declared this to be His divine manifestation. “vādaḥ pravadatām aham” – The three kinds of scriptural debate are:  
1. **jalpa** – a polemical argument where one advances one’s own position and refutes the opponent, seeking victory for one side. 2. **vitandā** – a purely destructive debate that only attacks the opponent’s view without presenting any own position. 3. **vāda** – an unbiased discussion aimed solely at discerning the truth. Among these, **vāda** is the highest, and the Lord has identified Himself with this supreme discourse. *Difference between spiritual knowledge (adhyātmavidyā) and royal knowledge (rājavidyā)* – Spiritual knowledge emphasizes the nirguṇa (formless) aspect of the Supreme, while royal knowledge emphasizes the saguna (with attributes) aspect. Knowing the formless Brahman by transcending the world is adhyātmavidyā; knowing the ever‑present, ever‑manifest saguna Brahman in all places, times, objects, persons, circumstances, and events is rājavidyā.

* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *  
729

Appendix Note – Among worldly sciences, “Adhyatma Vidya” (spiritual knowledge, i.e., self‑knowledge) is the highest. In the floral anthology of the Gita’s chapters this is termed “Brahma Vidya”. Adhyatma Vidya is declared the author’s own glory because it is the simplest, the most accessible, and it is directly experienced by everyone. There is no difficulty in practising, understanding, or attaining it. In it, the acts of doing, understanding and attaining do not even arise, for it is ever‑present, constantly available in waking, dreaming, deep sleep and all other states. Self‑knowledge is more immediate than the world itself; the world is never as manifest to us as self‑knowledge is. One should understand this as follows: when we look at our childhood and at the present condition, the body is no longer the same, habits have changed, language has changed, conduct has changed, place has changed, time has changed, companions have changed, actions have changed, thoughts have changed – everything has altered. Yet, in our essential being we have not changed, and we say, “I am the same as I was in childhood.” The implication is that what has changed possesses a different nature, and what has remained unchanged possesses another nature. The unchanged is our true nature, i.e., the Atman, while the changed is the body. This is self‑knowledge. **Verse 33**  
*akṣarāṇām‑ākāro ’asmi dvandvaḥ sāmāsikasya ca*  
*aham‑eva‑akṣayaḥ kālo dhātā‑ham‑viśvato‑mukhaḥ*

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- akṣarāṇām – of the letters (the immutable)  
- ākāraḥ – the vowel “a” (the primal sound)  
- ’asmi – I am  
- dvandvaḥ – dual (the “dvandva” compound)  
- sāmāsikasya – of the compound (sāmāsa)  
- ca – and  
- aham – I  
- eva – indeed, only  
- akṣayaḥ – imperishable  
- kālaḥ – time, eternity  
- dhātā – sustainer, cause  
- ham – I (repeated for emphasis)  
- viśvato – of the whole universe  
- mukhaḥ – facing, pervading

**Interpretation**  
The speaker declares: “I am the ‘a’ that pervades all letters, the dual‑compound, and I alone am the imperishable time, the sustainer who faces the whole universe.”

Explanation – “akṣarāṇām‑ākāro ’asmi” refers to the vowel “a” that is primary in the alphabet; because the vowel is essential for pronouncing consonants, the Lord identifies it as His own glory. In a dvandva compound, both words share equal importance; the Lord likewise presents this as His own glory. “aham‑eva‑akṣayaḥ kālaḥ” – The time that never decays, the timeless, infinite (Anadi‑Anant) is identified with the Lord. While ordinary calculations of creation and dissolution are based on the sun, at the great dissolution even the sun merges; then the measurement of time is performed only by the Supreme Self. Hence the Supreme Self is the imperishable time. “dvandvaḥ sāmāsikasya ca” – When two or more words combine to form a single word, it is called a sāmāsa (compound). There are several types: avyayībhāva, tatpurusha, bahuvrīhi, and dvandva – the four principal kinds. In a compound of two words, if the first word holds the primary meaning, it is an avyayībhāva compound; if the second word is primary, it is a tatpurusha compound (as in the third‑verse phrase “kālaḥ kalayatām aham”). If both words are equally significant, it is a dvandva compound. The “kāla” mentioned here is not a fixed instant; it is ever‑changing. In the great dissolution, even Brahmā merges. The duration of the great creation equals the lifespan of Brahmā, and the duration of the great dissolution equals that same span. Therefore, the calculation of such vast periods is performed only by the imperishable time, i.e., the Supreme Self.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

[Verse 34]
“dhātā aham viśvato mukhaḥ” – because He is the face of the whole universe, God’s gaze rests upon every living being. Consequently He is extremely vigilant in sustaining all creatures. He carefully determines which being should receive which object at what time, and promptly delivers that object. For this reason He continually assumes different divine manifestations. He is the foundation of time and astrology; He has disclosed His own nature, and from that the measurement of worldly time is derived. The “Akṣaya Kāla” mentioned here is the immutable aspect of the Supreme Soul; it never changes. Akṣaya Kāla consumes everything yet remains exactly as it is, without any alteration. This unchanging Akṣaya Kāla is presented here as His divine manifestation. In Chapter 11 God also declares “kālo ’asmi” (11.32) to signify Akṣaya Kāla. **Sanskrit verse (34)**

```
sarvaharaḥ mṛtyuḥ ca aham udbhavaḥ ca bhaviṣyatām |
kīrtiḥ śrīḥ vāk ca nārīṇāṁ smṛtiḥ medhā dhṛtiḥ kṣamā || 34 ||
```

- **kṣamā** – “forgiveness, tolerance”

**Commentary**

The phrase “mṛtyuḥ sarvaharaś ca aham” signifies that the one who annihilates death is supreme among all women. The quality **kīrti** possesses such extraordinary power that after death no memory remains; everything is withdrawn. This power does not belong to death itself but to the Supreme Soul. If the divine power to erase all and cause oblivion were absent in death, a person’s anxiety about his relatives in this life would be exactly the same as the anxiety concerning relations of a previous birth. Humanity has undergone innumerable births; if the recollection of those births persisted, the anxieties and attachments would never cease. Because death brings total forgetfulness, concerns about ancestors, family, property, etc., disappear. Hence the ability of death to extinguish worry and attachment is wholly God’s. The expression “udbhavaḥ ca bhaviṣyatām” echoes the earlier statement that the Lord is the sustainer of all; here it adds that He is also the cause of the origin of everything that will arise. In other words, He is the creator, maintainer, and destroyer of the universe. The seven feminine names **kīrti, śrī, vāk, smṛti, medhā, dhṛti, kṣamā** are identified as the daughters of the Prajāpati Dakṣa (the five daughters of Dakṣa) together with the daughters of the sage Bṛhaspati (Śrī) and of Brahmā (Vāk). These seven qualities, each personified as a woman, are renowned throughout the world. - **kīrti** denotes fame and reputation. - **śrī** denotes wealth, beauty, and auspiciousness; it represents both immovable and movable wealth (land, house, money, cattle, horses, camels, elephants). Both kinds of wealth are called **śrī**. - **vāk** is the speech that confers fame and makes a person a scholar or learned one. - **smṛti** is the recollection of old, heard teachings. - **medhā** is the stable power of intellect that retains knowledge correctly. - **dhṛti** is the steadfastness that upholds one’s principles and convictions. - **kṣamā** is the capacity for forgiveness and for enduring hardships. These seven feminine attributes are celebrated in the world for their virtuous influence. The commentary concludes by emphasizing that the divine power to dissolve all attachments and delusions resides exclusively in God, and that the immutable Akṣaya Kāla, the timeless aspect of the Supreme, governs the cosmic order without ever undergoing change.

[ Verse 35 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

The power that prevents one from being distracted from the teacher is called **dhṛti** (steadfastness). It is not merely a human quality; it is a divine (God‑like) attribute. When anyone commits a crime without cause, the punishment that arises within him is a manifestation of the divine. Even though one possesses the power to give punishment, refusing to punish creates worldly pride, leading to downfall, because in the after‑life no penalty is meted out for that crime. Such pride is the source of all demonic (asuric) qualities. The attitude of forgiving despite this is called **kṣamā** (forgiveness). **kīrti**, **śrī**, and **vāk** are three qualities that appear outwardly in beings, whereas **smṛti**, **medhā**, **dhṛti**, and **kṣamā** are four qualities that manifest within beings. The Lord has declared these seven qualities as His own divine manifestations. When these special qualities are described as “divine manifestations,” the intention is to direct attention toward the Lord alone. If such qualities appear in a person, they should be regarded not as the person’s own attributes but as the Lord’s attributes, invoking remembrance of the Lord. Recognizing them as the Lord’s qualities brings constant, unending joy. Any special ability or characteristic observed in a seeker should be attributed to the Lord, not to the object or individual. For example, the curse of the sage Lomaś turned the Brahmin Kākabhushundi into a bird; yet he felt no fear, no misery, no thought, only delight, because he considered the incident not a fault of the sage but a divine inspiration. (Manas 7.113.1). In the same way, all objects, persons, events, and circumstances ultimately rest in the Lord, expressed as **bṛhat‑sām**, **sāmnāṁ**, and **gāyatrī‑chandasāmham**. **mārgashirsho ’hamṛtūnāṁ kusumākaraḥ** – “I am the month of Mārgashirsha, the blossom‑maker of the seasons.”

Breakdown of terms (Roman transliteration + English meaning):

- **māsānāṁ sāmnām** – “of the months, of the chants” (referring to the verses sung in the Samaveda)  
- **gāyate jānēvālī** – “that which is sung”  
- **śrutīyoṁ me chandasām** – “in all meters of the hymns”  
- **mārgashirshaḥ** – “the month of Mārgashirsha (and)”  
- **gāyatrī** – “the Gāyatrī meter”  
- **ṛtūnām** – “of the six seasons”  
- **ahaṁ** – “I am”  
- **kusumākaraḥ** – “the maker of blossoms (spring)”  
- **māsānām** – “of the twelve months”  
- **ahaṁ** – “I am”

**bṛhat‑sām tathā vyākhyā** – “‘bṛhat‑sām and sāmnāṁ’ refers to a hymn in the Samaveda that sustains the people, describing the grain that appears each year. Through this hymn the deity Indra‑form of the Supreme is said to originate in the month of Mārgashirsha, when new grain is praised. It is a night‑sacrificial hymn and a yajña is performed. In the Mahābhārata era, the new year began with this hymn because the Samaveda is considered the highest; thus the Lord initiated the bṛhat‑sām with Mārgashirsha. The Lord has declared **Mārgashirsha** as His own manifestation. **gāyatrī‑chandasāmham** – Among all metrically‑structured verses of the Vedas, the Gāyatrī is pre‑eminent. The Gāyatrī is called the “mother of the Vedas” because the Vedas themselves emerged from it. The Smṛtīs and Śāstras extol the great glory of the Gāyatrī. Since the form, prayer, and meditation of the Gāyatrī are all aspects of the Supreme, it leads to the realization of the Supreme Self; therefore the Lord has declared the Gāyatrī as His manifestation. **ṛtūnām kusumākaraḥ** – In the spring season, without any rain, trees, vines, leaves, and flowers become abundant. The season is neither excessively hot nor excessively cold, and the Lord has called the spring season His manifestation. All these manifestations point to the exclusive greatness of the Lord. Hence contemplation should be only on “māsānāṁ mārgashirsho ’ham” – “I am the grain of the month of Mārgashirsha, the source of the whole.”

*In the twenty‑second verse of the tenth chapter, the Lord identified the Samaveda itself as His manifestation; likewise, in the thirty‑fifth verse he identified the “bṛhat‑sām” of the Samaveda as His manifestation.*

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Deceiver, gambler

**Verse 36**  
dhyutam‑chalayatamasmi tejas‑tejasvinām aham | jayaḥ asmi vyavasāyo’smi sattvaṁ sattvavatām aham || 36 ||

*Translation*: “I am the one who, by deceit, overcomes the gambler; I am the brilliance of the brilliant. I am victory, I am activity, I am the essence of purity, I am the pure‑natured.”

**Commentary**

The term “dhyutam‑chalayatamasmi” denotes the special power that seizes another’s kingdom, wealth, and possessions through deceit; this power is called *jūā* (gambling). The Lord declares this as one of His divine manifestations. *Doubt*: If the Lord describes *jūā* as His own manifestation, why is there any fault in playing it? If there is no fault, why do the scriptures forbid it? *Resolution*: The injunction “do this and do not do that” is a scriptural prohibition, not a description of divine powers. Here the focus is on the Lord’s *vibhūti* (divine display). When Arjuna asks, “Where should I contemplate you?”, the Lord answers by revealing His thoughts in the form of divine powers, indicating that contemplation becomes effortless through these displays. Hence, wherever a person’s vision falls, he should look beyond the material world and see the Lord, for the Lord says the entire universe is pervaded by Him (Gita, Chapter 9, Verse 4). If a seeker once habitually played *jūā* but now devotes himself to the Lord’s worship, the memory of gambling may arise. By abandoning the contemplation of *jūā* and focusing on the Lord, the gambler’s mindset dissolves and the thought of the Lord arises. Observing another’s gambling and its wins and losses, one should regard the power of winning and losing as the Lord’s power, not as a mere game, because the game ends while the Supreme Being remains ever‑present. Thus, the reference to gambling and similar powers signifies the Lord’s contemplation. The individual soul is a direct fragment of the Supreme, yet it mistakenly identifies itself with the transient body and world. If one regards the apparent greatness, distinction, and splendor of the world as the Lord’s and meditates on the Supreme, the soul moves toward liberation (Gita, Chapter 8, Verse 14). Conversely, if one treats those qualities as merely worldly and meditates on the world, the soul descends into decline (Gita, Chapter 2, Verse 56). Therefore, these divine displays are described solely for the purpose of contemplating the Supreme and knowing Him directly. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- *sattvavatām* = of the sattvic (pure‑natured) persons  
- *sattvaṁ* = purity, essence  
- *aham asmi* = “I am”

Thus, “I am the pure‑natured essence of the pure‑natured.”

**Further explanation of “tejas‑tejasvinām aham”**

The term *tejas* (divine brilliance) refers to the celestial influence of great souls that even sinners hesitate to invoke. The Lord declares this brilliance as His own divine display. Consequently, the Lord’s thought is that “jaya‑asmi” (I am victory) – the characteristic of winning and losing in a game belongs to the Lord. Victory is His attribute. If a doubt arises regarding any passage of a scripture, a complete study from beginning to end, understanding the author’s purpose, goal, and intent, resolves the doubt. In Chapter 7, the Lord also enumerates His divine displays, including the same line “tejas‑tejasvinām aham” (7.10).
