[ Verse 37 ]

The Lord has declared His own divine manifestations. *Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani* (the elixir for the seeker). One should not indulge in the pleasure that follows personal victory, but should cultivate divine wisdom, for the Lord appears in the form of victory. “Vyavasayo ’smi” – the word *vyavasaya* signifies a firm resolve. In this single resolve the Lord sings great glory in the Gita; for example, the resolute intellect of the karmayogi is one (Chapter 2, Verse 41), whereas the resolute intellect is absent in those attached to sense‑enjoyment and wealth (Chapter 2, Verse 44). “Now I will only chant the Lord’s name” – by the power of this single resolve even a wicked person is called a saint by the Lord (Chapter 9, Verse 30). Thus the determination to move toward the Lord is described by Him as His own divine manifestation. The implication of calling resolve a divine manifestation is that the seeker must retain such resolve, but must not regard it as his own quality; rather he should consider it a manifestation of the Lord, received through His grace. “Sattvam sattvavatam aham” – the *sattva* quality, attitude and conduct found in sattvic persons are also the Lord’s manifestation. The meaning is that by suppressing *rajas* and *tamas*, the rising sattvic disposition should be regarded not as the seeker’s own merit but as the Lord’s manifestation. When brilliance, resolve, sattvic disposition, etc., appear in oneself or in others, the seeker should not treat them as personal attributes or as attributes of any object or individual, but should attribute them to the Lord. When the mind turns toward those qualities, one essentially sees the Lord and should remember Him. **Verse (Sanskrit transliteration + meaning)**

vṛṣṇīnāṁ vāsudevo ’smi – “I am Vasudeva among the Vrishni.”  
pāṇḍavānāṁ dhanañjayaḥ – “I am Dhanañjaya (Arjuna) among the Pandavas.”  
munīnām api ahaṁ vyāsaḥ – “Even among the sages, I am Vyāsa.”  
kavīnām uśanā kaviḥ – “Among poets, I am the foremost poet (Śukracārya).”  
— 37 —

**Explanation of the verse**

* vṛṣṇīnāṁ vāsudevo ’smi – Here the Lord identifies Himself as the supreme remainder among the Vrishni lineage. * dhanañjayaḥ – The special quality that belongs to Arjuna among the Pandavas is, in fact, the Lord’s own quality; therefore He calls Arjuna His manifestation. * munīnām api ahaṁ vyāsaḥ – Vyāsa, the chief among the sages, is presented as the Lord’s manifestation; all divisions of the Vedas, the Puranas, the Mahābhārata and other Sanskrit literature are the result of Vyāsa’s grace, which ultimately originates from the Lord. * kavīnām uśanā kaviḥ – All scholars who master the scriptural principles are called “poets.” Among them, Śukracārya, the knower of the life‑giving science (*sanjeevani*), is foremost. Because of his many virtues, the Lord calls him a manifestation of Himself. Thus every attribute mentioned—Vasudeva of the Vrishni, Dhanañjaya of the Pandavas, Vyāsa among the sages, Śukracārya among the poets—is presented as a divine manifestation. When such attributes are observed, the seeker should recognize that they are not merely worldly qualities but reflections of the Lord’s own nature, which ultimately is the Supreme Self (*Atman*). The greatness of these manifestations points to the Lord’s presence; even a newly created work today is a result of Vyāsa’s grace and cannot be merely a worldly creation.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

[ Verse 38 ]  
**Sanskrit:** dando damayatamasmi nītir asmi jigīṣatām; maunaṁ caiva asmi guh yānāṁ jñānaṁ jñānavatām aham

**English translation:** I am the punitive power for those who oppress, the guiding principle for those who seek victory, the silence that pervades hidden realms, and the knowledge that belongs to the wise. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- *jñānavānām* – among the knowledgeable, I am the **punishment** (danda). - *damayatām* – for the oppressors, I am the **punitive policy**. - *nītir* – the **principle** or **policy**. - *jigīṣatām* – for those who **desire victory**. - *maunaṁ* – **silence**. - *ca* – also. - *asmi* – I **am**. - *guh yānām* – of the **secret, hidden** states. - *jñānaṁ* – **knowledge**. - *jñānavatām* – of the **knowledge‑possessing**. **Commentary (translation)**  
The verse declares four of the Lord’s divine manifestations. First, He is the **punitive principle** (danda‑nīti) that subdues the wicked; this discipline is essential for rescuing souls and guiding them onto the righteous path. Second, He is the **knowledge** that pervades all who are learned; any insight—whether of worldly arts or of ultimate philosophy—when recognized as His manifestation, is regarded as His divine attribute. Third, He is the **policy** (nīti) that grants victory to those who earnestly seek it; success is attained only through adherence to divine principle. Fourth, He is the **silence** that governs all secret, concealed emotions; the power of restraint and inner quiet is the hallmark of these hidden qualities, for the one who remains silent perceives the supreme reality beyond personal identification. [ Verse 39 ]  
**Sanskrit:** arjuna yac cāpi sarvabhūtānāṁ bījaṁ tad aham arjuna; na tad asti vina yat syām mayā bhūtaṁ carācaram

**English translation:** Arjuna, even the seed of all beings is I; there is nothing else besides Me that is the cause of the animate and the inanimate. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- *arjuna* – “O Arjuna”. - *yac ca api* – “even that which”. - *sarvabhūtānām* – “of all beings”. - *bījaṁ* – “seed” or **causal principle**. - *tad* – “that”. - *aham* – “I”. - *na* – “not”. - *tad asti* – “that exists”. - *vina* – “without”. - *yat* – “that”. - *syām* – “may be”. - *mayā* – “by Me”. - *bhūtaṁ* – “the created”. - *carācaram* – “the moving and the unmoving”. **Commentary (translation)**  
In this verse the Lord identifies Himself as the **seed (bīja)** of every manifestation. He is both the material cause that gives rise to the universe and the efficient cause that sustains it. Thus the entire cosmos, in its mutable and immutable aspects, originates from and is pervaded by the Divine. The commentary notes that from verse 20 through verse 48 the Lord enumerates a total of eighty‑two divine manifestations, allocating four per verse in many cases, thereby illustrating the comprehensive scope of His divine attributes. ---

[ Verse 39 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

It is that I remain exactly as I am, yet I appear in the form of the world, and even after appearing as the world I remain equally pervasive within it. The term “seed” (beej) is used here only to indicate a seed. Its purpose is not to describe a literal seed but to point out that whenever any object, person, event, or circumstance arises, the contemplation must be of the Lord alone. This is because Arjuna’s original question was: “How can I know you while contemplating you, and in what moods should I contemplate you?” (Verse 17). In answer, the Lord gave a brief description of His divine manifestations so that one may contemplate Him. “na tad asti vinaa yatsyam mayaa bhutam chara‑charam” – Nothing, whether animate or inanimate, can exist without Me. All that exists is Me; I am the sole reality. By realizing this fundamental principle, the seeker’s senses, mind, and intellect, wherever they go, or whatever worldly recollection arises in mind‑intellect, are to be regarded as the form of the Lord. Holding this view, the seeker contemplates only the Lord, not any other, because apart from the Lord there is no other reality. Here the Lord says that apart from Him there is nothing, animate or inanimate; therefore He is everything. In Chapter 18, Verse 40 it is stated that only the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—exist, meaning that all activity is the work of the qualities. This indicates that the present discussion belongs to the section on devotional yoga. In this section Arjuna asks where he should contemplate the Lord; the Lord replies that whatever the mind contemplates, that is Himself. In Chapter 18, Verse 40, however, the subject is Sankhya yoga, which emphasizes the discrimination between Prakriti (nature) and Purusha (spirit) and the separation from material nature. Because creation is the work of Prakriti, the world is three‑fold (tri‑guna). Hence, nothing exists free of the three qualities. **Special Note**  
Just as the Lord enumerated His divine manifestations to Arjuna in the Gita, He also enumerated His manifestations to Uddhava in the Srimad Bhagavatam (Canto 11, Chapter 16). Some manifestations mentioned in the Gita do not appear in the Bhagavatam and vice‑versa. Where the same manifestation appears in both, the description is identical; where they differ, the purpose is not to list objects or persons but to direct the devotee’s contemplation toward the Lord. Thus, whether in the Gita or the Bhagavatam, the essential task is to contemplate the Lord’s presence. Wherever a particular attribute of an object or person is highlighted, the seeker should ignore that attribute and focus solely on the Lord’s attribute. From “aham atmaa Gudakesh” (10.20) to “beejam tad aham arjuna” (10.39), the eighty‑two manifestations mentioned by the Lord signify the range from the smallest to the greatest, from the most excellent to the mediocre, and even the lowest. **Appendix (Parishisht Bhaav)** – The origin of all living beings is said to arise from four sources (khaanas):

1. **Jarayuj** – beings born from the womb such as humans, cows, buffaloes, sheep, goats, etc. 2. **Andaja** – beings born from eggs such as birds, snakes, squirrels, lizards, etc. 3. **Udbhijja** – beings that emerge upward by breaking through the earth, such as trees, vines, reeds, grass, grains, etc. 4. **Svedaja** – (the text ends here). 1. “idam gunamayam viddhi trividha mayaaya kritam” (Śrīmad‑Bhāgavatam 11.28.7) – Know that this is composed of the three qualities, created by Maya. “yac ca kin chi jagat sarvam drishyate shruuyate api va; antarbahi shcha tat sarvam vyaapya Narayanah sthitah” – Whatever is seen or heard in the world, both internal and external, is pervaded by Narayana.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 10 ]

From sweat arise lice, maggots, etc., and from the earth during the rainy season arise earthworms and similar creatures. From these four habitats arise 2,48,000 yoni (sources of life). Within these yoni there are two categories of beings—stationary and mobile. Trees, vines, reeds, grass, and similar organisms that remain in one place are the “stationary” beings, while humans, animals, birds, and the like that move about are the “mobile” beings. Among these beings some dwell in water, some in the sky, and some on the earth. Apart from the 2,48,000 yoni there are many other yoni such as devas, ancestors, gandharvas, ghosts, spirits, demons, Brahmarakshasas, Pootna, infant planets, etc. The seed, i.e., the primal cause of all these yoni, is God. The implication is that in the infinite universes there are infinite beings, but their seed is one! Hence in every form there is one God—*Vasudeva is all*. Just as agriculture proceeds from a seed, the entire world proceeds from one God. As millet produces only millet, wheat produces only wheat, animals produce only animals, and humans produce only humans, likewise God produces only God; the world therefore appears as God. Gold‑made ornaments are gold in nature, iron‑made tools are iron in nature, clay‑made vessels are clay in nature, cotton‑made garments are cotton in nature; similarly the world created from God is divine in nature. With ordinary seeds only one kind of crop is produced: wheat seed yields wheat, not millet, moth bean, or mung bean. Each seed is distinct. The seed that is God, however, is so extraordinary that from that single seed innumerable varieties of creation arise ([ Chapter 14 ] [ Verse 4 ]). Yet none of these creations become distorted; they remain exactly as they are because that seed is *avyaya* (imperishable) ([ Chapter 9 ] [ Verse 18 ]) and *sanātana* (eternal) ([ Chapter 7 ] [ Verse 10 ]). **Relation** – In the following verse the Lord concludes His description of His divine manifestations. nanto ’sti mama divyānāṁ vibhūtīnāṁ parantapa  
eṣa tūddeśataḥ proktō vibhūter vistaraḥ mayā || 40 ||

*Transliteration*: nanto ’sti mama divyānāṁ vibhūtīnāṁ parantapa | eṣa tūddeśataḥ proktō vibhūter vistaraḥ mayā || 40 ||  
*Translation*: “There is no end to My divine manifestations, O Arjuna. This is the detailed exposition of My divine manifestations that I have spoken.”

Breakdown of key terms:  
- **proktah** – said  
- **eṣaḥ** – this  
- **parantapa** – O Arjuna (the destroyer of enemies)  
- **n** – negation, “not” (here forming “there is no”)  
- **āsti** – is, “exists”  
- **mama** – my  
- **divyānām** – of the divine  
- **vibhūtīnām** – of the manifestations  
- **parantapa** – address to Arjuna again  
- **eṣaḥ** – this (referring to the description)  
- **tūddeśataḥ** – for the purpose of instruction  
- **proktō** – spoken  
- **vibhūteḥ** – of the manifestation  
- **vistaraḥ** – expansion, detailed description  
- **mayā** – by Me

The Lord’s concluding statement emphasizes that the entirety of His divine manifestations is limitless and has been fully disclosed for the seeker’s understanding.

[ Verse 40 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

‘nāntaḥ asti’ – the Lord’s divine manifestations are endless; that is, they have no bottom, an unfathomably deep abyss. There is no limit. Because the Lord is infinite, his manifestations—such as the eighteenth quality, pastimes, etc.—are also infinite—‘Hari is infinite, Hari’s story…’ (Manas 1.140.5). Hence, when the Lord expands, he says that in both the process of manifestation and its dissolution there is no end to the expansion of his manifestations. He also states that the expansion of his manifestations has no terminus. At Arjuna’s request, the Lord graciously described his manifestations in the Srimad Bhagavatam. Yet this expansion is such that “the number of atoms counted by Me over time is only from a worldly viewpoint.” Therefore the Lord can say here, but the countless universes created by Me… the expansion described here cannot be said to have an end. The expansion is only from your perspective; from My perspective it is actually very brief (merely nominal), because My manifestations have no end. Thus the Lord is infinite, boundless and immeasurable. Numerically the Lord is “infinite” meaning his count cannot be completed even to a half. From the standpoint of limits the Lord is “boundless.” In this chapter the manifestations described have two kinds of limits—time‑bound (kala‑kṛta) and region‑bound (deśa‑kṛta). Some do not apply, but many other manifestations arise and persist for a certain period—these are not described here. Hence a temporal limit exists; and from here to there the seeker should recognize where a particular attribute has a regional limit. The Lord is not bound by such limits. The mind is drawn, here and there, to that attribute; from the Lord’s own view the Lord is “immeasurable.” In the word *agādh* (immeasurable) contemplate the root *gādh* and the Lord; whether the manifestation here is called “bottom,” like the bottom of water. Whether spoken by the Lord or not, the sense remains. **Appendix (Pariśiṣṭa Bhāva)** – In the Gītā the Lord mentions as cause 17 manifestations (Chapter 7, verses 8‑12), as effect 33 manifestations (Chapter 9, verses 16‑19), as feeling 20 manifestations (Chapter 10, verses 4‑5), as personified 25 manifestations (Chapter 10, verse 6), as principal and sovereign 81 manifestations (Chapter 10, verses 20‑28), as essence 1 manifestation (Chapter 10, verse 49), and as influence 13 manifestations (Chapter 15, verses 12‑15). All this indicates that there is nothing but one Lord. In every form there is only the Lord—Lord alone is the totality. The mutable (asat) is changeable and the immutable (sat) is unchangeable. Both sat (higher) and asat (lower) are manifestations of the Lord—“I am sat‑cit‑ānanda, Arjuna” (Gītā 9.19). The implication is that the Lord Himself is directly present as manifestation. Hence whatever attracts us is actually the Lord’s attraction; however, because of sense‑pleasure that attraction turns not into divine love but into desire and attachment, which bind us in the world. In the Gītā the Lord also calls Brahmā “mām” (my form) (Chapter 8, verse 13), calls the Devas “mām” (Chapter 9, verse 23), calls Indra “mām” (Chapter 9, verse 20), calls the supreme speed “mām” (Chapter 7, verse 18), calls the knower of the field—the jīvātmā—as “mām” (Chapter 13, verse 2), calls the Antaryāmi residing in all bodies “mām” (Chapter 16, verse 18), calls the seed of all beings “mām” (Chapter 7, verse 10), etc. The implication is that with attributes and without attributes, with form and formless, human, deity, animal, bird, ghost, demon, and everything else together constitute the Lord’s total form; i.e., all are manifestations of the Lord, His sovereignty. 1‑saṅkhyānaṁ paramāṇūnāṁ kālen kriyate mayā. na tathā me vibhūtīnāṁ sṛjato’ṇḍāni koṭiśaḥ  
(Śrīmad Bhagavatam 11.16.39) – “The number of atoms is created by Me over time; yet the countless particles I create are not limited.”

sarve ca devā manavasamastās saptarṣayo ye manuṣūnvaś ca. indraś ca yo’yaṁ tridaśeśabhūto viṣṇor aśeṣās tu vibhūtayas tāḥ  
(Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.1.46) – “All the gods, all mankind, the seven sages, the humans, Indra, the three‑world ruler, and all the inexhaustible manifestations of Viṣṇu are indeed His manifestations.”

738  
Divine manifestations are imperishable (indestructible). * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 10 ]

[Verse 41]
Here a doubt arises: if the whole universe itself is the form of Bhagavan, what is the purpose of describing the divine manifestations? The answer is that Arjuna’s very question was exactly this—where should I contemplate You (the seventeenth verse of this chapter). In truth everything is the total form of the Lord, but the object in which a particular quality appears is easier for a human to see the Lord and to meditate on Him, because that quality is imprinted in the mind and the mind automatically turns toward it. Hence the Lord enumerated His manifestations. While describing the principal manifestations the Lord said that I am the beginning, middle and end of all beings and of creation itself (verses 20 and 32 of chapter 10), I am the seed of all beings; without Me there is no animate or inanimate creature (verse 49 of this chapter), and the entire world resides in a single fragment of Me (verse 42 of this chapter). What then remains apart from the Lord? Nothing remains! All is the Lord—“Vasudevah sarvam” (Gita 7.19). In the Gita the description of manifestations is not a subsidiary topic; it is the principal means of attaining the Lord, whose realization is expressed in “Vasudevah sarvam”. Because wherever a particular quality appears in the world, if we regard that quality as the Lord’s own, our attraction will be toward the Lord rather than toward the object, person, etc. The attraction of attachment and affection is what binds man—“Kāraṇaṁ guṇasaṅgo ’sya sad‑sādhyoni‑janmasu” (Gita 13.21). Therefore the purpose of the description of manifestations is to remove the world’s existence, importance and affection and to make the seeker experience “Vasudevah sarvam”, which is the special aim of the Gita. The world’s existence, importance and relation are what bind a person. Consequently, wherever a person’s greatest attraction lies in the world, when his enjoyment‑mind is replaced by divine wisdom, the inner heart will no longer hold the world’s existence, importance and relation but the Lord’s existence, importance and relation. **Relation** – In verse 18 Arjuna asked the Lord to explain both manifestations and yoga. The Lord first described His manifestations and now, in the following verses, He proceeds to describe yoga. **Sanskrit verse (41)**  
*yadyad‑vibhūtimat‑sattvaṁ śrīmadu‑rjitam‑eva vā*  
*tattad‑eva‑avagaccha tvam mama tejoḥ aśa‑sambhavam*

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- yadyad – whatever  
- vibhootimat – possessing divine manifestations, endowed with splendor  
- sattvaṁ – being, entity  
- śrīmadu – glorious, radiant  
- rjitam – energized, empowered  
- eva – indeed, precisely  
- vā – or  
- tat – that  
- tad – that (again)  
- eva – exactly  
- avagaccha – understand, perceive  
- tvam – you  
- mama – my  
- tejoḥ – of My energy, brilliance  
- aśa‑sambhavam – inexhaustible, never‑ending

**Translation**  
“Whatever being possesses divine manifestations, whether glorious or empowered, understand that it is precisely a fragment of My inexhaustible energy.”

Explanation: Any living or non‑living entity, event, circumstance, quality, feeling, or action that displays splendor, beauty, or power is to be recognized as originating from a portion of the Lord’s energy. The distinctive excellence of those things comes from My yoga, power, and influence—this is what you should comprehend. All devas, Manu, the seven sages, the sons of Manu, Indra the king of the gods, and everything else are manifestations of Lord Vishnu. **Sanskrit quotation**  
*na reṣv abhikṣṇaṁ mad‑bhāvaṁ puṁso bhāvayatocira‑āt*  
*spardhā‑sūyā‑tirskārāḥ sāha‑ṅkārā viyanti hi*

**Transliteration**  
na reṣv abhikṣṇaṁ mad‑bhāvaṁ puṁso bhāvayatocirāt  
spardhā‑sūyā‑tirskārāḥ sāha‑ṅkārā viyanti hi

**Translation**  
“When the devotee’s mind constantly contemplates only Me in all women and men, that is, when he sees only Me, then immediately the mind’s jealousy, contempt, disdain, and ego‑based faults disappear completely.”

[ Verse 41 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

You are the source of my brilliance. Without me, no one else can be regarded as the power of lightning; such uniqueness does not exist elsewhere. A human being must recognize the special quality in each object, person, or action as the special quality of the Supreme (Parmatma) and contemplate the Supreme only. If any other object, person, etc., is thought to possess a special quality apart from the Supreme, it leads to downfall. Just as a devoted wife who, in her mind, attributes special qualities to a man other than her husband breaks her vow of fidelity, likewise, when the mind clings to the special quality of any entity other than the Supreme, the fault of infidelity arises; the vow of exclusive devotion to the Supreme is broken. In the world, whether the smallest or the greatest object, person, or action appears to have importance, beauty, or pleasantness, or seems beneficial, it is in fact not a worldly thing at all. If it were, it would exist constantly and be visible to everyone, but it neither persists nor is ever fully visible. Hence it is proved that it does not belong to that object. So whose is it? The underlying basis of that object belongs to the Supreme (Parmatma). The glimpse of the Supreme is what manifests as beauty, pleasantness, and other forms in that object. However, when a person’s disposition does not turn toward the glory of the Supreme but remains fixed on the object, the person becomes trapped in the world. While trapped, he obtains neither anything nor satisfaction. There is no happiness, no contentment; even after such experience, the illusion of the object’s pleasantness does not disappear. One must carefully and thoughtfully examine how an object that perishes every moment can appear to give happiness. If the object is being destroyed moment by moment, how can its apparent importance or beauty belong to it? Just as a radio produces sound only because it is connected to electricity, a person may marvel at the voice coming from the device, but in reality the power in the radio is entirely electricity. Without electricity, the device cannot produce sound. An ignorant person attributes that power to the device itself; a knowledgeable person, however, attributes any apparent quality of an object, person, substance, or action to the Supreme. In the eighth verse of this chapter, the Lord says that everything is born from Him and all possess His power. The implication is that wherever you see special quality, importance, beauty, strength, etc., it is His, not the object's own. For example, a courtesan sang in a very beautiful voice; a saint, hearing her, exclaimed, “How splendid a throat the Lord has given! What a beautiful voice!” The saint’s attention did not go to the courtesan but to the Lord, recognizing that the attraction and sweetness of her voice belong to the Lord. Similarly, when one sees a flower, one should rejoice, “Wow, how beautiful the Lord has placed here!” When someone teaches another excellently, the power of excellent teaching is the Lord’s, not the teacher’s. The gods favor Brihaspati, the Raghu dynasty reveres Vasistha, some admire the lion’s majesty, others love money; the attraction, affection, and pull they feel toward those qualities all stem from the Lord’s power, not from the objects themselves. Hence, wherever any special quality appears, it should be seen as the Lord’s. Therefore, the Lord has described many kinds of divine manifestations (vibhutis). This means that the attraction to each manifestation will differ according to one’s faith and taste; the same manifestation will not appeal equally to everyone, but the power behind all of them is the Lord’s. Although every special quality in any object is ultimately the Supreme’s, we must be grateful to those from whom we have received or are receiving benefit, and we should serve them. Yet we must not become trapped by regarding their personal qualities as ultimate, and we must exercise caution. **Special Note**

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Here, in verse 41, the term **avagaccha** is employed to express the idea of “knowing.”

[ Chapter 10 ]

In the twenty‑fourth and twenty‑seven‑th verses the word **viddhi** appears, meaning “understand.” The guru explains through love, while the king explains through force and fear. The guru’s explanation emphasizes liberation; the king’s explanation emphasizes adherence to worldly propriety. In verse 27 the descriptions of **Uccaiḥśrava** and **Airāvata** are presented; both are signs of the king’s splendor. Horses, elephants, etc., are the king’s possessions, and a king who possesses such wealth governs. Hence the use of **viddhi** in that verse is directed specifically toward the king. In verse 41 the word **avagaccha** signifies the true understanding that everything that appears as a special quality actually belongs to the Lord. The use of **asmi** (“I am”) points to the underlying principle of all divine manifestations: the source of all manifestations is the Lord Himself. In verse 17 Arjuna asked how he could know the Lord; the Lord responded with **asmi**, indicating that one should recognize the Self in every manifestation. The two occurrences of **viddhi** aim to make the human mind vigilant and discerning. A person becomes discerning through two means—knowledge and governance. Knowledge is obtained from the guru; governance is exercised by the king. Therefore, in verse 24, where the guru describes **Bṛhaspati**, the instruction **viddhi** means: “You must understand, through the guru, the true nature of my divine manifestations, twice by **viddhi** and once by **avagaccha**.” The purpose of this instruction is that the fruit of understanding the nature of the manifestations—through both guru and king—is steadfast devotion, even when the individual still clings to personal preferences (see verse 7 of this chapter). If one does not truly comprehend the reality described in verse 27, one will not accept the king’s counsel. Where the king is described, **viddhi** indicates that the guru’s knowledge and the king’s rule must be applied; otherwise the king’s governance will be ineffective. Ultimately, one must accept oneself and thereby purify one’s life, aligning with the righteous path. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – Beyond the previously mentioned divine manifestations, the seeker should, wherever personal attraction appears, see the Lord Himself, recognizing that such qualities belong to the Lord. This firm conviction leads to the dissolution of the material world, just as gold ornaments disappear when they are identified as gold intelligence, and wooden toys vanish when recognized as wooden intelligence. In reality, the world does not truly exist; only living beings, through their likes and dislikes, sustain the illusion of the world—“yad yad dhāryate jagat” (Gita 7.5). The essential point is that the seeker must ultimately realize **Vāsudevaḥ sarvam** (the Lord is everything). Hence the Lord, through the description of divine manifestations, enables the experience of **Vāsudevaḥ sarvam**; seeing the Lord in the manifestations causes the Lord to appear everywhere, shifting attraction from material form to divine form. Any special quality or distinction that arises in a person actually originates from the Lord. If the Lord possessed no special qualities, how could they appear in a person? Something that is not present in a part cannot arise in that part. Humans err by arrogantly claiming such qualities as their own and ignoring their divine source. All objects, beings, etc., of creation are moving toward dissolution. The beauty, strength, and other qualities we admire in objects or persons will one day vanish. Thus every element of creation seems to teach: “Do not look at me; I will not remain. Look instead toward the creator and the created.” The beauty, power, and uniqueness we perceive are not ours; they belong to the creator. Recognizing this removes our attachment to objects and beings, and we begin to see the Lord in all. When this realization occurs, worldly enjoyment ceases, and a spontaneous union (yoga) with the Lord arises.

[ Verse 42 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

The Supreme Self (Parmatma) is a unique repository of all powers, arts, sciences, and the like. Powers cannot remain in inert nature; they can exist only in the conscious Supreme Self. How can the knowledge that drives action stay in inertness? Even if one assumes that all powers reside in nature, one must still admit that nature lacks the capacity to manifest and employ those powers (creation, formation, etc.). For example, a computer, though inert, performs many miraculous tasks, but its creation and operation are performed by a conscious being (human). Without being made, taught, and operated by a human, the computer cannot function. The computer is not self‑existent; it is artificial, whereas the Supreme Self is self‑existent. If the Supreme Self had no special quality, how could it appear in the world? The quality that is present in a seed also appears in the tree. A quality absent in the seed cannot appear in the tree. The Supreme Self’s poetic power appears in the poet, its eloquence in the orator, its literary power in the writer, its generosity in the giver. Liberation, knowledge, love, etc., are all gifts of that Supreme Self; they are not the work of nature. If the statement “I am of liberated form” is true, then from where did bondage arise, how, when, and why? If the statement “I am of knowledge‑form” is true, then from where did ignorance arise, how, when, and why? How can a night of new‑moon occur in the sun? In reality, knowledge belongs to the Supreme Self, but when one claims it as one’s own, ignorance appears. “I am of knowledge‑form, knowledge is mine” – this “I” and “mine” (ego‑attachment) is the very ignorance that brings about liberation, knowledge, love, etc. Because the seeker’s gaze does not turn toward the giver, it seems as if liberation, knowledge, love belong to the seeker. This is the unique characteristic of the giver (the Supreme Self): the recipient perceives the gift as his own. This singular quality of the Supreme Self is a great ideal that seekers must honor. Humans often make the grave mistake of taking the received object as their own while never directing their sight toward the source that gave it. They see the object but not the giver; they see the action but not the power that caused it. In truth the object is not theirs; the giver alone is. It is only by the power given by the Lord that a human becomes a karmayogi; by the knowledge given by the Lord a human becomes a jnanayogi; and by the love given by the Lord a human becomes a bhaktyogi. Every special quality that appears in a human is wholly a gift of the Lord. Even after giving everything, the Lord does not reveal Himself – that is His nature. Relation — Having answered Arjuna’s questions up to this point, the Lord now makes a special statement:

**Verse (translation and word‑by‑word)**

atha vā bahunaitena kim jñātena tavārjuna |  
vistabhya aham idaṁ kṛtsnam ekāṁśena sthito jagat || 42 ||

*Transliteration*:  
atha vā – or otherwise  
bahunaitena – by this multitude  
kim – what  
jñātena – is known  
tavārjuna – by you, O Arjuna  
vistabhya – pervading  
aham – I  
idaṁ – this  
kṛtsnam – the whole  
ekāṁśena – by one part  
sthito – situated  
jagat – the world

*Meaning*:  
Or, O Arjuna, what do you think by this multitude? By pervading the whole, I am situated in one part of the universe. **Explanation of the verse (Hindi commentary rendered in English)**

Thus, O Arjuna, what do you require? The entire universe is pervaded by me, yet I am present in a single fragment of it. In other words, the infinite cosmos is contained within one portion of my being. 1. Knowledge or the power of knowing does not belong to nature. Nature is not static; it changes every moment. If knowledge were in nature, that knowledge would also be subject to change and would not be eternal; it would be impermanent. Whoever says that knowledge resides in nature is actually calling that nature the Supreme Self—only the word differs. Hence, knowledge is not in nature; if it is, it is the Supreme Self itself. 2. “I am the peacock, you are Maya. Those who have merely fashioned the living being…” (Manas, Aranya 15.1). This verse emphasizes that the material illusion (Maya) is distinct from the true self, which remains beyond creation. ---

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Commentary – By presenting this immutable verse, the Lord seems to tell Arjuna, “According to the question you asked, I have already given the answer; now I will disclose a specially important essence for you.”

“Bahunaitena kiṁ jñātena tva‑Arjuna” – Brother Arjuna, why do you feel the need to know so many things? I sit before you holding the reins and the whip of the horses. Though I appear small, every particle of my body contains countless universes, both the great creation and the great dissolution. I am seated before you with all those, obeying your command. Hence, when I am directly before you, why do you need to know many more things? [ Chapter 10 ]

Infinite creations exist – “in every atom a crore‑crore of universes” (Manas 1.201). Yet none of those creations is a part of the Lord; even in any portion of the Lord there remains empty space for all those creations. For example, the material nature is a minute fragment of our intellect. Even though the intellect may possess knowledge of many languages, scripts, and arts, we cannot say that the intellect is filled with that knowledge; there is still room for another language, script, etc. The point is that even when the intellect contains knowledge of many languages, it still remains empty, and no amount of learning can fill it. Thus, if the tiny fragment of nature that is intellect cannot be filled by knowledge of many languages, how can any fragment of the past, infinite, boundless, and immeasurable Lord be filled by infinite creations? It remains even more empty than the intellect. Appendix meaning – This verse signifies that the Lord Himself is the world‑form; both the pervading and the pervaded, the subtle and the great, the real (Sat) and the unreal (Asat) are all the Lord. The Lord is infinite; therefore infinite universes reside in any single part of Him – “ekāṁśena sthito jagat” (the world is situated in one part). “viṣṭabh yāham idaṁ kṛtsna‑ekāṁśena sthito jagat” – I pervade the entire universe with a single fragment. This means that in any fragment of the Lord, the Lord’s declaration is that everything is Himself. When one looks from the Lord’s side, no manifestation remains apart from Him. When the source, refuge, illuminator, and seed (fundamental cause) of all manifestations sit before you, why contemplate the manifestations at all? Om tat sat – In the Upaniṣadic portion of the Srimad Bhagavad Gītā, within the treatise on Brahma‑knowledge and Yoga‑Shastra, the dialogue of Krishna and Arjuna contains the tenth chapter titled “Vibhūti‑Yoga” (Chapter 10). Thus, the utterances “Om, Tat, Sat” – the sacred names of the Lord – complete the tenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, which is the “Vibhūti‑Yoga” chapter. Wherever a special quality appears, it is the Lord’s own manifestation; recognizing this establishes a yogic (relationship) experience with the Lord, which is why the tenth chapter is called “Vibhūti‑Yoga”. Ten‑chapter verses, letters, and utterances:

(1) In this chapter there are three “atha dashamo ’adhyāyaḥ” headings, six “Arjuna uvāca” headings, five hundred sixty‑six verses, and thirteen verses of the poet Puṣpika. The total number of verses amounts to five hundred seventy‑eight. (3) The chapter contains three “uvāca” statements – two “Śrī‑Bhagavān uvāca” and one “Arjuna uvāca”. Meter used in the tenth chapter:

Among the forty‑two verses, the second and twenty‑fifth verses begin with “na‑gaṇa”, producing the “na‑vipulā” meter; the seventh verse’s first line, as well as the fifth and thirty‑second verses’ third lines, begin with “ma‑gaṇa”, yielding “ma‑vipulā”; the eighth verse’s first line and the twenty‑sixth verse’s third line start with “bha‑gaṇa”, giving “bha‑vipulā”; and the sixth verse’s first line starts with “ra‑gaṇa”, forming “ra‑vipulā”. These are the named meters. The remaining thirty‑six verses:

The seven “atha dashamo ’adhyāyaḥ” headings, twenty “Arjuna uvāca” headings, one thousand three hundred forty‑four letters, and sixty‑six letters of Puṣpika together total one thousand four hundred seventeen letters. These conform to the characteristics of the “pāṭhyāvakta” Anuṣṭup meter.

[ Chapter 11 ]  
[ Appendix ]

[Verse 1]
At the close of Chapter 10, the Lord, extending special grace toward Arjuna, declared that the whole universe—that is, the infinite creations—are contained in some part of Me, and that I am seated as your charioteer, holding the reins and the whip of your horses, and obeying your command. When I, the great source of all powers and yoga (effect), am seated before you, why do you need to learn about the various powers separately? Hearing this, Arjuna’s vision is filled with the Lord’s magnificent grace; he becomes overwhelmed with wonder and exclaims—

**Madanugrahāya**  
Arjuna said:

**Paramam guhya‑madhyātma‑saṅjñitam. Yat tvayoktaṁ vacas tena moho’yam vigataḥ mama.**  
[ Verse 1 ]

*Word‑by‑word breakdown*  
- **mad‑anugrahāya** – for the grace bestowed on me  
- **kevala** – only  
- **mujh‑par** – upon me  
- **kṛpā** – compassion  
- **guhyam** – secret  
- **tvayā** – by you  
- **yat** – which  
- **paramam** – supreme  
- **adhyātma‑saṅjñitam** – designated as spiritual  
- **vacas** – word  
- **uktam** – spoken  
- **Arjuna‑uvāca** – Arjuna said  
- **gopanīya** – confidential, secret  
- **adhyātma‑viṣayaka** – pertaining to the spiritual realm

*Explanation* – Having experienced the Lord’s grace, Arjuna becomes emotionally intoxicated. In his ecstatic utterance he forgets the strict metrical rules; consequently this verse contains thirty‑three syllables, whereas verses in the Gita composed in the Anuṣṭup meter have thirty‑two syllables. The implication is that extreme joy makes one lose attention to the rules. ‘**Madanugrahāya**’ – By extending grace to my devotees, I dispel the darkness born of their ignorance (Gita – Chapter 10, verse 11). The Lord uttered this solely under the influence of grace. This had a profound effect on Arjuna, prompting him to praise the Lord:

*“tena … mama … moha … vigataḥ”* – “By that, my delusion has been destroyed.”

From verses 12 to 15 of Chapter 10 onward, Arjuna continues this praise. Such a hymn of praise had not appeared earlier in the Gita. By focusing on this purpose, Arjuna says that the Lord spoke these words only to grant him grace. ‘**Paramam guhyaṁ**’ – After enumerating the chief manifestations, the Lord, at the end of Chapter 10, declares that He pervades the entire universe, the countless billions of worlds, in some part of Himself (Chapter 10, verse 42). Thus the Lord gave a self‑description of His nature, which Arjuna regards as the supreme secret. ‘**Adhyātma‑saṅjñitam**’ – (refers to Chapter 10, verse 7). From the first chapter up to this point, everything the Lord has said has been spoken under the influence of grace. In reality, all of the Lord’s actions are suffused with grace, but humans fail to recognise it. When one recognises the Lord’s grace, the experience of the divine reality becomes swift and effortless. When Arjuna turns toward divine grace, he exclaims that his delusion has been destroyed by that grace.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

The commentary continues: The Lord declared that anyone who truly knows, by direct experience, that He is the source of all manifestations and that every creation appears only through His power and ultimately merges back into Him, becomes steadfast in unwavering devotional yoga. Arjuna is said to be recognizing this spiritual truth. “Yattvayoktaṁ vacastena moho’yaṁ vigato mama” – the whole universe is contained in a single aspect of the Lord. Earlier Arjuna had no vision of this and was ignorant of it; that ignorance was his delusion. When the Lord said that He pervades the entire world in one fragment and sits before him, Arjuna’s delusion vanished, and he realized that his previous ignorance was merely delusion. Hence Arjuna declares that his delusion has completely disappeared. Yet the Lord does not accept this claim, for in the fifty‑fifth verse He tells Arjuna not to be afflicted by sorrow or delusion – “mā te vyathā mā ca vimūḍhabhāvaḥ.”

Appendix – Arjuna says that the words spoken by the Lord are granted to him out of grace, not to display His erudition; there is no motive other than grace. The Lord is the origin, middle and end of all beings (Chapter 10, Verse 20), the seed of all beings (Chapter 10, Verse 49), and every object endowed with splendor, power and beauty arises from a fragment of His yoga (Chapter 10, Verse 40). By extending a single fragment of Himself, He pervades the whole universe (Chapter 10, Verse 42). Hearing these statements, Arjuna feels that his delusion has been destroyed, though only a partial dissolution has occurred, not a total one. Connection – How the delusion is removed is explained in the following verse:

[ Verse 2 ]  
bhavāpyayau hi bhūtānāṁ śrutau vistaraśo mayā  
tvattaḥ kamalapatrākṣa māhātmyaṁ api ca avyayam

* bhavā‑apyayau – the creation and dissolution (of the world)  
* hi – indeed  
* bhūtānāṁ – of all beings  
* śrutau – as heard (from the Lord)  
* vistaraśo – in full detail  
* mayā – by Me  
* tvattaḥ – from You  
* kamalapatrākṣa – O lotus‑eyed One (address to the Lord)  
* māhātmyaṁ – greatness, majesty  
* api – also  
* ca – and  
* avyayam – the imperishable

Translation of the verse: “Indeed, the processes of creation and dissolution of all beings are described in detail by Me; O lotus‑eyed One, even Your greatness is imperishable.”

Explanation – The verse means that all phenomena of birth and death arise from the Lord Himself. The Lord earlier said, “I am the origin and dissolution of the whole universe; there is no cause other than Me” (Chapter 7, Verse 6). The modes of goodness, passion and ignorance also stem from Him (Chapter 7, Verse 12). All living beings are His, and all their actions are His (Chapter 10, Verse 8). He is the beginning, middle and end of all creatures (Chapter 10, Verse 20) and likewise of all creations (Chapter 10, Verse 1). All the teachings on devotion that the Lord has given are the most secret spiritual instructions. While delusion persists, knowledge of delusion does not arise; only when delusion departs does true knowledge appear, and with knowledge delusion ceases.

[ Verse 3 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The thirty‑second verse is being discussed. Arjuna says that one who truly knows the essence becomes steadfast in the path of devotional yoga. He affirms that I have also heard of the greatness (mahātmyam) of knowing Your divine power (vibhūti) and yoga (yoga) from the source. I have listened in detail to Your description of the origin and dissolution of all beings. This does not merely refer to hearing about creation and destruction; rather, it means that all beings arise from You, dwell in You, and merge back into You—essentially, everything is You. ‘Mahātmyam api ca avyayam’ – In Chapter 10, Verse 7 you explained that the greatness of My divine power and yoga, as well as the devotion and love toward them, are immutable. The term ‘avyayam’ (imperishable) indicates that the devotion, love, and oneness with the Lord that arise from truly knowing the divine power and yoga are all unchanging, because the Lord Himself is eternal and immutable. **Appendix meaning** – In this verse Arjuna explains why the illusion of the eye is destroyed. The phrase ‘mahātmyam api ca avyayam’ with the particle ‘api’ implies that Arjuna has heard both the perishable (changing) and the imperishable aspects of the Lord’s greatness. ‘Bhav‑apyayo hi bhūtānām’ denotes the perishable, mutable greatness of the Lord. When a person forms any relationship with the Lord, it leads to welfare; this is the imperishable, unchanging greatness of the Lord. Hence, both the real (sat) and the unreal (asat) are the Lord—‘sada‑sacca‑aham’ (Gita 9.19). **Connection** – In the next two verses Arjuna prays to the Lord for a vision of His universal form. Thus, O Supreme Person, I desire to behold You, O Supreme Person! You are the Self‑existent, the form‑embodied, the Supreme Lord. **Explanation** – The address ‘purushottama’ (Supreme Person) is used to convey that there is none equal to You in this world; You alone are the highest. In Chapter 15, Verse 18 the Lord also declares that He is beyond the perishable and surpasses the imperishable, and therefore He is known in the scriptures as ‘purushottama’. ‘Evam etad yathā‑tathā tvam ātmānam’ – O Supreme Person! The description you gave (from Chapter 7, Verse 10 onward) of your transcendental power and ability is exactly as stated. The world originates from You and merges back into You (Chapter 7, Verse 6); apart from You there is nothing else (Chapter 7, Verse 19); Brahman, the soul, action, the elemental, the divine and the priestly aspects are all You (Chapter 7, Verses 29‑30); the supreme truth attainable through exclusive devotion is You (Chapter 8, Verse 22); the entire universe pervades You, yet You are not the universe (Chapter 9, Verses 4‑5); all forms, both real and unreal, are You (Chapter 9, Verse 19); You are the primal cause of the world and the source of its vitality (Chapter 10, Verse 8); the whole creation resides in a single fragment of You (Chapter 10, Verse 42).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

‘Parameshvara’ – Arjuna had earlier heard from the Lord that “I am the great God of all beings and all worlds – *bhūtānām īśvaro ’pi* (4.6); *sarvaloka-maheśvaram* (5.29).” Consequently, Arjuna, overwhelmed by the Lord’s extraordinary power, addresses Him as “Parameshvara,” meaning “O Supreme Lord, you truly are the ultimate God, the owner of all prosperity.”

[ Chapter 11 ]

In the opening of this page the commentary continues: Arjuna says that whatever he has previously declared about himself is the ultimate truth (the 19th and 40th verses of the tenth chapter). Therefore the Lord gives only a brief description of His divine manifestations. When Arjuna expresses the desire to see one form of the Lord – “dṛṣṭum icchāmi te rūpam” – the Lord later (in the fifth verse) replies that one who greedily demands many forms from the giver diminishes the giver’s generosity, whereas one who asks modestly receives greater generosity. In the same manner Arjuna explicitly asks the Lord to enumerate all His manifestations; the Lord replies that He will summarize His manifestations. This prompts Arjuna to be cautious that his words do not become inappropriate. Hence, Arjuna modestly says that if his vision can encompass the Lord’s universal form, the Lord should reveal it. Seeing this hesitation, the Lord magnanimously says, “You may behold my countless forms.”

‘dṛṣṭum icchāmi te rūpam’ – Arjuna declares that he has heard the Lord’s supreme influence together with His greatness and now his heart is firmly convinced. “The entire universe resides in a fragment of my body” – hearing this, his mind burns with an intense longing to see that form. Another sense is that, despite the Lord’s incomparably vast greatness, He holds deep affection and intimacy toward Arjuna, fulfilling every request exactly as Arjuna asks. Because there is no slightest hesitation in speaking or asking, Arjuna’s desire to see the form that contains the whole universe in one fragment grows stronger. In the sixteenth verse of the tenth chapter Arjuna had said, “Speak all your manifestations completely; leave nothing unsaid – *vaktumarhasya śeṣeṇa*,” to which the Lord responded. A further sense is that, seated in Arjuna’s chariot, the Lord says, “The part of my body you are seeing contains the entire cosmos (which includes innumerable universes).” The implication is that the Lord’s body is minute, yet within a single part of that tiny body the whole universe is pervaded. Therefore Arjuna wishes to see that particular aspect – his reference to “rūpam” (one form) while describing the manifestations. Appendix meaning – Arjuna’s statement signifies that after hearing the Lord’s words he fully understands and harbors no doubt. Everything is the Lord; now only the divine form associated with the Lord remains to be seen. Teaching occurs in two ways – by speaking and by demonstrating. Earlier, in the tenth chapter, the Lord described His all‑encompassing form, stating that He pervades the whole universe through a single fragment of Himself. In this chapter Arjuna petitions to directly witness that form. manyase yadi tachchakyam mayā draṣṭum iti prabho | yogeśvara tato me tvaṁ darśayātmānamavyayam ||4||  
Translation: “Lord, if you think that I am capable of seeing that [form] by myself, O Lord of Yoga, then please reveal to me your imperishable self.”

[ Verse 5 ]

* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

O Lord! If by my own effort I might be able to behold that divine form of yours, then it is possible. If you deem yourself the eternal Self (Atman), O Lord of Yoga, please reveal that imperishable nature to me. **Explanation** – The address “Prabho” (Lord) denotes the all‑powerful One; therefore He is the master of every yoga—Hatha, Raja, Laya, Mantra, etc. By His supra‑mundane yogic power He can display His universal form. The sense of this address is: if you consider that I am capable of seeing your universal form, that is fine; otherwise grant me the capacity to perceive your divine (Ishvara‑related) aspect. The phrase “manyase yadi tachchakyam mayā draṣṭum iti” means that even if you do not reveal that form, I will still accept that your nature is as you describe, though I am not qualified to see it. Thus Arjuna harbors no doubt about the Lord’s words; his faith is firm, which is why he asks to be shown the universal form. In Chapter 10, Verse 17 Arjuna addressed the Lord as “Yogin” (the yogi). Here he addresses Him as “Yogeshvara” (Lord of all yogas), indicating a shift in Arjuna’s perception after the beginning of Chapter 10. The line “tato me tvam darśaya ātmānam avyayam” points to the Lord’s imperishable nature, the source of endless creation. By calling Him “Yogeshvara,” Arjuna acknowledges that all yogas reside in, and are absorbed by, that immutable essence. He thus requests a vision of that indestructible self. **Appendix (Parishishta‑Bhaav)** – Referring to the Lord’s universal form as “avyaya” (imperishable) establishes that the whole cosmos is His manifestation. Because He is immutable, there is no absolute lack in Him (see Gita 15.1). The combination of the mutable (asat) and the immutable (sat) constitutes the Lord’s total reality—“Sat‑chit‑ānanda” (the eternal truth, knowledge, bliss). Apparent inertia arises only from attachment and ignorance. **Connection (Sambandh)** – Hearing Arjuna’s humble prayer in the preceding verse, the Lord now grants permission to behold the universal form. **Shloka**  
*Śrībhagavān uvāca*  
*paśy me pārtha rūpāṇi śataśo ’tha sahasraśaḥ*  
*nanā‑vidhāni divyāni nanā‑varṇākṛtīni ca*

Translation: “The Supreme Lord said: O Partha, behold My forms—hundreds and thousands of them—various divine shapes and myriad colors.”

Breakdown:  
- *paśy* – “see, behold”  
- *me* – “my”  
- *pārtha* – “O son of Pritha (Arjuna)”  
- *rūpāṇi* – “forms”  
- *śataśo ’tha* – “hundreds and”  
- *sahasraśaḥ* – “thousands”  
- *nanā‑vidhāni* – “various kinds of”  
- *divyāni* – “divine”  
- *nanā‑varṇākṛtīni* – “of many colors and shapes”  
- *ca* – “and”.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Explanation – “See, O Partha, my forms, a hundredfold; a thousandfold.”  
Upon hearing Arjuna’s hesitant prayer, the Lord became exceedingly pleased and, addressing Arjuna as “Partha,” said, “Observe my forms.” He did not limit the vision to a few forms; He urged Arjuna to behold hundreds, even thousands, i.e., innumerable manifestations. Just as the Lord has declared that the list of His divine manifestations is endless, here He emphasizes the infinitude of His forms. “Various divine forms, various colored shapes.”  
Now the Lord describes the characteristics of those forms: they possess countless varieties of appearance. Their colors are manifold—some are yellow, some red, and so on. Each individual form may display many hues. Their shapes are also diverse—some are small, some stout, etc. [ Chapter 11 ]

Just as a tiny particle of earth is still earth, a minute fragment of the Lord’s boundless, infinite cosmic form makes this world itself a manifestation of the cosmic form. Yet this divine cosmic form is not revealed to everyone as a divine vision; it appears only as the world of material existence. Human perception is drawn toward the perishable world rather than toward the Lord. When the Lord incarnates, He does not always appear before all as the supreme divine form (see Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 7, Verse 25); He appears in human form. Likewise, the cosmic form of the Lord is perceived by all as the world‑form; each person sees the cosmic form only through the lens of the material world. In this passage, however, the Lord, revealing His immutable divine cosmic form directly, invites Arjuna to “see My divine forms.”

Appendix – Arjuna, feeling inadequate, had asked the Lord to show him a single divine form. The Lord, following His own will, instead instructed him to contemplate hundreds, even thousands, of forms. This demonstrates that the benefit a seeker receives from surrendering to the Lord’s will does not arise from personal desire or intellect. No matter how many sciences, arts, or scriptures a person masters, the intellect remains limited. The more simple, humble, and ego‑free a seeker is, the greater his capacity to know the Lord. Pride obstructs true knowledge; the more one thinks himself wise, the more he becomes a slave to that very wisdom. True humility, free from the arrogance of intellect, fosters genuine understanding. Relation – In the preceding verse the Lord spoke of seeing various colors and shapes in His cosmic form. The next verse directs the seeker to behold the divine beings. [ Verse 6 ]

[ Verse 7 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

Har, Bahurūpa, Tryaṁbaka, Aparājita, Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu – behold all these forms in My universal form. Kāpardī, Raivat, Mrigavyādha, Śarva and Kapāli – these eleven are the Rudras (Harivamsa, first Parva, third chapter, verses 51‑52). The twelve Ādityas, eight Vasu, eleven Rudras and the two Ashvini‑Kumāras constitute thirty‑three crore (thirty‑three types) of deities who are principal among all gods. Among the gods the two Ashvini‑Kumāras are counted as Marut‑ganas. These two brothers belong to the gods, but they are also physicians of the ninety‑one Marut‑ganas of the thirty‑three types. Sattvajyoti, Āditya, Satyajyoti, Tiryajjyoti, Sajyoti, Jyotiṣmān, Harit, Ṛtajit, Satyajit, Suṣeṇa, Senajit, Satyamitra, Abhimitra, Harimitra, Kṛta, Satya, Dhruva, Dhartā, Vidhartā, Vidhāraya, Dhvānta, Dhuni, Ugra, Bhīma, Abhiju, Sākṣip, Īdṛk, Anyādṛk, Yādṛk, Pratikṛt, Ṛk, Samiti, Saṁrambha, Īdṛkṣ, Puruṣa, Anyādṛkṣ, Cetas, Samitā, Samidr̥kṣ, Pratidṛkṣ, Maruti, Sarata, Deva, Diśa, Yajuh, Anudṛk, Sāma, Mānusha and Viś – these ninety‑one are the Maruts (Vāyu‑Purāṇa, sixty‑fourth chapter, verses 123‑130). They are regarded as distinct from other deities because they originated from demons; therefore the Lord also designates them separately with the term “tathā”. “Bahūnyadr̥ṣṭapūrvāṇi paśyāścaryāṇi Bhārata” – you have never before seen these forms with the eyes, heard them with the ears, contemplated them with the mind, or imagined them with intellect. Your inclination has never turned toward these unprecedented forms. Now behold these many unseen manifestations directly. The very sight of them astonishes, “Ah! Such are the forms of the Lord! Observe these marvelous appearances.”

**Parishisht Bhaav** – In the previous verse the Lord mentioned that in His universal form He appears in countless varieties, colors and shapes. This verse expands that statement in detail. The meaning is that all deities are My forms; i.e., I am present in the guise of every god (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 9, Verse 23). **Sambandh** – After the Lord commands Arjuna to behold the universal form, Arjuna may wonder where to see it. Hence the Lord says:

*Gudākēśa ihaiḥkṣaṁ jagatkṛtsnaṁ paśyādya sacharācaram |  
Mama dehe Gudākēśa yac cān yad draṣṭum icchasi || 7 ||*

“O Gudākēśa (the conqueror of sleep), behold the entire universe, both moving and immobile, right now. In My body, Gudākēśa, whatever else you wish to see, see it.”

Word‑by‑word breakdown:

- **ihaiḥkṣaṁ** – “in this one place”  
- **jagatkṛtsnaṁ** – “the whole universe”  
- **paśyādya** – “to behold”  
- **sacharācaram** – “the moving and the unmoving”  
- **mama** – “my”  
- **dehe** – “in the body”  
- **yac** – “that which”  
- **ān** – “else”  
- **icchasi** – “you desire”

Explanation – By attaining mastery over sleep (Gudākēśa), Arjuna’s mind is ready to perceive the universal form. The Lord addresses Arjuna as Gudākēśa, urging him to watch the universal form with utmost alertness. In the concluding part of Chapter 10 the Lord declared that He pervades the entire cosmos in every fragment. Accordingly, Arjuna, holding the reins of his horses and his bow, is asked to view the whole creation—living beings and inanimate entities—within the single “country” (portion) of the Lord’s body. Wherever his gaze falls, the infinite cosmos will be revealed: humans, gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ghosts, animals, birds, as well as trees, vines, grasses and plants that move and stand.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

The opening of this page reminds us that the Lord’s body contains everything that has ever existed, everything that is existing now, and everything that will exist in the future—mountains, earth, sand, and all other inert matter. He says, “Look at my entire universe right now, in this very moment; there is no time for delay.”  
He adds, “Whatever else you wish to see, see it.”

Arjuna, still doubting whether victory in the battle would belong to us or to the Kauravas, asks, “What else do I want to see?” (Gita – Chapter 2, Verse 6). The Lord replies that Arjuna may also behold everything that resides in a single fragment of His body. **Special point** – The whole cosmos is contained in one fragment of the Lord. If this were not declared, Arjuna would not have desired to see the Universal Form. Without desire there would be no prayer for its manifestation, and without prayer the Lord could not reveal His form. Thus it is evident that the Lord, out of grace, wishes to show His Universal Form to Arjuna of His own accord. A similar grace appears at the very beginning of the Gita. When Arjuna asks the Lord to place his chariot between the two armies, the Lord positions the chariot before the ancestors Bhishma and Drona and says, “Behold the Kuru lineage” – “Kuruṁ paśya” ([ Verse 1.25 ]). This indicates that the Lord, by grace, intends to disclose the Gita. Had He not spoken, Arjuna would have felt no sorrow and the teaching of the Gita would not have commenced. Hence the Gita is revealed through the Lord’s benevolence. In Chapter 10 the Lord says, “Who truly knows My divine power and yoga becomes firmly attached to Me in devotion.” Hearing this, Arjuna praised the Lord and, after prayer, asked for divine manifestations. Likewise, after hearing that “the whole world resides in a single fragment of Me,” Arjuna prayed to see the Universal Form. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – The Lord commands that the entire universe can be seen in a single part of His body. This proves that Lord Krishna is all‑encompassing and that the whole cosmos exists within Him. As the poet Manas writes, “crores upon crores of universes cling to each atom” (Manas, Bal 201). When the entire universe is contained in one fragment of the Lord, nothing remains apart from Him; everything is the Lord. Therefore the Lord tells Arjuna that whatever he wishes to see, he can see in the Lord’s Virat‑Rūpa. Arjuna wanted to see the outcome of the war, and he perceived it in the Virat‑Rūpa (Gita – Chapter 11, Verses 26‑27). **Relation** – In three verses the Lord uses the imperative “paśya” (see) four times to command Arjuna to view His form. Accordingly, Arjuna strains his eyes to look, yet sees nothing. Consequently, in the following verse the Lord explains why Arjuna cannot see and grants him divine eyes to behold the Universal Form. **Verse 8 (Chapter 11, Verse 8)**

*Transliteration*  
tu anena na tu māṁ śakye dṛṣṭum anenaiva svacakṣuṣā |  
divyaṁ dadāmi te cakṣuḥ paśya me yogam aiśvaram ||8||

*Word‑by‑word translation*

- **tu** – but  
- **anena** – by this (means)  
- **na** – not  
- **tu** – you (emphatic)  
- **māṁ** – Me  
- **śakye** – can  
- **dṛṣṭum** – see  
- **anenaiva** – only by this  
- **svacakṣuṣā** – with your own eyes  
- **divyaṁ** – divine  
- **dadāmi** – I give  
- **te** – to you  
- **cakṣuḥ** – eye(s)  
- **paśya** – behold / see  
- **me** – of Me  
- **yogam** – Yoga (the supreme spiritual power)  
- **aiśvaram** – lordship, divine sovereignty

*Full translation*  
“By this means you cannot see Me; with your own eyes you are unable to behold Me. I grant you a divine eye; behold My supreme Yoga.”

[ Verse 8 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

**Explanation** – “You cannot behold Me with these mortal eyes.”  
Your ordinary “skin‑eyes” (the limited sense of sight) have very little power. Because they are material, they can perceive only trivial natural phenomena: the forms of ordinary humans, animals, birds, their distinctions, and the play of light and shadow. They cannot, through mind, intellect, or the senses, perceive the transcendental form of the Lord. “I give you divine eyes; behold My yogic majesty.” – I grant you a supernatural, supra‑sensory vision, endowing your ordinary eyes with divine power so that you may see not only material objects but also their divine nature. Although the divine vision is not a matter of the eyes but of the intellect, the Lord says that with the divine eyes He gives you, you will also perceive the divine aspect—His supreme, other‑worldly influence. In other words, to see the Virat‑Rupa (the Cosmic Form) one needs the divine eyes. The verb “paśya” has two meanings: to see with the intellect (discernment) and to see with the physical eyes. In Chapter 9, Verse 5 the Lord said “paśya me yogam‑aiśvaram,” referring to seeing with the intellect (knowing). Here, “paśya me yogam‑aiśvaram” is used in the sense of seeing with the eyes. **Special note**  
Just as the words “Śrīmad‑Bhagavad‑Gītā” appear on a page, those who have no knowledge of the alphabet see only black lines, while those who know the alphabet see letters. A person who has read, written, and deeply contemplated the Gītā, when he sees “Śrīmad‑Bhagavad‑Gītā” on the page, instantly perceives all the chapters, verses, and meanings. In the same way, when the Lord gave Arjuna the divine eyes, he began to see the cosmic, supra‑sensory form and its divinity—something beyond ordinary intellect. This ability was due solely to the divine eyes bestowed by the Lord. Now a question arises: when Arjuna, in the fourth verse, said, “If I can see Your universal form, then show it to me,” the Lord could have replied in the eighth verse, “With these mortal eyes you cannot see My universal form; therefore I give you divine eyes.” Instead, the Lord repeatedly said “paśya, paśya” (see, see) before even granting the divine eyes. When Arjuna could not see, the Lord explained why he could not and then resolved the issue by giving the divine eyes. Why this apparent complication? The Lord’s compassion unfolds gradually toward the devotee. He first instructs Arjuna, transforming his inner attitudes and revealing His divine manifestations. By knowing these manifestations, Arjuna attains a unique exaltation and declares that even after hearing the Lord’s nectar‑like words, his satisfaction is not complete. The Lord then describes countless divine manifestations, stating that infinite Brahman (the Supreme Consciousness) resides in a single fragment of Himself, and that fragment contains infinite universes. Desiring to behold that Virat‑Rupa, Arjuna prays. The Lord reveals His universal form and repeatedly commands Arjuna to look. When Arjuna still cannot see, the Lord bestows the divine eyes. In summary, the Lord Himself manifested the curiosity to see the Virat‑Rupa, expressed the desire to show it, fulfilled the desire by revealing the form, and, when the vision failed, supplied the divine eyes. Thus, when one surrenders to the Lord, He assumes full responsibility for accomplishing the devotee’s tasks. **Appendix note** – The verb “paśya” carries two senses: to know and to see. In Chapter 9, Verse 5, “paśya me yogam‑aiśvaram” conveys the sense of knowing the Lord; here, “paśya me yogam‑aiśvaram” directs the devotee to see the Lord’s Virat‑Rupa with the eyes.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

The subject of “seeing” is introduced. The implication is that the one who is known is also God, and the one who is seen is also God. Nothing exists apart from God. In this eleventh chapter the uniqueness is not the analysis of the divine form but the extraordinary experience of beholding God’s supernatural form. Consequently, at the end of the Gita Sanjaya mentions both the uniqueness of “dialogue” and the uniqueness of “form” (verses 66‑70 of Chapter 18). Because the universal form of God is supramundane, He gave Arjuna divine eyes in order to see it. **Relation** – After receiving the divine sight, Arjuna’s vision of God’s form is described by Sanjaya in the verses that follow. Sanjaya said:

> **Sanjaya Uvāc**  
> “Having spoken thus, the king, the great lord of yoga, Hari,  
> displayed to Partha (Arjuna) the supreme divine form.”  
> **[ Verse 9 ]**

**Sanjaya’s commentary on the verse**  
- *Rajan* = “O king!”  
- *evam uktva* = “having said thus”  
- *mahayogeshvaraḥ* = “the great lord of yoga”  
- *Hari* = “the Supreme (God)”  
- *paramam rūpam aiśvaram* = “the supreme divine form”  
- *tataḥ* = “then”

Krishna, by granting Arjuna divine eyes, enabled him to perceive the divine‑related yoga of the Supreme. The phrase “evam uktva” refers back to the earlier verse in which the Lord said that Arjuna could not see Him with ordinary eyes, therefore He gives him the divine eye so that he may behold the divine aspect of the Supreme. *darshayāmāsa* = “displayed” (the universal form). The boundless power of the Lord fulfills all. In the third verse Arjuna called this form “rūpam aiśvaram”; here Sanjaya calls it “paramam rūpam aiśvaram,” indicating that the universal form of God is exceedingly extraordinary. The great Supreme God, Krishna, manifested an astonishing, supernatural, wondrous universal form. In the fourth verse Arjuna called the Lord “yogeshvara” (lord of yoga); Sanjaya calls Him “mahayogeshvara” (great lord of yoga). The divine vision granted to Arjuna also allowed him to perceive the Lord’s terrifying aspect, signifying that the Lord had to reveal more of His universal form after Arjuna’s earnest prayer (verse 17) and his fear (verse 45). Even a slight devotion (verse 55) prompted the Lord to assure Arjuna that He was fully present. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhāva)** – Calling the Lord “mahayogeshvara” means that He is the deity of all yogas. There is no yoga whose master is not the Lord; all yogas are encompassed within Him. Arjuna had earlier called the Lord “yogeshvara” (verse 4 of this chapter); Sanjaya calls Him “mahayogeshvara” because Sanjaya’s knowledge of the Lord exceeds Arjuna’s. Even Veda‑Vyasa, the great sage, knew the Lord through his grace (Gita 18.75). Ultimately, the Lord knows Himself better than anyone (Chapter 10 verses 2 and 15). **Relation** – Sanjaya now proceeds to describe the Lord’s supreme, divine form in the next two verses. Sanjaya, having also received divine sight from Veda‑Vyasa, had witnessed the universal form together with Arjuna (Chapter 18 verse 76). He now narrates that vision to Dhritarashtra.

[ Verse 10-11 ]

**Sanskrit verses (transliterated with literal meaning)**

- aneka‑divya‑abharaNam – “many divine ornaments.”  
- *sAdhaka‑sanjIvani* – “the elixir that sustains the seeker.”  
- aneka‑vaktra‑nayana – “many mouths and eyes”; aneka‑adbhuta‑darshanam – “many wondrous visions.”  
- divya‑mAlya‑ambara‑dharaM – “clothed in divine garlands and celestial robes.”  
- divya‑aneka‑odita‑yudhham – “bearing a multitude of divine weapons.”  
- divya‑gandha‑anulepanam – “anointed with divine fragrances.”  
[Verse 11]
- sarv‑ashcharyamayaM deva anantaM vishvato‑mukham – “the all‑wonderful God, infinite, whose face is turned toward the whole universe.”

**English rendering of the verses**

The Lord is described as possessing countless divine ornaments, the life‑giving elixir for the aspirant; He has innumerable faces and eyes and displays countless marvelous visions. He is robed in celestial garlands and divine attire, and He holds many divine weapons in His hands. He is anointed with heavenly scents, and He is the all‑marvelous, infinite deity whose countenance faces every direction of the world. **Commentary (translated in the order it appears on the page)**

The description “many faces and eyes” refers to the Lord’s universal form (Viraatrūpa) in which countless mouths, eyes, hands, feet and other limbs appear; every such part is divine because the Supreme Himself manifests them. “Many wondrous visions” means that in the universal form countless shapes, colors and strange configurations are seen, all of them astonishingly marvelous. “Many divine ornaments” indicates that the countless jewels, necklaces, crowns, etc., that adorn the hands, feet, ears, nose and throat in the universal form are all divine, for the Lord Himself appears as the very ornaments. “Many divine weapons” points to the various arms—discus, mace, bow, arrows, etc.—that the Lord holds in His universal form; each of these weapons is divine. The concluding line “the all‑marvelous God, infinite, whose face is turned toward the whole universe” expresses that the Lord, in His boundless, multi‑faced universal manifestation, displayed His supreme, radiant form to Arjuna, dazzling the mind of the beholder. Just as a person, seated far away, imagines himself bathing in the Ganges at Haridwar and mentally visualizes the river, the bridge, the ghats and the people there, the mind creates those images even though the physical places are absent; similarly, the Lord appears in countless forms—adorned with divine jewels, wielding various weapons, clothed in myriad garlands and celestial garments—so that everything in His universal form is divine. The phrase “divya‑mAlya‑ambara‑dharaM” signifies that the Lord’s neck is surrounded by divine flowers, gold, silver, pearls, gems and other ornaments, just as the Bhagavata Purana recounts that when the supreme Brahmā wore many garlands, the demons seized the calves; then Lord Krishna, Himself divine, transformed His body into calves and calves of various colors, each adorned with divine clothing, and even their horns, flutes, garments and ornaments became divine. Finally, “divya‑gandha‑anulepanam” refers to the anointing of the Lord’s forehead and shoulders with sacred fragrances, as described in Chapter 13, Verse 19 of the Bhagavad‑Gītā.

The illumination of the great Lord cannot be compared to the light of a thousand suns rising together in the sky. The reason is that the light of the sun is physical, while the light of the Lord is divine. No matter how great the physical light may be, it is insignificant compared to the divine light. The physical and divine lights are of different kinds, and therefore, they cannot be compared. However, the physical light can be used to indicate the divine light, like a finger pointing to the moon. Here, Sanjaya uses the imagination of the physical light of a thousand suns to describe the illumination of the Lord's Vishvarupa. Explanation - 'divi suryasahasya' - Just as the combined light of thousands of stars in the sky cannot be compared to the light of one moon, and the combined light of thousands of moons cannot be compared to the light of one sun, similarly, the combined light of thousands of suns in the sky cannot be compared to the light of the Lord's Vishvarupa. In other words, the light of thousands of suns is not sufficient to compare with the Lord's illumination. Appendix / Parishishta Bhaav - The light of thousands of suns combined cannot equal the Lord's illumination, because the light of the sun also comes from the Lord (Gita - 15.12). Even if the light of thousands of suns were combined, it would still be physical, whereas the Lord's illumination is not physical but divine. Connection - Having described the divine form, limbs, and radiance of the Lord's Vishvarupa in the previous verses, Sanjaya now describes how Arjuna saw the Lord's Vishvarupa. [ Verse 14 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *  
Seen in a clear form. **Commentary (continuation of the previous page)**  
In that vision the whole universe, though appearing as a single body, is divided into many categories: gods, humans, animals and birds, the earth, the seas, the sky, the stars, etc., together with all other divisions (not compressed, but fully expanded). Arjuna, using the divine eyes given by the Lord, directly perceived the entire animate and inanimate world as a part of the Lord’s body. The implication is that even the smallest portion of Lord Krishna’s body contains the whole moving and unmoving cosmos. That cosmos itself is manifested as countless universes, as many realms of deities, as innumerable individuals and substances, all differentiated and expanded. Thus even the gods have a master‑owner. The phrase “apashyad‑deva‑devasya śareere pāṇḍavas tatha” means that “at that moment when the Lord, by granting divine sight, displayed His universal form, Arjuna saw it.” The word *apashyat* indicates that Arjuna saw exactly the form that the Lord showed. Sanjaya had earlier described the Lord’s appearance; Arjuna now witnessed the same. Just as the human world is vastly different from the divine world, the divine world is infinitely more wondrous than the Lord Himself, because all worlds (including the divine world) are of the mode of nature, whereas the Lord is beyond nature. Hence the Lord is called *deva‑deva* (the supreme of gods). In the Lord’s body Arjuna saw, in a single place, the worlds of the egg‑born, the womb‑born, the sweat‑born, the stationary‑moving, the sky‑dwelling, the water‑dwelling, the earth‑dwelling, eighty‑four lakhs of wombs, fourteen bhuvanas, and many other divisions. Even though the world is infinite, it is contained within a single fragment of the Lord (Bhagavad Gītā 10.44). Wherever Arjuna directs his gaze into the Lord’s body, the infinite universe appears. **Relation** – After beholding the Lord’s supernatural universal form, Sanjaya describes Arjuna’s state in the following verse. ---

**Verse**  
tataḥ saḥ vismayāviṣṭo hṛṣṭaromā dhanañjayaḥ  
pranamya śirasā devaṁ kṛtāñjaliḥ abhāṣata

*Translation*  
Then, bewildered and delighted, Arjuna, the son of Dhananjaya, bowed his head, folded his hands, and spoke. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- *tataḥ* – then  
- *saḥ* – he  
- *vismayāviṣṭaḥ* – filled with amazement (very astonished)  
- *hṛṣṭaromā* – delighted with wonder (hṛṣṭa = delighted, roma = astonishment)  
- *dhanañjayaḥ* – Arjuna (son of Dhananjaya)  
- *pranamya* – bowing, having paid homage  
- *śirasā* – with his head  
- *devaṁ* – the Lord  
- *kṛtāñjaliḥ* – with folded hands (gesture of reverence)  
- *abhāṣata* – spoke

**Commentary on the verse**  
*vismayāviṣṭaḥ* – Arjuna was extremely astonished at the Lord’s universal form. *tataḥ* – subsequently, after that astonishment,  
*saḥ* – he,  
*hṛṣṭaromā* – became delighted because of the wonder,  
*dhanañjayaḥ* – Arjuna, the son of Dhananjaya. He (Arjuna) joined his hands in reverence, bowed his head toward the supreme deity, and expressed his feelings. *pranamya śirasā devaṁ kṛtāñjaliḥ abhāṣata* – Having bowed his head and placed folded hands before the Lord, Arjuna spoke. Arjuna’s inner feeling was: “Having witnessed the Lord’s extraordinary grace, how can I express my gratitude? I have nothing to offer except my devotion. I have come to the Srimad‑Bhāgavatam to recount how Yashodā once saw the universal form in the tiny mouth of little Kanhaiya. In that one universe among countless others, there is a continent, within it Bharat, within it a Mathura region, within it a Vraja region, within it a village called Nandgaon, within it a house called Nand‑Bhavan, and there stands a small Kanhaiya. When Yashodā, brandishing a stick, demanded, ‘Why did you eat the mud? Show me your face!’ Kanhaiya opened his mouth, and in that tiny mouth Yashodā saw the entire world—Nandgaon, Nand‑Bhavan, and herself—‘sahātmanam’ (the self‑same). In the same way, Arjuna saw the whole universe within a fragment of the Lord’s body.
