* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

Connection — Arjuna, astonished by the Lord’s wondrous universal form, proceeds to describe it in the next three verses while offering praise. Arjuna said:

“I see all the demigods in Your body, as well as the various assemblies of living beings, the serpents and the divine sages.” — [ Verse 15 ]

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- devah: O god! - bhuta‑viśeṣa: particular living beings (the myriad creatures)  
- īśam: the Lord (Shankara)  
- saṅghān: groups, communities of beings  
- sarvān: all  
- ṛṣīn: sages  
- ca: and  
- divyān: divine  
- uragān: serpents (celestial snakes)  
- paśyāmi: I see  
- dehe: in the body  
- sarvān: all  
- devān: gods  
- tathā: also  
- kamalāsana‑stha: seated on the lotus seat  
- brahmāṇam: Brahma

**Explanation** — Arjuna’s divine vision, granted by the Lord, is so extraordinary that the realms of the gods are displayed before him. Not only the three worlds (heaven, earth, and netherworld) appear, but also the supreme beings who preside over them—Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva—are directly visible. Thus Arjuna declares that he sees the entire host of deities, the myriad assemblies of creatures, and the supreme Lord Brahma and Shiva. “Brahmāṇam īśam kamalāsana‑stha” — Arjuna observes Brahma seated on the lotus. This indicates that he also perceives the navel of the Lord, the source from which the divine serpent‑like energy (Vishnu, reclining on the cosmic serpent Shesha) emanates, as well as Shiva on his mountain Kailāsa and the sacred banyan tree that stands there. “Ṛṣīn ca sarvān uragān ca divyān” — He beholds every earthly sage and the celestial serpents that dwell in the netherworld. **Special note** — When the Lord says that the entire universe resides in a single part of Him, Arjuna prays to be shown that aspect. In response, the Lord instructs, “Behold the whole moving and unmoving creation situated in one place of My body” (11.7). The sage Sanjaya, who also possesses divine sight, affirms, “There the entire universe is present in one place within the Lord’s body” (11.13). Here Arjuna states, “I see all beings and their assemblies in Your divine body.” The term “ekastham” (one place) appears in the Lord’s and Sanjaya’s statements, but not in Arjuna’s own words, as demonstrated by this verse.

[ Verse 16 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

It is said that when Arjuna’s vision entered any single spot on the Lord’s body, the Lord’s universal form (Vishvarupa) began to appear there. At that moment Arjuna’s sight did not turn toward the charioteer‑form of the Lord. Wherever Arjuna’s gaze fell, infinite creations started to be seen; therefore his vision flowed only toward that direction and he could not say “Ekastham” (one‑place). One can say “Ekastham” only when, together with the universal form, the charioteer‑form of the Lord’s body is also visible. Arjuna saw only the universal form, so he described only that form. The universal form appeared to him as boundlessly vast, without any limit of region or time. In other words, as long as Arjuna’s vision did not reach an end of the universal form, how could his sight turn toward the seated charioteer‑form of the Lord? The Lord is displaying the universal form within a single region of His body; therefore He uses the term “Ekastham.” Sanjaya, seated in the charioteer‑form, sees both the Lord and the universal form that resides in one region of the Lord’s body, and thus Sanjaya also uses the word “Ekastham.”

Now the question arises: in the visions of the Lord and Sanjaya, which single place was the one where Arjuna saw the universal form? The answer is that it cannot be determined exactly which spot in the Lord’s body Arjuna beheld the universal form. This is because innumerable universes (ananta‑koti) reside in every cell‑cavity of the Lord’s body. The Lord himself said, “In one region of My body you may behold the whole creation, together with the moving and the immovable” (verse 7 of this chapter). Hence, wherever Arjuna’s gaze fell once, the entire universal form unfolded before him. **Parishishta (Appendix) meaning** – In the Lord’s cosmic form Arjuna sees a multitude of deities, beings, Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, sages, serpents, etc. The implication is that while Arjuna is seated in the realm of death, he simultaneously perceives the realms of the gods, Brahmaloka, Vaikuntha, Kailasa, Nagaloka, and so on. Consequently, everything that can be spoken or heard resides as a fragment within the Lord’s one‑part. Whether the Lord is manifest or formless, great or small, His infinitude never ceases. The whole creation originates from Him, dwells in Him, and merges back into Him, yet He remains unchanged. **Verse 16 (Sanskrit transliteration and literal meaning)**

*anekā‑bāhū‑dara‑vaktra‑netram paśyāmi tvāṁ sarvato’‑ananta‑rūpam*  
*na‑antaṁ na‑madhyaṁ na punas‑tavā‑diṁ paśyāmi viśveśvara‑viśvarūpa*

- *anekā‑bāhū*: many‑armed  
- *dara*: belly, abdomen  
- *vaktra*: face, mouth  
- *netram*: eyes  
- *paśyāmi*: I see  
- *tvām*: you  
- *sarvato*: from all sides  
- *ananta‑rūpam*: form of the infinite

- *na‑antaṁ*: not the end  
- *na‑madhyaṁ*: not the middle  
- *na punas‑tavā‑adiṁ*: nor again (any) beginning  
- *paśyāmi*: I see  
- *viśveśvara*: Lord of the universe  
- *viśvarūpa*: universal form

**Literal translation:** “I see you, O Lord of the universe, with many arms, belly, faces and eyes, in an infinite form from all directions; I see no end, no middle, nor any beginning.”

**Interpretation:** The seer beholds the Lord as an all‑encompassing, boundless manifestation, beyond any limit of time or space. **Glossary of terms used in the explanatory notes**

- *Vishvarupa*: “O universal form!”  
- *Vishveshvara*: “O Lord of the universe!”  
- *sarvataḥ (tathā)*: from all sides  
- *ādīm*: the primal, original  
- *na*: not  
- *tvām*: you (the object of seeing)  
- *anekā‑bāhū‑vaktra‑netram*: many‑armed, many‑bellied, many‑faced, many‑eyed (i.e., the Lord)  
- *ananta‑rūpam*: of infinite forms  
- *madhyam*: middle  
- *punar*: again

**Footnotes**

1. The appearance of the word “Ekastham” in the statements of the Lord and Sanjaya implies that Arjuna also perceived the entire universal form within a single region of the Lord’s body. 2. (i) “In each cell‑cavity of the Lord’s body innumerable universes reside” (Manas 1.201). (ii) “How many countless universes flutter in each pore of the body, like tiny atoms of fire moving through the lattice of a window‑pane illuminated by sunlight” (Śrīmad‑Bhāgavatam 10.14.11).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

“na‑anta na madhya na punas tva‑adim” – there is no knowledge of where your end is, where your middle is, or where your beginning is. Explanation – the epithets **Vishvarūpa** (Universal Form) and **Viśveśvara** (Lord of the Universe) signify that everything that can be seen appears infinite; all that is seen is you, and you are also the master of this world. The bodies of ordinary humans are inert and contain both the physical and the conscious, but in your Virat (cosmic) form there is no distinction between body and consciousness. In the Virat form body and consciousness are one and the same, so everything is purely consciousness (cintamaya). Thus, by addressing you as “Vishvarūpa” Arjuna says you are the body, and by addressing you as “Viśveśvara” he says you are the consciousness, the lord of the body. “anekabahū‑dara‑vaktra‑netram” – when I look toward your hands I see many hands; toward your belly I see many bellies; toward your face I see many faces; and toward your eyes I see many eyes. The meaning is that your hands, bellies, faces and eyes are endless, all infinite. “paśyāmi tvāṁ sarvato ’nantarūpam” – you are infinite in all directions, beyond space and time. The expression “na‑anta” indicates that when one looks at something, the gaze first reaches the object’s limit. For example, when looking at a book the eye first notes its length and breadth. Likewise, when Arjuna beheld the Virat form, his sight first went to its limit (the end). Not finding an end, his gaze moved to the middle; then to the beginning, yet he could locate no end, middle, or beginning of the Virat form. Hence the phrase “na‑anta na madhya na punas tva‑adim” is placed in sequence to describe the infinite nature of the Lord’s Virat form. Even a fragment of the Lord contains infinity; just as there is no place in ink without a script, nor a place in gold without a jewel, so there is nothing lacking in the Lord—by nature, everything exists in Him. [ Verse 17 ]

The phrase “kirīṭinam gadhinam cakriṇam ca” describes you as wearing a crown, holding a mace, and bearing a discus (the conjunction “ca” also includes the conch and lotus). dyutim‑aprameyam – a form that shines intensely like a blazing fire and the sun; even the universal form cannot be fully perceived. This is the radiant form of the Lord. Your brilliance is such that, just as eyes are dazzled before the intense light of the sun, they are likewise dazzled when looking at you. Hence you are difficult to behold; you cannot be seen clearly. You are boundless from all sides, i.e., you are beyond measurement. Direct perception, inference, analogy, word, meaning, or any other proof cannot reveal you, because the power of proof resides in you. Here is a great wonder: the Lord gave Arjuna divine sight, yet even the divinely‑sighted Arjuna could not fully see the Lord’s universal form. This shows that even the power granted by the Lord is insufficient to fully know Him. The Lord Himself does not fully know Himself; if He did, how could He remain infinite? Relation – In the next verse Arjuna praises the Lord while seeing Him in the attributeless‑formless, attributeless‑form, and with attributes‑form. **Sanskrit verse (Bhagavad‑Gītā 11.18)**  
tvam akṣaraṁ paramaṁ veditavyaṁ tvam asya viśvasya paraṁ nidhānam |  
tvam avyayaḥ śāśvata‑dharmagoptā sanātanaḥ tvam puruṣo mato me || 18 ||

*Translation* – You are the imperishable, supreme, to be known; you are the supreme treasure of this universe. You are the immutable protector of eternal dharma, the eternal person; I consider you to be that. **Break‑down of the verse**

- *param* ashraya hain – you alone are the supreme refuge. - *tvam akṣaraṁ paramaṁ* – you alone are the supreme imperishable. - *tvam asya viśvasya paraṁ nidhānam* – you are the ultimate treasure of the entire universe. - *akṣara* (akṣara‑tva Brahma) – the imperishable, i.e., the eternal Brahman. - *śāśvata‑dharmatva* – the eternal dharma. - *tvam goptā asya* – you are the protector of this. - *sanātana dharmake rakṣaka hain* – the protector of the eternal dharma. - *tvam avyayaḥ* – you are immutable. - *sanātanaḥ* – eternal. - *puruṣaḥ* – person. - *me mato* – I consider. - *(and) you alone are the indestructible eternal person – thus I believe.*

**Explanation** – “tvam akṣaraṁ paramaṁ veditavyaṁ” indicates that you are the supreme, imperishable principle to be known, the ultimate repository of this world. By these words Arjuna praises the Lord using references from the Puranas, Smṛtis, saints’ sayings, and philosophical treatises, describing the supreme, attribute‑less‑formless aspect (the “akṣara‑Brahma”) as the source of all knowledge. “tvam asya viśvasya paraṁ nidhānam” means that whatever is seen, heard, or understood in this world, its highest support and foundation is you. When the great dissolution occurs, the entire creation merges back into you, the cause of all causes. “tvam śāśvata‑dharmagoptā” signifies that when righteousness declines and unrighteousness rises, you incarnate to destroy unrighteousness and protect eternal dharma. By these verses Arjuna extols the Lord’s manifest, attribute‑filled form. “avyayaḥ sanātanaḥ tvam puruṣo mato me” declares that you are immutable, without beginning or end, the eternal person, and I accept you as such. **Pariśiṣṭa‑bhāva (supplementary sense)** – The phrase “tvam akṣaraṁ paramaṁ veditavyaṁ” conveys the attributeless‑formless aspect; “tvam asya viśvasya paraṁ nidhānam” conveys the attributeless‑form aspect; and “tvam śāśvata‑dharmagoptā” conveys the attribute‑filled‑form aspect. Together they present the Lord’s complete nature: attributeless‑formless, attributeless‑form, and attribute‑filled‑form.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

After attaining knowledge of Him, nothing else remains to be known (Bhagavad Gita – Chapter 7, verse 2), because apart from Him there exists no other entity. Relation – having described the astonishing divine form from verses 15 to 18, the next two verses present Arjuna’s description of the ferocity, power and capability of the universal form. **Verse 19**  
*anādimadhyānta‑mananta‑vīrya‑mananta‑bāhuṁ śaśi‑sūrya‑netram | paśyāmi tvāṁ dīpta‑hutāśava‑kṛtam svatejasā viśvam idaṁ tapaṁtaḥ*

“I see You, whose nature is beyond beginning, middle and end, possessing infinite vigor and countless arms, eyes like the moon and the sun; I behold You radiant, fire‑offering, fierce‑mouthed, and by Your own brilliance this whole universe is blazing.”

Explanation of the terms:

- **anādimadhyānta** – “beyond beginning, middle and end”; there is no countable limit to Him. - **mananta‑bāhu** – “endless‑armed”; He has no boundary of arms, indicating limitless power. - **svatejasā** – “by His own brilliance”. - **śaśi‑sūrya‑netram** – “eyes like the moon and the sun”; the moon and sun that illuminate the world are His eyes, so the entire cosmos receives light from Him alone. - **dīpta‑hutāśava‑kṛtam** – “the fire‑form that receives all offerings made in sacrifice”; He is the radiant fire‑mouth that absorbs every sacrificial fire. - **tapaṁtaḥ viśvam** – “the universe that burns with His own energy”; all beings, objects and circumstances are scorched by the boundless vigor (anantavīrya) that emanates from Him. Arjuna’s earlier statement in verse 16 that he does not see any beginning, middle or end of the Lord is reiterated here with a different aspect: the earlier description concerned the “country‑created” (deśakṛta) infinity, while here the “time‑created” (kālakṛta) infinity is emphasized. Thus, concepts such as country, time, object, etc., cannot limit Him; they are all encompassed within Him, and He cannot be measured by any of them. The phrase **śaśi‑sūrya‑netram** signifies that the moon and sun, which illuminate the world, are His eyes, so the world receives its light solely from Him. **dīpta‑hutāśava‑kṛtam** denotes the blazing fire‑mouth that receives every fire offered in yajña, homa and similar rites; this fire‑form is Himself. **svatejasā viśvam idaṁ tapaṁtaḥ** means that by His own brilliance He scorches the entire universe. Consequently, every individual, object or circumstance that faces adversity encounters the limitless power (anantavīrya) residing in Him; that same power both scorches and is scorched, revealing His infinite, boundless, and supreme strength. The countless arms (anantabāhu) are the limbs of His universal form. Appendix meaning – this verse conveys that the Lord is infinite in every respect. The world that is scorched by His brilliance is not separate from the Lord; therefore, the scorcher and the scorched are both manifestations of the Divine form. **Verse 20**  
*dyāvā‑pṛthivyor idamantaraṁ hi vyāptaṁ tvayākena diśaś ca sarvāḥ | dṛṣṭvā‑adbhuta‑rūpam‑ugraṁ tavedaṁ loka‑trayaṁ pravyathitaṁ mahātmānaḥ*

“The space and the earth, the interval between them, and all directions are pervaded by You alone; having beheld Your wondrous and fierce form, O great‑souled one, the three worlds are agitated.”

Commentary on verse 20:

Arjuna again notes that the Lord’s form is “many‑armed, many‑faced, many‑eyed” (as in verse 16). This is not a mere repetition; the earlier description dealt with the divine (deva) aspect of the universal form, whereas the present verses describe the fierce (ugra) aspect. The appearance of the phrase “viśvam idaṁ tapaṁtaḥ” in verse 19 and the expression “dṛṣṭvā‑adbhuta‑rūpam‑ugraṁ” in verse 20 follow naturally from the transition to the fierce manifestation.

[ Verse 20 ]

mahātman = O great soul! diśaḥ idam = this direction  
dyāvā‑pṛthivyor = between heaven and earth (the sky and the earth)  
antaram ca sarve = the whole interval between them  
pṛthvīke = of the earth  
ekena tvayā hi vyāptaṁ = it is entirely pervaded by you alone  
* sādaka‑sañjīvani * = *Sādaka‑Sañjīvani* (the life‑giving elixir for the seeker)  
diśāḥ = the directions  
eka‑tvāt = from you alone

**Explanation – “mahātman”**  
The address “mahātman” means that no one’s nature can ever equal yours, has ever equaled yours, will ever equal yours, nor can it ever possibly do so. Hence you are “mahā‑ātmā”, the one of great, supreme nature. **Interpretation of “dyāvā‑pṛthivyor idam antarṁ hi vyāptaṁ tvayā ekena diśaḥ sarvāḥ”**  
The space that lies between heaven and earth, the whole expanse, is completely filled by you. The ten directions—east, west, north, south; between east‑north the direction “Īśāna”, between north‑west “Vāyavya”, between west‑south “Nairṛtya”, between south‑east “Āgneya”, and the upward and downward directions—are all pervaded by you. In each of these directions you alone are present and radiant. **Reference to the verse “dṛṣṭvā‑adbhutaṁ rūpam‑ugraṁ tavedaṁ lokatrayaṁ prayathitam”**  
In the nineteenth verse and the first half of the twentieth, the fierce form of the Lord is described. From the second half of the twentieth up to the twenty‑second verse, Arjuna narrates the effect of that fierce form. Seeing your marvelous, extraordinary, super‑natural, astonishing, brilliant and terrifying fierce form, all beings that dwell in the three worlds—heaven, the world of the dead, and the netherworld—are distressed and frightened. Although this verse mentions only heaven and earth (dyāvā‑pṛthivyor), Arjuna’s use of “lokatrayam” (the three worlds) also includes the netherworld. Arjuna’s vision penetrates a single region of the Lord’s body, yet the scene he sees alternates among the netherworld, the world of the dead, and heaven. Your wondrous, fierce form, when beheld, agitates the three worlds. (761) The wondrous and fierce form, when seen, causes all three worlds to become agitated. Thus, in Arjuna’s sight, the various scenes appear without any sequential order. A question arises: if the three worlds are disturbed by seeing the universal (Vīrāṭa) form, how could they have seen it without divine sight? The Lord granted divine vision only to Arjuna. Who gave the three worlds the divine sight required to perceive the Vīrāṭa form? Ordinary mortal eyes cannot perceive this form, yet Arjuna speaks of the three worlds being “sankata” (distressed) and “prayathita” (agitated) on seeing it, citing the verses “viśvam idaṁ tapaṁtaṁ” (11.19) and “lokatrayam prayathitam”. The resolution is that the distressed three worlds are themselves part of the Vīrāṭa form; they are its limbs. Sanjaya and the Lord speak of seeing the Vīrāṭa form in a single region (ekastham), but Arjuna does not say he saw it in a single region. While observing the Vīrāṭa form, Arjuna’s attention does not turn to the Lord’s bodily form; his gaze remains fixed on the universal form. When even the charioteer‑aspect of the Lord’s body does not attract Arjuna’s eye, how could his vision shift toward the mundane world that the distressed beings inhabit? This demonstrates that the distressed and the distressing, the agitated and the agitating, are all aspects of the same Vīrāṭa form. Arjuna perceives that the three worlds are disturbed and frightened by the Vīrāṭa form, but in reality, within the scope of the universal form, he is not sequentially viewing heaven, then netherworld, then again heaven. Using the divine sight granted by the Lord, he simultaneously beholds heaven, the earth, the netherworld, and all their inhabitants: the gods on the celestial realm, the various classes of beings, Brahmā seated on the lotus, Śiva on Kailāsa, all the sages, the divine serpents (11.15), etc. Though Arjuna’s utterance of these observations takes some time, the simultaneous vision of all realms does not. Consequently, his statements do not follow a fixed order of heaven, death, or netherworld.

762  
* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

The terrifying feelings that arise when one sees a lion, a tiger, a snake or death disappear when one grows older; in fact, the larger one becomes, the more the three worlds become frightened. Stones and rocks do not attract him; similarly, when a person’s vision is limited to material enjoyment, the prevailing attitude in the world persists, but it vanishes when that material vision disappears. Those whose vision is limited to material enjoyment perceive only the worldly truth; those whose vision is not limited perceive the world as the divine form of the Lord. Just as a single woman appears to a child as a mother, to a father as a daughter, to a husband as a wife, and to a lion as food, the world appears as true through “skin‑vision,” mutable through “discriminative vision,” divine through “emotional vision,” and as a tiny fragment of the Lord’s universal form through “divine vision.” The entire universe that can be seen, heard, and understood is a small part of the Lord’s divine universal form. The rigidity, changeability, and apparent non‑divinity that we see in the world are in fact merely a glimpse of the divine universal form, a play of that form. The divinity of the universal form possesses independent power, whereas the apparent non‑divinity of the world has no independent power. Arjuna beheld the Lord’s universal form with divine vision, while devotees, through emotional vision, see the world as the divine form—“Vāsudevaḥ sarvam” (Vāsudeva is everything). This means that, just as a child in his early years sees emotions in stones and rocks, the same principle applies. **Appendix meaning** – In this verse the word “tvayairkena” signifies that, although the Lord manifests in countless forms, He is essentially one—“Vāsudevaḥ sarvam.” No one can count His innumerable forms, yet He is one in all of them. The Lord possesses innumerable wondrous aspects; He is infinite with respect to country, time, object, person, form, knowledge, yoga, and every other perspective. Everything that we have not seen, heard, known, understood, or even imagined falls under the universal form. **Relation** – Now, before Arjuna’s eyes (in the universal form) the visions of heaven and other realms appear, and they are described in the next two verses. [ Verse 21 ]  
*amī hi tvāṁ surasaṅghā viśanti kechida‑bhītāḥ prāñjalayo gṛṇanti. svastītyuktvā maharṣi‑siddhasaṅghāḥ stu‑vantī tvāṁ stutibhiḥ puṣkalābhiḥ*

Breakdown:  
- amī = they  
- hi = indeed  
- tvāṁ = you  
- surasaṅghā = assembly of gods  
- viśanti = enter, approach  
- kechida = some  
- bhītāḥ = fearful  
- prāñjalayaḥ = with folded hands (salutation)  
- gṛṇanti = salute, bow to  
- svastī = “may you be well,” an auspicious greeting  
- it = thus (used to introduce the quotation)  
- maharṣi‑siddhasaṅghāḥ = the assembly of great sages and perfected beings  
- stu‑vantī = praising, extolling  
- tvāṁ = you  
- stutibhiḥ = with hymns of praise  
- puṣkalābhiḥ = abundant, plentiful

Explanation – “Amī hi tvāṁ surasaṅghā viśanti” means that when Arjuna had gone to heaven, the gods he had previously met are now seen entering the Lord’s form. All these deities originate from Him, reside in Him, and merge into Him. “Kechida‑bhītāḥ prāñjalayo gṛṇanti” indicates that some of the sages, though initially fearful, fold their hands in reverence. “Maharṣi‑siddhasaṅghāḥ stu‑vantī tvāṁ stutibhiḥ puṣkalābhiḥ” says that the great sages and perfected beings praise Him with abundant hymns of exaltation.

[ Verse 22 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

All of them are parts of the Supreme’s universal form; yet Arjuna, surrounded by the great sages— the Saptarishis, Devrishis, Maharishis, Sanakas, etc.— seems to be praising the Lord only after beholding His universal form, and the gods are also offering salutations (may there be welfare and auspiciousness). Their reverence is expressed through the highest hymns, and the assembled sages and perfected beings extol You with praises. **Appendix meaning** – The deities, Maharishis, Siddhas, and all such beings are themselves limbs of the Lord’s universal form. Consequently, those who enter, those who are frightened, those who chant the Lord’s names and qualities, and those who offer praise are also the Lord; the same applies to those who are being entered, who are being frightened, whose names and qualities are being chanted, and whose praises are being offered. This is the unique feature of the Lord’s saguna (with attributes) aspect. **Shloka (transliteration + meaning)**  
*rudrādityā vasavo ye ca sādhyaḥ viśve ’śvinau marutaś ca uṣma‑pāś ca*  
*gandharva‑yakṣa‑asura‑siddha‑saṅghā vīkṣante tvā vismitāś caiva sarve*

“The eleven Rudras, the twelve Adityas, the eight Vasus, the two Ashvins, the winds, and the hot‑food‑offering beings; the assemblies of Gandharvas, Yakshas, Asuras and Siddhas all behold You, astonished.”

**Explanation of the enumerated beings**

- *Rudrādityā* – the eleven Rudras and the twelve Adityas. - *Vasavo* – the eight Vasus. - *Sādhyaḥ* – the two Ashvins (the twin horse‑men). - *Marutaḥ* – the ninety‑five winds (Marud‑gan). - *Uṣma‑pā* – the “hot‑food” beings, whose name derives from the offering of warm food to the ancestors. These names are listed in the commentary on Chapter 6, Verse 6 of the Gita; see that passage for details. Further enumerations from the Vayu Purāṇa (Chapter 6, verses 15‑16) give twelve “sādhyas”: mind, consent, life‑force, man, vehicle, consciousness, horse, guidance, swan, Narayana, prosperity, and sovereignty. Ten “viśve‑devas” (Chapter 6, verses 31‑32) are: Kratu, Daksha, Shrava, Satya, Kala, Kama, Dhuni, Kuruvan, Prabhavan, and Rochaman. The phrase *vīkṣante tvā vismitāś caiva sarve* means “all these deities, ancestors, Gandharvas, Yakshas, etc., are astonished as they look upon You.”

The seven “pitṛs” (ancestors) associated with the universal form are: Kavyavāha, Anala, Soma, Yama, Aryama, Agni‑svāt, and Barhisat. **Appendix meaning (continued)** – Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, the Sādhyas, and the viśve‑devas are all limbs of the one Supreme Being. Hence, both the seer and the seen are the same Paramātmā. **Relation (Sambandh)** – In the next three verses Arjuna will describe the Lord’s magnificent, terrifying universal form and its consequences. *Note on the term “asura”* – The word contains the negative prefix “na‑” (as in “na sura asurāḥ”), indicating that Asuras are the opposers of the gods.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]  
[ Verse 23 ]

**Mahabaho** – “O great‑armed one!”  
Seeing your form, which has many mouths, many eyes, many arms, many legs, a vast belly, and many fierce tusks, the worlds are distressed, and I too am distressed. **Mahabaho =** O great‑armed! **Your form =** the appearance you display. **Seeing =** when beheld. **Bahuvaktra‑** many‑mouths, **bahu‑netra‑** many‑eyes, **bahu‑bāho** many‑arms, **bahu‑bāhu‑rūpād** many‑legs, **bahū‑udaram** many‑bellies, **bahu‑daṇṣṭra‑karāla‑** many‑fierce‑tusks. **Lokāḥ pravyathitāḥ** – all beings become agitated. **Aham** – I also (become agitated). **Bahubāhu‑rūpād =** many arms and legs. **Mahat =** great. *Explanation (commentary on verses 15‑18, 19‑22, and 23‑30 of the universal form):*  
From verses 15 to 18 the universal form is described as the “Deva” (divine) aspect; from verses 19 to 22 it is described as the “Ugra” (terrible) aspect; and from verses 23 to 30 it is described as the “Ati‑Ugra” (extremely terrible) aspect. **Bahuvaktra‑netram** – Your mouths do not all look alike. Some mouths are gentle, some are fierce; some are small, some are large. Likewise, your eyes are not uniform: many are gentle, many are fierce; some are small, some are large, some are long, some are wide, some are round, some are crooked, and so on. **Bahubāhu‑rūpād** – The shape, colour, and function of the hands are extraordinary; the thighs are varied and the feet are of many kinds. **Bahū‑udaram** – The bellies are not identical; some are large, some are small, some are terrifying, and many other kinds exist. ---

(2) **Arjuna’s reaction to the universal form** – Seeing the cosmic manifestation, Arjuna became terrified, astonished, bewildered, and distressed to the extent that he could not recall what Krishna had said or was saying. (3) Earlier Arjuna mentioned the distress of the three worlds; here he adds that *all* beings and even himself are distressed. (4) The repeated utterance of the same words by Arjuna is a sign of his fear and amazement. In the world, whenever a person experiences fear, joy, sorrow, or surprise, his mouth naturally repeats certain words or phrases:  
- On seeing a snake, one repeatedly cries “Snake! Snake! Snake!”  
- On the arrival of a noble person, one exclaims “Come! Come! Come!” in joy. - On the death of a beloved, one repeatedly laments “He is dead! He is dead! Darkness has fallen in the house!”  
- When a sudden disaster strikes, one shouts “I am dead! I am dead! I am dead!”

Similarly, in the vision of the universal form, before this verse Arjuna repeatedly uttered words expressing fear and awe because each new aspect of the form presented fresh terror, delight, or sorrow. Repetition here is not considered a flaw. **Bahudanshṭrā‑karālaṁ dṛṣṭvā lokāḥ pravyathitās tathāham** – The many fierce tusks (terrifying beards) cause all beings to become agitated, and I too become agitated. **Parishishta‑bhaav (Supplementary meaning)** – All creatures that see and are seen, those who cause distress and those who experience distress, including Arjuna himself, are encompassed within the Lord’s universal form.

[ Verse 24 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

**Sanskrit verse (transliteration)**  
nabhaspṛiśaṁ dīptam anekavarṇaṁ vyāttānanaṁ dīpta‑viśāla‑netram |  
dṛṣṭvā hi tvāṁ pravyathitānta‑rātmā dhṛtiṁ na vindāmi śamaṁ ca viṣṇo ||24||

**English rendering**  
“Your form, shining like the sky, is radiant with many colours; your mouth is spread wide, and your eyes are blazing and vast. Seeing you, my inner self, which is already agitated, finds no steadiness nor peace, O Viṣṇu.”

---

**Commentary translation (top‑to‑bottom)**

Because, O Viṣṇu, your luminous countenance spreads far and wide; the inner self that is terrified looks upon you, yet cannot obtain courage or calm. The verse describes the boundless magnitude of Viṣṇu’s universal form. In Chapter 20 Arjuna narrated both the length and breadth of the cosmic manifestation; here only the length is emphasized. ‘Viṣṇu’ denotes the all‑pervading Supreme who incarnated as Krishna to relieve the earth of its burden. ‘Dīptam‑anekavarṇaṁ’ – He possesses countless hues—black, yellow, dark, white, etc.—all brilliantly shining. ‘Nabhaspṛiśam’ – His appearance is so vast that it touches the sky. The touch is metaphorical: just as the eye reaches the heavens and then meets darkness beyond, the divine vision also meets the infinite. Thus the cosmic form is limitless, and even the highest human sight is confined. ‘Vyāttānanaṁ dīpta‑viśāla‑netram’ – Like a terrifying beast that opens its mouth wide to devour prey, Viṣṇu’s mouth is spread to encompass the whole universe, and his eyes blaze with immense radiance. ‘Śamaṁ ca viṣṇo’ – Seeing this, the inner self becomes deeply disturbed; it cannot find steadiness or peace. A question arises: Arjuna possesses both his own power and the divine vision granted by the Lord, yet he is frightened by the universal form, whereas Sanjaya remains unshaken. The reason is that sages such as Bhīṣma, Vidura, Sanjaya, and Kuntī had a special understanding of the Lord’s nature; consequently Sanjaya already comprehended the Lord’s essence and influence, while Arjuna’s delusion (moh) had not yet been completely dispelled (see Chapter 11, Verse 89). Because of this lingering delusion, Arjuna felt fear. Sanjaya, free from delusion, did not experience fear. This analysis demonstrates that divine grace especially favours those who are spiritually qualified; unqualified persons cannot fully perceive it. Just as a mother’s affection is greater for a small child than for an older boy, the Lord’s love is especially intense for innocent, simple‑hearted cowherds, gopas, and cows, but not as intensely directed toward liberated great souls, who already know the Lord intrinsically. Thus, the radiant, vast eyes of Viṣṇu reveal the supreme reality that Sanjaya, having already internalised the divine truth, perceives without anxiety, whereas Arjuna, still entangled in doubt, cannot yet attain steadiness or peace.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

The Lord, moved by Arjuna’s yearning, displayed His universal form. Because of this divine grace, Arjuna’s delusion was ultimately destroyed—just as Sanjaya had foretold that “delusion is destroyed by Your grace” (Bhagavad Gita 18.73). In that moment Arjuna, still a novice, realized the intimate relationship with the Lord, and the delusion of the ungrateful (kṛpā‑pātra) was completely eradicated. Hence the Lord’s mercy was especially abundant toward Arjuna. Appendix (Parishishta Bhāva) – The word “nabhah‑sparśam” (touching the sky) signifies the infinite nature of the cosmic (virat) form. Wherever Arjuna’s eyes could reach, he beheld only the virat form—“sā kāṣṭhā sā parā gatiḥ” (Katha 1.3.11), meaning that the Supreme Atman is the ultimate destination and the ultimate motion for all. Verse 25

Explanation – The phrase “daṁṣṭrā‑kārāla‑ni ca te mukhāni dṛṣṭvaiḥ” (the twelfth verse) describes faces that are as terrifying as the fire of dissolution (kāla‑agni) which consumes the three worlds at the end of the great cosmic cycle. The Lord’s faces, likened to that fire, are extremely fearsome because of their dreadful beards. Simply seeing them inspires overwhelming terror; no being can withstand their power. Consequently, I am unable to discern the directions, and the sight of those monstrous faces deprives me of any peace or happiness. “prasīda deveśa jagannivāsa” – You are the Lord of all deities, and the entire universe resides within you. Thus, whenever a deity or a human is frightened, they will call upon you alone; no one else can be invoked, and no one else will hear. Therefore I also call out, “O Lord of the gods! O inhabitant of the world! Please be pleased.”

Seeing the Lord’s terrifying form, Arjuna feels as if the Supreme is in a great rage. Overcome with fear, he prays that the Lord may be pleased. “diśo na jāne na labhe ca śarma” – The sight of those monstrous faces leaves me without knowledge of the directions. Knowledge of the directions normally comes from the rising and setting of the sun, but the sun itself has become part of the Lord’s eyes, subsumed within His virat form. Apart from that, an intense, all‑pervading light surrounds Him (Appendix of Chapter 11, verse 44), indicating that the Lord reveals His virat form only when He is pleased. Yet the ferocity of the form makes Arjuna fear that the Lord is displeased, prompting his prayer for the Lord’s satisfaction. Connection – In the next two verses Arjuna describes how the principal warriors enter the Lord’s universal form.

[Verse 26-27]
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *  
[ Verse 26‑27 ]

**Shloka 26**  
*Transliteration:*  
amī ca tvāṁ dhṛtarāṣṭrasya putrāḥ sarve sahaiva‑avanipāla‑saṅgaiḥ |  
bhīṣmo droṇaḥ sūtaputrastathā‑sau sahāsmadīyairapi yodha‑mukhyaiḥ ||

*Translation:*  
And these, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all together with the troops of the forest‑guard,  
Bhīṣma, Drona, Karna, and also the chief commanders of our side, are entering the battle. **Shloka 27**  
*Transliteration:*  
vaktraāṇi te tvaramāṇā viśanti daṁṣṭrā‑karālāni bhayānakāni |  
kecid vilagnā daśan‑āntareṣu saṁdṛśyante cūrṇitair uttamāṅgaiḥ ||

*Translation:*  
Their faces rush forward, fierce and terrible like fanged beasts. Some, with broken limbs, are seen amid the fighting, their bodies shattered. ---

**Commentary (English)**

The passage describes the forces that have entered the battlefield on the side of the Kauravas. “Our side” (as‑madīyaḥ) refers to the Kaurava army, whose chief warriors (yodha‑mukhyaiḥ) include the foremost commanders such as Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and Drupada, who fight out of duty (Dharma). The “sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra” are the princes of the Kaurava lineage. They are accompanied by the “troops of the forest‑guard” (avanipāla‑saṅgaiḥ), the soldiers who protect the forest regions that surround the battlefield. Three eminent elders—Bhīṣma, Drona, and Karna—are also present. Their participation underscores that even the most venerable and experienced warriors have taken up arms in fulfillment of their duty. Bhīṣma is famed for his lifelong vow of celibacy and his steadfast adherence to his promise, even when it required him to fight against his own father’s wishes. Drona, the preceptor of the Kauravas, fights because he perceives it as his duty to protect his students, though he later regrets the loss of his own son, Ashvatthāmā. Karna, bound by his friendship with Duryodhana, remains loyal to the Kaurava cause despite Krishna’s revelation of his true parentage; he declares that he will not harm the five sons of Kunti (Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula, Sahadeva, and himself) but will only confront Arjuna. The description of “faces rushing forward, fierce like fanged beasts” (vaktra‑āṇi…daṁṣṭrā‑karālāni) conveys the terrifying appearance of the combatants. The mention of “some, with broken limbs, seen amid the fighting” (kecid vilagnā…cūrṇitair uttamāṅgaiḥ) indicates that even the most powerful warriors suffer injury and dismemberment in the ferocious clash. Thus, verses 26‑27 portray the massive and formidable assembly of Kaurava forces, highlighting both their heroic stature and the grim reality of war.
[Verse 27]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

These are the sons of Dhritarashtra, together with the assembly of forest‑protectors, the kings who stand on Duryodhana’s side and wish to please him in battle (Gita – Chapter 1, Verse 23). They are not offering counsel that benefits Duryodhana. Along with those royal groups, Dhritarashtra’s sons Duryodhana, Dushasana, etc., a hundred fierce warriors with massive beards, because of their terrifyingly large beards, are rushing into your mouths with great speed— “vaktṛāṇi te tvaramāṇā viśanti daṁṣṭrākarālāni bhayānakāni.”

In the Virat (cosmic) form they may appear to enter the Divine or the Divine’s mouths; it is the same divine play. Their motions seem different according to the mood, but whether they go into the Divine or into the mouths, they remain in the Virat form. “kecid vilagnā daśanāntareṣu sandṛśyante cūrṇitai‑ruttamāṅgaiḥ” – some appear, after the teeth are separated, as finely pulverized, superior limbs. Just as certain foods, when chewed, pass straight to the stomach, while other foods become trapped between the teeth and the beard, so too many of those entering your mouths go directly inside (to the stomach), whereas others, together with crushed heads, seem lodged between your teeth and beards. [ Chapter 11 ]

A question arises: the warriors are presently standing on the battlefield, so how can they be seen entering Arjuna’s mouths in the Virat vision? The answer is that the Divine, in the Virat form, is showing Arjuna a vision of the imminent future. When the Divine displayed the Virat form, He said to Arjuna, “You may also see whatever else you wish to see in this Virat form” (Verse 7). Arjuna doubted whether the victory would belong to us or to the Kauravas (Chapter 2, Verse 6). To dispel that doubt, the Divine showed Arjuna a preview of the forthcoming outcome, indicating that the victory would be ours. In later questions Arjuna poses, the Divine repeats the same assurance (from verses 32 to 34). Appendix (Parishishta Bhāva) – Arjuna is witnessing the imminent future in the Divine’s Virat form. Because the Divine is timeless, past, present and future are all present (Gita – Chapter 7, Verse 26). Connection – Those who have taken up arms out of a sense of duty (Dharma) and who seek the realization of the Supreme (Atman) are described by Arjuna, in later verses, as entering the Virat form through the analogy of rivers. “yathā nadīnāṁ bahavo ’mbuvegāḥ samudrameva‑abhimukhā dravanti | tathā tavāmī nara‑lokavīrāḥ viśanti vaktṛāṇi abhivijvalanti” – [ Verse 28 ]

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- yathā – just as  
- nadīnāṁ – of the rivers  
- bahavo – many  
- ’mbuvegāḥ – swift currents (‑vega = speed)  
- samudrameva – toward the ocean alone  
- abhīmukhā – facing, directed  
- dravanti – flow, run  
- tathā – likewise  
- tavāmī – your (plural)  
- nara‑lokavīrāḥ – heroic men of the mortal world  
- viśanti – enter, penetrate  
- vaktṛāṇi – mouths  
- abhivijvalanti – shining, blazing forth

**Literal translation of the verse**  
Just as many swift currents of the rivers run straight toward the ocean, so too the heroic mortals of your world enter your mouths, shining brilliantly. The commentary explains that, leaving aside the names and the form of the flow, the rivers become the ocean itself. The water has no separate, independent existence apart from the ocean; it only appears distinct when it assumes the form of a river. In reality the rivers never possessed an independent existence; they seemed separate only because they took the shape of flowing water. Thus, the warriors who enter the mouths of the divine vision are like rivers that ultimately merge into the ocean, losing their individual identity and becoming one with the supreme whole.
[Verse 28]

[ Verse 29 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

The commentary begins:  
Warriors such as Bhishma, Drona and other heroes of the mortal world have entered the radiant, knowledge‑embodied faces of the Supreme. They shine like rivers; only the living being who has taken up the desire for the path of attaining the Supreme Soul runs straight toward the Supreme. But through error, by assuming a relationship with the perishable body, they become attached to worldly accumulation and sensual pleasure and start to regard themselves as a separate existence. Among the people who appear before them, those who truly desire the Supreme are the real warriors; such worldly seekers are rare and few. Hence, for them, the body is designated with the indirect pronoun “ami” (they) so that they are not absorbed in collection and enjoyment. Relation—those who have entered the battle driven by the lust for kingdom and praise, and who are engrossed in acquiring worldly wealth and pleasures—are described by Arjuna in the following verse using the vast form of moths as an analogy. **Shloka (Verse 29)**  
*yathā pradīptaṁ jvalanaṁ pataṅgā viśanti nāśāya samṛddhavegāḥ*  
*tathāiva nāśāya viśanti lokās tava api vaktrāṇi samṛddhavegāḥ*

*Word‑by‑word breakdown*  
- **yathā** – as  
- **pradīptaṁ** – illuminated, lit up  
- **jvalanaṁ** – fire, flame  
- **pataṅgā** – moths (the attracted insects)  
- **viśanti** – go toward, enter  
- **nāśāya** – for destruction, to perish  
- **samṛddhavegāḥ** – with great speed, swift‑moving  
- **tathāiva** – likewise, in the same way  
- **lokās** – the worlds, the people  
- **tava** – your (referring to the Supreme)  
- **api** – also, even  
- **vaktrāṇi** – mouths, faces (metaphor for the beings)  
- **samṛddhavegāḥ** – moving with rapid speed

*Translation of the shloka*  
Just as brightly lit fire draws moths, which fly toward it with swift speed for their own destruction, likewise all the worlds—your very faces—also rush forward with rapid speed toward ruin. **Explanation of the metaphor**  
The fire (jvalanam) represents the dazzling, alluring worldly pleasures. Moths, blinded by desire, rush toward the flame with great velocity (samṛddhavegāḥ). Some are consumed completely; others are merely singed and cease to fly, yet their longing remains fixed on the flame. If a person extinguishes the flame out of compassion, the moths become deeply distressed, feeling deprived of the great benefit they expected. Similarly, those driven by the desire for material enjoyment and accumulation run with accelerated worldly momentum toward their own downfall—toward the abyss of 84 lakh yonis and the realms of hell. In ordinary life, humans chase after sensual pleasure, comfort, honor, and respect day and night. In the pursuit of these, they encounter insult, criticism, loss, anxiety, inner burning, and the gradual exhaustion of their lifespan, yet they remain internally eager for further fleeting pleasures and possessions. **Bhartṛhari’s verse (Vairāgya‑śataka)**

*ajānanaṁ dāhātmyaṁ patati śalabhō dīpadahanē*  
*sa mīno'pyajñānādvaḍiśayutamaśnāti piśitam*  
*vijānanto'pyete vayam iha vipajjalajatilān na muñcāmaḥ*  
* kāmān ahaḥ gahano moham ahimā*

*Translation*  
Not knowing the burning nature, the moth falls into the flame; even a fish, out of ignorance, swallows the piece of meat attached to the lamp. Though we are aware of it, we do not free ourselves from the tangled net of misfortune woven by desires; alas, the glory of illusion is profound.

Appendix / Parishishta Bhaav - In the previous verse, the example of rivers was given, and in this verse, the example of moths is given. Moths, due to infatuation, voluntarily enter the fire to burn themselves, whereas rivers flow into the ocean to give themselves up. Therefore, those who have the desire to "take" are like moths, and those who have the desire to "give" are like rivers. The feeling of taking is inert, and the feeling of giving is conscious. The feeling of taking leads to inauspicious actions (Karma), and the feeling of giving leads to auspicious actions. For those who have the desire to take, there is heaven, and for those who have the desire to give, there is Moksha (liberation). This is because the feeling of taking is binding, and the feeling of giving is liberating. Connection - Having described the two communities through two examples in the previous two verses, now the description of the terrifying form of Lord Vishnu, who devours all the worlds, is given. You are licking up all the worlds on all sides with your flaming mouths, and having filled the entire universe with your radiance, your fierce splendor is scorching everything, O Vishnu. (30)

viṣṇo: O Vishnu. 'Tejobhirāpūrya jagatsamagraṁ bhāsastavogrāḥ pratapanti viṣṇo' - The radiance of Lord Vishnu in His universal form is very fierce. It is filling the entire universe and scorching everything. Explanation - 'Lelihyase grasamānaḥ samantāt lokān samagrān' - No living being can escape being licked up by Your tongue. 'Samagrān vadanaijvaladbiḥ' - You are destroying all living beings and, to prevent anyone from escaping, You are repeatedly licking them up with Your flaming mouths. This means that Lord Vishnu, in the form of time, is destroying everything. Appendix / Parishishta Bhaav - Here, 'lokān samagrān' (all worlds) and 'jagat samagram' (the entire universe, including inert and conscious beings) imply that all this is included in the universal form of the Lord. In the Gita, the Lord is also called 'samagran' - 'asaṁśayaṁ samagraṁ mām' (7.1), actions are also called 'samagran' - 'yajñāyācarataḥ karma samagran' (4.23), and in this verse, the universe is also called 'samagran'. This means that everything is a form of the Lord. Connection - Lord Vishnu, in His universal form, is showing His various wondrous forms. Seeing all living beings, including the warriors on both sides, being engulfed in His fierce and extremely terrible mouths, Arjuna becomes very frightened. Therefore, to understand the true nature of the fiercely formed Lord, Arjuna asks:

Please tell me, who are you with this fierce form? O greatest of gods, I offer my obeisance to you; please be gracious. I wish to know you, the original one, for I do not know your actions. (31)

[ Verse 32 ]

Prasida (grant your grace)  
Adyam (the first)  
You are (Bhavantam)  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjivani (nectar for the seeker) *  
by the principle (Tatvase)

(You) are pleased – may you become known. I wish to know; I (the speaker) ask because I do not fully understand. Explanation of the primordial form – tell me, O gracious one, salutations to you, O best of the gods, Prasida. You appear both in a divine form and in a fierce form; therefore, who are you who assumes such forms? Seeing the extremely fierce Virat (cosmic) form, Arjuna, out of fear, bows only a salutation. When Arjuna becomes completely unable to comprehend this terrifying Virat form, he finally says, “O supreme among the gods, salutations to you.”

The Lord, with his tongue, repeatedly licks all his mouths, a terrifying conduct that makes Arjuna pray, “May you be pleased.”

—

Your disposition (tava pravṛttim) – I do not know your disposition well. Opposing warriors keep entering the battlefield; therefore, what do you truly intend to do? In other words, who are you and what is your purpose? I wish to know this, and I ask you to explain it clearly. A question arises: the Lord’s first incarnation appeared as Virat (the cosmic) form in the world, and now Arjuna sees a Virat form in a particular region. Are these two Virat forms the same or different? The true answer is known only to the Lord, but contemplation suggests that the Virat form seen by Arjuna already contained the world‑like Virat within it. As is said, the Lord is all‑pervading; this does not only mean that He pervades the entire universe, but also that He pervades beyond the universe. The world is a part of Him, and countless creations are parts of Him. Likewise, the Virat form that Arjuna sees also contains this world. The statement “I wish to know you, O primordial one, but I do not truly know your disposition” refers to the Lord’s first incarnation as Virat (the cosmic) form. Hence Arjuna says, “Adi‑Narayana! I do not know you clearly, nor do I understand why you have manifested here, nor what is in your mouths besides our side and many other things.”

**Appendix** – Seeing the Lord’s majestic fierce form, Arjuna becomes so frightened that he asks his own friend Shri Krishna, “Who are you?”

**Connection** – The question Arjuna earnestly asked in the previous verse receives its true answer from the Lord in the following verse. Shri Bhagavan said:

*kālo ’smi loka‑kṣhaya‑kṛit pravṛiddho lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ | ṛte ’pi tvām na bhaviṣyanti sarve ye ’vasthitāḥ pratyānīkeṣu yodhāḥ || 32 ||*

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- kālo ’smi – I am Time  
- loka‑kṣhaya‑kṛit – the destroyer of worlds  
- pravṛiddho – having become great/aged  
- lokān – the worlds  
- samāhartum – to destroy  
- iha – here  
- pravṛttaḥ – engaged (in action)  
- ṛte ’pi – even without  
- tvām – you  
- na – not  
- bhaviṣyanti – will exist  
- sarve – all  
- ye – who  
- avasthitāḥ – are situated, stand  
- pratyānīkeṣu – on the opposite side  
- yodhāḥ – warriors

**English rendering of the verse**

“I am Time, the great destroyer of worlds, grown old, and now I am engaged in destroying the worlds. Even without you, all the warriors who stand on the opposite side will not exist.”

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

Commentary – The Lord’s universal form, whether contemplated or not, makes no difference, because I am intent on the destruction of all. You have already witnessed this in the Virat form, where the armies of both your side and the opposing side are entering my terrifying mouths. It appears extraordinary, for even Arjuna’s divine vision is unable to fully perceive it, and the universal form is described as difficult to behold – “durnirīkṣyaṃ samantāt” [ Verse 17 ]. Here the seekers ask the Lord, “Who are you, O fierce‑form?” It is implied that, had Arjuna not asked out of fear, the Lord would have continued to reveal ever more wondrous manifestations. Yet, when Arjuna posed the question, the Lord ceased showing further forms and began answering his query. “kālo ’smi loka-kṣhaya‑kṛt pravṛddhaḥ” – In the previous verse Arjuna asked, “Who are you, O fierce‑form?” In reply the Lord, in his Virat aspect, declares: I am the great, terrifying, ever‑growing Time, the inexorable destroyer of all worlds. “lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ” – Arjuna had said, “I do not understand your purpose” (i.e., “I do not know why you are here”). The Lord answers that he has come solely to annihilate both armies. “ṛte ’pi tvāṃ na bhaviṣyanti sarve ye ’vasthitāḥ prati‑ānikeṣhu yodhāḥ” – You earlier declared that you would not fight – “na yotsye” (2.9). Yet, will the opponents not die without your fighting? A doubt arises because Arjuna had seen, in the Lord’s mouths, the destruction of both his own and the Kaurava forces. Why then does the Lord speak only of the opponents’ demise without your fighting? The resolution is that if Arjuna fights, he will kill only the opponents; if he refrains, the opponents will still perish, for Time (Kāla) will consume everyone. Hence the Lord’s meaning: the destruction of all is inevitable; you merely fulfill your duty as a warrior. Another doubt: the Lord says the opponent’s warriors will not remain even without your fighting, yet warriors such as Ashvatthama survive the battle. The explanation is that the Lord referred only to those warriors whom Arjuna is capable of killing and those he will later kill. Thus the Lord’s statement means: the warriors you can kill will die even without your direct action; the warriors you will kill have already been slain by Me – “mayai‑vate nihataḥ pūrve‑meva” [ Verse 33 ]. Relation – In the previous verse the Lord said that the opponent’s warriors will not remain even without your killing. What should Arjuna do in such a situation? The answer is given in the next two verses:

“tasmāt tvam uttiṣṭha yaśo labhasva jitvā śatrūn bhūṅkṣva rājyaṃ samṛddham”  
“mayai‑vate nihataḥ pūrve‑meva nimitta‑mātraṃ bhava savyasācin” [ Verse 33 ]

Translation of the verse (11.33) with word‑by‑word rendering:

- **tasmāt** – therefore  
- **tvam** – you (for battle)  
- **uttiṣṭha** – arise, stand up  
- **yaśaḥ** – fame, glory  
- **labhasva** – obtain, acquire  
- **jitvā** – having conquered  
- **śatrūn** – the enemies  
- **bhūṅkṣva** – enjoy, partake of  
- **rājyaṃ** – the kingdom  
- **samṛddham** – prosperous, abundant

- **mayai** – by Me  
- **vate** – indeed  
- **nihataḥ** – slain, destroyed  
- **pūrve‑meva** – already beforehand  
- **nimitta‑mātraṃ** – merely as a cause, for the sake of  
- **bhava** – become, be  
- **savyasācin** – O Arjuna, the one who shoots arrows with both hands

Thus, the Lord urges Arjuna: “Therefore, arise, obtain glory, defeat the enemies, enjoy the prosperous kingdom; know that those enemies have already been slain by Me, so act only as a cause.”

[ Verse 33 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjivani *

Interpretation – “Therefore, arise and obtain fame,” O Arjuna, means that you must fire arrows with both hands, i.e., devote your full strength to the battle, but you must become only a mere instrument (nimitta‑mātra). “Being only an instrument” does not imply that you should withhold your power, intellect, or valor; rather, you must apply them carefully and completely. Yet you must not boast, “I have killed, I have won,” because those enemies were already destined to be slain. Hence you are to act merely as an instrument, without undertaking any new work. When you have realized that the opponents will not survive even without your direct killing, tighten your resolve and stand ready for battle, and you will acquire fame effortlessly. This signifies that the result is inevitable and has already been shown to you. Consequently, if you fight, fame will come without cost, and people will say, “Arjuna has achieved victory.”

The phrase “obtain fame” does not mean that you should exult, “Wow, I have won!” after gaining fame. Rather, understand it as: just as the opponents are already destined to die by my hand, the fame that is to arise will also arise inevitably. If you consider fame as something you must earn through personal effort, you become bound to the fruit (“phale sakto nibadhyate” – Gita 5.12). The implication is that profit‑loss, fame‑disgrace, all lie in the Lord’s hands. Therefore a person should not attach himself to them, because they are merely transient. “Having conquered the enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom” – a prosperous kingdom has two aspects: (1) it is free from obstruction, i.e., no enemy or adversary remains to trouble it; and (2) it is abundant in wealth and resources, so that the people possess ample riches—elephants, horses, cows, land, houses, water‑reservoirs, and sufficient food. Only when both conditions are met is the kingdom truly complete. The Lord tells Arjuna that by defeating the enemies you will enjoy such an unobstructed and wealth‑filled realm. Here “enjoying the kingdom” does not refer to sensual pleasure, but to the ordinary notion of enjoying a state that ordinary people consider a reward, which you will obtain effortlessly. “By Me these have already been slain earlier” – the Lord explains how you will obtain fame and the kingdom without effort: all those who have arrived here have already had their lifespan ended; in other words, time‑forms have already been destroyed by Me. “Become only a nimitta‑mātra, O Savyasācin” – because you fire arrows with both the left and right hands, Arjuna earned the epithet “Savyasācin” (the ambidextrous one). Addressing him by this name, the Lord says:

When acting as a mere instrument, there must be no deficiency on your part; you must apply your full strength carefully. No trace of pride should remain in the accomplishment of the work. For example, when Lord Krishna lifted the Govardhan mountain, He told the cowherd boys to press their sticks against the mountain’s base. All the boys placed their sticks and believed that the mountain was held up by their collective effort. In reality, the mountain rested on the tip of Krishna’s left little finger. When the boys became proud, Krishna lowered His finger slightly; the mountain began to descend, and the boys cried, “O father, it is falling!” Krishna urged them to exert greater force, yet even with all their combined strength they could not raise the mountain. Then Krishna raised the mountain again with a mere movement of His finger. Similarly, a seeker must apply his strength, intellect, and capability completely in the quest for the Supreme Self, leaving no slightest deficiency, yet must not become proud of the effort. The experience of the Supreme is solely due to the Lord’s grace. As the Lord says in the Gita: “By My grace one attains the eternal, imperishable position” (Gita 18.56) and “With My grace, a pure mind overcomes all difficulties” (Gita 18.58). Thus, merely becoming a nimitta‑mātra leads the seeker to the realization of the Supreme. “u bhau me dakṣiṇau pāṇi gāṇḍīvasy vikārṣaṇe | tena devamanuṣyeṣu savyasācīti māṁ viduḥ” (Mahā Virāṭa 44.19) – “Both of My right hands, when wielded as the bow‑string of the Gandiva, are known among gods and men as Savyasācin, that is how they call Me.”

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

When the aspirant regards his own power as the means of practice, the very belief in his own strength causes repeated failure and delays the attainment of the Truth. If the aspirant does not entertain even the slightest pride in his own power, success is attained instantly, because the Supreme Self (Parmatma) is ever‑present; only the aspirant’s pride in his own effort prevented his experience of that presence. The purpose of the phrase “nimittamātraṁ bhava” is precisely to remove this pride of personal effort. Only ignorance has caused this self‑imposed accusation. If a person abandons pride and the desire for fruit, and, in accordance with the attained condition, performs his duty‑action as a mere instrument, his liberation is automatically assured. What is destined will happen inevitably; no one can prevent it by his own strength, and what is not destined will not happen, regardless of any personal power or intellect. Hence, while remaining indifferent to success or failure, one should perform his prescribed duties; liberation then follows automatically. Bonds, the acquisition of hell, the attainment of eighty‑four lakh wombs—these are all results of action, whereas liberation, welfare, divine attainment, divine love, and the ego‑driven belief “I act, therefore it happens; if I do not act, it will not happen,” are all self‑evident. Appendix Note – “nimittamātraṁ bhava savyasācin” – Becoming merely an instrument does not mean performing actions for the sake of a name; rather, it means exerting one’s full strength without considering oneself the cause, i.e., without limiting one’s effort or harboring pride. The Lord has bestowed upon us strength, knowledge, aptitude, etc., for us to apply them, yet even by applying all our power we cannot obtain Him; attainment comes only by His grace. The Lord’s grace toward us is limitless. Just as a calf drinks milk from a single udder, the Lord has given the cow four udders; similarly, He bestows grace from all directions. We must become merely instruments. Arjuna faced a battlefield, therefore the Lord tells him to fight as a mere instrument; victory will be his. In the same way, the world is before us; if we practice as mere instruments, we shall triumph over the world. [ Chapter 11 ]

[ Verse 34 ]  
**Sanskrit (transliteration):**  
droṇaṁ ca bhīṣmaṁ ca jayadrathaṁ ca karṇaṁ tathānyāni yodhavīrān mayā hatāṁ tvam hani mā vyathaṣṭhā yudhyaḥ svajetāsi raṇe sapatnān

**Word‑by‑word meaning:**  
- *droṇaṁ* – Drona  
- *ca* – and  
- *bhīṣmaṁ* – Bhishma  
- *ca* – and  
- *jayadrathaṁ* – Jayadratha  
- *ca* – and  
- *karṇaṁ* – Karna  
- *tathānyāni* – as well as the others  
- *yodhavīrān* – warrior‑heroes  
- *mayā* – by Me  
- *hatāṁ* – having been slain  
- *tvam* – you  
- *hani* – kill  
- *mā* – do not  
- *vyathaṣṭhā* – be distressed  
- *yudhyaḥ* – fight

**Full English rendering:**  
“Kill Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha, Karna, and all the other warrior‑heroes whom I have already slain; do not be distressed, fight, and you shall surely win the battle against the foes.”

Explanation – The verse declares that the great warriors—teacher Drona, elder Bhishma, the mighty Jayadratha, Karna, and all other renowned opponents—have already been destroyed by the Lord’s will; therefore Arjuna is instructed to strike them down without anxiety, for victory is assured. In the earlier verse the Lord said, “These have already been slain by Me.” Bhishma, Drona, and Karna were famed for their heroic prowess, making them seemingly difficult to defeat. Jayadratha, though not as celebrated, possessed a boon that caused a hundredfold retaliation to anyone who struck his head; this made him appear formidable. The commentary clarifies that all these warriors have already been eliminated in the divine form, and Arjuna is urged to finish the task.

[ Verse 34 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjivani *

The phrase “by Me those already slain, you slay” means: defeat your opponents, but do not become conceited about the victory, because all of them have already been destroyed by Me. Arjuna’s anguish over killing his venerable elders—Bhishma, Drona, Karna—was expressed in “Do not be distressed, fight.” He regarded killing them as a sin. Hence the Lord tells him not to feel that distress; there is no need to contemplate violence or any other fault. He should perform his Kshatriya‑Dharma, i.e., wage war, and not abandon it. “Jetaṣi raṇe sapatnān” – you will defeat the enemies in battle. Earlier, in the sixth verse of the second chapter, Arjuna had said that it was uncertain whether we would win or lose; doubt lingered in his mind. At the beginning of chapter eleven, the Lord granted Arjuna the vision of the universal form and said, “See whatever else you wish to see” (seventh verse), including whose victory and whose defeat will occur. In that divine vision, the destruction of Bhishma, Drona, and Karna was shown, and the Lord now declares unequivocally that Arjuna’s triumph is assured. **Special note**  
A seeker, when obstructed by the allure of perishable objects and persons, may become anxious that his practice is ineffective. The Lord reassures him with the verses “Mayaivete nihataḥ pūrveva” and “Mayaḥ hantaḥ tvam jahi,” indicating that everything that appears attractive in the seeker’s path—objects, relationships, deteriorating habits—has already been annihilated by the Divine and is therefore of no importance. When the seeker worries, “My vices and misconduct do not cease; what shall I do?” the root cause is his own ego. The thought “They should disappear quickly” reveals a lack of faith, trust, and surrender to the Lord. Vices are not inherently bad; the error lies in the anxiety about them. Consequently, the seeker must never be anxious. “Kill those already killed by Me” raises the question: if the Lord, in his cosmic form, has already slain everyone, then any act of killing in the world is merely the killing of those already slain by the Lord, and the killer should not incur sin. The resolution is that no human has the right to kill or cause suffering; a human’s sole right is to serve all and bring happiness to all. If a person possessed the right to kill, the injunctions of the scriptures—perform auspicious actions, avoid inauspicious ones—would become meaningless. The prohibition would have no referent, and any act of killing or inflicting pain would be sinful because it is an unauthorized, hatred‑driven action. However, when a Kshatriya engages in a scripturally sanctioned war, abandoning selfishness and ego while performing his duty, no sin accrues, for this is his Svadharma (personal duty). **Appendix (Parishishta‑Bhava)**  
The Lord tells Arjuna that all those warriors have already been slain by Him. This implies that the seeker’s own anger, hatred, lust, and wrath have likewise been pre‑destroyed; they are without independent existence. We have mistakenly granted them status and importance by accepting them as part of ourselves. In reality, they possess no independent reality—“Nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ” (Gita 2.16). **Connection (Sambandh)**  
After witnessing the Lord’s terrifying universal form, Arjuna asked in verse 31, “Who are you and why have you come here?” In verse 32 the Lord replied, “I am the enlarged Time, come to annihilate all.” In verses 33‑34 the Lord assured Arjuna that he will strike down only those already killed by the Lord, guaranteeing his victory. What Arjuna subsequently did is narrated by Sanjaya in the following verses.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 19 ]

[ Verse 35 ]  
Sanjaya said: “Having heard this utterance of Keshava, the crown‑wearer (Kiriti) trembling, again with folded hands bowed to Krishna, trembling with fear.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
keshavasya kritanjaliḥ: with folded hands (hands joined) to Keshava  
vepamānaḥ kirītī: the crowned one (Kiriti) trembling  
namaskṛtvā bhūya eva aha kṛṣṇaṁ sagadgadaṁ bhītabhītaḥ praṇamya: again, with reverence, he bowed to Krishna, whose voice is “gagad‑gād” (shaking), being terrified

**Commentary (top continuation)**  
Arjuna was already frightened, and then the Lord declared, “I am Time; I shall devour all.” By uttering this, the Lord intensified Arjuna’s terror. The implication is that the Lord, as “I am Time,” foretells universal destruction—from “I am the destroyer” to “by Me you are slain.” Hearing this, Arjuna began to shiver and repeatedly offered salutations with folded hands. When Arjuna had previously slain demons such as Kāla, Kañja, etc., with Indra’s assistance, Indra, pleased, bestowed upon him a radiant divine crown (kiriti) comparable to the sun’s brilliance. Hence the name “Kiriti” was given to Arjuna. The term “Kiriti” here signifies that those who have slain great demons for Indra’s aid—Arjuna among them—are now trembling before the Lord’s universal form. Arjuna’s voice, though trembling, is not completely paralyzed; his speech remains “gagad‑gād” (shaky) both from joy and fear. If he were utterly terrified, he could not speak at all. Thus his continued chanting shows that his fear, while great, is not absolute. **Relation to the following verse**  
From the next verse onward, Arjuna proceeds to extol the Lord. Arjuna said:  
[ Verse 36 ]  
“By your fame, O Lord of the universe, the world rejoices and is drawn toward you; the fearful demons flee in all directions, and the assembled sages bow down.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
hṛṣīkeśa tava prakīrtyā jagat praḥṛṣyaty anurajyate ca: by your glorious name, O Lord of the senses, the world becomes delighted and attracted to you  
rakṣāṁsi bhītāni diśo dravanti sarve namasyanti ca siddha‑saṅghāḥ: all the fearful demons run away in every direction, and the assembled perfected beings bow down

**Commentary on Arjuna’s utterance**  
“Hṛṣīkeśa” addresses the Lord as the inner controller. The verse declares that the Lord’s reputation fills the whole universe with joy and love, causing even the most terrifying demons to retreat, while the assembled sages (siddha‑saṅghāḥ) prostrate themselves. **Cited passage**  
In the Mahabharata, Virata Parva, chapter 44, verse 17, it is recorded: “Earlier, with Indra’s favor, I was given a crown to fight the demon‑army; the crown shone like the sun upon my head.” This passage explains the origin of the name “Kiriti” for Arjuna.

[ Verse 36 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The fearful beings (demons, ghosts, etc.) are dispelled by the chanting of the Lord’s names and qualities, especially the chanting of the primordial (Adi). As they flee in all directions they bow and offer salutations to Him. In every place, in every direction, the whole universe is rightly filled with this phenomenon; it is the assembled Siddhas (realized saints) who perform it. In worldly experience it is observed that a person who becomes delighted by the Lord’s name, pastimes and attributes becomes extremely frightened; such a state is beyond ordinary speech. Arjuna, on seeing the Lord’s terrifying universal form, was indeed filled with terror. Yet, from the 36th verse onward up to the 48th verse, he still praised the Lord. The resolution is that although Arjuna was terrified by the Lord’s fierce (terrifying) form, he was simultaneously exhilarated, as he later declares: “adṛṣṭapūrvaṁ hṛṣito ’smi dṛṣṭvā bhayena ca pravyathitaṁ mano me” (11.45). This shows that his terror was not so overwhelming as to prevent him from extolling the Lord. ‘Hṛṣīkeśa’ – the term combines “hṛṣīka” (the senses) and “īśa” (Lord). The address signifies that the Lord, residing in the hearts of all, energizes the senses, the inner mind and all other faculties. ‘tava prakīrtyā jagatprāhṛṣyaty anurajyate ca’ – turning away from worldly attachment, devotees chant the Lord’s names and qualities, sing of His pastimes, recount and listen to His deeds; consequently the whole world rejoices. The implication is that worldly pursuits generate jealousy and hatred, whereas those who turn toward the Lord and chant His glories attain peace and delight. When the Lord incarnates, all stationary and mobile, inert and conscious realms—trees, vines, deities, humans, sages, celestial beings, animals, birds, rivers, lakes, etc.—become joyous. The chanting of Adi’s (the primordial) names and qualities affects everyone and makes all rejoice. When a person’s mind becomes delighted and absorbed in the Lord through such chanting, his inclination (vṛtti) turns toward the Divine, and love for the Lord blossoms. ‘rakṣāṁsi bhītāni diśo dravanti’ – all demons, ghosts, spirits, and other malevolent beings, frightened by the chanting of the Lord’s names and qualities and by the recitation of His deeds, flee. Their flight is not caused by the Lord’s names or qualities themselves but by their own sins. Because of their sins they cannot endure the sacred hymns praising the Lord’s virtues; wherever such hymns are sung they cannot remain. If any of them does remain, he is reformed, his evil nature is abandoned, and his welfare is restored. ‘sarve namasyanti ca siddha‑saṅghāḥ’ – all communities of Siddhas, saints, great souls and seekers who move toward the Lord, upon hearing the chanting of His names, qualities and pastimes, salute Him. All these scenes belong to the Lord’s eternal, divine, supra‑mundane, cosmic form, in which countless pastimes are enacted simultaneously. ‘sthāne’ – this is exactly as it ought to be and indeed is so, because turning toward the Lord brings peace, bliss and delight, removing obstacles. *Verse from Śrīmad‑Bhāgavatam 10.6.3*  
na yatra śravaṇādīni rakṣoghnaṇi svakarmasu |  
kurvanti sātvatāṁ bhartur yātudhānyaś ca tatra hi ||

Translation: “Where the hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch are not employed in one’s own actions, there the Lord, the sustainer of the world, is present, and there the righteous prosper.”

Thus, wherever people neglect the daily practice of hearing, chanting and reflecting upon the Lord’s names, qualities and pastimes, the power of demonic forces persists; where such devotional activities are performed, those forces are dispelled.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

The commentary begins by stating that when the individual part (a fragment of the divine) is destroyed, sorrow arises; the very presence of that fragment has captured the sense of loss. Consequently, as nature unfolds, only suffering and unrest increase. In other words, when your fragment‑self (the individual soul) is in the sight of the Supreme, it experiences happiness, and qualities such as peace, forgiveness, humility, etc., become manifest. When it turns away from the Supreme, sorrow follows—this is entirely appropriate. The mind inclines toward the opposite side; consequently, the desire for accumulation and enjoyment grows. In order to acquire possessions and pleasures, the mind works harder, and at the same time lack, unrest, pain, irritation, torment, and similar afflictions increase. Yet, when the individual soul withdraws from worldly life and repeatedly comes before God, it becomes ever more joyous. This soul stands between the Supreme (Paramātmā) and the world; by its very nature it is a direct fragment of the Supreme and, as it aligns with nature, its suffering gradually disappears. ---

**Appendix (Pariśiṣṭa) Note** – The word “sthāne” (in place) must be understood for verses that appear both before and after this passage. In verses 32, 33, and 34 the Lord said something that Arjuna now refers to in this verse: “All the opponents have been slain by me; you only become the instrument.” Whatever you have declared is therefore appropriate. By chanting your name, virtues, etc., the world rejoices, and the demonic beings flee in terror. All of this is happening exactly as it should, by your divine play, not by me. **Connection (Sambandh)** – The justification given by the word “sthāne” in the preceding verse is confirmed in the next four verses. **Verse 37**

*Transliteration*  
kasmācca te na nameram mahātmān garīyase  
brahmaṇo ’pi adikartre | ananta deveśa jagannivāsa  
tvam akṣaraṁ sada‑sattā tṛpṛam yat

*English rendering*  
“Why should you not bow to this great‑souled one? Even Brahman, the primal creator, bows to Him. O infinite Lord of the universe, you are the imperishable, the ever‑existent, the supreme beyond all.”

**Explanation (Vyākhyā)** – The verse asks why the great‑souled one (the Supreme) should not be saluted. Even Brahman, the original cause of creation, is described as “adi‑kartṛ” (the primal creator). Hence, the sages (the “siddha‑gaṇa”) ought to offer salutations to Him. It is proper for eminent beings to bow to Him, just as a disciple bows to a teacher who imparts knowledge and illumination, and as a child bows to his parents and elders who gave him birth, age, and learning. Arjuna declares that the Supreme is also the guru of the gurus. The term “ananta” (infinite) indicates that, from any perspective—country, time, object, or person—there is no beginning or end to Him. Viewed as a nation, there is no identifiable start or finish; viewed as time, He has always existed and will forever exist; viewed as an object or person, He transcends all limits. Patanjali Maharaj has said that the Supreme (Parameśvara) is the teacher even of the primordial deities such as Brahmā, etc. (“pūrveṣāmpi guruḥ” – the Supreme is the guru of the earlier beings). (Yoga‑darśana 1.26)
