[ Verse 38 ]  
* Sadhak – Sanjivani *

From the primordial viewpoint, you are the “Jagan‑nivas” – the resident of the whole universe. All forms have no beginning or end; through every eye you appear infinite. When any faculty of perception tries to grasp you, that faculty ceases, yet you remain unending. Hence you are boundless, immeasurable, and unfathomable from every side. The title “Devesh” (Lord of the gods) applies because you are the master, controller, and ruler of all deities such as Indra, Varuna, etc., described in the scriptures. “Tvam akṣaraṃ sad‑sattā‑tattva‑yat” – you are the imperishable, beyond‑existence‑and‑non‑existence form. The self‑existent, independent reality (Sat) is you; the reality that depends on the independent (Asat) also appears as you. You transcend both Sat and Asat, beyond any description by mind, intellect, or senses; you are beyond all conceivable imagination. Thus no being exceeds you; none can be greater, nor can any other be imagined. Consequently, reverence to you is appropriate. “Jagan‑nivas” – countless creations dwell in various portions of you, yet each portion remains incomplete and empty; you are limitless. The supplemental theme introduced in Chapter 9, verse 9.19 (“sadas‑cchāham”) and the present verses “sadas‑sattā‑tattva‑yat” reveal the infinite, all‑encompassing nature of the personal form of the Supreme. Sat and Asat are relative and therefore worldly; that which is beyond them is absolute and therefore transcendental. Both the worldly and the transcendental are aspects of the total Supreme. The Supreme’s higher and lower natures are not beyond Sat‑Asat, yet the Supreme also transcends Sat‑Asat, as expressed in Bhagavad‑Gita 7.7: “There is nothing higher than Me, O Arjuna.”

Within the qualified (sagun) aspect, the unqualified (nirguna) can appear, but not vice‑versa. The qualified aspect does not deny the unqualified, whereas the unqualified aspect denies all qualities. Hence the unqualified is one‑dimensional, admitting nothing within it, while the qualified embraces everything, leaving nothing excluded. Accordingly, Arjuna’s reference to “sadas‑sattā‑tattva‑yat” implies that you are Sat, you are Asat, and whatever else may arise in our imagination is also you. The indescribable principle that is neither Sat nor Asat, expressed in Bhagavad‑Gita 13.12 (“na sattān nāsadu­cyate”), is likewise you. In other words, apart from you there is no past, present, future, or potential existence—only you, alone. **Shloka (Verse 38)**  
*Transliteration:*  
tvam‑ādidevaḥ puruṣaḥ purāṇas tvam‑asya viśvasya para‑ni dhānam |  
vetta‑asi‑vedyam ca para‑ca dhāma tvayā tataḥ viśva‑anant‑rūpaḥ || 38 ||

*Translation:*  
You are the primal deity, the primordial person, the ancient one; you are the supreme abode of this universe. You are the knower, the known, and the supreme dwelling; by you the whole world assumes its infinite form. **Explanation of the Shloka**  
- *tvam* = you (the same)  
- *ādidevaḥ* = the original deity  
- *puruṣaḥ* = the primordial person  
- *purāṇaḥ* = ancient, timeless  
- *tvam‑asya* = you are of this  
- *viśvasya* = of the world/universe  
- *para‑ni dhānam* = the supreme abode, the ultimate treasure  
- *vetta‑asi* = you are the knower (the shelter of all)  
- *vedyam* = the known, that which is to be known  
- *para‑ca dhāma* = the supreme dwelling  
- *tvayā tataḥ* = by you therefore  
- *viśva‑anant‑rūpaḥ* = the world takes the form of the infinite. Thus, you alone are the original god, the timeless person, the ultimate repository of the cosmos, the source of knowledge and the supreme sanctuary, through whom the entire creation manifests as infinite. *Interpretation:* “Tvam‑ādidevaḥ puruṣaḥ purāṇaḥ” declares that you are the original god and the primordial person of all deities; the first manifestation is you. You are the “purāṇa‑puruṣa” because you are ever‑existing and ever‑remaining. Earlier, Arjuna addressed the imperishable Brahman as “Tvam‑akṣaraṃ paramam veditavyam” (BG 11.18); here the same attribute is expressed as “Tvam‑akṣaraṃ”.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

‘You are the supreme repository of this universe’ – in seeing, hearing, understanding and knowing everything that the world presents; and in the origin, condition, dissolution, etc., of the world, you are the ultimate foundation of all that. Only you are knowable. [ Chapter 11 ]

‘Parama Dham’ – the supreme abode that is called liberation, the highest state, where one goes and never returns, and upon attaining which there remains nothing to do, to know or to obtain; you are that supreme abode. ‘Vettasi’ – you are the knower of the entire universe, i.e., past, future and present, as well as all lands, objects, and the innumerable forms manifested from the universal form (Vishvarupa); there is no one beyond you who knows all. Your infinite forms pervade from every direction. You alone are. ‘Tvaya tatam vishvam’ – the whole world is pervaded by you. ‘Vedyam’ – you are the object of the Vedas, the scriptures, the saints and great souls; you pervade every particle of creation. Appendix meaning – Arjuna is merely repeating what the Lord has said: ‘Adideva’ – the Lord called this ‘Aham adir hi devānāṁ maharṣīṇāṁ ca sarvaśaḥ’ (10.2). Although Prakriti is also anadi (13.19), it remains subordinate to the Supreme Self, because Prakriti is the mutable power of the Supreme Self, while the Supreme Self is independent of any power and is self‑effulgent. ‘Purana’ – the Lord referred to this as ‘Purāṇam’ (8.9). No one is older than the Lord, for He is timeless. ‘Parama Nidhānam’ – the Lord called this ‘Nidhānam’ (9.18). Creation is infinite, yet it resides within the Lord’s singular realm. ‘Vetta’ – the Lord expressed this in verses such as ‘Vedāham samatītāni’ (7.26). ‘Vedyam’ – the Lord used the term ‘Vedyam’ (9.17). ‘Parama Dham’ – the Lord said, ‘Yaṁ prāpya na nivartante taddhāmaṁ paramaṁ mama’ (8.21). ‘Tvaya tatam vishvam’ – the Lord declared, ‘Yena sarvaṁ idaṁ tatam’ (8.22) and ‘Mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ’ (9.4). You are:

- Vāyu (Air) – the life‑giving breath that sustains all beings. - Yama (Lord of Discipline) – the sovereign of the realm of restraint who governs the entire universe. - Agni (Fire) – the pervasive energy that gives power, manifests light, and as digestive fire processes food. - Varuṇa (Lord of Water) – the ruler of the waters through which all life receives sustenance. - Śaśāṅka (Moon) – the lunar deity. - Prajāpati (Lord of Creation) – the creator. - Prapītāmah (Grandfather of the Gods, i.e., Brahmā, the father of the divine lineage). Verse 39 (translation):

“Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Śaśāṅka, Prajāpati, you are also Prapītāmah. Salutations, salutations to you; may you be honored a thousand times, and again and again, salutations.”

Explanation of each:

- Vāyu – the breath that animates all creatures; you are Vāyu. - Yama – the ruler of the city of restraint whose governance extends over the whole world; you are Yama. - Agni – the all‑pervading force that provides power, reveals light, and as the digestive fire processes food; you are Agni. - Varuṇa – the sovereign of the waters that gives life to all; you are Varuṇa.

[ Verse 40 ]

* seeker – sanjeevani *

‘Shashankah’ – the moon itself, the source of nourishment for all herbs and plants; it is the moon. ‘Prajapati’ – the creator of progeny, the skilled originator of all beings; Prajapati is you. ‘Prapitamah’ – the great-grandfather who reveals even Brahma; when one has no power left, you become the great‑grandfather. ‘Namo namaste’ … repeated thousands of times – all the gods, Indra and the like, are you. You are the infinite form. How can I praise you, how can I sing your glory? I have no duty left; now I only offer salutations, surrendering myself completely to the Divine. Hence all actions of doing and causing belong to the refuge (the Divine) alone, not to the seeker. **Shloka**  
namo namaste’ astu sahasrakṛtvaḥ punas ca bhūyo ’pi namo namaste  
sarvat evam sarvaḥ — you are the all‑encompassing, infinite heroic power; you pervade everything, and thus you are everything. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- namah – salutation  
- purastād atha – from the front, also  
- pṛṣṭhataḥ – from the back, also  
- te – to you  
- namo ’stu – may salutations be  
- te – to you  
- sarvat – from all directions (tenfold)  
- eva – indeed  
- sarva – all

- sarvam – everything  
- samāpnoṣi – you have gathered, embraced  
- tvam – you  
- sarva – all  
- iti – thus

- ananta‑vīrya – infinite vigor  
- amita‑vikramaḥ – boundless heroic power  
- tvam – you

- sarvaṁ – everything  
- samāpnoṣi – you have encompassed

**Explanation**  
The verse “namah purastād atha pṛṣṭhatas te namo ’stu te sarvat eva sarva” expresses Arjuna’s terror. He cannot find words, so he offers salutations from every direction—front, back, all ten quarters. ‘Ananta‑vīrya amita‑vikramaḥ tvam’ – your strength (ananta‑vīrya) and heroic power (amita‑vikrama) are limitless. ‘Sarvaṁ samāpnoṣi tato ’si sarvaḥ’ – you have embraced the whole universe; nothing exists outside you. It means that even light, force, and all cosmic attributes are subsumed in you. **Appendix (Pariśiṣṭa‑bhāva)**  
Seeing the Divine’s magnificent universal form, Arjuna says that you scorch the world with your own brilliance – “svatejasā viśvam idaṁ tapa‑nantam” (11.19). The scorching and the scorched are both aspects of that universal form. The fierce aspect of the Divine causes agitation in the three worlds – “lokatraiṁ prayathitaṁ mahātmān” (11.20); thus the distressed three worlds are also parts of that form. Gods, trembling, extol the Divine – “kecid bhītāḥ prāñjalayo gṛṇanti” (11.21); demons, frightened, flee in all ten directions – “rakṣāṁsi bhītāni diśo dravanti” (11.36). Hence the frightened gods and demons are also limbs of the Divine’s universal manifestation. They were not physically present on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra; rather, they appeared to Arjuna within the Divine’s colossal form.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, Rudra, Aditya, Vasu, the group of Sādhyas, the universal gods, the Ashvini twins, the Maruts, the ancestors, the serpents, the Gandharvas, the Yakṣas, the Rakṣasas, the Asuras, the Rishis‑Maharishis, the Siddhas, Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the moon, the sun, etc., and besides them Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, Jayadratha and all the royal families— all of these are limbs of the same divine, universal form. Not only that, Arjuna, Sanjaya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra as well as the Kaurava and Pandava armies are also limbs of that same universal form— “You attain everything, and then you are everything.” The implication is that whatever is seen, heard or thought in the material world, whether moving or immobile, is none other than the imperishable God. To experience this, the seeker must firmly accept that whether I understand it or not, whether I experience it or not, whether it is accepted or not, the truth remains the same. Just as a single drop of water and the whole ocean are both filled with the same water‑element, likewise every smallest or largest object is filled with the same Supreme Soul. Keeping this in mind, one should constantly, in mind, salute everyone. When he sees his beloved God in a tree, river, mountain, stone, wall, or anything else, he should pray, “O Lord! Grant me your love; O Lord! My salutations to you.” By doing so, God will appear everywhere to him, because in reality everything is God. Relation – In the next two verses Arjuna, while praying to the Lord, asks for forgiveness. [ Verse 41 ]  
**Transliteration:**  
*sakhEti matva prasabhaM yad uktam he kṛṣṇa he yādava he sakhEti | ajānata mahimānam tave’daM mayā pramādāt praṇayena vāpi || 41 ||*

**English meaning:**  
“Considering you as a friend, O Krishna, O Yadava, O friend, I have spoken this. Not knowing your greatness, I have said this out of folly or out of affection.”

**Commentary:**  
Arjuna, recalling his earlier informal conduct with Krishna in his fierce universal form, feels frightened and therefore turns to Krishna’s personal aspect, seeking forgiveness for his earlier disrespect. He forgets momentarily who the fierce form is, asks, “Who are you in this fierce form?” When the memory of Krishna as the Supreme Lord returns, he realizes that the same Lord is being addressed, and thus he humbly petitions for pardon. [ Verse 42 ]  
**Transliteration:**  
*yac chāvahāsārtham asatkṛto’si vihāra‑śayyā‑āsana‑bhojanēṣu | ekō’thavāpyacyuta tatsaṁkṣaṁ tattkṣāmaye idam mahimān = tvām aham apramēyam || 42 ||*

**English meaning:**  
“Because of my frivolous laughter and disrespect in the presence of friends, family and in places of rest, seat, and food, I have acted improperly. Even if I were alone before you, I would still seek forgiveness for this great offense, for you are immeasurable.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown:**

- **sakhEti** – *sakhE* (friend) + *iti* (thus) → “as a friend”  
- **matva** – *mat* (consider) + *va* (imperative) → “considering”  
- **prasabhaM** – *prasabha* (splendor, brilliance) → “splendid”  
- **yad** – “that which”  
- **uktam** – *ukta* (said) → “said”  
- **he** – vocative particle “O”  
- **kṛṣṇa** – “Krishna” (the Supreme Personality of Godhead)  
- **yādava** – “Yadava” (member of Krishna’s clan)  
- **sakhEti** – “friend” (repeated for emphasis)  
- **ajānata** – *a‑* (not) + *jānata* (knowing) → “not knowing”  
- **mahimānam** – *mahimā* (greatness) + *‑nam* (genitive) → “your greatness”  
- **tave’daM** – *tava* (your) + *idam* (this) → “this of yours”  
- **mayā** – “by me”  
- **pramādāt** – *pramāda* (folly) + *‑āt* (by) → “out of folly”  
- **praṇayena** – *praṇaya* (affection, love) + *‑ena* (by) → “out of affection”  
- **vāpi** – “or also”

- **yac** – “because”  
- **chāvahāsārtham** – *cha* (and) + *avahāsa* (laughter) + *‑ārtham* (for the purpose of) → “for the sake of frivolous laughter”  
- **asatkṛto’si** – *asat* (non‑truth) + *kṛta* (done) + *‑asi* (you are) → “you are the one who has done a false act” (i.e., I have acted improperly)  
- **vihāra‑śayyā‑āsana‑bhojanēṣu** – *vihāra* (recreation), *śayyā* (bed), *āsana* (seat), *bhojanēṣu* (in meals) → “in places of recreation, bed, seat and meals”  
- **ekō’thavāpyacyuta** – *eko* (alone) + *‑atha* (then) + *api* (also) + *acyuta* (you) → “even if I were alone before you”  
- **tatsaṁkṣaṁ** – *tat* (that) + *saṁkṣam* (immediate) → “that very moment”  
- **tattkṣāmaye** – *tat* (that) + *kṣāmaye* (grant forgiveness) → “grant forgiveness for that”  
- **idam** – “this”  
- **mahimān** – “greatness” (referring to the offense)  
- **tvām** – “you” (accusative)  
- **aham** – “I”  
- **apramēyam** – *a‑* (not) + *pramēya* (measurable) → “immeasurable” (referring to the Lord)

Thus Arjuna acknowledges his disrespectful conduct in laughter and in the presence of companions, and earnestly seeks the Lord’s forgiveness, recognizing the Lord’s boundless, immeasurable nature.

[ Verse 41-42 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The commentary begins by noting that the author sometimes addresses the Lord with familiar terms such as “you,” “Maharaj,” etc. In the context of meals he treats the Divine as an equal friend, calling Him at times “O Krishna,” at other times “O Yadava,” in moments of laughter or casual conversation, and sometimes simply “O friend.” These variations arise during activities such as lying on a couch, waking and sleeping, or rising and sitting on a seat. The author wonders why, when he uttered seemingly disrespectful words while eating, he thought he was insulting the Lord’s glory and form, or calling Him “O Achyuta!” without realizing that the Lord is singular and uniquely magnificent. He confesses that he was unaware that at any moment, or through his friends, family, and noble persons, countless billions of universes are manifested. He therefore seeks forgiveness for all the contempt he has shown, saying, “I have become one, even Achyuta has departed. I never imagined who you truly are; I am now seeking your boundless forgiveness.”

Although Arjuna had previously known the Lord’s form, glory, and influence, he had not fully comprehended them. He had accepted the unarmed Lord after abandoning his mighty army of Akshauhini. Yet the Lord’s body contains within it innumerable billions of universes, and Arjuna had not perceived this vast influence, form, and glory. When the Lord mercifully revealed His universal form (Vishvarupa), Arjuna’s sight turned toward that divine power, and he began to perceive the Lord. A strange feeling arose in him: “Where am I, and where is the deity of deities?” Yet, driven by impulsive love or mistake, he blurted out, “Maya pramādāt praṇayena vāpi” (by my mistake or affection again), without any caution. The relationship between Arjuna and the Lord is described as that of two friends playing together. At times Arjuna would splash water over the Lord while bathing, and the Lord would splash water over Arjuna. Sometimes Arjuna would run after the Lord, and other times the Lord would run after Arjuna. They would laugh together, display each other’s special skills, and when the Lord fell asleep Arjuna would tease, “You have fallen so deeply; will anyone else sleep? Are you alone?” When the Lord sat on a seat, Arjuna would ask, “Will you sit alone? Will you allow anyone else to sit? You have taken sole dominion—move aside a little.” Thus Arjuna interacted with the Lord in an extremely intimate manner. Recalling these episodes, Arjuna says, “O Lord! I have committed countless acts of contempt toward you, many of which I cannot even recall. Though you never minded my disrespect, many of my offenses have been directed at you, and therefore I seek forgiveness for all such contempt, invoking your incomprehensible (aprameya) nature.” The term “aprameya” (incomprehensible) indicates that even when one is in the divine posture of meditation, one does not fully fall under divine vision. In reality, no one can fully know the Lord’s glory because it is infinite; if it were fully known, its infinitude would cease and become limited. Since the manifestations (vibhutis) arising from the Lord’s power are endless, the Lord’s own glory cannot have an end—it is beyond termination. **Explanation of “mahimanam tava idam”**  
1. The word *idam* here is not an adjective of *mahimanam*; *mahimanam* is masculine, while *idam* is neuter. Hence *idam* is understood as “form” or “essence.” Consequently, “mahimanam tava idam” means “your glory and form.”  
2. The verse cited (Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 1.15.19) reads:  
   *śayyāsanāṭanavikatthanabhōjanādi‑svai­khyād vayasyṛtavāniti vipralabdhaḥ*  
   “One who is bewildered by the unity of lying, sitting, standing, eating, etc., is considered a learned person.”  
   Arjuna reflects that his conduct with Lord Krishna—sleeping, sitting, wandering, conversing, and sharing meals—became so natural that he would sometimes chide the Lord affectionately, saying, “O friend, you speak the truth!” Yet the Supreme Lord, in His greatness, tolerated all Arjuna’s inadvertent disrespect just as a friend tolerates a companion’s or a father tolerates his son’s slight.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

Appendix – Arjuna felt a friendly affection toward the Lord, but when he beheld the Lord’s divine majesty he forgot that affection, was astonished, and became frightened. He had never imagined that the Lord could be like this! Relation – In the following two verses Arjuna describes the Lord’s greatness and influence and again prays for forgiveness. [ Verse 43 ]  
**Sanskrit:**  
pitas i lokasya charācharasya tvam asya pūjyaś ca gurur garīyān  
na tvatsamo ’sty abhyadhikaḥ kuto ’nyo lokatraye ’py apratim‑prabhāva

**English translation:**  
You are the father of the world, of both the moving and the unmoving; you are worthy of worship and a teacher surpassing all teachers. There is none equal to you, let alone greater; how could there be any other in the three worlds who possesses an incomparable influence? **Word‑by‑word breakdown:**  
- *pita‑asi* – “father (of)”; *lokasya* – “of the world”; *charācharasya* – “of the animate and inanimate”. - *tvam* – “you”; *asya* – “of this”; *pūjyaḥ* – “worthy of worship”; *ca* – “and”; *guruḥ* – “teacher”; *garīyān* – “superior to teachers”. - *na* – “not”; *tvatsamaḥ* – “equal to you”; *asti* – “exists”; *abhyadhikaḥ* – “greater”. - *kuto* – “how”; *anyo* – “any other”; *lokatraye* – “in the three worlds”; *api* – “also”; *apratim* – “incomparable”; *prabhāva* – “influence”. **Commentary:**  
‘*pita‑asi lokasya charācharasya*’ emphasizes that the Lord is the supreme father who creates and sustains every moving creature (human, animal, bird, etc.) and every immobile entity (tree, vine, etc.) in the cosmos. He alone is worthy of worship and is the greatest of all teachers. ‘*na tvatsamaḥ asti abhyadhikaḥ*’ declares that no one can equal the Lord, and none can surpass Him; consequently, there can be no other being in the three worlds whose influence matches His. The phrase ‘*guruḥ garīyān*’ signifies that wherever a human seeks instruction in conduct or ultimate truth, no teacher can compare with the Lord. The appendix further explains that, from a worldly perspective, Arjuna acknowledges that there is no other like the Lord in the three worlds, and therefore no one can be greater. From the ultimate perspective, however, nothing exists apart from the Lord, so the very notion of “greater” or “equal” becomes meaningless. ---

[ Verse 44 ]  
**Sanskrit:**  
tasmāt praṇamya praṇidhāya kāyaṁ prasādaye tvām aham īśam īdyam  
piteḥ putrasya sakhyeḥ sakhyaḥ priyaḥ priayārhaḥ devah sodhum

**English translation:**  
Therefore, bowing down and offering my body as a humble offering, I pray that you, the Supreme Lord, may graciously accept it. As a father is dear to his son, as a friend is dear to his friend, you are worthy of devotion, O God, and I desire to serve you. **Word‑by‑word breakdown:**  
- *tasmāt* – “therefore”; *praṇamya* – “having bowed”; *praṇidhāya* – “having offered”; *kāyam* – “the body”; *prasādaye* – “may please, may accept”. - *tvām* – “you”; *aham* – “I”; *īśam* – “the Lord”; *īdyam* – “as a humble offering”. - *piteḥ* – “of a father”; *putrasya* – “of a son”; *sakhyeḥ* – “of a friend”; *sakhyaḥ* – “friendship”. - *priyaḥ* – “dear”; *priyārhaḥ* – “deserving of love”; *devah* – “O God”; *sodhum* – “I wish to serve”. **Commentary:**  
Arjuna declares that, because the Lord is the supreme father of all creation, he offers his very body as a reverent sacrifice, seeking the Lord’s gracious acceptance. Just as a father loves his son and a friend loves his companion, the Lord is deserving of the deepest affection and devotion. Arjuna’s prayer is a heartfelt desire to serve the Lord, who is the ultimate source of all love and protection.

[ Verse 45 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

Beloved – the insult of a wife that the Divine endures; thus, O God! You are worthy of the insult that I have incurred through my own effort. You are capable of bearing, i.e., forgiving, such an insult. Arjuna says that just as a father tolerates the insult of his son, a friend tolerates the insult of a friend, and a husband tolerates the insult of his wife—i.e., forgives them—so, O Lord, you are capable of bearing my insult; therefore I ask you for forgiveness. Explanation – “Therefore, having bowed down, I offer my body to you for your grace; even neglect is performed, but the husband naturally…”. You are the Lord of infinite universes. Hence you alone are worthy of praise by all. Your qualities, influence, and greatness are limitless; therefore the sages, great seers, deities, and great souls continuously extol you, yet they cannot attain the ultimate. How can I, who lacks the power to praise you, do so? I have no strength or capacity to sing your praises; therefore I can only prostrate myself at your feet like a humble servant and hope to please you by that act. In verses 41‑42 Arjuna mentioned three causes of insult: “pramādāt” (through negligence), “avahāsārtham” (through mockery or frivolity), and “praṇayena” (through love). He illustrates each cause with a metaphor: the father‑son relationship for negligence, the friend‑friend relationship for mockery, and the husband‑wife relationship for love. In Chapter 11 the eleven rasas (aesthetic flavors) are described. The insult of a person arises from three main reasons: (1) negligence (pramāda), (2) mockery or lack of seriousness (hāsya‑dillagi), and (3) the intimacy of closeness that makes one overlook the value of the companion. For example, a small child in a mother’s lap, out of ignorance, pulls the father’s beard, slaps his face, or kicks him; the father, seeing the child’s antics, feels pleased rather than offended. Similarly, a friend’s teasing remarks—“You speak great truth! You are a man of great promise! Now you have become proud! Today you seem like a king!”—are taken in good humor, because the friends consider themselves equals. In the husband‑wife relationship, the husband tolerates the wife’s occasional neglect or playful behavior, such as the wife sitting on a higher seat while the husband sits low, or indulging in light‑hearted banter. The eleven rasas of Chapter 11 are enumerated as follows: the description of the divine form yields “śānta‑rasa” (verses 15‑18); the universal, all‑pervading form produces “adbhuta‑rasa” (verse 20); the terrifying, time‑like aspect that devours all gives “raudra‑rasa” (verses 30‑32); the fierce, monstrous form creates “bībhatsa‑rasa” (verses 33‑25); the warrior aspect inspires “vīra‑rasa” (verse 34); the humble, prostrate posture evokes “dāsya‑rasa” (first half of verse 44); the sight of the Lord’s face by chief warriors and kings brings “karuṇa‑rasa” (verses 28‑29); the tolerance of insult in the relationships of friend‑friend, father‑son, and husband‑wife corresponds respectively to “sakhya‑rasa”, “vātsalya‑rasa”, and “mādhurya‑rasa” (second half of verse 44). The next two verses contain Arjuna’s prayer to see the four‑armed form of the Lord. adṛṣṭapūrvaṁ hṛṣito'smi dṛṣṭvā bhayena ca pravyathitaṁ mano me | tadeva me darśaya devarūpaṁ prasīda deveśa jagannivāsa || 45 ||  
Translation: “I am delighted beyond any previous experience, yet my mind is disturbed with fear upon seeing. O Lord of the universe, please reveal to me your divine form; be pleased, O Lord of the worlds.”

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

Having never before beheld that unprecedented form, I am filled with joy at seeing it; yet fear has caused my mind to become extremely agitated. O Lord of the gods, O inhabitant of the world, please be pleased with me. In the same sense, Arjuna’s words “adṛṣṭapūrvam hṛṣito’smi dṛṣṭvā bhayena ca pravyathitaṁ mano me” express that the divine, awe‑inspiring, colossal manifestation he now witnesses is something he has never imagined could exist. He feels that he lacks any qualification to perceive such a form and acknowledges that it is shown to him solely by the Lord’s grace. Consequently, he regards himself as exceedingly fortunate and rejoices, trembling with delight at the Lord’s mercy; at the same time, the fierce aspect of the divine appearance fills his mind with intense fear, anxiety, and trembling. The term “tat” (that) is used indirectly; therefore “tadeva” (that indeed) implies that Arjuna had previously seen the divine (Vishnu) form, which is not presently manifest. When Arjuna beheld the universal form, his first vision was of Brahmā seated on a lotus throne: “paśyāmi devān tava deva dehe ca.” From this it follows that the Vishnu aspect he saw within the universal form is the very one he now asks to be shown again. Thus “devarūpam” here means that, having already seen the Vishnu aspect in the Virāṭa (cosmic) form, Arjuna now requests to see only the divine (Vishnu) aspect, excluding the Virāṭa and human forms. In verse 46 he again uses “tenaiva” to deny the Virāṭa and human manifestations and to pray for the four‑armed Vishnu form. The address “prasīda deveśa jagannivāsa” combines two titles: “jagannivāsa” points to the universal form, while “deveśa” refers to the four‑armed form. By invoking both, Arjuna declares that the entire universe resides in the Lord—he has already witnessed the universal form and continues to see it. Now he asks the Lord, who is the master of the gods and the Vishnu aspect, to appear as the divine form. Special note: The Lord’s universal form is divine, imperishable, and inexhaustible. It contains infinite universes, and the creators, sustainers, and destroyers (Brahmā, Vishnu, and Śiva) of those universes are likewise infinite. From this eternal universal form arise countless worlds that continually merge into it. The verse “brahmāṇamīśaṁ kamalāsanastham” (11.15) shows that Arjuna also perceives the four‑armed Vishnu seated on the lotus. In verse 17 Arjuna says he sees the Lord bearing the crown, mace, discus, conch, and lotus—signs that the universal form remains unchanged. Later, in verse 46 the word “punar” and in verse 50 the word “bhūyaḥ” are used by Sanjaya to indicate that the same four‑armed form is again displayed within the universal manifestation. [ Verse 12 ]  
adṛṣṭapūrvam hṛṣito’smi dṛṣṭvā bhayena ca pravyathitaṁ mano me  
— “Having never before seen (such a form), I am delighted on seeing it, yet fear has greatly disturbed my mind.”

[ Verse 46 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The universal form (Vishvarupa) is so divine and supra‑mundane that no material comparison can contain it. Even when Krishna appeared to Arjuna in his human incarnation, a fragment of his two‑armed body displayed the vast Vishvarupa. The light of the sun is but a dim reflection of its radiance. Consequently, without the “divine eye” no one can behold this universal form. The “eye of knowledge” perceives the essential reality of the Supreme (Param‑Atma) that underlies the world, and the “eye of feeling” reveals the world as the Lord’s divine form, yet neither of these eyes can grant a vision of the Vishvarupa. The “eye of the skin” (carmachakshu) gives neither knowledge of the truth nor a view of the world as the Lord’s form, and it certainly does not reveal the Vishvarupa, because it is merely an instrument of material perception and can only perceive gross material activities. Lord Krishna possesses infinite, boundless divine qualities—splendor, sweetness, beauty, generosity, and other celestial attributes. The Vishvarupa of the Lord is composed of all these infinite divine qualities. Whenever the Lord shows any being his universal form, he first grants that being divine vision. According to the recipient’s capacity, merit, and inclination, the Lord then reveals the appropriate levels of his universal form. In chapters 11, verses 15 through 30, the Lord manifests the Vishvarupa in successive stages: first the divine (deva) form (verses 15‑18), then the fierce (ugra) form (verses 19‑22), and finally the extremely fierce (ati‑ugra) form (verses 23‑30). When Arjuna became frightened by the extremely fierce aspect, the Lord ceased to display further levels of his transcendental universal form; thereafter, in Arjuna’s fearful state, the Lord remained in his two‑armed form, because he chose not to reveal the higher manifestations. Nevertheless, when the Lord wishes to display a portion of his divine majesty, he reveals to Arjuna those levels that correspond to Arjuna’s suitability, authority, and emotional disposition. In doing so, the Lord also reveals his own vast universal form. In reality, all of the Lord’s forms—two‑armed, four‑armed, thousand‑armed, etc.—are equally divine and immutable. Likewise, all of the Lord’s qualified‑form (saguna‑nirakar), formless‑qualified (nirguna‑nirakar), and qualified‑manifest (saguna‑sakar) aspects are all divine and immutable. **Verse (46)**  
*aham tvām – kirīṭinam gadinam cakrahastam icchāmi tvāṁ draṣṭum ahaṁ tathaiva*  
*tenaiva rūpena caturbhujena sahasrabāho bhava viśvamūrte*

- aham tvām – “I desire to see you, O you who bear the crown (kirīṭi) and the mace (gada) and hold the discus (chakra) in hand.”  
- kirīṭinam gadinam cakrahastam – “crowned, mace‑bearing, discus‑handed.”  
- icchāmi tvāṁ draṣṭum ahaṁ tathaiva – “I wish to behold you in exactly this manner.”  
- tenaiva rūpena caturbhujena – “by that very form, the four‑armed one.”  
- sahasrabāho bhava viśvamūrte – “become the thousand‑armed, O form of the universe.”

**Parishishta (Appendix)**  
*idam astu sannikṛṣṭe samīpatara‑vartī ca itado rūpam. adas astu viprakṛṣṭe tad iti parokṣe vijānīyāt*

- idam astu sannikṛṣṭe samīpatara‑vartī ca itado rūpam – “Let this (idam) refer to the form that is near, immediate, and present.”  
- adas astu viprakṛṣṭe tad iti parokṣe vijānīyāt – “Let that (adas) refer to the form that is distant, remote, and to be known indirectly.”

**Connection (Sambandh)**  
In the Vishvarupa description, the pronouns follow this pattern: the near form is indicated by “idam,” the very near by “etad,” the remote by “adas,” and the indirect or far‑off by “tat.” Because the universal form becomes progressively nearer in verses 18‑19, the term “idam” appears when the Vishvarupa is almost touching Arjuna, as with the presence of deities like Bhishma and Drona within the form. By verse 33, the term “etad” is used because the divine vision granted to Arjuna shows the Vishvarupa at a greater distance, with gods appearing far away. In verses 21, 26, and 28, “adas” is employed when the earlier, more immediate four‑armed Vishnu aspect is no longer directly visible, rendering it indirect. Consequently, Arjuna uses “tat” for the most remote, indirect perception of the universal form.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ] – Commentary

The prayer “kirīṭinam gadinam cakrahastam icchāmi tvām” (I desire you crowned, bearing a mace and a discus) uses the particle “eva” to forbid the “virāṭarūpa” (the universal form). The petitioner therefore asks to see the Lord only in a specific aspect. In “dṛṣṭum ahaṁ tathāiva” the speaker says that the Lord, with a divine crown on his head and the mace and discus in his hands, is the very form he wishes to behold. The word “tathāiva” indicates that by expressing the desire “dṛṣṭum icchāmi te rūpam” (see you, I wish, as in 11.3) Arjuna has already caused the appearance of the virāṭarūpa. Consequently he abandons any further wish and declares: “I wish to see you exactly as the gentle four‑armed form I have already observed in your virāṭarūpa – icchāmi tvām dṛṣṭum ahaṁ tathāiva.”

In the preceding verse the particles “tadeva”, “tathāiva” and “tenaiva” all convey Arjuna’s terror at the universal form. By repeating the particle “eva” three times he implores the Lord to reveal only the Vishnu aspect, not the all‑encompassing form. Hence he asks the Lord to appear as the four‑armed deity. The address “sahasrabāho” (thousand‑armed) informs the listener that the Lord, who is described as having a thousand arms, should now manifest as the four‑armed universal form. In verses 15 and 17 the virāṭarūpa is already described as four‑armed; the epithet “viśvamūrte” (universal form) indicates that the previously shown Vishnu aspect is being set aside, and the Lord is requested to be one‑form. **Appendix (parishiṣṭa bhāva)** – Although the original verse mentions the Lord holding a mace and a discus, the term “caturbhujena” (by four arms) implies that the four arms also bear a conch (śaṅkha) and a lotus (padma) together with the mace and discus. **Connection (sambandh)** – In verse 31 Arjuna asks who the fierce form is; the Lord replies that He is Kāla (Time), the destroyer of all. Hearing this and witnessing the terrifying aspect, Arjuna feels that the Lord is in great anger, and therefore he repeatedly prays for the Lord’s pleasure. To dispel this anxiety the Lord says:

*Śrī Bhagavān uvāca*  
“Maya prasannena tavarjune idaṁ rūpaṁ paraṁ darśitam ātmayogāt;  
tejomayam viśvam anantam ādyaṁ yan me tvad anyena na dṛṣṭapūrvam.” (Verse 47)

**Translation of the verse** – “The Supreme Lord said: By my gracious will I have shown you this supreme, radiant form, the infinite source of the universe, which none other than I have ever displayed before.”

**Explanation of the verse** –  
- “Maya” = by me. - “prasannena” = with pleasure, by my benevolent disposition. - “tavarjune” = to you, Arjuna. - “idaṁ rūpaṁ” = this form. - “paraṁ” = supreme. - “darśitam” = shown. - “ātmayogāt” = by my own power (self‑effort). - “tejomayam” = full of brilliance. - “viśvam” = the universe. - “anantam” = infinite. - “ādyaṁ” = the original source. - “yan” = which. - “me” = of me. - “tvad anyena” = by any other. - “na dṛṣṭapūrvam” = has never been seen before. Thus the Lord assures Arjuna that the dazzling, all‑encompassing form he is now witnessing is a unique, divine manifestation that no other being has ever shown.

[ Verse 47 ]
* Sadhaka - Sanjivani *

He asked, what is the purpose of you knowing so much? To see, to show such a form before Kausalya and others, to hear, to understand—what the world presents in hearing and comprehension was not even complete, and they could not have seen that form. I pervade the world as a part of myself; consequently they lacked the capacity to perceive such a form. The second meaning is: why do you need to know my divine manifestations and yogic power? All manifestations depend on my yogic power, and I, supported by that power, sit before you. I expressed this only by special grace. Because of this, your desire to behold the universal form arose, and I gave you divine eyes and showed you the universal form. This is merely my pure delight. The implication is that, apart from my grace, there is no other motive for displaying this universal form; your desire to see is merely a pretext. ‘From self‑yoga’ – I displayed this cosmic form without any assistance, solely by my own power. ‘Supreme’ – this cosmic form of mine is exceedingly supreme. ‘Radiant’ – my universal form is intensely luminous. Hence, even after receiving divine sight you called this form “unseeable” (verse 17). ‘Universal’ – you addressed this form as Vishvarupa, Vishwamurti, etc. My form is all‑pervading. ‘Infinite and beginningless’ – the realm and time of my universal form are neither beginning nor end. It is the source of all and itself is without origin. ‘No one else has seen it before’ – How could the Lord say that no one besides you has seen my universal form? In the Ram avatar Mother Kausalya saw it; in the Krishna avatar Mother Yashoda saw it; and in the Kaurava assembly Bhishma, Drona, Sanjaya, Vidura, and the sages witnessed the Lord’s cosmic form. The Lord, using the term “evam rūpaḥ” (11.48), indicates that such a terrifying universal form, whose faces contain great warriors and commanders, had not been seen previously. The Lord did not say that no one sees the universal form now; He said that previously no one had seen it. Indeed, both Arjuna and Sanjaya are witnessing the Lord’s universal form. If Sanjaya had not seen it, he could not have said at the end of the Gita that repeatedly recalling the Lord’s wondrous cosmic form fills me with great amazement and repeated joy (chapter 18, verse 78). **Special point**

The Lord’s statement, “I have shown you this universal form solely by my pleasure and grace,” reveals a unique sentiment: the seeker perceives only a fraction of the Lord’s grace, whereas the Lord’s actual grace is many times greater. The seeker lacks the capacity to fully acknowledge the Lord’s boundless grace. Often the seeker equates the Lord’s grace with favorable objects, persons, or circumstances—finding good company, smooth practice, proper conduct, a mind that feels aligned with the Lord. This confines grace within limits, preventing experience of its infinitude. Accepting only that limited grace is a consumption of grace. The seeker should neither confine grace nor treat it as a consumable experience. The pleasure that arises when practice proceeds smoothly, and being content in that pleasure, is also a form of consumption that creates bondage—“Association with happiness binds, association with knowledge liberates” (Gita 14.6). Experiencing happiness or knowledge of happiness is not sinful; rather, attaching to it, becoming delighted, is sinful. Such attachment to sattvic pleasure hinders transcendence of qualities. Therefore the seeker must carefully remain unattached to this pleasure. A seeker who remains attached…

The Lord's eternal, immutable, and divine universal form can be seen only by His grace. The idea is that none of these means - the study of the Vedas, the performance of sacrifices, charity, or the practice of austerities - has the power to reveal the universal form. The vision of the universal form is possible only by the Lord's grace. Commentary - 'Kurupravira' - The address 'Kurupravira' is used here to imply that among all the Kurus, you, Arjuna, have the desire to learn from Me, to see My form, and to know Me. This is your excellence among the Kurus. The idea is that the desire to see and know the Lord is the true excellence of a human being. In the Gita, the three - yajna (sacrifice), dana (charity), and tapas (austerity) - are often mentioned. In the 28th verse of the 8th chapter and in the 57th verse of this chapter, the four - Veda, yajna, dana, and tapas - are mentioned, and here, the five - Veda, yajna, dana, tapas, and kriya - are mentioned. In the 28th verse of the 8th chapter, the genitive plural and in this verse, the instrumental plural are used, whereas usually, the nominative singular is used. 'Na vedayajnadhyanair na danaih na cha kriyabhir na tapobhir ugrai' - The study of the Vedas, the performance of sacrifices, the study of scriptures, the practice of charity, the practice of severe austerities, and the performance of auspicious deeds like pilgrimages and vows - none of these can be the cause of the vision of the universal form. The reason is that all these actions have a beginning and an end. Therefore, the fruit obtained from them is also limited. The idea is that each of these means - Veda, yajna, dana, etc. - is limited. Therefore, even if they are performed repeatedly or all of them are performed, they cannot reveal the Lord's infinite, boundless, and immutable universal form. The vision of the universal form is possible only by the Lord's grace, because the Lord is eternal, and His grace is also eternal. If the phrase 'Vedayajnadhyanaih' is interpreted as 'the study of the Vedas and the performance of sacrifices', then the study of scriptures is included in the study of the Vedas, because all scriptures follow the Vedas. However, to clarify, the study of scriptures is mentioned separately here.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 11 ]
[ Verse 49 ]
The vision of the Lord's universal form is not the result of any action. It is not attainable through any means. His grace is also unconditional. Many people say that the universal form can be seen through the Vedas, sacrifices, and other means, but this is not true. The Lord has shown Arjuna His universal form, and Arjuna has seen the entire universe in the Lord's body. The Lord has said that His universal form can be seen only through devotion, and that it is not attainable through any other means. The Lord's universal form is a unique and wondrous sight, and it is not possible to see it through ordinary eyes. The Lord has given Arjuna divine eyes to see His universal form, and Arjuna has seen the entire universe in the Lord's body. The Lord has said that His universal form is not attainable through any means, but only through His own grace. Sanjaya has also said that he has seen the Lord's universal form through the grace of Vyasa, and that it is not attainable through any other means. The Lord's universal form is a sight that is beyond human comprehension, and it is not possible to see it through ordinary means. Connection - To remove Arjuna's fear, the Lord commands him to see His gentle form in the next verse. mā te vyathā mā ca vimūḍhabhāvo dṛṣṭvā rūpaṁ ghoramīdṛṅ mam edam |
vyapetabhīḥ prītamanāḥ punas tvam tad eva me rūpam idaṁ prapaśya || 49 ||
Translation:
"Do not be disturbed, and do not be bewildered by seeing this terrible form of Mine. With a peaceful mind, and without fear, see again this same form of Mine."

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 11 ]
The Lord says, "You were delighted to see my gracious form, which is proper, but this lamentation of yours is not proper." 
The reason for your lamentation is the egoistic attachment to your body, which is subject to birth and death. This attachment is the root of ignorance and demonic tendencies. However, those who move towards the Lord have no attachment to their bodies and are filled with devotion to the Lord. They are fearless and have a divine nature. The Lord is saying, "I am showing you this form out of my grace, so you should not be deluded by it." The Lord is pleased and is showing this form to Arjuna out of his own pleasure. Arjuna's repeated request to the Lord to be pleased is a sign of his delusion, which he should give up. Arjuna had said earlier that his illusion had been dispelled, but in reality, it had not. He should give up this illusion and see the Lord's divine form with a fearless and pleased mind. The conversation between the Lord and Arjuna should be filled with pleasure and love, without any fear or illusion. The Lord says, "Have you seen any imperfection in me? Have I changed in any way?" Arjuna should not see any imperfection in the Lord's universal form. The fear that Arjuna is experiencing is due to his egoistic attachment to his body, which is a sign of his ignorance. He should give up this attachment. The Lord says, "Be free from fear and be pleased in mind. See my divine form again, which I had shown you earlier." The Lord is asking Arjuna to see his divine form, which includes the four-armed form that he had shown him earlier. The Lord is saying, "See my divine form, which is the same as the form of Vishnu, along with Brahma, Shiva, and other gods." The Lord is using the word "idam" to refer to the form that he is about to show Arjuna. How long did Sanjaya and Arjuna have divine vision? Sanjaya was given divine vision by Vedavyasa at the beginning of the war, which allowed him to narrate the events of the war to Dhritarashtra. Arjuna considers the Lord to be unchanged in all circumstances, which is why he uses the term "Achyuta" to address the Lord in the beginning, middle, and end of the Gita (in verses 21 of Chapter 1, 42 of Chapter 11, and 73 of Chapter 18). As stated in the Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, verses 9-10: "This Sanjaya, O King, will narrate to you the account of this war. With divine vision, he will be all-knowing and will tell you about the war."

[ Verse 49 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
However, when Sanjaya was overcome with grief at the death of Duryodhana, his divine vision (divya-drishti) was lost. This happened because Arjuna's divine vision had also been lost when he was frightened by the terrifying form of the Lord. When Arjuna had requested the Lord to show him His universal form, the Lord had given Arjuna divine vision, saying, "I grant you divine eyes; behold My divine power" (11.8). Arjuna then saw the Lord's divine, terrible, and other forms. When the extremely terrifying form appeared before him, Arjuna became afraid and, while praising and praying to the Lord, said, "My mind is distressed with fear; please show me your four-armed form." 
Another reason for the loss of Arjuna's divine vision can be that initially, Arjuna had a strong desire to see the Lord's universal form - "I wish to see your form" (11.3). Therefore, the Lord gave Arjuna divine vision. However, here Arjuna no longer had the desire to see the universal form and, being frightened, he desired to see the four-armed form. Thus, his divine vision was lost due to the lack of need for it. If Sanjaya and Arjuna had not been distressed by grief and fear, their divine vision would have remained for a long time, and they would have seen much more. But due to being overcome with grief and fear, their divine vision was lost. Similarly, when a person becomes attached to the world due to delusion (moha), the discriminative vision (viveka-drishhti) given by the Lord does not function. For example, if a person has excessive attachment to money, they may start stealing, and as their attachment increases, they may even commit robbery and, ultimately, murder for the sake of money. In this way, as attachment increases, one's discriminative vision ceases to function. If a person does not get entangled in attachment and instead values their discriminative vision, they can attain liberation and become a savior of the world. When Arjuna, frightened, asked the Lord to show him His four-armed form, the Lord showed him that form and then appeared in His two-armed form. This proves that Arjuna's divine vision remained until this point (the 49th verse). In the 51st verse, Arjuna himself says, "I have become composed and regained my natural state after seeing your gentle human form." 
A doubt arises here: Arjuna had been distressed earlier as well - "The worlds are distressed, and so am I" (11.23), "My heart is distressed within me" (11.24). Therefore, his divine vision should have been lost at that point. The solution to this is that Arjuna was not as frightened then as he is now. Here, Arjuna is frightened and repeatedly bows to the Lord, requesting Him to show His four-armed form. Appendix - Arjuna, frightened, told the Lord, "I beg your pardon" (11.42). The Lord says here that whether He appears in a peaceful or terrifying form, He is still Arjuna's friend. Arjuna's fear is due to his own foolishness and lack of firmness in their friendship. Whatever is visible is all the Lord's play (lila). What is there to be afraid of in this? In friendship, who is great and who is small? The Lord has manifested Himself in the form of the world; therefore, this world is called the Lord's original incarnation - "The first incarnation is the Supreme Person" (Srimad Bhagavatam 2.6.41). Just as the Lord has taken incarnations in the forms of Rama and Krishna, He has also taken incarnation in the form of the world. This is called an incarnation because, in it, the Lord appears in a visible form. At the time of incarnation, the Lord appears in a worldly form, but He remains transcendental (alaukika). However, due to attachment and aversion, the ignorant see the Lord as worldly (Gita 4.6, 7.24-25, and 9.11). Whether the Lord appears in a peaceful or terrifying form is His will. A beautiful scene, fragrant flowers, and a pleasant smell are all the Lord's form, and flesh, bones, filth, and foul smell are also the Lord's form. As stated in the Mahabharata, "O sinless king! I have become grief-stricken due to the death of your son and the loss of the divine vision given to me by Rishi Vyasa" (Mahabharata, Sauptika 9.62).

[ Chapter 11 ]
[Verse 50]
The Lord is the only reality; He has taken various forms like Rama, Krishna, etc., and also forms like Matsya, Kurma, Varaha, etc. Whatever form He takes, He is the Lord. The form is the Lord's, and the action is His divine play. If someone appears to be committing a sin or injustice, it should be understood that the Lord is enacting His divine play in the form of the Kali Yuga. He performs actions according to the form He assumes. Having assumed the form of an idol (Archavatara), He remains still like an idol, for it is not befitting for an idol to perform actions; otherwise, it would not be an idol. The Lord, having assumed the form of a boar (Varaha), acts like a boar, and having assumed the form of a human, He acts like a human. Whatever form He assumes and whatever actions He performs, they do not cause any impurity in the hearts of His devotees, for in their vision, there is nothing except the Lord. The world that we see is not the Lord's divine universal form (Virat Rupa), because the Virat Rupa is divine and imperishable, whereas the world we see is material and perishable. Just as we see the material Vrindavana, but not the divine Vrindavana within it, similarly, we see the material world, but not the divine world (Virat Rupa) within it. The reason for this is the desire for sensual enjoyment. Due to the desire for enjoyment, there is a sense of dullness, materiality, and impurity. If there were no attraction to the world due to the desire for enjoyment, everything would be seen as the divine Virat Rupa. When one attains spiritual knowledge, the world appears as the divine Virat Rupa to the wise, but to the loving devotee, it appears as the embodiment of sweetness (Madhurya Rupa). When one sees the world as Madhurya Rupa, there is a natural affection for all living beings, just as there is a natural affection for one's own body. However, Arjuna saw the Lord's Virat Rupa as the embodiment of majesty (Aishwarya Rupa), because that is what he desired to see - "I wish to see Your majestic form, O Supreme Person" (11.3). There is a special affection in sweetness and a special influence in majesty. The divine Virat Rupa, though one, appears in various forms according to the devotee's attitude, and though it appears in various forms, it remains one. This is the Lord's unique and divine characteristic. Connection - In the previous verse, the Lord had instructed Arjuna to behold His divine form, and now the Lord shows His Vishnu form to Arjuna - this is described by Sanjaya in the next verse. Sanjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vasudeva (Krishna) again showed him His own form and consoled the frightened Arjuna, assuming His gentle, two-armed human form. (50)

Vasudeva = Vasudeva, the Lord Krishna
Arjunam = to Arjuna
Iti = thus
Uktva = having spoken
Svam = His own
Rupam = form
Darshayamasa = showed
Bhuyah = again
Ashvasayamasa = consoled
Bhitam = frightened
Enam = this Arjuna
Cha = and
Punah = again
Saumya-vapuh = assuming His gentle, two-armed human form
Mahatma = the great soul, Lord Krishna
Bhutva = having become

Commentary - Having spoken thus to Arjuna, the Lord Krishna showed him His own form again and consoled the frightened Arjuna, assuming His gentle, two-armed human form. As it is said: "Just as an actor, having donned various costumes, performs various roles, but remains the same person, similarly, the Lord, having assumed various forms, performs various actions, but remains the same." (Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 72)

[ Verse 51 ]
* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
Being pleased, you should see this form of mine (49th verse). The Lord's statement has been mentioned here with the words 'ityarjunam vasudevas tathoktva'. The word 'tatha' means that just as the Lord showed his universal form out of compassion, he also showed his four-armed form out of compassion. It is not that Arjuna had any qualification or means to see this four-armed form, but it was only the Lord's compassion. The word 'bhuyah' means that the Lord showed Arjuna the same divine form (four-armed form) that he had seen earlier within the universal form (15th and 17th verses) and for which Arjuna had prayed (45th-46th verses). The Lord, having become compassionate, consoled the frightened Arjuna and showed him his gentle human form again. The Lord, who is great, appeared in his two-armed form (human form) and reassured Arjuna, who was frightened by seeing the universal form. Was the Lord two-armed or four-armed? The answer is that the Lord always remained in his two-armed form, but at appropriate times, he would take on his four-armed form. In the 10th and 11th chapters, the Lord described his own greatness, power, and influence while narrating his glories, and he also showed his extraordinary universal form. If a person comes to know or understands the Lord's great influence, they will not be attracted to the world. They will be forever free from worldly bondage. The Lord showed immense compassion to Arjuna by first showing him the universal form, then the divine form (four-armed form), and finally taking on his human form (two-armed form). Along with this, the Lord has also shown extraordinary compassion to us by allowing us to contemplate his universal form and glories whenever our minds wander. In this terrible time, the opportunity we have to contemplate the Lord's glories and universal form is not due to our efforts or qualifications, but solely due to the Lord's compassion. We should be pleased to see the Lord's compassion. Even in the past, only a few people, like Sanjaya, had the opportunity to hear and contemplate the Lord's glories and universal form. We have been given this opportunity today, and we should not let it go to waste. Connection - When the Lord, having taken on his human form, consoled Arjuna, Arjuna said:

Srimad Bhagavad Gita

[ Chapter 11 ]
I have now become composed, my mind is stable - 'Idanimsam samvrittah'. When I saw the extraordinary and vast universal form of the Lord, I came to my senses and thought, where am I and where is the Lord's wondrous and vast universal form? I have no qualification or authority to see this form. It is only due to the Lord's grace that I have been able to see it. The fear that arose in me when I saw the universal form has now disappeared, all my distress has gone, and I have attained my true state - Prakrtim gatah. The word 'sacetah' means that when Arjuna's fear had subsided, he was able to see the Lord's gentle, two-armed form, which he referred to as the human form. Lord Sri Krsna was two-armed. The Brahmavaivarta Purana states: 
"Tvaeva bhagavanadyo nirgunah prakrteh parah. Ardhangah dvibhujah krsno 'py ardhangena caturbhujah" (Prakrti 12.15)
You are the Supreme Lord, beyond the gunas and prakrti, and you have appeared in two forms: as two-armed Krsna and as four-armed Visnu. "Dvibhujas radhikanatho laksmikanthas caturbhujah. Goloke dvibhujas tisthau gopair gopibhir avrtah" (Prakrti 35.14-15)
[Verse 52]
The two-armed Krsna is the lord of Radha, and the four-armed Visnu is the lord of Laksmi. Krsna resides in Goloka, surrounded by the gopas and gopis, while Visnu resides in Vaikuntha with Laksmi. Both Krsna and Visnu are the same, identical in all respects. The meaning is that the two-armed form (Krsna), the four-armed form (Visnu), and the thousand-armed form (the universal form) are all the same, complete Lord. Connection - Approving Arjuna's gratitude, the Lord says: 
Sri Bhagavan uvaca 
Sudur darsam idam rupam drstavan asi yan mama. Deva apy asya rupasya nityam darsanakanksinah (11.52)
The Lord said: You have seen my form, which is very difficult to see. Even the gods are always eager to see this form. Explanation - The word 'sudur darsam' refers to the four-armed form, not the universal form or the two-armed form. The reason is that the Lord says that this four-armed form of mine is very difficult to see, and even the gods are always eager to see it. The universal form is not difficult to see, and the two-armed form is easily accessible to humans. Therefore, the word 'sudur darsam' refers to the four-armed form of Lord Visnu, which can only be seen through unalloyed devotion. Now, a question arises: if the Lord says that even the gods are eager to see this form, then how can it be seen? The answer is that the Lord's four-armed form can be seen through devotion, and not through other means like tapas, yajna, or dana.

[ Verse 53 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
When there is a constant longing to have a vision of the Lord, that is exclusive devotion. The solution to this is that the constant longing of the gods is not exclusive devotion. If they have a longing, why do they not have a vision? They do not have a vision because they have pride in their divinity and position. Due to this pride, and the power of their position, they cannot have a vision of the Lord. Therefore, Arjuna said in the fourteenth verse of the tenth chapter that "Neither the gods nor the demons know my manifestation." In this way, Arjuna has put the gods and demons in the same category for not knowing the Lord. This means that just as the gods have prosperity, the demons have various kinds of Maya, Siddhis, etc., but they cannot know the Lord through their power. Similarly, even if the gods have a longing for a vision, they cannot have a vision due to their divine power, because divinity is not the cause of the Lord's vision. The meaning is that the Lord cannot be seen through divine power, nor through sacrifices, penance, charity, and other virtuous actions (this chapter, verse 47). He can only be seen through exclusive devotion (verse 54). Both gods and humans can see the Lord through exclusive devotion. The meaning of having a constant longing is that one should always have a longing for the Supreme Being and no other longing. Even a very wicked person can become a devotee of the Lord and attain Him if he has such a longing. However, the gods do not have such an exclusive longing, because they have become gods primarily to enjoy worldly pleasures, and their main objective is to enjoy these pleasures. Then what kind of longing do they have? The kind of longing that most devout people have, that "we should have a vision of the Lord, we should attain liberation," such a desire is present in them, but their inclination towards worldly pleasures and accumulation remains the same. The meaning is that just as people wish to attain liberation incidentally, like finding a gem while walking on the path, in the same way, the gods wish to have a vision of the Lord incidentally. The statement "even the gods" means that the gods cannot have a vision of the Lord through the power of their virtuous actions, which have given them a high position and divine pleasures. The meaning is that virtuous actions have no value in having a vision of the Lord. Although the body of the gods is divine, the body of the Lord is even more extraordinary. The body of the gods is physical and full of light, while the body of the Lord is made of consciousness. The Lord's body is eternal, full of bliss, and extremely divine. Therefore, even the gods are eager to see the Lord. Just as ordinary people have a desire to see new places, the gods have a desire to see the Lord, but it is not out of love. The meaning is that just as devotees want to see the Lord out of love, the gods do not want to see Him out of love. Therefore, the Lord is under the control of loving devotees, but not under the control of the gods. Connection - The Lord confirms the statement made in the previous verse in the next verse. I am not capable of being seen through the Vedas, nor through penance, nor through charity, nor through sacrifice. You have seen me as I am, which is not possible for others (Verse 53). 1. If we attain liberation while walking on the path, it is a great gain. 2. Your body is full of consciousness and bliss. One who knows this is worthy (Ramayana, Ayodhya 127.3). karpanya-dosha-upahata-svabhavah: a heart afflicted by cowardice

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

I = 798

Just as you have seen Me, I am not visible by the Vedas, nor by austerities, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice; even the form with four arms cannot be seen by those means. [ Chapter 11 ]

**Explanation** – “You have seen Me” means that by a mere resolve you have instantly created countless universes in the form of My four‑armed manifestation. It is only by My grace that My vision can be attained; no qualification or merit can bring it about. “The statement ‘I am not visible by the Vedas, nor by austerities, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice’ is a principle that whatever is bought with a price is worth less than that price. For example, a shopkeeper sells a watch for one hundred rupees; he has bought that watch for a lower price, and therefore he can sell it for one hundred rupees. In the same way, studying many Vedas, performing great penance, giving huge donations, or conducting massive sacrifices does not guarantee the appearance of the Lord. No matter how great the action or how eminent the qualification, the Lord cannot be purchased. Even the combined effort of all such deeds does not constitute the price of attaining the Divine; they cannot confer any right over the Lord. Arjuna, in the thirty‑fourth verse of this chapter, clearly states that in the three worlds there is none equal to You; therefore how could anyone be superior to You? The implication is that without being superior to You, no one can claim any authority over You. In worldly matters a more qualified person may dominate a less qualified one, a more intelligent person may outshine a less intelligent one, a richer person may display his abundance over the poor; but the Lord cannot be bought with any force, intelligence, qualification, person, or object. How could the Lord, who pervades an entire universe, be purchased by any fragment of that universe—by any thing or person? The implication is that the attainment of the Lord is possible only through the Lord’s grace. Such grace is received when a human completely surrenders his capacity, time, understanding, and material resources to the Lord, experiences utter helplessness and unworthiness, and harbors no pride in his own strength or qualifications. When one, utterly powerless, dedicates himself wholly to the Lord and calls upon Him with exclusive devotion, the Lord manifests instantly. As long as the human heart clings to material objects, abilities, strength, or intellect, the Lord, however near, appears distant. The rarity mentioned in this verse applies solely to the four‑armed form, not to the universal form. If it were applied to the universal form, it would repeat the statement already made in the forty‑eighth verse concerning the rarity of the universal form. In the following verse the Lord declares that He can be seen only through exclusive devotion. Such exclusive devotion is impossible in the universal form, because even a heroic warrior like Arjuna, after receiving divine sight, was terrified upon beholding the universal form; in that overwhelming manifestation, exclusive devotion, exclusive love, or attraction cannot arise. **Relation** – When no means, qualification, or material can obtain you, how can you be obtained? The Lord answers this in the next verse. [ Verse 54 ]

bhaktyā tv ananyayā śakyaḥ ahaṁ evam vidhiro arjuna — by exclusive devotion alone I am able, O Arjuna,

jñātuṁ draṣṭuṁ ca tattvena praveṣṭuṁ ca parantapa — to be known, to be seen, and to enter into the truth, O supreme‑spirit.

[ Verse 54 ]
Oh Parantap Arjuna, I, who am of this kind, 
can be known, seen, and entered into through 
unwavering devotion (ananyaa bhakti) alone. The word "tu" (but) is used here to indicate a 
different means from the ones mentioned earlier. The Lord says, "Oh Arjuna, the four-armed form 
you have seen, which holds the conch, disc, mace, 
and lotus, cannot be seen through sacrifices, 
charity, or austerity, but only through 
unwavering devotion."

Unwavering devotion means having only the Lord 
as one's refuge, support, hope, and faith. One 
should not have even the slightest reliance on 
one's own abilities, strength, or intellect. This unwavering devotion arises spontaneously 
and is not a result of the mind, intellect, or 
senses. The essence is that one should have an intense 
longing for the Lord, and without His vision, 
one should not have a moment's peace. This 
inner restlessness is the primary cause of 
attaining the Lord. In this state of 
restlessness, the countless sins of countless 
births are reduced to ashes. The Lord has said, "I am easily attainable by 
that devotee who constantly thinks of Me with 
an unwavering mind" (Gita 8.14), and "I take care 
of the welfare of those devotees who worship Me 
with unwavering devotion" (Gita 9.22). Another meaning of unwavering devotion is that 
one should not have even the slightest reliance 
on one's own efforts or abilities for 
self-realization. Then, what is the purpose of 
performing spiritual practices? It is only to 
remove one's ego, the notion that "I can attain 
self-realization through my own efforts."

The Lord's attainment is not possible through 
spiritual practices, but rather through the 
dissolution of the ego. When the ego is 
dissolved, the Lord's pure grace descends, and 
there is no obstacle to receiving that grace, 
leading to the attainment of the Lord. "Through unwavering devotion alone can I be 
known, seen, and entered into." One can also 
attain the Lord through knowledge (Gita 18.55), 
but the Lord is not bound to grant a vision. The phrase "to know" means that one comes to know 
the Lord as He truly is. This does not mean that 
the Lord comes within the limitations of one's 
intellect, but rather that one's capacity to 
know is perfected by the Lord. This means that 
one comes to know the Lord as "Vasudeva, the 
all-pervading" (Gita 7.19) and "the eternal, 
unchanging reality" (Gita 9.19). The phrase "to see" means that one can see the 
Lord in any form they desire, whether it be as 
Vishnu, Rama, Krishna, or any other form. The phrase "to enter into" means that one 
experiences oneness with the Lord, or enters 
into the Lord's eternal play. The devotee's 
desire and the Lord's will are the primary 
factors in entering into the Lord's eternal 
play. As stated in the Dohavali (277) by Tulsidas, 
"One who has only one support, one strength, one 
hope, and one faith, has the Lord as their 
closest companion."

And as stated in the Ramayana (3.10.4), "The 
word of the compassionate Lord is dear to 
those who have no other recourse."

Special Note
[ Chapter 11 ]
[Verse 55]
When a devotee's all desires are fulfilled, then there is nothing left to do, know, or attain. It is a unique quality of the Lord that He fulfills the desire of the devotee to participate in His divine play. The Lord not only fulfills the spiritual desires of the devotee but also fulfills their worldly desires. For example, Dhruva received a kingdom of 36,000 years before having the Lord's darshan, and Vibhishan received a kingdom for a kalpa. The point is that the Lord fulfills the devotee's desires and then, according to His will, grants them true fulfillment, after which the devotee has nothing left to attain. The Lord immediately appears before the devotee. The intense longing of the devotee has such power that it creates a longing in the Lord to meet the devotee. No one can obstruct this longing of the Lord. When the Lord's grace flows towards the devotee, it removes all obstacles, disregarding the devotee's worthiness or unworthiness, and even subjugates the Lord Himself. Appendix - Where the Lord has described the ultimate stage of knowledge, He has mentioned only two things: knowing and entering - "tato mam tattvato jnatva visate tadanantaram" (Gita 18.55). However, here, He mentions three things: knowing, seeing, and entering through devotion. Devotion can also lead to the Lord's darshan, which is a special quality of devotion. Even if one attains the ultimate stage of knowledge, they may not have the Lord's darshan. Therefore, devotion has a special glory, and it leads to the attainment of the ultimate. Connection - Now the Lord describes the means of exclusive devotion. The verse is: 
"mat-karma-krit mat-paramo mad-bhaktah sangavarjitah, 
nirvairah sarvabhuteshu yah sa mam eti Pandava" (55)
Pandava, he who performs actions only for Me, who has Me as his supreme goal, who is My devotee, who is free from attachment, and who is without enmity towards all beings - he attains Me. Breakdown: 
mat-karma-krit: one who performs actions only for Me
mat-paramah: one who has Me as his supreme goal
mad-bhaktah: My devotee
sangavarjitah: free from attachment
nirvairah: without enmity
sarvabhuteshu: towards all beings

Explanation - This verse mentions five things, also known as the "sadhana-panchak" (five means of attainment). These five things are divided into two categories: (1) intimacy with the Lord and (2) detachment from the world. The first category includes "mat-karma-krit", "mat-paramah", and "mad-bhaktah", while the second category includes "sangavarjitah" and "nirvairah sarvabhuteshu". "Mat-karma-krit" refers to one who performs actions such as japa, kirtan, meditation, satsang, and self-study, and also worldly actions according to their varna, ashrama, place, time, and circumstances, solely for the Lord's pleasure. In essence, all actions, whether spiritual or worldly, have only one intention: to be performed for the Lord alone. This means that the devotee performs all actions, whether physical, mental, or intellectual, solely for the Lord. The reason is that everything the devotee has, including their body, mind, intellect, senses, abilities, and understanding, belongs to the Lord.

[ Verse 55 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

The power described is both given by and inherent in the Lord; He Himself regards it as His own will and grace. Such a devotee belongs wholly to the Lord. He is described as “nirvairah sarvabhuteshu” – free from enmity toward all beings – because he acts solely in accordance with the Lord’s command, using only the divine power that has been bestowed upon him. This is what is meant by “mat‑karmakrit”. **mat‑paramaḥ** – one who regards the Lord as the supreme, the ultimate goal, the sole refuge; such a devotee is “mat‑parama”. **mad‑bhaktaḥ** – one who is exclusively the Lord’s devotee, having formed an unshakable bond with Him: “I am only the Lord’s, and the Lord is only mine; I belong to no other, and no other belongs to me.” This exclusive relationship awakens intense love, because what is one’s own naturally feels dear. In the awakening of love, belongingness is the central element. Such a devotee constantly perceives the Lord as fully present in every country, in every age, in all objects and beings, and also within himself. From this viewpoint, the Lord’s presence in all lands, all times, all entities, and in the devotee himself is affirmed – this is the essence of “mad‑bhakta”. **saṅgavarjitaḥ nirvairah sarvabhuteshu yaḥ** – By performing actions only for the Lord, remaining solely devoted to the Lord, and becoming only the Lord’s devotee, one becomes “saṅgavarjita” (free from worldly attachment). Attachment, affection, and desire are the ties that bind a person to the world. When exclusive love for the Lord arises, these ties disappear entirely. When the devotee realizes “I am a fragment of the Lord” (the ultimate reality), his love for the Lord awakens. This awakened love eliminates all passion (rāga). With the complete absence of passion and the pervasive presence of divine consciousness, no amount of physical abuse, beating, or harm can generate even a trace of hostility in his heart toward the aggressor. He remains “saṅgavarjita” and “nirvairah sarvabhuteshu”. The phrase “saṅgavarjita” and “nirvairah” together signify a total severance of all worldly relationships, which automatically leads to the self‑realization of the Supreme Self. **sa‑mām eti** – The devotee attains the Lord Himself. In “sa‑mām eti”, knowledge, vision, and attainment of the ultimate truth are all realized, as explained in the preceding (34th) verse. The purpose for which human birth occurs is thereby completely fulfilled. **Special note**  
The Lord concluded Chapter 9 with the verse:

*manmana bhava madbhakto madyaji mam namaskuru | mamevaishyasi yuktva ivam atmanam matparayanah |* (9.34)

“Become steadfast in mind, be my devotee, perform sacrifice for Me, and bow to Me; you will obtain Me alone, having united your self with Me, being wholly devoted to Me.”

Even after uttering these words, the Lord wondered how to explain the entirety of His mystery. To elucidate this, He gave the Tenth and Eleventh chapters. The living being, being subject to birth, death, and constant change, relies on the body‑world for support, which creates a sense of separation from the immutable, eternal Lord. The purpose of the Tenth and Eleventh chapters is to eradicate this sense of separation and bring the soul before the Lord. Human beings possess two faculties: the power of thought and the power of perception. The faculty of thought must be directed toward the Lord’s divine manifestations. In other words, whenever a quality, greatness, uniqueness, or supernatural aspect is observed in any object or person, that attribute should be recognized as belonging to the Lord, and contemplation should be fixed on Him. This is the teaching of the Tenth chapter. The faculty of perception should likewise be fixed on the Lord. Just as the Lord’s divine, imperishable, universal form appears in countless shapes and appearances, the seeker’s eye should see the Lord in all such manifestations.
