* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 11 ]

[Verse 11]
The world is described as a manifestation of the same universal form; similarly, this material existence is portrayed as a manifestation of the Supreme’s cosmic form. At the beginning of Chapter 11 Arjuna says, “I wish to behold Your form,” and the Lord reveals His universal form and grants Arjuna divine eyes to perceive it. The Supreme is a single entity that possesses innumerable names, shapes, and appearances; in the primordial aspect, the Supreme (Parmatma) is complete in Himself. From this perspective, all beings are seen as embodiments of the Supreme. Hence the Lord designates this chapter as the eleventh. The implication is that the seeker should devote all contemplation and vision exclusively to the Lord; no other object should consume the mind’s power. When the seeker thinks, the thought must be of the Supreme; when he looks, he must see only the Supreme. Arjuna, for both modes of vision, offered prayer twice. In verse 17 of Chapter 10 Arjuna asks, “O Lord, in what moods should I contemplate You?” The Lord responds by directing the power of contemplation toward His divine manifestations, so that the seeker perceives only the Supreme’s nature. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – The devotion that enables one to see the Lord in His four‑armed form is explained as follows: the human must sever all ties with worldly existence and become wholly devoted to Me. “Mat‑karmakṛt” – devotion through the gross body; “Mat‑paramaḥ” – devotion through the subtle and causal bodies; and “Madbha‑ktaḥ” – self‑directed devotion, because “I am the Lord and the Lord is I” – a declaration of self‑realization. The term “samāmeti” denotes the attainment of the whole. Om tat sat – In the Srimad Bhagavad‑Gītā‑Upaniṣad, within the Brahma‑vidyā of the Yoga‑śāstra, the dialogue of Krishna and Arjuna, the eleventh chapter is titled *Viśvarūpa‑darśana‑yoga* (Verse 11). Thus, by uttering the sacred names Om, Tat, Sat, the precise Brahma‑knowledge and Yoga‑scripture of the Srimad Bhagavad‑Gītā‑Upaniṣad are completed in the eleventh chapter, *Viśvarūpa‑darśana‑yoga*. Having obtained divine sight from the Lord, Arjuna declares:

> “Having heard the description of the universal form I beheld, I accept the Lord’s influence; thus the experience of yoga (relationship) with the Lord arises. Consequently, the eleventh chapter is named *Viśvarūpa‑darśana‑yoga*.”

**Counts of verses, words, and letters**

1. In this chapter the three occurrences of “athaikādasho’dhyāyaḥ”, the twenty‑two occurrences of “Arjuna uvāca” and similar headings, eight hundred fifty‑one verses, and thirteen verses of the *Puṣpika* section together total eight hundred ninety‑nine verses. 2. The seven occurrences of “athaikādasho’dhyāyaḥ”, seventy occurrences of “Arjuna uvāca” and similar headings, two thousand one hundred ninety‑three verses, and fifty letters of the *Puṣpika* section together total two thousand three hundred twenty letters. Among the fifty verses of the chapter, the first verse contains thirty‑three letters; verses fifteen through fifty each contain forty‑six letters; the remaining eighteen verses each contain thirty‑two letters. **Meter (Chandas) employed in Chapter 11**

The chapter comprises fifty verses. Nineteen verses are composed in the *anuṣṭup* meter, three verses in the *upendravajrā* meter, and thirty‑three verses in the *upajāti* meter. In the nineteen *anuṣṭup* verses, the first and fifty‑fifth verses begin with the syllable “bha‑” (as in “bhaga‑”), producing a “bh‑” (broad) effect; the eleventh and thirty‑third verses begin with “na‑” (as in “naga‑”), producing a “na‑” (narrow) effect; the tenth verse starts with “na‑” in the first foot and “bha‑” in the third foot, yielding a “narrow‑broad” pattern. The remaining fourteen verses (from the second to the ninth, the twelfth to the fourteenth, the fifty‑first, the fifty‑second, and the fifty‑fourth) conform precisely to the characteristic features of the *pāthya‑avaktra* form of the *anuṣṭup* meter. Among the remaining thirty‑six verses, the twenty‑eighth, twenty‑ninth, and forty‑fifth verses are in the *upendravajrā* meter, while the other thirty‑three verses (from the fifteenth to the twenty‑seventh, the thirtieth to the forty‑fourth, and the forty‑sixth to the fiftieth) strictly follow the *upajāti* meter. **Occurrences of “uvāca”**

The chapter contains eleven instances of “uvāca”: four spoken by Arjuna (“Arjuna uvāca”), four spoken by the Supreme (“Śrī‑Bhagavān uvāca”), and three spoken by Sanjaya.

[ Chapter 12 ]

Preface –  
The commentary first recounts how, in the fourth chapter, verses 33 and 34 extol the superiority of Jñāna‑yoga and inspire the seeker toward knowledge. It then describes the glory of knowledge itself. Afterwards it explains, from chapter 5 verses 16, 17 and 24‑26, and from chapter 6 verses 24‑28, and from chapter 8 verses 11‑13, the importance of worshiping the attributeless, formless Brahman. In chapter 6 verse 47 the greatness of the aspirant‑devotee is praised, and from chapter 7 verse 1 through chapter 11 verses 45‑55 the significance of the personal (saguna‑sākār) and the impersonal (saguna‑nirākār) worship is repeatedly emphasized by the use of words such as “aham”, “mām”, etc. Finally, in chapter 11 verses 45‑55 the glory of exclusive devotion, together with its fruits and its true nature, is described. From the foregoing, Arjuna’s mind becomes curious: which worshiper is superior, the devotee of the personal God or the worshiper of the attributeless Brahman? With this doubt Arjuna asks:

**Arjuna said**  
“Thus, ever‑steady are those devotees who worship you, O Lord. They, though unmanifest and beyond letters, are the best in yoga.” (Verse 1)

The earlier chapters that describe the worship of the personal God are introduced by the following verses and their meanings:

- **Chapter 6, Verse 47** – “The faithful who, with their inner self merged in Me, sing My praises.”  
- **Chapter 7, Verse 1** – “The mind attached to Me, engaged in yoga, takes refuge in Me.”  
- **Chapter 2, Verses 29‑30** – “Those who, taking shelter in Me, strive forward; the one of steady mind.”  
- **Chapter 7, Verse 8** – “One who offers his mind and intellect to Me.”  
- **Chapter 7, Verse 14** – “The devotee whose heart is wholly fixed on Me, ever remembering Me.”  
- **Chapter 9, Verse 14** – “Devotees who constantly chant My name and qualities, with firm resolve, strive for My grace.”  
- **Chapter 9, Verse 20** – “Those who, with exclusive thought, contemplate Me, are the true worshippers.”

804  
* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

These devotees—  
Thus—  
— the devotee that Arjuna calls “you” (tvaam). In this way, the devotees who worship the personal (saguna‑sākāra) aspect of the Lord, as prescribed in the fifty‑fifth verse of Chapter 11, remain continuously attached to the imperishable, unchanging (akṣara) and indestructible (avinaśī) Brahman. [ Chapter 12 ]  
Even the formless (nirguṇa‑nirākāra) is worshipped; among those two, the one who is the best knower of yoga (yogavittam) is asked: “Who is he?”

**Explanation** – The expression “continually attached, these devotees” (evam satata‑yuktā ye bhaktāḥ) appears in Chapter 11, Verse 55. It means that a devotee acknowledges the Lord, yet in practical activities he regards his relationship with the world as primary. This mistake arises because, at different moments, the seeker’s purpose varies. As long as motives such as wealth, fame, family welfare, etc., remain, the seeker’s connection with the Lord is not continuous. If the sole purpose of one’s life becomes the attainment of the Supreme (Bhagavat‑prāpti), then the terms “yaha” and “saḥ” used in Chapter 11, Verse 55 refer specifically to the seeker who worships the personal (saguna‑sākāra) form of the Lord. Hence the phrase “ye bhaktāḥ” (these devotees) is applied to all seekers who worship the personal aspect. The word “evam” points to Chapter 11, Verse 55. When one truly identifies oneself as “I am the Lord,” every action becomes a means to Bhagavat‑prāpti, and the seeker becomes a means (sādhan). After the purpose of Bhagavat‑prāpti is established, all japa, remembrance, meditation, etc., are performed in relation to the Lord; likewise, even during worldly activities one must consider oneself constantly attached to the Lord. A seeker who has complete faith in the Lord has only one aim: Bhagavat‑prāpti. Consequently, in every activity—whether spiritual (japa, meditation, etc.) or practical (physical work, livelihood)—the seeker’s relationship with the Lord remains perpetual. The term “satata‑yuktāḥ” (continually attached) therefore describes such devotees. A common error of the seeker is to think that the relationship with the Lord exists only at the beginning and end of a worldly action. In reality, the remembrance of the Lord (Bhagavat‑smṛti) must be maintained continuously throughout the action. For example, just as a merchant adds entries to his ledger with unwavering focus, the seeker must keep his mind fixed on the Lord. **Earlier description of the formless worshippers** (from chapters preceding this one) is introduced as follows:

- **[ Chapter 4, Verse 34 ]** – *tad‑viddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā* : “Understand that knowledge by approaching the enlightened teachers with humility, by asking respectful questions, and by serving them.”

- **[ Chapter 4, Verse 39 ]** – *śraddhāvān labhate jñānam* : “A faithful person attains knowledge.”

- **[ Chapter 5, Verse 8 ]** – *naiva kiñcit karomīti yukto manyet tattvavit* : “The knower of the ultimate truth (tattva‑yogi) certainly thinks, ‘I do nothing,’ yet he is aware that the immutable (akṣara) is spoken of by the Vedic scholars.”

- **[ Chapter 5, Verse 13 ]** – *yad akṣaraṁ vedavidho vadanti* : “What the Vedic scholars call the imperishable.”

- **[ Chapter 5, Verse 24‑26 ]** – *brahma‑nirvāṇaṁ* : “Attainment of the supreme, formless Brahman (nirvāṇa).”

- **[ Chapter 6, Verse 25 ]** – *ātma‑saṁsthaṁ manaḥ kṛtvā* : “Having established the mind in the Self.”

- **[ Chapter 8, Verse 11 ]** – *om ity ekākṣaraṁ brahma vyāharann* : “By uttering the single syllable ‘Om’, one practices the Brahman.”

- **[ Chapter 8, Verse 13 ]** – *om ity ekākṣaraṁ brahma vyāharann* (repeated)

- **[ Chapter 9, Verse 15 ]** – *om ity ekākṣaraṁ brahma vyāharann* (repeated)

- **[ Chapter 9, Verse 15 ]** – *jñānayajnena ca anye yajanto mām upāsate* : “Others worship Me by offering the sacrifice of knowledge.”

- **[ Chapter 9, Verse 15 ]** – *na karomi* : “I do nothing (i.e., I do not act, nor cause action).”

- **[ Chapter 9, Verse 15 ]** – *nirvāṇa‑brahma prāptam* : “One attains the formless, immutable Brahman.”

- **[ Chapter 9, Verse 15 ]** – *manas paramātma‑stha* : “The mind is established in the Supreme Self.”

- **[ Chapter 9, Verse 15 ]** – *vedānāṁ jñātā puruṣaḥ paramapad‑khyātaḥ akṣaraḥ* : “The knower of the Vedas, who calls the supreme state ‘akṣara,’”

- **[ Chapter 9, Verse 15 ]** – *om ity ekākṣara‑rūpa brahma‑ucchāraṇaṁ mām nirguṇa‑brahma‑smaraṇam* : “By chanting the single syllable ‘Om’, one remembers the formless, attribute‑less Brahman, which is Me.”

Thus, the yogic devotee worships the formless, attribute‑less Brahman through the sacrifice of knowledge (jñānayajña) and thereby attains My worship.

[ Verse 1 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjivani *

The seeker becomes absorbed in the question “Who am I?” and in the act of adding numbers, while considering even the smallest detail insignificant. He does not retain knowledge of his own existence; his attention remains fixed only on the numerals he is adding. Before beginning the addition, the mind holds the notion “I am a certain merchant and I am adding for a certain purpose.” As soon as the addition is finished, the same sentiment resurfaces: “I am that merchant and I was performing that task.” Consequently, even while he is fully absorbed in the addition, the apparent forgetting of “I am that merchant and I was performing that task” is not regarded as true forgetfulness. In the same way, if at the beginning and the end of a duty‑action the practitioner’s attitude is “I belong to the Lord and I am performing this duty for the Lord,” and he harbors no doubt about this, then when he becomes fully absorbed in his duty‑action, any apparent forgetting of the Lord is likewise not considered genuine forgetfulness. “tvām paryupāsate” – the word *tvām* refers to all the saguna (with qualities) and sṛṣṭi‑manifest forms that devotees, according to their wishes, take up at various times, including the forms assumed by the Lord in his different incarnations and the divine form that dwells in the celestial abode, which devotees address by many names and forms. “paryupāsate” means “to worship completely, with full devotion.” Just as a devoted wife offers her body in service to her husband, contemplates him in his absence, serves his relatives, prepares his meals, and performs all household duties, thereby constantly worshiping him, so too does the seeker‑devotee sometimes immerse himself in the Lord, sometimes chant, remember, and contemplate the Lord, sometimes regard all worldly beings as the Lord and serve them, and sometimes perform worldly actions according to the Lord’s command. Such continuous worship is the proper worship. In the heart of such a worshipper, the transient substances and actions that arise and perish are…

“ye cāpakṣaram avyaktam” – here the pronoun *ye* denotes the worshippers of the nirguṇa (formless, attributeless) aspect. In the first half of the verse Arjuna used *ye* for the saguna (with qualities) worshippers; in this line the same pronoun is applied to the nirguṇa worshippers. *akṣaram* denotes the imperishable, sat‑citi‑ānanda‑filled Supreme Brahman (its explanation appears in the third verse of this chapter). It is beyond the objects of the senses and is called *avyakta* (unmanifest). The adjective *avyaktam* qualifies *akṣaram*, indicating the formless, attributeless Brahman. *api* suggests that a comparison is being drawn between the saguna worshippers and the nirguṇa worshippers, the latter regarding the formless Brahman as supreme. *teṣāṁ kē yogavitthamāḥ* – the pronoun *teṣām* applies to both saguna and nirguṇa worshippers. In the fifth verse of this chapter *teṣām* refers to the nirguṇa worshippers, while in the seventh verse it refers to the saguna worshippers. Arjuna’s question is which of these two kinds of worshippers is superior. Thus Arjuna asks, “Who is superior among the worshippers of the manifest and the unmanifest?” The Lord’s answer, when examined deeply, reveals the significance of Arjuna’s question. From the second verse of this chapter up to the twentieth verse of the fourteenth chapter, the Lord speaks continuously. The seventy‑three verses form a single, extensive passage in the Gita, indicating that the Lord intends to convey a matter of great importance. He wishes the seekers to realize the unity of the manifest and unmanifest forms, to understand the comprehensive mystery of the means that bring both forms into the heart, as described for the perfected devotees (verses 13‑19 of chapter 12).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 12 ]

And for the wise (the Gita—from the twenty‑second to the twenty‑fifth verses of the fourteenth chapter) it arouses special interest. The implication is that in the Lord’s heart there are supreme, highly secret and most exalted sentiments for the souls, and it is the Lord’s grace that reveals them up to Arjuna’s verses, so that they become familiar with the ideal qualities and the special importance of renunciation from the world becomes clear to them—these are the purposes that the Lord seeks to accomplish. This is the Bhagavata‑inspired question. Appendix meaning – because the Gita is a “Yoga‑Shastra”, yoga is the main theme. Hence the question: who is the true knower of yoga? This is Arjuna’s question. There are three categories of yoga‑knowers: (1) yogavit meaning a yogi; (2) yogavittara meaning the superior yogi among two; and (3) yogavittama meaning the supreme yogi among all yogis. Arjuna has no doubt concerning yogavit and yogavittara, but he is doubtful about yogavittama. Relation – In answer to Arjuna’s question about the superiority of Saguna and Nirguna worshippers, the Lord gives a decision. **Verse (2)**  
The Supreme Lord said:  
“Those who, having fixed their minds upon Me, ever constantly worship Me, they, uplifted by faith, are, in My view, the most attached to Me.”

*Word‑by‑word breakdown*  
- **mAy-yA vesh-ya** – having fixed (the mind) on Me  
- **manah** – mind  
- **ye** – who  
- **mAm** – Me  
- **nitya‑yukta** – ever attached, constantly  
- **upasate** – worship  
- **śraddhayā** – by faith  
- **parayopetāḥ** – uplifted, endowed  
- **te** – they  
- **me** – to Me  
- **yuktatama** – most attached  
- **matāḥ** – in My opinion

Explanation – [The Lord’s decision should be taken as is and applied in life without doubt.] He had already given this decision in the 47th verse of the sixth chapter. However, because Arjuna had no personal question on that subject, he could not grasp that decision. When one has no personal question, even heard teachings seldom reach the goal. Therefore, he posed this question in the first verse of this chapter. Similarly, when the mind lacks a complete desire and yearning to know a subject, and there is no personal question, the moving and important teachings heard in holy company or read in the scriptures seldom reach the aspirant’s goal. If the same teaching is explained when they ask a question, they accept it reverently as being specially addressed to them. Usually they disregard what they have heard or read, not internalizing it, even though the latent impressions remain and can be awakened by a strong yearning. Therefore, seekers should internalize what they hear and read, for the mind attaches where love resides. Where love is present, contemplation arises automatically. ‘Nitya‑yukta’ means that the seeker should constantly attach himself to the Lord. “The Lord is mine and I am the Lord’s” – this is the true self‑attachment to the Divine. When the firm purpose is the attainment of the Divine, mind and intellect automatically become attached to the Lord. Conversely, if the purpose is not the Divine, even earnest effort to attach mind and intellect to the Lord does not result in full attachment. However, when one regards oneself as the Lord, mind and intellect naturally become immersed in the Lord. The seeker is the doer and mind‑intellect are the means; the means depend on the doer. When the doer becomes the Lord, the means (mind‑intellect) automatically attach to the Lord. [ Verse 2 ]  
* Seeker – Sanjivani *

It is difficult to apply (the practice). Therefore, when the seeker fully recognises his genuine relationship with the supreme Being, who is both conscious and eternal, he can never forget the supreme Being in any condition. Then, whether rising or sitting, eating‑drinking, sleeping‑waking, the remembrance, contemplation and meditation on God arise automatically in every state. A complaint often arises that the mind and intellect do not fix upon God. When mind and intellect become one‑pointed, achievements such as samādhi become possible, but true welfare arises only when one’s own being is attached to God. The purpose of worship is to offer oneself to God, to realise “I am of God and God is of me.” By offering oneself to God, practices such as name‑chanting, contemplation, meditation, service, worship and scripturally prescribed actions are performed automatically for God alone. The body is a part of nature, and the soul (Atman) is a fragment of the supreme Being. The functions of nature are carried out by the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect and the ego. One who does not indulge in selfishness, affection or desire, and who recognises only God as his own, can say “I am God, God is mine.” Such a declaration does not create a new relationship with God; because of the conscious‑eternal nature of the soul, the relationship with God is already self‑evident. However, by forgetting this eternal, real relationship, the soul mistakenly assumes its relationship to be with nature and its functions (the body), which is unreal. Hence, as long as the relationship with nature is assumed, the need to consider one’s relationship with God persists. When the assumed relationship with nature breaks, the true, eternal relationship with God manifests; its memory is regained—“the delusion is destroyed, memory obtained” (Gita 18.73). Because of the inertia of nature—i.e., the continued enjoyment of worldly pleasures—the embodied soul adds a “I‑am‑the‑body” relationship, believing “I am the body.” Consequently, through this assumed bodily relationship, the soul naturally identifies with caste, ashrama, varna, name, occupation, childhood, youth, etc., without consciously recalling them, and does not regard itself as separate from them. The seeker whose aim is not the accumulation of worldly enjoyments but the sole attainment of the supreme Being must, by this understanding, consider his relationship with God as established. After fully recognising this relationship, the seeker no longer feels any desire, through mind, intellect, senses or body, to acquire or hoard worldly pleasures. In reality, while the soul, being wholly God, may desire a portion of nature’s pleasure, it fails to grasp the divine relationship with equal firmness; the same portion remains attached to nature. Therefore the seeker should turn away from nature, regard himself solely as God, and remain before Him. “Faith, when fully developed, is the best opinion for me” (Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā). The seeker’s faith will be that which he judges to be supreme. When faith arises—i.e., when intellect is applied—he will live naturally according to the principles he has set and will never deviate from them. Where love exists, the mind engages; where faith exists, intellect operates. In love, the quality of affection is primary; in faith, obedience to command is primary. When love is directed toward the sole God, the devotee experiences an uninterrupted, perpetual relationship with God and never feels separation. Hence, in God’s view, such devotees are truly the best yogic scholars. Here, the phrase “the best opinion for me” is in the plural form, referring to the soul’s bodily and worldly identification (a mistaken statement, similar to that made in Chapter 6, verse 47). The conviction of that identification remains so strong that, even without explicit mention, it is constantly remembered. In Chapter 11, verse 45, the Lord says that through exclusive devotion a seeker can see Him directly, know Him by truth, and obtain Him; whereas in Chapter 18, verse 55, the Lord tells the formless worshippers that they may know and obtain Him by truth, not that they will receive a vision. This makes clear that devotees of the personal (saguna) form of God do receive divine vision, which is their distinctive characteristic.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 12 ]

Appendix: “s yogi paramo matah” (Gita 6.32), “s me yuktatama matah” (Gita 6.47), “te me yuktatama matah” (Gita 12.2) – the Lord’s statement of superiority means that, irrespective of whether a person follows Karma‑yoga, Jnana‑yoga or any other path, the truly supreme one is the one who has already attained devotion. The Karma‑yogin and the Jnana‑yogin eventually acquire devotion, but the Bhakti‑yogin is engaged in devotion from the very beginning (which is the fruit of Karma‑yoga and Jnana‑yoga); therefore he is the highest. Both knowledge and devotion are equally effective in removing the sorrows of the world; however, the glory of devotion exceeds that of knowledge. Knowledge leads to the attainment of the indivisible (akhandarasa), whereas devotion leads to the attainment of the infinite (anantārasa). In infinite rasa there is a constantly growing, wave‑like, surging delight that is extraordinarily unique. Just as worldly knowledge such as “these are rupees; this is a watch” merely dispels ignorance, so does philosophical knowledge only eliminate ignorance. When ignorance is destroyed, suffering, fear, and the cycle of birth and death disappear. Yet love (bhakti) is even more extraordinary than knowledge. Knowledge does not reach the Lord, but love does. The experiencer of knowledge is the individual self, whereas the experiencer of love is the Lord Himself; those who know the Lord are the Lord. The Lord is never hungry for knowledge, but is ever hungry for love. When liberation is attained, the Jnana‑yogin becomes satisfied and content (see Gita, Chapter 3, Verse 17). When love is attained, however, the devotee does not become merely satisfied; rather, his joy continually increases. Hence the ultimate principle is love, not liberation. Just as the knowledge “these are rupees” removes ignorance, the desire to acquire more (“more, more”) introduces a special rasa. In the same way, devotion brings a special rasa. The point is that, in the world, the power to attract through rupees lies in greed; similarly, the power to attract the Lord lies in love, not in knowledge. Greed for wealth leads to greater downfall, whereas love elevates beyond knowledge. The rasa that draws one to an object is absent in the object itself and in the knowledge of the object. In the path of discrimination (Jnana‑yoga), the simultaneous acceptance of sat (truth) and asat (untruth) allows the subtlest form of ego (sukshma ahamkara) to persist alongside the subtle self. This subtle ego remains even after the removal of gross karmic impressions; it does not cause birth‑and‑death, but it obstructs complete union with the Divine. Consequently, while philosophers and scholars may attain liberation through Jnana‑yoga, they are not guaranteed the intimate union (love) with the Divine. This subtle ego is the source of philosophical disagreements. In contrast, the path of faith (Bhakti‑yoga) begins with the devotee recognizing no independent existence apart from the Divine. Hence the devotee becomes inseparable from the Divine. When this inseparability (the arising of love) occurs, the subtle ego and all philosophical disputes—dualism, non‑dualism, qualified non‑dualism, etc.—are completely erased. All such viewpoints merge into the reality of Vasudeva, who is everything. Therefore, a lover‑devotee who experiences “Vasudeva is all” harbors no attachment to any single doctrine; he respects all equally, and no disrespect arises from any particular view. The unity of love surpasses the unity of knowledge. In knowledge, the distance and distinction from the Supreme are removed, but complete union does not occur. In love, distance, distinction, and difference are all eliminated; thus true non‑duality resides in love. Love possesses such power that the devotee even becomes the beloved of the Lord. Practitioners of the knowledge path regard liberation as the highest goal; how then can they comprehend that beyond liberation lies love (pre‑loving devotion or supreme devotion)? Liberation contains a complete rasa, but love contains an ever‑increasing, infinite rasa. Love surpasses liberation, philosophical knowledge, self‑realization, and even the state of absolute freedom (kaivalya). In the forty‑seven‑th verse of Chapter 6, the Lord declares that a seeker who holds faith‑love for His personal form is the greatest among all yogis. The implication is that the seeker who regards the Lord as his own and remains devoted to Him is especially dear to the Lord. 1 – “Prem bhakti jal binu raghurayi. [ Verse 3-4 ]  
* Practitioner’s Elixir *

Karma‑yoga and Jñāna‑yoga are both worldly loyalties (see Gita Chapter 3 Verse 3), but Bhakti‑yoga is not a worldly loyalty, i.e., not the loyalty of the individual soul. When one becomes attached to the Lord, that attachment is to the Divine (Bhagavān) and is therefore transcendental. Both the means (sādhana) and the goal (sādhya) of Bhakti‑yoga are the Lord Himself. Hence Bhakti‑yoga is simultaneously the means and the end, as expressed in “bhaktyā sañjātayā bhaktyā” (Srimad‑Bhāgavatam 11.3.31): devotion begets devotion. The nine forms of “sādhana‑bhakti” are: śravaṇa (listening), kīrtana (chanting), smaraṇa (remembrance), pāda‑sevana (serving the Lord’s feet), ārchana (offering), vandana (salutation), dāsyam (servitude), sakhya (friendship) and ātmāniveśa (self‑surrender). Beyond these is “prema‑lakṣaṇā‑bhakti,” the “sādhya‑bhakti,” which is the ultimate object of both Karma‑yoga and Jñāna‑yoga (see Gita Chapter 18 Verse 24). This sādhya‑bhakti is the supreme, attainable principle. In Jñāna‑yoga the practitioner gives priority to the discrimination between sat (the real) and asat (the unreal) and abandons asat. Because the abandonment of asat creates a great distance between the renounced and the still‑existent, the complete relinquishment of asat occurs only after a long delay. In Karma‑yoga the practitioner does not regard asat objects as relinquishable but treats them as material for service. While the relinquishment of inferior objects is easy, giving up good objects is difficult; therefore it is easier to redirect the good object toward the service of others. Self‑less service to others quickly and smoothly eliminates asat. In Bhakti‑yoga, by regarding the world as the form of the Lord, the asat (the unreal) disappears almost instantly, leaving only the Divine. Consequently, compared with Jñāna‑yoga, Karma‑yoga brings about a rapid abandonment of asat (inertia); and compared with Karma‑yoga, Bhakti‑yoga brings about an even faster abandonment of asat, because in devotion asat does not remain—“sarva‑saccāham” (Gita 9.19). Thus Karma‑yoga is superior to Jñāna‑yoga—“tayoḥstu karmasannyāsāt karma‑yogo viśiṣyate” (Gita 5.2)—and Bhakti‑yoga is superior to Karma‑yoga—“yoginām api sarveṣāṁ mad‑gatenān‑tārmaṇāḥ; śraddhāvān bhajate yo māṁ sa me yuktatamo mataḥ” (Gita 6.47). **Relation** – In the preceding verse the Lord declared that devotees who worship with form (saguṇa) are the supreme yogis. A question may arise: are formless (nirguṇa) worshippers not the supreme yogis? The Lord answers:

*“ye tv akṣara‑m anirdeśyam avyaktaṁ paryupāsate  
sarvatra‑gama‑cin tyam ca kūṭastha‑m acalaṁ dhruvaṁ”* (Verse 3)

*“sanniyamye indriya‑grāmam sarvatra sama‑buddhayaḥ  
prāpnuvanti mām eva sarva‑bhūta‑hite ratāḥ”* (Verse 4)

Translation:  
“Those who worship the imperishable, indescribable, and unmanifest, who pervade everywhere, who are beyond thought, who are immovable and eternal—such beings, having fully restrained the senses, and whose intellect is equally steady everywhere, attain me alone, being devoted to the welfare of all beings.”

Thus, the worship of the unmanifest, all‑pervading Divine leads directly to union with the Lord. Before true knowledge, dualistic illusion entangles the mind; after realization, devotion embraces a beauty that surpasses even the accepted dual‑nondual synthesis. The nine devotional practices are again enumerated:

*śravaṇa, kīrtana, viṣṇoḥ smaraṇa, pāda‑sevana, ārchana, vandana, dāsyam, sakhya, ātmāniveśa* (Srimad‑Bhāgavatam 7.5.23).
[Verse 4]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 12 ]

Explanation – “tu”: here the word *tu* denotes the personal (sākāra) worshipper, who cannot be grasped by the limited mind‑intellect‑senses. It is introduced to show the distinction from the formless worshipper. “sanniyamye‑indriya‑grāmam” – by using the prefix *sam* and *ni* together with the root *sanniyam* (to restrain), the Lord indicates that all the senses must be properly and completely brought under control so that they do not turn toward any other object. When the senses are not fully mastered, worship of the attributeless (nirguṇa) principle becomes difficult. In worship of the with‑attributes (saguṇa) Lord, the object of meditation is the personal God, so the senses can be attached to Him because in His saguṇa form the senses find their object. Hence, although sense‑control is required in saguṇa worship, it is not as stringent as in nirguṇa worship. In nirguṇa worship, because there is no object for contemplation, the senses, if not strictly restrained, can still cling to objects, leading the mind to wander among them and increasing the risk of downfall (see Gita, Chapter 2, verses 52‑63). Therefore, a nirguṇa devotee must withdraw the senses completely from all objects and keep them fully under mastery. This mastery is not only external; internally, the practitioner’s heart must also be free of attachment to objects, for as long as attachment remains, attaining Brahman is difficult (see Gita, Chapter 15, verse 11). The emphasis on sense control in the Gita is far greater for nirguṇa worship and for Karma‑yoga than for saguṇa worship. “achintyam” – because the mind‑intellect have no object, the term *achintyam* (inconceivable) refers to the attributeless, formless Brahman. The mind‑intellect are functions of Prakṛti and therefore cannot become the object of the all‑pervading Supreme; likewise, the Supreme, being beyond Prakṛti, cannot become an object of the material world. Only material substances are objects of thought; the Supreme, being transcendent of all material thought‑objects, is beyond description. Hence the Supreme can be known only through self‑realization (action‑independent knowledge), not through the operations of mind‑intellect (action‑dependent knowledge). “sarvatra‑gam” – the Supreme pervades every country, time, object, and individual. “anirdeśyam” – that which cannot be described by language or speech is *anirdeśyam*. A sign can be given only to that which is defined by caste, quality, action, and relation and is separate from country, time, object, and person; but the all‑pervading, subtle principle cannot be indicated by any concrete language or speech. “kūṭastha” – this term denotes the immutable, ever‑unchanging, sat‑citi‑ānanda‑filled Brahman. Though it resides in all countries, times, objects, and beings, it remains ever‑unchanged and unattached. No alteration ever occurs in it, just as a well‑crafted jewel, weapon, or tool remains exactly the same while various objects are fashioned in a workshop. Likewise, despite the creation, existence, and destruction of myriad beings and substances, the Supreme remains ever‑the‑same. “acalam” – this word describes Brahman as completely free from any motion of coming and going. Prakṛti is in motion; Brahman is immovable. “dhruvam” – that whose existence is certain (truthful) and eternal is called *dhruva*. The sat‑citi‑ānanda‑filled Brahman is eternally existent everywhere, thus *dhruva*. Among the eight adjectives of nirguṇa Brahman, *dhruva* is the most important, because negative adjectives such as “anirdeśyam” or “achintyam” might be misinterpreted as implying non‑existence. By affirming *dhruva*, the text asserts the definite existence of that principle, which is never absent anywhere. Its existence gives existence to the unreal (the world of illusion). “akṣaram” – that which never undergoes decay or loss, that which is never deficient, is the sat‑citi‑ānanda‑filled Brahman, *akṣara*. “avyaktam” – that which is not expressed, i.e., not an object of mind‑intellect‑senses and has no form or shape, is called *avyaktam*. “paryupāsate” – here it indicates that because nirguṇa worshippers are complete, Brahman is *sarvatra‑gam* (present everywhere). Its all‑pervasive nature is the true indicator of proper worship. The body together with all material substances... (the commentary continues on the next page).

[ Verse 3-4 ]  
* Sadhaka - Sanjivani *

And in actions the lack of lust, the lack of ego‑sense, and the form of existence have arisen for the Jiva (individual soul). In the dense of Sat‑citi‑ānanda that is the Paramatma (Supreme Soul), remaining constantly, steadfastly, and inseparably is the very act of worship. In these verses, by means of eight adjectives a particular object has been pointed out as the ultimate reality, and the object that is understood from it is the nature of Buddhi‑vishishta Brahman (the Brahman distinguished by intellect), which is not complete; because the form of Nirguna‑Nirvishesha Brahman (devoid of qualities and attributes, beyond intellect) cannot in any way be a subject of intellect or similar. Indeed, worship performed with the aim of these adjectives is worship of the Nirguna Brahman, and the result attained is also of the Nirguna Brahman. Special note: To explain the nature of Paramatma two kinds of adjectives are given—negative (Nishedhatmak) and affirmative (Vidhyatmak). Adjectives such as akshara (imperishable), anirdeshya (indescribable), avyakta (unmanifest), achintya (inconceivable), achala (immovable), avyaya (unchanging), asima (boundless), apar (infinite), avinashi (indestructible) are Nishedhatmak; while adjectives like sarvavyapi (pervading all), kootastha (transcendental), dhruva (fixed), sat (existence), chit (consciousness), ananda (bliss) are Vidhyatmak. The negative adjectives indicate the non‑association of Paramatma with Prakriti, whereas the affirmative adjectives indicate the independent existence of Paramatma. The essence of Paramatma is beyond both worldly activity and renunciation (it is naturally withdrawn) and illuminates both equally. To set the goal of this impartial Paramatma and to bring the intellect nearer to Paramatma, various adjectives are employed to describe (the goal of) Paramatma. In the Gita, the description of the nature of Paramatma and Jiva is largely identical. The adjectives given for Paramatma here are the same as those given for Jiva in the Gita; for example, in Chapter 2 verses 24‑25 the adjectives *sarvagataḥ* (pervading all), *achala* (immovable), *avyakta* (unmanifest), *achintya* (inconceivable) appear, and in Chapter 15 verse 16 the adjectives *kootastha* and *akshara* are applied to Jiva. Similarly, in Chapter 7 verse 25 the adjective *avyayam* is used for Paramatma and in Chapter 14 verse 5 the same adjective *avyayam* appears. Even in the worldly realm, Paramatma and Jiva are described as equally pervasive; for instance, in Chapter 8 verse 22 and Chapter 18 verse 46 the phrase *yena sarvam idaṁ tatam* (by which all this is that) and in Chapter 9 verse 4 the phrase *mayā tatam idaṁ sarvam* (by Me all this is) declare Paramatma as pervading the entire universe. Likewise, in Chapter 2 verse 17 the same phrase *yena sarvam idaṁ tatam* indicates that Jiva also pervades the whole cosmos. Just as the vision of the eyes does not clash with each other, and even when sound spreads widely the words do not collide, similarly (according to dualistic philosophy) even though the entire universe is uniformly pervaded, the non‑material nature of Paramatma and Jiva prevents any conflict in their all‑pervading presence. *Sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ* – in the practice of Karma‑yoga the primary emphasis is the renunciation

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 12 ]

In the first practice, merely learning that “everything is Brahman” does not establish firm devotion to knowledge. As long as the heart harbors passions such as desire, anger, and other disturbances, attaining steadfastness in knowledge remains extremely difficult. Just as a karmayogi must be devoted to the welfare of all beings in order to eradicate his passions, a practitioner of nirguna worship must likewise be devoted to the welfare of all living beings; only then can the passions be eliminated and devotion to knowledge be realized. The expression “sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ” (engaged in the welfare of all) is introduced to convey this purpose. When one’s service becomes boundless, the underlying principle that remains after all material objects are set aside—without attachment, affection, or similar tendencies—is the Atman or Brahman. One should regard all creatures as the embodiment of that principle and devote oneself to their service, because they constitute the totality of matter. When such an infinite attitude arises, complete detachment from the inert material world occurs, granting the seeker immediate access to the supreme principle (Paramātman). The tendency to treat material objects as personal possessions creates division (ekadeśīyatā) and disparity within a person. By refusing to see matter as personal and by cultivating concern for the welfare of all beings, those divisions disappear. Conversely, an ordinary person who limits his service to beloved beings retains attachment and affection toward both the objects and the beings he serves; consequently, because of this limited mindset, he cannot attain the infinite divine principle. Therefore, attaining the infinite divine principle requires an all‑encompassing love (prīti‑rūpa) directed toward the welfare of all living beings. The phrase “sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ” precisely expresses this attitude. A yogi of jñāna‑yoga wishes to sever all ties with the inert world, yet as long as his heart respects perishable material things, it is difficult for him to abandon them by merely regarding them as illusory or dream‑like. In contrast, a karmayogi can more readily relinquish material objects by dedicating them to the service of others. For the jñāna‑yogi, a strong vairāgya (dispassion) is required for such renunciation; the karmayogi, even with a modest degree of dispassion, can renounce material objects in the service of others. Proper use of material things for the benefit of all beings facilitates a smooth, effortless detachment from the inert world. By declaring “sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ,” the Lord indicates that devotion to the welfare of all living beings engenders respect for material reality while maintaining an attitude of self‑less service. In another practice, a seeker who remains indifferent to the world and contemplates the ultimate principle in solitude finds that mere renunciation of actions aids him, but renunciation of actions alone does not guarantee success (see Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 3, Verse 4). To achieve the goal, a profound dispassion toward sensual enjoyment and a complete relinquishment of identification with body, senses, mind, and intellect are indispensable. Hence, vairāgya (detachment) and the absence of selfishness require the attitude of “sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ.”

A jñāna‑yogi often distances himself from society, which leaves his individuality intact; to dissolve that individuality, an attitude of concern for the welfare of the world is essential. Once such concern is present, detachment from the inert world will occur effortlessly. For the welfare of all living beings, karmayoga remains the most accessible means. Among the various internal distinctions in the practice of nirguna worship, two principal differences remain: (1) everything that appears as moving or immovable, conscious or unconscious, is ultimately Atman or Brahman; (2) everything that appears in the visible realm is transient, fleeting, and unreal. Consequently, true disassociation must begin with the body. When one becomes estranged from society, the ego (ahaṅkāra) solidifies and does not dissolve. Until the seeker experiences a clear separation from his own body, mere withdrawal from the world does not achieve the goal, because the body itself is part of the world, and the absence of identification and affection toward the body constitutes genuine separation. To eradicate identification and affection, the seeker must act for the welfare of all living beings. Moreover, it is impossible for a seeker to remain perpetually in solitude, since the body requires engagement in the world for sustenance. A reduction in dispassion can lead to rigidity in conduct due to pride, and such rigidity prevents the dissolution of the ego, making the attainment of the ultimate principle difficult. To avoid rigidity in conduct, it is also necessary that the seeker maintain an attitude of concern for all beings.

[ Verse 3-4 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

The practitioner who remains absorbed in the welfare of all beings, engaged in the yoga of knowledge, does not encounter difficulty in remaining constantly devoted to the Supreme Self that pervades all substances; nevertheless the Lord says that such difficulty can arise because the Supreme Self is impartial (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 5, Verse 19). Both Saguna‑worshippers and Nirguna‑worshippers must cultivate a feeling of universal welfare. When one regards personal welfare as separate from the welfare of all beings, the sense of “Aham” (individuality) persists, later becoming an obstacle for the aspirant. True welfare arises only when the sense of “Aham” is completely eradicated. Because one’s own means of advancement keep the “Aham” alive, every action—eating, drinking, sleeping, as well as chanting, meditation, recitation, self‑study, etc.—must be performed solely for the benefit of the world. One’s own welfare is inherent in the welfare of the world. The Lord’s mere power operates in the service of others; therefore, whatever is done for the welfare of all, the Lord’s power accompanies it. Service is not merely giving material objects to others or physically serving them; it is acting with the attitude that, without desiring anything for oneself, one seeks the happiness of the other. One should not even entertain the notion of being called a servant. Service becomes possible only when the servant regards the one he serves as inseparable from himself (as his own body) and expects nothing in return. Just as a person, without any instruction, naturally tends to his own body with great care and without pride, similarly, when the divine intellect pervades everywhere, the devotee automatically remains absorbed in the welfare of all (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 6, Verse 32). By his presence, even the smallest creatures receive benefit, yet his mind never harbors the feeling that he is doing anyone a favor. The sense of “Aham” disappears entirely; therefore, such liberated great souls become ideals for aspirants, who should, by exercising self‑realization everywhere, never cause even the slightest suffering to any creature and remain naturally devoted to their welfare. The expression “Sarvatra Samabuddhayaḥ” (universally equal‑minded) conveys that worshippers of the formless, attributeless Brahman view every being as the same. Here the author uses this phrase to indicate that, for seekers of knowledge, solitary contemplation of the absolute is not the sole means; the significance of “Samabuddhayaḥ” manifests especially in practical life. Removing oneself from the world and placing the body in a deserted place is not true solitude, because the body itself is a part of the world. Seeing body and world as separate is a distorted perception; only by perceiving them as one can equal‑mindedness arise. True solitude is achieved when, apart from the Supreme Self, all other entities—body and world—are absent. Solitude can aid practice, but a practitioner who relies entirely on isolation may err in daily conduct. The absence of attachment to the body constitutes genuine solitude. Hence the aspirant should aim at true solitude by relinquishing ego‑attachment to body, senses, mind, and intellect, and remain inseparably merged with the all‑pervading Brahman. Such a practitioner truly possesses equal‑mindedness. In the Gita, “Samabuddhi” means “equal vision,” not “equal conduct.” In Chapter 5, Verse 18, the Lord enumerates a learned, humble Brahmin together with a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a Chandala, stating that complete equality in dealing with these five beings is impossible. The term “Samadarshinaḥ” (one who sees equally) is used there, implying that uniform treatment of all cannot be achieved. No one can, nor should, behave identically toward everyone; differentiation in conduct is essential. While the practitioner’s view of various beings and substances may differ according to their forms and utilities, his ultimate vision remains fixed on the Supreme Self that pervades them. Just as different ornaments do not alter the essence of gold, varied modes of conduct do not affect the practitioner’s essential perspective. An inner equality toward all beings persists. The term “Samabuddhayaḥ” thus denotes this inner equality.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The goal is set solely toward inner equilibrium. In the view of the perfected sages, because there is no other reality besides the Supreme Atman, they are always and everywhere of “equal intellect.” The self‑realized state of the perfected sages themselves becomes the ideal for seekers, and they proceed by aiming at that ideal. In the seeker’s view, apart from the Supreme Atman, every other substance possesses only a fragmentary existence; consequently, the intellect does not remain balanced in proportion to those fragments. Hence, as the independent existence of other substances diminishes in the seeker’s mind, his intellect becomes increasingly uniform. The seeker strives, with his intellect, to perceive the Supreme Atman everywhere, whereas in the intellect of the perfected sages the Supreme Atman is so densely pervading that nothing else exists for them. Therefore, the object of their intellect is not the Supreme Atman; rather, their intellect itself is saturated with the Supreme Atman. Thus they are “equally‑intelligent everywhere.”

“Those who attain Me” – worshippers of the Nirguna (formless) principle sometimes misunderstand that the Nirguna reality is one thing and the Saguna (with qualities) is another. Hence the Lord clarifies that the Nirguna Brahman is not different from Him (Gita – Chapter 9 verse 4 and Chapter 14 verse 27). Both Saguna and Nirguna are merely aspects of His own nature. [ Chapter 12
What it is and (4) what the seeker attains. (1) In the latter part of the first verse of this chapter, Arjuna asked about the Nirguna principle, using the adjectives “Aksharam” (imperishable) and “Avyakta” (unmanifest). To elaborate on that principle, the Lord gave six additional adjectives, making a total of eight: five negative qualifiers (Aksharam, Anirdeshyam, Avyakta, Achintyam, and Achalam) and three positive qualifiers (Sarvatragam, Kootastha, and Dhruvam). (2) When the vision rests upon the all‑pervading principle that pervades every country, time, object, and being, the Nirguna worshipper attains equal intellect everywhere. Because they regard the body’s pride and the pleasures as separate, independent existences, desire for pleasure arises and is pursued. However, for these Nirguna worshippers, no separate independent existence exists apart from the Supreme Atman; consequently, pleasures have no significance in their intellect. They therefore master the senses with ease. Their universal equality of intellect makes them devoted to the welfare of all beings; they are “devoted to the welfare of all creatures.”

(3) For the seeker, constantly keeping the gaze on the Nirguna principle (remaining before the principle) constitutes “worship.”

(4) The Lord says that for such seekers who attain Nirguna Brahman, “I am that.” The implication is that Saguna and Nirguna are one and the same reality. In these two verses the Lord conveys four points for Nirguna worshippers: (1) the nature of the Nirguna principle, (2) the state of the seeker, (3) the nature of worship, and (4) the characteristic of the appendix (Parishishta Bhava). The attributes of Brahman that the Lord enumerates here—Achintya (unthinkable, see Chapter 2 verse 25), Kootastha (transcendental, see Chapter 15 verse 16), Achala (unchanging, see Chapter 2 verse 24), Akshara (imperishable, see Chapter 15 verses 16 and 18), Avyakta (unmanifest, see Chapter 2 verse 25), etc.—are the same attributes ascribed to the Jiva Atman. This parallelism indicates that the soul and Brahman are identical in essence. The “Jiva” is the soul bound to the body in many forms, while “Brahman” is the same essence free from bodily association. Thus the soul is distinct only because of the body‑identification; otherwise it is Brahman itself. Consequently, upon attaining Brahman, the worshipper automatically attains “sadharma” (spiritual equality): “Having taken refuge in this knowledge, I have attained spiritual equality” (Gita 14.2). “Those who attain Me” – both Saguna (with qualities) and Nirguna (without qualities) refer to the same underlying reality; therefore the Lord also declares that the Nirguna worshippers achieve Him. The meaning is that the formless, attribute‑less form is also His, not separate from His totality. “Devoted to the welfare of all creatures”—the world, the individual soul, and the Supreme Atman are seen as one from all three perspectives. Because the entire body belongs to the supra‑material nature and the entire soul likewise belongs to the supra‑material nature, when the seeker’s intellect becomes uniformly equal toward all beings—“equally‑intelligent everywhere”—he regards all creatures as his own.

[ Verse 5 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

When one truly believes the statement “He who sees the whole universe as a reflection of the Self, O Arjuna” (Bhagavad‑Gita 6.32), love for the welfare of all beings arises spontaneously. Because he regards every creature as his own body, he neither thinks anyone is bad nor wishes ill for anyone, nor harms anyone. Thus, with the abandonment of evil, his own concern for others is automatic. Likewise, if a tooth were to cut one’s own tongue, no one would become angry at the tooth and break it; similarly, one who regards all beings as his own does not entertain any desire to do harm, even if someone harms him – “Uma saints extol this greatness; one who harms the good is himself harmed” (Manas, Sundar 41.4). When evil is abandoned, the service rendered to others becomes a donation greater than any merit (punya). Therefore, the renunciation of evil is the root of all goodness. Only the one who has given up evil can truly be “engaged in the welfare of all beings.”

Relation – In response to Arjuna’s question, the Lord first praised the saguna worshippers as supreme, and in the next two verses described the attainment of the nirguna worshippers. The following three verses explain the subtle differences, difficulties, and ease of the two modes of worship. **Unmanifest‑attached minds**  
“klEsho ’adhikataraḥ teṣām avyakta‑āsakta‑cetasām  
avyaktā hi gatir duḥkhaṁ dehavad bhir avāpyate” 5

*Word‑by‑word breakdown*

- avyakta‑āsakta‑cetasām – of those minds attached to the unmanifest  
- klEshaḥ – suffering, distress  
- adhikataraḥ – is greater, predominates  
- teṣām – of them  
- avyakta – the unmanifest (the nirguna, formless Brahman)  
- hi – indeed  
- gatiḥ – progress, attainment  
- duḥkham – sorrow, pain  
- dehavad bhir – by those who are attached to the body (body‑identifying)  
- avāpyate – is obtained, experienced

Thus, for those whose consciousness is attached to the unmanifest, the predominant affliction is suffering; the very progress toward the unmanifest brings sorrow when pursued by those who cling to the body. **Commentary**

The phrase “klEsho ’adhikataraḥ teṣām avyakta‑āsakta‑cetasām” indicates that seekers whose minds are attached to the unmanifest have not become fully immersed in the nirguna principle. Hence they are still “attached minds” (cetasām) rather than “immersed minds.” Such seekers consider the nirguna worship superior, yet their consciousness has not entered the formless reality. To enter the formless reality, a seeker must possess three qualities: interest (ruchi), faith (vishvasa), and capacity (yogyata). Hearing the glory of the nirguna principle from scriptures and teachers may spark interest and lead to earnest practice, but a lack of vairagya (dispassion) and lingering body‑identification prevent the mind from entering the ultimate principle. Consequently, the term “avyakta‑āsakta‑cetasām” is used for these aspirants. Note that the adjective “āsakta” (attached) is employed instead of “avishita” (immersed) to stress that their attachment remains in the body, even though they are drawn to the unmanifest by hearing its greatness. Their attachment is bodily, not in the unmanifest. In Chapter 13, Verse 5, the word “avyaktam” is used in its natural‑world sense, but here “avyakta” denotes the nirguna, formless Brahman, the opposite of the manifested form (saguna). Earlier in this chapter, Arjuna asked about the personal (saguna) and impersonal (nirguna) aspects of the Supreme. The object of worship is the Supreme (Paramatma), not nature; nature and its activities are to be renounced. Therefore, the Lord employs “avyakta” specifically to refer to the formless, attributeless aspect of the Divine. In verses 27‑28 of Chapter 6, the Lord explains that a seeker who is “brahmabhuta” (identical with Brahman) attains Brahman with ease and joy. In the present verse, the expression “klEshaḥ adhikataraḥ” clarifies that seekers whose minds are not yet like those of the brahmabhuta, because they are still attached to the body, experience greater distress when pursuing the unmanifest.

Nature cannot be taken. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

In the fourth verse of Chapter 9 the expression “avyaktam‑mūrtinā” is used for the saguna‑nirākāra (with‑qualities, formless) aspect. One might wonder whether the phrase “avyaktāsakta‑cetasām” here could also be taken to mean “the person whose mind is attached in the saguna‑nirākāra state.” That interpretation, however, is not admissible, because in the first verse of the same chapter Arjuna’s question uses the word “tvām” for the saguna‑sākāra (with‑form) sense and the combination “avyaktam” with “akṣaram” for the nirguṇa‑nirākāra (without‑qualities, formless) sense. What is Brahman? – In answer to Arjuna’s question, Chapter 8, verse 3 already states that “parama‑akṣara = Brahman,” i.e., the word “akṣara” there also denotes the nirguṇa‑nirākāra (without‑qualities, formless) Brahman. [ Chapter 12 ]

Thus, when Arjuna asked about the nirguṇa Brahman using the terms “avyaktam akṣaram,” the same answer applies here: because “akṣara” functions as an adjective, the term “avyakta” must be understood as referring to the nirguṇa‑nirākāra Brahman, not to a saguna‑nirākāra form. The sense of the phrase “kleśo ’dhikataraḥ” is that practitioners whose minds are not immersed in the nirguṇa principle experience special difficulty in their practice because of bodily ego‑identification. In a subsidiary sense, the phrase indicates that from the initial to the final stage of practice, all nirguṇa worshippers encounter greater difficulty than saguna worshippers. Special note

Now the ease of saguna worship and the difficulty of nirguṇa worship are examined. Advantages of Saguna Worship

1 – Because the object of worship is saguna‑sākāra (with‑qualities, with form), the practitioner’s mind and senses have a concrete basis in the Lord’s form, name, pastimes, stories, etc. Devotion to the Lord makes the mind and senses readily engage in contemplation of the Lord’s form and pastimes, listening to narratives, serving the Divine, and worship (see Gita, Chapter 8, verse 14). Consequently, the tendency toward worldly contemplation is reduced. 2 – Worldly attachment is the source of distress in practice. Yet the saguna devotee relies on the Lord to remove this attachment, considering the Lord’s power as his own. Practitioners are essentially of two types –

Difficulties of Nirguna Worship

1 – In nirguṇa worship the object of worship is nirguṇa‑nirākāra (without‑qualities, formless), leaving the practitioner’s mind and senses without a concrete support. The lack of support, together with insufficient vairāgya (dispassion), increases the likelihood of sensory engagement with worldly subjects. 2 – The greater the attachment to the body, the greater the distress experienced in practice. The nirguṇa practitioner strives to remove this attachment through viveka (discrimination). Relying on viveka, he values his own inner strength as the primary aid in practice. Practitioners are broadly classified as follows:

* The first group consists of those who, through association with the holy, listening, and scriptural study, become inclined toward practice; they experience relatively more distress in their practice. * The second group comprises those whose practice is naturally motivated and who possess an innate dispassion toward the world; they encounter comparatively less distress. A question may arise: why are practitioners only of two kinds? The answer lies in the Gita’s description of the two possible courses of a yogic‑deviated person:

1 – Some yogic‑deviated individuals attain the worlds of merit, enjoy the pleasures there, return, are born into the families of virtuous persons, and again engage in practice to attain the Supreme (see Gita, Chapter 6, verses 41, 44, 45). 2 – Other yogic‑deviated individuals are directly born into the lineage of enlightened yogis and, after practice, attain the Supreme. Birth in such a lineage is rarer (see Gita, Chapter 6, verses 42‑43).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 12 ]

[ Verse 10 ] – Even while the heart respects material objects, if even a tiny trace of attachment remains, the aspirant’s sense of personal accomplishment binds him to the chain of karma. When the mind is occupied with serving sentient beings, any deficiency in renouncing material objects prevents actions from being offered as natural sacrifice, and the aspirant’s pride in his deeds keeps him trapped in karmic bondage. There is no difficulty in performing actions; for the worthy, renouncing material objects is even easier. For the Divine, renunciation of material objects can be accomplished with utmost ease. [ Verse 11 ] – In this practice, discernment and intense detachment are not required as much as love and faith. For example, even while harboring hostility toward the Kauravas, Draupadi’s mere call would bring the Divine forth, because she regarded the Divine as her own. The Divine looks only at the love and faith of the devotee, not at his faults. Forming a sense of belonging with the Divine is not difficult (because belonging to the Divine is self‑evident). The terms ‘avyaktā hi gatiḥ duḥkhaṁ dehavadbhir avāpyate’, ‘dehī’, ‘dehabhṛt’ are ordinarily understood as “the embodied man”. Contextually they can also mean “the living soul” or “the Atman”. Here ‘dehavadbhir’ should be rendered “persons who are attached to the body”. In the preceding half‑verse of the same shloka, the phrase ‘avyaktāsakta‑cetasām’ appears, indicating that the worshippers of the attributeless (Nirguna) consider that path superior; however, because of their bodily pride, their minds have not entered the attributeless reality. Bodily pride is the chief source of their suffering in practice. In Nirguna worship, bodily pride is the principal obstacle. [ Verse 10 ] – As long as the aspirant’s mind harbors even the slightest reverence for material objects and clings to the body and name as his own, he will find it difficult to regard material objects as illusory and to renounce them. [ Verse 11 ] – Only after becoming worthy can the aspirant attain the ultimate reality. Becoming worthy demands discernment and intense detachment, which are hard to acquire while attachment persists. The verse ‘dehābhimānini sarve doṣāḥ prādurbhavanti’ is quoted by the Divine specifically to draw attention to this obstacle. To remove bodily pride, the Divine, without waiting for Arjuna’s question, introduced Chapters 13 and 14; the first verse of Chapter 13 likewise addresses the eradication of bodily pride. The attainment of the attributeless, formless nature of Brahman is described here as ‘avyaktā gatiḥ’. Ordinary humans exist in the manifested form (the body); therefore they experience difficulty in situating themselves in the unmanifest. If the aspirant does not identify himself as a body‑holder, his transition to the unmanifest becomes smooth and swift. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – In Nirguna worship, the one who possesses a body is the ‘upāsaka’ (the living soul), while the one without a body is the ‘upāsya’ (Brahman). The perceived relationship with the body is a special impediment to the unity of the living soul and Brahman. Consequently, for those attached to the body, the achievement of Nirguna worship is delayed and difficult. In Saguna worship, however, the devotee’s turning away from the world, not bodily pride, is the obstacle. Thus the Saguna devotee, having withdrawn from worldly life, becomes dependent on the Divine rather than on any practice, and the Divine promptly grants his liberation. *Note on the term “deha”* – In the phrase ‘bhūmanindā‑prashansāsu nitya‑yoge ’tiśāyane; saṁsarge ’sti vivakṣāyāṁ bhavanti matubādayaḥ’, the word ‘saṁsarga’ (association) is interpreted from the Pāṇinian sutra ‘matup‑’ as “that which is associated”. Hence ‘dehavadbhir’ means “those humans who maintain a firm relationship with the body”. In Chapter 6, verse 27, the state of being “Brahma‑bhūta” (embodied in Brahman) is described as a pleasant attainment, whereas here the state of being “deha‑bhūta” (embodied in the body) is linked with a painful attainment of Brahman.

* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The fourteenth verse of the seventh and eighth chapters. This passage highlights the distinct character of Sagun worship. In Sagun worship the devotee does not regard the world as unreal nor does he stress renunciation, because in his view the root‑conscious, sat‑asat and everything are identified with the Lord – “I am the Sat‑Sat‑I‑Am, Arjuna” (Gita 9.19). Hence Sagun worship is a worship of the whole. The Gita treats Sagun as the whole and includes Brahma, Jiva, Karma, Adhibhuta, Adhidaiva and Adhijna as aspects of the universal Lord (Gita – seventh chapter, verses 29‑30). Consequently, when one looks at the Gita it appears that Nirgun worship (worship of Brahma) is the worship of one limb of the universal Lord, while Sagun worship itself is the worship of the whole Lord – “You worship Me” (Gita 12.1), “They worship Me by meditating on Me” (12.6). Whoever worships a single limb of the whole Lord ultimately attains the whole – “They obtain Me alone” (12.4), “Having known Me truly, they become established in Me thereafter” (18.55). Therefore, a person who is inclined toward Nirgun should practice Nirgun worship, but he must not disparage Sagun while insisting on Nirgun. Disparaging, denigrating, or refuting Sagun is highly detrimental to a Nirgun worshipper; it obstructs the fruition of his practice because the higher nature belongs to the Lord, and insulting it amounts to insulting the Lord. Refuting the qualities brings the reality of those qualities into being, which becomes an obstacle; without acknowledging their existence, how can the practitioner eradicate them? Hence, if a practitioner refrains from criticizing or despising others and devotes himself earnestly to his own practice, eventually all practitioners become one, for the underlying principle is singular. Ignoring Sagun may free the practitioner, but the differences do not disappear. When Sagun is not ignored, differences vanish and the practitioner attains the whole. “ye tu sarvani karmani mayi sannyasya matparah; ananyenaiva yogena mam dhyayata; yogena mam dhyayata upasate” (12.8)

- ye = these  
- tu = however  
- sarvani = all  
- karmani = actions  
- mayi = in Me  
- sannyasya = having abandoned  
- matparah = those attached to the mind‑object  
- ananyena = by exclusive devotion  
- eva = only  
- yogena = by yoga (union)  
- mam = Me  
- dhyayata = meditate  
- upasate = worship

Translation of the verse: “But those who, having abandoned all actions in Me, are devoted solely to Me by exclusive yoga, meditate on Me and worship Me.”

Explanation – In the fifty‑fifth verse of the eleventh chapter the Lord enumerated three affirmative qualities of the exclusive devotee (‘mat‑karmakrit’, ‘mat‑parama’, ‘mad‑bhakta’) and two prohibitive qualities (‘sangavarjita’, ‘nirvair’). The present verse alludes to those terms as follows:

1. ‘ananya‑yoga’ indicates the exclusive relationship (mat‑karmakrit). 2. ‘matparah’ points to ‘mat‑parama’. 3. ‘ananyenaiva yogena’ signals ‘mad‑bhakta’. The commentary further clarifies:

- Because the devotee remains exclusively attached to the Lord, he has no attachment elsewhere; therefore he is ‘sangavarjita’ (free from association). - Absence of any attachment prevents any feeling of enmity, hatred, or anger toward anyone, thus he is ‘nirvair’ (free from hostility). The phrase “ye tu sarvani karmani mayi sannyasya” is highlighted by the Lord, and the discussion proceeds to the thirteenth ‘mat‑karmakrit’. The term ‘matparah’ denotes the supreme of mind‑object, while ‘ananyenaiva yogena’ denotes the devotee of the Lord. The sages say that the true nature of the Lord is described by the terms “Brahma”, “Paramatma”, and “Bhagavan”. Hence, the practitioner must harbor no hatred toward anyone. “ye tu sarvani karmani mayi sannyasya” – now this is the dual knowledge, called Brahma, Paramatma, and Bhagavan. ( Srimad Bhagavata 1.2.11 )

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

From this point onward, the ease of worshiping the Saguna (with attributes) form is contrasted with the difficulty of worshiping the Nirguna (formless) form; all of these are actions performed for the sake of the Lord. The particle “tu” is used to distinguish the sections. Although the word “karmani” itself is plural, indicating the totality of actions, the adjective “sarvani” is added to include every activity of mind, speech, and body that is worldly (pertaining to livelihood and material existence) as well as spiritual (pertaining to japa, meditation, etc.) as prescribed in the scriptures (Gita, Chapter 9, Verse 27). Here, the phrase “mayi sannyasya” does **not** imply renouncing the very nature of action. First, renunciation of the very nature of action is impossible (Gita, Chapter 3, Verse 5 and Chapter 18, Verse 11). Second, if a Saguna‑worshipper, out of delusion, abandons the scriptural actions in their true nature, that abandonment is of the **tamas** quality (Gita, Chapter 18, Verse 7); and if he abandons them out of fear of physical suffering, considering them a source of pain, that abandonment is of the **rajas** quality (Gita, Chapter 18, Verse 8). Hence, such a mode of renunciation does not free one from the bond of action. Liberation from karmic bondage requires that the aspirant relinquishes **mama‑tṛṣā** (attachment to the self), **āsakti** (clinging), and **phale‑icchā** (desire for results), because actions performed with these motives are the very ones that bind. If the aspirant’s goal is the attainment of the Supreme (Bhagavat), he does not desire material objects, and by recognizing himself as the Lord, his attachment shifts from the body and other material entities to the Divine alone. When one offers himself wholly to the Lord, all his actions become offerings to the Divine. There are several categories of actions performed for the Lord, named in the Gita as **madarpaṇa‑karm** (actions initially intended for another purpose but later offered to the Lord), **madartha‑karm** (actions performed from the outset for the Lord or as service to the Divine), and **mat‑karm** (actions undertaken as if they are the Lord’s desire, encompassing both worldly duties such as business or employment and devotional duties such as japa and meditation). Regardless of how actions are performed, their sole purpose must be the attainment of the Supreme. An aspirant who attains perfection through any of the three types—madarpaṇa‑karm, madartha‑karm, or mat‑karm—has no longer any connection with action, because there is no longer any desire for results, no sense of personal accomplishment, and no attachment to material bodies, mind, intellect, or senses. When the instruments of action—body, mind, intellect—are no longer identified as “mine,” attachment to action cannot arise. Complete freedom from action is therefore true surrender. The deeds of perfected beings are automatically surrendered, and a seeker, aiming at total surrender, naturally strives to act in that manner. Just as a bhakti‑yogi frees himself from karmic bondage by offering all his deeds to the Lord, a jñāna‑yogi attains the same freedom by perceiving actions as natural expressions of Prakṛti, feeling completely detached and unrelated to them. The term **matparāḥ** (devoted to the Supreme) signifies seeing the Lord as the ultimate and supreme object of worship and maintaining a constant attitude of surrender toward Him. A Saguna‑worshipper who is wholly devoted to the Lord regards all auspicious deeds as performed by the Lord, and because he no longer seeks worldly enjoyment, no desire for pleasure arises, and consequently no inauspicious deeds occur. The verse “ananyenaiva yogena māṁ dhyāyanta upāsate” contains both **iccha‑related** and **upāya‑related** exclusivity: the devotees’ desired object is the Lord alone; no other goal is considered, and the Lord alone is their refuge for attainment. They regard divine grace as the sole means of success, not their own effort or personal ambition. They consider the means (upāya) and the object (upeya) to be the Lord Himself, and they worship—through japa, meditation, kirtan, etc.—with a single aim: the Lord. The statement “my dear, my only Giridhara‑Gopal, none else” exemplifies **ananya‑yoga**—the exclusive relationship with the Lord alone. [ Chapter 12 ]

* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *  
[ Verse 7 ]

**Shloka (transliterated)**  
tesham aham samuddharta mrityu‑samsara‑sagaraat  
bhavāmi na‑ciraat partha mayy‑aveshita‑chetasām

**Shloka (English rendering)**  
I become the swift rescuer of those devotees, delivering them from the ocean of death‑world. Soon, O Arjuna, I shall appear to those whose minds are immersed in Me. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
partha = “O Arjuna!”  
tesham = “of those devotees”  
mayy = “in Me”  
aveshita‑ = “immersed, possessed”  
aham = “I”  
mrityu‑samsara‑ = “death‑world” (the cycle of birth and death)  
chetasām = “of minds”  
na‑ciraat = “soon”  
samuddharta = “rescuer, deliverer”  
bhavāmi = “become”

**Commentary**

The verse means: “I become the savior of those, quickly delivering them from the ocean of death‑world.” The phrase “mayy‑aveshita‑chetasām” refers to those seekers whose sole aim, purpose and devotion have become the Lord Himself, whose hearts are wholly fixed on Him. Just as only water exists in the sea, only death exists in the world of existence. Nothing that arises in the world ever escapes even a moment’s touch of death; every created thing moves constantly toward death. Hence the world is called the “ocean of death‑world.”

If a seeker‑devotee offers all his favorable qualities to the Lord, establishing an exclusive love for the sole Supreme, and performs all unfavorable actions in the world merely as service, thereby turning away from the desire for personal gain, he can be liberated from this worldly bondage very quickly. The presence of both favorable and unfavorable tendencies is itself the cause of bondage in the world. The Lord’s universal principle is: “He who takes refuge in Me with a certain feeling, I also give refuge with the same feeling” (BG 4.11). Therefore, although He remains equally present in all beings—“I am the same in all creatures” (BG 9.29)—He especially rescues those who regard Him as their sole beloved, who perform all actions for Him, and who constantly meditate on Him. For such devotees He swiftly and perfectly lifts them out of the ocean of death‑world, allowing both favorable and unfavorable tendencies to be transformed. The conditions of the world, its circumstances, and the interplay of beings and material nature generate favorable and unfavorable tendencies, producing attachment (rāga) and aversion (dveṣa) that bind the human being in the world (BG 7.23). It is observed that even seekers become victims of rāga‑dveṣa when they develop sectarian or saintly preferences, preventing them from crossing the ocean of existence quickly. Sectarian bias is a serious obstacle for a seeker who truly longs for the ultimate reality. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – In Chapter 6, Verse 5, the Lord said that every ordinary seeker can save himself: “One should uplift oneself by one’s own effort” (BG 6.5). Here He adds that for devotees He Himself performs the rescue—“I am the rescuer of those.” This implies that initially each seeker strives on his own; those who rely on the Lord are rescued by Him because their trust is placed wholly in Him. **Illustrative citations** – “Nir‑dvandvaḥ” (2.45); “Nir‑dvandvo hi mahābāho” (5.3); “Te dvandva‑mohanir‑muktāḥ” (7.28); “Dvandvair‑vimuktāḥ” (15.5); “Na dveṣṭy‑akushalaṃ karma kuśale nānuṣajjate” (18.10); “Rāga‑dvēṣau vyudasya ca” (18.51). **Further explanation of “samuddharta bhavāmi”** – The Lord’s statement also conveys that the gracious devotee, through His grace, overcomes all obstacles in the practice, attains the desired goal, dispels the darkness of ignorance with the inner knowledge of the Supreme, and is liberated from all sins (BG 18.56). ---
