[ Verse 15 ]  
* Sadhaka – Sanjeevani *

The verse “Śānto brahmabhūyāya kalpate” (Chapter 18 Verse 53) and the line in Bhakti‑yoga “Nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ sama‑duḥkha‑sukhaḥ kṣamī” (Chapter 12 Verse 13) illustrate a special point: in reality our true nature is free of ego‑ism (aham‑tā) and of attachment (mam‑tā). Both ego‑ism and attachment are merely imagined qualities; they are not the essence of our being. If they were real, we could never become truly merciless (nirmam) and ego‑less, and the Lord would not describe Himself as merciless and ego‑less for everyone. Yet we *can* become merciless and ego‑less, and that is why the Lord makes such statements. In Karma‑yoga the first step is the renunciation of desire (kāmanā); thereafter the karmic yogi automatically becomes merciless and ego‑less (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 2 Verse 71). In Jñāna‑yoga the first step is the renunciation of ego (ahaṅkāra); then the jñāna yogi automatically becomes merciless (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 18 Verse 33). In Bhakti‑yoga the devotee offers himself to the Lord; by the Lord’s grace he automatically becomes merciless and ego‑less. “Mayyarpitamano‑buddhir yo mad‑bhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ” – here the phrase “mayyarpitamano‑buddhiḥ” refers to the person who has offered himself (himself) to the Lord. By offering oneself, the mind and intellect are also offered to the Lord. When one is offered, nothing remains apart from the offering, because the self is primary and body, mind, intellect, etc., are secondary. The devotee is primary; the human being is secondary. Once offered to the Lord, the mind‑intellect no longer retain independent existence; only the Lord remains. The Lord has an equal relationship with both the higher (para) and lower (apara) natures, but the living entity (para) does not have such a relationship with the lower nature. The living entity is superior to the lower nature and is a portion of the Lord; therefore its relationship is with the Lord. “Mayyarpitamano‑buddhiḥ” thus means that the living entity does not consider the lower nature (mind‑intellect) as its own, but regards the Lord alone as its own. The Lord is of the nature of knowledge and eternally complete. Hence He has no hunger for knowledge (curiosity), but He does have a thirst for love (prema‑pīpāsā). Therefore the Lord says that the devotee who offers his mind‑intellect to Him is dear to Him. Apart from such a devotee, no one can be dear to the Lord. Just as a king’s son who begins to beg from others does not suit the king, likewise the portion of the Lord that is Sat‑citta‑ānanda (existence‑consciousness‑bliss) does not suit the Lord when the living entity, being bound by the unreal, inert, sorrowful world, clings to hope in the Lord; it appears unlovely because the living entity’s great harm remains. The Lord loves only that which has no hope in anything else and in which the living entity’s supreme welfare is present – the embodiment of compassion. “Ek bāni karunānidhān kī. So priya jāke gati na ān kī” (Manas, Aranya 10.4). **Relation (Sambandh)** – This is the second section on the characteristics of the established devotee, describing six qualities, which appear in the following verse. **Verse (Bhagavad‑Gītā)**  
Yas‑mān‑na‑udvijate loko lokān‑na‑udvijate ca yaḥ  
Harṣa‑marṣa‑bhayo‑dvegair‑mukto yaḥ sa ca me priyaḥ || 15 ||

*Transliteration:*  
yas‑mān‑na‑udvijate loko lokān‑na‑udvijate ca yaḥ  
harṣa‑marṣa‑bhayo‑dvegair‑mukto yaḥ sa ca me priyaḥ

*Literal meaning:*  
He who is not disturbed by the world, and the world is not disturbed by him;  
who is free from joy, envy, fear and anxiety;  
such a one is dear to Me. **Bottom commentary**  
In this passage “man” includes both the mind‑stream (citta) and the ego‑sense (ahaṃkāra) that resides under intellect. The devotee who is untouched by worldly agitation and who does not cause agitation in the world, who is free from all emotional turbulence, is precisely the one whom the Lord calls dear.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The commentary explains that a true devotee (bhakta) sees the Supreme Lord everywhere and in everyone. Consequently, in the devotee’s vision, all actions of mind, speech, and body are performed solely for the pleasure of the Lord (Gita 6.31). In such a state, how could the devotee cause any creature distress? Yet, in the character of devotees one observes that their glory, honor, and even their gentle demeanor sometimes provoke envy in some people, who then develop baseless hatred and opposition toward the devotees. If one examines the relationship between people and the distress caused by devotees, it becomes clear that the actions of a devotee never become the cause of anyone’s distress, because the devotee sees only the Divine in every being—“Vāsudevaḥ sarvam” (Gita 7.19). The devotee’s actions are naturally intended for the ultimate welfare of all beings. He never, even inadvertently, acts against anyone’s interest. Those who feel disturbed by him do so because of their own attachment‑driven, demonic nature. Their own defective disposition makes even the devotee’s benevolent actions appear disturbing. What fault lies with the devotee? Bhartṛhari says:

* mṛgamīna‑sajjanānāṁ tṛṇa‑jala‑santoṣa‑vihita‑vṛttīnām |  
* lubdhakadhīvara‑piśunā niṣkāraṇa‑vairiṇo jagati || (Bhartṛhari, Nīti‑śataka 61)

Translation: “Deer, fish, and virtuous persons subsist on grass, water, and contentment without saying anything to anyone; yet the diseased, the turtles, and the wicked people become hostile to them without cause.”

Thus, the question of devotees causing agitation in other humans does not arise. Conversely, there are episodes in the lives of devotees where even those who initially harbored hatred become devotees themselves after experiencing the influence of the devotee’s thought, presence, touch, and conversation. The generous nature of the devotees is the cause of such transformation. Uma‑saint says:

* umā‑santa kai iha‑i baṛāī |  
* manda‑karata jo karai bhalaī || (Mānas 5.41.4)

Translation: “O saint, how great is the praise here; one who performs good deeds gently.”

Nevertheless, it is not a universal rule that all who oppose devotees gain benefit. [ Chapter 12 ]

The text notes that the absence of enemies or friends for a devotee does not imply that the categories of enemy‑friend, honor‑disgrace, blame‑praise, etc., are identical for the devotee (as mentioned later in verses 18‑19). The implication is that, because of their demonic nature, people may feel agitation even from the devotee’s beneficial actions and may act against the devotee, considering themselves his enemies; yet, from the devotee’s perspective, there is no enemy and no inclination to disturb anyone. The verse “lokān nodvijate ca yaḥ” (the Lord previously said that a devotee does not cause distress to any being) now indicates that the devotee himself also does not become distressed by any being. Two reasons are given:

1. Even actions and events that arise against the devotee’s body, mind, senses, or principles occur without his desire or aversion. Because the devotee fully realizes reality and loves the Lord intensely, he remains immersed in divine love, perceiving the Lord’s presence everywhere and in everyone. Hence, even the actions of other beings (however adverse) appear to him as the Lord’s play, and he never feels agitation from any action. 2. A human becomes agitated by others only when his own desires, beliefs, practices, or perceptions are opposed. The devotee is completely fulfilled in his desire for the Divine; therefore, there is no cause for agitation from others. The verse “harṣāmārṣabhayodvegair mukto yaḥ sa ca me priyaḥ” (the one liberated from joy, sorrow, fear, and distress is dear to Me) signifies that a perfected devotee is free from all mental disturbances such as joy, sorrow, etc. This does not mean the devotee is devoid of joy; rather, his joy is constant, unique, and transcendental, not dependent on the fleeting, perishable, and changing material circumstances. Because his consciousness is ever immersed in the Divine, he constantly experiences the pleasure of beholding his beloved God and the Lord’s pastimes. If one assumes that a devotee never causes distress to anyone’s progress (or that any action against the devotee is called “amarsa”), the text proceeds to discuss further nuances, but the essential teaching remains: a true devotee, immersed in the vision of the Supreme, neither creates nor experiences agitation.

[ Verse 15 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

The abundance of comforts, wealth, learning, fame, honor and respect makes one see only divine play. Yet, when a person perceives the Lord’s divine play within his own heart, how can fear arise in the ordinary mind? Envy toward the Lord begins, because the mind cannot tolerate the exaltation of others. Often, when a seeker witnesses or hears of another seeker’s spiritual progress and happiness, a slight feeling of jealousy may arise. The devotee, however, is completely free from this defect; his vision admits no independent power except that of his beloved Lord. Consequently, he has no reason to feel resentment toward anyone, nor any motive to do so. If, upon seeing another’s spiritual advancement, a seeker develops the desire that he too may attain such progress, this feeling aids his practice. But if the heart generates the notion “Why has his progress occurred?” a harmful attitude arises, leading to a feeling of resentment that can cause downfall. The anxiety that results from the separation from the beloved (the “desired”) and the conjunction with the undesirable is called “fear.” Fear arises from two sources: (1) external causes—such as lions, snakes, thieves, bandits, or any anticipated worldly loss; and (2) internal causes—such as theft, falsehood, deceit, adultery, and other actions or emotions that contradict the scriptures. The greatest fear is the fear of death; even the most discerning men are often haunted by it. A seeker also commonly fears the frailty of the body that may result from practices like satsanga, bhajan, meditation, etc. He may worry that, if he becomes completely detached from the world, how will his body and family be sustained? An ordinary person fears stronger individuals who can obstruct the attainment of desirable objects. All these fears arise from attachment to the body (its rigidity). The devotee, being wholly dependent on the Lord’s feet, remains perpetually free of fear. Likewise, a seeker retains fear only until he becomes completely dependent on the Lord’s feet. A perfected devotee is ever, everywhere, united with his beloved Lord. When the mind ceases to be steady and becomes agitated, it is called “udvega” (disturbance). In this fifteenth verse the word “udvega” appears three times. The first occurrence explains that no action of the devotee ever becomes the cause of another person’s disturbance. The second occurrence states that no deed of other people can disturb the devotee’s heart. Besides these, many other causes can disturb a human being: repeated attempts that still fail to complete a task, not receiving the desired fruit of an effort, involuntary seasonal changes, earthquakes, floods, and other calamities, or obstacles to one’s wishes, beliefs, principles, or means of practice. The third mention of “udvega” emphasizes that the devotee is entirely free from all such disturbances. In the devotee’s heart there is no entity called “udvega.” Such agitation originates from ignorance‑driven desire and an asura (demonic) nature. Because the devotee is completely devoid of ignorance, no independent desire remains, and the asura nature is destroyed at the stage of practice. The devotee’s will is identical with the Lord’s will. He perceives the Lord’s gracious ordinance in every result of his actions or in any involuntary favorable or unfavorable circumstance, and remains immersed in continual bliss. Hence, the devotee is utterly devoid of “udvega.”

The term “mukt” (liberated) means completely free from all mental disturbances. When the heart retains attachment to the world, i.e., when the mind and intellect are still partially fixed on the Supreme, emotions such as joy, sorrow, fear, and agitation arise. In the devotee’s view, because no independent power or significance exists apart from the Lord, these disturbances never arise, and natural virtues and moral conduct prevail. In this verse the Lord uses the word “mukt” instead of “bhakta,” indicating that the devotee is entirely free from all vices and misconduct. Pride in one’s virtues invites the emergence of vices. * svarasavāhī viduṣo'pi tathārūḍho'bhiniveśaḥ — “Even a learned person who clings to the sound (of the scriptures) remains bound by his inner disposition.” (Patanjala Yogadarshana 2.9)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 12 ]

The devotee usually lacks even the slightest awareness that any virtue resides within him. If he ever perceives a quality in himself, he attributes it to God, not to himself. Because of this lack of pride in one’s own qualities, the devotee is freed from all vices, misdeeds, and mental disturbances. The devotee is dear to God, and therefore God is dear to the devotee (Gita – seventh chapter). When a quality arises in a person, pride‑based vice is generated; how then can that quality be called a true quality? Divine qualities (sattvic virtues) can never give rise to demonic qualities (rajasic or tamasic vices). If demonic qualities could arise from divine ones, the statement “Divine wealth leads to liberation” (Gita 16.5) would be meaningless, for it would imply that a person could become free while still attached to pride. In reality, the pride that accompanies virtues is actually a reduction of virtue and an increase of vice. Pride fuels the growth of vices, because all vices—misdeeds, immoral conduct—stem from pride (see Verse 17). Appendix meaning – Disturbance, jealousy, fear, etc., arise only when one gives importance to another entity. In the devotee’s view, apart from the Supreme, no other power exists; therefore, from what source could he feel disturbance, jealousy, or fear, and why would he? – “One sees only the Lord as the true master; all else is opposition” (Manas, answer 112‑k). Connection – The third chapter, which describes the six qualities of a perfected devotee, appears in the following verses. **Verse 16**  
*Anapekṣaḥ śuciḥ dakṣaḥ udāsīnaḥ gatavyathaḥ  
Sarvārambhaparityāgī yo mad‑bhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ*

Word‑by‑word translation:

- **Anapekṣaḥ** – without expectation, free from desire for reward  
- **Śuciḥ** – pure, immaculate  
- **Dakṣaḥ** – skillful, competent, adept  
- **Udāsīnaḥ** – indifferent, detached, unperturbed  
- **Gatavyathaḥ** – beyond all distress, free from suffering  
- **Sarvārambha‑parityāgī** – one who completely renounces all beginnings, abandons every new undertaking  
- **Yo** – who  
- **Mad‑bhaktaḥ** – my devotee, one who is devoted to Me  
- **Sa** – he  
- **Me priyaḥ** – is dear to Me

Thus the verse declares: “He who, without expectation, pure, skillful, indifferent, beyond all distress, who has renounced every new undertaking, is My devotee, is dear to Me.”

Interpretation – “Anapekṣa” signifies that the devotee regards the Supreme alone as the highest; no benefit surpasses the attainment of the Divine. Consequently, he feels no attachment to any worldly object. Moreover, even his own body, senses, mind, and intellect are not regarded as his own; he sees them as belonging to the Lord, who in truth is the owner of all. Hence he has no concern for material sustenance. What further expectation can he have? He is free from all desire, longing, and craving for any object. Even when great obstacles arise for the devotee, knowledge of the obstacle does not disturb his mind. In the most terrifying circumstances, he remains absorbed in the divine play of the Lord and does not seek any favorable condition. Perishable material objects do not truly exist; their separation is inevitable, while the imperishable Supreme Self never separates. Knowing this, the devotee naturally loses any longing for transient things. It is important to note that there is no rule that merely wishing for material needs brings them, nor that not wishing deprives them. In reality, the material requisites for bodily existence are provided automatically, because the Lord has already arranged the necessary provisions for the living being. Desire actually hinders the acquisition of needed items. If a person clings to a strong inner desire—“How will I obtain that object? Where will I find it? When will I get it?”—the expansion of that desire is blocked.

* Sadhak - Sanjivani *

In other words, his desire does not reach the hearts of other people; because of this, the devotee’s body becomes extremely pure. Since the inner self is free from attachment‑aversion, joy‑sorrow, desire‑anger and similar disturbances, his inner self also becomes extremely pure. Such a devotee, who is pure both outwardly and inwardly, sanctifies others through his sight, touch, conversation, and contemplation. Pilgrimage sites purify all people; however, such a devotee also confers sanctity upon the pilgrimage sites, i.e., the sites become pure through his foot‑touch (yet the devotee harbors no such ego). With the supreme purity “Pavitrānāṁ Pavitram” (the purest of the pure) residing in his heart, through the Lord’s influence he makes even the pilgrimage sites great tirthas as he moves about. tīrthī kurvanti tīrthāni pahunch pāti. – “Pilgrims become the pilgrimage places and attain them.”

For this reason, there is no desire or impulse in the hearts of others to give that necessary object. It is often observed that those who have a strong desire to take—such as thieves—find no one willing to give. Conversely, one who has no desire for any object, a renunciate, experiences the needs of a child spontaneously, and others gladly provide for his bodily sustenance. Thus it is proved that by not desiring, the essential means of livelihood are obtained automatically without asking. Hence desiring objects is merely folly and leads to needless suffering. The realized devotee has no expectation even of the body that is called his; therefore he is completely self‑less. Some devotees do not even expect the Lord’s vision! Whether the Lord grants vision or not, they remain in bliss, because they are ever delighted by the Lord’s pleasure and grace. Such self‑less devotees are constantly followed by the Lord himself. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

A realized devotee possesses practical (worldly) competence, but to regard the test of worldly competence as the criterion for transcendental (parāmārthika) standing is essentially to insult the realized devotee. ‘Udasīnaḥ’ – the word *udāsīna* means “ut + āsīna”, i.e., seated above, neutral, free from bias. A person who remains completely neutral toward two disputants is called *udāsīna*. The term denotes detachment. Just as a man standing on a high mountain is unaffected by fire or flood below, a devotee remains unaffected by any condition, event, or circumstance; he is ever detached. One who wishes the devotee’s welfare and acts in his favor is considered his friend; one who wishes the devotee’s harm and acts against him is his enemy. This distinction may be evident in the devotee’s external conduct toward friends and foes, but in the devotee’s inner heart there is no discrimination at all. He remains wholly indifferent—detached—in both situations. The devotee’s inner self has no independent power; he regards the entire universe, including his own body, as the Supreme Self (Paramātmā). Consequently his behavior is free of partiality. ‘Gatavyathaḥ’ – whether one receives or is denied, whether anything comes or goes, the devotee’s mind never experiences the agitation of sorrow, anxiety, or grief; such a person is described as *gatavyatha*. Here *vyatha* does not merely denote sorrow; the mental agitation that arises from pleasure when circumstances are favorable, or from distress when they are not, is also *vyatha*. Thus the complete absence of mental fluctuations—attachment, aversion, joy, sorrow—arising from favorable or adverse conditions is what is meant by *gatavyatha*. ‘Sarvārambhaparityāgī’ – actions undertaken for the purpose of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and accumulation (*saṅgraha*) are called *ārambha* (new undertakings). For example, acquiring new household items for comfort, buying clothes, opening new shops to increase wealth, or starting a new business. The devotee completely renounces such merely instrumental actions. A person whose aim is worldly gain and who distinguishes himself by caste, ashrama, learning, intellect, ability, position, or authority is not a devotee. The devotee is devoted to the Lord; therefore his body, senses, mind, intellect, actions, and results are all offered to the Lord. In reality, the Lord is the true owner of the body and all its functions. Nature and its operations belong to the Lord. Hence the devotee regards no one else as his own. He never does anything for himself; his actions are performed solely for the Lord’s pleasure. He never engages in deeds motivated by wealth, comfort, honor, or prestige. Whoever is sincerely devoted to the realization of the Supreme Self (Paramātmā), regardless of the path he follows, never initiates a new *ārambha* for the sake of enjoyment or accumulation. ‘Yo mad‑bhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ’ – the Lord possesses such an inherent, magnificent attraction that the devotee is automatically drawn to Him and becomes His beloved. ātmārāmāś ca munayo nirgṛnthā apyurukrame | kurvanti ahaityukīm bhaktimittabhūtaguṇo hariḥ || ( Srimad Bhagavata 1.7.10 )  
*Translation*: The sages who delight in the Self, though unattached, still perform self‑less devotion; the qualities of the Lord Hari draw beings toward Him. By knowledge, those whose dense mental knots have been cut, even the self‑delighting sages practice self‑less (nirguṇa) devotion, because the Lord’s qualities irresistibly attract all beings. A question may arise: if the Lord’s attraction is so great, why do not all humans automatically gravitate toward Him and become His lovers? In truth, every living being is a fragment of the Lord; therefore an innate attraction toward the Lord exists in each. Yet those who truly belong to the Lord are described in the following verse:

anārambha aniket amānī | anagha aroṣa dacc bigyānī || ( Manas 7.46.3 )  
*Translation*: He who is without beginning, without abode, without measure; pure, unblemished, and ever‑wise.

[ Verse 17 ]  
* Sadhak – Sanjeevani *

The human being does not regard the self‑body, mind, intellect and the senses as his own; his attachment is only to the objects of the senses, i.e., to sensual enjoyments. Because he does not see the Divine hidden in those objects, he takes them as his own. Consequently, his attraction toward material sustenance and fleeting pleasures wanes, and he is drawn automatically toward the Divine. In the world he becomes turned away from God. Yet even a minute attachment that remains should not be taken as a real separation for the devotee, because the Divine is self‑loving. A devotee whose love for God is exclusive is called *mad‑bhakta* (intimate devotee) when he is drawn toward perishable enjoyments; the apparent distance is only an illusion, for a devotee who loves God exclusively perceives God in every enjoyment, and God remains ever‑present and beloved. **Appendix – “Anapekṣa” (unexpectant)**  
Anapekṣa means that the devotee does not entertain the expectation “if this object is absent, how will desire be satisfied?” In the devotee’s vision everything is God alone, so no expectation toward anything else arises. *Śuci* (purity) – the devotee’s sight, touch and speech purify others; even the air that touches his body is pure. Although such purity also exists in a jñāna‑yogi great soul, the devotee possesses a special purity from the beginning because of his universal friendliness (friendliness, compassion). *Dakṣa* – the devotee has performed the appropriate work; he has become the accomplished, the known, the to‑be‑known and the attained, therefore he is called *dakṣa* (competent). *Sarvārambhaparityāgī* – this epithet appears in Chapter 14, Verse 25 for a *guṇātīta* (beyond‑qualities) great soul: “One who is beyond qualities is called *sarvārambhaparityāgī*.” Because a *guṇātīta* being has no personal agency, he renounces all beginnings; likewise a devotee, free of selfishness and pride, renounces all beginnings. The devotee has nothing left to do for himself, so what “beginning” can he undertake? He may initiate action, but without attachment, desire, purpose or compulsion; whether the action occurs or not, he remains balanced in both cases. **Relation – the fourth chapter on the five qualities of a perfected devotee appears in the following verses.**

Yo na hṛsyati na dveṣṭi na śocati na kāṅkṣati. Śubhāśubhaparityāgī bhaktimān yaḥ sa me priyaḥ. — 17

*Word‑by‑word breakdown*  
- **yo**: he who  
- **na**: not  
- **hṛsyati**: rejoices  
- **na**: not  
- **dveṣṭi**: hates  
- **na**: not  
- **śocati**: grieves  
- **na**: not  
- **kāṅkṣati**: desires  
- **śubhā‑śubha‑parityāgī**: one who renounces both auspicious and inauspicious actions  
- **bhaktimān**: devoted, full of devotion  
- **yaḥ**: who  
- **sa**: he  
- **me**: to me  
- **priyaḥ**: beloved

**Explanation** – “He who does not rejoice, does not hate, does not grieve, and never desires the Divine” – the four principal afflictions are (1) attachment (rāga), (2) the feeling of perpetual separation (viyoga) which never truly occurs, (3) hatred, (4) joy, and (5) grief. In a perfected devotee none of these arise, remain, or can arise; therefore worldly disturbances do not affect him. He experiences that there is no independent entity – this is the realization of ultimate reality. (In ordinary language the word “śoka” denotes sorrow caused by another’s death; here it denotes the inner mental disturbance, i.e., *vikāra*.)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 12 ]

After attaining the divine vision, just as the sun shines without any attachment to material inertia, the devotee’s experience of his eternal, established relationship with the Lord remains immutable. Consequently, his inner self becomes completely free from attachment, aversion, and similar mental disturbances. When the Lord is realized, these disturbances disappear entirely. Even in the practice stage, as the aspirant progresses in his means, attachment, aversion, and related tendencies gradually diminish. What diminishes also ceases to exist. Therefore, when these tendencies begin to lessen during practice, it can be safely inferred that in the state of perfection they will be wholly absent, having been completely eradicated. Joy and sorrow are both results of attachment and aversion. Joy arises from the union with that toward which one feels attachment and from the separation from that toward which one feels aversion. Conversely, sorrow arises from the separation (or the fear of separation) from that toward which one feels attachment and from the union (or the fear of union) with that toward which one feels aversion. In a perfected devotee, the extreme absence of attachment and aversion automatically creates a continuous state of equanimity, rendering the mind entirely free of disturbances. Such a person never experiences these disturbances; he becomes perfectly fulfilled and therefore has no need for worldly existence. The term “renouncer of both auspicious and inauspicious” (śubhāśubhaparityāgī) signifies that, being free from affection, attachment, and desire for results, the devotee’s actions become essentially non‑action (akarma). Hence he is described as a renouncer even of virtuous deeds. Because attachment and aversion are completely absent, inauspicious actions do not arise. The primary causes of inauspicious deeds are desire, affection, and attachment, all of which are entirely lacking in the devotee; therefore he is also called a renouncer of inauspicious deeds. The devotee feels no attachment toward auspicious actions and no aversion toward inauspicious actions. He naturally performs scripturally prescribed virtuous deeds and abandons prohibited or undesirable deeds, not out of attachment or aversion but out of pure renunciation. Only one who wholly abandons attachment and aversion can be called a true renouncer. Human beings are not bound by actions themselves; rather, it is attachment and aversion within actions that bind them. The devotee’s complete set of actions is free from attachment and aversion, making him a renouncer of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds. Thus, the expression “renouncer of both auspicious and inauspicious” can be understood as one who relinquishes the fruits of both good and bad actions. In the first half of the verse, the statements “does not rejoice, does not develop aversion, does not mourn, does not desire” refer to the renunciation of both favorable (auspicious) and unfavorable (inauspicious) results. Consequently, the meaning of the term must be taken as the renunciation of attachment and aversion toward both auspicious and inauspicious outcomes. Just as, at night, one wishes to light a lamp; lighting the lamp brings joy, the one who extinguishes it evokes aversion or anger, and one worries about how the lamp will burn again. Darkness creates all four mental states. In contrast, when the midday sun shines, there is no desire to light a lamp, no joy in lighting it, no aversion toward the one who puts it out, and no anxiety about the lack of light. Similarly, when one turns away from the Lord and turns toward the world, one desires material comforts, circumstances, and objects for bodily sustenance and pleasure; their attainment brings joy, obstacles to their attainment provoke aversion or anger, and their absence generates anxiety about how the devotee can maintain exclusive love for the Lord. However, the devotee who is dear to the Lord—“the devotee is dear to Me”—experiences an innate, spontaneous contemplation, remembrance, and singing of the Lord. Such a devotee is called “bhaktimān” (one endowed with devotion). The appendix notes that joy (hṛṣyati) and sorrow (śocati), desire (kāṅkṣati) and aversion (dveṣṭi) constitute a duality. In the devotee, no such duality remains; he becomes non‑dual. As expressed in the Narada Bhakti‑Sutra:

“Having attained, he desires nothing, mourns nothing, bears no aversion, does not delight, and is not eager for any object.”

Thus, the perfected devotee is free from all mental fluctuations.

[ Verse 18 - 19 ]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *
[Verse 19]
Connection— Now, in the next two verses, the fifth and final chapter describing the ten characteristics of a perfected devotee is being discussed. He who is the same towards a foe and a friend, and also towards honor and dishonor, and who is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and who is free from attachment. He who is the same in praise and blame, and who is silent (i.e., self-controlled), and who is content with whatever comes his way, and who has no home (i.e., is not attached to any place), and who has a steady mind, and who is devoted to Me, is dear to Me. = (He who) is the same towards an enemy and a friend, and also towards honor and dishonor, and who is the same in cold and heat (i.e., remains equanimous in the face of physical discomfort), and who is free from attachment, and who is content, and who has no abode (i.e., is not attached to any place), and who has a steady mind, and who is devoted to Me, is dear to Me. Explanation— 'He who is the same towards a foe and a friend' - Here, the Lord has said that the devotee makes an impartial distribution (i.e., without favoritism). Therefore, even though the devotee's decision may seem biased, it is actually impartial. The characteristic of a devotee, being the same towards all individuals, has been described. Due to the presence of divine consciousness and the absence of attachment and aversion, a perfected devotee does not have feelings of enmity or friendship towards anyone. People may perceive the devotee's behavior as friendly or hostile based on their own nature, but the devotee remains always equanimous. Even careful seekers may have feelings of friendship or enmity towards the perfected devotee, but the devotee's heart never harbors such feelings. Suppose two individuals, one with a hostile attitude and the other with a friendly attitude towards the devotee, come to the devotee with a dispute related to the distribution of wealth. If the devotee were to make a decision, he might give more wealth to the hostile person and less to the friendly person. Although the devotee's decision may seem biased, it is actually impartial. The above verses also prove that people behave towards the perfected devotee with either hostility or friendship, and they consider themselves to be either the devotee's friend or enemy based on the devotee's behavior. This is why the devotee is described as being the same towards friends and enemies, rather than being without friends and enemies. 'And also towards honor and dishonor' - Honor and dishonor are actions that affect the body. The devotee does not have a sense of ego or attachment towards their body. Therefore, when the body is honored or dishonored, the devotee's inner self remains unaffected and equanimous. 'He who is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain' - These words describe the devotee's equanimity in two situations: (1) being the same in cold and heat, i.e., remaining unaffected when the senses come into contact with their respective objects, and (2) being the same in pleasure and pain.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 12
(2) To remain equanimous in happiness and distress, and to remain unaffected by the acquisition or non-acquisition of worldly objects, is the true meaning of 'sukha-duhkha-samata'. The term 'shita-ushna' refers to 'heat and cold'. Heat and cold are the subjects of the skin and sensory organs. A devotee does not remain equanimous only in the subjects of the skin and sensory organs. He remains equanimous in all subjects. Therefore, in this context, the term 'shita-ushna' refers to all subjects. When each sensory organ comes into contact with its respective subject, the devotee is aware of the (favorable or unfavorable) subject, but he does not experience any disturbance in his mind. He remains equanimous at all times. An ordinary person experiences happiness and distress due to the acquisition of favorable worldly objects and the non-acquisition of unfavorable objects. However, even in the acquisition or non-acquisition of these objects, the mind of a realized devotee remains unaffected. He remains equanimous in all situations. The term 'sukha-duhkha-samata' and 'sukha-duhkha-samatah' have the same meaning in the Gita. Happiness and distress are inevitable; therefore, it is impossible to remain unaffected by them. Hence, a devotee remains equanimous in all situations. However, it is possible to remain unaffected by the disturbances of happiness and distress. In this context, the Gita refers to remaining equanimous in all situations, and in another context, it refers to remaining unaffected by the disturbances of happiness and distress. The term 'sang-vivarjitah' means 'free from association' or 'free from attachment'. It is impossible for a human being to completely sever all relationships with the world, as long as he is alive, his body, mind, intellect, and senses are all associated with him. However, it is possible to renounce certain objects that are separate from the body. If a person renounces the association of worldly objects, but still has a slight attachment to them in his mind, then he is still associated with them. On the other hand, if a person has no attachment to worldly objects in his mind, then he is not associated with them, even if they are present in front of him. If renouncing worldly objects completely led to liberation, then every person who dies would be liberated, as they have already renounced their bodies. However, this is not the case. Even after renouncing worldly objects, a person's attachment to them remains in his mind, and this attachment binds him to the world. Therefore, it is the attachment to the world that binds a person, not the association with worldly objects. Renouncing worldly objects is one of the means to eliminate attachment. However, the primary need is to eliminate attachment completely. If a person has even a slight attachment to the world, then he will inevitably think about it. This attachment can lead the seeker to desire, anger, foolishness, and other negative qualities, which can ultimately lead to his downfall (Gita, Chapter 2, Verse 59-63). The Lord has stated in the second chapter, Verse 55, that after attaining the Lord, attachment is completely eliminated. However, it is possible to eliminate attachment even before attaining the Lord. In fact, attachment is completely eliminated in the Lord Himself. However, it is not a rule that attachment is completely eliminated in the seeker before attaining the Lord. A seeker can attain the Lord even if attachment is not completely eliminated in him (Gita, Chapter 5, Verse 21 and 22). Attachment does not exist in the pure consciousness of the Supreme Being, nor does it exist in the inert world. It exists in the 'I' - sense of the individual, which is a combination of the conscious and the inert. Attachment manifests itself in the mind, intellect, senses, and objects. If the 'I' - sense of the individual is eliminated, then attachment will automatically be eliminated. The cause of attachment is ignorance. If a seeker does not give importance to his own discrimination, then he will remain attached. A devotee does not remain attached. Therefore,

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
He is completely free from attachment. * Sadhak Sanjivani *
Due to ignorance, one turns away from the Lord and considers the world as one's own, resulting in attachment to the world. When the sense of ownership towards the world is completely eradicated, the intellect becomes balanced. As the intellect becomes balanced, one becomes naturally free from attachment. A profound statement
In reality, every living being has a natural affection (love) for the Lord. As long as there is a sense of ownership towards the world due to ignorance, this affection does not manifest and instead appears as attachment to the world. The attachment to the world does not diminish the affection for the Lord. As soon as the affection for the Lord becomes apparent, attachment (like darkness at sunrise) disappears completely. As one becomes detached from the world, the affection for the Lord becomes more apparent. It is a rule that after eliminating attachment, detachment also subsides, just like a fire that burns wood. In this way, when attachment and detachment are absent, the natural affection (love for the Lord) begins to flow spontaneously. No effort is required for this. Then, the devotee becomes completely surrendered to the Lord, and all their actions are done for the pleasure of the Lord. The Lord, being pleased, bestows His love upon the devotee. The devotee then dedicates this love back to the Lord, which delights the Lord even more, and He again bestows His love. The devotee once again dedicates it to the Lord. In this way, the exchange of ever-increasing love between the devotee and the Lord continues. "Tulya-nindastuti" - criticism and praise are primarily based on names. This is also an external action. People criticize or praise the devotee according to their nature. The devotee has no ego or attachment to their name or body; therefore, criticism or praise has no effect on them. The devotee does not have any affection for those who praise them or any aversion towards those who criticize them. They remain equanimous in both situations. Ordinary people have a desire for praise, so they feel unhappy when criticized and happy when praised. In contrast, the devotee remains cautious when criticized and feels ashamed when praised. However, since the devotee has no attachment to their name, they are unaffected by both and remain equanimous. They may, however, behave like a seeker (cautious when criticized and ashamed when praised) for the sake of worldly interactions. The devotee's constant awareness of the Lord also prevents them from discriminating between those who criticize or praise them. This lack of discrimination is evident in their equanimity towards criticism and praise. The devotee cannot perform any inauspicious actions, and they attribute any auspicious actions to the Lord alone. Therefore, whether someone criticizes or praises them, it does not create any disturbance in their mind. "Mouni" - the perfected devotee is constantly engaged in the natural contemplation of the Lord's nature. Hence, they are called "Mouni" or contemplative. In every thought that arises in their mind, they see "Vasudeva sarvam" (the Lord is everything). Therefore, they are always contemplating the Lord. Here, the term "Mouni" does not mean one who observes silence of speech, because if that were the case, devotees who spread devotion through speech would not be considered devotees. Moreover, if observing silence of speech were enough to make one a devotee, it would be very easy to become a devotee, and there would be countless devotees in the world. However, the number of devotees in the world is not seen to be very high. Additionally, a person with a demonic nature can also forcibly observe silence of speech. But here, we are describing the characteristics of a perfected devotee who has attained the Lord. Therefore, it is reasonable to interpret "Mouni" as one who contemplates the Lord's nature. "Santhushto yena kenachit" - the devotee appears to be content with whatever they receive for the sake of maintaining their body, according to their destiny. However, in reality, the devotee's contentment is not due to any worldly object or circumstance. The sole reason for their contentment is the Lord alone.

[ Chapter 12 ]
He always goes to the Lord, being in love with Him, and remains satisfied with the Lord. Due to this satisfaction, he remains equal in every favorable or unfavorable circumstance of the world, because in his experience, every favorable or unfavorable circumstance comes from the Lord's auspicious will. Therefore, due to being always satisfied in every circumstance, he is called 'santushto yena kenachit' (one who is satisfied in any way). 'Aniketah' - it is not that one who has no abode is 'aniktet'. Whether one is a householder or a monk, one who has no attachment or affection for one's place of residence is 'aniktet'. A devotee has no attachment or affection for his place of residence or his body (gross, subtle, and causal). Therefore, he is called 'aniktet'. 'Sthiramati' - the devotee's intellect has no doubt or misconception about the existence and nature of the Lord. Therefore, his intellect is never distracted from the knowledge of the Lord. Hence, he is called 'sthiramati'. To know the Lord, he does not need any evidence or scriptural consideration, self-study, etc., because he is naturally absorbed in the Lord. The desires are the obstacle to having a steady mind (Gita 2.44). Therefore, it is possible to have a steady mind only by renouncing desires (Gita 2.55). As long as there is a desire for worldly happiness in the heart, there is attachment to the world. This attachment does not disappear even when one knows the world to be unreal. Therefore, as long as there is a desire for worldly happiness, the attachment to the world does not disappear, and the independent existence of the world becomes firm. When the desire for worldly happiness disappears, the attachment disappears, and the independent existence of the world disappears, and the intellect becomes steady in the Lord. 'Bhaktiman' - the word 'bhakti' is used with the suffix 'matup' in the sense of constant union. This means that man has a natural love for the Lord. The mistake of man is that he leaves the Lord and starts loving the world. Therefore, he does not get the taste of natural love for the Lord, and his life remains dull. A perfect devotee is always absorbed in the taste of devotion. Therefore, he is called 'bhaktiman'. Such a devotee is dear to the Lord. The word 'narah' means that one who has made his human life successful by attaining the Lord is the one who is worthy of being called a human being. One who is engaged only in worldly enjoyment and accumulation, having obtained a human body, is not worthy of being called a human being. [ These two verses describe the devotee's state of being always equal. To be equal in the five dualities - enemy and friend, honor and dishonor, cold and heat, happiness and sorrow, and censure and praise - is the state of being perfectly equal. ]

Topic Connection
Special Topic Connection
The Lord described the characteristics of perfect devotees in the thirteenth and fourteenth verses of the first topic and said, 'Yo madbhaktah sa me priyah' (he who is my devotee is dear to me). In the second topic, He said, 'Yah sa cha me priyah' (he who is that is dear to me) at the end of the fifteenth verse. In the third topic, He said, 'Yo madbhaktah sa me priyah' (he who is my devotee is dear to me) at the end of the sixteenth verse. In the fourth topic, He said, 'Bhaktiman yah sa me priyah' (he who is devoted to me is dear to me) at the end of the seventeenth verse. And in the fifth topic, He said, 'Bhaktiman me priyo narah' (he who is devoted to me is dear to me, that man) at the end of the eighteenth and nineteenth verses. Thus, the Lord has divided the characteristics of perfect devotees into five parts by using the phrase 'me priyah' (dear to me) five times. Therefore, the characteristics of perfect devotees described in seven verses should not be considered as part of a single topic. The main reason for this is that if it were a single topic, the same characteristic would not be repeated, and the phrase 'me priyah' would also be used only once.

[ Verse 20 ]
* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
In all the five sections, the characteristics of devotees have been described, and the absence of attachment and aversion, as well as joy and sorrow, has been mentioned twice. If we consider the characteristics of devotees as one section, then there would be repetition, as the word "nirmamah" (without attachment) indicates the absence of attachment, and the word "advesta" (without aversion) indicates the absence of aversion. It is not possible for the words of the Lord to be repetitive. Therefore, it is said that the subject of all seven verses is one. In the first section, the absence of attachment is indicated by the word "nirmamah", and the absence of aversion is indicated by the word "advesta". In the second section, the absence of attachment and aversion is indicated by the words "harshamarshabhayodvegaih" (fear, anger, and aversion). In the third section, the absence of attachment is indicated by the word "anapekshah" (without expectation), and the absence of aversion is indicated by the word "udasinah" (indifferent). In the fourth section, the absence of attachment is indicated by the words "na kankshati" (does not desire), and the absence of aversion is indicated by the words "na dveshti" (does not hate). In the fifth section, the absence of attachment is indicated by the word "sangavivarjitah" (without attachment), and the absence of aversion is indicated by the word "santushtah" (content). Thus, all five sections are independent, and each section describes the characteristics of devotees. The reason for describing different characteristics in each section is that the nature of devotees varies due to differences in their spiritual practices, past actions, caste, stage of life, country, time, and circumstances. However, the absence of attachment, aversion, joy, and sorrow, as well as the state of equilibrium, is the same for all devotees. A seeker should follow the section that is most suitable for them, according to their taste, faith, and nature. If a seeker is unable to attain all the characteristics of a devotee, they should not be discouraged. If there were only one section describing the characteristics of devotees, it would not be necessary to repeat the absence of attachment, aversion, joy, and sorrow. Appendix - In these two verses, the Lord has described the places where it is difficult to maintain equilibrium. If a devotee can maintain equilibrium in these situations, it will not be difficult to maintain it in other situations. Equilibrium means being unaffected by external circumstances. Although a devotee sees only the Lord and no other reality, others may see the devotee as a friend or enemy. Even when they know that someone is their enemy or friend, they remain equanimous. A devotee remains equanimous in both pleasant and unpleasant situations, and in both favorable and unfavorable circumstances. They are not attached to pleasant situations nor averse to unpleasant ones. The words "yo madbhaktah sa me priyah" (he who is my devotee is dear to me) and "bhaktiman me priyo narah" (he who has devotion is dear to me) mean that devotees are dear to the Lord because of their devotion, not because of their qualities. Devotion is the primary thing, not qualities. Connection - In the previous seven verses, the Lord has described thirty-nine characteristics of devotees. Now, in the next verse, the Lord will answer Arjuna's question clearly. This nectar of righteousness, as described, is worshipped by devotees who have faith and are devoted to me. They are extremely dear to me. (20)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 12 ]
The Lord says: But those who are devoted to Me, having faith in Me, 
and are My devotees, 
they are very dear to Me. The word 'ye' here refers to those devotees who were mentioned by Arjuna in the first verse, 
and about whom the Lord had said in the second verse that they are the best among the yogis. The Lord had then explained the means of worshiping the Personal God and later described the characteristics of a perfected devotee. Now, the Lord is concluding that topic. As it was said, the word 'ye' here refers to those most faithful devotees who take the characteristics of a perfected devotee as their ideal and strive to attain them. The word 'tu' is used to separate the topic of perfected devotees from that of devotees who are still striving. This word indicates that the striving devotees are more dear to the Lord than the perfected ones. The characteristic of faith is not mentioned among the qualities of a perfected devotee, 
because once one has a constant experience of the Lord, there is no need for faith. Therefore, this word should be understood to refer to the striving devotees who have faith. Such faithful devotees strive to assimilate the Lord's teachings, which are full of nectar-like divine truths, 
with the aim of attaining the Lord. Although faith and love are essential for the practice of devotion, 
and discernment is essential for the practice of knowledge, 
it should not be understood that discernment is not necessary for devotion, 
or that faith is not necessary for knowledge. In reality, both faith and discernment are essential for all spiritual practices. Discernment accelerates the practice of devotion, 
and faith in the scriptures and in the Supreme Truth is necessary for the practice of knowledge. Therefore, both faith and discernment are helpful in the practices of devotion and knowledge. [ Verse 12 ]
Those who worship Me with devotion, 
who are intent on Me, 
and who are My devotees, 
they are very dear to Me. The word 'mat-paramah' means that the striving devotees have a most exalted devotion to the Lord. They have a superior intellect and follow the characteristics of a perfected devotee with reverence. By meditating on the Lord and depending solely on Him, 
they naturally develop all the divine qualities. The Lord has emphasized the importance of being devoted to Him in the 55th verse of the 11th chapter, 
using the word 'mat-paramah', and again in the 6th verse of this chapter, using the word 'mat-parah'. This repetition emphasizes that devotion to the Lord is the primary means of achieving spiritual growth. When one is devoted to the Lord, the Lord's grace automatically provides the means, 
and the obstacles to spiritual growth are removed. The phrase 'dharmyamritam idam yathoktam' means that the divine nectar-like teachings, 
as described earlier, are full of righteousness and free from any trace of unrighteousness. Since these teachings are free from any obstacles to spiritual growth, 
they are like nectar, and their practice is possible only when the striving devotee's goal is solely to attain the Lord, 
without any desire for wealth, honor, fame, or worldly pleasures. Each set of characteristics described is a divine nectar, 
and the striving devotee who takes them as their ideal and practices them is following the divine nectar. The characteristics of a devotee, such as being non-envious and friendly to all living beings, 
are present to some extent in the striving devotee, 
but they are also accompanied by some impurities and bad habits. Every living being has both good and bad qualities, 
and the striving devotee is no exception.

[ Verse 20 ]
* Sadhaka Sanjivani *
The defects can be completely abandoned, but the virtues will manifest and the vices will be destroyed as the seeker approaches God. It is not possible to completely abandon virtues, as the accomplished person has a balance of virtues according to their means and nature, but they do not have even a slight trace of defects. The virtues have been divided into five categories due to their varying degrees, but the defects are completely rejectable, so they cannot be categorized. The seeker practices good company, but bad company also occurs simultaneously. They practice self-control, but lack of self-control also occurs simultaneously. They practice spiritual disciplines, but the lack of spiritual disciplines also occurs simultaneously. As long as spiritual disciplines are accompanied by lack of disciplines or virtues are accompanied by defects, the seeker's spiritual practice is not complete. This is because those who are not seekers also have spiritual disciplines accompanied by lack of disciplines or virtues accompanied by defects. The seeker should be extremely cautious in this matter. If any defective tendency arises in their spiritual practice, they should not neglect it but try to remove it promptly. If it does not go away even after trying, they should pray to God with urgency. All good qualities, good conduct, and good feelings are related to the Supreme Being. Similarly, all bad qualities, bad conduct, and bad feelings are related to the unreal. Even in the most wicked person, there is no complete absence of good qualities, as every living being has an eternal relationship with the Supreme Being due to being a part of it. When one attains the Supreme Being, they are completely disconnected from the unreal, and all bad qualities, bad conduct, and bad feelings are destroyed. Attachment, aversion, joy, sorrow, lust, and anger are mental afflictions, not virtues (Gita, 13.6). The virtuous person has an eternal relationship with virtue, just like the sun has an eternal relationship with heat. Without a virtuous person, there is no virtue, and without virtue, there is no virtuous person. These mental afflictions are not always present in ordinary people, decrease in those who practice spiritual disciplines, and are completely absent in accomplished persons. If these afflictions were virtues, they would always remain the same and never be destroyed as long as the mind exists. Therefore, they are not virtues but rather temporary afflictions. As the seeker approaches God, these afflictions decrease and are completely absent when God is attained. In the Gita, God has instructed seekers to completely abandon these afflictions, saying "they should not come under the control of these" (3.34), "those who are free from attachment and aversion" (2.64), and "having abandoned attachment and aversion" (18.51). If these afflictions were virtues, it would be impossible to abandon them, and God would not have instructed seekers to do so. The Gita describes accomplished persons as being completely free from these afflictions. For example, in this chapter, from the 13th to the 19th verse, God describes accomplished devotees as being completely free from attachment and aversion. Therefore, these afflictions are not virtues but rather defects. The accomplished persons, who are completely free from these defects, have a mind that is free from even a trace of these afflictions. If these defects were present in their minds, what would they be liberated from? God has described the characteristics of the accomplished persons, who are free from these defects, as "Dharmyamrit" and has instructed seekers to follow these characteristics to attain God. The good qualities, good conduct, and good feelings are God's properties, so they are the characteristics of the accomplished persons.

* 
Srimad Bhagavad Gita 
*
[ Chapter 12 ]
The characteristics of devotees who are dear to the Lord have been described in the phrase 'pariupasate'. In the fifty-fifth verse, the nature of exclusive devotion has been described as the characteristics of His devotees. Arjuna asked in the first verse of this (twelfth) chapter which of the worshippers of the Lord with attributes and form, and the worshippers of the Lord without attributes and form, is superior. The Lord answered this question in the second verse, stating that those who worship the Lord with attributes and form, with their minds fixed on Him and with great faith, are superior. Here, in the conclusion, the word 'bhaktah' refers to those very devotees. The Lord considers these devotees, who are endowed with devotion, to be extremely dear to Him. Due to their natural attraction to the Lord, they possess divine qualities, or good qualities, which come to them naturally. Nevertheless, these devotees have a natural sense of reverence for the great qualities of perfected beings and strive to cultivate those qualities within themselves. This is what is meant by the devotees' adoption of those qualities. In this chapter, from the thirteenth to the nineteenth verse, the description of 'dharmyamrit' has been given in seven verses. The word 'pariupasate' is used here to mean the faithful and thorough adoption of that description. The adoption of these qualities means that the devotee should not possess even a trace of bad qualities. For example, even if a devotee does not fully possess compassion towards all living beings, they should not have any cruelty towards any living being. Since devotees do not possess all these qualities, they are advised to adopt them. If they do, they will become perfected beings. When a devotee has intense longing and eagerness for the attainment of the Lord, their bad qualities are automatically destroyed, because longing and eagerness consume the bad qualities and also bring about the means to attain the Lord. As a result, the devotee attains the Lord quickly and easily. The word 'bhaktah' is used here for the devotees who follow the path of devotion and are sheltered by the Lord. The Lord states in the fifty-seventh verse of the eleventh chapter that His vision is difficult to attain even through the study of the Vedas, austerity, charity, sacrifice, and so on. The reason for considering perfected devotees as 'dear' and devotees as 'extremely dear' is as follows: 
(1) Perfected devotees have already attained the experience of the Lord, whereas devotees, even though they have not attained the Lord, are still faithful and devoted to Him. Therefore, they are extremely dear to the Lord. (2) Perfected devotees are like the Lord's elder sons, while devotees are like His younger, ignorant children. A young child is naturally dear to everyone, and therefore, devotees are extremely dear to the Lord. (3) The Lord considers Himself indebted to the devotees because, even though He has not given them a direct vision of Himself, they still have simple faith in Him and are devoted to Him alone. Appendix - Duty is called 'dharma'. One who does not deviate from duty is called 'dharmya'. The idea that everything is the Lord is unparalleled; hence, it is 'dharmya' (Gita, 9.2). Devotees have faith, whereas perfected beings have experience, because in their experience, there is nothing except the Supreme Being; everything is the Supreme Being. Therefore, what need do they have for faith? In the view of the devotee, there exists another reality, and so they worship (pariupasate), that is, they mold their life in that way, but their attitude remains that if there is anything besides the Lord, it is also the Lord's play.

[ Verse 20 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

Even though a practitioner may acknowledge other deities, his devotion remains fixed on the Supreme Lord; no one else can capture his love. Consequently, the Lord becomes exceedingly dear to him. Until he experiences the realization that “everything is the Lord,” the Lord remains his benefactor. In the Śrīmad‑Bhāgavatam the Lord declares:

**yāvat sarveṣu bhūteṣu mad‑bhāvo nopajāyate**  
**tāvadeva‑mupāsīta vāṅ‑manaḥ kāya‑vṛttibhiḥ** (11.29.17)

“While the consciousness of Me does not arise in all beings, one should worship Me through mind, speech, and bodily actions.”

Thus, as long as the true conviction “all is the Supreme Self” has not yet taken root in every creature, one continues worship with all mental, verbal, and physical activities. **sarvaṁ brahmātmakam tasya vidyā‑ātmamanīṣayā**  
**paripaśyann‑uparmet sarvato mukta‑saṁśayaḥ** (11.29.18)

“All that is Brahman‑like is known by the intellect alone; having fully perceived this, one becomes free from doubt everywhere.”

Consequently, the devotee who has practiced the foregoing method attains the firm conviction that “everything is the form of the Supreme.” By means of this spiritual knowledge (Brahma‑vidyā) he becomes completely free of all doubt and, seeing the Supreme everywhere, he no longer needs to contemplate “everything is the Supreme”; the Supreme Himself appears directly before him. **om tatsaditi Śrīmad‑Bhagavad‑Gītā‑Upaniṣad‑sū‑brahmavidyā‑yoga‑śāstre Śrī‑Kṛṣṇārjunasaṁvāde bhakti‑yogo nāma dvādaśo’‑adhyāyaḥ** 12

“The verse ‘Om Tat Sat’ marks the conclusion of the twelfth chapter, titled ‘Bhakti‑yoga,’ in the Bhagavad‑Gītā‑Upaniṣad, the treatise on Brahma‑knowledge and Yoga‑scripture, which records the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.”

Thus, by the proper utterance of the divine names Om, Tat, Sat, the Brahma‑knowledge and Yoga‑scripture embodied in the Bhagavad‑Gītā‑Upaniṣad reach their completion in the twelfth chapter, ‘Bhakti‑yoga.’

In this twelfth chapter numerous methods of practice are described. The opening “Uvāca” verses number thirteen; the six‑hundred‑forty‑four verses together with the description of devotional qualities amount to forty‑five letters of the poet Puṣpika. The total of the chapter’s introductory and concluding sections equals seven‑hundred‑five letters. All of these are found within the devotional passages of the chapter. Only the third, fourth, and thirty‑second verses consist of thirty‑two letters each. The fifth section—comprising three verses—describes the means of attaining knowledge, yet it does so by juxtaposing devotion and knowledge to demonstrate the superiority of devotion; hence the chapter is named ‘Bhakti‑yoga.’

**Verses, letters, and “Uvāca” in the twelfth chapter**  
(1) The chapter contains three instances of “atha dvādaśo’‑adhyāyaḥ,” four “Arjuna uvāca” passages, two hundred‑forty‑four verses, and thirteen verses of Puṣpika, giving a total of two hundred‑sixty‑four verses. (3) Two “uvāca” statements appear: “Arjuna uvāca” and “Śrī‑Bhagavān uvāca.”

**Meter used in the twelfth chapter**  
Among the twenty verses, the ninth verse’s third line employs the meter “bhagaṇa,” producing a “bh‑vipulā” pattern; the nineteenth verse’s third line uses “na‑gaṇa,” yielding a “na‑vipulā” pattern; and the twentieth verse’s first line uses “na‑gaṇa” while its third line uses “bhagaṇa,” creating a “saṅkīrṇa‑vipulā” pattern. The remaining seventeen verses follow the regular “pathyā‑vaktra” meter. The headings “atha dvādaśo’‑adhyāyaḥ” appear seven times, and the “Arjuna‑anuṣṭup” meter is employed in seven verses, each characterized by the features of the Anuṣṭup meter.

Om Shri Paramatmane Namah

[ Chapter 13 ]

Preface – At the beginning of the twelfth chapter Arjuna asked which worship is superior: that of the personal (saguna‑sākāra) or that of the impersonal (nirguṇa‑nirākāra). The Lord declared worshippers of the personal form to be superior, and added that those who worship the impersonal form also attain Him; however, because of bodily ego they encounter greater difficulty in worship. He then described the worship of the personal form in detail. Now, to describe in detail the worship of the impersonal form and to remove the principal obstacle of bodily ego, the Lord commences the subject of the thirteenth chapter. First He introduces the distinction between the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). Shloka 1  
“i daṁ śarīraṁ kauntēya kṣetram ityabhidhīyate | etadyo vetti taṁ prāhuḥ kṣetrajña iti tad‑vidaḥ || 1 ||”

[Verse 1]
Translation – “This body, O son of Kunti, is called the field. He who knows this is called the knower of the field; that one is the wise.”

Word‑by‑word breakdown  
i‑daṁ – this; śarīraṁ – body; kauntēya – O son of Kunti; kṣetram – field; ity – ‘as’; abhidhīyate – is called; etad‑yo – who knows this; vetti – knows; taṁ – him; prāhuḥ – is called; kṣetrajña – knower of the field; iti – ‘thus’; tad‑vidaḥ – the wise. Commentary – The phrase “i daṁ śarīraṁ kauntēya kṣetram ityabhidhīyate” means that the material body, which we identify as “this” (i‑da), is designated the field. Human beings label physical entities—animal, bird, tree, etc.—as “this” (i‑da). The same body is also referred to as “I” or “mine” in ordinary speech, yet in reality the body that is called “my body” is also merely “this”. Whether it is the gross body, the subtle body, or the causal body, each is a manifestation of i‑da. The gross body (sthūla‑śarīra) is the aggregate of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—produced from the parents’ seed. It is also called the “annamaya‑kośa” (food‑filled sheath) because it originates from food and subsists on food; hence it is literally “food‑sheath”. Since it is the object of the senses, it is termed i‑da. The subtle body (sūkṣma‑śarīra) consists of the seventeen constituents: five sense‑indriyas, five motor‑indriyas, five prāṇas, the mind (manas), and intellect (buddhi). Because the prāṇas predominate, this sheath is called the “prāṇamaya‑kośa”; because the mind predominates, it is the “manomaya‑kośa”; because the intellect predominates, it is the “vijñānamaya‑kośa”. Being an inner sheath, it too is designated i‑da. The causal body (kāraṇa‑śarīra) is identified with ignorance (ajñāna). Human intellect provides knowledge, but beyond intellect there is no further knowledge; therefore this condition is termed ignorance. Ignorance is the cause of all bodies, so the causal body is called the “kāraṇa‑śarīra”. As stated in the Upaniṣadic commentary (Adhyātma, Uttara 5.9), “ajñāna‑eva‑hi mūla‑kāraṇam” – ignorance alone is the root cause. Consequently, the causal body is also described as nature, habit, and disposition.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

This is also called the “Anandamaya‑kosha”. In the waking state, according to one’s actions, the embodied soul repeatedly assumes a gross body (sthūla‑śarīra) and simultaneously carries a subtle body and a causal body. In the dream state the subtle body predominates, while the causal body remains present as well. In deep sleep the knowledge of the gross body (the annamaya‑kosha) is absent, and the knowledge of the subtle body (the prāṇamaya, manomaya and vijñānamaya koshas) is also absent; the intellect becomes immersed in avidyā (ignorance). Hence deep‑sleep is the state of the causal body. In waking and dreaming one experiences pleasure and pain, but in deep‑sleep pain is not experienced and only bliss remains. Therefore the causal body is termed the “Anandamaya‑kosha”. Because the causal body is also an object of itself and is known by itself, it is called “idam” (this). The three bodies mentioned above are called “śarīra” (body) to indicate that they are constantly perishing. They are called “kosha” (sheath) to convey that, just as a sword placed in a leather sheath acquires the designation “blade”, the soul’s identification with these three bodies gives them the designation “kosha”. Calling this body “kṣetra” (field) signifies that it is destroyed and transformed every moment, changing so rapidly that it cannot be seen again once the gaze has passed—it has already changed. The second sense of “kṣetra” is that of a cultivated field: just as various seeds are sown in a field, the human body, driven by ego‑attachment, performs diverse actions. The impressions (saṃskāras) of those actions lodge in the inner consciousness; when those impressions ripen as results, a different body—be it that of a deity, animal, bird, insect, etc.—is obtained. As the seed sown determines the grain produced, the actions performed in this body determine the next body, circumstances, and so on. In other words, this body enjoys the fruits of its deeds; hence it is also called a field. What appears different from its true nature is this body made of prākṛta (material) elements, actions, varṇa‑āśrama, etc.; it is merely “idam” (the visible). Mistaking this “idam” for “aham” (the self), the soul becomes trapped. The soul is a portion of the Supreme Self (Paramātmā) and pure consciousness, the greatest reality. Yet when it begins to regard itself as important because of gross, visible objects (“I am rich”, “I am learned”, etc.), it actually diminishes its own greatness and disgraces itself; the apparent greatness belongs only to wealth, knowledge, and similar material attributes, not to the soul itself, which is imperishable. When the soul accepts those material attributes, they appear significant; otherwise they are not. Thus the Lord, by saying “idam śarīraṁ kṣetram”, instructs us to view the body and other material entities as distinct from the self. **etadyo vetti** – the soul knows this body, i.e., “this body is mine, the senses are mine, the mind is mine, the intellect is mine, the life‑force is mine.” The soul sometimes calls the body “I” and sometimes “this”, meaning both “I am the body” and “this body is mine”. In the first half of the verse the body is referred to by the term “idam”, and in the second half by the term “etat”. Although both are proximate demonstratives, “etat” is even nearer to the speaker than “idam”. Hence “idam” points to the designated collection of bodies, while “etat” points to the “I‑ness” present within this body. **taṁ prāhuḥ kṣetrajña iti tad‑vidaḥ** – just as in Chapter 2, verse 16, those who discern the reality of sat‑asat are called “tattvadarśī” (realizers of truth), here those who comprehend the nature of field and knower of the field are called “tad‑vidaḥ” (knowers of that). Those who have realized what “kṣetra” (field) and “kṣetrajña” (knower of the field) are are true philosophers. Although the verb “prāhuḥ” (they say) would normally require the second case for “kṣetrajña”, the subsequent particle “iti” (thus) makes “kṣetrajña” appear in the first case. **Footnotes**  
1 – “śṛ hiṁsāyām” (dhatu) → forms the word **śarīra** meaning “body”. 2 – “kṣa kṣaye” (dhatu) → forms the word **kṣetra** meaning “field”.

[ Verse 1 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

It is by keeping the gaze fixed on the field (kṣetra) and by maintaining a relationship with the field that the wise great souls call this individual soul **Atman (the eternal soul)** “kṣetrajña” (knower of the field). If the Atman does not retain its relationship with the field, the designation “kṣetrajña” ceases and it merges into the form of **Paramatman (Supreme Soul)** (Gita — Chapter 13, Verse 31). **Key point** – 861

Great souls refer to the Atman as “kṣetrajña”. The implication is that even the tongue and the nostrils are objects of perception. The mind, which alternates between agitation and calm, stability and restlessness, is known through the intellect; therefore the mind itself is also an object of perception. The intellect, which sometimes grasps correctly, sometimes partially, and sometimes not at all, is likewise an object of perception, known through the Atman. Hence intellect is also visible. The intellect’s original seer is the Atman itself; it has never undergone change, does not change, will not change, and cannot possibly change. It remains ever‑unchanging; consequently it can never be an object of anyone’s perception. **Fundamental rule** – wherever bondage originates, only its removal can bring liberation. Thus bondage arises from the human body, and liberation from bondage can be attained only through the human body. If a person has no ego‑like (pride‑like) relationship of “I‑am‑the‑body” with his body, he is already free from worldly existence. Therefore, to sever the ego‑like identification with the body, the Lord calls the body “kṣetra” (field) and advises to view it as **idam‑tā** (separate). In reality it is indeed separate. Seeing the body as idam‑tā is not only for aspirants who seek their own welfare; it is absolutely essential for every human being, because the right and opportunity for one’s own deliverance reside within the human body. This is why, at the very beginning of the Gita’s teaching, the Lord first describes the body and the distinction of the bodily field. The word **idam** means “this”, i.e., that which appears distinct from the self. The first thing that appears is the gross body composed of earth, water, fire, air, and ether. It is visible and mutable. The organ that sees it is the eye. Just as colors, shapes, states, and uses of a visual object constantly change while the eye that sees them remains the same, likewise the objects of the senses—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—continuously change while the sense organs—ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nostril—remain unchanged. Variations in visual clarity—clear, dim, or completely absent—are changes of the eye recognized by the mind; similarly, changes in hearing, touch, taste, and smell are also known by the mind. Hence the five sense organs (ears, skin, eyes, tongue, nostrils) can each know their respective objects, but the objects themselves cannot know the subtle, superior, and illuminating sense organs. In the same way, sense organs and objects cannot know the mind; the mind, sense organs, and objects cannot know the intellect; and the intellect, mind, sense organs, and objects cannot know the self. The primary reason for this ignorance is that the sense organs, mind, and intellect are **relative seers**—they perceive only the gross form of the self with each other’s assistance. In contrast, the Atman, being infinitely subtle and superior to body, senses, mind, and intellect, is an **absolute seer**—it perceives without any external aid. Although the discussion above calls the sense organs, mind, and intellect “seers,” it must be understood that they can be seen only when they remain in the presence of the Atman. Since mind, intellect, etc., are functions of the inert (prakṛti) nature, they cannot be independent seers. Hence the Atman alone is the true seer. Even though the material body (the visible substance), the faculty of seeing (eyes, mind, intellect), and the seer (Atman) differ in qualities, there is an underlying metaphysical unity. Without this metaphysical unity, the attraction of seeing, the capacity to see, and the propensity to see could not be established. One may wonder: if the Atman is conscious, how does it perceive the inert intellect and other aspects with which it lacks metaphysical unity? The answer is that the Atman, by assuming the subtle nature of the inert, includes the inert within itself and thus becomes the “I‑self.”

*Rūpaṃ dṛśyaṃ locanaṃ dṛk taddṛśyaṃ dṛk tu mānasam |  
dṛśyā dhīvṛttayaḥ sākṣī dṛgeva na tu dṛśyate ||* (Vākya‑sudhā 1)

**Transliteration:**  
rūpaṃ dṛśyaṃ lócanaṃ dṛk tad‑dṛśyaṃ dṛk tu mānasam |  
dṛśyā dhī‑vṛttayaḥ sākṣī dṛgeva na tu dṛśyate ||

**Translation:**  
Form is visible, the eye is the seer; the eye itself is visible to the mind. The activities of the intellect that are visible become the witness; the eye alone is not seen.
