* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

The commentary assumes that the “I” is neither inert (Jada) nor purely conscious (Chetana). Because of its inherent nature, the inert aspect (the tendency toward inertia) becomes the seer of the material qualities such as intellect, ego, etc. The rule is that seeing is possible only within the same category: the visible, the act of seeing, and the seer must belong to the same class; otherwise seeing cannot occur. From this rule we understand that as long as the individual soul (Jivatma) remains the seer of intellect and similar faculties, it is still bound to the inert (material) nature. This assumed relationship is the root of all miseries. Because of this assumed relationship, the entire inert nature—intellect, mind, senses, objects of the mind, body, and material elements—becomes the object of the seer. When the special quality of the inert is observed, it merges with the inert and declares, “I am wealthy; I am learned,” etc. When the special quality of the conscious is observed, it merges with the conscious and declares, “I am Atman (the eternal soul); I am Brahman (Supreme Consciousness),” etc. This is the embodied person (Prakriti‑sthita Purusha) who, together with the qualities of nature, repeatedly takes birth in higher and lower wombs (Bhagavad Gita Chapter 13 Verse 21). The implication is that the embodied person contains both inert and conscious portions. The conscious portion aspires to the Supreme Soul, but through error it identifies itself with the inert portion. In that identification, the inert portion is attracted to the appendix concept “Idam” (the field). Under this field lie infinite universes. In each universe there are bodies that are “para” (the living entity, the field‑knower) and “apara” (the material world, the field). The living entity knows the world and acknowledges the Supreme Soul. The knower is expansive; therefore, within a single aspect of the field‑knower there are infinite universes—“yena sarvam idam tatam” (Bhagavad Gita 2.17). The seeker must realize: I am not the field; rather, I am the knower of the field. The visible is contained in some aspect of the seer. For example, even after seeing everything with the eye, the eye is never satisfied; thus, in reality the eye becomes larger than the visible. No matter how much the intellect learns, it never becomes full; it remains empty, constantly being filled and emptied. Hence the intellect expands. The origin, state, and dissolution of Brahman are also encompassed within our intellect’s knowledge. The gross, subtle, and causal bodies are visible; likewise, the gross, subtle, and causal creation is visible. This entire visible seer (field‑knower) resides in some aspect. Just as a person is called “wealthy” because of wealth, when wealth ceases the person remains, but the designation “wealthy” disappears. Similarly, one is called “field‑knower” because of the field; when the field ceases, the knower remains, but the title “field‑knower” disappears. The meaning is that a single luminous principle, when related to the field, is called “field‑knower”; when related to the perishable, it is called “imperishable”; when related to the body, it is called “bodily”; when related to the visible, it is called “seer”; when related to evidence, it is called “witness”; and when related to cause, it is called “agent.” In reality that principle has no name; it is only experiential. Relation – what is the nature of that field‑knower? The next verse explains. [ Verse 2 ]  
**Sanskrit:** kṣetra‑jñaṁ ca api mām viddhi sarva‑kṣetreṣu Bhārata  
**Transliteration & meaning:**  
- **kṣetra‑jñaṁ** – the knower of the field (field‑knower)  
- **ca** – also  
- **api** – indeed  
- **mām** – Me (the Supreme)  
- **viddhi** – know/understand  
- **sarva‑kṣetreṣu** – in all fields (in every domain)  
- **Bhārata** – O Bhārata (address to Arjuna, descendant of the Bharata dynasty)

**Interpretation:** “O Arjuna, also know Me as the field‑knower in all fields.”

**Breakdown of the explanatory notes:**  
- **Bhārata** = “O descendant of Bharata, Arjuna!”  
- **api** = indeed  
- **jñānam** = knowledge, understanding  
- **viddhi** = to know, to comprehend  
- **tat** = that (the same)  
- **sarva‑kṣetreṣu** = in all fields (in every domain)  
- **ca** = and  
- **mama** = my  
- **kṣetra‑jña‑m** = field‑knower (the knower of the field)  
- **mām** = me (the Supreme)  
- **kṣetra‑kṣetra‑jñayoḥ** = of the field and the field‑knower  
- **yad** = that which is  
- **mat‑tattva‑m** = my true nature, my knowledge

Thus the verse teaches that the Supreme declares Himself to be both the field and its knower, and the seeker must recognize this unity in every realm.

[ Verse 2 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

If the sense of “I am” ceases, the word “am” disappears, while the word “is” continues to exist. This is because one affirms his own unity. The knower of the field (kshetrajna) is united with the Supreme Self (Paramātma) by the verb “is”; through the relation of “I” with that “is”, the expression “am” arises. Hence, in reality the kshetrajna (“am”) is one with the Paramātma (“is”). The Lord is therefore telling us that in all fields you should consider me alone as the knower of the field. When a person knows an object, the object to be known is called the *jñeya* (that which is to be known). He knows that *jñeya* only through a *kāraṇa* (cause). There are two kinds of causes—external cause (*bahya‑kāraṇa*) and internal cause (*antaḥ‑kāraṇa*). A man knows objects through external senses (ear, eye, etc.) and knows the internal cause through the inner faculty (mind, intellect, etc.). The inner faculty has four components: mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), consciousness (*citta*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Among these, ego is the subtlest and is one‑pointed. This ego, which is the perceiver and the known, is the luminous knower of the field (*kshetrajña*). Recognize even that ego‑less knower as my own nature. The word “viddhi” here means, “O Arjuna, just as you consider the body to be yourself and the body to be yours, likewise consider yourself to be in Me and consider Me to be yours.” Because you have taken unity with the body, you must now take unity with Me in order to relinquish that former unity. In the same way the Lord says, “kṣetrajñaṁ cāpi māṁ viddhi” (know also Me as the knower of the field), elsewhere in the Gītā He declares unity. For example, in Chapter 17, Verse 7 He says of the pervading principle of the whole world, “avinaśi tu tad‑viddhi yena sarvam idaṁ tatam” (Know that which is imperishable, by which all this is pervaded). And in Chapter 9, Verse 4 He says, “mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ jagad‑avyakta‑mūrtinā” (All this manifested universe is pervaded by Me). Thus the Lord identifies the knower of the field (*kshetrajña*) with Himself, and later in this chapter, Verse 34, He will describe the unity of the body‑world (*kārya*) with its cause (*kāraṇa*). The implication is: the body is a fragment of nature; therefore you should become completely detached from it, while you are a fragment of Me, therefore you should turn toward Me. The body has a natural unity with the world. Yet the living being, by regarding the body as separate from the world, still maintains a natural unity with the world while simultaneously, by regarding the body as separate, distances himself from the Paramātma. Both the notion that the body is separate from the world and the notion that the self is separate from the Paramātma are false. Consequently, through the command “viddhi,” the Lord orders you to understand that the knower of the field is one with Me. In other words, the unity you have taken with the body, take the same unity with Me, which is the true unity. Scriptures describe *prakṛti* (nature), *jīva* (individual soul), and *Paramātma* (Supreme Self) as distinct. Yet by the word “api” the Lord points to a unique meaning: the all‑pervading form of the Paramātma described in the scriptures is none other than Me, and likewise the apparently separate knower of the field in every region is also Me. Hence the sense of the verses is that the knower of the field is the Paramātma itself. When the seeker realizes this, his experience of oneness with Me is distinct from the world yet inseparable from the Paramātma. Therefore, knowledge of the world arises only when one experiences complete separation from it. In other words, only by becoming free of desire for the world can one know the world’s true nature. However, true knowledge of the Paramātma arises only through oneness with Him. Thus the Lord points out his inseparability with the knower of the field so that the aspirant may attain authentic knowledge of the Paramātma. When this inseparability is fully realized, genuine knowledge of the Paramātma is attained. The statement “kṣetra‑kṣetra‑jñayoḥ jñānaṁ yat‑tad‑jñānaṁ mataṁ mama” can be rendered as:

- kṣetra‑kṣetra‑jñayoḥ jñānaṁ — the knowledge of the field and the knower of the field,  
- yat‑tad‑jñānaṁ — that which is that knowledge,  
- mataṁ — my view,  
- mama — my own. Thus, the unity of the body (*kṣetra*) with the whole world and the unity of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña* – the individual soul) with Me constitute the true “knowledge” in My opinion. When the Lord says “mataṁ mama,” He means that the myriad sciences, languages, scripts, arts, the three worlds and the fourteen lokas, though called knowledge, are not true knowledge. They are merely worldly knowledge that, while useful in material activity, entraps one in ignorance. True knowledge is that which severs the individual's attachment to the body, prevents rebirth in the world, and ends the bondage of worldly existence. This is the authentic knowledge in the Lord’s view.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

Parishisht Bhaav – Kshetrajna (Jeev) and Brahman are one. By relation to a field, he is “Kshetrajna”; when devoid of relation to all fields, he is “Brahman”. “Idam shareeram Kauteya kshetram” (this body is the field) proves that the body (field) is in unity with infinite universes (creation only) and “Kshetrajna chaapi ma vidhi” (know me also as Kshetrajna) proves that the self (Kshetrajna) is in unity with infinite, vast, limitless Supreme Soul. Therefore, any object far from us is body and any object close to us is Supreme Soul. The implication is that body and world are one and self and Supreme Soul are one (Gita – 15th chapter, 7th verse). This is knowledge. For Brahman, saying “mām” means that Brahman and Ishvara are not two, but one – “māya tatam idam sarva jagad vyaktamurti-nā” (Gita 9.4) “All this world is pervaded by my formless nature.” In infinite universes, that which is omnipresent with detached form is Brahman and the owner of infinite universes is Ishvara. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The Nourisher of Seekers *

Thus, in the context of the field, there are four things to be known, and in the context of the knower of the field, there are two things to be known - its nature and its effect. You should listen to me briefly about these two things. One should consider both the field and the knower of the field. The meaning is that the field, which is born from the knower, should also be considered in this context. Why not say that the field, as it is, with its defects and the one from which it is born? The solution to this is that the effect of the field, which is ever-changing in form, cannot be permanent. In the internal organ of the embodied being, the importance of material objects like wealth remains, and that is why the effect of the field (material objects) appears in the world. In reality, the field has no independent effect. Therefore, its effect cannot be described. Although in the beginning of this chapter, the first two verses have described the field and the knower of the field in a nutshell, which has been called 'knowledge' by the Lord, the detailed discussion of the division of the field and the knower of the field has been started in this third verse. Therefore, the Lord advises to listen to it carefully. In this verse, the Lord has given permission to listen to four things about the field, but only two things about the knower of the field - its nature and its effect. From this, a doubt may arise that why the effect of the field is not mentioned, and why the nature, defects, and virtues of the knower of the field are not described separately. The solution to this is that the nature of the knower of the field is also birthless and deathless, and therefore, its nature has been described under the category of its nature itself. Due to the relationship with the field, the knower of the field appears to have desires and aversions, otherwise, the knower of the field (by nature) is completely free from defects. Therefore, it is not possible to describe the defects of the defectless knower of the field. The knower of the field is unique, eternal, and uncreated. Therefore, the question of who was born from whom does not arise. Parishishta Bhaav - The meaning of the Lord's words 'tatsamasaena me shrinu' is that the seeker does not need to know more. Knowing more will only waste time, but the practice will be less. Sambandh - In the previous verse, it was briefly mentioned that one should listen to it, and now, in this verse, the detailed discussion of the division of the field and the knower of the field has been started. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

The commentary that I am giving in a concise form about the Brahma‑Kshetra‑Kshetrijna is also described by the sutra‑verses in terms of the essence of the Kshetra‑Kshetrijna. In this shloka, the Lord’s intention is made clear: if one wishes to see it in detail, he can look in the aforementioned texts. In the third shloka of the “Sambandha” section, six points were given for a brief hearing about the Kshetra‑Kshetrijna. Two of those points—its nature and its distortions—are described in the next two shlokas. ---

[ Verse 5 ]

**Indriya‑ani dashakaṃ ca pañca cendraiyogocarāḥ**  
*Indriya‑ani* – “the senses”  
*dashakaṃ* – “ten”  
*ca* – “and”  
*pañca* – “five”  
*cendraiyogocarāḥ* – “sensory objects”

*Translation:* “The ten senses and the five sensory objects.”

**Commentary**

*Avyaktameva* – “only unmanifest.”  
*Avyaktam* is the name of the original nature (mūla prakṛti). Because the original nature is the cause of the collective intellect (samāśṭi buddhi) and has no independent action, it is merely “nature.”

*Buddhi* – the collective intellect (samāśṭi buddhi). From this intellect the ego (ahamkara) arises; hence it is “nature,” and because it is the work of nature it becomes “distortion” (vikṛti). Thus this intellect is “nature‑distortion.”

*Ahamkara* – the collective ego (samāśṭi ahamkara). It is also called the sense of self (ahamābhāva). Because the five mahābhūtāni (earth, water, fire, air, and ether) are its cause, this ego is “nature,” and because it is the work of intellect it becomes “distortion.” Hence this ego is “nature‑distortion.”

*Mahābhūtāni* – the five great elements: earth, water, fire, air, and ether. The mahābhūtāni are of two types: *pañcīkṛta* (five‑fold) and *apañcīkṛta* (not five‑fold). When each mahābhūta is divided into five parts, the resulting mixture is called *pañcīkṛta mahābhūta*. The five senses have five subjects—this is the “field” of twenty‑four elements. When the divisions of these five mahābhūtāni are absent, they are called *apañcīkṛta mahābhūta*. The term *mahābhūtāni* refers to these. These mahābhūtāni are also called *pañcatamātra* and *sūkṣma mahābhūta*. Because the ten senses, the mind, and the words are causes of these mahābhūtāni, they are “nature”; because they are the work of ego, they are “distortion.” Thus the five mahābhūtāni are “nature‑distortion.”

*Indriya‑ani* – the ten senses: hearing, skin, eye, tongue, and smell (the five sensory senses), and speech, water, foot, presence, and breath (the five action senses). These ten senses are produced from the *apañcīkṛta mahābhūtāni* and have no independent cause, so they are only “distortion.”

*Ekaṃ ca* – the mind, produced from the *apañcīkṛta mahābhūtāni* and having no independent cause, is only “distortion.”

The ether has two divisions: half remains in its own form, and the other half is divided into four parts, which are given to air, fire, water, and earth. Air has two divisions: half remains in its own form, and the other half is divided into four parts, given to ether, fire, water, and earth. Fire has two divisions: half remains in its own form, and the other half is divided into four parts, given to ether, air, water, and earth. Water has two divisions: half remains in its own form, and the other half is divided into four parts, given to ether, air, fire, and earth. Earth has two divisions: half remains in its own form, and the other half is divided into four parts, given to ether, air, fire, and water. Thus, the five mahābhūtāni are mixed in a five‑fold manner, and this is called *pañcīkṛta mahābhūta*.

[ Verse 6 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

‘panc indriya‑gocharaḥ’ – the five sense‑objects: sound, touch, form, taste and smell. The fundamental nature is only prakṛti, and there are ten indriyas; one of them is smell. These are the five objects of the five jñāna‑indriyas. The un‑refined mind and the objects of the five jñāna‑indriyas – these sixteen arise solely from the five mahā‑bhūtas and are not vikṛti (distortions) by any cause. Because the aggregate of the twenty‑four elements is called kṣetra, these five objects become only vikṛti. Kṣetra is the trivial portion that is the human body, which the Lord called ‘idaṁ śarīram’ in the first verse and ‘tat‑kṣetram’ in the third verse. From this it is concluded that the five mahā‑bhūtas, one ahaṅkāra and one buddhi – these seven constitute the prakṛti‑vikṛti of desire, aversion, happiness, sorrow, body, consciousness and resolve. icchā = desire, wish  
dveṣaḥ = aversion, hatred  
sukhaṁ = happiness, pleasure  
duḥkhaṁ = sorrow, pain  
saṅghātaḥ = body (the aggregate of the twenty‑four elements)  
cetanā = consciousness (prāṇa‑śakti)  
dhṛtiḥ = steadiness, resolve

Thus the field (kṣetra) is briefly defined as a collection of distortions. Explanation – ‘icchā’ means the longing for a particular object, person or circumstance; it is the primary vikṛti named by the Lord among the field’s distortions. Desire is the root distortion because every sin and suffering originates from worldly desires. ‘dveṣaḥ’ arises when desire and pride are obstructed, producing anger. The subtle inner form of that anger is called dveṣa; the term also includes overt anger. ‘sukhaṁ’ is the pleasant feeling that arises when favorable conditions appear, i.e., a situation that pleases the mind. ‘duḥkhaṁ’ is the agitation that arises when adverse conditions appear, i.e., a situation that displeases the mind. ‘saṅghātaḥ’ is the name for the body‑form composed of the twenty‑four elements. The very manifestation of the body and its continual change are themselves distortions. ‘cetanā’ refers to the prāṇa‑śakti (life‑force) present in the body; it constantly changes, for example when a sattvic disposition arises. Ordinary people call the living as cetanā and the lifeless as acetanā; hence the term is used here for prāṇa‑śakti. ‘dhṛtiḥ’ means the faculty of holding or sustaining. It also varies: a person sometimes maintains patience, and at other times, when faced with adversity, abandons it. The amount of patience fluctuates, and a person may hold positive or negative thoughts. Therefore dhṛti is also a distortion of the field. [ In Chapter 18, verses 33 to 35, the three modes of dhṛti — sattvic, rajasic and tamasic — are described. Sattvic dhṛti is essential for moving toward the Supreme (Paramātmā). ]

‘etatkṣetraṁ samāsena savikārām udāhṛtam’ – just as in the first verse the Lord said ‘idaṁ śarīram’ to distinguish the body from the perceiver, here the term ‘etad’ is used to separate the viewer from the field and its distortions. In the fifth verse the Lord described the whole of creation; in this sixth verse He describes the distortions of the body‑field.

This is because in the collective world, afflictions such as desire (ichha) and aversion (dvesha) arise. To experience one’s eternal union (nityasanyoga) – the unity – one must not only perceive the body (vyasti sharira) as separate from the collective world (samasti sansara), but also understand that the body and the afflictions within it are not distinct from the collective world; they are one and the same. In the second shloka of this chapter, the Lord shows His unity with the knower of the field (kṣetra‑jnāna). Likewise, here the Lord explains that the body (vyasti sharira) and the afflictions within it are united with the collective world. In shloka 21, the Lord does not describe the soul (puruṣa) in the body but in nature, saying, “puruṣaḥ prakṛtisthā hī.” This further proves that the state (sambandha) of the soul in the body is the same as its state in the collective nature, because the body and the collective nature are one and the same. In reality, the body does not exist independently; only the collective exists. The body is merely a mistaken notion, just as separating waves from the ocean is a mistake. **Special point**  
When the knower of the field (kṣetra‑jnāna) mistakenly identifies himself with the field, afflictions such as desire and aversion arise. The true nature of the knower of the field is completely impassive. The afflictions that arise from the union of the field and the knower can be entirely eliminated, because this union is only a perceived one. To dissolve this perceived union, the Lord, in the first shloka of this chapter, instructs the seeker to see the body as separate from Himself, and in the second shloka to see the Supreme Self (paramātmā). Once this experience is attained, the perceived unity with the field disappears entirely, and no afflictions can arise. When the knower of the field (kṣetra‑jnāna) becomes fully detached from the body, desire and aversion are completely eradicated. Knowledge of pleasure (sukha) and pain (duḥkha), i.e., the knowledge of favorable and unfavorable circumstances, remains, but no afflictions arise in the inner self. Thus, a liberated great soul (mahāpurūṣa) who is freed from the body is neither happy nor sad. Knowing pleasure and pain is not a fault; the effect of that knowledge (the arising of afflictions) is the fault. The liberated great soul’s “association” (saṅghāta) – that is, the slightest sense of “I” or “mine” with the body – is absent. Even if the body is great and pure, it remains as it is according to its nature. As long as the body exists, consciousness (prāṇāśakti) also exists. When effort (parishrama) is present, restlessness arises; otherwise it remains calm. The virtuous quality (śāntā) that existed in the state of practice remains even after realization. However, because there is no identification with the inner self, the great soul’s consciousness and virtuous quality are not affected by afflictions. In other words, the afflictions that arise from identification with the body do not occur once realization is attained. Even if association, consciousness, and virtuous quality persist, they have no effect on the soul. **Appendix**

[Verse 7]
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *

[ Verse 7 ]

kshantir arjavam. sthayiram atma vinigrahah. (Forgiveness and humility; steadiness and self‑restraint.)

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- amanitvam apne mein shreshthata ka kshanti = forgiveness in the sense of lack of pride  
- arjavam = humility  
- acharya upasana = devotion to the teacher  
- shouch = cleanliness  
- = kshanti = forgiveness  
- = saralta = simplicity  
- sthayiram = steadiness  
- = (aur) bhav na hona = no attachment  
- adambhitvam = lack of ostentation  
- ahimsa = non‑violence  
- guru ki seva = service to the guru  
- atma vinigrah = self‑restraint  
- = man ka vash mein hona = being under control of the mind  
- bahar‑bhiantar ki shuddhi = purification inside and outside  
- vyakhya – amanitvam – apne mein maani pan ke abhaav ka arth = explanation – lack of pride in oneself

**Commentary**

By aligning oneself with the body, desires, hatred, and other afflictions arise, and these afflictions affect oneself automatically. Therefore, to destroy the identification with the body, the Guru explains the twenty essential means of “knowledge” in the next five verses. The first verse, “kshantir arjavam. sthayiram atma vinigrahah,” teaches that forgiveness and humility, steadiness and self‑restraint are the foundations of the path. The term *amanitvam* means the absence of pride or self‑importance. When a seeker feels superior because of caste, stage of life, qualifications, knowledge, qualities, rank, or any other factor, he thinks, “I am worthy, I am respected.” This feeling arises only when the seeker identifies with the impermanent body. The more he clings to this sense of superiority, the less real knowledge he attains. The less pride he harbors, the less attachment to the body he will have, and the faster he will progress toward the divine. To reduce pride, the seeker should associate with great souls—those who are higher than himself, who have attained liberation (tattvajña). By staying in their company, adopting their attitude, and becoming like them, the sense of pride disappears. In addition, many faults are removed smoothly through such companionship. Goswami Tulsidas says, “Sabhi maṇaprad aapu amāni” (Manas 7.38.2), meaning that saints give respect to everyone and are themselves free from the desire for respect. Likewise, a seeker should always give respect, honor, and praise to others. This attitude can only develop when the seeker regards others as superior in some way. Every person, though in different circumstances, possesses some special quality—caste, stage of life, qualities, knowledge, intelligence, qualifications, rank, authority, etc. By always respecting those qualities, the seeker naturally develops the habit of giving respect. When this habit becomes internalized, the desire for personal respect fades away. The seeker’s aim should be to eliminate pride within himself, not to seek respect from others. **Special note**

In the Bhagavad Gita, the Lord first removes the fear of the devotee’s path—“abhayam” (16.1)—and finally removes pride—“na atimanita” (16.3). In the path of knowledge, the lack of pride is removed first—“amanitvam” (13.7)—and the fear is removed last—“tattvajñāna‑arth‑darśanam” (13.11). This means that, just as a child becomes fearless when he sees his mother, a devotee on the path of devotion sees his Lord everywhere from the very beginning and thus becomes fearless. The devotee, by maintaining the habit of giving respect to others from the start, gradually becomes free of pride. In the end, the body‑based sense of unity dissolves on its own, and he becomes completely free of pride. In the path of knowledge, the seeker does not accept the unity with the body from the beginning (as in the first verse of this chapter). Therefore, he becomes free of pride from the start; because accepting unity with the body brings pride. In the end, by seeing the Supreme Soul everywhere, he becomes fearless. *Adambhitvam* means the quality of ostentation. When people see good qualities in us, they respect us.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13

We will wear garlands, perform our worship, and seat us on a high throne; to do, to cause someone else to do violence, and to approve it. Even if one does not possess such a quality within oneself, one can still approve violence (support it). To display a quality, even when one has little of it inside, and to make it appear more outwardly – all of this is ostentation. One may have virtue, purity, sanctity within, but if one displays sanctity before people, they will mock and criticize us. Thinking that way, abandoning one’s sanctity and becoming like the others is also ostentation. For example, at modern weddings and other occasions, at club or hotel receptions, or while traveling by airplane, even a person of pure conduct may be seen taking impure food for the sake of hospitality. That too is ostentation. Likewise, a wicked man, when he enters a community of good people, seeks honor, hospitality, fame, reputation, etc., and starts presenting himself as a saint, devotee, servant, philanthropist, etc., that too is ostentation. A practitioner, sitting alone in a closed room, chanting, meditating, and also taking laziness and sleep. But when a voice of reverence and respect from outside comes, upon hearing that voice he becomes alert and starts chanting and meditating, and his sleep and laziness go away. That too is a subtle ostentation. Even if one becomes alert upon hearing a voice, that is not a fault, but the feeling that this man will not have faith in me, that feeling is a fault. In that place, one should feel that the Lord has done a great good by making me alert and engaging me in chanting and meditation. The absence of all these types of ostentation is called *adambhitva* (non‑ostentation). **Upaya** – The practitioner should keep his sole aim as attaining the Supreme Self and should not even show a little to people. If vanity enters, his practice will become lax, hindering the attainment of the goal. Therefore, he should not think about any good, bad, high, low, whatever he may consider; he should remain focused on his practice. By maintaining such caution, ostentation disappears. The above three types of violence arise from three emotions – anger, greed, and attachment. That means that from anger there is also performed, caused, and approved violence; from greed there is also performed, caused, and approved violence; and from attachment there is also performed, caused, and approved violence. Thus violence becomes nine types. In the above nine types of violence there are three degrees – mild, moderate, and severe. Giving a little pain to someone is mild violence; giving more pain than mild is moderate violence; and severely injuring or killing is severe violence. Thus, by distinguishing mild, moderate, and severe, violence becomes twenty‑seven types. The above twenty‑seven types of violence arise from three causes – body, speech, and mind. Thus violence becomes one‑eleven types. The name of not performing any type of violence is *ahimsa*. Ahimsa also has four types – geographic, temporal, situational, and personal. In a certain pilgrimage, in a certain temple, in a certain place, one should not cause pain to anyone – that is *geographic ahimsa*. On the days of new moon, full moon, eclipses, etc., one should not cause pain to anyone – that is *temporal ahimsa*. When meeting a saint, on the day of a son’s birth, on the day of a father’s death, one should not cause pain to anyone – that is *situational ahimsa*. One should not cause pain to cows, deer, teachers, parents, children, etc. – that is *personal ahimsa*. In any country, time, or age, by not causing pain to anyone with body, speech, or mind, from anger, greed, or attachment, this universal ahimsa is called *Mahavrata*. **Upaya** – Just as a normal being seeks the pleasure of his body, a practitioner should regard his pleasure, the welfare of all, and his service to all as the same. That is, one should not separate one’s pleasure, welfare, and service from those of others. *All are of the same nature* – by keeping such discernment awake, one will never perform an act of causing pain, and in that, *ahimsa* – never causing any pain by mind, speech, or body – is the name of ahimsa. The three types of violence from the doer’s perspective are performed (self‑violence) – ahimsa nature will arise spontaneously.

[ Verse 7 ]

'Kshanti' – The term *kshanti* means tolerance or forbearance, i.e., the quality of forgiveness. By practicing it, one dispels rigidity and the practitioner naturally becomes humble. Even if one is capable, the person who commits a fault becomes simple and modest. Holding the attitude that no punishment, even a small one, should be received, and not seeking revenge or having someone else inflict punishment, is what *kshanti* is. **Methods**  
(1) Tolerance is inherent in its nature; it never becomes distorted. Therefore, if at any time a thought arises such as “someone has caused me pain or committed a fault,” one should automatically think that no one can truly harm us, that no distortion can arise within us, and that such a thing cannot reach our nature. By having this thought, the feeling of forgiveness naturally arises. (2) For example, when eating, if one accidentally cuts one’s own tongue with one’s own teeth, one does not become angry at the teeth or punish them. One may think that the tongue will heal, but the thought of breaking the teeth never arises. Because if one were to break the teeth, a new pain would arise, i.e., the pain would double, causing suffering and misfortune for oneself. Similarly, if someone wrongs us without reason and gives us pain, if we punish or inflict pain upon them, it will ultimately bring misfortune to ourselves, because they too are of the same nature. (Reference: Gita, 6th chapter, 39th shloka). 'Arjavam' – Simplicity or straightforwardness is called *arjavam*. The practitioner’s body, mind, and speech should be simple and straightforward. There should be no pretense in bodily adornment, simplicity in conduct and natural straightness in manner, and no stiffness or arrogance; this is *simplicity of the body*. Absence of deceit, hypocrisy, jealousy, hatred, and presence of honesty, gentleness, friendliness, and compassion constitute *simplicity of the mind*. Not engaging in sarcasm, criticism, gossip, or speaking hurtful or insulting words, and speaking simple, pleasant, and beneficial words is *simplicity of speech*. **Method** – By considering oneself as a single country, that is, by relating to the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, one sees a special quality in oneself compared to others. This leads to a certain stiffness or awkwardness in actions such as walking, standing, or sitting. Therefore, by not recognizing the relationship with the body and by looking toward one’s own nature, the worship of the teacher, *acharyopasana*, is invoked. The teacher who imparts knowledge and good instruction is also called *acharya*, and serving him brings benefit; but here the term *acharya* refers to the speaker of the supreme reality, the liberated great soul. Paying homage, respecting, and making the teacher’s body comfortable is also his worship, but truly living according to his principles and feelings is his true worship. Because serving the body of a bodily‑prideful person is done by serving his body, but serving only the body of a transcendent great soul is not complete service. The divine attributes of the Lord do not give the title *acharyopasana* in the knowledge path; here it is given in the means of knowledge. It reveals a special secret that the need for a teacher in the path of knowledge is as great as the need in the path of devotion. In the path of devotion, the practitioner entirely depends on the Lord and practices; therefore the Lord himself bestows grace, removes his shortcomings and obstacles, and grants him realization of the ultimate truth. In Chapter 4, Verse 34, the Lord also told Arjuna: “Go to those who are realized, self‑realized, liberated great souls; bow to them with reverence, serve them, and humbly ask questions to satisfy your curiosity, and those enlightened sages will impart to you the teaching of knowledge.”

Thus, by practicing, those great souls can remove those subtle deficiencies that the aspirant himself does not recognize, and effortlessly enable him to experience the Supreme Self. From the outset, the aspirant should thoughtfully approach a teacher or saint‑great soul. What should the teacher (guru) be like? The following points should be kept in mind—

[ Chapter 13 ]

(1) He appears to the aspirant as truly enlightened, a knower of the ultimate truth. (7) Whose every effort is solely for the welfare of seekers. (8) By being in their presence, our dedication toward the goal naturally increases. (9) In their company, through sight, discourse, remembrance, etc., our vices and misconduct are removed, and divine qualities of virtue arise spontaneously. (10) Apart from them, no one else exhibits such transcendence or uniqueness. One should stay with such teachers and saints and relate to them solely for one’s own liberation. What they do, what they do not do, why they act in certain ways, how they treat others—none of this should be analyzed with the intellect; one should not apply reasoning to their actions. The aspirant must remain under them, act only according to their commands and disposition, and serve them with devotion. If those great souls do not wish, there is no need to establish a practical guru‑disciple relationship. However, there is no objection to reverently considering them as gurus in the heart. If such great souls are not found, the aspirant should devote himself entirely to the Supreme Self, engage in meditation, contemplation, etc., and trust that the Supreme Self will inevitably grant him a guru. In reality, after becoming completely dependent on the Supreme Self, the guru’s role is fulfilled by the Supreme Self (2) who perfects the practices of Karma‑yoga, Jnana‑yoga, Bhakti‑yoga, and so on; because even the guru ultimately knows precisely. The separation of attachment occurs, and one becomes one with the Guru‑tattva; not deviating from it is called “sthiryam” (stability). One must firmly decide to attain tattva‑knowledge, and even when obstacles arise, remain undisturbed and diligently pursue one’s practice according to that determination—this is what is called “sthiryam” here. It becomes so, meaning that gravitas (importance) comes into it. When one separates from worldly attachments, liberation is attained, and when one becomes one with the Guru‑tattva, devotion is achieved. When gravitas enters a disciple, the disciple‑ness ceases. The scriptures and their authority no longer govern him. If a disciple does not perform his duty, he will still be called a disciple, but he will not possess disciple‑ness. Without disciple‑ness, he will not separate from worldly ties and will not acquire gravitas. Thus, he remains a slave to the world. Holding the feeling that the Guru should only serve my welfare is also a bondage for the disciple. The disciple should not desire anything for himself and should be completely devoted to the Guru, finding his own will within the Guru’s will. The Guru’s duty is to ensure the disciple’s welfare. If the Guru does not fulfill his duty, he will still be called a Guru, but he will lack gravitas. Without gravitas, the disciple remains a slave. [ Chapter 13 ]

**Shloka**  
“Indriyārtheṣu vairāgyaṁ anahaṅkāraḥ” – In the objects of the senses there is renunciation and no ego. **Commentary**

The view that one should maintain dispassion (vairāgya) toward the objects of the senses and that there is no sense of “I‑am” (anahaṅkāra) is explained as follows. Because the world of the senses and the world beyond are both perceived, the individual constantly feels a sense of personal identity. When the mind is not drawn toward any sensory object, the senses remain free from attachment; this is the true sense of dispassion toward sensory objects. Even when the senses are employed for the purpose of livelihood, the seeker must not develop raga (attachment), āsaṅgi (clinging), or priya (preference) for those objects. **Method (Upāya)**

1. When attachment to objects arises, the objects appear important, attraction is created, and consequently all sins are generated. If our mind remains attached to objects, how can we realize the true nature (tattva‑bodha) or attain the state of the Supreme Self (Paramātmā)? By relinquishing attachment, the mind becomes detached from objects, leading to vairāgya. 2. Consider the great wealthy, heroic warriors, kings, and emperors who have enjoyed countless pleasures. In the end, what remained for them? Nothing. Their bodies grew weak and everything departed. Reflecting on this also produces dispassion. 3. Those who have never tasted worldly pleasures, who possess no material possessions, and who are detached from the world appear distinct from those who have indulged in many pleasures and continue to do so. In reality, there is no special distinction; the latter are immersed in sorrow and anxiety. Such contemplation also generates vairāgya. **Anahaṅkāra**

In every individual’s experience there is a habit of thinking “I am …”. This habit, together with the body, creates the notion “I am the body”, producing a one‑sided sense of self‑identity, i.e., ego (ahaṅkāra). Because of this, the soul identifies with body, name, action, material, feeling, knowledge, renunciation, place, time, etc., and thus is born and dies in higher and lower wombs (as stated in the twenty‑first verse of the thirteenth chapter). In practice, this ego remains far from the seeker. In reality it has no substantive existence, yet the term is used in the teachings of the Lord to indicate the complete removal of the ego that is imagined in the body and mind. When the true nature of the inert‑conscious (jñāna) is realized, the ego disappears entirely. Only a human being can be completely ego‑free; therefore the Lord, by using the term “anahaṅkāra”, instructs the abandonment of ego. When pride (abhimāna) and ego are employed together, they give rise to distinct feelings. Pride arises from attachment to worldly things. Likewise, pride also arises when one admires one’s own renunciation, knowledge, etc. Identifying the body as one’s true form also creates ego. Hence, the term “anahaṅkāra” should be understood as the total absence of both pride and ego. Upon waking, the first knowledge that arises is the sense “I am” (aham). Then the mind adds identification with a particular body, name, caste, ashrama, etc., producing pride. This is a sequential process. In the supreme path, the destruction of ego follows a similar sequence. First, the pride attached to the gross body and material wealth disappears. Next, the sense of doership attached to the organs of action (karmendriyas) is eradicated. Then the intellectual pride of “I am the knower” fades. Finally, the primary “I‑am” witness consciousness (aham) also dissolves. At that point, the all‑pervading, blissful, conscious reality (Sat‑citan‑ānanda) remains spontaneously. 1. Pride arises from the feeling of superiority. It appears when a person looks at others and thinks they are inferior. For example, if there is only one millionaire in a village, he feels proud of being a millionaire. If everyone else is also a millionaire, his pride disappears. To eradicate the fault of pride, the seeker must see the lack of superiority in others. (The commentary continues beyond the provided excerpt.)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

One should never look at others, but rather see one's own defects and remove them. (1)

The same Atman (the eternal soul) that pervades this body is also present in all other bodies - 'sarvagatah' (Gita 2.24). However, due to ignorance, humans consider the omnipresent Atman to be limited to their own body and say, "I am this body." Just as a person considers only the money they have deposited in their own bank account to be their own, and not the entire bank's money, similarly, a person considers only their own body to be "I" and not the entire universe. They also consider themselves to be related to time, saying "I am in this time," to place, saying "I am in this place," to intellect, saying "I am intelligent," and to speech, saying "I am a speaker." This kind of relationship is not to be accepted, and it is the way to be free from ego. (2) The scriptures describe the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman) as 'saccidananda' - 'sat' (existence), 'cit' (knowledge), and 'ananda' (bliss). These three are not different forms of Brahman, but rather three names of the same Brahman. Therefore, a seeker can focus on any one of these qualities and become unattached. When one becomes unattached, one experiences one's own self-existent state in Brahman, and ego is completely destroyed. To understand this, consider the following:

(a) 'Sat' - Brahman has always existed, exists now, and will always exist. It is not created, destroyed, or modified. When one thinks about this with the intellect and becomes unattached, one's intellect is separated from the ego, and one experiences one's true state in Brahman. When this experience occurs, ego does not remain. (b) 'Cit' - Just as the body and other objects are seen in the light of the intellect, similarly, the intellect itself is seen in the light of the Supreme Consciousness. When one becomes unattached and experiences the Supreme Consciousness, one's intellect is separated from the ego, and one experiences one's true state in Brahman. (c) 'Ananda' - Seekers usually try to understand the Supreme Consciousness through the intellect, but this is a mistake. The intellect can only understand the material world, not the Supreme Consciousness. The Supreme Consciousness is the source of light for the intellect, and it cannot be understood through the intellect. To understand the Supreme Consciousness, one must separate oneself from the intellect. 'Janmamrityujaravyyadhidukhadoshanudarshanam' - This means to see the defects of birth, death, old age, and disease repeatedly. Just as a pot is cooked in the womb, similarly, a child is cooked in the mother's womb. The child's body is affected by the mother's food, which contains salt, chili, and other acidic substances. The child's body is burned by these substances. 1. Whatever the Lord does, it is all right, whether good or bad. 'Narayan' sits in your house, and you should clean your house. 2. A seeker has no purpose in thinking about the world, and the incomprehensible Supreme Consciousness does not enter into thought. 3. A merchant heard that a certain shop had made a profit, and he also heard that another shop had incurred a loss. Although there is a difference between profit and loss, the knowledge of both is the same. If there were no single knowledge, how could one know the difference between profit and loss? Similarly, the knowledge of 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' is the same. The light that illuminates 'I' also illuminates 'you', 'this', and 'that'. There is no difference in the light. If there is a relationship with the light, it is with all four, and if there is no relationship, it is with none.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 13 ]
The tiny creatures that live in the body also harm the child. "In the hospital of diseases." Many kinds of diseases are born in the body due to wind, phlegm, etc., and there is great pain in the body due to these diseases. Seeing the sufferings of diseases again and again. The pain that a mother feels during childbirth cannot be estimated. Similarly, the pain that the child feels when it comes out of the womb is the same. In this way, by repeatedly thinking about the sufferings of birth, one should become firm in the thought that there is only suffering. Whoever is born, has to die - this is a law. No one can escape it. When the breath leaves the body at the time of death, it is as if thousands of scorpions are stinging the body at the same time - such is the pain. When the separation from the wealth accumulated over a lifetime, the house lived in for a lifetime, and the family occurs, and there is no possibility of reunion, then a very heavy sorrow occurs due to attachment and attachment. When the key to the treasure chest, which was kept hidden from the family, is seen in the hands of the family members, a unbearable pain occurs in the mind. In this way, by repeatedly seeing the sufferings of death, one should become firm in the thought that there is only suffering. In old age, the power of the body and its limbs becomes weak, and there is difficulty in walking, sitting, etc. Not every kind of food is digested. Because of being old, one wants respect from the family, but since there is no purpose, the family members disrespect and insult. Then the thoughts of the past come to mind, "I have earned wealth, I have raised and nurtured this family, but now they are insulting me!" Due to these thoughts, a great sorrow occurs. In this way, by repeatedly seeing the sufferings of old age, one should become firm in the thought that there is only suffering. This body is a house of diseases and illnesses - "This body is a house of diseases."

Here, the meaning of repeatedly seeing is not that one should think about it again and again, but rather that one should think about it. By repeatedly thinking about the sufferings of birth, death, old age, and diseases, one's attachment to worldly objects decreases, i.e., one develops detachment from worldly objects. The meaning is that by repeatedly thinking about the sufferings of birth, death, etc., one develops detachment from worldly objects. Because attachment to worldly objects is natural in the case of birth, death, etc., and whoever is born, that person has to suffer from all kinds of sufferings. The Lord has described rebirth as a place of suffering - "Punarjanma duhkhalayamashashvatam" (Gita 8.15). By considering the body and other material objects as one's own, by giving importance to them, by taking refuge in them, all kinds of defects are produced - "Dehabhimani sarve dosah pradurbhavanti." The jiva-atma is itself pure and faultless because it is a part of the Supreme Being - "Chetan amal sahaj sukh-rasi" (Mans 7.117.1). This is the reason why the jiva-atma does not like suffering and defects, because they are not its own kind. The jiva-atma suffers from defects and sufferings due to the defects it has created itself. Therefore, the Lord is advising to consider the defects of birth, death, etc. and to remove the root cause of these defects, i.e., dehabhimana. Parishishta Bhaav - There is a 'suffering of experience' and a 'suffering of effect'. To experience suffering and to search for the cause of suffering and to remove it is 'suffering of effect'. Here, the suffering of effect is called 'dukhadoshanudarshanam'. By experiencing suffering, i.e., by being sad, the discriminative faculty is lost. But by the effect of suffering, the discriminative faculty is not lost, but rather the person searches for the cause of suffering with discriminative vision and removes it. The desire for happiness is the cause of all sufferings. When the cause is removed, the effect also disappears. Therefore, by removing the desire for happiness, all sufferings are destroyed. [ Verse 9 ]

**Asaktiḥ** – to be free from attachment. **Sādhaḥ‑sanjīvani** – the life of the seeker. **Anabhishvangaḥ** – not having a close relationship (oneness) with the objects of attachment, in the attainment of adversity. In the realms of son, daughter, house, etc., and in the realms of son, daughter, house, etc., the desire for good and the desire for bad are always present, and the mind remains steady, i.e., the mind remains unperturbed by favorable or unfavorable circumstances. **Explanation – “Asaktiḥ”** – the attachment that arises in worldly matters and is not kept for the purpose of taking. The purpose is to keep the attachment to the object, person, event, circumstance, etc. that one loves. That attachment is called **sakti**. The state of being free from that attachment is called **asakti**. From worldly objects, persons, etc., the desire to take pleasure, the hope for pleasure, and the enjoyment of pleasure create attachment and affection in a person. Because a person does not see pleasure except through association, he finds worldly pleasure attractive. But true pleasure arises from the separation from association (Gita – Chapter 6, Verse 23). Therefore, for a seeker, it is essential to renounce worldly attachment. **Remedy** – Worldly pleasure initially appears like nectar, but in the end it becomes like poison (Gita – Chapter 18, Verse 37). The person who enjoys worldly pleasure ultimately suffers sorrow – this is the rule. Therefore, by keeping an eye on the results of worldly pleasure, attachment does not remain. **Anabhishvangaḥ** – the state of not having a close relationship (oneness) with son, daughter, house, wealth, land, animals, etc. The attachment that arises from the unity with a son, for example, causes the mother’s body to weaken when the son becomes ill. Similarly, when a son or a wife dies, a person says “I have died”; when wealth is lost, a person says “I have been killed.” This lack of unity is why the term **anabhishvanga** is used. **Remedy** – If one sees a close relationship with someone, serve them, bring them pleasure, but keep the aim of removing attachment (tadātmya). If one intends to take service from them, then attachment will arise. Even if one has to serve them for their happiness, one should not be satisfied; because satisfaction leads to attachment. The point is to be very careful not to become involved with anyone. **Always and steady equanimity in favorable and unfavorable circumstances** – “Iṣṭa” means the favorable object, person, circumstance, event, etc.; “an-iṣṭa” means the unfavorable object, person, etc. When a favorable thing is obtained, the mind should not become enraptured with joy, pleasure, etc.; when an unfavorable thing is obtained, the mind should not become envious, sorrowful, distressed, etc. The point is that the mind remains constantly balanced, unaffected by favorable or unfavorable circumstances. God also says this in the verse “siddhyasiddhyoḥ samō bhūtvā” (2.48). **Remedy** – A person who receives favorable material treats it as his own and enjoys pleasure – this is a great obstacle. Because worldly material is obtained only for service in the world, not to bring pleasure to the body and senses. Likewise, the unfavorable material that a person receives is not for suffering, but to renounce worldly pleasure, to free the person from worldly attachment, desire, affection, etc. The point is that both favorable and unfavorable circumstances are given to elevate a person beyond pleasure and sorrow, to attain the Supreme Self. By firmly believing this, the seeker’s mind will remain balanced in the attainment of favorable and unfavorable situations. Treating son, daughter, etc. appropriately, not taking a sense of belonging with them, and serving them is not **abhishvanga**; rather, it is detachment, non‑attachment, which brings the experience of immortality.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 13 ]

**Verse 13.10**  
mayi cha ananyayogena bhaktiravyabhicharini  
*In the Lord, by exclusive (ananya) yoga, devotion remains free from attachment.*

**Verse 13.11**  
viviktadeshsevittumaratirjan-samsadi  
*By serving in a secluded place, the devotee dies in the world of birth.*

**Top Commentary**  
The word *mayi* means “in me” or “in the Lord.”  
The phrase *bhaktiravyabhicharini* indicates that devotion, when taken exclusively, does not become attached. The commentary explains that the devotee’s ego persists because he takes refuge in the world; this ego is the chief obstacle to knowledge. To remove it, the Lord shows the means of exclusive devotion. Thus, devotion can remove ego. The nature of living is not to be attached to others. The commentary distinguishes two kinds of knowledge: *sadhan‑jnana* (knowledge of the means) and *sadhya‑jnana* (knowledge of the goal). Both are essentially the same. The devotee should choose the means that suit the predominant quality of his nature—whether action, knowledge, or devotion. The sole purpose must be to attain the Supreme Self, not the nature or its work. With such a purpose, the devotee obtains the Supreme Self by that very means. **Exclusive Relationship with the Lord**  
The desire to obtain anything from anyone other than the Lord is forbidden. Only the Lord alone can provide experience. The devotee must have an exclusive relationship with the Lord and none with any other. This is the essence of *avyabhicharini bhakti* (unattached devotion). **Means and Goal of the Supreme**  
The means of attaining the Supreme Self should be the Lord alone, and the goal should also be the Lord alone. This is the exclusive devotion of the Lord. The commentary notes that even in the transcendental qualities, the Lord is the exclusive devotee (Gita 14.26). **Question and Answer**  
*Why does the verse say that devotion leads to knowledge, while Chapter 18 verses 44‑55 say that knowledge leads to devotion?*  
The answer: There are two types of devotion—*sadhan* (means) and *sadhya* (goal). A devotee of knowledge (*jijñāsu*) can be of two types:  
1. **Emotionally‑driven (bhakti‑pradhān)** – seeks the Supreme by taking refuge in the Lord (see Gita 7.16 and 13.18). 2. **Rationally‑driven (jnana‑pradhān)** – seeks knowledge without the pronoun *asmad* (I). Thus, the verses that use *asmad* refer to the emotionally‑driven devotee, describing the means of devotion within the knowledge path. The verses that do not use *asmad* refer to the rational devotee, describing the goal of devotion. **Bottom Commentary**  
The commentary concludes that the devotee who takes refuge in the Lord alone, with the aim of attaining knowledge, can attain knowledge only by this exclusive means. It also reminds that the devotee should use the seven virtues (sattvic food, ghee for nourishment, etc.) as part of the path.

Everywhere, at all times, with equanimity, the meaning is to focus the human being on the Supreme Being, to bring the human being to the Supreme Being – after making this decision, one should contemplate the ultimate truth as much as it has been understood. The logic is that the ultimate truth, the Supreme Being, was present in the form of existence before, it is present now, and it will remain present in the future. However, the world was not present before and will not be present in the future, and it is constantly disappearing in the present moment. The world's birth and destruction occur, but its foundation, the illuminator, the Supreme Being, remains eternal and continuous. There is no independent existence of the world apart from the Supreme Being. The world appears to have an independent existence due to the presence of the Supreme Being. In this way, contemplating the absence of independent existence of the world and the eternal and continuous presence of the Supreme Being is 'Adhyatma-jnana-nityatvam'. Upaya– Reading and reciting the spiritual scriptures, listening to and asking questions about the ultimate truth from the great personalities who have realized the ultimate truth. 'Tattva-jnana-artha-darshanam' – The ultimate truth is the meaning of knowledge. Seeing the Supreme Being everywhere, experiencing the Supreme Being everywhere is 'Tattva-jnana-artha-darshanam'. The Supreme Being is present in all places, in all times, in all things, in all beings, in all events, and in all circumstances. The sadhak's vision, his goal is only the Supreme Being at all times, whether in solitude or in interaction. The sadhak's nature becomes to see only the Supreme Being – this is 'Tattva-jnana-artha-darshanam'. After this is established, the sadhak experiences the ultimate truth. 'Etaj-jnanam iti proktam ajnanaM yadato'nanyatha'
The first twenty means of realization, from 'Amanitvam' to 'Tattva-jnana-artha-darshanam', are all called 'Jnana' because they are means of realizing the ultimate truth and are helpful in achieving the ultimate truth. The opposite of these means, such as egoism, pride, violence, etc., are all called 'Ajnana' because they increase egoism and are obstacles to realizing the ultimate truth. Special Note
If the sadhak develops such intense discrimination that he can renounce the relationship with the body, then this means of realization – the community – becomes self-evident to him. Then he does not need to perform the individual practices of these means. The main thing is to experience the body as separate from one's own self – this is the fundamental means. Though a seeker may not experience this at first and may see flaws within himself, after some time their complete absence becomes apparent. During practice, a seeker may sometimes see vices within himself. But in reality, before engaging in practice, the vices that were present appear as if they are leaving. The rule is that both those who come through the door and those who leave are seen. If, while practicing, one sees vices increasing within himself, one should understand that vices are coming. But if one sees vices decreasing, one should understand that vices are leaving. In such situations, the seeker should not despair; rather, he should remain steadfast on his purpose and diligently continue practice. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

**Explanation** – In this shloka the Lord says “I will explain” (pravakṣyāmi). He also says that “Parama Brahman” is a single Supreme Soul; there is no other vast, impersonal, eternal principle beyond which. That is what is called “Parama Brahman”. To describe this knowable principle the Lord has made a promise:  
- “amṛtamashnute” (to attain immortality) indicates the fruit of knowing it;  
- “anādimat” (without beginning) indicates its characteristic;  
- “Parama Brahman” gives its name; and  
- “na sattannāsu chyate” (cannot be called either “sat” or “asat”) describes it. **“jñeyaṃ yattatpravakṣyāmi”** – Here the Lord, in an attempt to describe the knowable principle, promises that he will give a clear description of the knowable principle that is the object of human effort. The human body exists only for the attainment of this principle, which has been described in the Upanishads, scriptures, and other texts. I will describe this knowable principle in detail. **“jñeyaṃ” (to be known)** – The meaning is that not every subject, matter, science, art, etc., in the world is necessarily knowable. The only thing that is necessarily knowable is the Supreme Soul. Even if one knows all worldly subjects, there will still be something left to know. Knowledge of worldly subjects does not erase birth and death. But once the Supreme Soul is known, nothing remains to be known, and birth and death are eliminated. Therefore, in the world, there is no other thing that is knowable besides the Supreme Soul. **“yajñātvamashnute”** – When this knowable principle is known, the experience of immortality (amṛta) is attained; that is, the attainment of the self‑realized principle is achieved. Once it is attained, there is nothing left to know, do, or obtain. In reality, the Self is already immortal, but by identifying with the mortal body it has taken on the role of a being that is born and dies. Knowing the Supreme Soul dispels this illusion, and the Self recognizes its true nature, thereby experiencing immortality. **“anādimat”** – The world is created, exists, and ultimately dissolves within this principle. Yet it remains unchanged at the beginning, middle, and end. Hence it is called “anādi” (without beginning). **“na sattannāsu chyate”** – This principle cannot be called “sat” (truth) nor “asat” (non‑truth). Because the concept of “sat” cannot be applied to it without the notion of “asat” (the absence of truth), and the principle is never lacking; therefore it cannot be called “asat” either. The implication is that the Supreme Soul has no tendency toward the words “sat” or “asat”; it is a neutral principle. For example, on Earth there are day and night. We call the absence of day “night” and the absence of night “day”. But in the Sun there is no day or night. Because there is no night in the Sun, we cannot call it “day”; the word “day” is used in relation to the absence of night. If the essence of night were absent, we could not speak of day or night. Similarly, the word “asat” is used in relation to the absence of “sat”, and the word “sat” is used in relation to the absence of “asat”. Where the Supreme Soul is called “sat”, it is in relation to the absence of “asat”. But where “asat” is extremely lacking, we cannot call the Supreme Soul “sat”, and a Supreme Soul that is constantly “sat” cannot be called “asat”. Therefore, the words “sat” and “asat” are not used for the Supreme Soul. Just as the Sun is unique in being neither day nor night, the knowable principle is unique in being beyond “sat” and “asat”. **Second point** – The judgment of “sat” versus “asat” is made by the intellect, and such a statement is made only when it concerns mind, speech, and intellect. But the knowable principle is entirely beyond mind, speech, and intellect; therefore it cannot be described as “sat” or “asat”. The Supreme Soul is also called “Parama Brahman” (the Supreme Consciousness) in the Vedas. **Appendix** – Calling the Supreme Soul “knowable” means that it is possible to know it, that one should know it, and that it is possible to know it. In reality, the Supreme Soul does not come into knowledge because it is beyond nature; it is not grasped by nature. But it can be attained by oneself. **Ram, the embodiment of consciousness, bliss, and delight** –  
Ram sacchidananda dinesa: the Lord of consciousness, bliss, and delight. Nahi tah moha nisa lavlesa: He is not a source of delusion or attachment. **Sahaj prakāsa-rūpa Bhagavān** – the Lord who is naturally luminous. Nahi tah pun bi gyan bihāna: He is not a source of ignorance. (Manas 1.116.3)

[ Verse 13 ]
* Sadhak Sanjivani *
 
Prakriti (nature) and Purusha (the soul) - both are said to be anadi (beginningless) (Gita - 19th verse of this chapter); therefore, the Supreme Self is called 'anadimat' (beginningless) as the master of both. In the 4th and 5th verses of the 7th chapter, the Lord has said that the lower nature (apara prakriti) is 'mine' and the higher nature (para prakriti or jiva) is 'my higher self', thus showing that both are under His control. Therefore, the Lord is the master of both. The Upanishad also says - 
'Ksharam pradhanam amritaksharam harah, ksharatmanav ishate deva ekah' (Shvetashvatara 1.10). 'Prakriti is kshara (perishable), and the Purusha (jiva) who enjoys it is amritaswarupa (immortal) and akshara (imperishable). One God controls both prakriti and purusha.'

In the Gita, the Supreme Self has been described in three ways - 
(1) The Supreme Self is both sat (existence) and asat (non-existence) - 'sadasachaham' (9.19). (2) The Supreme Self is sat, asat, and also beyond sat and asat - 'sadasattatparam yat' (11.37). (3) The Supreme Self is neither sat nor asat - 'na sat tan nasad uchyate' (13.12). - The meaning of this is that, in reality, there is nothing except the one Supreme Self. It is beyond the reach of the mind, intellect, and speech, and therefore, cannot be described, but it can be attained. In reality, the Supreme Self cannot be described in words. It is called sat (existence) in relation to asat (non-existence), nirmala (pure) in relation to vikara (impurity), and sarvadishi (all-pervading) in relation to ekdeshi (limited space), but in reality, these words do not apply to it. The reason is that all words are used in relation to prakriti (nature), but the Supreme Self is beyond prakriti and independent. Names are given based on place, time, object, person, state, and qualities, but the Supreme Self has no place, time, etc., so how can it be named? Therefore, it is said here that the Supreme Self cannot be called sat (existence) or asat (non-existence). The Supreme Self has no beginning (adi). How can something that has always existed have a beginning? All things are inferior (apara), and the Supreme Self is superior (para). It is neither sat nor asat. The distinction between adi-anadi (beginning and beginningless), para-apara (superior and inferior), and sat-asat (existence and non-existence) is in relation to prakriti. The Supreme Self is beyond these distinctions. In this way, what the Lord has said about the knowable Supreme Self is not a description, but rather an indication (lakshya) that points to it. The meaning is to give an indication of the knowable Supreme Self, not just to describe it. Therefore, the seeker should also consider it from the point of view of indication, not just from the point of view of learning. - In the previous verse, it was said that the Supreme Self 'cannot be called sat (existence) or asat (non-existence)' - thus describing the knowable Supreme Self in its nirguna-nirakara (formless and attributeless) form. Now, in the next verse, the same knowable Supreme Self will be described in its saguna-nirakara (formless but with attributes) form. sarvatah panipadam tat sarvato 'kshishiro-mukham, 
sarvatah shrutimat loke sarvam avritya tishthati. The Supreme Self has hands, feet, eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere (in the universe). It has ears everywhere and pervades the entire universe. * The phrase 'anadimat param brahma' can also be interpreted as 'anadi, mat param brahma', meaning 'the Supreme Self, which is my ultimate resort' - 'Brahmano hi pratishtaham' (Gita 13.27).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 13 ]

Just as ink absorbs the material, the Lord consumes the substance there (Gita, Chapter 9, Verse 26). Explanation – “Sarthat paṇipādaṃ tat” – All kinds of scripts exist everywhere; therefore a writer can write all kinds of scripts with ink. In gold, all kinds of ornaments exist everywhere; thus a goldsmith can make any ornament from any part of the gold. Likewise, the Lord has hands and feet everywhere; therefore, wherever a devotee wishes to offer whatever he wants to give into the Lord’s hands, the Lord’s hands are present at that very place to receive it. Whether the devotee offers from the outside or from the heart, from the east or the west, from the north or the south, the Lord’s hands are present there to receive it. Similarly, when a devotee, in water, land, or fire, calls upon the Lord in any crisis, the Lord’s hands are ready there to protect him; the Lord protects him with His hands at that very place. Wherever a devotee wishes to apply sandalwood to the Lord’s feet, offer flowers, or bow, the Lord’s feet are present there. If thousands or lakhs of devotees wish to worship the Lord’s feet in different ways at the same time, the Lord’s feet are present there according to their feelings. “Sarvato akṣiśiro mukhaṃ” – wherever a devotee lights a lamp for the Lord or performs arati, the Lord’s eyes are there. When a devotee dances with body or mind, the Lord sees his dance there. The implication is that the Lord, who sees everywhere, is never hidden from the devotee’s sight (Gita, Chapter 6, Verse 30). Wherever a devotee wants to apply sandalwood to the Lord’s head or offer flowers, the Lord’s head is there. Where a devotee offers food to the Lord, the Lord’s mouth is there. In other words, the devotee, by offering “Sarthat śrutimatt” (the entire heard), whether loudly, softly, or mentally, the Lord hears with His ears there. All the parts of a human are not present everywhere; where there are eyes, there are no ears, and where there are ears, there are no eyes; where there are hands, there are no feet, and where there are feet, there are no hands, etc. But the Lord’s senses and parts are everywhere. Therefore the Lord can hear with His eyes, speak, receive, etc. The implication is that He can perform all actions with all His parts, because all His parts contain all parts. Even in the smallest fragment of Him, all senses are present. The statement that the Lord has hands, feet, eyes, head, mouth, and ears everywhere implies that the Lord is not any creature. Because the Lord exists perfectly in all realms, times, objects, persons, events, and circumstances. The saints say: “In all directions, arati and worship; in all directions, Rama and not the worldly man. Just as a worldly person sees the world everywhere, inside and outside, up and down, nothing else but the world, likewise a person who knows the essence of the Supreme Self sees the Supreme Self everywhere.”

“Lokē sarvamāvitṛya tiṣṭhati” – there are infinite creations, infinite universes, infinite wealth, and within all of them, realms, times, objects, persons, etc. are infinite; all are under the Supreme Self. The Supreme Self pervades and resides in all. In Chapter 10, Verse 42, the Lord also says that He pervades and resides in all of the world with a single part. Appendix: In the Supreme Self, everything exists everywhere. For example, in a pen and ink, there is no place where a particular script does not exist; a knowledgeable person can write many scripts with that single pen and ink. In a piece of gold, there is no place where a particular ornament does not exist; a goldsmith can produce many ornaments from that single piece. Likewise, in iron, there is no place where a particular tool or weapon does not exist; in clay and stone, there is no place where a particular statue does not exist. Similarly, in the Supreme Self, there is nothing that does not exist. All creation arises from the Supreme Self, resides in it, and ultimately dissolves into it. [ Verse 14 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

If the aspirant accepts the teaching with firm resolve, the Supreme Self (Paramātmā) will begin to appear, because in reality only the Supreme Self exists; nothing else exists. The Lord says:

“ahame‑vāsa‑meva‑āgre nānyad‑yat sad‑asat param | paścād‑ahaṁ yad‑etac‑ca yo’va‑śiṣyet so’‑asmi‑aham ||” (Śrīmad‑Bhāgavatam 2.9.32)

‘Before creation I alone existed; nothing else was. After creation, everything that is seen in this world is also Me. Beyond truth, untruth, and the truth‑untruth dichotomy, whatever can be imagined is also Me. Apart from creation, I am the only reality; when creation is destroyed, I alone remain.’  
Thus the essence is that there is only one reality. Because we remain entangled in dualities, we fail to experience it. **Relation –** In the previous verse the Lord described the personal (saguna) and impersonal (nirguna) aspects; in the next three verses He expounds His uniqueness, all‑pervasiveness and omnipotence. **Sanskrit verse (14)**

*Transliteration and word‑by‑word meaning*

- sarve‑indriya‑guṇābhāsaṃ – the manifestation of all qualities through all senses  
- sarve‑indriya‑vivarjitam – free from all senses  
- asaktaṃ – unattached  
- sarva‑bhṛc‑caiva – also the sustainer of the whole world  
- nirguṇaṃ – beyond qualities  
- guṇa‑bhoktṛi ca – the enjoyer of qualities

**Translation:** “The Supreme Self appears as the illumination of all qualities through all senses, yet is beyond all senses; He is unattached, the sole sustainer of the universe, beyond all qualities, and the enjoyer of all qualities.”

**Commentary**

‘Asakta‑m’ means free from attachment; ‘asakti‑rahit’ means without any attachment to qualities. ‘Nirguṇa‑m’ denotes being beyond qualities. ‘Sarve‑indriya‑vivarjitam’ indicates that the Supreme Self is beyond the complete set of senses. ‘Sarva‑bhṛc’ refers to the one who nourishes the entire creation. ‘Guṇa‑bhoktṛi’ denotes the one who partakes of all qualities. The living‑and‑dying bound soul, when it attains the Supreme Self, is said to become ‘guṇātīta’ (beyond qualities). How then can the Supreme Self be bound by qualities? He is always beyond qualities. Consequently He is free from the material senses (hand, foot, eye, head, mouth, ear, etc.) like ordinary worldly beings, yet He is fully capable of receiving the objects of those senses. For example, although He is without ears, He hears the call of devotees; without skin, He embraces them; without eyes, He continuously beholds the living beings. **Explanation of “sarve‑indriya‑guṇābhāsaṃ sarve‑indriya‑vivarjitam”**

First comes the Supreme Self; then His power, Prakṛti, follows. The functions of Prakṛti are: the great‑importance (mahattva) of action, the ego (ahaṅkāra) arising from that importance, the five great elements (pañca‑mahābhūta) arising from ego, the mind arising from the elements, the ten sense organs, and the ten objects of the senses. All these are functions of Prakṛti. The Supreme Self is beyond Prakṛti and its functions. Whether He appears with qualities (saguna) or without (nirguna), with form (sākāra) or formless (nirākāra), He always remains transcendent of Prakṛti. Even when He incarnates, He remains beyond Prakṛti, mastering it at the time of incarnation. A being who thinks himself bound by qualities, even after realizing his freedom, still enjoys the pleasures offered by devotees. 1. Knowledge of objects comes through the senses; the senses reveal the objects, therefore objects are functions of the senses. 2. “apāṇi‑pāda‑ja‑van‑o grāhītā paśyaty‑acakṣuḥ sa śṛṇoty‑akarnaḥ” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19) – “He who is the receiver of the breath and the feet, sees with the eye and hears with the ear.”

Thus the Supreme Self, though without hands and feet, can still grasp and move swiftly; He sees without eyes and hears without ears. 3. “binu pada calai sunai binu kānā | kara binu karm karai vidhi nānā” – “Without feet He walks, without ears He hears; without hands He works, in many ways.”

4. “ānana rahita sakala tana binu paras nayan ras bhogī | binu bānī bakata baṛ jogī | binu dekha | grahī ghrān binu bās aseṣā” (Mānas 1.118.3‑4) – “Without a mouth, without a body, without eyes, He enjoys the essence; without speech He is the great yogi; without seeing He perceives, without smelling He is present.”

These verses illustrate that the Supreme Self, though devoid of material senses, fully perceives and acts, confirming His transcendence of all sensory limitations.
