* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 13 ]
The Lord performs all actions, and so on. In this way, even without the senses, He perceives the words, touch, and other objects of the Supreme Lord. Knowing this fully, the Lord performs all actions. Similarly, even without speech, He converses with His dear devotees, and even without feet, He runs to answer the calls of His devotees, and even without hands, He accepts the offerings given by His devotees, and so on. In this way, even without the senses, the Lord performs all the functions of the senses. This is the way the Lord illuminates the objects of the senses even without the senses. He provides the objects of the senses as and when needed in a suitable manner. Whether a living being is on earth, in the ocean, in the sky, or in heaven, that is, in any of the three worlds, the Lord takes care of all living beings. The Lord nourishes all living beings as their well-wisher. By means of favorable and unfavorable circumstances, He destroys the sins and virtues of living beings and keeps them pure and holy. "'Nirgunam gunabhoktr cha'—The Supreme Lord is devoid of all qualities and yet enjoys all qualities. This means that just as parents are pleased to see the mere actions of their child, similarly, the Lord is pleased to see the mere actions of His devotees, that is, the Lord is the enjoyer of all the actions of His devotees. 'Asaktam sarvabhritchaiva'—The Lord has a sense of belonging and love for all living beings, but He is not attached to anyone. Although He is not attached to anyone, He nourishes all living beings from Brahma to an ant. Just as parents nourish their child, the Lord nourishes all living beings to a much greater extent. Who can be more than this? —Parishishta Bhaav: Although Brahma is emphasized in this chapter, the present shloka describes the Supreme Lord as 'Samagri' (the all-inclusive). This 'Samagri' is the ultimate truth to be known. Therefore, the emphasis on 'Samagri' is found in both knowledge and devotion—'Vasudeva sarvam' (Gita 7.19), 'Sarvam Khalvidam Brahma' (Chandogya 3.14.1). The meaning of this shloka is that there is no existence other than the Supreme Lord. Whatever we say, it is not separate from the Supreme Lord. The Supreme Lord is devoid of everything and yet is everything. Bahirantashcha bhootanam charam charameva cha. Sukshmatvata tad avijnayam durastham cha antike cha tat. Tat
Bhootanam
= The Supreme Lord is the very essence of all living beings. Evam
= In this way. Charam charam
= The Supreme Lord is present in all living beings, from the smallest to the greatest. Cha
= And. Bahirantashcha
= The Supreme Lord is present outside all living beings. Antashcha
= The Supreme Lord is present inside all living beings. Durastham cha
= The Supreme Lord is present even in the most distant places. Antike cha
= The Supreme Lord is present even in the nearest places. Tat
= The Supreme Lord. Sukshmatvata
= Due to His subtlety. Tad avijnayam
= The Supreme Lord is not perceivable. Explanation: The description of the ultimate truth is presented in the next 12 shlokas, from the 12th to the 17th, that is, in 6 shlokas. The meaning of this shloka is that just as the water in the ice cubes is present both inside and outside the ice cubes, similarly, the Supreme Lord is present both inside and outside all living beings, from the smallest to the greatest.

[Verse 15]

[ Chapter 15 ]

As the water in the vessels is nothing but water, so also in the world, there is nothing but the Supreme Being. This is what the Lord has said in the vision of the great souls as 'Vasudeva sarvam' (Gita 7.19) and in His own vision as 'Sada Sachchham' (Gita 9.19). The Supreme Being is the very essence of all. This is the meaning of it. There is no void. That water, in its atomic form, remains in the sky and when it becomes gross, it appears as droplets, hailstones, etc. Similarly, the Supreme Being, being extremely subtle, cannot be perceived by the senses, mind, and intellect. Because they are beyond them, they are past them. Due to the ignorance of the living beings, they cannot perceive the Supreme Being. Just as the word 'Shrimad Bhagavad Gita' is written at a distance, so also the Supreme Being is beyond the threefold perception - the perception of the country, the perception of the object, and the perception of the time. The perception of the country is that it is far away, the perception of the object is that it is far away, and the perception of the time is that it is far away. The Supreme Being is far away from all three perceptions. Even in the country, the Supreme Being is present, and even in the object, the Supreme Being is present. Even in the time, the Supreme Being is present. Even in the past, the Supreme Being was present. Even in the future, the Supreme Being will be present. The Supreme Being is present in all. For those who are engaged in the collection of worldly objects and the enjoyment of worldly pleasures, the Supreme Being is far away, even if it is near in reality. But for those who are face to face with the Supreme Being, the Supreme Being is near. Therefore, the seeker should renounce worldly desires and the collection of worldly objects and cultivate the desire to attain the Supreme Being alone. When there is a strong desire to attain the Supreme Being, the attainment of the Supreme Being takes place, and there is a constant experience of the Supreme Being. The Supreme Being is extremely subtle, and therefore, it is not perceivable by the senses and the intellect. It is not perceivable by the senses and the intellect because it is beyond them. Now, the question arises that if it is not perceivable, then it must be non-existent. But it is not non-existent. Just as the atomic water is not perceivable by the eyes, but it is not non-existent, similarly, the Supreme Being is not perceivable by the senses and the intellect, but it is not non-existent. The Supreme Being is called 'Jneya' (the twelfth and seventeenth shlokas of this chapter) and 'Avijneya' (the fifth shloka of this chapter) as well. The meaning of this is that it can be known by itself, and therefore, it is 'Jneya', and it cannot be known by the senses and the intellect, and therefore, it is 'Avijneya'. To know the Supreme Being, who is present everywhere, it is necessary that the seeker should consider the Supreme Being as present everywhere. This consideration is also a kind of knowledge. Just as the knowledge gained by perception cannot be erased, similarly, the consideration 'the Supreme Being is present everywhere' cannot be erased. Just as the worldly perceptions 'I am a Brahmin', 'I am a saint', etc. cannot be erased, similarly, the spiritual perceptions cannot be erased. The Supreme Being is far away from the worldly perceptions, and the worldly perceptions are far away from the Supreme Being. The Supreme Being is far away from the perception of the earth, the perception of the water, the perception of the fire, the perception of the air, the perception of the sky, the perception of the prakriti, and the perception of the paramatma. The Supreme Being is far away from the perception of the prakriti, and the prakriti is far away from the perception of the paramatma. The Supreme Being is far away from the perception of the paramatma, and the paramatma is far away from the perception of the Supreme Being. Similarly, the Supreme Being is near to the perception of the prakriti, the prakriti is near to the perception of the sthula sharira, the sthula sharira is near to the perception of the sukshma sharira, the sukshma sharira is near to the perception of the karan sharira, the karan sharira is near to the perception of the aham, and the aham is near to the perception of the Supreme Being. The Supreme Being is near to the perception of the aham, and the aham is near to the perception of the Supreme Being. The Supreme Being is as near as possible, and there is no one else who is as near as the Supreme Being. -

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

Who can erase what is real? The implication is that when one firmly embraces this conviction, that very conviction becomes a means. Knowledge does not remain merely a form; the senses, mind and intellect—beyond form—also possess great glory when one believes. The Atman (the eternal soul) is omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and its experience will arise. Appendix note — In the twelfth verse the Atman is described as “jneya” (to be known). In this verse it is called “avijñeya” (unknowable), meaning that although the Atman is knowable, it is not knowable in the same way as the world. Just as the world is known through the senses, mind and intellect, the Atman is not known through those faculties. The senses, mind and intellect are functions of Prakriti, whereas the Atman is beyond Prakriti. The functions of Prakriti cannot be fully known even by Prakriti itself; therefore the Atman, which is beyond Prakriti, cannot be known by ordinary cognition. The Atman must be accepted by faith, because acceptance resides in the self, not in the causes (mind‑intellect‑senses). * The self is united with the Atman; consequently, attainment of the Atman also occurs through acceptance, not through contemplation, reflection or description. The body has never been united with the world, is not, will not be, and cannot be. The self has never been separated from the Atman, is not, will not be, and cannot be. **[ Verse 16 ]**  
*avibhaktam ca bhuteshu vibhaktam iva ca sthitam*  
*bhutabhrtru ca taj jneyam grasishnu prabhavishnu ca*

Translation:  
“The Atman, though undivided, appears as divided among beings; He who sustains all beings, He who is to be known, He who creates, He who nourishes, He who destroys.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- avibhaktam – undivided, indivisible  
- ca – also, and  
- bhuteshu – in all beings  
- vibhaktam – divided, separated  
- iva – as if  
- ca – also, and  
- sthitam – situated, present  
- bhutabhrtru – the sustainer of beings  
- ca – and  
- tat – that (the Atman)  
- jneyam – to be known, knowable  
- grasishnu – the creator, one who brings forth  
- prabhavishnu – the nourisher, one who sustains  
- ca – and

**Interpretative breakdown**  
The verse states that the Atman, though fundamentally indivisible, seems to be divided among all creatures. This apparent division is only a perception. Just as the sky, clouds, and mountain appear as separate forms yet are one in essence, the Atman appears in the various bodies of different beings yet remains one in reality. In Chapter 13, verse 27 the phrase “samam sarveshu bhuteshu tishthantam parameshvaram” declares that the Supreme Lord (Atman) pervades all beings equally. In Chapter 18, verse 20 the words “avibhaktam vibhakteshu” describe the same undivided reality, and this undivided view is termed “sattvic knowledge.”

The clause “bhutabhrtru ca taj jneyam grasishnu prabhavishnu ca” echoes the instruction “viddhi” (know) found in another verse of this chapter and the promise of “jneya” (to be known) in the twelfth verse. Here the Atman is identified with Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, indicating that the conscious principle (Atman) is one. Acceptance of this principle is internal; therefore statements accepted by the self are never forgotten—e.g., “I am a Brahmin,” “I am married.” In contrast, concepts formed in the mind‑intellect are easily forgotten. Acceptance carries no doubt and no opposite feeling.

The one who nourishes and sustains all beings in the form of Vishnu and is the embodiment of the tamoguna, is said to be the supreme light. It is essential to understand that the Supreme Being, although accepting various qualities for the creation and sustenance of the universe, is not bound by those qualities. He has complete control over them. By accepting primacy, He is said to be the one who destroys all beings in the form of Rudra. The meaning is that the same Supreme Being assumes the names of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva due to His power to create, sustain, and destroy the universe. This shloka describes the comprehensive form of the Supreme Being. Just as the world appears to be one from a physical perspective, similarly, the ultimate reality (Supreme Being) is also one and indivisible. However, just as the world, despite being one, appears in various forms as material and immaterial, living and non-living entities, etc., similarly, the Supreme Being, despite being one, appears in various forms. Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The knowledge that remains is not found in life or in conduct. It does not reside within itself. The knowledge that resides within itself does not depart. Therefore, the light of the intellect (the illuminator) is 'itself' (the self). The self is also a part of the Supreme Being, and the Supreme Being is a part of the self. Knowledge and light come from the Supreme Being only. Therefore, the light of the self (the illuminator) is the Supreme Being. No one can illuminate the Supreme Being, who is the self-luminous Supreme Being. The implication is that the light of the Supreme Being (knowledge) arises from within itself. The light of the self illuminates the intellect, the light of the intellect illuminates the mind, the light of the mind illuminates the senses, and the light of the senses illuminates the objects. Ultimately, the light in all these comes from the Supreme Being only. Therefore, the light of all these illuminators is the Supreme Being itself. Just as students sitting behind one another can see the one sitting in front of them, but not the one sitting behind them, similarly, the ego, intellect, mind, and senses can see the one in front of them, but not the one behind them. Just as the student sitting at the back can see all the students sitting in front of him, similarly, the Supreme Being, who is the ultimate illuminator, can see all, including the ego, intellect, mind, and senses, and illuminate them, but none can illuminate Him. The Supreme Being is the impartial illuminator of the entire universe - 'yasya bhāsā sarvam idaṃ vibhāti sacarācaram' (Srimad Bhagavat 10.13.55). There is no triad of illuminator, light, and illuminated in Him. . He is called the Supreme Being, who is beyond ignorance and extremely detached and unattached. In the ego, mind, intellect, and senses, knowledge and ignorance both arise and subside; but in the Supreme Being, who is the ultimate illuminator of all, ignorance never arises, nor can it arise, nor is it possible for it to arise. Just as darkness never arises in the sun, similarly, ignorance never arises in the Supreme Being. Therefore, the Supreme Being is said to be beyond ignorance. 'Jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ jñānagamyam' - In the Supreme Being, ignorance never arises. He is the embodiment of knowledge, and from Him, knowledge is obtained by all. Therefore, the Supreme Being is called 'jñāna' (knowledge), i.e., the ultimate reality that is beyond all subjects and objects. *
(1) The subject, the living being, and all else are encompassed by the Supreme Being, who is the ultimate reality and the knowledge that is beyond all subjects and objects. The knowledge that arises from the senses, mind, and intellect is not complete knowledge, because even after knowing it, there is still more to know. In reality, the only one who is worthy of being known is the Supreme Being - 'avasi dekhiahi dekhana jogu' (Mānasa 1.229.3). After knowing the Supreme Being, there is nothing else to know. In the 15th chapter, the Lord has said, 'I am the only one who can be known through the entire Vedas' (15th verse); 'He who knows me becomes all-knowing' (19th verse). Therefore, the Supreme Being is called 'jñeya' (the one to be known). Through the knowledge of the Supreme Being, one can transcend the ignorance of the world and know the ultimate reality. Therefore, the Supreme Being is called 'jñānagamyam' (the one who can be known through knowledge). 'hr̥di sarvasya viṣṭhitam' - The Supreme Being resides in the heart of all beings. The implication is that although the Supreme Being is omnipresent, all-pervading, and infinite in all aspects, His abode is the heart. The way to experience the Supreme Being in one's heart is as follows:
(1) A person knows all subjects and objects, but in that knowledge, both truth and untruth coexist. To distinguish between the two, the seeker should experience that although the various stages of life, such as wakefulness, sleep, and childhood, and the various circumstances, such as happiness and sorrow, and the union and separation of the world, have changed, I have remained the same. Although the country, time, object, person, and event have changed, I have remained the same. The implication is that although the various stages and circumstances have changed, the one who has remained the same is not different from them. To experience this, one should separate the one who has remained the same from the various stages and circumstances. By doing so, one can experience the one who resides in the heart of all beings, who is the same as the ultimate reality. * Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

(2) Just as an extremely hungry person cannot remain without food, and one who is intensely eager to obtain the Supreme Soul becomes restless, his heart cannot stay without thirst; in the same way the experience of that Supreme Soul arises. One cannot live without the Supreme Soul; one becomes agitated. Without Him there is no hunger, no thirst, and no sleep. Apart from that Supreme Soul no other activity can proceed. Thus, once the experience of the Supreme Soul is established in the heart, the seeker feels that “the Supreme Soul is everywhere.” This is the true experience. Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav) – The subject (jñeya) described from verses 12 to 17 is the total form of the Lord (“Vāsudevaḥ sarvam”). It includes the three modes: nirguṇa‑nirākāra (verse 12), saguna‑nirākāra (verse 13) and saguna‑sākāra (verse 16). ‘jñāna‑gamyam’ – The Supreme Soul is known only through the knowledge of His essence; it cannot be known through action, object, or any other means. Apart from jñāna‑gamyam there is no other means to know Him. Whether a person follows karma‑yoga, jñāna‑yoga, dhyāna‑yoga or any other path, the realization of the Supreme Soul ultimately comes through the knowledge of His essence. Faith, devotion, divine grace, etc., also lead to Him only through that knowledge, because knowledge is the source of knowing. Here the term ‘jñāna‑gamyam’ can also be understood as “attainable through the community of means,” a description that occupies verses 7 to 11 of this chapter. Relation (Sambandh) – The field (kṣetra), knowledge (jñāna) and the object of knowledge (jñeya) described from verse 1 to verse 17 are now concluded, together with their results, in the following verses. Thus

kṣetram iti kṣetraṁ tathā jñānaṁ jñeyaṁ ca oktaṁ samāsataḥ  
mad‑bhaktaḥ = in this way = field = and = having known this = jñeya = attains my state (verse 18)

Explanation – “Thus the field, the knowledge and the object of knowledge are spoken of as a whole.” In verses 5 and 6 the “field” is described; from verses 7 to 11 the “community of means” (knowledge) is described; from verses 12 to 17 the “object of knowledge” (the Supreme Soul) is described. In this compact manner the field, the knowledge and the object of knowledge have been presented. By knowing the field, the community of means (knowledge) and the object of knowledge (the Supreme Soul) through their essence, one attains my feeling. When the field is fully understood, the sense of separation from the field disappears. When the community of means (knowledge) is fully understood and adopted, the ego‑identification (personal identity) vanishes. When the object of knowledge (the Supreme Soul) is fully known, it is attained, resulting in an inseparable experience with the Supreme Soul. “mad‑bhakta‑etad‑vijñāya‑mad‑bhāvāy‑upapadyate” – “My devotee, having known this, attains my state.”

Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav) – The phrase “mad‑bhakta‑etad‑vijñāya” implies that the total knowledge of the Supreme Soul can be obtained only through devotion; therefore the seeker must become a devotee. The expression “mad‑bhāvāy‑upapadyate” appears in the Gītā in several forms, e.g., “mad‑bhāvam‑āgatāḥ” (4.10), “mam‑sādharmyam‑āgatāḥ” (14.2), “mad‑bhāvam‑so ’dhigacchati” (14.19). “mad‑bhāv” means “my loving devotion.”

[ Verse 19-20 ]  
* Sadhak Sanjivani *  
-

Air, fire, water and earth, as well as sound, touch, form and taste, are the elements; likewise, nature itself is eternal. Only by not considering the relationship between these two can one be freed from qualities. There is no difference in the eternal nature of the two; but there is a difference in their forms. “In the activity, causation, and agency, the purpose is that nature is described.” Space, for example, is nature endowed with qualities, whereas the soul is entirely devoid of qualities; nature has defects, but the soul does not; nature becomes the cause of the world, whereas the soul does not become the cause of anyone; nature has the sense of action and causation, whereas the soul is devoid of the sense of action and causation. “Both” means that nature and the soul are separate. Therefore, just as nature and the soul are eternal, this difference (discrimination) between them is also eternal. In the first verse of this chapter, the words “Idam shariram kshetram” direct the gaze toward the human body; that is, the understanding is of the human body itself, and from the word “kshetrajnaḥ” the understanding is of the person who knows the body. Therefore, to make the understanding of nature and its mere activity, the word “prakritim” is used, and to make the understanding of the mere field‑knowers, the word “purusham” is used. In the second verse of this chapter, the word “viddhi” was used to know the unity of the field‑knower with the Supreme Self, and here the word “viddhi” is used to know the difference of the soul from nature. The implication is that the human considers himself and the body as one; therefore, the Lord commands Arjuna with the word “viddhi” that these two are entirely separate—understand this correctly. “Vikaraanscha‑gunaanscha eva viddhi prakritisambhavan”—understand that the seven defects: desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, attachment, consciousness, and determination, as well as the three qualities: sattva, rajas, tamas, are produced by nature. The implication is that the soul has no defects or qualities. In the twelfth verse of the seventh chapter, the Lord says that the qualities arise from Himself, whereas here it says that the qualities arise from nature. The implication is that because of the devotee’s situation, the Lord says that the qualities arise from Himself and offers His refuge to escape the illusion of qualities. But here, because of the context of knowledge, the qualities are said to arise from nature. Therefore, the ten (Mahabhut and subjects) that are produced by the soul are called “action.” The thirteen (external and internal organs) are called “causation.” All the actions performed by these are produced by nature as the cause. What is produced is called “action,” and what brings about the accomplishment of action is called “causation”; that is, all the instruments (means) for performing an action are called “causation.” Causation comes in three types: (1) the five sense organs, (2) the five mental faculties, and (3) mind, intellect, and ego. The sense organs are gross, the mental faculties are subtle, and mind, intellect, and ego are extremely subtle. The sense organs and mental faculties are called “external causation,” while mind, intellect, and ego are called “internal causation.” The sense organs are the ones that perform actions, and the ones that govern the sense organs and mental faculties are mind, intellect, and ego. The implication is that the sense organs are governed by the mental faculties, the mental faculties are governed by mind, mind is governed by intellect, and intellect is governed by ego. Without mind, intellect, and ego, the sense organs and mental faculties do not work. When the mind becomes associated with the mental faculties, knowledge of objects arises. From the knowledge of objects by the mind, intellect decides which object is acceptable and which is to be rejected, which is correct and which is incorrect

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 13 ]  
By identifying with the external nature, one becomes the master of one’s own intellect, i.e., becomes both the doer (Karma) and the experiencer (Bhakti). The self, being situated in nature, indeed enjoys the qualities of nature – “Purushaḥ prakṛtisthō hi bhūnte prakṛti‑jangūnānaḥ” (Gita 13.21). But when the knowledge of the Self is realized, one is neither the doer nor the experiencer – “Śarīrasthō'pi Kaunteya na karoti na lipyate” (Gita 13.31). Thus, all actions performed by the body of a self that is devoid of both doership and experienership arise solely from the ego‑driven mind. The Gita describes these ego‑driven actions in many ways:  
- “All actions are performed by nature” (Chapter 13, Verse 21). - “All actions are performed by the qualities of nature” (Chapter 3, Verse 27). - “The qualities are present within the qualities” (Chapter 3, Verse 28). - “Apart from the qualities, there is no other doer” (Chapter 14, Verse 19). - “The senses are active in their respective objects” (Chapter 5, Verse 9). In short, all actions performed by the external and internal senses arise from nature. [ Chapter 13 ]  
The self, after identifying with the external (inert) nature, also creates a separate independent existence in the form of “Prakṛtisthā Purusha” (Gita 13.21), which is called “aham” (I). In this “aham” both the inert and the conscious aspects are present. The disturbances of pleasure and pain occur in the inert part, but because the inert part is identified with the self, the conscious part takes on the result of these disturbances. Thus the conscious part accepts the disturbance as “I am happy” or “I am unhappy.”  
For example, a shopkeeper may feel a loss, yet he says, “I have incurred a loss.”  
Heat appears in the body, yet one accepts, “I have a fever.”  
Heat does not arise within the self; if it did, it would never disappear. The result of pleasure and pain is borne by the conscious part; only then does the self desire liberation from pleasure and pain. If one is neither happy nor unhappy, the desire for liberation cannot arise. The desire for liberation arises from the inert aspect, because by accepting the inert aspect one is bound. The one who considers himself happy or unhappy seeks liberation from the disturbance of pleasure and pain, and that is his liberation. In other words, in the desire for liberation (kalyaan), the conscious part is dominant, whereas in the desire for pleasures, the inert part is dominant. Therefore, ultimately the partner of liberation is the conscious part, not the inert part. The self is called the experiencer of pleasure and pain – “Purushaḥ sukha‑duḥkhānāṁ bhōktṛtvē hetur ucchitaḥ” – becoming content (raji) when favorable circumstances arise is the enjoyment of pleasure, and becoming upset (nārāja) when unfavorable circumstances arise is the enjoyment of pain. This enjoyment of pleasure and pain occurs only in the self (consciousness), not in nature (inertness), because nature does not have the capacity to be happy or unhappy. Hence the self is the experiencer of pleasure and pain. If the self does not become content or upset in the presence of favorable or unfavorable circumstances, it cannot become an experiencer of pleasure and pain. In Chapters 7, verses 4–5, the Lord describes his two natures as “apara” (inert) and “para” (conscious). These two natures are the Lord’s own qualities, so they naturally tend toward the Lord. However, the para‑nature (consciousness), which is a part of the Supreme Self and whose natural inclination is to seek the Supreme, is attracted to immediate pleasures and keeps attributing its disturbances to itself. Only the inert part contains the distortion; the conscious part does not. Thus, truly being happy or unhappy is not the duty of the conscious part; rather, the conscious part, by identifying itself as happy or unhappy with the inert part, becomes the nature of the knower. In other words, the conscious part does not become happy or unhappy; it merely accepts the state of happiness or unhappiness arising from the interaction of the pleasure‑creating and pain‑creating aspects. The conscious part cannot have two opposing states of pleasure and pain simultaneously; such duality can exist only in the mutable nature. What is not mutable cannot have two forms. Therefore, all disturbances can exist only in the mutable. The conscious part, while remaining as it is, is accompanied by the mutable nature. “Ātmānaṁ ced vijānīyādayam asmīti pūrūṣaḥ. Kimicchann kasyā kāmāya śarīra‑manusanjvarēt.”  
(The self says, “I am the knower of the self.” What desire does the body have, for what work does it burn?)

* Sadhak‑Sanjivani *

Parishishtha Bhaav – Bhagavan again describes the nature of the field (Kshetra) and the knower of the field (Kshetrajna) using the terms Prakriti and Purusha. The field and the knower of the field are the manifestations (Vyakti) and Prakriti and Purusha are the collective (Samasti). There is one division of Prakriti and one division of Purusha. Body and the world belong to the Prakriti division, while soul and Paramatma belong to the Purusha division. Just as Prakriti and Purusha are eternal, the knowledge of their difference, i.e., discrimination (Viveka), is also eternal. From the perspective of discrimination, these two divisions are completely unrelated; there is no connection whatsoever between them. Prakriti is non‑existence (Asat), root and sorrow‑like, while Purusha is existence (Sat), consciousness (Chit) and bliss‑like. Prakriti is perishable, changeable and active, whereas Purusha is indestructible, unchanging and inactive. The constant dissolution of Prakriti and the constant attainment of Purusha are their characteristics. In the beginning of the Gita, Bhagavan also described this division using terms such as body and body‑self (Sharir and Shariri), form and form‑self (Deh and Dehi), Sat and Asat, etc. Therefore, a precise understanding of this division is essential for every seeker and leads to quick realization. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

They are the ones who eat. From these three qualities (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas) all substances and actions arise. When a Prakriti‑bound Purusha (the soul) takes these qualities as his own, they become the cause of birth in his higher and lower wombs. **Explanation** – “Purusha (the soul) is Prakriti‑bound” means that the soul is not merely present in the body (Prakriti), but when he identifies the body as “I” and “mine,” he is said to be in Prakriti. Such a Prakriti‑bound Purusha, taking the conditions created by the qualities as pleasant or unpleasant, becomes happy when favorable conditions arise and unhappy when unfavorable conditions arise. This is the soul’s becoming a consumer of Prakriti’s qualities. Just as in a motor accident both the motor and the driver are involved, in the execution of an action only the motor (the body) is dominant, but the consequence (punishment) is borne by the driver (the doer). Likewise, in worldly activities both Prakriti and Purusha are involved; in the execution of actions only the body is dominant, but the pleasure or pain is borne by the Purusha who has associated himself with the body. If he does not associate himself with the body and regards all actions as performed by Prakriti alone (see Gita Chapter 13 Verse 29), he will not become the one to suffer the fruits of those actions. “Because of the association with the qualities, the soul is born in the wombs of the higher and lower realms.” The wombs that are abundant in pleasure are called “Sat‑yoni” and those abundant in pain are called “Asat‑yoni.” The reason for the soul’s birth in Sat‑ and Asat‑yoni is the association with the qualities. Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas are the three qualities that arise from Prakriti. Once the soul is in Prakriti, he becomes a consumer of Prakriti’s qualities, and this association, attachment, and affection lead the soul to be born in higher and lower wombs. If he is not Prakriti‑bound, does not indulge in the body (Prakriti), remains in his own nature, he will never become a consumer of pleasure and pain; he will be equal in pleasure and pain, and will be healthy (see Gita Chapter 14 Verse 24). Thus he can be in Prakriti and also in his own nature. The difference is that being in Prakriti is a state of bondage, while being in his own nature is a state of natural freedom. Bondage is unnatural for him, and liberation is natural. Therefore bondage does not suit him, and liberation does. Where there is a distinction (discrimination) between Prakriti and Purusha, there is ignorance of associating with Prakriti. From this ignorance the soul becomes associated with Prakriti. By becoming associated, the soul considers himself as Prakriti‑bound, i.e., as residing in Prakriti (the body). Being Prakriti‑bound gives the body a sense of “I” and “mine.” This is the association with the qualities. This association binds the soul (see Gita Chapter 14 Verse 5). Once bound by the qualities, the soul moves according to the qualities (see Gita Chapter 14 Verse 18). **Appendix** – In the latter half of Verse 19 and the first half of Verse 20, the Lord describes Prakriti, and in the latter half of Verse 20 and in Verse 21, he describes Purusha. The relationship with the object, person, and action is the “guna‑sang” (association with the qualities), which is the cause of birth and death. The association with the qualities is impermanent, and disassociation is permanent. Disassociation is our nature – “Asango hyaya Purusha” (Brihadaranyaka 4.3.15). If we do not hold onto the impermanent (association with the qualities), birth and death cannot occur. “I” is the root (Prakriti), “am” is the conscious (Purusha), and “I am” is the association of the root and consciousness. In this “I am” there is both the doer and the consumer. If “I” is absent, “am” is absent, and “is” remains. Just as iron and fire are associated, the term “Prakriti‑bound” means “body‑bound.” From Verse 19 the cycle of Prakriti and Purusha is in motion, so here the soul is called Prakriti‑bound. In reality, the soul is not Prakriti‑bound or body‑bound. By not considering himself healthy, i.e., by not experiencing his own state in the self, he considers himself body‑bound.

[ Verse 22 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

When iron is left unattended it remains on the earth, while fire merges into the formless element of fire. In the same way, the sense of “I am” (aham) stays only in nature, and the sense of “am” (is), being the form of “has‑been”, dissolves into “is”. “Is” contains no sense of doer‑hood or enjoyer‑hood. Hence, in worldly experiences the “I‑am” is drawn into pleasure and pain, whereas “is” is not. The “I‑am” becomes both the actor and the experiencer; “is” never becomes either. Therefore the seeker must not identify with “I‑am” but must recognize and experience “is”. All beings experience the coming and going of happiness and sorrow and the fact of their own existence. Even a sinful person experiences this. Yet, when such experience arises, the person, together with the incoming happiness‑sorrow, becomes both happy and sorrowful. This happens because attachment to happiness and fear of sorrow create the false notion “I am separate and happiness‑sorrow are separate”. Discrimination does not work in that case. In reality the self is not independently happy or sorrowful; it merely assumes happiness or sorrow in conjunction with the body. Thus happiness‑sorrow exist only on the basis of an un‑discriminating belief. **Relation** – In verses 19, 20 and 21 the nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) were described. In the following verses the special attributes of the person are explained. **Sanskrit shloka**  
*upadarṣṭān‑anumantā ca bhartā bhoktā maheśvaraḥ*  
*paramātmēti cāpyukto dehe ’smin puruṣaḥ paraḥ*

**Word‑by‑word**  
- upadarṣṭān – the seer, the one who observes  
- anumantā – the grantor, the one who gives permission  
- ca – and  
- bhartā – the sustainer, the one who nourishes  
- bhoktā – the enjoyer, the consumer  
- maheśvaraḥ – the great lord, the supreme controller

- paramātmē – as the supreme soul (Atman)  
- iti – thus  
- ca – also  
- apyukto – is called  
- dehe – in the body  
- ’smin – in this  
- puruṣaḥ – the person  
- paraḥ – the supreme

**English translation of the shloka**  
“The seer, the grantor, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the great lord – this being is also called the supreme soul (Paramātmā) even while residing in this body.”

**Explanation** – Because this person is ever‑present, pervading everywhere, immutable and eternal (as stated in the 24th verse of the second chapter of the Gita), when he turns his attention toward nature and its functions, i.e., when he acknowledges his relationship with them, the designation “upadarṣṭā” (seer) becomes applicable. The person, being without any external relation, is therefore called “bhartā” (sustainer). By associating with the body, he regards favorable circumstances as making him happy and adverse circumstances as making him sorrowful; consequently the term “bhoktā” (enjoyer) is appropriate. He regards the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect and wealth as his possessions; thus he is called “maheśvara” (great lord), the one who gives consent for every action. Hence the name “anumantā” (grantor) is used. He, together with the embodied object, partakes of food, water, etc., and protects it from heat and cold. The phrase “paramātmēti cāpyukto dehe ’smin puruṣaḥ paraḥ” declares that the person is the highest, the supreme soul; therefore the scriptures refer to him as “Paramātmā”. Even while residing in the body, he remains free from any bodily attachment. (Continuation of the chapter follows.)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

In the thirty‑first verse it is explained that this description must be understood. In reality there is no distinction; it neither resides in the body nor becomes attached. It is not. Just as the same person is addressed by different titles—father, uncle, brother, etc.—according to different relationships, similarly the same Purusha (the conscious principle) is called by many names, yet in reality it is one. Appendix meaning—In fact the Purusha is “para” (transcendent), but in relation to others he becomes the observer, the authorizer, etc. For example, a man is “father” in relation to his son, “son” in relation to his father, “husband” in relation to his wife, “brother” in relation to his sister, and so on. These relations exist only for the performance of duty, not for affection. The true nature is “para”, i.e., completely without relation. Here the many titles such as observer, authorizer, Ishvara, etc., signify the unity that the conscious principle is actually one. In the chapter on knowledge the description of Prakṛti (nature) and Purusha is the main theme. Therefore all the words that appear here—observer, authorizer, Ishvara, etc.—should be understood as referring to Purusha. Connection – From verse 19 to verse 22 the analysis of Prakṛti and Purusha is given; the following verses explain the fruit of knowing them as a reality. [ Verse 23 ]

**Sanskrit (Roman transliteration) – word‑by‑word**  
- ya – who  
- evam – thus  
- vetti – knows  
- puruṣam – the Purusha (the conscious principle)  
- prakṛtim – nature (Prakṛti)  
- ca – and  
- guṇaiḥ – with qualities  
- saha – together  
- sarvathā – in every way  
- vartamāno – existing, present  
- api – also  
- na – not  
- sa – he  
- bhūyo – again  
- abhijāyate – is born

**Translation**  
He who thus knows the Purusha together with nature and its qualities, even while existing in every way, is not born again. Explanation – In the previous verse “dehe’smin puruṣaḥ paraḥ” declares Purusha as beyond the body, i.e., without relation. Here the word “evam” says that the seeker who knows Purusha as beyond the body and nature, i.e., relation‑free, also realizes that everything that appears in the world as modification, action, cause, object, etc., is merely the work of Prakṛti and its qualities. Consequently, even while performing duties appropriate to his varna, ashrama, and circumstance, he does not take birth again. The cause of birth is the association with the qualities (Gita 13.21). In the phrase “sarvathā vartamāno’pi na sa bhūyo’bhijāyate” one must not take prohibited conduct, because one who experiences himself as free from bodily relation and perceives nature with its qualities as separate from himself cannot develop desire for unreal objects. Without desire, prohibited conduct cannot arise, since desire is the cause of prohibited conduct (Gita 3.33). Here the Lord cautions the seeker to know his true nature, so that he clearly understands that in that nature there is essentially no action. Therefore he is not the doer of any action, and because he is not the doer, he is also not the enjoyer. When the seeker realizes himself as non‑doer, his pride of agency disappears automatically and the attachment to the fruits of action also ceases. Yet the scripturally prescribed actions continue to occur automatically. Because he is beyond the qualities, he does not acquire rebirth.

[ Verse 24 ]

* Sadhak-Sanjivani *

**Appendix – Explanation of the phrase “dehe‑asmīn puruṣaḥ paraḥ” found in the preceding verse**

The shloka explains that when a person’s discernment (viveka) awakens, the experience “dehe‑asmīn puruṣaḥ paraḥ” (the soul is beyond the body) comes to him. Even while performing all actions in accordance with his varna‑ashrama, he remains detached. In reality, the mere human form is detached; it becomes entangled only when it is accompanied by qualities (gunas). Thus the soul repeatedly births and dies (see the 21st verse of this chapter). The qualities are associated with nature, not with the soul (see the 19th–20th verses of this chapter). The word **apī** in the phrase “sarvathā vartamāno‑api” means that, like an attached human, he behaves in all ways yet remains impassive (see Gita – 3rd chapter, 25th verse). **“na sa bhūyo‑abhijāyate”** – Just as butter that has been extracted from buttermilk does not become curd again when mixed back, a person does not become bound to qualities after detaching from them. His relationship with Brahman becomes pure. Just as Brahman has no birth or death, so too does he have none. In the 31st verse of chapter 6, the shloka says “sarvathā vartamāno‑api sa yogī mayi vartate” (even though fully present, the yogi dwells in Me). Here it says “sarvathā vartamāno‑api na sa bhūyo‑abhijāyate” (even though fully present, he does not become attached). In the former, the yogi attains **prīti** (love); in the latter, he attains **bodhi** (understanding). In both, the soul does not remain with the qualities. The difference is that in **bodhi** liberation from birth‑death is achieved, whereas in **prīti** there is both liberation and union with the Lord. **Connection –** The preceding verse explained that the Lord’s birthlessness is due to the true knowledge of nature (prakriti) and the soul (puruṣa). Now the question arises: is there any other way to be free from birth‑death? The Lord answers in the next two verses with four methods. ---

**Shloka 24**

*dhyanena‑ātmani paśyanti kechida‑ātmanam ātmanā. anya saṅkhya‑ena yōgen karmayoga‑ena cāpare. 24.*

**Translation:**  
Some see their own soul within themselves by meditation; others, by Sankhya and by Karma yoga, see it within themselves. **Commentary**

*Some by meditation, others by Sankhya, etc.* – The commentary explains that those who meditate experience the soul within themselves. Others, through Sankhya and Karma yoga, also experience the soul within themselves. In such states, the mind, world, body, habits, and thoughts are transcended. At that moment, the meditator, satisfied with the experience within himself, is content (see Gita – 6th chapter, 19th–20th verses). **Explanation –** “dhyanena‑ātmani paśyanti kechida‑ātman” – In the state where the mind is restrained, the soul is seen within oneself. This is described in the 27th–28th verses of the 5th chapter, the 10th–28th verses of the 6th chapter, and the 8th–14th verses of the 8th chapter, where the attention to qualities, non‑qualities, form, and formlessness is described. Depending on one’s interest, faith, and ability, many practitioners, by focusing their attention accordingly, experience the supreme soul within themselves. The detachment of the relationship between nature and the soul occurs by knowing them separately; this detachment also occurs through meditation. Meditation does not occur in a dull or distracted mind. It begins in a distracted mind. When the mind becomes concentrated in its form, samādhi is attained. When concentration is achieved, the mind becomes restrained. *“anya saṅkhya‑ena yōgen”* – In the 11th–30th verses of the 2nd chapter, the 31st–43rd verses of the 4th chapter, the 8th, 9th, and 13th–26th verses of the 5th chapter, and the 4th–5th verses of the 12th chapter, it is said that many practitioners, by Sankhya yoga, experience the supreme soul within themselves. Sankhya yoga is called *viveka* (discernment). By this discernment, the judgment of *sat‑asat* is made: “*sat* is eternal.”

**Further Commentary**

The phrase “sarvathā vartamāno‑api” indicates that even when fully present, the yogi remains detached. The phrase “na sa bhūyo‑abhijāyate” emphasizes that attachment does not arise even when fully present. The yogi, through love, experiences union with the Lord; through understanding, he attains liberation from birth‑death. Both states are free from the qualities, but love brings union with the divine, whereas understanding brings liberation.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

It is omnipresent, has a steady nature, is immovable, and is unmanifest. It acts only for the welfare of the world. Yajna, Dana, Tapas, Tirtha, and Vrat are its actions; it is inconceivable. And “Asat” is moving, impermanent, defective, and changeable. In such a way, the Sankhya yogi becomes completely distinct from nature and its actions through discernment and thought, and experiences the Atman (the eternal soul) within himself. “By Karma Yoga also” – from the 42nd to the 31st verse of the second chapter; from the 7th to the 19th verse of the third chapter; from the 16th to the 32nd verse of the fourth chapter; from the 6th–7th etc. verses of the fifth chapter, it is stated that many practitioners experience the Atman within themselves through Karma Yoga. Whatever one does, one does it only for the welfare of living beings, not for oneself. By doing so, one becomes detached from those actions, matter, body, etc., and experiences the Atman within oneself. Human beings naturally accept the body within themselves, believing it. To dispel this belief, one must see the Atman within oneself, i.e., to regard the Atman within oneself instead of the body. Seeing the Atman within oneself is independent of action. Knowledge that is action‑dependent arises from the relationship with nature. Therefore, a practitioner does not exist in the Atman by means of any action; rather, one is situated in the Atman itself. The state of being situated in one’s own Atman, which arises from the separation of nature and Purusha, also arises from the separation of relation by Karma Yoga. A Karma Yogi cannot have anything done by any action. Appendix: Just as the previous shloka explained the importance of discernment as a means of liberation, here other means such as Dhyana Yoga are explained. In the Gita, the attainment of the Atman through Dhyana Yoga is mentioned in Chapter 6, Verse 28; the attainment through Sankhya Yoga is mentioned in Chapter 2, Verse 15; and the attainment through Karma Yoga is mentioned in Chapter 2, Verse 71. All these are independent means to attain the Atman. Others, knowing only themselves, after hearing, worship others. Even they, by following the mind, are devoted to death according to what they have heard. **Commentary on Verse 2.25**  
Thus, those who are devoted to what they have heard act according to what they have heard. Others, after hearing, worship others. They do not know death. Explanation:

[ Verse 26 ]  
* Sadhak – Sanjeevani *

According to the preceding discussion, a person who moves with ardent enthusiasm, without any worldly desire, and whose sole purpose is to attain the ultimate reality (Atman), will naturally attain the supreme self by the grace of the divine. The reason is that wealth, when possessed by a person who has attained the supreme self, becomes a means of attaining the supreme self; because the Lord knows and is under the control of that person, but the supreme self is not under anyone. The body is bound to death; when a person becomes devoted to the great sages, the bond with the body is released. Therefore they transcend death; they no longer consider the death of the body as their death, and they are freed from that belief. **Three categories of śruti‑parāyaṇa sādhakas**

1. If a sādhaka has no desire for worldly pleasures, only a keen longing for the attainment of the ultimate reality, and he follows the command of the great sage, he is an experienced great sage; then the sādhaka will quickly attain the supreme self. 2. If a sādhaka still has a desire for pleasure, then by merely following the command of the great sage, that desire will be destroyed and he will attain the supreme self. If, for some reason, a sādhaka becomes skeptical or has a negative view towards the great sage, he will see only defects and no virtues. This is because the great sage is beyond both virtues and defects (guna‑atīta). When a person has doubt, his own feeling is revealed. The person sees the world from the feeling he has, and that feeling becomes his bond. Seeing defects makes the bond with defects. Therefore a sādhaka should not focus on the actions or conduct of the great sage, but should remain neutral towards them. The one who can gain more from the great sage is the one who keeps no worldly relationship with them and only maintains a spiritual (sādhanā) relationship. Also, the sādhaka must be careful not to criticize the great sage. If he criticizes them, he will not progress. 3. The sādhakas who follow the command of the great sage but are not experienced great sages, and who have even a slight attachment, are those who do not understand the scriptures, have weak discernment, but have a keen desire to escape death. Such people also transcend death by following the command of the living liberated great sages. **Story of Satya‑Kama**  
Satya‑Kama, the son of Jabal, went to Gautama Rishi to receive instruction. The Rishi gave him four hundred weak and frail cows and told him to follow them. Satya‑Kama, with enthusiasm, said that he would return only when their number reached one thousand. He then took the cows into the forest and began to rear them. After many years, when their number reached one thousand, a bull told him that their number had reached one thousand and that he should bring them to the teacher. The bull then gave Satya‑Kama the first teaching of Brahma. The next day, Satya‑Kama set out with the cows toward the guru‑college. On the way, a fire offered the second teaching of Brahma, a laughing bird offered the third teaching of Brahma, and a water‑bird (madgu) offered the fourth teaching of Brahma. Thus, by acquiring Brahma‑knowledge on the way, he reached Gautama Rishi. When the guru asked, he told the whole story and requested that the guru give him instruction from his own mouth. Gautama Rishi then instructed him (Chandogya 4th chapter, sections 4 to 9). In this way, by simply following the command of the living liberated great sage, Satya‑Kama attained Brahma‑knowledge. **Relationship**  
The previous verse said that śruti‑parāyaṇa sādhakas also transcend death. The question now is: what is the cause of birth and death? The Lord answers this in the following verse. **Verse**  
yāvat sañjāyate kiñcit tattvaṃ sthāvarajñāgamam |  
kṣetra kṣetra jñāna saṃyogāt tadviddhi bharatārṣabh || 26 ||

*Translation:*  
As long as a certain principle is known, the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetra‑jñāna) are joined together; that is, the knowledge of the field and the knower of the field are the same, O Bharata.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Chapter 13
The Interaction of the Field and the Knower of the Field

O, Arjuna, son of the Bharata dynasty, know that all beings, whether stationary or mobile, are born from the interaction of the field (kshetra) and the knower of the field (kshetrajna). Explanation: As long as the interaction of the field and the knower of the field continues, stationary beings such as trees, creepers, grass, shrubs, skin, bamboo, and mountains, as well as mobile beings like humans, gods, animals, birds, insects, butterflies, fish, and tortoises, are all born. The field (kshetra) is the perishable material substance, and the knower of the field (kshetrajna) is the imperishable, eternal, and unchanging essence that knows the field. The interaction of the field and the knower of the field is the cause of the birth of the jiva (the individual self). This interaction is the result of the jiva's identification with the body and its attachment to the material world. As long as the jiva identifies with the body and its material possessions, it is born and dies. But when the jiva realizes its true nature and its relationship with the knower of the field, it is no longer born and dies. Note: The term "kshetra" refers to the material world, including the body, and "kshetrajna" refers to the knower of the field, which is the eternal and unchanging essence that knows the field. Appendix - The Commentary:

In this context, the term "yavatsanjayate" refers to all living beings, including those born from eggs, womb, sweat, and other means. The seventh chapter of the Gita also mentions this in the sixth verse: "Etad-yoni bhutani" (all these beings are born from this source). In the context of devotion, the Lord says that both the higher and lower nature are His own nature, and that all living beings are born from the interaction of these two natures. However, in the context of knowledge, the Lord says that all living beings are born from the interaction of the field and the knower of the field. The question arises: how can the knower of the field (the eternal and unchanging essence) interact with the field (the material world)? The answer is that the knower of the field has the power to attract and interact with the material world, just as the sun attracts and interacts with the earth. This power is given to the knower of the field by the Lord Himself. However, the knower of the field has misused this power and has identified itself with the material world, leading to birth and death. This is the cause of the jiva's bondage to the cycle of birth and death. Connection:

The previous verse explained that the jiva is born and dies due to its identification with the body and its material possessions. Now, the question arises: how can the jiva escape from this cycle of birth and death? The answer will be given in the next verse. Verse 13.1:

[ Verse 27 ]

**Shloka (Transliteration + Meaning)**  
Yah vinashyatsu sarveṣu bhūteṣu sādhaka‑sanjīvani samam sarveṣu bhūteṣu tiṣṭhantaṃ parameśvaram |  
Vinashyatsva vinashyantaṃ yah paśyati sa paśyati || 27 ||

*Yah* – he who; *vinashyatsu* – destroying; *sarveṣu bhūteṣu* – in all beings; *sādhaka‑sanjīvani* – the eternal life of the seeker; *samam* – equal; *tiṣṭhantaṃ* – standing; *parameśvaram* – the Supreme God. Thus: **“He who, in all beings, is the eternal life of the seeker, who stands as the Supreme God in all beings, sees the one who is destroying and is destroyed, sees that one.”**

**Commentary (English Translation)**

The phrase *samam sarveṣu bhūteṣu* means that the Supreme Soul (Atman) is present in all beings in a uniform, unchanging form. All living beings are diverse—solid or moving, pure (sattva), passionate (rajas), or dull (tamas), small or large, tall or short, of many colours. Yet the Supreme Soul is equally situated in every one of them; it is neither small nor large, nor does it vary in any way. In the second verse of this chapter, the Lord explained that He is one with the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetreṇa). Here the same idea is expressed: the Supreme Soul is uniformly situated in all beings. *tiṣṭhantaṃ* refers to the three states of all beings—creation, preservation, and dissolution. Beings are born, exist, and are destroyed; they rise and fall, move in various directions, and are never still. The Supreme Soul, however, remains constantly and uniformly present in all these changing beings. *Parameshvaram* denotes that every being regards some deity or master as its God. The Supreme Soul, however, is the ultimate God of all beings and of the entire material‑conscious world. The phrase *vinashyatsva vinashyantaṃ yah paśyati sa paśyati* means that among those beings who are constantly moving toward destruction, the one who sees the Supreme Soul as indestructible and equal is truly seeing. A person who identifies with the changing body and sees himself as such is not truly seeing; only the one who sees himself as inseparable from the unchanging Supreme Soul is truly seeing. In the second verse of this chapter, the Lord said that knowledge of the field and its knower is the only knowledge in His view. Here it is stated that the knowledge of seeing the Supreme Soul as indestructible and equal in all beings who are subject to destruction is the true knowledge. Just as the field is always changing while its knower remains unchanged, all beings are born and destroyed, but the Supreme Soul remains uniformly present in all states. In the twenty‑sixth verse, the Lord explained that all beings are created by the union of the field and its knower. The field is never still, but the knower never changes. Therefore, experience the constant separation of the field from its knower. In the twenty‑seventh verse, the Lord says that in all beings that are born and destroyed, the Supreme Soul remains indestructible and uniformly present; experience unity with it. **Appendix (Illustration)**  
Just as the sky may be illuminated by the sun, darkened, filled with smoke, clouded, struck by lightning, rained upon, or struck by hail, yet the sky itself remains unchanged, the same is true of the entire reality. Whether there is creation and dissolution, birth and death, famine, flood, earthquake, or war, the reality remains indifferent, unchanged, and unperturbed. This indifference is natural; the disturbances (sangha) are artificial and imagined. Whether one is bound or free, sinful or righteous, the indeterminate reality is uniformly present in both.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 ]

Just as the Ganga river flows continuously, the foundation over which it flows remains steady as ever. The water of the Ganga may be clear at times and murky at others; it may become scarce or flood; it may warm when rain falls on a hot mountain or cool when it does not; it may roar with a swift current or become calm. Yet the foundation remains unchanged, unaffected by any difference. Likewise, fish may appear in the water, snakes and other creatures may come, floating logs may drift, flowers may flow, garbage may appear, mud may accumulate, dung may be seen, a corpse may drift, a living person may float. All these come and go, but the foundation remains unmoving and impassive. In the same way, the entire country, time, objects, persons, actions, states, circumstances, events, etc. flow continuously, but the Self (the luminous reality) remains unchanged. Change and destruction occur in country and time, not within the Self. “Who sees, sees” – this phrase appears in Chapter 5, Verse 5 on the subject of practice, and in the present verse on the subject of attainment. It is further mentioned in Chapter 18, Verse 16, that the one who sees the self as the doer does not see the deluded mind – “The deluded mind does not see.”

**Shloka (Verse 28)**

samam pashyanni sarvatra samavsthitam ishvaram. na hinastyaatmanaatmanam tato yati param gati. (28)

*Word‑by‑word breakdown*  
- samam (equally)  
- pashyanni (seeing)  
- sarvatra (everywhere)  
- samavsthitam (equally present)  
- ishvaram (the Supreme Being). - na (not)  
- hinastyaatmanaatmanam (does not kill the self)  
- tato (then)  
- yati (goes)  
- param (ultimate)  
- gati (motion). **Commentary (after the shloka)**

Because the Supreme Being is equally present everywhere, the one who sees Him everywhere does not kill the self. The phrase “samam pashyanni” means that the person who sees the Supreme Being, who is equally present in all beings—whether immovable, movable, inert, conscious, in the lower or higher realms, in the three worlds—experiences his own inseparability with that Supreme Being. He does not kill himself. To “kill” here means to be caught in the cycle of birth and death; he does not experience the disturbances of the world and body. In reality, one cannot kill oneself by losing one’s own nature; one cannot become deficient, nor desire to become deficient. To align oneself with the perishable body is to kill oneself, to fall, to bring oneself into the cycle of birth and death. By aligning with the body, one grows with the body, shrinks with the body, becomes ill when the body is ill, becomes healthy when the body is healthy, and considers the body’s birth as his own birth and the body’s death as his own death. Thus, he keeps wandering in the lower and higher realms, repeatedly experiencing the body’s disturbances as his own. When he experiences his inseparability with the Supreme Being, he no longer brings the Supreme Being into the cycle of birth and death. Instead, he attains the eternally realized Supreme Being. The sight turns away from the body and focuses only on the omnipresent, all‑mighty Supreme Being. He then realizes that his Supreme Self is present in all countries, in all times, in all…

[ Verse 28 ]  
* Sadhak Sanjivani *

It exists in individuals, in all objects, in all events, in all circumstances, in all actions. In all of them it is present in a single form, in the same manner, perfectly as it is. If attaining it is difficult, how can it be easy? Wherever you wish, attain it there. In reality, what appears as “the world” is not the world. The world does not remain even for a moment. It is only change, change itself. It is only a cluster of change. Just as a fan spinning rapidly appears as a circle, but in reality there is no circle; rather the blades of the fan appear as a circle. Similarly, the world appears as “not” yet as “is”. In reality, only one Atman (the eternal soul) exists as “is”. Consider: the bodies that appear now, were they present a hundred years ago? And will they remain a hundred years later? They were not before and will not exist after; therefore they are not even in between. But Atman existed before the creation was born, and will remain after the creation is dissolved; thus Atman is perfect even at the time of creation. What was not before will not exist later; what existed before will exist later. Therefore, what appears as “the world” is a mistake. The Atman appears as “is”. It is only through the truth of that Atman that this illusory world appears as if it were real due to illusion (foolishness). Being entangled in the world is not humanity, but animality. One must abandon this animal nature – “Pashubuddhimimā jāhi” (Srimad Bhagavata 12.5.2). Therefore, God says that seeing the indestructible Atman among the destroyable beings is right. But seeing the destroyable and not seeing the indestructible is self‑killing. If one is not a pure soul, one is not attained. What sin is not committed by one who, though being of an indestructible nature, regards the soul as a destroyable one? (Mahabharata, Udyoga 42.37). One who does not see the destroyable world but sees the all‑pervading Atman everywhere in the same form is not self‑killing; he does not kill himself, and thus attains the supreme goal. But one who does not see the all‑pervading Atman and sees the world‑body instead is self‑killing, does not attain the supreme goal, and keeps being reborn and dying repeatedly. Therefore, man must save himself by his own effort and avoid his own downfall (Gita – Chapter 6, Verse 5). Suffering: Just as a mirror shows a face even when there is no face, and a dream shows an elephant even when there is none, the world appears even when it does not exist. If one does not look toward the world, the world will not appear as “is”. Only the Atman appears as “is”. The seeker must firmly believe that this is true, even if it does not appear now; later it will begin to appear. Just as the seeker sits in Vrindavan, he does not need to remember Vrindavan. While sleeping, eating, or doing any work, he does not recall Vrindavan; yet he says “I am in Vrindavan”. He has no doubt. He remembers without remembering. Similarly, even if the Atman does not appear now, the seeker can firmly believe that “is” is only the Atman, not the world, and later he will experience it. Because how long will a false object remain “is” (Atman) without experiencing “not”, and how long will the true object remain hidden? If illusion is gone, the world will not appear; only the Atman will appear – “Vasudevaḥ sarvam” (Gita 7.19). Since Atman existed, will exist, and no other will appear in between, just as gold existed in jewelry and will remain gold; thus between gold there is no other. Jewelry is only for description; fundamentally it is gold. Similarly, the world is only for description; fundamentally it is Atman. Experiencing that Atman is the success of human birth.

Explanation - 'Prakrityeva cha karmanni kriyamanani sarvashah' - In reality, the conscious principle is naturally, naturally, and naturally unchanging, peaceful, and tranquil. The power of the conscious principle is the natural, spontaneous, and active nature. In it, there is always continuous activity - 'Prakarshen karmanam (bhavelyut) iti prakritih' (the nature is always active). Although nature is said to have two states - active (in the state of creation) and inactive (in the state of dissolution), a subtle consideration reveals that even in the state of dissolution, its activity does not cease. The reason is that when the dissolution begins, nature moves towards the state of creation. In this way, nature's subtle activity continues. The subtle activity of nature is called inactivity; because in this state, no creation takes place. However, when the great creation takes place, nature moves towards the state of creation from the beginning to the middle of creation, and then towards the state of dissolution. If we consider pralaya and mahapralaya as inactive, then how will the beginning, middle, and end of pralaya and mahapralaya be? Just as the sun rises, then moves to the middle, and then sets, from which we understand that in the morning, the light increases from sunrise to noon, and from noon to sunset, the light decreases. After sunset, darkness increases until midnight, and from midnight to sunrise, darkness decreases. In reality, the subtle connection between light and darkness is at noon and midnight, but it is visible at the time of sunrise and sunset. In this way, the activity of light and darkness does not cease, but continues uninterruptedly. Similarly, in creation and dissolution, in great creation and great dissolution, nature's activity continues uninterruptedly. When this person establishes a relationship with nature, then the natural activities of the body (due to the connection with nature) become apparent to him. 'Yah pasyati tatha-atmanam akartaram sa pasyati' - When this person sees the Self as the non-doer, he sees (experiences). * In great creation, the sun is the means of calculating time; but in great dissolution, the sun also becomes latent. Therefore, the calculation of time in great dissolution begins from the time of great creation. The only means of calculating time in great dissolution is the eternal, conscious, and indestructible Supreme Self.

[ Verse 30 ]  
* Sadhaka – Sanjivani *

All activities—eating and drinking, walking and moving, rising and sitting, falling and growing, shaking and wandering, sleeping and waking, thinking, being in meditation, etc.—are performed only by Prakṛti (Nature); the Self (Ātman) performs no action, because the Self does not act. The one who sees, i.e., experiences, truly sees. By such seeing one experiences akartṛtva (non‑action) within oneself. Here the actions are described as caused by Prakṛti, elsewhere as caused by the guṇas, and elsewhere as caused by the indriyas (senses). These three statements are identical. Prakṛti is the ultimate cause; the guṇas are the functions of Prakṛti; and the indriyas are the instruments of the guṇas. Consequently, every action that appears to be produced by Prakṛti, by the guṇas, or by the indriyas is ultimately an action of Prakṛti. **Appendix meaning** – Every action, whatever it may be, belongs wholly to the domain of Prakṛti. The Jīva (individual soul) has no hand in it. The Gita sometimes refers to these as “actions of the guṇas” and sometimes as “actions of the indriyas.” For example:

- *prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ* (3.27): “All works are performed by the qualities of Prakṛti.”  
- *guṇā guṇeṣu vartante* (3.28): “The guṇas operate within the guṇas.”  
- *nānyam guṇebhyaḥ kartāram yadi draṣṭānapashyati* (14.19): “When one sees, there is no doer other than the guṇas.”  
- *indriyāṇi indriyārtheṣu vartante* (5.9): “The senses act on sense‑objects.”

The implication is that action is purely Prakṛti‑generated. Hence Prakṛti is never inert, and the Puruṣa (spiritual principle) never performs any action. Thus the Gita states that the Sāṅkhya‑yogi who knows the Truth thinks:

- *naiva kiñcit karomīti yukto manyeta tattvavit* (5.8): “One who truly knows the Truth thinks, ‘I do nothing at all.’”  
- *naiva kurvan kārayan* (5.13): “The Self neither acts nor causes action.”  
- *śarīrastho ’pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate* (13.31): “Even while residing in the body, O Kaunteya, the Puruṣa neither acts nor becomes attached.”  
- *tatraivaṁ sati kartāram ātmānaṁ yadi* (18.16): “One who regards the Ātman as the doer is of misguided intellect, because his wisdom is not pure.”

**Verse 30**

*yadā bhūtapṛthag‑bhāvaṁ brahma sampadyate tadā* – “When one perceives the distinct existence of all beings, Brahman is attained at that moment.”

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**

- *yadā* = when  
- *bhūta‑pṛthag‑bhāvaṁ* = the separate existence of beings  
- *brahma* = the Supreme Reality (Brahman)  
- *sampadyate* = is attained  
- *tadā* = then

**Explanation** – Prakṛti has two aspects: action (kriyā) and substance (dravya). When the seeker (sādaka) perceives the distinct states of all beings, he simultaneously perceives Brahman. The separation of beings into various forms—egg‑born, womb‑born, germ‑born, sweat‑born—in the three worlds, together with their gross, subtle, and causal bodies, all arise from a single Prakṛti. The names, forms, dispositions, qualities, disorders, origins, conditions, and dissolution of all material and mobile beings are produced by that one Prakṛti. All bodies remain situated in, sustained by, and merged back into Prakṛti. By this vision the seeker attains Brahman, i.e., the transcendental Self beyond Prakṛti, which is already his true nature; it merely becomes realized when the mind ceases to identify action with the individual self.

The Bhagavad Gita 
[Verse 31]
In the thirteenth chapter, it is stated that the self (Atman) (the eternal soul) remains in its own state only when it considers its relationship with the body. The self (Atman) does not get corrupted by the influence of nature (Prakriti), but when it sees everything as emerging from and situated in nature (Prakriti), it experiences its own inherent nature. Although it may not be visible, the self (Atman) always remains unattached. When the seeker (Sadhak) has a clear understanding of this, they attain the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman) (liberation). It is a rule that when one considers their relationship with nature (Prakriti), they develop a sense of self-interest, a desire for enjoyment, and a desire for happiness, which leads to different feelings towards living beings. When one has affection, they see the good qualities, and when they have aversion, they see the faults. In this way, the veil of affection and aversion covers the true nature of things, and one cannot experience reality. However, when the seeker (Sadhak) sees the origin, existence, and destruction of all bodies, including their own gross, subtle, and causal bodies, as taking place in nature (Prakriti) and sees their own absence in them, the veil of affection and aversion is lifted, and they experience the Supreme Self (Paramatman) (the Supreme Consciousness). Just as all the bodies and changes that take place in them, whether stationary or moving, occur on the earth, similarly, all the qualities, corruptions, and changes that occur in them take place in nature (Prakriti). In other words, just as the substances produced from the earth remain on the earth and ultimately merge into it, becoming one with the earth, similarly, the entire world produced from nature (Prakriti) remains in nature (Prakriti) and ultimately merges into it, becoming one with nature (Prakriti). In the same way, the conscious essence (Chetan Tatva) that exists in the form of stationary and moving living beings is constantly experienced as the Supreme Self (Paramatman) (the Supreme Consciousness). Appendix - In the previous verse, the topic was the individual, and in this verse, the topic is time. In the chapter on devotion, the Lord has stated that all feelings arise from Him - "Bhavanti bhava bhutanam matta eva prthag-vidhah" (10.5), but here, in the chapter on knowledge, all feelings are attributed to nature (Prakriti). The meaning is that where a distinction is made between the real and the unreal, all feelings are said to be unreal, and where the all-encompassing aspect is described, all feelings are said to be part of the Supreme Self (Paramatman). In reality, everything, whether real or unreal, is the Supreme Self (Paramatman) - "Sadasachaham" (9.19). Connection - The verse that follows describes the true nature of the person who was said to be beyond the body in the twenty-second verse and was said to attain the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman) (liberation) in the thirtieth verse. व्याख्या–—अनादित्वान्निर्गुणत्वात्परमात्मायमव्ययः
-
इसी अध्यायके उन्नीसवें श्लोकमें जिसको अनादि कहा है,
उसीको यहाँ भी ‘अनादित्वात् ' पदसे अनादि कहा है अर्थात्
यह पुरुष आदि-(आरम्भ - ) से रहित है । अब प्रश्न होता
है कि वहाँ तो प्रकृतिको भी अनादि कहा है, इसलिये
प्रकृति और पुरुष – दोनोंमें क्या फरक रहा? इसके उत्तरमें
भगवान् कहते हैं—‘निर्गुणत्वात्' अर्थात् यह पुरुष गुणोंसे
रहित है। प्रकृति अनादि तो है, पर वह गुणोंसे रहित नहीं
प्रत्युत गुणों और विकारोंवाली है। उससे सात्त्विक,
राजस और तामस—ये तीनों गुण तथा विकार पैदा होते
हैं। परन्तु पुरुष इन तीनों गुणों और विकारोंसे सर्वथा रहित
(निर्गुण और निर्विकार) है। ऐसा यह पुरुष साक्षात्
अविनाशी परमात्मस्वरूप ही है अर्थात् यह पुरुष विनाशरहित
परम शुद्ध आत्मा है।
'शरीरस्थोऽपि कौन्तेय न करोति न लिप्यते'-
यह पुरुष शरीरमें रहता हुआ भी न कुछ करता है और
न किसी कर्मसे लिप्त ही होता है। तात्पर्य है कि इस
पुरुष - ( स्वयं -) ने न तो पहले किसी भी अवस्थामें कुछ
किया है, न वर्तमानमें कुछ करता है और न आगे ही कुछ
कर सकता है अर्थात् यह पुरुष सदासे ही प्रकृतिसे
निर्लिप्त, असंग है तथा गुणोंसे रहित और अविनाशी है।
इसमें कर्तृत्व और भोक्तृत्व है ही नहीं
।
यहाँ 'शरीरस्थोऽपि' कहनेका तात्पर्य है कि यह पुरुष
जिस समय अपनेको शरीरमें स्थित मानकर अपनेको
कार्यका कर्ता और सुख - दुःखका भोक्ता मानता है, उस
समय भी वास्तवमें यह तटस्थ, प्रकाशमात्र ही रहता है ।
सुख-दुःखका भान इसीसे होता है; अत: इसको प्रकाशक
कह सकते हैं, पर इसमें प्रकाशक - धर्म नहीं है ।
-
९०९
यहाँ‘अपि' पदसे ऐसा मालूम होता है कि अनादिकालसे
अपनेको शरीरमें स्थित माननेवाला हरेक (चींटीसे ब्रह्मापर्यन्त)
प्राणी स्वरूपसे सदा ही निर्लिप्त, असंग है। उसकी शरीरके
साथ एकता कभी हुई ही नहीं; क्योंकि शरीर तो प्रकृतिका
कार्य होनेसे सदा प्रकृतिमें ही स्थित रहता है और स्वयं
परमात्माका अंश होनेसे सदा परमात्मामें ही स्थित रहता है
स्वयं परमात्मासे कभी अलग हो सकता ही नहीं । शरीरके
साथ एकात्मता माननेपर भी, शरीरके साथ कितना ही
घुल-मिल जानेपर भी, शरीरको ही अपना स्वरूप
माननेपर भी उसकी निर्लिप्तता कभी नष्ट नहीं होती, वह
स्वरूपसे सदा ही निर्लिप्त रहता है। अपनी निर्लिप्तताका
अनुभव न होनेपर भी उसके स्वरूपमें कुछ भी विकृति
नहीं होती । अतः उसने अपने स्वरूपसे न कभी कुछ किया
है और न करता ही है तथा वह स्वयं न कभी लिप्त हुआ
है और न लिप्त होता ही है।
यद्यपि पुरुष अपनेको शरीरमें स्थित माननेसे ही कर्ता
और भोक्ता बनता है, तथापि इक्कीसवें श्लोकमें भगवान्ने
कहा है कि 'प्रकृति' में स्थित पुरुष ही भोक्ता बनता है
और यहाँ कहते हैं कि 'शरीर' में स्थित होनेपर भी पुरुष
कर्ता - भोक्ता नहीं है । ऐसा कहनेका तात्पर्य यह है कि
कर्ता-भोक्ता
प्रकृति और उसका कार्य शरीर - दोनों एक ही हैं । अतः
पुरुषको चाहे प्रकृतिमें स्थित कहो, चाहे शरीरमें स्थित
कहो, एक ही बात है । एक शरीरके साथ सम्बन्ध होनेसे
मात्र प्रकृतिके साथ, मात्र शरीरोंके साथ सम्बन्ध हो जाता
है। वास्तवमें पुरुषका सम्बन्ध न तो व्यष्टि शरीरके साथ
है और न समष्टि प्रकृतिके साथ ही है । अपना सम्बन्ध
शरीरके साथ माननेसे ही वह अपनेको कर्ता-भोक्ता मान
लेता है। वास्तवमें वह न कर्ता है और न भोक्ता है ।
परिशिष्ट भाव — पुरुष अनादि है, पर शरीर आदिवाला है। पुरुष निर्गुण है, पर शरीर गुणमय है । पुरुष परमात्मा
है, पर शरीर अनात्मा है। पुरुष अव्यय है, पर शरीर नाशवान् है । इसलिये अज्ञानी मनुष्यके द्वारा पुरुष (आत्मा) - को शरीरमें
स्थित माननेपर भी वास्तवमें वह शरीरमें स्थित नहीं है अर्थात् शरीरसे सर्वथा असम्बद्ध है—' न करोति न लिप्यते' । कारण
कि शरीरका सम्बन्ध तो संसारके साथ है, पर पुरुषका सम्बन्ध परमात्माके साथ है। अतः वास्तवमें पुरुष कभी शरीरस्थ
हो सकता ही नहीं। परन्तु इस वास्तविकताकी तरफ ध्यान न देनेके कारण मनुष्य उसको शरीरस्थ मान लेता है ।
'निर्गुणत्वात्'– पुरुष स्वयं निर्गुण होते हुए भी गुणोंका संग करके बँध जाता है (गीता - इसी अध्यायका
इक्कीसवाँ श्लोक)। दीखता तो ऐसा ही है कि बन्धन स्वतः - स्वाभाविक है और मुक्ति कृतिसाध्य है, पर वास्तवमें
मुक्ति स्वतः - स्वाभाविक है और बन्धन कृतिसाध्य है । गुणोंका सम्बन्ध पुरुषके साथ नहीं है, प्रत्युत प्रकृतिके साथ
है (गीता १३। २३) इसलिये 'अनादि, निर्गुण, परमात्मा, अव्यय' और 'न करोति न लिप्यते'- ये स्वतः-स्वाभाविक
हैं। साधकको इस स्वाभाविकताका अनुभव करना है।
जैसे मकानमें रहते हुए भी हम मकानसे अलग हैं, ऐसे ही शरीरमें रहते हुए माननेपर भी हम शरीरसे अलग हैं।
