[ Verse 31 ]  
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *

Explanation: — anāditya‑annirguṇatvā‑paramātmā‑amavyayaḥ (from the eternal, from the formless, the Supreme Self is indestructible). In the 19th verse of this chapter, the word “Anadi” is used. Here too the term “Anaditya” is employed to mean “Anadi,” that is, the Atman is without a beginning. The question then arises: nature is also called Anadi, so what distinguishes nature from the Atman? God answers, “from the formless,” meaning this Atman is devoid of qualities. Nature is Anadi, but it is not devoid of qualities; it possesses qualities and defects. From nature arise the three qualities—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—and their defects. Yet the Atman is entirely free from these qualities and defects (formless and unaffected). Thus the Atman is the indestructible Supreme Self, the truly pure, indestructible soul. Even when situated in the body, the Atman neither acts nor is involved in any action. This means that the Atman has never performed any act in any state, does not act in the present, nor can it act in the future. The Atman is always detached from nature, unassociated, devoid of qualities, and indestructible. There is no sense of doership or enjoyment. The phrase “sarira‑stho‑api” indicates that even when the Atman considers itself situated in the body and regards itself as the doer of actions and the experiencer of pleasure and pain, it remains truly neutral, merely a light. The perception of pleasure and pain arises from this. Hence, it can be called a light-bringer, but it is not a light-bringer of Dharma. The word “api” here implies that from the beginning, every being—from the ant to Brahma—who considers itself situated in the body remains ever detached and unassociated. The Atman has never been united with the body; the body, being a function of nature, remains in nature, and the Atman, being a part of the Supreme Self, remains in the Supreme Self. The Atman can never be separated from the Supreme Self. Even if it believes itself united with the body, even if it mixes with the body, even if it regards the body as its own form, its detachment is never destroyed; it remains ever detached from its own form. Even without experiencing this detachment, there is no distortion in its form. Therefore, it has never acted upon its own form, nor does it act, nor has it ever been involved, nor will it ever be involved. Although the Atman becomes a doer and experiencer by considering itself situated in the body, in the 21st verse God says that the Atman who resides in nature becomes the experiencer. Here it is stated that even when situated in the body, the Atman is not a doer or experiencer. This means that the doer‑experiencer, nature, and its work, the body, are the same. Thus, whether one calls the Atman situated in nature or in the body, it is the same. Having a relationship with the body merely creates a relationship with nature or with bodies. In reality, the Atman’s relationship is neither with the individual body nor with the collective nature. By assuming a relationship with the body, it mistakenly considers itself a doer‑experiencer. In truth, it is neither a doer nor an experiencer. Appendix: The Atman is Anadi, but the body is Adi. The Atman is formless, but the body is endowed with qualities. The Atman is the Supreme Self, but the body is the non‑self. The Atman is indestructible, but the body is perishable. Therefore, even when an ignorant person considers the Atman to be situated in the body, in reality it is not situated in the body; it is entirely detached from the body—“does not act nor is involved.” The body is related to the world, but the Atman is related to the Supreme Self. Hence, the Atman can never truly be situated in the body. However, because one does not focus on this reality, a person mistakenly regards it as situated in the body. From the formless, the Atman, though formless, becomes bound by qualities (Gita, this chapter, 21). It appears that bondage is natural and liberation is achievable, but in reality liberation is natural and bondage is achievable. The qualities are not associated with the Atman; they are associated with nature (Gita 13.23). Therefore, “Anadi, formless, Supreme Self, indestructible” and “does not act nor is involved” are natural. The seeker must experience this naturalness. Just as we live in a house yet remain separate from the house, even when we consider ourselves residing in the body, we remain separate from the body.

[ अध्याय १३
'न करोति न लिप्यते' – यह साधनजन्य नहीं है, प्रत्युत स्वतः - स्वाभाविक है। तात्पर्य है कि स्वरूपमें लेशमात्र
भी कर्तृत्व-भोक्तृत्व नहीं है - यह स्वत: सिद्ध बात है । इसमें कोई पुरुषार्थ नहीं है अर्थात् इसके लिये कुछ करना नहीं
है। तात्पर्य है कि कर्तृत्व- भोक्तृत्वको मिटाना नहीं है, प्रत्युत इनको अपनेमें स्वीकार नहीं करना है, इनके अभावका
अनुभव करना है; क्योंकि वास्तवमें ये अपनेमें हैं ही नहीं ! इसलिये साधकको अपनेमें निरन्तर अकर्तृत्व और
अभोक्तृत्वका अनुभव करना चाहिये । अपनेमें निरन्तर अकर्तृत्व और अभोक्तृत्व (निष्कामता-निर्ममता) - का अनुभव होना
ही जीवन्मुक्ति है। इसीको गीताने स्मृति प्राप्त होना कहा है- 'नष्टो मोहः स्मृतिर्लब्धा' (१८ । ७३)
अगर स्वरूप कर्ता और भोक्ता नहीं है तो फिर कर्ता और भोक्ता कौन है ? यह विचार किया जाता है। पहले
यह विचार करें कि कर्ता कौन है ? शरीर कर्ता नहीं है; क्योंकि यह प्रतिक्षण अभावमें जा रहा है । मन, बुद्धि, चित्त
तथा अहंकार- ये चार करण हैं, जिनको 'अन्तःकरण' कहते हैं । यह अन्तःकरण भी कर्ता नहीं है; क्योंकि करण
कर्ताके अधीन होता है। परन्तु कर्ता स्वतन्त्र होता है - 'स्वतन्त्रः कर्ता' (पाणि० अ० १।४।५४) । करण तो क्रियाकी
सिद्धिमें अत्यन्त सहायक होता है - 'साधकतमं करणम्' (पाणि० अ० १ । ४ । ४२), इसलिये करणके बिना किसी
क्रियाकी सिद्धि होती ही नहीं । जैसे, कलम स्वतन्त्रतासे नहीं लिखती, प्रत्युत वह तो लिखनेका एक साधन (करण)
है, जो लेखक (कर्ता) के अधीन होता है। अतः करण कर्ता नहीं होता और कर्ता करण नहीं होता। दूसरी बात,
यदि करणमें कर्तापन है तो फिर सुखी - दुःखी स्वयं क्यों होता है ? यदि करण सुखी - दुःखी होता है तो हमें क्या नुकसान
है? सत्-स्वरूप भी कर्ता नहीं है; क्योंकि मैंपन तो प्रकृतिका कार्य है, वह प्रकृतिसे अतीतमें कैसे सम्भव है? यदि
स्वरूपमें कर्तापन होता तो वह कभी मिटता नहीं; क्योंकि स्वरूप अविनाशी है । इसलिये भगवान्ने यहाँ स्वरूपमें
कर्तापनका निषेध किया है—' न करोति' । आगे अठारहवें अध्यायमें भी भगवान् ने कहा है कि जो आत्माको कर्ता
मानता है, वह दुर्मति ठीक नहीं समझता; क्योंकि उसकी बुद्धि शुद्ध नहीं है (गीता - अठारहवें अध्यायका सोलहवाँ
श्लोक) । वास्तवमें जो भोक्ता ( सुखी - दुःखी) होता है, वही कर्ता होता है ।
।
-
अब यह विचार करें कि भोक्ता कौन है ? भोक्ता न सत् है, न असत् है । सत् भोक्ता नहीं हो सकता; क्योंकि
सत्में कभी अभाव नहीं होता - ' नाभावो विद्यते सतः', जबकि भोक्तापनका अभाव होता है - ' न लिप्यते ' । असत्
भी भोक्ता नहीं हो सकता; क्योंकि असत्की सत्ता ही नहीं है - ' नासतो विद्यते भाव: ' । असत् में चेतनता भी नहीं
है। अतः उसमें भोक्तापनकी कल्पना ही नहीं हो सकती । तात्पर्य यह हुआ कि कर्तापन और भोक्कापन न तो सत्में
है और न असत्में ही है । सत्-असत् के संयोगमें भी कर्तापन और भोक्तापन नहीं है; क्योंकि जैसे दिन और रातका
संयोग असम्भव है, ऐसे ही सत् और असत्का संयोग भी असम्भव है । अतः कर्तापन - भोक्तापन केवल माने हुए हैं-
'कर्ताहमिति मन्यते ' ( ३ । २७) । जब साधक विवेकपूर्वक शरीरसे सर्वथा सम्बन्ध-विच्छेद कर लेता है अर्थात् मैं-
मेरापनको मिटा देता है ( जो कि वास्तवमें है नहीं), तब न कर्ता रहता है, न भोक्ता रहता है, प्रत्युत एक चिन्मय
सत्ता रहती है। इस प्रकार अपनेमें कर्तापन और भोक्तापनके अभावका अनुभव होनेपर साधक मुक्त हो जाता है अर्थात्

The phrase *na karoTi na lipyate* – “not doing and not being involved” – is not a result of effort; it is inherent and natural. The implication is that even a mere trace of *karta* (doer) or *bhakta* (devotee) is absent in the true nature. This is a self‑evident truth. There is no *purusharth* (human effort) required; nothing must be done for it. [ Verse 33 ]  
* Sadhak-Sanjivani *

**Translation of the Commentary**

The commentary begins by explaining that in the preceding verse the Lord has described the absence of *Karma* (action) first, using the word “n‑karoti”, and then the absence of *Bhakti* (devotion) with the word “n‑lipyate”. In this verse, however, the Lord first speaks of the lack of *Bhakti* in the soul, and in the following verse he will speak of the lack of *Karma*. The reason for this reversal is that although *Bhakti* follows *Karma*—one first performs an action and then enjoys its fruit—every human being acts with a goal in mind. The mind first holds a desire for a result (a *siddhi*), and only then does the action follow. Thus, from the Lord’s perspective, the first prohibition is against *Bhakti*; when attachment to the fruit is abandoned, the attachment to the action itself also disappears. The commentary then discusses the nature of space (*Akasha*). Space is said to be present in the four material elements—air (*Vayu*), fire (*Tejas*), water (*Jala*), and earth (*Prithvi*)—but the four elements are not present in space; rather, they are contained within space. The reason is that the four elements are gross, whereas space is subtle. The elements are limited, finite, and subject to change, whereas space is infinite and eternal. The elements are afflicted by defects, but space is free from defects. The phrase “sarvatra avasthito dehe tathātmā nopalyate” means that even though the self (*Atman* (the eternal soul)) resides everywhere, it is not attached to any body. The self, though perfect in all bodies, does not dissolve into any of them. It remains completely detached at all times because the self is itself eternal, omnipresent, immovable, unchanging, and beyond thought. (See Gita 2.24 and 2.25.) From this indestructible self, the functions of space—air, fire, water, and earth—arise. Hence the world is pervaded by space (Gita 2.17). **Appendix Commentary**  
The “Chinmay” (all‑pervading) soul is one, but it appears different because of the *aham* (I‑ego). The living being is called a “part” because it holds the *aham*; if it does not hold the *aham*, there is only one reality. All other concepts are merely imagination. The Chinmay soul is the foundation, support, light, and refuge of all imagination. It is not localized; it is all‑pervading like space. All creation—actions and matter—falls under this reality. Creation is continually produced and destroyed, but the reality remains unchanged. Thus the Chinmay soul is neither bodily nor natural; it is everywhere, both inside and outside all bodies and creation. It is our very nature and the ultimate reality. Therefore, the one reality is universal. It is the yoga of yogis, the knowledge of sages, and the God of devotees. The seeker’s goal is always to remain in that reality. **

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 13 (Atman) ]  
[ Verse 21 ]

Bhārat, O son of the Bharata dynasty, Arjuna! This bright, radiant, all‑encompassing sun illuminates the entire world, just as a single sun illuminates the world. Just as a single sun shines upon the field, the field is illuminated. The field‑knowledge (Atman) illuminates the entire field. Explanation: as the sun illuminates each bright world, the bright world is illuminated. In its illumination, the gross world has its actions. The sun, seen by the eyes, illuminates the entire world, and the material world is illuminated by a single sun. All actions of the world are under the sun’s illumination; but the sun does not act as “I illuminate everyone.”  
Just as the sun’s light allows a Brahmin (Brahman) to read the Veda and a hunter to kill animals, the sun’s light does not cause the reading of the Veda or the hunting. Here the word “world” refers only to the material world (the fourteen realms). Because whatever is light in the material world (moon, stars, fire, gems, herbs, etc.) is all from the sun. “Field‑knowledge illuminates the field, O Bhārat” — like the sun, a single field‑knowledge (Atman) illuminates all fields, meaning that all actions in all fields occur in the light of the field‑knowledge; but the field‑knowledge does not cause those actions. The field‑knowledge does not illuminate only the gross field (the world), but rather it illuminates the gross, subtle, and causal fields, and in its light all actions of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies occur. Just as the sun, after illuminating the entire world, does not feel pride in illuminating everyone, and after illuminating various actions does not feel distinction, similarly the field‑knowledge, after illuminating all fields and giving them vitality, does not feel pride or agency, and after illuminating various actions does not feel distinction. The field‑knowledge remains detached and unconnected. No action or object exists without support, and no perception exists without light (knowledge). The field‑knowledge illuminates only the gross world; it is the support and light. Appendix: Just as the sun illuminates the entire visible world and in its light all good and bad actions occur, the sun neither becomes the doer nor the consumer of those actions. Similarly, the field‑knowledge illuminates all bodies of all worlds, giving them vitality, but in reality it does nothing and remains detached; it has no agency or consumption. Thus, the field‑knowledge has no pride in being a light‑giver. Responsibility for action lies with that which can act. Just as a skilled painter cannot paint without materials (paint, brush, etc.), a person (consciousness) cannot act without the aid of nature. Therefore, a person cannot be responsible for action. All experience shows that without the body we cannot act. Hence the body is used only for doing something. If we do not want to do anything, what is the use of the body? If we do not want to see anything, what is the use of the eye? If we do not want to hear anything, what is the use of the ear? The gross body is used for gross actions; the subtle body is used for thinking and meditation; the causal body is used for stillness and samādhi. If we do nothing, what is the use of the three bodies? The body and its actions are only for the world. Our nature is only the luminous being; thus for it the body and its actions are useless. The luminous being is complete; it has no deficiency; therefore we need nothing for ourselves. There is no other besides the luminous being; because there can be only one being, not two. Thus we need no companion. Thus there is no relationship with action (agency). Samādhi and vyutthāna both exist in the causal body. When the causal body is detached from the relationship, “natural samādhi” or “natural state” occurs.

[Verse 34]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Yes, if there is no relationship with the unattained (kāmā) and no relationship with the attained (mamatā), then there will be no identity with nature. Without identity with nature, there will be activity in nature, but there will be no doer and no enjoyer. (This is the thirty-fourth verse of this chapter.)

Connection - Now, the Lord explains the result of knowing the distinction between the field (kshetra) and the knower of the field (kshetrajña), and concludes the discussion. With the eye of knowledge. The distinction between the field and the knower of the field, and liberation from the nature of the past, those who know this attain the supreme. Thus,

Those who know the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, and liberation from the nature of the past, attain the supreme. Explanation - [The path of knowledge begins with discrimination, and it is only through true discrimination that it is completed. When true discrimination is achieved, there is a complete separation from nature, and one attains the ultimate reality.]

'Kshetra-kshetrajñayor eva mantram jñānacakṣuṣa' - The 'eye of knowledge' (viveka) is the name of the knowledge that distinguishes between the field (sat) and the non-field (asat), the eternal and the non-eternal. This field is subject to change, and it is never one and the same. It is constantly changing, and there is no moment when it remains the same. However, the knower of the field, who resides in the field and knows it, remains one and the same. The knower of the field is not subject to change, nor will it change, nor is it possible for it to change. This is what it means to know the distinction between the field and the knower of the field through the eye of knowledge. 'Ye viddur yānti te param' - When true discrimination is achieved, there is a complete separation from nature, and one attains the ultimate reality. The Lord had earlier said that those who worship the formless attain Him - 'te prāpnvanti mām eva' (12.4). He had also said in the eighteenth verse of this chapter, 'madbhāvāyopapadyate' (18.54), and in the twenty-third verse, 'na sa bhūyo 'bhijāyate' (18.66). And now, He says, 'yānti te param' (18.55). They know (the ultimate reality) and attain it. The ego is the main obstacle on the path of knowledge. To remove this obstacle, the Lord had said in the beginning of this chapter, 'idam śarīram' (13.2), to experience the separation of the self from the body. In the second verse, He said, 'kshetra-kshetrajñayor jñānam' (13.2), to know the knowledge of the distinction between the field and the knower of the field. He then described the distinction between the field and the knower of the field in various ways. Now, He concludes the discussion by saying that knowing the distinction between the field and the knower of the field is the ultimate knowledge. The knower of the field has considered itself separate from the ultimate reality and has considered itself one with the field. Therefore, it is necessary to say both that the knower of the field is one with the ultimate reality and that it is completely separate from the field. Just as a brave person, by lighting a lamp in a dark room, dispels the darkness and the ghosts that were perceived in it, so too, by knowing the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, one attains complete separation from the field.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 13 ]

However, as soon as these fears are dispelled by the light, they vanish. Similarly, only the Supreme Self, in the form of light, remains. To dispel darkness, one needs to bring in light, but to attain the Supreme Self, one does not need to bring it from anywhere. It is complete in all places, times, objects, individuals, and circumstances. Therefore, when one is completely detached from the world, the experience of the Supreme Self arises naturally. When one is detached from the Supreme Self, who is the embodiment of light, and is surrounded by darkness, the independent existence of the world appears, and various fears start to torment. However, when one attains true knowledge, the independent existence of the world does not remain, and all fears vanish. A subsidiary thought - the knowledge of the distinction between the field (kshetra) and the knower (kshetrajna) is called 'viveka'. Those who, by giving importance to this viveka, understand the distinction between the field and the knower, and experience the world and its activities (the body) as completely separate from themselves, attain the Chit (conscious) Supreme Self. In their vision, there is nothing but the Chit (conscious) Supreme Self. The Lord has mentioned the attainment of the saguna (with attributes) in the verse 'madbhavayopapadyate' (13.18), and here, the attainment of the nirguna (without attributes) is mentioned in the verse 'ye viduryanti te param'. In reality, the attainment of 'madbhav' and 'param' is the same (Gita - 8th chapter, 21st verse, and 14th chapter, 27th verse). Om tat sat - the recitation of these names of the Lord, along with the knowledge of Brahman and the yoga shastra, completes the 13th chapter of the Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Upanishad. Thus, the 13th chapter, 'Kshetra-kshetrajna-vibhag-yoga', is complete. (13)

Om Shri Paramatmane Namah

[ Chapter 14 ]

Preface –  
At the end of the thirteenth chapter, Lord Krishna said that one who sees with the eye of knowledge the distinction between field (kṣetra) and knower of the field (kṣetrajña) attains the Supreme Atman. The question then arises: what is that knowledge, what is its glory, and what is the simple means of attaining it? To describe this, the Lord now begins the subject of the fourteenth chapter. Bondage arises from two causes— from Prakṛti and from the modes of material nature (guṇas). To free oneself from the bondage of material nature, the Lord had already explained the theme of the thirteenth chapter. Now, to free oneself from the bondage of the modes of material nature, the Lord starts the fourteenth chapter and, in the first two verses, describes the magnificence of that knowledge. Shri Bhagavān said:

“param bhūyaḥ pravakṣyāmi jñānānāṁ jñāna‑uttamam |  
yaj jñātvā munayaḥ sarve parāṁ siddhim ito gatāḥ || 1 ||”

**[ Verse 1 ]**

*Word‑by‑word translation*

- **param** – supreme, highest  
- **bhūyaḥ** – again, further  
- **pravakṣyāmi** – I shall declare, I will explain  
- **jñānānāṁ** – of all knowledge  
- **jñāna‑uttamam** – the best of knowledge, the supreme knowledge  
- **yaj** – which, that which  
- **jñātvā** – having known, having realized  
- **munayaḥ** – sages, enlightened ones  
- **sarve** – all, every  
- **parāṁ** – supreme, ultimate  
- **siddhim** – perfection, liberation (moksha)  
- **ito** – henceforth, from this point  
- **gatāḥ** – have gone, have attained

*Combined meaning*: “Again I shall declare the supreme of all knowledge, the highest knowledge; having known it, all sages have attained the supreme liberation.”

**Explanation** – The phrase “param bhūyaḥ pravakṣyāmi jñānānāṁ jñāna” appears together in verses 18, 23 and 34 of the thirteenth chapter, where the Lord had spoken of the discriminative knowledge (viveka) of field and knower of the field, of Prakṛti and Purusha. By using the words “again I shall declare,” the Lord re‑affirms that this same discriminative knowledge is the subject of the present chapter. All worldly and transcendental knowledge— the various sciences, arts, languages, scripts, etc.— are inferior to the knowledge that distinguishes Prakṛti from Purusha, that transcends material nature, and that leads to the realization of the Supreme Atman. No other knowledge can equal it, nor can any comparable knowledge arise, because all other knowledge entraps beings in the world of bondage. Although the words “uttamam” (best) and “param” (supreme) convey the same sense, each emphasizes a different aspect: “uttamam” stresses that this knowledge severs the connection with material nature and the body, while “param” stresses that it is the means of attaining the Supreme Atman, making it the utmost. “yaj jñātvā munayaḥ sarve parāṁ siddhim ito gatāḥ” – The knowledge that, when realized, frees great sages from worldly existence and enables them to attain the Supreme Atman, I shall now describe. When this knowledge is attained, no sage remains unenlightened; all who acquire it become liberated, free from the bondage of the world and its dominion, and they attain the Supreme Atman. One who contemplates the true nature (tattva) and no longer feels identification with his body is called a muni (sage).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *  
[ Chapter 14 ]

The phrase **paraṁ siddhim** (the ultimate perfection) means that the worldly forces which cause death, bind us, and obstruct the attainment of the supreme Self are merely obstacles. Yet the perfection that is the attainment of the supreme Self is far greater than all other achievements such as wealth, fame, and dignity; it is the supreme perfection. When this is attained, all worldly births and deaths are transcended, and the person is freed from the cycle of birth and death. **Appendix Note** – This fourteenth chapter is a supplement to the thirteenth chapter. The knowledge of the *kṣetra‑kṣetra‑jñāna* (the knowledge of the field and the knower of the field) is superior to all worldly and transcendental knowledge. This knowledge is the most effective means to attain the nature of the supreme Self; therefore, anyone who obtains this knowledge becomes liberated and attains the supreme Self. The meaning of the phrase **jnānānāṃ jñānam uttamam** is that this final knowledge is superior to all other kinds of knowledge—whether it be *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas* knowledge, or worldly and transcendental knowledge. No other knowledge can bring about the ultimate perfection except this supreme knowledge. Experiencing the supreme Self is the attainment of ultimate perfection. When ultimate perfection is attained, action and matter become almost nonexistent, and only a single luminous being remains, which is the true reality. **Shloka 2**  
*idam jñānamupāśritya*  
*sādharmaṃgāṭhā*  
*sarga‑epi nopajāyante*  
*pralayena na vyathanti*

**Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
- *idam* – this  
- *jñānamupāśritya* – having taken refuge in knowledge  
- *sādharmaṃgāṭhā* – the person has attained my nature (sādharma)  
- *sarga‑epi* – even in creation  
- *nopajāyante* – do not arise  
- *pralayena* – in dissolution  
- *na* – not  
- *vyathanti* – are troubled

**Translation of the shloka**  
Having taken refuge in this knowledge, the person attains my nature. Even in creation they do not arise, and in dissolution they are not troubled. **Explanation**  
*Idam jñānamupāśritya* – In the preceding verse, the Lord says that a yogi’s power is limited, but the knowledge that is described as supreme and ultimate is the refuge that must be taken. Experiencing this knowledge removes all doubt and makes one a being of knowledge. *Sa‑dharmaṃgāṭhā* – By taking refuge in this knowledge, a person attains my nature, meaning that just as I am free from the dualities of doership and enjoyment, so too does the person become free from those dualities. The wise, great souls become detached and impartial like the Lord, but they cannot perform the functions of creation, sustenance, and dissolution that the Lord does. Though a yogi may acquire some power through practice, that power is not equal to the Lord’s inherent power. The yogi is a *yujana‑yogi* (one who has practiced), whereas the Lord is a *yukta‑yogi* (one whose power is self‑sufficient). *Sa‑rga‑epi nopajāyante* – The word *epi* indicates that even at the beginning of the great creation, these great souls are not born. In the primordial stage of the great creation, the fourteen worlds and their rulers are created, but these great souls are not born; hence they do not have to take a body through karma. *Pralayena na vyathanti* – In the great dissolution, all beings—moving and stationary—are consumed by the fire of the destroyer. The earth sinks as the sea rises, and all beings suffer and perish. Yet these great souls are not troubled, for there is no disturbance in the nature they have attained. If there is no disturbance in that nature, how can they be troubled? They cannot be. They are capable of existing even in the great creation and of remaining untroubled in the great dissolution—*karmā‑karmā‑anyathā kṛtuṃ samarthaḥ* (capable of doing and not doing in any way). Nature and its inherent qualities are completely detached from the bonds of relation. When this detachment occurs, sorrow, agitation, and the influence of nature cease. Therefore, in the great souls who are free from the bonds of nature, birth, death, sorrow, and other afflictions do not arise. **Appendix** – By detaching from the causal body one attains the state of *nirvikalpa* (unconditioned state). When the causal body is detached, one experiences *nirvikalpa‑bodha* (unconditioned awareness). The state of *nirvikalpa* may change into a conditioned state, but the awareness of *nirvikalpa* never changes; it remains as it is. This is expressed by the verse “sarge apni nopajayante pralaye na vyathanti cha.”

Great creation and great dissolution occur within nature. When the fundamental principle (Atman (the eternal soul)) is attained, the great creation and dissolution have no effect, because the bond with nature is no longer present. The detachment from nature is also called “ultimate dissolution.” Thus, when a person is bound by the activities of nature, he becomes subject to birth and death; but when he detaches from the activities of nature, he becomes free, lives a detached life, and is liberated from birth and death forever. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Nothing happens to Me, nor am I perturbed even in the great dissolution. This original nature is called 'yoni' (womb) because it is the source of all creation. From this original nature, infinite universes are born and merge into it. Infinite worldly powers are born from this original nature. To refer to this original nature, God says, 'This nature is Mine.' 
Therefore, My authority over it is also Mine. Without My will, this nature cannot do anything on its own. Whatever it does, it does under My supervision (Gita - 9th Chapter, 10th Verse). I am the Supreme Self, the Parabrahman, who is even greater than the great Brahman (Mahad Brahman) - 
this is what God says to explain that He is the Supreme Self. One should not consider oneself fallen. [ Chapter 14 ]
'In Him I place the embryo' - here, 'embryo' refers to the collective group of living beings along with their accumulated karma. God does not establish a new embryo. Since time immemorial, living beings have been flowing through the cycle of birth and death, 
and at the time of the great dissolution, they merge into the nature along with their accumulated karma (Gita - 9th Chapter, 7th Verse). When the karma of the merged living beings ripens and becomes ready to bear fruit, 
God establishes a special relationship between them and the nature, which was already present as a causal body - 
this is what God does by establishing the embryo of living beings in the nature, which is the womb (yoni). 'Possible for all beings, from that, you will come to be, O Bharat' - 
after establishing the embryo of living beings in the nature through His own divine part, 
God says that He is the father of all beings, who have come into existence through the womb (yoni) of the nature. Even though living beings are separated from the Supreme Self and are associated with the nature, 
they are still a part of the Supreme Self. Their dharma, their unity is with the Supreme Self, not with the body. - Parishishta Bhaav (Appendix)
The meaning of God's statement is that even though living beings are bound by the cycle of birth and death, 
they are still a part of the Supreme Self. - Sambandh (Connection)
The previous shloka described the creation of the collective universe, 
and now the next shloka will describe the creation of individual bodies. O Kunti's son, in all wombs, those that are born, 
I am the seed-giving father, the womb (yoni) is the mother, and I am the father. 4. = O Kunti's son, 
= in all wombs, 
= those that are born, 
= I am the seed-giving father, 
= I am the womb (yoni), 
= the mother, 
= and I am the father. - Vyaakhya (Breakdown)
'In all wombs, O Kunti's son, those that are born, 
I am the seed-giving father, the womb (yoni) is the mother, and I am the father' - 
all living beings are born through four types of wombs: 
jarayu (born from a womb, humans, animals, etc.), 
andaja (born from an egg, birds, snakes, etc.), 
svayedaja (born from sweat, insects, lice, etc.), 
and udabhija (born from the earth, plants, trees, etc.). These four types of wombs are the four sources of creation of all living beings.

[ Verse 5 ]  
* Sadhak - Sanjeevani *

Places. From each of these four places, millions of yoniyaan (vessels) are produced. From those millions of yoniyaan, each yoni gives rise to beings, and each of those beings has a different form. In a single yoni, the beings born in a single caste also differ in form, whether gross or subtle; thus no two beings have exactly the same shape. For example, in a human yoni, billions of bodies have been produced for billions of years, yet to date no two human forms are identical. In this regard, a poet has said:

pag bhaag vaani prakriti, aakriti vachan vika. (“The foot, the part, the speech, the nature, the form, the word, the thought, the power, and the letters of writing are all different even between two people.”)

Thus, among the 42 lakh yoniyaan, all the bodies that have been produced since ancient times have different forms. Apart from the 42 lakh yoniyaan, deities, ancestors, gandharvas, ghosts, spirits, pishachas, brahmarakshasas, child planets, immovable, movable, aquatic, terrestrial, celestial, living, egg‑born, plant‑born, sweat‑born, etc. should also be considered under the term “sarvayonish” (all vessels). In various bodies with different colors and forms, God establishes His conscious part‑essence seed. This shows that the part of the Supreme Soul (Parmatma) present in each creature appears differently due to the differences in bodies. In reality, the same Supreme Soul exists in all beings (Gita, Chapter 13, Verse 2). This is explained with an illustration. Though the illustration does not occur in all aspects, it helps bring the intellect closer. Cloth and earth both have the same dominant element. If cloth is immersed in water, it sinks to the lower part. Cloth is woven from warp (long thread) and weft (horizontal thread). Between each warp and weft there is a tiny hole. Cloth has many such holes. When it remains in water, water fills all the threads and the various holes. Even after removing the cloth from water, the threads and countless holes still contain the same water, perfectly filled. In this illustration, cloth represents “prakriti” (nature), the numerous holes represent “body,” and the water filling cloth and its holes represents “Parmatma‑tattva” (the essence of the Supreme Soul). The implication is that from a gross perspective, each body shows a different Parmatma‑tattva, but from a subtle perspective, all bodies, all of creation, contain the same perfect Parmatma‑tattva. “tasaam brahma madhyoniyonam beejpradah pita” – The above four places, i.e., the 42 lakh yoniyaan, are the places of birth of bodies, and the origin of all these yoniyaan (in the mother’s place) is “Mahadbrahma,” i.e., the primordial nature. In that primordial nature, the one who establishes the seed of life is the father, i.e., I am the one. Appendix: The 42 lakh yoniyaan, deities, ancestors, gandharvas, ghosts, spirits, pishachas, brahmarakshasas, child planets, immovable, movable, aquatic, terrestrial, celestial, living, egg‑born, plant‑born, sweat‑born, etc. should all be considered under the term “sarvayonish.” This is also mentioned in Chapter 7, Verse 6: “etadyonini bhutani sarvanit yupadhari” and Chapter 13, Verse 26: “yavatsanjayate kintisattvam sthavara jngam.”

Here, the word “murti” means body. It includes both manifest and unmanifest bodies. Earth, water, and fire are manifest. Air and sky are unmanifest. Since the body is air‑dominant, ghosts, spirits, and pishachas are also unmanifest. God has explained in the first two shlokas that without a relationship with nature, there is no birth and death, and in the third and fourth shlokas that with a relationship with nature, birth and death occur. The third and fourth shlokas are expanded upon from the fifth to the eighteenth shloka. Relationship – how the Supreme Soul and its power, when combined with nature, bind living beings with natural qualities – this is discussed in the following shlokas. sattvam rajastam iti gunaah prakritisambhavaah. nibadhnanti mahabaahoh dehe dehinamavyayam. (“The qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, inherent in nature, bind the body (deha) and the unchanging (amavya) body.”)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

O Mahabahu! Rajaḥ (passionate quality) and Tamaḥ (dull quality) are the qualities of the dehīnam (body‑possessing one), i.e., satva (the good quality). These three qualities bind the body. The qualities arise from prakṛti (nature). Satva, raja, and tama are produced from the same fundamental nature, which is called “Mahā Brahma.”

The word “iti” indicates that from these three qualities infinite creations arise, and the balance of the three qualities gives rise to many differences among living beings. There are not two or four qualities, but only three. “nibadhnanti mahabahu dehe dehīnam avyayam” – these three qualities bind the indestructible body into the body. In reality, these three qualities do not bind anyone by themselves; rather, it is the person who, by associating with these qualities, becomes bound. The implication is that when a living being regards material wealth, family, body, nature, habits, circumstances, actions, etc. as its own, it becomes bound even though it is indestructible; it becomes subject to the destructive material, wealth, etc. Even though it is completely free, it becomes dependent. For example, a person who regards wealth as his own is affected by the increase or decrease of that wealth; a person who regards others as his own is affected by their birth and death; a person who regards the body as his own is affected by its increase or decrease. This is how the qualities bind the indestructible body. It is a great surprise that this body, even while remaining in its indestructible form, becomes, under the influence of the qualities and their tendencies, itself satva, raja, and tama. Goswami Tulsidas says: “Ishvara ansa jīv abhināsi. Chetan amal sahaj sukharāsi” (Manas 7.117.1). The indestructible nature of the living being never binds itself to the qualities. However, when it regards the destructive body as “I,” “mine,” and “for me,” it becomes bound to the qualities because of its own belief, and it cannot know its indestructible nature beyond the three qualities. Even when bound in the body by the qualities, the living being’s real indestructible nature remains unchanged, which is the goal of God, as indicated by the word “avyayam.”

Here the word “dehīnam” means that when the body possesses self‑attachment, affection, and desire, the three qualities bind this person into the body. If the body lacks self‑attachment, affection, and desire, then it is the supreme soul itself. Special point: The living being attaches itself to the body in two ways – (1) by non‑differentiated feeling, placing itself in the body, so that it appears as “I am the body”; and (2) by differentiated feeling, placing the body within itself, so that it appears as “the body is mine.” By attaching itself to the body in a non‑differentiated way, the living being regards itself as the body, which is called “ahamta” (ego). * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

There will be no desire to remain eternally and no fear of death either. Therefore, as long as there is a desire to remain eternally and a fear of death, he is bound by virtues. You are experiencing separation, and what difficulty and effort is there in separating from it? The effort is only to not grasp the thing that is going to be separated from itself. It is the self that is immortal and the body that is mortal. By not grasping the mortal body, one will experience the separation from one's own immortal, attributeless nature at every moment. This will be experienced by oneself. Due to being born from the nature-principle, the three gunas - sattva, rajas, and tamas - are present in the nature-principle itself. However, due to considering the body as 'I' and 'mine', these gunas bind the immortal conscious self to the mortal body, i.e., they create the ego 'I am the body and the body is mine'. The implication is that all vices are born from the relationship with nature. There is no vice in the sattvic nature itself - 'Asamgo hyayam purushah' (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.15), 'Dehe'smin purushah parah' (Gita 13.22). Due to vices, birth and death occur. Actually, the gunas do not bind the jiva, but the jiva binds itself to them (21st shloka of this chapter). If the gunas were binding, then no one could escape from them even while they exist, nor could anyone attain liberation from them! In the previous shloka, the Lord mentioned that the three gunas - sattva, rajas, and tamas - bind the body. In the next shloka, He will explain the nature and the binding nature of the sattva guna. There
Sattva is called the illuminating and pure one due to its purity. It binds through association with happiness and through association with knowledge, the unblemished one. Translation of the shloka:

Hear, O sinless Arjuna! There
Sattva
Sattva guna
Due to its association with happiness
Illuminating and pure
And
Through association with knowledge
Binds
The unblemished one
Translation of the commentary:

In the previous shloka, the Lord mentioned that the three gunas - sattva, rajas, and tamas - bind the body. In those three gunas, sattva guna is pure and unblemished. The implication is that sattva guna is not tainted like rajas and tamas gunas. It is pure and clean. Due to its purity, it helps in gaining knowledge of the Supreme Reality. Sattva guna is called 'prakashakam' (illuminating) because it is pure and clean. Just as a lamp illuminates objects, sattva guna illuminates the vices of rajas and tamas gunas. The vices of rajas and tamas gunas, such as lust, anger, greed, pride, and jealousy, are clearly visible due to the presence of sattva guna. When sattva guna is predominant, the senses are illuminated, and there is a sense of lightness and clarity. The intellect functions properly, and one can understand both spiritual and worldly subjects clearly. There is a great enthusiasm to work. There are two types of sattva guna - (1) pure sattva, in which the goal is the Supreme Reality, and (2) impure sattva, in which the goal is worldly pleasure and accumulation. In pure sattva guna, the goal is the Supreme Reality, and therefore, there is a natural inclination to move towards the Supreme Reality. In impure sattva guna, the goal is worldly pleasure and accumulation, and therefore, there is an inclination towards worldly tendencies, which binds the individual. Even in impure sattva guna, the intellect is capable of understanding worldly subjects clearly. However, since the goal is not the Supreme Reality, it is called 'malin sattva' (impure sattva). In impure sattva guna, rajas guna is present along with it.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The way to understand it is to realize that the increase of sattvic qualities is the only way to achieve scientific inventions; but its purpose is not to attain the Supreme Consciousness, hence it remains bound to the world due to ego, pride, and attachment to wealth. 'Anamayam' - Sattvic qualities are free from attachment to rajas and tamas. In reality, it is the work of nature, hence it is not entirely free from attachment. Only the Supreme Consciousness, which is beyond all qualities, is entirely free from attachment. To help attain the Supreme Consciousness, God has also declared sattvic qualities to be free from attachment. ' Sukhasangena badhnati jnanasangena cha anagha' - When there is a sattvic quality in the heart, there is no attachment, then one gets happiness, peace, and tranquility. At that time, the seeker thinks that this happiness, peace, and tranquility should be permanent. However, when this happiness, peace, and tranquility do not remain, the seeker does not like it. This liking and disliking is the attachment to sattvic qualities, which binds. When the seeker has a clear understanding of the three qualities - sattva, rajas, and tamas, and their characteristics, and when the seeker has knowledge of many wonderful things that were not known before, then the seeker thinks that this knowledge should be permanent. This attachment to knowledge is also binding. 'I know more than others' - this pride is also binding. |
[ Chapter 14 ]
In this way, sattvic qualities bind the seeker with attachment to happiness and knowledge (asakta - ) and do not allow him to become beyond qualities. This attachment is rajas, which is binding (Gita - 13th chapter, 21st verse). If the seeker does not attach himself to happiness and knowledge, then sattvic qualities do not bind him, but rather make him beyond qualities. In other words, if there is no attachment, the seeker rises above sattvic qualities and experiences his true nature. When the seeker experiences happiness and knowledge due to sattvic qualities, he should be cautious that this happiness and knowledge are not his goal. These are not to be enjoyed by him. They are the means to attain the goal. His goal is to attain the Supreme Consciousness, which illuminates happiness and knowledge. All sattvic qualities are the characteristics of the heart. They come and go, but the true nature remains unchanged. In it, there is no increase or decrease. Therefore, the seeker should always remain detached and indifferent to sattvic qualities. He should not enjoy them. If he does not enjoy them, he will not be attached to happiness and knowledge. If the seeker does not attach himself to the happiness and knowledge that arise from sattvic qualities, he will attain the Supreme Consciousness quickly. But if he does not give up attachment to them, then, due to the goal of attaining the Supreme Consciousness, he will develop a distaste for them and attain the Supreme Consciousness. Parishishta Bhaav - Here, God has declared sattvic qualities to be anamay (free from attachment) - this is the uniqueness of sattvic qualities. The reason is that sattvic qualities are very close to being beyond qualities. Although sattvic qualities are free from attachment, they become attached due to attachment - 'Sukhasangena badhnati jnanasangena cha anagha'; because attachment is the nature of rajas - 'Rajo raagatmakam viddhi' (Gita 14.7). Happiness and knowledge are not obstacles, but their attachment is an obstacle. Attachment is - to consider them as one's own. In reality, sattvic qualities are not one's own, they are the characteristics of nature. In humans, rajas has predominance - 'Rajas in pralayam gatva karma sangishu jayate' (14.15), 'Madhye tisthanti rajasah' (14.18). Therefore, as long as attachment remains, liberation does not occur; because the true nature is unattached. God has declared sattvic qualities to be anamay and the Supreme Abode to be anamay - 'Padam gachchhanti anamayam' (2.51). From this, it should be understood that sattvic qualities are relatively anamay and the Supreme Abode is absolutely anamay. Although the three qualities are born of nature, rajas is born of attachment and tamas is born of ignorance (this chapter's 7th and 8th verse); but sattvic qualities are only born of nature. In other words, sattvic qualities are born of nature, but not born of any vice. Therefore, it is called 'anamay'. Sattvic happiness and sattvic knowledge are also not one's own, but are the characteristics of nature, hence they are 'par' (belonging to others) and are under the control of others. [ Verse 16 ]
The sattvic qualities are the characteristics of nature, hence they are not one's own.

[Verse 7]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

There is happiness in being a slave to others, but not in being happy with one's own nature. - The difference between sattvic knowledge and knowledge of reality is that sattvic knowledge has the attachment 'I am knowledgeable', whereas knowledge of reality is completely unattached, i.e., when one has knowledge of reality, knowledge remains, but 'I am knowledgeable' does not remain. In sattvic knowledge, one sees and there is a sense of specialness in oneself; but in knowledge of reality, there is no seer and there is no sense of specialness or deficiency in oneself, nor is there a sense of specialness; because there is no individuality. The experience of specialness is attachment. The experience of specialness is to accept 'I am knowledgeable' - like this. When one has knowledge of reality, one experiences the bliss of one's own nature. In the 27th verse of the 13th chapter, the description of sattvic knowledge and the 28th verse of the same chapter describe the knowledge of reality. Connection - What is the nature of the rajo guna and how it binds? This is explained in the next verse. Rajo ragatmakam viddhi tishnasa sangasamudbhavam
Tannibadhnati kaunteya karmasangena dehinam 7

Hear, O son of Kunti! (kaunteya) 
Tishnasa sangasamudbhavam = born of attachment and 
Rajo ragatmakam = rajo guna, which is of the nature of attachment
Karmasangena dehinam = through attachment to actions
= the embodied one (jiva)
Viddhi = understand
That = it
Nibadhnati = binds
Karmasangena = through attachment to actions
= the embodied one (jiva)
= it binds. Explanation - 'Rajo ragatmakam viddhi' - This is the rajo guna. The command is to give up rajo guna and do duty. Rajo ragatmakam = rajo guna, which is of the nature of attachment, i.e., the attachment that arises in a person, thing, situation, event, action, etc. is the nature of rajo guna. 'Ragatmakam' means that just as ornaments made of gold are of the nature of gold, similarly rajo guna is of the nature of attachment. Duty done without attachment is liberating (3.25). In the 22nd verse of this chapter, the Lord says that even when the tendency to act arises, the guna-atit person does not have attachment in it. The implication is that even the guna-atit person is affected by the influence of rajo guna, but the action is not done with attachment. The guna-atit person is also bound by attachment to sattva guna, which is the attachment to happiness and knowledge. This proves that attachment is the cause of bondage. In the Yoga Sutras (2.18), 'prakashakriyasthitisheelam bhootendriyam bhogapavartham drishyam' (the activity of illumination is the nature of the senses, the object of enjoyment and the object of liberation). One of the unique features of the Srimad Bhagavad Gita is that it presents its own views on a subject without criticizing any particular school of thought. In the Gita, the Lord has called action both rajo guna (14.12) and sattvic (18.23). Therefore, the fault is not in the actions themselves, but in attachment or desire. It is the attachment or desire that binds a person, not the actions themselves. If actions were the only cause of bondage, then even liberated great souls would be bound, because they also perform actions (14.27). The Lord creates the universe through action and even He performs actions (leelas) in His incarnations, but He is not bound by actions because He has no attachment (9.9). In the 23rd, 24th, and 25th verses of the 18th chapter, the Lord has described three types of actions - sattvic, rajas, and tamas. If actions were only rajo guna, then how would there be a distinction between sattvic and tamas actions? This proves that the Gita mainly calls attachment rajo guna.

'

To understand the true nature of Rajoguna, the Lord is saying that in the beginning of the creation, the Supreme Being had the thought 'Bahusyam Prajayey' (I shall create many beings). This thought is Rajoguna in nature. The Gita has referred to this thought as 'Karma' (action) in the 8th chapter, 3rd verse. Just as ghee and buttermilk separate from curd, similarly, the creation of the universe is influenced by this Rajoguna thought, resulting in the manifestation of Prakriti (nature), which in turn gives rise to Sattvaguna (good quality) and Tamoguna (dark quality) as separate entities. Sattvaguna gives rise to the mind and the senses of knowledge, Rajoguna gives rise to the vital force and the senses of action, and Tamoguna gives rise to the gross material objects, the body, etc. The manifestation of all other objects in the universe is due to the three Gunas. Thus, the Lord's creative action in the beginning of the creation is entirely devoid of attachment (Raga) (Gita - 4th chapter, 13th verse). -
'Trishnasaṅgasaṃudbhavam' - The thought of 'I shall get more and more' arises from the attachment to the already obtained objects, persons, situations, events, etc. This attachment gives rise to the thought of 'I shall get more and more' (Jimi Pratilabha Lobha Adhikari). This attachment in turn gives rise to the attachment to the objects, persons, situations, events, etc. -
[ Chapter 14
The attachment to the objects, persons, situations, events, etc. does not bring about the opportunity for one's own salvation or liberation. Thus, the attachment to the Rajoguna actions binds the embodied being (Dehin) to the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, the seeker should perform the duties (Karmas) in a detached manner, according to the circumstances, but should not initiate new actions for the sake of accumulation and enjoyment. The word 'Dehin' implies that the embodied being, who identifies himself with the body, is bound by the attachment to the Rajoguna actions. There is a pleasure in performing actions with attachment (Sakama Bhava), and there is also a pleasure in enjoying the fruits of actions (Fala Asakti). The attachment to the actions and their fruits binds the human being. To get rid of this attachment, the seeker should think that these objects, persons, situations, events, etc. will not remain with him for long. Because all visible things are constantly disappearing, life is constantly approaching death, the world is constantly approaching destruction, and the great creation is constantly approaching the great destruction. The stages of life, such as childhood, youth, etc. that have passed, will not come again. There are two meanings to this - (1) The time that has passed, which gave rise to attachment and attachment, will not come again. The last stage of great kings, emperors, and wealthy people is a great example of this. (2) The attachment and attachment that arise from the attachment to the objects, persons, situations, events, etc. will not come again. Just as a seed and a tree are interdependent, i.e., a seed gives rise to a tree, and a tree gives rise to many seeds, similarly, the attachment to the objects, persons, situations, events, etc. increases the attachment and attachment, and the attachment and attachment increase the attachment to the objects, persons, situations, events, etc. Therefore, both meanings are correct. -
'Tannibadhnaati Kaunteya Karmasaṅgena Dehinam' - The attachment to the Rajoguna actions binds the embodied being to the cycle of birth and death. As the attachment and attachment increase, the tendency to perform actions also increases. The tendency to perform actions increases, and the embodied being starts performing new actions. He remains engaged in this tendency day and night. The seeker should think that the state of the people who have become ruins is the same state that will befall his body, wealth, house, etc. But I have wasted my power, intelligence, and time by getting trapped in their allurements. This is a great loss. Such thoughts will arise in the seeker's mind, and he will rise above the attachment to actions. If I remain engaged in performing new actions day and night, my human birth will be futile, and I will be born in various wombs and die in various ways. Therefore, I should not initiate new actions for the sake of accumulation and enjoyment, but should perform the duties in a detached manner, according to the circumstances. Such thoughts will also arise in the seeker's mind, and he will rise above the attachment to actions. 1 - From which (state) the attachment and attachment arise. 2 - Of which (state) the attachment and attachment arise. |

[ Verse 8 ]  
* Saadhak‑Sanjeevani *

Appendix meaning — Rajoguna (the mode of passion) binds a person when it is associated with actions. Consequently, even sattvic actions become binding when they are associated. If there is no association, actions are not binding (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 18, Verse 17). Therefore liberation is attained through Karma‑yoga, because Karma‑yoga is the non‑association of actions with their results (Bhagavad‑Gītā, Chapter 6, Verse 4). Relation — The nature of tamoguna (the mode of darkness) and the way it binds are explained in the following verse. **Verse (Bhagavad‑Gītā 8.8)**  
tamastva‑jñāna‑jaṁ viddhi mohanam sarvadehinām |  
pramād‑ālasya‑nidrābhiḥ tannibadhnāti bhārata ||

*tamastva‑jñāna‑jaṁ* – “that which is born of darkness and ignorance”  
*viddhi* – “understand”  
*mohanam* – “the delusion”  
*sarvadehinām* – “of all embodied beings”  
*pramād‑ālasya‑nidrābhiḥ* – “by negligence, laziness and sleep”  
*tannibadhnāti* – “binds him”  
*bhārata* – “O Arjuna”

Thus: “O Arjuna, understand that the delusion born of darkness and ignorance binds all embodied beings through negligence, laziness and sleep.”

Explanation of the terms used in the verse:

- **pramād‑ālasya‑nidrābhiḥ** = by *pramāda* (negligence), *ālasya* (laziness) and *nidrā* (sleep). - **bhārata** = address to the descendant of Bharata (Arjuna). - **tamah** = tamoguna, the mode of darkness. - **jñāna‑jaṁ** = produced from ignorance. - **nibadhnāti** = binds (together with the body). Commentary (continued):

Arjuna, the “delusion” that binds all embodied beings arises from tamoguna, which is generated by ignorance. The particle **tu** in the original text emphasizes the extremely low quality of tamoguna when contrasted with sattva and rajas. The binding effect of tamoguna operates in two ways:

1. **Non‑performance of appropriate duties** – refraining, because of negligence, from actions that are beneficial to oneself and the world, both now and in future results. 2. **Performance of un‑worthy actions** – engaging in deeds that cause harm to oneself and the world, both now and in future results. Tamoguna is born of *ajñāna* (lack of true knowledge) and *moha* (delusion). It clouds the judgment of all embodied beings, preventing discrimination between *sat* (truth) and *asat* (falsehood), and between duty and non‑duty (lack of discernment). Moreover, it obstructs the enjoyment of worldly pleasures and the accumulation of material wealth; it even prevents the enjoyment of rajas‑type pleasures, let alone the higher, sattvic happiness. In reality, the delusion produced by tamoguna primarily affects humans, because other creatures are naturally immersed in tamoguna. The expression **sarvadehinām** underscores that humans who lack the discrimination between *sat* and *asat* (knowledge of duty versus non‑duty) are, despite being human, comparable to the 84 lakhs of lower‑born beings (animals, birds, etc.) that eat, drink and sleep without discernment. The line **pramād‑ālasya‑nidrābhiḥ tannibadhnāti bhārata** states that tamoguna, through negligence, laziness and sleep, binds all embodied beings. Two categories of **un‑worthy work** are described:

1. **Wasteful expenditure** – spending money on cigarettes, bidis, bhang, cannabis, or on entertainment such as movies and games. **Futile activity** – playing cards, engaging in sport without purpose, causing needless suffering to animals and birds, harassing living beings, or destroying small trees and plants without any selfish motive. **Laziness (ālasya)** also appears in two forms:

1. **Inaction** – sleeping, idly sitting, neglecting necessary work, and postponing duties with the thought “I will do it later.” This type of laziness binds the person. **Pre‑sleep heaviness** – a state where the body feels heavy, mental tendencies become heavy, and the power of understanding diminishes. This is not a culpable laziness, because it arises without the person’s volition. **Sleep (nidrā)** likewise has two kinds:

1. **Necessary sleep** – the regular sleep required for bodily health. *Pramāda* (negligence) also has two aspects:

1. **Negligence that leads to lightness of the body**, making the mind agile; (the text is truncated here).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 19
|
It is essential to have a calm mind, and for that, one needs to be free from the attachment to worldly pleasures and knowledge. Therefore, the sattvic quality is associated with 'sukha-sang' (attachment to pleasure) and 'jnana-sang' (attachment to knowledge), while the rajasic quality is associated with 'karma-sang' (attachment to action). However, in the tamasic quality, there is no attachment mentioned; because tamasic quality is associated with attachment. It binds a person by its very nature. In other words, sattvic and rajasic qualities bind a person through attachment, but tamasic quality binds a person by its very nature. Sleep is not to be rejected and is not a fault. God has not considered regular sleep as a fault, but rather as a helpful factor in yoga practice - 'yuktasvapnavabodhasya' (6.17) and (2). Unnecessary sleep - which is taken for the sake of sleep, leading to excessive drowsiness, a heavy body and mind, and a lack of memory - is to be rejected and considered a fault. God has also rejected unnecessary sleep - 'na caiti svapnashilasya' (6.16). In this way, tamasic quality binds a person through laziness, procrastination, and sleep, and prevents their worldly and spiritual progress. Special Note
If there is no attachment to pleasure and no pride in knowledge, then pleasure and knowledge do not bind a person, but rather make them gunatita (beyond the gunas). Similarly, if there is no attachment to action and its fruits, then action becomes a means to attain the ultimate reality (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 3, Verse 19). The three gunas are the natural functions of prakriti, and the jiva (individual soul) is completely free from prakriti and its gunas. The three gunas - sattva, rajas, and tamas - bind a person due to their association with them. However, the way they bind a person is different. Sattvic quality binds a person through attachment to pleasure and knowledge, while rajasic quality binds a person through attachment to action. Tamasic quality binds a person by its very nature. [ Verse 9 ]
O descendant of the Bharta dynasty, Arjuna! Sattva binds a person through attachment to pleasure and knowledge, and through attachment to action, rajas binds a person. But tamas binds a person through ignorance and laziness. Explanation - 'Satva-sukhe-sanjayati' - This verse says that sattvic quality binds a person through attachment to pleasure and knowledge. However, here it is said that sattvic quality's victory is only in pleasure, not in knowledge. The implication is that a person is actually bound by attachment to pleasure. When a person has knowledge, an ego arises, 'I am a knower!' This ego also brings a sense of pleasure, and through this pleasure, a person becomes bound. Therefore, sattvic quality binds a person through attachment to pleasure alone. When sattvic pleasure arises, a person becomes attached to it, and this attachment binds them, preventing them from progressing further in their spiritual practice, and thus they cannot become gunatita (beyond the gunas).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

'When rajas (passion) is in action, O Bharata, it makes a man fond of work, attached to it, and enthusiastic about it. It makes him victorious in the field of action.' This means that God likes to see man engaged in action, and He is pleased with it. Just as a child is made to work by being given a toy, so also rajas (passion) makes man enthusiastic about work and engages him in it. Therefore, when a man is engaged in work, he is not attached to it, nor is he enthusiastic about it. On the other hand, when he is not engaged in work, he feels miserable. This is the nature of rajas (passion). 'When tamas (ignorance) arises, it covers the knowledge (discernment) of the distinction between right and wrong, and the knowledge of what is beneficial and what is not.' When tamas (ignorance) arises, it makes man dull and ignorant, and it does not allow him to understand the distinction between right and wrong, and the knowledge of what is beneficial and what is not. It makes him lazy and sleepy, and it does not allow him to understand the knowledge of the scriptures. The sattva (goodness) quality gives rise to the two qualities of knowledge (discernment) and light (purity). The tamas (ignorance) quality is the enemy of these two qualities, and it covers them. Therefore, it makes man dull and ignorant, and it does not allow him to understand the knowledge of the scriptures. The sages say, 'You have no right to the fruits of your actions.' This means that one should not be attached to the fruits of one's actions. On the other hand, the sages say, 'You have the right to perform actions, but you should not be attached to them.' They say, 'He who wants to attain yoga should perform actions without attachment.' Therefore, one should perform actions without attachment. The attachment to the fruits of actions is the bondage of the sattva (goodness) quality. The attachment to the actions themselves is the bondage of the rajas (passion) quality. The tamas (ignorance) quality is the bondage of the very nature of ignorance. 'When I am happy, I am in the company of good qualities.' This is the company of good qualities. 'When I am engaged in good actions, my actions are good.' This is the company of good actions. The company of good qualities and good actions is the bondage of the sattva (goodness) quality. The company of good qualities is the bondage of the rajas (passion) quality. The tamas (ignorance) quality is the bondage of its very nature. Rajas (passion) increases when it overcomes tamas (ignorance), and sattva (goodness) increases when it overcomes rajas (passion). Tamas (ignorance) increases when it overcomes sattva (goodness), and rajas (passion) increases when it overcomes tamas (ignorance). 10. O Arjuna, son of the Bharata dynasty,
Rajas (passion) becomes sattva (goodness),
Sattva (goodness) becomes rajas (passion),
Tamas (ignorance) becomes sattva (goodness),
And sattva (goodness) becomes tamas (ignorance). Thus, the three gunas (qualities) are mutually opposing each other.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Commentary: 'Rajas and Tamas are subdued, and Sattva prevails, O Bhārata' - Sattva increases by suppressing the tendencies of Rajas and Tamas, i.e., the tendencies of attachment, activity, new endeavors, restlessness, desire, worldly enjoyment, and accumulation, and the tendencies of negligence, laziness, unnecessary sleep, and ignorance. 'Raśas (Rajas) is Sattva, and Tamas is also Raśas' - Rajas increases by suppressing the tendencies of Sattva and Tamas, i.e., the tendencies of knowledge, light, detachment, and generosity, and the tendencies of negligence, laziness, unnecessary sleep, and ignorance. 'Tamas is Sattva, and Raśas is also Tamas' - Similarly, Tamas increases by suppressing the tendencies of Sattva and Rajas, i.e., the tendencies of purity, cleanliness, light, generosity, and the tendencies of restlessness, attachment, and desire. [ Chapter 14 ]

The Lord has presented the opposite order here, i.e., first, the binding of the other, then the victory, and then the increase of one over the other. The purpose of this order is that the Lord first explained in the second verse that those great souls who have severed their relationship with nature are not born in the great creation and are not affected in the great destruction. Because both the great creation and the great destruction are due to the relationship with nature. But those who join their relationship with nature, their nature-born qualities bind them (Fourteenth Chapter, fifth verse). It is natural to ask what the nature of these qualities is and how they bind the human being. The Lord has explained the nature of the three qualities, Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, and how they bind the human being in the sixth to eighth verses. Now, the question arises as to what the three qualities do before they bind the human being. The Lord has explained that the increased quality conquers the human being, then binds him (Fourteenth Chapter, ninth verse). Now, the question arises as to how the quality conquers the human being. The Lord has said that one quality conquers the human being by suppressing the other two (Fourteenth Chapter, tenth verse). In this way, it is understood that the Lord has presented the order from the sixth to the tenth verse. The nature of the qualities is that when one quality increases, its predominance becomes, and the other qualities become secondary. This is the nature of the qualities. [ Connection ]

When one quality increases, what are its characteristics - to explain this, first, the characteristics of the increased Sattva quality are described. In all the doors of this body, light is born. When one knows that Sattva has increased, it is said. 11. When in this body, in all the doors (senses and mind), light is born, and one knows that Sattva has increased, it is said.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

- Commentary: 'sarvadvarEsu dehe'smin jnAnaM yadA' – This refers to the activity, characteristics of the sattvic gunas. When sattvic gunas increase, and rajasic and tamasic tendencies are suppressed, then clarity and purity manifest in all the senses and the mind. Just as the sun's light makes all objects appear clear, similarly, when the mind and senses are pure, one gains true knowledge of the five objects of perception. One's mind is clear and focused on any subject. Clarity and purity of the mind and senses enable one to understand the true nature of things. One gains clear knowledge of what is real and what is not, what is to be done and what is not to be done, what is beneficial and what is detrimental, and what is conducive to one's well-being and what is not. This clarity of knowledge is called viveka. Here, 'dehe'smin' means that this opportunity for sattvic gunas to increase, and for clarity and purity to manifest in the mind and senses, is available only in the human body, not in other bodies. The Lord has used the phrase 'sarvadehinAm' (14.8) for those bound by tamasic tendencies, implying that rajasic and tamasic gunas can increase in other bodies, but sattvic gunas can only increase in the human body. Therefore, it is essential for humans to strive to conquer rajasic and tamasic gunas and rise above them by cultivating sattvic gunas. - 'tadA vidyAd vivRiddhaM sattvam ityut' – When the mind and senses are clear and pure, the sattvic gunas have increased, and the rajasic and tamasic gunas have decreased, the aspirant should realize that sattvic gunas have become prominent. The aspirant should not develop the ego that 'I have become knowledgeable, I have become wise,' or that 'I have acquired the qualities of sattvic gunas.'

Here, 'iti vidyAt' means that the changes in the gunas, such as the increase, decrease, and predominance of one guna over the other, occur only in the gunas themselves, not in their essence. However, humans often fail to appreciate the importance of viveka and instead attribute the qualities of sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic gunas to themselves. - It is essential for humans to understand that the gunas are constantly changing and that they themselves are not subject to change. If humans were also subject to change, then who would observe the changes in the gunas? When sattvic gunas increase, the mind and senses become clear and pure, and viveka awakens. The attachment to the world decreases, and detachment increases. Restlessness disappears, and peace arises. Greed disappears, and generosity increases. The actions become selfless and motivated by a sense of duty. One's perception becomes clear, and one's actions become careful and well-planned. Mistakes decrease, and one's actions become more accurate. When sattvic gunas increase, one gains clear knowledge of what is real and what is not, what is to be done and what is not to be done, and what is beneficial and what is detrimental. - Therefore, when sattvic gunas increase, the aspirant should focus on devotion, meditation, and other spiritual practices. Even a little effort in these practices can bring significant benefits. Parishishta Bhaav: 'prakaSha' and 'jnaana' are two distinct concepts. 'prakaSha' refers to the clarity and purity of the mind and senses, which is the absence of rajasic and tamasic tendencies. 'jnaana' refers to the knowledge of viveka, which is the understanding of what is real and what is not, what is to be done and what is not to be done, and what is beneficial and what is detrimental. Samabandh: The next shloka will describe the characteristics of increased rajasic gunas. LobhaH pravRittirArambhaH karmANAmashmaH spruHah |

But to act without attachment and aversion is not a fault; because such a tendency is also found in great souls who are beyond gunas (Gita-14th Chapter, 22nd Verse). But to act with attachment, i.e., with the desire for pleasure, comfort, wealth, etc. is a fault. 'Armbha'—The name of 'Armbha' is the beginning of actions. But to start new actions for the sake of wealth, prestige, etc. is 'Armbha'. There is a difference between Pravritti and Armbha. According to the situation, some actions are tendencies and some are nivritti. is Armbha. 'Asam'—The name of 'Asam' is the state of the mind where there is unrest, turmoil. When the desired things do not come, then there is unrest, turmoil in the mind. When the attachment to desires is given up, this unrest does not remain. 'Spriha'—The name of 'Spriha' is the attachment to things. Just as when hunger comes, the attachment to food, when thirst comes, the attachment to water, when cold comes, the attachment to clothes, etc. is necessary. But to have attachment to food, water, clothes, etc. is not a fault; but to have attachment to these things is a fault. The sadhaka should give up this attachment; because no thing is under the control of attachment. -
' Rajasy etani jayante vivriddhe Bharatarshabha'—When rajo guna increases in the mind, then the tendencies of lobe, pravritti, etc. increase. At that time, the sadhaka should think that his life is being maintained, what else does he need? Thinking like this, he should remove the tendencies of rajo guna and become detached from them. Manusya janma prapt hone par, only the goal of attaining the Paramatattva should be, not the goal of enjoyment and accumulation. In this view, in Bhakti Yoga and Jnana Yoga, the 'sarvarambhparityagi' (12th Chapter, 16th and 14th Verse) is said to give up all beginnings. In Karma Yoga, actions are started, but in the background, the light of satva guna and knowledge is suppressed. Rajo guna is the enemy of asangata (non-attachment); 'Rajo ragatmakam viddhi' (Gita-14.7). Because of the attachment to action and material, rajo guna does not allow a person to become yogarudha. Because a person becomes yogarudha only when he is detached from action and material (Gita-6th Chapter, 4th Verse). -
|
Samnabdha—What are the symptoms of increased tamoguna? This will be told in the next verse. Aprakasha apurvritti ca pramado moha eva ca. Tamasy etani jayante vivriddhe Kurunandana. 13.

Explanation–‘aprakashaH' — when the tamas guna increases by suppressing the sattva guna (the purity-) tendency,
then there is no purity in the senses and the mind. The power of understanding in the senses and the mind is lost due to the increase of tamas guna, i.e., the first thing is that one does not remember and new wisdom is not born. This tendency is described here as 'aprakasha' and its opposite is 'prakash' (purity) tendency. Light | Recognition is only possible through tendencies; because tendencies are gross,
they become the subject of the senses and the mind. Therefore, the Lord has described the tendencies of the three gunas in the 11th, 12th, and 13th shlokas, respectively,
so that the subtle gunas can be recognized and the sadhak can carefully discard the rajo guna and tamas guna and increase the sattva guna. Pungent Point
'apravrittiH ' – when the tamas guna increases by suppressing the rajo guna's tendency 'pravritti' (activity),
then there is no desire to work. The mind is only interested in idle sitting or lying down. There is no interest in doing necessary work. This is the work of 'apravritti' tendency. ‘pramadaH - getting involved in unnecessary work and not doing necessary work,
and getting involved in activities that do not lead to spiritual growth or worldly growth or social work,
and which are not even necessary for the body—such as smoking, drinking, playing cards, watching movies, etc. is the work of 'pramada' tendency. 'mohaH ' — when the tamas guna increases, then the 'moha' tendency arises,
then the opposing tendency of wisdom is born in the mind. The mind does not work according to wisdom, but is filled with foolishness,
so that there is no ability to do spiritual or worldly work. 'eva cha’—in addition to these, one should also take rest, waste one's life, waste one's wealth, etc. all such useless activities. 'Tamasyetani jayante vivritte kurunandana' – these are the symptoms of increased tamas guna,
i.e., when these darkness, indolence, etc. are seen, one should understand that the sattva guna and rajo guna have been suppressed and the tamas guna has increased. Sattva, rajo, and tam—these three gunas are subtle and ati-indriya (beyond the senses),
i.e., they are not the subject of the senses and the mind. Therefore, these three gunas are not visible, and their true nature is not known. The knowledge of these gunas is not direct, but is obtained through their tendencies. The tendencies of the three gunas are natural and are born, destroyed, and increased. These are all changeable. The sadhak also experiences the change of these tendencies in his life. This proves that the tendencies of the three gunas are changeable and those who know their change are never changed. The tendencies of the three gunas are visible, and the person who sees them is the seer. The seer is different from the visible, this is the rule. The seer is called so because he has a gaze towards the visible. If there is no gaze towards the visible, the seer is without the name of seer. The mistake is that one attributes the visible to oneself and says, 'I am a doer', 'I am angry', etc. Attributing vices like kama and krodha to oneself is to invite them and make them permanent.
