* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The vices arise not in the self, but in the mind and intellect. However, when a person engages in work, these vices become changeable and the self, along with the mind and intellect, considers them to be its own. If the self does not consider them to be its own, then the relationship with the vices is severed. In that case, it is not necessary to remove the vices; rather, they automatically disappear. For instance, when anger arises, the self should think, "I am the same; I can never be associated with the arising and departing anger." If this thought becomes firm, the intensity of anger will decrease, and it will arise less frequently than before. Ultimately, it will completely disappear. [ Chapter 14
The Purusha (the individual self) is a part of the Paramatma (the Supreme Self) and is, therefore, unchanging. The Purusha and Prakriti (nature) are mutually exclusive. How can there be a state of oneness between the two, one of which is changeable and the other is not? By having a vision of this reality, the tamas and rajas (dark and active gunas) are suppressed, and the sattva (pure) guna naturally increases in the self. However, due to the presence of the sattva guna, which is associated with the pleasure of enjoying the world, this sattva guna also becomes a hindrance to its own transcendence. Therefore, the self should not enjoy the pleasure arising from the sattva guna. The enjoyment of sattvic pleasure is a characteristic of the rajas guna. When the rajas guna increases, attachment arises, and when attachment arises, it leads to anger and delusion. As a result, the self falls into the tamas guna and meets its downfall (Gita - The second Lord speaks in the following three shlokas about the characteristics of the increase of the sattva, rajas, and tamas gunas, warning the self to be cautious that the self's association with the gunas is the cause of the gunas' activities, which appear to be its own, whereas in reality, the self has no connection with them whatsoever). Parishishta Bhaav - Darkness and inactivity are opposed to the sattva and rajas gunas, and ignorance and attachment are the characteristics of the tamas guna. Sambandh - The following two shlokas explain the consequences of the temporary increase of the gunas. When the sattva guna is increased, the self (deh-bhrit) meets its destruction. In that state, it attains the pure worlds (amal lokan) of the great knowers (uttam-vidam). 14. Translation of the shloka: 
When the sattva guna is increased, the self (deh-bhrit) meets its destruction. Explanation: When the sattva guna temporarily increases, and the self (deh-bhrit) meets its destruction, it attains the pure worlds (amal lokan) of the great knowers (uttam-vidam). The meaning is that the self, which has been associated with the temporary increase of the sattva guna, attains the pure worlds of the great knowers, who are engaged in only good deeds and never commit any evil deeds. The pure worlds of the great knowers are the highest and most elevated worlds, which are attainable only by those who have been engaged in good deeds throughout their lives. The self, which has been associated with the temporary increase of the sattva guna, attains the pure worlds of the great knowers, who are engaged in only good deeds and never commit any evil deeds.

[Verse 15]
* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

It is evident that the virtues that arise from virtues lead to actions. These virtues take a person to higher realms. They are not weak. Therefore, the sattvic virtues are also as excellent as virtuous actions. From this perspective, the importance of the attitude is also present in the virtuous actions prescribed by the scriptures, not just the virtuous actions themselves. Therefore, the sattvic attitude has a very high place. The four - matter, action, attitude, and goal - are sequentially higher from each other. The meaning of 'amal' is that the sattvic nature is pure; therefore, when the sattvic virtues increase, the deceased person attains the pure realms. There is a doubt here that if the virtuous people who have done good deeds throughout their lives attain certain realms, then how will the deceased person go to those realms when the sattvic virtues increase? The Lord has a special exemption that the person's fate at the time of death is the same as his intellect (Gita - 8th Chapter, 6th Verse). Therefore, when the sattvic virtues increase, the person who leaves the body goes to the higher realms - there is no doubt about this. The sattvic virtues are subtle and extensive. In the world, the consumption of subtle things is less than the gross; just as the gods are subtle and are satisfied with only fragrance. However, the power of the subtle is certainly greater than the gross. This is the reason why the predominance of subtle virtues does not lead to an increase in sattvic virtues at the time of death. Parishishta Bhaav—'tad-uttam-vidāṁ lokān amalān' - The wise person is the best of the best. If he considers sattvic virtues as his own and does not immerse himself in them and remains in the presence of the Lord, then the sattvic person will go to the Lord's supreme abode, becoming beyond the gunas. Otherwise, the sattvic person will go to the higher realms up to Brahmaloka, having a connection with sattvic virtues. 'Amalān' - In the realms up to Brahmaloka, there is relative purity, but in the Lord's supreme abode, there is absolute purity. rajasī
rajasī pralayam gatvā karma-saṅgiṣu jāyate |
tathā pralīna-stamasi mūḍha-yoniṣu jāyate || 15 ||
= When the rajas guna increases, 
pralayam = the deceased person
gatvā = goes to
karma-saṅgiṣu = the company of those who are attached to actions
= becomes a person in human form
jāyate = is born
pralīnaḥ = thus
tathā = similarly
tamasi = when the tamas guna increases
mūḍha-yoniṣu = in the company of foolish people
jāyate = is born

Explanation—When, at the time of death, due to any reason, rajas guna's lust, attachment, restlessness, and other qualities arise in any person, and his body leaves, then the deceased person is born in the company of people who are attached to actions. If a person who has done good deeds throughout his life, who has good virtues, dies due to the increase of rajas guna, then even after being born in human form, his virtues, behavior will be good, he will be a virtuous person. If a person who has a simple life dies due to the increase of rajas guna's lust and other qualities, then even after being born in human form, he will be a person who is attached to worldly things, persons, and actions. If a person who is mainly attached to kama and krodha dies due to the increase of rajas guna, then even after being born in human form, he will be a person who is especially attached to asuric qualities. The meaning is that even after being born in human form, people become three types due to the balance of gunas - three types of people with different natures. However, there is a special thing to be noted that even after being born in human form, the person who dies due to the increase of rajas guna will have the divine gift of discrimination. Therefore, every person should give importance to this discrimination, and by doing sat-sang, self-study, etc., they should purify this discrimination and rise to the highest, attain the supreme self. This discrimination is the reason why all people can attain the supreme self.

All human beings become eligible to attain God by their actions. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

"In the end, when a person is overcome by the darkness of ignorance, he is reborn in a lowly species, such as an animal, bird, insect, or even a tree or a creeper. In these lowly species, ignorance is present to a lesser or greater degree. For example, the degree of ignorance in a tree or creeper is less than that in an animal or bird."

-

*
[ Chapter 19
If a person who has been doing good deeds dies at the time of their downfall, when their temporary darkness of ignorance increases, they will still be good in their new birth, their behavior will be good, and their nature will be to do good deeds. For example, when Bharata Muni's body was overcome by the darkness of ignorance, he was reborn as a deer. However, the self-sacrifice and austerities he had done in his human birth remained the same in his deer birth. He did not stay with his mother, nor did he eat green leaves, but only ate dry leaves, and so on. Such caution is rare even in humans, and Bharata Muni had it in his deer birth.]

Parishishta Bhaav — The 'Raga' aspect of Rajas Guna is the one that binds and gives birth, whereas the 'Kriya' aspect is not. It is said that 'He is born in the company of actions' because of Raga. The Kriya aspect of Rajas Guna is present even in the transcendental, as it is said, 'It shines and it moves' (Gita 14.22). If there is Raga in a thing, action, or person, then that person will be born in the company of actions. A human being is naturally a doer of actions; because the right to perform actions is only in the human birth—'Actions bind one to the human world' (Gita 15.2). Sambandh–Why do the actions of people who die at the time of their downfall lead to such births? This will be explained in the next shloka. The wise men have said that the fruit of good deeds is pure and clean, and the fruit of Rajas Guna is painful and ignorant. 16. Viveki Purushon ne—

The fruit of Tamas Guna's actions is said to be ignorance, and the fruit of Rajas Guna's actions is said to be pain and ignorance. Vivriti—

In reality, actions are not Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic. All actions are just actions. It is the doer who is Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic. The action done by a Sattvic doer is Sattvic, the action done by a Rajasic doer is Rajasic, and the action done by a Tamasic doer is Tamasic. 'Karmanah Sukritasyaahuh Sattvikam Nirmalam Phalam'—The nature of Sattva Guna is pure, clean, and unchanging. Therefore, the action done by a Sattvic doer will be Sattvic, and the fruit of that action will also be pure and clean. As long as the Sattva Guna is associated with the doer, even if the doer does not desire the fruit of the action, the action will still be Sattvic, and its fruit will be pure and clean. However, when the association with Sattva Guna is completely severed, the doer is no longer Sattvic, and the actions done by the doer become actions without a doer. ' Rajas tu Phalam Duhkham Ajnaanam'—The nature of Rajas Guna is Raga-atmaka. Therefore, the action done by a Raga-atmaka doer will be Rajasic, and the fruit of that action will be painful and ignorant. In other words, the doer will experience pleasure and pain in the world, and will enjoy the fruits of their actions in their body. The meaning is that the doer will experience pleasure and pain in the world, and will enjoy the fruits of their actions in their body.

[Verse 17]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

In the presence of any situation, a sattvic person will not experience any sorrow. Similarly, a rajasic person will not experience any happiness in any situation. On the other hand, a tamasic person will not be able to awaken his discriminative faculty, but will remain in a state of ignorance. There will be the attainment of the pleasures of the heavenly worlds, but all these worldly pleasures are the causes of sorrow - 'These sensual pleasures are the causes of sorrow and birth' (Gita 5.22). Therefore, the Lord has described the fruit of rajasic karma as sorrow here. Two things are produced by the rajas guna - sin and sorrow. A rajasic person commits sin in the present and suffers the consequences of those sins in the form of sorrow in the future. In the thirty-sixth shloka of the third chapter, when Arjuna asks, "Why does a person commit sin even when he does not want to?" the Lord explains that the root cause of sin is the desire born of ignorance. 'Ignorance is the fruit of tamas' - ignorance is the nature of tamas, which is characterized by delusion. Therefore, a tamasic person, who is deluded and does not see the consequences of his actions, will perform tamasic karma, which will lead to the attainment of ignorant birth. In accordance with his karma, he will be born in a state of ignorance, such as that of an animal, bird, insect, or a tree, where ignorance is predominant. The nature and circumstances of a person are determined by his karma. As long as the guna and karma are related, a person cannot be happy in any situation. When the guna and karma are not related, a person cannot be unhappy in any situation and will not be bound. The main factor in birth is the thought at the time of death, and the root of this thought is the growth of guna. The growth of guna is determined by karma. Therefore, a person's thought at the time of death will be in accordance with his guna and karma. In this way, the main factor in birth is the thought at the time of death. - Appendix / Parishishta Bhaav -

The nature of rajas is attachment, and it is this attachment that causes sorrow - 'The fruit of rajas is sorrow' (Gita 3.37). All the sorrows and sins in the world are caused by attachment. Attachment is the cause of the birth of desire - 'Desire, anger, and attachment are born of rajas' (Gita 3.37). - Sambandh / Connection -

In the previous shloka, the Lord explained the nature of the gunas and their effects. Now, the Lord will explain the gunas that are the root of sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic karma. From satva guna, knowledge is born. From rajas guna, attachment is born. From tamas guna, ignorance, carelessness, and delusion are born. 17. Translation of the shloka:

Explanation: 'Satva guna from which knowledge is born' - from the satva guna, the discriminative faculty is awakened, and a person performs good and virtuous actions. The fruit of those good actions is sattvic, pure.

'rajaso lobha eva ca' - Rajas guna se lobha adi paida hote hain. Loba ko lekar manushya jo karma karta hai, un karmaon ka phal dukh hota hai. Jitna mila hai, uski vridhi chahane ka naam loba hai. Loba ke do roop hain—uchit kharch na karna aur anuchit reetise sangrah karna. Uchit kamonmein dhan kharch na karna se, usse ji churaane se manushyakay manmein ashant, halchal rehti hai aur anuchit reetise arthata jhooth, kapat adise dhan ka sangrah karna se paap bante hain, jisse narakonmein tatha chaurasi lakh yoniyonmein dukh bhogna padta hai. Is drishti se rajas karmaon ka phal dukh hota hai. 'pramadamoha u tamaso bhavato'jnanameva ca' - Tamogunase pramad, moha aur ajnana paida hote hain. In teenon ke buddhim anese vivik-viruddh kaam hote hain (Gita - Aatharavadi Adhyayaka batteesva shlok), jisse ajnana hi badhta hai, dridh hota hai. Yahaan to tamogunase ajnana ka paida hona bataya hai aur isi adhyayake aathave shlokmein ajnane se tamogun ka paida hona bataya hai. Iska tatparya yah hai ki jaise vrikshase bij paida hote hain aur un bijonse aage bahut-se vriksh paida hote hain, aise hi tamogunase ajnana paida hota hai aur ajnane se tamogun badhta hai, pust hota hai. Pehle aathave shlokmein Bhagavan ne pramad, aalas aur nidra—ye teen bataye. Parantu terehve shlokmein aur yahaan pramad to bataya, par nidra nahin bataya. Isse yah sidh hota hai ki avashyak nidra tamogunee nahin hai aur nishiddh bhi nahin hai tatha baandhnevali bhi nahin hai. Kaaran ki sharirake liye avashyak nidra to satvik purushako bhi aati hai aur gunaateet purushako bhi! Vastavmein adhik nidra hi baandhnevali, nishiddh aur tamogunee hai; kyonki adhik nidraase sharirmein aalas badhta hai, pad rahe rahe man karta hai, bahut samay barbaad ho jata hai. Vishesh baat—

Yah jeev sakshat paramatmak aans hai karte hue bhi jab prakritike saath sambandh jod leta hai, tab iska prakritijanay gunonke saath sambandh jud jaata hai. Phir gunonke anusar uske antahkaranmein vrittiyan paida hoti hain. Un vrittiyonke anusar karma hote hain aur inhi karmaonka phal unch-nich gatiyan hoti hain. Tatparya hai ki jeevit avasthame anukool-pratikool paristhitiyan aati hain aur marneke baad unch-nich gatiyan hoti hain. Vastavmein un karmaonke moolmein bhi gunonki vrittiyan hi hoti hain, jo ki punarjanmke hone me khas kaaran hain (Gita—Terehve Adhyayaka ikkisva shlok). Tatparya hai ki gunonka sang karmaonse kamjor nahin hai. Jaise karma shubh-ashubh phal dete hain, aise hi gunonka sang bhi shubh-ashubh phal deta hai (Gita - Aathave Adhyayaka chhathva shlok). Isilee pehle chaudhavme-se aatharavadi shlok takke is prakaranmein pehle chaudhavme-panchavadi shlokonmein gunonki tatkalik vrittiyonke badhane ka phal bataya aur jeevit-avasthame jo paristhitiyan aati hain, unko solahavadi shlokmein bataya tatha aage aatharavadi shlokmein gunonki sthayi vrittiyonka phal batayenge. Atah vrittiyon aur karmaonke hone me gun hi mukhya hain. Is poore prakaranmein gunonki mukhya baat isi (satrahvadi) shlokmein kahi gayi hai. Jiska uddeshy sansar nahin hai, pratitut paramatma hai, wah sadharan manushyonki tarah prakritime sthit nahin hai. Atah usme prakritijanay gunonki parvashata nahin rehti aur sadhan karte-karte aage chalakar jab ahantha parivartit ho kar lakshaki dridhata ho jaati hai, tab usko apne svatah sidh gunaateet swaroopka anubhav ho jaata hai. Isike naam bodh hai. Is bodhke vishayme Bhagavan ne is adhyayaka pehla-dusra shlok kaha aur gunaateetke vishayme baivadi-se chabivadi shlok kaha. Is tarah yah poora adhyay gunonse atit svatah sidh swaroopka anubhav karane ke liye hi kaha gaya hai. Parishisht bhaav - Jnana (vivek) satvagunase prakat hota hai aur sang na karna par badhate-badhte tatvabodhtak chala jaata hai arthata tatvabodhmen parinat ho jaata hai. Parantu loba, pramad, moha, ajnana badhte hain to koi nuksaan baaki nahin rehta, koi dukh baaki nahin rehta, koi muuddh yoni baaki nahin rehta, koi naraka baaki nahin rehta. Sambandh—Tatkalik gunonke badhane par marnevalonki gatikaa varnan to chaudhavme-panchavadi shlokonmein kar diya; parantu jinkon jeevanme satvagun, rajogun athva tamogunki pradhanata rehti hai, unki (marne par) kya gati hoti hai - iska varnan aage shlokmein karte hain.

[Verse 18]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Those who are established in the mode of goodness, go higher and higher, those who are established in the mode of passion remain in the middle, and those who are established in the mode of ignorance go down. = Those who are established in the mode of goodness, go to higher realms,
=
those who are established in the mode of passion, remain in this world,
=
and those who are established in the mode of ignorance, go down. Explanation of the commentary: 'Those who are established in the mode of goodness' - Those whose lives are characterized by the predominance of the mode of goodness, and who have thus renounced worldly pleasures; who have performed auspicious deeds such as pilgrimages, vows, charity, and other virtuous actions; who have established wells, food distribution centers, and other facilities for the benefit of others; who have planted trees for the benefit of animals and birds; who have established cow shelters, such people are called 'those who are established in the mode of goodness'. When the body of such people is released from the world, they go to higher realms due to their association with the mode of goodness, their attachment to the mode of goodness, and their subsequent birth in higher worlds. The description of these higher worlds is given in the 14th verse of this chapter. Those who are established in the mode of passion, remain in the middle - Those whose lives are characterized by the predominance of the mode of passion, and who have thus accumulated wealth and sensual pleasures; who have lived a life of luxury and comfort; who have been attached to worldly possessions and people; such people are called 'those who are established in the mode of passion'. When the body of such people is released from the world, they are reborn in this world due to their attachment to the mode of passion, and they acquire a body that is characterized by a predominance of the mode of passion. The phrase 'remain in the middle' implies that such people are reborn in this world in the same state as they were in their previous life. They do not undergo any significant change, and they continue to live a life of luxury and comfort. They do not engage in any sinful or immoral activities, but they are still attached to worldly possessions and people, and they are reborn in this world due to their attachment to the mode of passion. Those who are established in the ignorance, go down - Those whose lives are characterized by the predominance of the mode of ignorance, and who have thus wasted their wealth and time on useless pursuits; who have been lazy and lethargic; who have neglected their duties and responsibilities; who have harmed others and caused them suffering; who have committed sinful and immoral acts such as theft, deception, and violence; such people are called 'those who are established in the mode of ignorance'. When the body of such people is released from the world, they go down due to their association with the mode of ignorance, their attachment to the mode of ignorance, and their subsequent birth in lower worlds. There are two types of downward paths - the path of specific birth and the path of specific place. The path of specific birth refers to the birth of animals, birds, insects, and other creatures, while the path of specific place refers to the birth in hellish realms such as Vaitarani, Asipatravana, Lalabhaksha, Kumbhipaka, Raurava, and Maharaurava. Those whose lives are characterized by the predominance of the mode of goodness or passion, but who are overcome by the mode of ignorance at the time of death, are reborn in the path of specific birth. Those whose lives are characterized by the predominance of the mode of ignorance, and who are overcome by the mode of ignorance at the time of death, are reborn in the path of specific place. In summary, the ultimate destination of a person is determined by their final thoughts and actions, but the experience of pleasure and pain is determined by their karma. Just as a dog may be reborn as a dog, but may still experience pleasure and pain, so too does a person experience pleasure and pain based on their karma, regardless of their final destination.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

If one performs actions according to their nature, they will receive great happiness and comfort. However, the ultimate thought of a person has already become bad, so they will become bad according to their ultimate thought; but they will receive a terrible situation as the fruit of their actions. They will have diseases in their bodies. They will face difficulties in getting food, water, and clothes. A seeker should engage in reading the true scriptures (Sat-Shastra), increase the sattvic qualities by doing so. They should eat and drink sattvic food, and avoid rajasic and tamasic food. They should associate with sattvic people, live with them, and follow their instructions. They should serve pure and sacred places, and avoid places where there is noise, and places where eggs, meat, and liquor are sold. The morning and evening times are considered sattvic, so they should utilize these times for spiritual practices like bhajan and dhyana. They should perform only those actions that are prescribed by the scriptures, and avoid prohibited actions. They should never perform rajasic or tamasic actions. A person should follow their own duties according to their varna and ashrama. They should meditate on God only. They should recite only sattvic mantras. By doing all these things, the old sanskaras (impressions) will be destroyed, and sattvic sanskaras (qualities) will increase. In the Srimad Bhagavatam, ten causes of increasing qualities are mentioned:

Agaṃo 'paḥ prajā deśaḥ kālaḥ karma cha janma cha
Dhyānaṃ mantraṃ atha saṃskāro daśaite guṇa hetavaḥ (11 | 13 | 4)

"These ten things - scriptures, food, people, place, time, actions, birth, meditation, mantras, and sanskaras - if they are sattvic, increase sattvic qualities; if they are rajasic, increase rajasic qualities; and if they are tamasic, increase tamasic qualities."

Special Note

At the time of death, when the rajasic quality increases, a person takes birth in the human world (this chapter's 15th verse) and a person who is predominantly rajasic dies and takes birth again in the human world (this chapter's 18th verse). From these two things, it is clear that all humans in this world are rajasic. Satvic and tamasic qualities are not present in them. If this is the case, then why does the Bhagavan say that when the satvic quality increases, a person dies and takes birth in the higher worlds (this chapter's 14th verse and 18th verse), and when the tamasic quality increases, a person dies and takes birth in the lower worlds (this chapter's 15th verse and 18th verse)? And why does the Bhagavan say that the entire universe is tri-guṇa (18th chapter, 40th verse)? The answer to this doubt is that in the upward path, satvic quality is predominant, but along with it, rajasic and tamasic qualities also exist. Therefore, even the gods have sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic natures. Therefore, even in the upward path, there are subtle differences in the satvic quality. Similarly, in the middle path, the rajasic quality is predominant, but along with it, satvic and tamasic qualities also exist. Therefore, even humans have sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic natures. In the downward path, tamasic quality is predominant, but along with it, satvic and rajasic qualities also exist. Therefore, even animals, birds, and other creatures, and even the inhabitants of hell, have different natures. Some have a gentle nature, some have a moderate nature, and some have a cruel nature. The meaning is that wherever there is a relationship with any quality, all three qualities will exist. Therefore, the Bhagavan says that there is no being in the three worlds who is devoid of all three qualities (18th chapter, 40th verse). In the upward path, the satvic quality is predominant, the rajasic quality is secondary, and the tamasic quality is very secondary. In the middle path, the rajasic quality is predominant, the satvic quality is secondary, and the tamasic quality is very secondary. In the downward path, the tamasic quality is predominant, the rajasic quality is secondary, and the satvic quality is very secondary. The meaning is that even in those who are predominantly satvic, rajasic, or tamasic, each quality exists in greater, moderate, or lesser amounts. In this way, the three qualities bind the indestructible body (5th verse of this chapter). The entire universe is deluded by the three qualities (13th verse of the 7th chapter). The three types of doers are sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic (26th to 38th verses of the 18th chapter). The entire three worlds are tri-guṇa (40th verse of the 18th chapter), and so on. [ Chapter 14 ]

[ Chapter 14 ]

[Verse 20]
Becoming free from the miseries of birth, death, decay, and old age, the embodied being, transcending these three qualities, attains immortality. Explanation - 'Gunaanetaanatitya trine dehee dehasamudbhavaan' 
Although the wise man's connection with the body is not, yet, in the eyes of people, he is called 'dehee' (embodied being) because of being associated with the body. The qualities that give rise to the body are the very qualities themselves. The man who associates himself with a particular quality is born in high or low wombs according to that quality (Gita - 13th Chapter, 21st Verse). The words 'etan trine gunaan' have come here for the three qualities mentioned from the 5th to the 18th verses of this chapter. The wise man transcends these three qualities, i.e., he does not associate himself with them, nor does he consider himself to be related to them. The reason is that he has a clear understanding that all qualities are changeable, born, and destroyed, and that they never get entangled with their own nature. It is worth noting that the person from whom these qualities arise also has no connection with them. Then how can there be a connection with qualities? "When the embodied being transcends these three qualities, he is no longer born, does not die, and does not experience the miseries of old age." - When the seeker transcends these three qualities, he is no longer born, does not die, and does not experience the miseries of old age. Because the cause of birth, death, and old age is the association with qualities. These qualities are always changing, and their nature is always changing. The qualities are sometimes sattvic, sometimes rajasic, and sometimes tamasic, but their own nature is never sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic. The self (svarupa) remains unattached. This unattached self never takes birth. When birth does not occur, death also does not occur. The reason is that the death of a person is the death of the same person, and the old age of a person is the old age of the same person. The association with qualities is the cause of the experience of the miseries of birth, death, and old age. He who experiences the detachment from all qualities attains the experience of his own self-realization. The association with the body is the cause of the experience of the miseries of death. Man considers himself to be mortal because of his association with the body. The greatest misery is death. Man is immortal by nature, but due to his attachment to worldly possessions and his association with the body, which is constantly changing, he does not experience immortality. The wise man experiences immortality when he is detached from the body. In the previous verse, 'madbhavam so 'dhigachchhati' was mentioned, and here 'amritamashnuthe' is mentioned - in fact, both are the same thing. In the Gita, 'jaramrityumokshay' (7.29), 'janmamrityu-jaravyadhidukhadoshanudarshanam' (13.8), and 'janmamrityujaradukhairyvimuktah' (14.20) - on all three occasions, instead of mentioning 'balya' and 'yuvavastha', the name 'jar' (old age) has been used. The reason is that man does not experience much misery in the stages of childhood and youth, because in these stages, the body has strength. But in old age, the body does not have strength, and man experiences more misery. Similarly, when a man's life force leaves his body, he experiences great misery. But he who transcends the three qualities experiences immortality.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

As one transcends, he accepts birth, death, and sorrows as eternal. The body is freed from the sufferings of old age due to the absence of the productive qualities of the body. Born, he becomes. Due to the absence of the productive qualities of the body, a great soul, who is beyond qualities, is freed from all sufferings related to the body. In this human body, when one becomes aware, there is no question of his birth. However, his old age and death will certainly come, but he will not suffer from old age and death. Only by considering oneself to be one with the body in the present moment does rebirth occur, and due to the body's suffering from minor diseases, etc. Therefore, every human being should first experience his unqualified nature before death. Due to being unqualified, one is freed from all kinds of sufferings, such as old age, disease, and death, and one experiences immortality. Then, his rebirth does not occur. Parishishta Bhaav - There is a feeling in the human being that 'I should remain forever, I should not die.' He wants to be immortal. This desire for immortality is proved to be true, as it is said, 'This is the same eternal world' (Gita 8.19). However, when a human being, due to his ignorance, considers himself to be one with the mortal body, i.e., 'I am the body,' then fear of death and the desire for immortality arise in him. When he considers his intellect to be important, i.e., 'I am not the body; the body is always in death, and I am always in immortality,' then he experiences his own self-proved immortality. The body's vices and changes are always experienced by oneself while remaining one and the same. Therefore, the seeker should give importance to his being, his immortality, rather than the vices and changes. This shloka is the essence and summary of the fourteenth chapter. Sambandh - Hearing that the unqualified person is freed from sufferings and attains immortality, Arjuna's curiosity arose to know the characteristics of the unqualified person. Therefore, he asks the Lord in the next shloka. Arjuna said,
O Lord, by what characteristics does one transcend these three qualities? What is the conduct of one who has transcended these three qualities? How does one transcend these three qualities? 21. Arjuna asked the Lord,
O Lord, by what characteristics does one transcend these three qualities?

Is the daily routine of a person of great virtues the same as that of a person who is awake at night? Or is it something extraordinary? Is the daily routine of a person of great virtues the same as that of a person who is awake at night, or is it something extraordinary? The behavior of a person, like us, is determined by the three gunas. What is the way of life, the food, and the behavior of a person of great virtues? Can a person of great virtues be achieved by following a certain path or method? Relation - In the answer to the first question of Arjuna, the Lord describes the characteristics of a person of great virtues in the next two shlokas. The Blessed Lord said:
Pandava, I do not hate those who are engaged in their duties, nor do I desire those who have renounced them. 22. Pandava - O Pandava! Sampravritti - (These) all (good) actions
Ch - are (being) engaged in
Tarhaas - in this way

Kankshati - I do not desire (those who have renounced their duties). Explanation - 'Prakasam' - The light of the senses and the mind. 'Pravritti' - The tendency to engage in actions. The Blessed Lord said:
O Pandava, I do not hate those who are engaged in their duties, nor do I desire those who have renounced them. The Lord has already described the two tendencies of the satva guna in the eleventh shloka - prakas and jnana. Here, only the prakas tendency is being referred to, which means that the satva guna is the main one. As long as the senses and the mind do not have prakas, there is no purity and clarity, and therefore, there is no jnana (discernment). It is only when prakas arises that jnana is awakened. 'Pravritti' - As long as there is a connection with the gunas, there is the tendency to engage in actions, which is the result of the rajo guna. This tendency is characterized by attachment, desire, and restlessness. However, when a person becomes gunatita, this tendency does not arise. But even a gunatita person engages in actions, and this is what the Lord refers to as 'pravritti'. 'Moham' - Attachment is of two types - (1) the attachment to the eternal and the non-eternal, the good and the bad, the obligatory and the non-obligatory, which is a lack of discernment, and (2) the attachment that arises from ignorance, such as considering a faultless person to be faulty and a faulty person to be faultless, and so on. The first type of attachment does not arise in a gunatita person, as it is mentioned in the fourth chapter of the Gita (35th shloka). However, the second type of attachment, which arises from ignorance, does arise in a gunatita person. 'Na dvetsi sampravritti na nivritti kankshati' - Even though the three gunas are fully active, a gunatita person does not hate those who are engaged in their duties, nor does he desire those who have renounced them.

The one who has realized the Self does not get affected by the rise and fall of these tendencies. The meaning is that a great soul's vision does not go towards them; because his vision is that 'why are these tendencies being generated?' To see them as they are, they can again rise; these tendencies can remain' – He does not harbor attachment for this. 'To do' is under the category of 'to do', and 'to see' is under the category of 'to be'. Due to being beyond the gunas, it is not affected by the tendencies of the gunas that arise and subside. To see the defects is to do, and to see them as they are is not to do. Therefore, the seeker is not affected by them. Even if a bad tendency appears in his heart, he remains detached by nature. He should not be frightened by this. The tendencies that appear as they are (to be seen) are the ones that he should see as they are. The seeker commits a mistake by seeing the tendencies as they are and getting entangled in them. Lord Rama says-

There is one 'to be' and one 'to do'. 'To be' is a collective phenomenon, and 'to do' is an individual phenomenon. The responsibility for what 'happens' in the world does not lie on us. The responsibility for what 'we do' lies on us. The power that governs the entire universe is the same power that governs our body, senses, mind, and intellect (which are all parts of the universe). When we do not feel the good or bad effects of the actions that happen in the world, then how can we feel the good or bad effects of the actions that happen in our body, senses, mind, and intellect? But when a person gets attached to the actions that happen in the world with attachment or hatred, then he becomes the doer of those actions, and he has to suffer the consequences of those actions. - does not perform any action. Explanation: The term 'udasiinavadaasiinah' refers to two people who are engaged in a dispute. The one who remains indifferent to the dispute is called a 'madyastha' (a mediator), and the one who takes sides is called a 'pakshapati' (a partisan). However, the one who observes both parties but does not take sides or express any opinion is called an 'udasiin' (an indifferent person). Similarly, a person who sees the world and the universe as being devoid of qualities appears to be indifferent like an 'udasiin'. In reality, the universe is not independent, but is dependent on the Supreme Consciousness. Therefore, when a person who has transcended qualities sees the universe, he does not see any qualities, and hence appears to be indifferent like an 'udasiin'. 'Gunaairyaha vichalyate' - Although the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas are present in his inner self, he is not agitated by them. The implication is that just as the presence of qualities in another person's inner self does not affect him, similarly, the presence of qualities in his own inner self does not affect him. This is because his inner self is constantly aware of the absence of the universe and the presence of the Supreme Consciousness. 'Guna varant ityeva yo avatisthiti' - The qualities are present in the qualities, and thus he remains established in his own nature, untouched by them. 'Neingate' - This phrase indicates that he does not perform any action. The reason is that the Supreme Consciousness is beyond all actions and is unchanging. [ The 22nd and 23rd verses of this chapter describe the state of a person who has transcended qualities.]

Parishishta Bhaav - The three phrases 'na vichalyate', 'avatisthiti', and 'neingate' convey the same meaning, which is that a person who has transcended qualities remains in a state of stability and non-attachment. He is not agitated by anything, nor is he affected by anything. The three concepts 'karna' (doing), 'hona' (being), and 'hai' (is) are interconnected. When 'hona' and 'hai' are combined, the ego is completely eliminated. A person who is attached to the concept of 'karna' (doing) thinks, 'I am doing this', and thus creates the ego. A person who has transcended qualities, on the other hand, experiences only 'hona' and 'hai', and thus remains egoless. A person who has not attained self-realization thinks, 'I am doing this', and thus creates the ego. A person who has attained self-realization, however, experiences only 'hona' and 'hai', and thus remains egoless. A person who has attained self-realization experiences only the state of being, 'yo avatisthiti neingate'. He is the Supreme Consciousness, which is the ultimate reality. All actions are present in Him, and He is the ultimate reality.

[Verse 25]
As it is. The vision of a great person remains on the ultimate consciousness ('is') itself, not on actions. Vivaran - Dhīraḥ, samaduhkha-
sukhaḥ ' – knowing the truth of the eternal and the non-eternal, the real and the unreal, etc. and remaining in one's own self-existent nature, a person beyond the gunas is said to be steady-minded. =
- is said to be
remains the same in happiness and sorrow;
puts mica in its place, stone in its place, and gold in its place (in the treasury, etc.). The meaning is that although he does not experience joy or sorrow in the acquisition or non-acquisition of these, he remains the same, yet he behaves appropriately with them. The name of the favorable and unfavorable circumstances that come according to one's past deeds is called happiness and sorrow, i.e., according to the prarabdha, the favorable circumstances of the body, senses, etc. are called 'happiness' and the unfavorable circumstances are called 'sorrow'. A person beyond the gunas remains the same in both. The meaning is that the external circumstances of happiness and sorrow cannot create any vikara in his internal consciousness, nor can they make him happy or unhappy. The knowledge of mica, stone, and gold is not samata. Samata is that even with the knowledge of these three, there should be no attachment or aversion to them. Knowledge is never a fault, it is the vikara that is a fault. ' Tulyapriyāpriyaḥ '– remains the same in the success and failure of actions, i.e., in the immediate fruits of actions, whether they are obtained or not. ' Tulyanindātma-
saṃstutiḥ ' - the main thing is praise and blame. A person beyond the gunas has no connection with name; therefore, whether someone praises or blames him, there is no sadness in his mind and no joy. Similarly, he has no attachment or aversion to those who praise or blame him. ' Svasthaḥ'– his nature is such that there is no happiness or sorrow in it. The nature is revealed by happiness and sorrow. Therefore, a person beyond the gunas does not become a consumer of coming and going happiness and sorrow, but remains steady in his own eternal and unchanging nature. ' Samaloṣṭāśmakāñcanaḥ ' – he has no attraction (raga) or aversion (dvesha) to mica, stone, and gold. However, in behavior, he does not have raga towards mica.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
It is a common habit of ordinary people that they feel bad about their criticism and good about praise. However, those who rise above virtues, have knowledge of criticism and praise, and they also behave appropriately with everyone, but they do not feel sad or happy due to criticism and praise. The reason is that they are situated in a reality where virtuous criticism and praise do not reach. Criticism and praise - both are external actions. Being pleased or displeased with these actions is a mistake. The reason is that a person speaks according to his nature and perception. If he speaks according to our liking and does not criticize us, it is not justice, i.e., it is not right to force him to speak in our favor. It is injustice. What right do we have to ask others not to criticize us and only praise us? Another thing is that if someone criticizes us, a seeker should be pleased that my sins are being cut, I am becoming pure. If someone praises us, our virtues are being destroyed. Therefore, one should not be pleased with praise; because being pleased with praise is a danger. 'Man and disrespect are equal' - the body's main concern is with praise and disrespect. A person who is beyond virtues does not have a connection with the body. Therefore, whether someone respects him or disrespects him, praises him or disrespects him, it has no effect on him. Criticism and praise, and respect and disrespect - a person who is beyond virtues remains the same in both these external actions. Having knowledge of these external actions is not a fault, but being sad due to criticism and disrespect, and being happy due to praise and respect is a fault; because these are natural vices. A person who is beyond virtues has knowledge of criticism and disrespect, but due to the separation from virtues, he does not have a connection with the name and body, and therefore he is not happy or sad. The reason is that he is situated in a reality where these vices do not exist. That reality is beyond virtues, it is unchanging. 'Equal to friends and enemies' - in reality, a person who is beyond virtues remains equal to friends and enemies. Although a person who is beyond virtues does not consider anyone as a friend or enemy, others consider him as a friend or enemy according to their feelings. Even ordinary people can consider someone as a friend or enemy according to their feelings; but when they come to know about this, it affects the person, and they may develop attachment or aversion. But a person who is beyond virtues is not affected even when others come to know about this. In fact, the feeling of friendship and enmity is the cause of bias in behavior. A person who is beyond virtues does not have the feeling of friendship and enmity in his heart, and therefore, he does not have bias in his behavior. A person who has friendship with a great person and another person has enmity with him. When they get an opportunity to judge someone, they tend to favor the person who has friendship with him more than the person who has enmity with him. For example, when distributing things, he gives less to the person who has friendship with him (as much as he can tolerate with pleasure) and gives more to the person who has enmity with him. This is also considered equality; because it is necessary to be just with friends and generous with enemies. 'The one who abandons all beginnings' - a great person is one who abandons all beginnings of actions. In other words, he does not start any new action for the sake of accumulating wealth and enjoying its fruits. His behavior is according to the circumstances that arise naturally, i.e., his behavior is free from desires, attachment, and ego, and his inaction is also free from the desire for fame and praise. 'He is called beyond virtues' - here, the word 'uchyate' implies that the person who is beyond virtues is not beyond virtues by nature, but he is called so due to the characteristics of his body and heart. In reality, if someone is beyond virtues, he cannot have characteristics. Characteristics are only of virtues; therefore, if someone has characteristics, how can he be beyond virtues? But Arjuna has asked for the characteristics of a person who is beyond virtues, and God has also described the characteristics of a person who is beyond virtues. The meaning is that people first consider the body and heart of a person who is beyond virtues to be in a certain state, and then they attribute those characteristics to him, saying that this person is beyond virtues.

[Verse 26]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Those who possess the following eight characteristics are considered to be beyond the realm of material qualities. These characteristics are so difficult to attain that even sages may not possess them. However, one who possesses these eight characteristics finds it easy to maintain equanimity in all situations. The Lord now explains the names of these eight difficult-to-attain characteristics, which are inherent in a person who is beyond material qualities. The qualities of nature are its attributes, and the attributes of qualities are the body, senses, mind, and intellect. Therefore, it is not possible to fully describe the attributes of qualities through the intellect and mind, and even less so is it possible to describe the nature of nature, which is beyond all qualities. One who is beyond all qualities cannot be described by the intellect and mind. In reality, these eight characteristics are not inherent in a person who is beyond material qualities; rather, they are considered to be so when the ego and attachment are destroyed from within. Through the medium of the purified heart, these characteristics are described as the signs of one who is beyond material qualities. The Lord has mentioned the characteristics of one who is beyond material qualities in the twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth verses of this chapter. Parishishta Bhaav - The vices of attachment and aversion do not reside in the inert or the conscious, nor are they the inherent nature of the heart. Rather, they reside in the ego of the body. The ego itself is not real, but is considered to be so due to a lack of discrimination and understanding. The meaning is that vices do not actually reside within a person, but a person considers them to be so due to a lack of understanding. A person experiences the presence and absence of vices, as well as their own nature, but does not give importance to this experience. If a person were to understand and experience the absence of vices through discrimination and understanding, then they would not become a victim of vices. Sambandh - Arjuna had asked for a way to become beyond material qualities as his third question. The Lord will answer this question in the next verse. Māṃ ca yo 'vyabhicāreṇa bhaktiyogena sevate,
Sa guṇān samatītyaiteān brahmabhūyāya kalpate. 26

Translation: And one who, with unswerving devotion, serves Me through the path of devotion, transcends these qualities and becomes eligible for the state of Brahman. Explanation - The words "yad yah" indicate the devotee, "mām" indicates the object of devotion, and "avyabhichāreṇa bhaktiyogena sevate" indicates the act of devotion. The meaning is that one who serves Me through unswerving devotion becomes eligible for the state of Brahman. Vyakhya - Although the Lord had explained the three concepts of devotee, object of devotion, and devotion in the nineteenth and twentieth verses of this chapter, Arjuna asked for a way to become beyond material qualities in the twenty-first verse. This indicates that Arjuna wants to know a way to become beyond material qualities other than the one mentioned earlier. Therefore, the Lord, considering Arjuna to be a devotee, explains the way to become beyond material qualities through devotion.

In this way, the term 'avvyabhicharen' refers to taking shelter of others. [ Chapter 19 ]
[Verse 27]
The second point is that the scriptures say that one who takes shelter of the Lord through 'bhaktiyogen' (devotional service) and worships only the Lord, is eligible to take shelter of the knowledge of the different stages (bhoomikaaon). The word 'sevate' means that one should worship the Lord through avvyabhichari bhaktiyogen (unwavering devotion), take shelter of the Lord, and follow the Lord's path. ' Sa gunaans samatityaitean' - One who takes shelter of the Lord alone, without any attachment to others, does not have to transcend the gunas (qualities), but rather, the Lord's mercy makes him transcend the gunas (Gita - 12th chapter, 6th-7th verse). 'Brahmabhuyaay kalpate' - He becomes eligible to attain Brahman (the ultimate reality). When the Lord is explaining the importance of devotion, He should have said that He is the one who is eligible to attain Brahman, but instead, He says that one who is devoted to Him becomes eligible to attain Brahman. The reason for this is that Arjuna had asked about the means to attain gunatit (beyond the gunas), and therefore, the Lord is explaining that devotion to Him is the means to attain Brahman. There is no need for any other means or effort; rather, the knowledge of the different stages (bhoomikaaon) becomes established on its own. The Lord is saying that one who worships Him through avvyabhichari bhaktiyogen does not need any other means to become eligible to attain Brahman, but rather, he becomes eligible to attain Brahman on his own. However, that devotee does not become satisfied with attaining Brahman; rather, his desire is to please the Lord. His happiness lies in pleasing the Lord, and the Lord's pleasure is his pleasure. In other words, one who is devoted to the Lord alone, and is attracted to the Lord alone, becomes eligible to attain Brahman on his own. Whether he considers Brahman to be of great importance or not is a different matter; however, he becomes eligible to attain Brahman on his own. Thirdly, the realization of the ultimate truth that is achieved through jnana yoga, karma yoga, and other means can also be achieved through devotion. Although there may be differences in the means, there is no difference in the realization of the ultimate truth. Through devotion, the seeker achieves whatever he desires. If the seeker desires to attain mukti (liberation) or to attain the ultimate truth, he achieves it through devotion, because the ultimate truth is the Lord Himself (Gita - 13th chapter, 27th verse). The ultimate truth is the very essence of the Lord, and it is the Lord's own form (Gita - 7th chapter, 28-29 verse). In the 10th verse of the 13th chapter, devotion is also mentioned as a means to attain knowledge. In the Shrimad Bhagavatam, the worship of the Lord with qualities (sagun) is considered to be beyond the gunas (nirgun), just like 'manniketam tu nirgunam' (11.25.25), 'matsevayaan tu nirgunaa' (11.25.27) etc. Therefore, one who worships the Lord with qualities becomes beyond the gunas. The Lord with qualities is not bound by the gunas, but rather, the gunas are bound by Him. One who is bound by the gunas of sattva, rajas, and tamas is not called sagun, but rather, one who has infinite and eternal divine qualities such as beauty, charm, and majesty is called sagun. The Lord's actions can be sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic, but they are not bound by those gunas. Through devotion to the Lord, the devotee becomes beyond the gunas and attains the Lord's very essence. Moreover, he attains knowledge of the Lord's entire form. Connection - How can one worship the Lord and become eligible to attain Brahman? The answer to this is given in the next verse. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[Verse 27]
Because I am the Supreme, the imperishable, the immortal,
The support of all that is eternal and imperishable,
The refuge of all that is blissful and eternal,
The abode of all that is eternal and imperishable,
The support of all that is blissful and eternal,
The abode of all that is eternal and imperishable,
I am the foundation of all that is eternal and imperishable,
And I am the foundation of all that is blissful and eternal. Explanation: The meaning of 'Brahmano hi pratishtaham' is that I am the foundation of Brahman, and I am one with it. Just as fire is both visible and invisible, so too is Brahman. From the point of view of devotion, Brahman is the ultimate reality, and from the point of view of knowledge, it is the ultimate truth. But in reality, Brahman and I are one and the same. Just as a meal has a fragrance and a taste, and yet it is one and the same, so too is Brahman and I one and the same. The word 'Brahman' is used in the Gita to refer to the ultimate reality, and the word 'Avyaktamurti' is used to refer to the invisible form of Brahman. The meaning is that the visible and invisible forms of Brahman are one and the same. The phrase 'Amritamashnuti' (13.12, 14.20) means that I am the one who gives immortality. 'I am the foundation of eternal dharma' means that I am the foundation of eternal righteousness, and eternal righteousness is my foundation. The meaning is that eternal righteousness and I are one and the same. The Gita says that I am the protector of eternal righteousness (11.18), and I take avatars to protect it (4.7-8). 'I am the foundation of bliss' means that I am the foundation of bliss, and bliss is my foundation. The meaning is that bliss and I are one and the same. In this verse, the words 'Brahmano hi', 'Amritasya', etc. are used to convey the idea of non-duality. The meaning is that Brahman, immortality, etc. are not separate from me, but are one and the same. The four main religions of the world - Hinduism, Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam - have a large following. The founders of these religions are Buddha, Jesus, and Muhammad. These three religions are relatively recent, but Hinduism is eternal and has no human founder. It is the result of the search and inquiry of various sages. The search and inquiry of those who already exist is the only kind of search and inquiry that is possible. Hinduism is eternal, infinite, and timeless, just like God. Therefore, God has declared in the Gita (14.27) that Hinduism is his own nature. Whenever Hinduism is in decline, God takes an avatar to establish it (4.7-8). The meaning is that God takes an avatar to protect and preserve Hinduism, not to create it. In fact, all other religions and sects have originated from Hinduism. Therefore, the practices and rituals of these religions should also be considered as part of Hinduism. If one performs these practices and rituals with a sense of detachment, one can attain benefit. The principles of Hinduism are entirely scientific and beneficial.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 14 ]
Whatever is called Brahman, or whatever is called Krishna, or whatever is called Krishna, or whatever is called the ultimate bliss; and whatever is called the imperishable nectar, or whatever is called Krishna, or whatever is called the ultimate bliss - all these are one and the same thing. There is no difference in this. Therefore, the imperishable nectar, or whatever is called the ultimate bliss, or whatever is called the eternal Dharma, is one and the same thing. Hence, the worship of Krishna, or the worship of Brahman, or the worship of the ultimate bliss, or the worship of the eternal Dharma - all these lead to the attainment of Brahman. Parishishta Bhaav - 'I am the refuge of Brahman and the imperishable nectar' - this is the teaching of the attributeless and the knowledge of the Self. 'I am the refuge of the eternal Dharma' - this is the teaching of the divine and the knowledge of action. 'I am the refuge of the ultimate bliss' - this is the teaching of the divine and the knowledge of meditation. The implication is that by worshipping Me (the divine), by taking refuge in Me, the three yogas - knowledge, action, and meditation - are all accomplished. The attainment of the ultimate truth, which is called 'samagri', is achieved through all three. All the divine attributes are the manifestations of the divine. Brahman is also one of the divine attributes. Therefore, the Lord says, 'Brahman is My abode'. In the Padma Purana, it is said that the ray of the divine's nail is Brahman. "Whatever is the divine attribute of the divine's nail, which is the object of contemplation for the gods, including Brahma, is the divine attribute that transcends the three gunas. I bow down to the Lord Krishna, the ruler of Vrindavan."

(From the Patala 77, 60)

(The Lord Shankar says - ) I, the Lord Shankar, bow down to the Lord Krishna, whose nail's luster is the divine attribute that the gods, including Brahma, contemplate. Om tat sat iti shriimad bhagavad gitaasupanishatsu brahmvidyayaam yogashastre shrii krishnaarjunasamvade gunatrayavibhagayogo nama chaturdashaadhyaah 14. Thus, with the utterance of the divine names Om, Tat, and Sat, the Brahma Vidya and the Yoga Shastra, the Srimad Bhagavad Gita Upanishad, the conversation between Lord Krishna and Arjuna, the 'Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga' chapter, the 14th chapter, is complete. In this chapter, the division of the three gunas - Satva, Rajas, and Tamas - is described. When one transcends these three gunas, when one is free from their influence, one experiences the eternal union with the Supreme. Therefore, this chapter is named 'Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga'. The characteristics of the 14th chapter are as follows:

(1) This chapter has three introductory words - 'Ath Chaturdashaadhyaah', three hundred and twenty-two shlokas, and thirteen words in the Puspika. The total number of words is three hundred and forty-five. (2) All the shlokas in this chapter have thirty-two words. (3) There are three Uvacha in this chapter - two 'Shri Bhagavan Uvacha' and one 'Arjuna Uvacha'. The meter used in the 14th chapter is as follows:

In twenty-seven shlokas, the meter is 'Sankirna-Vipula', which is used when the word 'Nagana' is used. In the remaining twenty shlokas, the meter is 'Pathya-Avaktara', which is used when the word 'Ragana' is used.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The question of who is superior among devotees of the Saguna and Nirguna forms was answered by the Lord in the first verse of the twelfth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, where He declared the Saguna devotees to be the supreme yogis. In the fifth verse, the Lord compared the Saguna and Nirguna forms of worship, stating that for those attached to the body, the worship of the Nirguna form is difficult. The Lord discussed this topic and the Nirguna form in the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters. In the twenty-first verse of the fourteenth chapter, Arjuna asked for the characteristics and behavior of those who are beyond the gunas, as well as the means to become so. In response, the Lord described the characteristics and behavior of those who are beyond the gunas in verses 22 to 25, and in the twenty-sixth verse, He declared that the 'unwavering practice of devotion' is the means for those who worship the Saguna form to become beyond the gunas. This means that the devotee who is exclusively devoted to the Lord (who has no other attachment) can easily become beyond the gunas. In this twenty-sixth verse, the Lord described the 'unwavering practice of devotion' as a practice that is free from the fault of attachment (to the world), 'he' (the devotee) and 'me' (the Lord). Therefore, the Lord will now explain the meaning of the three subjects - the world, the individual, and the Supreme - in this fifteenth chapter. Although the individual is by nature beyond the gunas (being a part of the Supreme), due to the ignorance of being eternal, it is affected by the gunas and is bound to the world (the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc.) through attachment, possessiveness, and desires. As long as it does not know the Supreme's influence, it cannot be completely free from the influence of the gunas. Therefore, the Lord begins this fifteenth chapter to explain His most confidential and special influence, which is the means to attain devotion. The individual is a part of the Supreme (Gita - 15th chapter, 7th verse). Therefore, its only relationship is with the Supreme. However, due to ignorance, it mistakenly considers its relationship to be with the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc., which are foreign substances and were never, are not, will never be, and cannot be its relationship. Considering these foreign substances as 'I', 'mine', and 'for me' is the fault of attachment. This fault is the main obstacle to unwavering devotion. To remove this obstacle, the Lord will give instructions in the first five verses of the fifteenth chapter, describing the world tree and ordering its destruction. *
The Lord said:
[Verse 1]
He who knows this (the world tree) is the knower of the Vedas. This tree has its roots above and its branches below, and it is eternal. Its leaves are the Vedas, and it is the source of all that is pure and sacred, and it is the ultimate goal of all knowledge. All beings are sustained by it, and none can transcend it. This is the ultimate truth. (Katha Upanishad 2.3.1)

Ordinarily, the roots of a tree are below and the branches are above; but this world tree is a peculiar tree, with its roots above and branches below! The abode of the Lord is such that one who goes there does not return to the world. The Supreme Being is above all worldly existence. The main branch (trunk) of the world tree is Brahma, because at the time of the creation of the world, Brahma is the first to be born. Therefore, Brahma is the main branch of the world tree. Brahma's world is lower than the abode of the Lord. In all respects - place, qualities, status, age, etc. - the abode of the Lord is superior to Brahma's world. Therefore, Brahma's world is described as 'Adha-shakha' (below the branches). This world tree has its roots above. The root of a tree is the most important part. The Supreme Being is the root of this world tree. Just as the root of a tree is the foundation, similarly, the Supreme Being is the foundation of the entire universe. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The more one identifies with the body and its attachments, the more one is bound and the more one experiences birth and death. This is like the branches of a tree spreading downwards. The three modes of nature - sattva, rajas, and tamas - are all part of this downward growth (Gita - 14th Chapter, 18th Verse). This world is a direct manifestation of the Supreme Being, for all living beings, except Brahma, are devoid of the desire for pleasure and are thus free. However, for those who desire pleasure from the world, this world is a home of suffering. The reason is that the world itself is eternal and unchanging, while the world tree is constantly changing and ephemeral. Therefore, one can never be satisfied with it, but instead, one keeps taking birth and dying in a cycle of birth and death. Hence, one should not have any attachment to the world and should only serve it. -1

'Asvattham' - The term 'Asvattham' has two meanings - (1) something that does not last even for a day, and (2) the peepal tree. According to the first meaning, the term 'Asvattham' implies that the world is not stable for even a moment. It is a collection of changes. When a new form appears, it is called birth; when it remains stable for a while, it is called existence; and when its form changes again, it is called destruction. However, in reality, birth, existence, and destruction do not occur. Therefore, the world is constantly changing and is never stable for even a moment. It is visible only for a moment and then disappears. This is the reason why the world is called 'Asvattham'. According to the second meaning, the world is like a peepal tree. The scriptures have praised the peepal tree highly. Even God Himself has described the peepal tree as His own form and has said that it is the most sacred and worthy of worship - 'Asvatthah sarva-vrksanam' (Gita 10.26). The peepal, banyan, and tulsi trees are all worthy of worship because they are manifestations of God. 'Prayahuravyayam' - The world is called 'avyay' or eternal. The reason is that its beginning and end cannot be known, and it is constantly flowing due to the eternal nature of God. Just as the water of the ocean evaporates into the air, becomes clouds, and then falls back to the earth as rain, and then flows back into the ocean, the world is also constantly changing and flowing. This cycle of the world has no end. However, in reality, the world is not eternal. If it were eternal, then the description of its nature in the 3rd verse of this chapter would not be true, and it would not be subject to detachment. The world is not eternal, and it is not worthy of worship. 'Chhandansi Yasya Parnani' - The Vedas are the leaves of this world tree. Here, the Vedas refer to the part of the Vedas that describes the performance of rituals. The meaning is that the world is born from the Supreme Being, and He is the ultimate cause of the world. Therefore, the world tree is also a manifestation of the Supreme Being and is worthy of worship. The worship of the world tree is to serve it without desiring pleasure from it. -

' Svah' paryantram na tisthatiti asvatthah' - The term 'Asvattham' refers to something that does not last even for a day. The term 'Svah' is a word that refers to the day that is yet to come. The term 'Asvattham' means that which does not last even until the day that is yet to come. 2 - The philosophers have analyzed the concept of 'kshan' or moment as follows: when a needle is pressed on a lotus leaf, it takes three moments - the moment of touch, the moment of cutting, and the moment of passing through. 3 - The Vedas contain 80,000 mantras that describe the performance of rituals, but only 20,000 mantras are liberating. Among these, 4,000 mantras are related to knowledge, and 16,000 mantras are related to worship.

*
Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 15 ]
A person knows that a tree in which beautiful flowers and leaves are present but no fruits are there is useless; because true satisfaction comes from fruits, not from flowers and leaves. Similarly, the world tree appears beautiful and attractive from the outside, but one who seeks pleasure and happiness from it does not attain eternal bliss or great joy. If one performs rituals and actions as per the Vedas with the intention of attaining heaven and other divine realms, it is better than performing prohibited actions, but it does not lead to liberation. Because, after enjoying the fruits of these actions, the merit of the actions is lost, and one has to take birth again in the world (Gita - 9th Chapter, 21st Verse). In this way, both the tree of worldly actions and its fruits are born and perish. Therefore, the seeker should remain detached from both and attain the ultimate reality of the Supreme Self alone. Leaves are born from the branches of a tree and are responsible for its protection and growth. The tree appears beautiful and strong due to its leaves. Similarly, the Vedas are the main branches of the world tree, and they are born from the Supreme Lord Brahma. The growth and protection of the world are possible only through the performance of actions as per the Vedas. Therefore, the Vedas are considered to be the leaves of the world tree. Through the performance of worldly actions, one can attain heavenly realms and other divine abodes - this is the growth of the world tree. The heavenly realms are like a beautiful garden, with beautiful airplanes and beautiful nymphs - this is the beauty of the world tree. Through the performance of worldly actions, one experiences repeated birth and death - this is the strength of the world tree. The Lord is saying that the seeker should not get entangled in the worldly actions and their fruits, but should take refuge in the ultimate reality of the Supreme Self. By taking refuge in the Supreme Self, one can understand the true nature of the Vedas. The true nature of the Vedas is not the world or heaven, but the Supreme Self itself (Gita - 15th Chapter, 15th Verse). The Lord says, "He who knows this tree is a knower of the Vedas" (1). The world tree is known by one who knows its true nature. Knowing the world tree as ephemeral, one should not have any hope or desire for pleasure and happiness from it - this is the true knowledge of the world tree. In reality, the world tree is ephemeral, and one cannot attain pleasure and happiness from it. As long as one considers the world and its objects as permanent, one has hope and desire for pleasure and happiness, and one takes refuge in the world. But when one realizes that the world is ephemeral, one's desire for pleasure and happiness disappears, and one experiences the ultimate reality of the Supreme Self. The ultimate reality of the Supreme Self is the true meaning of the Vedas. One who experiences the ultimate reality of the Supreme Self, having renounced his attachment to the world, is the true knower of the Vedas. The Lord has called Himself a knower of the Vedas in the 15th verse of this chapter. Here, the Lord is saying that the person who knows the true nature of the world tree is a knower of the Vedas. The meaning is that the human being, having the power of discrimination, can know the true nature of the world tree and become a knower of the Vedas, just like the Lord. The true relationship of the individual self is only with the Supreme Self, and not with the world. The individual self has forgotten its true relationship with the Supreme Self due to ignorance. By realizing this ignorance through the power of discrimination, one can renounce one's attachment to the world and experience the ultimate reality of the Supreme Self. One who experiences the ultimate reality of the Supreme Self is the true knower of the Vedas. The Lord says, "The Vedas proclaim the Supreme Self, the ultimate reality, again and again" (2). The Lord also says in the 14th chapter, 2nd verse, "Those who have approached me with a similar nature" (Gita - 14.2). The same thing is said here.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Parishishta Bhaav — The World, the Living Being, and God - All Three are in the Form of Vasudeva - 'Vasudeva Sarvam' - This is described here in the form of a tree. Although the world is constantly changing, saying that it is 'avyaya' (unchanging) means that there is no expenditure or end to it. Just as the water in the ocean remains the same despite the rise and fall of the waves, the world also remains unchanged despite the constant changes. The reason is that the world is the work of the power of God, 'apara prakriti', and is therefore the form of God - 'Sadasatchaamarjuna' (Gita 9.19). Apara prakriti, which is the changing world, and para prakriti, which is the unchanging world, are both the form of God. This world is the waves of God. Just as there are no waves in the ocean itself, but only on its surface, so too, despite the changing world, there is a peaceful and calm God within. The meaning is that the world is not unchanging in its worldly form, but is unchanging in its divine form. The world is a reflection of God. The seeker's vision should be on God, not on the reflection. Looking at the reflection is to attribute independence and importance to it and to connect with it, which is bondage. One of the meanings of saying that the world is 'avyaya' is that whoever connects with the world will also be connected with birth and death, which will never end. Just as a long path may have an end, but a circular path does not, so too, birth and death are a circular path. The world is 'avyaya' because its seed is also 'avyaya' - 'Bijam Avyayam' (Gita 9.18). Sambandh — In the previous shloka, the Lord showed the seeker the tree of the world. Now, in this shloka, the Lord will describe the tree of the world in detail, along with its branches. Adhah Svoradhvaṁ Prasritās Tasya Śākhā Guṇapravṛddhā Vṛttipravālāḥ |
Adhaḥ Mūlāni Anusantatāni Karmanubandhīni Manuṣyaloke || 2 ||

The branches of the tree of the world are:

- The branches that have grown upwards (towards the divine) are the branches of the world that have been enriched by the three gunas (satva, rajas, and tamas). - The branches that have grown downwards (towards the material) are the branches of the world that are attached to the material. - The branches that have grown in the middle (between the divine and the material) are the branches of the world that are connected to the actions of the living beings. The roots of the tree of the world are also connected to the actions of the living beings. The explanation is that the main branch of the tree of the world is Brahma. From Brahma, the entire creation, including the gods, humans, and other living beings, has originated and expanded. Therefore, all the gods, humans, and other living beings in all the worlds are the branches of the tree of the world. Just as the branches of a tree grow when it is watered, so too, the branches of the world grow when they are nourished by the three gunas. The world is full of the three gunas, and therefore, it is full of life. The living beings are born in the three types of yonis (high, middle, and low) due to the influence of the three gunas. There is no place, thing, or person in the entire creation that is not influenced by the three gunas (Gita - 13th chapter, 21st and 14th shlokas).

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The state of the world is related to the qualities. The experience of qualities is generated by the qualities and the objects that arise from them. Therefore, to abandon the relationship with qualities, which is considered as 'gunapravritta', the Lord has said here that as long as there is even a slight relationship with qualities, the branches of the world tree will continue to grow. Therefore, to cut the world tree, one should not keep even a slight relationship with qualities; because, as long as one is related to qualities, separation from the world is not possible. 'Vishayapravala' - Just as the new, tender leaves that grow from the branches of the tree are called 'praval' (bud), in the same way, the objects of the world, from the qualities to the visible objects, are called 'vishayapravala' here. The trunk of the tree gives rise to the main branch, the main branch gives rise to the branches, and the branches give rise to the buds. In this world tree, the objects of the world are the buds. The objects of the world arise from the three qualities. Just as the branches of the tree grow from the water of the qualities, in the same way, the objects of the world also grow from the qualities. Just as the water in the buds is not visible, in the same way, the qualities are not visible in the objects of the world. Therefore, the qualities are known through the objects of the world. The meaning of the word 'vishayapravala' is that the relationship with the world cannot be severed even when one is engaged in thinking about the objects of the world (Gita - 2nd chapter, 63rd and 73rd shlokas). In the end, the person who leaves the body with the thought of the objects of the world attains that very thought (Gita - 8th chapter, 6th shlok). This is the sprouting of the buds of the world. The objects of the world appear to be beautiful and attractive, but they are not actually so. They appear beautiful and attractive due to one's attachment to them. Therefore, the detachment from attachment is the real detachment. Just as the tender buds can be destroyed without any effort, in the same way, the objects of the world can be given up without any difficulty. The objects of the world appear beautiful and attractive only when one has attachment to them. In reality, they are like the sweetmeats that are filled with the objects of the world. Therefore, to cut the world tree, it is necessary to give up the attachment to the objects of the world and the attachment to the objects of the world. 3

'Adhashchordhvamparsrita' - Here, the word 'ch' refers to the middle world, i.e., the human world. The word 'urdhva' refers to the world of Brahman, which is above the human world. There are two paths to reach the world of Brahman - the path of the gods and the path of the ancestors (which is described in the 24th and 25th shlokas of the 8th chapter of the Gita). The word 'adha' refers to the hells, which have two types - the hells of specific yonis and the hells of specific places. The meaning of these words is that the branches of the world tree are spread out in all directions, from the lower world to the upper world. The human world is the main branch, because it is the only world where one can perform new actions. The other branches are the worlds of suffering, where one can only experience the fruits of past actions. From this main branch, one can go down (to the lower world) or up (to the upper world), and by cutting the world tree, one can reach the highest (the world of Brahman). 1

The objects of the world are like a poisonous snake, which is more deadly than the poison of the snake. The poison kills the one who consumes it, but the objects of the world do not spare even the one who sees them. (Vivekachudamani 79)

If you have a desire for liberation, then give up the objects of the world from a distance, just as one gives up poison. (Vivek 84)

There is a discrimination in the human body, which is given importance by the living being. This discrimination is not only limited to this life but also extends to the afterlife.
