[ Chapter 15 ]
This chapter is also referred to as 'tam eva cha adyam purusham prapadye' in the fourth verse of this chapter. The abundance of worldly pleasures and the pursuit of them have led to the loss of discrimination in those very yonis (species) where they are found. Therefore, it is not possible to see one's own self (the true nature) separate from these defects in those yonis. Only in the human yoni, due to the presence of discrimination, can one experience that one is free from the defects of tattva (identification), moha (attachment), and kama (desire). In the human world, karma (action) binds one to tattva, moha, and kama, which are present in all the lower and higher worlds, and in all yonis. Even in animals and birds, there is tattva (identification) with their bodies, moha (attachment) to their offspring, and kama (desire) for good food when hungry. Similarly, in the gods, there is tattva (identification) with their divine bodies, moha (attachment) to the things they have obtained, and kama (desire) for things they have not obtained. In this way, the defects of tattva, moha, and kama are present in all yonis, but only in the human yoni do they bind one. Although the human yoni is the only one where these defects bind one, it is also the only yoni where one can see the results of one's actions. If one does not see the results of one's actions, it is as if one is a beast, and to call such a person a beast is to condemn them to the animal yoni. * The Nectar of the Seeker *

The easiest way to sever ties with the world is to not consider the things obtained from it (such as the mind, intellect, senses, body, wealth, and possessions) as 'mine' or 'for myself', and instead use them for the service of the world. Even if one acquires as many worldly pleasures as one can, such as a wife, children, fame, wealth, property, and a long life, and even if all the worldly pleasures of the world are bestowed upon one person, still, one cannot be satisfied with them. This is because the living being itself is eternal, and the worldly pleasures are ephemeral. How can the ephemeral satisfy the eternal? A person may wander around, enchanted by the various things on display in a grand exhibition, and the various topics discussed by philosophers, but in reality, the exhibition is just a display, and the topics are just topics. However, our relationship with the world is illusory, and its end is unknown. Therefore, it is essential to sever ties with the world - this is the consensus among all philosophers. If one considers the world to be one's own and is attached to its pleasures, one cannot understand the beginning, middle, and end of the world. The means (senses, mind, and intellect) that a person has to understand the world are all part of the world itself. According to a principle, a thing can be dissolved into its cause, but it cannot be understood. Just as a pot made of clay cannot contain the earth within it, similarly, the individual senses, mind, and intellect cannot comprehend the world and its workings. Therefore, it is only when one severs ties with the world that one can understand its true nature, which is the Supreme Self. In reality, the world has no independent existence; it is merely a sequence of birth and death. The world appears to have a stable existence due to the sequence of birth and death. In fact, there is no birth; there is only destruction. If something's form does not remain even for a moment, how can the world, which is devoid of a stable existence, have a reputation? When one severs ties with the world, its end is achieved, and one's true nature, which is the Supreme Self, is established. A special note

No scientist has been able to discover the beginning, middle, and end of the world, nor can they do so. If one tries to find the beginning, middle, and end of the world while being attached to it or while enjoying its pleasures, it is like a donkey trying to move a millstone - one will keep wandering around, but nothing will be achieved. In reality, there is no need to discover the beginning, middle, and end of the world. The need is to sever ties with the world, which is considered to be one's own. The phrase 'ashvattham enam suviruḍhamūlam' means that the world appears to be a sturdy tree, even though it is devoid of a stable existence, due to attachment, love, and desire. When attachment, love, and desire arise in a person, object, or action, the worldly bond becomes stronger and stronger. A person starts to consider the things and people they are attached to as their own nature. For example, when a person is attached to wealth, they feel happy when they acquire it and think, 'I am a wealthy person.' When the wealth is lost, they consider themselves to be lost. As their attachment to wealth increases, they start to do unjust and sinful things to acquire it. Eventually, they become convinced that wealth cannot be acquired without deceit, falsehood, and other sinful acts. They do not even think about the consequences of their actions, such as, 'I will acquire wealth through sinful means, but it will be of no use to me in the end. The wealth will remain with the body, but the sinful acts will accompany me to the afterlife and bring me suffering.'

The world is endless, and a person becomes so attached to it that they start to advise others to acquire wealth at any cost, saying, 'One cannot acquire wealth without deceit, falsehood, and other sinful acts.' They do not even consider the fact that the wealth they acquire through sinful means will be of no use to them in the end, and the sinful acts will accompany them to the afterlife and bring them suffering. * Wealth remains in the treasury, animals remain tied up, women remain in the house, children remain in the cremation ground, and the body remains until the end. Only the soul, accompanied by its accumulated karma, goes to the afterlife.*

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

It is said that there is no harm in doing wrong deeds; it is just a business, and in this business, lying, cheating, etc. are all proper (Gita - 17th Chapter, 3rd Verse). This is the very nature of attachment, the firm establishment of the roots of attachment and desire. Due to the firm establishment of these impure feelings, a person becomes like that (Gita - 17th Chapter, 3rd Verse). These attachments, desires, and roots of attachment are so firmly established in the inner self that they are not completely destroyed even by reading, listening, and thinking (vivēchan) about them. Sadhaks (spiritual seekers) usually say that when they listen to discussions and talks about the truth, they feel that it is good and easy to give up these vices; but in practice, it does not happen that way. They want to give up these vices, but they do not leave them. The main reason for this is the desire to enjoy worldly pleasures. The sadhak forgets that he also wants to enjoy worldly pleasures and at the same time wants to be free from vices. Just as a greedy person wants to enjoy the sweetness of worldly objects and at the same time wants to avoid poison, it is not possible. If one does not have even a slight hope of enjoying worldly pleasures, then the root of attachment is automatically destroyed. Another thing is that 'attachment, desire, and attachment are very difficult to give up' - this is the sadhak's belief, which does not allow these vices to be given up. In reality, these vices are automatically being destroyed. These vices are not always present in a person; they are born and destroyed; but due to their own belief, they appear to be permanent. Therefore, the sadhak should not consider it difficult to give up these vices. The Lord says, 'With the sword of detachment, which is firm and unattached, cut off' (Gita - 17th Chapter, 3rd Verse). Although the roots of attachment in this world are very firm, they can be cut off with the sword of detachment. Attraction to any person, thing, or situation, and considering oneself to be big and happy due to their association; feeling happy when one gets or accumulates material objects - this is called 'sang' (attachment). Its absence is called 'asanga' (detachment) or 'vairagya' (dispassion). There are two types of detachment - (1) ordinary detachment and (2) firm detachment. Firm detachment is also called 'uparati' or 'par vairagya'. Special points related to detachment

Detachment has many forms, which are as follows:

*
[ Chapter 15
The first type of detachment is from wealth, house, land, etc. If one gives up these material objects, but still has a sense of their importance in the mind and has the ego of being a renouncer, then it is not true detachment. True detachment is when there is no attachment to material objects in the heart, and no attraction to them. The second type of detachment is from one's family - mother, father, wife, brother, sister, etc. One should consider their service and happiness as the reason for their association, not for one's own happiness. Not considering any attachment to them for one's own happiness is detachment from family. The third and true detachment is from the body. If one has attachment to the body, then one has attachment to the whole world, because the body is a part or seed of the world. Detachment from the body means detachment from the world. Attachment (identification with the body, i.e., ego) is destroyed by giving up the desire for name, fame, wealth, etc. Even after giving up these desires, if one has attachment to one's name, then the desire for fame, praise, and respect remains. This is why, even after death, subtle desires like the desire for one's name, the desire to become a monument, etc. remain. Sometimes, the sadhak's heart is filled with envy when he hears praise of others or sees others being praised. Therefore, it is necessary to destroy this envy as well. After destroying the above desires, attachment to the body remains. This attachment remains even after death. This is why, even after burning the dead body, if the bones are thrown into the Ganges, the soul (which had attachment to the body) gets further progress. When 'vivek' (discrimination, i.e., the knowledge of the difference between the individual self and the body) awakens, attachment is destroyed. After destroying attachment and desire, the ego (identification with the body) is almost destroyed. The absence of ego is the attainment of love for God.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
When a person himself experiences that 'I am separate from the world, therefore, our incompatibility is self-evident - one should firmly believe in this reality. Regardless of how well-established the world may be, by not associating with it, it automatically separates itself; because it is not associated with us, but only perceived as such. Therefore, by not associating with the world, its separation is achieved - the seeker should not have any doubt about this; whether it appears so in the beginning or not. I am not the body; the body is not mine', then desire, attachment, and identification - all three disappear. This is the true detachment. One who has firm detachment within himself, his inner self is completely free from all desires. By not associating with one's own nature (jada) - body, senses, mind, intellect, etc. - and considering 'May all be happy, may all be free from disease, may no one suffer any sorrow' - this feeling is the characteristic of firm detachment. The one that is known by the form 'this' (idam) - the gross, subtle, and causal bodies along with the entire world - is called 'I' (aham). 'This' (the known object) and 'I' (the knower) can never be one - this is the rule. In this way, the world and the body are destroyed, and I (myself) am immortal - by respecting this discrimination, one should experience oneself as completely separate from the world and the body - this is the asanga (non-association) weapon by which the world tree is cut down. Due to not giving importance to this discrimination, the world appears to be firmly established. The absence of worldly objects is not possible, but the absence of attachment to them is possible. Therefore, the meaning of 'cutting' is not the destruction of worldly objects, but rather removing attachment from them. When separation from the world is achieved, the world's absence for oneself becomes absolute, which is also called 'atyantik pralaya' (ultimate destruction). The one that is not our true nature and with which we do not have a real association - its rejection (cutting) is done. We are essentially conscious and immortal, and the world is material and destructible; therefore, our association with the world is unreal and based on a mistake. We are inherently separate from the world. One who is inherently separate, remains separate - this is the rule. From the beginning, the mistake was made of considering the body-world as one's own association. Therefore, the responsibility of cutting this association also lies with the individual. Therefore, the Lord is saying to cut this association. Some easy methods for separating from the world:

(1) Without any desire to take anything, use the resources obtained from the world for the service of the world. (2) Completely give up the desire for worldly pleasures and accumulation. (3) Completely give up the dependence on the world. (4) Completely remove the sense of 'I' and 'mine' from the body-world. (5) Firmly believe in the reality that 'I am the Lord's; the Lord is mine'. (6) Decide firmly that one should move only towards the Supreme Lord. (7) Perform one's own duties as per the scriptures (svadharma). (8) Recognize that the body, objects, circumstances, knowledge, strength, etc. that existed in childhood are no longer the same, but I (myself) remain unchanged - give importance to this experience. (9) Remove the good faith (sattabhava) of the perceived association with the world. Parishishta Bhaav - The Lord has said - 'I am the beginning, middle, and end of all beings, and the ultimate reality' (Gita 10.20), 'I am the origin, middle, and end of all creations' (Gita 10.32), and here He says about the world - 'There is no beginning, no end, and no establishment'. The meaning is that the Lord is present in the beginning, middle, and end, but the world is not present in the beginning, end, or middle; it does not exist at all - 'There is no existence of what does not exist' (Gita 2.16). Therefore, one should have the firm resolve - 'May all be happy, may all be free from disease, may no one suffer any sorrow' (1.35), 'One should renounce attachment, and by the knowledge of the scriptures, one should narrate the path of liberation' (Mans 3.16.1).

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 15 ]

The word 'chitta' in the phrase 'asangashastrena dhriddena chittva' does not mean to cut or destroy, but to sever the relationship. This is because the world is an unchanging, eternal entity, being the unmanifested material nature of God. Its essence is unattached, as it is said, 'asango hyayam purushah' (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.15). The world is not attached to its inherent qualities. It is only through attachment to qualities that birth and death occur, as it is said, 'karanam gunasango'sya sad-asad-yoni-janmasu' (Gita 13.21). Therefore, by experiencing the world's unattached nature, its non-attachment, and its timelessness, one should establish oneself in it, which is to cut through the world like a sharp sword. The world appears to be full of attachment. Wherever attachment exists, the existence and importance of that thing are perceived. If attachment does not exist, the existence is perceived, but not the importance. Therefore, the phrase 'asangashastrena dhriddena chittva' means to completely eliminate attachment to the world, i.e., to not consider any other entity as one's own or for one's own benefit. In reality, the existence of the world is not binding; it is the attachment to it that is binding. Existence is not a hindrance, but attachment is. Therefore, some philosophers describe the world as unreal, real, or a combination of both, but God says to sever the relationship with the world. After severing the relationship with the world, the seeker should know what to do next – this is discussed in the next verse. Tat padam tat parimargitavyam yasmadgata na nivartanti bhuyah. Translation of the commentary:
'That which should be searched for, then, is the Supreme (God), from which the original creation has originated and spread. I surrender to that original person (God), from which the original creation has originated and spread.'

Explanation: 'That which should be searched for, then, is the Supreme (God)' – God has said in the previous verse that one should sever the relationship with the world. This establishes that searching for the Supreme (God) is essential before severing the relationship with the world. This is because the Supreme (God) is present everywhere, in all time, in all things, in all events, and in all situations. Due to the attachment to the world, the experience of the Supreme (God) is hindered. The world's attachment causes delay in searching for the Supreme (God), and even after performing rituals, worship, and study, no special benefit is obtained. Therefore, the seeker should primarily focus on severing the relationship with the world. The seeker should surrender to the Supreme (God), who is the origin of the original creation. The seeker should realize that the Supreme (God) is the ultimate reality, and that the world is an illusion. The seeker should understand that the world's existence is not a hindrance, but the attachment to it is. The seeker should search for the Supreme (God), who is the origin of the original creation.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Here, the search for the Supreme Being does not mean searching for Him with the help of any particular means or rituals. It means to take refuge in Him who is always present, within oneself, and has always been present, without taking refuge in the world (body, family, wealth, etc.) which was never, is not, and will never be one's own. The Supreme Being is eternal and omnipresent. Therefore, just as it is possible for a person to forget the knowledge they have acquired due to a stroke (paralysis), it is not possible to forget the memory of the Supreme Being once it has been acquired (Gita - Chapter 2, Verse 72 and Chapter 4, Verse 35). On the contrary, the memory of the Supreme Being remains forever. Just as a person does not forget their own existence ('I am') even after a stroke, it is not possible to forget the Supreme Being because one has never been associated with the world and has never been separated from the Supreme Being. It is essential for a seeker to engage in spiritual practices (sadhana) because there is no better activity than this. However, it is not correct to think that one can attain the Supreme Being through spiritual practices. The Supreme Being is attained through His grace. He cannot be bought with any means or rituals. The purpose of spiritual practices is to eliminate the unspiritual (asat) - attachment to the world, ego, and desires - which is one's own creation. Therefore, the importance of spiritual practices should be understood as eliminating the unspiritual. If one has a strong desire to eliminate the unspiritual, one will also receive the strength to do so through the Supreme Being's grace. The common notion among seekers is that just as one can attain worldly objects through hard work, one can attain the Supreme Being through spiritual practices. However, this is not the case. The attainment of the Supreme Being is not the result of any action (sadhana, tapasya, etc.), no matter how excellent it may be. The reason is that the beginning and end of even the most excellent action are limited. Therefore, how can the result of such an action be eternal? The result of an action is also limited and ephemeral. Therefore, the attainment of the Supreme Being is not possible through any action. In reality, the elimination of attachment to the world and the body (tyaga, tapasya, etc.) is what happens through spiritual practices. This is what is mistakenly thought to be the attainment of the Supreme Being. When one eliminates attachment to the world and the body, one experiences the Supreme Being, who is omnipresent, eternal, and always attainable. One's memory of the Supreme Being becomes awakened. Arjuna also says at the end of the complete teaching, "I have attained memory" (18.73). Although forgetfulness is also eternal, it is limited and ephemeral. There is a great difference between the memory of the world and the memory of the Supreme Being. It is possible to forget the memory of the world after it has been acquired, but not the memory of the Supreme Being. To experience the Supreme Being, one must realize that the body and the world have no connection with oneself, and that one is a part of the Supreme Being. This is the true search for the Supreme Being. In reality, the elimination of attachment to the world results in the eternal experience of the Supreme Being. "Just as a drop of water merges with the ocean and cannot separate from it again, similarly, the individual self (jiva) cannot separate from the Supreme Being after attaining it" (6.6). Just as a drop of water cannot separate from the ocean after merging with it, the individual self cannot separate from the Supreme Being after attaining it. The reason is that the individual self is a part of the Supreme Being. When a person eliminates attachment to the world and the body, they eliminate the cause of rebirth (13.21). Therefore, there is no question of rebirth after attaining the Supreme Being. "The Prakriti (nature) and its qualities are the cause of rebirth" (13.21). The creator of the universe is one Supreme Being. He is the support and light of the universe. A person is attracted to worldly objects and forgets the Supreme Being due to ignorance. If the Supreme Being, who is the creator of the universe, is so dear, how much more dear should He be? Although the attraction to created objects is a kind of attraction to the creator (10.41), a person forgets the Supreme Being due to ignorance.

*
Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 15 ]
One who is not successful in his worldly endeavors, even after making great efforts, should not consider himself a failure. Instead, he should take refuge in the Lord and consider himself weak. If he does so, the Lord's mercy will certainly remove his defects, and he will attain the Lord. Therefore, a seeker should never lose hope of attaining the Lord. He should take refuge in the Lord and become fearless and free from anxiety. When one takes refuge in the Lord, the Lord's mercy removes obstacles and leads to the attainment of the Lord (Gita - 18th Chapter, 24th and 64th Verse). The nature of a living being is to take refuge in and be attached to that which he considers the greatest and most desirable. Just as people in the world are eager to acquire wealth and are busy accumulating it, because they expect to get all their desired objects through it, similarly, when a seeker realizes that there is nothing greater than the Lord and that His attainment gives a joy that surpasses all worldly pleasures (Gita - 6th Chapter, 22nd Verse), he becomes eager to attain the Lord (Gita - 15th Chapter, 19th Verse). One should take refuge in the Lord, who has no beginning but is the beginning of all (Gita - 10th Chapter, 2nd Verse). There is no other refuge that can provide lasting protection. Taking refuge in anyone other than the Lord is, in fact, a source of destruction, just as a crocodile is a source of destruction for a person drowning in the ocean. Therefore, a seeker should not take refuge in the worldly attachments, but rather in the Lord, who is the only true refuge. A seeker should renounce all attachments, just as he renounces worldly attachments. Even after renouncing worldly attachments, a seeker may still harbor a subtle sense of 'I am separate' (parichchinna tatva), which can only be removed by taking refuge in the Lord. Taking refuge in the Lord means surrendering all objects of attachment, including the body, senses, mind, intellect, ego, wealth, family, and home, to the Lord, and renouncing all attachment to them. A devotee who has taken refuge in the Lord has two feelings: 'I am the Lord's' and 'The Lord is mine.' However, the feeling 'I am the Lord's and for the Lord's sake' is superior. This is because, in the former feeling, there is a sense of expectation from the Lord, whereas in the latter feeling, there is only a sense of devotion to the Lord. When a seeker has this feeling, he becomes free from all attachments and expectations, and his devotion to the Lord becomes unshakeable. When a seeker takes refuge in the Lord, his devotion to the Lord becomes unshakeable and unending. This devotion is beyond all limitations and is not affected by gain or loss, pleasure or pain. It is a devotion that grows with each passing moment and is filled with an infinite and boundless joy. This devotion is so great that it brings joy to the Lord Himself. *
When one applies one's full strength and yet cannot remove his defects, then devotion to the Lord is the only means to remove them. *
When I called out to the invincible Lord Rama, He came to me, half of His name. I have heard of the invincible Lord Rama's strength.

* The Seeker - The Reviver *

965
The meaning of the word 'eva' is that one should renounce all other sources of refuge and take refuge in the Supreme Being alone. One should take refuge in the one and only God by saying 'I' with Him. This is the same sentiment that is expressed in the Gita, which is why 'ha' has been changed to 'hūm'. If 'I' is said to be the one who takes refuge in the Supreme Being, as in 'mām eva ye prapadyante' (7.14) and 'tam eva śaraṇaṃ gaccha' (18.62), and 'mām ekam śaraṇaṃ vraja' (18.66), then 'ha' would remain, but 'hūm' would not. As long as it has appeared in the words. The relationship between 'I am' and 'He is' is based on the association of the self, intellect, mind, senses, and body. As long as one considers oneself to be associated with these, one is not in a state of exclusive devotion. The meaning of 'prapadye' is 'I take refuge'. There may be a doubt here as to how the Lord can say 'I take refuge'. Does the Lord also take refuge in someone? If He takes refuge, then in whom does He take refuge? The solution to this is that the Lord does not take refuge in anyone, because He is supreme. He says this to the devotee in the language of the devotee, for the sake of worldly education, that the devotee should have the feeling of 'I take refuge'. -

As the living being is an aspect of the Supreme Being, it is actually always dependent on the Supreme Being. However, after becoming detached from the Supreme Being (due to forgetfulness of one's true nature), one starts taking refuge in the fleeting and ephemeral world, which is never stable. Therefore, one experiences suffering. Therefore, the seeker should recognize that one is actually the Supreme Being and that one is taking refuge in oneself, and not in the world. The relationship between 'I am' and 'He is' should be understood. The world is always transient and ephemeral, so it is renounced. The Supreme Being is always attainable, so one should seek Him. The difference between creation and seeking is that creation is the making of something that did not exist before, while seeking is the discovery of something that already exists. The Supreme Being is always present and self-existent, so one should seek Him, not create Him. When the seeker accepts the existence of the Supreme Being, then seeking begins. There are two types of seeking: one is to search for something that is not present, and the other is to search for something that is present but forgotten. The seeking of the Supreme Being is like searching for something that is present but forgotten. The Supreme Being is not lost, but one's attention is not directed towards Him due to attachment to the world. The absence of attention towards the Supreme Being is what is meant by forgetfulness. The forgetfulness of the Supreme Being is eternal and unending. Just as two people may not recognize each other, so the existence of the Supreme Being is not recognized. Just as we do not know the existence of the Sanskrit language, so the existence of the Supreme Being is not recognized. The existence of the Supreme Being is always present, but its recognition is not present. The forgetfulness of the Supreme Being is what is meant by the absence of recognition. The seeking of the Supreme Being is the means to overcome this forgetfulness and attain Him. The means to seek the Supreme Being is to renounce what does not exist, i.e., to renounce the world. The world is renounced, and the Supreme Being is sought. This is stated in the Bhagavata: 'Atat-ti-jantu mṛgayanti santah' (10.14.28). 'Tam eva ca ādyam puruṣaṃ prapadye' - When one renounces the world, one attains a state of being in the form of existence, and the seeker is liberated. Liberation means that one's attachment to the world is renounced, but one's love for the Supreme Being is not renounced. The Brahma Sutra states: 'Muktopaśṛpyavyapadeśāt' (1.3.2). 'The Supreme Being, who is the embodiment of love, is attainable even for the liberated souls.' The attainment of love for the Supreme Being is the fulfillment of human life. The Supreme Being is the embodiment of love, and one's love for Him is the means to attain Him. The relationship between 'I am' and 'He is' should be understood in this context.

* The Nectar of the Seeker *

The ultimate goal is not to attain material possessions, but to be free from desires. 967
The desire for unattainable things arises. However, for those who are devoted, to crave worldly desires and hope for happiness is a great delusion. One can never attain peace while desires remain - 'na kāmāni kāmāya mā gṛhṇāti' (Gita 2.56). Therefore, the cessation of desires is the only means to attain supreme peace. Hence, one should strive for the cessation of desires, not for their fulfillment. Attachment to the body gives rise to desires, such as "May my body remain healthy, may it not fall ill; may it remain strong, may it not weaken."
This is how numerous worldly desires, such as wealth, material possessions, and houses, are born. When attachment to the body ceases, the desires of devotees vanish. Devotees experience that the body, senses, mind, intellect, and ego - all belong to God alone. God is the only one who possesses them; nothing belongs to them. Such devotees' desires are completely and utterly destroyed. Therefore, they are called 'viniṣṭakāmāḥ' (those who have abandoned all desires). Special Point

In reality, the separation from the body and other material possessions is happening every moment. The seeker should simply accept this separation. If one considers the separation from these material possessions as union, then desires are born. From birth till now, our vital energy is constantly being destroyed, and our body is constantly separating from us. When the body dies one day, people will say, "Today it has died."
However, in reality, the body has not died today; rather, the death of the body, which is constantly happening, has been completed today! Therefore, for the cessation of desires, the seeker should consider the body and other material possessions as permanent and not associate with them. In reality, the fulfillment of desires never occurs. As long as one desire appears to be fulfilled, numerous other desires arise. When one desire is fulfilled, a person experiences happiness, and then he starts to strive for the fulfillment of other desires. However, this is a rule that no matter how many worldly pleasures and possessions one obtains, the fulfillment of desires is never possible. New desires are born from the pleasure of worldly possessions - 'jimi prati-lābh loha adhikāi' (Gita 2.55). The entire world, along with all its possessions, cannot fulfill the desires of even one person, let alone a limited number of possessions. The pleasure of worldly possessions is considered to be the cause of desires. This is the common notion - "The pleasure of worldly possessions is the cause of desires."
The more intense the desire, the greater the pleasure one experiences from obtaining the desired object. In reality, the fulfillment of desires does not bring happiness. When a person considers the absence of a thing as a cause of sorrow and associates with it through desire, then upon obtaining the thing, or upon the separation from it, happiness or sorrow does not arise. If one did not have desires in the first place, then upon obtaining the thing, neither happiness nor sorrow would arise. There is no inherent existence of desires in the ultimate reality because if the thing desired does not have an independent existence, then how can its desire exist? Therefore, all seekers are capable of being nishkāma (without desires). Those who are devoted are free from the dualities of pleasure and pain, happiness and sorrow, attachment and aversion, etc. - 'dvandvair vimuktāḥ sukha-duḥkha-saṅjñaiḥ' (Gita 2.14). The reason is that they consider everything that happens to them as the grace of God. Their vision remains focused on the grace of God alone, not on the favorable or unfavorable circumstances. Therefore, they experience that whatever happens is a part of God's benevolent plan - "Whatever happens is a part of our beloved Lord's benevolent plan."
This mindset helps them to easily overcome the dualities. God is the well-wisher of all beings - 'suhṛdaṁ sarva-bhūtānām' (Gita 5.29). Nothing can be detrimental to their own essence (jīva-ātma). Whatever circumstances arise from God's benevolent plan are for their ultimate benefit. Therefore, devotees remain pleased with God's plan. Even when they experience favorable or unfavorable circumstances, they do not experience any dualities, such as "Why did this happen?" or "This situation is not good."
Their minds remain free from such thoughts.

968
Special Point
* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Duality (raga-dveshadi) is the root of all inequalities, which give rise to all kinds of sins. Therefore, the seeker should remove the perceived importance of ephemeral things from his heart. There are two types of duality:
(1) Coarse (vyavaharik) duality - pleasure-pain, favor-disfavor, etc. This coarse duality is seen in humans, animals, birds, trees, etc. People desire pleasure, favor, etc., but do not desire pain, disfavor, etc. (2) Subtle (adhyatmik) duality - although it is necessary and beneficial to give respect and importance to one's own worship and the worshiped, and to consider them as the best, yet to criticize, condemn, and degrade the worship of others and the worshiped is 'subtle duality' which is harmful to the seeker. -
In reality, the ultimate goal of all worship is to completely separate oneself from the world (jada-ta) and its attachments. The seeker's interest, faith, and qualifications vary in different worship practices, which is also correct. Therefore, the seeker should not look at the differences in worship practices but should focus on the unity of the ultimate goal. By not looking at the worship practices of others and being fully engaged in one's own worship, the 'subtle duality' related to worship will automatically disappear. In the Gita, 'coarse duality' is called 'mohakalilam' (2.52) and 'subtle duality' is called 'shrutivipratipanna' (2.53). As long as the attachment to the world (jada-ta) remains in the seeker's heart, these dualities will remain. The 'coarse duality' gives special importance to the world. Therefore, it is very necessary to eliminate 'coarse duality'. -
In reality, looking at duality within oneself is itself ignorance. Raga-dvesh, sukha-duhkha, harsh-shok, etc. are dualities that exist in the heart, not in one's own nature. The heart is also not related to 'oneself' (svarupa). This is an illusion created by one's own perception. Everyone's experience is that when sukha-duhkha, etc. dualities arise, we remain the same. It does not happen that when sukha arises, we become something else, and when duhkha arises, we become something else. However, due to ignorance, we become happy and unhappy by mixing with these sukha-duhkha, etc. If we remain in our own nature (svarupa) without mixing with these changing states, we will be free from these dualities. Therefore, the seeker should not look at the changing states (sukha-duhkha, harsh-shok, etc.) but should always look at their own nature, which is beyond all states. The Gita has given a very easy way to be free from raga-dvesh, etc. dualities, which is to recognize that anukulata-pratikulata, etc. are hidden in them. To avoid them, the seeker should be careful not to be under their control (Gita, third chapter, 34th shloka). The meaning is that even when raga-dvesh appear, the seeker should not act according to them, because by acting, they become stronger. -
'Gachchhantyamoodha padamavyayam tat' - the desire or effort to attain changing objects and to be happy or unhappy due to them is 'ignorance'. In reality, the world is constantly changing, and the Supreme is eternal. The world's existence is perceived due to the existence of the Supreme. However, to consider the existence of the eternal Supreme and the changing world together as 'the world' is ignorance. Just as ignorant people clearly see 'the world', in the same way, enlightened devotees clearly experience 'the Supreme'. The world appears as it is, and the Supreme appears as He is. To consider the world as permanent is ignorance (moha). Those devotees who have overcome this ignorance are called 'amoodha' (free from ignorance). After ignorance is overcome, the effect of sukha-duhkha, etc. dualities does not occur. The Supreme is the illuminator of the conscious and the unconscious. Therefore, the one who is not affected by sukha-duhkha, etc. dualities is the Supreme. The meaning of 'shrutivipratipanna' is to be unable to make a decision or take a stand on any particular idea or concept, such as jnana, karma, and bhakti, duality, non-duality, etc., and to be confused about the various ideas and concepts, such as Vishnu, Rama, Krishna, Shiva, Shakti, Ganesha, etc., and to be unable to make a decision or take a stand on any particular idea or concept.

[Verse 6]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

A person who has renounced worldly attachments does not return to the transitory world. He becomes a candidate for liberation (Gita - Second Chapter, Fifteenth Verse). One who attains this eternal abode is certainly liberated, and that is why the Lord has emphasized the renunciation of ignorance in this verse by mentioning it twice ("nirmamooha" and "amoodha"). Ignorance has two forms: (1) attachment to the world and (2) not knowing the Supreme Being properly. In this verse, the Lord first mentions the renunciation of worldly attachment through the phrase "nirmamooha" and then the proper knowledge of the Supreme Being through the phrase "amoodha". The Supreme Being, who was described as "Urdhva-moolam" in the first verse of this chapter and who was the subject of the Lord's encouragement to seek in the fourth verse and the description of His glory in the sixth verse, is now referred to as "Avyayam Padam". Those who are pure in heart, free from attachment, and devoid of all vices, attain that Supreme Being. In reality, the human being is already a part of that eternal abode, but due to lack of awareness, he does not experience it. This can be understood through an example. Suppose we are traveling by train and our train stops at a station. We see another train standing on the adjacent track, and it suddenly starts moving. At that moment, due to our gaze on the moving train, we may think that our train is also moving. However, when we look away from the moving train and focus on the station, we realize that our train is still standing at the station. Similarly, when a person is attached to the world, he sees himself as being active like the world. But when he looks within and focuses on his true nature, he realizes that he is still and unchanged. Parishishta Bhaav - Bhakti is not included in Jnana Yoga and Karma Yoga, but both Jnana Yoga and Karma Yoga are included in Bhakti (Gita - Tenth Chapter, Tenth and Eleventh Verses). Therefore, we can interpret the phrase "Adhyatma-nitya" as Jnana Yoga and the phrase "Vinitrata-kama" as Karma Yoga. Sambandh - In the previous verse, the Lord described the eternal abode that the devotees attain. Now, the Lord explains the nature of that eternal abode. The sun, the moon, and fire do not illuminate that abode. One who attains that abode does not return to the world. That is my supreme abode. Vyakhya - [The sixth verse is a continuation of the fifth and seventh verses of the sixth chapter. The Lord says that the jiva is also a part of me, and therefore, it is inseparable from me. In these verses, the Lord explains that the jiva's inseparability from the eternal abode is due to its being a part of me. The eternal abode is my own abode, which is inseparable from me and is attained by me every moment. Just as one who knows the nirguna reality becomes amoodha (free from ignorance), so does one who firmly believes in the saguna-sakara (the Supreme Being with attributes) become amoodha (Gita - Fifth Chapter, Twentieth Verse; Tenth Chapter, Third Verse; and Fifteenth Verse).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

We are already situated; however, due to our identification with the material body and its various attachments, we do not experience our natural state of being. Due to attachment and desire, we are unable to attain or remain in that state. Commentary: We are parts of God - 'mamaivansho jeevaloke' (Gita 15.7). Therefore, God's abode is also our abode. This is why, upon attaining that abode, we do not have to return to the world. As long as we do not reach our true abode, we will continue to wander in various forms and realms, unable to find rest anywhere. Even if we go to the highest realm of Brahmaloka, we will still have to return to the world - 'abrahmabhuvallokah punaravartino 'arjuna' (Gita 8.16). This is because the entire world is a foreign land, not our own. It is a foreign home, not our own. Our wandering and wandering in various forms and realms will cease only when we reach our true home. The idea that one will not return to the world after attaining the supreme abode is mentioned three times in the Gita - 
1. 'Yam prapya na nivartante tad-dham paramam mama' (8.21)
2. 'Tat padam tat parimargitavyam yasmadgata na nivartanti bhuyah' (15.4)
3. 'Yadgatva na nivartante tad-dham paramam mama' (15.6)

The Lord has said that through the path of knowledge, one can attain the state of no return - 'gachchanti punaravrittim jnananirdhootakalmashah' (Gita 5.17). However, through the path of devotion, one can attain the supreme abode - this is the special characteristic of devotion. In the supreme abode, there is a special experience of love. The supreme abode cannot be illuminated by the light of the material world (sun, moon, etc.) or the light of the divine world (eyes, mind, etc.). This is because it is self-illuminating, with no distinction between the light and the source of light. The word 'gatva' implies movement, not action. This is because the movement of a part towards its part is natural, not forced. Action is forced, not natural. Action is driven by ego, whereas movement is egoless. Movement is natural and effortless, whereas action is forced and laborious. Movement is driven by the self, whereas action is driven by the ego. Movement is infinite, whereas action is limited. Movement liberates, whereas action enslaves. Movement is driven by the desire to enjoy and accumulate, whereas movement is driven by the desire to give and serve. The origin of movement is 'sat' (being), whereas the origin of action is 'asat' (non-being). Just as the Ganges River flows naturally towards its source, movement is the natural flow of the self towards its source. Movement can be in two ways - either by turning away from the world and its attachments, or by moving towards the ultimate goal of the self. The distance between the self and the ultimate goal is considered to be a state of separation, which is overcome by movement. Movement brings about the realization of the true nature of the self and its unity with the ultimate goal. The devotee experiences that their thoughts and actions have become more refined and elevated over time, which is a sign of their movement towards the ultimate goal. In the state of liberation, the devotee's movement is characterized by an intense experience of love, which is free from even the subtlest traces of ego. This is because the ego is inversely proportional to the distance between the self and the ultimate goal. The closer the self is to the ultimate goal, the more the ego is eliminated.

* The Seeker - The Reviver *

We should always keep in mind that the body and other material things are like actors performing on a stage. They are following their respective roles in this world-theatre, and we should always maintain the feeling of 'I am a part of God' within ourselves. We cannot bring them along, nor can we change them according to our wishes, nor can we keep them stable at our will, nor can we remain with them forever, nor can we take them along with us. Yet, we consider them as our own - this is our greatest mistake! In childhood, our mind, intellect, senses, and body were like this, but now they are not the same. They have all changed, yet we still believe that 'I am the same person I was in childhood.'

The reason for this is that even though there are changes in the body and other material things, there is no change in us. In this way, it is clear that there is a change in the body and other material things. Whoever sees a change in themselves is actually changeless themselves. Therefore, the things of the world and individuals are not our companions. -
Maintaining the feeling of 'I am a part of God' is to attribute oneself to God. The mistake that seekers make is that they try to attribute their mind and intellect to God instead of attributing themselves to God. They forget the reality that 'I am a part of God' and instead believe that 'I am a brahmin, I am a saint, etc.' and try to attribute their mind and intellect to God. This confusion will never be resolved, and even after great effort, their mind and intellect will not be able to attribute themselves to God as they should. God has also said in the fourth verse of this chapter that 'I am a part of the Supreme Being' is the only thing that is true. Goswami Tulsidas also says that first, one should consider oneself a part of God and then perform name-jap and other spiritual practices. This can improve one's situation even after many births -

The spoiled birth of many can be corrected now itself. Become a devotee of Ram, and leave the company of the wicked. (Dohavali 22)

In other words, it is better to attribute oneself to God rather than expecting to attribute one's mind and intellect to God. By attributing oneself to God, one's mind and intellect will automatically and easily attribute themselves to God. Just as an actor on stage says, 'I am Ravana's son Meghanad' and performs external actions like Meghanad, but within himself, he always maintains the feeling that this is just a role and that he is not actually Meghanad. Similarly, seekers should also maintain the feeling that 'I am eternal' (sanatanah). God has never abandoned the jiva, nor has He become distant from it. The jiva also cannot abandon God. Just as a gold ornament is not separate from gold, the jiva is also not separate from God. The wise person's great mistake is that he is becoming distant from God, his own part. He does not even think that God is so kind, merciful, and loving that He loves us even when we do not love Him, knows us even when we do not know Him. God is so generous and kind that He cannot be described in words, emotions, or intellect. It is foolish for a wise person to abandon God and consider other perishable material things as his own. God is so kind that He guides us even when we are in a state of sin, cleanses us from our old sins, and prevents us from committing new sins. Whether the jiva is in hell or heaven, in a human or animal body, God considers it as His own part. This is God's great kindness, generosity, and greatness. When God sees the jiva's downfall, He is grieved and says that the jiva has the right to come to Him, but it is going to hell without coming to Him (Gita - 16th chapter, 20th verse). God does not allow the jiva to remain in any state; He always attracts it towards Himself. When there is any change in our normal state (suffering or happiness, respect or disrespect, etc.), we should believe that God is remembering us specially and giving us a new opportunity. When a person follows God's instructions and performs his duties, God gives him such advancement that his life becomes successful, and the bondage of birth and death is destroyed forever. When a person commits a prohibited act (sin) due to ignorance, God sends him suffering, cleanses him from his old sins, and prevents him from committing new sins. -
God considers the jiva as His own part, whether it is in hell or heaven, in a human or animal body.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The circumstances are creating problems; they are pulling us towards themselves. Even God is subject to them! It is believed that the seeker remains engrossed in the special circumstances, seeing the blessings of the Lord, and never forgets the Lord. There is no difficulty or delay in obtaining a part; there is difficulty and delay because the parts have considered themselves separate from their parts, considering those bodies and others as their own, which are not theirs. Therefore, their attainment is automatically established in the presence of the Lord. Being present in front of the Lord is the living being's duty; because the living being has become distant from the Lord. The Lord considers the living being as His own; the living being should consider the Lord as its own—this is being present in front of the Lord. It is a great mistake of the human being that he considers the person, object, or circumstances that have not yet come or whose meeting is not certain, and even if they meet, they will not remain forever, as his complete effort and progress. This is a great deception of the human being! In reality, the attainment of the Supreme Being, who is always attainable and one's own, is the human being's ultimate effort, bravery. We may acquire as many worldly objects and wealth as we like, but ultimately they will either not remain or we will not remain. Ultimately, only 'not' will remain. In reality, attaining the eternal Supreme Being, who is always 'is', is the bravery. The living being is as worthless as the perishable objects it values, and it goes down as much as it values them, and as much as it values the eternal Supreme Being, it rises up. Because the living being is a part of the Supreme Being. The human being can never become great by acquiring perishable worldly objects. It is only a delusion or deception that he becomes great, and in reality, he remains deprived of the real greatness—attaining the Supreme Being. The greatness due to perishable worldly objects is never lasting, and the greatness due to the Supreme Being is never lost. Therefore, the living being, who is a part of the Supreme Being, becomes great only by attaining the Supreme Being. It becomes so great that even the gods respect and desire that it should come to their world. Not only that, the Supreme Being Himself says—
'He (the living being) is attracted to the objects of the senses, which are situated in the material nature'—The Lord has said in this very verse, in the first half, that the living being is not situated in Him, but is His part. In the same way, in the second half of the verse, He has said that the mind and senses are situated in the material nature, not as His parts, but as parts of the material nature. The meaning is that the Lord's part, the living being, is always situated in the Lord, and the mind and senses, situated in the material nature, are parts of the material nature. Considering the mind and senses as one's own, considering a relationship with them, is to attract them. Here, the implication is that the word 'mind' includes the intellect (which is a characteristic of the inner organ) and the five sense organs, and the five working sense organs, and the five pranas. The Lord says in the above words that His part, the living being, remains situated in Him, but due to ignorance, it considers its situation to be in the body, senses, mind, and intellect. Just as the body, senses, mind, and intellect, being parts of the material nature, are never separate from the material nature, similarly, the living being, being the part of the Lord, is never separate from the Lord. However, the living being has forgotten the Lord due to ignorance. Here, the mention of the mind and the five knowledge senses implies that the living being is bound by linking with these six. Therefore, the seeker should give the body, senses, mind, and intellect to the service of the world, i.e., engage in the service of the world, and offer himself to the Lord. Special point
(1)
The human being, due to ignorance, considers the perishable objects such as the body, woman, son, wealth, house, prestige, greatness, etc. as his own and his own, and becomes unhappy. This is a lower thing that he considers these objects as his own and considers himself great by enjoying and accumulating them; whereas, in reality, by considering them as his own, he becomes their slave. We may or may not know, we consider those objects necessary, in which we see some speciality or importance, or in which we have a desire, those objects (wealth, knowledge, etc.) are greater than us and we are insignificant in front of them. The value we understand in the acquisition of objects is actually insignificant, whether the objects are acquired or not acquired. [ Chapter 15 ]

दास ही बनाते हैं। वास्तवमें भगवान्‌को अपना जानकर
उनके शरण हो जानेसे ही मनुष्य बड़ा बनता है, ऊँचा
उठता है। इतना ही नहीं; भगवान् ऐसे भक्तको अपने से भी
बड़ा मान लेते हैं और कहते हैं-
“
अहं भक्तपराधीनो ह्यस्वतन्त्र इव द्विज ।
साधुभिर्ग्रस्तहृदयो भक्तैर्भक्तजनप्रियः ॥
(श्रीमद्भा० ९। ४ । ६३)
हे द्विज ! मैं भक्तोंके पराधीन हूँ, स्वतन्त्र नहीं
भक्तजन मेरेको अत्यन्त प्यारे हैं । मेरे हृदयपर उनका पूर्ण
अधिकार है। कोई भी सांसारिक व्यक्ति, पदार्थ क्या हमें
इतनी बड़ाई दे सकता है ?
यह जीव परमात्माका अंश होते हुए भी प्रकृतिके अंश
शरीरादिको अपना मानकर स्वयं अपना अपमान करता है
और अपनेको नीचे गिराता है। अगर मनुष्य इन शरीर,
इन्द्रियाँ, मन आदि सांसारिक पदार्थोंका दास न बने, तो
वह भगवान्का भी इष्ट हो जाय - 'इष्टोऽसि मे दृढमिति'
(गीता १८। ६४) । जिन्होंने भगवान्‌को प्राप्त कर लिया
है, उनको भगवान् अपना प्रिय कहते हैं (गीता - बारहवें
अध्यायके तेरहवेंसे उन्नीसवें श्लोकतक ) । परंतु जिन्होंने
भगवान्‌को प्राप्त नहीं किया है; किंतु जो भगवान्‌को
प्राप्त करना चाहते हैं, उन साधकोंको तो वे अपना
अत्यन्त प्रिय' कहते हैं - ' भक्तास्तेऽतीव मे प्रियाः'
(गीता १२ । २० ) । ऐसे परम दयालु भगवान्‌को, जो
साधकोंको ‘अत्यन्त प्रिय' और सिद्ध भक्तोंको केवल
'प्रिय' कहते हैं, मनुष्य अपना नहीं मानता - यह उसका
कितना प्रमाद है!
(२)
।
संसारका एक छोटा-सा अंश शरीर है और परमात्माका
अंश स्वयं (जीवात्मा) है । भूल यह होती है कि
परमात्माका अंश संसारके अंशके साथ मिलकर संसार
और परमात्मा—दोनोंको अपने अनुकूल बनाना चाहता है!
साधकका काम है— इस भूलको मिटाना । इसके लिये वह
शरीरको तो संसारके अनुकूल बना दे और स्वयं
परमात्माके अनुकूल बन जाय । तात्पर्य है कि शरीरको
संसारपर छोड़ दे कि जैसी संसारकी मरजी हो, वैसे रखे ;
संसारकी चीज संसारको दे दे और परमात्माकी चीज
परमात्माको दे दे – यह ईमानदारी है। इस ईमानदारीका नाम
ही 'मुक्ति' है। जिसकी चीज है, उसको न दे; संसारकी
चीज भी ले ले और परमात्माकी चीज भी ले ले - यह
बेईमानी है। इस बेईमानीका नाम ही 'बन्धन' है।
संसारकी चीज संसारपर और परमात्माकी चीज
परमात्मापर छोड़कर निश्चिन्त हो जाय। अपनी कोई
कामना न रखे । न जीनेकी कामना रखे, न मरनेकी ।
भगवान् ऐसा कर देते तो ठीक रहता; भगवान् वर्षा कर
देते तो ठीक रहता; गरमी ज्यादा पड़ रही है, थोड़ी कम
कर देते तो अच्छा था; बाढ़ आ गयी, वर्षा कम करते
तो ठीक रहता - इस तरह मनुष्य परमात्माको भी अपने
अनुकूल बनाना चाहता है और संसारको भी। इस बातको
छोड़कर अपने-आपको सर्वथा भगवान्‌के अर्पित कर दे
और भगवान् से कह दे कि हे नाथ! आप मेरेको पृथ्वीपर
रखें या स्वर्गमें रखें अथवा नरकोंमें रखें; बालक रखें या
जवान रखें अथवा बूढ़ा रखें; अपमानित रखें या सम्मानित
रखें; सुखी रखें या दुःखी रखें; जैसी परिस्थितिमें रखना
चाहें, वैसे रखें, पर मैं आपको भूलूँ नहीं ।
मनुष्य जिस घरको अपना मानता है, जिस
कुटुम्बको अपना मानता है, जिन रुपयोंको अपना मानता
है, उनकी ही चिन्ता उसको होती है । संसारमें लाखों-
करोंड़ों घर हैं, अरबों आदमी हैं, अनगिनत रुपये हैं, पर
उनकी चिन्ता नहीं होती; क्योंकि उनको वह अपना नहीं
मानता । जिनको अपना नहीं मानता, उनसे तो मुक्त है ही ।
अतः ज्यादा मुक्ति तो हो चुकी है, थोड़ी-सी ही मुक्ति
बाकी है!
विचार करना चाहिये कि जिन थोड़ी-सी चीजोंको
हम अपनी मानते हैं, वे कौन-सी सदा साथ रहनेवाली हैं !
चीजें तो रहेंगी नहीं, पर बन्धन ( उनका सम्बन्ध) रह
जायगा, जो जन्म-जन्मान्तरतक साथ रहेगा। इसलिये
साधकको चाहिये कि वह या तो शरीरको संसारके अर्पण
कर दे, जो कर्मयोग है; चाहे अपनेको शरीर-
संसारसे सर्वथा अलग कर ले, जो ज्ञानयोग है; और चाहे
अपनेको भगवान्‌के अर्पण कर दे, जो भक्तियोग है ।
इन तीनोंमेंसे कोई भी साधन अपना ले, तीनोंका फल एक
ही होगा ।

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The Lord says to His devotee, "I am the one, and give up yourself to the Supreme Being, just as a devotee of the Supreme Being is My crown jewel!" However, those who please themselves, keep them as they are. We are servants, but they never say, "The greedy is My crown jewel!" They only make us their servants. In reality, a person becomes great and elevated by taking refuge in the Supreme Being, knowing Him as their own. The Supreme Being considers such a devotee even greater than Himself and says, "I am bound by My devotees, just as a twice-born person is bound by good people. I am pleased with devotees and am dear to them."

O twice-born person! I am bound by My devotees, I am not independent. My devotees are very dear to Me. They have complete control over My heart. What can any worldly person or material thing do for us? Although the jiva is a part of the Supreme Being, it considers itself a part of the material world and thus commits self-destruction and falls. If a person does not make his body, senses, mind, etc. his servants, then he becomes dear to the Supreme Being - "You are dear to Me, I am firm in this" (Gita 18.64). Those who have attained the Supreme Being call Him their beloved (Gita, Chapter 12, verses 13-19). However, those who want to attain the Supreme Being, the Supreme Being calls them His "very dear" - "These devotees are very dear to Me" (Gita 12.20). Such a merciful Supreme Being, who calls devotees "very dear" and siddhas "beloved", is not recognized by a person as their own - this is their great foolishness! (2)

The body is a small part of the world, and the jiva is a part of the Supreme Being. The mistake is that the jiva wants to make the world and the Supreme Being both favorable to itself! The duty of a sadhak is to remove this mistake. For this, he should make his body favorable to the world and himself favorable to the Supreme Being. In other words, he should give up his body to the world, as per the world's will, and give himself to the Supreme Being. This is honesty. The name of this honesty is 'mukti' (liberation). If one gives up what belongs to someone else and takes what belongs to oneself - this is dishonesty, and the name of this dishonesty is 'bandhan' (bondage). Leave the world's things to the world and the Supreme Being's things to the Supreme Being, and remain detached. Do not have any desires. Do not desire to live or die. If the Supreme Being were to do this, it would be fine; if the Supreme Being were to give rain, it would be fine; if the heat were to decrease, it would be good; if the flood were to decrease, it would be fine - in this way, a person wants to make the Supreme Being favorable to itself and the world. Leave this thought and completely offer yourself to the Supreme Being and say, "O Lord! You keep me on earth or in heaven, or in hell, or as a child or as an old man, or humiliated or honored, or happy or unhappy; keep me as you please, but I will not forget you."

A person is concerned about the house he considers his own, the family he considers his own, and the money he considers his own. There are millions of houses, billions of people, and countless rupees in the world, but he is not concerned about them because he does not consider them his own. One who does not consider anything his own is already free. Therefore, there is already a lot of freedom, and there is only a little bit of freedom left! We should think about which of the things we consider our own are eternal companions. Things will remain, but their relationship will remain with us, which will be with us for birth after birth. Therefore, the sadhak should either give his body to the world, which is karma yoga; or separate himself from the body and the world, which is jnana yoga; or give himself to the Supreme Being, which is bhakti yoga. Any of these three paths will have the same result.

*
श्रीमद्भगवद्गीता
*
[ अध्याय १५
परिशिष्ट भाव—यहाँ भगवान्ने जिसको अपना अंश कहा है, उसीको सातवें अध्यायके पाँचवें श्लोकमें अपनी 'परा
प्रकृति' कहा है। इसलिये दोनों ही जगह 'जीवभूत' (जीव बना हुआ) शब्द आया है- 'जीवभूतः', 'जीवभूताम्' । परा
और अपरा—दोनों भगवान्‌की शक्तियाँ हैं (गीता - सातवें अध्यायका चौथा - पाँचवाँ श्लोक) । जबसे पराकी दृष्टि भगवान्से
हटकर अपराकी तरफ चली गयी, तबसे परा जन्म-मरणके चक्रमें पड़ गयी । इसी बातको सातवें अध्यायमें 'ययेदं धार्यते
जगत्' पदोंसे और यहाँ 'मनःषष्ठानीन्द्रियाणि प्रकृतिस्थानि कर्षति ॥' पदोंसे कहा गया है।
यद्यपि अपरा भी भगवान्‌की है, तथापि उसका स्वभाव अलग (परिवर्तनशील ) है । इसलिये भगवान् ने अपनेको अपरासे
अतीत बताया है—‘यस्मात्क्षरमतीतोऽहम्' (गीता १५ । १८ ) । परन्तु परा और भगवान् एक स्वभाववाले (अपरिवर्तनशील)
हैं। इसलिये ‘ममैवांशः’ पदमें 'एव' कहनेका तात्पर्य है कि जीव केवल मेरा (भगवान्का) अंश है, इसमें प्रकृतिका अंश
किंचिन्मात्र भी नहीं है। जैसे शरीरमें माता और पिता — दोनोंके अंशका मिश्रण होता है, ऐसे जीवमें मेरा और प्रकृतिके
अंशका मिश्रण (संयोग) नहीं है, प्रत्युत यह केवल मेरा अंश है । अतः इसका सम्बन्ध केवल मेरे साथ है, प्रकृतिके साथ
नहीं। प्रकृतिके साथ सम्बन्ध तो यह खुद जोड़ता है—' मनःषष्ठानीन्द्रियाणि प्रकृतिस्थानि कर्षति ॥'
-
अपरा प्रकृति परमात्माकी है, पर जीवने उसको अपना मान लिया और उससे सुख लेने लग गया, तभी वह
बन्धनमें पड़ा है। अपनी न होनेके कारण ही न वस्तुएँ ठहरती हैं, न सुख ठहरता है।
स्थूल, सूक्ष्म और कारण - शरीरके साथ अपना सम्बन्ध मानना ही अनर्थका कारण है। जीव शरीरको अपनी तरफ
खींचता है ( कर्षति ) अर्थात् अपना मानता है, पर जो वास्तवमें अपना है, उस परमात्माको अपना मानता ही नहीं ।
यही जीवकी मूल भूल है ।
जीव ब्रह्म (निर्गुण)-का अंश नहीं है, प्रत्युत ईश्वर ( सगुण ) - का अंश है - ' ईस्वर अंस जीव अबिनासी'
(मानस ७ । ११७ । १) । कारण कि ब्रह्म चिन्मय सत्तामात्र है; अतः उसमें अंश - अंशीभाव हो सकता ही नहीं । जीवकी
ब्रह्मसे एकता (साधर्म्य) है अर्थात् अनेक रूपसे जो जीव है, वही एक रूपसे ब्रह्म है। शरीरके साथ सम्बन्ध होनेसे
वह जीव है और शरीरके साथ सम्बन्ध न होनेसे वह ब्रह्म है। अतः वास्तवमें जीव और ब्रह्म - दोनों ही समग्र भगवान्‌के
अंश हैं। इसलिये भगवान् ने अपनेको ब्रह्मकी प्रतिष्ठा (आधार) बताया है - 'ब्रह्मणो हि प्रतिष्ठाहम्' (१४। २७)
और ब्रह्मको अपने ही समग्र रूपका एक अंग बताया है - ' ते ब्रह्म तद्विदुः " (७। २९-३०)।
,
मन और इन्द्रियाँ जिसके अंश हैं, उसीमें रहते हैं - ' प्रकृतिस्थानि' । इससे जीवको यह शिक्षा लेनी चाहिये कि
मैं भी जिसका अंश हूँ, उसीमें निरन्तर रहना चाहिये, उसीके साथ सम्बन्ध जोड़ना चाहिये । यह सम्बन्ध स्वयंको
ही जोड़ना पड़ेगा, दूसरा नहीं जोड़ेगा । कारण कि स्वयंने ही जगत्से सम्बन्ध जोड़ा है और स्वयं ही परमात्मासे विमुख
हुआ है। जगत्के सम्मुख होने ( सम्बन्ध जोड़ने ) - में जगत् कारण नहीं है और परमात्मासे विमुख होनेमें परमात्मा कारण
नहीं हैं, प्रत्युत दोनोंमें स्वयं ही कारण है । परमात्माका अंश होनेसे जीव स्वतन्त्र है और इसी स्वतन्त्रताका उसने दुरुपयोग
किया है। इसलिये इसका सदुपयोग स्वयंको ही करना पड़ेगा – 'उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानम् ' ( गीता ६ । ५) ।
प्रकृतिके साथ मन और इन्द्रियोंका नित्य और वास्तविक सम्बन्ध है, पर मन और इन्द्रियोंके साथ स्वयं (आत्मा)-
का अनित्य और माना हुआ सम्बन्ध है । अनित्य सम्बन्ध कभी स्थायी नहीं रहता, प्रत्युत बदलता और मिटता रहता
है। स्वयंका नित्य सम्बन्ध परमात्माके साथ है, जो कभी बदलता और मिटता नहीं । परन्तु अनित्य सम्बन्धको स्वीकार
कर लेनेसे उस नित्य सम्बन्धसे विमुखता हो जाती है, जिससे उसका अनुभव नहीं होता ।
'ममैवांशो जीवलोके' पदोंसे यह भाव निकलता है कि हम तो प्रभुको अपना मानते हैं, पर प्रभु हमें अपना
जानते हैं! जब जीव भगवान्‌के शरण हो जाता है, तब वह भी प्रभुको अपना जान लेता है—' मामेव ये प्रपद्यन्ते
मायामेतां तरन्ति ते' (गीता ७। १४)।

*
Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 15
Parishishta Bhaav—Here, the Lord has referred to the one He called His part as His 'para prakriti' in the fifth verse of the seventh chapter. Therefore, both places have the word 'jiva-bhoot' (jiva-made) - 'jiva-bhootah', 'jiva-bhootam'. Para and apara—both are the powers of the Lord (Gita - seventh chapter, fourth - fifth verse). Since the para vision of the Lord has moved away from Him and gone towards the apara side, since then the para has fallen into the cycle of birth and death. This is also mentioned in the seventh chapter with the words 'yayedam dharyate jagat' and here with the words 'manah-sasthaani indriyaani prakritisthaani karshati'. Although apara is also the Lord's, yet its nature is different (changeable). Therefore, the Lord has described Himself as beyond apara—‘yasmadksaramatito 'ham' (Gita 15.18). However, para and the Lord are of the same nature (unchangeable). Therefore, the meaning of the word 'mamevaansho' is that the jiva is only my (Lord's) part, and there is no part of prakriti in it at all. Just as the mixture of the parts of the mother and father is in the body, similarly, the jiva is only my part, and there is no mixture of the parts of prakriti in it. Therefore, its relation is only with me, not with prakriti. Prakriti itself establishes a relation with it—'manah-sasthaani indriyaani prakritisthaani karshati'. Apara prakriti is the property of the Supreme Being, but the Lord has taken it as His own and has started enjoying it, and that is why it has fallen into bondage. Due to not being His own, it does not remain in anything, nor does it remain in happiness. Considering the body as one's own and relating with it is the cause of all troubles. The jiva relates with the body (karshati) i.e., considers it as its own, but the one who is actually its own, the Supreme Being, it does not consider as its own. This is the fundamental mistake of the jiva. The jiva is not a part of the Nirguna-Brahm (the Supreme Being without attributes), but it is a part of the Saguna-Ishwar (the Supreme Being with attributes) - 'Ishwar ansh jiva abinasi' (Manas 7.117.1). Because the Nirguna-Brahm is merely consciousness, therefore, it cannot have a part-part relationship. The jiva has a unity (sadrmya) with the Nirguna-Brahm, i.e., the one who is many forms is the same as the one who is one form. Due to being related with the body, it is the jiva, and due to not being related with the body, it is the Nirguna-Brahm. Therefore, in reality, both the jiva and the Nirguna-Brahm are the parts of the Supreme Being. Therefore, the Lord has described Himself as the foundation of the Nirguna-Brahm - 'Brahmano hi pratishtaham' (14.27) and has described the Nirguna-Brahm as one of His own parts - 'te brahm tadviduh' (7.29-30). The mind and the senses, which are its parts, reside in it—'prakritisthaani'. From this, the jiva should learn that it should always reside in the one in whom it is a part, and should establish a relation with it. This relation will have to be established by itself, not by another. Because it has established a relation with the world itself and has become distant from the Supreme Being itself. Being present in front of the world (establishing a relation) is not due to the world, and becoming distant from the Supreme Being is not due to the Supreme Being, but due to itself. The jiva is independent due to being a part of the Supreme Being, and it has misused this independence. Therefore, it will have to use it properly itself—'udhareda atmanatmanam' (Gita 6.5). The mind and the senses have a constant and real relation with prakriti, but the relation of the self (atma) with the mind and the senses is temporary and assumed. The temporary relation does not remain constant, but changes and disappears. The self's constant relation is with the Supreme Being, which never changes and disappears. However, accepting the temporary relation makes one distant from the constant relation, and thus its experience is not obtained. The phrase 'mamevaansho jiva lokhe' implies that we consider the Lord as our own, but the Lord knows us as His own! When the jiva takes refuge in the Lord, then it also comes to know the Lord as its own—'mameva ye prapadyante mayam etam taranti te' (Gita 7.14). The jiva is the eternal part of the Lord; therefore, relating with the Lord is the real goal of the jiva. The goal achieved through the body is a means for the world, and it is only for the world. But the goal achieved through the self is the real goal. Therefore, being free from evil, being detached, and considering the Lord as one's own are the goals of the self. Being free from evil makes a person useful for the world.

[Verse 7]

* The Saviour of the Seeker *

The body becomes useful for oneself by being detached from the world. It becomes useful for God by considering God as one's own. A person cannot be useful for the world without being detached from the world. The body cannot be useful for oneself without being detached from the world. One cannot be useful for God without being connected to God. To feel the need to become free from vice, to become detached, and to become a devotee of God is itself an effort. However, the seeker should first accept that one can become free from vice, detached, and a devotee of God. For this, the seeker should know that we are all one in the world, one in the self, and one in the Supreme Self. Therefore, just as one has a sense of concern for one's own body, one should have a sense of concern for all bodies. Or, just as one remains detached from all bodies, one should remain detached from this body. One can become free from vice by considering all bodies as one. One can become detached by leaving all bodies and remaining in one's own form. One can become a devotee of God by leaving all bodies and remaining in the Supreme Self. We are related to the Supreme Self - 'mamaivansho jivaloke', therefore, we are in the Supreme Self. However, the body, senses, mind, and intellect are related to the inferior nature - 'prakritisthani'. 'Vikaranca gunancaiva viddhi prakritisambhavan' (Gita 13.19). We have never been, are not, and will never be related to the body. We have never been, are not, and will never be separate from the Supreme Self. The farthest thing from us is the body, and the nearest thing to us is the Supreme Self. However, due to the cause of desire, attachment, and identification, the person sees the body as near and the Supreme Self as far. The body appears to be attainable, and the Supreme Self appears to be unattainable. To renounce the relationship with the body, the seeker should accept three things - 1. The body is not mine; because I do not have control over it. 2. I do not need anything, and 3. I do not do anything for myself. As long as the seeker considers himself related to the three bodies - gross, subtle, and causal, he is bound by the three - 'karma', 'chintan', and 'sthirata' (nirvikalpa avastha). However, when the seeker renounces the relationship with the three bodies, he is not bound by the three. To awaken the awareness of the eternal relationship with God, the seeker should accept three things - 1. God is mine, 2. I am God's, and 3. everything is God's. When the awareness of the eternal relationship with God is awakened, the seeker attains the love of God. The attainment of the love of God is the fulfillment of human life. A person has three desires - the desire for enjoyment, the desire for knowledge, and the desire for love. The desire for enjoyment is 'kama', the desire for knowledge is 'jijnasa', and the desire for love is 'pipasa' (abhilasha). The desire for enjoyment is related to the body, the desire for knowledge is related to the self, and the desire for love is related to the Supreme Self. Considering the body as one's own is a mistake; because the body is a part of the inferior nature. Therefore, the desire for enjoyment related to the body is not one's own, but a mistake. However, the desire for knowledge and the desire for love are one's own, not a mistake. Therefore, by dedicating the body to the service of the family, society, and the world, or by intensifying the desire for knowledge, the mistake is removed. The mistake removed is the desire for enjoyment. The desire for enjoyment removed is the fulfillment of the desire for knowledge. The seeker attains the natural state of being, and he becomes a jivanmukta. Then, the desire for love related to the Supreme Self is awakened. Since the jiva is a part of the Supreme Self, the ultimate desire of the jiva is love. Love is a universal desire. The attainment of love makes human life complete. There is nothing left after that. Connection - The Lord describes an example to show how the jiva, along with the mind and senses, goes through many births due to considering them as one's own.

The Bhagavad Gita is a sacred text that teaches us about the nature of the self and the universe. It is a dialogue between Lord Krishna and Prince Arjuna, in which Krishna explains the concept of the self and its relationship with the material world. Just as the wind carries scents from one place to another, the self (jiva) carries the material body and senses with it, just as the wind carries scents from one place to another. The wind does not retain the scent, but rather carries it away, just as the self does not retain the material body and senses, but rather carries them with it to a new place. The self is like the wind, which is not affected by the scent it carries. Similarly, the self is not affected by the material body and senses it carries. However, due to ignorance, the self identifies itself with the material body and senses, just as the wind is identified with the scent it carries. Just as the wind carries scents from one place to another, the self carries the material body and senses with it, just as the wind carries scents from one place to another. The self is not bound to the material body and senses, just as the wind is not bound to the scent it carries. The self has the power to choose its associations, just as the wind can choose which scents to carry. The self can choose to associate with the material body and senses, or it can choose to transcend them. The self has the freedom to choose its path, just as the wind has the freedom to choose which scents to carry. The self is not bound by the material body and senses, just as the wind is not bound by the scent it carries. The self can transcend the material world and achieve liberation, just as the wind can transcend the scent it carries and return to its natural state. The three words used by Lord Krishna as examples are: wind, scent, and place. The wind is like the self, the scent is like the material body and senses, and the place is like the material world. Just as the wind carries the scent from one place to another, the self carries the material body and senses with it, just as the wind carries scents from one place to another. The self has three main mistakes:

1. It identifies itself with the material body and senses, thinking that it is their owner, when in fact it is their servant. 2. It forgets its true owner, the Supreme Being, and identifies itself with the material body and senses. 3. It does not give up its association with the material body and senses, even though it has the freedom to do so. The Supreme Being has given the self the freedom to use the material body and senses for its own benefit, not to become their owner. However, the self makes a big mistake by not using them for its own benefit, but rather identifying itself with them and becoming their servant. The self can give up its association with the material body and senses only when it realizes that it is their servant and not their owner. This realization is the key to liberation, and it is the only way to achieve true freedom.
