* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

One experiences a sense of 'deficiency' when one comes to know that one is not the owner of these things, and at the same time, one considers oneself as 'orphaned'. He who finds the idea of being the master or owner pleasing, cannot attain the Supreme Being; because the one who becomes the owner of any person, thing, or object, forgets his own master - forgets his own master - this is a rule. For instance, when a child considers only his mother as his own and wants her alone, he cannot live without her at that time. But when the same child grows up and becomes a householder, and starts considering himself as the owner of his wife, children, etc., he does not find it pleasant to be near his mother. This is the result of becoming the owner! In the same way, this jiva-atma also forgets its real master, the Supreme Being, by becoming the owner of the material objects like the body, etc. - by becoming the owner of the material objects like the body, etc. - as long as this forgetfulness or detachment remains, the jiva-atma continues to suffer. The word 'api' with the word 'Ishwar' has a special meaning that this jiva-atma, although created by Ishwar, is not powerless, inert, or dependent like air. This jiva-atma has the capacity and discrimination to give up the relationships it has accepted and to experience the eternal relationship with the Supreme Being. However, due to the desire for the fleeting pleasures of the world, it does not give up the relationships it has accepted and does not even want to give them up. The jiva-atma cannot leave the material objects even after becoming detached from them - it cannot leave the material objects even after becoming detached from them - just like a lump of gandhaki cannot take the bodies with it when it leaves them. The jiva has two powers - (1) the power of life, by which it experiences the process of breathing, and (2) the power of desire, by which it desires to enjoy the objects of the world. The power of life is constantly decreasing (due to the process of breathing). The destruction of the power of life is known as death. Due to attachment to the material objects, the power of desire remains active. If the power of life remains and the power of desire is destroyed, then the person becomes liberated. If the power of life is destroyed and the power of desire remains, then the person has to take birth again. The power of desire remains the same in the new body, and the power of life is obtained anew. The expenditure of the power of life should be in the destruction of desires. By being selfless and devoted to the welfare of all living beings, desires can be easily destroyed. Here, the word 'grihita' means - to have attachment, affection, or fondness for things that do not belong to us. The jiva-atma, by accepting attachment to the mind and senses, carries them along with it, but they do not say, "We are yours, and you are ours." The jiva-atma cannot control them; it cannot change them as it pleases; yet it keeps them attached to itself, which is a mistake. In reality, the attachment to things is the bond that binds us. Whether the thing is obtained or not, whether it is good or bad, whether it comes in the way or not, whether it is near or far, if we consider it as our own, then a relationship is established with it. This relationship is not broken even after death. Therefore, by throwing the dead body into the Ganges, the jiva's journey continues. We are completely free and powerful to give up this relationship. If we can give up this attachment even while living, we can attain liberation. The greatest fault is to consider what is not one's own as one's own and what is one's own as not one's own. This is the reason why progress is not made on the path of spirituality. In this shloka, the word 'etani' refers to the six senses (including the mind) and the five knowledge senses. Here, the word 'etani' is also a symbol of the subtle body and the causal body - the nature. The jiva-atma takes all these with it and goes to another body. Just as a person gives up old clothes and takes on new ones, the jiva-atma gives up the old body and takes on a new one (Gita - 13th chapter, 24th verse). In reality, it is not possible for the pure consciousness (atma) to acquire or give up any body; because the atma is immobile and equally present everywhere (Gita - 2nd chapter, 17th and 24th verses). The acquisition and giving up of bodies is limited (to a particular place and time). The jiva-atma can acquire and give up bodies only through a particular principle (tattva), whereas the atma cannot be limited to any particular place, time, or object. However, when the atma identifies itself with the material objects and becomes a part of the prakriti, it can acquire and give up bodies.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The mind is the source of life and the means of experiencing the world. It is the instrument through which we perceive the world, and it is the source of our thoughts, feelings, and actions. The mind is the seat of our consciousness, and it is the means by which we experience the world. The mind is the source of our perception, and it is the means by which we experience the world. When the mind is in a state of calmness and clarity, we are able to perceive the world in its true form. But when the mind is clouded by thoughts and emotions, our perception of the world becomes distorted. The five senses - hearing, seeing, touching, tasting, and smelling - are the means by which we experience the world. But the mind is the source of our perception, and it is the means by which we interpret the information that we receive through our senses. The sense of hearing is the ability to perceive sound. We have heard many different types of sounds in our lives - sweet and harsh, pleasant and unpleasant. But when we hear a sound, it is the mind that interprets it and gives it meaning. The sense of sight is the ability to perceive light and color. We have seen many different types of objects and scenes in our lives - beautiful and ugly, pleasant and unpleasant. But when we see an object, it is the mind that interprets it and gives it meaning. The sense of touch is the ability to perceive physical sensations. We have felt many different types of sensations in our lives - soft and hard, warm and cold. But when we touch an object, it is the mind that interprets it and gives it meaning. The sense of taste is the ability to perceive flavors. We have tasted many different types of foods and drinks in our lives - sweet and sour, salty and bitter. But when we taste something, it is the mind that interprets it and gives it meaning. The sense of smell is the ability to perceive odors. We have smelled many different types of fragrances and odors in our lives - pleasant and unpleasant. But when we smell something, it is the mind that interprets it and gives it meaning. The five senses are connected to the five organs of action - the tongue, the hands, the feet, the anus, and the genitals. The senses and the organs of action are connected to the five elements - earth, water, fire, air, and ether. The sense of hearing is connected to the element of ether, and it is the means by which we perceive sound. The sense of sight is connected to the element of light, and it is the means by which we perceive light and color. The sense of touch is connected to the element of earth, and it is the means by which we perceive physical sensations. The sense of taste is connected to the element of water, and it is the means by which we perceive flavors. The sense of smell is connected to the element of fire, and it is the means by which we perceive odors. The sense of hearing is the means by which we perceive two types of knowledge - direct and indirect. Direct knowledge is the perception of sound, and indirect knowledge is the perception of objects and events through sound. The sense of hearing is the most important sense, and it is the means by which we perceive the world. The sense of hearing is the means by which we perceive the world through sound. We hear many different types of sounds in our lives - sweet and harsh, pleasant and unpleasant. The power of sound is beyond human comprehension, and it is the means by which we perceive the world. Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The five elements' combined sattva-guna - portions make up the mind and intellect, the rajo-guna - portions make up the vital force, and the tamo-guna - portions make up the body. One
'Vishayanupasevate' - just as a merchant, due to some reason, takes down his shop from one place and sets it up in another, similarly, the jiva-atma leaves one body and takes birth in another; and just as he used to enjoy worldly objects with attachment in the previous body, similarly, he starts enjoying them with attachment in the new body. Due to this, the jiva-atma keeps wandering in various high and low wombs, getting attached to worldly objects again and again. The Lord has given this human body for self-realization, not for enjoying worldly pleasures. Just as when a brahmin is given a cow as a donation, we can give him food and water, but we cannot drink the milk of the donated cow, similarly, it is our duty to use this body properly, but we cannot consider it as our own and enjoy worldly pleasures. Special Point
The result of serving worldly objects is that attachment to them increases, which is the cause of rebirth and all kinds of suffering. In reality, there is no happiness in worldly objects. It appears to be so in the beginning due to ignorance (Eighteenth Chapter, Thirty-eighth Verse). If there were happiness in worldly objects, then the wealthy, the pleasure-seekers, and the powerful would have been happy, but in reality, they are seen to be unhappy and restless. The reason is that worldly objects do not give happiness, have not given happiness, will not give happiness, and cannot give happiness. The desire to enjoy worldly objects has destroyed patience, destroyed attention, created diseases, created anxiety, created restlessness, created regret, created shame, destroyed strength, destroyed wealth, and destroyed peace, and generally, suffering, sorrow, and anxiety arise (as seen in a thoughtful person). Just as thirst in a dream is not quenched by drinking water, similarly, worldly objects do not give peace, nor do they quench the thirst of the mind. A person thinks that if he has a lot of wealth, a lot of accumulation, and a lot of things, then he will get peace, but even after getting them, peace does not come, and instead, the desire for more things increases. The desire for worldly objects continues to increase, and the person keeps thinking, 'And I will get this, and I will get that.' But even if a person gets all the worldly objects, he will not be satisfied. The reason is that the jiva is an immortal part of the Supreme Being and is conscious, while worldly objects are perishable and are unconscious. The hunger of the conscious cannot be quenched by the unconscious. Hunger is in the stomach, and if we tie a sweet dish on the back, how can the hunger be quenched? Even if we give a delicious halwa to a person who is thirsty, how can the thirst be quenched? 1 - We have not enjoyed worldly objects, worldly objects have enjoyed us; we have not practiced austerities, we have been practiced; time has not passed, we have passed; thirst has not decreased, we have decreased (Bhartrihari's Vairagya Shataka). 2 - Desire is not satiated by the enjoyment of desires; just as the fire is not extinguished by pouring ghee, but rather it is strengthened (Manu 2.94; Shrimad Bhagavat 9.19.14). 3 - Whatever wealth, grain, animals, and women are on this earth, they are not sufficient for one person; therefore, one should give up desire (Vishnu Purana 4.10.24; Mahabharata, Adi Parva 85.13)

The thirst of the living being cannot be quenched. Similarly, the living being has a thirst to move in a particular direction, but it cannot make a firm decision (Gita- Ch. 2, Verse 42). The Supreme Consciousness, however, wants to quench this thirst of the living being. The living being cannot be satisfied by material objects, as it is not possible to attain satisfaction through them. The more the living being takes on material objects, the more its thirst increases. This is a great mistake of the living being! A seeker should make a firm decision today that he will not engage in sensual activities. His firm resolve should be that no matter how much the world offers him, he will not be satisfied. When the seeker makes this firm decision, his senses become detached from worldly objects, and his mind becomes unattached. When the mind becomes unattached, the intellect becomes calm, and when the intellect becomes calm, the seeker experiences the Supreme Consciousness directly (Gita- Ch. 5, Verse 19). The Supreme Consciousness is always present, but the seeker does not experience it due to his attachment to worldly objects. The attachment to worldly objects and the attachment to accumulating wealth are two things that a person becomes attached to. However, the form of the Supreme Lord and the name of the Lord are always dear to a person. Saints have also experienced this and have said:

"Leave aside the taste of Maya, which is sweet like nectar. Drink the nectar of the name of the Lord again and again. The Lord is dear to me."

The attachment to worldly objects makes a person's own self insignificant, and the body becomes the most important thing. Therefore, a person becomes like the world itself (Gita- Ch. 7, Verse 13). * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The devotee is considered the best yogi among yogis (Gita - 6th Chapter, Verse 2). It is as if the Lord says that a person who is overcome by attachment is a servant of the Tamas guna (the third guna). He is so engrossed in the enjoyment of worldly objects that he does not even think about the consequences. He is only concerned with enjoying and accumulating wealth. The knowledge of such a person is shrouded by the Tamas guna. Therefore, he cannot understand the distinction between the body and the Self. In the process of becoming gunatita (beyond the gunas), one's own efforts are helpful (because one's own discrimination is helpful). However, in the process of attaining love (prema), the grace of the Lord is the only factor. - 'Vimudha nana upashyanti' - Just as we remain the same despite performing various activities, similarly, even after giving up the body and taking on another body, and while enjoying worldly objects, 'the Self' remains the same. The implication is that change occurs in actions, but not in the Self. However, one who identifies the Self with various actions (as mentioned in the 23rd verse of the 3rd Chapter) is called an ignorant person (tattva-jnaanee). Dull people are so attached to enjoyment and accumulation that they do not even think about the fact that the body and its objects are not permanent. They do not consider the consequences of their actions. In the 17th Chapter of the Gita, the Lord has described the objects that are dear to sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic people. In this, the consequences of sattvic objects have been described first, the consequences of rajasic objects have been described last, and the consequences of tamasic objects have not been described at all (Gita - 17th Chapter, Verses 8-10). The reason for this is that the sattvic person considers the consequences of his actions before performing them, the rajasic person performs actions first and then considers the consequences, and the tamasic person does not even consider the consequences. *
Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
-
The jiva (conscious) entity, having disregarded the gift of discrimination given by God, remains unchangeable. In it, the concepts of 'you are', 'this is', and 'that is' are considered to be the body (jada), and 'I am' and 'my' are considered to be the relationship with the body. This is what is said, but 'I am' is not said to be the body; rather, it is said that 'I am bound to the jiva.' The reason for this is that the relationship 'I am' is considered to be the cause of 'I am.' This relationship has arisen due to the fact that 'I am' is considered to be the cause of 'I am.' As long as 'I am' exists, 'I am' is firm, and it is not released even after death. It is as crude as the concept of one-sidedness or limitation. 'I am' can be released at any time. When it is released, only 'is' remains. The jiva is completely free to form or break relationships. Using this freedom, the jiva considers itself to be related to non-related substances such as the body and other objects. By not giving importance to its own discrimination (the knowledge of its difference from the body), discrimination is suppressed. When discrimination is suppressed, the body (jada-tattva) becomes prominent, and it appears to be true. As discrimination develops through the practice of sat-sang, self-study, etc., the relationship considered with the body is gradually released. When discrimination is awakened, the jiva experiences its true relationship with the Supreme Consciousness (Chinmay-tattva), and it experiences its natural state in it. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Atmani avasthitam.'

The concept of 'I am' (ahanta) arises due to the relationship with the world of vikar (samsara). This ahanta is of two types: (1) acceptance through hearing, such as 'I am so-and-so' or 'I am of such-and-such varna', and (2) acceptance through action, such as giving lectures, teaching, or practicing medicine. These two types of ahanta are not permanent, but 'is' is a permanent reality. When the concept of 'I am' is given up, the concept of 'is' is also given up, and the yogi experiences his true state in the permanent reality of 'is.' This is the experience of realizing one's own essence. Marmik baat
The meaning of 'Atmani avasthitam' is that 'is' is present in 'I am,' and 'I am' is present in 'is.' In other words, the individual (vyakti) is present in the universal (samasthi), and the universal is present in the individual. Just as the ocean and the waves cannot be separated from each other, 'is' and 'I am' cannot be separated from each other. However, just as the ocean and the waves are not separate in reality (they are both the same water), 'I am' and 'is' are not separate in reality (they are both the same Supreme Consciousness). To experience this is to experience one's own essence. The concept of 'I am' (ahanta) is the cause of not experiencing the Supreme Consciousness in oneself. Therefore, due to the concept of 'I am,' one experiences distance or separation from the Supreme Consciousness and has to wander from place to place to attain it. The more objects one sees as separate from oneself, the more one experiences separation. However, one who experiences the Supreme Consciousness in oneself does not experience separation. Jagah-jagah
Experiencing the Supreme Consciousness in oneself is not a supporter of duality (dvaitabhav), but rather a destroyer of it. In reality, the concept of 'I am' is the supporter of duality. Man has forgotten the concepts of limitation, dependence, absence, ignorance, etc. (vikar) and has considered them to be his own. To remove these vikar, one has to experience the Supreme Consciousness in oneself. These vikar exist as long as the sanchalak sees 'I am' and not 'is.' When 'is' is seen in place of 'I am,' there is no vikar; because 'is' has no vikar at all. The world is changing. Due to being a part of the world, the concepts of 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' are said to be related to the world, and their basis is the Supreme Consciousness ('is'). These four are constantly changing, but 'is' is eternal. 'I' is also changing, such as 'I am a child' or 'I am a young man.'

* Tamatmasthan ye'nupashyanti dhiraas te'shvatam sukham shaashvatam netare'sham *

Those wise men who constantly see the Supreme Consciousness (Atman) in themselves alone attain eternal happiness, and not others.

The self-proclaimed 'I' says, 'I am old', 'I am sick', 'I am healthy', and so on. Just like the world, 'I' too is born and destroyed. As the world does not exist, so 'I' do not exist. What is, is beautiful, what is not, is not beautiful. Do not see what is not, see what is. 'Is' is always there and 'is not' never exists. 'Is' does not appear when seen, but 'is not' appears when seen; because the one by whom we see 'is not' is also a part of 'is not'. To see 'is not' in the three states (jagrat, swapna, and sushupti) is a form of similarity, i.e., the knowledge that arises from the three states is a form of similarity. Therefore, 'is not' can only be seen by 'is not' itself, not by 'is'. The knowledge of 'is' is independent of the three states. Although 'is not' has no independent existence, its existence is only apparent due to the existence of 'is'. 'Is' is the illuminator and foundation of 'is not'. Just as we can see the world through the eyes, but not the eyes themselves, similarly, the one who knows everything cannot be known through any means. The one who is illuminated by 'is' cannot illuminate 'is' itself. This is not possible through 'is not'. It is only through one's own self that one can experience the self. No external help is needed to experience the self. One cannot know the self through the senses, mind, or intellect. Because all these are the products of nature and are therefore limited. One can only experience the self by transcending the limitations of nature. The biggest mistake of the seeker is that he wants to know the self in the same way as he knows the world. But the way to know the self is different from the way to know the world. The world can be known through the senses, mind, and intellect, but the self cannot be known in this way. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Verse 11 ]
* The Nectar of the Seeker *

Those who know the Supreme Lord as their own and the Supreme Lord as the ultimate reality, the yogis with eyes of knowledge, experience the Supreme Lord, separate from the body, senses, mind, and intellect, within themselves. However, those who consider the body as their own and the body as the ultimate reality, the bewildered and unenlightened people, cannot experience the Supreme Lord, even after making great efforts with the body, senses, mind, and intellect. (2)
The Lord has said in the phrase 'avasthitam' that He is situated in the Self of all beings (omnipresent). To experience this, the seeker must firmly believe in the following four things:
1. The Supreme Lord is present here. 2. The Supreme Lord is present now. 3. The Supreme Lord is present within me. 4. The Supreme Lord is mine. Since the Supreme Lord is omnipresent, He is present here; since He is present in all three times, He is present now; since He is present in all beings, He is present within me; and since He is present in all, He is mine. From this perspective, since the Supreme Lord is present here, there is no need to go to another place to attain Him; since He is present now, there is no need to wait for the future to attain Him; since He is present within me, there is no need to search for Him outside; and since He is mine, there is no need to consider anyone else as mine. They will naturally be very dear to me. The above four things are extremely important and beneficial for every seeker. The seeker must firmly believe in these four things. This is the essence of all spiritual practices. There is no need for any qualification, practice, or virtues. These things are self-evident and true, so everyone is eligible, worthy, and capable of accepting them. The only condition is that they must desire only the one Supreme Lord. Those who have not purified their inner self are called 'akritatmanah' (unenlightened). The reason for this is that they do not give importance to the knowledge of the distinction between the real and the unreal (viveka). 989
Those who have a sense of importance for worldly objects and people and who consider the body as their own and seek pleasure and wealth from it are 'akritatmanah' and 'achetasa' (unenlightened). Such people may engage in spiritual practices like meditation, study, and prayer, but they do not experience the Supreme Lord because their inner self is still attached to worldly objects. Although their efforts are not entirely fruitless, they do not experience the Supreme Lord in the present moment. The experience of the Supreme Lord can only be had by completely renouncing worldly attachments. The rule is that one cannot abandon the one whose refuge they have taken. Therefore, the seeker cannot renounce worldly attachments by taking refuge in the body, mind, and intellect, which are worldly objects. Besides, the seeker's subtle ego remains attached to these worldly objects, and it is only by renouncing this ego that it is eliminated. The easiest way to renounce worldly attachments is to take refuge in the one Supreme Lord, that is, to accept the reality that 'I am the Supreme Lord, and the Supreme Lord is mine.' There is no need to make any effort or practice for this. It is enough to firmly accept the truth.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 15 ]
[Verse 12]
Commentary - Always, pleasure and wealth do not stay with a person, nor does the accumulation of wealth stay with him - this discrimination is innate in a man. However, the person who, even after reading scriptures, engaging in good company, and practicing spiritual disciplines, does not pay attention to his own discrimination, does not experience separation from pleasure and wealth, is an 'akritatma' (one without self-awareness). Such a person is called 'akritabuddhi' and 'durmati' in the sixteenth verse of the eighteenth chapter. Although attaining the Supreme is not difficult, yet due to attachment, desire, and a sense of pleasure, they do not know the Supreme even after practicing spiritual disciplines. The reason is that the person who is attached to pleasure and wealth does not have a steady discrimination. In the previous verse, those who were called 'vimoodhah' are now called 'achetasah', because they are deluded by attachment to qualities and do not know the distinction between the objects of the world and their own nature, i.e., the distinction between the union and separation of objects and their own nature. Up to the eleventh verse of this chapter, the Lord wants to explain that my essence, the jiva-atma, is completely separate and the material (body, etc.) which it considers as its own is also completely separate - 'prakritisthan'. Just like the division between the sun and the night, their division is completely different. Their mutual union is not even possible. Only the one who sees the division of both the jiva and the material as completely separate is a jnani (one with knowledge) and a yogi. But the one who sees them as united is an ignorant and worldly person. Connection - The fifteenth chapter has five-five verses, divided into four sections. This third section is from the twelfth to the fifteenth verse, including the sixth verse, which makes five verses complete. This third section is especially meant to reveal the Lord's power and importance. In the sixth verse, the subject (the sun, moon, and fire cannot illuminate the supreme abode) was not clearly explained, and now the Lord explains it clearly in the next verse. Yadādityagataṃ

पदार्थ कोई नहीं है। चन्द्र, अग्नि, तारे, विद्युत् आदि जितने

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 10 ]
[ Verse 12 ]

'The Lord is the teacher of all ancestors; for His power is not bound by time.'

There is no physical entity in the entire material world that is as radiant as the sun. The moon, fire, stars, electricity, and other luminous objects all derive their light from the sun. Since the sun's radiance is so extraordinary and powerful, it is only natural to assume that the Lord Himself is even more extraordinary and powerful. This thought naturally draws one towards the Lord. The sun is the deity presiding over the eyes. Therefore, the light (ability to see) in the eyes should be understood to have originated from the Lord Himself. 'Yad chandraṃsi' – just as the sun's luminous and fiery energies are derived from the Lord, similarly, the moon's luminous and nourishing energies are also bestowed by the Lord. Just as the Lord's radiance is 'āditya' (solar), similarly, His radiance is also 'candra' (lunar). The moon's luminous and nourishing qualities, along with its coolness, sweetness, and nourishing properties, are all manifestations of the Lord's power. The moon is the deity presiding over the mind. Therefore, the light (ability to think) in the mind should be understood to have originated from the Lord Himself. Fire is the deity presiding over speech. Therefore, the light (ability to speak) in speech should be understood to have originated from the Lord Himself. 'Tat tejo viddhi māmākam' – the radiance that is present in the sun, moon, and fire, and that is reflected in other luminous objects (stars, planets, electricity, etc.), should be understood to be the Lord's radiance. The Lord is saying that a person should recognize His presence in every radiant object that attracts him. Just as the sweetness in a laddoo is not its own, but that of sugar, similarly, the radiance in the sun, moon, and fire is not their own, but that of the Lord. The entire world is illuminated by the Lord's radiance – 'Tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṃ vibhāti' (Katha Upanishad 2.2.15). He is the light of all lights – 'Jyotiṣām api taj jyotiḥ' (Bhagavad Gita 13.17). The sun, moon, and fire are respectively the deities presiding over the eyes, mind, and speech, and are the ones that illuminate them. A person uses his eyes, mind, and speech to express and understand his thoughts. These three senses are the ones that radiate the most light, and not the other senses. The light that is present in the eyes and speech is not their own, but that of the Lord. 'Yad agnau' – just as the Lord's radiance is 'āditya' (solar), similarly, His radiance is also 'agni' (fiery). The implication is that they are external instruments, and the mind is the internal instrument. The instruments (senses) derive their power from the Lord, and not the other way around. The radiance that is present in fire, electricity, lamps, and other objects is not their own, but that of the Lord. Parishishta Bhaav – The Supreme Lord is the source of all powers. There is a story in the Kena Upanishad that illustrates this point. Once, the Supreme Lord granted victory to the gods over the demons. However, the gods became arrogant and thought that they had achieved victory through their own power. To correct their misconception, the Supreme Lord appeared before them in the form of a yaksha. The gods were amazed and wondered who this yaksha was. They asked Agni, the fire god, to find out the yaksha's identity. Agni replied that he was the famous fire god, Jataveda, and that he could burn down the entire earth if he so desired. The yaksha then asked Agni to burn a small twig, but despite Agni's best efforts, he could not burn it. Agni was embarrassed and returned to the gods, saying that he could not identify the yaksha. The gods then sent Vayu, the wind god, to find out the yaksha's identity. The yaksha asked Vayu to blow out a small flame, but Vayu could not do so. The gods then realized their mistake and understood that the Supreme Lord was the source of all powers.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

After explaining the significance of the word 'Soma' in the previous shloka, now the Lord explains in this shloka that the power of Soma is that it has the power to nourish and give life. The power of Soma is that it brings forth the nectar from the moon and then it is distributed to the earth. The moon is the nourisher of all plants and trees. The moon is the provider of nourishment to all living beings. The moon is the one who gives life to all living beings. Here, the word 'Soma' refers to the moon, not the moon's orbit. The moon that we see with our eyes is the moon's orbit. The word 'Oushadhi' refers to all kinds of grains, such as wheat, barley, etc. The power of the moon is that it nourishes all living beings, including humans, animals, birds, etc. The power of the moon is that it gives life to all living beings. The power of the moon is that it nourishes all living beings. The moon's power of nourishment is not its own, but it is the power of the Lord. The Lord is the one who creates the moon and its orbit. The Lord is the one who nourishes all living beings through the moon. The Lord is the one who gives life to all living beings. Parishishta Bhaav - The earth, the moon, etc. are all the Lord's aparapratya (material) nature (Gita - 7th chapter, 4th shloka). Therefore, everything that sustains, produces, protects, and nourishes these aparapratya is the Lord Himself. The Lord's power is such that the aparapratya is inseparable from the Lord. Here, the word 'Soma' refers to the moon, which is above the sun. Sambandh - After explaining the power of the moon in the context of the collective power, now the Lord explains the power that is operating in the individual world. Praaninam

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
-

Special Point Related to Paramatma's Acquisition
Explanation— 'sarvasya ca aham hrdi sannivishtah' * — The Supreme Being is obtained in the 'heart'. (Gita - Thirteenth Chapter, Verse 14)
After describing His own glories, the Lord now reveals the secret that I am present in the hearts of all beings. Although the Lord is present in the body, senses, mind, intellect, etc., He is especially present in the heart. The heart is the main organ of the body. All kinds of emotions arise in the heart. Emotions are the main factor in all actions. The purity of emotions leads to the purity of all objects, actions, etc. Therefore, the importance lies in emotions, not in objects, persons, actions, etc. The heart's importance arises from the fact that it is the seat of emotions. As the heart is the seat of the sattvic quality, the Lord is especially present in the heart. The Lord says that I am extremely close to every human being in his heart; therefore, no seeker should be disheartened by the experience of separation from Me. Therefore, whether one is a sinner or a virtuous person, a fool or a wise person, poor or wealthy, sick or healthy, etc., any man or woman, regardless of caste, creed, profession, country, time, or circumstances, is eligible for the acquisition of the Supreme Being. The only necessity is a strong desire, eagerness, and anxiety for the acquisition of the Supreme Being, without which one should not remain. The Supreme Being is actually attainable by man, but due to the attachment to the world, the attachment is directed towards the world, and the Supreme Being, who is always attainable, appears to be unattainable. As soon as the attachment to the world is completely severed, the Supreme Being, who is present everywhere, becomes self-evident. The actions, discussions, and contemplations that are done for the sake of the Supreme Being are done with the help of attachment (to the world). This is because it is impossible to perform these actions without the help of attachment. The purpose of these actions is to sever the attachment to the world. As long as these actions are done for one's own benefit, the attachment to the world is not severed. It is a wrong notion that the acquisition of the Supreme Being depends on some special means, qualities, qualifications, characteristics, etc. The principle is that the thing obtained in exchange for some value is of lesser value. Therefore, if the acquisition of the Supreme Being is considered to depend on some special means, qualities, etc., then the Supreme Being would be of lesser value, whereas the Supreme Being is not of lesser value than anything else. (Gita - Eleventh Chapter, Verse 43)
Therefore, the Supreme Being is all-pervading and equally present everywhere, yet He is obtained in the heart. Just as milk is present in the entire body of a cow, yet it is obtained from the cow's udder, or just as water is present everywhere in the earth, yet it is obtained from a well, etc., similarly, the Supreme Being is present in the sun, moon, fire, earth, etc., yet He is not obtained from them. Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
If the attainment of the Supreme Being is considered to be in exchange for value (means, qualifications, etc.), then what benefit would we get from them? Because we already have more valuable things (means, etc.) than them! Just as worldly things are obtained through actions, the attainment of the Supreme Being is not obtained through actions; because the attainment of the Supreme Being is not the fruit of any action. The origin of every action is egoism, and the attainment of the Supreme Being is when egoism is destroyed. Because egoism is a creation (action), and the Supreme Being is uncreated. How can an uncreated entity be obtained through a creation - 'na asti krtah krtena' (Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.12). The meaning is that the attainment of the Supreme Being is not through the means of the mind, intellect, senses, body, etc. (jada substances), but rather through the rejection of jada-ness. As long as the mind, intellect, senses, body, place, time, object, etc. are taken as a refuge, the Supreme Being cannot be taken as a refuge. The attainment of the Supreme Being will be through the rejection of the mind, intellect, senses, body, etc. - this is the fundamental mistake of the seeker. If the refuge and faith in jada-ness are lost, and only the Supreme Being is taken as a refuge and faith, then there will be no delay in the attainment of the Supreme Being. *
* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The forgetting (vismriti) of the three - nishkama bhava (karma yoga), svarupa bodha (jnana yoga), and bhagavat prema (bhakti yoga) - is present in the jiva from time immemorial. Once their remembrance (smriti) arises, forgetting does not occur again; because this remembrance is awakened in the 'svarupa' (the Self). The worldly remembrance (buddhi's weakening) that occurs in the 'buddhi' can be destroyed, but the remembrance that occurs in the 'svarupa' is never destroyed. The knowledge of a subject is called 'jnana'. All the worldly and paraarthik knowledge is the appearance of the Supreme Being, the Jnana-svarupa. Therefore, the Lord says that this knowledge is His own. In reality, knowledge is that which is known from the 'svarupa' itself. Due to being anantha, purna, and nitya, there is no doubt or delusion in this knowledge. Although the knowledge obtained through the senses and intellect is also called 'jnana', it is limited, imperfect, and changeable, and therefore doubt or delusion remains in it; just as the sun appears small in the sky, etc. The knowledge that was previously understood through the intellect, appears wrong when the intellect becomes more developed or purified. The meaning is that the knowledge obtained through the senses and intellect is karana-sapaksha and limited. The limited knowledge is called 'ajnana'. In contrast, the knowledge of the 'svarupa' is not dependent on any karana (senses, intellect, etc.) and is always complete. The removal of doubts, delusions, and contradictions, etc. is called 'apohan'. The Lord says that these defects are also removed by His mercy. The scriptures are true or false? Who has seen the Lord? The world is true, etc. - these doubts and delusions are also removed by the Lord's mercy. The perception of one's own benefit in worldly things, the perception of happiness in obtaining them, the perception of the world's existence, etc. are also contradictory views, which are the parts of the Supreme Being, but the jiva, due to ignorance, becomes detached from the Supreme Being and starts to consider its relationship with the world. The destruction of this ignorance, and the direct experience of 'I am the Lord's own, not the world's' is the 'smriti' (Gita 18.73). In smriti, there is no new knowledge or experience, but only the removal of the defects by the Lord's mercy. The Gita's teacher says in the end

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Arjuna also destroyed his attachment due to the mercy of God. Even the wise do not take a decision (they accept the realization of the Supreme and the destruction of doubt - Gita - Second Smriti). Therefore, only by taking refuge in God, who is the knower of the true meaning of the Vedas, can they understand the true meaning of the Vedas and be free from 'shruti-vipratipatti' (doubt about the Shruti) and 'shruti-vipratipatti' (contradiction with the Shruti). (Eighteenth Chapter, 73rd Verse). 'Vedaischa sarvairevam eva vedyah' - Here, the word 'sarvairevam' refers to the Vedas and all other scriptures that are in harmony with the Vedas. The ultimate purpose of all scriptures is to reveal the true knowledge of the Supreme or to attain it. Here, God makes it clear that the true meaning of the Vedas is to attain Him, not to attain worldly pleasures. The reason that the Shruti (scriptures) describes the samskaras (dispositions) of the kamik (worldly) people in detail is that the number of kamik people is more in the world. Therefore, the Shruti (scriptures) also follows them. Only one, the Supreme, is worthy of being known, and when He is known, there is nothing else to be known. Without knowing the Supreme, the knowledge of the world is incomplete and always remains incomplete. Arjuna had a special desire to know God. Therefore, God says that I, who am the knower of all the Vedas and scriptures, am present before you. 'Vedantakrit' - The Vedas were revealed by God Himself (Gita - Third Chapter, 15th and 17th Verses). Therefore, only He can explain the ultimate meaning of the Vedas and reconcile the apparent contradictions in the Vedas. Therefore, God says that I am the one who truly understands the ultimate meaning of the Vedas and can reconcile the apparent contradictions. 'Vedavid eva cha aham' - God alone truly understands the meaning, spirit, and purpose of the Vedas. He alone knows what is said in the Vedas, what is the spirit behind it, and what is its ultimate purpose. Because the Vedas were revealed by God Himself, He alone knows the true meaning of the Vedas. In this (15th) Chapter, the first verse, God had called the person who knows the true nature of the world 'Vedavit'. Now, in this verse, God calls Himself 'Vedavit'. The meaning of this is that a great person who knows the true nature of the world becomes one with God. The meaning of knowing the true nature of the world is - 'The world is not independent, and the power of the Supreme is supreme.' By knowing this, one leaves the relationship with the world and establishes a relationship with God. Special point related to the topic

God has described His various glories in four chapters of the Shrimad Bhagavad Gita - in the 7th Chapter, from the 8th to the 12th verse, God has described 17 glories of the Supreme as the cause of the primary substances of the world, and has established His omnipresence and all-pervasiveness. In the 9th Chapter, from the 16th to the 19th verse, God has described 37 glories of the Supreme as the cause of action, behavior, substance, etc., and has established Himself as all-pervading. The 10th Chapter is itself called 'Vibhuti Yog'. In this chapter, in the 4th and 5th verses, God has described 20 glories of the Supreme as the disposition of living beings, and in the 6th verse, He has described 25 glories of the Supreme as the individual. Then, from the 20th to the 41st verse, God has described 62 primary glories of the Supreme in detail. In this 15th Chapter, from the 12th to the 15th verse, God has described 13 glories of the Supreme to establish His power. * Even if one studies the Vedas in detail, if he does not know the Supreme, who is the object of knowledge of the Vedas, he is a fool who only bears the burden of the Vedas. * (Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, 318.50)

The description of the divine qualities has been given. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The purpose of describing the divine qualities in the four previous chapters is that the seeker should experience the truth that 'Vasudeva: sarvam' (Gita 7.19) 'everything is Vasudeva' (i.e., the ultimate reality is one with God). Therefore, when describing their divine qualities, the Lord has especially proven their omnipresence, as if—

'Mattah parataram na anyat kinchidasti' (7.7)
'There is nothing greater than me in this world.'

'Sadasatchaham Arjuna' (9.19)
'I am the truth and the untruth.'

* Chapter 15
The one who is the source of light and the foundation of everything. Knowledge (the self-luminous Paramatma) is present in every object before it is perceived. Therefore, even though the world is said to be pervaded by Paramatma, in reality, the world comes later, and its foundation is Paramatma, i.e., Paramatma is perceived first, and then the world. However, due to attachment, a person's vision does not go to the source of light (Paramatma). There is no existence of the world without the existence of Paramatma. However, due to the lack of attention towards Paramatma and attachment to worldly objects, a person perceives the existence of those objects as separate from Paramatma. If attachment or attachment to worldly objects were to cease entirely, then the true existence of Paramatma would be perceived. The meaning of the description of divine qualities is that 'Na tadasti vina yatsyam maya bhutam characharam' (10.39)
'There is nothing in this world that exists without me.'

The implication is that when a person focuses their attention on any object, they should remember only the one God, i.e., they should see God in every object (Gita – 10th chapter, 41st verse). 'Ahm sarvasya prabhavo mattah sarvam pravartate' (10.8)
'I am the cause of the origin of everything, and everything functions through me.'

'Chari and achari, no being is such that it exists without me; all beings are my very form.'

In the same way, in this 15th chapter, the Lord concludes the description of their divine qualities by saying—

'Sarvasya chaaham hrdi sannivishtah' (15.15)
'I am situated in the hearts of all beings.'

The implication is that all beings, objects, and things are endowed with the existence of Paramatma. There is no separate existence of anything other than Paramatma. Just as a thing is not visible in the absence of light, every object is perceived only in the presence of the source of light. When a person sees an object, they first perceive the light, and then the object is perceived. Every object is perceived only in the presence of the source of light. Similarly, the knowledge of any object, action, or quality is possible only in the presence of a unique and unobstructed light, i.e., knowledge. 1. The thirteen divine qualities described in this chapter are:

(1) The splendor of the sun, (2) the splendor of the moon, (3) the splendor of fire, (4) the power of sustenance of the earth, (5) the power of nourishment of the moon, (6) the sun, (7) the inner controller, (8) memory, (9) knowledge, (10) negation, (11) the one who is known through the Vedas, (12) the creator of the Vedas, and (13) the one who knows the Vedas. 2. In reality, considering oneself small or big based on the number of rupees is a sign of downfall. The number of rupees does not do any work; it is the things bought with rupees that do the work. However, people have given more importance to the increase in the number of rupees rather than its use. Therefore, a person with more rupees considers himself more important in society. A person who gives importance to rupees alone cannot understand the importance of Paramatma. How can such a person develop the desire to attain Paramatma? A person who thinks that he cannot live without rupees or that he cannot do anything without rupees has a fixed idea in his mind.

[ Verse 16 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The seeker cannot comprehend; he cannot understand that the influence of the Divine is required. Consequently, as long as the living being can function adequately even without material wealth, the influence of the qualities (the world) is operative, and therefore a profound need arises to recognize the Lord’s influence. Just as a merchant, whose sole aim is the acquisition of money, sees money in every commercial activity—buying, selling, and all trade‑related actions—so too, the aspirant whose exclusive purpose is the realization of the Supreme Self perceives the Divine essence in every object, action, and principle. This leads to the conviction that nothing exists apart from the Supreme. Describing His own influence, the Lord (from verses 12 to 15 of this chapter) declares that He alone illuminates the entire universe; He alone enters the earth and sustains all living beings; He alone generates food on the earth and nourishes it; when a human consumes that food, He alone, in the form of the cosmic monkey, digests it, and He alone imparts memory, knowledge, and absorption (apohana) to the human. This description proves that, from the beginning, Arjuna in Chapter 14 asked how one may transcend the modes of material nature, and the Lord answered that all actions of the whole creation are ultimately His. The soul becomes entangled in the world only through association with the qualities; therefore, internally, all activity proceeds by their power. To eradicate the ego‑driven attachment to the qualities, the Lord here assumes Himself as the doer of those actions, thereby treating even minor influences as personal deeds and becoming bound by them. **Appendix (Parishishta Bhaav)** – The concluding remark of the opening verse of this chapter is given in this verse. **Significant observation** – In the first three verses the Lord described His powers in terms of influence and action; in the present verse He describes Himself directly. The meaning is that this verse contains a self‑description of the Lord, not a description of his manifestations as Aditya‑born, Chandra‑born, Agni‑born, or Vaishvanara‑born. The underlying principle is singular; only the mode of description differs. From the earlier statement “mamaiva‑aṃśo jīvaloke” it is established that the Lord is “His own”; from “sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭaḥ” it follows that the Lord is “within Himself”. Accepting the Lord as “one’s own” naturally engenders love, and recognizing Him as “within oneself” eliminates any need to seek Him elsewhere. The term “apohanam” means “removal of doubt” (literally, “the removal that has arrived”). “Vedanta” signifies the ultimate conclusion of the Vedas – the essence, as expressed in “ubhayor api dṛṣṭo ’ntaḥ” (Gita 2.16). The Lord says that although there are many Vedas, the knowable reality is one and the same, and He alone is the knower of all. Hence, everything is He. **Relation** – From the first to the fifteenth verse of this chapter (in three sections) the Lord successively expounded the world, the individual soul, and the Supreme. The present two verses summarize that discussion by explicitly naming the three as the perishable (kshara), the imperishable (akshara), and the Supreme Person (purushottama). **Sanskrit verse with word‑by‑word transliteration and meaning**

- **dvāv imau puruṣau** – “two persons” (dvau = two, imau = these, puruṣau = persons)  
- **lokē** – “in the world” (lokē = in the realm)  
- **kṣaraś ca akṣara eva ca** – “the perishable and the imperishable alike” (kṣaraḥ = perishable, ca = and, akṣaraḥ = imperishable, eva = indeed, ca = also)  
- **kṣaraḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni** – “the perishable comprises all beings” (kṣaraḥ = the perishable, sarvāṇi = all, bhūtāni = beings)  
- **kūṭasthaḥ akṣaraḥ ucyate** – “the imperishable, who dwells in the heart, is called ‘Akshara’ ” (kūṭasthaḥ = situated in the heart, akṣaraḥ = imperishable, ucyate = is called). Thus, the verse states: “In this world there are two persons, the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable includes all created beings; the imperishable, residing in the heart, is called Akshara.”

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 15 ]

Exposition: 'The two persons in the world are the perishable and the imperishable' (the perishable is called 'kshara' because it is subject to destruction). Here, the word 'loke' should be understood as referring to the entire world. In this very chapter, the word 'jiva-loke' also occurs in the seventh verse in the same sense. In this world, there are two divisions that are known - the perishable (jada) and the imperishable (chaitanya) living beings. As is clear from reasoning, one is the visible body and the other is the living being residing within it. The living being is the one that makes the life force function, and the body is controlled by it. As soon as the life force leaves the body, the body's functioning comes to an end, and it starts to decay. People burn the body. This is because the importance lies not in the perishable body but in the imperishable living being residing within it. In reality, there is no such thing as 'vyasti' (a particular entity); it is only called 'vyasti' because it is considered a part of the 'samasthi' (the entire world). The difference between the world and the body, etc. is only a matter of attachment (raga-mamatva) and is not real. Only the material and actions are natural. Therefore, the actions of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies are all for the benefit of the world, not for themselves. The imperishable living being is described here by the word 'akshara'. Nature is perishable, and the living being (being a part of the Supreme Consciousness) is conscious. In this very chapter, the third verse, the Lord had said that the destruction of this world (kshara) is to be known. And in the seventh verse, the Lord had said that the living being (akshara) is His part. Here, the world is described by the word 'kshara', and the living being is described by the word 'akshara'. All the material objects (such as the five elements - space, air, fire, water, and earth) that are formed from the five elements are perishable and jada. The gross body is one with the gross world, and the subtle body is one with the subtle world. The causal body is one with the causal world. [Verse 17]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The seer sees no sex in it, and no sex is perceived by the intellect. * The Saviour of the Seeker *

Both the perishable and the imperishable are called 'Purushottam' for the sake of attaining the highest state. Here, the Lord has called both the perishable and the imperishable 'Purush' (the Supreme Being). 'Kshara' is the name given to the perishable world, which was described in the beginning of this chapter as the tree of the world, and whose destruction was urged. Here, 'Bhootani' refers to the gross, subtle, and causal bodies of living beings. This is because here the impermanence of the bodies of living beings is stated. The bodies of living beings are impermanent, but the living beings themselves are not. Therefore, the term 'Bhootani' refers only to the gross bodies. 'Kuta-stho' Akshara Uchyate' - In the seventh verse of this chapter, the Lord described His eternal and imperishable part, which is the individual soul. Here, the individual soul is called 'Akshara' (the imperishable). The individual soul, whether it takes on many bodies or goes to various worlds, remains unchanged and unaltered. It is always the same (Gita - 8th chapter, 19th and 13th verses). Therefore, it is called 'Kuta-stha' (the imperishable). In the Gita, the descriptions of the nature of the Supreme Being and the individual soul are almost identical. Just as the Supreme Being is called 'Kuta-stha' (the imperishable) and 'Akshara' (the imperishable) in the 12th chapter, 3rd verse and the 8th chapter, 3rd verse, respectively, similarly, the individual soul is also called 'Kuta-stha' and 'Akshara' in the 15th chapter, 16th verse. There is a fundamental and essential unity between the individual soul and the Supreme Being. The individual soul is always unchanging and unaltered in its nature; however, due to ignorance, it identifies itself with the body and the material nature, and thus it is called 'Jiva' (the living being). If it were not so, it would be the Supreme Being itself (Advaita Siddhanta). Parishishta Bhaav - In the 6th verse and then from the 12th to the 15th chapters, the Lord described the transcendental nature of the Supreme Being, stating that it is independent and not bound by the laws of nature. The nature of the Supreme Being is transcendental, and the nature of the world is bound by the laws of nature. The world is illuminated by the light of the Supreme Being. All the effects and phenomena that are seen in the world are the result of the Supreme Being's transcendental nature. **********

The world (Kshara) and the individual soul (Akshara) are both bound by the laws of nature and are therefore 'Laukik' (worldly). The Supreme Being, however, is beyond the laws of nature and is therefore 'Alaukik' (transcendental). (Gita 15.17)

The path of Karma Yoga and the path of Jnana Yoga are both worldly (Laukik) - 'Lokasmin dvividha nishtha' (Gita 3.3). Karma Yoga is based on the perishable (Kshara), and Jnana Yoga is based on the imperishable (Akshara). However, Bhakti Yoga is transcendental, and it is based on the Supreme Being. In the 7th chapter, the 'Para Prakriti' (the higher nature) is called 'Kshara', and the 'Apara Prakriti' (the lower nature) is called 'Akshara'. UttaamaH

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Here, the word 'anya' is used to distinguish the Supreme Being (Paramatma) from the eternal soul (jiva-atma) not in the sense that they are different, but in the sense that they are unique. Therefore, the Lord has described Himself as 'nashvan' (transitory) and 'kshar' (impermanent) in the eighteenth shloka, and as 'uttam' (superior) and 'akshar' (eternal) in the eighteenth shloka. Even though the Supreme Being is a part of the jiva-atma, the jiva-atma's perception or attraction is towards the transitory kshar. Therefore, the Lord is described as unique here. 'Paramatmetyudahritah' - the Supreme Being is referred to as 'Paramatma' (the ultimate person). The word 'Paramatma' is considered to be a symbol of the nirguna (beyond attributes) and is used to denote the supreme soul or the soul of all beings. In this shloka, both 'Paramatma' and 'Ishwar' (Lord) are used, indicating that the nirguna and saguna (with attributes) are one and the same. 'Yo lokatrayamavishya bibharti vyaaya Ishwarah' - the ultimate person (Paramatma) pervades all three worlds (the material, the subtle, and the causal) and is the sustainer of all beings. Here, the word 'bibharti' means that the Paramatma is the actual sustainer of all beings, but the jiva-atma mistakenly attributes its own sustenance to the material world and its inhabitants. This results in the jiva-atma experiencing unnecessary suffering. The Lord is described as 'avyaya' (imperishable), meaning that despite sustaining all beings, the Lord does not experience any loss or depletion. The word 'Ishwar' is considered to be a symbol of the saguna (with attributes) and is used to denote the Lord who governs. A poignant point
Although parents care for their child, the child is not aware of who is caring for it, how it is being cared for, and why it is being cared for. Similarly, although the Lord is the sole sustainer of all beings, the ignorant person is not aware of who is caring for them. Only the Lord's devotee who has taken refuge in Him knows that the Lord is the sole sustainer of all beings. The Lord does not show any bias or partiality in caring for His devotees and non-devotees, sinners and virtuous persons, believers and non-believers alike. This is evident from the way the sun shines equally on all, the earth sustains all equally, the fire in the stomach digests all food equally, the air is available equally to all, and food and water satisfy all equally. 'He who is greater than the greatest, hidden, infinite, and the ultimate reality, in whom both knowledge and ignorance reside, is the Supreme Being.'

The perishable material world is referred to as 'avidya' (ignorance), and the imperishable jiva-atma is referred to as 'vidya' (knowledge). The one who governs both knowledge and ignorance is the Supreme Being, who is unique and beyond both. (2) 'Ksharam pradhanamritaksharam harah ksharAtmanavishate deva ekah' - 'The perishable material world is the primary, and the imperishable jiva-atma is the ultimate reality. The one God governs both.'

1 - The concept of sustenance is relevant only in the path of devotion, not in the path of knowledge. This is because the path of devotion recognizes the distinction between the jiva-atma and the Paramatma. 2 - 'Ayuham uttamah ayam adhamah jatyA rUpena samptA vayasA. Shlaghyo'shlaghyo vettham na vetthi BhagavAnanugrahAvasare' - 'The one who is superior or inferior in birth, wealth, or age is not known to the Lord when He is pleased.'

The inner self is the consumer of inner feelings, just like the great cloud is the consumer of the rain. Does the cloud think about whether it is raining over the khadira (acacia) or the champak (champak) tree? (From the commentary of Prabodhasudhakar, 252-253)

Continuation of Commentary - The meaning of 'anya' (other) is that the Purushottam (Supreme Being) is beyond the mundane (laukik) and the transcendental (alaukik) both. Therefore, the Supreme Being is not a subject of thought, but a subject of faith and trust. The proof of the existence of the Supreme Being is the Bhakt (devotee), the saint, the great soul, the Vedas, and the Shastras. The explanation of 'anya' is given by the Lord in the next shloka. The meaning of the words 'yo lokatrayam aavishya...' (which covers the meaning of the 12th to 15th shlokas) is that the duty of a human being is in the human world, but the duty of the Lord is in all three worlds. In reality, the Lord has no duty, but He performs duty for the benefit of the jivas (living beings) (Gita - 3rd chapter, 22nd, 23rd, and 24th shlokas). Connection - The previous shloka described the unity of the supreme person with himself, and now, the incarnate Lord Sri Krishna reveals his most confidential secret. Chottamah. Ato 'smi lokeshu vedesu cha prathitah purushottamah. 18. Yasmat

Explanation - 'Yasmat ksharamatito 'ham' - The meaning of these words is that the Lord incarnates (takes an avatar) (Gita - 4th chapter, 6th shloka), while the jiva (soul) remains unchanged, unchanging, and unattached (Gita - 8th chapter, 19th shloka). Therefore, I am beyond the imperishable (Kshar). This is the reason why I am beyond the perishable (Kshar). (3) The Supreme Being is always unattached (Gita - 4th chapter, 14th and 9th shlokas), while the jiva has to make an effort to become unattached (Gita - 4th chapter, 18th and 7th shlokas). The senses are superior to the body, the mind is superior to the senses, and the intellect is superior to the mind (Gita - 3rd chapter, 42nd shloka). In this way, the body, senses, mind, and intellect are all of the same nature, being material (jada). However, the Supreme Being is far superior to all these, for He is conscious (chetan) and not material (jada). 'Aksharad api chottamah' - Although the jiva (soul) is a part of the Supreme Being (Akshar), the Lord considers Himself to be superior to the jiva. The reason for this is - (1) Even though the jiva is a part of the Supreme Being, it identifies itself with the perishable (Kshar) and gets attached to its qualities, whereas the Supreme Being is beyond the perishable (Kshar) and is never attached (Gita - 7th chapter, 13th shloka). (2) The Supreme Being is beyond the perishable (Kshar) and is not affected by its qualities. The fact that the Lord declares Himself to be beyond the perishable (Kshar) and superior to the imperishable (Akshar) indicates that there is a difference between the two. If there were no difference, the Lord would either be beyond both or superior to both. Therefore, it is established that just as the Lord is beyond the perishable (Kshar) and superior to the imperishable (Akshar), so also the imperishable (Akshar) is beyond the perishable (Kshar) and superior to it. 'Ato 'smi lokeshu vedesu cha prathitah purushottamah' - Here, the word 'lokeshu' means the Puranas, Smritis, etc. The Lord is famous as 'Purushottam' in the Shastras. The name 'Ved' means pure knowledge, which is eternal. This knowledge has been revealed in the form of the Rigveda, Yajurveda, etc. in the past. The Lord is famous as 'Purushottam' in the Vedas as well.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The previous shloka mentioned that the Kshara (transient) and Akshara (eternal) are not at all responsible. There is a superior person who is beyond both of them. The Lord reveals this secret, saying that He Himself is the superior person, the Purushottam. A special note:
(1) The physical creation is Kshara (transient), while the eternal essence of the Supreme Being, the Jiva-atma (individual soul), is Akshara (eternal). Although Akshara is superior to Kshara, it has mistakenly associated itself with Kshara. This is the greatest fault, mistake, or error. This association is merely assumed, and in reality, it does not exist even for a moment. Just as the body has changed completely from childhood to the present, yet we say, "I am the same." We cannot even determine the exact day when childhood ended and youth began, because the body is constantly flowing like a river, while the Akshara (Jiva-atma) remains stationary and unchanged like a rock in the river. If the Akshara (Jiva-atma) were also constantly changing and transient like Kshara, then its calamity would be averted. However, even though the Akshara (Jiva-atma) is immutable and eternal, it mistakenly associates itself with Kshara. This is the calamity that needs to be averted. The solution is to make Kshara (the body and the world) serve Kshara (the world) itself, just as a gardener tends to the garden. [ Chapter 15
(2) In the 15th chapter, the Lord first described the Kshara-sansara (transient world) tree. Then, after cutting it down, He encouraged Arjuna to seek refuge in the Supreme Person, Paramatma, and to renounce attachment to the world. After that, the Lord described the nature of the Akshara (Jiva-atma) and its eternal essence. The Lord then described His own power, stating that His effulgence is present in the sun, moon, and fire; that He pervades the entire universe with His power; that He nourishes all living beings through the moon's rays; that He digests the food consumed by living beings through the fire of digestion; that He resides in the hearts of all living beings as the Antaryami (the inner controller); that He is the source of memory, knowledge, and the destruction of ignorance; that He is the object of knowledge and the ultimate reality that can be known through the Vedas; and that He is the one who decides the ultimate truth and is the knower of the Vedas. After revealing His power, the Lord reveals this most secret truth in this shloka, saying that the one who possesses this power is the Purushottam, the Supreme Person, who is beyond Kshara and Akshara. The Lord has revealed this secret to Arjuna out of special mercy, just as a father reveals his hidden wealth to his son or as a person reveals his identity to a lost traveler, saying, "You are searching for me, but you have not found me because you have not served me. Instead, you have served these transient objects, which are not worthy of being served. Your duty is to serve others, not to identify yourself with them."

Parishishta Bhaav:
The Lord has used the word "Yasmat" (from which) to draw attention to His transcendental nature. The word "Akshara" refers to the Jiva-atma (individual soul) as well as Brahman (the Supreme Being). In the Gita (8.3), it is said, "Aksharam Brahma Paramam" (the Supreme Being is the ultimate, unchanging reality). This word is used to refer to consciousness everywhere, but it is never used to refer to the inanimate. Kshara and Akshara do not have independent existence; only the Supreme Being has independent existence. Both Kshara and Akshara exist within the Supreme Being. However, the Jiva (individual soul) associates itself with Kshara and becomes subservient to it, as it is said, "Yayedam Dharyate Jagat" (the world is sustained by this). The Supreme Being remains untouched and unassociated with Kshara. Therefore, the Supreme Being is superior to the Jiva (individual soul). If the Jiva (individual soul) were to associate itself with the Supreme Being instead of Kshara, it would become one with the Supreme Being, as it is said, "Jnani Tva Atmaiva Me Matam" (the wise one knows that I am the ultimate reality).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

19]
* The Nectar of the Seeker *

1005
Liberation is situated in the form of the imperishable (Brahman), but in devotion, the attainment of the Supreme Being (Purushottama) is even better. The Imperishable is a part, the Supreme Being is the Supreme (Purushottama). Connection - In the twenty-sixth verse of the fourteenth chapter, the Lord had spoken about the unadulterated devotion (avyabhicharini bhakti) and in this fifteenth chapter, a detailed analysis of the world, the living being, and the Supreme Being has been made to attain that devotion. Now, in the next verse, the Lord will summarize it. O descendant of Bharata! He who knows Me as the Supreme Being (Purushottama) in this way,
He worships Me with all his being, O Bharata! 19

Translation:
O descendant of Bharata! 19

Explanation - 'Yo mām evaṁ asammūḍhaḥ' - The jiva-atma (the individual self) is the eternal and unchanging part of the Supreme Being (Paramatma). To consider oneself as a part of the Supreme Being is to know the Lord in His true form. Therefore, to experience the real relationship with the Supreme Being (Paramatma) is to be free from ignorance (asammūḍhaḥ). The connection between the world and the Supreme Being or the understanding of the true nature of the world is obstructed by ignorance (moha). One can gain knowledge of the true nature of a thing only when one has no attachment or aversion towards it. To have attachment or aversion towards worldly things is ignorance (moha). When one understands the world in its true nature, one experiences the unity with the Supreme Being, and when one understands the Supreme Being in His true nature, one experiences the separation from the world. In other words, understanding the world in its true nature leads to the destruction of the attachment to the world, and understanding the Supreme Being in His true nature leads to the experience of the real relationship with the Supreme Being. The attachment to the world is the defect of attachment (vyabhichar-dosha) in devotion. To be free from this defect of attachment is to understand the above-mentioned words. To know the Supreme Being (Purushottama) is to understand. Whatever is seen or heard in the world is all the manifestation of the Supreme Being (Purushottama). To consider this as the truth is to destroy the attachment to the world completely. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 15 ]

When a person understands the Supreme (God), his intellect (faith) is only for the sake of pleasing the Supreme (God). His every thought and action then becomes a worship of the Supreme (God) itself. In this way, to worship the Supreme (God) in all ways is what is called 'avvyabhicharini bhakti' (unwavering devotion). As long as a person considers himself to be related to worldly objects like the body, senses, mind, and intellect with attachment, he cannot worship the Supreme (God) in all ways. This is because wherever attachment is present, the thought (mind) automatically goes there. “

The main thing in the path of knowledge is 'to know' and in the path of devotion is 'to believe'. In devotion, to firmly believe in something without even a slight doubt is what is called 'to know'. After considering the Supreme (God) to be the highest, the devotee worships the Supreme (God) in all ways (Gita - 10th Chapter, 8th Verse). After considering the Supreme (God) as 'Purushottam' (the highest), a person becomes 'sarvavit' (all-knowing), and then worships the Supreme (God) in all ways. By firmly believing in the fact that 'I am the Supreme (God) and the Supreme (God) is mine', one automatically worships the Supreme (God) in all ways. Then, the devotee's actions (eating, sleeping, speaking, walking, etc.) are all worship of the Supreme (God). Parishishta Bhaav – "Yo maam evam sammoohdho jaanaati purushottamam" - He who knows the Supreme (God) is the only truth, is not confused (Gita - 10th Chapter, 3rd Verse). But he who does not know the Supreme (God) is confused - "Avajananti maam muudhaa" (Gita 9.11). 'Sarvavid bhajati maam sarvabhavena Bharat' - Both the ephemeral and the eternal are parts of the Supreme (God); therefore, a person who knows them is not all-knowing (sarvavit). He who knows the Supreme (God) who is beyond the ephemeral and the eternal, is the only all-knowing (sarvavit) person. Such an all-knowing devotee remains attached to the Supreme (God) in all ways - 'Sarvatha varatamoapi sya yogi mayi vartate' (Gita 6.31); because in his view, there is no one else but the Supreme (God). In the Gita, the word 'sarvavit' has come only for the devotee. The devotee knows the entire universe, both the worldly and the transcendental; therefore, he is all-knowing. The worldly cannot be included in the transcendental, but the transcendental can include the worldly. Therefore, a person who knows the transcendental (nirguna tatva) is not all-knowing, but a person who knows the Supreme (God) is all-knowing. Sambandh – According to the 'Arundhati-darshan-nyay' (from the gross to the subtle), the Supreme (God) has explained in this chapter first 'kshar' (the ephemeral) and then 'akshar' (the eternal), and finally described 'Purushottam' (the highest). What is the purpose and meaning of this description? The Supreme (God) will explain this in the next verse. Thus, O sinless Arjuna, the most confidential knowledge has been told to you by Me. Having known this, one becomes wise and accomplished in work, O scion of Bharata. 20.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Verse 20]
* The Saviour of Seekers *

Explanation: 'Angha' - Arjuna was called sinless because he was free from the vice of envy. The vice of envy is a sin. It makes the heart impure. Only one who is free from the vice of envy is a fit candidate for devotion. A confidential matter is only revealed to one who is free from the vice of envy. If a person with envy is told a confidential matter, it has an adverse effect on him. He starts seeing faults in the one who revealed the confidential matter, and also in himself. He starts seeing faults in others as well, saying that the one who revealed the confidential matter is self-praising; 
he is trying to deceive others, etc. This results in great loss to the person with envy. The main reason for envy is pride. A person's pride is based on his own shortcomings. He sees the shortcomings in others. If a person is proud of his own virtues, he sees faults in others. If a person sees faults in others, he develops pride in his own virtues. If the Lord Himself tells a person with envy that He is the Supreme (Purushottam), he will not believe it. On the contrary, he will think that the Lord is self-praising. 'He does not know his own ignorance, and thus he does not recognize the Lord.' (Mansag 7.73.5)
The Lord's presence is not recognized by a person with envy. Therefore, the Lord and the saints do not reveal confidential matters to a person with envy. (See Gita 18.66)
In fact, confidential matters are never revealed to a person with envy. The term 'Angha' can also be used to describe Arjuna because in this chapter, the Lord has revealed a very confidential and mysterious power. This power can only be revealed to a simple and sinless person like Arjuna. 'Idam guhyatam shashtram idam' - After describing the faultless devotion in the 14th chapter, the Lord described the 15th chapter in the 26th verse of the 14th chapter. In this chapter, the Lord has described the 15th chapter from the 1st to the 19th verse. This chapter is a complete and perfect description of the goal and the means to achieve it. In this chapter, the Lord has described the three aspects of the universe - the world, the individual soul, and the Supreme Soul. The Lord has described His own unique power (from the 12th to the 15th verse). Then, the Lord has revealed a confidential matter - that the one who has this power is the Supreme (Purushottam) Himself. The Lord incarnates on this earth in the same way as an actor takes on a role. He behaves in such a way that an ignorant person cannot recognize Him. He does not reveal His true nature, but keeps it a secret. However, in this chapter, the Lord has revealed His true nature in the 18th verse, and has thus revealed a very confidential matter - that He is the Supreme (Purushottam). This chapter is called 'Guhya' because the Lord has revealed a very confidential and mysterious power. It is also called 'Shashtram' because it describes the three aspects of the universe - the world, the individual soul, and the Supreme Soul. In the Gita, which is a complete and perfect scripture, this chapter is the only one to be called 'Shashtram'. The reason for this is that this chapter describes the Supreme (Purushottam) in detail. Therefore, this chapter is called 'Guhya Shashtram'. In this chapter, the Lord has described six ways to attain Him:

(1) To understand the world in its true nature (first verse). (2) To renounce all worldly relationships and take shelter in the Lord (third and fourth verses). (3) To know the Supreme Soul who resides within oneself (eleventh verse). (4) To understand the true nature through the study of the Vedas (fifteenth verse). (5) To know the Lord as the Supreme and to worship Him in all ways (nineteenth verse). In the first verse of the ninth chapter, the Lord had promised to reveal the most confidential knowledge to Arjuna, who was free from envy. In this chapter, the Lord has revealed an even more confidential matter. Therefore, it is appropriate to interpret 'Angha' as 'Anasuya' (free from envy).
