*
Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 15
(6) The essence of the entire chapter is to know the truth (because there is no need to know anything else; for He has explained the knowledge of the supreme being, the Purushottam, in this chapter) (Verse 6) ]. The chapter in which the Lord has described such easy ways to attain Him is indeed a 'Shastr' (scripture). 'Maya ukta' - The Lord says in these words that the entire physical world is illuminated and established by Him, who resides in the hearts of all beings, and is known through the Vedas, and is superior to both the transitory and eternal. This most secret scripture has been explained by Him with great mercy. As I say, no one else can say. Because, the other will first know me (due to my mercy), then he will say something about me, while I am not unaware of myself. In reality, no one else can know the Lord completely except Himself (Gita - 10th chapter, 2nd and 15th verses). In the 42nd verse of the 6th chapter, Arjuna had said to the Lord that no one else can remove his doubts except you. Here, the Lord seems to be saying that there is no possibility of any doubt remaining in the matters that He has explained. 'Etat budhva buddhimann asya atkritakrityash cha bharat' - The Lord has described in this entire chapter the reality of the world, the nature of the individual soul, and His own unparalleled power and secrecy. The instruction to this most secret scripture is given here by the word 'etad'. The person who knows this scripture from the essence of truth becomes a wise person, i.e., one who knows the knowable and the knowable. He has no need to know anything else. The knowledge of the ultimate truth makes a person free from ignorance. Even if one acquires all worldly knowledge, languages, arts, etc., ignorance does not disappear without the knowledge of the ultimate truth, because all worldly knowledge is limited and imperfect. All worldly knowledge is born and dies, and is incomplete. As all worldly knowledge is born from the ultimate truth, how can it reveal the ultimate truth? The person who knows the ultimate truth, even without knowing worldly knowledge, is indeed wise. In the 19th verse, the Lord has called the devotee who is free from attachment and ego 'sarva-vit' (all-knowing). Here, He is called 'buddhimann' (wise). Here, the word 'ca' is a repetition of the previous verse, indicating the result (prapti-praptavyata) of the previous verse. In the previous verse, the Lord has especially mentioned the importance of devotion to Him, which is the greatest benefit. There is no other benefit like devotion to the Lord - 'labhu ki kichhu hari bhakti samana' (Mans 7.112.4). Therefore, the person who acquires devotion to the Lord becomes prapt-praptavy (one who has achieved and has the potential to achieve). The uniqueness of the Lord's nature is that by the practice of karma yoga, jnana yoga, or bhakti yoga, one can achieve three things: krtakrttya (fulfillment), jnata-jnativya (wisdom), and prapt-praptavya (achievement). Therefore, the person who knows the Lord's nature has no need to know anything else, achieve anything else, or do anything else. His human life becomes successful. Parishisht Bhav - The Lord has revealed Himself in this chapter as Purushottam, i.e., the supreme being, and therefore, it is called 'Guhya-tam Shastr' (most secret scripture). A person becomes krtakrttya (fulfilled) by the practice of karma yoga, jnata-jnativya (wise) by the practice of jnana yoga, and prapt-praptavya (achieving) by the practice of bhakti yoga. If a person experiences that he has nothing to do for himself, he becomes krtakrttya. If a person experiences that his body is not his, that he has no control over his body, and that he has no connection with his body, he becomes jnata-jnativya. If a person experiences that he needs nothing, he becomes prapt-praptavy. In this verse, the word 'buddhimann' (wise) indicates the experience of jnata-jnativya. In the previous verse, the word 'sarva-vit' (all-knowing) indicated the experience of prapt-praptavy. In this verse, the word 'ca' indicates the experience of prapt-praptavy. The worldly, transitory, and eternal are prapt-praptavy (achievable). Therefore, the person who knows the ultimate truth, even without knowing worldly knowledge, is indeed wise. *
So, one who knows you, O Lord, is the one who has known you. You know yourself, and thus you become known to yourself. (Mans 2.127.2)
Your mercy is your own, O Raghunandan. The devotees know you, O Lord, and the devotees know the devotees as the sandalwood on their forehead.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The Supreme Being alone is to be attained. This shloka conveys the idea that the devotee attains the fruit of both knowledge yoga and karma yoga, i.e., he becomes jnata (known) and jnayate (to be known) and krtakrti (self-realized) (Gita - 7th chapter, 31st-32nd and 10th chapter, 10th-11th shloka). Om tat sat iti shriimad bhagavad gitaasupanishatsu brahmvidyayaam yogashaastre shriikrishnarjunasamvade purushottamayogo nama pancadaso'dhyayah 15. In this way, with the utterance of the names of the Lord, Om, Tat, and Sat, the Brahma Vidya and Yoga Shastra, in the form of the Shrimad Bhagavad Gita Upanishad, the conversation between Shri Krishna and Arjuna, the 15th chapter, 'Purushottam Yoga', is complete. 15. Understand the topics discussed in this chapter in their true form, as it is written in words. The remaining 15 shlokas have 32 words. If one reads them, one experiences the eternal union with the Supreme Being (3). In this chapter, there is a dialogue, 'Shri Bhagavan uvacha' (3). Therefore, this chapter is named 'Purushottam Yoga'. The 15th chapter has 300 and 6 words in total. The meter used in the 15th chapter

In this chapter, of the 20 shlokas, the second, third, and fourth shlokas are in the 'Upajati' meter, and the fifth and 15th shlokas are in the 'Indravajra' meter. The remaining 15 shlokas have 7th shloka's first and third lines in 'Jati-paksha-vipula', 9th shloka's first line in 'Jati-paksha-vipula', 20th shloka's third line in 'Maga-paksha-vipula', and 19th shloka's third line in 'Maga-paksha-vipula'. The total number of words in this chapter is 576. In this chapter, of the 20 shlokas, the second, fourth, fifth, and 15th shlokas are in the 'Nagana' meter, which is a meter with the suffix 'N-vipula'. The remaining 10 shlokas (1, 6, 8, 10-14, 16-17) have 42 words each, and the third shloka has 45 words, which is exactly like the 'Pathya-avaktra' meter, which has the characteristics of the 'Anushtub' meter. The essence of the 15th chapter

The Lord has described his two natures, Apara and Para, in the 7th chapter (7.4-5). The Apara nature has eight types of divisions - earth, water, fire, air, sky, mind, intellect, and ego. The Para nature, which has taken the form of the universe, is the Jiva (the individual self). Apara and Para are both the nature of the Lord, i.e., His own nature. In the 15th chapter, the Lord describes Apara, Para, and Himself in detail. In the 15th chapter, first, the Lord describes Apara in the form of a tree of the universe, then, from the 7th to the 11th shloka, He describes Para in the form of His own parts, then, from the 12th to the 15th shloka, He describes His own influence. Finally, the Lord describes Apara, Para, and Himself as Kshara, Akshara, and Purushottam, respectively, and concludes the chapter. In the 7th chapter, the Lord has described both Apara and Para as His own nature, i.e., as His own - 'itiyam me' (7.4), 'me param' (7.5). However, in the 18th shloka of the 15th chapter, the Lord describes Himself as beyond Apara (Kshara) and superior to Para (Akshara). This means that as long as the seeker considers Apara and Para as separate entities, the Lord is beyond Apara and superior to Para. But when the seeker's perception is such that Apara and Para are not separate entities, then Apara, Para, and the Lord are one - 'vasudevah sarvam' (7.19), 'sad sach chaham' (9.19). The middle of the 15th chapter describes the meaning of the word 'Akshara' (the individual self). The individual self has one side of Kshara (the universe) and one side of Purushottam (the Supreme Being). The individual self has a relationship with the Supreme Being - 'mamevansho jeevlok' (3.27). Because just as the sparks of a fire are not separate from the fire, the individual self is not separate from the Supreme Being.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 15 ]

The Supreme Consciousness (Paramatma) is eternal, imperishable, and unchangeable. Similarly, the living being (jiva) is also eternal, imperishable, and unchangeable. The relationship of the body with the world is like this: "The mind and the senses are situated in the material nature" (Manas: the mind, and the senses are situated in the material nature). Just as the world is material, perishable, and changeable, the body is also material, perishable, and changeable. The living being cannot be separated from the Supreme Consciousness, and the body cannot be separated from the world. The Supreme Consciousness is described as that which is present everywhere, is all-pervading, is all-powerful, is extremely merciful, and is unique. There is no need to wait for the future to attain it, because it is present now. Since it is present everywhere, there is no need to search for it anywhere. Since it is all-pervading, it is also present in oneself; therefore, there is no need to go anywhere to find it. Since it is all-pervading, it is also one's own; therefore, there will be self-love for it. Since it is all-powerful, there will be no need to be afraid of it. Since it is extremely merciful, there will be no need to be disappointed. Since it is unique, there will be no need to identify or describe it. The reason for not attaining the Supreme Consciousness is that we do not accept its existence and greatness, and we do not consider it as our own. If we accept its existence, greatness, and our relationship with it, then it will not seem unattainable. The Supreme Consciousness becomes dear to us because we accept it as our own. The only way to attain love for the Supreme Consciousness is to accept it as our own. The performance of great pious deeds like yajna, dana, tap, tirtha, and vrat does not lead to love for the Supreme Consciousness, but only accepting it as our own does. The Supreme Consciousness has said, "I am the only part of the living being in this world" (15.7). This means that the living being is only a part of the Supreme Consciousness, and there is no mixture of any other entity. This proves that our relationship is only with the Supreme Consciousness. When we are only a part of the Supreme Consciousness, then how did the body become a part of the material nature? Therefore, the Supreme Consciousness is our own, and no other entity is our own. Because we are only a part of the Supreme Consciousness, we cannot be separated from it, and we cannot leave it. The all-powerful Supreme Consciousness also cannot be separated from the living being, and it cannot leave it. If the Supreme Consciousness leaves the living being, then the living being will become a new Supreme Consciousness, and the Supreme Consciousness will not be one, but many, which is impossible. Since we cannot leave the Supreme Consciousness, we do not even ask about its nature. Therefore, we should love the Supreme Consciousness without thinking about its nature. When a person considers the body as his own and the world as his own, he becomes bound. When he considers the Supreme Consciousness as his own, he becomes free and becomes a devotee. The greatest mistake of a person is that he considers the body, which belongs to the world, as his own, and he forgets the Supreme Consciousness, which is his own. When a seeker accepts the truth that the body is not his own and is not meant for him, then he serves the world automatically. When he accepts the truth that the Supreme Consciousness is his own and is meant for him, then he has love for the Supreme Consciousness. The seeker does not need anything in return for his service, because if he gives everything to the world, then what has he spent? What new endeavor has he made? He does not need anything in return for his love, because there is no such thing that is dearer to him than love, and he needs it. The Lord is for me, so I should offer myself to Him, and I should not take anything from Him. If I take something from Him, then I will be separated from Him, and if I offer myself to Him, then I will be inseparable from Him. Service leads to liberation, and love leads to devotion. Liberation leads to a life without attachment, and devotion leads to a life full of joy.

प्रार्थना की। विभूतियोंका वर्णन करते हुए भगवान्ने दसवें अध्यायके अन्तिम श्लोकमें अर्जुनसे कहा कि 'तुझे
अधिक जाननेसे क्या मतलब? मैं तो सारे संसारको एक अंशमें व्याप्त करके स्थित हूँ।' इसपर उस स्वरूपको
(जिसके एक अंशमें सारा संसार स्थित है ) देखनेके लिये उत्सुक हुए अर्जुनने ग्यारहवें अध्यायके आरम्भमें
भगवान् से अपना विश्वरूप दिखानेके लिये प्रार्थना की।
अर्जुनको अपना विश्वरूप दिखाकर भगवान्ने ग्यारहवें अध्यायके चौवनवें- पचपनवें श्लोकोंमें अनन्य-
भक्तिकी महिमा एवं उसका स्वरूप बताया। इसपर सगुण और निर्गुण - उपासकोंकी श्रेष्ठताके विषयमें अर्जुनने
बारहवें अध्यायके पहले श्लोकमें प्रश्न किया । अतः भगवान्ने बारहवें अध्यायमें सगुण-उपासकोंका वर्णन करके
तेरहवें अध्यायसे चौदहवें अध्यायके बीसवें श्लोकतक निर्गुण-विषयका वर्णन किया। फिर अर्जुनने चौदहवें
अध्यायके इक्कीसवें श्लोकमें गुणातीतके लक्षण, आचरण एवं गुणातीत होनेका उपाय पूछा। उन प्रश्नोंका उत्तर
देते हुए भगवान्ने छब्बीसवें श्लोकमें 'मां च योऽव्यभिचारेण भक्तियोगेन सेवते' पदोंसे अव्यभिचारिणी
भक्तिको गुणातीत होनेका उपाय बताया अर्थात् अव्यभिचारसे दैवी सम्पत्तिका और व्यभिचारसे आसुरी सम्पत्तिका
संकेत किया। वह अव्यभिचारी भक्ति कैसे प्राप्त हो— यह बतानेके लिये पन्द्रहवें अध्यायका आरम्भ हुआ ।
पंद्रहवें अध्यायके तीसरे श्लोकमें भगवान्ने 'असंगशस्त्रेण दृढेन छित्त्वा ' पदोंसे आसुरी सम्पत्तिके
कारणरूप ‘संग’-(संसारकी आसक्ति-) का त्याग करके असंगतासे प्रकट होनेवाली दैवी सम्पत्तिकी बात कही।
फिर चौथे श्लोकमें 'तमेव चाद्यं पुरुषं प्रपद्ये' पदोंसे शरणागतिरूप दैवी सम्पत्तिका वर्णन किया और अर्थान्तरमें
जो शरण नहीं होते, उन आसुरी सम्पत्तिवालोंका संकेत किया। फिर उन्नीसवें श्लोकमें 'स सर्वविद् असम्मूढः
मां सर्वभावेन भजति' पदोंसे दैवी सम्पदावालोंका अर्थात् अधिकारियोंका वर्णन किया और अर्थान्तरमें जो
भगवान्‌का भजन नहीं करते, उन आसुरी सम्पदावालोंका अर्थात् अनधिकारियोंका वर्णन किया।
इस प्रकार अर्जुनके अन्य प्रश्नोंके कारण अबतक भगवान्‌को दैवी और आसुरी सम्पदापर विस्तारसे
कहनेका अवसर प्राप्त नहीं हुआ। अब अर्जुनका कोई प्रश्न न रहनेसे भगवान् इस सोलहवें अध्यायमें दैवी और
आसुरी सम्पदाका विस्तारसे वर्णन आरम्भ करते हैं।

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The Avatarnika (Introduction) –
The Lord has described the people with bad qualities and those who have taken to the path of the asuras (those who have taken to the path of the demonic) in the 15th verse of the 7th chapter, saying, "The foolish and the wicked who are lost to themselves do not surrender unto Me." (Those who have bad qualities and have taken to the path of the asuras do not surrender unto Me.) Similarly, in the 16th verse of the 7th chapter, He has described the people with good qualities and those who have taken to the path of the divine in the 16th verse, saying, "The devotees who have taken to the path of the divine surrender unto Me." (The devotees who have taken to the path of the divine surrender unto Me.)

In the 7th chapter, Arjuna had asked seven questions on the last two verses, and in response to those questions, the 8th chapter was completed. The Lord had promised to explain the knowledge along with the science of the Self in the beginning of the 7th chapter, and for this purpose, the subject of the 9th chapter was started. In the 12th verse of the 9th chapter, He has described the people with bad qualities and those who have taken to the path of the asuras in the 12th verse, saying, "Those who have taken to the path of the asura." (Those who have taken to the path of the asura.) Similarly, in the 13th verse, He has described the people with good qualities and those who have taken to the path of the divine in the 13th verse, saying, "Those who have taken to the path of the divine surrender unto Me." (Those who have taken to the path of the divine surrender unto Me.)

After the 11th verse of the 10th chapter, the Lord was supposed to describe the divine and asura qualities in detail, but due to the influence of the Lord's power, Arjuna began to praise the Lord and requested Him to describe His glories. The Lord, while describing His glories, said in the last verse of the 10th chapter that, "What is the use of knowing more about you? I am present in all the living beings." (What is the use of knowing more about you? I am present in all the living beings.) Arjuna, being eager to see that form, requested the Lord in the beginning of the 11th chapter to show him His universal form. The Lord, by showing Arjuna His universal form, described the glory of unalloyed devotion and its form in the 24th to 31st verses of the 11th chapter. Arjuna then asked a question in the first verse of the 12th chapter about the superiority of the devotees of the Saguna and Nirguna. Therefore, the Lord described the devotees of the Saguna in the 12th chapter and the devotees of the Nirguna from the 13th to the 20th verse of the 14th chapter. Arjuna then asked a question in the 21st verse of the 14th chapter about the characteristics and behavior of the one who is beyond the gunas and the way to become one. In response to that question, the Lord said in the 26th verse that the one who serves Me with unalloyed devotion is beyond the gunas. (The one who serves Me with unalloyed devotion is beyond the gunas.) To explain how this unalloyed devotion is obtained, the 15th chapter was started. In the 3rd verse of the 15th chapter, the Lord said that one should renounce the 'sang' (attachment to the world) with the sword of detachment and that the divine quality will then be revealed. (One should renounce the 'sang' (attachment to the world) with the sword of detachment and that the divine quality will then be revealed.) In the 4th verse, He described the quality of devotion as 'sharanagati' (surrender) and in the inner meaning, He indicated the quality of the asuras who do not surrender. In the 19th verse, He described the devotees who have taken to the path of the divine as 'sarva-vid' (all-knowing) and 'asammoodh' (unbewildered) and who surrender unto Me with all their being. (The devotees who have taken to the path of the divine as 'sarva-vid' (all-knowing) and 'asammoodh' (unbewildered) and who surrender unto Me with all their being.) In the inner meaning, He indicated the devotees who do not surrender unto Me. In this way, due to Arjuna's questions, the Lord had not yet had the opportunity to describe the divine and asura qualities in detail. Now, since Arjuna has no more questions, the Lord begins to describe the divine and asura qualities in detail in this 16th chapter.

* The Saviour of Seekers *

When one attains this, then injustice, evil deeds, and all fears disappear, and one becomes completely fearless. This is because one's goal is never diminished and is never destroyed. (1) When a person's behavior is not good, and he is involved in injustice, cruelty, etc., then he feels fear. Just as Ravana was feared by humans, gods, yakshas, rakshasas, etc., but when he went to kidnap Sita, he himself felt fear. Similarly, when the drums of the Kaurava army's eleven akshauhinis were beaten, it had no effect on the Pandava army (Gita, Chapter 1, Verse 13), but when the drums of the Pandava army's seven akshauhinis were beaten, the hearts of the Kaurava army were shattered (Gita, Chapter 1, Verse 19). The implication is that those who engage in injustice and cruelty have weak hearts and are fearful. When a person gives up injustice and cruelty and purifies his behavior and thoughts, his fear disappears. (2) A person cannot be completely fearless as long as he has not fulfilled his duties, acquired knowledge, and achieved his goals. As long as he has not done so, he will always be afraid. The more a devotee trusts and relies on God, the more he becomes fearless. He thinks to himself, "I am a part of God, and therefore I am immortal. Why should I be afraid?" And since the body and all other material things are constantly being destroyed, why should I be afraid?" When a person has this clear understanding, his fear disappears, and he becomes completely fearless. When a person does not consider himself to be the doer of his actions, he does not have attachment to his body, family, etc. Without attachment, there is no fear of death, and the person becomes completely fearless. "Satvashuddhi" means the purification of the mind. What is purification of the mind? It is to be detached from worldly desires and to develop love for God. When a person's thoughts, feelings, intentions, and goals are all focused on achieving God, his mind becomes pure. This is because the desire to acquire worldly things creates three types of defects in the mind: mal, vikshepa, and avarana. To remove these defects, the scriptures recommend doing selfless work, worship, and gaining knowledge. However, the best way to purify the mind is to not consider oneself to be the doer of actions. A seeker does not need to perform many rituals to purify himself of past sins or to remove new sins committed due to circumstances. He should only focus on his spiritual practice with enthusiasm and dedication. In this way, all his known and unknown sins will be removed, and his mind will become pure. A seeker develops a mindset that spiritual practice and worldly activities are two separate things. He thinks that spiritual practice is one thing, and worldly activities like business and trade are another. He knows that in worldly activities, he may have to engage in deceit and hypocrisy, which can pollute his mind. Therefore, he should always be cautious and not mix spiritual practice with worldly activities. The worldly things that we possess can be a source of fear. We fear that they may be lost, that we may be humiliated, that we may be attacked, that we may become old, that we may be defeated in arguments, that we may be insulted, and that we may die. The only thing that can free us from these fears is detachment. 1. Our goal is already set. We have obtained a human body, and now we need to recognize and fulfill our goal. 2. "Rama died, so I will die. I am a child of the immortal, so I will not be killed."

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

A seeker, due to ignorance, considers himself guilty of the wrongs committed and also considers the person who has caused him harm as guilty, thereby making his inner self impure. To remove this impurity, the seeker should take a firm vow not to commit the wrongs done out of ignorance again, and without asking for forgiveness, he should forgive the person who has caused him harm and pray to God, saying, "Oh Lord! Whatever bad has happened to me is the result of my own wrongdoings. That person has done it out of ignorance and without any malice. He is not at fault. Please forgive him." By doing so, his inner self becomes pure. 'Jnana-yoga-vyavasthiti' - To be established in yoga for the sake of knowledge means to have knowledge (realization) of the Supreme Reality, whether it is saguna or nirguna. This knowledge is essential for yoga. The meaning of yoga is to remain equanimous in the midst of worldly pleasures and pains, to remain unaffected by praise or blame, to remain unaffected by happiness or sorrow, and to remain calm and peaceful in the midst of all worldly activities. 'Dana' - According to worldly perception, the things that are considered valuable are to be given to others, keeping in mind the time, place, and circumstances, and according to one's ability, is called 'dana'. There are various types of dana, such as bhumi-dana, go-dana, suvarna-dana, anna-dana, and vasa-dana, etc. Among these, anna-dana is the most important. However, even more important than anna-dana is abhaya-dana. There are two types of abhaya-dana:

(1) To give fearlessness to a person who is afraid of worldly troubles, obstacles, and circumstances, to give him assurance, and to help him, is called abhaya-dana. This abhaya-dana is related to the physical body and worldly possessions. (2) To free a person from the cycle of birth and death by narrating the stories of God, is also called abhaya-dana. To publish and distribute the scriptures like the Gita, Ramayana, and Bhagavata, and to narrate their stories in simple language, and to give them to people at a low cost, or to explain them to those who understand, so that their welfare may be achieved, is also a form of abhaya-dana. God is very pleased with such a dana, because God is all-pervading. Therefore, the more the welfare of the living beings is achieved, the more God is pleased. This is the highest form of abhaya-dana. In this, the devotee should be careful while narrating the stories of God to others, that he should not consider himself superior to others, but should consider it as the result of God's mercy that God is using him as a medium to benefit the listeners. The above-mentioned dana should not be associated with the devotee's own relationship, but the devotee should consider that whatever he has, whether it is wealth, ability, or qualifications, is given by God for the service of others. Therefore, whatever is given to others, whether it is a little or a lot, should be considered as a dana, and it should be given with the intention of pleasing God. 'Dama' - The control of the senses is called 'dama'. The meaning of this is that no worldly activity should be done that is prohibited by the scriptures. Even the activities that are permitted by the scriptures should be done for the benefit of others, and not for personal gain or pride. By such a behavior, the senses, the mind, and the body remain pure and unattached. The seeker's goal is to control the senses, and therefore, he should not engage in activities that are prohibited by the scriptures, and he should engage in activities that are beneficial to others. 1. The Panchatantra says, "Just as the wise people say that the greatest dana is the dana that gives fearlessness, so also the greatest dana is the dana that gives fearlessness." (Mithra-bhed 313)

2. The Shrimad Bhagavat says, "Oh Lord! Your nectar-like story is the elixir of life for the suffering souls, it is the destroyer of all sins, it is the nectar that is relished by the poets, it is the purifier of the listeners, and it is the greatest dana on this earth. The people who narrate your story are considered to be the greatest dana-givers." (10.31.9)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Pursuit is taking place, and in it, self-interest, pride, attachment, and other impurities have never been absent. Only the impurities of the tendencies do not remain. If one never experiences the true nature of any action, self-interest arises, and it is suppressed, and thus the impurities are eliminated, and purity is established, and eventually, self-control is achieved. 'Yajna' – The word 'yajna' means offering oblations. Therefore, performing homa, balivaishvadeva, and other rituals according to one's varna and ashrama is 'yajna'. Besides, according to the Gita's vision, performing any duty that one obtains at any time, according to one's varna, ashrama, and circumstances, without attachment to self-interest and pride, with a sense of devotion to God or for the benefit of others, is 'yajna'. Furthermore, all actions related to livelihood, such as business, agriculture, and bodily maintenance, such as eating, drinking, walking, sleeping, giving, and taking, performed with devotion to God, are 'yajna'. Similarly, obeying the orders of one's mother and father, guru, and other elders, serving them, and making them happy by providing them with mental, verbal, and physical comfort, and worshiping and honoring cows, brahmins, gods, and the Supreme Being are all 'yajna'. 'Tapas' – Enduring hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and other hardships is also a form of tapas. However, in reality, tapas is to endure difficulties, obstacles, and afflictions that arise due to one's past karma, with equanimity and a sense of devotion, and to cultivate a new strength and power in oneself. A sadhaka should be cautious not to use this tapas to bless others, curse others, or fulfill one's own desires. Rather, one should use this power to increase one's ability to endure difficulties and obstacles in one's spiritual practice. When a sadhaka practices, he encounters various obstacles. He thinks that if he had a quiet place to practice, he could do it, or if the atmosphere were favorable, he could practice. He should not be attached to these favorable conditions. Rather, he should be content with the circumstances that arise and practice with devotion and equanimity. 'Svadhyaya' – The term 'svadhyaya' refers to the study of the scriptures, such as the Gita, the Bhagavata, the Ramayana, and the Mahabharata, and the repetition of the name of God. However, in reality, svadhyaya means to study one's own tendencies and circumstances correctly. A sadhaka should not use his tendencies as a yardstick to measure his circumstances, nor should he be bound by his tendencies. Since tendencies are constantly changing, it is natural to ask whether one can purify them. In reality, a sadhaka's duty is to purify his tendencies, and this purification is achieved by not identifying with one's tendencies and by cultivating a pure heart. This is because identifying with one's tendencies is the root of all impurities. 'Arjavam' – Simplicity and straightforwardness are referred to as 'arjavam'. This simplicity is a special quality of a sadhaka. If a sadhaka wants others to consider him good, he should not pretend to be simple, as this would be a form of hypocrisy. This would lead to artificiality in the sadhaka, whereas he should be straightforward and simple. Even if others consider him foolish or ignorant, he should not be concerned, as this is the highest form of tapas, as stated in the Boddhsar: "One should welcome what comes one's way, not obstruct those who are going, and accept what one gets, and this is the highest form of tapas."

A hypocrite's nature is not simple, but that of a devotee of 'Narayan' is simple, like a boat tied to the shore. [ Chapter 16
Therefore, the behavior of a seeker's body, speech, and mind should not be artificial; it should be natural and straightforward. . Non-violence, truth, absence of anger, self-control, tranquility, compassion, and forgiveness are the qualities of a noble soul. 2. Non-violence = non-violence,

Explanation–‘Non-violence’–is in the body, mind, speech, behavior, and so on; because a person who is attached to worldly pleasures and thinks only of his own self-interest and happiness, does not harm anyone or anything, and does not wish to harm anyone or anything, is called ‘non-violence’. In reality, complete non-violence is when a person turns away from the world and moves towards the Supreme Being. Through this, non-violence is naturally practiced. However, a person who is attached to worldly pleasures and enjoys them with a sense of attachment, can never be completely non-violent. He not only destroys himself but also destroys the objects he enjoys. A person who considers the limited objects of the world as his own, even when they are not, and enjoys them with a sense of attachment, commits violence. This is because considering the objects of the world as one's own, for one's own enjoyment, is violence. If a person considers the objects of the world, which are meant for the service of the world, as belonging to the world itself, and serves the world without attachment, then he can avoid violence and be non-violent. A person who enjoys worldly pleasures with a sense of attachment, causes suffering to those who do not get these pleasures – the unfortunate ones. This is their violence, and their indifference to the suffering of others. However, if a person sees a saint or a great soul who serves others for their benefit, he may feel some suffering, but it will not be considered violence. This is because such a person does not serve others for his own benefit, but for the benefit of others. He does not enjoy worldly pleasures, as he says, 'A person who performs only physical actions, acquires sin' (Gita 4.21). Only a person who moves towards the Supreme Being, and not one who is attached to worldly pleasures, is non-violent. This is because the latter serves worldly objects with a sense of attachment, whereas the former does not serve them at all. A seeker who moves towards the Supreme Being never causes suffering to anyone through his body, mind, or speech. If someone suffers due to his external actions, it is due to his own nature. A seeker should never have the intention to cause suffering to anyone, even slightly. His intention should always be to benefit everyone – 'He who is engaged in the welfare of all beings' (Chapter 12). If someone creates an obstacle in a seeker's spiritual practice, he should not feel angry or have the intention to harm him. This intention is violence. However, if an obstacle arises in his practice of moving towards the Supreme Being, he may feel some suffering, but it will not be like worldly suffering. A seeker, when faced with an obstacle, calls out to the Lord, saying, 'The minds, words, and actions of the great souls are all the same; but the minds, words, and actions of the wicked are all different.'

* The Nectar of the Seeker *

"Oh, Lord! Where have I made a mistake, which is causing the obstacle?"
Thinking this, he might cry; but he cannot harbor anger or hatred towards the one causing the obstacle. When an obstacle arises, the seeker becomes more vigilant and cautious. If he harbors hatred towards the one causing the obstacle, then the extent of hatred is inversely proportional to the extent of his vigilance and caution, and his eagerness to practice. A seeker has two qualities: one is vigilance and the other is eagerness. Vigilance makes him interested in his practice, and eagerness makes him attached to his practice. When he is interested, he becomes aware of the shortcomings in his practice and has the power to remove them, and he also makes an effort to remove them. However, when he is attached, there is a possibility of harboring hatred towards the one who creates obstacles. In reality, it is seen that the obstacle arises due to a lack of interest in our practice. If we are not interested in our practice, then the other person will not create obstacles for us; rather, he will ignore us, thinking that we are stubborn and will not listen. Just as the fragrance of a flower spreads on its own, similarly, the seeker's spiritual essence spreads on its own, and the atmosphere becomes pure. This results in a great benefit and happiness for all living beings. On the other hand, the one who pollutes the atmosphere with his own evil deeds and vices is guilty of harming living beings. "'Satyam' - Truth is to speak and act in accordance with what one has understood and experienced, after considering the well-being of others, without any personal interest or pride. When one's ultimate goal is to attain and know the Supreme Truth, then one's words, actions, and behavior become truthful and beneficial to all. One who seeks to know the truth remains in the presence of truth itself. Therefore, all his thoughts, words, and actions are directed towards the pursuit of truth. "'Akrodha' - Anger is the feeling of resentment that arises in one's heart when one thinks of harming others. However, as long as one does not harbor the intention to harm others, one is not angry; one is merely disturbed. A person who seeks to attain the Supreme Truth does not wish to harm anyone who is causing him harm. He understands that the person who is causing him harm is actually harming himself. This harm is the result of his own past mistakes, and it is purifying him. Just as a doctor cuts off a diseased part of the body to cure it, similarly, the person who is causing harm is helping the seeker to become pure and clean. Those who are beneficial to the seeker and serve him do not cause him any harm. Instead, they bring him happiness and destroy his good deeds. However, the seeker does not harbor anger towards them. He thinks that their good intentions and noble behavior are praiseworthy. However, the destruction of his good deeds occurs when he enjoys the benefits of their service. In this way, the seeker's perception is focused on the good intentions and noble behavior of those who serve him. "'Tyaga' - True renunciation is to become detached from the world. A seeker should renounce both the external and internal worldly attachments. Just as one should renounce external vices and pleasures, one should also renounce internal desires and attachments. In this, renouncing internal desires is more superior. When one renounces all desires, one attains peace immediately - 'Tyagaachchhaantiranantaram' (Gita 12.12). The seeker's greatest obstacle is his desire for things that are born and perishable. Therefore, one should renounce all desires completely. When is renunciation considered to be true?

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

When a seeker's goal is to attain the Supreme Being alone, why should he reveal the defects of others? As a result, his desires fade away. This is because worldly pleasures and accumulation are not his goals. Therefore, he gives up the desires for worldly pleasures and accumulation and proceeds with his spiritual practice. 'Peace' – the absence of turmoil in the mind due to attachment and aversion; because attachment and aversion towards the world create turmoil in the mind, and the absence of these creates a peaceful and happy mind. The destruction of old merits due to favorability and the possibility of deterioration of one's nature are more in favorability, but the destruction of sins and improvement of one's nature occur in adversity. Understanding this, one remains peaceful even in adversity. If a seeker sometimes develops attachment or aversion towards a situation, turmoil arises in his mind, and he immediately becomes cautious, thinking that attachment and aversion are not his goals. This thought brings peace, and with time, it becomes stable. A devotee sees his Lord everywhere, a knower sees his own nature, and a yogi sees his servant. Therefore, a seeker cannot harm anyone by speaking ill of them, criticizing them, or gossiping about them. 'Dayā Bhūteṣu' – the feeling of compassion to remove the suffering of others. The compassion of God, saints, seekers, and ordinary people is different. (1) God's compassion – God's compassion is for the purification of all. The devotees consider this compassion to have two aspects – mercy and compassion. Sending unfavorable circumstances to humans to purify them from their sins is 'mercy,' and sending favorable circumstances is 'compassion.'

(2) Saints' compassion – Saints are sorrowful to see the suffering of others and happy to see their happiness. However, they do not actually suffer from the suffering of others or their own suffering. This is because, in reality, there is neither suffering nor happiness. Just as waves appear on the surface of the ocean but there are no waves inside, saints appear to be sorrowful but their inner nature is peaceful. They do not actually suffer from the suffering of others but remove their suffering by their actions. When they face unfavorable circumstances, they see God's mercy, and when others suffer, they take their suffering upon themselves to bring happiness to them. For example, Indra beheaded Dadhichi without any fault, but when he asked for his bones for protection, Dadhichi gladly gave them to him. Similarly, saints do not tolerate the suffering of others but give their happiness and even their lives to bring happiness to others. 'Apaiśunam' – revealing the defects of others in front of others to create hatred towards them is cruelty, and its complete absence is 'apaiśunam.' Since the goal is to attain the Supreme Being alone, a seeker never speaks ill of others. As his practice advances, his tendency to see defects and hatred towards others decreases, and he naturally develops a good attitude towards others. He does not think, 'I am practicing and these others are ordinary people,' but sees everyone's true nature, that they are not bound by worldly attachments. Therefore, he does not harm anyone. Just as the skin of Karna, the meat of Shibi, the bones of Dadhichi, and the life of Jīmūtavāhana were given, it is true that nothing is unacceptable to the great souls for the benefit of others.

[Verse 2]
The compassion of great souls is especially pure and unadulterated. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

(3) A seeker's heart is filled with the desire to alleviate the suffering of others, and he makes efforts accordingly. When he sees others suffering, his heart melts, because he understands their pain as if it were his own. Therefore, his attitude is to wish for the happiness of all, the well-being of all, and the liberation of all. He makes similar efforts from his side, but he does not harbor pride in doing so, because he considers his actions as a natural part of his character. Hence, he does not feel proud. The one who does not follow the path of the Lord, who is engaged in evil deeds, who commits wrongs against others, and who brings about his own downfall – such a person does not evoke anger in the seeker. Instead, the seeker feels compassion for him. Therefore, the seeker always strives to help such people rise above their evil deeds and attain the path of the Lord. Sometimes, the seeker prays to the Lord, saying, "Oh Lord, please help these people to overcome their flaws and become Your devotees."

(4) The compassion of ordinary people is slightly tainted. When they make an effort to benefit someone, they think, "I am so kind! I have brought happiness to this person, and I am so good! Not everyone is as kind as I am; some people are like this, and some are like that." They think in this way, and with a sense of self-importance, they exhibit compassion, which is mixed with a sense of pride. This type of compassion is also tainted with attachment and bias. Those who are even lower than this are the ones who show compassion only to benefit themselves and their own interests. They are the ones who pretend to be kind to others, but their actions are driven by their own selfish desires. 'Aloluptva' – The absence of attachment to worldly objects and the tendency to be distracted by them is called 'aloluptva'. The opposite of this is 'lolluptva', which is the tendency to be attracted to worldly objects and to be distracted by them. The means to achieve 'aloluptva' are:

(1) A seeker must be cautious not to get attached to worldly objects through his senses and must not harbor the thought that he has control over his senses. He must not think, "I am the master of my senses, and I can do whatever I want."

(2) A seeker must be constantly aware of the dangers of attachment and must pray to the Lord, saying, "Oh Lord, if I ever get attached to worldly objects, I will fall and become separated from You."

(3) A seeker must not see or engage in any activities that are related to sensual desires, such as those of men and women or animals. If he sees such things, he must think, "This is a path that leads to 84 lakh types of births and deaths. This is a path that is common to all living beings, from humans to animals, from demons to spirits. But I want to rise above this path and attain liberation. I do not want to be bound by the cycle of birth and death."

A seeker must maintain this awareness and avoid engaging in any activities that are related to sensual desires. 'Mardava' – The absence of harshness and cruelty towards others, and the natural tendency to be gentle and kind is called 'mardava'. A seeker's heart is filled with gentleness and kindness towards all. Even if someone is harsh or cruel towards him, his gentleness remains unaffected. Ordinary people may show compassion, but their compassion is limited to those who are close to them, such as family members or those who share their beliefs.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 16 ]
If I give him that harsh answer, it will be beneficial for him. Therefore, I give him such answers in private or alone. But later, he thinks in his mind, "Why did I behave harshly with him? I could have understood him with love or some other means."

This kind of thought makes the harshness disappear and gentleness increases. Although the sages have gentleness in their thoughts and speech, yet due to their different natures, there is not the same gentleness in all their speech. However, there is a gentle feeling in their hearts towards all. Similarly, due to the difference in the nature of those who practice karma yoga, jnana yoga, and bhakti yoga, etc., their behavior is different towards all; therefore, there is not the same gentleness in their behavior towards all, but there is a great gentleness in their hearts. "Why can I show it to people?" - due to this shame, the sages avoid bad actions and their behavior becomes correct. When the sages change their ego to "I am a servant, I am an inquirer, I am a devotee," it is natural for them to feel shame in doing actions contrary to their ego. Therefore, every sages who have a spiritual goal should change their ego to "I am a sages, I am a servant, I am an inquirer, I am a devotee of God" in such a way that they can avoid actions contrary to their goal and attain their goal quickly. 'Acapalam' - not being hasty in any work, i.e., not having impatience, is 'acapalam'. Being hasty (chanchalata) does not make the work done quickly. The sattvic person does all work with patience; therefore, his work is done properly and at the right time. When the work is done properly, there is no restlessness or worry in his heart. Not being hasty does not make the work prolonged, but it makes him ready for all work, so that all work is done properly. 'Hrih' - the shame of doing work contrary to the scriptures and social norms is called 'hrih' (shame). The sages feel shame in doing actions contrary to their goal. This shame does not come from the fear of being seen by people, but it arises in their mind itself, "Oh Ram, how can I do such an action? Because I am a devotee of God, and people also consider me as a devotee of God."

[Chapter 9]
* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Even though one has the ability to forgive, yet to bear the offenses of others is called 'dhriti' (patience). And to pardon them is called 'kshama' (forgiveness). This kshama is done due to attachment, fear, or self-interest, as in the case of a father forgiving his son's offense. However, this is not pure forgiveness. Similarly, when a powerful and cruel person commits an offense against us, we remain silent out of fear, which is not pure forgiveness. When an inspector comes to check our wealth, we are intimidated and do not speak out of fear of loss, which is also not pure forgiveness. True forgiveness is that which has the intention of not punishing the person who has caused harm, both in this world and the next. Forgiveness can be sought in two ways:

(1) We have committed an offense against someone, and we do not want to be punished for it - this is done out of fear, but it is not pure forgiveness. (2) Someone has committed an offense against us, and we do not want to commit such an offense again in the future - this is done with the intention of self-improvement and is pure forgiveness. If a person's nature is sattvic, then patience is maintained, but if it is rajasic or tamasic, then patience is not maintained. Just as a pilgrim to Badrinath does not stop due to favorable or unfavorable circumstances, but continues with determination and patience, similarly, a sadhak should not be distracted by favorable or unfavorable circumstances, but should maintain patience and determination. A person who has the intention of achieving his goal does not see the joys and sorrows that come his way, as it is said:

Manasvi karyaarthi na ganyati duhkham na ca sukham (Bhartrhari Nitisataka)

The term 'shoucham' refers to external purity and internal purity. A sadhak who has the intention of achieving self-realization maintains external purity, as it leads to internal purity. As Patanjali Maharaj said:

Shouchat svangjugupsa parairasamsargah (Yoga Sutras 2.40)

External purity leads to a sense of disgust towards one's own body and a desire to avoid association with others. To cultivate forgiveness in oneself, one should not have the expectation of happiness from external purity, and one should have the knowledge that the body of the person who has caused harm is impure. If one does not have a sense of disgust towards the impurity of another's body, then forgiveness will not arise. When one has the knowledge that all bodies are the same, then one's attachment to other bodies is removed, and one remains steadfast in one's own position. 1. What is the difference between kshama (forgiveness) and akrodha (angerlessness)? Forgiveness involves a special consideration for the person who has committed the offense, that they should not be punished, whereas angerlessness involves a consideration for oneself, that one should not feel anger, resentment, or agitation. Although forgiveness may involve a degree of angerlessness, the two are not the same. 2. Here, the term 'shoucham' refers only to external purity, as internal purity has already been mentioned in the previous shloka.

The desire to acquire (material possessions) is eliminated. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

External purification occurs in four ways: (1) physical, (2) verbal, (3) domestic, and (4) economic. (1) Physical purification - The body becomes impure due to laziness, indolence, love for comfort, and attachment to sensual pleasures. Conversely, by engaging in necessary work with a sense of duty, self-discipline, and simplicity, the body becomes pure. Similarly, physical purification also occurs through the use of water, earth, and other substances. (2) Verbal purification - The tongue becomes impure due to speaking lies, harsh words, unnecessary talk, criticism, and gossip. Conversely, by speaking truth, being kind, and speaking words that benefit others (which leads to their spiritual growth and the well-being of the country, village, neighborhood, family, and community), and refraining from unnecessary talk, verbal purification occurs. (3) Domestic purification - Providing good education to children, adopting good behavior, fulfilling one's duties towards family members, treating them with justice, and showing equal concern for all family members - this is domestic purification. (4) Economic purification - Using wealth in a just and truthful manner, benefiting others, and donating to those in need, the poor, the sick, the afflicted, and the hungry - this is economic purification. Donating to the service of saints, great souls, and the propagation of sacred scriptures, and making them available at a low cost, also leads to great economic purification. Chapter 16

This practice helps one to renounce egoism and attachment to the body. In this way, it becomes a means for attaining the ultimate goal. 'Adroha' - Not harboring a sense of revenge against someone who has caused harm, is 'Adroha'. A common person, if harmed by someone, develops a grudge in their heart, thinking, "I will take revenge when the opportunity arises." However, one whose ultimate goal is to attain the ultimate reality does not harbor a sense of revenge, even if someone causes them harm. This is because the practitioner of karma yoga performs duties for the benefit of all, the practitioner of jnana yoga sees everyone as their own self, and the practitioner of bhakti yoga sees everyone as their beloved Lord. Therefore, they cannot harbor a sense of revenge against anyone. (Manas 7.112 Kh)

'Natimanaata' - There is 'mananaata' (a sense of self-importance) and 'atimanaata' (an excessive sense of self-importance). A common person's desire for respect from others is 'mananaata', and their desire for respect from those they admire and aspire to emulate is 'atimanaata'. The absence of both 'mananaata' and 'atimanaata' is 'natimanaata'. There are two types of 'mananaata' from a superficial perspective - (1) worldly 'mananaata' - A sense of superiority over others due to wealth, knowledge, virtues, intelligence, abilities, authority, position, caste, and stage of life. For example, "I am not like ordinary people; many people respect me, and they show me respect because I am worthy of it." (2) spiritual 'mananaata' - A sense of superiority over others due to one's spiritual practices and achievements. When one's ultimate goal is to attain the ultimate reality, their worldly 'mananaata' is eliminated. As a result, their body, speech, family, wealth, and other external factors become pure and sacred. Others also consider them to be pure and sacred, and they are revered as a person who has achieved spiritual purification. Krodha (anger) and Drish (hatred) - There is a difference between the two. The feeling of anger that arises immediately when someone causes harm is called 'krodha'. The feeling of hatred that arises within, which is the desire to harm someone in the future, is called 'drish'.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

As long as a person has a sense of individuality (one-sidedness, limitation), he shows a sense of specialness in relation to others. However, as soon as this individuality fades away, the sense of specialness in relation to others also fades away. Ultimately, when all these attributes are absent, the divine quality of 'naitimita' (non-attachment) manifests in the sadhak. There are some who praise this quality, saying, 'This is a divine quality.' This is indeed a divine quality, for it reveals a sense of individuality, but in reality, it is not a quality of any individual. If it were a personal quality, it would be evident due to a lack of siddhi (spiritual power) in the sadhak. This quality remains within oneself, not in any other person. The manifestation of this quality is a paraarthik (transcendental) attribute. If one considers this quality as personal, then ego arises. Ego is the main characteristic of asuri (demonic) quality. All the vices of asuri quality remain in the shadow of ego. If asuri quality arises from divine quality, then it will never disappear. However, divine quality never gives rise to asuri quality; rather, the vices of asuri quality arise from the ego, which is a result of considering one's own siddhi as a personal quality. Just as a person who has an ego of being truthful may also speak lies, so ego arises from considering one's own siddhi as a personal quality. The meaning is that ego arises from considering one's own siddhi as a personal quality and from the vices of asuri quality remaining with the virtues. In reality, ego can never arise from divine quality. The virtues of divine quality are numerous, and they are all present in the sadhak. The sadhak's goal is to awaken these virtues fully. However, due to the differences in nature, some people may have a deficiency in some virtues. But this deficiency is felt by the sadhak, and he takes refuge in the Lord, and with his effort, he strives to attain siddhi. As the deficiency decreases, the possibility of the virtues increasing also increases. As a result, the vices and evil deeds are completely destroyed, and the divine quality manifests. The Lord says, 'These are the characteristics of people who have acquired divine quality, O Arjuna.' When the goal is to attain the Lord, these divine qualities naturally manifest in the sadhak. Some of these qualities are awakened due to the samskaras of past births. However, the sadhak does not consider these qualities as his own and does not consider them as acquired through his own effort. Rather, he attributes them to the Lord's grace. Sometimes, the sadhak thinks, 'I did not have such virtues in the past, I did not have such qualities. How did they arise in me?' As a result of this thought, he experiences the Lord's grace, and he does not develop ego. The meaning of divine quality is that it is the Lord's quality. Therefore, when one has a relationship with the Lord, when one takes refuge in the Lord, this quality naturally manifests in the sadhak. Just as Lord Rama said to Shabari, 'I will tell you about the nine types of devotion. Listen carefully, and keep it in your mind. One who has these nine types of devotion is dear to me, and he is the most excellent of all beings.'

The nine types of devotion are: devotion to the Lord as the ultimate reality, devotion to the Lord as the ultimate goal, devotion to the Lord as the ultimate refuge, devotion to the Lord as the ultimate friend, devotion to the Lord as the ultimate father, devotion to the Lord as the ultimate mother, devotion to the Lord as the ultimate guru, devotion to the Lord as the ultimate servant, and devotion to the Lord as the ultimate lover. In all living beings, whether human or divine, whether animate or inanimate, there is a desire to live, to preserve one's life, and to maintain one's existence. This desire is the asuri quality. Even a tyagi (renouncer) or a vairagi (one who has renounced worldly attachments) has a desire to live, but he does not have the desire for prana-poshana (preservation of life) or indriya-lolupata (attachment to the senses), because his goal is the Lord. He does not consider the divine qualities as his own, that is, the qualities of the body and the world. The Lord says, 'Even if the body is decaying, the desire to live is stronger.' (Shrimad Bhagavatam 10.14.53)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 16 ]
When a devotee develops love for the Lord, then attachment to objects and individuals ceases to exist. This is why, when the husband dies, the devoted wife happily becomes a sati (self-immolates) in her grief. In other words, when one develops exclusive love for the Lord, then attachment to one's life, body, and possessions ceases to exist. With the cessation of attachment to one's life, body, and possessions, the asuric (demonic) wealth is completely destroyed, and the divine wealth manifests itself naturally. Gosaumi Tulsidas Maharaj has indicated this fact in the following verse:

Preme bhagati jal binu raghurai. He loves the Lord more than his life. With the cessation of attachment to his life, his life becomes dependent solely on the Lord. Therefore, he addresses the Lord with the following terms: 'Pran Nath! Praneshwar! Pranpriya!' etc. He cannot bear the separation from the Lord, and his life itself may be lost. The reason is that a person who considers something more precious than his life will gladly give up his life for it; just as a devoted wife considers her husband more precious than her life, and therefore, she gladly gives up her life for him. - (Manas 7.49.3)

[Verse 4]
Connection - So far, the divine wealth of those who have only one goal, the Supreme Being, has been described. However, those who have the goal of enjoying worldly pleasures and accumulating wealth, what kind of wealth do they possess? This will be explained in the next verse. Arjuna

* साधक - संजीवनी *
१०२५
बड़प्पनका अनुभव होता है, उसका नाम 'अभिमान' है' || बात है कि क्रोधी व्यक्ति जिसका अनिष्ट करता है, उसका
किन्हीं दुष्कर्मोंका जो फल भोगरूपसे आनेवाला है, वही
होता है अर्थात् उसका कोई नया अनिष्ट नहीं हो सकता; परंतु
क्रोधी व्यक्तिका दूसरेका अनिष्ट करनेकी भावनासे और
अनिष्ट करनेसे नया पाप-संग्रह हो जायगा तथा उसका
स्वभाव भी बिगड़ जायगा । यह स्वभाव उसे नरकोंमें ले
जानेका हेतु बन जायगा और वह जिस योनिमें जायगा, वहीं
उसे दुःख देगा।
जैसे - मैं जाति-पाँतिमें कुलीन हूँ; मैं वर्ण- आश्रममें ऊँचा हूँ;
हमारी जातिमें हमारी प्रधानता है; गाँवभरमें हमारी बात चलती
है अर्थात् हम जो कह देंगे, उसको सभी मानेंगे; हम जिसको
सहारा देंगे, उस आदमीसे विरुद्ध चलनेमें सभी लोग भयभीत
होंगे और हम जिसके विरोधी होंगे, उसका साथ देनेमें भी
सभी लोग भयभीत होंगे; राजदरबारमें भी हमारा आदर है,
इसलिये हम जो कह देंगे, उसे कोई टालेगा नहीं; हम न्याय -
अन्याय जो कुछ भी करेंगे, उसको कोई टाल नहीं सकता,

करणमें जो जलनात्मक वृत्ति पैदा होती है, उसका नाम

अध्यायके इक्कीसवें श्लोकमें भगवान्ने क्रोधको नरकोंका

‘पारुष्यम्’– कठोरताका नाम 'पारुष्य' है। यह कई
प्रकारका होता
प्रकारका होता है; जैसे- शरीरसे अकड़कर चलना, टेढ़े
चलना - यह शारीरिक पारुष्य है। नेत्रोंसे टेढ़ा - टेढ़ा देखना-

संकट, दुःख आनेपर भी उनकी सहायता न करके राजी होना
आदि जो कठोर भाव होते हैं, यह हृदयका पारुष्य है ।
जो शरीर और प्राणोंके साथ एक हो गये हैं, ऐसे
मनुष्योंको यदि दूसरोंकी क्रिया, वाणी बुरी लगती है, तो
उसके बदलेमें वे उनको कठोर वचन सुनाते हैं, दुःख देते
हैं और स्वयं राजी होकर कहते हैं कि 'आपने देखा कि
नहीं ? मैंने उसके साथ ऐसा कड़ा व्यवहार किया कि उसके
दाँत खट्टे कर दिये ! अब वह मेरे साथ बोल सकता है
क्या ?' यह सब व्यवहारका पारुष्य है।

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The experience of greatness is called 'abhimana' (pride). The fact is that a person who is angry with someone else, who is about to suffer the consequences of their own evil deeds, will suffer the same consequences; there will be no new misfortune for them. However, due to their anger, they will accumulate new sins and their nature will also deteriorate. This nature will become a reason for them to go to hell, and the suffering they will face in the next birth will be due to this nature. For example, I am from a high caste, I am from a high varna (social class), our caste is superior, everyone in the village respects us, everyone will accept what we say, everyone will be afraid to oppose us, and everyone will be afraid to disagree with us. Even in the royal court, we are respected, so no one will be able to stop us from doing what we want, no one will be able to oppose us, and no one will be able to disagree with us. I am a great scholar, I know about the Siddhis (supernatural powers) such as Anima, Mahima, Garima, etc., so I can disturb the entire world, etc. 'Krodha' (anger) is the name of the burning feeling in the heart that arises due to the desire to harm others. When a person does something that is contrary to their nature, a burning feeling arises in their heart due to the desire to harm others, which is called 'krodha' (anger). Anger and irritation are different. A child is stubborn, does not listen, and is punished by his parents - this is their 'kshobha' (irritation), not anger. Because they do not have the intention to harm the child, but rather to benefit him. But if a person is irritated and harms others, causing them suffering, then this is 'krodha' (anger). This is the nature of those who have an asuric (demonic) nature. A person who is controlled by anger does not hesitate to do things that are not worthy of being done, which ultimately leads to his own suffering. An angry person harms others, but their own harm is not reduced; because they cannot harm others without harming themselves. Anger ultimately burns itself. An angry person does not have a good reputation in society, but rather is despised. Even their own family members are afraid of them. In this chapter, the 21st verse of the Gita says that anger is the door to hell. When a person's ego and pride are obstructed, anger arises. Then anger leads to delusion, delusion leads to the destruction of intelligence, and the destruction of intelligence leads to the downfall of a person (Gita - 2nd chapter, 61st-63rd verse). 'Parushyam' (coarseness) is the name of harshness. It has many forms, such as:

- Walking with a stiff body
- Walking with a twisted gait
- Looking at others with a twisted gaze
- Speaking harshly, which frightens others
- Not helping others in times of trouble, but rather being satisfied with oneself
- Other harsh feelings

A person who is attached to their body and life, if they see someone else's actions or words as bad, they will respond with harsh words and actions, and will say, "I have treated him so harshly that he will not dare to speak to me again." This is an example of harsh behavior. Wherever pride and arrogance both exist, they are both under the category of pride. But where they both exist independently, there is a slight difference between them. 'Mamta' (attachment) is related to pride, and 'Ahanta' (ego) is related to arrogance. 1. Wherever pride and arrogance both exist, pride is the overarching category, and arrogance is a subcategory. 2. 'Krodha' (anger) is the first enemy of humans, which is present in the body and destroys the body. Just as fire present in wood burns the wood, similarly, the fire of anger present in the body burns the body.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
To prove his point, he has to cause suffering to others through his actions, and some calamity will befall them - he cannot even think about these things. Due to a hard-hearted disposition in his heart, he only sees his own interest and his mind, speech, body, behavior, etc. are all hard-hearted. His self-interest-oriented nature becomes more and more prominent, and he even resorts to violence, etc. as a result of which cruelty becomes a natural part of his nature. Cruelty arising, there is no gentleness in his heart. Without gentleness in his heart, his behavior and dealings are naturally hard-hearted. Therefore, he is always engaged in getting money from others, causing suffering to others, etc. He does not even think about whether this will bring him happiness or suffering. ' Ajñānam ' - Here ' Ajñānam ' means lack of discernment. The person lacking discernment does not have the knowledge of what is right and wrong, what is good and bad, what is duty and what is not duty, etc. Because their vision is always focused on the enjoyment and accumulation of perishable things. Therefore, they do not even think that these perishable things will last for some time and we will be with them for some time. Like animals, they are only engaged in the maintenance of their life and do not know what is their duty and what is not their duty, and they do not even want to know. They consider only the temporary pleasure that arises from the conjunction of circumstances as pleasure and consider the conjunction of circumstances unfavorable to the body and senses as suffering. Therefore, they work only for pleasure and, as a result, they get more suffering than they had before. Despite this, they do not realize that this will have a bad effect on us. They are attracted by the allurements of fame, pleasure, wealth, and property, and they even start doing things that are not worth doing, which have a bad effect on them and the world. *
Chapter 16
' Abhijātasya pārtha sampadāsaurīm ' – O Partha! These are the characteristics of the people who have acquired this asurī wealth. The people who consider their body as one with death and think, 'I will never die; I will always live and enjoy,' have these characteristics in their hearts. In the 40th verse of the 18th chapter, the Lord says that no ordinary person is completely free from the influence of the qualities of nature. This proves that every living being, being a part of the Supreme, is born with a connection with nature. The connection with nature means the relationship of 'I' and 'mine' with the body and attachment, desire, and greed for objects. The relationship of 'I' and 'mine' with the body is the fundamental characteristic of asurī wealth. The person who has a primary connection with nature is said to have acquired asurī wealth. The connection with nature is the relationship of 'I' and 'mine' with the body and attachment, desire, and greed for objects. As long as a person is attached to the body, his attachment increases, and asurī wealth increases. When asurī wealth increases, a person starts harming others for his own benefit and even for his own survival. He does not even hesitate to kill others. 1- karmanya ārabhamāṇānāṃ duḥkha-hatyai sukhayā ca | pācyet pāka-viparyāsaṃ mithunī-cāriṇāṃ nṛṇām || (Shrimad Bhagavat 11.3.18)
O king! The men who are bound by relationships like husband and wife, etc. perform actions for the sake of pleasure and the removal of suffering. But the person who wants to cross over the world, should consider how his actions will have a reverse effect. They get suffering instead of pleasure, and their suffering increases instead of decreasing. 2- Here, the word 'asurī' does not mean the opposite of the gods, but 'asur' means the person who is attached to the senses and the life force, i.e., the person who is attached to the temporary pleasure that arises from the conjunction of circumstances. The people who do not have the goal of attaining the Supreme and who want to enjoy the body by enjoying the senses are called 'asur'. Their wealth is called 'asurī wealth'.

[Verse 5]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

When a man considers the temporary as permanent, then, without being invited and without being asked, the vices and evil tendencies of the asuric wealth, the group of evil deeds, come to him of their own accord, which are detrimental to the attainment of the Supreme. The implication is that the association with the untruth leads to being detached from the truth and being led to downfall. Connection: Now, the Lord explains the fruits of both the divine and asuric wealth. Divine Wealth
For liberation
Asuric Wealth
For bondage
Divine wealth is considered to be for liberation, and asuric wealth is considered to be for bondage. You, O Pāṇḍava, are not of the divine wealth. 5

Explanation: 'Divine wealth' - it is the path that leads to the Lord. As soon as this feeling becomes clear in the sadhaka, he becomes present before the Lord. Being present before the Lord leads to detachment from the world. Detachment from the world leads to a decrease in the evil tendencies and evil deeds of the asuric wealth, and an increase in the good qualities and good deeds of the divine wealth. This leads to an interest in the Lord, His name, form, pastimes, qualities, and character. It is essential to note that the more the sadhaka's goal is firm, the more the eternal relationship with the Supreme will be revealed, and the relationship with the world, which is considered to be, will be destroyed. What is destroyed is what has been considered to be the relationship all along! In reality, there is no relationship with nature. It is only this life that has been considered to be the relationship. The good intention behind this considered relationship is 'I am the body and the body is mine' - this good intention is what has kept the world going. As soon as this good intention is destroyed, the considered relationship with the world will be destroyed, and the complete good qualities of the divine wealth will be revealed, which are meant for liberation. The divine wealth is not meant only for oneself, but for the benefit of all. Therefore, do not worry. There are many big, old, and other members in the family, but the head of the family (grihastha) himself works for their upbringing, just like how the Lord has created man for the upliftment of the world. What is man, after all? By the extraordinary power given by the Lord, man can, by being present before the Lord and serving the Lord, bring the Lord under his control. What a wonderful power has been given to man! Therefore, man should perform all the means of salvation, such as yajna, dana, tapa, tirtha, vrat, japa, dhyana, svadhyaya, satsanga, etc., for the benefit of the infinite number of living beings in the infinite number of universes, and with firm determination, he should pray, 'O Lord! May the benefit be for the living beings, may the living beings attain liberation, may the living beings become Your exclusive devotees; but, O Lord! This will happen only by Your mercy. I can only pray, and that too by the mercy given by You.' Keeping this feeling, one should offer all one's body, senses, mind, intellect, wealth, etc., to the Lord for the benefit of the world. By doing so, one's body, senses, mind, intellect, wealth, etc., will be revealed to be in a state of unity with the Lord, and not separate from the world. This is for the benefit of all living beings. Just as the grihastha works for the benefit of all the members in the family, the Lord has created man for the benefit of all living beings.

The term 'yogi' has been applied to sakama purushas (those who seek worldly pleasures) as well (in Gita - 8th chapter, 25th verse). Otherwise, sakama purushas cannot be called yogis. The second fruit of asuri-sampatti (the quality of being demonic) is - 'patanti narke'shuchau' (Gita 16.16). Those who are controlled by their desires and commit papa (sin), anaya (injustice), durachar (immorality), etc., attain the specific hells as a result of their actions. The third fruit of asuri-sampatti is - 'asurishv eva yonisv', 'tato yantyadhamam gatim' (Gita 16.19-20). Those in whom durguna-durbhav (evil tendencies) reside, and who are sometimes inspired by them to commit durachar, are said to attain asuri yoni (demonic birth) and then, according to their actions, the lowest path (adham gati) - the attainment of hells. ' Ma shuchah sampadam daivim abhijato'si pandava' - The divine sampatti (quality) of the one who is devoted to the eternal Paramatma (Supreme Consciousness) is the one that brings liberation and freedom from the cycle of birth and death. The worldly sampatti (quality) of those who seek to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of the world is the one that binds them to the cycle of birth and death. This is what the Lord says to Arjuna, so that he may not harbor any doubts about his own sampatti. The Lord says, 'Arjuna, you have been blessed with divine sampatti; therefore, do not grieve or harbor doubts.' * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 16
(1.45) ]. It is very essential for one to repeatedly renounce one's asuric possessions even in the battlefield. They ask for the good thing, saying, "Tell me what is certain good, and I will do it" (2.7); "Tell me one thing that is certain, by which I may attain good" (3.2); "Tell me one thing that is certain, by which I may attain good" (5.1). This is due to the presence of divine possessions in them. On the other hand, those who possess asuric possessions, such as Duryodhana, have such a great attachment to the kingdom and wealth that they do not even look at the sin of destroying their family (the thirty-eighth shloka of the first chapter). In this way, Arjuna had divine possessions from the beginning. The asuric possessions, in the form of Moha, entered him later, which was later destroyed by the grace of God - "My delusion is destroyed, my memory is regained by your grace, O Acyuta" (18.73). That is why God says here, "Brother Arjuna, do not worry; because you possess divine possessions."

Arjuna does not see divine possessions in himself, so God tells Arjuna that you possess divine possessions. The reason is that the great persons do not see good qualities in themselves and the bad qualities do not remain in them. The reason for not seeing good qualities is that they are inseparable from their good qualities. Just as the collyrium applied to the eyes does not appear to the eyes because it becomes one with the eyes, similarly, the divine possessions become one with the person and do not appear. As long as good qualities appear in oneself, it means that they have not become one with the person. Good qualities appear when they are separate from oneself. Therefore, God reassures Arjuna that you possess divine possessions by nature, even if you do not see them, so do not worry. Marmik Baat
God has given us the human body, so we should pay special attention to our emotions and behavior for its success. Because the body's fate is unknown, when will the breaths leave the body. In such a situation, one should take refuge in divine possessions and

*
|
Divine possessions are the possessions of the divine, and the word 'dev' is the symbol of the Supreme Being. Their possessions are called 'divine possessions' - 'devasya idam daivi'. The divine possessions are inherent in the jiva by nature, as it is an eternal part of the Supreme Being. When the jiva turns away from its part, the Supreme Being, and becomes associated with the perishable material world, then asuric possessions enter it. The reason is that all the bad qualities, such as greed, anger, lust, attachment, pride, hatred, etc., are born from the association with perishable things. The word 'asur' is the symbol of those who are attached to the perishable world - 'asurah praneshu ramante iti asurah'. Therefore, the desire to live happily - 'I want to live happily' - is a special characteristic of asuric possessions. . -
Divine and asuric possessions are found in all living beings (sixteenth chapter of the Gita, sixth shloka). There is no ordinary living being in whom these two possessions are not found. However, the liberated and wise great persons are completely free from asuric possessions. But no one can be completely free from divine possessions. The reason is that the jiva is an eternal part of the Supreme Being, so it has divine possessions by nature. Asuric possessions are predominant, so divine possessions are suppressed, but they do not disappear. Because the truth cannot be destroyed. Therefore, no one can be completely wicked, completely merciless, completely dishonest, completely immoral. All the bad qualities cannot be present in anyone. Even if someone is very wicked, he will have some good qualities with him. Divine possessions are revealed, and asuric possessions disappear. Because divine possessions are eternal and asuric possessions are perishable. The liberated and wise great persons are free from perishable things and are established in the eternal Supreme Being. Therefore, they do not have any fear of death or attachment to life. They are established in their true nature, so they have good qualities by nature. They are above divine possessions, so their good qualities are natural and serve as an ideal for seekers.
