* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[Verse 5]

The eternal soul, being a part of the Supreme Consciousness, always thinks, "I must always exist; I must never die." It wants to possess divine qualities, such as truthfulness, non-violence, and compassion. It wants to be all-knowing, never ignorant; it wants to be always happy, never unhappy. This is how the eternal soul, with a heart full of truth, consciousness, and bliss, remains in every living being. However, there is a mistake in this. The eternal soul wants to fulfill its desires through worldly possessions, such as a body, knowledge, and happiness. It wants to preserve its body, become knowledgeable through its intellect, and experience happiness through its senses and body. It wants to complete its desires in this fleeting world. Due to its attachment to life, the eternal soul remains with the qualities of the asura (demonic) nature. A significant point is that the eternal soul always desires to exist eternally, and this desire can make it eternal. It desires not to die, and this desire can prevent it from dying. It is natural to want to live, and it is unnatural to die. Similarly, ignorance is undesirable, and it is unnatural to be ignorant. Suffering is undesirable, and it is unnatural to suffer. From this, it is clear that the eternal soul's nature is sat (truth). Its nature is not asat (untruth). Despite being sat, it desires asat because it has identified with the fleeting, perishable body and its attributes and has become attached to them. This means that even though the eternal soul is sat, it has a desire for sat due to its acceptance of asat. Similarly, even though it is jnana (knowledge), it has a desire for jnana due to its acceptance of ignorance. Even though it is sukha (happiness), it has a desire for sukha due to its acceptance of suffering. However, it wants to fulfill its desires through the asat, jada (insentient), and dukha (suffering) nature of the world. It wants to maintain its name and form even after death. In this way, the asura nature arises from its association with asat. On the other hand, by renouncing the association with asat, the asura nature is destroyed, and the divine nature is revealed. It wants to acquire its qualities through its own efforts. This is a principle that what is acquired through duty and one's own efforts is not natural but artificial. Moreover, due to the acquisition of qualities through one's own efforts, there is a sense of pride, such as "I am a great truth-speaker," "I am a great person," and so on. All the vices and bad behaviors are in the shade of pride, and they are strengthened by pride. Therefore, as long as one is engaged in efforts to acquire divine qualities, the asura nature does not leave him. Ultimately, he becomes hopeless or his enthusiasm decreases, and he thinks, "This is not within my power." The reason for this is that he has not yet realized that the asura nature arises from association with the fleeting and perishable. The asura nature is the result of association with the fleeting and perishable. As long as this association remains, the asura nature will remain. He does not give up this association, so the asura nature does not leave him. Therefore, if he wants to acquire divine qualities, he must renounce the association with the fleeting and perishable. When he renounces the association with the fleeting and perishable, the divine nature will reveal itself naturally, because the eternal soul is a part of the Supreme Consciousness, and the divine nature is inherent in it. It does not need to be acquired through duty and one's own efforts. There is another significant point. The divine qualities are natural and inherent in the eternal soul. No one can abandon them. How can one realize this? Just as one can think, "I will always speak the truth," and one can always speak the truth, similarly, one can think, "I will always be knowledgeable," and one can always be knowledgeable. However, when one thinks, "I will always be ignorant," one cannot remain ignorant. Similarly, when one thinks, "I will always suffer," one cannot remain suffering. In the Gita, the phrase "dehavadbhi" (12.5), "dehinam" (3.40; 14.5, 7), and so on refer to those who are attached to the body and are, therefore, included in the asura nature.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 16 ]

One who is not truthful cannot speak the truth. Even if one has acquired divine wealth, if one thinks that one cannot speak the truth, then one can suffer from unhappiness. However, one who thinks that one will speak lies will find it difficult to eat, drink, speak, and move about. If one is hungry and says that one is not hungry, then life becomes difficult. If one makes a promise that one will speak lies, even if one has to die, then this promise will become true. Therefore, either the promise will be broken and truth will emerge, or the promise will become true. Truth can never be lost; because truth is natural to man. Similarly, all the divine qualities that one has acquired are permanent and natural. One has to only give up the association with the transitory and unnatural things. The wealth of the demons is transitory and unnatural. The bad qualities and bad behavior are completely transitory and unnatural. A person who is happy is not said to be happy because of that, but a person who is unhappy is said to be unhappy because of that. Happiness is natural, and unhappiness is unnatural. Therefore, a person who has good behavior is not said to be good because of that, but a person who has bad behavior is said to be bad because of that. Therefore, good qualities and good behavior are permanent and natural, and bad qualities and bad behavior are transitory and unnatural. Arjuna had divine qualities in particular. When cowardice arose in him, then Lord Krishna said with surprise, "Where did this cowardice come from in you?" This means that cowardice was not natural to Arjuna, but it was acquired. Initially, Arjuna did not have this defect. Arjuna says, "Tell me something that will bring me certain happiness." Even in the context of war, Arjuna has this desire. Therefore, it appears that Arjuna had divine qualities in his nature from the beginning, otherwise, rejecting Urvashi, a celestial nymph, would not have been a trivial matter for any ordinary person. Arjuna thinks, "Do I have divine qualities or not? Am I entitled to them or not?" Therefore, Lord Krishna consoles him, saying, "Do not grieve; the 'I' consciousness arises from the identification of the self with the eternal and the non-eternal." A person, whether he does a good or bad deed, does it with a sense of 'I'. When a person moves towards the Supreme, his 'I' consciousness is predominantly of the eternal, and when he moves towards the world, his 'I' consciousness is predominantly of the non-eternal. Therefore, a person is said to be entitled to divine qualities if his 'I' consciousness is predominantly of the eternal, and he is said to be a non-entitled person if his 'I' consciousness is predominantly of the non-eternal. The human body has been given to man to destroy the non-eternal aspect of his 'I' consciousness. Therefore, man is not weak, nor is he a slave, but he is completely powerful and free. The non-eternal aspect of his 'I' consciousness is always being destroyed, but he retains his connection with it. This is a mistake. He retains his connection with the non-eternal aspect of his 'I' consciousness, and therefore, the absence of divine qualities is not absolute. The 'I' consciousness arises from the connection with the non-eternal. The connection with the non-eternal is destroyed, and the 'I' consciousness is destroyed. The connection with the non-eternal is established through the attachment to the non-eternal. The non-eternal aspect of his 'I' consciousness is made up of both the eternal and the non-eternal. Due to the identification with the non-eternal, the 'I' consciousness arises. The eternal and the non-eternal are both present in the 'I' consciousness. The eternal aspect of the 'I' consciousness is the conscious aspect, and the non-eternal aspect is the unconscious aspect. Due to the identification with the non-eternal, the 'I' consciousness is formed. The attachment to the non-eternal is the cause of the 'I' consciousness. The attachment to the non-eternal is the cause of the 'I' consciousness, and the attachment to the eternal is the cause of the destruction of the 'I' consciousness. The attachment to the non-eternal is the cause of the 'I'

* The Seeker - Reviver *

When I am in front of the Lord, the living being becomes one with me, and the countless sins of birth are washed away. The consumer of happiness and sorrow cannot be a mere material part. It seems that only the conscious being, who knows the result, becomes the consumer. As many actions take place, they all take place in nature (Third Chapter, Twenty-Third and Thirteenth Verses of the Fourteenth Chapter). But due to the sense of oneness, the conscious being considers itself the doer. In the sense of oneness, the conscious being (Paramatma) has the main aspect of its own will, and the material (samsar-) has the main aspect of its own will. When the conscious being's will is predominant, divine wealth comes, and when the material's will is predominant, demonic wealth comes. Even if the material is in a state of oneness with the conscious being, the desire for sat, chit, and ananda remains in the conscious being. There is no desire in the world that does not include these three desires (to always exist, to know everything, and to always be happy). This is the mistake of trying to fulfill these desires through the material (samsar-). The material and demonic wealth have been accepted by the conscious being itself. The material cannot remain stable on its own; it is always changing. If the conscious being does not hold it, it will escape on its own. Because the conscious being is never affected by vikar. It always remains the same. But the unreal nature is always changing, always changing, and never remains the same. The conscious being has accepted the relationship with nature. It accepts the power of this relationship in the form of 'I' and 'mine'. Therefore, the material's relationship and the demonic wealth that arises from it are temporary. If it were permanent, it would never be destroyed; because the permanent one is never destroyed, and the idea of giving up demonic wealth never arises. Although it is impermanent, it appears to be permanent due to its relationship with the conscious being. Due to its relationship with the permanent one, the impermanent one appears to be permanent. Therefore, the person in whom demonic wealth exists can give up demonic wealth and, by adopting virtuous behavior, can attain Paramatma (Sixteenth Chapter, Twenty-Second Verse). Because 'janm koti agh' (countless sins of birth) have arisen from accepting the relationship with nature. If you do not accept nature, then how will birth and death occur? Birth and death are due to the relationship with nature - 'karanam gunasango'sya sad-asad-yoni-janmasu' (Gita 13.21). But the jiva-atma (individual soul) considers the actions of nature as its own and considers the work of nature as 'I' and 'mine' in the body, due to which it is born and dies. In reality, it is neither the doer nor the one who is entangled - 'Sharirastho'api kaunteya na karoti na lipyate' (13.31). To experience this reality is to see 'karma in akarma' and 'akarma in karma'. The meaning of these two is that, while doing karma, it is completely unentangled and a non-doer, and while being unentangled and a non-doer, it does karma. That is, it does karma at the time of doing karma and does not do karma at the time of not doing karma. It remains eternally and constantly unentangled and a non-doer. Only the one who experiences this reality is wise among humans (Fourth Chapter, Eighteenth Verse). The one in whom there is no sense of doership and whose intellect is not entangled, that is, who has no desires, even if he kills all living beings, no sin will be incurred (Eighteenth Chapter, Seventeenth Verse). Arjuna asked what inspires a person to commit sin. Then the Lord said - due to desire (Third Chapter, Thirty-Sixth to Thirty-Seventh Verses). All sins arise due to desire. The desire for enjoyment and accumulation arises due to the sense of oneness with the body. Therefore, the association of the material (mahattva) is the sole cause of all sins (asuric wealth). If the material's association does not exist, divine wealth is automatically established. Arjuna is the representative of the seeker. Therefore, the Lord reassures the seeker through Arjuna that do not worry; if demonic wealth appears in you, do not be afraid; because your divine wealth is automatically established in front of Paramatma. It is natural for any person to not like to be considered guilty; because in this world, being guilty is considered a shame, and in the next world, one has to suffer in 84 lakh yonis and hells. But a person, being under the control of the desires born of the association with the ephemeral material, starts doing actions that are forbidden by the scriptures. Therefore, the result of that action does not match the desire of the doer (the person), and the doer becomes guilty and sinful.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Do not lament, O Pandava, you are born of divine wealth. (16.5)

The sense is that the seeker must never lose hope of attaining the supreme, transcendental goal, because being a fragment of Parmatma (Supreme Self) means that the divine wealth (Parmatma’s property) resides within every human being. When the purpose is the attainment of Parmatma, divine wealth manifests automatically. [ Chapter 16 ]
Since the seeker is a fragment of Parmatma, he must never become disheartened in his quest for Parmatma; Parmatma, by His grace, has given the human body precisely for that purpose. Therefore, the resolve of Parmatma is essentially for our welfare. If we keep no separate personal resolve and instead merge our resolve with the resolve of Parmatma, then welfare follows automatically by His grace. Appendix: The living being has, on one side, God and, on the other, the world. When he moves toward God, divine wealth arises; when he moves toward the world, asuri (demonic) wealth arises. Divine wealth is accompanied by a theistic (āstika) attitude, whereas asuri wealth is accompanied by a non‑theistic (nāstika) attitude. Although all means of liberation (Karma Yoga, Jñāna Yoga, Dhyāna Yoga, etc.) fall under divine wealth—‘for liberation through divine wealth’—the primary element within divine wealth is devotion (bhakti). Hence, the Lord says in the devotional section:

“Mahātmānas tu māṁ Pārtha daivīṁ prakṛtim āśritāḥ |
Bhajanty ananyam anaso jñātvā bhūtādim avyayam ||” (Gita 9.13)

“Great‑souled ones, O Arjuna, who are attached to the divine nature, worship Me without any other thought, knowing Me as the immutable source of all beings.”

Later the Lord also says, “Having attained Me, O Kaunteya—” (16.20). All means of liberation are encompassed within devotion. Those who love their own life‑force become attached to the world and possess asuri wealth. Those who love God more than their own life‑force possess divine wealth. Acting for the happiness of others or desiring others’ happiness is ‘consciousness’ (cetanā); acting for one’s own happiness or desiring one’s own pleasure is ‘inertia’ (jaratā). Even bhakti and meditation performed for personal comfort, bodily ease, or honor are forms of inertia. Consciousness primarily generates divine wealth; inertia primarily generates asuri wealth. The root defect, which gives rise to all asuri wealth, is the acceptance of the body and the world’s existence and importance, thereby creating attachment to them. The root virtue, which reveals all divine wealth, is the acceptance of God’s existence and importance, thereby creating attachment to Him. These root defect and root virtue appear in many forms due to positional differences. As long as qualities (guṇa) coexist with their opposites (avaguṇa), the importance of the qualities is evident and pride arises. If no opposite qualities remain, pride disappears. Pride is the seed of asuri wealth. Because of pride, a person begins to see his own traits as superior to others—this is asuri wealth. Pride also turns divine wealth into a force that expands asuri wealth. When qualities exist without opposites, the importance of the qualities is no longer perceived, and pride does not arise. When the importance of qualities is not seen, the seeker’s attention does not turn to his own qualities, causing him to become anxious. This is why Arjuna, unable to see any divine wealth in himself, becomes frightened. To dispel such anxiety, the Lord says, “Do not lament, O Pandava, you are born of divine wealth.”

*

Once a distressed ascetic exclaimed, “I have no faith in the Gita; what will become of me?” He quoted the Lord’s words: “The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish” (4.40). I replied that the one who lacks faith meets destruction—where is this written? He answered, “In the Gita.” I said that the anxiety caused by the verses of the Gita shows his lack of faith; what then is the Gita without faith? Upon hearing this, he became delighted.

[Verse 6]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Connection - In this world, there are two aspects - consciousness and insentience - present in all living beings. Many living beings are focused on consciousness (the Supreme) and many are focused on insentience (worldly desires and attachments). In this way, living beings are divided into two categories, which the Lord will explain in the next verse. There are two types of creation in this world, O Partha, and both are present in this world. I will explain the divine in detail, and you, O Partha, listen to me about the demoniac. 6. Translation of the verse: "dvaau bhootsar-gau loke'smin daiva eva ca | daivaH vis-tarah pr-oktaH aasuram parth me sh-rinu || 6 ||"

Breakdown of the verse:
- "dvaau" = two
- "bhootsar-gau" = types of creation
- "loke'smin" = in this world
- "daiva" = divine
- "eva" = indeed
- "ca" = and
- "aasuram" = demoniac
- "parth" = O Partha
- "me" = to me
- "sh-rinu" = listen

Commentary:
The Lord begins to explain the demoniac nature in detail, starting with the fact that there are two types of creation in this world - divine and demoniac. The divine nature is the eternal soul (Atman) and the demoniac nature is the insentient aspect of the world. When the eternal soul is confronted with the changing insentient aspect, the demoniac nature arises. When the eternal soul is focused on the Supreme alone, the divine nature is awakened. The word "dev" means the Supreme. All the means to attain the Supreme, such as good qualities and virtues, are divine. Just as the Supreme is eternal, so are the means to attain Him. The Supreme has called the means to attain Him "avyaya" or eternal. "Imam vivasvate yogam proktavananham avyayam" (Gita 4.1). In the phrase "dvaau bhootsar-gau", the word "bhoot" can refer to all living beings, including humans, gods, demons, animals, plants, and even inanimate objects. However, the ability to renounce the demoniac nature is mainly present in the human form. Therefore, humans should renounce the demoniac nature completely. When they do, the divine nature will manifest automatically. A wise saying from the Puranas: "Krur-se krur kasai mein bhi daya rehti hai, chor-se chor mein bhi saahukari rehti hai." (In a butcher who kills, there is still compassion; in a thief who steals, there is still honesty.) Similarly, no one can be completely devoid of divine nature, as every living being is a part of the Supreme. The divine nature is inherent and natural, while the demoniac nature is acquired. Those who sincerely follow the path of devotion will find the demoniac nature constantly bothering them and will try to get rid of it. However, those who engage in worldly activities and attachments, thinking them necessary, are not true devotees. The reason is that both divine and demoniac natures are present in even the lowest of creatures. A special note: One should be aware that the tendency to act in accordance with one's ego is the root of all behavior. The strength of one's ego determines one's behavior. If one's ego is strong and says, "I am a truthful person," then that person will speak the truth. However, if one's ego is weak and says, "I am a worldly person and my purpose is to enjoy and accumulate wealth," then that person will be prone to lying and deceit.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 16 ]

The one who adopts deceitful means cannot succeed in his endeavors, nor can he achieve anything by pretending to be merciful. (Manu 7.44.3)

In today's world, it is indeed necessary to adopt such a means, and no one can escape this. In this way, the Lord creates humans from those who are egoistic, and it is only due to their downfall that they are unable to escape from wicked deeds. The Lord believes that these people will achieve their own salvation (deliverance) due to this reason. Therefore, people find it difficult to give up wicked qualities and vices. The Lord considers it impossible. The Lord has especially given humans the means and qualifications for achieving their goals, and also the power of discrimination. Therefore, the phrase 'loke'smin' specifically refers to humans. However, the Lord is equally present in all living beings - 'samahm sarva-bhuteshu' (Gita 9.29). Wherever the Lord resides, His wealth also resides. Therefore, the phrase 'bhutas-sargau' is used. This proves that all living beings can move towards the Lord. No one is barred from moving towards the Lord. As the part of the Supreme, no one can be devoid of good qualities. And, as a human being, one cannot be completely free from egoism and attachment to the body. Even if downfall occurs, the seed of good qualities is never destroyed, because good qualities are 'sat' (eternal) and 'sat' can never be absent - 'na abhavo vidyate sat' (2.16). On the other hand, wicked qualities are born from bad company and are not eternal - 'na asato vidyate bhava' (2.16). Human behavior is primarily determined by the predominance of good or wicked qualities. When good qualities predominate, one behaves well, and when wicked qualities predominate, one behaves wickedly. In other words, when the goal is to attain the Supreme, good qualities predominate, and wicked qualities are eliminated. But when the goal is to accumulate worldly wealth and possessions, wicked qualities predominate, and good qualities are suppressed. The phrase 'loke'smin' means that new opportunities are available only in this world. In this world, especially in the land of Bharat (India), unique opportunities are available. The gods have praised the people born in Bharatvarsha - *. The opportunity for salvation is available only in human life. Therefore, one should be cautious and awaken the divine wealth in this life. The Lord has especially given humans this human body - *

Those humans who are completely engaged in wicked deeds are more sinful than the lowest of creatures, such as chandalas, animals, birds, insects, and worms. The reason is that the lowest of creatures are born in their respective species due to their past sins and suffer the consequences of those sins. However, wicked humans engage in bad behavior knowingly and intentionally, thereby committing new sins. The lowest of creatures suffer the consequences of their past sins and move towards advancement, whereas wicked humans move towards downfall by committing new sins. Even such wicked humans can achieve eternal peace if they take shelter of the Lord and worship Him with devotion - (Gita 9.31-32). Similarly, even the most sinful person can attain salvation by crossing the ocean of ignorance with the boat of knowledge - (Gita 4.36). The meaning is that even the most wicked and sinful person can achieve salvation if they take shelter of the Lord and worship Him with devotion. The gods praise the people born in Bharatvarsha, saying, 'Ah! What have these people done to deserve such good fortune? Or has Lord Hari Himself become pleased with them? We too are always eager to attain such good fortune.' (Srimad Bhagavatam 5.19.21)

The gods praise the people born in Bharatvarsha, saying, 'The people born in Bharatvarsha are blessed. They become eligible for the path of heaven and liberation. They become eligible for the path of heaven and liberation due to their birth in Bharatvarsha.' (Vishnu Purana 2.3.24)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

One can attain salvation by acquiring devotion and knowledge, which is natural. Then, how can the mind be devoted to God for the sake of other sinful births? Therefore, the word 'bhoot' (all living beings) has been used here. In this way, divine qualities are seen in animals and birds. However, it is true that the field and capacity for the development of these divine qualities are not present in them. The field and capacity for their development are only present in the human body. Many instances are heard, read, and seen about the presence of divine nature in non-human living beings. Such examples are seen in animals, birds, plants, trees, creepers, and so on. In all these living beings, both divine and demonic qualities are present. Many dogs are seen that are wealthy. Humans protect all these living beings. They observe fasts on Amavasya, Ekadashi, and so on, and they should do so on these days only, as it is necessary for the protection of all living beings. They do not eat food on these days. Humans are created for the purpose of socializing with other living beings. In social gatherings, one has heard of the stories of animals and birds. Even snakes are seen in social gatherings. Sattvic animals, birds, plants, and so on are present, and their protection is necessary, as it benefits us. In Gorakhpur, when the kirtan was held for twelve months, special care was taken for their protection, as their protection benefits us. In the Kirtan Mandal, a black dog used to roam and sit wherever divine wealth increases. Just as the cow is our revered mother, in the place of satsang, it used to sit. In Rishikesh (Swaragashram), we should protect and care for the cow, as there was a saint there. The cause of the entire creation is - 'Gavo vishvasya matrah'. One day, the saint told the snake to stop, and it stopped. The yajna is performed with the ghee of a cow, but not with the ghee of a buffalo. The saint taught the snake the Gita, and it sat quietly. The Gita is a shower of knowledge. Knowledge is born from the shower, and from knowledge, living beings are born. The snake left that place and never returned. In the same way, other animals and birds are present, and their protection is necessary, as they are beneficial for us. For agriculture, the need for oxen arises. Oxen are present there. The oxen used to come there. (In this way, animals and birds have such a nature, which is due to their previous karma.)

In the Shanti Parva of the Mahabharata, there is a story about a hunter named Shakuni. His main work was to kill animals and birds. One day, he went to the forest to hunt. He roamed around the whole day, but he did not get any food. Suddenly, the sky became dark, and a storm with heavy rain started. The hunter took shelter under a tree. A pair of doves, a male and a female, lived on that tree. They had gone out to search for food, but due to the rain, the female dove returned quickly. Her wings were wet, and she fell down, so the hunter caught her and put her in his cage. When the male dove returned, he started crying, saying, 'My dear husband, why are you crying? You should perform your duty. I have come to your place as an atithi (guest). You should protect me.' The female dove replied, 'My dear husband, I am in the cage. You should not worry about me. I will take care of your hunger.' The male dove thought for a while, but he could not think of any other way to save his wife except by throwing himself into the fire. He went around the fire three times and then jumped into it. Seeing the hunter's cruelty, the male dove realized that he was a cruel and inhuman person. He thought, 'This dove has shown me so much respect, and I, a human being, am doing such a cruel act! From now on, I will never do such a sinful act again.' Saying this, he released the female dove from the cage. The female dove also jumped into the fire, crying, 'My dear husband, how will I live without you?' A chariot came, and the two doves boarded it and went to the heavens. Seeing the doves going to the heavens, the hunter threw away all his weapons and decided to renounce the world and practice devotion and self-control. He thought, 'I will not eat anything, but I will practice devotion and self-control.' Saying this, he went to the forest, where there were thorns everywhere. His body was scratched by the thorns. A forest fire was burning all around him. He jumped into the fire and died. At the time of his death, he was thinking of the Lord, and so he attained salvation.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 16 ]

The cultivation of the land by ploughing and irrigating it with the water from wells and other sources is the origin of the divine wealth. The produce of the land, such as grains, clothes, and other necessities, is the means of sustenance for all living beings, including humans, animals, and birds. The ghee and milk, which are essential for our food and drink, are also obtained from the land. These substances give us physical strength and spiritual purity. Similarly, the herbs and plants that grow in the land have the power to heal and rejuvenate the body. Therefore, we must take special care of the sattvic animals, birds, and herbs, so that our life in this world and the next may be improved. The Lord says, "I have described the divine wealth in detail." This includes the 26 characteristics mentioned earlier. Before this, the characteristics of the gunatita (beyond the three gunas) were described in the 14th chapter, from the 22nd to the 25th verse. The 20 means of knowledge were described in the 13th chapter, from the 7th to the 11th verse. The characteristics of the devotees were described in the 12th chapter, from the 13th to the 19th verse. The characteristics of the karma yogi were described in the 6th chapter, from the 7th to the 9th verse. And the characteristics of the sthitaprajna (one who has attained a steady state of consciousness) were described in the 2nd chapter, from the 71st to the 73rd verse. The Lord says, "Now, O Partha, listen to the description of the asuric wealth." This refers to the people who are solely concerned with their physical survival and do not know what is right and wrong. They do not know what is good and bad behavior, what is purity and impurity, what is truth and falsehood. They do not know how to cultivate good habits, how to maintain cleanliness, how to behave with respect towards elders and juniors, and how to speak the truth. As a result, they become detached from the divine and do not recognize the existence of God, dharma, and other spiritual principles. They believe that the origin of the world is the union of man and woman. Following this materialistic view, they cause suffering to others and ultimately lead themselves to a great downfall. Asurāḥ
Jana:
Pravṛttim
Pravṛttiṃ ca nivṛttiṃ ca jana na vidurāsuras. Na śaucam nāpi cācāro na satyaṃ teṣu vidyate. 7

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Commentary - People do not know what is right behavior and what is wrong behavior in today's chaotic environment, influenced by food, education, and other factors. They do not want to know either. If someone tries to explain it to them, they do not believe it, but instead, they laugh at them, consider them foolish, and think themselves to be wise due to their pride. Some people do know what is right behavior and what is wrong behavior, but due to the influence of asuric wealth, they do not follow their prescribed duties and do not abstain from prohibited actions. Therefore, the asuric wealth comes first, and they do not know right behavior and wrong behavior. How can one know right behavior and wrong behavior? It can be known through the guidance of a guru, a scripture, or a wise person. Additionally, if a person faces a calamity, gets stuck in a difficult situation, or experiences a strange event, their discriminative power awakens. If a person meets a great soul, their nature changes due to their past impressions, or if they visit places where powerful saints have resided, their discriminative power awakens. The discriminative power resides in all living beings. However, in animal and bird species, it is limited to their physical bodies only. In contrast, humans have the ability to develop and utilize their discriminative power not only for their own well-being but also for the well-being of their family and other living beings. Humans can abandon their bad qualities and adopt good qualities. Humans are completely free in this regard, as they are the sattvic species. However, animals and birds are not free, as they are the tamasic species. When humans have a special nature even in their eating and drinking habits, they do not have the awareness of their duties and non-duties. Such humans have a hidden divine wealth, which does not manifest in front of them. Even such humans are considered to be humans, as they have the potential to manifest divine wealth. Special Note

From verse 16.7 to verse 16.19, the words used by the Lord do not mention the term "man" or "human." This implies that even though humans have the potential to abandon asuric wealth and adopt divine wealth, those who remain asuric and do not adopt divine wealth are not worthy of being called humans. They are even lower than animals and hellish beings, as animals and hellish beings are moving towards purity, while these asuric humans are moving towards further sin and ignorance, wasting the human body they have obtained due to their past merits. The Lord has described the characteristics of asuric humans without using the term "animal" or "beast." Instead, He has used the terms "ashubhan" and "narahadhaman." This is because animals and beasts are not as sinful as asuric humans, and their presence does not lead to sin. However, the presence of asuric humans leads to sin and impurity. In verse 22 of this chapter, the Lord has used the term "narah" to indicate that only those who have abandoned the doors of hell and are engaged in selfless actions are worthy of being called humans. This is also confirmed in verse 23 of chapter 5. "There is no purity, no good behavior, and no truth among them" - Asuric humans do not have the awareness of purity and impurity. They do not have the awareness of their behavior towards others, such as how to behave with their elders and other humans. They do not have truth in their words and actions. They speak lies and act falsely. This is the meaning of being asuric. They are like animals, and their behavior is like that of animals. They only think of how to satisfy their own desires and live comfortably, saying "I will live and enjoy."

[ Chapter 16 ]
The idea is that due to the influence of demonic tendencies, they do not pay attention to their purity and good conduct. When even those who are engaged in rituals and other duties prescribed by the scriptures, in accordance with the rules, cannot make up their minds about the Supreme Self, then what to say about those who are overly engaged in unjust enjoyment and accumulation of wealth? The Lord has stated in the 44th verse of the second chapter that even those who follow the Vedic procedures for worldly enjoyment and accumulation of wealth find it extremely difficult to have a firm conviction about the Supreme Self. Appendix - As demonic tendencies increase, discretion is lost. Being addicted to worldly pleasures, demonic people cannot distinguish between what should be done and what should not be done. Their devotion is not even worldly, let alone spiritual; it leads them to hell. Demonic people are solely concerned with their own bodily comfort and self-interest. They are inclined towards whatever brings them pleasure and averts whatever brings them pain, based on their own selfish desires. In reality, the scriptures are the authority for determining what to do and what to avoid (Gita 16.24); however, demonic people do not follow the scriptures due to their attachment to their bodies and lives. They do not listen to the scriptures, and even if they do, they cannot understand them - "Even while striving, those who have not controlled their minds do not perceive Him" (Gita 15.11). Connection - Where there is no inclination towards virtuous actions, noble qualities are also disregarded, i.e., they are suppressed. Now, this will be explained. Verse 8:
They say that the world is unreal, without a basis, and born of mutual union, and that it is driven by lust. What else could be the cause? anishvaram = without a ruler

Commentary - Demonic people say that the world is unreal, meaning that nothing in it is true. They do not consider virtuous actions like sacrifices, charity, penance, meditation, self-study, pilgrimage, and vows to be real. They think these are just deceptions. They also say that the world is without a ruler, meaning that there is no God, no creator, and no one to govern it or dispense the fruits of good and bad deeds. 1. The natural tendency of the wicked is to not engage in devotion. (Ramayana 5.44.2)
2. The birth that occurs after death, whether in the mortal world or any other realm, or in any specific species, is all referred to as the afterlife.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The people who do not respect the social norms and traditions of their family, but instead consider only their own selfish interests as right, their courage and wisdom become so weak that they start thinking that their own selfishness is a virtue. They consider immorality as morality and think that they have no debt to their parents. They consider morality as immorality and think that they have no relation with good things. They consider falsehood, deceit, and cunning as good and consider truth as falsehood. They think that by accumulating wealth, they can save it. etc. are the misconceptions of such people. Parishishta Bhaav - In the third chapter, the Lord has also said that this worldly life is a great devourer - 'Mahashan' (3.37) and is like fire, which is never satisfied - 'Dushpurenaanalena cha' (3.39). Therefore, it is impossible to fulfill all worldly desires. Therefore, those who consider the fulfillment of desires as their goal, never get peace. There is great subjugation in the fulfillment of desires, but the asuric people experience freedom in this subjugation, thinking that if they get wealth and other material possessions, they will be free. They do not respect the scriptures, gurus, God, and dharma, so they do not take refuge in anyone except their own desires. Sambandh - Now, in the next two shlokas, we will explain the nature, behavior, and actions of those asuric people who are devoid of good deeds, good behavior, and good thoughts. Chinatamapareeyam cha pralayantamupashritah |
Kamopabhogaparama etavatiti nishchitah || 11 ||

They are always dependent on the endless worries of worldly life and are always engaged in accumulating wealth and material possessions, thinking that this is the only thing that will give them satisfaction. Pralayantam (those who are dependent on worldly life) and apareeyam (endless) chintaam (worries) upashritah (dependent on) = They are always dependent on the endless worries of worldly life. Kamopabhogaparama (engaged in accumulating wealth and material possessions) etavat (only this much) iti (thinking) nishchitah (convinced) = They are convinced that accumulating wealth and material possessions is the only thing that will give them satisfaction. Pralayantam (those who are dependent on worldly life) = Those who are dependent on worldly life will have to face the same fate as the worldly possessions they have accumulated. Their children will have to face the same fate as the wealth they have accumulated. Their wives will have to face the same fate as the wealth they have accumulated. Their relatives will have to face the same fate as the wealth they have accumulated. Their friends will have to face the same fate as the wealth they have accumulated. Their servants will have to face the same fate as the wealth they have accumulated. Their wealth will have to face the same fate as the wealth they have accumulated. Vyaakhya - 'Chinatamapareeyam mupashritah' - The asuric people have endless worries, which have no end or limit. As long as they are alive, these worries do not end. The fruit of these endless worries is also endless, i.e., they have to face death again and again. There are two types of worries - one is spiritual and the other is worldly. The spiritual worry is about one's own salvation and the other is about one's own worldly life. Those who have spiritual worries are superior. But the asuric people do not have spiritual worries. They are worried about their own worldly life, thinking about how they will live, how they will earn their livelihood, how they will be dependent on others, how they will maintain their prestige, how they will maintain their honor, how they will maintain their reputation, how they will maintain their name, etc. A person who is dependent on worldly life is worried about his own worldly life, thinking about how he will live, how he will earn his livelihood, how he will be dependent on others, how he will maintain his prestige, how he will maintain his honor, how he will maintain his reputation, how he will maintain his name, etc. He is worried about his own worldly life, thinking about how he will live, how he will earn his livelihood, how he will be dependent on others, how he will maintain his prestige, how he will maintain his honor, how he will maintain his reputation, how he will maintain his name, etc.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 16 ]

The rich man leaves the key outside and finds it inside the house. If he doesn't do this, he will have to starve to death. He went out and carelessly locked the door. Now, without the key, the door won't open, and he will die from lack of food, water, and air. He writes, "I am dying with so much wealth; I am dying with so much wealth, even though I have it all, because I am not getting food, water, or air inside." One will not die from the absence of food and other necessities, but one will die in the same way even with them. Just as a doctor won't give medicine to a patient even if food is available when the patient is suffering from a disease, a person will die in the same way even with necessities available. Those who do not collect even a single coin are blessed with more than what they need according to their past deeds. Therefore, one's life is not dependent on material things. However, people with an asuric nature cannot understand this truth. They think that we worry, desire, think, and work, and only then do we get things. Those who are devoted to the enjoyment and consumption of worldly things are always eager to accumulate wealth and enjoy it. Their only desire is to collect and enjoy wealth and material possessions. They think that wealth is necessary for enjoying worldly pleasures, for becoming famous in the world, and for satisfying their desires. In other words, they think that there is nothing more important than enjoying worldly things. Their conclusion is that enjoying and accumulating wealth is the only purpose of life. They believe that this is the only truth in the world. They think that there is no life after death and that the only thing that matters is enjoying life as long as the body is alive. They do not believe in the concept of karma, rebirth, and the afterlife. Commentary—A person who is devoted to enjoying and accumulating wealth becomes blind. He cannot understand the world or the Supreme Being. His vision is limited to the material world, and he considers it to be the only reality. He thinks that the material world is permanent, while the Supreme Being is impermanent. He cannot understand how the impermanent material world can provide satisfaction to the eternal Supreme Being. Ashapasha-shatair-baddhah: (Those who are bound by hundreds of fetters of desire and attachment)

(3) One does not get grains or money by worrying. Ramdas sits in meditation, and everything comes to him in abundance. 2. Similarly, those who believe in the existence of heaven also say that there is nothing more important than heaven. Their only desire is to go to heaven after death and enjoy its divine pleasures. They think that the pleasures of heaven are greater than the pleasures of the world. 3. As long as one lives, one should live happily. One should drink ghee (clarified butter) by taking a loan. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

People are bound by the noose of hope. It is the duty of those who are bound by the noose of hope to control others with anger, otherwise people will take away our entire wealth. Then we will have no existence at all, and so on. Even if we have millions or billions of rupees, their greed does not subside. Their only hope is that they will get something from saints, from God, from humans, from animals, birds, trees, creepers, mountains, and oceans, and so on. In this way, they remain constantly in the state of 'I will get, I will get'. Such people's worldly hopes are never fulfilled (Gita – 9th Chapter, 12th Verse). If their hopes are fulfilled, it will not be of any benefit; because if they live, the object of their hope will be destroyed, and if the object of their hope remains, they will die, or both will be destroyed. Those who are bound by the noose of hope can never remain stable at one place, and those who have escaped from this noose of hope live happily at one place – 'Aśā nām manuṣyāṇāṃ kācid aścary śṛṅkhala' (The hope of humans is a strange chain that binds them). Those who are bound by this chain run about, and those who are free from it remain stable. Their ultimate goal, their abode is Kāma (desire) and Krodha (anger) – that is, their life is only for fulfilling their desires and tormenting others with anger. They are convinced that without desires, a human being becomes dull. Without anger, their energy does not remain. All their actions are for fulfilling their desires, otherwise, why would they work? Without desires, their life would become a burden. In the world, Kāma (desire) and Krodha (anger) are the only things that matter. Without them, people would not let us live in the world. It is through anger that the government runs, otherwise, who would obey the government? The asuric natured people's aim is to accumulate wealth and enjoy worldly pleasures through unjust means, such as cheating, deception, and theft. They believe that in today's world, one can only accumulate wealth through unjust means. They think that honesty and justice are mere words, and they cannot be put into practice. If we work honestly and justly, we will suffer and it will be difficult to sustain life. This is the conviction of those with asuric nature. However, even those who have accumulated wealth through unjust means can, if they wish, make a resolve to attain the Supreme and become devoted to spiritual practice. There is no restriction on anyone to make such a resolve; because human birth is meant for attaining the Supreme. However, those who have accumulated wealth through unjust means cannot have the conviction of attaining the Supreme, because their minds are not pure. The phrase 'āśāpāśaśatāir badhhāḥ' means that as long as there is a connection with the world, the noose of hope does not break. In the 42nd verse of the 2nd chapter, it is said, 'Bahushākhā hy anantāśca buddhyo 'vyavasāyinām' (The minds of those who are not devoted to spiritual practice are infinite and have many branches). This is because they have turned away from the eternal and have attached themselves to the ephemeral and have formed a connection with it. The asuric natured people consider Kāma (desire) and Krodha (anger) to be their natural tendencies. They do not see anything beyond Kāma and Krodha. These are their ultimate goal, their abode. A human being thinks that by getting angry, he can control others. But the one who is helpless and weak will not remain under our control for long. As soon as he gets a chance, he will harm us. Therefore, the result of anger is always bad. In this chapter, the 10th verse says that 'Dambha, Māna, and Mad' are their companions, and here it is said that 'Kāma and Krodha' are their refuge.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 16
The Proud and the Wealthy
We are wealthy,
similar to others,
I am not,
there are many others,
who are more,
who can be happy? There is a man who thinks this way about us. We will perform many yajnas,
we will give much in charity,
and we will enjoy ourselves,
in this way,
those who are deluded by ignorance,
remain so.]

Explanation—A person with an asura nature will be proud of the yajnas they have performed, the charity they have given. They will think, "We are wealthy, we have so much gold and silver, houses, land, and many good people on our side. We have so much power and influence that we can do whatever we want." They will think, "There is no one else like me, I am unique." They will think, "We will perform such grand yajnas, give such large amounts in charity, that everyone will be impressed." They will think, "What is the use of performing small yajnas, giving small amounts in charity, and feeding a few brahmins? We will perform yajnas and give charity on a grand scale, like no one has ever done before." They will think, "We will make our name famous in the newspapers, and build a temple in a dharmashala with our name on it, so that people will remember us."

In this way, people with an asura nature are always thinking, "We will do this, we will do that," but they never actually do anything. They will perform yajnas and give charity, but only for show, to impress others. They are deluded by ignorance and remain so, because of their foolishness. [ Connection—The asuras, who are deluded by ignorance, experience anxiety, jealousy, and suffering in this life. But what happens to them after death? This is explained in the next shloka.]

Distracted by many thoughts,
deluded by the net of ignorance,
they are drawn to sensual pleasures,
and fall into the filthy hell. 16. Explanation—People who are distracted by many thoughts, and are deluded by the net of ignorance, are drawn to sensual pleasures and fall into the filthy hell. They are like a person who is caught in a spider's web and cannot escape. [ Verse 16 ]

Commentary—Those people whose minds are distracted by many thoughts, and who are deluded by the net of ignorance, are always thinking about many things and are never satisfied. They are always thinking about how to fulfill their desires, and their minds are always wandering. The net of ignorance refers to the tendency to be deluded by one's own ignorance and to be caught in the cycle of birth and death. Those who are deluded by ignorance are always thinking about sensual pleasures and are never satisfied. In this way, people who are deluded by ignorance are always thinking about sensual pleasures and are never satisfied.

[Verse 17]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Those who are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and their enjoyment, and who are excessively proud of their wealth, status, and comforts, are extremely attached to these things. They consider themselves superior to everyone else and think that they deserve to be worshiped and revered. They are so engrossed in their own ego and pride that they are unaware of their own downfall. Just like a fish trapped in a net, they are caught in the net of their own desires and cannot escape. They are unaware of the suffering that awaits them due to their own actions. They are trapped in the net of their own ego and pride, and they are unaware of the consequences of their actions. Their desires are not limited to one side; they have desires on both sides. They think, "I will get this much wealth, but then I will face this obstacle." "I will get this much status, but then I will face this problem." They are always worried about the consequences of their actions, but they are unable to escape the net of their own desires. Asuric people, who are attached to worldly pleasures and their enjoyment, are always accompanied by greed, anger, and pride, along with fear. They are never certain about their actions, and they are always trapped in the net of their own desires. Parishishta Bhaav – In reality, asuric people are already in hell due to their attachment to worldly pleasures and their enjoyment. They are burning in the fire of their own ego and pride. As a result, they suffer from severe suffering and fear in this life, and in the next life, they will face even more severe suffering and fear. 'Patanti narake'shauca' - The net of their own desires is already a hell for them, and after death, they will face even more severe suffering in places like Kumbhipaka, Maharaurava, etc. They will fall into even more severe suffering and fear in those hells. The phrase 'narake'shauca' means that they will fall into hells where they will suffer from unbearable suffering and fear. This is because their actions in this life will determine their fate in the next life. It is not the physical location or actions that determine their fate, but their attitude and behavior. The value of their attitude and behavior determines their actions. Therefore, the Lord has described the attitude and behavior of asuric people. Samabandh – The Lord will now describe the consequences of the actions of asuric people, who are attached to worldly pleasures and their enjoyment. He will explain how their actions will lead to suffering and fear in this life and the next life. Aatma-sambhavitah: Those who consider themselves superior to everyone else. Dhanamana-mad-anvitah: Those who are proud of their wealth and status. Avidhi-purvakam: Those who perform rituals and worship without any sense of devotion. Yajante namayajnais: They perform rituals and worship with a sense of pride and arrogance. Tebhyah: Those who are proud of their wealth and status. Stabdhah: Those who are stubborn and inflexible. Dambhen: Those who perform rituals and worship with a sense of pride and arrogance. Yajante: They perform rituals and worship. 17. Translation of the shloka: Those who consider themselves superior to everyone else, who are proud of their wealth and status, and who perform rituals and worship without any sense of devotion, are performing rituals and worship with a sense of pride and arrogance. Vyaakhya – 'Aatma-sambhavitah' means that they consider themselves superior to everyone else and think that they deserve to be worshiped and revered. They are proud of their wealth and status and think that they are above everyone else. Narake'shauca: Those who are proud of their wealth and status will fall into hells where they will suffer from unbearable suffering and fear.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 16 ]
It is desirable that we should be praised. The varna, ashrama, vidya, buddhi, and bhavas are all in accordance with their behavior. We are superior in all respects in terms of pad, adhikar, yogya, and so on; therefore, all people should follow us. ' Stabdhah ' - They do not bow down to anyone, nor do they bow down. Even if a great saint or an avataric God comes in front of them, they will not bow down to them. They consider themselves to be superior, so why should they bow down to anyone? If they are forced to bow down to anyone due to some reason, they will do so with pride. In this way, they have a lot of arrogance. ' Dhanamanamadavitah ' - They are always intoxicated with wealth and fame. They have a mad (intoxicated) state of mind due to wealth, their family, land, property, and house. If they get recognition from someone, they also get intoxicated with that. They think, "We have connections with big ministers, and we have such power that we can get whatever we want, and we can destroy whatever we want." In this way, wealth and fame are their only support. They are intoxicated with these things, and they consider them to be superior. ' Yajante namayajñas te dambhen ' - They perform name-based yajnas (rituals) with pride. They perform yajnas only to show off to others and to increase their own prestige. They do this with the intention that others will be impressed by them and will be influenced by their power. They want people to know about their greatness, and they want to be famous. They will publicize their name through yajnas, and they will distribute pamphlets and other materials to promote their name. They will even give less food to brahmins so that they can save money and still get recognition. They will also give more food to brahmins in a way that will make a big impression on others. In this way, they perform yajnas and other rituals with pride, without following the scriptures. When a big festival or fair is held in a temple, and many people are expected to attend, they will decorate the temple nicely, dress up the priests nicely, and give them expensive gifts so that many people will come and give them donations. In this way, the priests will get a lot of recognition, but the real purpose is to attract people and get their donations. If a big minister or official is coming to the temple, they will decorate the temple nicely and give them a lot of respect, and they will give them a special mala and prasad so that they will be pleased and will help them in their business and other matters. In this way, the priests are performing a superficial puja (worship) of the deity, but the real purpose is to attract people and get their donations. Similarly, the managers of gau-sevi (cow protection) organizations will keep only healthy cows that give a lot of milk in the goshala, and they will give them a lot of food. They will not keep old, lame, blind, or milkless cows, and if they do keep them, they will give them less food. But they will publicize the goshala as a great place for cow protection, without showing its real condition. They will print pamphlets, write articles, and give advertisements to promote the goshala, so that they can get more money and less expenses. Similarly, the managers of dharmic (religious) organizations will use the organization's money to run their own business. They will think about how to make a profit, how to run their business, and how to get more money. They will perform superficial rituals and activities, without following the scriptures, and they will do everything just to show off to others. Even the people who perform sadhana (spiritual practices) will do so just to show off to others, without any real devotion or spiritual growth.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

- 
We will sit down after assuming a posture, start chanting and meditating, but where can we talk about the nature of those who are born of nature? We will start rotating the rosary. However, if no one is watching, they will engage in discussions about the scriptures in an unscriptural manner - those people who are of an asuric nature will engage in playing cards or dice, or they will not even believe in the scriptures. They will always engage in activities that are forbidden by the scriptures. They will engage in such activities. This kind of devotion and worship is only done so that others may consider us good, consider us devotees, and praise us. They will give donations, but they will not give them to the worthy, they will give them to the unworthy. They will respect us, they will consider us worthy, and they will praise us. They will keep company with the unworthy and will keep unity with them. This is the way they will engage in devotion and worship. This kind of devotion and worship is only done for the sake of name and fame. It is only done for the sake of name and fame. In reality, this kind of devotion and worship is done by those who are of an asuric nature. It appears to be a virtuous activity, but it is actually a vicious activity. (Gita 18.32)

Parishishta Bhaav - 
Asuric natured people are in competition with others and therefore they perform yajnas so that no one may consider them inferior to others. They perform yajnas only to gain fame among people, they do not have faith in the fruits of their actions. When someone else performs a yajna, they think that he also performs it only for the sake of fame. They do not have faith in the existence of God and the next world, therefore their vision is not in accordance with the scriptures. They think only about what is written in the scriptures, not about what is beneficial for them. They are of the opinion that if someone performs a certain action, then a certain fruit will be obtained. -
All the activities of asuric natured people are superficial. However, they have a sense of pride that they will perform better yajnas than others. They have a sense of pride that they are knowledgeable and others are ignorant. In reality, they are full of foolishness. =

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 16 ]
Those who are opposed to the Supreme Lord residing in their heart, who reject the good thoughts that arise in their heart, who reject the good principles of the scriptures, and who do not accept the good qualities of others, are considered to be inimical to the Lord. A person who opposes the Lord and engages in enmity with Him is certainly a lowly wretch and will fall into the hells. Even the sages and great souls who are now in the hells were once great sages and great souls. The worldly-minded people say that the sages and great souls are also afflicted with the defects of attachment, aversion, greed, and egoism, and that they are also subject to the same weaknesses as ordinary people. But this is all a pretence. We have also seen that the sages and great souls who have practiced self-control, devotion, and austerities have not attained any real benefit. They have only suffered pain and their time has been wasted. The worldly-minded people are also deceived by the false claims of the sages and great souls. They say that the sages and great souls are also subject to the same weaknesses as ordinary people and that they are not really self-controlled.

[Verse 20]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The excessive attachment to worldly possessions in the body, due to the influence of nature, makes a person fall into the asuric (demonic) state. This is why the Lord says, 'I cast them into the asuric wombs' (asurishu eva yonishu kshipami). The Lord has described attachment (raga) as the cause of all sins (tisri adhyay ka sathvar shlok). As attachment increases, the asuric wealth also increases. Just as excessive attachment to wealth leads to an increase in vices like deceit, cunning, and falsehood, and an intense desire to acquire more wealth, similarly, the attachment to worldly possessions leads to an increase in cruelty and a desire to acquire wealth by any means. This eventually leads to a person becoming a thief, a robber, or even a murderer. As a result, their nature becomes more and more cruel, and they are eventually born in the asuric wombs of animals, insects, or other creatures. The Lord's intention in casting them into the asuric wombs is not to abandon them, but to purify them. The Lord has compassion on all beings, even those who are cruel and wicked. Just as a teacher disciplines his students to make them wise and virtuous, the Lord disciplines those who are ignorant of Him and His glory, and who are engaged in sinful activities. The Lord says, 'I cast them into the asuric wombs, where they are born again and again in a state of ignorance.'

Hence, the Lord says, 'Kshipamy ajastram ashubhan asurishu eva yonishu' - I cast them into the asuric wombs, where they are born again and again in a state of ignorance. The Lord's intention is to purify them, to make them realize their true nature, and to lead them to the path of righteousness. The Lord says, 'Aasurim apanna muuda janmani janmani' - Those who are born in the asuric wombs, and who are ignorant of Me, are born again and again in a state of ignorance. They do not attain Me, even in their human birth, and they are thus led to the path of destruction. The Lord says, 'Mam aprapy eva kaunteya tato yantyadhamam gatim' - Even in their human birth, when they have the opportunity to attain Me, they do not do so, and are thus led to the path of destruction. [Verse 20]

Oh, son of Kunti! Those who are ignorant and do not attain Me, are born again and again in the asuric wombs, and are led to the path of destruction. Translation of the verse:

Oh, son of Kunti! Commentary:

The Lord has already mentioned that those who are born in the asuric wombs are born again and again in a state of ignorance. Now, He says that even in their human birth, when they have the opportunity to attain Him, they do not do so, and are thus led to the path of destruction.

*
Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
'To me alone' - The Lord says this with great compassion, 'I have given human bodies to living beings and given them the opportunity to attain salvation, but these wretched beings have become so foolish and unfaithful that they have not attained salvation through the very body that was meant for it. They have instead taken the path of the wicked. Regardless of how a person behaves after attaining a human body, they can still attain the Lord if they wish, even in a short time (Gita - 9th Chapter, 31st Verse) or at the end of their life (Gita - 8th Chapter, 5th Verse). This is because the Lord has said, 'I am equal to all beings' (Gita 9.29), making salvation accessible to all living beings. However, it is possible that some animals and birds may not have the capacity to attain the Lord. But from the Lord's side, there is no prohibition for anyone. Despite having the opportunity to attain the Lord, these wicked humans do not attain Him and instead take the path of the wicked. Seeing this, the compassionate Lord is filled with sorrow. 'Then they go to the path of the wicked' - Even after taking the path of the wicked, their sins are not completely destroyed. Therefore, they have to suffer the consequences of their remaining sins in the form of even more wicked paths, such as hell. There may be a question here - If the wicked humans who have taken the path of the wicked do not have the capacity to attain the Lord in their current form, then why did the Lord say that they will not attain Him even if they do not take the path of the wicked? The answer is that the Lord's statement is made before they take the path of the wicked, while they are still in their human form. In other words, even after attaining the human form and having the opportunity to attain the Lord, they do not attain Him and instead take the path of the wicked. The special thing is that
[ Chapter 16
Even after attaining the human form for the purpose of attaining the Lord or for one's own well-being, a person becomes a slave to their desires, ego, and pride and engages in sinful activities such as theft, robbery, lying, cheating, deception, violence, etc. The consequences of these actions are of two types - (1) external fruit - part and (2) internal samskaras - part. When someone causes suffering to others, they suffer the same harm that was destined for them; however, the person who causes suffering is guilty of a new sin, which they will have to suffer in hell. Moreover, the seeds of new sins are sown through sinful activities, which lead to the growth of evil tendencies in a person's heart. For example, a person who commits theft becomes a thief themselves, as they will continue to steal and the tendency to steal will become deeply ingrained in their heart. This is how evil tendencies are created through sinful activities. These tendencies lead to a person's downfall and cause them to commit more and more sinful acts, ultimately leading them to suffer in hell. As long as a person does not attain their own well-being and does not remove the evil tendencies that have taken root in their heart, these tendencies will continue to cause them to commit sinful acts and lead them to suffer in hell. Even after they have suffered in various forms of existence and hells, if they are reborn as humans, their evil tendencies will still be present in their heart, causing them to commit sinful acts and suffer in hell. It is observed in all forms of existence and hells that some beings are gentle and peaceful, while others are cruel and violent. This difference in nature is due to the pure or impure ego that they have created for themselves. Even after experiencing the consequences of their actions in various forms of existence and hells, their nature remains the same. Moreover, even after experiencing all forms of existence and hells, if a being is reborn as a human, their evil tendencies will still be present in their heart, causing them to commit sinful acts and suffer in hell. 'Durabhav from which durachar are born, and durachar from which durabhav are strengthened.'

[ Verse 21 ]  
* Sadhak‑Sanjeevani *

The same holds for those who, driven by the desire for heaven, perform good deeds here: their nature does not change, i.e., there is no transformation in their innermost self. The opportunity to modify and purify one’s nature exists only in the human body. After death, they go to heaven according to those deeds; the fruits of their actions are enjoyed there, but the relationship—mentioned in the previous verse—remains: the Lord says that these souls, even after attaining the chance to reach Him in the human body, do not attain Him, and therefore He must send them to a lower womb. The fundamental cause of their descent into the lower womb and the lower realm (hell) is explained by the Lord in the following verse. **Shloka (Verse 21)**  
trividhaṁ narakasya idaṁ dvāraṁ nāśanam ātmanah  
kāmaḥ krodhas tathā lobhas tasmād etat trayaṁ tyajet

*Translation:* There are three doors to hell, which bring about the destruction of the self: desire, anger, and greed; therefore one should abandon these three. **Word‑by‑word breakdown**  
trividhaṁ – three kinds  
narakasya – of hell  
idaṁ – this  
dvāraṁ – door, gateway  
nāśanam – ruin, destruction  
ātmanah – of the self  
kāmaḥ – desire (the craving for sense‑objects)  
krodhas – anger (the fiery agitation)  
tathā – as well as  
lobhas – greed (the clinging to accumulation)  
tasmād – therefore  
etat – this  
trayaṁ – trio  
tyajet – should be abandoned

The commentary explains that “kāmaḥ, krodhas, tathā lobhas” are the three enemies that cause downfall and must be renounced. The phrase “lobhas trividhaṁ” (greed in three forms) is linked to the twelfth verse of Chapter 5 of the Gita, where the Lord describes how a person becomes bound. In Chapter 3, verse 36, Arjuna asked about “narakasya idaṁ dvāraṁ.” The Lord had earlier said in Chapter 5, verse 5, that divine wealth leads to liberation while demonic wealth leads to bondage. Demonic wealth arises where worldly desire exists. The accumulation of worldly pleasures—material possessions, honor, prestige, comfort—appears attractive, and it is precisely this attraction that draws a person toward hell. Hence desire (kāma), anger (krodha), greed (lobha), illusion (moha), pride (mada), and jealousy (matsara) are classified as the six enemies. Sometimes three, sometimes two, sometimes one of them are cited to answer why a person, even without wanting to, commits sin. The Lord identifies “kāma” and “krodha” as two foes, but emphasizes “kāma” as the primary cause, because obstruction of desire gives rise to anger. Thus desire, anger, and greed are the three enemies. The implication is that the tendency toward enjoyment is “kāma,” while the tendency toward accumulation is “lobha.” When “kāma” appears alone, it includes the other two; they are inter‑mixed, of the same metal, and the desire for enjoyment and accumulation arise together. Yet “kāma” remains the root because desire itself generates both. Greed and desire arise independently, leading to the pursuit of enjoyment. **Ancient citations**

1. “Atyanta‑kopaḥ kaṭukā ca vāṇī daridrata ca svajanesu vairaḥ. Nīcaprasangaḥ kulahīna‑sevā cihnāni dehe narakasthitānām.”  
(Chanakya Nīti, 7.17)  
*Translation:* Among those who have come from hell are the marks of extreme anger, harsh speech, poverty, hostility toward one’s own, association with the lowly, and service to the lineage‑less. 2. “Svargasthitānām iha jīvaloke catvāri cihnāni vasanti dehe. Dāna‑prasangaḥ madhurā ca vāṇī devārchanaṁ brāhmaṇa‑tarpanaṁ ca.”  
(Chanakya Nīti, 7.16)  
*Translation:* Those who return from heaven and dwell in the human world bear four marks in the body: a disposition toward charity, sweet speech, worship of the deities, and satisfaction of the Brahmins.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 16 ]

The desire for enjoyment and the desire for accumulating wealth lead to the emergence of 'Kama' (lust) and 'Lobha' (greed), respectively. These two are obstacles to one's progress. When 'Kama', 'Krodha' (anger), and 'Lobha' all increase, 'Moha' (attachment) arises. Kama gives rise to Krodha, and Krodha leads to Moha (attachment) (Gita - Chapter 2, Verse 62-63). If there is no obstacle to Kama, then Lobha arises, and Lobha leads to Moha. In reality, Kama assumes the form of Krodha and Lobha. When Moha arises, the Tamo-guna (darkness) manifests. Then, the entire Asuri (demonic) wealth is acquired. The three - Kama, Krodha, and Lobha - are the causes of a person's downfall. Those whose goal is to enjoy and accumulate wealth think that they are doing the right thing. Their mindset is that they will enjoy life, live comfortably, and accumulate wealth. This mindset itself leads to their downfall. 'Tyajet' - these three - Kama, Krodha, etc. - are the gates of hell. Therefore, a person should renounce them. How to renounce them? In Chapter 3, Verse 34, the Lord has said that in every sense object, there is a tendency to be attracted and a tendency to be repelled. The Sādhanā (spiritual practitioner) should not be under the control of these two tendencies. Being under their control means that one should not act with the intention of enjoying sensual pleasures or accumulating wealth, as this would lead to the downfall of a person, contrary to the teachings of the scriptures, Dharma, and social norms. Parishishta Bhaav - Enjoying sensual pleasures is 'Kama'. Accumulating wealth is 'Lobha'. When there is an obstacle to enjoying and accumulating, 'Krodha' (anger) arises. These three are the roots of Asuri (demonic) wealth. All sins arise from these three. A person and his wealth are lost, but the demonic mindset leads people to hell. Sambandh - Now, the Lord will explain the glory of being free from Kama, Krodha, and Lobha:

Etair Vimuktah Kaunteya Tamodvare Trinbhir Narah
Acharaty Atmanah Shreyo Tatha Yati Param Gati

Translation:

[Verse 22]
Oh, son of Kunti! He who is free from these three - Kama, Krodha, and Lobha - and is under the control of the three gates of hell, performs the actions that lead to his own good and attains the supreme state. Vyakhya - 'Etair Vimuktah Kaunteya Tatoh Yati Param Gati' - One who is free from Kama, Krodha, and Lobha and performs actions that lead to his own good attains the supreme state. Therefore, the Sādhanā should be very careful not to be under the control of these three. Because, one who is under their control is not a true Sādhanā. A true Sādhanā is one who does not allow these three to be with him. These three always trouble him, because allowing them to be with him is a great mistake. Gati - In the previous shloka, the three - Kama, Krodha, and Lobha - were referred to as the gates of hell. Here, they are referred to as 'Tamodvare' (gates of darkness). 'Tam' is the name of darkness, which arises from ignorance - 'Tamastvajnanajam viddhi' (Gita 14.8). The meaning is that due to Kama, etc., one thinks, 'These wealth, women, men, house, etc. were not with me before, will not be with me in the future, and are not with me now. Therefore, I should not be attached to them.' This thought does not arise in the mind, and therefore, there is darkness in the intellect. Therefore, people who are Sādhanās pay attention to their spiritual practice, but they are under the control of Kama, etc. How much harm they cause to themselves!
