* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The sages who practice yoga are less attentive to this side (of the world). Without this detachment, no benefit will be obtained. This is the reason why, even after years of practicing yoga, the practitioner does not see their true progress, and they do not experience any special change within themselves. Once they are free from these defects, purity comes naturally. The impurity in the living being has arisen due to attachment to the world; otherwise, being a part of the Supreme, it is inherently pure—

While practicing yoga, one also develops good behavior and bad behavior; good qualities and bad qualities coexist. By performing japa, dhyana, kirtan, satsang, self-study, pilgrimage, and vows, etc., we can purify ourselves - this is the special attitude of the practitioner; but the thought of removing the bad qualities and bad behavior that are harming us is less in the practitioner's mind, therefore—

From the moment one wakes up until one falls asleep, and from the moment one realizes their true nature until death, one should dedicate all their time to contemplating the Supreme Reality (with attributes and without attributes). Give no opportunity to worldly desires and other passions, no matter how small. This does not mean that when we are free from bad qualities and bad behavior, we will then practice yoga; but the practitioner should keep the main goal of attaining the Lord in mind and also strive to be free from them. Because, even if we have good behavior, such as truthfulness, honesty, and self-control, as long as we are attached to worldly desires, passions, and vices, new impurities and new sins will arise, and our practice of yoga will be ineffective—

The Lord is the imperishable Self, conscious, and the embodiment of bliss. (Manas 7.117.1)

The meaning of "shreyah acharati" is that one should not engage in behavior that involves worldly desires, anger, and greed; one should be free from worldly behavior (asat-sanga) and cultivate pure behavior. If any worldly tendency arises within, do not allow it to manifest in one's actions. One should only strive to eliminate worldly tendencies from within. If they cannot be eliminated, one should call out to the Lord, "O Lord! O Lord! O Lord!" Gosaiani Tulasidas Maharaj says—

My Lord, You reside in my heart. Many thieves reside there. They make it difficult for me to live. They do not listen to my prayers. (Vinay Patrika 125.2-3)

Parishishta Bhaav - The meaning of "etair vimuktah" is to be free from worldly desires, anger, and greed. The goal is to renounce these and not be under their control. Even if good actions are performed due to worldly desires, anger, or greed, they do not lead to spiritual growth. Therefore, one should pay special attention to renouncing these. If one is controlled by worldly desires, anger, and greed, even if one performs spiritual practices (such as japa and dhyana), spiritual growth will not occur; because these are the root causes of all sins (Gita, third chapter, thirty-third shloka). Worldly desires, anger, and greed destroy dharma and social norms, causing great harm to the world. People with an asuric nature are attached to worldly desires, anger, and greed. They perform good actions, such as yajna and dana, only for show, without any intention of spiritual growth. On the other hand, divine beings who are practicing yoga are not under the control of worldly desires, anger, and greed, and they perform actions that lead to their own spiritual growth, benefiting the world. Asuric people consider these divine beings to be foolish and harbor ill will towards them, but the divine beings have compassion for them and pray to the Lord to grant them good sense. Relation - Those who follow the path of the scriptures and act for their own benefit will attain the ultimate goal, but those who do not follow the path of the scriptures and act according to their own whims will have what fate? This is explained in the next shloka. One who abandons the path of the scriptures and acts according to their own desires will not attain perfection, nor happiness, nor the ultimate goal. 23.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The person who abandons the path of scripture and acts according to his own desires, is not successful in achieving self-purification (siddhi) - that is, he does not attain purity of the heart. He does not attain happiness (sukha) - that is, he does not attain peace. He acts in accordance with his own desires, and thus he does not attain happiness. Explanation: [ This is similar to the 18th verse of the 17th chapter. ]

The people who abandon the path of scripture and act according to their own desires, are those who, despite following the prescribed rituals and performing good deeds, do so without any regard for the scriptural path. They perform yajnas, give donations, and engage in various other good deeds for the benefit of the world, but they do so without any regard for the scriptural path. They act according to their own desires, without any consideration for the scriptural path. The reason for this is that they are not concerned with the inner qualities of their heart, such as greed, anger, and attachment. They are only concerned with their external actions, and they consider themselves to be great due to these external actions. Others also consider them to be great due to their external actions. However, very few people are aware of the inner qualities of their heart. In reality, the inner qualities of the heart are of great importance. If a person has inner qualities such as greed, anger, and attachment, and yet appears to be a great ascetic or a great yogi, he will ultimately fall into ruin. He will become arrogant and will start to criticize others. His virtues will be transformed into vices, and his glory will be transformed into infamy. His renunciation will be transformed into attachment, and his detachment will be transformed into attachment to worldly pleasures. He will ultimately fall into ruin. Therefore, it is only when a person has inner qualities such as greed, anger, and attachment that he abandons the scriptural path and acts according to his own desires. He does not attain self-purification (siddhi) - that is, he does not attain purity of the heart. He does not attain the supreme goal (param gati) - that is, he does not attain liberation. Just as a person who is suffering from a disease may abandon the path of health and start to follow a path that is detrimental to his health, and thus his health will deteriorate further. Similarly, a person who is on the path of spirituality may abandon the scriptural path and start to act according to his own desires, and thus he will fall into ruin. [ Chapter 16 ]

In other words, you should perform your duty according to the scriptural injunctions. Commentary—'Therefore, the scripture is the authority for determining what is to be done and what is not to be done.'—For those who are attached to their lives and are proceeding with the hope of the next world, not knowing the duty and what is not to be done, i.e., pravritti and nivritti, they are especially inclined towards demonic tendencies. Therefore, you should consider the scripture as the authority for determining your duty. Those whose glory has been sung by the scriptures and whose conduct is in accordance with the scriptural principles, following the conduct and words of such saints is also considered as following the scriptures. This is because those great men have respected the scriptures and have become great by following them. In fact, the scriptures are formed from the conduct, ideals, and emotions of those who have attained the Supreme Reality. The scripture is the authority in determining what is to be done and what is not to be done. 'Knowing the ordinance of the scripture, you ought to perform your duty in this world.' A person who is devoted to the maintenance of his life does not know the scriptural injunctions (as to what to do and what to avoid); therefore, he does not attain perfection, etc. The Lord tells Arjuna that he has attained divine tendencies, so he should know the scriptural injunctions and follow his duty. Arjuna used to say earlier, based on his own conviction, that by fighting the war, he would incur sin, whereas, for the fortunate and great Kshatriyas, the war that comes of its own accord is a gateway to heaven (Gita, 2.32). The Lord says, "Brother! You are determining sin and virtue according to your own mind; you should consider the scripture as the authority in this matter."
The meaning of 'scripture is the authority' is that in this world, the human body is obtained only for performing noble deeds and attaining the Supreme Reality. Therefore, do not let this opportunity go to waste. Appendix / Parishishta Bhaav – The demonic men consider themselves accomplished and happy due to pride – 'I am accomplished, I am strong, I am happy' (Gita 16.14), but in reality, they are not accomplished and happy – 'they do not attain perfection, nor happiness'. The fire of pride and hatred burns in their hearts! Connection—By abandoning the scriptural injunctions, one does not attain perfection, etc. Therefore, what should one do? * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 16 ]

It is essential to understand the command of the scriptures before performing one's duty. A person who performs actions with a selfless attitude, free from personal interests, should perform his duty. This implies that the action that binds is not the war-like activity, but rather the action performed with self-interest and pride (such as performing rituals like yajna and dana), which binds. On the other hand, actions performed in a whimsical manner (contrary to the scriptures) lead to downfall. Even though the war-like activity appears to be cruel and violent, it is not considered sinful (Gita – 18th Chapter, 43rd Verse). The implication is that one does not attain sin by performing actions in accordance with one's natural disposition, as ordained by the scriptures (for a brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, or shudra). Sin arises from self-interest, pride, and thinking ill of others. The purpose of human life is to attain the ultimate goal of realizing the Supreme Self, free from attachment to the body and its life forces. One should perform actions ordained by the scriptures with this ultimate goal in mind. Parishishta Bhaav – In the 7th verse, the Lord said that those with an asura nature do not understand what is right and wrong. Here, the Lord explains that this asura nature can be eliminated by following the scriptures. A question may arise as to how those who have not studied the scriptures can understand their duty. The answer is that if their intention is to attain their own well-being, they will naturally understand their duty; because necessity is the mother of invention. However, if their intention is not to attain their own well-being, even after studying the scriptures, they will not understand their duty, and instead, their ignorance will increase, thinking that they know more. Om tat sat iti. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the Upanishad, the Bhagavad Gita, in the science of the ultimate truth, the Yoga Shastra, the dialogue between Shri Krishna and Arjuna, on the division of divine and asura wealth, known as the sixteenth chapter. 16. In this manner, with the recitation of the names of the Lord (Om, Tat, Sat), the Bhagavad Gita, in the form of the Upanishad, the science of the ultimate truth, and the Yoga Shastra, the dialogue between Shri Krishna and Arjuna, the sixteenth chapter, known as the 'division of divine and asura wealth', has come to an end. (2) In this chapter, there are seven 'Ath Shodasho Adhyayah', seven 'Shri Bhagavan Uvaach', seven hundred and sixty-four shlokas, and forty-two letters in the pushpika. In this way, the total number of letters is eight hundred and thirty-four. All the shlokas in this chapter have thirty-two letters. The name of this sixteenth chapter is 'Daiva Asuri Sampad Vibhag Yog'; because in this chapter, the description of both types of wealth is given, which are mutually opposite. The divine wealth is beneficial, while the asura wealth is binding and leads to lower birth and hell. The one who understands these two divisions correctly will abandon the asura wealth completely. As soon as the asura wealth is abandoned, the divine wealth will manifest automatically. When the divine wealth manifests, one will be connected with the Supreme Self alone. Details of the sixteenth chapter, its words, and letters:

(1) In this chapter, there are three 'Ath Shodasho Adhyayah', two 'Shri Bhagavan Uvaach', two hundred and thirty-six shlokas, and thirteen letters in the pushpika. In this way, the total number of letters is three hundred and fifty-two. (3) In this chapter, there is one 'Uvaach' – 'Shri Bhagavan Uvaach'. The meter used in the sixteenth chapter:

In this chapter, out of the twenty-four shlokas, in the first quarter of the sixth shloka, in the third quarter of the tenth shloka, and in the first quarter of the twenty-second shloka, the word 'Magan' is used, making it a 'M-Vipula' meter. Similarly, in the third quarter of the eleventh, thirteenth, and nineteenth shlokas, the word 'Nagan' is used, making it a 'N-Vipula' meter. The remaining eighteen shlokas are in the 'Pathya Avaktar' meter, which is a characteristic of the Anushthup meter.

The question that Arjuna raises in this chapter is about the nature of people who follow their own path, without adhering to the principles of the scriptures. This question is relevant to the context of the previous verse, where Arjuna had asked about the nature of those who follow their own path, without knowing the scriptures. Arjuna's Question:

Arjuna said:

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 17 ]
In the coming generations, the knowledge of scriptures will be very less. The people of asuric nature are those who are materialistic. Their devotion is based on material possessions. It will be difficult for them to get good company; because even in the previous yugas, there were fewer good saints, and in the kaliyuga, there will be even fewer. Even if they are less, if they have a desire to get good company, they can get it. But the difficulty is that in the kaliyuga, there will be more hypocrisy and pretentiousness, so many hypocrites and pretenders will become saints. Therefore, it is difficult to recognize the true saints. First, it is difficult to meet the saints, and even if they meet them, it is not easy to recognize which saints are true. Without recognizing them, it is not possible to get special benefits by associating with them. Therefore, those who do not know the scriptures and do not get the association of real saints, but who perform rituals and worship with faith - what kind of devotion do they have? Is it sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic? Of asuric nature. It means that a person's thoughts, behavior, and views are like his nature, and his nature determines his position (devotion). The position determines the future progress. You say that by abandoning the scriptural path and following one's own way, one cannot attain perfection, happiness, and ultimate liberation. If their devotion is not known, then how can their progress be known? Therefore, you explain their devotion, so that it can be known whether they are sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic. The Supreme Lord said:

There are three types of faith in human beings, which are inherent in their nature. One is sattvic, the second is rajasic, and the third is tamasic. Listen to this. (2)

Listen. (2)

1 - The difference between the three gunas is tenfold. Just as one is ten times greater than ten, and ten is ten times greater than one hundred, similarly, tamoguna (1) is ten times greater than rajoguna (10), and rajoguna is ten times greater than sattvaguna (100). The meaning is that tamoguna and rajoguna are close to each other, while sattvaguna is far from both. 2 - The cause of anger is rajoguna, and the action is tamoguna.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 17 
Born from the association with a particular caste, a particular profession, a particular ashram, or a particular sect, the inclination to learn from them, the inclination to follow the instructions of a guru - 
whatever be the country, whatever be the person, however they may be - all have a natural faith of three types. 'This person is faith-based' - this man is faith-based. Therefore, as his faith will be, so will be his form. From him, the tendency will be as per his faith. ,
‘Whatever faith a person has, he is that’ - the person with such faith will have the same devotion and his actions will be in accordance with his faith. His every thought and action will be in accordance with his faith. As long as he remains connected with the world, his form will be in accordance with his heart's faith. Ponderable Point
A person's worldly tendency arises from believing in the reality of worldly objects, seeing them, hearing about them, and experiencing them, and their spiritual tendency arises from having faith in the Supreme Being. The person who has faith in the Supreme Being, whom he has not experienced personally, but has faith in due to the natural tendencies of his past lives, the teachings of scriptures, and the words of saints and sages, is said to have faith. It is through faith that one enters the spiritual path, whether it is the path of karma yoga, jnana yoga, or bhakti yoga. Without faith in both the goal and the means, spiritual progress is not possible. -
In human life, faith has a great significance. A person is as his faith is - 'Whatever faith a person has, he is that' (Gita 17.3). He may not appear to be so today, but he will become so with time. . It has become very difficult for seekers to recognize their natural faith today. The reason is that there are many different opinions and theories. Some say that knowledge is the most important thing, some say that devotion is the most important thing, some say that yoga is the most important thing, and so on. As a result of reading and listening to such different theories, a person becomes confused and does not know what to do. He is unable to determine his true goal, his true objective, and what path he should follow. In such a situation, he should deeply reflect on his inner thoughts and actions and find out what is his natural inclination, which is not created by external associations, scriptures, or teachers. The root of all inclinations is the natural inclination to be free from all suffering and to attain eternal happiness. This is the natural inclination of all living beings, and it is more prominent in humans. The natural inclination of humans is influenced by their past lives, their upbringing, their education, their surroundings, and the things they hear and see. As a result, they develop a certain faith, which is either sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic. The sattvic faith is directed towards the Supreme Being, while the rajasic and tamasic faiths are directed towards the world. In the Gita, wherever sattva is described, it is described as being directed towards the Supreme Being. Therefore, sattvic faith is spiritual and divine, while rajasic and tamasic faiths are worldly and demonic. The seventeenth chapter of the Gita is meant to reveal the divine faith and to discard the demonic faith, because it is beneficial for a person who desires his own well-being to have a divine faith, and it is detrimental for him to have a demonic faith. A person who desires his own well-being has a sattvic faith, a person who desires worldly pleasures and happiness in this life and the next has a rajasic faith, and a person who is like an animal, living a life of ignorance and indulgence, has a tamasic faith. The first step towards sattvic faith is to have faith in the existence of the Supreme Being, which arises from hearing about it from scriptures, saints, and gurus, and having a sense of reverence for it. Wherever faith is present, it is present in the form of reverence.

. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Preman sva: ho jata hai. Kaaran ki jis Paramatma mein shraddha ke siddhantko svikar kar hi liya, chaahe vah Ishvar ko hoti hai, usi Paramatma ka ams yah jivaatma hai. Atah mana ya na mana. Isliye aayu, vidya, gun, buddhi, yogya, shraddha hoti hi yah Paramatma ki taraf khinchta hai. Abhi yah samarthy, pad, adhikar, aishvaryadi mein se ek-ek se Paramatma se vimukh hokar jo sansaramen lagaa hua hai, vah dekhete, to badeppan dekhete-dekhete ant mein badeppan ki jahan bhi sansaramen shraddha-vishvas honese hi hai. Par yah samapti ho, vahi Ishvar hai; kyonki bade-se-bade Ishvar hai. Vastavik shraddha nahin hai, pratitut shraddhaka durupayog hai. Usse bada koi hai hi nahin- jaise, sansaramen yah rupiyon par vishesh shraddha karta hai ki inse sab kuch mil jata hai. Yah shraddha kaise hui? Kaaran ki bachpan mein khane aur khelne ke padarth paise se milte the. Aisa dekhete-dekhete paise ko hi mukhya maan liya aur usi mein shraddha kar li, jisse yah bahut hi patankari taraf chala gaya. Yah sansaarak shraddha hui. Isse oonchi dharmik shraddha hoti hai ki main amuk varn, ashram adikaa hoon. Parantu sabse oonchi shraddha paramaarthik (Paramatma ko lekar) hai. Yahi vastavik shraddha hai aur isse kalyan hota hai. Shastron mein, sant-mahatmamon mein, tattvajnya-jivanmuktomon mein jo shraddha hoti hai, vah bhi paramaarthik shraddha hi hai. Jinko shastron ka jnana nahin hai aur sant-mahatmamon ka sang bhi nahin hai, aise manushyon ki bhi poorv-sanskaare ke kaaran paramaarthik shraddha ho sakti hai. Iski pehchaan kya hai? Pehchaan yah hai ki aise manushyon ke bhitar svaabhavik yah bhav hota hai ki aisi koi mahaan cheez (Paramatma) hai, jo dekhatee to nahin, par hai avashya. Aise manushyon ko svaabhavik hi paramaarthik baaton ko bahut pyaar lagta hai aur ve svaabhavik hi yajna, daan, tap, teerth, vrat, sat-sang, svadhyaya adi shubh karmaon mein pravrit hote hain. Yadi ve aise karma na bhi karein, to bhi sattvik aahaar mein svaabhavik ruchi honese unki shraddhaki pehchaan hoti jati hai. Manushya, pashu-pakshi, lata-vriksh adi jutne hi sthaavar-jangam prani hain, ve kisi-n-kisi ko (kisi-n-kisi amsmen) apne se bada avashy manaate hain aur bada manaakar uska sahaara lete hain. Manushya par jab aafat aati hai, tab vah kisi ko apne se bada manaakar uska sahaara leta hai. Pashu-pakshi bhi apni raksha chahte hain aur bhaybhoot hone par kisi ka sahaara lete hain. Lata bhi kisi ka sahaara lekar hi oonchi chadhti hai. Is prakaar jisne kisi ko bada manaakar uska sahaara liya, usne vastav mein 'Ishwaravad' kiyaa. Wah Paramatma sabke poorvajon ka bhi guru hai; kyonki uska kala se avachched nahin hai arthatah vah kalaaki seemase bahar hai. Is prakaar pratyek manushya apne dhrishthi se kisi-n-kisi ko bada manaata hai. Badeppan ki yah maanayata apne-apne antahkaran ke bhavon ke anusaar alag-alag hoti hai. Is kaaran unki shraddha bhi alag-alag hoti hai. Shraddha antahkaran ke anuroop hi hoti hai. Dharna, maanayata, bhavana adi sabhi antahkaran mein rehte hain. Isliye antahkaran mein sattvik, rajas ya tamas jis gunki pradhanata rehti hai, usi gun ke anusaar dharna, maanayata adi banati hai aur us dharna, maanayata adik anusaar hi teen prakaariki (sattviki, rajasii ya tamasi) shraddha banati hai. Sattvik, rajas aur tamas - teenon gun sabhi praniyon mein rehte hain (Gita - Aatharvah shlok). Un praniyon mein kisimein satvagun ki pradhanata hoti hai, kisimein rajogun ki pradhanata hoti hai aur kisimein tamogun ki pradhanata hoti hai. Atah yah niyam nahin hai ki satvagun ki pradhanataavale manushyamen rajogun aur tamogun na aaye, rajogun ki pradhanataavale manushyamen satvagun aur tamogun na aaye, tatha tamogun ki pradhanataavale manushyamen satvagun aur rajogun na aaye (Gita – Chaudhavah shlok). Kaaran ki prakriti parivartanashil hai-'prakarshen karanaam (bhavay lyut) iti prakritih'. Isliye prakritijanya gunon mein bhi parivartan hota rehta hai. Atah ekamatra Paramatma-praptike uddeshyavale sadhak ko chahiye ki vah un aane-jane wale gunon se apna sambandh maanakar unse vichalit na ho. Jivamatra Paramatma ka ams hai. Isliye kisi manushyamen sansaarak shraddha 'bhog' ki, dharmik shraddhamen 'bhav' ki aur paramaarthik shraddhamen 'tattv' ki pradhanata hai.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 17 ]
[Verse 4]
The predominance of the quality of passion or the quality of darkness should not be considered as inferior. The faith of a person becomes sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic, depending on the quality he comes into contact with. Therefore, a person should always associate with sattvic people, scriptures, thoughts, and the atmosphere, and so on. By doing so, his inner self and his faith, which is in accordance with his inner self, will become sattvic, which will be his means of salvation. On the other hand, a person should never associate with rajasic or tamasic people, scriptures, and so on; because, by doing so, his faith will also become rajasic or tamasic, which will be his means of downfall. It is observed that a person's nature is the same as the nature of the company he keeps. A person should have two kinds of feelings: one should be towards the divine, and the other should be towards the mundane. This is because it is impossible to know in advance which person will be prosperous at a particular time. The reason is that the Atman (the eternal soul), which is the part and parcel of the Supreme Being, is pure in all beings. However, the quality of a person's inner self is determined by the company he keeps, scriptures, thoughts, and so on. As a result, the faith of a person is also determined by the quality of his inner self. The faith that leads a person towards the divine is called sadbhava, and the faith that leads a person towards the mundane is called asadbhava. The predominance of sadbhava is found in divine wealth, and the predominance of asadbhava is found in demonic wealth. ' I am a seeker' - If the predominance of asadbhava is found in this statement, it is a sign of ego, and if the predominance of sadbhava is found, it is a sign of self-respect. Ego leads to demonic wealth, and self-respect leads to divine wealth. If a person looks for special qualities in others, it is a sign of ego, and if a person looks for his own duties, it is a sign of self-respect. A person who is egoistic will engage in activities that are against the path of devotion, whereas a person who has self-respect will not engage in such activities. A person who has self-respect will be sattvic, and a person who is egoistic will be rajasic or tamasic. Connection - Now, we will explain how the devotion of a person can be identified by their worship of their Ishta (deity). Those who are sattvic worship the gods (devas), those who are rajasic worship the yakshas and raksasas, and those who are tamasic worship the ghosts and spirits. (4)

Sattvic people worship the gods,
Rajasic people worship the yakshas and raksasas,
Tamasic people worship the ghosts and spirits. Explanation - 'Yajante sattvika devan' - Sattvic people worship the gods, i.e., those who are in divine wealth. Here, the word 'devan' refers to the five types of gods, namely, Vishnu, Shiva, Ganesha, Shakti, and the Sun. In divine wealth, the word 'deva' is a symbol of the Supreme Being, and this wealth is the means of liberation, as mentioned in the scripture: 'Dharmasya tattvam nihitam guhyatam (16.5)'. The sattvic people, in whom this divine wealth is manifest, are identified by their natural faith, and this is why the phrase 'yajante sattvika devan' is used here. Those who are tamasic worship the ghosts and spirits. The devotees of the Supreme Being have different faiths in different gods. Some have faith in Lord Vishnu (Rama, Krishna, etc.), some in Lord Shiva, some in Lord Ganesha, some in the Goddess Shakti, and some in the Sun God. They worship the gods in whose form their natural faith is manifest. They worship the gods with great devotion and dedication. Even worshiping the thirty-three gods mentioned in the scriptures, such as the twelve Adityas, eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, and two Ashvini Kumaras, without any expectation of reward, is also an example of 'yajante sattvika devan'.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

It is to be understood in this context that 'yaksharaksansi rajasah' - the rajasic men worship yakshas and raksasas. Yakshas and raksasas are also born in the divine realm. Yakshas are primarily engaged in the accumulation of wealth, and raksasas are primarily engaged in the destruction of others. Rajasic men worship yakshas and raksasas due to their desire to fulfill their own desires and to destroy others. 'Tamasa janah pritan bhutaganaanscha anye yajante' - tamasic men worship the spirits of the dead and the ghosts. Those who have died are called 'preta', and those who have gone to the realm of ghosts are called 'bhuta'. Here, the word 'preta' does not include one's own ancestors. Those who understand their duty and worship their ancestors with a selfless attitude are not tamasic, but rather sattvic. The Lord has not prohibited the worship of one's own ancestors - 'pitrunyanti pitravratah' (Gita 9.25). The meaning is that those who worship their ancestors with a self-serving attitude, thinking that they will protect us or that we will perform shraddha and tarpan for them, are not sattvic, but rather rajasic. However, those who worship their ancestors with a selfless attitude, thinking that their ancestors will perform shraddha and tarpan for them, are sattvic. Those who understand their duty and worship their ancestors with a selfless attitude are the true 'pitrvratah', and they are the ones who will attain the realm of the ancestors. However, one's own ancestors will not be attained by worshiping them. Even if one feeds dogs, crows, and other animals with a selfless attitude, as per the scriptures, their birth in those species will not be attained. This is because they are not their ishta (dear ones). They are simply following the scriptural injunctions. Similarly, performing shraddha and tarpan for the dead, as per the scriptural injunctions, with a selfless attitude, will not lead to birth in the realm of the dead. It is only by following the scriptural injunctions or the Lord's command that their salvation will be attained. Therefore, one should not consider the performance of shraddha and tarpan for the dead, as per the scriptural injunctions, with a selfless attitude, as tamasic. These are essential actions performed for the salvation of the dead, and every individual should perform them as per the scriptural injunctions. We perform yajnas and other auspicious actions, and in them, we first worship Ganesha, the nine planets, the sixteen mother goddesses, and others, following the scriptural injunctions with a selfless attitude. This is not the worship of Ganesha and the nine planets, but rather the worship of the scriptural injunctions. Just as a woman's well-being is attained by serving her husband, so too is a person's well-being attained by serving his ishta (dear one). Vivah (marriage) is possible for every person, even a raksasa or an asura. They can also become husbands. However, true well-being is not attained by serving one's husband, but rather by following the command of the scriptures, the sages, and the Lord. The fate of those who worship the gods and goddesses will be the same as that of the worshipers - this is stated here for the sake of explanation. Arjuna had asked about the devotion of those who worship the gods and goddesses with faith, following the scriptural injunctions, and not following the scriptural injunctions. Therefore, the devotion of the worshipers is determined by their ishta (dear one), and this is explained here. Parishishta Bhaav - Sattvic men who worship the gods and goddesses will attain the realm of the gods after leaving their physical bodies. Rajasic men who worship yakshas and raksasas will attain the realm of yakshas and raksasas, and tamasic men who worship the spirits of the dead and the ghosts will attain the realm of the dead and the ghosts (Gita 9.25). In the Gita, the word 'yajna' is very comprehensive, encompassing all duties and actions, including yajna, dana, tapas, and vrat (Gita 4.24-25). Therefore, in this context, the word 'yajante' should be understood to include all duties and actions, with yajna being the primary one. The spirits of the dead and the ghosts are our ancestors, and others' ancestors are their spirits. Worshiping one's own ancestors is not tamasic, but worshiping the spirits of the dead and the ghosts is tamasic.

[ Chapter 17 ]
Connection - So far, the discussion has been about those people who, due to ignorance of the scriptural method, abandon it (without understanding) but have faith in their chosen deity and its worship. Now, the description of the actions of those people who, in opposition to the scriptural method, abandon it without faith, will be given in the next two verses. Those who perform such intense and inauspicious austerities, being united with pride and ego, and being endowed with the power of lust and attachment, cause suffering to the body. 5. Those who are devoid of intellect, and who consider me and the self within the body to be demons, should be known as demoniac. 6. Those people, who are devoid of faith, and who are united with pride and ego, and who are endowed with the power of lust and attachment, and who are attached to worldly objects, and who are engaged in the practice of austerities with force and obstinacy, are said to be performing inauspicious austerities. 7. Explanation - 'Ashastri-vihitam ghoraṃ tapyante ye tapo janāh' - Those people, who are engaged in inauspicious austerities, which are not prescribed in the scriptures, but are prohibited, have a tendency to perform them. This is because they have a tamasic intellect (as mentioned in the 32nd verse of the 18th chapter of the Gita). They do not understand the scriptures and do not accept the advice of others. They are proud of their own knowledge and consider themselves to be wise. ' Dambhāhaṅkārasaṃyuktāḥ' - They have a deep-seated feeling that all the rituals, meditation, and study of scriptures performed by others are mere show and pretence. They themselves also pretend to be pious and consider themselves to be knowledgeable. They think that they can guide others and that they are superior to others. 'Karśayantaḥ śarīrasṭhaṃ bhūtagrāmam' - They consider the practice of austerities to be the practice of inflicting pain on the body and consider the five elements (earth, water, fire, air, and ether) to be demons. 'Anantahkaranam sthitividyā mām chaiva antaḥ śarīrasṭham tān vidyāsura-niścayan' - You should know that those people who are devoid of faith and are united with pride and ego, and who consider me and the self within the body to be demons, are demoniac. Explanation - 'Kāmarāga-balānvitāḥ' - The word 'kāma' refers to worldly objects. Those people who are attached to worldly objects and are engaged in the practice of austerities with force and obstinacy, are said to be performing inauspicious austerities. In this way, they are always attached to worldly objects and are engaged in the practice of austerities with force and obstinacy.

[Verse 7]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The people who consider the acts of giving, serving, and charity as good, but do not consider the acts of the Lord and the scriptures as good, are considered to be of the demonic nature. They perform the acts that are against the scriptures, such as fasting, sleeping on thorns, hanging upside down, standing on one leg, and performing fire rituals against the scriptures. They also cause pain to their body, mind, and senses in various ways. The description of the acts of the body, speech, and mind is given elsewhere, where there is no mention of causing pain to the body. That act of tapas is done with great peace, but this act of tapas is a great act against the scriptures and is done by causing pain to the body in an improper manner. The Lord says, "Māṃ ca evaṃ antaḥ śharīrastham" - He says that these people also cause pain to the eternal soul, which is situated within the body, by not following His command and not following the path of the scriptures. Arjuna had asked which type of people these are - are they sāttvika, rājasika, or tāmasika? Are they of divine or demonic nature? The Lord says that they should be considered as people of demonic nature - "tān vidhi āsura-niścayān". Here, the term "āsura-niścayān" does not refer to people of demonic nature in general, but specifically refers to those who are extremely low and non-believers. Special Note

In the 16th chapter, 23rd verse, it is mentioned that even though one knows the scriptures, if one does not follow them and instead performs acts of charity, service, and other good deeds, it is not a bad thing. However, in this case, it is mentioned that one considers the acts that are not mentioned in the scriptures as good and performs them in one's own way, which is against the scriptures. What is the difference between the two? In the 23rd verse, it is mentioned that the acts of charity, service, and other good deeds will not lead to spiritual growth, but in this case, it is mentioned that performing such acts will lead to a lower birth and hellish existence, as they are accompanied by pride and other demonic qualities. These people do not follow the scriptures and do not listen to them, and even if someone tries to explain the scriptures to them, they do not listen. In the 4th verse, the term "yajante" was used to describe the acts of worship performed by people who do not know the scriptures, but have faith. However, in this case, the term "tapyanthe" is used to describe the acts of worship performed by people who do not follow the scriptures and do not have faith. The reason for this is that the demonic people consider tapas as their worship and consider causing pain to the body as their tapas. The characteristic of their tapas is to cause pain to the body and to make it suffer. This type of tapas is not mentioned in the scriptures of the rājasika and tāmasika nature. In the 16th chapter, 23rd verse, it is mentioned that the scriptures are neglected, and in this chapter, the 1st verse, it is mentioned that the scriptures are neglected due to ignorance, and in this case, it is mentioned that the scriptures are neglected due to opposition. Further, in the tāmasika yajña and other acts, the scriptures are also neglected. However, in this case, there is opposition to the scriptures, faith, the community of living beings, and the Lord. Therefore, the Lord begins to explain the difference between the three types of acts - food, worship, and charity - and says:

"Ahāras tv api sarvasya trividho bhavati priyah,
Yajñas tapas tatha dānam
Teṣāṃ bhedam imam bhedam imam śṛṇu" 7

The food of all beings is of three types, and so are the worship and charity. Listen to the difference between them. Ahāraḥ:

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 17
Commentary – The food of every person is of three types. It is the same with all the scriptural duties. The interest, preference, and affection of people in yajna, tapas, and other duties vary. Here, the word "tatha" implies that just as there are three types of worship and three types of food, there are also three types of scriptural duties. From this, it also becomes clear that whatever comes in front of a person, whether it is scripture, association with the good, discussion, conversation, story, book, vow, pilgrimage, or a person, what is sattvic will be liked by a sattvic person, what is rajasic will be liked by a rajasic person, and what is tamasic will be liked by a tamasic person. The word "priyah" – in the fourth shloka, the Lord explained to Arjuna the three types of yajna, tapas, and dana according to the inquiry of Arjuna for the examination of the faith of humans. However, how can the faith of those people be identified who do not have faith in yajna-puja? For this, it is said that just as people have to eat food for the maintenance of the body, whether they are atheists or theists, whether they are Vedic or Christian, Parsi, Jew, Greek, etc., of any sect, they all have to eat food. Here, the word "ahara-stvapi" is used to say that the identification of faith is not only in yajna-puja, but also in the taste of food. A person's mind naturally likes the food in which it is attracted, that is, when it hears, sees, and tastes the food, its mind is attracted to it. According to this, its sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic faith is considered. 'Tesam bhedam imam shrinu' – Listen to the difference of yajna, tapas, and dana. That is, listen to the natural inclination, tendency, and happiness of a person in what. Just as a Brahmin likes to donate according to his inclination, and another ordinary person likes to donate, and some people befriend those who have pure behavior, and some befriend those whose behavior is not pure, etc. The meaning is that the inclination of sattvic people is in sattvic food, behavior, work, society, and person, and they like to be with them. The inclination of rajasic people is in rajasic food, behavior, work, society, and person, and they like to be with them. The inclination of tamasic people is in tamasic food, behavior, and association with low people, and they like to be with them. It seems that this chapter is to explain how sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic food is. However, it is not just about food, but about the inclination of food. Therefore, this chapter has come to explain how the faith of food can be identified. Here, the words "sarvasya" and "priyah" are used to say that generally, all people have a liking for some food, from which their sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic faith can be identified. Similarly, the words "yajna-tapas-tatha dana" are used to say that generally, people have a tendency in their behavior according to their nature. Appendix – The actions of a person according to his nature are of two types – practical and scriptural. Therefore, here, "ahara" under the practical actions and "yajna-tapas-dana" under the scriptural actions should be understood. 1 - Although the word "yajna" here refers to the homa yajna, it is not a comprehensive term for all duties (because yajna, tapas, and dana have come separately), but from the secondary point of view, other duties like pilgrimage, vow, etc. can also be included. 2 - "Mrga mrgaih sangamanuvrjanti gavash cha go bhisturagasturangaih. Mookhash cha mukhaih sudhayah sudhibhih samanshilavyasaneshu sakhyam" (Panchatantra, Mitra-bhed 305) - Just as animals move with animals of the same kind, cows with cows, horses with horses, and foolish people with foolish people, and wise people with wise people, because friendship is only in similar habits and behavior.

[ Chapter 17
(The Consumable, Potable, Lickable, and Digestible) Foods are dear to the Rajas Man; in the mouth, when they cause a burning sensation, they are loved. This is a sign of his devotion. Alas, this is a sorrow. After eating, there is no joy in the mind. 'Dukh-shoka-amaya-pradaah' - However, such foods, in the end, cause suffering, but a natural sense of worry remains, this is a sorrow. Such foods and diseases are caused by them. Sour, pungent, and spicy foods often cause diseases in the body.]

Explanation: 'Yātayāmam' - Foods that are not fully cooked, like pickles, jellies, and sweets that have not been cooked properly, or foods that have been cooked for too long, or foods that have been stored in the fridge after the season has passed, or foods that have been stored without proper preservation. 'Gatarasam' - Foods that have lost their natural moisture due to heat, or foods that have been processed and their natural essence has been extracted. 'Pūti' - Foods that have been spoiled due to fermentation, like spoiled wine, and foods that have a natural foul smell, like onions and garlic. 'Ucchiṣṭam' - Leftover food, or food that has been touched by animals, birds, or insects. “Amēdhyam” - Meat, fish, eggs, etc. that are impure and have been killed by the Rajas guna, and are very impure. 'Paryuṣitam' - Foods that are stale, like vegetables and fruits that have been stored for a long time. However, it is said that one should also consume foods that are forbidden by the scriptures, like:

1 - The scriptures call a person who drinks wine a great sinner. The Chāndogya Upanishad (5.10.9) says: "A person who steals gold, a person who drinks wine, a person who commits adultery with a guru's wife, and a person who kills a brahmin - all these four are great sinners, and the fifth one who associates with them is also a great sinner."

This proves that drinking wine is completely condemnable, and eating meat is even more condemnable and leads to downfall. The Ganges river is said to purify everyone, but if a wine cup is placed in it, it will not become pure. If a wine cup, which is used to hold wine, becomes impure, then a person who drinks wine will become even more impure. The harm caused by drinking wine is that it destroys the seeds of dharma in the heart. This means that the divine feelings, the sense of righteousness, and the good habits that a person has, are all destroyed by drinking wine. This leads a person to a great downfall. 2 - Here, the word 'amēdhyam' is used to describe the foods that are dear to the Tamas guna, and it seems that the Lord is reluctant to even mention their names.

* The Revitalizer of Seekers *

Certain foods have been considered forbidden, such as lentils, carrots, and turnips. 1073

The foods that are forbidden are those of the 'Rajas' and 'Tamas' varnas, as mentioned in the tenth verse. The words 'priya' (dear) and 'ishta' (desired) also appear in the tenth verse, which are indicative of one's inclination. If this were only a description of food, then the Lord would not have used the words 'priya' and 'ishta' in this context. Instead, He would have used phrases such as 'these are sattvic foods', 'these are rajasic foods', and 'these are tamasic foods'. 'bhajanam tamaspryam' - such food is dear to a person of tamas nature. This is how one can identify their faith. If sattvic food is eaten with attachment, it becomes rajasic, and if eaten excessively, it becomes tamasic. Similarly, if a beggar receives alms in the form of dry, stale, and spicy food, which is rajasic-tamasic, but eats it with devotion and the name of the Lord, then even that food becomes sattvic. Prakaran-Sambandhi

A special point related to the context

In this chapter of four verses, the description of sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic foods is seen, but in reality, this is not a description of food, but rather a description of the inclination of the 'aahari' (one who eats). Therefore, the description of the inclination of the 'aahari' is given here, and the following points can be inferred:

(1) In the 23rd verse of the 16th chapter, Arjuna asked, "How can one identify the faith of those who act according to their own whims and fancies?" The Lord replied in the 2nd verse of this chapter that faith is of three types, and in the 3rd verse, He explained that faith is according to one's own nature. In the 4th verse, He explained that faith is according to one's worship. In the 7th verse, He used the word 'sarvasya' (of all) and said that food is of three types, dear to each person according to their own nature. From this, it is clear that one's faith is identified by what one considers dear. The word 'priya' (dear) is used only in the 7th verse, but it is also used in the 8th verse as 'sattvikpriyah' and in the 9th verse as 'sattvikpriyah'. (2) Another powerful point is that sattvic foods are described first as 'ayuh sattvabal arogyasukh pritivivardhanah' (increasing life, strength, health, happiness, and joy), and then the description of the food itself is given. This is because a sattvic person is always thoughtful and considers the consequences of their actions. Therefore, their attention is first drawn to the results of their actions. A rajasic person, on the other hand, is drawn to the food itself, and therefore, the description of the food is given first, followed by its consequences in the 10th verse as 'duhkhoshokamayapradah' (causing suffering, sorrow, and disease). The implication is that if a rajasic person were to consider the consequences of their actions, they would be hesitant to eat rajasic food, as it would lead to suffering, sorrow, and disease. However, due to their attachment, they do not consider the consequences. The consequences of sattvic food are described first, and the consequences of rajasic food are described later, but the consequences of tamasic food are not described at all. This is because a tamasic person is foolish and does not consider the consequences of their actions. They do not consider whether the food is just or unjust, whether it is in accordance with the scriptures or not, and whether it will increase their mental and intellectual strength or not. They eat like animals, without any consideration. A sattvic person is divine, and a rajasic or tamasic person is asuric.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 17 ]
It is said that food prepared with purity is eaten; the effect of food is in the mind (6.5.4). By offering food and thinking of God and chanting His name while eating, the food becomes sattvic. If one earns money with the intention of self-interest and pride, without considering the truth and falsehood, then the food prepared with such money is rajasic. If one earns money by any means, such as by deceit, theft, robbery, or cheating, and buys food without considering purity and impurity, and prepares food without following any rituals and eats it without washing hands and feet and wearing shoes, then such food is tamasic. However, the Lord has described here only the types of food that are pleasing to sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic persons, so that their preferences can be known. In the Gita, wherever the topic of food is discussed, only the description of food is given, such as 'niyataharaH' (4.30), where the one who eats a regular diet is described, and 'yuktahara-viharaH' (6.16-17), where the one who eats more and the one who eats a regular diet are described. Similarly, in the 9th chapter, the verse 'yadashnasi' (9.27) describes the one who offers food to God, and 'laghvashi' (18.52) describes the one who eats less. In the same way, in the 7th verse of this chapter, the word 'tatha' (in the same way) is used, which means that those who perform yajna, tapas, and dana also perform their actions according to their own (sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic) nature. The discussion from the 11th to the 22nd verse of this chapter also describes the nature of those who perform yajna, tapas, and dana. The necessary considerations for food

In the Upanishads, it is said that as the food is, so is the subtle essence of the mind (antahkaran), the second part becomes the semen, the third part becomes the blood, and the fourth part becomes the stool, which is excreted. Therefore, to purify the mind, the food should be pure and sacred. The purity of food makes the mind pure - 'ahara-shuddhau satva-shuddhiH' (Chandogya 2.26.2). The place where food is eaten, the atmosphere, the sight, and the seat on which one sits should also be pure and sacred. Because, when one eats, the prana (life force) takes in the food and also takes in the particles of the surrounding environment. Therefore, the place, atmosphere, etc. should be such that the prana takes in the particles in the same way, and the mind becomes the same. The food preparer's thoughts and intentions should also be pure and sattvic. Before eating, wash the five parts of the body - the two hands, two feet, and the mouth - with pure water. Then, facing east or north, sit on a pure seat and read the following verse: 'patram pushpam phalam toyaH yo me bhaktya prayacchati, tadaham bhaktya-upahritam ashnami prayata-atmanah' (Gita 9.26). Offer the food to God. After offering, read the following verse: 'brahma-arpanam brahma-havir brahma-agnau brahma-nyahutam brahmaiva tena gantavyam brahma-karma-samadhina' (Gita 4.24). Then, take the first bite of food after chanting the name of God. While chewing each bite, recite the following mantra: 'Hare Rama Hare Rama Rama Rama Hare Hare, Hare Krishna Hare Krishna Krishna Krishna Hare Hare.' Repeat this mantra twice, either mentally or by chanting the name of one's Ishta (chosen deity). This mantra has 16 names, and by repeating it twice, it becomes 32 names. There are also 32 teeth in our mouth. Therefore, by repeating the mantra 32 times with each name, the food becomes easily digestible and healthy, and one becomes satisfied with a small amount of food, and the taste of the food also becomes pleasant, and the food itself becomes a form of worship. The mind becomes pure by chanting the name of God while eating - 'annamayam hi somya manah' (Chandogya). By repeating this mantra, the defects of the food also disappear. * One who repeats the name of Rama, again and again, while eating, does not get affected by the defects of the food.*

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Those who are filled with envy, fear, and anger, and who are greedy, and who are suffering from diseases and poverty, and who are full of malice, the food they eat does not digest properly, i.e., it becomes indigestible. * Therefore, a person should keep his mind calm and happy while eating. He should not let the vices of lust, anger, greed, attachment, etc. enter his mind. If they do enter, he should not eat at that time; because the vices have an effect on the food and the mind becomes accordingly. It is also said that when cowherds milk cows, they first leave the cow and then tie it up after seeing the cow's anger. They then milk the cow and give the milk to the soldiers who become fierce. Similarly, the effect of milk also falls on living beings. Once, someone experimented by giving buffalo's milk to some horses and cow's milk to some other horses. One day, all the horses were going somewhere. On the way, they came across a river. The horses that had drunk buffalo's milk sat down in the river, while the horses that had drunk cow's milk crossed the river. In the same way, a buffalo and a cow were made to fight each other, but the buffalo would defeat the cow. However, if both are yoked to a cart, the buffalo would stick out its tongue in the sun, while the cow would keep moving. This is because the milk of a buffalo does not have sattvic power, while the milk of a cow has sattvic power. Just as the vices of living beings have an effect on food, similarly, the vision of living beings also has an effect. The vision of a bad person or a hungry dog falls on the food, making it impure. Now, how can that food become pure? One should feel happy that God has come, and then offer the first portion of the food to Him. After offering it to Him, one should eat the remaining pure food, and the defect of the vision will be removed, making the food pure. Another thing is that people do not give the cow its full milk and take it all for themselves. That milk is not pure because the cow's right is involved. Give the cow its full milk and then take the remaining milk, which is very pure, no matter how little it is. The attitude of the person eating and the person offering food also affects the food. For example, (1) if the person offering food is more happy than the person eating, then the food is considered to be of higher quality. (2) If the person offering food is very happy, then the food is considered to be of medium quality, but if the person eating has the attitude of "I have saved so much money, I will get stronger," then the food becomes of lower quality. (3) If both the person offering food and the person eating have the attitude of "I have to spend money, I have to cook, I have to serve food," then the food becomes of the lowest quality. In this context, the Gita has said in a conclusive manner - "sarva-bhuta-hite ratah" (5.25, 12.4). The meaning is that the more a person is concerned with the welfare of all living beings, the more his actions, etc. will be pure. After eating, one should read these shlokas - "annad bhavanti bhutan parjanyad annasambhavah" (3.14). "Yajnady bhavati parjanyo yajnah karmasamudbhavah" (3.14). "Karma brahmodbhavam viddhi brahmasamudbhavam" (3.15). "Tasmad sarvagatam brahma nityam yajne pratishtitam" (3.15). Then, while eating, one should read "aham vaisvanaro bhutva" (15.14) and rotate the middle finger from the navel clockwise. Eating food offered by one who is filled with envy, fear, anger, and greed, and who is suffering from diseases and poverty, and who is full of malice, does not digest properly. (Bhavaprakash, Dinacharya Prakaran 5 | 228)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 17
Connection—The natural faith of those who, without knowing the scriptural method, give up the prescribed duties of worship and offerings and eating, is recognized by their natural inclination; but how can one recognize the natural inclination of those who engage in worldly activities such as trade, agriculture, etc., or those who perform the prescribed duties of yajna, etc., as ordained in the scriptures? To explain this, we begin to discuss the threefold division of yajna, tapas, and dana.]

The yajna performed by those who desire no fruit, as ordained in the scriptures, is considered sattvic, when the mind is firmly fixed on the idea that 'yajna is to be performed.'

yajna, to be performed, is the idea, 
that is to be thought of, 
is that yajna is to be performed, 
and that is the sattvic yajna, 
which is performed by those who are free from the desire for fruit. Translation: 'yajna, to be performed, is the idea, that is to be thought of, is that yajna is to be performed, and that is the sattvic yajna, which is performed by those who are free from the desire for fruit.'

Explanation: 'yajna, to be performed, is the idea' - When a man thinks, 'I have got a body, I have got respect, I have got honor, I have got a place in heaven, and I have got wealth in the next birth,' then his mind becomes attached to that yajna. The meaning is that the attachment to yajna arises from the desire for fruit. If one does not desire fruit, then his mind becomes attached to yajna. 'yajna is to be performed' - When one thinks, 'It is my duty to perform yajna,' then his mind becomes attached to yajna. 'that is to be thought of' - When one thinks, 'It is my duty to perform yajna,' then his mind becomes attached to yajna. 'is that yajna is to be performed, and that is the sattvic yajna' - When one thinks, 'It is my duty to perform yajna,' then his mind becomes attached to yajna. 'which is performed by those who are free from the desire for fruit' - When one does not desire fruit, then his mind becomes attached to yajna. When one thinks, 'It is my duty to perform yajna,' then his mind becomes attached to yajna. When one does not desire fruit, then his mind becomes attached to yajna. The sattvic yajna is performed by those who are free from the desire for fruit. Now, let us think about the meaning of sattvic. What is sattvic?

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The relation of the doer with the fruit of the yajna will not be there. Gita | This relation, which is considered to be like this, says—'kayena manasaa buddhya kevalair indriyairapi na hi chhoddhate, tabhak yah janma-maraṇa-roop bandhanam prāpte (5.11) i.e., the instrument (body, senses, etc.) remains - 'phale saktaḥ nibadhya te' (Gita 5.12). ( The material used for yajna and the place where yajna is performed)
There should be no relation with anyone else. A unique thing is that in Gita, the sattvic quality is said to be that which takes one away from the world and towards the Supreme Being, hence it is said to be 'sat' or 'nirguna'. The divine wealth also has all sattvic qualities. However, the one who possesses divine wealth will attain the Supreme Being only when he rises above the sattvic qualities, i.e., when the yajna-kriya begins and ends. Similarly, the fruit of the yajna also begins and ends. The action and its fruit are both born and destroyed, while the self remains eternal and unchanging; but it will be completely detached from the action and its fruit. But, O Arjuna, the yajna that is done with the intention of getting the desired fruit or with the intention of showing off is considered to be rajasic. (17.11) 'Yajña karmanā matrāḥ phalaṃ tyāgaḥ phalaṃ tyāgaḥ' (17.20) 'Karma kartavyam eva' (18.9) etc. words spoken by the Lord in Gita mean that the one who has the intention of doing yajna, donation, or duty alone, his action and the fruit of his action do not have any relation with nature and the work of nature, i.e., even the sattvic yajna, donation, etc. become 'nirguna'. In the last verse of the 17th chapter, the Lord has explained the meaning of the word 'sat' (17.27) while describing the three names of the Supreme Being 'Om, Tat, Sat'. The meaning is that all the actions done for the sake of the Supreme Being become 'sat' or 'nirguna'. The implication is that the karma-yogi's action and its fruit are detached from each other, and the bhakti-yogi's actions are connected with the Supreme Being, hence all their actions become 'nirguna'. In this way, both the statements become one, and therefore, the Gita does not describe 'nirguna' separately. In Gita, where sattvic quality is described as 'anamaya', it is also said that bondage occurs due to sattvic quality (14.6) and that the person who is situated in sattvic quality goes to the upper worlds (14.18). The implication is that bondage does not occur due to sattvic quality, but due to attachment to it - 'Sukha-sangena bandhnaati jñāna-sangena ca anagha' (14.6) and 'Kāraṇaṃ guṇa-saṅgo 'sya sad-asad-yoni-janmasu' (13.21). Similarly, considering oneself to be situated in sattvic quality is also bondage-causing - 'Sattva-sthāḥ' (14.18).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 17 ]

'Our enemies will be destroyed; our humiliation in the world will be taken away; the sacrifice that is performed for this purpose becomes rajas. Let there be no humiliation, no contempt, no adverse circumstances for us. Such are the desires for the removal of inauspiciousness.'

'Even if for the sake of prestige, people consider us to be good-natured, virtuous, self-controlled, austere, charitable, devoted to duty, and performers of sacrifices, and thus our reputation spreads in the world - such a showy sacrifice is considered rajas. In people who perform such showy sacrifices, all the statements like "I will serve" (16.15) and "They perform sacrifices with the name of sacrifice" (16.17) etc. become particularly relevant.'

[Verse 13]
'Consider this sacrifice as rajas, O best of the Bharatas, when it is performed with a desire for prestige.' - In this way, the desire for fruit and the show of prestige are to be avoided. The sacrifice in which the method of the scriptures is not followed is tamas. The sacrifice in which faith is not present is tamas. The sacrifice in which the mantras are not used is tamas. The sacrifice in which the gift is not given is tamas. The sacrifice in which the knowledge of the scriptures is not present is tamas. The tamas people have the idea that by offering oblations alone, the sacrifice is complete, the fragrance is obtained, and the impurities are destroyed. What is the need for mantras? etc. According to the explanation - 'Vidhiheenam' - There are different methods for different sacrifices, and there are different vessels, seats, and directions for sitting. Different materials are used for different deities, such as red clothes and red materials for the goddess. However, in tamas sacrifices, these methods are not followed, but rather, they are neglected. 'The sacrifice in which the food is not prepared' - The tamas people who perform material sacrifices do not give food to the Brahmins and others. They have the idea that if they give food for free, they will become lazy and will not work, and thus, uselessness will spread in the world. 'The sacrifice in which mantras are not used' - The Vedic and scriptural mantras are used in material sacrifices. However, in tamas sacrifices, these mantras are not used. 'The sacrifice in which the gift is not given' - The tamas people do not give gifts to the Brahmins and others. They have the idea that if they give gifts, the Brahmins will become lazy and will not work, and thus, uselessness will spread in the world. They do not think that by neglecting their scriptural duties and their duties, they themselves will become lazy. 17.13
The tamas people consider the sacrifice to be complete by offering oblations alone, and they do not follow the scriptural method. They do not use mantras, and they do not give gifts. They consider the sacrifice to be complete by neglecting the scriptural method.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The one who performs a sacrifice without faith is said to be in the mode of darkness, and the oblation given to him is also in the mode of darkness. (Gita 17.28) - This is the attitude of the tamasic people regarding the offering of gifts. They think that grains, ghee, barley, rice, coconut, and dates are the necessities of human life. It is foolishness to offer these necessities to the fire. * They perform sacrifices for their own fame and prestige, but without following the scriptures, without offering food, without chanting mantras, and without offering a fee. They do not have faith in the scriptures, the mantras, and the methods prescribed in them, nor do they have faith in the results of the sacrifices performed according to the scriptures. The reason is that they are foolish. They do not have their own intelligence, and if someone else explains it to them, they do not accept it. *

Therefore, if the performer, knowledge, action, faith, intelligence, association, scripture, and food are all sattvic, then the sacrifice will be sattvic. If they are rajasic, then the sacrifice will be rajasic. And if they are tamasic, then the sacrifice will be tamasic. Connection - In the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth shlokas, the sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic sacrifices are described respectively. Now, in the next three shlokas, the description of physical, verbal, and mental austerities will be given, which will be further divided into sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. The worship of gods, brahmins, gurus, and wise men, cleanliness, and non-violence are called physical austerities. (14)

Explanation - 'The worship of gods, brahmins, gurus, and wise men' - Here, the word 'dev' refers to the five types of gods. The main ones are Vishnu, Shiva, Ganesha, Shakti, and Surya - the one whom one has faith in, whom one worships more, that is the one who is the object of one's worship. * Just as the farmer who plows the field with the plow mixes the good seeds into the soil, and when the crop grows, it yields many times more grains than the seeds; similarly, the offering of oblations with the chanting of mantras is not a futile act. The seeds mixed into the soil are material, because the earth is material, but the oblation offered to the fire with the chanting of mantras is divine, because the gods are divine. Therefore, the oblation offered to the gods is like a shower of rain, which brings a great benefit. *

Manu has said - The oblation offered to the fire is offered to the sun, and the sun's rays become strong. From the strong rays, there is rain, and from the rain, there is food, and from the food, there is the creation of living beings. (Manusmriti 3.76)

In other words, the oblation offered to the fire strengthens the sun's rays, and from the strong rays, there is rain, and from the rain, there is food, and from the food, there are living beings. (This is also accepted by the physical scientists.)

The living beings are born from food, and food is born from water - 'Annamaya sadhanani parjanyam anna-sambhavah' (Gita 3.14). Therefore, water is the primary element in the creation. Rain is the result of the yajna - 'Yajnād bhavati parjanyah' (3.14).

It is essential to worship with a sense of detachment. *
*
Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Twelve Adityas, eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, and two Ashvini Kumaras - these thirty-three deities mentioned in scriptures also fall under the category of 'Deva'. In the context of yajna, tirtha, vrat, and other rituals, and on special occasions like deepamalika, and at the time of jatakarman, chudakarman, yajnopavita, and other samskaras, when the scriptures prescribe the worship of certain deities, we should also consider them as 'Deva'. It is the command of scriptures to worship these deities at the appropriate time. Therefore, we should understand our duty to be to preserve the limits of scriptures and worship these deities with detachment. In essence, it means that according to the scriptures, we should worship those deities on the specific days, occasions, and times mentioned. The term 'Dvija' refers to Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas, but in this context, it only refers to Brahmins. It does not refer to Kshatriyas and Vaishyas. Those from whom we receive education, our parents, elderly relatives, kulagurus, teachers, and those who are older than us in terms of age, ashram, and knowledge - we should consider them as 'Guru'. To follow the orders of Dvijas (Brahmins) and our parents, gurus, and to serve them, please them, and worship them with offerings like letters, flowers, and aarti - this is their worship. Here, the term 'Prajna' refers to a jivanmukta (liberated soul). If such a person were to be considered in terms of varna and ashram, they would be considered as Dvija, and if they were to be considered in terms of their physical form and knowledge, they would be considered as Guru. Therefore, the term 'Prajna' is used here for a jivanmukta who is not bound by varna and ashram and does not have a guru-disciple relationship. To respect the words and principles of such a jivanmukta and to live according to their teachings is the true worship of such a person. In reality, Dvijas and Gurus are worthy of respect and worship from a worldly perspective, but a Prajna (jivanmukta) is worthy of respect and worship from a spiritual perspective. Therefore, we should respect and worship a jivanmukta from the heart, as true respect and worship come from the heart, not from external gestures. 'Very cleanliness' - the name of making the body pure with water, earth, etc. - is 'shouch'. Physical cleanliness leads to the cleanliness of the mind. From cleanliness, there is aversion to the body, and from aversion to the body, there is separation from others. (Yoga Sutras 2.40)

From cleanliness, there will be a sense of disgust towards the body, that we keep this body clean day and night, but still, it produces waste, urine, sweat, nasal mucus, eye and ear secretions, saliva, and phlegm. This body is made up of bones, flesh, and marrow, which are all impure substances. Even if we clean this body thoroughly, there is no pure, clean, and fragrant substance in it. It is just a container for filth. It is only filled with filth and impurities. It is just a machine that produces waste and filth. When one understands the impurity and filth of the body, one becomes detached from it. When one becomes detached from the body, one does not have pride in one's varna, ashram, or age. People often say that those who maintain cleanliness are arrogant and contemptuous towards others. This is completely wrong, as the result of cleanliness is not to despise others, but to avoid contact with others. In reality, the body is just a container for filth, like a pot that is washed with water and eventually becomes useless. Even if we clean the body thoroughly, it will never be clean, as its fundamental nature is impure. In this context, the phrase 'parair asamsargah' means that one will avoid contact with others due to the impurity of the body. [Chapter 17
Therefore,
the worship of a Prajna (jivanmukta) is indeed worship. In the same way, some people worship Lord Vishnu, Lord Shiva, Lord Ganesha, Goddess Durga, and Lord Surya as the Supreme God. Therefore, in their own faith and devotion, they consider their own Ishta (deity) as the Supreme God and the other deities as subordinate.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

A person who is born from a place (the womb of his mother), from a seed (the union of his parents), nourished by the remnants of food (the food he has eaten), and is accompanied by the excretions of the body (urine, feces, sweat, etc.), and is destined for death (mortality), and is considered impure due to contact with water and earth (impurities), is considered impure by wise people. 'Arjavam' - The abandonment of the stiffness of the body (physical rigidity) and the adoption of a straightforward posture (physical ease) is called 'Arjavam'. Abundance of pride (ego) leads to physical stiffness. Therefore, one who desires his own well-being should not harbor pride in himself. By being free from pride, one's body becomes naturally easy and flexible in all its movements, such as sitting, standing, walking, speaking, and seeing, which is called 'Arjavam'. 'Brahmacharya' - The following eight actions are considered to be the destruction of Brahmacharya: (1) remembering a woman with whom one has had sex, (2) talking to women with attachment, (3) laughing and joking with women, (4) looking at women with attachment, (5) talking to women alone, (6) thinking of sex with women, (7) making a firm decision to have sex with women, and (8) actually having sex with women. These eight types of sex are mentioned by wise people. None of these actions should ever occur, and that is what is called 'Brahmacharya'. Brahmacharis, Vanaprasthis, and Sannyasis - These three should never have sex and should not even think about it. A householder who has sex with his wife according to the scriptures during his fertile period is considered a Brahmachari even while living in the household. Similarly, a widow who has followed the duty of pativratadharma (faithfulness to her husband) and has followed the duty of Brahmacharya after her husband's death is considered to be in the same state as a young Brahmachari. In reality, 'Brahmacharivratasthita' (Gita 6.14) - being established in the duty of Brahmacharya - is what is called Brahmacharya. However, if there is a nocturnal emission or if there is a discharge of semen due to a physical defect, it is not considered a breach of Brahmacharya. Only the mental disturbances that lead to such emissions are considered a breach of Brahmacharya. This is because Brahmacharya is related to the mind. Therefore, one who practices Brahmacharya should keep his mind pure and should never allow it to be drawn towards women. If the mind does wander, one should firmly think, "This is not my work, I will not do this; I am committed to practicing Brahmacharya."

'Ahiṃsā' - The absence of all types of violence is called 'Ahiṃsā'. Violence arises from selfishness, anger, greed, and delusion. For example, taking someone else's wealth by force, causing harm to someone, or killing someone - these are all forms of violence arising from selfishness. Causing harm to someone due to anger, killing someone due to anger, or causing harm to someone due to greed - these are all forms of violence arising from anger. Killing an animal for its skin or meat, or killing someone for wealth - these are all forms of violence arising from greed. However, if someone hits a dog, breaks a tree branch, or kills a grasshopper, it is not due to anger, greed, or a desire for wealth - it is due to delusion. Ahiṃsā is the absence of all these forms of violence. 'Shārīraṃ tapa ucyate' - The five types of physical austerity are: worship of gods, cleanliness, Arjavam, Brahmacharya, and Ahiṃsā. In addition to these, one should also practice pilgrimage, vows, and self-control. When one suffers hardships, that is considered austerity. However, the physical austerities mentioned above do not involve suffering hardships. Therefore, these austerities are not considered true austerities. 1. Smaranam (remembrance), Kirtanam (chanting), Kelih (service), Prakshanam (gazing), Guhyabhashanam (secret speech), Sankalpo (resolution), Adhyavasaya (determination), and Kriyanishpati (action) - these eight are considered the eight limbs of Maithuna (sex) by wise people. The opposite of Brahmacharya is what should be practiced by those who seek liberation. 2. Here, 'Ahiṃsā' is included under physical austerity, so only physical Ahiṃsā is considered, not mental or verbal Ahiṃsā.
