* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

There are two types of diseases - Adhi (mental disease) and Vyadhi (physical disease). Adhi has two subtypes - one is Shok, Chinta, etc. and the other is Pugalpan (madness). Chinta, Shok, etc. occur due to ignorance, and Pugalpan occurs due to Prarabdha (past karma). Therefore, when one has knowledge, Chinta-Shok, etc. disappear, but Pugalpan can occur according to Prarabdha. However, even if one is mad, a knowledgeable person does not commit any inappropriate or prohibited act. (5) What is the difference between Akasmi (sudden death) and Akal Mrityu (untimely death)? If a person dies due to a snake bite, falls from above, drowns in water, or dies due to heart failure, it is his Akasmi death. Even Akasmi death occurs according to Prarabdha (past karma), just like natural death. For example, if someone is to be hanged at exactly 10 o'clock, the person who hangs him will also be hanged, as the government had given the order to the hangman. However, the hangman does not remember that he is taking revenge for the person's past karma. Therefore, it is the hangman's fault. No one has the right to kill another person. No one wants to die. Killing another person is a disrespect to one's own conscience. A human being has the power of discrimination, and according to that, he is free to do good or bad deeds. Therefore, disrespecting one's own conscience and killing another person is a fault. If people continue to take revenge for each other's past karma, this cycle will never end, and humans will never be liberated. If a person attempts to commit suicide, but does not die, it is because his Prarabdha is linked to another person's Prarabdha. Therefore, he is saved due to his Prarabdha. Similarly, if a person has a good deed or a good karma in his future life, or if he has to suffer a great suffering in this life, he will not die even if he attempts to commit suicide. (6) If one person kills another, he is taking revenge for the past enmity, and the person who dies is suffering the consequences of his past karma. Therefore, why is the killer at fault? The killer is at fault. The duty of punishing is of the ruler, not of the common man. If a person is to be hanged at 10 o'clock, the person who hangs him will also be hanged, as the government had given the order to the hangman. If a person takes revenge for another person's past karma, he can do so in other animal species, but not in the human species. However, it is possible that the person who takes revenge may not be liked by us, but we should not harbor hatred or cause suffering to him, as it is a new karma. (7) What is the difference between Prarabdha and Bhagwat Kripa (God's grace)? Whatever a person gets, it is according to his Prarabdha, but the ruler of Prarabdha-Vidhan is God Himself. The reason is that karma is inert and cannot give independent results, but it gives results according to God's will. For example, a person works in someone's field all day, and at the end of the day, he gets paid according to his work, but he gets paid from the field owner. Money is earned by working, but does it come without working?

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18 ]
The Master Will Give Money to Whom? If someone goes to the forest and does all work, will he get money if he works hard all day? No, he will not get money. It will be seen who did the work on whose instructions and whose responsibility it was. Those who are more generous; however, the one who does all work completely devoted to God, God also becomes a devotee of that devotee.* In the world, no employer makes a servant his master; but if a servant works with great zeal and skill, the employer only makes him his servant. Such generosity is only found in the Lord. The Lord gives more than what a servant deserves and makes him a partner in his business. He also gives him a share in his property. Similarly, the Lord is pleased with a man who has a pure and devoted mind. He gives him more than what he deserves and makes him a partner in his business. The Lord is pleased with a man who has a pure and devoted mind. In the world, no employer makes a servant his master; but if a servant works with great zeal and skill, the employer only makes him his servant. Relation - Just as in the path of Karma Yoga, there is no relation with actions, similarly in the path of Sankhya Siddhanta, there is no relation with actions - this will be explained further. Panchaitani Mahabaho Karamani Nibodha Me
Sankhye Kritante Proktani Siddhey Sarvkarmanam 13

[Verse 13]
Oh Mahabaho! The five causes of all actions have been explained in Sankhya Siddhanta for the attainment of the ultimate goal of all actions. Explanation - 'Panchaitani Mahabaho Karamani Nibodha Me' - Oh Mahabaho! If you understand these five causes deeply, you will immediately experience the truth. These five causes have been explained in Sankhya Siddhanta for the attainment of the ultimate goal of all actions. These five causes are:

1. Svayam (Swaroop) - The Self, the doer, is not the cause of actions. 2. Prakriti (Nature) - The material cause of actions. 3. Karma (Action) - The action itself is the cause of actions. 4. Dravya (Material) - The material cause of actions. 5. Karta (Doer) - The doer of actions. When a person has a sense of doership in actions, there is both the attainment of the fruit of actions and the accumulation of actions. But when a person does not have a sense of doership in actions, there is only the attainment of the fruit of actions, not the accumulation of actions. Just like the changes that occur in the world, such as the flow of rivers, the movement of the wind, and the growth of trees, etc. - these actions are mere activities, but they do not lead to the accumulation of actions. Similarly, in Sankhya Siddhanta, there is no relation with actions. Evam Svabhaktayo Rajan Bhagavan Bhaktabhaktiman (Shrimad Bhagavat 10.86.59)

[Verse 14]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The meaning of this is that they are not binding. In other words, the meaning is that only through the sense of doership (kartrutva-abhimana) does the accomplishment of actions and the accumulation of actions take place. When the sense of doership is removed, the four causes of action - the substratum (adhisthana), the doer (kartar), the instrument (karana), the effort (cheshtha), and the divine (daiva) - are the only causes that remain (Gita - this chapter's 14th verse). Here, the description of the Sankhya Siddhanta is being given. In the Sankhya Siddhanta, the predominance of discrimination (vivek) is there, and then why has the Lord mentioned 'sarva-karma-nam siddhiye' (for the accomplishment of all actions) here? The reason is that Arjuna is facing the situation of war. As a Kshatriya, war is his duty. Therefore, one should perform such actions through the yoga of action (karma-yoga) or the yoga of Sankhya (sankhya-yoga), so that one remains detached from actions even while performing them - this is what the Lord wants to say to Arjuna. Arjuna has asked about the essence of Sankhya, so the Lord begins to explain how to perform actions through the Sankhya Siddhanta. He wanted to explain to Arjuna that the acceptance and rejection of actions are not causes of well-being. The causes of well-being are the separation of the eternal and imperishable self from the perishable and changing nature. There are two procedures for this separation - karma-yoga and sankhya-yoga. In karma-yoga, the main thing is the rejection of the attachment to the fruits of actions, and in sankhya-yoga, the main thing is the rejection of the ego. However, the rejection of the ego itself leads to the rejection of attachment, because attachment also arises from the ego. For example, 'my opinion should prevail, my opinion should not be rejected' - this is also a form of attachment to the ego. Therefore, by rejecting attachment, the ego also gets rejected. In karma-yoga, one performs actions with the feeling 'I have nothing, I don't need anything, and I don't have to do anything for myself.' This is done for the benefit of the world. By doing so, attachment gets rejected. When attachment is rejected, the ego also gets completely rejected. In karma-yoga, the actions performed through the gross body are for the benefit of the world, the thoughts of detachment from the world are performed through the subtle body, and the stability (one-pointedness) is performed through the causal body. Therefore, while performing actions for the benefit of others, one's thoughts are also focused on the benefit of others. As a result of this, stability arises, and with stability, the ego and attachment both get rejected, and peace is obtained. The peace obtained by rejecting the world is not the ultimate goal or the object to be attained, but it is a means - 'yogarudhasya tasyaiva shama karanam uchyate' (Gita 6.3). However, the peace obtained by attaining the Supreme Self is the ultimate goal, which is the nature of the Supreme Self - 'shanti nirvana-paramam' (Gita 6.15). Now, the seeker should be cautious not to enjoy this peace obtained through the means. If one enjoys it, one will get stuck in it.

is. Explanation– 'Adhisthanam' - The body and the place where it is situated - the skin - touching, the tongue - tasting, the nose - smelling, the ears - hearing - these two are 'adhisthan'. 'Karta' - All actions are performed by nature and the actions of nature - whether they are collective or individual - but the doer is not 'oneself'. Only a person who is deluded by ego and has no knowledge of the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious - such an ignorant person - when he attributes the actions of nature to himself, becomes the 'karta'. Such a 'karta' becomes the cause of the accomplishment of actions. 'Karana cha pithagvidham' - There are thirteen kinds of karana. The five organs of action - the hands, the feet, the tongue, the anus, and the genitals - and the five organs of knowledge - the ears, the eyes, the skin, the tongue, and the breath - these ten are the 'bahih karana' and the mind, the intellect, and the ego - these three are the 'antah karana'. 'Vividhashcha pithakcheshta' - The different actions of the above-mentioned thirteen karana are - for example, the hands - taking and giving, the feet - walking and running, the tongue - speaking, the anus - excretion, the genitals - excretion, the ears - hearing, the eyes - seeing, the skin - touching, the tongue - tasting, the mind - thinking, the intellect - deciding, and the ego - pride and egoism. 'Devam chaivaatra pancham' - The fifth cause in the accomplishment of actions is called 'deva'. Here, 'deva' means samskaras. A person does a particular action, and according to that action, a samskara is formed in his antahkarana. A good action forms a good samskara, and a bad action forms a bad samskara. These samskaras create the impulse to perform actions. The more a person has a samskara for a particular action, the easier it is for him to perform that action, and if a person does not have a samskara for a particular action, he may face difficulty in performing it. In the same way, a person listens, reads books, and thinks, and all these actions are performed according to his samskaras. The meaning is that a person's antahkarana has good and bad samskaras, and according to those samskaras, he performs actions. In this shloka, five causes of the accomplishment of actions are mentioned - adhisthan, karta, karana, cheshta, and deva. The reason for this is that without a basis, no action can be performed. All actions are performed by nature - this is described in the Gita in many ways - for example:

(1) All actions are performed by nature - 'Prakrityeve cha karmanni kriyamanani sarvashah' (13.29), all actions are performed by the qualities of nature - 'Prakriteshu kriyamanani guneshu karmanni sarvashah' (3.27). (2) The qualities perform actions among themselves - 'Gunah guneshu vartante' (3.28), the seer does not see any other as the doer except the qualities - 'Nanyam gunebhyah kartaram yadadrashtanupashyati' (14.19). (3) All the senses perform their respective actions - 'Indriyani indriyarthesu vartante' (5.9). (4) In this shloka (18.14), the five causes of the accomplishment of actions - adhisthan, etc. - are mentioned. The meaning of all these is that nature and the person - in these two, only nature performs actions, not the person. When a person identifies himself with nature, he attributes the actions of nature to himself. Just as a person sitting in an airplane thinks that he is flying in the airplane, when in fact the airplane is flying, in the same way, a person attributes the actions of nature to himself - 'Ahankaravimoodhatah kartahamiti manyate' (3.27). A person who has knowledge of the truth and is not deluded by ego experiences that all actions are performed by nature and nature's actions, and he does not perform any actions - 'Naiva kimchit karmeti yukto manyeta tat tvavit' (5.8).

[Verse 15]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Why does the term 'adhisthana' (support) come? Because it is without a doer. Why does the term 'cheshtha' (effort) come? Who will perform the actions? Hence, the term 'kartaa' (doer) comes. The actions will be performed according to the samskaras (impressions). The samskaras are the means (karana) for performing actions, and hence the term 'karana' comes. When the means for performing actions are available, the term 'daiva' (divine) comes. In this way, even if these five are present, the action will not be performed, and then how will the fruit of action be obtained? The fruit of action is obtained. Parishishta Bhaav - The 'kartaa' (doer) is the ego (ahankar), which is the inferior nature, and the 'jiva' (individual) is the superior nature. The jiva is related to the Supreme Self, but it identifies itself with the ego and considers itself the doer. 'Daiva' - Good or bad samskaras are present in everyone - 'sukhmati kumati sabke ur rahin' (Mans, Sundar 40.3). The company, scriptures, and thoughts - these three give strength to good or bad samskaras, leading to new actions. A man begins to act by means of body, speech, and mind. Whether the action is righteous or unrighteous, it is due to these five causes - body, speech, mind, doer, and the means (effort). Explanation - The five causes mentioned in the previous shloka (14) are present in these words - 'shariravaangmanobhih' (body, speech, and mind), 'narah' (man), 'viparitam' (unrighteous), 'yad' (which), 'nyayyam' (righteous), and 'vah' (or). These five causes are present in the actions performed by man. Whether the action is righteous or unrighteous, it is due to these five causes - body, speech, and mind. These three are the means of all actions. The actions performed by them are called kayaik (bodily), vaachik (verbal), and maanasik (mental) actions. The impurities in these three lead to bondage. Therefore, the kayaik, vaachik, and maanasik tap (austerities) are described in the 14th, 15th, and 16th shlokas of the 17th chapter. The meaning is that one should not perform any action that is prohibited by the scriptures, but only perform actions that are ordained by the scriptures. That is 'tap'. It is said in the 17th shloka of the 17th chapter that the tap performed without any attachment is sattvic (pure). Sattvic tap is liberating, but rajas (passionate) and tamas (dark) tap are binding. When one considers the body, speech, and mind as one's own and performs actions for one's own benefit, impurities arise in them. Therefore, without purifying them, one can understand the philosophical discussions of the Sankhya system through reasoning and intellect. However, one cannot have a clear understanding that 'I have no connection with actions whatsoever.' In such a situation, the sadhak (spiritual seeker) should not consider the body, etc., as one's own and should not perform any actions for one's own benefit. Then, the body, etc., will become pure quickly. Therefore, one can either purify them through the practice of karma yoga (action yoga) and then break the connection with them, or through the practice of Sankhya yoga (philosophical yoga).

One should break the connection with these (the senses) by the power of strong discrimination. However, where one does not consider oneself the doer, there the separation of the connection with the means and the work of nature along with the nature itself takes place, and the real truth is experienced. No accumulation of karma takes place there. Only actions take place there. Therefore, those actions are not productive of fruit and do not bind. For example, growing from childhood to youth, the coming and going of breath, the digestion of food, and the transformation of food into essence, etc., are actions that take place naturally and spontaneously without the sense of doership, and there is no accumulation of karma, i.e., no good or bad karma. Similarly, when there is no sense of doership, all actions take place through the power of nature. The collective power that makes all the actions of the universe take place, makes the actions of the individual body also take place naturally and spontaneously. Because of not giving importance to discrimination, a person considers himself the doer of actions such as eating, drinking, standing, sitting, sleeping, and waking, etc. In such a case, there is accumulation of karma, i.e., those actions become binding. Parishishta Bhaav - Having attachment, aversion, joy, sorrow, etc. in the mind is a mental karma. 'Niyayam' means - sattvic actions, actions prescribed by the scriptures, or good actions. 'Vipareetam' means - rajasic, tamasic actions, actions prohibited by the scriptures, or bad actions. 'Niyayam vaa vipareetam vaa' means - only actions. Connection - What is the intention of explaining the five causes of actions in the context of explaining the Sankhya philosophy? This is described in the next shloka. Thus,

= i.e., he has not given importance to discrimination. Explanation - The phrase 'tatraiva sati' means - even if the self is present as the doer. The phrase 'pasayatya-kritabuddhitvaat' means - because his intellect is not pure. The phrase 'durmatih' means - a dull-minded person. The phrase 'akritabuddhitvaat' means - because his intellect is not pure. The meaning is that the dull-mindedness of the person is due to the impurity of his intellect, i.e., he has not given importance to discrimination. If he had given importance to discrimination, he would not have been dull-minded. The phrase 'tatraiva sati' means - even if the self is present as the doer. However, even if the self is present as the doer, a person does not see (the reality) because his intellect is not pure, i.e., he has not given importance to discrimination. The self does not do anything, nor does it get attached to anything - 'na karoti na lipyate' (Gita 13.31); but due to the sense of identification, the thought 'I do not do anything' does not arise. The cause of this is 'akritabuddhi', i.e., the person has not made his intellect pure. Therefore, he considers himself the doer, whereas the pure self does not have the sense of doership.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Verse 16 ]
* The Nectar of the Seeker *

The word 'kevalam' (only) is present in both Karma Yoga and Sankhya Yoga. Karma Yoga and Sankhya Yoga proceed based on the discrimination between nature and the individual. In Karma Yoga, all actions are performed through the body, mind, intellect, and senses, but they are not associated with attachment. The absence of attachment leads to the experience of unity with the body, mind, and other senses. This unity is experienced when one realizes their true nature. Therefore, in Karma Yoga, the word 'kevalam' is used in relation to the body, mind, intellect, and senses - 'kayena manasa buddhya kevalair indriyairapi' (Gita 5.11). One considers oneself the doer. The attachment is eliminated through discrimination. How can one consider oneself the doer when attachment is eliminated? This means that one experiences their true nature. Therefore, in Sankhya Yoga, the word 'kevalam' is used in relation to the true nature - 'kevalam atmanam'. Now, there is a special point to be noted here. In Karma Yoga, the word 'keval' is used in relation to the body and mind, and it implies that the body and mind are associated with the concept of 'aham' (I), which is a service to the world. In Sankhya Yoga, the word 'keval' is used in relation to the true nature, and it implies that one is 'nirlep' (untainted), 'shuddh-buddh-mukt' (pure, intelligent, and liberated). In Sankhya Yoga, the emphasis is on the subtle distinction between 'aham' and the true nature. The more one is aware of this distinction, the more one will experience the true nature. However, the attachment to the concept of 'aham' will remain, and one will not be able to experience the true nature. The attachment to the concept of 'aham' is due to the ignorance of the true nature. The true nature is not the doer, nor is it the enjoyer. The doer and the enjoyer are both attributes of the individual, and they are not present in the true nature. The true nature is the witness, and it is not involved in any action. The individual is the doer, and the individual is the enjoyer. The individual is the one who is attached to the concept of 'aham'.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18 ]

Do not abandon actions, but do not consider yourself the doer of them. Consider them as happening through you and for your benefit. The importance of actions, whether worldly or spiritual, is actually the same as the importance of a stone. Due to their scriptural origin, spiritual actions have a special importance in the mind, but this importance is also like the importance of a stone, and it is an obstacle for the seeker. Spiritual actions become beneficial when they are related to the Supreme Being. As the importance of actions decreases and their relationship with the Supreme Being increases, so does their benefit. When actions are considered as the main thing, even years of practice do not bring benefit. Therefore, the importance of actions should not be considered, but rather the pleasure of the Supreme Being. Pleasing the Supreme Being is devotion, not actions. A person whose mind is devoid of discrimination is called a 'durmata' (a person with a wrong understanding). Discrimination is the cause of knowledge, not the mind. The mind becomes pure through discrimination. The purity of the mind is also achieved through good deeds, but not to the same extent as through discrimination and thought. Not giving importance to discrimination is as much a fault as the faults of malice, attachment, and ignorance. Discrimination is eternal and constant. Therefore, even with the presence of malice, attachment, and ignorance, discrimination can be awakened. Discrimination is not destroyed by sin, but it is not awakened. The reason for not giving importance to discrimination is the importance given to actions and objects. Relation - The previous shloka said that a person who sees the pure form as the doer is not seeing correctly. So, who is the one who sees correctly? This is described in the next shloka. [Verse 17]
A person whose mind is free from the ego and whose mind is not tainted, even if he kills, does not kill and does not get bound. Explanation - A person whose mind is free from the ego and whose mind is not tainted, even if he kills, does not kill and does not get bound. This means that such a person does not have the thought 'I am the doer' and 'I will get the fruit of this action.' This is because the ego and the mind are both tainted by the thought 'I am the doer.' When the ego and the mind are free from this thought, the doer and the enjoyer both disappear, and the person experiences the reality of not being the doer and the enjoyer. The state of being without ego and the mind being free from taint is like a light in which all actions, whether scriptural or forbidden, take place. The light is not the doer of the actions and does not cause them to be done. In the same way, the Supreme Being is the substratum of all actions, and it is not the doer of the actions and does not cause them to be done. A person who experiences this reality does not have the thought 'I am the doer of the actions.'

The work of nature is going on naturally, changing and remaining in its own form, and its light is the substratum of all actions. A person who remains in his own form, considering the work of nature as going on naturally, does not have the thought 'I am the doer of the actions.' This is because the thought 'I am the doer' arises from accepting the body as one's own. In the worship of the Supreme Being, the pleasure of the Supreme Being is the main thing, and the seeker's doer-ship is not involved. The four things - action, karma, worship, and discrimination - are all separate. 'Action' does not relate to anyone. 'Karma' relates to the favorable or unfavorable circumstances of the fruit. 'Worship' relates to the Supreme Being. 'Discrimination' separates the gross and the subtle.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The savior - the elixir - is obtained by doing it. When the egoistic feeling is completely eliminated, there is no trace of the thought "I have obtained the fruit" in the mind; that is, there is no desire for the fruit. Egoistic feeling is a mental attitude. Although it is a mental attitude, it remains in the self; because the self accepts both the attitude of being the doer and the attitude of not being the doer. - "Even if he kills all these living beings, he does not kill them, nor is he bound" - even if he kills all these living beings, he does not kill them; because there is no sense of being the doer in him, and he is not bound; because there is no sense of being the enjoyer in him. The meaning is that he has no connection with actions and their fruits. In reality, nature itself is transformed into action and fruit. However, due to the lack of experience of this reality, the person (the conscious being) becomes the doer and the enjoyer. Because when actions are performed with egoism, the doer, the instrument, and the action - all three come together, and then the accumulation of karma takes place. But in the one in whom the egoistic feeling does not remain, only the universal consciousness, the source of light, and the general consciousness remain; then how can he kill anyone, and how can he be bound to anyone? It is not possible for him to kill or be bound (Gita - 2.19). What is killing all living beings? It is the one in whom the egoistic feeling does not exist and in whose mind there is no stain - such a person's body, which is in a particular varna and ashrama, is in a situation that arises in front of him according to that varna and ashrama; when he acts according to that situation, he does not incur sin. For example, if a jivanmukta kshatriya gets a situation of self-war, he kills everyone in that situation, but he neither kills nor is bound. Because there is no sense of pride and self-interest in him. Here, there is a situation of war in front of Arjuna too. Therefore, the Lord has inspired Arjuna to fight with the word "hataapi". The meaning of the word "api" is - "Even if he is engaged in action, he does not do anything" (Gita 4.20). "Even if he is engaged in action, he is not attached to it" (Gita 6.31). "Even if he is engaged in action, he remains in me" (Gita 13.31). The meaning is that he is engaged in action completely. The reality is that the nature of the self remains unchanged whether one is engaged in action or not. Because the division of action is in nature, not in the self. In reality, it is the egoistic feeling (personality) that creates distinction in a person. If the egoistic feeling does not exist, then there is no distinction with the Supreme. Then, only the universal consciousness, the source of light, and the general consciousness remain. He does not become the doer of actions, and he does not become the enjoyer of fruits. He was never the doer of actions or the enjoyer of fruits. He accepted the egoistic feeling, considering it to be a relation with the body. There are two types of 'aham' - 'aham sphurta' and 'aham kriti'. As soon as a person wakes up from a deep sleep, he first experiences his existence - this is called 'aham sphurta'. After that, he attributes to himself - "I am such and such a name, varna, ashrama, etc." - this is the false relation. This false relation leads to the thought "I do it" when he performs actions related to the body, this is called 'aham kriti'. The 'aham' related to 'aham sphurta' may have a slight sense of distinction (personality). However, this distinction is not binding; that is, even if there is a sense of distinction, 'aham sphurta' is not guilty. Because, without the sense of being the doer, one does not attribute virtues and vices to oneself. It is only when 'aham kriti' arises that one attributes virtues and vices to oneself, which leads to the creation of good and bad karma. When one realizes, the slight sense of distinction in 'aham sphurta' disappears, and only the spark remains. In such a state, a person neither kills nor is bound. What is the meaning of "he does not kill, nor is he bound"? It is a state of non-dualism, and it is a state of non-dualistic awareness. Non-dualistic awareness is a means to an end, and its rise is also possible. When there is a discrepancy in this non-dualistic state, one experiences the self-existent non-dualistic awareness. Non-dualistic awareness is not a means to an end, and it is not possible for it to be non-dualistic.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18 ]

[Verse 18]
In the state of equilibrium, there is no change, nor can there be any change, nor is it possible for any change to occur. This means that in the state of equilibrium, there is no agitation or disturbance. This is the meaning of 'na hanti na nibadhyate'. The fruits of actions, which are obtained as a result of karma, also come and go. In this way, both action and its fruits are constantly coming and going. However, the Self remains unchanged, like a lamp that remains the same in its radiance. When one experiences this equilibrium through discrimination and reasoning, then the egoistic attitude and the egoistic attitude in the intellect cease to exist. What is the means to prevent the egoistic attitude and the egoistic attitude in the intellect from existing? The egoistic attitude and the egoistic attitude in the intellect do not exist in the intellect. The change occurs only in the nature, not in the intellect. Commentary - The meaning of not having an egoistic attitude is to be free from ego and the intellect not being attached. The meaning of the intellect not being attached is to be free from desires, attachment, and selfishness. Arjuna had said that killing these enemies would be a sin - 'papameva ashrayed asman hatva etan atatayinah' (Gita 1.36) and killing the wise and noble gurus would be a sin - 'gurun hatva hi mah anubhavans' (Gita 2.5). Therefore, the Lord says that there is no sin in killing them, because the reason for sin is ego and the attachment of the intellect. The intellect is attached to desires, attachment, and selfishness. Just as the Ganges does not become impure if someone drowns in it, and it does not become pure if someone bathes in it, drinks its water, or cultivates its banks, similarly, the year does not become impure if many living beings die in it, and it does not become pure if many living beings are born in it. The reason is that the Ganges and the year do not have ego and the intellect is not attached. If a doctor does not have desires, attachment, and selfishness in his intellect, then even if he cuts off a limb during an operation, it will not be a sin. If he does not have ego, then what is the question of sin? The destruction of egoistic attitude is achieved through the path of knowledge, and the destruction of the attachment of the intellect is achieved through the path of action. When one of these two is destroyed, the other is also destroyed. The egoistic attitude is the cause of the desire for pleasure and liberation. When the egoistic attitude is destroyed, the desire for pleasure also disappears - 'buddhir yasya na lipyate'. When the desire for pleasure disappears, the desire for liberation is automatically fulfilled, because liberation is self-existent. Relationship - It is not the knowledge and the tendency (action) that are to be blamed, but the egoistic attitude is to be blamed, because it is the egoistic attitude that leads to the accumulation of karma - this is explained in the next shloka. jnanam jneyam parijanata trividha karmachodana |
karanam karma karteti trividha karmasangraha || 18 ||

The motivation for action is the result of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the one who knows. The threefold motivation for action is the result of the threefold knowledge, and the threefold accumulation of karma is the result of the threefold knowledge. Commentary - [This is explained in the same chapter, where the Lord has explained the five causes of the formation of karma - adhisthana, kartar, karana, cheshta, and daiva (samskara). Even in these five causes, the root cause is the kartar. To destroy this root cause, the Lord has severely criticized those who have the attitude of kartar in the sixteenth shloka, and has praised those who do not have this attitude in the seventeenth shloka. The attitude of kartar should not exist at all.]

[Verse 19]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The one who is born, then quenches thirst with water. The one who is the cause of water and other things is called 'karan'. Eating, drinking, sitting, standing, and other actions are called 'kriya'. The one who has knowledge of these actions is called 'jneya'. The one who knows these actions is called 'parijnaata'. The one who has knowledge, is called 'karma'. The one who has karan and kriya, and is the one who knows these actions, is called 'karta'. The one who has these three, is the one who has the motivation to perform karma. If any one of these three is missing, then there is no motivation to perform karma. The one who is called 'parijnaata' is the one who knows all kinds of actions. He is only a 'jnaata' (one who knows), he has knowledge only of the actions, and there is no desire or pride in performing the actions. Any action is born in a particular individual. Therefore, there can be many 'kartas' (doers) in the form of one who hears, one who touches, one who sees, one who tastes, and one who smells. But there is only one 'parijnaata' (one who knows) who knows all of them. The Lord is explaining here how karma-sangraha (accumulation of karma) happens. That is, how the doer (karta) binds karma. The Lord is explaining the three causes of karma-banana (accumulation of karma) by mentioning the doer (karta). If there is no doer (karta), then there is no karma-sangraha, only actions are performed. 'Karan' is not the cause of karma-sangraha, because karan is under the control of the doer (karta). The doer (karta) wants to perform a particular action, and that action is performed. Therefore, 'karma' is also not the cause of karma-sangraha. According to the Sankhya philosophy, the special cause of karma-sangraha is 'ahankritbhava' (false ego) and this is the cause of karma-sangraha. If there is no false ego, then karma-sangraha does not happen, and karma is not fruitful. The Lord has mentioned the doer (karta) after mentioning karan and karma, in order to explain the root cause of karma-sangraha, that is, false ego. Therefore, the three causes of karma-sangraha are karan, karma, and karta. These three work together to complete karma. The doer (karta) performs karma with the help of certain means (sadhana), and these means are the actions of the senses (indriyas). Parishishta Bhaav - Arjuna had expressed his desire to know the truth of jnaana-yoga and karma-yoga (18th chapter, first shloka). Therefore, the Lord explained karma-yoga up to the 12th shloka. Then the Lord explained the five causes of karma-siddhi (18th chapter, 13th, 14th, and 15th shlokas) from the point of view of jnaana-yoga. Now, the Lord is explaining karma-prerana and karma-sangraha in a different way. When a person has a false ego and attachment, then the motivation to perform karma arises, that is, 'I will perform this action and get this fruit'. This motivation is called 'karma-prerana'. Karma-prerana leads to the accumulation of karma, that is, the accumulation of papa (sin) and puunya (merit). The Lord will explain in detail how these papa and puunya karma arise in the 20th shloka. Sambandh - The Lord is now starting the discussion on the objects of the three gunas (qualities) with the next shloka, with the intention of becoming guna-tita (beyond the three gunas). Jnaanam karma cha kartaa cha tridhaiva guna-bhedatah |
Procyate guna-sankhyane yathavacchrunu taan api || 19 ||

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18
Commentary - 'It is said that the knowledge of the qualities' – In the scripture where this is mentioned, the goal of trying to know, to acquire these subjects is the 'satisfaction' that remains in relation to the different aspects of the qualities of each thing. The feeling of studying remains the same in the study of knowledge, as per the same scripture, I am telling you that I will know, that I will get more knowledge, that I will get more wealth by studying more, that I will get more respect, that I will get more happiness by doing more work, and that I will be happy by doing such work. Similarly, the goal of every work is always 'satisfaction'. Therefore, God has described the three aspects of the knowable (jneya) as 'satisfaction' (sukha) in the scripture (Guna Sangkhyana) from the thirty-sixth to the forty-second verse. 'Jnanam karma cha karta cha tridhaiva gunabhedaat'
In the next verse, God has described the three reasons for the motivation of work and the three reasons for the formation of work. In this way, six things have been described in the scripture up to the formation of work. Now, in this verse, God is only talking about the analysis of the three things - knowledge, work, and the doer. In the division of the motivator of work, only 'knowledge' has been taken, because in the motivation of any work, knowledge always comes first. After knowledge, the work begins. In the division of the collection of work, only 'work' and 'doer' have been taken. Although the doer is the main one in the formation of work, the reason for taking work along with the doer is that the collection of work takes place only when the doer performs the work. If the doer does not perform the work, then the collection of work will not take place. The meaning is that in the motivation of work, 'knowledge' and in the collection of work, 'work' and 'doer' are the main ones. If these three - knowledge, work, and doer - are sattvic, then a person can remain detached, but if they are rajasic or tamasic, then he cannot remain detached. Therefore, in the division of the motivator of work, 'the knower' and 'the knowable' have not been taken, and in the division of the collection of work, 'the instrument' has not been taken. Why has the analysis of the 'knower' and 'the knowable' not been done in the division of the motivator of work? The reason is that when the knower is related to the action, he is called the 'doer', and the doer has three aspects (sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic) under the three aspects of the doer. But when the knower is only the knower, then he does not have three aspects, because he does not have the association of qualities. The association of qualities makes his three aspects. Therefore, the knowledge - the intellect - is sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic. The thing that is to be known is called 'the knowable'. Since there are many things to be known, its different aspects have not been described. However, the ultimate goal of knowing all these knowable things is to get 'satisfaction'. Just as a person studies to get knowledge, a person earns money to get wealth, a person tries to get a position to get respect, similarly, God has not described the three aspects of the instrument (karana) because all the instruments (such as the senses) are only means. Therefore, their three aspects are not there. However, in all these instruments, the 'intellect' has the highest importance, because a person does all his work through the intellect, thinking carefully. Therefore, God has described the three aspects of the instrument (karana) as 'the intellect' from the thirtieth to the thirty-second verse. The intellect is strengthened by 'dhriti' (steadfastness). God has mentioned 'dhriti' along with the intellect in two places (in the 25th verse of the 6th chapter and in the 41st verse of the 18th chapter) in the path of knowledge. This shows that in the path of knowledge, the intellect and steadfastness have a special need. Therefore, God has described the three aspects of 'dhriti' (steadfastness) from the 33rd to the 35th verse. The word 'tridhaiva' (in three ways) means that these three aspects are only three, not two or four. The reason is that the three qualities - sattva, rajas, and tamas - are the only three qualities that are produced by nature - 'Satvam rajas tam iti gunah prakriti-sambhavah' (Gita 14.5). Therefore, these three qualities are the only three aspects. 'Yathavat' - I am telling you this subject as it is described in the scripture (Guna Sangkhyana), without adding or subtracting anything from it. 'Shrinu' - Listen to this subject with attention, because the sattvic things are those that separate the relationship of work and give the knowledge of the Supreme Self, the rajasic things are those that give birth and death, and the tamasic things are those that lead to downfall and take a person to hell or lower birth. Therefore, listening to the description of these three, one can understand the motivation of work and the collection of work. The motivation of work is subtle, and the collection of work is gross, that is, knowledge, the knowable, and the knower - these three are subtle material, and work, instrument, and doer - these three are gross material.

Verse 20 ]
To accept sattvic things and to renounce rajasic and tamasic things is desirable. 'Those' – there is no connection of these (jñāna etc.) with your nature. Your nature is always pure and unattached. 'Api' – there is also a great need to know their distinctions; because, by knowing them properly, the experience of 'yasya nāhankṛto bhāvo ....... na hanti na nibadhyate' (18.17) will be obtained, i.e., the realization of one's own nature will be obtained. Explanation – 'sarvabhūteṣu yenaikam avyayam' – what is seen in all living beings, which is the same in all, is not the individual, but the all-pervading Paramātman. The individual's independent existence is not seen; because, in every moment, there is a change in the individual. No individual is such that there is no change in it; but due to ignorance, its existence appears to be independent. When ignorance is removed and knowledge arises, the seer's vision turns towards the unchanging reality, which is the source of all existence. When knowledge arises, the seer's vision turns towards the unchanging reality, which is the source of all existence (Gita – 13th chapter, 23rd verse). Then the seer sees the unchanging reality in all changing objects, persons, situations, and events (Gita – 13th chapter, 16th verse). The seer sees the unchanging reality in all changing objects, persons, situations, and events (Gita – 13th chapter, 16th verse). This means that, despite the diversity of objects, persons, situations, and events, the seer sees the same unchanging reality in all. This is the hallmark of the seer's vision. 'tajjñānaṃ viddhi sāttvikaṃ' – know this knowledge as sattvic. This knowledge is sattvic because it is related to the changing objects, persons, and situations. The seer sees the unchanging reality in all changing objects, persons, and situations. The sattvic knowledge is also known as 'vāsṭavik bodha' (true realization), which is the knowledge of the ultimate reality, as described by the Lord – 'jñeyam yattatpravaṣyāmi yaj jñātvāmṛtam aśnute' (Gita 13.12). The knowledge of the world is obtained through the senses, the knowledge of the senses is obtained through the mind, and the knowledge of the mind is obtained through the 'I' (the ego). The 'I' knows the three – the mind, the senses, and the objects. But the 'I' also has a light, which is the source of the 'I's' existence. This light is all-pervading and infinite, whereas the 'I' is limited and one-sided. In this light, the 'I' is seen, and in this light, the 'you', the 'this', and the 'that' are also seen. This light is not the subject of any object. In reality, this light is nirguṇ (beyond the gunas), but due to its association with the gunas, it is called sattvic knowledge. This sattvic knowledge can also be understood in another way – the four – 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' – all function in a light. All living beings are included in these four, which are separate and distinct. But the light, which is the source of their existence, is not separate and distinct. It is all-pervading and unchanging. The speaker says 'I', the listener says 'you', and the one near says 'this', and the one far says 'that'. The speaker says 'I' because he is the speaker, the listener says 'you' because he is the listener, and the one near says 'this' because he is near, and the one far says 'that' because he is far. The speaker, the listener, and the one near and far are all included in these four – 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'this'. But the light, which is the source of their existence, is not included in these four.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18 ]

The one who says 'this' to the one near him and 'not this' to the one far away, in reality, gets power from him. He says 'that' to himself. Due to the reason of identification, what was 'you' becomes 'I', and what was 'I' becomes 'you', 'this', and 'that'. However, the knowledge of the distinction between 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' does not arise. The one who is the source of light, is self-luminous, and remains the same always. 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' are the forms of the divided beings, and the one who is the real source of light is beyond division. This is the true 'sattvic knowledge'. If 'I' becomes 'you', and 'this' and 'that' remain the same, in the same way, if 'this' becomes 'I', then 'you' becomes 'this', and 'I' becomes 'you'. 'That' remains in its place due to being beyond perception. If 'that' becomes 'I', then in its view, 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' all become 'that'. In this way, 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' can all become each other in each other's view. This knowledge is the illuminator of all objects, and it is itself pure and free from vices. Therefore, it is called 'sattvic'. In reality, this 'sattvic knowledge' is called 'the knowledge of the illuminator' from the view of the illuminator, and 'the knowledge of the undivided' from the view of the divided. When it is free from the illuminator and the divided, then it is the 'true knowledge' that is beyond qualities and is unattached. From this, it is established that 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' are all changeable and do not remain the same. If they were true, they would remain the same. The true one is the illuminator and the refuge, whose light makes 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' apparent. In the view of the seeker, this 'sattvic knowledge' (discernment) is called 'sattvic knowledge' because of the presence of the power of the living beings. If, in his view, the power of the living beings does not remain, and only the eternal power remains, then it is the 'knowledge beyond qualities' (the realization of Brahman). That eternal power is present everywhere in the same form. Our natural unity is with that power. Connection—

Now, the description of 'rajasik knowledge' is given. In all beings, the knowledge that knows the different forms of the different beings, and knows the different characteristics, is the 'rajasik knowledge'. Example: Ram, Shyam, Govind, and Gopal are four individuals. Ram and Shyam are facing each other, Govind is near them, and Gopal is far away. Ram says 'I' to himself, 'you' to Shyam, 'this' to Govind, and 'that' to Gopal. If Shyam says 'I', then Ram will say 'you' to him, Govind will say 'this', and Gopal will say 'that'. In the same way, if Govind says 'I', then he will say 'this' to Shyam and 'you' to Ram, or 'you' to Shyam and 'this' to Ram, and 'that' to Gopal. If Gopal says 'I', then he will say 'that' to Ram, Shyam, and Govind. In this way, Ram, Shyam, Govind, and Gopal can all become 'I', 'you', 'this', and 'that' in each other's view. [ Verse 21 ]

But, O Arjuna, the knowledge that knows the different forms of the different beings, and knows the different characteristics, is the 'rajasik knowledge'.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

A person understands the eternal and indestructible Self, which is the essence of all, in a different way in each of them. Shloka 22
Commentary - A person who has a different understanding of the Self in each of them, taking into account their nature, name, form, qualities, etc., is called a 'Rajas' person. In Rajas knowledge, the predominance of 'Raga' (attachment) is seen - 'Rajo Raga-atmakaṃ viddhi' (Gita 14.7). The rule of Raga is that it creates attachment and aversion to someone, and attachment and aversion to someone else. Due to this Raga, a person considers humans, gods, Yakshas-Rakshasas, animals, birds, insects, plants, etc. as different from each other. In Rajas knowledge, there is no distinction between the living and the non-living. 'Vetti sarveshu bhuteshu tajjñānaṃ viddhi rājasam' - Similarly, the knowledge that a person has, which considers all living beings as different from each other, due to their internal organs, nature, senses, life, etc., is called 'Rajas'. Because of attributing reality and attachment to both the action and the object, they appear different. Connection - Now, the description of Tamas knowledge is being given. What is the knowledge that is present in the entire work, tied to a single work, and is devoid of any purpose or reason? That Tamas knowledge is being mentioned. 22. But

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18 ]

Why has the description of the ignorant, unwise, and extremely foolish been mentioned? Because the Lord has initiated the discussion of the three types of knowledge in the nineteenth verse, and the ignorant are said to be given importance. Since the ignorant do not have knowledge and the Lord has hesitated to call it 'knowledge' even after describing the sattvic and rajasic knowledge, it was necessary to mention it as 'ignorant'. Parishishta Bhaav - The asuric wealth is especially present in the ignorant knowledge. The meaning of not using the word 'knowledge' in this verse is that it is not knowledge, but rather ignorance. This is the ignorant nature of humans, which is called 'animal intellect' - 
'Tvam tu raajan marisyeti pasubuddhimimam jahi. Na jatah pragaabhootta adya dehavattvam na nashyasi' 
( Shrimad Bhagavat 12.5.2 )
( Shri Shukadevji said - ) 'O King! Now leave this animal intellect that I will die. Just as the body was not present before, was born, and will die, similarly you were not present before, were born, and will die - this is not the case.'

Connection - Now the Lord will describe the sattvic karma. The karma that is done without attachment, without attachment to the fruits of action, and without any expectation of reward, is called sattvic. 23. Explanation - 'Niyata' means that the karma is done according to the scriptural injunctions and is free from attachment. 'Sangarahitam' means that the karma is done without the sense of doership. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Free from attachment, one performs action, that is, action without attachment. A person with a desireless mind performs action, that is, action without desire. The action is not done with attachment, nor is it done with aversion, and one remains unattached to other things, performing action without attachment. The means (body, senses, and mind) by which one performs action are called sattvic if they are free from attachment and aversion. The present verse "aragadveshat" indicates the absence of attachment, and the future verse "aphalaprepsuna" indicates the absence of attachment in the future. The implication is that the present verse is describing rajasic action. Sattvic action remains sattvic as long as there is a subtle connection with nature. When there is a complete separation from nature, it becomes "akarma" (inaction). Yattu kamepsuna karma sahangkaraen va punah |
krayate bahulayaasam tadrajasamudahritam || 24 ||

That is, one performs action with attachment, or one performs action with a sense of pride, that is, rajasic action. Explanation: "Yattu kamepsuna karma" - We will perform action, taking into account our own special qualities (ahankara). If we perform action with a sense of pride, we will get material possessions, enjoyments, and honors, etc. "Sahangkaraen" - When we perform action in front of others, people see it and praise us, and we develop pride. "Va punah" - Or, we perform action with a sense of pride even when we are alone, because we see our own special qualities and abilities. "Krivate bahulayaasam" - When we perform action, every person experiences physical strain, but the person who is primarily motivated by the desire for material possessions experiences more physical strain. The person who is primarily motivated by the desire for material possessions experiences physical strain because his mind is focused on fulfilling his desires, and his physical body is a hindrance to achieving his goals. However, if a karma yogi experiences a sense of pride, it will not be a major obstacle, because his sense of pride is only related to performing his duty, and it is not a permanent attachment. The word "tu" is used here to distinguish rajasic action from sattvic action.

The meaning is that when the primary focus is on the body's comfort and relaxation, the disregard for the desire for fruit (of action) arises, and when the primary focus is on the desire for fruit, the disregard for the body's comfort and relaxation arises. When a person performs actions in front of others and receives a dose of egoistic pleasure, and the body's comfort and relaxation are not the primary focus, then the Rajas type of person does not find much effort in performing actions. However, when a person performs actions alone and does not receive a dose of egoistic pleasure, and the body's comfort and relaxation are the primary focus, then the Rajas type of person finds a lot of effort in performing actions. Parishishta Bhaav - The Rajas type of person increases his needs excessively, so that he needs more things for every task. To gather more things, he has to put in more effort. The Rajas type of person expands his actions, so he also has to put in more effort. Due to attachment to the body, the Rajas type of person wants the body's comfort, which makes him feel that even in small tasks, he has to put in a lot of effort. Sambandh - Now, the description of Tamasa karma is being given. The karma that is done without considering the consequences, the loss, and the harm to oneself and others, is called Tamasa karma. Yat tat tamasam uchyate = That which is done without considering the consequences, the loss, and the harm to oneself and others, is called Tamasa karma. Anubandham kshayam hinse anavetsy cha paurusham = The karma that is done without considering the consequences, the loss, and the harm to oneself and others, is called Tamasa karma. Vyakhya - 'Anubandham' - The one who has a desire for the fruit of action, that person does karma with the intention of getting the fruit, but the Tamasa person does not consider the consequences, the loss, and the harm to oneself and others, and starts the work without thinking. 'Kshayam' - The one who does this karma, does not consider the loss and harm to oneself and others, and starts the work without thinking. Dhritiutsaha-vyakhya - 'Muktasangah' - just like a sanyasi who does not get attached to his actions, a sattvic doer is also free from attachment. He does not get attached to objects, people, positions, situations, events, etc., due to his relationship with them. A sattvic doer is completely free from attachment. 'Anahnavadi' - the tendency to feel a sense of superiority due to the possession of objects, people, positions, etc. is a very lowly quality. A sattvic doer does not have this tendency. Instead, he says, "I am detached, I am free from ego, I am unattached, I am neutral, I am selfless."

'Dhritiutsahasamnvitah' - a sattvic doer has the quality of being steadfast and enthusiastic, just like a person who is full of hope and enthusiasm, even in the face of obstacles and failures. 'Siddhyasiddhyor nirvikarah' - a sattvic doer remains unaffected by success or failure. He remains calm and composed, whether he achieves his goal or not. 'Kartah sattvika uchyate' - such a person is called a sattvic doer. * Without thinking, whoever does something, later regrets it. *
* The work gets spoiled, and the person becomes a laughing stock in the world. *

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
Free from attachment, fear, and anxiety, and endowed with success and failure; devoid of egoism, possessed of determination, enthusiasm, success, and failure. The one who remains unattached is called 'Sattvic'. Among these, the first two are devoid of, and the middle two are endowed with. In this shloka, six things are mentioned— being with, and the last two things for remaining unattached. Parishishta Bhaav— The idea of remaining unattached in success and failure has been mentioned three times in the Gita— 'Siddhyasiddhyoḥ samō bhūtvā' (2.48), 'Samō siddhāvāsiddhau ca' (4.22), and here 'Siddhyasiddhyor nirvikaḥ' . The meaning is that success and failure are not a big deal, but remaining unattached in them is a big deal. What is a big deal, that needs to be corrected. 'Anahamvadi' - A Sattvic person is one who says, 'I can do this, but the other cannot do it in the same way.' He neither speaks from outside nor from inside. He experiences his own speciality, which is speaking from inside. Sambandh— Now, the characteristics of the Rajas type of doer are being described. Ragī karmaphalaprēpsur lubbhō hiṃsātmanāśuciḥ |
Harṣaśokānvitāḥ kartā rājasā parikīrtitaḥ || 27 ||

Vyākhya— 'Ragī'— The Lord has mentioned the word 'Ragī' first in the characteristics of the Rajas type of doer, because Raga is the nature of Rajoguna. Raga means— attachment to actions, attachment to the fruits of actions, and attachment to objects, etc. The one in whom these things are attached, is called 'Ragī'. 'Karmaphalaprēpsuḥ'— The Rajas type of person will do any action, but he will do it with the desire for some fruit. For example— I am doing this ritual, I am giving this donation, and from this I will get wealth, respect, and fame in this world, and in the next world, I will get heaven, etc. I am taking these medicines, and from these, my body will remain healthy, etc. 'Lubbhō'— The Rajas type of person is not satisfied with whatever he gets. Rather, he is always eager to get more and more. For example— 'If I get this much, I will be satisfied, but if I get more, I will be even more satisfied.' 'If I get this much respect, I will be satisfied, but if I get more respect, I will be even more satisfied.' 'If I get this much wealth, I will be satisfied, but if I get more wealth, I will be even more satisfied.' This kind of attachment and greed always remains in him. Parikīrtitaḥ = is said
'Hīṃsātmanāḥ' - He is of a violent nature. He does not care about the suffering of others for his own benefit. As he accumulates more and more wealth, he creates suffering in the hearts of those who do not get it. The reason is that no wealth can be obtained without violence. The meaning is that the Tamasic person commits violence in his actions, and the Rajas type of person is himself violent. 'Aśuciḥ' - The Ragī person is impure. He is attached to the objects and the fruits of actions through his senses and the intellect.

Vyakhya - 'Ayuktah' - tamas guna makes a person foolish. 'Prakrit' means uneducated. (Gita - 14th chapter, 8th shloka) . Therefore, at what time should we do what work? * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
'Anaiskrtikah' - One who has received some benefit from someone, is also sattvic, rajasic or tamasic. The one who has the nature of repaying the benefit is called 'anaiskrtik'. However, the tamasic person, even after receiving benefit from others, does not repay them, but instead harms them, hence he is called 'anaiskrtik'. 'Alasah' - Although the tamasic person has obtained the necessary duties according to his varna and ashram, due to foolishness, he does not find it good to perform the duties, but instead finds it good to indulge in worldly, meaningless things or to sleep. Therefore, he is called 'alas'. 'Visadi' - Although the tamasic person does not think about what is duty and what is not, and how much his power, valuable time, and life are being wasted in sleep, laziness, and negligence, yet, due to being away from the good path and duty, he naturally has a sense of sorrow (dissatisfaction, unrest) within himself. Therefore, he is called 'visadi'. 'Dirghasutri' - He who does not think about how to do a task in a good and efficient way, and therefore, does a task without wisdom, and takes a lot of time to complete a task that can be done quickly, is called 'dirghasutri'. The sattvic doer, by making his actions, intellect, etc. sattvic, experiences sattvic happiness and becomes one with the Supreme Consciousness, 'duhkhantam cha niggchhati' (Gita 18.36). Because the sattvic doer's goal is the Supreme, he becomes one with the Supreme Consciousness, free from the bondage of doer-ship and enjoyer-ship, as he was already one with the Supreme in his true nature. However, the rajasic and tamasic doers, being attached to rajasic and tamasic actions, intellect, etc., are entangled in rajasic and tamasic happiness and cannot become one with the Supreme Consciousness. Because the goal of the rajasic and tamasic doers is not the Supreme, and they are also more bound by ignorance. Now, a question may arise that if the doer is sattvic, then how can the actions be sattvic? The answer is that if the doer does not have attachment, ego, or desire for the fruit of the action, then the action becomes sattvic. Such sattvic actions bring great benefit to oneself and the world, and purity arises in all the things, people, and objects related to that action, because purity is the nature of the sattvic quality, 'tatra sattvam nirmalatvat' (Gita 14.6). Another point is that Patanjali Maharaj has considered rajo-guna as only kriyātā (active), 'prakashakriyāsthitiśīlaṁ bhūtendriyātmakaṁ' (Yoga Darshan 2.18). However, the doer is called 'tamasic'. Special note
The things said in the 26th, 27th, and 28th shlokas are all about the doer. The characteristics of the doer are the same as the characteristics of the actions. The doer accepts certain qualities, and according to those qualities, the actions take their form. The doer's actions, instruments, etc., are also in accordance with the doer's nature. The meaning is that just as the doer is, so are the actions, instruments, etc. The Gita considers rajo-guna as only rāgātmaka (attached to desire), 'rajo rāgātmakaṁ viddhi' (14.7). In reality, it is 'rāga' (desire) that binds, not 'kriyā' (action). In the Gita, actions are classified into three types: sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic (up to the 23rd shloka of this chapter). If the doer's attitude is sattvic, then the actions become sattvic; if the attitude is rajasic, then the actions become rajasic; and if the attitude is tamasic, then the actions become tamasic. Therefore, the Lord has not considered only 'kriyā' (action) as rajo-guṇī (active). Parishishta Bhaav - The term 'visadi' should be in rajo-guna, but it has come in tamas-guna here. The tamasic person has a natural opposition to the wisdom of the vritti (mental state), hence he has more sorrow.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Connection - All actions are performed with careful consideration. Now, I will explain the differences in these actions, which are determined by the predominance of the intellect and the power of resolve. Listen fully, O Arjuna, to the differences in the intellect and the power of resolve, which are threefold due to the threefold nature of the qualities. The differences in the intellect and the power of resolve are to be understood in their entirety, separately. O Arjuna, listen fully to the differences in the intellect and the power of resolve, which are threefold due to the threefold nature of the qualities. Explanation - In this chapter, the eighteeneenth shloka has mentioned the three causes of the accumulation of actions - the instrument, the action, and the doer. Among these instruments, the senses, etc., do not have threefold differences - sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. The predominance of the intellect remains in these senses, and all the senses function according to the intellect. Therefore, here, the differences in the intellect are being explained in relation to the differences in the instruments. The power of resolve, which is the ability to hold on to one's decision, is called dhriti. Without the power of resolve, the intellect cannot remain firm on its decision. Therefore, it is necessary to explain the threefold differences in the power of resolve along with the intellect. A person does whatever he does with careful consideration, i.e., he is engaged in a particular activity after proper thought and consideration. Even when he is engaged in that activity, he requires a lot of patience and determination. His intellect has a strong power of reasoning, and his power of resolve is superior, so his intellect does not get distracted from its determined goal. When the intellect remains firm on its goal, the person's work is successful. It is essential for the seeker to know what kind of intellect and power of resolve can hinder him from rising above the world - this is a very important thing to know. Therefore, the Lord has explained the differences in the intellect and the power of resolve. The Lord's intention in explaining the differences is that the seeker can rise above the world only with sattvic intellect and power of resolve, not with rajasic or tamasic intellect and power of resolve. 'Dhananjaya' - When the Pandavas performed the Rajasuya yajna, Arjuna had brought a lot of wealth by defeating many kings. This is how he got the name 'Dhananjaya'. Now, the Lord tells Arjuna that acquiring sattvic intellect and power of resolve is the real wealth, and one should acquire this wealth, which is the true fulfillment of one's name 'Dhananjaya'. 'Buddherbhedaṃ dhṛteścaiva guṇataḥ trividhaṃ śṛṇu' - The Lord says that the intellect is one and the power of resolve is one, but due to the predominance of the qualities, the intellect and the power of resolve have threefold differences - sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. I will explain these differences in detail and briefly mention a special point, and you should listen carefully, O Arjuna. In the ongoing discussion on the causes of the accumulation of actions, the importance of knowledge, action, and the doer has been emphasized. Similarly, in the seeker's practice, the importance of determination and the senses as instruments has not been emphasized. Therefore, the Lord is explaining the differences in the intellect and the power of resolve, using the word 'chava' to emphasize that just as the intellect requires special consideration, I will explain the threefold differences in the intellect, and similarly, I will explain the threefold differences in the power of resolve. Only by knowing this can the seeker rise above the world. What kind of intellect and power of resolve can hinder him from rising above the world - this is what he should know. From a superficial view, it may seem that the power of resolve is just a quality of the intellect. However, in the Sankhya yoga, the intellect and the power of resolve are both essential, and in all other means of attaining the Supreme, the intellect and the power of resolve are also essential. Therefore, in the Gita, both the intellect and the power of resolve are mentioned together, as in 'shanaih shanair uparamet buddhya dhritigrihitaya' (6.25) and 'buddhya vishuddhyaa yukto dhrityaatmanam nityam cha' (18.51).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18 ]

The distinction between the intellect and the will is a quality of the intellect itself. However, the will and the intellect of the seeker are both sattvic, and they are distinct and unique; because the will is the doer itself. It is due to the will that a person can make proper use of the intellect. The more will be the will's sattvic quality, the more stable will be the intellect of the seeker in the practice. In the practice, the necessity of the intellect's stability is as much as the necessity of the will's stability is not. However, in the acquisition of the minor siddhis like anima, there is a necessity of the will's stability. But in the spiritual progress, there is a greater necessity of the intellect's stability on its own objective. Only then will the seeker be firmly engaged in the practice. Therefore, the necessity of knowing the distinction between these two is essential. 'I will explain their distinction separately, that is, what are the differences between the intellect and the will, and I will also explain those.'

[Verse 30]
'Prauchyamanasheshen' - The Lord says that I will fully explain all the necessary things about the intellect and the will, and after that, there will be nothing left to be known. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The purpose of being engaged and disengaged is only to attain the ultimate truth. Not having any relation with worldly attachments is 'Moksha' or liberating. Being engaged is done for the service of all living beings, and being disengaged is done for attaining the state of supreme peace or one's true nature. 'Karyakarye' - according to the scriptures, varnas, and ashrams, the work that is done is 'kary' (duty) and the work that is done against the scriptures is 'akary' (non-duty). The work that we can do, which is necessary to be done, and which brings benefit to the living being, is 'kary' or duty, and the work that we should not do, which causes bondage, is 'akary' or non-duty. The work that we cannot do is not 'akary', it is simply our inability. 'bhayabhaye' - one should observe the causes of fear and fearlessness. The work that causes fear and harm to oneself and the world in the present and future is 'bhay' or fearful, and the work that causes benefit and happiness to oneself and the world in the present and future is 'abhay' or fearless. When a person is engaged in non-duty and is deviated from his duty, fear arises in his mind due to the fear of loss of prestige and criticism. However, the one who is always established in his duty and does not wish any harm to anyone and is always attached to the Supreme, has fearlessness in his mind. This fearlessness itself makes a person attain the state of being fearless and attains the Supreme. A person experiences the absence of things he does not have due to his desires for them. He considers himself to be a slave of those things and considers himself to be free when he has them. He thinks that he has become free due to having things, but actually, he becomes a slave again. The difference between the absence and presence of things is that the absence of things seems like a slavery that is apparent and painful, and the presence of things seems like a slavery that is hidden and sweet, but both are slavery. The poison that kills is the poison of attachment to worldly things. The conclusion is that attachment to worldly things is bondage, and not desiring anything except the Supreme is liberation. If there is a desire in the mind, then having the thing is bondage and not having it is bondage. If there is no desire in the mind, then having the thing is liberation and not having it is liberation. 'Buddhih sa parth saattvikii' - the intellect that knows the true nature of engagement and disengagement, duty and non-duty, fear and fearlessness, and bondage and liberation is sattvic intellect. What does it mean to know the true nature of these things? It means to understand them deeply and to know that the things that are not related to us should not be related to us, and the things that are inherently related to us should be related to us. It means to know the Supreme, who is the basis and light of all things, in its true nature. 'Bandham moksham cha ya vetti' - the one who performs external duties like yajna, dana, tirtha, and vrat, but internally desires and craves for worldly things and heavenly pleasures, all these external duties become 'bandham' or bondage for him. The one who has a relationship with the Supreme alone and does not have any relationship with the world, knows the true nature of things. The essence is that knowing the true nature of worldly things and their relationship with us is not knowing at all, but rather it is learning. It means to understand that the relationship with the world is not a relationship at all, but rather it is a bondage. There is one desire and one necessity. The desire is for the world, and the necessity is for the Supreme. The desire is never fulfilled, but it is always extinguished, whereas the necessity is always fulfilled. The necessity for the Supreme arises due to the desire for the world. The necessity for the Supreme is not present when the desire for the world is absent, and the Supreme is attained. Parishishta Bhaav - The meaning of knowing the true nature of engagement and disengagement, duty and non-duty, fear and fearlessness, and bondage and liberation is to cut off the relationship with the world. If there is no cutting off of the relationship with the world, then it is not true knowledge, but rather it is learning.

(Man)
The one whose intellect is like this is called Rajasic. Explanation: 'Yaya Dharmam Adharmam Cha' - whatever has been ordained by the scriptures is 'Dharma', i.e., whatever has been commanded by the scriptures and leads to salvation in the next world is Dharma. Whatever has been prohibited by the scriptures is 'Adharma', i.e., whatever has not been commanded by the scriptures and leads to suffering in the next world is Adharma. For example, serving one's parents, elders, and taking care of others' happiness by dedicating one's body, mind, wealth, and abilities is 'Dharma'. On the other hand, taking away others' wealth, causing harm to others, and killing others is 'Adharma'. In reality, Dharma is that which brings about the welfare of the living being, and Adharma is that which binds the living being. 'Karyam Cha Akaryam Evacha' - whatever work has been ordained by the scriptures according to one's varna, ashrama, country, time, and social norms is 'Karyam' or 'Duty'. Not doing what is ordained and doing what is not ordained is 'Akaryam' or 'Non-duty'. For example, a Brahmin's duty is to perform yajnas, weddings, and other rituals, but it is non-duty for a Kshatriya, Vaishya, or Shudra. Similarly, whatever work has been ordained by the scriptures for each varna and ashrama is their duty, and whatever has been prohibited is their non-duty. In the workplace, dedicating one's full time to work with honesty, performing tasks efficiently, and doing work in such a way that it benefits the employer is the duty of employees. On the other hand, getting distracted by one's own interests, not working diligently, causing harm to the employer by taking bribes, and causing harm to the employer for a few rupees is the non-duty of employees. In the government, officials are appointed to manage the affairs of the state and to benefit everyone. Therefore, doing work that benefits everyone, bringing happiness and peace to everyone, and putting the interests of the state above one's own interests is the duty of officials. On the other hand, causing harm to the state and its people for one's own interests and pride is the non-duty of officials. The intellect that does not know what is to be done and what is not to be done, and does not know what is duty and what is non-duty, is Rajasic.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The tendency to be mentioned in sattvic intellect - renunciation, fear, and aversion - when these two are associated with the world, the relationship is established here. Here, the concepts of fearlessness and bondage-liberation are also taken with the words 'eva ca'. 'Ayathavat prajanati buddhih sa parth rajashee'
Due to attachment, the intellect becomes rajasic, and in it, self-interest, bias, and inequality, etc. defects arise. With these defects, the intellect cannot know the true nature of dharma-adharma, karma-akarma, fear-fearlessness, bondage-liberation, etc. Therefore, what is dharma for which varna-ashrama and in which circumstances, and what is adharma? What becomes a duty for which varna-ashrama and what becomes an adharma? From whom fear arises and from whom man becomes fearless? The intellect that cannot know these things is rajasic. When a man is associated with the world, he cannot know the world. Similarly, when a man is separate from the Supreme, he cannot know the Supreme. One can know the world by being separate from it, and one can know the Supreme by being one with Him. This oneness can be through love or through knowledge. The sattvic intellect is the one that makes one realize this oneness, as it is the one in which the power of discrimination is awakened. However, in the rajasic intellect, this power of discrimination is dull due to attachment. Just as the clarity and purity of water are lost when mud is mixed in it, similarly, the clarity and purity of the intellect are lost when the rajasic quality is mixed in it. Therefore, it becomes difficult to understand dharma-adharma, etc. When a man has a rajasic intellect, he finds it difficult to understand any subject he enters. Without understanding the virtues and defects of a subject, he cannot accept or reject it in his behavior. That is, he cannot accept or reject any object. When attachment (asakti) arises in worldly objects, persons, events, situations, actions, or substances, it becomes a cause of hatred towards others. Then, the person who has attachment cannot see the defects of the one in whom attachment arises, and the person in whom hatred arises, he cannot see the virtues of that one. He cannot accept or reject any object. Parishishta Bhaav - The one who does not know dharma and adharma, and also does not know what is duty and what is not duty, how can he know bondage and liberation? He cannot know it. The intellect that is attached becomes incapable of knowing these things; because, due to the predominance of attachment, it does not give importance to discrimination. The power of discrimination is lost due to the attachment to worldly objects that are subject to birth and destruction. Samabandh - Now, we will describe the characteristics of the tamasic intellect.
