* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The idea of considering scriptures as a hindrance to action is a misconception - this is a misunderstanding of the concept of Dharma; it is a notion that is based on one's own education, knowledge, and understanding; it is an 'adharma' (unrighteousness). The tamasic (dark) nature of the mind leads people to think that the sages and Brahmins have created their own importance and have imposed various rules and regulations on people, thereby making India subservient; as long as these scriptures and sacred texts exist, India will not progress, and it will remain tied to its subservient state, and so on. Therefore, they consider the destruction of moral values as the ultimate goal of Dharma. [ Chapter 18 ]

As many saints and great souls have emerged, considering one's own opinion as superior to theirs; instead of focusing on true happiness, considering the fleeting pleasures of life as true happiness; considering only those actions as one's duty that are not worthy of being done; considering impure things as pure - this is the complete reversal of all things. "Buddhih sa partha tamsi" - the tamasic (dark) intellect, which considers unrighteousness as righteousness, and righteousness as unrighteousness, and good as bad, and bad as good, is the tamasic intellect. This tamasic intellect is the one that leads a person to downfall - "adhogachchhanti tamsah" (Gita 14.18). Therefore, one should not consider one's own self as the ultimate reality, but rather the body; one should not consider God as the ultimate reality, but rather the visible world; one should consider others as inferior and oneself as superior; one should consider the one who is seeking liberation as inferior - one should completely abandon this tamasic intellect. Parishishta Bhaav - The one whose intellect is tamasic, sees everything in a reversed manner in both behavior and spiritual pursuits. This can be seen clearly in the present time. For example, the production of meat is called 'meat production'! Abortion, which is a great sin, and the destruction of a person's creative power is called 'family welfare'! The promiscuity of women, which destroys social norms, is called 'women's liberation'! Earlier, women were the queens of the home (grihalakshmi), but now they are considered to be the servants of many men (naukar) in the name of 'women's independence'! In this way, subjugation is considered to be independence. Moral decay is considered to be a sign of progress. Barbarism is considered to be a sign of civilization. Irreligiosity is considered to be a sign of religiosity, and religiosity is considered to be a sign of irreligiosity. When the time of destruction is near, such a tamasic intellect is born - 'vinashakale vipareetabuddhih', 'buddhinashat pranashyati' (Gita 2.63). Sambandh - Now, the Lord will describe the characteristics of sattvic (pure) determination. O Partha, by the power of yoga, one should cultivate a determination that is free from attachment, and by which one's mind, life force, and senses remain steady. Through yoga, one should cultivate a determination that is free from attachment, and by which one's mind, life force, and senses remain steady. This determination is sattvic (pure). Yogaen avyabicharinyaa dhritihaa sa partha sattvikee || 33 ||

The one who has this determination, which is free from attachment, and by which one's mind, life force, and senses remain steady, is said to have sattvic (pure) determination. Vyaakhya - Determination (dhriti) is the one that is free from attachment (vyabhichara) - the attachment to worldly pleasures and pains, honor and dishonor, success and failure, and so on. The one who has this determination is said to have sattvic (pure) determination.

The power of unshakeable resolve, which is the strength of the mind, is called 'Dhriti'. Through the unshakeable and unwavering Dhriti, which is yoga, the mind, life force, and senses are controlled. The mind is free from thoughts of attachment and aversion, and it can be focused on whatever it desires and can be withdrawn from whatever it does not desire. This control of the mind's activities through Dhriti is the same as controlling the life force's activities through Dhriti. The unshakeable Dhriti is the power of steady breathing, where the exhalation and inhalation do not go against the rules. The senses are not distracted by the objects of the senses, and they are focused on the desired objects and withdrawn from the undesired objects. This control of the senses' activities through Dhriti is the same as controlling the life force's activities through Dhriti. When practicing pranayama, the exhalation should not be accompanied by the inhalation, and the inhalation should not be accompanied by the exhalation. The external retention of the breath should not be accompanied by the inhalation, and the internal retention of the breath should not be accompanied by the exhalation. This is the sattvic Dhriti, O Arjuna! Explanation - A person with a Tamas nature does not give up sleep, fear, grief, despair, and pride. This is the Tamas nature. The willpower of a person who is extremely lazy and whose intellect is clouded by ignorance and foolishness is Tamas in nature. He is not able to give up sleep, fear, grief, despair, and pride. He is always immersed in these emotions. Sometimes he is overcome by sleep, sometimes he is afraid of death, disease, loss of reputation, insult, poverty, and loss of wealth. Sometimes he is overcome by grief and sorrow, sometimes he is immersed in pain and suffering, and sometimes he is proud and arrogant due to the acquisition of desirable things. In addition to sleep, fear, grief, and pride, one should also consider the following vices and evil deeds as Tamas in nature: laziness, pride, hypocrisy, hatred, jealousy, and other evil qualities. A person with a Tamas nature is not able to give up these vices and evil deeds. The Lord has described the Sattvic and Rajas willpowers in the 33rd and 34th shlokas, using the word "dhārayate" (to hold or to possess). However, in this context, He has not described the Tamas willpower. The reason is that a person whose intellect is extremely clouded by ignorance and foolishness, and whose willpower is extremely weak, is not able to give up these vices and evil deeds. A person with a Tamas nature is not able to give up sleep, fear, grief, and pride. He is naturally immersed in these emotions. The willpower of a person is classified into three categories: Sattvic, Rajas, and Tamas. In the case of Rajas and Tamas willpowers, the person is described as "phalākāṅkṣī" (desiring the fruit) and "durmehā" (foolish), respectively. However, in the case of Sattvic willpower, the person is not described as "phalākāṅkṣī" (desiring the fruit). The reason is that in Sattvic willpower, the person is not attached to the fruit of his actions. However, in Rajas and Tamas willpowers, the person is attached to the fruit of his actions. Special Note
Human beings are endowed with the faculty of discrimination. A person who performs any action does so with full awareness and discrimination. As soon as he performs an action with full awareness and discrimination, his faculty of discrimination becomes clear. A Sattvic person's willpower is characterized by clear discrimination, and he knows that he should only follow the path of the Supreme Being. A Rajas person's willpower is characterized by attachment to worldly pleasures, and his faculty of discrimination is not clear. However, in this life, he follows the path of righteousness and performs actions that are in accordance with the scriptures. However, a Tamas person's willpower is characterized by attachment to worldly pleasures, and his faculty of discrimination is not clear. He is not able to give up sleep, fear, grief, and pride, and he is naturally immersed in these emotions.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Dhriti in which vivek is completely suppressed. In tamas nature, the goal is present, and actions are performed accordingly. When its strength becomes so great that there is no need to hold onto those emotions. He is immersed in tamas nature such as sleep, fear, etc. The thing itself remains, it never changes. For the firmness of the goal, the necessity of sattvic intellect is required, and for the sattvic intellect to keep the decision of the intellect unshakeable, the necessity of sattvic dhriti is required. Therefore, in the next six verses, the Lord, using the term "Pārtha" six times, reminds Arjuna, the representative of the seeker, that "O Pritha's son! Do not worry about worldly objects and people, and firmly hold onto your goal. Remain vigilant so that you never get affected by rajas and tamas emotions."

[Verse 37]
Action does not work as much as the purpose does in the paramarthic path. The predominance of gross action is in the gross body, the predominance of thought is in the subtle body, and the predominance of stability is in the causal body. All these actions are actions. "Action takes place in the bodies, but I have to walk only on the paramarthic path" - such a purpose or goal remains in itself (consciousness). As such, the auxiliary emotions - sleep, fear, worry, sorrow, pride, etc. - will remain, and cannot be removed - such a person is called "Durmedha". Such a person does not even think of giving up their defects, nor do they have the courage to give them up, but instead, they naturally hold onto them. Excessive sleep is a hindrance. Necessary sleep, in accordance with the circumstances, is not a hindrance (Gita - 6th chapter, 16th-17th shlokas). Connection - The tendency of humans to engage in actions is due to the greed for pleasure, i.e., the purpose of accumulating pleasure-karma. Therefore, in the next four shlokas, the distinction between types of pleasure is explained. Listen, O Arjuna, to the three types of pleasure that have been attained by abhyasa (practice) and in which the end of suffering is reached. That pleasure which is like poison at the beginning, and like nectar in the result, is called sattvic pleasure, born of the grace of the intellect. O Arjuna, you are not one who will be attached to rajas and tamas pleasures; because you have already won over rajas pleasure; just as you have won over the beautiful apsara Urvasi of the Svarga, who is as beautiful as the goddess Lakshmi.

You have rejected this. In the same way, you cannot be detached from the tamasic pleasure. Therefore, the Lord says, "Brother, that victory has been achieved; because you have conquered the tamasic pleasure, which is necessary for all living beings."
This is why your name is 'Gudakesh' (Gudakesh means one who has conquered sleep). 'Sukham tu idanam' - After explaining the threefold distinction of knowledge, action, doer, intellect, and determination, the Lord says here, using the word 'tu', that pleasure is also of three kinds. There is a special point to be noted here, that all the aspirants who are walking on the path of paramartha (spiritual path) have a high status or have not experienced the ultimate reality, if there is any obstacle or hindrance, then it is the desire for pleasure. Pleasure is of three kinds, listen to them and accept the sattvic pleasure and reject the rajasic and tamasic pleasures. Because sattvic pleasure is helpful in moving towards the ultimate reality, and rajasic and tamasic pleasures are binding and lead to downfall in the world. ‘Abhyasādramate yatra’ - In sattvic pleasure, there is a tendency to get immersed in practice. Ordinary people do not experience this pleasure without practice. In rajasic and tamasic pleasures, there is no need for practice. In them, there is a natural attraction of the living being. In rajasic and tamasic pleasures, there is a natural attraction of the senses towards objects, the mind and intellect towards enjoyment and accumulation, and towards sleep and other things when tired. All these pleasures are naturally attractive to living beings. Even animals, who are lowly creatures, are pleased if they are respected, and they become angry if they are disrespected, and they become unhappy. The meaning is that in rajasic and tamasic pleasures, there is no need for practice; because this pleasure is naturally obtained by all living beings in other births. Sattvic pleasure also becomes a binding factor due to attachment. The meaning is that if the pleasure obtained through practice and concentration is also taken, it becomes a binding factor. Not only that, if the pleasure of samadhi is also taken, it becomes an obstacle to the attainment of the ultimate reality - 'Sukhasangena baddhanti' (Gita 14.6). In this matter, someone may say that if the pleasure of the ultimate reality is obtained, then why should we not take it? In reality, the pleasure of the ultimate reality is not taken, but it is experienced naturally (Gita - Fifth Chapter). In sattvic pleasure, what is the practice? Listening, reflection, and practice (21st and 18th verses of the 21st and 18th chapters) are all practices. Understanding the scriptures is also a practice, and so is the practice of the shlokas. Abandoning the rajasic and tamasic tendencies is also a practice. The pleasure that is naturally obtained is the eternal pleasure. The Lord is pointing out the natural tendency of living beings towards pleasure, and is saying that this tendency is different from the new tendency that is being created. The word 'tu' is used to indicate this new tendency. 'Abhyas' is the practice. In sattvic pleasure, practice is necessary, but enjoyment is a hindrance. The meaning of 'idanim' is that Arjuna wants to know the truth of renunciation and detachment, so the Lord has explained the threefold distinction of renunciation, knowledge, action, doer, intellect, and determination. But in all these, the goal is pleasure. Therefore, the Lord says, "Listen to the distinction of pleasure for the sake of achieving that goal."

-
'Trividham shrinu me' - People are always engaged in rajasic and tamasic pleasures and consider them to be the real pleasure. Therefore, the Lord says, "Listen to me, there is a sattvic pleasure beyond rajasic and tamasic pleasures."

'Abhyasādramate' - The meaning is not that sattvic pleasure should be enjoyed, but that there should be a tendency to get immersed in practice in sattvic pleasure. 'Duhkhantam cha nigachchhati' - As the tendency to get immersed in practice in sattvic pleasure increases, the result is that the destruction of suffering and the increase of happiness, pleasure, and joy (Gita - Second Chapter, 60th verse). -
The word 'cha' is used to indicate that as long as there is a tendency to get immersed in practice in sattvic pleasure, the result is the destruction of suffering and the increase of happiness, pleasure, and joy. 'Abhyasādramate yatra' - In sattvic pleasure, there is a tendency to get immersed in practice.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The sattvic pleasure is born from the satisfaction of the divine intellect, 'ātmbuddhiprasādajam.' Whatever is born will certainly perish. How can there be an end to suffering from such pleasures? Therefore, one should not be attached to sattvic pleasure either. By rising above sattvic pleasure, a person attains the end of suffering, becomes beyond the gunas. There will not be an extreme absence of suffering until then. Because the renunciation of rajas and tamas pleasures is like poison. Just as, when a child is forced to give up play and games and is made to study, he feels imprisoned in his studies and does not enjoy it. If he is not allowed to play and run around, he finds studying to be like poison. But if the child studies and passes one or two exams, then he starts to enjoy his studies. His interest and liking for studying increase. 'ātmbuddhiprasādajam' – The intellect in which there is no importance given to worldly fame, respect, wealth, and sensual pleasures, but only the thought of the Supreme is present, that intellect's satisfaction is the birth of sattvic pleasure. In other words, the pleasure that arises from being immersed in the thought of the Supreme, free from worldly attachments, is sattvic pleasure. 'Yattadagre vishamiv' – Here, 'yattat' means that sattvic pleasure is yet to be experienced. It is only a goal, whereas rajas and tamas pleasures are already being experienced. Therefore, it is difficult to renounce the pleasures that are already being experienced, and the effort made to attain the sattvic pleasure, which is yet to be experienced, seems like poison at the beginning. People who have experienced rajas and tamas pleasures in many lives and are experiencing them in this life as well, remember the pleasure they have experienced in the past. Therefore, they naturally get attached to rajas and tamas pleasures. However, sattvic pleasure has not been experienced by them, so they do not get attached to it easily. This is why sattvic pleasure seems like poison at the beginning. In reality, sattvic pleasure is not poison, but it is only for those who have a natural attachment to rajas and tamas pleasures. However, those who have a natural aversion to worldly pleasures, who have a natural interest in spiritual studies, scriptures, and devotion, and whose knowledge, actions, intellect, and determination are sattvic, experience sattvic pleasure as nectar from the very beginning. They do not feel any difficulty, hardship, or labor in it. 'Parinamem amritopam' – Through practice, the sattvic guna arises in the sadhaka. When the sattvic guna arises, purity, cleanliness, the light of knowledge, peace, and detachment manifest in the senses and the mind. This manifestation of sattvic gunas is the result of sattvic pleasure, which is like nectar. If this pleasure is not enjoyed, then the attainment of eternal and imperishable bliss is achieved. In the end, sattvic pleasure raises one above rajas and tamas pleasures and breaks the bond of attachment to worldly things, and since one is not attached to it, one attains the Supreme in the end. Therefore, this is like nectar. 'Tatsukham sattvikam proktam' – The pleasure that arises from sadhana, study, chanting, japa, meditation, and contemplation is not related to worldly attachments, such as fame, respect, comfort, wealth, and sensual pleasures, nor is it related to laziness, sleep, and idleness. It is related to the Supreme. Therefore, it is called sattvic pleasure. Sattvic, rajas, and tamas – these three gunas exist in the mind in an imperceptible form. Their presence can be inferred from the nature of one's thoughts, which is described from the eleventh to the thirteenth shlokas of the fourteenth chapter.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18 ]

- Appendix / Parishishta Bhaav – In the fourteenth chapter, it was said that the sattvic pleasure binds (14.6), but here it is said that it destroys suffering (duality). This means that sattvic pleasure, when enjoyed, becomes a binding factor, i.e., it does not allow one to transcend the gunas. If one does not enjoy it, then it becomes a destroyer of suffering. Enjoying pleasure does not destroy suffering. It is only by renouncing pleasure that one attains yoga. Therefore, one should remain detached from sattvic pleasure as well. Attachment leads to the emergence of the rajasic guna. The emergence of the rajasic guna in the sattvic guna leads to downfall. Because of not giving importance to discrimination, sattvic pleasure initially appears like poison. A rajasic person does not respect discrimination. Therefore, sattvic pleasure initially appears like poison due to rajasic nature. In other words, sattvic pleasure is not painful, but due to the rajasic nature of the person, it appears painful. The intention is to attain sattvic pleasure, but there is a rajasic tendency within. Connection – Now, the description of rajasic pleasure is being given. Verse 38

If one indulges in objects, then suffering and pain arise, the mind does not remain in happiness, therefore, this rajasic pleasure appears like amrit at the beginning. Explanation – 'Vishay-indriya-sanyogaat' - The dislike for objects and sense organs arises. The pleasure that arises from the union of sense organs and objects is not practiced. The reason is that this living being goes to any yoni, and there it experiences pleasure due to the union of sense organs and objects. The pleasure of the five objects - sound, touch, etc. - is experienced by all living beings, including animals, birds, insects, and worms. Therefore, in this pleasure, the natural practice of the living being remains. In human life, it is natural to be happy in favorable circumstances and to be unhappy in unfavorable circumstances. Therefore, in this rajasic pleasure, there is no need for practice. 'Yattadagre'mritopam' – The description of rajasic pleasure as amrit-like at the beginning means that the possibility of obtaining worldly objects creates a sense of happiness in the mind. However, the pleasure of enjoying objects does not remain the same even when they are obtained. Initially, there is a sense of happiness and satisfaction, but after some time, this happiness does not remain, and when the capacity to enjoy objects decreases, there is no happiness. On the other hand, the description of rajasic pleasure as amrit-like means that when the mind is attracted to objects, they appear to be very dear. The pleasure of hearing about objects and their enjoyment is greater than the pleasure of enjoying them. Therefore, in the Gita, it is said, "Yamimam pushpitam vacham pravadanthy vipashchitah" (2.42); a rajasic person is attracted to the pleasure of enjoying heavenly objects, and he becomes greedy for it. In other words, the pleasure of enjoying heavenly objects appears to be very dear to him even from a distance, but when he enjoys it, he does not experience the same pleasure, and it does not appear to be as dear. 'Parinaame vishamiva' - Initially, objects appear to be very beautiful, and they create a sense of happiness. However, when they are enjoyed, the pleasure becomes dull and uninteresting.

* The Nectar of the Seeker *

1165
It becomes, in that happiness, a complete aversion develops, then | it does not kill like poison, but rather, it shows like poison, that very happiness is like a poison. It becomes. In that, the interest that was there in the beginning does not remain the same, i.e., that happiness becomes like poison, it is not actually poison. In the world, as many living beings are imprisoned, as many are in forty-eight lakh yonis and hells, if we see the reason, they have enjoyed worldly objects, they have taken pleasure in them, and because of this, they are experiencing suffering in prison, hells, etc. Because the result of rajas (passion) is always suffering - 'Rajas tu phalam duhkham' (Gita 14.16). Even today, those who are trembling, suffering, are doing so due to the cause of attachment to worldly objects. The one who has become poor after being rich, to the extent that he is suffering and tormented, to that extent, the poor one does not suffer because his inner nature is not afflicted with the seeds of happiness. But the rich one has enjoyed rajas (passion) more, his inner nature is more afflicted with the seeds of happiness, therefore, he suffers more due to the lack of wealth. Just as a person who eats various types of food, if there is even a slight deficiency in his food, it bothers him a lot, "Today, there is no chutney, no pickle, no sweet dish, no such and such thing" - in this way, he is constantly bothered by "no, no". But a common man, eating coarse, dry bread, does not bother at all about the deficiency of any food item. The meaning is that the more happiness is obtained from worldly objects, the more the experience of their absence is felt. The experience of absence is always painful. The one who desires something, makes efforts to obtain it. Efforts are made, but it is uncertain whether the desired thing will be obtained or not. If the desired thing is not obtained, then the pain of its absence is felt, and if the desired thing is obtained, then the desire to obtain even more of that thing arises. In this way, the fulfillment of desire becomes the cause of the birth of new desire, and the fulfillment of desire and the birth of desire - this cycle continues, and it has no end. The meaning is that desire never subsides, and the pain of absence continues to bother. This absence is like poison, i.e., it is painful. Why is rajas (passion) like poison? Because poison kills in one birth, but rajas (passion) kills in many births. A person who is attached to rajas (passion) and enjoys worldly pleasures, even if he goes to heaven by doing good deeds, he does not find happiness and peace there. In heaven, he sees people of higher status and feels envy, "Why have they become higher than me?" He feels sorrow seeing people of equal status, "Why have they become equal to me?" And he feels pride seeing people of lower status, "I am higher than them!" In this way, envy, sorrow, and pride continue to reside in his mind, and where is happiness and peace? Moreover, when his good deeds decrease, he has to come back to the mortal world - 'Kshine punye martyalokam vishanti' (Gita 9.21). He comes here, does good deeds again, and goes to heaven. In this way, he is stuck in the cycle of birth and death - 'Gatagatam kamakama labhante' (9.21). If he becomes involved in sinful deeds due to attachment to rajas (passion), then in the result, he falls into forty-eight lakh yonis and hells, and he is born and dies countless times, and there is no end to it. Therefore, this happiness is called like poison. 'Tatsukham rajassmritam' - In the thirty-seventh shloka, it is said that sattvic (pure) happiness is 'proktam' (spoken), but here, the word 'smritam' (remembered) is used for rajas (passion) happiness, meaning that humans have previously experienced the result of rajas (passion) as suffering, but due to attachment, they again become attracted to the association. Because the effect of association is already present on him, and he does not accept the effect of the result. If he accepts the effect of the result, then he will not be trapped in rajas (passion) happiness. Many stories are found in smriti, shastra, puranas, etc., in which humans have suffered due to the cause of rajas (passion) happiness. This is mentioned here to remind them of this fact. If rajas (passion) happiness is like poison, then all those who enjoy it should die after experiencing its result. But rajas (passion) happiness looks at the result of every subject.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[ Chapter 18 ]

The person who is attached to temporary pleasures does not pay attention to them. However, in the present moment, he seems to enjoy them, but he does not look at the consequences of his actions, which are harmful. He says, 'These sensual pleasures, which arise from contact, are the sources of pain and are fleeting, and they only give temporary happiness.' (Gita 5.22) Therefore, the seeker remains detached from the world. A person of passion should have a connection with the world, but he should not get attached to worldly pleasures. Parishishta Bhaav - The pleasure of worldly desires is like nectar at the beginning and like poison at the end. The ignorant person gives importance to the beginning, but the beginning is always temporary, and its desire remains forever, which is the cause of all sorrows. However, the wise person looks at the end and does not get attached to worldly pleasures. He says, 'The wise man does not enjoy them.' (Gita 5.22) Only a human being has the ability to see the consequences. Not seeing the consequences is like being an animal. In reality, the beginning (sanyog) is not the main thing, but the end (viyog) is the main thing. A person likes the beginning, but it does not last, because every union has a separation, which is a rule. The beginning is temporary, but the end is eternal. The desire for the temporary is the cause of the birth of sorrows. The separation from the world is eternal. However, due to the nature of passion, the union seems good in the present moment. If a person does not give importance to the pleasure of the beginning, then sorrow will never come. Seeing the beginning leads to pleasure, and seeing the end leads to yoga. The pleasure that seems to exist in the union of the world is mixed with sorrow. However, the pleasure that arises from the separation from the world is beyond sorrow and pleasure, and it is eternal bliss. Sambandh - Now, we will describe the pleasure of tamas. If a person is in a state of lethargy and indolence, and if his pleasure arises from it, then that pleasure is said to be tamas. (39)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The Saviour of the Seekers

To think, to act; to smoke cigarettes, to drink liquor, to take bhang, to sleep - all these are essential. To be addicted to vices like playing cards, watching movies, and to be involved in theft, robbery, lying, cheating, and adultery, and to indulge in such evil deeds - this is 'active negligence'. Due to negligence, the tamasic people waste their time and get pleasure in telling lies, cheating, and being dishonest. Just as laborers or employees get their full wages, but do not work properly, doctors do not treat their patients properly, so the patients keep coming and paying them. The milk sellers mix water with milk to increase their earnings. They do not stop mixing water even if they are paid more. In this way, the tamasic people get the worst hell due to such sinful negligence. When the tamasic negligence comes, it covers the discriminative knowledge and wisdom of the sattvic people. When the tamasic sleepiness and laziness come, it covers the illuminating knowledge of the sattvic people. When discriminative knowledge is covered, negligence occurs, and when illuminating knowledge is covered, sleepiness and laziness occur. The tamasic people get pleasure in sleepiness, laziness, and negligence - therefore, the tamasic pleasure is said to be born from these three. Special Note

-

There are two types of sleep - yukta-nidra and ati-nidra. (1) 'Yukta-nidra' - In sleep, a person gets relaxation. Relaxation brings a sense of well-being in the body, mind, intellect, and heart. It brings freshness, cleanliness, and clarity. Due to this freshness, a person gets the strength to perform spiritual practices and worldly activities with enthusiasm. Therefore, yukta-nidra is not a fault, but it is essential for everyone. The Lord has also said that yukta-nidra is essential - 'yuktasvapnavabodhasya yogah bhavati duhkhah' (Gita 6.17). Relaxation alone is essential for the seeker. If a seeker does not have worldly desires, he falls asleep quickly, and if he is very desirous, he does not fall asleep quickly. This shows that the worldly relationship does not allow a person to enjoy the pleasure of sleep. Sleep is essential because in sleep, the stable principle gives a person the strength to perform spiritual practices and worldly activities. Although sleep is tamasic, its unconsciousness is to be avoided, and its relaxation is to be accepted. However, every person cannot get relaxation without unconsciousness; therefore, their unconsciousness is also acceptable. But those who have risen to a higher level through spiritual practices can get relaxation without unconsciousness. (2) 'Ati-nidra' - Sleeping at the right time and waking up at the right time is yukta-nidra, and sleeping too much is ati-nidra. Ati-nidra and its effects, such as laziness, remain in the body. Due to excessive sleep, a person becomes lazy and lethargic. In the 14th chapter, 8th verse, the Lord has mentioned that the first is negligence, the second is laziness, and the third is sleep - 'pramad-alasya-nidrabhis tan nibadhnati bharta' (Gita 14.8). But here, the first is sleep, the second is laziness, and the third is negligence - 'nidra-alasya-pramadotham' (Gita 14.8). The reason for this reversal is that in the previous context, the Lord was talking about binding a person with these three, and in this context, the Lord is talking about the downfall of a person due to these three. Negligence is the most binding factor, so it is mentioned first. It makes a person indulge in sinful activities, leading to downfall. Laziness only stops a person from good behavior, so it is mentioned second. Sleep is essential, so it is not a binding factor, but ati-nidra is a binding factor, so it is mentioned third. The intention here is that sleep is not as harmful as it is thought to be. Sleep leads to laziness, and laziness leads to negligence. If a person sleeps too much, he will get a lower birth, like an animal. The seekers should not sleep to get relaxation. Their attitude should be that they used to worship the Lord while working, and now they will worship the Lord while sleeping. The 39th verse

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
Laziness and procrastination will lead to a person abandoning their duty and engaging in immoral behavior, and that pleasure becomes as intoxicating as nectar - one will have to go to hell by indulging in it. 'parinamena'mritopam' - 
'Yadagre chanubandhe cha sukham mohananmatmanah' - sleep, laziness, and procrastination, born from these, are the initial and final causes of pleasure, which is an intoxicating and deluding force. In this pleasure, there is no discernment in the beginning and no discernment in the end, i.e., this pleasure does not allow discernment to awaken. Just as animals, birds, insects, and other creatures do not think about the beginning and end of their actions due to the lack of discernment, similarly, a person who is indulging in this pleasure cannot think about the consequences of this pleasure, what benefits or harms it will bring, what good or evil it will bring, and what happiness or unhappiness it will bring. This pleasure is called 'tamas' - 'tattamasudahritam'. Special Note
(1) Nature and the individual are both eternal, and the understanding of their distinction is also eternal. This understanding resides in the individual, not in nature. When the individual disregards this understanding and, due to a lack of understanding, associates with nature, then a sense of attachment arises in the individual. When attachment is subtle, understanding is strong. When attachment increases, understanding is suppressed, but it does not disappear. However, if understanding is awakened properly, then attachment does not persist, i.e., attachment is absent, and at that time, the individual is considered liberated. Due to this attachment, a person becomes attached to the natural pleasures. While being attached to these pleasures, if a person tries to attain sattvic pleasure for some reason, then he finds it difficult to give up rajasic and tamasic pleasures - 'yattadagre vishamiva'. It is due to attachment that rajasic pleasure appears to be as intoxicating as nectar in the beginning. However, that pleasure turns out to be as poisonous as poison for living beings in the end, causing great suffering. Due to attachment to natural pleasures, there is no end to the chain of suffering. When the same attachment takes on the form of tamoguna, then a person's qualities become heavy. Then, a person wastes time in sleep and laziness and becomes detached from essential duties and gets involved in non-essential activities. However, tamas makes the person feel happy in these very things. Therefore, this tamas pleasure is an intoxicating and deluding force. (2) That which is constantly disappearing is, in reality, 'not' present. However, that which reveals 'not' and is its basis is, in reality, the 'existent' truth. This truth is called 'satchidananda'. Due to its constant existence, it is called 'sat', due to its knowledge-form, it is called 'chit', and due to its bliss-form, it is called 'ananda'. As this satchidananda is the essence of the Supreme, this living being is also satchidananda in nature. However, when the living being desires an unreal thing, i.e., a particular thing, then its natural bliss-satisfaction is covered. When this desire is removed, then that natural bliss-satisfaction becomes apparent. The eternal and constant truth, which is blissful, becomes apparent when the sattvic intellect becomes absorbed in it. When the intellect becomes pure and clean, then the experience of this natural bliss-satisfaction becomes apparent. When the connection with the intellect is broken, then the true bliss-satisfaction remains. The tamoguna quality, which is laziness, only prevents good behavior from arising and engages a person in ordinary, frivolous activities like play and recreation. However, when attachment joins laziness (which is the form of rajoguna), then desire is born. From desire, various kinds of vices and evils arise, which have a terrible outcome. 2. Attachment gives rise to various vices, but all these vices arise in nature, not in the individual. Due to the association with nature, the individual considers these vices to be his own, and thus, the individual becomes a sensualist. However, when the individual comes to understand that vices arise and pass away, are born and destroyed, but the individual's eternal nature remains unchanged, then the individual becomes a yogi.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Shloka 39
The state of 'sukha' (happiness) is called 'sattvic' when it is free from attachment. However, when separation occurs, its natural 'sattvic' state is lost. This happiness is an illusion, and it is called the 'sukha' of sleep. However, due to the impurity of the mind, it does not experience the natural happiness in the same way. The implication is that due to the influence of tamoguna (darkness) in the mind, there is no clarity, and therefore, the happiness is not experienced clearly. Hence, it is called 'tamas' (darkness) in the context of sleep. When a person desires to attain something, that thing settles in the mind, and the mind and intellect become associated with it. When the desired object is obtained, it leaves the mind, and the association with it is broken. The implication of this is that when a sattvic person is detached from the world, the suffering that arose from the absence of the object is replaced by happiness, and the natural, inherent happiness is experienced. On the other hand, a rajasic person experiences happiness due to the presence of the object, which is a temporary experience. The happiness of a tamasic person is due to the absence of the object, which is a result of forgetfulness and laziness. In reality, the inherent, natural happiness is experienced when the association with the object is broken, and the intellect is free from the influence of tamoguna. The three causes of happiness are attachment, attraction, and enjoyment. However, these causes are obstacles to spiritual growth, and they lead to forgetfulness of the object. The detachment from the object is essential in the state of sleep, as it leads to the breaking of the association with the object. The tamasic person is always attached to the object, and his intellect is clouded by ignorance. The implication of this is that the tamasic person is not aware of the beginning or the end, as his intellect is clouded by ignorance. The state of sleep is called 'tamas' (darkness) because the intellect is clouded, and there is no awareness of the world. If the intellect is not clouded, this state is called 'samadhi' (meditation), and it leads to rest and relaxation. However, the happiness experienced in this state is not the ultimate happiness, which is experienced when the intellect is free from the influence of tamoguna. The nature of the universe is constantly changing, but the ultimate reality is unchanging, peaceful, and stable. In the state of sleep, the intellect becomes one with this ultimate reality, but the attachment to worldly objects remains, and the person is drawn to them again after waking up. The ultimate reality is not experienced due to the attachment to worldly objects, and the person is not able to derive any benefit from it. The state of sleep only provides temporary relief from fatigue, but it does not lead to the ultimate happiness. If the person renounces attachment to worldly objects and desires, the state of sleep and wakefulness will be the same, and the ultimate reality will be experienced in its true form. Parishishta Bhaav - The tamasic person is always attached to the world, and his intellect is clouded by ignorance. This ignorance is the cause of bondage, and it prevents the intellect from becoming aware of the ultimate reality.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

One should not have attachment to knowledge; because one should renounce pleasure and tamas. Renunciation of these leads to attachment to knowledge. Therefore, renunciation of these is the only means of spiritual practice. By renunciation, one attains detachment from the material world and rises to the level of sattva guna. This is the reason why the discussion of gunas has been brought up here. Sattva is very essential. Because in it, the light of discrimination is awakened, which helps in liberation from the material world. In reality, it is the means of becoming asanga (free from attachment). The seeker should focus on sattvic knowledge, actions, doer, intellect, and happiness, and shape his life accordingly, and with caution, renounce rajasic tendencies. In the tenth chapter, the Lord had explained that from His perspective, all things are born from Himself, 'na tadasti vina yatsyam maya bhuta characharam' (10.39). Here, the Lord explains that all things are born from the gunas of nature, as seen from the perspective of discrimination. Because in the perspective of discrimination, both sat and asat exist, but from the perspective of a devotee, only the Lord exists - 'sad asatchaham arjuna' (9.19). In the path of discrimination, renunciation of asat and gunas is the main thing, but in the path of devotion, the main thing is the relationship with the Lord. The idea that any object in the world is devoid of the three gunas is a view of the ignorant, but not of the wise. The wise person's perspective is focused on the essence of the self, which is naturally nirguna (gunas-less) (Gita - 13th chapter, 30th verse). In the discussion of detachment, the Lord had explained that renunciation of prescribed duties is not proper. Renunciation of prescribed duties in a foolish manner becomes tamas, and renunciation of prescribed duties due to fear of physical pain becomes rajasic, and renunciation of attachment to fruits and attachment to prescribed duties becomes sattvic (this is explained in the 7th, 8th, and 9th verses of this chapter). In the Sankhya yoga, the five causes of the fulfillment of all actions are explained, and in it, the description of sattvic action is given, and it is mentioned that the action should be done by a person who is free from ego, attachment, and desire for fruits (23rd verse of this chapter). The Lord now begins a new discussion to explain which actions are prescribed duties for which varna and how they should be performed, and also to explain the path of devotion. O Parantapa! The actions of brahmins, kshatriyas, and vaishyas, and of shudras, are divided according to their inherent nature and gunas. Translation of the shloka: 
'brahmanakshatriyavisham shudranam parantap | 
karmani pravibhaktani svaabhavaprabhavair gunaih || 41 ||'

Translation of the commentary:
'brahmanakshatriyavisham shudranam parantap' - whatever actions are done, are divided according to the three gunas that have arisen from their inherent nature. Here, the term 'brahmanakshatriyavisham shudranam' refers to the four varnas - brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, and shudra. The term 'parantap' is an address to Arjuna. The term 'karmani pravibhaktani' means that the actions are divided. The term 'svaabhavaprabhavair gunaih' means that the division is according to the gunas that have arisen from their inherent nature. The commentary explains that the four varnas - brahmin, kshatriya, and vaishya - have a certain samskara (impression) that is formed due to their past actions, and this samskara determines their inherent nature. The term 'shudra' refers to those who do not have this samskara and are not considered to be of the three varnas. The commentary explains that the actions of brahmins, kshatriyas, and vaishyas are divided according to their inherent nature, and the actions of shudras are also divided according to their inherent nature. The division of actions is according to the gunas that have arisen from their inherent nature.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
If the qualities and virtues present in a human being are of a certain kind, then that kind of action (karma) manifests. All the means and resources are just that. There are two types of actions (karma) - (1) actions that determine birth in high or low castes, and (2) actions that bring about happiness or suffering. The actions that result in birth in high or low castes are called 'janma-arabhak karma', and the actions that bring about happiness or suffering are called 'bhoga-dāyak karma'. Bhoga-dāyak karma creates favorable or unfavorable circumstances, which are referred to as anishṭ, iṣṭ, and miśra in the Gita (18th chapter, 12th verse). Upon closer examination, it can be seen that only bhoga-dāyak karma is responsible for happiness or suffering. That is, happiness or suffering also arises from janma-arabhak karma. For example, a person born in a noble family is respected, honored, and receives good treatment, while a person born in a lowly family is disrespected, humiliated, and receives bad treatment. Similarly, favorable circumstances bring respect and honor, while unfavorable circumstances bring disrespect and humiliation. The point is that happiness or suffering arises from both janma-arabhak and bhoga-dāyak karma. However, the happiness or suffering that arises from janma-arabhak karma is secondary, as it is not always present. On the other hand, the happiness or suffering that arises from bhoga-dāyak karma is primary, as it is always present. The use or misuse of bhoga-dāyak karma is entirely up to the individual. That is, a person can either use favorable circumstances for the benefit of others or for their own happiness, or they can use unfavorable circumstances to renounce their desires for happiness. Serving others and renouncing one's desire for happiness are both means. (1)
According to the scriptures, a person's good deeds lead to rebirth in heaven, while bad deeds lead to rebirth in hell, and a balance of good and bad deeds leads to rebirth as a human being. However, no one can be entirely good or entirely bad. That is, no one can be entirely virtuous or entirely wicked. Even in the case of a person who is reborn as a human being due to a balance of good and bad deeds, there is a balance of virtues and vices. That is, some people have more virtues, while others have more vices. Similarly, there is a division of virtues and vices in the case of the three gunas (satva, rajas, and tamas). People with a predominance of satva guna are reborn in the upper worlds, those with a predominance of rajas guna are reborn as humans, and those with a predominance of tamas guna are reborn in the lower worlds. Even within these three categories, there are many sub-divisions based on the balance of virtues and vices. In the case of brahmins, who are born with a predominance of satva guna, there are sub-divisions based on birth and circumstances. That is, some brahmins are considered higher or lower based on their birth, and the consequences of their actions are also varied. Therefore, it is necessary to consider the sub-divisions of the three gunas. Similarly, kshatriyas, vaishyas, and shudras are also divided into sub-categories based on birth and circumstances. In this way, the three gunas are present in all human beings, and there is a balance of virtues and vices in each person.

[ Chapter 18
The way to use one's abilities - This means that the natural tendencies and the absence of any virtues in them are to be experienced (well understood) - this is called 'Vijnan' (Knowledge). 'Aastikyam' - The Supreme Being, the Vedas, and other scriptures, and the afterlife, etc. are revered in the heart, faith is established, and there is no doubt about their truth, and one's behavior is in accordance with them, this is called 'Aastikyam' (Faith). -
'Brhamkarman Svabhavajam' - These are the natural tendencies of the Brahmins, such as self-control, etc. (These are the inherent qualities of the Brahmins), i.e., the Brahmins do not have to exert themselves to maintain these qualities. Or, even if there is a deficiency in any of these qualities, it is easy for them to make up for it. The creation of the four varnas is based on the balance of qualities, so the qualities manifest naturally in each varna according to their nature, and the other qualities become secondary. For example, in the Brahmins, the predominance of the quality of Sattva (purity) makes self-control, etc. (the qualities of the Brahmins) natural, and the qualities related to livelihood become secondary, and in the other varnas, the predominance of the qualities of Rajas (passion) and Tamas (ignorance) makes the qualities related to livelihood natural. In this way, in the Gita, the natural tendencies of the Brahmins are described as self-control, etc. (without mentioning the qualities related to livelihood). -
Parishishta Bhaav - If the varna-parampara (the tradition of the varnas) is correct, then these qualities are natural in the Brahmins. However, due to varna-sankara (mixing of varnas), these qualities do not become natural, and there is a deficiency in them. In the previous shloka, 'Svabhavaprabhavair gunaih' was said, so here the natural tendencies are described. The formation of one's nature is mainly in the previous birth, and then in the subsequent births, the company (sang) is the main factor. Due to sang, self-study, practice, etc., one's nature changes. . Samabandh - Now, the natural tendencies of the Kshatriyas are described. Shouryam Tejo Dhritir Dakshyam

'Tejo' - The power to inspire others, the ability to make a positive impact on the world, the ability to overcome obstacles and challenges, the ability to achieve great things, the ability to make a difference in the world, this is called 'Tejo' (Energy). ' Dhritih ' - The ability to remain calm and composed in the face of adversity, the ability to stand up for one's principles, the ability to perform one's duties without hesitation or fear, the ability to remain patient and composed even in the face of great challenges, this is called 'Dhritih' (Patience). 'Dakshyam' - The ability to govern the people, the ability to lead and guide others, the ability to make wise decisions, the ability to act with compassion and empathy, the ability to perform one's duties with skill and expertise, this is called 'Dakshyam' (The ability to govern the people). 'Apalayanam' - The ability to remain calm and composed in the face of danger, the ability to stand up for one's principles, the ability to perform one's duties without hesitation or fear, the ability to remain patient and composed even in the face of great challenges, this is called 'Apalayanam' (Not running away). 'Kshatram' - The ability to perform one's duties with skill and expertise, the ability to make wise decisions, the ability to act with compassion and empathy, the ability to govern the people, the ability to lead and guide others, this is called 'Kshatram' (War). 'Danam' - The ability to give charity, the ability to help others, the ability to make a positive impact on the world, the ability to overcome obstacles and challenges, the ability to achieve great things, this is called 'Danam' (Giving charity). ' Ishwarabhaavah' - The desire to rule, the ability to lead and guide others, the ability to make wise decisions, the ability to act with compassion and empathy, the ability to perform one's duties with skill and expertise, this is called 'Ishwarabhaavah' (The desire to rule). These are the natural tendencies of the Kshatriyas.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The term 'dāna' (charity) has originated in the nature of the kshatriyas (warriors). The special quality or expertise of the kshatriyas is called 'dākṣya' (cunning or skill). 'Yudhācāpyapalāyanam' - never show one's back in war, never accept defeat in one's mind, and never flee from the battlefield - this is what is called 'apalāyan' (fleeing) in war. -

'Īśvarabhāvaśca' - it is inherent in the nature of the kshatriyas to rule and govern. When they see people acting against the norms of morality, justice, and dignity, they naturally think, "Why are these people behaving in this manner?" and they wish to guide them according to the norms of morality and justice. They have a desire to govern people according to their respective dharma (duties). This desire to rule is not accompanied by pride or arrogance, as kshatriyas are known for their humility, simplicity, and other noble qualities. 'Dānam' - when kshatriyas give charity, they do not stint or hold back; they give generously and liberally. In contrast, the vaisyas (merchants) of today have a tendency to give charity, but they do so with a sense of limitation, thinking, "If we give this much, it will suffice; why give more?" This is due to their attachment to wealth. This attachment to wealth creates obstacles in the path of dharma (righteous living), leading to a decrease in the quality of charity. As a result, the sāttvika dāna (charity motivated by purity of heart) becomes difficult to perform (Gita, chapter 17, verse 20). However, kshatriyas are known for their daanveerata (generosity). Parishishta Bhaav - Kshatriyas (Rajputs) are known for their bravery and valor. However, due to jealousy, a king who came to power tried to suppress the enthusiasm of his Rajput subjects, preventing them from rising to power and potentially overthrowing him. As a result of this jealousy and the suppression of their enthusiasm, the Rajputs became weak, and the non-dharmic people were able to conquer India. 'Kṣātram karma svabhāvajam' - one who protects the people from suffering is called a kshatriya. The kshatriya's natural duty is referred to as kṣātrakarma. Sambandh - Now, the natural duties of the vaisyas and shudras are being described. Agriculture, animal husbandry, trade, and service - these are the natural duties of the vaisyas and shudras. Kṛṣigaurakṣyavaṇijyam vaiṣyakarma svabhāvajam |
Paricaryātmakaṃ karma śūdrasyāpi svabhāvajam || 44 ||

[ Chapter 18
The duties of a king. The king, Manu, died after being bitten by a snake while protecting cows. The Manusmriti (1.90) says that the protection of cows is a duty. Here, the Lord (as mentioned in the previous verses) seems to be saying that if you cannot protect all animals, at least protect cows and their protection is a must. If you cannot increase the number of cows, it does not matter, but their protection is a must, so that our wealth (gods) does not decrease. Therefore, the Vaisya community should dedicate their body, mind, and wealth to the protection of cows, and should not save their strength for this purpose. Gauraksha is a special duty. For humans, cows are to be protected in all respects. Cows give us four types of purusharthas - artha, dharma, kama, and moksha. In today's materialistic era, cows are extremely useful. By cow protection, we get milk, ghee, cow dung, and other things, which increase our wealth. Our country is an agricultural country. Therefore, the importance of cows in agriculture is as much as that of bulls. Cows can also be used for agriculture, but bulls can do more work in the fields. Bulls are stronger than cows, but they can withstand the heat. Cows, on the other hand, cannot withstand the heat and their tongue comes out when they walk in the sun. This is because cows do not have sattvic power, while bulls have sattvic power. Cows are less than bulls in this respect. Similarly, camels are also used for agriculture, but they are less than cows and very expensive. No one can afford to buy a camel. Nowadays, good bulls are being killed, so bulls are also becoming expensive. However, they are not as expensive as camels. If cows are kept in homes, then bulls are born in homes and do not need to be bought. Foreign cows are not suitable for work in the fields, as their legs are not strong enough to bear the load. A man was bitten by a snake and died. People took him to the bank of the Ganges, where a sage lived. The sage asked what had happened to the man. People replied that he had died after being bitten by a snake. The sage said that he had not died, bring some cow dung from the cow. Cow dung was brought. The sage applied cow dung to the man's entire body, except his nose. After half an hour, another layer of cow dung was applied. The man's breathing started and he regained consciousness. Cow urine is also very useful in removing heart diseases. Drinking two tola of cow urine every day can cure stomach diseases. A saint had a complaint of asthma, which was cured by drinking cow urine. Nowadays, many medicines are being made from cow dung and cow urine. Cow dung is also producing gas. The food produced from cow dung and cow urine is also pure. The soil becomes fertile due to the presence of cow dung and cow urine, just like the soil becomes fertile due to the presence of foreign chemical fertilizers. A farmer told that the yield of grapes increased manifold after applying cow dung, whereas the yield did not increase after applying foreign fertilizers. Foreign fertilizers can make the soil infertile in a few years, whereas cow dung and cow urine keep the soil fertile. In foreign countries, many fields have become infertile due to the use of chemical fertilizers, so people are importing cow dung from India and sending it to foreign countries by ships. Our cows are gentle and sattvic. Therefore, their milk is also sattvic, which makes the mind sharp and the temperament calm. The milk of foreign cows is more, but it is not sattvic. Drinking it makes a person's temperament cruel. The milk of buffaloes is also more, but it is not sattvic. Drinking it does not give sattvic power. The milk of horses is given to horses, which makes them strong. Once, some soldiers gave buffalo milk to some horses, which made them very strong. However, when the river was flowing rapidly, the horses could not cross it. Cows are pure. The air that touches their body is also pure. Cow dung and cow urine are also pure. Houses covered with cow dung do not get diseases like plague and cholera. This is not the only benefit, but even in times of war, houses covered with cow dung do not get damaged by bombs, whereas houses made of cement and other materials get damaged. Cow dung has a special power to absorb poison. A person in Kashmir was crossing a river on a horse, but the horse got into the water. The horse's tongue came out, and it died.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The cow is a life-giver for the devotees. In Gaya, even the milk of a donkey is produced, but it does not turn into curd or butter. Its milk is tamasic and leads to misery. In the memories of the people, the cow, dog, donkey, and others are considered impure. Sitting in the water, the same nature is found in horses as well. Therefore, it will be difficult to get food, water, and clothes for the body. If cows and their milk, ghee, dung, etc. do not exist, the people will suffer greatly. Without cows, the country will become weak and dependent. In the present time, the main reason for natural disasters like drought, floods, and earthquakes is the killing of cows. Therefore, it is our prime duty to protect cows with all our might and prevent them from being slaughtered in slaughterhouses. Cows have a special importance in all religious activities. In the sixteen sacraments, such as Jatakarma, Chudakarma, and Upanayana, the cow, its milk, ghee, and dung have a special connection. The yajna is performed with the ghee of the cow. The cow dung is used to purify the place. In the Shradh ceremony, the khichdi made from the milk of the cow is offered. The cow is sacrificed to save one from the hells. In the religious activities, the "Panchagavya" is used, which is made from the milk, curd, ghee, dung, and urine of the cow. In the yajnas performed for the fulfillment of desires, the ghee of the cow is used. In the Raghuvansha, the cow had a prominent place. In the nutritious and virility-enhancing substances, the milk and ghee of the cow have a prominent place. By serving the cow without any expectation, one gets liberation. By serving the cow, the inner self becomes pure. Lord Shri Krishna also performed the cowherd's play without wearing shoes, so his name is "Gopal". In the ancient times, the sages used to keep cows in the forest and their intellect became sharp and extraordinary due to the milk and ghee of the cow, and they used to compose big scriptures. Today, even those who understand those scriptures properly are rare. The sages used to live long due to the milk and ghee of the cow. Therefore, the ghee of the cow is also called "Ayus". Even the big kings used to go to their ashrams and take their advice to rule the kingdom. The stories of those who sacrificed their lives for the protection of cows are filled in the history and Puranas. It is a sad fact that in our country, thousands of cows are being slaughtered every day due to the greed for money. If this continues, one day the cows will be extinct. When the cows will be extinct, what will be the situation? What kind of calamities will come? It cannot be imagined. When the cows will be extinct, there will be no cow dung, and without cow dung, the soil will not be fertile. Without fertile soil, how will the agriculture be done? Without agriculture, how will the food and clothes be obtained? The people should take care of the cows and keep them in their homes. They should only consume the milk and ghee of the cows and not of the buffaloes. They should use the cow dung and gas in their homes. The cow shelters should be built for the protection of cows, not for the milk. The government should protect the cow shelters and the land used for cow grazing. The government's policy of killing cows should be opposed, and they should be requested to ban cow slaughter throughout the country immediately for the protection of the country. The service of the four varnas, the preparation of the service material, and the absence of any obstacle or hindrance in the work of the four varnas, so that everyone is happy and comfortable, is the natural duty of the Shudra. Here, a doubt arises that the Lord has said that the birth of the four varnas is due to the three gunas - satva, rajas, and tamas. In it, the birth of the Shudra is due to the predominance of tamas guna, and in the Gita, where the description of tamas guna is given, seven vices are mentioned - ignorance, negligence, laziness, sleep, darkness, inactivity, and attachment (Gita, 14th chapter, 8th, 13th, and 17th shlokas). Therefore, how can service be done from such a Shudra who is full of these vices? Because he will be lazy, negligent, etc., how will he be able to serve? Service is a very high-class work. The Lord has made such a provision for the Shudra, how? If we consider the gunas, then it is said in the Gita that the satva guna people go to the higher worlds, the rajas guna people go to the middle world after death, and the tamas guna people go to the lower world (Gita, 14th chapter, 18th shloka). In this also, it is said that the people of the tamas guna are born in the lower world. Therefore, how can service be done from such a Shudra who is born in the lower world?

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
In reality, if one observes, when the quality of Rajas increases, the one who dies, is reborn in a life form that is primarily driven by actions - 'Rajas in Pralaya, going to the company of actions, is born' (Gita 14.15). This implies that humans are primarily driven by Rajas. In those driven by Rajas, there are three qualities - Sattvic, Rajasic, and Tamasic - and these three qualities are responsible for the creation of the four varnas. Therefore, performing actions is the primary duty of all, and this is why humans are called 'Karmanyon' and in the Gita, the actions of the four varnas are referred to as 'Svabhavaj Karma', 'Svabhavaniyata Karma', etc. Therefore, the service of a Shudra, i.e., serving others, is 'Svabhavaj Karma', in which there is no effort required. Since humans are primarily driven by actions, even in Brahmans, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas, there is a special balance of discernment and purity, but in Shudras, due to the predominance of attachment, discernment is greatly suppressed. From this perspective, in the service of a Shudra, there is no predominance of discernment, but rather the predominance of obedience - 'Agya sam na susahib seva' (Mansa 2.301.2). Therefore, serving others according to the orders of the four varnas, and gathering happiness and convenience, is a natural duty for a Shudra. The actions of Shudras are service-oriented, i.e., in the form of service. All their physical, social, civic, and village-related actions are performed properly, from which all four varnas derive happiness, convenience, adaptability, and fulfillment of their needs. The meaning of natural actions
The conscious living soul and the inert nature have different natures. The conscious soul is naturally unchanging and inert nature is naturally changing. Therefore, their natures being different, their relationship is not natural; but the conscious soul has considered its relationship with the inert nature as natural, i.e., it has considered it as a relationship, and this is called the association of qualities, which is the cause of the soul's birth in good or bad wombs - 'The cause of the association of qualities is the soul's birth in good or bad wombs' (Gita 13.21). Due to this association of qualities, the soul's birth in the varnas is determined by the balance of qualities. The actions of the varnas are natural, spontaneous, and effortless, as per their nature and the nature of their actions; for example, the actions of Brahmans are shama, dama, etc., those of Kshatriyas are shourya, teja, etc., those of Vaishyas are agriculture, cattle-rearing, etc., and those of Shudras are service. The meaning is that the four varnas do not require effort in performing these actions, as their nature and the nature of their actions are in accordance with the qualities. Therefore, when humans perform these actions for their own benefit, i.e., for their own interests, desires, and pleasures, they become bound to these actions. When they perform these actions without attachment and ego, for the benefit of the world, it becomes 'Karmayoga', and they perform these actions in the name of the Supreme, or they perform actions related to the Supreme, such as japa, dhyana, satsang, etc., it becomes 'Bhaktiyoga'. When the association of qualities is completely severed, there remains only one Supreme Reality, in which the self-realization of the independence, unity, and changelessness of the great souls remains. Even then, their bodies, minds, intellects, and senses, according to their respective varnas and ashrams, perform actions as per the scriptures, which are natural and spontaneous, and are a model for the world. Being drawn to the Lord, love increases moment by moment, which is a form of infinite bliss. Is caste determined by birth or by actions? As many bodies as are obtained in the various castes, they are obtained according to the qualities and actions. Therefore, the caste of a human is determined by birth. Therefore, from the perspective of the gross body, actions such as marriage, food, etc. should be performed according to birth, i.e., according to one's caste. Another thing is that for a being whose purpose is worldly enjoyment, wealth, fame, comfort, pleasure, etc., it is necessary to perform duties according to one's caste and to follow the norms of one's caste. If it does not follow the norms of its caste, it becomes a sinner.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
The glory of the Lord has been sung in the ancient Puranas and in the epic Mahabharata, Ramayana, and other historical texts. A devotee of the Lord, regardless of his lowly birth, is superior to a learned but faithless Brahmin. *

[ Chapter 18 ]

The food, water, medicine, etc., offered to the devotees of the Lord, who are Brahmins, are like a nourishing diet for their entire body, and all their limbs become strong. Similarly, the collection of goods, their transportation, and the distribution of goods to places where they are needed, so that the people do not lack anything, is the duty of the Vaisyas. The collection of food and water for the body is for the benefit of the entire body, and along with it, the stomach also becomes strong; because a man does not fill his stomach only for his stomach. Similarly, the Vaisyas should collect goods only for the benefit of others, not for themselves. They give alms to Brahmins, pay taxes to Kshatriyas, maintain themselves, and give wages to Shudras. In this way, they serve everyone. If the Vaisyas do not collect goods, they will not be able to engage in agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. It has been said that the Brahmin is the face of the Lord, the Kshatriya is his hand, the Vaisya is his thigh, and the Shudra is his foot. The Brahmin is considered the face because he has the collection of knowledge, so he should teach the four varnas, give good education, and preach. In this sense, the Brahmin is considered superior. The Kshatriya is considered the hand because he protects the four varnas from their enemies. Protection is the main work of the hands, just as the hands protect the body from boils, wounds, etc., and also protect the body from external injuries, and also give injuries to others in self-defense, and also support the body when it falls. Therefore, the Kshatriya is considered the hand. When there is chaos, it becomes the duty of all four varnas to protect their people, wealth, etc. The Shudra is considered the foot because, just as the feet support the entire body and serve it, similarly, the Shudra serves everyone through his service work. It is worth noting that the Gita describes the natural duties of the four varnas, which are the duties of the Vaisya as the middle part because, just as the stomach collects food and water for the benefit of the entire body, and along with it, the stomach also becomes strong, similarly, the Vaisya collects goods only for the benefit of others, not for himself. (1) "Ah! That Chandal is superior, whose tongue-tip bears your name. Those who pronounce your name are superior, even if they have performed all the austerities, sacrifices, and studies." (Srimad Bhagavat 3.33.7)

(2) "I consider the Brahmin, who has twelve good qualities, to be inferior to the Chandal, who has dedicated his mind, speech, actions, wealth, and life to the Lord." (Srimad Bhagavat 7.9.10)

(3) "The Chandal, who is devoted to the Lord, is superior to the Muni; and the Brahmin, who is devoid of devotion to the Lord, is inferior to the Chandal." (Padma Purana)

(4) "The Brahmin, who is not devoted to the Lord, is inferior to the Chandal, who is devoted to the Lord; the Brahmin goes to hell, while the Chandal is liberated." (Brahma Vaivarta, Brahma 11.39)

(5) "The devotee of the Lord, who is a Shudra, is not a Shudra, but a superior Brahmin; and in all the varnas, the Shudra is he who is devoted to the Lord." (Mahabharata)

[Chapter 16]
* The Saviour of Seekers *

They are self-sufficient, meaning they do not require much effort to perform their duties. The writers have their own self-interest and pride. For the four varnas, there are other duties as well, which can be seen in the Smritis and followed accordingly (Gita - 16th Chapter, 24th Verse). In the present time, even if there is chaos in all four varnas, if we look at each varna separately, we will find that the brahmins possess more qualities like self-control, humility, etc. than the kshatriyas, vaishyas, and shudras. The kshatriyas possess more qualities like bravery, courage, etc. than the brahmins, vaishyas, and shudras. The vaishyas possess more qualities like trade, earning wealth, and managing wealth (not letting wealth show from the outside) than the brahmins, kshatriyas, and shudras. The shudras possess more qualities like service-oriented nature than the brahmins, kshatriyas, and vaishyas. The implication is that even if all four varnas are lawless and unruly, their inherent qualities are visible in their respective communities, indicating that these qualities are not individual but community-based. Those who do not know the deep secrets of the scriptures say that brahmins have pens in their hands, so they wrote that "brahmins are the most superior" and made them supreme. Those who had kingdoms said to the brahmins, "What are we? Are we nothing?" The brahmins replied, "No, no, you are also there, you are in the second position." The vaishyas said to the brahmins, "What will happen to our livelihood if you are supreme?" The brahmins replied, "Yes, yes, you are in the third position." Those who had neither kingdoms nor wealth rose to a higher position, and the brahmins said, "Your fate has not written you as kings or wealthy people. You should serve the brahmins, kshatriyas, and vaishyas, so you are in the fourth position." In this way, they deceived everyone by saying that they are superior due to their knowledge, kingdoms, and wealth. The solution to this is that brahmins have not written anywhere that they are supreme, so they should live comfortably, enjoy wealth and material possessions, etc. On the contrary, brahmins have written that they should renounce, bear hardships, and practice tapas. Even while living in a household, they should not accumulate wealth, and the accumulation of food should be minimal, like a pot filled with a little grain (kumbhidaan). They should not be attached to worldly pleasures and should accept alms only after performing their duties, such as yajna, homa, japa, and patha. If they accept alms, they should perform the atonement (prayaashchitta) for it. If a brahmin is invited to a shraaddha, he should give it on the first day, so that he can invite the yajamana's ancestors to his own self and live a life of brahmacharya and self-control during the night. On the second day, he should perform the pinddaan and tarpan of the yajamana's ancestors according to the proper rituals. After that, he should eat there. He should accept the invitation of only one yajamana and eat food at only one house. After eating the shraaddha food, he should purify himself by reciting the Gayatri mantra, etc. Accepting alms and eating shraaddha food is not a high status for a brahmin. The high status of a brahmin is renunciation. Brahmins accept shraaddha food and alms only out of a sense of compassion for the yajamana's ancestors, not out of self-interest; therefore, this is also a form of renunciation. The brahmins have described five types of livelihoods - rit, amrit, mrit, pramrit, and satyanrit - for their own livelihood*-

(1) Rit-vritti is considered the highest type of livelihood. It is also known as shiloshcha or kapota-vritti. Farmers go to the field, cut the grain, and take it away. The grain that falls on the ground is considered the property of the brahmins; therefore, they should collect it and use it for their own sustenance, thus making the fourth varna (shudra) subservient - this is 'shiloshcha-vritti' or the livelihood of collecting grain from the field. Ritamritabhyam jivet tu mritena pramritena va | Satyanritabhyam api va na shwavrittya kadacana || (Manusmriti 4.4)
"Live by rit, amrit, mrit, or pramrit, but never by shwavritti (the livelihood of service)."
