*
Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
There, the grains that have fallen on the earth are the property of the gods; | The welfare of the Shudra is achieved by serving alone. -
Therefore, choosing them and living by them is 'the profession of a bird' (i.e., one that is easy and effortless). (2) Without asking and without being asked, a patron comes and gives, so taking only the means of living is 'the immortal profession' (i.e., one that is free from attachment). This is also called 'unasked profession'. (3) Going to the village in the morning to beg and telling people the date, day, and auspicious moment, and then living by whatever is obtained by begging, is 'the dead profession'. The Lord has further said that by performing their respective varna-dharma (duties), the Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra attain the highest perfection— 'The human being attains perfection by performing his own duties' (18.46). In reality, welfare is not achieved by performing varna-dharma, but by worshiping without attachment. The Shudra's natural duty is service, which is a form of worship, so his worship is achieved by serving. (4) Therefore, living by trade is 'the profession of a hypocrite' (i.e., one that is based on deceit). (5) If the four professions mentioned above do not provide a means of living, then one should cultivate the land, but even that should be done with great difficulty and adherence to rituals, just as one should not plow the field with a single ox, or plow during the heat of the day, etc. This is 'the profession of a dead man'. If one lives by any of the above professions, one should perform the five great sacrifices, serve guests, and eat the leftovers of the yajna *. When considering the Srimad Bhagavad Gita, it is seen that the nine natural duties prescribed for the Brahmin are not meant to create a means of living. The seven natural duties prescribed for the Kshatriya include fighting and ruling, which are two duties that create a means of living. The three natural duties prescribed for the Vaishya include agriculture, cow protection, and trade, which are all means of creating a living. The Shudra's only duty is service, which is a means of living in itself. The Shudra has been given a lot of freedom in matters of food, living, etc. The Lord has said in the verse 'A person attains perfection by performing his own duties' (18.45) that the welfare of the Brahmin is achieved by performing the nine duties of self-control, etc., the welfare of the Kshatriya is achieved by performing the seven duties of bravery, etc., the welfare of the Vaishya is achieved by performing the three duties of agriculture, etc., and the welfare of the Shudra is achieved by performing the duty of service. However, the welfare of the Shudra will be achieved much faster and more easily than that of the Brahmin, etc. It is worth considering that the sages have given more importance to the salvation of the lower varnas, because the lower varnas are more deserving of salvation and have less burden. The sages have given more importance to the salvation of the Shudra and have given him more freedom in matters of livelihood. In reality, the higher the varna, the more difficult the rituals and rules prescribed by the scriptures. The difficulty of following these rules and rituals is more apparent. However, the lower the varna, the easier it is to achieve welfare. In this context, there is a story in the Vishnu Purana—once, many sages gathered at the house of the great sage Vedavyasa to decide who was the most superior. Vedavyasa respectfully seated all the sages and then went to bathe in the Ganges. While bathing, he said—'You, Kaliyuga, are blessed! You, women, are blessed! You, Shudra, are blessed! When Vedavyasa returned from bathing and came to the sages, they said—'Maharaj, how did you bless Kaliyuga, women, and the Shudra?' Then Vedavyasa said that in Kaliyuga, the Shudra and women can achieve welfare easily and quickly by following their dharma. There is another point to consider—what the scriptures have prohibited for the Brahmin and Kshatriya is not serving, but the profession of serving, i.e., the profession of a servant. They can serve the lowest of the low, just like a mother and father. The service of the lowly is their greatness. Therefore, it is the profession of serving that has been condemned, not the service itself. The condemnation is of serving for one's own selfish interests, not of serving selflessly.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
-
The service of a devotee should be done with the same attitude as worship, devotion to God, and devotion to the guru. It should be done with the same reverence and respect as worship, by offering flowers, incense, and garlands, and by performing the aarti. When done in this way, the service becomes a form of worship. From this, the devotee's heart becomes filled with joy, their mind becomes calm, and their body becomes filled with bliss. Their devotion to the devotee becomes evident, and they may even become a little lax in their service. However, as their devotion grows, their inner purity, love for God, and vision of God become established. In this context, the phrase "swa-swa karma" means that whatever work is done with a sense of duty and devotion becomes a form of service. Even if one does any work, whether it is one or many, with a sense of duty and devotion, it becomes a form of service. The word "karma" in this context means that the person's intention is to attain the ultimate goal of self-realization. The ultimate goal of self-realization is the only purpose of their work. Just as the Ganges River flows from the Himalayas to the Ganges Delta, and all the rivers, streams, and lakes merge into it, so too do all the person's actions merge into the ultimate goal of self-realization. However, if one is attached to their actions, they will want to achieve multiple results from one action, or multiple results from multiple actions. In this case, their intention is not to attain the ultimate goal of self-realization, and therefore their sense of duty and devotion is not one-pointed. (Gita - 2.41)

"Swakarma-niratah sidhim yatha vindati tachchrunu" - Listen to this and understand it well: a person who is devoted to their work, with a sense of duty and devotion, attains self-realization in the same way as one attains it. This is the message of the Gita. A special point to note is that the servant should be provided with the necessary comforts and facilities, and should be made to feel comfortable and at ease in their daily work. This is a service that even a paid servant can do, and does do. However, in the case of a paid servant, there is a sense of duty and a sense of time, i.e., the servant has to complete a certain amount of work within a certain time. Therefore, the work of a paid servant is not considered a form of service. However, if the servant is served with devotion and respect, then the work becomes a form of service. This devotion and respect can arise from various sources, such as birth, education, social status, or spiritual qualifications. Wherever there is a sense of devotion and respect, the servant feels comfortable and at ease, and their heart is filled with joy. The servant's service is not just a means of earning a living, but a way of attaining self-realization. In the case of worship, the devotee's body becomes filled with bliss, and their inner self becomes filled with a sense of joy and peace. Their devotion to the deity is evident, and their heart is filled with love and respect for the deity. In the case of service, the servant's body becomes filled with bliss, and their inner self becomes filled with a sense of joy and peace. Their devotion to the master is evident, and their heart is filled with love and respect for the master. Just as the jnani's attitude is "I do not do anything," so too is the bhakta's attitude "I do not do anything." Even though the bhakta performs many actions, their heart remains filled with devotion to God. Their ego disappears, and their heart becomes filled with love and respect for God.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Parishishta Bhaav - One should consider all the actions that have been accepted as one's own, under the category of 'Swa Swa Karma' (one's own actions). For instance, if a person considers himself a lawyer, servant, teacher, or doctor, then performing his duties with love, respect, and selflessness is also his 'Swa Karma'. When a person performs actions with attachment, driven by self-interest, bias, or desires, it is considered 'Asakti' (attachment). On the other hand, when he performs actions with love, detachment, and for the benefit of others, it is considered 'Abhirati' (devotion). The Lord has prohibited 'Asakti' in actions - 'Na Karmanusajjate' (Gita 6.4). A person should not consider himself superior or inferior based on his caste, but rather, like the parts of a clock, he should perform his duties according to his role and not criticize or condemn others. He should not have an inflated sense of self-importance, and then only will he be in a state of 'Abhirati'. In reality, it is not the 'Karma' (action) that is paramount, but rather the 'Bhaav' (attitude). If the attitude of the doer is pure, then the action will be beneficial, regardless of the caste of the doer. In actions, there is a predominance of caste, and in attitude, there is a predominance of divine or asuric (demonic) qualities. Therefore, divine or asuric qualities are not inherent in any particular caste, but can be present in all. Divine qualities lead to liberation, while asuric qualities lead to bondage. Hence, even if a Brahmin has an inflated sense of self-importance, he will become asuric and meet with destruction. Wherefrom the activities of all beings proceed, by which all this is pervaded, that Supreme Being, by performing one's own natural duties, is to be worshipped by men. 46. Explanation - The Supreme Being, from whom the activities of all beings proceed, by which all this is pervaded, that Supreme Being, who is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the universe, and who is present in all beings, should be worshipped by men through their natural duties. The natural duties of a Brahmin are to study, teach, and perform sacrifices, while those of a Kshatriya are to protect the people, give gifts, and perform sacrifices. The natural duties of a Vaishya are to engage in trade, commerce, and agriculture, while those of a Shudra are to serve the other three varnas. A person should perform his natural duties with love, detachment, and for the benefit of others, and thus worship the Supreme Being. In the Manusmriti, the following five duties are prescribed for Brahmins and Kshatriyas - studying, teaching, performing sacrifices, giving gifts, and protecting the people. For Vaishyas, the following six duties are prescribed - studying, teaching, performing sacrifices, giving gifts, protecting the people, and engaging in trade and commerce. For Shudras, the following nine duties are prescribed - studying, teaching, performing sacrifices, giving gifts, protecting the people, engaging in trade and commerce, and serving the other three varnas. 1. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
The seven inherent nature-based actions, such as eating and sleeping, become impure and are not fit for worship. All actions, including those of a warrior, should be performed as an offering to the Supreme Being. A Vaisya should perform yajna, study, give charity, and engage in trade and commerce, and a Shudra should serve others as ordained by the scriptures and according to their inherent nature. One should perform all actions, including eating, sleeping, and other daily activities, as an offering to the Supreme Being, with a sense of detachment and devotion. The scriptures prescribe various duties for humans based on their varna and ashrama. However, if one performs these duties with devotion and a sense of detachment, their actions become an offering to the Supreme Being. For example, when Arjuna's grandfather Bhishma was fighting in the war, he served as Krishna's charioteer and offered his arrows as a form of worship. One should perform both worldly and spiritual actions as an offering to the Supreme Being, without attachment to the means and instruments used. If one is attached to the means and instruments, their actions become impure and cannot be offered to the Supreme Being. The phrase "siddhim vindati manavah" means that a person who performs actions as an offering to the Supreme Being becomes free from the limitations of nature and attains their true self. In this state, the person's devotion to the Supreme Being becomes spontaneous, and they no longer need anything else. The word "manavah" does not refer only to Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas, and Shudras, but to all humans, regardless of their caste, creed, or profession. Anyone can perform actions as an offering to the Supreme Being, as they are all His children. Just as a mother is pleased with the actions of all her children, the Supreme Being is pleased with the actions of all humans. In this chapter, the Supreme Being has said to Arjuna that anyone can perform actions as an offering to Him, regardless of their varna or ashrama. The scriptures prescribe various duties for humans based on their varna and ashrama, but if one performs these duties with devotion and a sense of detachment, their actions become an offering to the Supreme Being. The following verses from the Manusmriti support this idea:

1. "The protection of animals, giving in charity, and studying the Vedas are the duties of a Vaisya. A Vaisya should engage in trade and commerce, and a Shudra should serve others." (Manu 1.90)
2. "The Supreme Being is the only duty of a Shudra. A Shudra should serve others with devotion and humility." (Manu 1.91)
3. "As I am the Supreme Being, I am the one who has been pierced by your sharp arrows. My skin is torn, and my armor is broken. My horses are tired, and my chariot is in disarray. I am the Supreme Being, Krishna, and I am in your heart." (Bhagavad Gita 1.9.34)
4. "Mamatamal jarai jai" (Mans 7.117)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

If I perform the sacrifice of knowledge through him, I will be worshiped by the sacrifice of knowledge. This proves that if one recites the Gita, studies it, the Lord considers him worthy of worship. Such is the case. He who turns away from worldly objects and faces the Lord is considered worthy of worship by the Lord. The special thing is that in Karma Yoga, detachment from worldly objects is achieved through actions, and in Bhakti Yoga, devotion to the Supreme Being is achieved without being attached to the world. The Karma Yogis attach their body, senses, mind, intellect, etc. to the service of the world, leaving aside their ego, selfishness, and desires. As a result, they become detached from their own possessions and completely separate from the world. The inherent detachment is revealed. The devotee worships the Supreme Being through his natural and ordained actions, as well as through spiritual actions (such as meditation, etc.) performed at the right time. Due to the difference in their attitudes, there is a difference between the two. The actions of the Karma Yogis become a means of benefiting all, and their actions come to a standstill, resulting in detachment. On the other hand, the actions of the devotee become offerings to the Supreme Being, and he becomes detached from the world, and his love for the Supreme Being increases. The devotee is already facing the Lord and offering himself to the Lord. Through self-surrender, all his worldly and spiritual actions become offerings to the Lord. It appears that there is a difference between the two, but in reality, there is no difference. The Karma Yogis and Jnana Yogis both become detached in the end. Just as the Karma Yogis detach themselves from worldly objects through their actions, and their actions become offerings to the world, and they themselves become detached. Similarly, the Jnana Yogis detach themselves from worldly objects through their knowledge, and their actions become offerings to nature, and they themselves become detached. The implication is that there is a difference in the way they offer themselves, but in detachment, both become one. In this detachment, both the Karma Yogis and Jnana Yogis become independent. There is no bondage of actions for them. The Karma Yogis' actions are completely absorbed in the performance of their duties (Gita - 4.23), and the Jnana Yogis' actions are completely destroyed by the fire of knowledge (Gita - 4.37). However, the one who is not satisfied with this independence, and whose independence leads to a state of inactivity, can have love for the Lord through the Lord's grace. Parishishta Bhaav - Here, the word 'pravruttih' in the phrase 'yatah pravruttir bhootaanam' should be interpreted as 'utpatti' (origin). Because all living beings originate from the Supreme Being, but there is no action. The action is due to the influence of the rajoguna - 'lobhaH pravruttir aarambhaH' (Gita 14.12). In the 15th chapter, 4th verse, the word 'pravruttih' is also used in the sense of 'utpatti' - 'yatah pravruttih prasrita puraani'. This world is the first incarnation of the Lord - 'aadyo avataaraha purusha parasya' (Shrimad Bhagavat 2.6.41). Therefore, this world is the form of the Lord, the divine embodiment. Just as we worship the Lord in the form of a murti, offer flowers, and apply sandalwood paste, our intention is not to worship the murti but the Lord. Similarly, we should worship the Lord through every action of ours. The listener should worship the speaker, and the speaker should worship the listener - in this way, everyone should worship each other through their actions. The gaze should be towards the Lord, not towards the brahmin, kshatriya, etc. The Lord praises Shri Rama, and the brahmins and muni praise the Lord. * It is essential for the practitioners of Karma Yoga, Jnana Yoga, and Bhakti Yoga to be detached from the world. In the Gita, it is said that the Karma Yogis should renounce attachment (5.11), the Jnana Yogis should be detached (18.26), and the Bhakti Yogis should be detached (11.55).

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]

Devotion (bhava) is offered by the Vaishnavas, not by the Kshatriyas. The essential point of worship is that everything belongs to the Lord and is for the Lord. Just as one worships the Ganga by using Ganga‑water, one must worship the Lord by using the Lord’s own objects. In reality every action is worship of the Lord; we only have to erase our own mistake. Offering the Lord’s own objects to the Lord eliminates selfishness, desire for enjoyment, and the wish for fruit, and by recognizing our own power as the Lord’s, the sense of doership also disappears and the experience of attaining the Lord arises. In truth, worship of the world in the mood of devotion to the Lord is even more valuable than idol worship. An idol does not appear to be pleased when worshiped, whereas beings become visibly happy when they are served. If individuals are regarded as manifestations of the Lord and are served with actions and material offerings, the world will vanish and only the Lord will remain—that is, the realization that “everything is the Lord.” When the illusion of a snake on a rope disappears, the snake is gone but the rope remains; similarly, when the illusion of the world disappears in the Lord, the world disappears as a worldly form while the divine form of the Lord remains. The world is a perception, but “the Lord is” is the reality. In the Srimad‑Bhagavatam the Lord says:

* nareṣv abhikṣṇaṁ madbhāvaṁ spardhāsūyātiraskārāḥ bhāvayato’acirāt | puṁso sāhaṅkārā viyanti hi || (SB 11.29.15)  
  *Translation:* “When the devotee’s attitude toward all men and women becomes constantly my attitude, and they see only Me, then swiftly envy, censure, contempt and other faults together with ego are removed from the mind.”

Thus, when the devotee’s mind is wholly fixed on the Lord in every person, all negative mental tendencies disappear. The Bhagavad‑Gita records the Lord’s declaration:

* ahaṁ ātmā guḍākeśa sarva‑bhūtāśaya‑sthitaḥ (10.20)  
  *Translation:* “I, the Self, am situated in the heart of all beings.”

Consequently, serving or honoring any creature as an expression of devotion is in fact service to the Lord. Disrespect or contempt toward any creature is disrespect or contempt toward the Lord, as expressed in the verse:

* karśayantah śarīrasthaṁ bhūtagrāmam acetasḥ (17.6)  
  *Translation:* “By destroying the body, the soul (the conscious principle) is left without a dwelling.”

In the path of knowledge, qualities remain within qualities (“guṇā guṇeṣu vartante”), while in the path of devotion the worship of the Lord’s objects is worship of the Lord Himself. The two paths differ greatly. “Guṇā guṇeṣu vartante” signifies a rootedness in inertia, which the jñāna‑mārga renounces; “svakarmṇā tam abhyarcya” signifies a rootedness in consciousness, which the bhakti‑mārga embraces. Hence, inertia is eliminated on the devotional path, the worldly illusion disappears, and the divine form of the Lord is revealed, because the Lord alone is real. If the seeker sees the world as a worldly form, he should serve it; if he sees it as the divine form, he should worship it. One should do nothing for oneself. Acting solely for oneself is bondage; acting for the world is service; acting for the Lord is worship. **Relation** – When one performs innate (sahaja) actions selflessly and with the consciousness of worship, even if some deficiency remains, the practitioner must not become despondent. This is explained in the next two verses. * śreyaḥ svadharmo viguṇaḥ para‑dharmāt sv‑anushṭhitāt | svabhāva‑niyataṁ karma kurvann āpnoti kilbiṣam (3.35)  
  *Translation:* “One’s own duty, even if imperfect, is better than the duty of another performed without devotion; performing one’s natural duty without attachment does not incur sin.”

To perceive the Lord in men and women, we often focus on their virtues and faults, which prevents the feeling of devotion. By looking beyond virtues and faults and seeing only the Lord in all beings and material objects, the mood of devotion arises smoothly throughout creation.

The duty performed by oneself, 
is superior to the duty performed by others, 
for it is done according to one's nature. Explanation: 
Here, the word 'swadharma' is taken in the sense of varna-dharma, i.e., the duty prescribed for one's varna. A person who is striving for the attainment of the Supreme, considers 'swa' or himself as a particular varna, and his duty or karma is 'swadharma'. For example, a person who considers himself as a man, his duty is to follow the duties of a man; a student considers his duty as studying, a teacher considers his duty as teaching, a devotee considers his duty as devotion, an inquirer considers his duty as inquiry, and a servant considers his duty as service. In this way, a person's duty is determined by his nature and the work he is assigned to do. Translation:
One who performs his duty, 
is not bound by the sin of it, 
for it is done according to his nature. Explanation:
If a person's duty is easy to perform and is done in accordance with his nature, then it is the best to perform one's own duty. The scriptures prescribe certain duties for certain varnas, and those duties are 'swadharma' for those varnas. For example, the duties of a brahmin, such as performing yajnas, accepting donations, etc., are 'swadharma' for him, but the same duties are 'paradharma' for kshatriyas, vaishyas, and shudras. However, in times of distress, the scriptures do not prohibit the performance of duties related to livelihood, and those duties become 'swadharma' for all varnas. For example, a brahmin can perform the duties of a kshatriya, such as fighting, and a kshatriya can perform the duties of a vaishya, such as trade. Translation:

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
This is a different matter that some virtues are suitable for some people's nature and some virtues are suitable for some people's nature. For example, some people's nature is mainly compassionate and some people's nature is mainly neglectful, some people's nature is self-forgiving and some people's nature is forgiving on request, some people's nature is naturally generous and some people's nature is generous with thought, etc. Such a distinction can be made. ,
'Svabhāvaniyataṃ karma kurvannāpnoti kilbiṣam'
There are two types of words in the scriptures - prescribed and prohibited. In these prescribed actions, there is a command to perform the actions and a prohibition to perform the prohibited actions. In these prescribed actions, the scriptures have appointed different actions for different varnas, ashrams, countries, times, events, circumstances, objects, conjunctions, and disjunctions, etc. These actions are called 'niyata karma' for a particular varna, ashram, etc. -
. Satva, rajas, and tamas - these three gunas form a person's nature, and the actions that are appointed according to that nature are called 'svabhāvaniyata karma'. These are also called svabhāvaprabhava, svabhāvaj, svadharma, svakarma, and sahaj karma. In essence, the person who is born in a particular varna, jati, etc. has the same gunas and actions that were present in him before birth. The actions are completed when performed, but the gunas - in the form of samskaras - remain. When born, the gunas and actions that are in accordance with his nature are naturally present in him, i.e., he does not need to acquire them from anywhere and does not need to exert himself for them. Therefore, they are called svabhāvaj and svabhāvaniyata. Although 'sarvārambhā hi doṣeṇa dhūmenāgnirivaāvṛtāḥ' (Gita 18.48) states that there is a defect in actions alone, yet if the actions prescribed by the scriptures for a particular varna are performed with the intention of benefiting others and not for personal gain or pride, then the person born in that varna will not incur the defect (pap) of those actions. Similarly, if one performs actions only for the sake of the body, he will not incur the defect - 'śārīraṃ kevalam karma kurvannāpnoti kilbiṣam' (Gita 4.21). Special Note
[ Chapter 18
A big doubt arises here that if a person is born in a butcher's house, then his natural (sahaj) action is to be a butcher. A person performing svabhāvaniyata karma is not considered to have committed a sin, so should he not renounce the action of a butcher? If he should not renounce the action of a butcher, then how will he avoid prohibited behavior? How will he attain happiness? The solution to this is that svabhāvaniyata karma is that which is prescribed, not prohibited in any way, i.e., it does not harm anyone. The actions that are harmful to anyone are not included in sahaj karma. They are performed due to attachment, desire, and ego. Prohibited actions, whether they are formed in this birth or in a previous birth, are defective. The defective part is to be renounced, because defect is asuric property, and virtue is divine property. Even if there is a tendency to indulge in evil behavior due to the samskaras of previous births, it does not necessarily lead to evil behavior. It can be removed by viveka, good thoughts, association with the good, and the scriptures. ,
It can also be seen with reason that no living being wants to harm himself, nor does he want to kill himself. Therefore, no one has the right to harm anyone else, to kill anyone else. A person wants to do good for himself, so he should also do good for others. The scriptures also state that the actions that are defective, sinful, unjust, are 'vikrita', not 'prakrita', i.e., they are formed due to vikara, not due to svabhava. In the third chapter, Arjuna asked that how does a person, who does not want to, commit sinful actions? Then the Lord said that a person commits sinful actions due to being under the control of desire (Gita 3.33-34). The actions that are performed due to desire, anger, ego, and self-interest are not pure, but impure. The actions that are performed with the intention of attaining the ultimate goal are different, but they are not defective. A person born in a brahmin's house will perform brahmin-like actions, and a person born in a shudra's house will perform shudra-like actions, but the defective part is not present in anyone.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

There will be no such thing. A person of a lowly birth or a person of a lowly nature cannot be a natural recipient of good qualities. Good qualities will naturally arise in him without being told or heard. However, a person who is prone to committing mistakes can still be a natural performer of his duties, but he cannot be a natural recipient of good qualities. If a Brahmin attains the realization of the Supreme Consciousness, he will still eat food in the same state of purity as he should; he will still live in the same state of purity as he should. Similarly, if an outcast attains the realization of the Supreme Consciousness, he will still eat leftovers; he will still live in the same state as he did before. However, a Brahmin will not do so because eating pure food is his natural duty, whereas an outcast eating leftovers is not considered a fault. Therefore, even the great sages have different kinds of actions, but they are not considered faults. Their nature is pure because they are free from attachment and aversion. In the Ramcharitmanas, it is mentioned that Lord Rama said to Shabari, "I will tell you about the nine types of devotion. Listen carefully and keep it in your mind." Then, after explaining the nine types of devotion, Lord Rama said, "All types of devotion are firm in you." The implication is that devotion has nine types, and Shabari was not aware of it. However, devotion of all types was natural to Shabari. Through the practice of sat-sang, bhajan, and meditation, we can acquire the qualities that we do not know about. Those who only remember to tell others about it will tell others, but they will not acquire the qualities in their behavior until they purify their nature and move towards the Supreme Consciousness. Therefore, a person should purify his nature and actions. There is no one who is dependent, weak, or unfit for this. No one is unworthy or ineligible. A person thinks that he is unable to perform his duties and acquire good qualities, but in reality, he is not unable. It is due to his attachment to worldly pleasures and his desire to accumulate material possessions that he feels unable. If a person was born in a butcher's family due to his past karma, it is not because he was born to commit sins, but because he has to suffer the consequences of his past karma. The consequences of karma are described as caste, age, and enjoyment, not as new karma. "The fruit of karma is caste, age, and enjoyment" (Yogadarshan 2.13). He is free to perform his actions. If his mind is purified, he will not be able to perform the actions of a butcher. A saint was asked, "If someone considers his duty to be killing animals, what can he do?" The saint replied firmly, "If he performs the name-japa of the Supreme Consciousness, and the name-japa of his Ishta-deva, with purity and devotion for three years, he will not be able to kill animals." The reason is that his past karma or the karma of this life has created a certain nature in him, and that nature is a fault. If he sincerely seeks the realization of the Supreme Consciousness, he will not be able to perform the actions of a butcher. He will feel ashamed, and he will be able to control himself. The realization of the Supreme Consciousness is the only means to attain liberation. "The path to liberation is the means to attain it" (Mansarovar 7.43.4). If it were impossible to purify one's nature, how could it be called the path to liberation? If a person cannot purify his nature, then what is the purpose of human life? Kuntah, do not abandon even a duty that is tainted with faults, for all beginnings are covered with faults, like a fire covered with smoke. 48. Hear, O Kunti's son, do not abandon even a duty that is tainted with faults, for all beginnings are covered with faults, like a fire covered with smoke.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18
Commentary - In the previous shloka, it was said that even if there is a deficiency of virtues in one's inherent nature and natural actions, a person performing the actions as ordained by the scriptures does not attain sin. This proves that even in natural actions, there is a possibility of sinful activity. If there were no sinful activity, then saying 'he does not attain sin' would not be justified. Therefore, here, the Lord says, 'One should not abandon even natural actions that have some defects; because all actions are enveloped by defects like the smoke that surrounds fire.'

'Even natural actions, O son of Kunti, should not be abandoned, even if they have defects.'

Natural actions are those that are inherent in one's nature and natural tendencies. For example, a Brahmin's actions like self-control and restraint, a Kshatriya's actions like bravery and heroism, a Vaishya's actions like agriculture and cattle-rearing, and a Shudra's actions like service. The actions ordained by the scriptures for each varna are also considered natural actions, such as a Brahmin's duty to perform yajnas and teach, a Kshatriya's duty to perform yajnas and give charity, a Vaishya's duty to perform yajnas, and a Shudra's duty to serve. The defects in natural actions are:

(1) Both the Supreme Being and His part are 'swa' (one's own), and nature and its activities are 'para' (other). However, the part of the Supreme Being becomes 'para' (dependent) due to being under the control of nature, i.e., it becomes bound by nature's activities and considers them as its own, thus becoming dependent. This dependence on nature is a great defect. (2) Every action has some inherent and unavoidable defects like violence, etc. (3) Any action is beneficial to some and harmful to others. Being harmful to others is also a defect. (4) Due to negligence, etc., there is a deficiency in performing actions or there is a mistake in the method of performing actions, which is also a defect. Even if there are defects in one's natural actions, one should not abandon them. The meaning is that just as the actions of a Brahmin are more gentle, the actions of other varnas are not considered gentle. However, even if they are not gentle, they are not considered defective. Similarly, the actions of a Kshatriya, Vaishya, or Shudra are not considered defective in comparison to those of a Brahmin. Therefore, one should not abandon natural actions. For a Brahmin, alms-giving is ordained. At first glance, alms-giving appears to be a defect-free action. However, there are defects in it. For example, if a beggar comes to a house while another beggar is already there, the householder is burdened. There is a possibility of rivalry among beggars. If a householder is not prepared to give alms, he suffers. If he does not give alms, the beggar becomes disappointed and leaves. As a result, the householder feels guilty and gets entangled in it. Similarly, even though there are defects in alms-giving, a Brahmin should not abandon it. For a Kshatriya, righteous war is ordained. If a Kshatriya gets an opportunity to fight a righteous war, he does not feel guilty about it. Although there are defects in war, such as killing humans, a Kshatriya does not feel guilty about it because it is ordained by the scriptures and is in accordance with his nature. Similarly, for a Vaishya, agriculture is ordained. Although there is a lot of violence involved in agriculture, a Vaishya does not feel guilty about it because it is ordained by the scriptures and is in accordance with his nature. It is true that natural actions do not entail sin; however, how can one attain liberation through these simple natural actions? In reality, natural actions do not hinder liberation. Bondage and sin arise due to desires, attachment, ego, and other such factors. Therefore, a person should perform natural actions without attachment, for the sake of the Lord, and thus attain liberation. 'All beginnings are enveloped by defects like the smoke that surrounds fire' - just as fire, when lit, is surrounded by smoke, all actions are surrounded by defects. Although there are defects in actions due to factors like time, place, circumstances, and the influence of others, the scriptures have ordained actions in accordance with one's nature. One should perform actions in accordance with the scriptures, without attachment, and thus attain liberation.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

A person engaged in action does not come under the category of one who suffers from the consequences of sin. This is because, as per justice, it is the duty of a warrior to engage in war. The Lord seems to be saying to Arjuna, 'Brother, you consider war as a great action, which is a warrior's duty; it is your duty' (Gita - Second Chapter, Verse 31). -

In the absence of attachment to prohibited actions or due to the reason that one is not enjoying the fruits of prohibited actions, the prescribed action appears to be difficult. In reality, the prescribed action is natural and effortless, and it does not require any effort. From the 42nd verse to this point, the words 'swakarma', 'swadharma', and 'sahajkarma' have been used. This proves that the Gita considers 'swakarma' and 'sahajkarma' as 'swadharma'. There is a defect in performing prescribed actions, but the defect does not arise due to the absence of desire, happiness, or the desire for enjoyment. The implication is that the defect or the lack of it depends on the intention of the doer; just as a doctor, whose intention is to serve, does not commit a sin by cutting off a part of the patient's body during an operation, but rather earns merit due to his selfless attitude and benevolent intention. Connection - Now, the Lord begins to describe the principles of Sankhya Yoga, first describing the characteristics of a Sankhya yogi. One who has a detached mind, who is victorious over his senses, and who has shed all attachment, attains the supreme goal of non-action through renunciation. 49. Translation:

sarvaatra = everywhere
vashamena = with control
kararakhaha = has kept under control
paramam = the supreme
asaktabuddhih = one whose mind is detached
vigata-spruhah = one who has shed all attachment
naishkarmya-siddhim = the goal of non-action
paramam = the supreme
san-nyaasena = through renunciation
adhigachchhati = attains

Explanation - A Sankhya yogi does not worry about the basic necessities of life. He does not worry about getting food, water, or clothes. He does not worry about the cold or the heat. He has transcended all these worldly concerns. The three characteristics of a Sankhya yogi are:

(1) 'Asaktabuddhih sarvatra' - One whose mind is detached everywhere, i.e., he is not attached to anything - country, time, event, situation, object, person, action, or substance. (2) 'Jit-atma' - One who has conquered his senses, i.e., he is not controlled by his senses, but rather controls them. He is not lazy or negligent, but rather, he is alert and active. (3) 'Vigata-spruhah' - One who has shed all attachment, i.e., he is not attached to anything, not even to the basic necessities of life. The implication is that a Sankhya yogi has transcended all worldly concerns and has become detached from everything. He has become a jivanmukta, one who has attained liberation while still living in the world. The phrase 'naishkarmya-siddhim paramam san-nyaasena adhigachchhati' means that a Sankhya yogi attains the supreme goal of non-action through renunciation. The reason is that when one is detached from all actions and their consequences, one becomes free from the cycle of birth and death.

Parishishta Bhaav – The meaning of Naiskarmya Siddhi is that one's actions become completely free from attachment, and one remains unaffected by the consequences of actions, as stated in the verse 'Karmaṇyakarma yaḥ paśyed akarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ' (Gita 4.18). Not performing actions is not Naiskarmya (Nishkarma), but rather performing actions is necessary for the seeker, as stated in the verse 'Karmaṇyakarma yaḥ paśyed akarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ' (Gita 6.3). -
-
The verse 'Asaktabuddhiḥ sarvatra jita ātmā vigata-spr̥hāḥ' is the Siddhi of Karma Yoga (Gita 2.50), which is achieved when one becomes detached from all desires. When this Siddhi is achieved, the Karma Yogī attains Sāṅkhya Yoga and from there attains Naiskarmya Siddhi. Thus, Karma Yoga leads to 'Naiskarmya Siddhi' – 'Na karmaṇāṃ anārambhān na naiskarmyaṃ puruṣo 'aśnute' (Gita 3.4). However, through Bhakti Yoga, one attains 'Param Naiskarmya Siddhi'. Karma Yoga and Jñāna Yoga are 'Nishtha' – 'Lok'eṣaṃ dvi-vidhā nishṭhā' (3.3), but the 'Para Nishtha' that is achieved through Bhakti is the highest Nishtha. In other words, 'Param Naiskarmya Siddhi' and 'Para Nishtha' are both achieved through Bhakti. -
Sambandh – Now, I will explain the method to attain that highest Siddhi. Siddhim prāpto yathā brahma tathā pṛāpti nibodha me |

Oh Kauṇṭeya, the one who has attained the highest Siddhi, which is the Supreme Consciousness, attains it in the same way as I will explain to you. The one who has attained the highest Siddhi, which is the Supreme Consciousness, is the one who has attained the highest Nishtha, which is the knowledge of the Supreme Consciousness. Vyaakhya – 'Siddhim prāpto yathā brahma tathā pṛāpti nibodha me' – Here, 'Siddhi' refers to the purification of the mind, which is described in the previous verse as 'Asaktabuddhiḥ', 'Jita ātmā', and 'Vigata-spr̥hāḥ'. The one whose mind is purified to such an extent that there is no attachment, no desire, and no ego, does not need anything, and is not bound by anything. This is the true Siddhi. In the world, people consider Siddhi to be the attainment of any desired object or power, but this is not true Siddhi. This is a bondage, not a liberation. [ Verse 51 – 53 ]  
* Sadhaka‑Sanjeevani *

Appendix meaning – the term “siddhim” here denotes the total purification of the inner self achieved through karma‑yoga as a means; after attaining this, the karmayogi may proceed to jñāna‑yoga or bhakti‑yoga at any point. Thus one should continue performing actions until either a detachment from sense‑pleasures arises or faith in the divine play (liṅga‑kathā) through hearing, chanting, etc., is established. If the practitioner bears the imprint of knowledge, the path will naturally turn toward jñāna; if the imprint is of devotion, the path will turn toward bhakti. When no single inclination dominates, karma‑yoga, jñāna‑yoga and bhakti‑yoga each function both as a means (sādhana) and as an end (sādya). As means they differ, but as ends they converge. Hence the Gītā sometimes states that knowledge is attained through devotion (the means‑devotion yielding the end‑knowledge), e.g., “mayi cānanyogaena bhaktiravyabhicāriṇī” (13.10), “māṁ ca yo’vyabhicāreṇa brahmbhūyāya kalpate” (14.26); elsewhere it says that devotion is attained through knowledge (the means‑knowledge yielding the end‑devotion), e.g., “sanniyamye ndriyagrāmaṁ sarvatra … sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ” (12.4), “brahmbhūtaḥ prasannātmā madbhaktiṁ labhate parām” (18.54). The Lord earlier declared, “svakarmāṇā tamabhyarcya siddhiṁ vindati mānavaḥ” (18.46), indicating that devotion is realized through karma‑yoga; the verse “siddhim prāpto yathā brahma” likewise points to the attainment of jñāna through karma‑yoga. Chapter 5 also mentions the rapid attainment of jñāna through the means of karma‑yoga: “yogyato munir brahma na cirenādhigacchati” (5.6). Connection – the next three verses explain what material (sādhana) is required for the supreme steadfastness (parāniṣṭhā) in knowledge. **Verse 51**  
buddhyā viśuddhayā yukto dhṛtyātmānaṁ niyamya ca  
śabdādīn viṣayān tyaktvā rāga‑dveṣau vyudasya ca

*Translation*: With a mind purified by wisdom, firmly resolved, one should restrain the self; having abandoned the objects of the senses (words, etc.), one should relinquish attachment and aversion. **Verse 52**  
vivikta‑sevī laghvāśī yatavāk‑kāyamāna‑saḥ  
dhyānayogaparo nityaṁ vairāgyaṁ samupāśritaḥ

*Translation*: The solitary practitioner, modest in diet, who controls body, speech and mind, ever devoted to meditation‑yoga, takes refuge in constant detachment. **Verse 53**  
ahaṅkāraṁ balaṁ darpaṁ kāmaṁ krodhaṁ parigraham  
vimucya nirmamaḥ śānto brahmbhūyāya kalpate

*Translation*: By relinquishing ego, strength, pride, desire, anger and grasping, one becomes free, utterly pure, peaceful, and attains the state of becoming Brahman. Breakdown of key terms (Roman transliteration with English gloss):

- **buddhyā viśuddhayā** – by a pure intellect (sattvic)  
- **yukto** – united, associated with the intellect  
- **dhṛtyā** – with steadfast resolve  
- **ātmanam** – the self  
- **niyamya** – restraining, controlling  
- **śabdādīn viṣayān** – objects of the senses such as words, etc. - **tyaktvā** – having abandoned  
- **rāga‑dveṣau** – attachment and aversion  
- **vyudasya** – having let go  
- **vivikta‑sevī** – one who serves in solitude  
- **laghvāśī** – modest eater (light diet)  
- **yatavāk‑kāyamāna‑saḥ** – one who subdues speech, body and mind  
- **dhyānayogaparo** – devoted to meditation‑yoga  
- **nityaṁ** – always, eternally  
- **vairāgyaṁ samupāśritaḥ** – taking refuge in detachment  
- **ahaṅkāraṁ** – ego‑sense  
- **balaṁ** – force, power  
- **darpaṁ** – pride  
- **kāmaṁ** – desire  
- **krodhaṁ** – anger  
- **parigraham** – grasping, attachment  
- **vimucya** – having been freed  
- **nirmamaḥ** – completely pure, without blemish  
- **śānto** – peaceful  
- **brahmbhūyāya kalpate** – becomes capable of attaining Brahman.

[ Chapter 18
Brahmabhuta (the state of unity with the Supreme Consciousness)
- is attained by the worthy. Explanation - 'Buddhya vishuddhaya yuktah' - He who is a Sankhya yogi, has a pure intellect. The intellect of the aspirant should be pure, i.e., sattvic (Gita - this chapter's 33rd verse). His intellect should be clear, and there should be no slightest doubt in it. In this Sankhya yoga chapter, the name of intellect came first. Its meaning is that the discriminative faculty, which is necessary for the Sankhya yogi, is revealed in the intellect. Through that discriminative faculty, he renounces the quality of grossness. 'Veeragya samupashritah' - Just as worldly people take the objects of pleasure, persons, etc. as their support, their refuge, and their means of livelihood, similarly the Sankhya yogi takes the support of detachment. That is, he remains naturally detached from the world, the society, and the place. He has a strong detachment from all worldly and transcendental enjoyments. 'Veekitasvee' - The nature of the Sankhya yogi is to remain in solitude. It is good to have a liking for solitude, but there should not be any eagerness for it. That is, if solitude is not available, there should not be any distraction or restlessness in the mind. If there is eagerness for solitude, and it is not available, the aspirant will become restless, and he will not be able to remain in the company of others. Therefore, the nature of the aspirant should be to remain in solitude, but if solitude is not available, there should not be any distraction or restlessness in the mind. Because, if there is distraction or restlessness in the mind, the importance of the world comes to the mind, and this is a hindrance to the practice of meditation. 'Ekantam seve' - By remaining in solitude, the practice of meditation becomes more. The mind becomes fixed in God, and the mind becomes pure. But, "In solitude, there will be no noise, no disturbance; wherever one sits, no one will see; there will be all kinds of comfort in solitude; and people will also praise and respect the one who remains in solitude" - these thoughts should not make the aspirant feel comfortable and attached to solitude. He should always remain vigilant. '
Laghvashi' - The nature of the aspirant should be to eat little, i.e., to eat sattvic food in moderation. Three things have been told about food - hit, mit, and medhya. 'Hit' means that the food should be suitable for the body. 'Mit' means that the food should not be excessive, nor should it be deficient; one should eat just as much food as is necessary for the maintenance of the body (Gita - 6th chapter, 16th verse). If one eats food with the idea that it will make the body strong, then one should not eat it; one should eat food only as a medicine to satisfy hunger, so that there may be no obstacle in the practice of meditation. 'Medhya' means that the food should be pure. '
Dhrityatmanam niyamya cha' - The aspirant should not let his intellect be distracted by worldly attractions, even if they are many; he should control his senses with the help of sattvic intellect (Gita - this chapter's 33rd verse). That is, he should keep his senses under control, and he should not allow them to do anything that is contrary to the practice of meditation. He should remain vigilant at all times, so that he may not do anything that is contrary to the practice of meditation through his senses. '
Yata vakkaya manasah' - The aspirant should also control his body, speech, and mind (Gita - 17th chapter, 14th, 15th, and 16th verses). That is, he should not move his body unnecessarily; he should not go on a journey for the sake of seeing and hearing; he should not talk unnecessarily; he should speak only when it is necessary; he should not speak untruth; he should not indulge in slander or backbiting; and he should not think of the world with attachment. He should think of God. '
Shabdadin vishayans tyaktva' - At the time of meditation, one should give up all external relationships, which are sensual in nature, and which come into contact with the senses, and which give rise to sensual pleasure (Gita - 17th chapter, 16th verse). Because, if one indulges in sensual pleasures, one cannot practice meditation. If one indulges in sensual pleasures, one's mind will not be fixed in God, and one will think of the world.

[Verse 54]

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

'Very soon, attachment and aversion will be destroyed' - This is the importance of worldly things. The attachment that is created for the sake of doing something is called 'anger'. The accumulation of things due to the desire for pleasure and comfort is called 'hoarding'. The attachment that is present in the heart due to the presence of false things is called 'attachment'. The attachment remains in the beginning, but when a person tries to acquire those false things, aversion arises towards them. If attachment arises in one part of the world, aversion arises in another part - this is the rule. For example, if attachment arises in the body, it arises only in things that are favorable to the body, and aversion arises in things that are unfavorable. Attachment and aversion both create a relationship with the world. The thought of attachment and aversion both arise. Therefore, the seeker should not have attachment and should not have aversion. 'Dhyanayogparo nityam' - The seeker should always be devoted to the practice of meditation, i.e., he should not engage in any other practice except meditation. During meditation, he should meditate, and at the time of work, i.e., while walking, eating, working, he should always maintain the thought that there is no independent existence in the world except the Supreme Being (Gita - This is the 20th verse of this chapter). The seeker gives up all the above-mentioned ego, strength, pride, desire, anger, and hoarding. 'Nirmamah' - There should be no attachment to the things that are available for sustenance and the means of work, such as the body, senses, etc. There should be no attachment to the things that we like, and there should be no desire for their existence. The person who is not attached to things that are not his own is called 'nirmamah'. The things that we consider our own today were not our own a hundred years ago, and they will not be our own a hundred years from now. Therefore, we can use or serve them, but we should not consider them our own. If we do not consider them our own, then what is the obstacle in considering them not our own? By not considering them our own, the seeker becomes nirmamah. 'Shantah' - The attachment to false things in the world creates unrest and turmoil in the heart. When there is a complete separation from the attachment to false things, there is no unrest or turmoil. Therefore, the seeker remains calm and peaceful always. 'Ahankar bal darpan vimuchy' - The special quality that is present in a person due to his virtues is called 'ahankar'. The insistence on doing something forcefully, or the insistence on doing something according to one's own will, is called 'bal'. The pride that arises due to the possession of external things, such as wealth and property, is called 'darpan'. The desire for pleasure and comfort is called 'kam'. The desire to harm others due to one's own ego and pride is called 'krodh'. 'Brahmabhuuya kalpate' - The person who is free from attachment and remains calm and peaceful becomes eligible to attain the Supreme Being. This is because when there is a complete separation from false things, the capacity to attain the Supreme Being arises. As long as there is a relationship with false things, there is no capacity to attain the Supreme Being. What happens when the above-mentioned means and materials are used with complete devotion? This is explained in the next verse. Brahmabhuuta prasannatma na shochati na kaankshati. Samah sarveshu bhuteshu madbhaktim labhate param. 54. 1. For brahmacaris, vanaprasthas, and sannyasis, the renunciation of accumulation is inherent in their nature. If a grihastha does not accumulate things for his own pleasure, but accumulates things only for the benefit of others, then it is not accumulation. 2. It is not a fault to have attachment to things for the sake of worldly transactions, but it is a fault to consider them one's own for all time.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
= He grieves not
= (And) does not desire
= (Such a) person
= Attains everything
= (And) is not attached to anything
Explanation: When the quality of destruction of worldly objects is removed from the mind, then the ego, pride, etc. of the mind are calm, i.e., they are abandoned. Then, there is no attachment to the objects that are present with him. The absence of attachment leads to no accumulation of objects due to the pleasure and enjoyment of the mind. When the pleasure and enjoyment of the mind are removed, then peace naturally arises in the mind. In this way, when the seeker rises above the unreal, he becomes eligible for the attainment of Brahman. Eligibility for the attainment of Brahman arises naturally. He does not need to do anything for it. In this state, he experiences that 'I am of the nature of Brahman and Brahman is my nature.' This state is described here as 'Brahmabhuta' and also in the 24th verse of the 5th chapter of the Gita. 'Pleased soul' - When the importance of unreal objects arises in the mind, then the desire to attain those objects arises. The desire to attain objects arises, and the peace of the mind is disturbed, and unrest arises. But when the importance of unreal objects is removed, then the seeker's mind remains naturally pleased. The cause of displeasure is removed, and therefore displeasure never arises again. Because the Sankhya yogi seeker's mind remains with the absence of the self and the presence of the Supreme Self. 'He grieves not, nor desires' - This is the identification of the pleased state that he does not grieve or worry. Even if a great loss occurs in the world, he does not grieve, and even if a certain situation is obtained - he does not desire it. This means that he is not affected by the birth and death of objects, and the change of situations, and the coming and going of people, etc. 'He is equal to all beings' - As long as the seeker has a little bit of joy and sorrow, attachment and aversion, etc. in the mind, he cannot experience the unity with the Supreme Self. He cannot experience the unity because he cannot see himself as a part of all beings. But when the seeker is completely free from joy and sorrow, attachment and aversion, etc., then he naturally experiences the unity with the Supreme Self. The experience of unity with the Supreme Self arises, and therefore he sees himself as a part of all beings. Just as the Supreme Self is present in all beings, 'I am also present in all beings' (Gita - 9th chapter, 29th verse). This is what is described here as 'He is equal to all beings'. He becomes equal to all beings in what way? Just as the mind creates various creations in the state of dream and imagination, and the mind itself assumes various forms, so the creation is mental. Similarly, just as the mind is present in all creations and all creations are present in the mind, so also the seeker is present in all beings and all beings are present in him. 'He attains My devotion' - When the seeker experiences the unity with the Supreme Self, then his mind is everywhere in a state of equality, and therefore his mind is naturally attracted to the Supreme Self. This attraction is described here as devotion.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The 24th verse of the 5th chapter describes the attainment of Brahmanirvana after the state of Brahman-bhuta. Similarly, this verse describes the attainment of Parabhakti after the state of Brahman-bhuta. Parishishta Bhaav–The one who is a seeker of Jnana Yoga and has the samskaras of Bhakti, does not consider Moksha (liberation) as the ultimate goal. He does not consider his own ego or attachment to be the ultimate goal. He does not consider the destruction or criticism of Bhakti to be the ultimate goal. Therefore, after attaining Moksha, he attains the state of Parabhakti (love). The one who has become Brahman-bhuta is not actually Brahman, but has become Brahman-like. After becoming Brahman-bhuta, the jiva (individual) attains a tattvika sambandh (a relationship of similarity) with Brahman – 'mama sādharmyam āgatāḥ' (Gita 14.2). This tattvika sambandh is the same as Moksha. Then, by merging oneself in the Supreme Consciousness, one attains a relationship of identity with the Supreme – 'jñānī tvātmaiva me matam' (Gita 7.18). This relationship of identity is the same as Parabhakti. In the path of Jnana Yoga, the renunciation of jada (inertness) is the main thing. The renunciation of jada is a siddhi (attainment) of viveka (discernment). However, even after renouncing jada, the samskaras of the rejected things can remain, which can lead to philosophical differences. But, after attaining Parabhakti, the samskaras of the rejected things do not remain, because the bhakta (devotee) does not reject anything, but considers everything to be the form of God – 'sad-asacchāham' (Gita 9.19). The attainment of Parabhakti is not a siddhi of viveka, but a siddhi of vishvas (faith). Faith is dependent on the mercy of God, therefore, the one who has the samskaras of Bhakti, does not get satisfied with Moksha, but the mercy of God makes the Moksha-ras (the taste of liberation) weak and provides the Anantarasa (the taste of love) of Bhakti. The relationship with the world causes anxiety, therefore, in the path of Karma Yoga, after renouncing the relationship with the world, one attains 'shanta-ananda' (peaceful bliss). In the path of Jnana Yoga, after attaining the state of nij-svarupa (one's own form), one attains 'akhanda-ananda' (unbroken bliss). In the path of Bhakti Yoga, after attaining the state of abhinna-ta (identity with God), one attains 'ananta-ananda' (infinite bliss). Sambandh–In the next verse, the fruit of Parabhakti is described. Through Bhakti, one comes to know Me as I am in reality. Knowing Me in reality, one enters into Me. 55. Translation of the shloka:

Through Bhakti, one comes to know Me as I am in reality. Explanation–When the ego is completely renounced, and the attraction to the ultimate reality is established, the seeker becomes completely surrendered to the ultimate reality, and becomes one with it. Then, his separate existence ceases to be, and he does not have even a subtle sense of 'I am'. Therefore, he attains the state of Parabhakti (love). Through Parabhakti, one attains the true knowledge of the ultimate reality. The ego, which is a subtle aspect of the individual, is destroyed when one becomes Brahman-bhuta. This ego is a product of the prakriti (nature), and prakriti is 'par' (other), therefore, the individual remains in a state of paradhina (subservience). This ego is destroyed only when one becomes attracted to the ultimate reality through Parabhakti. The destruction of this ego is the true knowledge of the ultimate reality. * Prem Bhagati jal binu raghurai. Abhi-antar mal kabahu na jai. * (Mans 7.49.3)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

‘Yavan’– In the beginning of the seventh chapter, the Lord told Arjuna to listen to the entire form of mine, whose mind has become attached to me, whose refuge is only me, and who maintains a strong relationship with me, unattached to anything else. Whoever comes to know my entire form in this way, listen to that from him. The Lord said in the end of the seventh chapter that those who take refuge in me and make an effort to attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death, come to know the Supreme Being, the entire spiritual realm, and the entire realm of action, that is, the entire realm of the attributeless. And along with the three aspects of the Supreme Being, the individual self, the divine, and the cosmic, they come to know me, the Supreme Being with attributes. In this way, the Supreme Being manifests in various forms, such as Rama, Krishna, Shiva, Ganesha, Shakti, the Sun, and others, and performs various pastimes. To know this is to know the Supreme Being in all its forms and aspects. ‘Yashchasmim Tatvath’ – The Supreme Being, who is the ultimate reality, manifests in various forms, various forms, various powers, and various activities, and it is the same Supreme Being who is worshipped in various forms and aspects in various sects, according to one's own feelings. In reality, the Supreme Being is one and the same. To know this is to know the truth. ‘Tato Mam Tatvato Jnatah Vishate Tad Anantaram’ – When one knows me in this way, the individual self immediately merges into me, that is, the individual self loses its sense of separation from me. The ignorance that was present in the individual self is completely eliminated, and the individual self merges into the Supreme Being. This is the ultimate goal, and this is the fulfillment of human life. Special Note

The love of the individual self for the Supreme Being is not limited by time. 1. The individual self has a natural love for the Supreme Being, which is a love that is not limited by time. However, when the individual self associates with the material nature, it becomes separated from the Supreme Being and becomes attracted to the material world. This attraction is known as vāsanā, sprha, kāma, āśā, tṛṣṇā, and so on. The object of this attraction is a transitory and changing thing, whereas the individual self is eternal and unchanging. However, due to its association with the material nature, the individual self becomes attracted to the changing and transitory things. As a result, it does not get anything, but it is under the illusion that it will get something. This illusion is the cause of the individual self's birth and death, and it is the source of great suffering. To escape from this suffering, the Lord has taught the path of yoga. The path of yoga is to separate the individual self from the material nature and to establish a relationship with the Supreme Being. The Gita mentions three types of yoga: karma yoga, jñāna yoga, and bhakti yoga. 2. The love of the individual self for the Supreme Being is present in all three types of yoga. In karma yoga, this love is known as 'kṛtavyarati', that is, the love that is present in the performance of one's duties. 'Sve Sve Karmānyabhiratah' (18.45). This love ultimately transforms into self-love. In jñāna yoga, this love is known as 'ātmaratī', that is, the love that is present in the self. 'Yo 'ntaḥ Sukho 'ntarāramah' (5.24). * The Seeker - The Reviver *

The best is (the Gita - the sixth chapter, the forty-second verse). The meaning is that, having a connection with the material world, even after performing a very heavy tapas (austerity), acquiring knowledge from many scriptures, and performing big yajnas (sacrifices), daans (donations), and tirthas (pilgrimages), whatever is obtained is all temporary, but for a yogi, the attainment of the eternal truth is permanent. Therefore, the tapasvi (one who performs austerity), the jnani (one who has knowledge), and the karmi (one who performs action) - all three are inferior to the yogi. Similarly, among all yogis, including karma yogi, jnana yogi, hatha yogi, laya yogi, etc., the Bhagavan (the Supreme Being) has declared the bhakti yogi (one who has devotion) to be the supreme (the Gita - the sixth chapter, the fortieth verse). This bhakti yogi comes to know the all-pervading form of the Bhagavan. The sanyasi yogi also comes to know the all-pervading form of the Bhagavan through parabhakti (supreme devotion). The description of this all-pervading form is given here by the word "yavan" (as much as). In the beginning of this chapter, it was said that the seeker, who has attained the state of purity of the antahkaran (the inner self), is the same as the one who has attained Brahman (the Supreme Being). It was also said that the seeker, who has become a devotee of the dhyana yoga (meditation), attains vairagya (detachment). Through vairagya, he gives up the ego and other impurities and becomes free from attachment. Then he becomes eligible to attain Brahman. When he becomes eligible, his state of being Brahman is established. When this state of being Brahman is established, all the dualities, such as attachment and aversion, joy and sorrow, etc., which were present in the world, are completely eliminated. Then he becomes one with all living beings. When he becomes one with all living beings, he attains parabhakti (supreme devotion). This parabhakti is the true love. Through this love, he comes to know the all-pervading form of the Paramatman (the Supreme Being). When he comes to know the all-pervading form, he enters into that state - "vishate tad-anantaram" (he enters into that state immediately). A man can know the Bhagavan in his true form, enter into him, and see him through ananya bhakti (unwavering devotion) (the Gita - the eleventh chapter, the twenty-fourth verse); but the sanyasi yogi, who knows the Bhagavan in his true form, cannot see him. The reason is that his sadhana (practice) has been vivec-pradhana (based on discrimination) from the beginning, so he does not have the desire to see him. Even if he does not see him, there is no deficiency in him. Therefore, one should not consider any deficiency. The entry into that state is the attainment of the inexpressible love. This love is described in the Naraad Bhakti Sutra as "guna-rahitam, kama-rahitam, pratikshan-varthaman, avichchinnam, suukshma-taram anubhavarupam" (free from gunas, free from desires, increasing every moment, unbroken, subtle, and of the nature of experience). This love is free from gunas, free from desires, increasing every moment, unbroken, subtle, and of the nature of experience.

Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
When one's own connection is established, then the egoistic feeling of 'I am' arises. When one becomes beyond the gunas, i.e., when one is completely detached from the gunas, there are no two states of forgetfulness and remembrance. It is not that one forgets in sleep and then remembers when one wakes up - such an experience does not occur. Instead, one experiences that the sleep has only occurred in the mind, and one's own nature has remained unchanged. This means that the occurrence of sleep and waking up are both natural phenomena, and one experiences this clearly. In the twenty-second verse of the fourteenth chapter, it is said that the light of knowledge, i.e., waking up from sleep, and the darkness of ignorance, i.e., the occurrence of sleep, both arise from the gunas. Even a small amount of guna-atit purusha's (the one who has transcended the gunas) good or bad deeds can cause the cycle of birth and death to begin. However, one who has a high level of spiritual practice, i.e., one whose mind is always in a state of Brahman, experiences the knowledge of the self in all places. But as long as the connection with the satva guna remains, when one wakes up from sleep, one immediately experiences the feeling of 'I am Brahman' or 'everything is the Supreme Being.' It seems as if one had forgotten this truth in sleep, and now one has regained it. There is no attachment or aversion in this state. Parishishta Bhaav - The statement 'I am as much as I am, and I am what I am' (yavat yashchasmi) is a characteristic of the saguna (with attributes) form. This is because 'yavat' (as much as) is not possible in the nirguna (without attributes) form, but only in the saguna form. In the Chatur-shloki Bhagavatam, the Lord has said, 'As I am, in my true form, with my attributes and deeds, may you have the knowledge of my true nature through my grace' (yavat yashchabhaavo yadrupagunakarmakah, tathaiva tat-tvavijnanamastu te madanugrahatah). The Lord has also described Himself as 'sadhya-sadhya-devam, sadhi-yajnancha ye viduh' (those who know me as the goal, the means, and the ultimate goal) in the thirty-first verse of the seventh chapter. This shows the characteristic and predominance of the saguna form. When one follows the path of knowledge, and then attains devotion, one experiences only two things: knowing (jnaatvaa) and entering (vishate) into the truth. There is no seeing (drishya) in it. There is no deficiency in these two, but the desire to see (darshan) is not there. However, from the beginning, one who follows the path of devotion experiences seeing (drishya) the Lord, in addition to knowing (jnaatvaa) and entering (vishate) into the truth (Gita - eleventh chapter, twenty-fourth verse). Therefore, in the path of knowledge, the saints do not talk about devotion, but only about knowledge. Just as people from different paths come together and enter the same door, similarly, those who follow different yogic paths come together and enter into the Lord, i.e., they become one. There is no subtle difference between them, as the egoistic feeling (ahamkAra) is completely absent in them. There are two states of love: (1) sometimes the devotee becomes completely immersed in love, and then the lover and the beloved become one, and (2) sometimes the devotee experiences a surge of love, and then the lover and the beloved become one, but for the sake of play, they become two again. This verse is explaining the first state. Sambandh - In the previous verse, Arjuna had asked about the nature of renunciation and detachment, and the Lord had explained the path of karma yoga from the fourth to the twelfth verse, and then from the forty-first to the forty-eighth verse. He had also briefly explained the path of devotion. Now, the Lord begins to explain the path of devotion, which is based on surrender. sarva-karmāṇi sadā kurvāṇo mad-vyapāśrayaḥ |

Parishishta Bhaav – For the yogi, the Lord has said that he should give up all worldly attachments and remain steadfast in meditation, then he becomes eligible to attain the state of Brahman, abandoning egoism, attachment, lust, anger, and other vices (verses 41, 42, and 43 of the 18th chapter). But for the devotee, it is said here that he attains the supreme state by performing all the duties prescribed for his varna and ashrama, and by taking refuge in the Lord's mercy; because he has taken refuge in the Lord – 'mad-vyapashraya'. The meaning is that taking refuge in the Lord's lotus feet is the easiest way to attain salvation. The devotee does not have to do anything himself; rather, he has to take refuge in the Lord alone, without relying on his own strength, knowledge, etc. Then the Lord's mercy alone will bring him salvation – 'mat-prasadaat avapnoti shashvatam padam avyayam'. The Lord also looks at the devotee's refuge alone, not at his faults. It is said in the Ramayana –
“ 
The Lord remains untouched by the devotee's faults. He is very merciful and kind to his devotees. ( Bala 29.3)
( Uttar 1.3)
The meaning of 'mad-vyapashraya' is – the Lord's special refuge, i.e., the refuge of the Lord alone, without relying on anyone else. The merciful Lord is one who does not show mercy to anyone else. ( Mansa, Aranya 10.4)
Connection – After explaining the general rule (niyam) in the previous shloka, the Lord now gives a special order to Arjuna in the next shloka. Chetasaa sarvakarmaani mayi sannyasya mat-parah |

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

'Param-parah' - I have taken refuge in the Supreme Lord alone, and there is nothing else for me. I have nothing to do, nothing to gain, and nothing to acquire from anyone. I have no purpose or attachment to anything - country, time, object, person, event, or situation. This is what it means to be devoted to the Supreme Lord. One should completely give up the feeling of attachment to them and realize that I am not a part of these situations. When happiness comes, one should attribute it to the will of the Supreme Lord. When a favorable situation arises, one should attribute it to the will of the Supreme Lord. Even when an unfavorable situation arises, one should attribute it to the will of the Supreme Lord. Therefore, I remain the same in happiness and unhappiness, in favorable and unfavorable situations, in gain and loss. I do not change with the changing situations. I remain the same always. One should remain established in oneself, in one's own self. When one remains established in oneself, one attains equanimity in happiness and unhappiness. This equanimity is the worship of the Supreme Lord - 'Samatvam Aradhana Achyutasy' (Vishnu Purana 1.17.90). That is why the Supreme Lord advises one to take refuge in the yoga of the intellect, which means to take refuge in equanimity. One should be careful about one thing - people consider wealth, family, and body as their own and think that they are their masters. However, this is a false notion and a great deception. When one considers something as one's own, one becomes a slave to it, and it becomes one's master. One cannot live without it. Therefore, all the things that people consider as their own, they become slaves to them and become insignificant. These things are all worldly and separate from oneself. To be under their control is to be a slave. The Supreme Lord is one's own, one's own. If one considers the Supreme Lord as one's own, then the Supreme Lord will become one's servant. The Supreme Lord has as much respect for His devotee as He has in His own heart. The Supreme Lord considers His devotee as His crown jewel and says, 'I am the servant of My devotee, My devotee is My crown jewel.'

However, the world will not consider a person as its servant and make them its crown jewel. It will only make them its servant and degrade them. Therefore, one should take refuge only in the Supreme Lord and become completely devoted to Him. 'Buddhi-yoga-upashritah' - In the Gita, it is seen that the glory of equanimity is very great. When a person attains equanimity, they become a sage, a yogi, a devotee, and a knower of the Self. However, if one does not attain equanimity, even if one has good qualities, the Supreme Lord does not consider them perfect. Equanimity is a natural quality of the human being. It arises and falls with the changing situations. Therefore, one should be cautious and remain equanimous in all situations. He who has completely dedicated himself to the Supreme Lord, his mind also becomes completely dedicated to the Supreme Lord. Then, the Supreme Lord's inherent and natural authority becomes manifest in him, and the Supreme Lord Himself resides in his heart. This is what it means to be 'mattah' - to be completely dedicated to the Supreme Lord. The word 'mattah' means to be completely dedicated to the Supreme Lord. The word 'satatam' means to be always in the Supreme Lord. One should remain constantly in the Supreme Lord. The Supreme Lord's constant remembrance will be there only when one's ego is completely dedicated to the Supreme Lord. When one's ego is dedicated to the Supreme Lord, one's mind also becomes naturally dedicated to the Supreme Lord. Just as a student becomes a student when they dedicate their ego to their teacher, and they remember their teacher constantly, similarly, when one dedicates their ego to the Supreme Lord, they remember the Supreme Lord constantly. In this way, one should remain constantly in the Supreme Lord. One should not let their mind be distracted by worldly activities. One should not let their mind be attached to worldly things. One should keep their mind firm and not let it be distracted by worldly things. However, one should engage in the remembrance of the Supreme Lord, the chanting of the Supreme Lord's name, the narration of the Supreme Lord's stories, and the practice of the Supreme Lord's yoga. One should remain constantly in the Supreme Lord, and one's mind should also remain constantly in the Supreme Lord. This is the meaning of 'mattah'.
