* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
[ Chapter 18 ]
The knowledge of one's own existence is not dependent on any proof. The memory of the Self, which is a function of the internal organ, is not based on any expectation of the senses. There is a great difference between the memory of the Self and forgetfulness, which are both like a corpse. The memory of the Self is dormant, not rigid, whereas the memory of forgetfulness is rigid. Only by paying homage to the rigid can the dormant memory of the Self remain hidden, i.e., remain unmanifest. When the covering (of the Self) is removed, the manifestation of the Self takes place, and it is called 'smritirlabdh' (obtained memory). The manifestation of the Self is the revelation of the existing truth, and the removal of the covering is called 'labdh' (obtained). According to the inclination of the seekers, the memory of the Self is divided into three categories: (1) Karma Yoga, i.e., the memory of the Self in a state of non-attachment, (2) Jnana Yoga, i.e., the memory of one's own nature, and (3) Bhakti Yoga, i.e., the memory of the relationship with God. When these three yogas are awakened, they are considered to be eternal and self-existent. When these yogas are considered as means, they are called 'sadhana' (means), but from the standpoint of the Self, they are eternal. Therefore, the realization of the eternal is called 'smriti' (memory). The implication is that the forgetfulness of these means has occurred, not their absence. The reverence for the transient objects of the world, i.e., the attribution of reality and importance to them, gives rise to attachment - this is the 'forgetfulness' (covering) of Karma Yoga. The forgetfulness of one's own nature, i.e., ignorance, is the 'forgetfulness' of Jnana Yoga. The forgetfulness of one's own nature, which is the essence of the Self, is the forgetfulness of Bhakti Yoga, i.e., the attachment to the world. The realization of the Self, i.e., the removal of forgetfulness, is the 'memory' of the Self. This realization is not the attainment of something that was previously unattainable, but rather the realization of something that was always attainable. The realization of the Self is not possible when there is forgetfulness, because the Self is always unchanged and unchanging. However, the memory of forgetfulness can be forgotten, because it is a function of the nature of the individual. The implication is that the world and the body are considered to be the Self, and the realization of the Self is the 'memory' of the Self. The memory of the Self is self-existent and does not require any effort or practice. It is not a function of the internal organ, but rather a direct realization of the Self. Therefore, the realization of the Self is not dependent on any external means or practice. The realization of the Self is a direct experience and not a product of practice. Therefore, once the memory of the Self is awakened, there is no need to repeat the practice. The realization of the Self is a gift of God's grace, which is obtained when one is in the presence of God and has renounced the world. As Arjuna said, "I will only follow your command" (Karishye Vachanam Tava), so too one should renounce the world and take refuge in God, saying, "O Lord, I will only follow your command."

The implication is that the realization of the memory of the Self is due to the seeker's presence in the presence of God and God's grace. Therefore, Arjuna considered God's grace to be the sole cause of the realization of the memory of the Self. God's grace is infinite, unbroken, and unshakeable, and when a person is in the presence of God, he experiences this grace.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The identification of the self with the body (the sense of “I‑ness”) and the identification of the body as the self (the sense of “my‑ness”) cause one to regard the birth and death of the unreal body as one’s own birth and death, and to consider the cause of the body as one’s own creator. If one asks whether the error precedes the relation with the unreal, or the relation with the unreal precedes the error, the answer is: from the beginning of time, the soul, caught in the cycle of birth‑and‑death, was liberated by the Lord so that it might attain eternal bliss. For that purpose the Lord gave the soul a human body. The Lord’s mind was not solitary—“the one who dwells alone does not delight” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.3)—hence He created the human body for Himself to play with. Play is possible only when both players are free; therefore, along with the body, the Lord bestowed freedom and discernment (knowledge of the real and the unreal). Had freedom and discernment not been given, the being would have been merely an animal, lacking any trace of humanity. Because of this discernment, the human, knowing the unreal as unreal, misused the freedom granted and became attached to the unreal (the pleasures of worldly experience and accumulation). Attachment to the unreal is the source of error. Why does the human, even while knowing the unreal as unreal, become attached to it? The mind is drawn toward the fleeting pleasure that appears to arise from the unreal, while it does not contemplate the consequences of that pleasure. (Those who keep their sight on the result are seekers; those who do not are worldly.) Hence the error originates from the relation with the unreal. The error is recognized when, having abandoned attachment to the transient worldly enjoyments, one stands before the Supreme Self; the memory awakens, proving that the error arose from attachment to the unreal while turning away from the Supreme. The error that arises from giving importance to the unreal is not natural; it is created by the human. A natural thing, even when altered, does not cease to exist; the error, however, can be completely eradicated. This shows that the error is self‑generated, because anything that is destined to perish is also destined to arise. Consequently, the responsibility for eliminating the error rests on the human, who can remove it with ease. In other words, only the human, who has produced the error, possesses the power to eradicate it; the Lord has already endowed Him with that capability. When the error disappears, the memory of one’s true nature awakens spontaneously, and the human becomes forever the doer of deeds, the knower of what is to be known, and the possessor of what is to be possessed. Up to now, the human has taken birth many times, encountering countless objects, persons, circumstances, states, and events; yet all of them have been separated from Him, and He has remained unchanged. The separation from the world is not accidental, whereas the encounter with the world is accidental. Thus, separation from the world is the only reality; there is no true conjunction. Since the beginning of time, continuous separation from objects has persisted, making separation the true state. Consequently, the experience of complete separation from the world is Yoga—“that which is known as the union of sorrow, conjunction, and separation is Yoga” (Gita 6.23). This Yoga is eternally established. Our eternal Yoga is with the true nature or the Supreme Self, while the body remains eternally separated from the world. The mere goodwill of worldly conjunction does not bring about the experience of eternal Yoga; when goodwill vanishes, the experience of eternal Yoga arises, never having been separated. Considering worldly conjunction as reality is “forgetfulness,” whereas experiencing perpetual separation from the world means that, in truth, there was never any conjunction with the world—nor is there any possibility of such a conjunction. This realization is “memory.”

Appendix: Worldly memory is spoken of as a form of forgetfulness, but the memory of the transcendental principle is not based on forgetfulness; it is a direct experience. The impartial memory of that principle—experience itself—is here called “smṛti‑labdha.”

* In Karma‑Yoga and Jñāna‑Yoga there is eternal Yoga with one’s true nature, and in Bhakti‑Yoga there is eternal Yoga with the Lord.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

[Chapter 13]
[Verse 73]

The truth is not forgotten, but rather, one becomes detached from it. This means that initially, there was knowledge, and then it was forgotten - this is not the case with the forgetting of the truth. If we consider this forgetting, then after gaining memory, forgetfulness would occur again! Therefore, it is said in the Gita - 'yajjñâtva na punarmoham' (4.35), i.e., after knowing it, there is no more delusion. By considering the unreal as real and giving importance to it, the attitude towards the truth has been lost - this is what is called forgetfulness. The departure and appearance of the attitude - this is also from the perspective of the seeker, not from the perspective of the truth. From the perspective of the truth, even if the attitude departs or one becomes detached, the truth remains as it is. If one considers the unreal as unreal, then the real truth will remain as it is. There are two types of thoughts. One is to think, and the other is for a thought to arise. The thought that is thought is an action, but the thought that arises is not an action. In thinking, the predominance of the intellect remains, but when a thought arises, there is a separation from the intellect. Therefore, the realization of the truth is not from thinking, but from the arising of a thought. This means that the realization of the truth is from the arising of a thought, with the intention of achieving the goal of realizing the truth. When one thinks about the real and the unreal, and the unreal is abandoned, then the thought of 'the world is not, it has not been, it will not be, it is not possible' arises. With the arising of this thought, the realization of the truth is achieved, and the world is destroyed, and the truth is revealed; the assumed thing is destroyed, and the reality remains. The inferior nature is of God, but we have made a mistake by considering it as our own and for our own use. This connection we have made, and we are responsible for giving it up. By considering the inferior nature as our own and for our own use, the forgetfulness of the eternal connection with God has occurred, and we have become bound. Therefore, the separation from the inferior nature is the means of our well-being. To give up the connection with the inferior nature, one must consider the body as not one's own and not for one's own use - 'sharīra mera aur mere liye nahīn hai' (my body is not mine, nor is it for my use). By giving importance to this discrimination, the realization of 'the inferior nature is not mine, nor is it for my use' is achieved. Arjuna has not experienced the truth of duality or non-duality, but has experienced the truth that is beyond duality and non-duality. The reason is that duality and non-duality are delusions, and Arjuna's delusion has been destroyed. The living being has been the property of the Supreme Being since time immemorial, and it is only necessary to abandon the shelter of the world. Arjuna has been reminded of the path of devotion. Karma yoga and jnana yoga are means, but devotion is the goal. Therefore, the realization of devotion is the true one. The realization of devotion is - 'Vāsudeva sarvam' (all is Vasudeva), i.e., everything is God. The realization of 'Vāsudeva sarvam' is 'smṛtir labdhā' (gained memory). This realization can only be achieved by the grace of God - 'tvaṭprasādāt' (by your grace). The words are limited, but the grace is infinite. In thinking, there is the sense of doership, but in realization, there is no sense of doership. The reason is that thinking is done by the mind, the intellect is beyond the mind, the ego is beyond the intellect, and the essence is beyond the ego, and in the essence, realization occurs. In thinking, we do it, but in realization, there is only a look in that direction. Even in the time of forgetfulness, the truth remains as it is. Therefore, a look in that direction is enough to achieve realization. 'I am free from doubts' - initially, it seemed right to fight according to the dharma of a warrior, but after meeting the elders, it seemed wrong to fight; but after gaining realization, all the doubts disappeared. I do not know what to do? Should I fight or not fight? - there was no doubt, no hesitation, no question. Now, there is nothing left for me to do, but to follow your command - 'karishye vachanam tava' (I will do your command). This is surrender. 1 - After gaining knowledge, there is no newness, i.e., initially, there was ignorance, and now there is knowledge - this does not seem to be the case. After gaining knowledge, it is experienced that knowledge has been there since eternity, and my gaze was not in that direction. If initially there was ignorance, and later there was knowledge - if we consider this, then there would be a sense of newness in knowledge, but knowledge is not new, it is eternal. What is new is what is limited, and what is eternal is infinite. 2 - 'Dvaitādvaitamahāmohaḥ' (great delusion of duality and non-duality) (Māheśvaratantra)
'Ahō māyā mahāmohau dvaitādvaitavikalpanā' (Avadhūtagītā 1.61)

Explanation - Sanjaya says, "Thus I have heard the dialogue of the great-minded Vasudeva and Partha, which is wonderful and thrilling, and just hearing it fills me with joy and thrill."
Here, the word 'Iti' means that Sanjaya begins the dialogue of the Gita in the twentieth verse of the first chapter with the words 'Ath Vyashtitan Drishtva Dhartarashtram Kapidhvajah' and concludes it with the word 'Iti' in this verse. The word 'Mahatmanah' is used to describe Arjuna, meaning that Arjuna is a great and extraordinary person, whose orders are followed by God himself! Arjuna says, "Oh Acyuta, place my chariot in the middle of both armies" (Gita - First Chapter, Verse 21), and God places the chariot in the middle of both armies (Gita - First Chapter, Verse 24). In the Gita, wherever Arjuna asks questions, God answers them lovingly and in detail. In this way, the dialogue between the great-minded Arjuna and God Vasudeva is what I have heard. - This
= dialogue

= What is wonderful and thrilling in this dialogue? It is said in the scriptures that only by renouncing the world can a person follow the path of righteousness and attain liberation. It is also believed by people that by renouncing the world and becoming a sanyasi, one can attain liberation. However, the Gita says that in any situation, in any condition, in any event, in any place, and at any time, one can attain liberation by utilizing it properly. Not only that, it can be in a good situation or a bad situation, in a peaceful situation or a violent situation, in a war-like situation where people are fighting and killing each other all day, one can still attain liberation, one can still be free. The reason is that the bondage of birth and death is due to attachment to the world (Gita - Thirteenth Chapter, Verse 21). To overcome this attachment, one has to utilize the situation properly, i.e., one has to perform one's duty without attachment and aversion (Gita - Fifth Chapter, Verse 3). This is the secret of this dialogue. - When every situation is to be renounced for liberation, then what is the difference between a good situation and a bad situation? It is said that the difference is in the way one utilizes the situation. One can utilize the situation in a way that leads to liberation, or one can utilize it in a way that leads to bondage. The difference is not in the situation itself, but in the way one responds to it. In reality, one who is bound is not free, and one who is free is not bound. What is freedom, then? Freedom is to renounce the bondage that one has accepted.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Oh King! This conversation between Lord Krishna and Arjuna is truly wonderful, sacred, and extraordinary. It is filled with so many secrets that even in the midst of the most intense war-like actions, one can attain the highest spiritual achievement. A person can save himself in every situation. I am filled with joy and happiness every moment, remembering this kind of conversation. [ Chapter 18 ]

Oh King, I am remembering this conversation again and again, and I am filled with joy and happiness. (Sanjaya says, understanding it in this way.) When a person is not fixed on one principle or one idea, his anxiety is very strange. Arjuna was also in a state of anxiety, unable to decide whether to fight or not to fight. Due to this anxiety, Arjuna was drawn to Lord Krishna, and he came before him. By coming before him, Arjuna received Lord Krishna's special mercy. Arjuna's single-minded devotion and eagerness caused Lord Krishna to become situated in the yoga of love, meaning that He became immersed in His own loving nature, and not in His opulence or other attributes. In this state, He explained the Gita to Arjuna. What can be said about the glory of this conversation between the eager Arjuna and the eternal Lord Krishna, who is situated in the yoga of love? The glory of this conversation is also very extraordinary. Even if one tries to describe its glory, it is impossible. Commentary:
The reason why people today do not have a special eagerness to learn about spiritual truths is that they are satisfied with temporary pleasures like wealth, family, fame, social status, education, knowledge, sensual pleasures, and material possessions. This satisfaction causes their eagerness to learn about the truth to be suppressed. 1. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The extraordinary thing is that the sages and saints go to hear it, and yet this (Gita) is a dialogue of a spiritual nature! In the Shrimad Bhagavatam, when Uddhava saw that Lord Krishna was giving answers to questions in a most extraordinary way, he then asked thirty-five questions together (Shrimad Bhagavatam, Eleventh Skandha, Nineteenth Chapter, from the 18th to the 32nd verse). - 'I am delighted again and again, for I have never heard such extraordinary things about karma, knowledge, and devotion anywhere else. Therefore, Sanjaya is delighted again and again upon hearing these. Sanjaya was aware of the Lord. When Dhritarashtra asked him the reason for this, Sanjaya told him, "I do not serve Maya (deception), O great king, nor do I perform vain (hypocritical) actions. My inner self has become pure through devotion; therefore, I know the Lord's form through the words of the scriptures." (Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 69.5)

Hail to the king! I never serve Maya (deception), nor do I perform vain (hypocritical) actions. My inner self has become pure through devotion; therefore, I know the Lord's form through the words of the scriptures.'

In this way, Sanjaya first knew the Lord through the words of the scriptures, but now he has come to know Him through the Lord's own words! O king! That (form) is indeed most wonderful, and remembering it again and again, I am filled with great wonder, and I am delighted again and again. 77. The form of Lord Krishna is most wonderful, and remembering it again and again, I am filled with great wonder, and I am delighted again and again. Sanjaya says, "O king! When I remember that form again and again, I am filled with great wonder, and I am delighted again and again."

The commentary explains, "That (form) is indeed most wonderful, and remembering it again and again, I am filled with great wonder, and I am delighted again and again." Sanjaya says this. Another point is that Arjuna had called the dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna "most wonderful" in the previous verse, but here Sanjaya calls the form of the Lord "most wonderfully wonderful." This means that the dialogue can still be read and thought about, but the form of the Lord cannot be seen now. Therefore, that form is most wonderfully wonderful. In the ninth verse of the eleventh chapter, Sanjaya had called the Lord "Mahayogeshvara." Here, "I am filled with great wonder, O king," even though the Lord had shown His divine form to Kausalya in the Ramavatara and to Yasoda in the Krishnavatara, and to the Kaurava assembly, including Duryodhana, yet that form was not so wonderful that many great warriors were stuck in its beard and that both armies were being destroyed. This kind of most wonderfully wonderful form is remembered, and the poet says that it is the form of the great yogeshvara, the Lord. I, the servant of the Lord, wish to hear your words, which are filled with dharma and artha, in the midst of the kings. You are the greatest of kings, and I wish to hear your words." (Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 83.68-69)

"(Parashurama said - ) O Mādhava, the destroyer of enemies! We wish to hear the words that you will speak in the assembly of the kings, which are filled with dharma and artha."

[Chapter 18]

The name 'Pārtha' has been used thirty-eight times in the Gita, and no other name has been used as many times for Arjuna. This shows that Lord Krishna likes the name 'Pārtha' very much. Similarly, Arjuna also likes the name 'Krishna' very much, and that is why the name 'Krishna' has been used nine times in the Gita. No other name of Lord has been used as many times in the Gita. Finally, Sanjaya has also mentioned both the names 'Krishna' and 'Pārtha' at the end of the Gita. The words 'Shri', 'Vijaya', 'Vibhuti', and 'Dhruva Niti' all refer to the divine qualities of Lord Krishna and Arjuna. Wherever Lord Krishna is, there will be infinite wealth, infinite beauty, infinite kindness, infinite courtesy, and infinite beauty. Similarly, wherever Arjuna is, there will be victory, bravery, and other kshatriya virtues. The question of Dhritarashtra about the victory of the Pandavas is answered by Sanjaya in a proper way. The meaning is that the victory of the Pandavas is certain, and there is no doubt about it. The Lord is the knower of all secrets, and He is the one who grants all desires. He is the one who is pleased with the devotees, and He is the one who is the charioteer of Arjuna. He is the one who is the friend of the devotees, and He is the one who is the savior of the devotees. Thus, the entire Gita, which is a dialogue between Lord Krishna and Arjuna, is a complete and perfect knowledge of the ultimate reality. It is a yoga-shastra, and it is a Brahma-vidya. It is a Upanishad, and it is a scripture that teaches the path of liberation. The name of this eighteenth chapter is 'Moksha-Sannyasa-Yoga', which means the yoga of liberation and renunciation. This chapter is complete, and it is the eighteenth chapter of the Gita. In this chapter, there are 179 verses, and the total number of words is 2135. The meter used in this chapter is Anushtubh, and it is a combination of Magan, Nagan, and Bhagan. Thus, the entire Gita is a complete and perfect knowledge of the ultimate reality, and it is a scripture that teaches the path of liberation. * Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The Lord said: "One who has no limbs, who is a listener, a Shudra, or a lowly person, is not to be approached. One who is ignorant of the fire's potency and falls into it is destroyed. The ignorant person, who is half-awakened, is bound by ignorance. Ignorance is the root cause of his downfall. The small and the great, the moving and the stationary, are all seen by the wise as equal. The wise one does not consider anyone superior or inferior. Due to excessive familiarity, one becomes contemptuous. Oh, what a wretched creature is a dog! Oh, what a sharp and bitter pain is the result of excessive anger! Oh, what a great illusion is the great delusion! What is the outcome of this? (3.5)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

Thus, O Madhava, those who know that imperishable syllable, they alone see the Self in its own form. I will also manifest that form. When one's mind is obstructed by the ego, one sees the beautiful form of the Lord. The one who is beyond both good and evil, the one who is beyond both pleasure and pain, is the one who is the ultimate reality. (15.19)

The object of desire is intense due to the presence of the ego. (6.23)

The sky, the moon, the sun, the stars, and the planets are all manifestations of the Lord's glory. (18.10)

The two birds, the individual self and the supreme self, are perched on the same tree, the body. (15.15)

The second fear is the fear of death. (18.66)

The knowledge of the ultimate reality is the purpose of the scriptures. (4.34)

The one who has two arms, Radha's beloved, is the ultimate reality. (11.51)

In the absence of remembrance of the ultimate reality, one becomes extremely agitated. (18.66)

The two letters, A and U, are the ultimate reality for those who are devoted to the Lord. (15.17)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

There is no caste or learning in them. They are not born of a good family, nor are they learned. They are not even aware of the Supreme Being. They are always engaged in the service of the Supreme Being. They are always calm and peaceful. They are always detached from worldly attachments. They are always self-controlled. They are always free from desires. They are always free from attachment to worldly objects. They are always free from the influence of the six enemies. They are always free from the influence of the three modes of nature. They are always free from the influence of the five elements. They are always free from the influence of the five senses. They are always free from the influence of the five organs of perception. They are always free from the influence of the five organs of action. They are always free from the influence of the five types of knowledge. They are always free from the influence of the five types of faith. They are always free from the influence of the five types of devotion. They are always free from the influence of the five types of detachment. They are always free from the influence of the five types of renunciation. [Chapter 18] [Verse 66]

Many have attained my lotus feet. I would have many children. Even if I am obstructed, my devotee is not obstructed. The Supreme Being is the ultimate goal of the Vedas. They are all in the Supreme Being. [Reference to other verses]

The body of a Brahmin is the temple of the Supreme Being. They say that the body of a Brahmin is the temple of the Supreme Being. The body of a Brahmin is the temple of the Supreme Being. The devotee who is devoted to devotion is devoted to devotion.

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *

The body is a temple of disease; the remaining part is known as the sheath. In the Shudra caste, if one has good fortune, cleanliness, contentment, and austerity, then one's body becomes pure. From purity, one develops aversion to one's own body. With tears and affection, one's relatives are released. (1)

With faith, one should give; without faith, one should not give. (2)

Listening to and chanting the name of Vishnu, as per the Shruti and Smriti, is my command. (3)

Having heard and touched, one should know that the ultimate truth is the essence of all virtues. (4)

In the course of time, the number of atoms is infinite. (5)

Association with the Supreme Self is to be renounced. (6)

The practice of circumambulation with the feet is the means of liberation. (7)

Sanjaya, the son of Ganges, is the embodiment of the Munis. (8)

The Sanjivani is the means of attaining life. (9)

One who is entangled in worldly duties should not be deluded. (10)

Knowledge arises from the mere impression of the past actions. (11)

He is the most wicked of all. (12)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
A person should not have deceit, cunning, or hypocrisy in their mind, i.e., they should be straightforward and simple, and this quality is called 'arjav' (18.42). Touching, piercing in the second moment, and transcending in the third moment (15.1 T). Attachment - attachment to things that are foreign to one's own nature (jada) (3.19)
Forgiveness - attraction to punishing someone who has committed a crime without a reason (3.19)

God - the word 'Ishwar' is considered to be a symbol of saguna, which means the ruler (15.17)

Indifferent - one who sits above, untouched, unbiased (12.16)

Disturbance - when the mind becomes agitated and restless (12.15)

Rishi - those who give importance to the knowledge (vivek) are called 'Rishi' (5.25)

Instrument - the five sense organs (pancha-indriya) and the five organs of knowledge (pancha-jnana-indriya) are the ten 'bahi-karana', and the three 'antah-karana' are the mind, intellect, and ego (18.14)

Duty - (1) that which can be done and should be done (3.19)
(2) only the work done for the benefit of others is considered duty. The work done for oneself is not duty, but only action (4.31)

Tolerance - to bear the troubles, calamities, and obstacles that come one's way, considering them as opportunities for spiritual growth (16.1)

Chetan and Jada - one who knows oneself and others is 'chetan', and one who does not know oneself and others is 'jada' (7.20 T)

World - the world is that which is constantly changing (7.6)

Caste - the word 'jati' is derived from the root 'janipradurbhave', which means birth. The word 'krti' is derived from the root 'dukarna', which means action. However, the protection of one's caste is only possible by performing one's duty (4.14)

Tap - to bear the difficulties of life, such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and rain, with equanimity (16.1)

Kam - (1) the desire for pleasure, wealth, and action (3.37)
(2) the attachment to worldly things, considering them as valuable (3.39)

Desire - the desire to acquire something that is not yet in one's possession (3.39)

Vasana - the subtle desires that are present in the mind (3.39)

Sphurha - the desire to acquire something that is necessary (3.39)

Asakti - the attachment to something that is considered valuable (3.39)

Ash - the hope of acquiring something (3.39)

Lobh - the excessive desire to acquire something (3.39)

Yachana - the request for something that is considered valuable (3.39)

Causal agent - those who have attained the state of God and reside in the divine abode are called 'karak purusha' (4.8 T)

(2) the ability to control the senses, so that they can perform the desired action, and the ability to withdraw the senses from their objects (18.42)

Dambh - the desire to show off one's status, prestige, and wealth, even if it is not actually present (16.4)

Compassion - (1) the feeling of sorrow for someone who is suffering (16.2)
(2) the two types of compassion, kripa and daya, as understood by the devotees. Kripa is the act of sending someone to a difficult situation, and daya is the act of sending someone to a favorable situation (16.2)

Kootasth - one who remains steady like a koot (a type of plant) (6.8)

Darpan - the pride of having wealth, property, and family (16.4)

Kshan - the time it takes for a needle to pass through a lotus leaf (16.4)

Dana - the act of giving away something that is considered valuable (16.4)

Note: The translation of the text is based on the Gita Press edition of the Bhagavad Gita.

* Glossary of Terms *

1295
The state of being a benefactor, along with the country, time, and circumstances, is pramad - (1) not doing work that is beneficial, and not doing work that is not beneficial, while considering the thoughts of others, and doing work that is beneficial for others as per their needs. (16.1)
Dvandva - to have two opposing views or feelings about the same thing or subject. (2.45)
Dharma -
(1) 'Dharma' refers to two things - (a) doing charitable work, building wells, and opening food distribution centers, etc. and (b) following one's duties and responsibilities as per the scriptures and the varna and ashrama system. (2.40)
(2) Whether it is called dharma or karman, it is the same thing. (2.39)
Dhriti (Serenity) - (1) The power to remain steadfast in any favorable or unfavorable circumstances is called 'dhriti'. (16.3)
(2) The power to firmly hold one's convictions and not be swayed from one's goal is called 'dhriti'. (18.29)
(3) The power to firmly hold one's beliefs, principles, goals, feelings, actions, and thoughts is called 'dhriti'. (18.33)
Naiskarmya - The state in which a person's actions do not bind them, is called 'naiskarmya'. (3.4)
Pandit - A person with a developed and discerning intellect is called a 'pandit'. (2.11)
Paramatman - The term 'paramatman' refers to the Supreme Being, who is beyond all qualities and attributes. (15.17)
Paraloka - 
(1) Doing work that is beneficial. (14.7)
(2) Engaging in activities such as smoking, playing cards, and watching performances. (14.13)
Bhaya - Fear is the feeling of anxiety and apprehension that arises from the fear of separation from the beloved and the fear of meeting with misfortune. (12.15)
Bhuta-Preta - The term 'bhuta' refers to beings that have passed away, and the term 'preta' refers to beings that have died. (17.4)
Bhog - The term 'bhog' refers to the enjoyment of the five senses - sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, as well as the enjoyment of the eightfold pleasure - the pleasure of the body, the pleasure of name and fame. (2.44)
Mad - The feeling of intoxication and elation that arises from one's own abilities and qualities is called 'mad'. (16.10)
Mahatman - A person who is free from ego, individuality, and attachment is called a 'mahatman'. (7.19)
Maharathi - A person who is skilled in both the scriptures and the art of warfare, and can control a thousand warriors single-handedly, is called a 'maharathi'. (1.6)
Man - The pleasure that arises from the respect and honor shown to one's body is called 'man'. The pleasure that arises from the praise and admiration of one's name is called 'badai'. (18.12)
Mardav - The quality of gentleness and compassion, even towards those who are cruel and hostile, is called 'mardav'. (16.2)
Moha - The attachment to the body and the attachment to worldly objects, such as one's mother, father, wife, children, and wealth, is called 'moha'. (2.52)
Yaksha-Rakshasa - The term 'yaksha' refers to beings who are primarily concerned with accumulating wealth, and the term 'rakshasa' refers to beings who are primarily concerned with destroying others. (17.4)
(1) According to the Gita, the term 'yajna' refers to the performance of one's duties. (3.9)
(2) The term 'paraloka' refers to the state of existence after death, whether it is in this world or in some other world, whether it is as a human being, an animal, or some other creature. (16.8)
Parigraha - The accumulation of wealth and material possessions, motivated by attachment and a desire for pleasure and comfort. (4.5)
Pishunata (Slander) - The act of revealing the faults of another person to others, with the intention of creating ill will towards that person. (16.2)
Prakriti - The term 'prakriti' refers to the natural order of things, in which everything is in a state of activity and movement. (18.11)
(2) The term 'yajna' refers to the performance of all worldly and scriptural duties, without any attachment or expectation of reward. (3.14)
Yajna-shesha - The remaining essence of the yajna, which is the state of yoga, or equanimity. (3.13)
Yajna-arth-karma - The performance of all actions with the intention of benefiting others and promoting their welfare. (3.9)

* Srimad Bhagavad Gita *
Effort - The inner zeal, which cannot remain without being fulfilled, is called 'yajna' (effort). It is the truth that is achieved by giving up one's own interests and pride and going only for the sake of others. (15.11)
Yoga - (1) - 1. 'Yujir yoge' - The eternal bond with the Supreme Being, 2. 'Yuj samadha' - The state of being in a state of equanimity, where one has seen, heard, read, understood, and decided as per the perspective of the well-being of others, and not more or less than that - to express it in the same way in words. (16.2)
-
-
-
Stability, i.e., being in a state of samadhi, and 3. 'Yuj sankalp - Sankalpa' - The power of self-control, strength, and influence. (Pr.)
(2) The eternal bond that the jiva (individual) has with the Supreme Being is called 'yoga'. (18.75)
Yoga-Kshema - (1) The name 'yoga' is for the acquisition of an unattainable thing, and the name 'kshema' is for the protection of an acquired thing. (2.45; 9.22)
(2) 'Yoga' is the name of the bond with the Supreme Being, and 'kshema' is the name of the well-being of the jiva. (9.22)
The color that appears on the mind due to attachment to worldly objects is called 'raga'. (2.56)
Shame - The feeling of hesitation to act against the scriptures and social norms. (16.2)
Loc - (1) It has three meanings - 1. Human world, 2. The living beings residing in those worlds, and 3. The scriptures (other than the Vedas). (3.20)
(2) Those whose essential unity or identity with the jiva is not, are called 'loc' (worlds) in the sense of nature and its activities. (15.7)
Varnasankar - When a person and a woman of different varnas (castes) have a child, that child is called 'varnasankar'. [The mixture of opposing principles is called 'sankar'.] (1.41)
Vyabhichar - Going anywhere except to the Supreme Being is 'vyabhichar', and going only to the Supreme Being is 'avyabhichar'. (18.33)
Sham - (1) Removing the mind from the objects of the senses. (4.33)
(2) The mind should be fixed where one wants to fix it, and removed from where one wants to remove it - this is called 'sham' (self-control). (18.42)
Shraddha - (1) Having faith in God, scriptures, etc. even in the absence of direct experience. (4.33)
(2) Having faith in something that one has not experienced oneself, but has heard from scriptures, saints, etc. and has a natural inclination towards it, is called 'shraddha'. (17.3)
Sanket - A note:
The various thoughts that arise in the mind due to circumstances, etc. are called 'sankalpa' (resolve) when they have the qualities of being pleasing, beautiful, and necessary. (6.24)
-
Sannyas - The name 'sannyas' means to give up something completely and to separate oneself from it through discrimination. (18.1)
And friend - One who is like a mother, without attachment, and who desires the well-being of all and works for it, is called a 'suhrid' (friend), and one who repays good with good is called a 'mitra' (friend). (6.9)
Spriha - (1) The need for the body, such as a country, time, object, person, etc. that appears necessary for the maintenance of life, is called 'spriha'. (2.71)
(2) The subtle desire for things that are necessary for the maintenance of life is called 'spriha'. (18.49)
-
Self-study - The study of the scriptures, such as the Gita, Bhagavat, Ramayana, Mahabharata, etc. for the realization of one's goal, is called 'svadhyaya'. In reality, it means to study one's own nature, one's own state, etc. thoroughly. (16.1)
Swabhiman - The feeling of superiority over others is called 'abhimana', and the feeling of one's own duty is called 'swabhiman'. If one has abhimana, one will act against one's duty, but if one has swabhiman, one will feel ashamed of acting against one's duty. (17.3)
-
-
-
Av. - Avatarnika, A. S. - Adhyayaka Sari, Ti. - Tippani, De. - Dekhe, Ni. - Sadhak-Sanjivani Parishishtaka Namr Nivedan, Par. - Parishisht, Pu. - Pushpika, Pr. - Prakathan, Ma. - Marma Bata, Vi. - Vishesh Bata, San. - Sambandh.
